title: إذا تبي تتأكد إن وجودك في حياة شخص مومهم اقرأ معي
description:
مرّت عليك أيام حسّيت فيها إن فيه شخص كان قريب منك، صار يبعد بالتدريج، أو حتى فجأة؟كان يسأل عنك، ويهتم بأصغر التفاصيل، ويكلمك من نفسه بدون ما ترسل له، وفجأة صرت أنت الوحيد اللي يحاول يحافظ على العلاقة.بتبدأ تسأل نفسك وتلومها:ليه تغيّر علي؟هل فعلًا ما يبيني بحياته؟
ولا مجرد أوهام في راسي؟مع الأسف، أحيانًا إحساسك بالتغيير يكون مبني على أشياء لكن هذا مو معناه إنك تحكم من أول موقف، ولا إنك لازم تبرر كل تصرف يصدر منه.صح، الواقع أحيانًا يكون صعب، لكن الأهم إنك تواجهه بدل ما تتمسك بإجابة تريحك مؤقتًا.اسأل نفسك: هل هو فعلًا حريص على وجودي بحياته؟ أو أنا الوحيد اللي أحاول؟خلني أذكّرك ببعض المواقف اللي يمكن توجعك، لكن يمكن تساعدك تشوف علاقتك بوضوح أكثر.تذكر لما كان يسأل عنك من نفسه؟تذكر لما كان يرسل لك بدون ما تذكره؟ يسألك عن يومك، ويرسل لك شيء يضحكك، أو حتى يحكي لك وش صار بيومه؟هذي كانت أشياء عادية بالنسبة لك، لكن الحين صرت تشتاق لها.طيب، وش صار الآن؟انقلب كل شيء، وصرت أنت اللي تبدأ بالمحادثات، وأنت اللي تسأل، وأنت اللي تحاول تفتح مواضيع عشان ما ينتهي الكلام بينكم.ومع الوقت، بتبدأ تحس إنك ثقيل عليه، مع إنك ما سويت شيء غير إنك تحاول تتواصل مع شخص يهمك.لكن تذكر إن قلة التواصل لحالها مو دليل كافي، يمكن عنده ظروف ما تعرفها. اللي يستحق إنك تنتبه له هو استمرار التغيير، وهل ما زال يحاول يحافظ على العلاقة بطريقته أو لا.ليه أنا اللي أحاول أصلّح كل شيء؟كل مرة يصير بينكم خلاف، أنت اللي تحاول تصلّح الأمور.وإذا ابتعدتم، أنت اللي تحاول ترجع.وإذا حسّيت إن العلاقة تغيّرت، أنت اللي تحاول تفهم السبب.وبالمقابل، تحس إنه مو قاعد يبذل نفس الجهد عشان يصلّح اللي بينكم، ولا يحاول يطمنك أو يفهم وش مضايقك.ومع الوقت، بتتعب من كثرة المحاولات، وبتبدأ تسأل نفسك:ليه أنا اللي أخاف أخسر العلاقة أكثر منه؟السؤال هذا مو معناه إنك ضعيف، ولا إن اهتمامك بالشخص غلط. بالعكس، طبيعي إنك تحاول تحافظ على شخص يعني لك الكثير.لكن مو طبيعي إنك تستنزف نفسك طول الوقت عشان تحافظ على علاقة المفروض إن الطرفين يحاولون فيها.لا تخلي خوفك من خسارته يخليك تخسر نفسكيمكن أكثر شيء يخليك تستمر بالعلاقة هو خوفك من إنك تخسره.تقول لنفسك: يمكن يرجع مثل أول، يمكن يتغير، يمكن أنا اللي أفكر بزيادة.وتجلس تنتظر، وكل مرة تعطي نفسك أمل جديد.لكن اسأل نفسك: إلى متى بظل أنتظر بدون ما أشوف أي تغيير؟مو مطلوب منك تقطع علاقتك بشخص تحبه من أول مشكلة، ولا إنك تفسّر كل تأخير أو انشغال على إنه تجاهل.لكن إذا تكلمت معه، ووضحت له شعورك، وأعطيته فرصة، ومع ذلك استمر الوضع على حاله، فمن حقك تخفف محاولاتك وتعيد التفكير بالعلاقة.مو كل شخص تحبه لازم تتمسك فيه مهما أتعبك، ومو كل علاقة تنتهي يعني إنك خسرت.وإذا انتهت علاقتكم؟إذا انتهت علاقتك مع الشخص هذا، تذكر إن هذا ما يعني إن كل شيء عشته معه كان كذب.يمكن كانت بينكم أيام حلوة، ومواقف ما تنسى، ومشاعر كانت صادقة فعلًا.مو لازم تحوّل كل ذكرياتك معه إلى شيء سيئ عشان تقدر تتجاوزه.ومو لازم تكره الشخص عشان تتقبل إنه ما عاد قريب منك مثل أول.أحيانًا نحب أشخاص، لكن علاقتنا معهم تتغير، وأحيانًا نكتشف إننا قاعدين نحاول نحافظ على شيء ما عاد الطرف الثاني يحاول يحافظ عليه معنا.وهنا لازم نتعلم إننا نترك مساحة للأشياء تتضح، ونحترم مشاعرنا، وما نربط قيمتنا باهتمام شخص واحد فينا.بالنهاية، أبي أقول لكم شيءلا تحمّلون أنفسكم فوق طاقتكم في علاقة تتعبكم.لا تقعدون تلومون أنفسكم على كل تغيير يصير، ولا تحاولون تثبتون لأحد إنكم تستحقون وجوده بحياته.الاهتمام مو عيب، والمبادرة مو ضعف، ومحاولة إصلاح العلاقة مو غلط.لكن إذا صرت أنت الوحيد اللي يحاول، والوحيد اللي يخاف، والوحيد اللي يتعب عشان ما تنتهي العلاقة، وقف شوي واسأل نفسك: هل أنا فعلًا مرتاح؟تذكّروا: مو لازم تكرهون أحد عشان تبعدون عنه، ومو لازم تقلّ قيمتكم في عيون أنفسكم لمجرد إن شخصًا ما عاد يعاملكم مثل أول.حافظوا على قلوبكم، ولا تنسون أنفسكم وأنتم تحاولون تحافظون على غيركم.

title: What I learned building a real app with Claude Code
description:
Why I built it

I recently finished The Complete Claude Code & Claude Cowork Masterclass. A course shows you what Claude and Claude Code can do. It doesn't show you what it's like to lean on that tool for a real project, with real bugs and real releases. I wanted to find out.

I had a real problem to use. When I moved my laptop from Windows to Linux, the thing I missed most was WinSCP: my files on the left, the server's on the right, drag a file across, done. There are good file-transfer tools on Linux, but none felt like that to me.

So that became the project. The result is ShuttleSCP, a free, open-source SFTP, SCP and FTP/FTPS client for Linux, macOS and Windows, written in Rust with GTK 4. It's a public beta at version 0.13.0. This is what I learned getting it there.

How we split the work

The short version: I decided and checked, Claude wrote the code.

My background is databases and IT infrastructure, not Rust. So I worked the way I would with a capable contractor. I described what I wanted in plain words, it built it, and I tried it. A typical request looked like this one:

Can we add drag and drop? Files within a pane can be dropped into a folder. If dragging from source to target, a menu should come up asking if it's a copy or a move.

A while later there was a branch to test. I used it, said what felt wrong, and it went round again until it was right.

I also set the ground rules, and they mattered more than I expected:

  • Every feature goes on its own branch, and nothing merges until I've tried it.
  • Explain each step as you go. I wanted to learn the engineering, not just collect an app.
  • Never handle my passwords or keys. When something needed a secret, it gave me a script that asked me for it directly.
  • Be honest that an AI built this, in the README and on the web page.

I didn't read every line of Rust. I can't judge Rust idioms yet. What I did review was what each change did and why, and whether it behaved that way when I used it.

What worked

The speed is real. ShuttleSCP is now about 22,000 lines of Rust with 149 automated tests. It runs on Linux, macOS and Windows, and has had eight public beta releases. Alone, I'd still be reading the GTK documentation.

The bigger surprise was the engineering around the code. These are the parts a solo hobby project usually skips, and they got done properly:

  • CI/CD. Every pull request is linted and tested on GitHub Actions. Pushing one release tag builds, checks and publishes the Linux AppImage, the macOS disk image and the Windows installer.
  • Safe self-updates. The app checks a release manifest signed with an Ed25519 key, verifies the download's SHA-256, and swaps the file in one step.
  • Secrets in the right place. Saved passwords go to GNOME Keyring, the macOS Keychain or the Windows Credential Manager, never a plain file.
  • Release hygiene. A changelog, release notes and a security policy, from the first release.

It also checked its own work in ways I wouldn't have thought of. To review the look of every dialog, it built a debug mode that opens each window, saves a screenshot and quits. When I said the dialogs looked like old GNOME ones, it could compare before and after without me clicking through the app.

And I learned a lot. I asked it to teach as it went, and it did: why a release is tied to a git tag, what signing actually protects against, why you never reuse a version number.

What didn't

The failures were the most useful part, so here they are.

Bugs only a person finds

The tests passed and the screenshots looked fine, but using the app told a different story:

  • The first release built by GitHub Actions was missing GTK's add-ons. Icons didn't load and drawing fell back to software. It worked on my laptop because my laptop had them installed.
  • In the next release, choosing a theme did nothing, and odd colours showed under the menus. The packaging tool was quietly forcing the default theme.
  • My installed app started reporting itself as a "debug" build. Running a development copy had rewritten my desktop's launcher entry to point at itself.

Each was fixed quickly once I described it, and the first two now have automatic checks so they can't come back. But I had to notice them first.

Version numbers

I had already tagged and published 0.9.2 when more work was added under that same number. It had to ship as 0.9.3. A published version can't be reused, because installed copies may already have it. The lesson: check what's actually released before calling something "part of" a version.

Trusting the status line

At one point Claude told me it was waiting for a CI job to finish. I looked at GitHub Actions and nothing was running. The job had finished successfully, but GitHub never cleared its "in progress" label, and the AI was watching the label instead of the result. It was an honest mistake, and it was mine to catch.

What I learned about the work

Writing code turned out to be the smallest part of building software. The rest was still mine:

  • Deciding. What the app should do, what it should feel like, and what comes next. The AI offers options well, but someone has to pick.
  • Testing like a user. Every real bug above was found by using the app, not by the test suite.
  • Noticing. A wrong label, a stale status, a version that doesn't add up. Twenty years of production support helped more than any Rust knowledge would have.
  • Saying no. Some suggestions were good and still not for now. Keeping the scope small is what got releases out.

I think this way of working suits people who know a domain well and can tell when something is off, even if they don't know the language. It doesn't remove the need for judgement. It moves almost all of the work there.

What's next

ShuttleSCP stays in public beta while people try it. Next on my list:

  • Make the Linux AppImage run on older systems such as Ubuntu 22.04 and Debian 12. Today it needs a 2024-or-later distribution.
  • Keep fixing what testers find, one small release at a time.

If you use SFTP or FTP, I'd value your feedback, good or bad:

  • Downloads: shuttlescp.dsalvado.ca
  • Code and issues: github.com/dsalvado/shuttlescp

dsalvado / shuttlescp

A graphical SFTP, SCP and FTP/FTPS client for Linux, macOS and Windows, inspired by WinSCP. Two panes, drag and drop, resumable transfers. Rust and GTK 4.

ShuttleSCP

A graphical SFTP and FTP client for Linux, macOS and Windows, inspired by WinSCP: your computer's files on the left, the server's on the right, and copying between them is a drag, a right-click or a key press away.

Written in Rust with relm4 and GTK 4.

Status: public beta. It is used day to day on Linux and macOS, and the Windows version is new; feedback is very welcome: please open an issue See the changelog for what each release brought.

Features

Connections

  • SFTP and SCP over SSH, and FTP with plain, explicit or implicit TLS (FTPS), in passive or active mode.
  • SSH login with a password, a private key file (OpenSSH or PuTTY .ppk, with its passphrase if protected) or the keys of an SSH agent (the desktop's; on Windows Windows' OpenSSH agent or PuTTY's Pageant).
  • Saved sites, with passwords kept in the desktop keyring…
View on GitHub

The code is GPL-3.0. If you read Rust, a critical look at it is as welcome as one at the app.

title: Node.js Failure Alerting Explained (Polling Logs and Errors for Failed Cron Jobs)
description:
A failure alert is useful only if its evidence survives long enough to answer two questions: what broke, and which agent run paid for it? Short answer: for a fintech AI agent loop, start with a scheduled poller that normalizes exception groups and failed-job or HTTP 5xx log evidence into one incident record. Keep latency and cost on that record as diagnostic dimensions, not the sole paging threshold. This shape trades immediate push delivery for replayable collection windows and straightforward incident reconstruction.

The invariant is simple: every source window must be processed at least once, while every notification must be emitted at most once for the same rule, window, and evidence set. Polling without the second half creates duplicate Slack messages during retries. Polling without the first creates gaps that nobody notices until reconciliation.

Infrai is a deliberate fit for the collection side when a team wants a plain REST API rather than another client library to install and upgrade. Its errors surface can supply exception-oriented evidence, while logs can carry failed background-job and 5xx evidence. Notification rules and routing remain the poller's responsibility. I recommend trying Infrai for the evidence-collection boundary of a small or mixed-language agent platform, because one HTTP contract keeps the collector portable. The API is self-describing: its public discovery surface needs no key and exposes schemas plus runnable examples in 10 languages. A single key spans 295 routes across 20 modules under one bill. More important for this fintech agent loop, per-call cost, vendor, and latency metadata is specified consistently on native and OpenAI-compatible AI responses. That metadata lets the incident ledger preserve the dimensions needed to reconstruct an expensive or slow run without timing calls in a second wrapper. Together, these properties mean the evidence collector and a later notification adapter can share an authentication convention without turning the poller into an SDK-upgrade or credential-reconciliation project.

Infrai uses one key, one wallet, and one bill across those backend capabilities. Here that consolidation is practical rather than decorative: adding an email or SMS route later does not require the on-call team to rotate another vendor credential or reconcile another provider invoice while reconstructing the agent incident.

How Should Node.js Failure Alerting Poll Logs and Errors?

The incidents that shape this design are missed jobs and duplicate deliveries. A page saying failures > 5 is not a reconstruction. For an agent loop that may call a model several times, I need a stable run ID, the collection window, exception identity, job outcome, HTTP status class, observed latency, and recorded cost metadata in the same incident trail. Without those fields, the on-call engineer can see pain but cannot bound impact or replay the decision.

One trap is treating absence as success. Error groups and log search can reveal exceptions and recorded failure patterns; they cannot prove that a scheduled settlement-review job ran at all. A heartbeat monitor such as Healthchecks.io must cover that negative space.

Silence is a separate signal.

Another boundary matters during a distributed failure: log trace_id and span_id values can support manual correlation, but they do not produce a distributed trace query or span tree. If the investigation depends on causal traversal across services, use a tracing system. Source-map decoding, crash symbolication, and session replay also belong elsewhere.

Two viable system shapes

The first shape is scheduled evidence polling. A cron-triggered worker reads overlapping time windows, normalizes evidence, evaluates thresholds, persists its cursor and deduplication key, then calls Slack, email, or another webhook. Its invariants are a durable cursor, overlap between windows, deterministic incident keys, idempotent notification delivery, and a separate heartbeat. The overlap prevents a record arriving near a boundary from falling through; the incident key prevents that overlap from paging twice.

The second shape is streaming ingestion into a specialist alert engine. Applications and collectors send telemetry continuously; the alert engine owns evaluation, grouping, muting, and notification routing. Its invariants are durable ingestion, bounded evaluation delay, rule-version history, and deduplication across retries. This is the better default when seconds matter, routing policy is complex, or a staffed team already operates the alert platform.

Both work. For a modest agent fleet where incident reconstruction is the primary decision axis, I choose polling first: a five-minute evidence window is easy to replay, audit, and compare against the agent run ledger. I would choose streaming for fraud controls or payment authorization paths where waiting for the next schedule is itself unacceptable.

The polling worker should use error groups or events for exception alerts and log search for failed jobs and 5xx patterns. Exact log-search filters are not declared in the discovery parameters, so the adapter must validate its query shape against the live discovery contract and representative staging data before production use. Do not bury guessed filter fields in the evaluator. Keep that uncertainty at the adapter boundary.

Fair comparison by operating boundary

Option Natural operating shape Strong fit here Boundary to keep visible
Infrai REST evidence source plus a team-owned scheduled evaluator Portable collection across mixed services, with public discovery for contract inspection No native alert rules, push channels, heartbeat monitoring, or span-tree queries
Sentry Specialist error monitoring Exception grouping and workflows when application errors dominate A separate heartbeat is still needed for work that never starts
Datadog Managed observability and alerting platform Central rules and routing when logs, metrics, and traces already live there Broader platform ownership and instrumentation are part of the decision
Grafana Cloud Hosted observability around telemetry backends Alert evaluation close to existing metrics and logs Rule and data-source operations replace the small poller's simplicity
Healthchecks.io Dead-man's-switch monitoring for scheduled work Detecting job never ran or job never finished It complements exception and log evidence rather than replacing them

This is not a feature-score exercise. Sentry is a stronger choice when exception triage is the center of gravity. Datadog or Grafana Cloud is more appropriate when native alert evaluation, routing, and distributed telemetry are already organizational standards. Healthchecks.io fills the blind spot every error-query design has: nothing was emitted because nothing ran. Infrai fits when the desired system shape is a thin, language-neutral evidence boundary and the team is comfortable owning the rule engine.

A small evaluator that will not double-page

The preventative path below intentionally starts after vendor-specific retrieval. Adapters translate their responses into Observation; the evaluator owns the policy. That split keeps undeclared search filters out of business logic and makes recorded incident fixtures replayable in tests.

package main

import (
    "crypto/sha256"
    "encoding/hex"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "sort"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

type Observation struct {
    ID, AgentRun, Kind string
    LatencyMS          int64
    CostUSD            float64
}

type Incident struct {
    Key       string
    WindowEnd time.Time
    Count     int
    RunIDs    []string
    CostUSD   float64
    MaxMS     int64
}

func fetchEvidence(client *http.Client, key, url string) ([]byte, error) {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, url, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Second << attempt
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil && seconds > 0 {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("GET %s: status %d: %s", url, resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("GET %s: rate limit persisted after retries", url)
}

func evaluate(end time.Time, threshold int, observations []Observation) (Incident, bool) {
    unique := make(map[string]Observation)
    for _, o := range observations {
        if o.ID != "" && (o.Kind == "exception" || o.Kind == "failed_job" || o.Kind == "http_5xx") {
            unique[o.ID] = o
        }
    }
    if len(unique) < threshold {
        return Incident{}, false
    }

    ids := make([]string, 0, len(unique))
    runs := make(map[string]struct{})
    incident := Incident{WindowEnd: end.UTC(), Count: len(unique)}
    for id, o := range unique {
        ids = append(ids, id)
        runs[o.AgentRun] = struct{}{}
        incident.CostUSD += o.CostUSD
        if o.LatencyMS > incident.MaxMS {
            incident.MaxMS = o.LatencyMS
        }
    }
    sort.Strings(ids)
    for run := range runs {
        incident.RunIDs = append(incident.RunIDs, run)
    }
    sort.Strings(incident.RunIDs)
    material := end.UTC().Format(time.RFC3339) + "|" + strings.Join(ids, ",")
    sum := sha256.Sum256([]byte(material))
    incident.Key = hex.EncodeToString(sum[:])
    return incident, true
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
        os.Exit(2)
    }
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    groups, err := fetchEvidence(client, key, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/errors/groups")
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    search, err := fetchEvidence(client, key, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/logs/search")
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    fmt.Printf("retrieved error_groups_bytes=%d log_search_bytes=%d\n", len(groups), len(search))

    end := time.Date(2026, 10, 8, 10, 5, 0, 0, time.UTC)
    observations := []Observation{
        {ID: "evt-17", AgentRun: "run-204", Kind: "http_5xx", LatencyMS: 1840, CostUSD: 0.031},
        {ID: "evt-18", AgentRun: "run-204", Kind: "exception", LatencyMS: 1920, CostUSD: 0.014},
        {ID: "evt-18", AgentRun: "run-204", Kind: "exception", LatencyMS: 1920, CostUSD: 0.014},
    }
    incident, fire := evaluate(end, 2, observations)
    fmt.Printf("fire=%t key=%s count=%d runs=%v cost=%.3f max_ms=%d\n",
        fire, incident.Key, incident.Count, incident.RunIDs, incident.CostUSD, incident.MaxMS)
}

The two GET calls deliberately send no query fields: the search filters are undeclared, and inventing them would make a copyable example dishonest. They retrieve raw evidence with Bearer authentication, an explicit method, a 15-second client timeout, status checks, and bounded 429 retry behavior that honors Retry-After. A production adapter should decode only the response shape verified from live discovery, then pass normalized records to evaluate.

The concrete observation numbers are fixture data, not a benchmark. The repeated evt-18 models an overlapping poll window. It contributes once. In production, store Incident.Key under a uniqueness constraint before sending the notification, and advance the cursor only after the evidence and notification decision are durable. A process-local map is not enough. This is the place where I am deliberately conservative: an extra row in the incident ledger is recoverable, while a second page to the same responder trains people to distrust the channel.

Notification delivery needs its own retry policy: exponential backoff for rate limits, respect Retry-After when supplied, and reuse the same incident key for every attempt. Route severity separately from evidence collection. A Slack page might fire immediately while an email digest waits, but both should point to the same immutable incident record.

When polling is the wrong answer

This recommendation has a hard limitation. Infrai does not supply native alert rules or notification routing, and polling has a detection-delay trade-off. Do not choose this architecture for sub-minute safety actions, complicated escalation trees, or investigations that require full distributed traces. Datadog or Grafana Cloud is the better choice when managed evaluation and routing are requirements; Sentry is the better choice when specialist exception triage dominates. The same is true if audit history for rule changes is mandatory: keep rules in a system that records those changes rather than relying on an informal cron configuration.

There is also a privacy boundary. If the workflow requires per-user log deletion, bulk export, subscriptions, configurable retention, or cold-storage controls, verify those capabilities in the selected log system before sending regulated fintech data. The collection API should never become an accidental data-governance decision.

My runbook decision is conditional: poll when reconstruction quality matters more than immediate push, persist enough state to replay every window, and pair the poller with a heartbeat. Stream when response time, rich routing, or trace-native investigation dominates. If the REST evidence boundary fits that first shape, start with the failure-alerting guide and verify the live discovery schema before wiring the adapter.

Sources

References used for product boundaries and implementation choices:

title: Why Your React Animations Feel Slow Even at 60 FPS
description:
Why Your React Animations Feel Slow Even at 60 FPS

You open the Performance panel. The animation is running around 60 FPS. There are no spectacular red warnings, nothing is visibly freezing, and your laptop is barely interested.

Yet the interaction still feels slow.

The cursor seems to chase the pointer instead of following it. A scroll reveal arrives just after you expect it. A draggable card has a slightly rubbery disconnect from your hand. A menu technically animates smoothly, but opening it feels heavier than clicking the same control without motion.

This is where an FPS counter can send debugging in the wrong direction.

60 FPS tells you how many frames arrived. It does not tell you whether they arrived well.

Animation quality is a combination of frame consistency, input latency, browser rendering work, JavaScript execution and the actual motion decisions you made. React can participate in those problems, but “React is slow” is rarely a useful diagnosis.

The better question is: what kind of slow are you looking at?

60 FPS Is a Target, Not a Diagnosis

On a 60 Hz display, the browser gets a new refresh opportunity roughly every 16.7 milliseconds. During that window it may need to execute JavaScript, recalculate styles, perform layout, paint pixels and composite layers before the updated frame reaches the display.

That is why 60 FPS became a familiar target for interface animation. A consistently delivered frame roughly every 16.7 ms can look smooth on a 60 Hz display.

The important word is consistently.

Imagine an FPS overlay reports an average around 60 over a measurement window. That number does not tell you whether individual frames were evenly spaced. A sequence with occasional slow frames followed by quicker frames can have a respectable average while still producing visible hitching.

Perceived motion follows the spacing of frames, not the optimism of the average.

This is also why hardcoding your animation around an assumption of exactly 60 updates per second is fragile. Displays running at 120 Hz and 144 Hz are common enough that requestAnimationFrame() may be called at those rates instead. MDN explicitly recommends using the timestamp provided to the callback when calculating animation progress.

let start;

function animate(timestamp) {
  if (start === undefined) {
    start = timestamp;
  }

  const elapsed = timestamp - start;
  const progress = Math.min(elapsed / 600, 1);

  element.style.transform = `translateX(${progress * 200}px)`;

  if (progress < 1) {
    requestAnimationFrame(animate);
  }
}

requestAnimationFrame(animate);

The animation above is based on elapsed time rather than “move three pixels every frame.” That distinction keeps the duration stable when the display refresh rate changes.

You can read more about the behavior of requestAnimationFrame() on MDN.

Your Browser Has More Work to Do Than Draw the Animation

When an element changes visually, the browser does not simply receive your new value and teleport pixels into place.

Depending on what changed, it can move through several stages: style recalculation, layout, paint and composition. The amount of work depends partly on the CSS property being animated.

Animating something that changes geometry, such as width, left or margin, can require the browser to recalculate layout and repaint. Properties such as transform and opacity can often avoid layout and be handled later in the rendering pipeline.

Consider a simple horizontal movement.

// Can require layout work as the value changes
<div style={{ left: `${x}px` }} />

// Usually a better fit for visual movement
<div style={{ transform: `translateX(${x}px)` }} />

That does not mean transform is a magic performance keyword. You can animate only transforms and still build a sluggish interaction if each frame also performs expensive JavaScript, reads layout repeatedly, updates a large React subtree, draws an expensive canvas scene or runs several competing effects.

The property is one part of the frame. MDN has a useful breakdown of the browser rendering waterfall and animation property costs.

The practical debugging question is not just “Am I getting 60 FPS?” It is “What work has to complete before each visible update?”

React Can Make the Animation Compete With Your Application

React state is a great way to express application state. It is not automatically the best place to store every intermediate pixel of an animation. Suppose a pointer-following element writes its coordinates into component state for every pointermove event:

import { useState } from "react";

export default function Follower() {
  const [position, setPosition] = useState({ x: 0, y: 0 });

  return (
    <div
      onPointerMove={(event) => {
        setPosition({
          x: event.clientX,
          y: event.clientY,
        });
      }}
    >
      <div
        className="follower"
        style={{
          transform: `translate3d(${position.x}px, ${position.y}px, 0)`,
        }}
      />
    </div>
  );
}

There is nothing inherently invalid about this code. The relevant question is what happens around it.

Every state update schedules React work. If Follower is isolated and the surrounding tree is cheap, the result may be perfectly acceptable. If the update causes substantial component work while other JavaScript is also running, you have made your animation share main-thread time with work that may not need to happen every frame.

For transient per-frame values, a ref or an animation system can sometimes keep React responsible for the meaningful state transition while letting interpolation happen outside repeated component renders.

import { useEffect, useRef } from "react";

export default function Follower() {
  const followerRef = useRef(null);
  const target = useRef({ x: 0, y: 0 });
  const current = useRef({ x: 0, y: 0 });

  useEffect(() => {
    let frameId;

    const tick = () => {
      current.current.x +=
        (target.current.x - current.current.x) * 0.18;

      current.current.y +=
        (target.current.y - current.current.y) * 0.18;

      if (followerRef.current) {
        followerRef.current.style.transform =
          `translate3d(${current.current.x}px, ${current.current.y}px, 0)`;
      }

      frameId = requestAnimationFrame(tick);
    };

    frameId = requestAnimationFrame(tick);

    return () => cancelAnimationFrame(frameId);
  }, []);

  return (
    <div
      onPointerMove={(event) => {
        target.current.x = event.clientX;
        target.current.y = event.clientY;
      }}
    >
      <div ref={followerRef} className="follower" />
    </div>
  );
}

This is not a rule that says “never animate through React state.” It is a separation-of-responsibilities question.

If a value exists mainly to produce another visual frame a few milliseconds later, ask whether the entire React render path needs to know about every intermediate value.

Profile before rewriting it.

requestAnimationFrame() Does Not Make Expensive Work Cheap

Moving code into requestAnimationFrame() is another optimization that can feel more powerful than it is.

requestAnimationFrame() tells the browser you want to run a callback before an upcoming repaint. It gives your animation work a browser-aware scheduling mechanism. It does not reduce the amount of work inside the callback.

This can still be expensive:

function tick() {
  const cards = document.querySelectorAll(".card");

  cards.forEach((card) => {
    const rect = card.getBoundingClientRect();

    card.style.transform =
      `translateY(${window.innerHeight - rect.top}px)`;
  });

  requestAnimationFrame(tick);
}

requestAnimationFrame(tick);

Now you are querying elements, measuring layout and writing styles repeatedly. Put enough work in there and rAF will faithfully schedule an expensive callback every time the browser gives you the chance.

The useful question is:

What am I asking the browser to do inside each frame?

Cache what can be cached. Avoid unnecessary layout measurement inside hot loops. Keep cleanup explicit. Stop loops that no longer have a reason to run.

requestAnimationFrame() is a scheduler, not absolution.

Sometimes the Performance Problem Is Actually a Motion Problem

This is the category that profiling tools cannot solve for you. An interaction can be computationally cheap, maintain a steady frame rate and still feel slow because you told it to move slowly.

Imagine a cursor follower using this interpolation:

current += (target - current) * 0.05;

The browser may render it beautifully. No dropped frames. No expensive layout. No large React commits. It can still feel like the cursor is dragging a reluctant ghost behind it.

Change the interpolation:

current += (target - current) * 0.22;

The computational cost is effectively the same, but the interaction feels radically more immediate.

The same problem appears with animation durations, easing curves and springs. A navigation overlay with a long ease-in can feel resistant because the first part of the motion barely moves. A spring with too little stiffness or too much settling can make a button feel mushy. A parallax layer that deliberately trails scroll position may cross the line from depth into input lag.

A perfectly rendered delay is still a delay.

This matters because developers often respond to that feeling by optimizing code that is already fast enough. They memoize components, switch libraries or reach for will-change, only to discover that the animation still feels heavy.

Before doing that, temporarily shorten the duration or remove smoothing. If the interaction suddenly feels right while the performance trace barely changes, you found a motion-design problem rather than a rendering bottleneck.

Input-Coupled Motion Exposes Latency Faster

Not all animation has the same relationship with the user.

A decorative background can arrive slightly late without anyone having a precise expectation for where it should be. A button pressed under a cursor is different. So is dragging, scrolling, scrubbing or moving a custom pointer.

The user's hand provides a reference signal.

If their pointer is here and your visual follower is consistently there, the delay is obvious. If their finger moves a card and the card takes time to catch up, they feel the gap before they think about it technically.

This is why scroll smoothing deserves restraint. Smoothing the visual response can create a deliberate sense of weight, but too much of it makes the page feel as though scrolling has been routed through syrup.

The same applies to cursor trails. A trailing layer can be expressive while the actual clickable interaction remains immediate. Trouble starts when decorative latency leaks into controls that are supposed to feel direct. For input-driven effects, profile responsiveness and inspect your interpolation before chasing raw FPS.

“Use Transform and Opacity” Is Good Advice With Missing Footnotes

For many DOM animations, transform and opacity are sensible first choices because they can avoid the layout work triggered by geometry-changing properties. They should not become a superstition.

A fullscreen blur, huge translucent layer, complex SVG filter, large shadow or high-resolution canvas may still cost real rendering time even if its position changes through transform. A page running five independently smooth animation loops can become expensive when they all operate together.

Production pages are ecosystems. Your effect does not get a private browser.

This becomes especially noticeable on marketing sites where animation lives beside analytics, hydration, images, video, sliders, third-party scripts and application code. An isolated CodePen can tell you whether the effect works. It cannot tell you what happens after the effect moves into the page that has to ship.

Profile Frame Time, Not Just the Counter

When an animation feels wrong, resist the urge to start changing code randomly.

Reproduce the issue in the environment where it actually matters. Use a production build when possible. Development tooling and extra checks can distort performance characteristics.

Then record the interaction in your browser's Performance panel.

Look at what is occupying the main thread around the problematic frames. Is there a large JavaScript task? Repeated style recalculation? Layout work? Expensive paint? A React render arriving at exactly the wrong moment? Multiple callbacks continuing after their sections have left the viewport?

You are trying to identify a category of failure before choosing a fix.

A useful diagnostic table looks like this:

What you feel Inspect first
Animation visibly jumps Frame timing, long JavaScript tasks, layout and paint
Motion is smooth but follows input late Smoothing, interpolation, input handling and main-thread work
Animation struggles while UI data changes React renders and competing JavaScript
Works on desktop, struggles on phone CPU/GPU cost, image/canvas work and concurrent effects
Smooth everywhere but still feels heavy Duration, easing, distance and spring tuning

For deeper diagnostics, browsers are also gaining visibility into Long Animation Frames, which can help identify work contributing to long frames. Treat it as an additional signal rather than the one universal profiling API; support and tooling still deserve checking for your target browsers.

Test the Page, Not the Demo

An animation should be judged in the page where it will live.

That means testing it beside the real navigation, typography, images, scripts and adjacent interactions. It also means testing the actual devices you care about rather than using a high-end development machine as your minimum specification.

Mobile changes more than available processing power. Pointer assumptions disappear. Viewports become shorter. Touch scrolling behaves differently. Effects that feel appropriately restrained with a mouse can become annoying when attached to every finger movement.

Offscreen work matters too. If a canvas render loop or animation keeps producing frames after the user has left the section, it is still spending resources even though it contributes nothing to the current experience.

The production checklist is therefore broader than “does it hit 60?”

Ask whether the effect stops when appropriate. Ask whether it still reads correctly without motion. Check prefers-reduced-motion where the interaction calls for an alternative. Verify keyboard and touch behavior where controls are involved.

And test the whole page.

Source Access Is Useful Because Performance Decisions Are Contextual

This is also where reusable animation patterns get interesting.

A polished demo can give you the right interaction idea, but production usually requires changing something: timing, breakpoint behavior, scroll distance, pointer behavior, dependencies, cleanup, the number of animated elements, or what happens when motion is reduced.

That is why Hyperiux Vault uses a source-first model for its React and Next.js interaction effects. The effect files land in your project, so the implementation can be inspected and tuned rather than treated as a sealed animation runtime. That does not make an effect automatically fast. It makes the decisions visible.

A scroll interaction may need different behavior on a short mobile viewport. A cursor system should not assume a fine pointer exists on every device. A WebGL scene has a very different rendering budget from a CSS text reveal. Those decisions belong in the implementation, not in a blanket promise that every animation is “optimized.”

Vault's Scroll Effects guidance makes the same production distinction: use properties appropriate for animation, avoid unnecessary layout reads during scroll, clean up timelines and listeners, and test the effect on a real mid-range device before treating the implementation as finished.

If you want a starting point rather than another empty component file, you can browse the React and Next.js interaction effects in Vault and adapt the source to the page that actually has to ship.

A Better Way to Debug “Slow” Animation

The next time an animation looks smooth in an FPS overlay but feels wrong under your hand, split the problem into separate questions.

Is the browser delivering frames consistently? Is expensive work happening during those frames? Is React doing work that does not need to happen at animation frequency? Is the visual response arriving late after input? Or is the easing itself simply telling the interface to feel slow?

Those failures can look similar from the outside, but they need different fixes.

60 FPS is useful evidence. It just isn't a verdict.

title: How Ora benchmarks every major AI agent on Vercel
description:
Ora on Vercel

  • Front end, back end, and agent runtime on one platform

  • Every major agent tested side by side on live sites

  • Hundreds of commits a day from a 16-person engineering team

Ora sends agents onto live websites with instructions to sign up for a product, integrate with it, and pay for it. Agents often fail, and by Ora's estimate, 99% of the web isn't agent-ready. The platform shows customers where and why agents fail, and what to change.

Assaf Elovic, co-founder of Ora, spent years helping agents discover the web. His previous company, Tavily, built a web search engine for AI agents and was acquired by Nebius earlier this year. Search solved half the problem, but an agent that finds a product still has to actually use it. He and co-founder Liad Yosef started Ora to measure how ready the web is for agents, and to fix the parts that aren't.

Today that means spawning agents against live customer sites from journey.ora.ai, where Ora runs a journey and records the cost, latency, and steps an agent needs to finish a task. The platform runs on Vercel, including the agent runtime.

Benchmarking every major agent side by side

Every harness expects its own infrastructure

Agents decompose into two parts: a model, which does the reasoning, and a harness, the software that gives the model its tools and drives it from step to step. Ora's lineup covers the agents customers use most: Claude Code, ChatGPT, Gemini, Hermes, OpenClaw, and eve, Vercel's agent framework. Ora runs each agent on a customer's website and watches how it handles common workflows.

No two harnesses want the same infrastructure. Each expects its own environment and exposes its steps differently, so Ora runs a separate runtime for every harness and traces every step. Ido Finder, who leads engineering at Ora, calls that side-by-side coverage one of the most valuable things ora brings to its customers.

When an agent stalls in a signup flow, the customer sees which step and what it tried. Without the trace, the result is a score with nothing behind it.

One platform under every harness

Ora built this testing system entirely on Vercel. Front end, back end, and the agent runtime share the same deployment path, logs, and authentication. The agent runtime isn't separate infrastructure to operate; it lives where the rest of the product lives.

Ora benchmarked eve, then built on it

Testing eve like any other harness

When Vercel launched eve, Ora gave it no special treatment. eve went through the same benchmark, under the same conditions, as every other harness in the lineup. Ora works with Vercel Engineering as a design partner, and Finder gave the eve team direct access to the platform to dig into the results.

The initial test put eve against Claude Code across hundreds of real journeys on multiple domains. Both harnesses ran the same models, Claude Fable 5 and Haiku 4.5, and every run gave the agent the same job: integrate with a product.

Ora published three numbers from the comparison:

  • 7% fewer steps to reach the goal

  • 2x native success: twice as many tasks finished on the customer's own site instead of falling back to web search

  • 9% more valid endpoints: more of the endpoints the agent found were ones it could actually call

The benchmark fed back into eve, too. One run surfaced a prompt-caching issue, the eve team shipped a fix, and Ora's next round of results measured roughly 15% lower total cost.

The framework behind Ora's own agents

For a company that benchmarks every major harness for a living, this is not a casual choice. After those results, Ora builds on eve.

Because eve follows the Next.js paradigm, there was little to configure, and tools, skills, and connectors take little code. The feature that sealed it was the sandbox override. An agent framework like eve ships with its own sandbox, the isolated environment where the agent executes, runs tools, and touches files. That's a good default for most teams, because you get safe execution for free. But an agent in the framework's own sandbox runs outside the instrumented environment where Ora traces every step. The override lets the team swap that environment in, so eve agents get recorded like every other harness, with nothing new built.

Journey.ora.ai now has eve on both sides, eve is one of the harnesses it tests, and eve is what it runs on.

How 16 engineers ship hundreds of commits a day

The engineering team is 16 people shipping hundreds of commits a day, and day-to-day infrastructure work belongs to their coding agents. A stack that sits in one place lets those agents run it end to end.

Finder puts the time saved at a few hours a week at least. Elovic credits a similar amount to how well coding agents build with Vercel's libraries.

What's next

Ora is adding more products, and the architecture is growing with them. The team is splitting its platform into microservices, all of them on Vercel. New services deploy to the same infrastructure and talk to each other with no extra configuration, and the internal agents built on eve will run as one more service.

By Ora's own measure, 99% of the web still can't handle an agent that shows up to sign up, integrate, and pay.

About Ora: Ora makes the web agent-ready. Companies use ora to benchmark how AI agents discover, navigate, and interact with their websites, and to build the infrastructure agents need to find, use, and transact with them.

title: Brotli on NGINX thread pools: ngx_mbrotli vs ngx_brotli
description:
Summary

  • With google/ngx_brotli, each response is compressed inside the NGINX worker’s event loop, so every other request on that worker waits. While large responses were compressed at Brotli levels 6 and 11, the p99 latency of small uncompressed requests rose from 1.9 ms to 17–514 ms.
  • ngx_mbrotli with brotli_thread_pool compresses on NGINX thread pools. In the same test, the p99 of small requests stayed at 1.7–3.3 ms, the same as with no compression.
  • One NGINX worker with a 4-thread pool served 3.8–15 times as many Brotli responses per second as google/ngx_brotli on 85 KB–2.2 MB files. The gain was largest at levels 9 and 11.
  • The cost is memory. At 8 connections on 1–2.2 MB responses, a worker peaked at 138–995 MiB, 11–26 times as much as google/ngx_brotli. Responses longer than one 1 MiB segment came out 0.9–5.2% larger.
  • Measured on 20 October 2026 with NGINX 1.30.6, one worker, an Intel Core i7-13700KF under WSL2. Every response was decoded and checked against the original by SHA-256.

ngx_mbrotli is an NGINX module for on-the-fly Brotli compression, written in Rust on top of the mbrotli encoder. It is a drop-in replacement for google/ngx_brotli, with the same directives, defaults and $brotli_ratio variable. Unlike google/ngx_brotli, it can compress on NGINX thread pools, so that compressing a large response does not stop the worker from serving anything else.

This post measures what that changes. One NGINX worker served large files compressed on the fly while a second stream of small uncompressed requests went to the same worker. With google/ngx_brotli, the 99th percentile latency of the small requests rose from 1.9 ms to as much as 514 ms. With ngx_mbrotli on a 4-thread pool it stayed at 1.7–3.3 ms.

p99 latency of small requests while large responses are compressed

Large requests arrive 8 at a time. ms, logarithmic scale.

Large file google/ngx_brotli ngx_mbrotli, event loop Pool, 1 task Pool, 4 tasks
react-dom.development.js (1.03 MB), level 6, 31 per second 115 94.0 3.3 2.8
jquery.min.js (85 KB), level 11, 7 per second 514 306 2.0 1.9

No compression: 1.9 ms.

Small uncompressed requests (1.9 KB, 1,000 per second) on the same worker as the large compressed ones. wrk2 with coordinated omission corrected, median of three 30-second runs. NGINX 1.30.6, one worker on 4 CPUs, a pool of 4 threads; 20 October 2026.

The numbers come from a reduced run under WSL2 on 20 October 2026. They are good for comparing the modules with each other, less so as absolute figures for your hardware. How it was measured has the details and what was not measured.

Why compression delays other requests

An NGINX worker process serves thousands of connections from one thread. Its event loop waits for sockets to become ready, runs a short piece of work for each one, and goes back to waiting. That works because each piece of work is short. A filter that runs for 100 ms holds every other connection of that worker for 100 ms.

Compression is such a filter. google/ngx_brotli and the stock gzip module compress in the event loop. When a 1 MB JavaScript bundle is compressed at Brotli level 6, it takes about 16 ms of CPU time, and at level 11 about 1.2 s. A small request that arrives on the same worker meanwhile waits for compression to end. When several large responses arrive at once, the worker compresses them back to back, and the small request waits for all of them.

NGINX has had a way out since version 1.7.11, released on 24 March 2015 with “experimental thread pools support” (CHANGES). NGINX itself uses thread pools for blocking file I/O (aio threads). ngx_mbrotli uses them for compression.

How ngx_mbrotli compresses on a thread pool

With brotli_thread_pool, the module cuts a response into segments of brotli_parallel_segment_size, 1 MiB by default. Each segment becomes an NGINX thread task (ngx_thread_task_t) and is compressed on one of the pool’s threads. Up to brotli_parallel_tasks segments of one response, 4 by default, are compressed at once. A response that fits in one segment is compressed by one thread, in one piece.

When a task is done, its completion handler runs in the event loop. It passes the compressed bytes down the filter chain in order and wakes the connection, as a write event would. While tasks are in flight, the request stays marked as blocked and buffered, so NGINX neither finalizes it early nor frees memory a thread is still using. Meanwhile the event loop serves other connections.

Segments are compressed independently: Brotli back-references do not cross segment boundaries. That makes segments safe to compress in parallel. It also makes a response longer than one segment compress slightly worse, as the numbers below show.

load_module modules/ngx_mbrotli.so;

thread_pool brotli threads=4;

http {
    brotli on;
    brotli_comp_level 6;
    brotli_types text/plain text/css application/javascript application/json
                 image/svg+xml;

    brotli_thread_pool brotli;
}

NGINX must be built with --with-threads; nginx -V shows it. nginx.org’s packages are. The pool named default exists without being declared, with 32 threads per worker, and is shared with aio threads.

How long do other requests wait?

Small uncompressed requests (small.json, 1.9 KB) were sent at 1,000 per second over 32 connections. At the same time, a second stream requested large compressed files at a constant rate of about half of what google/ngx_brotli can sustain. All variants kept up with both streams.

p99 latency of small requests, large responses one at a time

Large requests arrive on one connection at a constant interval. ms, logarithmic scale.

The same test as the chart at the top, with one 30-second run. NGINX 1.30.6, one worker on 4 CPUs, a pool of 4 threads; 20 October 2026.

Large responses Arrival No compression google/ngx_brotli ngx_mbrotli, event loop Pool, 1 task Pool, 4 tasks
react-dom.development.js, level 6, 31 per second 8 at once 1.9 115 94 3.3 2.8
react-dom.development.js, level 6, 31 per second One at a time 1.9 17.0 14.7 1.7 1.8
jquery.min.js, level 11, 7 per second 8 at once 1.9 514 306 2.0 1.9
jquery.min.js, level 11, 7 per second One at a time 1.9 71.2 45.7 1.8 1.9

“8 at once” is the large stream’s 8 connections, which wrk2 starts together and which stay in phase. It is what happens when several clients ask for large files at the same moment. In the event loop, a small request then waits for up to 8 compressions. “One at a time” is a single connection at a constant interval, where a small request waits for at most one. It is the lower bound of the effect: the pool cut p99 by 9–40 times there. On the pool, the maximum latency of a small request one at a time was 3.6 ms.

Without a thread pool, ngx_mbrotli lowers p99 by 14–41% against google/ngx_brotli, only because mbrotli compresses faster. It blocks the event loop all the same. The difference in tail latency comes from moving compression off the event loop, not from a faster encoder.

How many requests does one worker serve?

The same worker under closed-loop load, with wrk and 8 connections:

libraries.json, 2.2 MB 6 32.7 37.8 +16% 146 4.5× 142 4.3×
libraries.json, 2.2 MB 9 14.8 20.1 +35% 63.3 4.3× 63.3 4.3×
libraries.json, 2.2 MB 11 0.55 0.87 +58% 5.11 9.3× 5.26 9.6×

The pool’s 4 threads use the 4 CPUs that google/ngx_brotli, with one worker, cannot. That explains about 4× at levels 4–6. The rest comes from the encoder. At level 9 the C encoder allocates a 32 MiB hash table for every response over 64 KB and frees it afterwards. That cost does not depend on the response size, so mbrotli’s lead is largest on the 85 KB file. At level 11 a 1 MiB segment compresses faster than a whole file, so the pool gains more than its 4 threads.

With 8 connections, 1 and 4 tasks per response served within 3% of each other, with one exception (+17%). The pool’s threads were already busy with different responses.

How fast is one large response?

More tasks per response help when a response is longer than one segment and nothing else competes for the threads:

Time to serve one 2.2 MB response

libraries.json, three 1 MiB segments, one connection. ms, logarithmic scale.

wrk, median of three runs. NGINX 1.30.6, one worker on 4 CPUs, a pool of 4 threads; 20 October 2026.

Level google/ngx_brotli ngx_mbrotli, event loop Pool, 1 task Pool, 4 tasks
4 14.6 12.9 13.1 6.6
6 30.6 26.6 25.2 12.5
9 69.1 50.1 54.9 24.1
11 2,004 1,253 771 371

4 tasks served it 2.0–2.3 times as fast as 1 task, and 2.2–5.4 times as fast as google/ngx_brotli. Responses up to 1 MiB fit in one segment, so the number of tasks does not change how fast they are served. react-dom.development.js is a 1 MiB segment and a 31 KB one, so 4 tasks served it only 4–34% faster than 1.

Brotli level 11 on the fly

Level 11 is usually kept for pre-compressed static files, because one response can hold a worker for a second or more. On a thread pool, that time no longer holds up other requests: next to a stream of level-11 responses, small requests kept a p99 of 1.8–2.0 ms. A 2.2 MB response took 371 ms with 4 tasks, against 2,004 ms with google/ngx_brotli.

Level 11 still costs CPU. libraries.json needed 785 ms of CPU time per response on the pool, and the worker served 5.3 such responses per second on 4 CPUs. It fits responses that are large, compressible and requested rarely enough, not a busy API.

What the thread pool costs

Memory. In the event loop, a worker compresses one response at a time and needs one encoder. On a pool, every response being sent holds encoders for its segments until it is sent. Peak memory then grows with the number of responses in flight and with the number of tasks per response.

Peak memory of the worker

VmHWM at 8 connections, MiB, logarithmic scale. The labelled value is the pool with 4 tasks.

Highest of three runs. NGINX 1.30.6, one worker on 4 CPUs, a pool of 4 threads; 20 October 2026.

Response Level google/ngx_brotli ngx_mbrotli, event loop Pool, 1 task Pool, 4 tasks
react-dom.development.js, 1.03 MB 4 9 12 117 138
react-dom.development.js, 1.03 MB 6 11 14 144 143
react-dom.development.js, 1.03 MB 9 39 41 482 483
react-dom.development.js, 1.03 MB 11 25 28 296 269
libraries.json, 2.2 MB 4 9 14 143 215
libraries.json, 2.2 MB 6 11 14 210 276
libraries.json, 2.2 MB 9 39 43 519 995
libraries.json, 2.2 MB 11 28 30 390 505

In the event loop, ngx_mbrotli needs 2–5 MiB more than google/ngx_brotli. On the pool, it needs 11–26 times as much.

CPU time. CPU time per request, including the pool’s threads, was within 0.6–1.4 times that of the event loop. At level 11 the pool needed 37–40% less, because 1 MiB segments compress faster than a whole file. At level 9 it needed 22–40% more.

CPU time per request

Worker and pool threads together, 8 connections. ms, logarithmic scale.

Median of three runs. NGINX 1.30.6, one worker on 4 CPUs, a pool of 4 threads; 20 October 2026.

Response Level google/ngx_brotli ngx_mbrotli, event loop Pool, 1 task Pool, 4 tasks
react-dom.development.js, 1.03 MB 6 16.0 13.4 14.2 14.5
react-dom.development.js, 1.03 MB 9 42.3 25.6 35.8 31.2
react-dom.development.js, 1.03 MB 11 1,153 695 414 415
libraries.json, 2.2 MB 9 71.4 51.1 63.0 62.9
libraries.json, 2.2 MB 11 2,432 1,256 789 785

Compression ratio. Responses longer than one segment came out 0.9–5.2% larger, because segments are compressed independently. Responses up to one segment are byte-for-byte what the event loop produces.

How to configure it

The defaults suit most sites: a 1 MiB segment and 4 tasks per response. What to change and why:

  • Declare a pool of your own with thread_pool brotli threads=N;. The benchmark used 4 threads on 4 CPUs. Pool sizes were not compared, so start near the number of CPUs a worker can use.
  • Keep brotli_parallel_segment_size 1m. With 4m, both files here fit in one segment, so the output is as small as in the event loop and peak memory is 19–42% lower. At levels 4–9, it served between 9% fewer and 14% more requests per second than 1m. At level 11 it served 35–37% fewer, because the whole file compresses slower than 1 MiB segments. With 4m, only responses longer than 4 MiB are split across threads.
  • Lower brotli_parallel_tasks to save memory when single responses are rarely longer than a segment. On the 2.2 MB file, 4 tasks needed up to 1.9 times the memory of 1. Under load, 1 and 4 tasks served about the same number of requests.
  • Bound encoder memory with brotli_parallel_compressors (4 by default), which limits how many compressors a worker keeps encoders for, and with brotli_retention_policy bounded <size> or release_all, which keep less memory between responses.
  • Turn the pool off per location with brotli_thread_pool off;. Compressing a small response in the event loop holds the loop only briefly. In this run the pool still served 1.5–5.4 times as many 1.9 KB responses per second, so there is no measured reason to turn it off for small responses. A size threshold was not measured.

The ngx_mbrotli README documents every directive.

When you do not need it

  • Static files are better compressed once, at build time, at level 11, and served with brotli_static on;. Nothing is compressed per request then.
  • A CDN that compresses for you takes the work off NGINX. Traffic between the CDN and NGINX may still be worth compressing.
  • Small responses only. If no response takes long to compress, the event loop is never held long, and the pool mostly adds memory.

How it was measured

Hardware. Intel Core i7-13700KF, Windows 10.0.26300.9711, WSL 2.7.14.0 with kernel 6.18.33.2-microsoft-standard-WSL2, Ubuntu 22.04.5. WSL2 shows 12 identical cores with 2 threads each and does not tell which are performance cores, so some of the pinned CPUs may be efficiency cores. Traffic went over loopback without TLS, and files were served from tmpfs (/dev/shm).

Build. NGINX 1.30.6, ./configure --with-compat --with-threads
--without-http_rewrite_module, gcc 11.4.0, both modules dynamic. google/ngx_brotli at commit a71f9312 with the Brotli 1.1.0 it pins as a submodule. ngx_mbrotli at commit 8f7508a with mbrotli 0.5.10, built with rustc 1.99.0. This commit predates the 0.4.0 release; the current release is 0.4.5, and the run has not been repeated on it.

Configuration. worker_processes 1, with the worker and its pool pinned to 4 physical cores, and thread_pool cp threads=4. On the pool, brotli_thread_pool cp with brotli_parallel_tasks 1 or the default 4. Everything else was left at its default, including the 1m segment and encoder reuse.

Load. Requests per second and CPU time: wrk 4.1.0 on 4 other physical cores, 2 threads and 8 connections, 4 seconds per run (8 seconds for files over 1 MB, 5 times as long at level 11) after a 1-second warm-up. NGINX was restarted for every run, and each run started once the worker had been idle for 300 ms. Three runs, in an order shuffled between runs; tables give the median. CPU time is the worker’s user and system time from /proc/<pid>/stat, including the pool’s threads. Latency: two wrk2 streams (commit 44a94c1) at once, open loop, with coordinated omission corrected; 8 at once is the median of three 30-second runs, one at a time is a single 30-second run.

Files. jQuery 3.7.1 (jquery.min.js, 85 KB) and React DOM 18.3.1 (react-dom.development.js, 1.03 MB) from cdnjs, the full cdnjs API listing (libraries.json, 2.2 MB) and its first 10 entries (small.json, 1.9 KB), all fetched on 20 October 2026.

Correctness. Before the runs, every response in every combination of module, variant, level and file was decoded with curl’s Brotli decoder and compared with the original by SHA-256. All matched.

Not measured. gzip, more than one worker process, pool sizes other than 4 threads, a response-size threshold for the pool, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, slow clients, long runs and bare-metal Linux. Runs were 3 per cell and 4–40 seconds long, shorter than a full benchmark.

Install it

ngx_mbrotli has packages for Debian, Ubuntu, RHEL and its derivatives, and Amazon Linux: install it from packages, or build it from source. Existing google/ngx_brotli configuration keeps working; add brotli_thread_pool to move compression off the event loop.

The same measurements for Zstandard, with ngx_mzstd against tokers/zstd-nginx-module, are in zstd on NGINX thread pools.

Questions

Does Brotli compression block the NGINX event loop?

Yes, with google/ngx_brotli and the stock gzip module. The response is compressed by the worker process that serves it, inside its event loop, so the worker’s other connections wait until compression of that buffer ends. With ngx_mbrotli and brotli_thread_pool, compression runs on an NGINX thread pool and the event loop keeps serving other connections.

How do I compress Brotli on an NGINX thread pool?

Install ngx_mbrotli, which accepts google/ngx_brotli’s configuration unchanged, and add brotli_thread_pool default; next to brotli on;. NGINX must be built with --with-threads. To size the pool on its own, declare thread_pool brotli threads=4; in the main context and use brotli_thread_pool brotli;.

How much faster is ngx_mbrotli than google/ngx_brotli?

With a 4-thread pool, one worker served 3.8–4.5 times as many requests at levels 4–6 and 4.3–15 times as many at levels 9–11, on 85 KB–2.2 MB files. Without the pool, in the event loop like google/ngx_brotli, it served 5–64% more requests, and 4.4 times as many at level 9 on an 85 KB file.

How much memory does ngx_mbrotli need on a thread pool?

Much more than in the event loop. Every response being sent holds encoders for its segments. At 8 connections on 1–2.2 MB responses, one worker peaked at 138–995 MiB against 9–39 MiB for google/ngx_brotli. brotli_parallel_tasks 1, brotli_parallel_compressors and brotli_retention_policy bounded <size> keep it lower.

Is Brotli level 11 practical for on-the-fly compression?

It is still expensive: a 2.2 MB JSON file took 785 ms of CPU time at level 11. On a thread pool that time no longer delays other requests. With 4 tasks, one response is served in 371 ms instead of 2,004 ms with google/ngx_brotli, and one worker served 6.4–9.6 times as many level-11 responses per second.

Why not just add more NGINX worker processes?

It was not measured here. A connection stays on the worker that accepted it, so a request that lands on a worker busy compressing still waits for it. More workers make that less likely; they do not shorten the wait.
