title: Why OFFSET Pagination Is Killing Your PostgreSQL Queries (And How to Implement Keyset Pagination in Node.js)
description:
Almost every API starts with the same pagination code:

SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20 OFFSET 40;

It's simple, it works in development, and it ships. Months later, the table has millions of rows and you're seeing:

  • Page 1 loads in 5 ms. Page 5,000 takes 3 seconds.
  • A crawler or an export job walking through pages brings the database to its knees.
  • Users report seeing the same item twice, or missing items entirely, as they page through a live feed.

All three have the same root cause: OFFSET pagination doesn't scale and isn't stable. This post explains why, then builds the alternative, keyset pagination (also called cursor or seek pagination), step by step in Node.js and PostgreSQL, including a subtle timestamp bug that trips up most first implementations.

Why OFFSET gets slower with every page

OFFSET 100000 doesn't mean "jump to row 100,000." PostgreSQL has no way to teleport to the Nth row of a sorted result. It has to produce the first 100,020 rows in order and throw away the first 100,000.

So the cost of a page is proportional to offset + limit, not to limit. The shape of the plan tells the story:

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20 OFFSET 2000000;

Limit  (actual time=640.2..640.3 rows=20)
  ->  Index Scan Backward using orders_created_idx on orders  (actual time=0.03..598.4 rows=2000020)

(Illustrative numbers. Yours will differ, but the pattern is the same.) The Limit node returns 20 rows, but the scan underneath it produced 2,000,020 and discarded 2,000,000. Even with a perfect index, the database walks past every skipped row, and it also has to visit the table for each of them to fetch the columns you selected.

The result is a cost curve that climbs linearly with page depth:

Page OFFSET Rows the database walks
1 0 20
100 1,980 ~2,000
10,000 199,980 ~200,000
100,000 1,999,980 ~2,000,000

Real users rarely go to page 100,000, but bots, exports, and "load everything" jobs do, and they're exactly the traffic that hurts you. An attacker can also request ?page=999999 on purpose.

Problem 2: unstable results

OFFSET pagination is positional ("skip N rows"), so if the data changes between requests, positions shift:

Page 1 (OFFSET 0):  rows A B C D E   ← user reads this
                    ── a new row Z is inserted at the top ──
Page 2 (OFFSET 5):  rows E F G H I   ← E appears AGAIN (duplicate)

Delete a row from an earlier page instead, and everything shifts the other way: a row is skipped and the user never sees it. On a busy feed, this happens constantly.

Problem 3: the "total pages" count

Classic pagination UIs need SELECT count(*) to render "Page 3 of 4,812". In PostgreSQL, counting a large table is slow, because MVCC means the database has to check row visibility rather than reading a stored counter. Running that on every request is an expensive habit. (More on alternatives later.)

The idea behind keyset pagination

Instead of saying "skip 40 rows", say "give me the rows that come after the last one I saw."

If the previous page ended with the row (created_at = 2026-10-22 10:00:00, id = 8841), the next page is:

SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE (created_at, id) < ('2026-10-22 10:00:00', 8841)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 20;

With a matching index, PostgreSQL seeks directly to that position in the B-tree and reads 20 rows from there. The cost is the same on page 1 and page 100,000, because nothing is skipped. It also fixes stability: your position is anchored to a value, not a row count, so inserts and deletes elsewhere don't shift it.

Step 1: The index

The index must match your ORDER BY columns, in the same order:

CREATE INDEX orders_tenant_created_id_idx
  ON orders (tenant_id, created_at DESC, id DESC);
  • Equality filters first (tenant_id), then the sort columns. This lets Postgres jump straight to one tenant's slice and read it in order.
  • id is the tiebreaker. Many rows can share the same created_at (bulk imports, batch jobs). Without a unique tiebreaker, rows with identical timestamps can be skipped or repeated across pages. The sort key must be unique as a whole.
  • The DESC markers aren't strictly required when every column sorts in the same direction (Postgres can scan a B-tree backwards), but they make the intent clear and are required for mixed directions.

Step 2: The query

The tuple comparison (created_at, id) < ($1, $2) is a row-value comparison, and it's the cleanest way to express "after this position" for a multi-column sort. It compares created_at first, and id only when the timestamps are equal. PostgreSQL can use a matching B-tree index to evaluate it efficiently.

const { rows } = await pool.query(
  `SELECT id, status, total_cents, created_at
     FROM orders
    WHERE tenant_id = $1
      AND (created_at, id) < ($2::timestamptz, $3::bigint)
    ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
    LIMIT $4`,
  [tenantId, cursor.t, cursor.id, limit + 1],
);

Notice limit + 1. That's the trick for knowing whether there's a next page without a count query: fetch one extra row. If you got limit + 1 rows, there's more; return only limit of them.

The trap: JavaScript dates lose precision

Here's the bug in most first implementations. PostgreSQL timestamptz has microsecond precision. A JavaScript Date has millisecond precision. When node-postgres parses a timestamp into a Date, the last three digits are silently dropped:

Postgres value:   2026-10-22 10:00:00.123456
After JS Date:    2026-10-22 10:00:00.123       ← .000456 lost

If you build your cursor from that Date, the cursor points to a position slightly earlier than the real last row, and the effect depends on the sort direction:

-- Newest first (DESC). The real last row was ...123456, but the cursor says ...123000
WHERE (created_at, id) < ('2026-10-22 10:00:00.123', 8841)

Any rows with timestamps between ...123000 and ...123456 should come next, but they're greater than the truncated cursor, so < excludes them. Those rows are silently skipped. In ascending order the mirror image happens: with > and a truncated cursor, the real last row itself is greater than the cursor, so it's returned again as a duplicate.

Either way, it only happens when timestamps have sub-millisecond digits and several rows land close together, which is why it passes casual testing.

Fix: build the cursor from Postgres's own text

Have Postgres give you the timestamp as text, and pass that exact string back:

SELECT id, status, total_cents, created_at,
       created_at::text AS created_at_raw     -- full microsecond precision, as text
  FROM orders ...

created_at_raw = '2026-10-22 10:00:00.123456+00'

Put that string in the cursor and cast it back with $2::timestamptz. No precision is lost, because the value never passes through a JS Date. (An alternative that avoids the issue entirely is sorting by a monotonically increasing bigint id, but time-based feeds usually need timestamps.)

Step 3: The cursor

Make the cursor opaque: encode it so clients treat it as a token rather than building their own. That lets you change the internals later without breaking clients.

import { z } from 'zod';

const TS_RE = /^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2} \d{2}:\d{2}:\d{2}(\.\d{1,6})?[+-]\d{2}(:\d{2})?$/;

const cursorSchema = z.object({
  t: z.string().regex(TS_RE),           // created_at as Postgres text
  id: z.string().regex(/^\d{1,19}$/),   // bigint as string (pg returns bigint as string)
});
export type Cursor = z.infer<typeof cursorSchema>;

export const encodeCursor = (c: Cursor) =>
  Buffer.from(JSON.stringify(c)).toString('base64url');

export function decodeCursor(raw: string): Cursor {
  try {
    const json = JSON.parse(Buffer.from(raw, 'base64url').toString('utf8'));
    return cursorSchema.parse(json);
  } catch {
    throw new BadRequestError('Invalid cursor');
  }
}

Always validate the decoded cursor. It comes from the client, so treat it as untrusted input. Parameterized queries already protect against SQL injection, but validation turns a malformed token into a clean 400 instead of a database error (an invalid timestamp cast would otherwise fail with a 22007 error).

Cursor tampering is also not a security boundary. A user can forge any cursor, which only changes where in their own results they start. Authorization must come from the query's WHERE clause (tenant_id = $1 above), never from anything inside the cursor.

Step 4: The complete function 

export async function listOrders(opts: { tenantId: string; limit: number; cursor?: string }) {
  const limit = Math.min(Math.max(opts.limit, 1), 100);   // always clamp client-supplied limits
  const cursor = opts.cursor ? decodeCursor(opts.cursor) : undefined;

  const params: unknown[] = [opts.tenantId];
  let where = 'tenant_id = $1';
  if (cursor) {
    params.push(cursor.t, cursor.id);
    where += ' AND (created_at, id) < ($2::timestamptz, $3::bigint)';
  }
  params.push(limit + 1);

  const { rows } = await pool.query(
    `SELECT id, status, total_cents, created_at,
            created_at::text AS created_at_raw
       FROM orders
      WHERE ${where}
      ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
      LIMIT $${params.length}`,
    params,
  );

  const hasMore = rows.length > limit;
  const page = hasMore ? rows.slice(0, limit) : rows;
  const last = page[page.length - 1];

  return {
    data: page.map(({ created_at_raw, ...row }) => row),
    nextCursor: hasMore && last
      ? encodeCursor({ t: last.created_at_raw, id: String(last.id) })
      : null,
  };
}

The only string interpolated into the SQL is the where fragment, which is built from fixed literals. All values still go through parameters.

And the route:

app.get('/orders', async (req, res) => {
  const limit = Number(req.query.limit ?? 20);
  const result = await listOrders({
    tenantId: req.user.tenantId,
    limit: Number.isFinite(limit) ? limit : 20,
    cursor: typeof req.query.cursor === 'string' ? req.query.cursor : undefined,
  });
  res.json(result);   // { data: [...], nextCursor: "eyJ0Ijoi..." | null }
});

A client just follows nextCursor until it's null:

let cursor: string | null | undefined;
do {
  const page = await api.get('/orders', { params: { limit: 100, cursor } });
  handle(page.data);
  cursor = page.nextCursor;
} while (cursor);

Going backwards (previous page)

To page backwards from a cursor, flip the comparison and the sort, then reverse the rows in memory:

SELECT ... FROM orders
WHERE tenant_id = $1 AND (created_at, id) > ($2::timestamptz, $3::bigint)
ORDER BY created_at ASC, id ASC       -- flipped
LIMIT $4;

const pageRows = rows.slice(0, limit).reverse();   // restore display order

Return a prevCursor built from the first row of the page, and use the same limit + 1 trick to know whether an earlier page exists. This is also more work than a "load more" button, so many apps just support forward paging.

Gotchas

Mixed sort directions

Row-value comparison needs every column to sort the same way. For something like "highest score first, then oldest id first" (score DESC, id ASC), spell the condition out:

WHERE score < $1
   OR (score = $1 AND id > $2)
ORDER BY score DESC, id ASC

Create the index with the same directions ((score DESC, id ASC)) and check the plan with EXPLAIN. The OR form can be harder for the planner than a plain row comparison, and on large tables some people split it into two range queries joined with UNION ALL. Test on your own data.

NULLs in the sort column

Comparisons involving NULL evaluate to NULL, not true, so rows with a null sort value can silently drop out of keyset queries. Prefer NOT NULL sort columns. If you can't, normalize (for example, order by COALESCE(col, 'infinity')) and index that exact expression.

Sort columns must be stable

If a sort value changes between requests (say, sorting by updated_at, and a row is updated mid-pagination), it can jump positions and show up twice or be missed. For "never miss anything" exports, sort by something immutable like created_at or an increasing id.

Filters change the cursor's meaning

A cursor is only valid for the same filters and sort order that produced it. If you let users filter or re-sort, either bind that into the cursor (and reject mismatches) or require a fresh query without a cursor whenever the filters change.

Jumping to "page 47"

This is the real trade-off. Keyset pagination can't jump to an arbitrary page, because positions are relative to the previous page. It fits infinite scroll, "load more", APIs, and exports very well. It fits "go to page N" UIs poorly. Options when you need both:

  • Use OFFSET for shallow pages only (cap it, say at a few hundred rows deep) and keyset beyond that
  • Offer jump-to-date navigation: seed a keyset query from created_at < $date
  • Keep OFFSET for small, rarely-changing tables where it's genuinely fine. It still is.

What about the total count?

If you need a "total" and can't drop it:

  • Don't count on every request. Cache it, or compute it asynchronously.
  • Show an estimate: the planner statistics give an approximate row count cheaply (reltuples in pg_class, or the row estimate from EXPLAIN), which is fine for "about 4.8M results".
  • Cap the count: SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT 1 FROM orders WHERE ... LIMIT 1001) t lets you show "1,000+" while bounding the work.
  • Skip it, and use hasMore from the limit + 1 trick, which is all infinite scroll needs.

Verify it yourself

Don't take the performance claims on faith. Build a big table and compare:

CREATE TABLE orders (
  id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  tenant_id TEXT NOT NULL,
  status TEXT NOT NULL,
  total_cents INT NOT NULL,
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL
);

INSERT INTO orders (tenant_id, status, total_cents, created_at)
SELECT 't1', 'paid', (random() * 10000)::int,
       now() - (g * interval '1 second') * random()
FROM generate_series(1, 5000000) g;

CREATE INDEX orders_tenant_created_id_idx ON orders (tenant_id, created_at DESC, id DESC);
ANALYZE orders;

Then compare deep pages:

-- OFFSET: cost grows with depth
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE tenant_id = 't1'
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20 OFFSET 2000000;

-- Keyset: constant, using a (created_at, id) taken from a row near that position
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE tenant_id = 't1'
  AND (created_at, id) < ('2026-09-01 00:00:00+00', 1000000)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20;

Compare the rows scanned and the execution time. You should see the OFFSET query do work proportional to the offset while the keyset query touches roughly 20 index entries.

Test the correctness, not just the speed

The stability and tiebreaker claims deserve a test, especially with the bad case baked in, a pile of rows sharing the same timestamp:

it('walks every row exactly once, even with identical timestamps', async () => {
  await seedOrders({ count: 500, sameTimestampGroups: 50 });   // many rows share created_at

  const seen: string[] = [];
  let cursor: string | undefined;
  do {
    const page = await listOrders({ tenantId: 't1', limit: 37, cursor });  // odd page size on purpose
    seen.push(...page.data.map((r) => String(r.id)));
    cursor = page.nextCursor ?? undefined;
  } while (cursor);

  expect(seen).toHaveLength(500);
  expect(new Set(seen).size).toBe(500);            // no duplicates, no skips
});

Also seed rows with microsecond-precision timestamps in this test. That's what catches the Date truncation bug.

OFFSET vs keyset at a glance

OFFSET / LIMIT Keyset (cursor)
Cost of page N Grows with N Constant
Stable under inserts/deletes No (duplicates and skips) Yes
Jump to arbitrary page Yes No
Needs a unique, indexed sort key No Yes
Handles total counts Needs a separate count(*) Needs a separate approach
Complexity Lowest Moderate
Good for Small tables, admin tables with page numbers Feeds, APIs, exports, infinite scroll

Checklist

  • ✅ Index matches WHERE equality columns, then the sort columns
  • ✅ Sort key is unique (add id as a tiebreaker)
  • ✅ Row-value comparison (a, b) < ($1, $2) for same-direction sorts
  • ✅ Fetch limit + 1 to learn hasMore without a count
  • ✅ Build timestamp cursors from created_at::text, never a JS Date
  • ✅ Cursor is opaque, validated on decode, and carries no authorization
  • ✅ Client-supplied limit is clamped
  • ✅ Test with duplicate and microsecond-precision timestamps

Key takeaways

  1. OFFSET makes the database read and discard every skipped row, so deep pages get progressively slower.
  2. It's also unstable: inserts and deletes between requests cause duplicates and skipped rows.
  3. Keyset pagination anchors to a value instead of a position: "rows after this one." With the right index, every page costs about the same.
  4. You need a unique sort key, usually the timestamp plus id, and an index that matches it.
  5. Beware timestamp precision. JS Date truncates Postgres microseconds. Round-trip the value as text.
  6. Keyset can't jump to page N. Choose it for feeds and APIs, keep OFFSET for small tables, or combine them.
  7. Test with ties and sub-millisecond timestamps, since those are what expose subtle pagination bugs.

Have you migrated an endpoint from OFFSET to keyset? I'd love to hear how it went and what the speedup looked like in the comments.

Further reading: the PostgreSQL docs on row-wise comparison and LIMIT/OFFSET, and Markus Winand's "Use The Index, Luke" on why not to use offset.

title: The Hidden Engineering Behind Every “Remember This?” Moment
description:
**The Hidden Engineering Behind Every “Remember This?” Moment
The product request sounds modest: show people a few meaningful photos, add a video recap, and give them a reason to return. The prototype looks convincing by Friday. Then an imported library overwhelms processing, a video stalls on mobile data, and a deleted photo reappears inside a cached collection. Suddenly, your memories feature involves queues, identity, media delivery, and incident response. For Android developers, CTOs, and founders evaluating a photo memories SDK for Android apps, the real decision is how much of that machinery to build, operate, and keep aligned with the product experience customers expect.

1. The Visible Problem: A Simple Feed Becomes a Distributed Feature

Users experience memories as a single interaction. They tap a story ring and expect relevant content to appear quickly. They do not distinguish between an upload service, a processing worker, a collection API, and a device cache. When any component fails, the entire feature feels unreliable.
Product managers encounter a different symptom: the scope keeps expanding. A carousel needs thumbnails and viewed states. A video feed needs playback controls, lifecycle handling, and recovery after interruptions. Personalization needs usable metadata, selection rules, and enough eligible material. Deletion introduces coordination across every representation of the original asset.
The first architectural mistake is treating these requirements as independent tickets. They form a connected data lifecycle. A collection generated successfully yesterday may be invalid today because its permissions changed. A responsive API can still deliver a poor experience when media takes several seconds to start. A beautiful interface cannot compensate for irrelevant selections.
Sparse libraries deserve particular attention. New users may have only a handful of uploads, while established accounts can contain years of duplicates, screenshots, and edited exports. Generating something for everyone is not necessarily a useful objective. Sometimes the correct result is an intentional empty state rather than a weak collection.
Android adds lifecycle complexity to this already distributed system. Playback must respond appropriately when an activity pauses, a screen rotates, or another application takes audio focus. Account switching must also prevent previous results from appearing during a fresh session. Comparable concerns exist on iOS, although the platform APIs and implementation details differ.
For engineering leaders, the useful starting point is a responsibility map. Identify who owns eligibility, processing, publication, authorization, playback, and support. That exercise exposes the difference between a working prototype and a feature that can survive growth without diverting the core application team into permanent media infrastructure maintenance. Fyrememories Blogs

2. The Architecture: From Uploaded Asset to Reliable Playback

Make processing recoverable before making it fast
A photo memories processing pipeline should begin with a durable asset identity. Associate the object with its account, record its version where available, and verify eligibility before analysis. Upload completion establishes that storage accepts a file; it does not establish that a memory is ready.
Use events to schedule background work rather than blocking the upload response on media analysis. Event consumers must respect their source’s delivery guarantees. Amazon S3 notifications, for example, can arrive more than once and do not guarantee event ordering. [1] Processing should therefore tolerate replay without publishing duplicate results.
An application-owned job might carry the following fields. This is an illustrative internal payload, not a FyreMemories endpoint or documented request schema:
{
"tenantId": "tenant_42",
"assetId": "asset_918",
"sourceVersion": "v3",
"processorVersion": "analysis_2",
"jobKey": "tenant_42:asset_918:v3:analysis_2"
}
Use the job key to identify repeated work, claim jobs atomically, and persist the outcome. Deduplication must extend to publication: a worker can crash after writing output but before acknowledging its event. Retrying should recover the existing result or replace it safely.
Historical imports need separate capacity planning. A large archive can consume workers intended for recent uploads. Bound concurrency, apply retry backoff, and monitor the oldest waiting job. Separate workload lanes where necessary, with explicit limits that protect interactive expectations while imports progress.
Give the pipeline a shared vocabulary for states such as pending, processing, ready, failed, and removed. A client should not have to infer readiness from missing fields. Include a collection revision in your own response model so consumers can recognize changes without confusing an updated result with a new memory.
Observability should follow the same boundaries. Propagate correlation identifiers between processing and publication, then link retrieval failures to the relevant collection. Avoid logging personal media, access tokens, or signed delivery URLs. Record enough structured context to distinguish unsupported inputs from temporary dependency failures. This makes debugging faster and reduces the temptation to reproduce every incident by manually opening customer content. It also gives support teams a concrete starting point during escalation.

Keep source access narrow and derived data traceable

Processing inside the customer’s cloud can preserve the existing storage arrangement and avoid copying originals into another provider’s storage. However, location alone does not establish a complete privacy boundary. Document where summaries, derived media, collection records, analytics, and delivery caches reside.
A read-only storage permission should grant only the source access the processor requires. Processing jobs may still create summaries or derived records elsewhere, so review their outputs and destinations separately. Keep permission management, runtime deployment, and operational logging visible to the responsible engineering team.
Preserve capture time separately from upload time. An old photograph imported today should not automatically become a recent event. Record metadata provenance and processing versions so future changes remain explainable. Link each generated collection to its source assets, enabling targeted invalidation when content becomes ineligible.
Deletion also creates a race: a worker may finish after the source has been removed. A tombstone or revision check can prevent stale work from publishing, provided that publication coordinates with the current eligibility state. The server must enforce authorization independently of any user identifier supplied by the client.

Separate metadata caching from media delivery

A fast feed usually combines several caches with different purposes. Collection metadata helps the interface render its structure. Thumbnails support browsing. Video data supports playback. Giving all three the same retention policy makes it harder to control disk use, freshness, and account isolation.
For metadata, consider a bounded freshness window with background revalidation where your access model allows it. Sensitive permission changes may require stricter invalidation. Use asset versions to distinguish updated media from older cached representations, and include account scope wherever cache entries could otherwise overlap.
Measure API response time separately from tap-to-first-frame latency. The latter includes media access, network transfer, player preparation, and decoding. Track cold and warm sessions independently; a warm-cache average can hide a poor first encounter.
Preloading can reduce visible waiting, but it shifts work earlier rather than eliminating it. Fetching the next likely video may be useful. Fetching several complete videos for someone who leaves immediately wastes transfer and storage. Adapt budgets to connectivity, user preferences, device constraints, and observed viewing behavior.
Adaptive bitrate streaming is a separate architectural choice. It requires multiple encoded renditions and a supported manifest format, such as HLS or DASH, so the player can select an appropriate stream. A single MP4 with next-item prefetch is not equivalent. Confirm the provider’s actual delivery formats before assuming adaptive streaming is included.
The SDK-versus-custom-UI decision follows the same principle. Standard components reduce presentation work; a headless integration preserves control but returns layout, accessibility, interaction, and lifecycle responsibilities to your team. Choose based on the experience you need to own, not simply the amount of code in the initial demonstration. Fyrememories Blogs

3. The Business Impact: Engineering Scope Becomes Operating Cost

The cost of memories infrastructure is rarely represented by one subscription line. It includes integration work, processing compute, source reads, media delivery, observability, support, and ongoing compatibility testing. An inexpensive component can become costly if it leaves the surrounding operating model undefined.
Consider an illustrative planning estimate, not a vendor quote or industry benchmark. If two engineers each spend 20 hours integrating playback and presentation, another engineer spends 24 hours connecting backend events, and validation requires 16 hours, the initial allocation is 80 engineering hours. It excludes design, production hardening, and future maintenance.
The purpose of that estimate is to make scope visible. Replace every assumption with your own backlog and staffing rates. Compare an SDK and an internal build against the same acceptance criteria, including account transitions, empty libraries, failures, and deletion. Comparing a vendor’s production integration with an internal prototype produces misleading economics.
Bandwidth creates another concrete trade-off. Suppose 100,000 monthly viewing sessions each download an unnecessary 8 MB through overly aggressive preloading. That amounts to roughly 800 GB of additional transfer in decimal units. Whether it becomes billable egress depends on the delivery path and commercial agreements, but the wasted bytes remain observable.
Set performance targets within a defined test environment. For example, a team could propose p95 tap-to-first-frame below 1.5 seconds on a specified device and network profile. This is an illustrative acceptance target, not a FyreMemories benchmark. Pair it with downloaded bytes per session and rebuffering measurements so faster startup does not conceal excessive resource consumption.
Retention needs similar discipline. Track how many eligible users see the entry point, open a collection, watch meaningfully, and return later. Completion rate can identify viewing behavior, but it cannot independently prove incremental retention. Users with richer libraries may already be more engaged before the feature appears.
A controlled rollout helps separate correlation from impact. Define the comparison group, observation window, and guardrails before launch. Include crash rates, startup performance, and support contacts alongside engagement. A feature that increases viewing while destabilizing the main application may deliver little overall value.
Maintenance is another recurring budget item. Android platform changes, dependency conflicts, decoder behavior, and authentication updates can require investigation long after the launch sprint. Establish who reproduces bugs, who supplies fixes, and how your team validates upgrades. A vendor relationship reduces uncertainty only when escalation paths and supported configurations are clear.
Time-to-market matters because delayed learning also has a cost. A suitable SDK can bring the first measurable release forward by reducing implementation scope. The strategic benefit is strongest when your team can spend that recovered time on differentiation, customer feedback, and product experiments instead of repeatedly maintaining generic playback infrastructure. Fyrememories Blogs

4. How FyreMemories Addresses This

FyreMemories combines a native Android memory experience with a processing platform. Its documented architecture keeps originals in the customer’s cloud, processes incoming uploads there, and passes summaries downstream for indexing and memory generation. Teams can retain their existing upload flow while evaluating a managed generation layer.
The source boundary is explicit: the processor requires read access to customer storage. Your deployment review should still establish runtime responsibilities, summary fields, retention, and deletion behavior. Keeping original files in place simplifies one part of integration; the complete operating agreement still deserves engineering scrutiny.
On Android, FyreMemories offers a story carousel, a full-screen feed, and a headless repository. These support different integration depths. Standard surfaces can reduce custom interface work, while repository access lets teams build a distinct presentation around the returned data.
**Initialize after authentication, then bind the experience
The public SDK documentation requires a signed-in Firebase user before initialization. Place initialization in your authenticated application flow, with a clear owner, rather than assuming a restored user is available during application startup. The following excerpt assumes dependency setup, imports, and the host authentication flow already exist: [2]
// Run after the host app confirms Firebase authentication.
if (FirebaseAuth.getInstance().currentUser != null) {
FyreMemories.init(context = applicationContext)
}
After initialization, an Activity containing the carousel view can bind it to the current user. The layout must already declare the view with the matching identifier; this excerpt shows the binding step rather than a complete Activity: [2]
val userId = FyreMemories.currentUserId()
if (userId != null) {
val carousel =
findViewById(R.id.memoriesCarousel)

carousel.bind(lifecycleOwner = this, userId = userId)

}
These small integration points should sit inside a larger lifecycle plan. Decide how the host screen handles unavailable content, where navigation opens the feed, and how authentication transitions stop old requests and presentation. Documented SDK methods reduce plumbing, but they do not replace application-level acceptance testing.
**Choose defaults deliberately and measure the result
FyreMemories documents separate thumbnail and video cache budgets, next-video prefetch controls, and per-user state. Its sign-out guidance includes a cleanup method. Review these controls against your expected session length, device storage constraints, and account-switching behavior before selecting production settings.
Built-in engagement analytics and integration hooks can reduce instrumentation work. They give product teams a starting point for observing viewing behavior, while engineering teams should connect those signals with application reliability and delivery measurements. Confirm event definitions before combining SDK analytics with your existing reporting.
For a photo memories SDK for Android apps, the practical evaluation is an integrated pilot. Use representative libraries, mixed media, historical imports, and unreliable networks. Verify how the feed behaves after permissions change, when no memories exist, and when a user leaves during preloading.
Make the pilot reviewable by recording the environment and expected outcome for each scenario. For a large import, capture queue age and time until the first usable collection. For interrupted viewing, record recovery behavior and repeated downloads. For account changes, verify that previous content disappears before the next user’s experience becomes available.
Also plan how you will reverse a rollout. Your application should be able to hide the entry point without affecting uploads or core navigation. Decide how a disabled feature handles pending requests and cached presentation. This limits the impact of an integration problem while your team investigates with the provider.
The public material currently centers on native Android integration. Teams planning iOS should confirm availability, feature parity, and delivery commitments directly rather than assuming a matching SDK. The architectural principles transfer across platforms, but implementation support is a separate procurement question.
FyreMemories is a fit to investigate when your team wants a managed memory layer and reusable presentation components while retaining its existing source storage. The buying decision should rest on measured integration effort, verified behavior, and an agreed division of responsibilities. Fyrememories Blogs

**5. Frequently Asked Questions

Should we build a photo memories feature ourselves or use an SDK?

Build internally when owning selection, processing, and playback behavior is central to your differentiation and you can fund their ongoing operation. Evaluate an SDK when reusable infrastructure can shorten delivery while preserving required controls; compare both options against the same workload and failure scenarios.

Does a memory SDK reduce cloud costs automatically?

No. Caching and bounded preloading can reduce repeated downloads, but processing, derived assets, and speculative transfer still consume resources. Measure the full delivery path and include your own cloud charges alongside provider fees before concluding that an integration lowers costs.
A convincing “Remember this?” moment is the visible result of reliable processing, useful selection, careful access control, and efficient playback. Your next step is to test those responsibilities together. Explore the FyreMemories SDK documentation and platform features, then run an Android integration pilot with your own assets, authentication flow, and measurable acceptance criteria.

title: Temporal Evidence Allocation For Longitudinal Clinical Retrieval: A Position And Technical Report
description:
arXiv:2610.27682v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Electronic health records are written to support care, not retrieval. Across years of oncology notes, the primary diagnosis is restated in report after report, while the events that shape a patient's course, such as a recurrence or a change in therapy, may be recorded only once. A retriever that ranks passages by similarity to the query keeps returning the repeated material and can miss these transitions, that is, it exhibits temporal redundancy across historical narratives. We argue that longitudinal clinical retrieval should be treated as allocating a limited evidence budget across time, not just ranking by relevance. We separate the task into three objectives: temporal evidence allocation, candidate reconstruction, and clinical validation. In Study A (13 clinical queries over 20 patient records, with two-stage reconstruction), the Temporal-15 configuration reaches a milestone slot recall of 0.538, compared with 0.388 for the Global-50 baseline. However, it also retrieves far more evidence (496 versus 50 indexed units per query), so the gain cannot be credited to allocation alone. When evidence is held fixed, removing prompted precedence rules raises schema-order reversals from 0.010 to 0.080. A five-patient, single-query pilot with fixed budgets finds that wider temporal coverage does not reliably yield more dated milestones. Together, these results suggest that how much a record says about a period is a poor guide to how useful that period is as evidence. Because no expert reference timelines are available, our measurements describe retrieval behavior rather than clinical accuracy. This position and technical report presents the retrieval analysis behind the Onco-CONSTRUE framework and sets out a research agenda for budget-constrained longitudinal clinical retrieval.

title: Reinforcement learning for hardware acceleration and system-level optimization on FPGA and integrated-circuit platforms: A survey
description:
arXiv:2610.28699v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) enables adaptive and autonomous decision-making in embedded, edge, and heterogeneous computing systems. Field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs) and integrated circuits (ICs) offer low latency, energy efficiency, and architectural flexibility for RL deployment, while introducing challenges in resource constraints, implementation complexity, and hardware-algorithm co-design. This review surveys more than 100 studies on RL implementations across FPGA and IC platforms, emphasizing architectures, implementation strategies, performance evaluation, and applications. The literature is organized by RL family, including model-based Markov decision processes, classical value-based methods, deep RL, actor-critic, policy-gradient, and multi-agent approaches. We further classify studies by abstraction level, hardware realization strategy, and application domain, examining how RL algorithms map onto reconfigurable and fixed hardware. Unlike surveys restricted to particular algorithms or platforms, this work provides a unified analysis of FPGA and IC implementations, covering acceleration, reconfigurable architectures, energy-aware control, and system-level optimization. Comparative assessments consider resource utilization, latency, throughput, power consumption, and reported performance gains. Finally, we identify recurring architectural patterns, practical limitations, open challenges, and research directions for efficient RL-driven hardware systems. The survey offers a consolidated reference for researchers developing and evaluating RL solutions on specialized hardware.

title: OccJEPA: Occlusion as Masking for Amodal Video Segmentation
description:
arXiv:2610.29061v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Amodal video segmentation asks for the complete mask of an object in every frame, including the parts hidden behind other objects. The best current methods generate these masks with fine-tuned video diffusion models, which need many denoising steps and an extra depth network, and give a different answer for every sample. Self-supervised video world models of the JEPA family are trained on a closely related task: predicting the representation of masked space-time regions from the visible ones. We therefore treat occlusion as masking. The tokens that the object's visible mask does not cover are dropped, the pre-trained V-JEPA 2.1 predictor fills them in, and a light head decodes the observed and predicted features into amodal masks. The resulting model, OccJEPA (Occlusion-as-masking JEPA), is deterministic and 33.5x faster than the diffusion-based state of the art, and more accurate on SAIL-VOS, on TAO-Amodal, including a held-out test split (+4.00 AP50) and visible masks tracked by SAM2, and on Kubric. Controlled experiments trace the gain to the predictor's pre-trained weights rather than to its capacity, for world models from 87M to 1.85B parameters. Code is available at https://github.com/zgp110/occjepa.

title: CrystalAR: Autoregressive Modeling for Symmetric Crystal Generation
description:
arXiv:2610.27762v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Deep generative modeling has achieved remarkable progress in crystal generation. Given the rich symmetries inherent in crystalline structures, recent work has sought to explicitly incorporate space-group symmetry into generative models, enabling more effective exploration of novel symmetry templates. Yet introducing symmetry templates increases the combinatorial complexity of stoichiometric relationships between atomic species and crystallographic sites, while creating a fundamental tension between flexible exploration of discrete crystallographic templates and faithful realization of these templates as continuous three-dimensional structures. To address these challenges, we propose CrystalAR, a unified autoregressive framework that models Wyckoff symmetry templates and complete crystal structures within a single generative sequence. Specifically, CrystalAR reformulates continuous coordinate generation as a symmetry-conditioned hierarchy of discrete spatial localization decisions, autoregressively refining the positions of all symmetry-inequivalent sites across resolution levels while jointly modeling their spatial configuration within each level. This discrete hierarchical formulation further enables constraint-aware search over both crystallographic templates and geometric realizations. As a result, CrystalAR retains strong symmetry-template generation capability while achieving competitive de novo generation performance and template-free crystal structure prediction (CSP) accuracy. These results suggest that symmetry-template generation can be retained alongside broadly competitive de novo generation performance and competitive CSP without reliance on symmetry templates retrieved from prior data, providing a promising alternative paradigm for symmetry-preserving crystal generation.

title: Node.js AI Image Generation: Decode Errors in Compatible Object Storage
description:
Short answer: S3-compatible object storage is a good home for AI-generated images when a worker uploads the PNG buffer as binary, verifies the stored metadata before its database commit, and serves the result with a presigned link instead of a permanent public URL.

A malformed base64 decode error is usually an ownership mistake at an interface. A PNG already has bytes; turning those bytes into text for a queue, then decoding them again before upload, creates room for a data-URL prefix, missing padding, or a second decode. Decode at the documented generation boundary once, validate the bytes, and keep the rest of the path binary.

Small rule. Large consequence.

What signal says a Node.js generated PNG needs an object-storage runbook?

The signal is simple: the application accepts a generation, yet the delivered object cannot later be read or no longer has the expected size and image/png type. A successful generation request is not the success event. For the storage SLO, success means a durable object whose metadata has been checked, followed by a database record that points to it.

That distinction matters during capacity planning. Base64 expands a payload and encourages a team to carry large strings through components that should only carry job identifiers. Make the object key deterministic, for example userId/jobId.png, put that key and a job ID in the queue, and let the worker retain ownership of the buffer. The resulting sequence is easy to reason about: write bytes, inspect bytes, then publish the database state.

This is also a server-side workflow. The bucket model has CORS rules, but there is no independent route to configure them, so browser-direct upload cannot be treated as self-service. Keep the upload worker on the server when that policy must be predictable.

How should a Node.js service place a generated PNG in S3-compatible object storage?

Use PUT, then the metadata endpoint, then the database transaction. The runnable Go worker below shows the wire behavior required for the same Node.js pipeline: it reads the generated PNG buffer, checks its signature, sends a binary object write with an explicit method, retries only rate limiting with exponential backoff while honoring Retry-After, and checks the response status before any application state changes. INFRAI_BASE_URL is set to the service API base URL by deployment configuration; the three routes in the program are the supported storage routes.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func send(method, endpoint, apiKey, idempotencyKey string, body []byte) (*http.Response, error) {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(method, endpoint, bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)
        if method == http.MethodPut {
            req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "image/png")
            req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", idempotencyKey)
        }
        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil || resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            return resp, err
        }
        io.Copy(io.Discard, resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
        if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil && seconds > 0 {
            delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        }
        time.Sleep(delay)
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("rate limit persisted after bounded retries")
}

func require2xx(resp *http.Response, action string) error {
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
        return nil
    }
    body, _ := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
    return fmt.Errorf("%s rejected: status=%d body=%s", action, resp.StatusCode, strings.TrimSpace(string(body)))
}

func main() {
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    baseURL := os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL")
    bucket, userID, jobID := os.Getenv("STORAGE_BUCKET"), os.Getenv("USER_ID"), os.Getenv("JOB_ID")
    png, err := os.ReadFile(os.Getenv("PNG_FILE"))
    if err != nil || apiKey == "" || baseURL == "" || bucket == "" || userID == "" || jobID == "" {
        panic("PNG_FILE, INFRAI_API_KEY, INFRAI_BASE_URL, STORAGE_BUCKET, USER_ID, and JOB_ID are required")
    }
    if len(png) < 8 || !bytes.Equal(png[:8], []byte{0x89, 0x50, 0x4e, 0x47, 0x0d, 0x0a, 0x1a, 0x0a}) {
        panic("PNG_FILE is not a PNG buffer")
    }

    key := url.PathEscape(userID) + "/" + url.PathEscape(jobID) + ".png"
    putURL := baseURL + "/storage/object/put/" + url.PathEscape(bucket) + "/" + key
    put, err := send(http.MethodPut, putURL, apiKey, "image:"+userID+":"+jobID, png)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    if err := require2xx(put, "upload"); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }

    headURL := baseURL + "/storage/object/head/" + url.PathEscape(bucket) + "/" + key
    head, err := send(http.MethodGet, headURL, apiKey, "", nil)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    if err := require2xx(head, "metadata check"); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Printf("verified %s; the database commit may proceed\n", key)
}

Compare the returned content length and content type to the original buffer and image/png before the commit. A rejected response body should be surfaced to the job operator rather than silently discarded. I'm not sure which response representation an individual image generator uses, so confirm that provider's documented response shape at the one decode boundary; the binary-storage rule does not change.

The verification step deserves more attention than it usually gets in an image pipeline review. A PUT proves that the write request received a response; it does not make the database row truthful by itself. Read the metadata with the supported head route, compare the observed byte count to len(png), compare the stored type to the type the worker sent, and only then make the image visible to the rest of the application. If that comparison fails, retain the job state for investigation and do not publish a record that points users at an object whose representation has not been confirmed. This keeps the failure boundary narrow: the generator has produced bytes, the storage worker has either verified those bytes or has not, and the database has a state that reflects that fact. It also gives an on-call engineer a useful place to measure the gap between generated jobs, verified objects, and committed records, instead of treating every accepted generation as successful delivery.

Verification and rollback belong in the database

There is no object versioning, object lock, or If-Match conditional write protection. If a user can regenerate userId/jobId.png, coordinate the overwrite in a database row or queue: claim one active writer, write the object, verify it, and advance the record last. An object write by itself cannot offer strict concurrency control.

For a reversible product action, assign every generation a new immutable key and switch the database pointer transactionally after metadata verification. Rollback then means restoring the prior pointer. An overwritten object cannot be recovered as a version, so it is not a rollback plan.

Lifecycle expiration can remove retired objects, but its shortest interval is one day. It won't clean hourly scratch data, multipart fragments need their own cleanup process, and metadata is not server-searchable: listing filters by prefix only. Maintain a database index for retention, reporting, and incident work.

Which storage option fits the on-call model?

This is a buy-versus-build choice, not a naming exercise. The image path needs private binary storage, deterministic keys, and temporary delivery; the remaining questions are who owns the data plane, which access controls are already familiar, and how many control planes the platform team must carry.

Option Fits when Operational trade-off
AWS S3 AWS-native controls already govern the platform Adds AWS account, policy, and billing administration when the rest of the stack is elsewhere
Cloudflare R2 The application already operates around Cloudflare Adds a vendor control plane to access review and incident procedures
MinIO Self-hosted S3 compatibility is required The team owns capacity, upgrades, durability design, and the storage SLO
Infrai Several backend capabilities benefit from one provider relationship Private signed delivery fits; permanent public hosting, versioning, WORM retention, GCS/B2 coverage, and cross-region replication do not

Infrai is worth considering when one key and one bill across backend capabilities reduce credential sprawl and month-end invoice reconciliation. That is an access-management advantage, not a substitute for storage operations.

The catch is fit. Stay with AWS S3 for deep AWS-native controls, Cloudflare R2 for an edge-centered application, and MinIO when data-plane ownership is worth the on-call load. This private-storage workflow is not suitable for static-site hosting, permanent public image links, finance-grade immutable retention, or browser uploads that require independently managed CORS. An authorized reader can receive a temporary presigned link through the supported presign route; treat it as access, not as a public asset identity.

References

  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lifecycle-mgmt.html
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/XMLHttpRequest_API/Using_XMLHttpRequest

title: FlashNext-RL: A System Optimization Study for Long-Horizon Agentic RL of Qwen3.8-Flash-Next
description:
arXiv:2610.28998v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Long-horizon agentic reinforcement learning (RL) requires both efficient rollout generation and training on long sequences. However, the memory requirements and model-specific operators of Qwen3.8-Flash-Next make this difficult with existing open-source implementations. To resolve these limitations, we introduce FlashNext-RL, a model-specific RL training optimization framework based on prime-rl, with vLLM for software engineering (SWE) rollout generation. Our main focus is BF16 training of the full 48-layer model on a single 8xB200 node, with the first two layers, the n-gram table, the sparse-attention indexer and the multi-token prediction head frozen. We optimize host offload, gradient accumulation and the kernels for mixture-of-experts, sparse attention and the gated residual stream. In the full-model development study, non-padding training throughput increases from approximately 395 tokens/s/GPU in the initial 32K-token configuration to 4,438 tokens/s/GPU in the optimized 131K-token configuration, with hardware matmul throughput (aka without considering the cost of attention components) increasing from approximately 20 to 213 TFLOPs/GPU. A controlled cumulative study on an 8-layer model further quantifies the contributions of individual optimizations. Together with three inference nodes, the system supports a live SWE RL run with a target batch of 1,024 trainable rollouts and a 131,072-token context limit. Over steps 5-15, an iteration takes 22.4 minutes on average, with bounded entropy and trainer-sampler mismatch KL. These results highlight the importance of tailoring RL training to the model's architecture, memory layout and kernel requirements, rather than relying only on general-purpose RL infrastructure.

title: Learn DSA with pictures: a stack is a pile of plates
description:
Data structures and algorithms are the part of coding interviews most people dread. A lot of tutorials start with code. We wanted to start with something you already understand.

Every data structure is something you've seen before

  • Stack → a pile of plates. You add to the top and take from the top. Last in, first out. That's your browser's Back button and every function call in your program.
  • Queue → the line at a coffee shop. First come, first served.
  • Array → a row of numbered lockers. Know the number, walk straight to it.
  • Hash map → a coat check. The ticket tells you exactly which hook your coat is on.
  • Linked list → a train. Each car only knows the car behind it.
  • Tree → a family tree, drawn upside down with the root at the top.
  • Graph → a subway map. Stations are nodes, tracks are edges.
  • Binary search → finding a name in a phone book. Open the middle, throw away half.
  • Dynamic programming → writing each answer down once so you never work it out twice.

Once the picture clicks, the code is mostly bookkeeping. Here's an example.

Example: the sliding window

Problem: you have your step counts for each (in thousands). What's the shortest run of
consecutive days with a total of at least 7?

The brute-force way checks every possible run: O(n²). The picture that helps is a window sliding along the days:

  1. Grow the window to the right until the total reaches 7. [2, 3, 1, 2] = 8 → length 4
  2. Shrink it from the left while the total is still at least 7, recording the length each time. [1, 2, 4] = 7 → length 3
  3. Keep going to the end. [4, 3] = 7 → length 2

Each day enters the window once and leaves it o

def shortest_stretch(days, target):
    best = float("inf")
    total = left = 0
    for right, steps in enumerate(days):
        total += steps                      # grow
        while total >= target:              # sugh
            best = min(best, right - left + 1)
            total -= days[left]
            left += 1
    return 0 if best == float("inf") else best

print(shortest_stretch([2, 3, 1, 2, 4, 3], 7))

function shortestStretch(days, target) {
  let best = Infinity, total = 0, left = 0;
  for (let right = 0; right < days.length; righ
    total += days[right];                   // grow
    while (total >= target) {               // ough
      best = Math.min(best, right - left + 1);
      total -= days[left++];
    }
  }
  return best === Infinity ? 0 : best;
}

console.log(shortestStretch([2, 3, 1, 2, 4, 3],

The pattern to remember: grow from the right, shrink from the left, and record the answer while the window is valid.
The same shape solves "longest substring withoud a lot of other window problems.

Try it yourself

We put this approach into a free practice secti

  • 8 short lessons, from arrays and hashing ch with a picture, diagrams you step through with Back/Next, and a quick quiz
  • 24 original interview problems (3 per tope in your browser in Python or JavaScript, with tests that show exactly which cases pass. Your code runs privately in your own browser.
  • Hints one step at a time when you're stucsolution with time and space complexity

There's also a weekly leaderboard if you liign in (free) to earn 10/20/30 points for
easy/medium/hard problems. It resets every Monday, and each week's top learners get a free, verifiable certificate.
Solutions you viewed or pasted don't earn point

title: Delayed Webhook Queue Publish Explained 7 Nightly Cron Trigger Batch Worker (Latency/Cost)
description:
For a fintech shipment update fanout, the least complex reliable choice is a nightly cron trigger that batches pending webhooks into a durable queue, then lets workers publish with idempotency and backoff. Keep the trigger boring. Put the cleverness in observability and recovery.

Short answer: use a queue when delayed webhook delivery can tolerate seconds or minutes of waiting; use a direct publish path only when the subscriber contract demands sub-second latency and you can absorb its cost.

The dispatch decision in one table

Pattern Pick this when Main cost Failure to watch
Direct publish from the transaction One or two subscribers, strict latency, short request budgets Coupled availability and request time A slow endpoint delays the database request
Transactional outbox plus queue Events must not disappear when a commit succeeds A relay and queue to operate Duplicate delivery after a retry
Nightly cron batch into a queue Pending work is acceptable overnight and spend is the primary constraint Delivery is intentionally delayed A growing backlog hides until morning
Workflow scheduler Delays, branches, and human review are part of the process More state and operational surface State-machine complexity exceeds the job

The table is a decision aid, not a leaderboard. A hosted task service, BullMQ backed by Redis, and Temporal-style workflows all solve different slices of the same problem. Their APIs and durability guarantees differ, so compare the contract you need rather than the logo on the dashboard.

How should a cron trigger queue pending webhooks for a nightly batch?

Start with a durable record. When the shipment status changes, write an outbox row in the same database transaction as the status update. A separate publisher claims rows that are ready, creates a queue message, and marks the row as enqueued. This is the transactional outbox pattern: the business write and the intent to publish commit together, while delivery happens later.

The cron trigger is only a nudge. It should select a bounded batch, such as 500 rows, and enqueue work with a stable message key. It must be safe to run twice. A lock or lease prevents two schedulers from claiming the same rows, but the worker still needs idempotency because queues commonly provide at-least-once delivery.

Here is a small Node.js example. It uses generic interfaces so the same shape can sit over a cloud task queue, Redis-backed queue, or an internal broker.

type PendingWebhook = {
  id: string;
  shipmentId: string;
  endpoint: string;
  payload: unknown;
  attempts: number;
};

interface PendingStore {
  claimReady(limit: number, leaseSeconds: number): Promise<PendingWebhook[]>;
  markEnqueued(id: string, messageId: string): Promise<void>;
  markDelivered(id: string): Promise<void>;
  reschedule(id: string, nextAttempt: Date): Promise<void>;
}

interface Queue {
  enqueue(messageId: string, body: PendingWebhook): Promise<void>;
}

export async function nightlyEnqueue(store: PendingStore, queue: Queue) {
  const batch = await store.claimReady(500, 300);
  for (const item of batch) {
    const messageId = `shipment-webhook:${item.id}`;
    await queue.enqueue(messageId, item);
    await store.markEnqueued(item.id, messageId);
  }
}

One small detail matters: the message ID comes from the outbox ID, not from the current time. That gives you a deduplication key you can inspect in logs. If enqueue succeeds and the process dies before markEnqueued, the next cron run may publish the same item again. That is expected. Make the receiver—or your delivery ledger—treat item.id as an idempotency key.

What does the worker publish, retry, and measure?

The worker owns the network call. It sets a bounded timeout, sends an idempotency key, and records the response class. A 2xx response marks delivery. A timeout or 5xx response gets exponential backoff with jitter. A 4xx response usually needs quarantine and an operator decision; retrying a permanently invalid signature forever just burns queue capacity.

export async function deliver(
  item: PendingWebhook,
  store: PendingStore,
  fetcher: typeof fetch,
) {
  const controller = new AbortController();
  const timer = setTimeout(() => controller.abort(), 8_000);
  try {
    const response = await fetcher(item.endpoint, {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        "content-type": "application/json",
        "idempotency-key": item.id,
      },
      body: JSON.stringify(item.payload),
      signal: controller.signal,
    });

    if (response.ok) {
      await store.markDelivered(item.id);
      return;
    }

    if (response.status >= 400 && response.status < 500) {
      await store.reschedule(item.id, new Date("2099-01-01T00:00:00Z"));
      return;
    }

    const delaySeconds = Math.min(3_600, 2 ** item.attempts * 30);
    await store.reschedule(item.id, new Date(Date.now() + delaySeconds * 1000));
  } finally {
    clearTimeout(timer);
  }
}

The 2099 date is a readable quarantine sentinel for this example; production code should use an explicit dead-letter state. Do not hide that distinction in a generic retry helper.

Measure the path as a timeline: outbox_created, queue_enqueued, worker_started, request_finished, and delivered. The useful metrics are age of the oldest pending row, batch size, enqueue lag, delivery latency, retry count, and dead-letter count. Alert on age and error rate, not on a single slow request. Logs should carry shipment ID, webhook ID, message ID, attempt, and a trace ID. That lets an on-call engineer answer “where did this update stop?” without replaying the entire night.

Which queue shape fits latency versus cost?

If customers watch a shipment screen in real time, a nightly batch is the wrong shape. Use the outbox relay continuously and let workers drain small messages; the extra queue operations buy lower latency. If the webhook is a reconciliation hint consumed by a back-office job, a 15-minute or nightly batch can be rational. Your mileage may vary when subscribers are spread across time zones or have contractual delivery windows.

A queue service usually charges for requests and retained work; Redis-backed queues shift cost toward always-on capacity and operations; workflow engines charge for state transitions and add visibility for multi-step processes. I’m not sure which line item dominates for your traffic until you chart messages per shipment, retry probability, and retention hours. Cost belongs beside latency in the design review, never in place of a delivery guarantee.

The catch is operational ownership. A cron plus queue is not suitable when each webhook needs human approval, calendar-aware waits, or a long saga; stick with a workflow engine then. Conversely, a workflow engine is excessive for one POST and one retry policy. Keep the state model proportional to the failure modes you can actually explain.

Limits and a practical rollout

Begin in shadow mode: enqueue copies, measure lag, and compare the worker's result with the existing publisher. Then enable one subscriber group, cap concurrency, and document the replay command. Test duplicate messages, a full queue, a rotated signing key, and a database lease that expires halfway through a batch. These are ordinary paths, not exotic chaos tests.

Measure twice.

For a useful rehearsal, freeze the subscriber endpoint for ten minutes while a batch is in flight. The queue should retain the messages, the worker should record timeouts without losing payloads, and the age-of-oldest metric should climb. Restore the endpoint, watch retries drain, and verify that the delivery ledger contains one terminal result per webhook ID even if the same message was attempted several times. Run that exercise with 50 records first, then with the largest batch your database lease can hold; the point is to validate the handoff and the alert, not to manufacture a benchmark.

There is no exactly-once network delivery. There is only an idempotent receiver, a durable intent, and enough evidence to replay safely. If the business cannot accept delayed updates at all, move the decision earlier: publish from the committed outbox continuously and design the subscriber contract around bounded latency.

References

Further reading:

  • https://cloud.google.com/tasks/docs/dual-overview
  • https://microservices.io/patterns/data/transactional-outbox.html
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/AbortController
  • https://docs.bullmq.io/
  • https://docs.temporal.io/
