title: Enhancing Cross-Grade Generalization in Banana Variety Classification via Hybrid CNN-Transformers and Knowledge Self-Distillation
description:
arXiv:2610.29008v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In recent years, automated fruit classification systems have become a more critical component in precision agriculture for efficient yield estimation, quality control, and supply chain optimization. However, they still face significant challenges under varying quality, fruit maturity, illumination, texture degradation, morphological attributes, domain shift, and post-harvest handling conditions. In this study, we address the challenging issue of cross-grade banana variety classification. This is a real-world setting where models that have been trained on specific quality grades must generalize to unseen grades to handle significant domain shift. Under a rigorous Leave-One-Grade-Out evaluation protocol, we present a thorough comparative analysis of CNNs, ViTs, and dual-stream hybrid architectures using a large-scale dataset of 31,678 banana images with three varieties and three quality grades. Specifically, to address the drawbacks of single-paradigm frameworks, we present a dual-stream Swin ResNet hybrid framework enhanced with KL-divergence-based self-distillation to align probabilistic feature representations across the CNN and Transformer streams. Comprehensive experimental analyzes show that the presented hybrid framework with KL-divergence based self-distillation achieves better overall performance, i.e., it attains a mean accuracy of 81.25% and significantly surpasses CNN and Transformer baseline models. Qualitative analysis further confirms that the hybrid framework in this study improves discriminative feature transferability, improves attention localization, and stabilizes optimization.

title: Introducing Flat Rate CDN
description:
Over the past year, we have improved Vercel’s Pro pricing to better reflect how teams build, with expanded user roles, flexible credits, access to enterprise features, and more. But one area our customers continued to give us feedback on was CDN pricing.

CDN costs should be predictable, but viral launches, traffic bursts, or misconfigured routes sometimes turned an otherwise normal month into an unexpected bill. For teams building on Vercel, that uncertainty made growth feel like a problem at exactly the moment it should feel exciting.

Today, we are introducing Flat Rate CDN for Pro teams: a new way to pay for CDN usage with a predictable monthly bill, built-in spike protection, and service tiers designed for different traffic profiles.

What is Flat Rate CDN?

Flat Rate CDN is an alternative to usage-based CDN billing that provides you with a predictable monthly bill.

The model is designed around a simple idea: teams should be able to choose the CDN capacity that corresponds to their typical usage profile, pay a known amount monthly, and avoid surprise overages from temporary spikes.

Flat Rate CDN has several advantages over usage-based billing:

  • Fixed monthly price: Pay a fixed amount for Vercel CDN each month.

  • Covers traffic spikes: CDN Requests, Fast Data Transfer, and other resources are no longer billed directly, so spikes don't result in surprise bills.

  • No overages: Your bill will never increase because of temporary usage spikes.

Importantly, predictable pricing does not mean lower-quality bandwidth. Every request still runs on Vercel’s premium network, including private fiber that routes around congestion on the public internet, which can improve performance by up to 60%. Comparable routing is often sold as a premium add-on, but Vercel includes it by default for Pro teams, and performance isn't degraded during traffic spikes.

How it works

All new Pro teams have Flat Rate CDN enabled by default, and existing Pro teams can opt in. Usage is tracked at the team level and covers all projects, so you no longer need to manage capacity for them individually.

What’s included

On Flat Rate CDN, one fixed monthly fee covers:

  • CDN Requests

  • Fast Data Transfer

  • Blob Data Transfer

  • Observability events generated by CDN requests

The default tier is included with Pro. You can upgrade to a higher tier for increased request and data transfer capacity.

Your tier is fixed throughout any given billing period, so you never have to worry about charges from temporary traffic spikes.

What happens during a spike

The following team had a relatively normal usage profile that would fit comfortably in our $20/month Flat Rate CDN tier:

Only days after the above period, they experienced a viral product launch that generated a significant surge in traffic:

If the team had been on usage-based pricing, their CDN bill would have reached tens of thousands of dollars. On Flat Rate CDN, it stayed at $20 for the month.

No caps and no performance hit

Flat rate pricing from other infrastructure providers often places caps on usage when you reach your capacity, resulting in rapid performance degradation and request rejection. Flat Rate CDN is different in two ways:

  1. We recognize usage spikes and remove them when evaluating your CDN usage against capacity.

  2. We rightsize your Flat Rate CDN tier every month based on sustained usage.

This means we’ll never bring down your site when you’re going viral, and you don’t have to actively manage your tier when you’re growing quickly.

You can still monitor every covered resource on the Usage page or in the CLI, including traffic spikes absorbed by Vercel:

What we heard from customers during beta

Even though surprise bills are rare across our entire customer base, we’ve seen numerous stories from Pro customers about unexpected bills, many of which famously blew up on X. One team we interviewed was running hundreds of client sites and told us that CDN costs were “by far our largest line item, and the hardest to forecast,” especially when traffic spiked “from a client’s listing going viral, seasonal traffic, or bot traffic.”

In May, we released Flat Rate CDN to a small set of teams in limited beta. Over the last several months, it has changed how they operate on Vercel.

They worried less:

Flat Rate CDN eased our billing anxiety. With the recent increase in AI crawler traffic, we used to frequently check bot activity through Observability and monitor which bots were generating traffic. We now spend much less time doing that.

They built more:

Knowing that CDN usage is predictable makes us more willing to adopt caching-oriented approaches. We're now considering broader use of Cache Components and other caching strategies in our Next.js architecture, whereas previously we had to think more carefully about the potential cost impact of additional cache traffic.

This is exactly what we built Flat Rate CDN to do. No surprise bills, predictable pricing, and peace of mind to ship the next project.

Get started

All new Pro teams have Flat Rate CDN enabled by default. Existing Pro teams can opt in to the new plan:

  1. Select Billing in the navigation.

  2. Browse to Flat Rate CDN and toggle the setting to on.

  3. Choose a capacity tier that corresponds to your typical usage.

  4. Review your selection, which will show subscription costs if you chose a paid Flat Rate CDN tier.

  5. Select Enable to apply.

Learn more about Flat Rate CDN pricing in the documentation.

title: Multi-Scale Latent Temporal Compression Attention and Video-Text Cross Attention Fusion for Video Action Detection
description:
arXiv:2610.29176v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In video action detection, modeling the temporal dependencies in continuous video streams is crucial. Previous methods based on deep neural networks can perform frame-level video recognition tasks. However, these methods struggle to model dynamic temporal patterns, facing challenges such as redundant frame information, difficulty balancing global and local features, and insufficient fusion of visual and textual features. To address these issues, we propose a video temporal attention module based on the Multi-Scale Latent Temporal Compression Attention, which aggregates continuous temporal sequences into feature representations across diverse temporal scales while efficiently reducing redundancy. We also introduce a Video-Text Cross Attention Fusion module that leverages cross-attention at both latent and standard feature levels, achieving fine-grained fusion between video and textual features to enhance semantic alignment and feature interaction. Experimental results across multiple video recognition benchmarks demonstrate that our proposed methods achieve superior performance compared to existing methods, validating the effectiveness and generalization capability.

title: Extreme Low-State Quantized Transformer for Electricity-Load Forecasting
description:
arXiv:2610.28784v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Aggressive low-state weight quantization can substantially reduce neural-network representational flexibility, making predictive performance difficult to preserve when only a few discrete weight states are available. We investigate this regime for Transformer-based electricity-load forecasting using 3-, 5-, 7-, and 16-state weight quantization across feed-forward-only and attention-plus-feed-forward quantization. Two tasks predict either the next hour or the next 24 hours from the preceding 48 hours across two co-primary electricity-consumption datasets. Direct post-training quantization (PTQ) increased mean normalized root-mean-square error (NRMSE) relative to full precision by 6.25 and 7.04 percentage points in Datasets A and B, whereas quantization-aware fine-tuning (QAT-FT) recovered approximately 90.2% and 94.5% of these penalties. Quantization-aware training from random initialization (Scratch-QAT) also produced competitive low-state solutions, with particularly favorable behavior at three states. We further introduce accumulated-update thresholding, which accumulates optimizer-proposed weight changes before commitment. Relative to paired Scratch-QAT controls, this reduced committed shadow-weight updates by approximately 99.7% and discrete state transitions by approximately 77--80%, while mean NRMSE changed by only +0.042 and +0.197 percentage points. These results show that useful Transformer forecasting can be retained under highly discrete weight representations while strongly suppressing target-state activity, supporting a prospective route toward compact, low-activity edge forecasting using multilevel synaptic devices.

title: From Weather to Enhanced Weathering: Weather Foundation Models for Carbon Dioxide Removal at Operational Scale
description:
arXiv:2610.28973v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Enhanced Rock Weathering (ERW) is a carbon removal solution with the potential to remove gigatons of CO$_2$ per year, but quantifying that removal today requires dense soil sampling and laboratory analysis. We evaluate five weather Foundation Models (FMs) as frozen encoders feeding lightweight decoders, under a leave-one-field-out protocol on 5,192 chronosequences from 264 fields across Brazil and the US. To our knowledge, this is the first holistic evaluation of weather FMs for ERW and the largest evaluation on operational ERW data. We find that across weather FMs, representations transfer to ERW: our best model, TerraNova-ERW, built on Aurora 1.5, positively orders measurements within fields it has never seen. Zero-shot prediction of a new field's mean removal is not yet feasible, and we attribute this to data scale: the same architecture excels on $\sim$$10^5$ natural-weathering sequences, anchoring the scale we expect ERW data must reach. Few-shot prediction, blending the model with a few samples per field, is supported today: TerraNova-ERW recovers over 60% of the highest-removal fields with two samples per field, roughly halves the samples needed to estimate a field's mean removal, and can cut sampling on our densest fields by 28-98%.

title: “Real Developers Test in Production.” But Should They?
description:
You've probably heard this joke before. It pokes fun at developers who skip testing, push code straight to production, and let real users discover the bugs.

But there's a reason the joke exists. Software that works on a developer's machine can behave very differently when real requests, databases, and multiple services get involved.

A broken update endpoint could corrupt customer data. An unhandled error could take down a critical feature. A bad deployment could turn a routine release into hours of debugging, incident response, and frustrated users.

And fixing the code is only part of the problem. Someone has to identify what broke, reproduce the issue, assess its impact, roll back or deploy a fix, and verify that the same bug doesn't return. Depending on the organization, that work can involve developers, QA engineers, SREs, and incident responders.

So, should developers test in production?

Their are different types of Production testing which are done like A/B testing, Canary Releases, Feature Flags, Shadow Testing, Smoke testing etc.

But these testings are done for a specific purpose and that is to test the application in a production environment. But these testings are not enough to catch all the bugs that our existing tests miss before they affect real users.

Let's build a small application, break it deliberately, explore the testing techniques that help prevent these failures, and see how Keploy can turn recorded API interactions into reusable regression tests so we dont have to write the test cases and guess what scenarios to test.

Sample Application Setup

We have a sample Bookmark application with Go, Echo and PostgreSQL. It has all the CRUD operations for bookmarks along with a simple UI to interact with the application.

You need:

  • Go
  • Docker
  • Keploy CLI

Clone and run this sample application locally using:

git clone https://github.com/Namanv0509/bookmark.git && cd bookmark

go mod download

To start the application run:

docker compose up --build -d

Check the health of endpoint:

curl http://localhost:8080/health

Run the following command to stop it:

docker compose down

Let's Break Something First

We'll use bookmark, a simple bookmark manager built with Go, Echo, and PostgreSQL.

Users can save bookmarks, add notes and tags, view their saved links, update them, and delete them. The application has a small browser interface and a REST API.

Start the application locally and Open http://localhost:8080 and create a bookmark. You can also interact with the API directly.


curl -i -X POST http://localhost:8080/links \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "url": "https://www.google.com/",
    "title": "Google Search",
    "notes": "Sounds like a good search engine. It helps me find good blogs like this.",
    "tags": ["Search Engine"]
  }'

The application should save the bookmark and return its details.

Now let's imagine we're making a small improvement to the update endpoint. We change its SQL query, test that the application starts, and deploy the new version without checking whether the update behavior still works.

Here's the mistake we introduce:

UPDATE links
SET url = $1,
    title = $3,
    notes = $2,
    tags = $4,
    updated_at = NOW()
WHERE id = $5;

The title and notes parameters are swapped. We intended to assign the title from $2 and the notes from $3, but accidentally did the opposite.

Let's send an update request with distinct values to see the effect.


curl -i -X PUT http://localhost:8080/links/1 \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "url": "https://www.google.com/",
    "title": "Title",
    "notes": "Notes",
    "tags": ["updated"]
  }'

The endpoint still return a successful response. The application is running and everything looks fine. Yet the bookmark's title can now become notes.

We've introduced a bug without necessarily causing a crash.

Imagine the same mistake in a production application. Users might save incorrect information, downstream services might consume the corrupted data, and the problem might go unnoticed until someone reports it.

Let's imagine a different mistake: a database connection failure that causes requests to time out. That could make a feature unavailable, potentially affecting every user who relies on it.

These are different failure modes, but they reveal the same problem: a successful deployment doesn't guarantee correct behavior.

What Does “Testing in Production” Actually Mean?

The phrase gets used to describe several different practices, but they aren't interchangeable.

Skipping tests and deploying directly

This is the reckless interpretation of the joke: code goes straight to production without sufficient verification.

It might appear faster initially, but failures can become expensive. Developers may have to investigate unfamiliar production states, QA teams may need to reproduce issues, and operations teams may have to mitigate an outage.

Testing in a staging environment

A staging environment is a separate environment intended to resemble production. Teams can deploy a release candidate there and run tests before exposing it to users.

Staging is useful, but it isn't a perfect copy of production. Data volumes, configurations, integrations, and traffic patterns can differ.

Testing in production deliberately

Some teams perform controlled tests in production because certain conditions are difficult to reproduce elsewhere.

For example:

  • Canary releases send a small portion of real traffic to a new version before a wider rollout.
  • Feature flags let teams enable or disable features for selected users and gradually expand access.
  • A/B testing compares different versions of a feature with different user groups to measure outcomes such as engagement or conversion.
  • Shadow testing mirrors real requests to a candidate version so its behavior can be evaluated without using its responses for normal user-facing results.results.

The Different Layers of Software Testing

Different tests answer different questions. A practical testing strategy combines them rather than relying on a single tool.

Type Question it answers bookmark example
Unit testing Does this piece of logic work? Does URL validation reject ftp:// URLs?
Integration testing Do components work together? Can the API save a bookmark in PostgreSQL?
API testing Does the HTTP interface behave correctly? Does an invalid request return the expected status and response?
End-to-end testing Does a complete user workflow work? Can a user create a bookmark through the browser and see it in the list?
Regression testing Did a change break existing behavior? Does updating a bookmark still preserve its title and notes?
Load testing How does the application behave under traffic? Can the list endpoint handle concurrent requests?

These categories can overlap. For example, an API test that exercises the actual database is also an integration test. Regression testing describes the goal of detecting unintended changes, not a particular test level.

Let's look at what each approach gives us.

Unit Testing: Check the Small Pieces First

A unit test checks a small, isolated piece of code.

For our bookmark application, we want to verify that the validation logic accepts valid HTTP URLs, rejects unsupported schemes, and requires a title. The test cases are already available in main_test.go.

Run the following commands from your project directory:

go test ./...
go test -v ./...
go test -cover ./...

The first command runs the tests, the second displays individual test results, and the third reports code coverage.

You should see output similar to this:

=== RUN   TestValidateInput
=== RUN   TestValidateInput/valid_input
=== RUN   TestValidateInput/missing_title
=== RUN   TestValidateInput/unsupported_scheme
=== RUN   TestValidateInput/missing_URL
--- PASS: TestValidateInput (0.00s)
PASS
ok      linkvault       0.110s

All four test cases pass, confirming that our validation logic handles these inputs as expected. However, our overall code coverage is only 7% because we've tested just a small part of the application.

Unit tests help us verify individual pieces of logic, but they don't tell us whether our HTTP handlers and SQL queries work correctly together.

For that, we need to test how the application interacts with its dependencies.

Dependencies: What Does Your Application Rely On?

A dependency is something your code relies on to perform its job.

bookmark has dependencies at several levels:

  • Echo handles HTTP routing and middleware.
  • A PostgreSQL driver lets Go communicate with the database.
  • PostgreSQL stores bookmark data.
  • The frontend depends on the API returning data in the expected format.

Some dependencies are libraries. Others are external systems that must be running and correctly configured.

This distinction matters when testing. Our validation function can run without PostgreSQL, but creating a bookmark requires a database connection, a valid schema, and a working SQL query.

When a test fails, we want to know whether our own logic is wrong or a dependency is unavailable or behaving differently than expected.

One way to investigate this is to test with the real dependency. Another is to replace it with a test double.

Integration and API Testing: Bring the Pieces Together

Let's return to the running application.

An integration test can send a request to bookmark, let the actual handler execute its SQL query, and verify that PostgreSQL stores the expected data.

An API test focuses on the behavior exposed through HTTP. We might check that:

  • Creating a valid bookmark returns the expected response.
  • An invalid URL produces a validation error.
  • Retrieving an unknown ID returns the appropriate not-found response.
  • Updating a bookmark changes its fields correctly.
  • Deleting a bookmark removes it from subsequent results.

For example:

curl -i -X POST http://localhost:8080/links \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "url": "https://keploy.io",
    "title": "Keploy",
    "notes": "API testing tutorial",
    "tags": ["testing"]
  }'

Then inspect the result:

curl http://localhost:8080/links

These requests exercise more of the real application than our isolated unit tests.

The problem is that manually repeating these requests after every code change quickly becomes tedious. We also need to ensure the same scenarios are tested consistently.

Regression Testing

How do we know a code change hasn't broken behavior that already worked?

That's where regression testing comes in. It helps us verify that existing functionality continues to behave as expected after changes to the code.

Their are severl tools we can use for it like:

  • Keploy
  • Diffy
  • Pact

For our demo, we'll use Keploy to record API interactions and replay them after code changes. This lets us catch unexpected changes in application behavior without manually writing every test case.

Keploy can also mock supported dependency interactions during replay, reducing the need to run every dependency.

1. Record the API interactions

Start Keploy's recording workflow:

keploy record -c "docker compose up --build" \
  --container-name "linkvault-app" \
  --build-delay 60

Your Keploy logs should look something like this in keploy-logs.txt

🐰 Keploy: 2026-10-22T12:01:03.650059+05:30   [34mINFO[0m   Keploy agent is ready to record test cases and mocks.

With recording active, open http://localhost:8080 and exercise the application:

  • Create a bookmark.
  • Retrieve the bookmark list and an individual bookmark.
  • Update its title and notes.
  • Delete a bookmark.

We just performed an update to bookmark

🐰 Keploy: 2026-10-22T12:20:36.086862+05:30   [34mINFO[0m   🟠 Keploy has captured test cases for the user's application. {"path": "/Users/namanverma/Downloads/linkvault/keploy/test-set-0/tests", "testcase name": "post-links-1"}
🐰 Keploy: 2026-10-22T12:20:36.089196+05:30   [34mINFO[0m   🟠 Keploy has captured test cases for the user's application. {"path": "/Users/namanverma/Downloads/linkvault/keploy/test-set-0/tests", "testcase name": "get-links-1"}
🐰 Keploy: 2026-10-22T12:30:01.330101+05:30   [34mINFO[0m   🟠 Keploy has captured test cases for the user's application. {"path": "/Users/namanverma/Downloads/linkvault/keploy/test-set-0/tests", "testcase name": "post-links-2"}
🐰 Keploy: 2026-10-22T12:30:01.333557+05:30   [34mINFO[0m   🟠 Keploy has captured test cases for the user's application. {"path": "/Users/namanverma/Downloads/linkvault/keploy/test-set-0/tests", "testcase name": "get-links-2"}

Use distinct values for the title and notes so that incorrect updates are easier to detect.

Stop recording with Ctrl+C. Keploy captures the interactions and generates test cases according to the configured setup. keploy can be configured to mask senstitive information and handle noise.

2. Introduce a regression

Let's deliberately introduce a bug in the update handler's HTTP response.

In main.go, locate the end of updateLink().
Just before return c.JSON(200, link) add the following line:

// Intentional regression: swap title and notes in the response.
link.Title, link.Notes = link.Notes, link.Title
return c.JSON(200, link)

This simulates a response-mapping bug: the API returns the title as the notes and the notes as the title.

3. Replay the captured tests

With the regression in place, run:

keploy test -c "docker compose up --build" \
--container-name "linkvault-app" \
--build-delay 60 \
--delay 10

Heads up: non-deterministic fields. Fields like created_at, updated_at (set by NOW()), and auto-generated IDs change on every run, keploy detects them and mark them as noise fields.

Keploy replays the captured requests against the rebuilt application and compares the resulting HTTP responses with the recorded responses.

Because the values differ, Keploy should flag the response mismatch, provided those fields are included in its response comparison.

and for sure you can see that in the test summary as well

 <=========================================> 
  COMPLETE TESTRUN SUMMARY. 
        Total tests: 2
        Total test passed: 1
        Total test failed: 1
        Total time taken: "28.14 s"

        Test Suite Name         Total Test      Passed          Failed          Time Taken      Failed Testcases

        "test-set-0"            2               1               1               "28.14 s"       
<=========================================>

Your summary can vary depending on what and how many requests you have sent and your endpoint configs

We never had to write the test cases and we could catch the regression by replaying our traffic recorded previously. We can automate this testing with CI/CD, we will cover that in next article. 🐰

Conclusion

There's no single testing technique that catches every bug. Understanding when to use each approach helps us build more reliable software and catch problems before they reach production.

In the upcoming articles, we'll dive deeper into different types of testing, how they work, and when to use them.

If you'd like to explore further, here are two useful resources:

  • Microsoft Engineering Playbook — Automated Testing
  • Keploy Blog — Technology

Until next time, see you in the next one!

title: Liquid glass CSS — the Apple liquid glass effect with CSS only (plus SVG refraction)
description:
Originally published at webtricks.dev, where the liquid glass card snippet has a live playground.

Apple's Liquid Glass (introduced across iOS, iPadOS and macOS in 2025) is
the current reference for translucent UI. The good news: around 80% of the look
is plain, well-supported CSS. The catch: the bending refraction — where the
background visibly warps as it passes through the glass — needs an SVG
displacement filter that, today, only Chromium can feed into backdrop-filter.

This guide builds the effect in layers so you can stop at the layer your
support target allows. Every block is copy-paste ready; the control-driven
version lives in the liquid glass card snippet.

What "liquid glass" actually is

Look at a Liquid Glass control up close and you can separate five layers.
Each maps to one CSS feature:

Layer What it does CSS
Tint A faint white (or black) wash so the pane reads as a material, not a hole background: rgba(255,255,255,.1)
Blur + saturation Frosts what is behind and pumps its colors so the glass looks thick backdrop-filter: blur() saturate()
Specular rim A thin bright edge, strongest at the top, where light enters the pane inset box-shadow highlights + a 1px border
Sheen A soft diagonal gloss across the surface a ::after with a linear-gradient and mix-blend-mode: screen
Refraction The backdrop bends near the edges and ripples slightly backdrop-filter: url(#filter) with feDisplacementMap

Classic glassmorphism (the 2020 trend) is layers one to three. Liquid
glass adds the sheen and refraction, and uses stronger saturation so the
material looks lit from inside. If you only need the simpler flat version,
the glassmorphism card snippet is enough.

1. The cross-browser core (liquid glass CSS only)

Frosted glass is backdrop-filter. Liquid glass reads as a thick, lit pane,
and three ingredients do that: tint, blur with saturation, and a rim built
from inset shadows. This block works in every current browser:

.liquid-glass {
  position: relative;
  isolation: isolate;          /* keeps the ::after's z-index inside this box */
  padding: 28px;
  border-radius: 28px;
  color: #fff;

  /* 1. tint */
  background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.10);

  /* 2. frost — blur + saturation + a touch of brightness */
  backdrop-filter: blur(8px) saturate(180%) brightness(1.1);
  -webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(8px) saturate(180%) brightness(1.1);

  /* 3. specular rim: strong top highlight, softer on the other edges */
  border: 1px solid rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.18);
  box-shadow:
    0 8px 32px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.25),                 /* lift */
    inset 0 1px 1px rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.55),      /* top */
    inset 0 -1px 1px rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.30),     /* bottom */
    inset 1px 0 1px rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.20),      /* left */
    inset -1px 0 1px rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.20);     /* right */
}

Then add the diagonal sheen with a pseudo-element, so the surface looks
glossy rather than matte:

.liquid-glass::after {
  content: "";
  position: absolute;
  inset: 0;
  z-index: -1;                 /* below the text, above the tint */
  border-radius: inherit;
  pointer-events: none;
  background: linear-gradient(
    135deg,
    rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.45) 0%,
    rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.08) 28%,
    transparent 58%
  );
  mix-blend-mode: screen;
}

Why the asymmetric rim? Real glass catches light from above, so the top
inset is roughly twice as bright as the sides. Make all four equal and the
card flattens into an outlined box. If you want to tune the lift shadow and
the inset highlights visually, the box-shadow generator
builds layered inset shadows and copies the whole declaration.

A complete, working liquid glass card then looks like this:

<div class="liquid-glass">
  <h3>Liquid glass</h3>
  <p>Frosted, lit from the top, glossy across the surface.</p>
</div>

Put it over a busy, colorful background — a photo, or a few overlapping
radial gradients. Over a flat fill the blur has nothing to sample and the
effect vanishes (see Common mistakes below).

2. Light-mode variant

On a light background, white tint plus white highlights disappear. Flip the
tint toward the background color, lower the saturation boost, and switch the
rim to a mix of white (top) and dark (bottom) so the edge still reads:

.liquid-glass.light {
  color: #111;
  background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.45);
  backdrop-filter: blur(14px) saturate(140%);
  -webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(14px) saturate(140%);
  border: 1px solid rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.65);
  box-shadow:
    0 8px 24px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.10),
    inset 0 1px 1px rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.90),
    inset 0 -1px 1px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.06);
}

.liquid-glass.light::after {
  background: linear-gradient(
    135deg,
    rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.70) 0%,
    rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.15) 30%,
    transparent 60%
  );
  mix-blend-mode: normal;      /* screen does nothing useful over white */
}

Two rules of thumb for light mode: more blur (12–16px) because light
backgrounds have less contrast to frost, and a higher tint alpha (0.4–0.6)
because the text needs a more opaque surface to stay readable.
If you theme with tokens, drop your brand color into the
color converter to get it as rgb() so you can
append an alpha: rgb(14 165 233 / 0.12) makes a tinted glass in one line.

3. Real refraction with SVG displacement

To make the backdrop actually bend, displace it with an SVG filter.
Procedural noise from feTurbulence drives an feDisplacementMap:

<svg width="0" height="0" aria-hidden="true" style="position:absolute">
  <filter id="liquid" x="-20%" y="-20%" width="140%" height="140%">
    <feTurbulence type="fractalNoise" baseFrequency="0.008 0.012"
                  numOctaves="2" seed="9" result="noise" />
    <feGaussianBlur in="noise" stdDeviation="1.4" result="soft" />
    <feDisplacementMap in="SourceGraphic" in2="soft" scale="40"
                       xChannelSelector="R" yChannelSelector="G" />
  </filter>
</svg>

@supports (backdrop-filter: url('#liquid')) {
  .liquid-glass {
    backdrop-filter: blur(4px) saturate(180%) brightness(1.1) url('#liquid');
  }
}

How it works: feTurbulence produces an RGB noise image. feDisplacementMap
reads the red channel to shift each backdrop pixel horizontally and the
green channel to shift it vertically. A channel value of 0.5 means "no
move", so values above and below push pixels in opposite directions, and
scale sets how far (in user units) a full-strength value can move a pixel.
The feGaussianBlur in between softens the noise so the distortion looks
like water, not static.

Tuning the three numbers

Attribute Low values High values Good range for glass
baseFrequency Large, slow waves (0.002 — a single swell across the card) Fine ripples (0.05+ — looks like frosted texture, not liquid) 0.005–0.015; use two values (x y) for a slightly stretched, less "random" wobble
numOctaves 1 — smooth, blobby 4+ — adds fine detail on top of the big waves, much more expensive 1–2
scale 5–15 — barely visible shimmer 80+ — the backdrop tears into chunks 20–50

Change seed to get a different noise layout with the same character. The
filter region (x="-20%" etc.) is widened on purpose: displacement pulls
pixels in from outside the element, and with the default region the edges
clip to hard lines.

A static alternative: feImage

Noise gives you an organic, random wobble. Apple's real effect is not random:
the distortion is strongest at the edges (like a lens) and flat in the middle.
You get that by replacing the turbulence with a hand-made displacement
map — a PNG or inline SVG where the red/green channels encode the push
direction, grey in the center, ramping toward the edges:

<filter id="lens" x="0" y="0" width="100%" height="100%">
  <feImage href="lens-map.png" preserveAspectRatio="none"
           result="map" />
  <feDisplacementMap in="SourceGraphic" in2="map" scale="32"
                     xChannelSelector="R" yChannelSelector="G" />
</filter>

The map is stretched to the element with preserveAspectRatio="none", so one
image fits any card size. Paint it with a radial gradient from
rgb(128,128,128) in the middle to red/green-shifted corners, or generate it
from a small canvas script. This is the technique the in-depth walkthroughs at
LogRocket
and this Habr article build up to,
and it is much closer to the native look than raw noise.

Browser support

Two separate features matter: backdrop-filter itself, and whether a browser
accepts an SVG filter reference (url(#id)) inside backdrop-filter.

Feature Chrome / Edge Safari Firefox
backdrop-filter (blur, saturate…) 76+ 9+ with -webkit- prefix, 18+ unprefixed 103+
@supports (backdrop-filter: …) yes yes yes
url(#svg-filter) inside backdrop-filter yes no (declaration is dropped) not reliable — treat as no
url(#svg-filter) inside plain filter yes yes yes
prefers-reduced-transparency media query 118+ no behind a flag

The practical consequence: keep -webkit-backdrop-filter for older Safari,
and always gate the SVG refraction behind
@supports (backdrop-filter: url('#id')). Browsers that fail the check keep
the frosted layer, which already looks good. Do not combine the two in one
unguarded declaration — Safari rejects the whole backdrop-filter value if
any part of it is invalid, and you lose the blur too.

Accessibility

  • Contrast is unpredictable. Text over glass sits on whatever scrolls behind it. WCAG's 4.5:1 ratio must hold against the worst part of the backdrop, not the average. Raise the tint alpha, add a subtle text-shadow: 0 1px 2px rgb(0 0 0 / .4), or keep glass for chrome (toolbars, pills) and put long text on solid surfaces.
  • Respect reduced transparency. Users who turn on "Reduce transparency" in macOS or iOS expect opaque panels: 
@media (prefers-reduced-transparency: reduce) {
  .liquid-glass {
    background: rgb(28 30 38 / 0.92);
    backdrop-filter: none;
    -webkit-backdrop-filter: none;
  }
}
  • Reduced motion. If you animate the displacement (for instance by animating baseFrequency with an SVG animate element), disable it under prefers-reduced-motion: reduce. A rippling backdrop behind text is a real problem for readers with vestibular disorders.

Performance

backdrop-filter forces the browser to composite everything behind the
element into a texture, blur it, and re-composite every frame something
behind it moves. Three rules keep it smooth:

  1. Keep it off scrolling lists. One glass header over a scrolling page is fine; 50 glass cards inside a scrolling list means 50 blurs per frame. Use glass for the container, not the items.
  2. Blur radius is the cost knob. blur(8px) is cheap; blur(40px) on a full-width panel can drop a mid-range phone below 60fps. Liquid glass wants a small blur (4–10px) anyway — the saturation does the work.
  3. SVG displacement is the expensive layer. feTurbulence with numOctaves="2" recomputed every frame on a large element is noticeably heavier than any CSS filter. Keep displaced elements small (buttons, pills, a single card), keep numOctaves at 1–2, and never animate the noise on more than one element.

will-change: backdrop-filter is rarely useful: the element is already
promoted to its own compositor layer by the filter. Adding will-change:
transform to a glass element that moves (a draggable card, a slide-in
sheet) does help, because it stops the browser re-rasterizing the pane
while it moves.

Common mistakes

  • Flat background. The most frequent "it doesn't work" report. Glass only shows over variation. Test over a photo or stacked radial gradients first.
  • Forgetting isolation: isolate. The sheen uses z-index: -1. Without its own stacking context, the pseudo-element drops behind the parent's background and disappears — or, worse, behind the page.
  • ::after covering the text. If you set z-index: 1 instead, the gloss sits on top of the text and washes it out. Keep the sheen at -1 and the text at auto.
  • Missing position: relative. The inset: 0 on the pseudo-element is relative to the nearest positioned ancestor; without it the sheen stretches over the whole page.
  • overflow: hidden on the glass element. It clips the outer lift shadow. Use border-radius: inherit on children instead.
  • Equal highlights on all sides. Reads as an outline, not a rim. Keep the top highlight the strongest.
  • Blur too strong. Beyond ~16px the backdrop turns into a uniform smear and the material reads as "frosted plastic", not glass.

FAQ

Can I do liquid glass with CSS only, no SVG?

Yes. Tint, blur, saturation, the specular rim and the sheen are all plain
CSS and work in every current browser. You only lose the refraction (the
visible bending of the backdrop), which is the one part that needs an SVG
feDisplacementMap and currently works only in Chromium.

What is the difference between glassmorphism and liquid glass?

Glassmorphism is a translucent tint plus a blur and a thin border. Liquid
glass adds strong saturation, an asymmetric specular rim, a glossy sheen and
edge refraction so the panel looks like a thick lens rather than frosted
film. Compare the glassmorphism card and the
liquid glass card side by side.

Why does my backdrop-filter not work in Safari?

Older Safari needs the -webkit-backdrop-filter prefix (unprefixed support
arrived in Safari 18). Also, if any part of the value is unsupported — such
as url(#filter) — Safari discards the whole declaration, so put the SVG
part inside @supports.

Does liquid glass hurt performance?

A single glass element with a small blur is cheap. The cost scales with the
element's area, the blur radius, and how often what is behind it changes.
Avoid glass on many list items, keep the blur under ~10px, and reserve the
SVG displacement for small controls.

How do I make the glass tinted with my brand color?

Replace the white tint with your color at low alpha, for example
background: rgb(14 165 233 / 0.14), and keep the highlights white. Use the
color converter to get your hex as space-separated
rgb() so you can add the alpha channel.

Try it live

Open the liquid glass card snippet and drag
the blur, saturation, radius and tint controls, then copy the CSS with your
settings. Browse all snippets or subscribe via RSS.

title: GO: Introduction and core syntax
description:
Go (Golang) is Google's statically typed, compiled, cross-platform, open-source programming language that combines efficiency with ease of use. Its features include built-in concurrency via goroutines and channels. It has simple syntax, fast compilation, and a comprehensive standard library. It's popular for microservices, web servers, and cloud-native development.

Installation guide: Getting Started with Go — Install Go

Module One: Go Core Syntax

  • Package declaration and Imports
  • Variables and Types
  • Control Flow and Loops: for loops, range loops, and switch statements

Package declaration and Imports

A Go program is made of packages. Packages in Go are directories containing source files that work together to organize and reuse code. Every Go file belongs to a package, and that package is declared at the top of the file. A package like fmt (for formatted I/O) is one you bring in with an import.

A package can also be defined as a group of files that share one package name, usually in one folder. Every Go file starts with a package line that names it. A Go program starts in a package called main, and its function main is where the program starts running.

A package works like a folder of recipes in a cookbook section. Every recipe card in the folder says which section it belongs to. The section that starts the meal is the one the cook opens first.

// package line
package main
// import line
import "fmt"
func main() {
    fmt.Println("Hello, World!")
}

Expected output: Hello, World!

package main tells Go which package the file belongs to. The main package is special because it's the entry package for a program intended to run as an executable.

import "fmt" makes Go's standard library fmt package available to the file. It is used for formatted input and output, including printing text to the terminal.

func main() declares a function named main. When you run an executable program, execution begins in the main function.

fmt.Println("Hello, World!") calls the Println function from fmt to print text, followed by a new line. The dot accesses an exported name from a package, and the parentheses contain the arguments you're passing to the function.

How to Use Code That Belongs to Another Package (Import Another Package)

Our file often needs code from another package, which is listed in the import line. The import statement makes a standard library package available to the file. After importing, you call its functions using the package name, a dot, and the function name, such as fmt.Println. fmt is the package, and Println is the function inside it.

package main

// Makes the standard library package available to the file.
import "fmt"

// Declares the function where execution begins.
func main() {
    // Creates a variable named name as a string using the short variable declaration.
    name := "Ada"

    // Calls fmt.Println, which lives in the fmt package.
    fmt.Println("Hello", name)
}

Expected output:

Hello Ada

Naming Conventions in Go

As an example, we have fmt.Println("Train Name"). Under fmt, we have the package name, and under Println, we have the function name.

Note: Println starts with a capital letter. In Go, names beginning with a capital letter are exported and can be accessed from another package, while names beginning with a lowercase letter are unexported and can only be accessed within their own package. Go decides what other packages can use based on the first letter of a name.

Unused Imports and Compiler Errors

Go checks imports strictly. If a file imports a package and doesn't use it, the compiler stops with an error. If the file uses a package without importing it, the compiler also stops. The import block is an honest list that shows what a file depends on, and every imported package must be used.

Never use a package you haven't imported yet. Check whether an imported package is needed before importing it. You don't need to use every function inside an imported package, just one.

Incorrect:

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "strings"
)

func main() {
    name := "ada"
}

Go complains about fmt and strings being imported and not used. It also complains that name is declared and not used, because Go is just as strict about unused variables.

Correct:

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "strings"
)

func main() {
    name := "ada"
    fmt.Println(strings.ToUpper(name))
}

Go vs. JavaScript

JavaScript Go
const name = "Ada"; name := "Ada"
console.log("Hello", name); fmt.Println("Hello", name)

Lesson Takeaway

  1. Every Go file starts with a package line, and package main with the main function is where a program starts.
  2. An import statement brings in another package, and you can call its functions using the package name.
  3. A name starting with a capital letter is exported and can be used from other packages, while a lowercase name remains unexported.
  4. Go returns a compiler error for unused imports.

Variables and Types

A variable is a named storage location in memory used to hold a value of a specific type. It is a named box that holds a value.

In Go, variables are statically typed, meaning their type is known at compile time and cannot change.

Variables are declared using the var keyword, followed by the name, the type, and an optional value. The type says what kind of value the box can hold, and Go checks this. Any value written with the wrong type will be rejected by Go.

Kitchen analogy: There is a labelled jar in the kitchen. The label is the name, the jar's size and purpose are the type, while the contents are the value.

var itemCount int = 3
  • var — keyword
  • itemCount — name
  • int — type
  • 3 — value

Go also infers the type from the value. If you provide a value, you can leave out the type. In that case, 3 becomes an integer (int), 2.5 becomes a float64, "C" becomes a string, and true or false becomes a boolean.

The short assignment operator (:=) is used to declare a variable in Go, with the type usually inferred from the assigned value. It can only be used inside a function. Variables declared outside a function must use the var keyword.

Use var when you want to specify a type that cannot be inferred from the value, or when you want a zero value, which is the default value Go assigns to a variable when no value is provided. Inside a function, the short assignment operator (:=) is the usual choice for declaring a new variable.

Go vs. JavaScript

JavaScript Go
let item = 3; itemCount := 3

Type Inference in Go

Type inference is Go working out a variable's type from the value you give it. Go determines a variable's type from the initial value you assign to it. You don't write the type; Go infers it from the value, and the variable has a fixed type. So, the variable can't later hold a different kind of value. For example, if name is declared as a string using the short assignment operator (:=), assigning 5 to name later would be incorrect because name has already been defined as a string.

Kitchen analogy: A shelf is labelled by the first item placed on it. If the first item placed on a shelf is a book, then it can't also be used to store a banana.

// Type Inference in Go
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    // var declares itemCount with the type int and the value 3.
    var itemCount int = 3

    // price := 29.5 declares a new variable. Go infers float64 from 29.5.
    price := 29.5

    // name := "tea" declares a string. The := creates a new name here.
    name := "tea"

    // A plain = assigns to an existing variable. It does not declare a new one, so no := is needed.
    itemCount = itemCount + 6

    // Prints the three values in order: name, itemCount, and price.
    fmt.Println(name, itemCount, price)
}

Expected output:

tea 9 29.5

How does this compare to TypeScript?

If you're coming from TypeScript, this will feel familiar:

let name = "tea";
name = "coffee"; // Valid
name = 5;        // Type error

TypeScript infers that name is a string, much like Go does. The difference is that TypeScript's types disappear once it's compiled to JavaScript, while Go's types are part of the compiled program. Both languages help catch certain mistakes before your program runs. Here's the same thing in Go:

name := "tea"
name = "coffee" // Valid
name = 5        // Compile error

Go Variable Naming Rules

Go variable names can be short, like x and y, or descriptive, like age and price. They must start with a letter or underscore, cannot start with a digit, and can contain only letters, digits, and underscores. Variable names are case-sensitive, cannot contain spaces or be Go keywords, and have no length limit. Multi-word variable names can use camel case (myVariableName), Pascal case (MyVariableName), or snake case (my_variable_name).

Lesson Takeaway

  • The var keyword is used to declare a variable in Go.
  • The short variable declaration operator (:=) declares a variable with its type inferred from the assigned value.
  • The short variable declaration operator (:=) can only be used inside a function.

Control Flow and Loops

A quick note before we start: the snippets in this section leave out package main and import "fmt" to keep things short. If you want to run one, add those two lines at the top of the file.

for Loops

Many languages have a separate keyword for each loop type, but Go doesn't. It has only for, and what follows it decides the loop shape. The header sits between for and the opening brace, and the body is the code that repeats.

Kitchen analogy: A kitchen timer can count down a set number of minutes. When it reaches zero, it stops and is ready to be turned off. One tool, 3 uses.

func main() {
    // i := 1 happens once, before any check.
    // i <= 3 is checked before every pass, and the body only runs while it's true.
    // i++ adds 1 after each pass.
    for i := 1; i <= 3; i++ {
        fmt.Println(i)
    }
}

Expected output:

1
2
3
  • for — keyword
  • i := 1 — initialises i to 1
  • i <= 3 — condition
  • i++ — increments i by one
  • fmt.Println(i) — body, the code that repeats

A typical for loop has three parts, separated by semicolons.

  1. Initial statement: It runs once before the loop starts and usually creates a counter. 
i := 1;
  1. Condition statement: It is checked before each pass through the loop. 
i <= 3;
  1. Post statement: It runs after each pass and usually changes the counter. 
i++

So, i := 1 starts the counter at one, the loop runs while i is less than or equal to three, and i++ adds one after each pass.

Types of For Loops in Go

There are three major types of loops in Go:

  • Classic loop
  • Condition only loop
  • Infinite loop

1. Classic Loop

We use a classic loop when we want to repeat something a known number of times or track a counter.

for i := 0; i < 5; i++ {
    fmt.Println(i)
}

A classic loop has three parts: the initial statement, condition statement, and post statement. It runs five times in this example, printing 0 to 4.

2. Condition Only Loop

This works like a while loop in JavaScript or TypeScript.

count := 0
for count < 5 {
    fmt.Println(count)
    count++
}

Note: There's no semicolon in the loop header. It has only a condition and runs while the condition is true.

3. Infinite Loop

You use an infinite loop when you omit the condition. The loop continues indefinitely unless something inside stops it, usually with the keyword break or return.

for {
    fmt.Println("Still running")
    break
}

Note: break stops the loop after the first print. An infinite loop has no condition and runs indefinitely until it is stopped.

Go vs. JavaScript/TypeScript

Purpose Go JavaScript
Counter loop for i := 0; i < 3; i++ { } for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) { }
Condition loop for count < 3 { } while (count < 3) { }
Infinite loop for { } while (true) { }

Main difference: Go does not have a separate while keyword. It uses for for all loop types, and what follows for determines how the loop behaves.

Range Loop

Writing i := 0; i < 5; i++ can honestly be a bit long sometimes. So Go gives us a shorter way to write it using range.

for i := range 5 {
    fmt.Println(i)
}

This gives i values from 0 to 4, printing each value on a new line.

Expected output:

0
1
2
3
4

Note: range 5 iterates five times, producing values from 0 up to, but not including, 5. Ranging over a number like this needs Go 1.22 or newer, so if it doesn't compile, run go version to check what you have installed.

In a loop, continue skips the rest of the current iteration and moves to the next one, while break stops the whole loop.

func main() {
    for i := range 5 {
        if i == 2 {
            continue
        }

        fmt.Println(i)
    }
}

Expected output:

0
1
3
4

Lesson Takeaway

  1. Go has only one looping keyword, for.
  2. A classic loop has three parts, separated by semicolons: an initialisation statement that starts the counter, a condition statement that is checked before every pass, and a post statement that runs after every pass.
  3. A condition-only loop runs as long as the condition is true.
  4. An infinite loop runs indefinitely unless it is stopped using break or return.
  5. A range loop provides a shorter way to iterate over values, such as for i := range 5, which produces values from 0 to 4.
  6. continue skips the rest of the current iteration and moves to the next one, while break stops the loop.

Route Logic Using Typed Switch Statements

In JavaScript or TypeScript, there is a switch statement or an if-else statement. Go has both too. A switch statement in Go selects and executes one block of code from multiple possibilities based on the value or type of an expression. A switch statement provides a cleaner alternative to multiple if statements. It also supports both value-based and type-based branching.

How does it work?

A switch statement tells Go which values to examine. Then, each case defines a possible value. Go runs the code under the matching case. If no case matches, it runs default.

package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    day := "Monday"

    switch day {
    case "Monday":
        fmt.Println("Start of the week")
    case "Friday":
        fmt.Println("Almost the weekend")
    default:
        fmt.Println("Another day")
    }
}

Expected output:

Start of the week

Go supports two types of switch statements

  1. Expression switch
  2. Type switch

1. An Expression Switch

An expression switch evaluates an expression and executes the matching case block. This is useful when you have several possible options.

// Expression switch: evaluate the value, find a match,
// execute the matching case, and exit the switch.

func main() {
    route := "/profile"

    switch route {
    case "/":
        fmt.Println("Home page")
    case "/dashboard":
        fmt.Println("Dashboard page")
    case "/profile":
        fmt.Println("Profile page")
    default:
        fmt.Println("Page not found")
    }
}

An expression switch can also check more than one value in a single case. Just separate the values with a comma.

func main() {
    age := 25

    switch age {
    case 18:
        fmt.Println("Finally an adult")
    case 25, 30: // two values, one case
        fmt.Println("How's life?")
    case 35:
        fmt.Println("Oldie")
    default:
        fmt.Println("Another age")
    }
}

Expected output:

How's life?

The value in the switch and the values in the case expressions must be comparable under Go's type rules. E.g., an integer variable cannot be compared directly against a string.

func main() {
    age := 25

    switch age {
    case "25": // Error: cannot compare int with string
        fmt.Println("Twenty-five")
    }
}

This code produces a compile-time error because age is an integer (int), while "25" is a string. Go does not allow these incompatible types to be compared directly in a switch statement. The fix is to make both sides the same type, like case 25:.

Go also allows you to omit the value after switch. Each case can then contain a Boolean condition.

func main() {
    score := 75

    switch {
    case score >= 80:
        fmt.Println("Excellent")
    case score >= 60:
        fmt.Println("Passed")
    default:
        fmt.Println("Try again")
    }
}

Go evaluates the cases from top to bottom and executes the first case whose condition is true.

2. Type Switch

A switch checks the value, while a type switch checks what type a value is. This is useful when a variable has an interface type, such as any, and the value inside can be any data type. In Go, any is an alias for the empty interface, and it can hold a value of any type.

func main() {
    var value any = true

    switch v := value.(type) {
    case string:
        fmt.Println("This is a string:", v)
    case int:
        fmt.Println("This is an integer:", v)
    case bool:
        fmt.Println("This is a Boolean:", v)
    default:
        fmt.Println("Unknown type")
    }
}
  • value — a variable of type any.
  • .(type) — the syntax used to inspect the value's type in a type switch.
  • v — a variable declared in the switch that refers to the value inside each case, with its specific type.
  • case string — when the value is a string, v is a string.
  • case int — when the value is an integer, v is an integer.

Expression Switch vs. Type Switch

Feature Expression switch Type switch
What it checks A value or Boolean condition The type of a value
Typical use Routes, selectors, and codes Values whose types may differ
Example switch route switch v := value.(type)
Cases Values or Boolean conditions Types such as string, int, etc.
Matching Executes the matching case Executes the case matching the value's type
Type handling Cases must be compatible with the switch expression's type Go identifies the value's type in each case

Go vs. JavaScript

Feature Go JavaScript
Syntax switch expression { } switch (expression) { }
Case behaviour Exits the switch automatically after a matching case (use fallthrough if you want it to continue) Requires break to prevent fall-through

Lesson Takeaway

  1. Use an expression switch when one value can have several possible outcomes.
  2. Use a type switch when you need to identify a value's type.
  3. Use case to define options and default to handle anything unmatched.

Final Practice Exercise

Create a small program that combines what you've learned.

Your program should:

  1. Declare a variable called status and assign it "pending".
  2. Use an expression switch to print a message for "pending", "approved", or "rejected".
  3. Print "Unknown status" for any other value.
  4. Use a for loop with range 5 to print the numbers zero through four, but skip the number two using continue.

Next Module: Data Structures

title: SkillEval: Learning Interpretable Ability Profiles of LLMs via Cognitive Diagnosis Models
description:
arXiv:2610.28767v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Current evaluation of LLMs on benchmarks typically aggregates performance over individual examples into a single scalar score. This approach is overly coarse and ignores the diverse scope of skills covered by benchmark datasets. To address this limitation and better exploit benchmark data, we propose SkillEval, a new evaluation framework that performs cross-model, skill-level analysis. The framework integrates advances from two areas: (1) it leverages the meta-cognitive capabilities of LLMs to automatically discover interpretable skills from questions, and (2) it applies cognitive diagnosis models (CDMs) from psychometrics to estimate per-skill abilities of LLMs. We conduct experiments on 3,811 LLMs evaluated on 9,523 items across five benchmarks spanning diverse domains (MATH, BBH, GPQA, MuSR, IFEval). Compared to the traditional average-based evaluation paradigm, SkillEval produces reliable, more calibrated and informative yet concise model profiles that more accurately predict model behavior on unseen items. We also demonstrate the utility of SkillEval in two downstream tasks: (1) LLM routing, which dynamically assigns each query to a capable but efficient model, reducing inference cost by over 60% while achieving improved performance, and (2) Computerized Adaptive Testing (CAT), where an unseen model can be efficiently evaluated using a trained CDM. Furthermore, we show that these skill profiles provide useful insights, for example, how benchmarks share skills and how instruction-tuned models differ from their base models.

title: Unit-Aware Differentially Private Quantum Machine Learning for Clinical and Wearable Health Data
description:
arXiv:2610.28968v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Clinical registries and wearable sensors support early health-risk assessment, yet models trained on these records may leak sensitive information when released. Differential privacy (DP) bounds this leakage by injecting noise whose total magnitude grows with the number of trainable parameters, a cost especially severe for small health cohorts. This motivates parameter efficient models including quantum machine learning (QML), whose variational circuits can represent complex decision boundaries with few trainable parameters. It raises a question: at matched input dimensionality and privacy budget, does a quantum model retain more utility than a classical one? We investigate this question on three clinical cohorts and one wearable cohort, treating each clinical record or participant as a privacy unit. We compare capacity-matched quantum, multilayer perceptron, and logistic regression models across five privacy budgets and five seeds. The quantum model leads on three clinical cohorts by up to 0.104 ROC AUC averaged across budgets; however, trails on the wearable cohort, where the small number of participants requires substantial noise. No difference survives Holm correction across 24 tests, so these results indicate a trend rather than a quantum advantage. An analytic gradient bound shows that lower clipping thresholds can improve utility by reducing noise despite clipping bias. Finally, an experiment on IBM quantum computer (ibm_fez, a 156-qubit superconducting processor) using eight fixed test cases yields mean absolute probability errors of 0.046 (private) and 0.063 (non-private) relative to simulation, supporting the feasibility of inference on noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) hardware. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/TITANS-Lab-Artifacts/DP-QML-Health.

title: Master Java gRPC with Micronaut: Your First Microservice in Minutes
description:
gRPC is a powerful framework for communication between backend services. Combined with Java and Micronaut, it provides a practical foundation for building lightweight, strongly typed microservices.

In this tutorial, you'll learn how to get started with a Java gRPC service, build the project with Maven, and run a sample client-server interaction.

You can follow along using GRPCMicroService v1, the free starter project, available on GitHub under the MIT License. If you're looking for a more complete solution with additional features, GRPCMicroService v2 is available as a paid starter kit.

  • Free v1: Browse the GitHub repository
  • Paid v2: Discover the Complete Starter Kit

Why Use gRPC with Micronaut?

gRPC uses Protocol Buffers to define service contracts and exchange structured messages between clients and servers.

Some of its key benefits include:

  • Strongly typed contracts: Define service methods and message structures using .proto files.
  • Efficient communication: Use HTTP/2 and Protocol Buffers for remote procedure calls.
  • Code generation: Generate client and server classes from service definitions.
  • Microservice architecture: Build services with clearly defined interfaces.
  • Java ecosystem: Use familiar tools such as Maven and your preferred Java IDE.

Micronaut provides the framework for building JVM applications, while gRPC handles service-to-service communication.

Together, they offer a practical foundation for developing Java microservices.

Prerequisites

Before getting started, make sure you have:

  • JDK 21
  • Apache Maven
  • Eclipse IDE or another Java IDE (optional)
  • Basic knowledge of Java and Maven

Verify your environment by running:

java -version
mvn -version

Make sure your terminal and IDE are configured to use a compatible JDK.

Step 1: Get the Free Starter Project

For this tutorial, we'll use GRPCMicroService v1, a free starter project that demonstrates the essential components of a Java gRPC microservice.

Clone the repository:

git clone https://github.com/frekost/grpc-micronaut-starter-kit.git
cd grpc-micronaut-starter-kit

You can also download the source code directly from the GitHub repository.

Import the Project into Eclipse

If you're using Eclipse, follow these steps:

  1. Open Eclipse.
  2. Select File → Import.
  3. Choose Maven → Existing Maven Projects.
  4. Select the project directory containing pom.xml.
  5. Finish the import and wait for Maven dependencies to resolve.

You can also open the project in your preferred Java IDE.

Step 2: Build and Test the Application

Open a terminal in the project directory and run:

mvn clean compile test

This command cleans the previous build output, compiles the project, and executes the configured tests.

If everything is configured correctly, Maven should finish with:

BUILD SUCCESS

This confirms that the build and configured tests completed successfully.

Step 3: Run the Application

In Eclipse, locate the application's main class, Application.java, and select:

Run As → Java Application

The sample project uses gRPC port 50052.

Once the server is running, the included client runner can send a request to the Greeter service.

The expected output is similar to:

Processing request with name: "Micronaut"
Response from gRPC server: Hello, Micronaut!

The exact output depends on the implementation and application configuration.

For a more detailed walkthrough, follow the Free v1 Quick Start Guide.

Step 4: Understand the Project Structure

A typical Java gRPC microservice contains several important components.

Protocol Buffers

The .proto file defines the service contract, request messages, and response messages.

These definitions provide a structured interface between the client and the server.

Service Implementation

The server-side implementation contains the business logic executed when a client calls an RPC method.

This is where you can start adapting the example to your own requirements.

gRPC Client

The client connects to the server and invokes methods defined in the service contract.

In the sample project, the client demonstrates how to send a request to the Greeter service and receive a response.

Maven Configuration

The pom.xml file manages dependencies, build plugins, and Protocol Buffers code generation.

Maven helps keep the project build reproducible and makes it easier to manage dependencies as the application evolves.

Tests

Automated tests help verify application behavior and catch regressions as the project changes.

Together, these components provide a practical starting point for developing and extending a gRPC-based microservice.

What's Next?

Once your service is running, you can explore more advanced topics:

  • Adding new RPC methods
  • Defining additional Protocol Buffers messages
  • Implementing error handling and validation
  • Configuring deadlines and timeouts
  • Adding authentication and authorization
  • Integrating logging and observability
  • Introducing asynchronous event processing
  • Exploring messaging systems such as Apache Kafka
  • Containerizing and deploying your service

These are useful next steps when moving from a local example to a more complete microservice architecture.

You can implement these capabilities yourself, or start from a project that already includes some of the additional building blocks.

Free v1 vs. Paid v2

GRPCMicroService is available in two versions, designed for different needs.

GRPCMicroService v1 — Free

The free v1 project is designed for developers who want to learn how Java, Micronaut, gRPC, and Protocol Buffers work together.

It includes:

  • A working gRPC Greeter service and client
  • Protocol Buffers definitions
  • Maven build configuration and code generation
  • Micronaut application configuration
  • Error-handling components
  • Automated tests and technical documentation

The source code is available on GitHub under the MIT License, allowing you to use, modify, and redistribute it under the terms of that license.

Get started for free:

  • Free v1 GitHub Repository
  • Step-by-Step Quick Start Guide
  • v1 Documentation

GRPCMicroService v2 — Complete Starter Kit

If you need more than the basic example, GRPCMicroService v2 extends the starter-kit concept with additional features for building Java microservices.

Depending on your requirements, these capabilities can help you explore more advanced application patterns without assembling every component from scratch.

The v2 starter kit includes additional capabilities such as:

  • Event handling — Building blocks for event-driven workflows.
  • Apache Kafka integration — Exploring messaging and asynchronous communication between services.
  • Logging — Additional support for application diagnostics.
  • Error handling — Components for managing errors across the application.
  • Source code and automated tests — A more complete project to study, test, and adapt.

The paid v2 package is intended for developers who want a more complete starting point and prefer to spend less time assembling the initial project structure and supporting components.

Looking for the complete starter kit?

Discover GRPCMicroService v2 on Gumroad →

Review the product page for the package details and the applicable license terms.

Final Thoughts

Java, Micronaut, and gRPC are a useful combination for building services with clearly defined APIs and strongly typed communication.

Starting with a working example can help you understand the essential components before extending the service to meet your own requirements.

If you're learning gRPC or want a free foundation for your experiments, GRPCMicroService v1 is a good place to start.

If you're looking for additional capabilities, including event handling and Apache Kafka integration, GRPCMicroService v2 offers a more complete, paid starter kit.

Choose the version that fits your needs, explore the code, and start building your own Java gRPC microservices.

Have you used gRPC with Java or Micronaut? Share your experience and lessons learned in the comments!

title: One inbox for 8 networks: polling comments without burning API quota
description:
VeloxonHub Social has an Inbox that collects comments on your published posts from Facebook, Instagram, YouTube, Threads, Bluesky, Mastodon, DEV.to and WordPress, and lets you reply from one screen. Most of these networks don't push comments to you, so the Inbox is built on polling. Here's how we keep that cheap, correct and threaded.

Poll by post age, not on a fixed clock

Comments arrive fast while a post is new and almost stop after a couple of days. Polling every post every 15 minutes wastes quota: YouTube gives the whole app about 10,000 units a day, so a 15-minute comment poll for 14 days would cap us at roughly 100 videos.

So each published post has a cadence:

inboxCadence = repository.PollCadence{
    FreshFor: 2 * 24 * time.Hour, Fresh: 15 * time.Minute,
    Stale:    3 * time.Hour,      MaxAge: 14 * 24 * time.Hour,
}

Every 15 minutes for the first 2 days, then every 3 hours, and never after 14 days. The "is this post due?" check is a single SQL expression, so the worker asks Postgres for the next batch instead of keeping timers:

AND pt.published_at > now() - $2::interval            -- MaxAge
AND (pt.inbox_checked_at IS NULL OR pt.inbox_checked_at <
     now() - CASE WHEN pt.published_at > now() - $3::interval  -- FreshFor
                  THEN $4::interval ELSE $5::interval END)     -- Fresh / Stale
ORDER BY pt.inbox_checked_at NULLS FIRST

Posts that were never checked go first, and only posts on active accounts are polled.

Inserts that keep read state

Each poll returns the comments the network currently has, most of which we've already seen. They're saved with:

ON CONFLICT (social_account_id, external_id) DO NOTHING

An existing comment keeps its read and replied state, and RowsAffected() tells us exactly which comments are new. Only those trigger the bell notification (and a push alert in our iOS and Android apps, which are coming soon), so a re-poll never notifies twice.

Threads from one extra column

Networks return replies to comments as well as top-level comments. Storing the parent's external id (parent_external_id) is enough to build threads. The frontend groups the flat list into comment → reply → reply trees, sorts threads by their newest activity, and shows a reply on its own (with "Replying to …") when its parent is filtered out.

Rows saved before we tracked parents fill in on their next poll: if the insert hits a conflict and the network now reports a parent, we update just that column.

Replies: one interface per capability

Not every network lets an app reply, and fewer allow images in replies. Each network's client registers what it can do: a Replier, and optionally an ImageReplier. The API returns can_reply and can_reply_image per comment, so the UI only shows what will actually work. Where replies aren't possible, the UI says so and links to the comment on the network.

Before sending we check the network's character limit, and that an attached image is an image from the workspace's own media library. If the network rejects the reply, the user sees the network's own reason, plus "reconnect the account to grant reply permission" when it was a permissions error.

What we'd tell you if you're building something similar

  • Poll by age. Most comments arrive in the first two days.
  • Let the database decide what's due. One indexed query beats a scheduler per post.
  • Use ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING and count affected rows to find what's new.
  • Model capabilities per network, and expose them to the UI.

The Inbox is on every VeloxonHub Social plan, with a 7-day free trial: https://social.veloxonhub.com. Happy to go deeper on the per-network clients in the comments.

title: STAR-XPC: Set Transformer for Estimating X-ray Transmission in Polymer Composites
description:
arXiv:2610.28709v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Evaluating the energy transmission ratio of an X-ray beam through a polymer composite is a challenging task in radiation shielding studies. The reference solution with Monte Carlo transport simulation is highly accurate but computationally expensive: each of our reference simulations is capped at $4\times10^9$ photon histories and a 20,000 s (over 5 hours) time limit, while closed-form analytical methods fail to represent such complex scenarios. We present an artificial neural network model that maps the unordered multi-set of molecular constituents, their mass fractions, and four bulk physical descriptors directly to the transmission ratio $I(t)/I_0$ in 1-3 milliseconds. The model is a Set Transformer, which makes it permutation invariant by construction and accepts mixtures of different sizes up to 11 constituents within a fixed-size padded set. Each constituent is embedded with a chemistry-pretrained transformer language model, ChemBERTa. In our proposed method, training data are produced by an automated PENELOPE/penEasy pipeline using the radiation source at 30, 80, 100, and 120 kV tube voltages over polyethylene-based shielding composite slabs of thicknesses spanning 0.15-2.5 mm. After preprocessing, the dataset contains $n = 4697$ simulated configurations on which a leakage-free, jointly stratified 10-fold cross-validation is performed, attaining mean squared error MSE = $(1.12 \pm 0.56)\times10^{-4}$, normalized-MSE percentage NMSE% = 0.0294% $\pm$ 0.0147%, and $R^2 = 0.9988$. The corresponding per-sample percentage errors give an alpha-trimmed ($\alpha = 0.10$) absolute percentage error (APE) of 1.66% and a median APE of 1.15%. Our model's inference is several orders of magnitude faster than the underlying Monte Carlo simulation (sub-millisecond per query vs. several hours for the reference run) with effective accuracy in predicting $I(t)/I_0$.
