title: Caching Is Easy. Cache Invalidation Is Where Systems Break: A Practical Guide
description:
Adding a cache takes ten minutes. Debugging the bug it causes six months later takes a week.

Caching trades correctness for speed. The senior move is deciding how much correctness you're willing to give up, and making that decision explicit.

Start with the question, not the tool

Before you reach for Redis, answer three things:

  1. How stale can this data be? (seconds, minutes, never)
  2. What does a wrong answer cost? (a flicker, or a wrong invoice)
  3. What's the read-to-write ratio? (caches pay off on read-heavy data)

If you can't answer #1, you're not ready to cache it.

The four patterns 

CACHE-ASIDE (lazy)            WRITE-THROUGH
App -> Cache: hit? return     App -> Cache -> DB
      miss -> DB -> fill      (write both, in order)

WRITE-BEHIND                  READ-THROUGH
App -> Cache -> (async) DB    App -> Cache (cache loads DB itself)
Pattern Good for Risk
Cache-aside Most apps, default choice Stale reads, stampedes
Write-through Data read right after write Slower writes
Write-behind Write-heavy, loss-tolerant Data loss if cache dies
Read-through Simplifying app code Provider lock-in

My default: cache-aside with a TTL. It's simple, and failure is safe because the DB stays the source of truth.

Cache-aside in code 

async function getUser(id) {
  const key = `user:${id}`;

  const cached = await redis.get(key);
  if (cached) return JSON.parse(cached);

  const user = await db.users.findById(id);
  if (user) {
    // TTL + jitter so keys don't all expire together
    const ttl = 300 + Math.floor(Math.random() * 60);
    await redis.set(key, JSON.stringify(user), "EX", ttl);
  }
  return user;
}

async function updateUser(id, data) {
  await db.users.update(id, data);
  await redis.del(`user:${id}`); // invalidate, don't update
}

Delete on write, don't update. Updating the cache invites race conditions where an older write lands after a newer one.

The three failure modes

1. Cache stampede

A hot key expires and thousands of requests hit the database at once.

t=0   key expires
t=0+  [req][req][req][req][req] -> all miss -> all hit DB -> DB falls over

Fixes:

  • Request coalescing (single flight): one request rebuilds, the rest wait.
  • Lock on rebuild with a short timeout.
  • Stale-while-revalidate: serve the old value while one worker refreshes.
  • TTL jitter, as in the code above. 
const inflight = new Map();

function singleFlight(key, loader) {
  if (inflight.has(key)) return inflight.get(key);
  const p = loader().finally(() => inflight.delete(key));
  inflight.set(key, p);
  return p;
}

2. Cache penetration

Requests for keys that don't exist always miss and always hit the DB (bots love this).

Fix: cache the negative result briefly (null with a 30-60s TTL), or put a Bloom filter in front.

3. Stale data after writes 

Thread A: reads DB (old)  ............  writes cache (old)
Thread B:        updates DB (new), deletes cache
Result: cache now holds OLD data until TTL

Fixes: short TTLs as a safety net, versioned keys (user:42:v7), or event-driven invalidation from the write path.

Layers matter 

Browser cache -> CDN -> API gateway -> App memory -> Redis -> DB
   (fastest, least control) ------------------> (slowest, most control)

Push caching as close to the user as correctness allows. For public, static-ish data, HTTP headers do more than any Redis cluster:

Cache-Control: public, max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=300

What to measure

  • Hit ratio (below ~80% on a hot path means rethink the key design)
  • p99 latency with and without cache
  • Eviction rate and memory pressure
  • DB load during cold start: can you survive an empty cache?

That last one is the real test. If a cache flush takes you down, your cache isn't an optimization, it's a dependency.

Rules I follow

  • The database is the source of truth, always.
  • Every key has a TTL. No exceptions.
  • Invalidate by deleting, not by updating.
  • Design for a cold cache on day one.
  • Don't cache what you can't afford to be wrong.

Takeaway

There are only two hard things in computer science: cache invalidation and naming things. Treat invalidation as a design problem up front, and your cache stays a speed boost instead of becoming a source of mysterious bugs.

What's the nastiest caching bug you've shipped? Share it in the comments. 👇

title: The equals and hashCode contract in Java: Failure modes and the TreeSet twist
description:
1. The one idea to hold onto

Forget the formal wording for a moment and hold this picture instead.

Think of an object as a person's full name, like "Srinivas Reddy". Think of
hashCode() as that person's initials, "SR": a cheap little summary you can
compute from the full name in a second. And think of equals() as the slow,
careful check: do the two full names actually match, letter for letter?

With that picture, the two clauses of the contract stop being rules and become
common sense.

Clause one: equal objects must have equal hash codes. If two records are the
same person, their initials must come out the same. "Srinivas Reddy" gives you
"SR" every single time. It would be absurd for the identical name to produce
"SR" on one form and "TK" on another. So when the full thing is equal, any
summary derived from it is forced to be equal too. That is just what "summary of
the same thing" means.

Clause two: equal hash codes do NOT force the objects to be equal. Flip it
around. If I only tell you someone's initials are "SR", can you tell me who they
are? No. "SR" could be Srinivas Reddy, or Sara Roy, or Sam Rivera. Same
initials, completely different people. Matching initials is a hint that two
records might be the same, never a proof. You still have to read the full names.
Two different things sharing a summary has a name in the hashing world, a
collision, and it is completely normal and expected.

Here is a real collision from Java you can verify yourself. The two strings
"Aa" and "BB" are obviously different words, yet they produce the exact same
hashCode, the number 2112. It falls out of Java's string formula (each
character times 31, summed):

"Aa".hashCode();   // 65*31 + 97  = 2112
"BB".hashCode();   // 66*31 + 66  = 2112

Two genuinely different objects, one identical hash. That is clause two in the
flesh.

The one-way street. Initials are a summary, and a summary throws away almost
all the information in the name. Once you have thrown information away, different
things will occasionally collapse to the same summary. There simply are not
enough initials to go around. But the act of making the summary is fixed and
mechanical: the same name always yields the same initials, and two equal names
always yield equal initials. So the arrow only runs one direction. Equal name
guarantees equal initials. Equal initials guarantees nothing. Lossy, but
consistent, and that combination is the entire asymmetry.

The consistency clause. Your initials today are the same as your initials
tomorrow, unless you actually change your name. In code: as long as nothing
about the object changes, calling hashCode() again gives the same answer. It
does not wander.

If you want the single sentence that carries all of it: hashCode is a cheap
summary used to narrow down, and equals is the careful check used to confirm,
and the contract simply guarantees those two never contradict each other.

2. Why the contract exists: the two-step lookup

The reason clause one is non-negotiable becomes obvious once you see how a
HashMap actually finds things. It is secretly an array of slots called
buckets, and a lookup does two moves in sequence, never a full scan.

The first move: it calls hashCode() on your key and uses that number to pick
exactly one bucket. This is the shortlist step, how the map jumps straight to
the handful of entries that could possibly match instead of checking a million.
The second move: inside that one bucket, it calls equals() on each candidate
to find the exact match. This is the confirmation step.

So the roles are: hash narrows, equals confirms. Hash gets you to the right
shelf; equals reads the spine to find the exact book.

Now the asymmetry makes mechanical sense. Two different objects landing in the
same bucket is fine, because equals will sort them out once they are there.
That is a collision, and collisions are expected. But two equal objects landing
in different buckets is a catastrophe, because the confirmation step only ever
runs inside a single bucket. If your key is on the wrong shelf, equals never
even gets a chance to run. The librarian searching shelf seven will never find
the book sitting on shelf twelve, no matter how identical the two copies are,
because she never walks to shelf twelve.

That single sentence is the whole contract. Everything in the failure gallery
below is just that idea showing up in different disguises.

3. The contract, stated precisely

Now that you have the picture, the formal version reads as a summary rather than
a wall.

For hashCode:

  1. If a.equals(b) is true, then a.hashCode() == b.hashCode() must be true.
  2. If a.hashCode() == b.hashCode(), then a.equals(b) is NOT required to be true (collisions are legal).
  3. Called repeatedly on the same object with unchanged state, hashCode() must return the same value.

For equals, the method must be:

  • Reflexive: a.equals(a) is always true.
  • Symmetric: if a.equals(b) then b.equals(a).
  • Transitive: if a.equals(b) and b.equals(c) then a.equals(c).
  • Consistent: repeated calls give the same result while nothing changes.
  • Null-safe: a.equals(null) is always false and never throws.

The examples below are, in effect, a tour of what breaks when you violate one of
these.

4. The failure gallery

Each example is a complete, runnable snippet with the surprising output written
as a comment, followed by the reason it happens.

4.1 Override equals, forget hashCode (the classic)

This is the most common bug, and it is insidious because the code looks
perfectly reasonable.

class User {
    final String email;
    User(String email) { this.email = email; }

    @Override
    public boolean equals(Object o) {
        return o instanceof User u && u.email.equals(this.email);
    }
    // hashCode() NOT overridden
}

Map<User, String> map = new HashMap<>();
map.put(new User("a@b.com"), "Srinivas");
String name = map.get(new User("a@b.com"));   // returns null

When you put, the map calls hashCode() on your first User. You did not
override it, so it uses the one inherited from Object, which is based on the
object's identity (essentially its memory address, unique to that specific
object). Say that gives bucket 2, so the entry is filed there.

When you get with a brand new User that has the same email, the map calls
hashCode() on this different object. Different object, different identity hash,
say bucket 5. The map walks to bucket 5, finds it empty, and returns null. Your
carefully written equals is never called, because the search never reached
bucket 2 where the entry actually lives.

The entry is in the map. You just cannot get it out.

The same flaw wearing a different symptom in a HashSet:

Set<User> seen = new HashSet<>();
seen.add(new User("a@b.com"));
seen.add(new User("a@b.com"));   // should be a duplicate
System.out.println(seen.size()); // prints 2

The set looked in the second object's bucket, found nothing, concluded it was
new, and stored it. You now have two equal elements in a Set. The set has
quietly stopped being a set.

4.2 The mutable-key leak

Here hashCode and equals are both correct, but the fields they depend on can
change after insertion.

class Point {
    int x, y;
    Point(int x, int y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; }

    @Override public boolean equals(Object o) {
        return o instanceof Point p && p.x == x && p.y == y;
    }
    @Override public int hashCode() {
        return Objects.hash(x, y);
    }
}

Set<Point> set = new HashSet<>();
Point p = new Point(1, 1);
set.add(p);              // hash computed from (1,1), filed in that bucket
p.x = 99;                // mutate the key AFTER inserting it
set.contains(p);         // false, even though p is physically in the set
set.remove(p);           // also fails to remove it

When you added p, its hash was computed from (1, 1) and it was filed in the
matching bucket. Then you changed x to 99, so the hash is now computed from
(99, 1), which points at a different bucket. Every future lookup computes the
new hash and searches the wrong bucket. The object is stranded in its old
bucket, unreachable and unremovable.

That is not a metaphor. It is a genuine memory leak: the entry occupies space,
cannot be found, and cannot be deleted. This is the strongest argument for
making keys and set elements immutable.

4.3 A legal but terrible hashCode 

@Override public int hashCode() {
    return 42;   // constant
}

Here is the subtle part: this does NOT violate the contract. Equal objects do
return equal hashes, because every object returns 42. So lookups are correct.
They are just slow. Every entry now hashes to the same bucket, so instead of
jumping to a shelf with one or two items, the map dumps everything into one
giant bucket and walks the whole thing calling equals. Your O(1) map has
degraded toward O(n).

Modern Java softens this. Since Java 8, when a single bucket gets too crowded
(past a threshold, once the table is large enough), the HashMap converts that
bucket's internal linked list into a balanced red-black tree, making lookups
within it O(log n) instead of O(n). Better, but still a serious regression from
O(1), and it only helps if the keys implement Comparable so the tree has
something to sort by. The lesson: a correct hashCode is not enough, it also
needs to spread values out. A good hashCode distributes; a bad one clumps.

4.4 The symmetry trap

This one catches even experienced developers, and it is a favorite interview
question. It happens when you extend a value class and add a field to compare.

class Point {
    final int x, y;
    Point(int x, int y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; }

    @Override public boolean equals(Object o) {
        return o instanceof Point p && p.x == x && p.y == y;
    }
    @Override public int hashCode() { return Objects.hash(x, y); }
}

class ColorPoint extends Point {
    final String color;
    ColorPoint(int x, int y, String color) { super(x, y); this.color = color; }

    @Override public boolean equals(Object o) {
        return o instanceof ColorPoint c
                && super.equals(c) && c.color.equals(this.color);
    }
}

Point p = new Point(1, 2);
ColorPoint cp = new ColorPoint(1, 2, "red");

p.equals(cp);   // true   (Point.equals only checks x and y)
cp.equals(p);   // false  (ColorPoint.equals also demands a matching color)

equals is now asymmetric: p.equals(cp) and cp.equals(p) disagree. That
breaks the symmetry rule from Section 3, and it produces bugs that depend on
argument order, which are miserable to track down. Worse, a common "fix" (make
ColorPoint ignore color when compared against a plain Point) trades the
symmetry break for a transitivity break, so you cannot patch your way out.

The real resolution is a design rule: there is no way to extend an instantiable
value class with a new value component and preserve the equals contract. Two
clean options exist. Use exact-class matching instead of instanceof, so a
Point and a ColorPoint are simply never equal:

@Override public boolean equals(Object o) {
    if (o == null || getClass() != o.getClass()) return false;
    Point p = (Point) o;
    return p.x == x && p.y == y;
}

Or, better for most cases, favor composition over inheritance: give ColorPoint
a Point field and a method to expose it, rather than extending Point.

4.5 The TreeSet twist: compareTo must agree with equals

Everything so far has been about hash-based collections. Tree-based collections
play by a completely different rulebook, and knowing that difference is what
separates someone who memorized the contract from someone who understands it.

TreeMap and TreeSet do not call hashCode() at all. Not once. They are not
built on buckets. They keep elements in sorted order using either compareTo()
(if the type implements Comparable) or a Comparator you supply. So a
catastrophically broken hashCode, even return 42, causes a TreeSet zero
problems.

But a different contract governs them: compareTo should be consistent with
equals, meaning a.compareTo(b) == 0 in exactly the same situations where
a.equals(b) is true. Break that alignment and the tree quietly redefines
equality on your behalf, because to a tree, two elements are "the same" precisely
when compareTo returns zero, no matter what equals says.

The canonical demonstration is BigDecimal, because it is real, it is in the
standard library, and it disagrees with itself on purpose:

BigDecimal a = new BigDecimal("1.0");
BigDecimal b = new BigDecimal("1.00");

a.equals(b);        // false   equals also compares scale (1 vs 2 decimals)
a.compareTo(b);     // 0       compareTo compares numeric value only

Set<BigDecimal> hash = new HashSet<>(List.of(a, b));
Set<BigDecimal> tree = new TreeSet<>(List.of(a, b));

hash.size();   // 2   HashSet uses equals, which says they differ
tree.size();   // 1   TreeSet uses compareTo, which says they are identical

Identical input, two Set implementations, two different answers. If code ever
fills one kind of set from a list of BigDecimal and later switches to the
other, the element count silently changes and nothing throws.

The same trap with your own class, to show it is not special to BigDecimal:

class Person implements Comparable<Person> {
    String name; int id; int age;
    // equals and hashCode built from name + id (correct and consistent)

    @Override public int compareTo(Person other) {
        return Integer.compare(this.age, other.age);   // BUG: ordering ignores identity
    }
}

TreeSet<Person> set = new TreeSet<>();
set.add(new Person("Asha", 1, 30));
set.add(new Person("Ravi", 2, 30));   // different person, same age
System.out.println(set.size());       // 1  Ravi rejected as a "duplicate"

Two clearly different people who happen to share an age. The TreeSet compares
them with compareTo, gets zero, decides they are the same element, and refuses
to add the second. No error, no warning, just a missing record.

5. How to write them correctly

Now that you have seen every way it breaks, the rules for doing it right are just
the failures turned around.

Override hashCode and equals together, from the same fields. If equals
compares email and name, then hashCode must be derived from email and name, so
two objects equal in those fields are guaranteed to hash the same. The modern
helpers make this a two-liner:

class User {
    final String email;
    final String name;

    @Override public boolean equals(Object o) {
        if (this == o) return true;
        if (!(o instanceof User u)) return false;
        return Objects.equals(email, u.email) && Objects.equals(name, u.name);
    }

    @Override public int hashCode() {
        return Objects.hash(email, name);   // same fields as equals
    }
}

Objects.equals handles nulls on both sides, and the instanceof check makes
equals(null) return false for free, since null instanceof User is false.

Prefer immutable fields for anything used in hashCode, so you never hit the
stranded-key leak from Section 4.2.

If your type is Comparable, keep compareTo consistent with equals, so
you never hit the BigDecimal or Person surprises from Section 4.5.

Do not add a value component by extending an instantiable class, per the
symmetry trap in Section 4.4. Use composition, or exact-class equality.

Easiest correct path: use a record. A Java record generates a correct
equals, hashCode, and toString from its components automatically, and they
are always consistent with each other. For a plain immutable value holder, this
removes the whole class of bugs above:

record User(String email, String name) { }
// equals and hashCode are generated, correct, and mutually consistent

If you cannot use a record, let your IDE generate both methods together, or use
a library like Lombok's @EqualsAndHashCode. The danger is almost always
hand-writing one method and forgetting or mismatching the other.

6. Quick reference

A lookup table for after you have read the reasoning above. The value of each row
is the reasoning in the linked section, not the one-liner.

Symptom Cause Fix
map.get(equalKey) returns null (4.1) equals overridden, hashCode not Override both from the same fields
HashSet stores equal duplicates (4.1) same as above Override both from the same fields
Entry cannot be found or removed after a change (4.2) Key mutated after insertion Make keys immutable
Correct but slow lookups (4.3) hashCode returns few distinct values Distribute the hash across fields
Order-dependent equality bugs (4.4) equals is asymmetric via inheritance Composition, or getClass() equality
HashSet and TreeSet disagree on size (4.5) compareTo inconsistent with equals Make compareTo == 0 match equals == true
TreeSet silently drops distinct elements (4.5) compareTo returns 0 for unequal objects Same as above

Interview-ready one-liners, each of which the sections above let you defend:

  • A HashMap finds an entry in two steps: hashCode selects the bucket, then equals confirms inside it. Equal objects must hash equally, or the lookup searches the wrong bucket and equals never runs.
  • A bad hashCode that breaks the contract makes lookups wrong; a bad hashCode that merely collides a lot makes them slow. Only the first is a correctness bug.
  • Tree collections never touch hashCode; they order by compareTo, and there the rule is that compareTo must agree with equals. BigDecimal breaks that on purpose, so "1.0" and "1.00" give a HashSet of size two but a TreeSet of size one.
  • The cleanest way to get all of this right is a record, which generates consistent equals and hashCode for you.

title: SimHack: Predicting the onset of detectable reward hacking before RL training
description:
arXiv:2610.28707v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: When training LLMs to code with reinforcement learning, reward hacking is often detectable but difficult to prevent, since (a) environment hardening is increasingly difficult as training environments grow more complex; and (b) training-time interventions incentivize models to obfuscate hacking behavior to bypass detection.
  We instead study whether we can predict when detectable reward hacking becomes dominant before executing an RL run, enabling us to select lower-risk recipes in advance. We find that the initial hacking rate alone does not determine onset, which varies substantially across training recipes and repeated runs. We thus formulate this problem as predicting the distribution of the reward hacking onset step under a target training recipe.
  We introduce SimHack, a simulator that learns reward hacking training dynamics from a handful of smaller-scale reference RL runs and generates counterfactual simulation runs of unseen target recipes without costly retraining. Across unseen target recipes, SimHack predicts the median onset to a relative error of 11.3% and achieves across-recipe rank correlation of 0.85, while generalizing to differences in model scale, curriculum, number of rollouts, and learning rate between reference and target recipes. As an application, we show that SimHack can guide training decisions by screening candidate RL curricula, discovering curricula over the same set of scenarios that train for 96.6% longer without hacking.

title: TrainBridge: Agentic NPU Training Optimization Guided by GPU Compilation Evidence
description:
arXiv:2610.29171v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study how to improve training efficiency on Ascend NPUs. In the NPU training programs we study, framework-level compilation optimizations such as operator fusion are only partially applied, leaving fragmented computation and avoidable execution overheads. Profiling-guided tuning can address these inefficiencies, but it often requires costly trial and error. To make training on NPUs more efficient, we propose TrainBridge, an agentic approach for transferring GPU optimization guidance to NPU training. TrainBridge uses the highly optimized execution produced by mature GPU compilation stacks as a task-specific reference for NPU tuning. It extracts optimization intents from the GPU training execution to guide NPU program rewrites and further refines the rewritten program through iterative profiling. Our GPU-to-NPU migration experiments show that TrainBridge achieves an average 1.7x speedup across four workloads covering LLM pretraining, image classification, and vision-language training, and an average speedup of nearly 2.0x across 27 Modded-NanoGPT speedrun records with highly optimized GPU implementations.

title: Structured-Token Attention for Fine-Grained mmWave Liquid Identification
description:
arXiv:2610.27512v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Fine-grained liquid identification requires a classifier to distinguish similar substances from compact millimeter-wave measurements. We investigate structured-token attention, which represents a radar feature tensor through complementary antenna, feature, branch, and global views. The proposed StructAttn model embeds these views into eleven tokens and combines them with a three-layer transformer. Experiments on the public FG-LiquID data cover 30 liquids and 3,000 samples. Over five seeds on the released split, StructAttn achieves 96.70\% mean best-epoch accuracy, matching the original-recipe MMNet baseline and exceeding a scalar-token attention model by 1.50 percentage points. A five-seed probability ensemble reaches 97\%, corresponding to 18 errors among 600 test samples. Final-epoch and five-fold results complement the checkpoint-selected comparison, with StructAttn obtaining 95.30\% out-of-fold accuracy. Token and feature analyses show that structured views are useful for prediction, while residual confusions concentrate in water, soft-drink, and edible-oil classes. These results support structured tokenization as a practical design choice for attention-based liquid recognition.

title: Queue Push Webhook vs Worker Polling: Choose a Public HTTPS Subscriber Endpoint
description:
Short answer: choose queue push when your weekly digest can enter through a public HTTPS webhook, because a tiny authenticated intake handler gives you a clean recovery point; choose worker polling when the subscriber must remain private. In either design, verify the sender, durably claim an idempotency key, and acknowledge only after that claim succeeds.

For a one-person developer-tools SaaS, the deciding metric is recovery time, not trigger speed. A digest that arrives a minute late is usually tolerable. A duplicate digest sent to every active customer is not. The design should make Monday's question boring: which digest keys were accepted, which were completed, and which can be retried? Getting there requires five decisions in order: who may reach the edge, which dependency owns the queue contract, what an acknowledgement proves, where business state lives, and which requirement forces a migration.

This is where Infrai belongs on the shortlist, but within a narrow boundary. I would try its queue push for a small SaaS that already exposes a public edge and wants queue infrastructure behind the same key and bill as its other backend services. The supporting benefit is integration friction: it is a plain REST API, so the producer doesn't need another SDK or language-specific client. The catch is just as important. A private-only subscriber, a replay-heavy event system, or a multi-stage workflow needs a different tool.

Ship the recovery path first.

Access policy decides between push and polling

Imagine the digest publisher emits one task per account on Friday, with delivery intended for Monday. On Monday morning, support reports that account acct_1842 did not receive its digest. The useful system is the one that can answer three questions from application data: was digest:2026-W34:acct_1842 accepted, did a worker claim it, and did the final send complete?

The first choice is a security and network policy, not a queue preference. Push requires a public HTTPS target. If policy forbids public ingress, stop there and use polling from a private worker. If a hardened public edge already exists, keep its authority narrow: it may authenticate a delivery and create an intake record, but it may not query the full customer dataset or send mail. That boundary limits both request time and the work exposed at the edge.

Push and polling place the first transition in different locations. Push asks a public endpoint to authenticate the delivery and record the key. Polling asks a private worker to fetch, authenticate, and record it. Everything after that should be the same worker path. That symmetry matters because it keeps transport choice out of the business state machine. It also means the team can change transports later without changing what sent means, how an account is deduplicated, or which evidence support uses to answer a customer. The transport owns delivery attempts. The ledger owns business truth. Mixing those responsibilities may look economical during the first Friday build, but it makes every later recovery depend on vendor-specific delivery state.

No magic.

Set a dependency budget for the queue contract

Before exposing the subscriber, confirm that the configured queue is the queue the deployment expects. Infrai's relevant integration advantage is one REST API over pure HTTP, with no SDK to install. Its discovery surface is public without a key, so the request contract can be inspected before credentials enter the setup. In this workflow, that removes two small but recurring costs: a solo maintainer doesn't have to add a package just to perform a deployment check, and a future worker in another runtime can use the same HTTP boundary. That is a dependency-governance choice, not a claim that HTTP is inherently better than a client library; a specialist SDK is preferable when its types, local emulator, or framework integration repay the added package and release cadence.

The following preflight uses the verified verb-style route. It reads the key and queue name from environment variables, sets the method explicitly, reports non-success response bodies, and backs off on 429 while honoring Retry-After when the server provides it.

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
const queueName = process.env.INFRAI_QUEUE;
if (!apiKey || !queueName) {
  throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY and INFRAI_QUEUE are required");
}

function retryDelay(value: string | null, attempt: number): number {
  if (value) {
    const seconds = Number(value);
    if (Number.isFinite(seconds)) return Math.max(0, seconds * 1_000);
    const date = Date.parse(value);
    if (Number.isFinite(date)) return Math.max(0, date - Date.now());
  }
  return 250 * 2 ** attempt;
}

async function getQueue(attempt = 0): Promise<unknown> {
  const response = await fetch(
    `https://api.infrai.cc/v1/queue/get/${encodeURIComponent(queueName)}`,
    {
      method: "GET",
      headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}` },
    },
  );

  if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 4) {
    await new Promise((resolve) =>
      setTimeout(resolve, retryDelay(response.headers.get("retry-after"), attempt)),
    );
    return getQueue(attempt + 1);
  }
  if (!response.ok) {
    throw new Error(`Queue lookup ${response.status}: ${await response.text()}`);
  }
  return response.json();
}

console.log(await getQueue());

This is deliberately a read, not an invented subscription request. The live capability contract supplies the request schema for writes; guessing a familiar-looking REST body or path would make the example useless.

Can a Node.js public HTTPS webhook subscriber verify and ack queue push?

The handler should verify the signature over the raw bytes, parse and validate the event, insert its idempotency key under a unique constraint, and return success quickly. Slow customer queries and email delivery belong in a worker. If they run inline, the sender can repeat delivery while the first attempt is still busy, which turns a slow callout into a duplicate-risk problem.

Signature names and canonicalization are provider-specific. I'm not sure which header your current queue defines, so copying a made-up vendor header would be worse than leaving the boundary explicit. The runnable example below defines an application-owned HMAC contract named x-digest-signature: the publisher and subscriber sign the exact request bytes with the same secret. When a provider supplies its own documented verifier, replace only validSignature; keep the raw-body, durable-insert, and response ordering.

import { createHmac, timingSafeEqual } from "node:crypto";
import { createServer, type IncomingMessage, type ServerResponse } from "node:http";
import { DatabaseSync } from "node:sqlite";

type DigestTask = {
  idempotencyKey: string;
  digestWeek: string;
  accountId: string;
};

const secret = process.env.DIGEST_WEBHOOK_SECRET;
if (!secret) throw new Error("DIGEST_WEBHOOK_SECRET is required");

const database = new DatabaseSync("digest-intake.sqlite");
database.exec(`
  CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS digest_tasks (
    idempotency_key TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    digest_week TEXT NOT NULL,
    account_id TEXT NOT NULL,
    state TEXT NOT NULL,
    accepted_at TEXT NOT NULL
  )
`);

const insertTask = database.prepare(`
  INSERT OR IGNORE INTO digest_tasks
    (idempotency_key, digest_week, account_id, state, accepted_at)
  VALUES (?, ?, ?, 'accepted', ?)
`);

async function readRaw(req: IncomingMessage): Promise<Buffer> {
  const chunks: Buffer[] = [];
  for await (const chunk of req) chunks.push(Buffer.from(chunk));
  return Buffer.concat(chunks);
}

function validSignature(raw: Buffer, supplied: string | undefined): boolean {
  if (!supplied) return false;
  const expected = createHmac("sha256", secret).update(raw).digest("hex");
  const received = supplied.startsWith("sha256=") ? supplied.slice(7) : "";
  if (received.length !== expected.length) return false;
  return timingSafeEqual(Buffer.from(received, "hex"), Buffer.from(expected, "hex"));
}

function reply(res: ServerResponse, status: number, body = ""): void {
  res.writeHead(status, { "content-type": "application/json" });
  res.end(body);
}

createServer(async (req, res) => {
  if (req.method !== "POST" || req.url !== "/weekly-digest-intake") {
    return reply(res, 404, JSON.stringify({ error: "not_found" }));
  }

  const raw = await readRaw(req);
  const signature = req.headers["x-digest-signature"];
  if (!validSignature(raw, typeof signature === "string" ? signature : undefined)) {
    return reply(res, 401, JSON.stringify({ error: "invalid_signature" }));
  }

  try {
    const task = JSON.parse(raw.toString("utf8")) as Partial<DigestTask>;
    if (!task.idempotencyKey || !task.digestWeek || !task.accountId) {
      return reply(res, 400, JSON.stringify({ error: "invalid_task" }));
    }

    insertTask.run(
      task.idempotencyKey,
      task.digestWeek,
      task.accountId,
      new Date().toISOString(),
    );
    return reply(res, 204);
  } catch {
    return reply(res, 400, JSON.stringify({ error: "invalid_json" }));
  }
}).listen(Number(process.env.PORT ?? "3000"));

The order is the ack pattern. A bad signature gets 401. A malformed task gets 400. A new task and a duplicate of an already accepted task both get 204, but only after the database operation. INSERT OR IGNORE makes the duplicate harmless without a read-then-write race. The HTTP success response is the push acknowledgement; it does not claim that the email has already been sent.

Ack is a receipt.

Keep the endpoint public over HTTPS in deployment. Localhost and private VPC-only addresses cannot receive push deliveries. Also cap the body before it reaches this code. Queue messages are limited to 256 KB, and a digest task should usually contain identifiers rather than a rendered email or a full customer export.

The idempotency key sets the data ownership line

The queue transports work. The application ledger explains it. This ownership line should appear in the schema, the runbook, and the support query: queue metadata can describe attempts, while the application's key decides whether a customer-facing action already exists.

A useful digest record can move through accepted, processing, and sent, with the idempotency key unique across all three. The worker claims accepted rows, performs the slow customer lookup and callout, then records completion. If processing is interrupted, recovery operates on the same row instead of publishing a fresh identity. That distinction is small in code and huge during an incident: retrying work is allowed; inventing a second digest key is not.

Standard queue delivery is at least once, so duplicate delivery is part of the contract, not an exceptional corner. The application key should encode the business action, such as digest week plus account ID. A transport message ID is useful for tracing, but it cannot express the rule “one weekly digest for this account.” Likewise, FIFO deduplication lasts five minutes. It cannot enforce a business invariant that spans a week.

There is one uncomfortable edge worth naming. If the worker sends the email and stops before recording sent, the intake ledger alone cannot prove whether the external callout completed. The honest design needs an idempotency facility at the email boundary or a separate send ledger whose key is reused on every attempt. Your mileage may vary with the downstream provider's contract. Resolve that contract before claiming end-to-end exactly-once behavior, because the queue itself only promises at-least-once delivery.

Now the revenue-per-hour lens becomes practical. An operator can query one table and decide whether to resume an existing task. There is no need to correlate a scheduler page, an HTTP access log, and an email dashboard before making the first recovery decision. Outsource the undifferentiated transport; keep the business identity and completion evidence in the app.

Delayed publication has limits too. A delayed message can be scheduled at most seven days out. Retention is at most 30 days, and acknowledgement deletes the message, so the queue is not a permanent audit trail. Those limits reinforce the ledger design rather than weaken it.

Migration triggers are topology, replay, and private ingress

First, keep the public handler small. More workers should increase processing capacity without adding customer queries or email calls to the intake request. Test duplicate delivery, a 401 signature rejection, an interrupted worker after it marks processing, and a retry that reuses the same business key. These tests protect the migration boundary: another transport can preserve the same receipt states and business keys even when its delivery mechanics differ.

Then watch the topology. Infrai has no native DAG or fan-out/join primitive, no topic that sends once to many subscribers, and no Kafka-style replay or multiple consumer groups. It also has no native debounce or throttle. If the weekly digest becomes a graph of audience calculation, per-region rendering, approval, delivery, and reconciliation, stick with Temporal or Airflow for orchestration. If independent analytics and delivery consumers need to replay the same event stream, choose a streaming specialist. Those aren't minor configuration differences; they change the system's recovery model.

The alternatives are easier to judge once the receipt contract is fixed:

Option First durable recovery point Best fit Boundary that should change the choice
Infrai queue push Public HTTPS intake record Small app that values one key, one bill, and a direct REST integration Subscriber must be public; no workflow joins, replay, or multiple consumer groups
Worker polling Private worker claim record Ingress must stay inside a private network The app owns polling cadence and worker capacity
AWS SQS FIFO Consumer-side deduplication record FIFO ordering is a hard requirement A five-minute deduplication window does not replace weekly business idempotency
BullMQ Application-owned worker record The Node app should own a Redis-backed queue and worker The operator also owns that queue stack
Inngest Function-run state Event-driven application functions need managed steps and retries It introduces a workflow model beyond one intake receipt
Trigger.dev Task-run state Hosted background jobs fit the application It is a broader task platform than a single queue endpoint
Temporal Workflow history The digest becomes a coordinated, multi-stage workflow More operating surface than one delayed task and one worker
GitHub Actions schedule Workflow run Repository automation is the actual job It is not an application delivery ledger for customer tasks

This isn't a generic vendor ranking. AWS SQS FIFO is the clearer choice when ordering dominates. BullMQ keeps the machinery close to a Node application that is ready to operate its queue stack. Inngest and Trigger.dev fit teams that want hosted function or task abstractions. Temporal is the specialist when the job grows into orchestration, while GitHub Actions fits repository work. Queue push wins this comparison only when quick public intake plus a small recovery ledger is the whole problem.

For the original job, stay small: one scheduled publication, one queue task per active account, one fast public subscriber, and one worker path. The producer can use the documented queue API over HTTP, and the public discovery surface exposes the request schema before a key is needed. Don't infer REST-style paths from a noun; use the capability's discovered method and path. This keeps the integration inspectable without turning the application into a vendor SDK project.

The final decision rule is blunt. Use push when public HTTPS is acceptable and durable intake can finish quickly. Use polling when private ingress is non-negotiable. Choose an orchestration or streaming specialist when recovery requires workflow history, joins, replay, or multiple consumer groups. Then ship weekly.

References

  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-fifo-queues.html
  • https://docs.github.com/en/actions/using-workflows/events-that-trigger-workflows

Further reading

If this boundary fits your system, start with the Node push subscriber guide.

title: Distilling Multi-Teacher Scoring Principles for Unsupervised Time Series Anomaly Detection
description:
arXiv:2610.29063v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Time series anomalies take diverse forms, and individual detectors encode different anomaly scoring principles that rarely cover all anomaly types. Recent unsupervised time-series anomaly detectors provide complementary scoring signals, yet deploying them as an ensemble preserves the inference and maintenance cost of every individual detector. We study whether heterogeneous teacher detectors can be distilled into a single lightweight detector in the unsupervised setting, where no anomaly labels are available to define a shared target. AnoMix addresses this by extracting weak pairwise supervision from the training-set anomaly scores of frozen teachers. It normalizes each teacher score sequence independently and trains the student with CoRank, a multi-teacher ranking-distillation objective that converts teacher score gaps into pairwise supervision through teacher consensus. Across seven benchmark datasets, AnoMix successfully integrates complementary teacher scoring principles into a single deployable model, improving over individual detectors and static score ensembles while using a compact student with under 80k parameters on the benchmark settings. A zero-shot variant further shows that the distilled ranking signal transfers to unseen datasets and can outperform large pretrained time-series foundation models for anomaly detection.

title: Detect image formats from magic bytes in Node and Python
description:
Read the first bytes of the file and compare them with each format's signature: FF D8 FF is JPEG, 89 50 4E 47 0D 0A 1A 0A is PNG, RIFF plus WEBP at byte 8 is WebP, and an ftyp box with an avif or heic brand is AVIF or HEIC. A 20-line function in Node or Python does it from 64 bytes. On my 12 test files it named every format correctly; the file extension was wrong on 4 of them.

Here is the sniffer in both languages, and what sharp, Pillow and Python's imghdr said about the same files.

Why not trust the file extension or the Content-Type?

Both come from the client. A user renames screenshot.png to .jpg, a phone uploads HEIC as image.jpeg, and an attacker names an SVG avatar.jpg. Your decoder does not care what the name says. It reads the bytes, and some decoders accept more formats than you planned for.

That last case is the one to worry about. I wrote a 64 × 64 SVG to a file called svg-as.jpg and handed it to sharp:

files/svg-as.jpg         metadata=svg            decode=ok

sharp detected SVG from the content and rendered it. If your upload route only meant to accept photos, it just ran an XML renderer on user input. Sniff first, and refuse anything that is not on your list.

How do you sniff image magic bytes in Node?

Read a small head of the file, never the whole thing, and check each signature:

// sniff.mjs: node sniff.mjs files/*
import { open } from 'node:fs/promises';

const ascii = (b, start, end) => b.toString('latin1', start, end);

export function sniff(b) {
  if (b.length >= 3 && b[0] === 0xff && b[1] === 0xd8 && b[2] === 0xff) return 'jpeg';
  if (b.length >= 8 && b.subarray(0, 8).equals(Buffer.from([0x89, 0x50, 0x4e, 0x47, 0x0d, 0x0a, 0x1a, 0x0a]))) return 'png';
  if (ascii(b, 0, 6) === 'GIF87a' || ascii(b, 0, 6) === 'GIF89a') return 'gif';
  if (ascii(b, 0, 4) === 'RIFF' && ascii(b, 8, 12) === 'WEBP') return 'webp';
  if (ascii(b, 4, 8) === 'ftyp') {
    // ISO BMFF: a major brand, a minor version, then compatible brands, 4 bytes each.
    const size = Math.min(b.readUInt32BE(0), b.length);
    const brands = [ascii(b, 8, 12)];
    for (let i = 16; i + 4 <= size; i += 4) brands.push(ascii(b, i, i + 4));
    if (brands.some((x) => x === 'avif' || x === 'avis')) return 'avif';
    if (brands.some((x) => ['heic', 'heix', 'heim', 'heis', 'mif1'].includes(x))) return 'heic';
  }
  return null;
}

async function head(path, n = 64) {
  const fh = await open(path, 'r');
  try {
    const { buffer, bytesRead } = await fh.read(Buffer.alloc(n), 0, n, 0);
    return buffer.subarray(0, bytesRead);
  } finally {
    await fh.close();
  }
}

if (import.meta.url === `file://${process.argv[1]}`) {
  for (const path of process.argv.slice(2)) {
    const ext = path.split('.').pop();
    console.log(`${path.padEnd(24)} ext=${ext.padEnd(5)} sniffed=${sniff(await head(path))}`);
  }
}

The signatures come from the specs: the 8-byte PNG signature in RFC 2083, and the 12-byte RIFF header in Google's WebP container spec, which says a WebP file must begin with RIFF and the FourCC WEBP.

What it printed:

files/graphic.gif        ext=gif   sniffed=gif
files/not-an-image.jpg   ext=jpg   sniffed=null
files/photo.avif         ext=avif  sniffed=avif
files/photo.heic         ext=heic  sniffed=heic
files/photo.jpg          ext=jpg   sniffed=jpeg
files/photo.png          ext=png   sniffed=png
files/photo.webp         ext=webp  sniffed=webp
files/renamed-avif.png   ext=png   sniffed=avif
files/renamed-png.jpg    ext=jpg   sniffed=png
files/svg-as.jpg         ext=jpg   sniffed=null
files/transparent.png    ext=png   sniffed=png
files/truncated.jpg      ext=jpg   sniffed=jpeg

Why does AVIF need the brand list, not just the first brand?

AVIF and HEIC share one container, ISO BMFF. Both start with a box size and ftyp. Only the brands tell them apart, and the major brand alone is not enough. Our AVIF's header lists avif first, then mif1, avif and miaf as compatible brands. Another encoder can put mif1 first and avif further down. Check the whole list, and check avif before the generic mif1.

How do you do the same in Python?

The same logic in plain bytes slicing:

# sniff.py: python sniff.py files/*
import sys

PNG = b'\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n'

def sniff(b: bytes):
    if b[:3] == b'\xff\xd8\xff':
        return 'jpeg'
    if b[:8] == PNG:
        return 'png'
    if b[:6] in (b'GIF87a', b'GIF89a'):
        return 'gif'
    if b[:4] == b'RIFF' and b[8:12] == b'WEBP':
        return 'webp'
    if b[4:8] == b'ftyp':
        size = min(int.from_bytes(b[0:4], 'big'), len(b))
        brands = [b[8:12]] + [b[i:i + 4] for i in range(16, size - 3, 4)]
        if b'avif' in brands or b'avis' in brands:
            return 'avif'
        if any(x in brands for x in (b'heic', b'heix', b'heim', b'heis', b'mif1')):
            return 'heic'
    return None

if __name__ == '__main__':
    for path in sys.argv[1:]:
        with open(path, 'rb') as f:
            head = f.read(64)
        print(f"{path:<24} sniffed={sniff(head)}")

It printed the same 12 answers as the Node version.

What do sharp, Pillow and imghdr say about the same files?

File Sniffer sharp.metadata() Pillow Image.open imghdr.what
photo.jpg jpeg jpeg JPEG None
photo.avif avif heif/av1 AVIF None
photo.heic heic heif/hevc not identified None
renamed-png.jpg png png PNG png
svg-as.jpg null svg, decodes not identified None
not-an-image.jpg null error not identified None
truncated.jpg jpeg jpeg, decode fails JPEG, load fails None

Three results stand out:

  • imghdr missed a normal JPEG. Its JPEG test looks for the text JFIF or Exif at bytes 6 to 10. Our JPEG starts FF D8 FF DB with no APP0 or APP1 segment, so it returned None. The module is also gone: the Python docs deprecated it in 3.11 for removal in 3.13 (PEP 594).
  • sharp reports AVIF and HEIC both as heif. Read compression (av1 or hevc) to tell them apart. sharp read the HEIC's metadata here but failed to decode it.
  • Pillow 11.3.0 opened the AVIF with no plugin, and could not identify the HEIC.

Is sniffing slower than asking the decoder?

No. On the 9.8 MB camera JPEG, median of 5 runs each:

sniff 64 bytes    0.11 ms
sharp.metadata()  0.40 ms
full decode       123.53 ms

Sniffing costs less than a millisecond, so run it before anything else touches the file.

Note: Magic bytes tell you what a file claims to be, not that it is valid. truncated.jpg is the first 2,000 bytes of a real JPEG: it passed the sniffer and sharp.metadata(), then failed at decode with "premature end of JPEG image". Sniff to reject, then decode inside a try with pixel limits, and treat a decode failure as a bad upload.

Our engine sniffs every upload the same way before it decodes. If you want to see how a renamed or odd file is handled end to end, the image format guide covers what each of these formats is for.

How I measured

  • Files: photo.jpg, photo.png, photo.webp, photo.avif, photo.heic, transparent.png from packages/engine/tests/fixtures/; graphic.gif converted by sharp from graphic.png; two copies renamed; truncated.jpg (first 2,000 bytes of photo.jpg); two SVG text files named .jpg. Timing on apps/web/public/images/index/image-compressor-sample-camera-photo.jpeg.
  • Node 24.22.0 with sharp 0.35.4 (libvips 8.18.6). Python 3.9.6 with Pillow 11.3.0, in a venv.
  • Time: median of 5 runs, performance.now().
  • Apple M1 Pro, macOS, 2026-10-17.

What I did not test

TIFF, BMP, ICO, JPEG XL and animated AVIF (avis) files. I did not test the file-type npm package or python-magic.

I build Blinkimg, an image compressor and converter with a developer API. I wrote this article with help from an AI assistant (Claude), which ran the code on my machine; every number in it comes from those runs.

title: Commerce.com turns on WebMCP for nearly 100,000 storefronts
description:
Commerce.com has turned on WebMCP for almost 100,000 of its domains, working with Cloudflare, according to a Cloudflare blog post. The aim is to let AI agents shop a store through defined tools rather than by reading the page and guessing which button to press.

What changes for agents

Most shopping agents today work from a site's HTML. They look at the page, guess what each control does, click, and retry on failure. Cloudflare says this is slow, token-hungry and fragile, and that even a theme change can break it.

WebMCP is a Google-backed browser standard that gives a page structured tools, such as search_products. On an enabled Commerce.com store, an agent finds the tools in the browser and calls them directly. In the source's example, a request for a waterproof trail running shoe under $140 in size 10 becomes two calls: search_products, then add_to_cart.

The tools run inside the shopper's own browser session on the store's domain. The agent therefore sees the same prices and cart as the shopper, and no credentials go to a third party. The shopper clicks checkout personally, so payment details stay with them.

How the rollout works

Cloudflare launched edge WebMCP in beta in August. When it is enabled, Cloudflare injects a small script at the edge, and the site owner writes no code. Commerce.com's tool logic lives in its backend MCP server, and Cloudflare proxies tool definitions and actions unchanged. Commerce.com says WebMCP works alongside its server-side MCP, which serves agents that connect to a store directly.

Two changes were needed for a platform of this size:

  • Per-merchant opt-out. WebMCP was designed as one switch for a whole zone. Commerce.com turned it on for its main zone and added a Configuration Rule that checks custom hostname metadata. A merchant who flips the opt-out in the Commerce.com dashboard is skipped at the edge. According to Cloudflare, an opted-out store gets no extra latency, no remote lookup and no injected script.
  • Custom MCP path. The bridge assumed each MCP server sat at /mcp, while Commerce.com's is at /api/mcp. Cloudflare added a zone-level setting for the URL.

If a store's MCP server is offline or the visitor's browser lacks WebMCP support, the script exits and the storefront loads as normal.

Limits

WebMCP is an experimental, proposed standard in early preview. It is available behind a Chrome flag, in Chrome Origin Trials, in some agentic browsers and in developer environments such as Cloudflare Kitesurf. The source gives no figures on how many shoppers or agents use the tools. Cloudflare says it will next work on helping agents discover a site's tools more easily.

title: TriGeoBench: A Multimodal Mathematical Geometry Benchmark with Figures and TikZ
description:
arXiv:2610.27626v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models show strong vision-language capabilities, yet their geometry-centric reasoning remains insufficiently understood. Existing mathematical benchmarks typically rely on rasterized figures and cover limited geometric knowledge areas and response formats, making it difficult to assess whether models reason over geometric structures or exploit superficial visual patterns. We introduce TriGeoBench, a geometry-centric multimodal benchmark constructed from Chinese middle- and high-school mathematics examinations. TriGeoBench contains 7,000 question-answer pairs and 12,235 geometric figures with TikZ code, spanning plane geometry, solid geometry, analytic geometry, function, and vector geometry across diverse response formats. Each instance forms a {question-answer pair, image, TikZ} triplet: question-answer pairs are stored in LaTeX, images as RGB figures, and TikZ preserves geometric topology, symbolic annotations, and relational structure. We evaluate representative open- and closed-source MLLMs through image-to-TikZ and multimodal reasoning probes. Results reveal persistent fine-grained structure and image-text alignment challenges. Oracle experiments with human-curated reference TikZ suggest that accurate executable representations provide complementary geometric cues; they do not evaluate an end-to-end conversion pipeline. TriGeoBench offers a testbed for structure-aware mathematical reasoning.

title: Stop assembling audit evidence by hand 🛠️
description:
Spending the week before an audit pulling scattered logs out of multiple tools is a manual grind that does not actually make your systems safer.

The problem and fix:

  • Compliance evidence is usually scattered across CI systems, Git records, and access logs.
  • Drift happens when one-off configuration changes occur and records fall out of sync.
  • Automating evidence generation directly at the platform layer turns audit prep from a weeks-long research task into a simple lookup.
  • Pairing automated deployment logs with Git approval workflows gives auditors the change management proof they need.

Continuous evidence keeps releases from getting blocked by slow, manual verification steps. Check out the full post to read the complete technical breakdown:

Automated audit evidence generation | Upsun

Upsun Cloud logs every deploy, code push, and config change, turning SOC 2 and PCI DSS audit evidence into a byproduct of normal platform operation

title: Minimax-Optimal Predictive Flow Matching under Distribution Drift
description:
arXiv:2610.28898v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Flow matching learns a generative velocity field by regression, but under distribution drift a field must be deployed before the current data arrive. We study this predictive problem for a fixed, possibly nonconvex, neural class, with dynamic regret against the best represented field of each round. We propose DyProd-FM, which refits flow matching on dyadic historical prefixes and selects among the fits with a sleeping Prod master. Without knowing any drift budget, it attains regret $\widetilde{O}(\min\{N_\omega+1,1+\sqrt{T\Omega}\})$ in the relative velocity risk variation $\Omega$ and $\widetilde{O}(\min\{N_\mu+1,1+T^{1/3}V_\mu^{2/3}\})$ in the target-law variation $V_\mu=\sum_t W_2(\mu_{t+1},\mu_t)$, up to approximation and fitting costs. Matching lower bounds for fixed classes show that both rates are optimal in $T$ and in the budgets up to logarithmic factors. Prior optimal dynamic-regret guarantees rely on a convex decision set with strongly convex or exp-concave losses, whereas our class may be nonconvex and no curvature in its parameters is assumed. The target-law rate rests on a second-order link between the two variations, which the base noise of flow matching provides.

title: How the sidecar steals the traffic
description:
A sidecar proxy only works if the application never knows it's there. This post is part 1 of a 2-part series about the three times the kernel reminded me how hard that is.

Section 1: The Problem

You build an application that runs in Kubernetes, and it runs fine for some time. Then you need to add telemetry, and your manager wants mTLS, circuit breaking, and retries. Easy, right? Except you have 60 applications running in your cluster, they all need these features, and there are other features sitting in the backlog. So you decide to build a proxy that sits in the pod and does all of this for them. But that means every application has to be reconfigured to send its traffic through the proxy. The fix is to make the proxy transparent: catch the traffic without the app knowing. In this post we will discuss how to make that happen.

Section 2: What a packet goes through

To start off, we need to know what iptables are. At its core, iptables is a command-line tool that allows you to configure the Linux kernel's built-in network filtering system.
The rules used to set up the Ananse iptables are as follows:

# inbound: anything arriving at the pod, except the sidecar's own ports
iptables -t nat -A ANANSE_PROXY_INBOUND  -p tcp --dport 15006 -j RETURN
iptables -t nat -A ANANSE_PROXY_INBOUND  -p tcp --dport 15021 -j RETURN
iptables -t nat -A ANANSE_PROXY_INBOUND  -p tcp -j REDIRECT --to-ports 15006
iptables -t nat -A PREROUTING -p tcp -j ANANSE_PROXY_INBOUND

# outbound: anything the app sends, with three escapes
iptables -t nat -A ANANSE_PROXY_OUTBOUND -m owner --uid-owner 1337 -j RETURN   # the sidecar itself
iptables -t nat -A ANANSE_PROXY_OUTBOUND -d 127.0.0.1/32 -j RETURN            # app talking to itself
iptables -t nat -A ANANSE_PROXY_OUTBOUND -d $KUBE_API_IP -j RETURN            # the API server
iptables -t nat -A ANANSE_PROXY_OUTBOUND -p tcp -j REDIRECT --to-ports 15001
iptables -t nat -A OUTPUT -p tcp -j ANANSE_PROXY_OUTBOUND

We have two primary chains: PREROUTING for inbound requests and OUTPUT for outbound requests. We have one set of rules for each. REDIRECT rewrites the destination to this same machine, both the address and the port, and RETURN says this request is allowed to skip the redirect and go directly to its destination (on the outbound side, this is the sidecar's own user, localhost, or the API server).
The first two inbound rules leave the sidecar's own ports alone: 15006 for traffic and 15021 for health checks and metrics. Everything else arriving at the pod gets sent to 15006.
On the outbound side, after the REDIRECT, the sidecar accepts a connection whose destination now reads 127.0.0.1:15001. (Inbound connections land on 15006, addressed to the pod's own IP.) The address the app actually wanted is gone from the packet. It survives in only one place; the kernel's conntrack table, and that is where the sidecar gets it back using SO_ORIGINAL_DST.

Section 3: The Gotchas

Like everything in engineering, there are gotchas we need to look out for. Here is the first one.

The Loop (UID 1337)

I hit this one early. I don't remember exactly what the first symptom looked like, but the cause was simple: intercepting all traffic leaving the pod meant the sidecar's own requests were redirected straight back into it. I had built an infinite loop.
The fix relies on how Linux handles processes. In Linux, every process runs under a specific User ID (UID). By convention in the service mesh world (borrowed from Istio and Envoy), the sidecar proxy is configured to run as a dedicated, unique user ID: 1337. Once I figured out the loop, the solution was to update our iptables script to check for this ID. If the traffic is owned by UID 1337, it is allowed out directly, bypassing the redirect back to port 15001.
To orchestrate this in Kubernetes, the injector sets the sidecar container to run as user 1337. The init container, which applies the iptables rules before the app starts, is different. Ananse's init container runs as root with NET_ADMIN and NET_RAW capabilities, because changing the kernel's netfilter rules is a privileged operation:

SecurityContext: &corev1.SecurityContext{
    RunAsUser:    ptr(int64(0)), // Root (required for iptables)
    RunAsNonRoot: ptr(false),    // Override pod-level runAsNonRoot
    Capabilities: &corev1.Capabilities{
        Add:  []corev1.Capability{"NET_ADMIN", "NET_RAW"},
        Drop: []corev1.Capability{"ALL"}, // Drop everything else
    },
},

Why Outbound Uses UIDs and Inbound Uses Ports

This loop fix highlights a crucial detail about how the Linux networking stack works. You might notice that our outbound escape rules check the user, while our inbound escapes check the port.
The kernel only knows who owns a packet when that packet is created on this specific machine. Packets arriving from the outside world have no local owner attached to them. Because of this, outbound rules can cleanly filter by the local UID, but inbound rules are forced to rely on the destination port to figure out where the traffic belongs.

Summary

Right now we have a working intercept. By using a combination of PREROUTING, OUTPUT, and a dedicated 1337 user ID, Ananse can transparently hijack both inbound and outbound pod traffic without a single change to the application's configuration.
The network layer is fully rigged, but the packet is currently sitting at our sidecar, stripped of its original destination. In Part 2, we will dive into the Go implementation to extract that address from the conntrack table, and look at two more things that broke: the deadlock that occurs when you run the control plane inside the very same mesh it manages, and the health probe that dialled itself.

title: RoPT: Robust 6DoF Object Pose Tracking in Video
description:
arXiv:2610.28962v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Accurate 6-DoF object pose tracking is essential for robotic interaction, yet conventional monocular pipelines frequently suffer from catastrophic divergence under rapid object motion. We present RoPT, a robust tracking framework engineered to overcome this limitation by unifying visual perception, temporal kinematics, and global re-localization into a tightly coupled closed loop. Unlike existing open-loop trackers, RoPT delivers three critical capabilities that fundamentally alter system resilience. First, the visual perception component tracks object masks to robustly handle partial and severe occlusions. Second, a kinematic factor graph regularizes frame-to-frame updates, forecasts forward pose predictions, and drives a parallel multi-hypothesis verification scheme to bypass local minima. Finally, an active re-localization module transforms the pipeline into a closed-loop system, making it failure-aware and capable of deterministic self-recovery. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework across challenging benchmarks alongside real-world robotic demonstrations, achieving significantly higher tracking survivability under rapid motion.

title: Sandboxing Python: RestrictedPython vs Docker vs Pyodide
description:
Running "untrusted Python" means executing code you did not write, a user's formula, an AI agent's generated script, or a plugin, without letting it read your files, open network connections, or seize the machine. It matters because Python was designed for trusted developers, so the interpreter offers no security boundary and the isolation has to be built deliberately around it.

Key takeaways

  • The classic exec() with stripped builtins is not a sandbox: Python's introspection lets any object walk up to a class that still holds import.

  • RestrictedPython's own maintainers state it "is not a sandbox system or a secured environment": it stops accidents and casual mischief, not a determined attacker.

  • Pyodide gives strong isolation for pure computation in WebAssembly, but its Python-to-JavaScript bridge has been the route of real production escapes.

  • Docker with a seccomp profile and a read-only root filesystem suits broadly trusted code; adversarial code needs gVisor or a microVM because containers share the host kernel.

  • Pick the boundary from the threat model, and never rely on interpreter-level tricks as the only layer.

Every few months a team learns this the expensive way: a "run user code" feature ships with exec() and a trimmed builtins dict, a researcher spends an afternoon on it, and the postmortem reads like a magic trick. Python looks sandboxable because you can see the dangerous names. The trap is that those names are never the whole attack surface.

Why can't you just use exec() with restricted builtins?

The naive sandbox looks like this:

exec(user_code, {"builtins": {}})

Emptying builtins feels thorough. It is not. Python's introspection gives every object a ladder back out: ().class reaches tuple, .base reaches object, and .subclasses() lists every loaded class (opencomputer.dev). From there the code picks a class whose module kept normal builtins, reaches through init.globals to grab import, imports os, and calls system, all without naming anything your filter blocked.

Here is the uncomfortable fact stated plainly: CPython was never designed to run hostile code inside its own process. Audit hooks and resource limits each close one hole, but the introspection surface is too large to close hole by hole (opencomputer.dev). Any defence that lives inside the interpreter is playing whack-a-mole against the language's own object model.

So the security boundary has to move somewhere the interpreter cannot reach: out to the operating system, the browser, or the hardware. That is what the three serious options do, each at a different layer.

What does RestrictedPython actually guarantee?

RestrictedPython, maintained by the Zope Foundation, compiles a restricted subset of Python by rewriting the abstract syntax tree at compile time. Attribute access to names starting with underscores is blocked, dangerous builtins are removed from the namespace your code sees, and imports go through a guard you control. The official example shows both sides:

from RestrictedPython import compile_restricted
from RestrictedPython import safe_globals

Harmless code runs fine

source = """
def example():
return 'Hello World!'
"""
byte_code = compile_restricted(source, '', 'exec')
namespace = {}
exec(byte_code, safe_globals, namespace)
print(namespace'example') # 'Hello World!'

Hostile code is stopped at the import

evil = """
import os
os.listdir('/')
"""
byte_code = compile_restricted(evil, '', 'exec')
exec(byte_code, safe_globals, {})

ImportError: import not found

In production you layer more on top: a custom getattr guard and a vetted import hook that only allows the modules your use case needs. It powers formula fields and scripted templates in systems like Plone, where semi-trusted users extend an application the operator controls.

Now the honest part, in the maintainers' own words: RestrictedPython "is not a sandbox system or a secured environment, but it helps to define a trusted environment and execute untrusted code inside of it" (PyPI). It stops accidents and casual mischief: a user who writes a bad formula gets an error, not your filesystem. It was never designed to hold a hostile expression, and treating it as a security boundary against untrusted code is a misuse. Against an adversary, it is at most one layer, never the wall.

Does Pyodide provide real isolation?

Pyodide is CPython compiled to WebAssembly, running in the browser or Node.js. For pure computation the isolation is genuinely strong: WebAssembly modules have no ambient access to the host and receive only the capabilities you grant them.

The catch is the foreign function interface between Python and JavaScript, which is the whole point of embedding Pyodide in a page. Through the js module, Python code can reach JavaScript objects, and by default it sees the host runtime's global scope. One real escape (blog.barrack.ai, CERT VU#414811) is instructive: the sandbox handed Python a mock document built as a plain object literal, and because every such object inherits from Object.prototype, the payload walked .constructor.constructor to the Function constructor, evaluated "return globalThis", and landed in the real global scope. In Node.js that means process, require, and child_process.

This was not a one-off. Researchers disclosed CVE-2025-68668 against n8n's Pyodide-backed code node: n8n blocked risky functions by patching names, but two bypasses worked anyway, one using ctypes to call libc's system() directly, the other using _pyodide._base.eval_code() where the patches did not apply (cyera.com). The proof of concept was two lines. Earlier, Grist disclosed a CVSS 9.1 escape in its Pyodide formula engine (GHSA-7xvx-8pf2-pv5g), fixed in Grist 1.7.9 by running Pyodide under Deno: a real process boundary outside the interpreter.

The pattern is consistent: Pyodide has never claimed to be a security boundary, and the escapes happen at the bridge the embedder built, not in WebAssembly itself. For a browser playground, it is an excellent zero-server-cost choice. On a server, treat the JavaScript globals configuration as the actual security surface: anything reachable from Python is reachable by the attacker.

// Pin a version you have tested; the snippet below is illustrative
const pyodide = await loadPyodide();
// Runs in the visitor's browser: no server, no bill, no shared state
const result = await pyodide.runPythonAsync(
def fib(n):
a, b = 0, 1
for _ in range(n):
a, b = b, a + b
return a
fib(30)
);
console.log(result); // 832040

Is Docker enough for hostile code?

Containers move the boundary to the operating system: Linux namespaces and cgroups give the code its own filesystem view, process tree, network stack, and resource limits. For code you broadly trust, Docker with a hardened configuration is the workhorse answer:

docker run --rm \
--cap-drop=ALL \
--security-opt=no-new-privileges \
--security-opt seccomp=default.json \
--read-only --tmpfs /tmp:rw,noexec,nosuid \
--network none \
--memory 256m --cpus 0.5 \
--pids-limit 64 \
--user 1000:1000 \
python:3.13-slim \
python /app/user_code.py

Each flag closes a real door: no Linux capabilities, no privilege escalation through setuid binaries, a seccomp filter on syscalls, a read-only root filesystem, no network, and hard caps on memory, CPU, and processes so a fork bomb is a billing event rather than an outage.

The caveat is architectural: containers share the host kernel, so a kernel-level exploit escapes the container. For code you broadly trust, that risk is acceptable with a seccomp profile and a read-only root filesystem. For adversarial code, the boundary must move again: gVisor interposes a user-space kernel that intercepts syscalls, and microVMs such as Firecracker add a hypervisor, so an escape must defeat virtualisation rather than a single kernel bug (opencomputer.dev).

Production systems rarely bet on one layer. Cohere's Python interpreter documents a defence-in-depth stack: untrusted code runs in a WebAssembly sandbox, inside a Node.js process, inside a Docker container, inside cloud infrastructure, with network egress and the filesystem locked down at every level (Cohere North security docs). No single layer is trusted.

Which one should you use?

Start from the threat model, not the tool. The question is never "which sandbox is best" but "who is writing the code, and what happens if they turn malicious?"

  • Semi-trusted users extending your app (formulas, templates, workflow expressions): RestrictedPython fits: friendly errors instead of breaches, and fast in-process code your test suite can exercise. Still run the whole application in a container, since RestrictedPython is the guardrail, not the wall.

  • Public playgrounds and tutorials: Pyodide in the browser is hard to beat. Execution happens on the visitor's machine, so there is no server to attack and no compute bill. Keep the JavaScript bridge minimal and never expose Node.js globals server-side.

  • Customer or agent-generated code on your servers that you broadly trust: Docker with the hardening flags above, plus timeouts and output limits. This is the standard answer for a reason.

  • Adversarial or multi-tenant code: containers alone are not enough. Use gVisor or a microVM per execution, and treat the container image as untrusted input too.

Much of what remains unknown is operational: sandbox overhead depends on your workload, and public benchmarks measure different things, so treat vendor numbers as directional. What is settled is the principle every story here converges on: CPython cannot sandbox itself, so the boundary must live outside the interpreter. Choose the layer that matches your adversary, stack more than one, and test the configuration the way an attacker would.

title: Single-Image Food Mass Estimators Do Not Transfer Their Gram Scale Across Datasets
description:
arXiv:2610.29025v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Estimating food mass from a photograph is central to image-based dietary assessment, but whether trained models transfer to new cameras and foods is unclear. We fine-tuned DINOv2-base on 2,253 weighed Nutrition5k dishes to predict mass from one RGB photograph and compared it with a zero-shot vision-language model, Qwen3-VL-32B, on Nutrition5k and three external datasets: ASA24 studio portions, ECUSTFD whole foods and Food Portion Benchmark meal trays. In domain, the fine-tuned model's mean absolute error was 24.8 g, less than half of Qwen's. On external datasets it did not beat Qwen. For a food it had never seen, it ranked portions by size, but no better than a count of food pixels. Its gram scale was wrong in two ways: it changed with how much of the scene the photograph showed, and it was off by a different factor for each food. Training on other foods or trays from the tested dataset cut the external error by 38 to 65%. DINOv2-large, a larger backbone trained on the same dishes, did not reduce the external error. One labeled photograph of the same food cut the model's ASA24 error to 28.3 g, better than that photograph achieved alone. Prediction intervals that held the true mass for 90% of Nutrition5k dishes held it for at most half of external photographs. Nutrition5k often photographed the same plate several times, so a random test split shared near-identical photographs with training and overstated accuracy. Single-image mass estimators therefore need labeled photographs from the setting where they are used.
