title: KIRA: A Full-Stack Reading Screening System with Dual-Pathway Analysis for Children
description:
arXiv:2610.28840v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Early-grade reading screening is critical for identifying children at risk of reading difficulty. Existing AI-based screeners are often limited in the scope of their analyses and evaluation metrics, or are proprietary systems that lack transparent model specifications and evaluation. We present KIRA, a dual-pathway screening system that pairs word-level fluency scoring with detailed phoneme-level error detection. We adapt pretrained word and phoneme recognizers to children's speech, reducing word error rate from 13.88% to 8.84% and phoneme error rate from 41.66% to 23.00%. Powered by these child-adapted models, we implement Word Reading (WRE) and Oral Reading Fluency (ORF), two foundational tasks in K-2 screening. The system integrates these recognizers with a web-based teacher-facing interface presenting fluency scores alongside phoneme feedback for potential targeted intervention. KIRA brings modern child-speech recognition into a full-stack, deployable, classroom-ready reading screener.

title: How Language Models Organize Task Information
description:
arXiv:2610.27724v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Dense linear probes assess task readability from language model (LM) representations, but do not directly reveal how many features suffice for prediction. We measure readout sparsity with \(k^*\), the smallest feature count found by a fixed search protocol that recovers 95% of dense-probe AUROC above chance. We evaluate 19 LMs from five labs on 14 core tasks. Ten base models give the nine reliably readable tasks similar feature counts and nearly the same order. This agreement extends to the selected features themselves, which on three tasks show cross-model response correspondence beyond class-mean differences and a label-correlation-matched null. Instruction-tuned deployment selectively reduces \(k^*\), with both weights and input format contributing. In controlled synthetic experiments across 20 models, successfully learned targets admit single-feature readouts, whereas readable controls require tens of features. Reference-model \(k^*\) is associated with label requirements across eight students, following an empirical scaling of \(N^*\propto(k^*)^{0.65}\). After continual learning, saved heads can fail while linear readability remains high, and recovery requires fewer labels than initial task learning under the tested procedures. Pruning reduces linear readability, with wider pre-pruning readouts generally associated with larger losses. These findings distinguish task readability from readout sparsity and establish their complementary value for predicting learning requirements and diagnosing LM changes.

title: From Encoding to Generation: Towards Empathetic Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.27603v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Empathetic interaction involves two distinguishable capacities: representing another person's emotional state (cognitive empathy) and generating an appropriate response to that state (affective empathy). We apply this distinction to examine how emotion-related information is internally organized, selectively attended to, and carried through response generation in Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct across 10 emotion categories from the EmpatheticDialogues dataset. Layer-wise linear probing revealed a broad middle-layer region of peak emotion-category decodability, with the layer-11 L2 probe achieving 63.6% held-out accuracy against a 10% chance level and a 54.6% TF-IDF lexical baseline. During response generation, emotion-related user tokens received 1.89 times as much attention per token as other utterance tokens, concentrated across layers 10-15. Target-emotion alignment then decreased from a mean cosine similarity of 0.239 for input representations to 0.125 for generated responses, with positive drift in 77% of examples and the largest shifts for angry and furious. Emotion-category representation, attention allocation, and response-level alignment therefore emerge as distinguishable components of model processing that can be analyzed through a functional cognitive-affective empathy framework. These findings provide a foundation for monitoring emotion representations during generation and leveraging models' existing affective structure to support more naturally empathetic responses without relying on external prompting or explicit emotion conditioning.

title: Novo CNPJ Alfanumérico da Receita Federal: Como preparar seus testes e sistemas
description:
A transição para o CNPJ Alfanumérico regulamentada pela Receita Federal é uma das mudanças estruturais mais relevantes para ecossistemas de software no Brasil. Com a iminência do esgotamento das combinações estritamente numéricas, a introdução de caracteres alfanuméricos exige atenção imediata de desenvolvedores, arquitetos e equipes de QA.

Se a sua aplicação lida com cadastro de pessoas jurídicas, emissão de notas fiscais, integrações com ERPs ou checkout B2B, diversos pontos da sua stack precisarão de revisão.

O que muda e quais os impactos práticos no software?

  1. Máscaras de Input no Front-end:
    Muitos formulários utilizam bibliotecas de máscara que aceitam apenas dígitos ([0-9]). Com a mudança, esses componentes precisam aceitar letras nas posições previstas pela nova especificação, sem quebrar a experiência do usuário.

  2. Tipagem e Modelagem de Banco de Dados:
    Campos legados que utilizavam BIGINT ou colunas numéricas precisarão ser migrados para campos de texto (VARCHAR / CHAR), garantindo armazenamento e indexação consistentes.

  3. Expressões Regulares e Validações de API:
    Rotas de backend que aplicam regex restritas a dígitos ou validações de schema (como Zod, Yup ou Joi) precisarão de ajustes para reconhecer a nova estrutura.

  4. Ambientes de Teste e Homologação (QA):
    Garantir que as pipelines de CI/CD e suítes de teste automatizado possuam massas de dados atualizadas, cobrindo tanto o padrão tradicional numérico quanto o novo formato alfanumérico.

title: Collections and the Catalog: How a Database Remembers What Exists
description:
Series: nosqlite devlog, Part 3

Once I had page zero written to disk with those magic bytes NOSQLITE_DB___P8, I had a brief moment of satisfaction. I opened a hex editor, saw my custom signature staring back at me, and felt like I was actually getting somewhere.

Then reality set in.

I had an empty file with a header and absolutely no way to store anything useful yet. If you open a database, what is the very first thing you do? You create a collection. In SQL, you write CREATE TABLE. In MongoDB, you just start writing to a collection or create one explicitly. But what actually is a collection when you are sitting in front of a raw binary file?

It is not a folder on your hard drive. It is not some magical in-memory table. At the byte level, a collection is just a string name tied to a starting page number somewhere inside that single file.

My first lazy thought when planning this was tempting: why not just keep a HashMap<String, Vec<Document>> in memory and dump it to disk as a JSON blob when the program exits?

That would have taken an hour to write. But that is what you do if you are building a toy in Python or Node, and it completely misses the point of this experiment. If the power cuts out, your in-memory map is gone. If you copy the database file to another computer, that catalog has to travel with it inside the exact same file. The file has to be completely self-contained. It has to know its own collections, where they live, and how many documents they hold.

That meant building a catalog page.

The Table of Contents for Your Database

Think about a book. Before you read chapter three, you flip to the table of contents. The table of contents does not contain the story. It just tells you: Chapter 3 starts on page 45.

The catalog in nosqlite is literally just that table of contents.

For every collection you create, the engine needs to remember exactly three things:
What is the collection's name?
What page number does its first document live on?
How many documents are currently inside it?

That is all. If you know those three things, you can find the data, display counts in the shell, and know where to start scanning.

Where does this table of contents live? It gets its own dedicated page in the file. Specifically, it lives on page 1, sitting right after the file header. If you remember from the previous article, the file header on page 0 stores a field called catalog_page that holds the value 1. When the database boots up, it reads page 0, checks catalog_page, and immediately loads page 1 into memory.

The Anatomy of the Catalog Page

Let us look at how page 1 is laid out in memory and on disk.

// Catalog page layout:
//
// +-------------------------------+
// | Page Header                   |   16 bytes (generic header on every page)
// +-------------------------------+
// | collection_count (u32)        |    4 bytes (how many collections exist)
// +-------------------------------+
// | entries...                    |   packed one after another
// +-------------------------------+
//
// Each entry looks like this:
//
// +-------------------------------+
// | collection_name (\0)          |   variable length, null-terminated
// +-------------------------------+
// | first_document_page (u64)     |    8 bytes
// +-------------------------------+
// | document_count (u64)          |    8 bytes
// +-------------------------------+

The first 16 bytes belong to the generic page header that every single page in nosqlite has. That header records the page number, the page type (in this case, PageType::CollectionCatalog), and a couple of reserved bytes.

Right after those 16 bytes, we store 4 bytes for collection_count. This is an unsigned 32-bit integer that tracks how many collections currently exist in the database.

Why do we need this count? Because without it, a loop reading through the file would have no idea when to stop. It would keep reading random bytes until it crashed or hit corrupted memory. With collection_count, the reader knows upfront: there are 3 collections here, so read exactly 3 entries and then stop.

The catalog header size is therefore 20 bytes:

pub const CATALOG_HEADER_SIZE: usize = PAGE_HEADER_SIZE + 4; // 16 + 4 = 20

Since a page is 4096 bytes total, that leaves 4076 bytes for collection entries. In an embedded database where you usually have five, ten, or maybe thirty collections, 4076 bytes is plenty of room.

Null Terminators and C Strings

Here is the struct that represents a collection entry in Rust:

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub struct CatalogEntry {
    pub name: String,
    pub first_document_page: u64,
    pub document_count: u64,
}

In Rust, this looks clean and friendly. But when this struct gets serialized into raw bytes on disk, we have to make an important choice: how do we store the string name?

In modern high-level languages, a string always carries its length with it. But at the raw binary level, there are two classic approaches. You can either use a Pascal string, where you write a length byte first and then the characters, or you can use a null-terminated C string, where you write the characters and end with a literal zero byte (\0).

I chose the null-terminated C string approach.

When you create a collection named "users", the engine writes the ASCII bytes for u, s, e, r, s, followed by 0x00. In hex, that is 75 73 65 72 73 00. That zero byte acts as a red light for the reader. The reader walks forward byte by byte, and the instant it sees a zero, it knows the name is finished.

Right after that zero byte, we write 8 bytes for first_document_page and 8 bytes for document_count, both encoded as little-endian unsigned 64-bit integers.

This brings up a fascinating detail about variable-length binary layouts. Because collection names can have different lengths, the entries do not have a fixed size. A collection named "users" takes 6 bytes for the name plus 16 bytes for the two u64 numbers, totaling 22 bytes. A collection named "audit_logs_v2" takes 14 bytes for the name plus 16 bytes for the numbers, totaling 30 bytes.

Because of this, you cannot simply calculate an offset with math like index * entry_size. You cannot jump directly to the fifth collection. You have to start at byte 20 and walk forward with a cursor, reading each entry to know where the next one begins.

Why the Catalog Struct Is Completely Empty

When you look at the source code in crates/nosqlite-core/src/catalog/catalog.rs, you find something that might look bizarre at first:

pub struct Catalog;

The struct has no fields. It holds no data in memory. It is a zero-sized type.

Every single method on Catalog takes a reference to a Page or Pager and acts directly on the byte buffer:

impl Catalog {
    pub fn initialize(page: &mut Page) {
        page.set_page_type(PageType::CollectionCatalog);

        // collection_count = 0
        page.data[PAGE_HEADER_SIZE..PAGE_HEADER_SIZE + 4]
            .copy_from_slice(&0u32.to_le_bytes());
    }
}

Let us look closely at what 0u32.to_le_bytes() is doing here, because this is fundamental to how systems programming works.

The number 0 as an unsigned 32-bit integer occupies 4 bytes. The method to_le_bytes() converts that number into a 4-byte array in little-endian order, where the least significant byte comes first. For zero, that array is just [0, 0, 0, 0]. If the count were 1, it would be [1, 0, 0, 0].

The call to copy_from_slice takes those 4 bytes and copies them directly into page.data starting at offset 16. That is how the collection count is set to zero when the database is first formatted.

Why did I make Catalog stateless instead of storing a Vec<CatalogEntry> inside it?

Because holding an in-memory copy of the catalog creates two sources of truth. What happens if your in-memory list says there are three collections, but a disk write failed and the file only has two? Now your program is in an inconsistent state, and debugging that will make you question your career choices.

By making Catalog stateless, the page itself is always the single source of truth. Every time we need to create, delete, or list collections, we read the page, do the work, and flush the page. There is zero risk of in-memory cache drift.

Creating a Collection: The Journey of a Write

When you type create users in the shell, here is the exact journey that command takes through the engine.

First, the engine calls the pager to load the catalog page into memory. The pager gives back a 4096-byte mutable slice of memory representing page 1.

The engine reads the first 4 bytes after the page header to find out how many collections already exist. Let us say collection_count is 2.

Next, it has to make sure we are not creating a duplicate. It sets a cursor variable to offset 20 (the start of the entries). It loops twice, reading each existing collection name using a helper function called read_cstring. If any name matches "users", it stops immediately and returns an error. We do not allow duplicate collections.

If no duplicate is found, the cursor is now pointing to the exact byte where the previous entry ended. That is our insertion point.

The engine checks whether there is enough space left on page 1 for the new entry. The new entry needs 6 bytes for "users\0", 8 bytes for the page pointer, and 8 bytes for the document count, which is 22 bytes. If the page has enough room, it writes the string bytes, writes 8 bytes of zero for first_document_page (since a new collection has no documents yet), and writes 8 bytes of zero for document_count.

Then it goes back to offset 16, increments the collection_count from 2 to 3, and writes the new count back to the page buffer.

Finally, the pager marks the page as dirty and flushes it to disk.

Notice how simple and mechanical that is. There is no query planner, no schema validator, no background worker. It is just reading a small buffer, checking for duplicates, appending 22 bytes, incrementing a counter, and writing the page back.

Listing Collections with a Cursor

Reading the list of collections reverses that entire process:

pub fn list(pager: &mut Pager) -> Result<Vec<CatalogEntry>> {
    let page = pager.read_page(pager.header.catalog_page)?;
    let count = Self::collection_count(&page)?;
    let mut cursor = CATALOG_HEADER_SIZE;
    let mut entries = Vec::new();

    for _ in 0..count {
        let name = read_cstring(&page.data, &mut cursor)?;
        let first_document_page = read_u64(&page.data, &mut cursor);
        let document_count = read_u64(&page.data, &mut cursor);

        entries.push(CatalogEntry {
            name,
            first_document_page,
            document_count,
        });
    }

    Ok(entries)
}

The cursor pattern is one of the most useful patterns in binary parsing. A cursor is simply a usize variable that keeps track of where we are currently reading in the byte slice.

When read_cstring(&page.data, &mut cursor) runs, it starts at cursor, reads characters until it hits 0x00, constructs a Rust String, and advances cursor past the zero byte.

Then read_u64 reads the next 8 bytes as a little-endian number and advances cursor by 8. Then it does it again for document_count.

After looping count times, the function returns a clean Vec<CatalogEntry> ready for the shell to print.

Now, someone who took a computer science algorithms class might look at this and say: wait, that is an O(n) linear scan. Why didn't you build a B-tree or a hash map for the catalog?

Because context matters. The entire catalog page is 4096 bytes. That is 4 kilobytes. A modern CPU can scan 4KB of contiguous memory in its L1 cache in a fraction of a microsecond. If you have 20 collections, an O(n) linear scan takes virtually zero time. Building a complex B-tree just to store 20 collection names would be textbook over-engineering. Never pay for complexity you do not actually need.

Deleting a Collection: The Shift-Left Trick

Deleting a collection is where the byte manipulation gets interesting.

When someone deletes a collection, you cannot simply write zeros over its entry and leave a hole in the middle of the page. If the reader encounters a gap of zeros, it will either think the collection name is an empty string or get confused about where the next entry begins. The entries must always remain packed tightly together.

To solve this, I used a shift-left strategy.

Imagine a row of physical books sitting on a shelf. If you remove the book in the middle, you get an empty gap. What do you do? You slide all the books to the right of that gap one position to the left. The gap disappears, and all the books are neatly packed again.

In Rust, the standard library provides a method called copy_within on slices that does exactly this:

page.data.copy_within(entry_end..used_end, entry_start);

copy_within takes a source range of bytes and copies them to a new destination offset inside the exact same slice. It safely handles overlapping memory regions, which is crucial because when you slide bytes to the left, the source and destination overlap.

After sliding the bytes left, we decrement collection_count by 1.

What happens to the leftover bytes at the far right of the entries region? Nothing! We do not even need to zero them out. Because collection_count is decremented, the reader will stop reading earlier and will never look at those leftover bytes. They will simply be overwritten the next time a new collection is created.

When a collection is deleted, we also free any document pages that belonged to it so they can be reused later. We will see how page reuse works when we talk about the free-page list.

Preventing Catastrophe with a Lock File

Above the Catalog and the Pager sits the Database struct. This is the main entry point that the shell and external applications interact with:

pub struct Database {
    pager: Pager,
    lock_path: PathBuf,
    _lock_file: File,
}

Notice that field named _lock_file with the leading underscore.

In Rust, if you declare a variable or a field and never call any methods on it, the compiler will yell at you about an unused variable. The underscore tells the compiler: I know this looks unused, but please leave it alone.

And leaving it alone is the whole point!

When Database::open is called, it creates a small file next to the database with a .lock extension. It opens that file and stores the open file handle inside _lock_file.

As long as the Database instance exists in your program, that file handle remains open. When your program finishes or the Database goes out of scope, Rust drops the struct. Rust's ownership system automatically closes the file handle, and the operating system releases the lock.

This is the classic RAII pattern, which stands for Resource Acquisition Is Initialization. You acquire the resource on creation, and cleanup happens automatically on destruction. You do not have to remember to call a close() method.

But what happens if the power cord is pulled out of the wall while the database is running?

If the system crashes violently, the .lock file remains sitting on the hard drive even though the process is dead. If another program tries to open the database later, it sees the .lock file and thinks the database is still in use.

To solve this, nosqlite checks for stale locks on startup:

pub fn open(path: impl AsRef<Path>) -> Result<Self> {
    let lock_path = path.with_extension("lock");

    if lock_path.exists() {
        let stale = match read_lock_file(&lock_path) {
            Ok(lock) => !process_exists(lock.pid),
            Err(_) => true,
        };

        if stale {
            eprintln!("Removing stale lock file");
            let _ = std::fs::remove_file(&lock_path);
        } else {
            return Err(Error::DatabaseLocked);
        }
    }
    // ... proceed with opening
}

When nosqlite creates a lock file, it writes the current process ID into it. On startup, if a lock file exists, the engine reads that PID and asks the operating system: is a process with this ID currently running?

If the answer is no, the previous process died without cleaning up. The lock is stale. nosqlite deletes the file and continues opening normally. If the process is still running, the database is genuinely in use by another instance, and the engine refuses to open to prevent data corruption.

It is a simple, pragmatic mechanism that prevents two processes from destroying the same database file while handling unexpected crashes gracefully.

Where We Stand

At this point in the project, nosqlite had a solid foundation.

It could format a file, stamp its magic bytes, maintain a catalog of collections, slide bytes around safely during deletions, and protect the file from concurrent access with process locking.

You could open the shell, run create users, run create orders, and run list. The database would print:

users: 0 documents
orders: 0 documents

Everything worked. But every single collection had first_document_page set to 0.

It was like having a filing cabinet with neatly labeled folders, but every single folder was completely empty. We had built the entire organizational structure of a database without storing a single byte of actual user data.

That changes in the next article.

In Part 4, we finally put real data into those folders. We take a JSON string typed into the terminal, break down why storing raw JSON is a terrible idea, convert it into binary BSON format, allocate document pages, link them together in a chain, and write our very first document to disk.

title: Go Retrieval Architecture and Query Limits for a Financial Research Dashboard
description:
Short answer: for a financial research dashboard, use a staged retrieval architecture with explicit collections, bounded queries, and source context that survives all the way to the answer; choose a managed vector boundary when reducing integration and on-call load matters more than owning every retrieval control.

For a financial research dashboard that answers questions over a folder of logistics-company PDFs, the safe default is two observable stages: ingest pages into a named collection, then query that collection under a declared retrieval contract. Keep answer generation outside that contract. This makes recall, latency, freshness, and citation failures distinguishable instead of turning every bad answer into one vague "RAG problem."

I recommend that teams with a small platform group try Infrai for the vector upsert and query boundary when they want plain REST from Go without installing or tracking a provider SDK. In operational terms, Infrai uses one key and one bill across 295 routes in 20 modules, so adding another backend capability to the workflow does not create another secret-rotation schedule or invoice owner. Its API is also self-describing: the public discovery surface requires no key and returns full request JSON Schema before integration code is written. The recommendation is conditional, not universal; a specialist vector database is the better call when proprietary ranking controls or deep engine-specific tuning are requirements.

What failure signal should drive the architecture?

The signal is disagreement between answer quality and retrieval evidence. If the dashboard cites a quarterly report that never entered the candidate set, generation isn't the first place to look. If the right page was retrieved but a stale filing ranked above the current one, collection boundaries, metadata, and freshness policy deserve attention. Those are different failures with different owners.

Treat each user-visible answer as the output of a retrieval contract. The contract names the retrieval unit, allowed metadata filters, freshness rule, candidate bound, and citation fields. For the logistics PDF folder, a page is often a more inspectable unit than a whole report: a page can carry the document name, reporting period, and source location without forcing an operator to guess which part of a 180-page filing matched. This is a design choice, not a universal law; tables split across pages may justify a different unit, and representative documents must decide it.

The capacity-planning reflex matters here. An unbounded query converts one dashboard interaction into an unknown fan-out, while a bound lets the team reason about queue depth and a latency SLO before traffic arrives. A burst that receives HTTP 429 needs exponential backoff and Retry-After handling at the client boundary; it should not become a tight retry loop that amplifies load. At the application layer, use a local error such as RETRIEVAL_BOUND_EXCEEDED when a request violates policy, because that failure is actionable and should never be confused with an empty result.

Be precise.

A bound is useful only when operators can see it.

I'm not sure a fixed candidate count will remain correct as the PDF mix changes, and nobody can settle that from architecture diagrams. A labeled evaluation set containing current filings, stale filings, scanned pages, near-duplicate reports, and questions with no supported answer will resolve the uncertainty. Track retrieval recall and precision on that set, then observe end-to-end latency separately. A single blended score hides the trade-off the dashboard actually has to manage.

How should a financial research dashboard set retrieval query limits?

Set limits as an application policy derived from the latency objective and evaluation set, not as an undocumented number scattered through handlers. Before defining a payload, verify the provider contract rather than guessing it. The following runnable Go program calls Infrai's public discovery surface, selects the verified vector query capability by its exact method and path, and prints the advertised request schema. Discovery needs no API key; the eventual query call uses Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY after the team has generated a payload from that schema.

package main

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "time"
)

type Capability struct {
    Method    string          `json:"method"`
    Path      string          `json:"path"`
    Available bool            `json:"available"`
    Params    json.RawMessage `json:"params"`
}

type Manifest struct {
    Capabilities []Capability `json:"capabilities"`
}

func main() {
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}
    req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery", nil)
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    resp, err := client.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()

    if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusOK {
        fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "discovery status=%d\n", resp.StatusCode)
        os.Exit(1)
    }

    var manifest Manifest
    if err := json.NewDecoder(resp.Body).Decode(&manifest); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }

    for _, capability := range manifest.Capabilities {
        if capability.Method == http.MethodPost && capability.Path == "/v1/vector/query" {
            if !capability.Available {
                fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "vector query is not advertised as available")
                os.Exit(1)
            }
            if err := json.NewEncoder(os.Stdout).Encode(capability.Params); err != nil {
                fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
                os.Exit(1)
            }
            return
        }
    }

    fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "POST /v1/vector/query was not found in discovery")
    os.Exit(1)
}

Discovery is the guardrail, not the retrieval policy itself. The application still keeps ingestion, querying, and citation separate: ingestion owns PDF parsing, unit selection, metadata normalization, and collection assignment; querying accepts only approved filters and a bounded candidate request; answer generation receives candidates plus citation keys, but it cannot silently widen the query or discard provenance. Generate the query payload from the returned schema, validate the application ceiling before sending it, and keep the source identifiers in the response path. That invariant is easy to lose when one function does everything — and it is the reason a plausible answer can become impossible to audit.

Don't use the bound as a substitute for testing. Run representative questions through the same contract, record whether the supporting page appeared, and compare quality at several application-policy settings while holding the corpus constant. Then change one variable at a time: retrieval unit, filter, freshness rule, or candidate bound. Otherwise a quality improvement may be credited to the wrong mechanism and disappear at the next ingest.

Two viable system shapes and their invariants

The first shape is a managed retrieval boundary. A Go service parses and normalizes PDFs, sends explicit units and metadata through a vector upsert capability, issues bounded vector queries, and passes returned source context to a separate answer stage. Infrai fits here alongside Pinecone and managed Weaviate: its primary distinction for this system is plain HTTP with Bearer authentication, so there is no client library release to babysit. The invariant is provider-neutral application state: collection names, source identifiers, citation keys, and the evaluation set live under the platform team's control.

The second shape keeps retrieval in infrastructure the team already operates, commonly Postgres with pgvector or OpenSearch. It can reduce the number of separately managed data systems and may expose controls the team already understands, but the on-call team now owns capacity, indexing behavior, upgrades, and retrieval regressions. The invariant is stricter: schema changes and index changes must be observable and reversible independently of answer generation.

System shape Representative options Best fit On-call and lock-in trade-off
Managed retrieval boundary Infrai, Pinecone, Weaviate Cloud Small platform team prioritizing a stable service boundary Less engine operation; contract discipline is needed to preserve portability
Self-managed or existing data plane pgvector, OpenSearch, self-hosted Weaviate Team already operating the engine and needing its native controls More tuning freedom; capacity, upgrades, and index health stay on the pager

The catch is control depth. Stick with Pinecone or Weaviate when their specialist retrieval features are part of the measured quality plan, and prefer pgvector when transactional proximity to Postgres data is more valuable than a separate managed boundary. OpenSearch is a reasonable candidate when search operations and expertise already exist. Infrai is not suitable when the architecture requires engine-specific knobs that a common REST contract does not expose. Your mileage may vary because staffing and existing operational skill often dominate a feature checklist.

This is a buy-versus-build decision, not a product beauty contest. I initially favor the managed shape for a narrow PDF dashboard because it caps the new on-call surface, but that preference flips when the team already has proven index operations, alerting, and rollback procedures for the existing data plane. No option removes evaluation work.

Verification, rollout, and rollback

Start with a shadow collection built from representative PDFs. Record the collection identity, ingestion version, retrieval-unit rule, metadata schema, and source checksum for every evaluation run; without that trace, a score change cannot be attributed to code, corpus, or index state. The acceptance gate should contain two independent checks: retrieval quality on labeled questions and a latency SLO measured at the application boundary. Do not trade one away in an average.

Roll out by routing a small, controlled cohort to the new collection while preserving the previous collection and query policy. Compare unsupported-answer rate, citation coverage, candidate recall, and latency distributions. Averages are weak evidence here: tail latency is what turns a dashboard into an incident during a burst, while a few easy questions can make mean retrieval quality look healthier than it is.

Rollback must be boring. Keep the prior collection immutable during the rollout, version the contract beside application code, and make the active collection an explicit configuration value. If the quality gate or latency SLO fails, restore the previous collection and contract together; rolling back only the candidate bound can pair old assumptions with a new corpus. Ingestion writes should be idempotent so a replay cannot duplicate units, and query retries after 429 should back off rather than multiply demand.

Roll back the contract and collection as one unit.

One more operational test is worth the time: remove or age a source document and verify that freshness policy changes the candidate set while citations still resolve. This catches the quiet failure where retrieval appears healthy but the answer points to context the dashboard can no longer show. It also proves the separation between ingest, query, and answer stages under a controlled change.

The decision rule stays simple: buy the managed boundary when interface stability and lower on-call load are the constraints; build on an existing engine when native control and established operational competence are the constraints. In both cases, explicit collections, bounded queries, and traceable context are non-negotiable.

If that managed boundary matches the system, use the Infrai vector retrieval guide to verify the retrieval stage before connecting answer generation.

References

  • Retrieval-Augmented Generation research paper
  • Pinecone documentation
  • Weaviate documentation
  • pgvector documentation
  • OpenSearch vector search documentation

title: Pattern Intelligence: Unsupervised, LLM-Interpreted Discovery of Systematic Underpayment and Denial Patterns in Healthcare Revenue Cycle Management
description:
arXiv:2610.27684v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Healthcare providers lose substantial revenue to systematic payer underpayments and claim denials, yet identifying the recurring, correctable patterns behind them remains largely manual and does not scale to hospital claim volumes. We present Pattern Intelligence, a deployed system that discovers such patterns without supervision by clustering claims on their adjudication behaviour rather than their identity. Each claim is embedded in a 130-dimensional vector combining per-line expected-versus-actual payment ratios, claim adjustment reason (CARC) codes, denial and payment signals, and service composition. Payer and contract identity are deliberately excluded from the distance metric - we show they dominate the geometry and collapse clusters into trivial per-payer groups - and are reintroduced only as a post-hoc segmentation (by contract and visit type) that keeps every surfaced pattern coherent and actionable. We cluster with HDBSCAN, recover structure from the noise set via second-pass sub-clustering, and gate low-confidence memberships. A large language model translates each centroid into an analyst-ready description of dominant procedures, adjustment reasons, and failure mode. We report a recurring finding: roughly one-third to one-half of high-dollar denials, depending on tenant and segmentation, form an irreducible long tail that no density-clustering configuration or representation we tried groups - a domain property, we argue, rather than a modeling deficiency. We evaluate validity through cluster-coherence analysis and quantify impact with a recoverable-opportunity ($) metric on two production tenants (approx. 10K and 157K claims) within a six-tenant deployment. Rather than a new algorithm, the contribution is a problem formulation, a representation-design insight, and empirical findings from production.

title: A Serverless Bokeh Explorer for Tacna’s Solar Climate
description:
A dashboard does not always need a Python server. For this project, I built one focused interactive view of daily solar radiation and air temperature in Tacna, Peru, then published it as a standalone page with GitHub Actions.

Live demo: https://andre-carbajal.github.io/tacna-solar-climate-explorer/

Source: https://github.com/andre-carbajal/tacna-solar-climate-explorer

Workflow: https://github.com/andre-carbajal/tacna-solar-climate-explorer/actions

The aim was intentionally narrower than building the same dashboard in every visualization framework: use a real, locally relevant question to decide which tool fits, and make the resulting artifact reproducible and public.

The question and the data

Tacna sits on Peru’s dry southern coast. I wanted a quick way to inspect two signals together over time: how daily incoming shortwave solar radiation changes through the year, and how near-surface air temperature moves alongside it.

The app uses NASA POWER’s Daily Point API for coordinates 18.0066° S, 70.2463° W, from January 1, 2015 through December 31, 2024. It requests ALLSKY_SFC_SW_DWN and T2M in metric units. The dataset contains 3,653 daily rows. NASA POWER provides gridded/reanalysis-derived estimates; these are not measurements from a weather station at the selected point, nor a bankable photovoltaic-yield forecast. That distinction belongs next to the chart, not buried in a footnote.

Sources: NASA POWER API · NASA POWER

Why Bokeh—and why not a server framework?

The interaction needed here is small: choose one of two measures and a year, then compare daily values with a monthly mean. Bokeh can serialize plots, widgets, and data into standalone HTML. Its CustomJS callbacks run in the browser, so the published dashboard does not need a Python process, a database, or a live API key.

A tracked CSV snapshot makes the page deterministic: rebuilding the same commit does not depend on NASA’s API being available at build time. The trade-off is that data refreshes are deliberate; update the snapshot and metadata when you want newer observations.

Other tools solve different parts of the problem:

  • Seaborn is excellent for statistical charts in notebooks and reports, but it is not the dashboard runtime. Use it to explore distributions before choosing what should become interactive.
  • Bokeh fits this requirement because its standalone document supports browser-side interactivity without a Python server.
  • Dash and Shiny make more sense when an application needs server callbacks, shared state, or richer data workflows. That power also means hosting and maintaining a running service.
  • Streamlit is an approachable way to turn Python scripts into interactive apps, especially for data-centric prototypes. It likewise expects an app runtime on its hosting platform.

This is not a benchmark or universal ranking. It is a deployment decision: for two controls and a bundled dataset, the static artifact removes operational pieces the app does not need.

Build the dashboard

The repository keeps the moving parts visible:

build_dashboard.py       # reads CSV and writes index.html
requirements.txt         # Bokeh dependency
data/tacna_daily.csv     # pinned data snapshot
data/metadata.json       # source, units, coordinates, period
.github/workflows/pages.yml

The Python build script loads the CSV, prepares the selected year’s series and monthly averages, and wires both selectors to one CustomJS callback. When a control changes, the callback filters embedded arrays and updates the chart data sources. No request goes back to Python after the page loads.

To reproduce locally:

python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
python build_dashboard.py
python -m http.server 8000

Open http://localhost:8000. The generated index.html is a Bokeh document that loads BokehJS from its CDN; app data itself is embedded in the HTML.

Automate the build and deployment

A GitHub Actions workflow builds on every pull request, checks that the generated page exists and contains the standalone plot, and uploads it as a Pages artifact. On pushes to main (or a manual dispatch), a second job deploys that artifact to GitHub Pages. The workflow grants the Pages and OIDC permissions needed for deployment and keeps contents permission read-only.

The deployment pipeline is part of the example, not a hand-waved last step: inspect the workflow runs. The public result is hosted at GitHub Pages, a free static hosting option for a public repository. There is no container, server instance, cloud credential, or Azure bill to maintain.

What this approach gives up

A static page cannot securely hold private data, run Python callbacks after loading, or provide shared user sessions. The complete dataset is public and bundled into the artifact. For larger or confidential datasets—or server-side filtering, authentication, and live API integration—I would switch to Dash, Shiny, Streamlit, or a Bokeh server and deploy to a service designed to run an application process.

For this small public dataset, fewer runtime components are a feature. There is one published HTML file, one committed data snapshot, and one automated path from commit to site.

Try it and adapt it

Fork the repository, replace the CSV with a dataset you are allowed to publish, update data/metadata.json, and push to main. The page will rebuild and deploy. The project code is MIT-licensed; check the source provider’s terms and attribution requirements before reusing data.

Disclosure: This article was prepared with AI assistance and reviewed against the public repository, workflow, and deployed page.

title: Pioneers Across Europe Deploy NVIDIA Earth-2 Open Models to Power Real-World Weather and Climate Prediction
description: Weather forecasts shape more than daily plans; timely weather information is crucial for energy producers, insurers and transport operators to plan around changing conditions. A global forecast can show a storm taking shape, but decisions about solar farms, shipping routes or insured property depend on what happens locally. NVIDIA Earth-2 gives developers and researchers a […]

title: Map pointer coordinates into the canvas drawing buffer
description:
Convert the pointer position into drawing-buffer coordinates before drawing a marker on a resized canvas. The event reports viewport coordinates, while the drawing buffer has its own width and height.

For a canvas displayed at half its buffer width, one CSS pixel covers two buffer pixels. Subtracting the canvas position gives a local CSS coordinate. Multiply that value by the buffer-to-display ratio before drawing a marker or choosing a crop boundary.

function canvasPoint(canvas, event) {
  const rect = canvas.getBoundingClientRect();
  if (rect.width === 0 || rect.height === 0) return null;
  return {
    x: (event.clientX - rect.left) * canvas.width / rect.width,
    y: (event.clientY - rect.top) * canvas.height / rect.height
  };
}

This example assumes an axis-aligned canvas with no CSS border or padding and no rotation or skew. Put a decorative border on a wrapper. The bounding rectangle includes border and padding, so those would need separate handling if placed on the canvas itself.

The returned coordinates describe the canvas buffer. If the drawing context has a transform, or if the photo is letterboxed inside that buffer, mapping into the photo requires another step. Reject clicks outside the displayed photo before calculating a crop.

Check the mapping near both corners after resizing the page. If a marker follows the pointer near the upper-left corner but drifts near the lower-right, check the scale conversion. Read the current rectangle for the interaction; a rectangle saved before a layout change can be stale.

Reference: MDN

title: Policy Central: Detecting Conflicts, Redundancy, and Similarity in Deployed Police Policy
description:
arXiv:2610.29338v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Policy Central is a deployed system that helps police departments find relationships between sections of their written policy: whether two sections conflict, are redundant, are merely similar, or are different. We describe the system and compare two architectures. Retrieve-Judge, a retrieve-then-classify pipeline, runs as a cheap library-wide health signal; Screen-Confirm, a screen-then-confirm cascade, is a selective audit of the documents a reviewer chooses, checking them exhaustively against one another. On a 302-pair benchmark drawn from one department's ~84 real policy documents, given each pair Screen-Confirm reaches 0.795 aggregate recall and 0.885 on Conflict, so current models judge well. Finding the pair is the hard part: Retrieve-Judge's composed recall falls to 0.457, and Screen-Confirm recovers 0.472 (0.615 on Conflict). Today these pairs are found by reading the whole library, nearly 20,000 sections, checked against one another and re-checked after every revision. A scan that returns half of them in minutes, at low cost, and can be re-run on demand changes the economics of policy review even before recall improves.

title: MOSAIC: An Omni-Modal Benchmark for Long-Term Memory and Cross-Modal Reasoning in Conversational Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.29249v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Omni-modal assistants must remember not only what users say, but also what they show and convey. Existing long-term memory benchmarks are mostly text-and-image or report a single end-to-end score, so they cannot locate whether evidence is lost when it is represented, retrieved, delivered, or read. We introduce MOSAIC, a benchmark of 923 questions over persona-grounded histories of 11-24 sessions spanning text, image, video, and audio. MOSAIC constructs targeted spatial, temporal, and prosodic signals rather than decorative media, with the strongest causal validation for spatial information and selector-level validation for annotated prosody, and pairs them with a matched diagnostic protocol that freezes the question, reader, prompt, and budget while intervening on representation, retrieval, and delivery. Matched decomposition shows that representation loss is modality-dependent, residual reading dominates even under gold evidence, and abstention remains weak on these controls: strong answerable scores coexist with failures to refuse. MOSAIC thus turns omni-modal memory evaluation from a leaderboard into a diagnosis of write, retrieve, deliver, and read failures.

title: Tenant-Isolated Object Storage: Delete Old Thumbnails After Image Replace
description:
Tenant isolation changes the cleanup decision. For a customer-support service accepting private uploads, store each thumbnail generation under a tenant-scoped, image-scoped prefix, publish the complete replacement in the database, and only then enqueue deletion of the old generation. A one-day lifecycle rule can be a backstop, but it is not the replacement transaction.

That order is the answer. The storage system owns bytes; the database owns which bytes a support agent is allowed to request. Mixing those responsibilities creates a particularly unpleasant failure: a cleanup worker for tenant A can remove objects that a later retry, or even another tenant, still considers live.

How should you delete old thumbnails after an image replacement in object storage?

Use an immutable generation rather than overwriting keys such as thumbs/160.webp. A useful key shape is:

tenants/{tenant_id}/images/{image_id}/generations/{generation_id}/{variant}.webp

For tenant acme, image img_42, and generation g_18, the 160-pixel variant becomes tenants/acme/images/img_42/generations/g_18/160.webp. The application record stores the active generation or its complete prefix. It should never discover the active generation by scanning storage after the fact.

The write path has three durable boundaries:

  1. Validate that the caller belongs to the tenant and that the upload is private.
  2. Write every expected thumbnail under a new generation prefix.
  3. In a database transaction, publish that generation and record the old prefix as a cleanup job.
  4. Let a worker list the recorded old prefix and batch-delete only those returned keys.

The database commit is the visibility boundary. Before it, readers use the old set. After it, readers use the new set, even if the cleanup worker has not run yet. That temporary duplicate storage is an acceptable failure boundary; serving a thumbnail that has already been deleted is not.

The cleanup target must be captured at publication time. Imagine replacement A publishes g_18, then replacement B publishes g_19 before A's worker gets scheduled. A must delete the prefix belonging to g_17; it must not reread the row and calculate “everything except g_19.” That calculation can accidentally include the generation B had just published or a generation needed by a delayed reader. A recorded target makes retries narrow and auditable.

This is also where a Node.js implementation needs discipline. The client library, promise chain, or queue changes the syntax, not the state machine: prepare objects, publish the active pointer, enqueue the old prefix, list it, then batch-delete the listed keys. Keep the storage interface small enough that the application can test this order without a real bucket.

The architecture decision record

The invariants are more important than the particular object-storage API.

Decision Invariant Failure boundary
Prefix includes tenant, image, and generation A cleanup job has one explicit ownership scope A malformed or missing scope is rejected before deletion
New variants are written before publication The active database pointer never names a partial set An incomplete new generation is abandoned and later reaped
Publication and cleanup are separate A worker cannot make the live record disappear The old set may remain temporarily
Cleanup stores its target prefix A retry repeats the same deletion set A newer replacement does not change an older job's target
Batch deletion is idempotent Replaying a completed job is harmless An already-absent key is treated as success by the adapter

The tenant prefix is a security boundary in the naming scheme, not an authorization system. Every read and write still needs an authorization check against the tenant in the request and the tenant stored with the image. A prefix filter reduces the blast radius of a mistake; it does not prove that the caller is entitled to the prefix.

Object versioning is a separate recovery control. It can preserve prior object versions after an overwrite, but it does not tell the application which thumbnail generation is active, and it does not replace tenant checks. If rollback requirements depend on retaining old object versions, enable and test that feature deliberately; generation-scoped keys remain useful because they make publication and cleanup sets explicit. The general storage documentation for object versioning describes this distinction between a current version and retained prior versions.

There is a concurrency question here that storage alone cannot settle. Two image replacements need a database transaction, row lock, compare-and-swap field, or serialized queue, depending on the service's write rate and database. I'm not sure which coordination primitive fits without those details. The non-negotiable part is that a job records the version it replaced and never performs a broad “delete all non-current objects” scan.

A small, testable cleanup path

The following standard-library example models the critical path. Its adapter exposes prefix listing and batch deletion, while the database keeps the active generation and cleanup target. A production Node.js service can implement the same contract with its chosen object-storage client.

from __future__ import annotations

import sqlite3
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Iterable, Protocol


class ThumbnailStore(Protocol):
    def put(self, key: str, content: bytes) -> None: ...
    def list_prefix(self, prefix: str) -> list[str]: ...
    def delete_batch(self, keys: Iterable[str]) -> None: ...


@dataclass
class MemoryStore:
    objects: dict[str, bytes] = field(default_factory=dict)

    def put(self, key: str, content: bytes) -> None:
        self.objects[key] = content

    def list_prefix(self, prefix: str) -> list[str]:
        return sorted(key for key in self.objects if key.startswith(prefix))

    def delete_batch(self, keys: Iterable[str]) -> None:
        for key in keys:
            self.objects.pop(key, None)


def prefix(tenant_id: str, image_id: str, generation_id: str) -> str:
    return (
        f"tenants/{tenant_id}/images/{image_id}/"
        f"generations/{generation_id}/"
    )


def replace_image(
    db: sqlite3.Connection,
    store: ThumbnailStore,
    tenant_id: str,
    image_id: str,
    generation_id: str,
    variants: dict[str, bytes],
) -> None:
    row = db.execute(
        "SELECT active_prefix FROM images WHERE tenant_id = ? AND image_id = ?",
        (tenant_id, image_id),
    ).fetchone()
    old_prefix = row[0] if row else None
    new_prefix = prefix(tenant_id, image_id, generation_id)

    for variant, content in variants.items():
        store.put(f"{new_prefix}{variant}", content)

    with db:
        db.execute(
            """
            INSERT INTO images (tenant_id, image_id, active_prefix)
            VALUES (?, ?, ?)
            ON CONFLICT(tenant_id, image_id) DO UPDATE SET
                active_prefix = excluded.active_prefix
            """,
            (tenant_id, image_id, new_prefix),
        )
        if old_prefix and old_prefix != new_prefix:
            db.execute(
                "INSERT INTO cleanup_jobs (tenant_id, prefix, state) VALUES (?, ?, ?)",
                (tenant_id, old_prefix, "pending"),
            )


def run_cleanup_job(store: ThumbnailStore, prefix_to_remove: str) -> None:
    keys = store.list_prefix(prefix_to_remove)
    if keys:
        store.delete_batch(keys)

The example deliberately does not delete inside replace_image. A request can return after publication while a worker continues safely, and a worker can retry after a process restart. In production, the cleanup job should also carry an image identifier and generation identifier, record attempts, and use bounded batches so one unusually large upload does not monopolize the worker.

The database transaction shown here assumes the row and job tables have the matching uniqueness constraints. It also leaves a subtle production concern visible: writing objects and committing a database transaction are different systems. If the process dies after the object writes but before publication, the new prefix is orphaned. A periodic reaper may remove generations that are neither active nor referenced by a pending job, but that reaper must use the same tenant-scoped naming and authorization rules as the normal worker.

What can go wrong during listing and batch deletion?

Listing is a snapshot for a cleanup attempt, not a permanent inventory. New objects should not be written into an old generation prefix, and the worker should treat a repeated listing as normal after a retry. If the storage API paginates results, the adapter must consume every page before declaring the prefix empty. If batch deletion has a request-size limit, split the listed keys into bounded batches and persist progress or make replay safe.

The error policy should distinguish an already-absent stale key from an authorization failure, malformed request, or rate limit. A missing object can be success for an idempotent cleanup job. A permission failure must remain visible and must not trigger a retry loop that silently expands its target. A throttled request should back off according to the service response when possible. Never send the service's authorization header to a presigned download URL.

Observability should answer four questions for every job: which tenant owns it, which generation was published, which prefix is being removed, and how many keys remain after the attempt. Log identifiers and counts rather than private image contents. Alert on cleanup age and repeated authorization failures; a growing queue is a storage hygiene problem, while a database pointer to missing active objects is an availability and integrity problem.

The private-upload requirement also affects the download path. Return short-lived signed links only after checking tenant ownership, and do not treat an unguessable object key as permission. This design is not suitable for public static assets, permanent cache URLs, or a workflow that requires users to share immutable public links. For those cases, use a separate public-asset policy and keep it outside the private support-upload namespace.

Why a one-day lifecycle rule is only a backstop

Lifecycle expiration has a minimum age of one day in this decision. That is useful for abandoned generations, crash leftovers, and retention hygiene when delayed removal is acceptable. It is the wrong mechanism for an image replacement that should stop exposing the old generation as soon as the database publishes the new one.

The rejected lifecycle-only design has a clean boundary: it knows object age, not the database event that made a generation obsolete. Keep explicit prefix listing and batch deletion on the replacement path, then use lifecycle as a coarse safety net. The trade-off is extra worker code and more operational signals in exchange for a small, explicit deletion set and a clear tenant boundary.

Before shipping, test concurrent replacements for one image and for two tenants with similar image IDs. Test a crash after the last thumbnail write, a crash after publication, an empty prefix, a paginated listing, a repeated batch delete, and a rejected tenant authorization. Test the retention rule with a clock you control. Storage cleanup is uninteresting when it works; the test suite is what makes the destructive path trustworthy.

References

  • https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/66/r2/final
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/Versioning.html

title: Firefox 153 Local Mode: Open Local HTML Files Over HTTPS Without a Server
description:
Firefox 153 added Local Mode to DevTools: it maps a folder on your disk to an https:// origin. You don't run npx serve or python -m http.server, and you don't touch mkcert. Open DevTools, point it at a folder, and https://shop.localhost/index.html loads straight from ~/code/shop.

The official docs pitch it in one line: "This prevents having to spawn a HTTP server to test a web page." I spent a while trying to poke holes in it. My take is that the docs oversell the HTTPS part, which localhost already gave you, and undersell per-project origins, which fix something that annoys me every day. Below is the setup, plus the limits that will send you back to Vite.

What Firefox Local Mode actually does

You register mappings. Each one has two fields:

  • Origin: a hostname Firefox serves over https://, e.g. firefox.localhost
  • Local folder: the directory the files come from, e.g. /home/alex/app

After that, https://firefox.localhost/ loads /home/alex/app/index.html and gets a proper origin instead of null or file://, with the scheme, host and storage partition the rest of the web platform expects.

The docs list two goals. One is to "test all Web APIs, including the ones being restricted to Secure Contexts (i.e. using https)". The other is "having many distinct origins (domain) for each experiment / project" with "dedicated storage/cookies for each." The second one is the reason I'd keep using it.

How to set up Local Mode (three ways)

1. The DevTools Options panel

Open DevTools (F12) and go to the Options panel (the ⋯ menu, then Settings). Add a mapping with an origin and a folder, and add as many more as you need. This is the setup for projects you come back to.

2. The file:// notification bar

Drag an HTML file into Firefox, or open any file:// URL, with DevTools open. A notification bar appears at the top of DevTools with two buttons:

  • Add To Settings opens the Options panel with a permanent mapping for that file's location already filled in.
  • Try it creates a transient mapping for the current file or folder. It disappears when you close DevTools or Firefox.

"Try it" is what I'd use for a one-off: someone sends you a zip containing a demo, you unzip it, open index.html, click once, and you're on https.

3. about:config, for teams and dotfiles

Each mapping is stored as three prefs, where N is an incrementing integer:

devtools.local-mode.mappings.N.origin    = "shop.localhost"
devtools.local-mode.mappings.N.path      = "/home/alex/code/shop"
devtools.local-mode.mappings.N.disabled  = false   (optional)

Since they're ordinary prefs, you can put them in a profile's user.js and commit that to your dotfiles or an onboarding repo:

user_pref("devtools.local-mode.mappings.0.origin", "shop.localhost");
user_pref("devtools.local-mode.mappings.0.path", "/home/alex/code/shop");
user_pref("devtools.local-mode.mappings.1.origin", "admin.localhost");
user_pref("devtools.local-mode.mappings.1.path", "/home/alex/code/admin");

On Lobsters, kevincox already sets Firefox prefs through Nix and half-jokingly suggested deploying static sites straight into the Firefox config. The docs say the prefs exist "so that you can easily import and transfer them between profiles, or via automation." Paths are absolute, so a shared file only works if everyone keeps their checkouts in the same location.

Do you even need HTTPS on localhost? Usually not

The headline feature is "test HTTPS-only APIs without a server," and I don't fully buy it.

http://localhost is already a secure context. MDN's Secure Contexts page lists localhost, *.localhost, 127.0.0.0/8 and ::1 as potentially trustworthy, and it lists the file scheme as well. crypto.subtle and the async clipboard API already work on npx serve at localhost:3000. On Lobsters, majaha checked and found that window.isSecureContext is true on file:// in Firefox.

So if you're on one machine and already running a server, Local Mode doesn't unlock anything you didn't have.

It's more useful in the situation the feature is named for, where you skip the server entirely. A file loaded from disk can technically count as secure and still be unusable:

  • Service workers don't register from file://. The Service Worker spec rejects any script URL whose scheme isn't http or https. Local Mode gives you https, so registration works.
  • The bigger issue is the origin. Firefox has treated local files as their own origins since the CVE-2019-11730 fix in Firefox 68, because the previous behaviour let a downloaded HTML file read its neighbours. That fix is why fetch('./data.json') from a file:// page breaks. With a mapped origin, everything in the folder shares one origin.

So Local Mode is a good fix for "open a folder and have it behave like a website," and mostly irrelevant for testing secure-context APIs, where the localhost server you already run was fine.

Per-project origins are the part worth keeping

Everybody's localhost:3000 holds leftovers from six projects. There's an auth token from last week's prototype still in localStorage and a service worker registered by some other app still intercepting requests. Somewhere in there is a cookie named session that belongs to who knows what.

They collide because the origin is http://localhost:3000 whichever project happens to be on that port. Each Local Mode mapping gets its own hostname, so shop.localhost and admin.localhost have separate storage, cookies and service worker registrations. You don't have to clear site data before switching projects, and you don't get a stale SW from another repo serving a cached index.html.

You can get the same result with a server by giving each project its own port or a *.localhost hostname in Vite. In practice almost nobody does.

Where it falls short

First, it only works while DevTools is open. The docs say so directly: "These mappings are only functional when DevTools are opened." Close the toolbox and https://shop.localhost stops resolving. For debugging that's fine. As a general way to keep a local site around, it's annoying.

Only Firefox can use it. The docs present this as a security property: no other program on your machine or network can reach the mappings. That also means no curl, no Playwright running in Chromium, and no testing from your phone. In the thread, pocket_walrus and Pomax both said they'd reach for Caddy when they need local HTTPS, and for anything beyond one browser on one machine that's still my answer too.

It also just serves files. The docs say nothing about custom response headers, SPA fallback rewrites or live reload. If your app needs Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy for SharedArrayBuffer, or /dashboard has to fall back to index.html, you need a server.

And early reports are mixed. On Lobsters, kiwec hit "failed to load" errors and a security error with the default firefox.localhost name, then went back to cloudflared tunnel. BD103 had it working for a handful of PNGs. I'd treat it as a v1 feature for now.

Local Mode vs npx serve vs Vite vs Caddy

You want to... Local Mode npx serve / python -m http.server Vite Caddy / mkcert
Open a static folder on https, no process Yes No No No
Isolate storage per project Yes, one origin each Only via separate ports Configurable Configurable
Register a service worker Yes Yes (on localhost) Yes Yes
Use TypeScript, JSX, bare imports No No Yes No
HMR / live reload No No Yes No
Custom headers (COOP/COEP) Not documented serve via serve.json; http.server no Yes Yes
Reach it from a phone or another browser No LAN, http unless you pass serve --ssl-cert LAN, http by default Yes, once the device trusts the CA
Works with DevTools closed No Yes Yes Yes

My rule after reading through all this: if the project has a build step, Local Mode isn't for it. Keep Vite. If it's a static folder (a demo, a bug repro, a vanilla JS prototype, a PWA spike, a generated docs site), stop starting a server for it. Map the folder once with "Add To Settings" and be done.

The case I'd use it for most is bug reproductions. Someone files an issue with a zip, and instead of cd, npx serve, and "wait, port 3000 is taken," you open index.html, click Try it, and you have an https origin that won't touch anything else in your browser.

Try it today

  1. Update to Firefox 153 or later (153 shipped July 21, 2026).
  2. Open any local index.html with DevTools open.
  3. Click Try it in the notification bar.
  4. Put an empty sw.js next to it, then run isSecureContext and navigator.serviceWorker.register('./sw.js') in the console.
  5. If it holds up, click Add To Settings and choose a *.localhost name per project.

How do you test HTTPS-only APIs locally right now: mkcert, Caddy, a tunnel, or push to staging and hope? And is "DevTools must stay open" a dealbreaker for you, or a fair price for never typing npx serve again?

Sources

  • Firefox DevTools docs: Local Mode
  • Lobsters discussion: Firefox Local Mode
  • MDN: Secure contexts
  • MDN: Using Service Workers
  • W3C Service Worker spec: register algorithm
  • MDN: Firefox 153 release notes for developers
  • Arch Linux security tracker: CVE-2019-11730

title: What Is USFP? Ultra-Dense Small Form Factor Pluggable Optics for the AI Era
description:
AI training clusters are running out of three things at once: rack space, power, and fiber. A modern GPU cluster interconnects tens of thousands of accelerators, and the scale-out fabric that ties them together is built from pluggable optics. When every port is an OSFP or QSFP-DD module, a 1U switch tops out around 32 × 800G — and each module can draw 15–30 W. Multiply that across a 102.4T switch and the optics alone consume kilowatts, while the faceplate runs out of room and the fiber plant becomes a spaghetti wall of MPO trunks.

USFP attacks this directly. By shrinking the module to roughly half the width, USFP doubles faceplate density — up to ~64 × 800G per 1U — while targeting lower per-module power. The payoff is more fiber density and cable density per rack, fewer switches to reach the same GPU count, and a better watts per terabit figure for the whole AI data center.

What Exactly Is USFP?
USFP (Ultra Small / Ultra-Dense Small Form-factor Pluggable) is a very compact optical transceiver form factor defined by an industry MSA. Like OSFP and QSFP-DD, it is a hot-pluggable module that sits in a cage on the switch faceplate — but the cage and module are markedly narrower. USFP uses a short electrical reach to the host ASIC and is specified around 100G and 200G electrical lanes, carrying PAM4 signaling. An 800G USFP module aggregates eight 100G lanes or four 200G lanes, and the same mechanical platform is intended to scale toward 1.6T as 200G per lane matures (aligned with IEEE 802.3dj and OIF 224G work).

The defining idea is simple: more ports, less power, less fiber per bit. USFP does not invent new physics — it re-packages proven silicon photonics, lasers, and DSP/LPO electronics into a denser shell so that density, not raw reach, is the win.

Challenges and Caveats
Young ecosystem: fewer module and switch options than OSFP/QSFP-DD; validate interoperability.
Reach trade-off: density-optimized, so long-haul reach is not its game — keep OSFP/QSFP-DD for ZR/long DCI.
Thermals at the faceplate: more ports per RU concentrates heat; confirm switch airflow and cooling.
Fiber plant: higher density changes MPO/trunk counts and breakout planning — design the cabling, not just the switch.
How to Choose
Pick USFP when port density and power are your binding constraints — AI scale-out, dense leaf tiers, and short-reach DCI. Stay with OSFP/QSFP-DD for long reach, multi-vendor fabrics, and mature ecosystems. If you are power-limited at the rack edge, evaluate USFP + LPO, and pilot CPO where density justifies it.

Frequently Asked Questions
What does USFP stand for?
USFP stands for Ultra Small Form-factor Pluggable (often described as Ultra-Dense Small Form-factor Pluggable) — a compact pluggable optical transceiver form factor defined by an industry MSA for high-density, lower-power links.

How is USFP different from OSFP and QSFP-DD?
USFP is roughly half the width, doubling faceplate density (up to ~64×800G per 1U vs ~32) and targeting lower power — optimized for density and AI scale-out. OSFP and QSFP-DD are wider, higher-power, and stronger for long reach and multi-vendor interoperability.

Is USFP 800G or 1.6T?
USFP is shipping for 800G today (8×100G or 4×200G PAM4 lanes), with 1.6T the roadmap target as 200G-per-lane optics and SerDes mature.

How does USFP relate to CPO and LPO?
USFP is the pluggable bridge: its compact, low-power design is LPO-friendly today and delivers CPO-like density while remaining field-replaceable — a stepping stone toward near-packaged/co-packaged optics and optical I/O.

Is USFP a replacement for OSFP?
No — they coexist. Use USFP where density and watts dominate (AI scale-out, dense leaf); use OSFP/QSFP-DD for long reach, ZR/DCI, and where you need the broadest multi-vendor ecosystem.

title: Self-hosted Plausible analytics, in one command
description:
For a while, railyard.run ran with zero analytics. Not out of principle — we just hadn’t gotten to it, which meant every “is anyone actually reading this” question was a guess. Fixing it became the first real test of whether “self-hosted, one click” actually holds up for something we’d use ourselves, not just something we built for other people’s apps.

What we launched#
Plausible Community Edition, as a Railyard stack template: three services — Plausible itself, Postgres for its own app data, and ClickHouse for the actual analytics events — provisioned together on one of our own servers.

railyard launch plausible --server Copy
That’s the whole provisioning step. No separate ClickHouse setup, no wiring connection strings by hand — the template declares all three services and how they talk to each other, and Railyard deploys the set as one unit.

What came after the launch command#
The rest was the normal first-run of any self-hosted app, not anything Railyard-specific:

Open the app’s URL, sign up as the instance owner — Plausible’s own first-run flow, nothing to pre-seed.

  • Add a website, enter the domain being tracked. Copy the tracking snippet it generates and drop it in the site’s . No custom domain was even necessary — the app’s default *.apps.railyard.run URL was enough to run the dashboard and serve the tracking script. We only use that path because it’s genuinely simpler, not because anything was missing.

Where it actually broke, briefly#
It didn’t — which is itself worth saying plainly, since the point of posting this at all is to be honest about what self-hosting something actually costs in practice. The template launched clean, the three services found each other over Railyard’s private networking without any manual env var wiring, and the tracking script started showing pageviews in Plausible’s Realtime view within seconds of being added to the site.

The one thing worth knowing going in: a fresh launch creates a new app every time you run it, so launching twice means two full stacks running side by side, not an update to the first one. Easy mistake, easy fix — apps:rm --confirm in the CLI removes the extra one cleanly.

Why self-hosted instead of Plausible Cloud#
Plausible Cloud is a fine product and the simpler choice for most teams. We picked self-hosted specifically because it’s the same category of claim we make about everything else on Railyard: you should be able to run the tools you depend on, on infrastructure you control, without a second vendor relationship for every piece of your stack. Cookie-free, no consent banner, and the data never leaves a server we provisioned ourselves.

If you’re weighing the same tradeoff for your own site, the Plausible template is one click away, and Logs, metrics and alerts covers the rest of what Railyard surfaces about traffic without a separate analytics stack at all.
