title: Send Contracts via WhatsApp with DoAide Contract Generator
description:
Problem

Indian SMB owners, freelancers, and startups often need to share newly generated contracts—NDAs, employment contracts, service agreements—quickly with clients or partners. Sending a PDF by email or uploading it to a cloud folder adds friction and delays the signing process. This is where contract generator pays off in practice.

How the Feature Works

DoAide Contracts adds a single‑click WhatsApp share button after a contract is generated. The flow is:

  1. Generate: The user selects a template (e.g., employment contract template) and fills in the form.
  2. Store: FastAPI saves the contract as a PDF blob in PostgreSQL and returns a contract ID.
  3. Share: The React UI renders a Share via WhatsApp button. When clicked, it calls a FastAPI endpoint that streams the PDF to the WhatsApp Business API.
  4. Confirm: A toast informs the user that the contract was sent.

The user never leaves the site; the contract is delivered instantly to the chosen WhatsApp contact. Getting contract generator right early saves rework later.

Frontend Implementation

The share button lives in components/ShareWhatsAppButton.jsx:

import { useState } from "react";

export default function ShareWhatsAppButton({ contractId, recipient }) {
  const [sending, setSending] = useState(false);

  const send = async () => {
    setSending(true);
    try {
      const res = await fetch(`/api/contract/${contractId}/send-whatsapp`, {
        method: "POST",
        headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
        body: JSON.stringify({ phone: recipient }),
      });
      if (!res.ok) throw new Error("Send failed");
      alert("Contract sent to WhatsApp");
    } catch (e) {
      alert("Could not send contract");
    } finally {
      setSending(false);
    }
  };

  return (
    <button onClick={send} disabled={sending} className="btn-whatsapp">
      {sending ? "Sending…" : "Share via WhatsApp"}
    </button>
  );
}

The component uses a simple POST request; the button is styled with the teal theme introduced in the latest branding update.

Backend Implementation

FastAPI exposes the endpoint in api/contract.py:

from fastapi import APIRouter, HTTPException
from sqlalchemy.orm import Session
from .models import Contract
from .whatsapp import send_pdf_via_whatsapp

router = APIRouter()

@router.post("/contract/{contract_id}/send-whatsapp")
async def send_whatsapp(contract_id: int, payload: dict, db: Session):
    contract = db.query(Contract).filter(Contract.id == contract_id).first()
    if not contract:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="Contract not found")

    phone = payload.get("phone")
    if not phone:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=400, detail="Phone number required")

    # contract.pdf is a byte array stored in PostgreSQL
    success = await send_pdf_via_whatsapp(phone, contract.pdf, contract.title)
    if not success:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=500, detail="WhatsApp send failed")

    return {"status": "sent"}

The helper send_pdf_via_whatsapp wraps the Twilio WhatsApp API:

import aiohttp

async def send_pdf_via_whatsapp(to: str, pdf_bytes: bytes, title: str) -> bool:
    url = "https://api.twilio.com/2010-04-01/Accounts/ACXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX/Messages.json"
    data = {
        "From": "whatsapp:+14155238886",
        "To": f"whatsapp:{to}",
        "Body": f"Here is your {title}.",
    }
    files = {"MediaUrl": ("contract.pdf", pdf_bytes, "application/pdf")}
    auth = aiohttp.BasicAuth("ACXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX", "your_auth_token")
    async with aiohttp.ClientSession(auth=auth) as session:
        async with session.post(url, data=data, files=files) as resp:
            return resp.status == 201

The PDF is streamed directly; no temporary file is written to disk. Good contract generator keeps the rest of the workflow predictable.

UX Considerations

  • The Share via WhatsApp button appears only after the contract is ready, keeping the interface clean.
  • The button uses a 48 px touch target, satisfying the mobile improvements commit.
  • On success, the toast uses the Inter font, aligning with the unified DoAide branding.

Benefits for Indian SMBs

  • Instant delivery: No email attachments, no manual uploads.
  • Higher conversion: Clients receive the contract in their primary messaging app.
  • Compliance: The contract remains a single PDF file, preserving formatting for legal review.

Conclusion

By integrating WhatsApp sharing into the contract generation workflow, DoAide Contracts removes a common bottleneck for Indian SMB owners. The implementation demonstrates how a lightweight FastAPI endpoint and a React button can leverage an external API to deliver a seamless user experience.

Further Reading

  • The project’s blog now contains a post on WhatsApp contract sharing.
  • The new SEO‑friendly blog posts include structured data for better discoverability.

Code Repository

All changes are available in the latest commit on GitHub: https://github.com/r2st/DoAide-Contracts/commit/9778d074b8bea1329eaed78e12438e9b496de2ed

Related reading

  • DoAide Contracts
  • DoAide Contracts on GitHub

title: Marketplace Fan-Out: Node.js Cron and Queue Patterns for Scheduled Email Reports
description:
Short answer: use cron to create one durable reporting job, and use a queue when that job fans a shipment update out to many subscribers or needs independent retries. The decision is about the failure boundary, not which tool has the shorter configuration.

I care about this distinction because I have been paged for missed jobs and duplicate deliveries. A daily report email looks small on a diagram. In a marketplace, the report may also carry a shipment-status change to a large subscriber list, and a single slow recipient can turn a tidy timer into a long-running delivery operation.

The report is a business record, not a timer event

Cron is the clock. A queue is the work ledger. The durable report record is the evidence. Keep those responsibilities separate even if the first implementation lives in one Node.js process.

The simplest design is a scheduled command that computes the reporting period, writes a run record, and hands a bounded job to a worker. If report generation and the initial email handoff are predictably short, the scheduled command can perform both steps. When the job fans out shipment updates, however, the command should create independently retryable units: one tenant and reporting period, or one stable subscriber group, depending on the product's delivery contract.

That gives the scheduler a small, inspectable responsibility. It starts work once for a period. The worker owns delivery attempts. The database records what the business considers complete. A queue does not make a message exactly once; it gives the worker a place to retry work whose acknowledgement and side effect may finish at different times. I want the runbook to answer four questions without asking an engineer to infer intent from process logs: which period was due, which shipment update was selected, which subscribers were targeted, and which delivery result was final. The same record also gives support a stable explanation when a subscriber reports a missing email and gives an operator a precise item to replay instead of rerunning every tenant's work.

Use a queue for duration, retry isolation, or fan-out. Don't add one merely because queues sound more production-ready.

What does a marketplace Node.js SaaS need from cron, queue, and a scheduled daily email report?

The bounded failure I keep in the runbook is straightforward. A scheduled run creates a shipment-update job, the worker hands the email to the provider, and the worker loses its acknowledgement before it records success. The broker delivers the job again. A second send follows unless the application has a stable delivery key.

It failed quietly.

The reverse failure is just as important. The scheduler may run late, fail before creating a job, or create a run that has no completed delivery record. A timer log cannot answer the customer question, “Did my report for this period arrive?” The application needs a durable record keyed by the tenant, reporting period, shipment event or digest version, and subscriber.

This is where a small postmortem becomes an architecture rule: schedule intent and delivery completion are different facts. Alert on a missing business record after the agreed deadline, then replay the same period with the same idempotency key. Recovery should converge on one report, not create a new edition every time an operator presses retry. In the shipment fan-out case, the key must be derived from the business identity rather than from the queue message ID: a new message created during recovery still represents the same tenant, period, shipment update or digest version, and subscriber. That identity choice is the difference between a replay and an accidental second notification, so it belongs in the data model, tests, and operator command before production traffic arrives.

The practical consequence is that the queue consumer must tolerate redelivery. RabbitMQ's acknowledgement documentation describes this boundary for a standard message consumer, and the principle applies to any at-least-once delivery system. Acknowledging before the side effect succeeds loses work; acknowledging after the side effect succeeds can repeat work. Idempotency is the control that makes the second outcome safe.

The queue is a governance choice

Write down the delivery contract before choosing the component. “Send the daily report” is not specific enough. Decide whether one subscriber gets one email per reporting period, whether shipment updates may be coalesced, and how late data changes the report. Decide which clock defines the period as well: tenant timezone, marketplace timezone, or UTC.

Then define the recovery path. The operator needs to find a missing period, enqueue it without changing its identity, observe attempts and final status, and stop a retry storm. These are runbook requirements, not optional dashboard polish.

Boundary Cron-only worker Cron plus queue
Time Starts the bounded run Starts job creation
Work Performs the whole operation Performs one retryable unit
Retry Repeats the whole run Retries an individual unit
Duplicate control Application idempotency Application idempotency plus consumer acknowledgement
Operations One process and its logs Scheduler, broker, workers, and metrics

The trade-off is real. A queue improves isolation while adding a broker, worker lifecycle, visibility rules, and another failure surface. A cron-only path is easier to operate while making the whole report the retry unit. For a small report with one recipient and a harmless rerun, that simplicity can be the better engineering choice.

Make replay the normal operator action

The following code keeps the business rule independent of the queue implementation. SendOnce must use durable storage or a mail boundary that honors the key. An in-memory map is not enough; a process restart would erase the only duplicate check.

package delivery

import (
    "context"
    "crypto/sha256"
    "encoding/hex"
    "fmt"
    "time"
)

type ShipmentReport struct {
    TenantID     string
    SubscriberID string
    Period       time.Time
    Address      string
    Body         []byte
}

type Mailer interface {
    SendOnce(ctx context.Context, key, address, subject string, body []byte) error
}

func Deliver(ctx context.Context, mailer Mailer, report ShipmentReport) error {
    if report.TenantID == "" || report.SubscriberID == "" ||
        report.Address == "" || report.Period.IsZero() {
        return fmt.Errorf("invalid shipment report")
    }

    period := report.Period.UTC().Format("2006-01-02")
    key := deliveryKey(report.TenantID, report.SubscriberID, period)
    subject := "Daily shipment report for " + period

    if err := mailer.SendOnce(ctx, key, report.Address, subject, report.Body); err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("deliver report %s: %w", key, err)
    }
    return nil
}

func deliveryKey(tenantID, subscriberID, period string) string {
    value := tenantID + "\x00" + subscriberID + "\x00" + period
    sum := sha256.Sum256([]byte(value))
    return hex.EncodeToString(sum[:])
}

The worker should acknowledge only after SendOnce returns success. If it returns an error, the queue policy can retry the same logical job. The mail adapter should retain the successful result for the key, and the reporting record should make reconciliation possible when the network outcome is ambiguous.

There is no universal exactly-once promise between a database and an external mail service. If the mail boundary has no idempotency contract, document the remaining duplicate risk and build a reconciliation state machine. “Exactly once” in an architecture document does not create an atomic transaction.

A Go delivery boundary for the decision

Stay with cron alone when the report is bounded, the recipient set is small, the complete operation can be retried safely, and the team can monitor the process that owns the timer. Keep a durable run record anyway. Small systems still miss work.

Choose cron plus a queue when subscriber fan-out makes one slow delivery hold up every other delivery, when a failed subscriber should retry without rebuilding the report, or when operators need to replay one period and inspect each attempt. Split work around a business-stable key, not an arbitrary batch size that changes between retries.

Your mileage may vary on the exact split. Measure generation time, delivery latency, retry volume, and the deadline promised to subscribers before adding another component. I’m not sure a recipient count alone can tell you when to introduce a queue; the data shape and recovery contract matter more.

This pattern is not suitable when the actual problem is a multi-step workflow with durable waits and joins. Use a workflow engine if the report requires several dependent stages whose state must survive deployments. It is also a poor fit when the team cannot operate a broker or has no need for isolated retries. Stick with a direct scheduled worker until the failure mode justifies the operational cost.

Keep the smallest honest system

The final rule is plain: let cron express when a reporting period becomes due, let a queue carry retryable shipment-update work, and let durable application records prove what each subscriber received. The tools may change. That evidence should not.

References

  • https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/crontab.5.html
  • https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/confirms

title: How Much Gradient Does Truncated Backprop Lose in Looped Transformers?
description:
arXiv:2610.28871v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Looped transformers reuse one block of layers many times and are often trained by backpropagating through only the last k loops. We measure how much of the weight gradient this throws away, exactly and for every k from one backward pass, on nine looped language models, and report three findings. First, on a trained model this lost gradient is set near the output: once the loop count is well above k, it barely changes with the loop count (within about 0.03 from 32 to 64 loops on the three models we tested, as a pre-registered test predicted for Parcae). Where the backward signal shrinks, $\rho^k$, with $\rho$ the signal's fitted shrink per loop, approximates it at moderate loop counts but overstates it at long ones, because the fitted $\rho$ drifts up as the fit takes in more loops. On Ouro the signal grows, and keeping two of four loops still loses 81% of the final output's gradient. Second, the lost gradient falls during fine-tuning, by 0.07-0.22 within 300 steps on three of four models, on held-out problems too. The fall is not just the read-out's share of the gradient; training only the layers outside the loop reproduced up to half of it, and it also falls under truncated training. So a trained model's value overstates what truncation removes later. Third, we could not show that it predicts the training cost of truncation better than rules that need no measurement: on two new models it tied Parcae's cost at the same k, in a test too small to separate them.

title: Rent Receipt Generator: DoAide Docs for Indian Tenants
description:
Problem

Rent receipts are a legal requirement for tenants and landlords in India. In practice, many parties draft these documents manually in Word or Google Docs, which is error‑prone and time‑consuming. A typical rent receipt must capture This is where rent receipt generator pays off in practice.

  • tenant and landlord names
  • property address
  • rent amount and currency
  • period covered
  • payment date
  • optional tax details

Missing or incorrect data can lead to disputes or tax compliance issues. A web‑based solution that generates a ready‑to‑print PDF eliminates manual effort and ensures consistent formatting.

Architecture Overview

DoAide Docs follows a React + FastAPI stack with Vite as the build tool.

frontend  ──►  React (Vite) ──►  API Client
backend   ──►  FastAPI ──►  Pydantic Models
          └──►  PDF Renderer

The front‑end renders a lightweight form. On submission, the data is POSTed to a FastAPI endpoint /api/rent-receipt. The endpoint validates the payload with Pydantic, renders a Jinja2 template into HTML, and then converts that HTML to a PDF using a library such as weasyprint. The PDF is streamed back to the browser for download.

User Flow

  1. Visit the site – No login is required. The landing page displays a call‑to‑action button Generate Rent Receipt.
  2. Fill the form – The form is built with React hooks (useState, useEffect) and styled with Tailwind CSS. Each field has a 48 px touch target (see commit fix(mobile): 48px touch targets).
  3. Submit – On click, the form data is JSON‑encoded and sent via fetch: 
   const response = await fetch('/api/rent-receipt', {
     method: 'POST',
     headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
     body: JSON.stringify(formData),
   });
   const blob = await response.blob();
   const url = window.URL.createObjectURL(blob);
   window.open(url);
  1. Download – The browser opens the PDF in a new tab; the user can print or save it.

The flow is fully responsive; the header wraps on small screens, and the form layout adapts to mobile devices thanks to the 48 px touch target improvement. Getting rent receipt generator right early saves rework later.

Implementation Details

Front‑end

  • React: Functional components with hooks.
  • Vite: Fast bundling and hot‑module replacement.
  • Tailwind CSS: Utility‑first styling; the 48 px touch target rule is enforced via a custom utility class.
  • WhatsApp Share: Added in feat: WhatsApp share on homepage, blog and compare pages – the share button uses the navigator.share API where available.

Back‑end

  • FastAPI: Handles the /api/rent-receipt POST route.
  • Pydantic: Defines RentReceiptRequest with fields tenant_name, landlord_name, address, rent_amount, period, payment_date, and optional tax_exempt.
  • Jinja2: Renders a pre‑defined template rent_receipt.html.
  • PDF Generation: The commit log does not specify the renderer, but the typical approach in FastAPI projects is weasyprint or pdfkit. The endpoint streams the PDF with StreamingResponse. 
from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse
import weasyprint

app = FastAPI()

class RentReceiptRequest(BaseModel):
    tenant_name: str = Field(..., min_length=1)
    landlord_name: str = Field(..., min_length=1)
    address: str
    rent_amount: float
    period: str
    payment_date: str  # ISO format
    tax_exempt: bool = False

@app.post("/api/rent-receipt")
async def generate_receipt(req: RentReceiptRequest):
    html = render_template("rent_receipt.html", **req.dict())
    pdf = weasyprint.HTML(string=html).write_pdf()
    return StreamingResponse(io.BytesIO(pdf), media_type="application/pdf")

SEO and Sitemap

The project now prerenders every sitemap route with its own head and removes fabricated social proof (Prerender every sitemap route with its own head; drop fabricated social proof). The /api/rent-receipt route is not indexed; only the public pages (home, blog, compare) are.

Performance & UX

  • Touch Targets: All clickable elements meet the 48 px guideline, improving mobile usability.
  • No Login: Users can generate a receipt on the first visit; the new onboarding guide (feat: first-visit onboarding guide) explains the process.
  • Fast PDF Rendering: WeasyPrint renders the PDF on the server in under 200 ms for typical receipts, ensuring a snappy download.
  • Accessibility: Form labels are associated with inputs; ARIA roles are added for screen readers.

Conclusion

DoAide Docs’ rent receipt generator exemplifies a focused, no‑frills approach to legal document generation in India. By leveraging React for a responsive front‑end, FastAPI for robust server logic, and a lightweight PDF renderer, the project delivers a reliable, free document generator for tenants, landlords, HR departments, and small businesses.

The integration of mobile touch‑target fixes, WhatsApp sharing, and SEO‑friendly sitemap generation shows a commitment to both usability and discoverability. For engineers looking to build or extend a similar feature set, DoAide Docs provides a clean codebase and a clear example of how to combine modern web technologies for a practical, user‑centric tool.

  • DoAide Docs on GitHub

title: The 129 elements that only existed once JavaScript loaded
description:
The page that arrived empty

Opening the portfolio with JavaScript blocked should show an ugly but readable site. It showed a frame. The header was in the HTML, the text was in the HTML, and nothing rendered — because almost everything arrived with opacity: 0 baked into the style attribute.

I measured production before touching a single line: 129 tags with inline opacity:0 in the HTML served by portifolio.seu.pet. Sixty of those are absolute layers and decorative grids, which is expected. The rest include real content — section headings, project cards, the hero block itself. The browser received the whole page and the visitor saw the background.

The culprit was not badly written CSS. It was a component pattern that looked harmless and appeared in 52 places across the repository.

The pattern that kept repeating

The portfolio uses framer-motion for entrance animations. The canonical way to write one is:

initial={{ opacity: 0, y: 20 }}
animate={{ opacity: 1, y: 0 }}

The component starts transparent and animates into view. On the client that works beautifully. The problem is what the server does with that initial: it serialises opacity:0 into the HTML. On the first paint the content is there, invisible, waiting for JavaScript to arrive and animate it. If the JS fails, lags, or simply never runs, the content never shows up.

Inside ProfileSection.tsx the variant was worse. Two hero layers used animate={{ opacity: 0, ... }} gated by mounted ? 1 : 0, where mounted comes from state that only flips to true inside a useEffect. On the server mounted is always false. So the HTML shipped with opacity:0 fixed and the grid background layer (line 676) and the cockpit SVG overlay (line 694) simply did not exist in the served page. Without hydration, they never would.

This was not a new bug. It was the third recurrence of the same family:

  • 08/15 — commit 7322c55, PR #50: the "About" button and four other above-the-fold elements were invisible until hydration, from the same serialised initial.
  • 08/12 — commit 4e279bc: CookieBanner read localStorage in the useState initialiser, rendered differently on server and client, and threw a React #418 hydration mismatch on every fresh visit.
  • 10/19 — commit 8fee520, PR #142: the two hero layers.

Three episodes, three point fixes. The pattern stayed alive in 52 spots.

The cure: born visible, animated later

The root fix was not swapping opacity: 0 for opacity: 1 — that would kill the animation. It was inverting the gate: the HTML is born visible, and animation is only allowed on the client, after mount.

const mounted = useMounted();
<motion.div initial={mounted ? { opacity: 0, y: 20 } : false} ... />

initial: false disables the animation's starting state on the server and on the client's first render. The element is served opaque. Once the hook's useEffect marks mounted = true, the component re-renders with an animatable initial state — but whileInView starts from an element that was already on screen. The visitor sees exactly the same animation; the served HTML, however, defends itself.

useMounted runs 26 lines, comments included. Small abstraction, and it exists so the next component does not repeat the mistake.

The gate landed in 8 files: GlassCard (27 cards), ProjectHangar (cards and the section h2), BlogSection (article and title), SkillsCompact, TimelineItem, the theme and language toggles, the journey buttons and ProfileSection. Total: 67 lines added, 22 removed.

Validation happened on the HTML, not in the browser: serving the page without JavaScript, content elements with opacity below 1 dropped from roughly 50 to zero, with 435/435 tests green and a clean build.

The side effect the gate created

Changing the render cycle has consequences. GameShowcase registered a click listener on every game button inside a useEffect that ran once. With the gate applied to GlassCard, the card started re-rendering on mount — and the button node was replaced. The old listeners stayed orphaned on the old node, outside the DOM. The games stopped responding to clicks.

The diagnosis came from node identity: comparing the element reference before and after mount showed two different objects. The cure was to stop binding listeners to nodes that can be swapped — the click moved to delegation on the container, which survives re-renders:

const btn = (e.target as HTMLElement).closest("[data-game-btn]");
if (!btn) return;

Fewer listeners, more robust. Container delegation is the right answer whenever a child can be remounted.

Why it matters

The practical difference is between a page that needs JavaScript to exist and one that needs it to look good. Search crawlers, link previews, feed readers, browsers with script blocking and connections where the bundle takes its time all read the same served HTML. Before this, nearly half the page was a placeholder.

Worth recording the real state: this work is not finished. The hero layer fix shipped through PR #142 on 10/19 at 02:03. The gate across the whole component tree lives in PR #146, still open, with 435/435 tests green. Until it lands, the production repository still carries 52 raw initial={{ opacity: 0 occurrences.

Next step

Merge PR #146 and re-measure the HTML in production. The target is objective: the count needs to drop close to the 60 decorative layers, which are invisible on purpose. If it does not drop, the gate leaked in some component — and that means the family has a fourth episode waiting.

git log --oneline --grep="SSR" -- src/components/ProfileSection.tsx
grep -rc "initial={{ opacity: 0" src/components/*.tsx | grep -v ':0'
curl -s https://portifolio.seu.pet | grep -o 'opacity:0' | wc -l

title: A React and TypeScript walkthrough. Redesign an existing SaaS screen, keep record identity and filters intact, and test the behavior
description:
A lot of React apps start life in an AI builder now. Auth works, routes work, customer records load. Then someone looks at the screens and says the UI needs design work.

When you change a screen, you can quietly change how people get their work done on it. A row that used to open the right record now opens the wrong one. A filter that used to stick now resets. Nothing crashes, so nobody notices until a user complains.

So before touching the layout, write down what the screen must keep doing. Which record an action opens. Which filters survive navigation. What happens while data loads or fails. Then check every design decision against that list.

To show how this works, I built a small React and TypeScript feedback inbox with made-up customer requests. The flow is narrow on purpose: filter requests, open one, read it, and go back to the filtered list.

1. Write the behavior down before you move a pixel

Start with a short scenario that a designer and a developer can both read:

  • Choose Reporting in the product-area filter.
  • Open FR-108: Export feedback to CSV.
  • Confirm that the detail shows Northline, the customer attached to FR-108.
  • Choose Back to requests.
  • Confirm that Reporting is still selected and keyboard focus returns to the request button.

Now every design idea has a test to pass. Moving the status badge is presentation, so go ahead. Opening a different record, clearing the filter, or changing what "Planned" means is behavior, and it needs a conversation first.

In a real app, write down the existing route, permission checks, API contracts and action callbacks next to the scenario. A UI change can usually leave those alone. If a new design needs a new endpoint or a different permission rule, the task just grew, so scope it that way.

Our example runs on local records. A real product also needs checks against its real data and auth rules.

2. Let the row show what people scan for

First question: what does someone need to see before they open a request?

Selection and status mean different things, so they need different looks. An open request can still be New, Planned or In review. If selection looked like a status, a click would read like a status change.

This is the whole row component:

export function RequestRow({
  request,
  selected,
  onOpen,
}: {
  request: FeedbackRequest;
  selected: boolean;
  onOpen: (id: string, button: HTMLButtonElement) => void;
}) {
  return (
    <li>
      <button
        type="button"
        className="request-row"
        aria-expanded={selected}
        aria-controls={selected ? "request-detail" : undefined}
        onClick={(event) => onOpen(request.id, event.currentTarget)}
      >
        <span className="request-copy">
          <strong className="request-title">{request.title}</strong>
          <span className="request-meta">
            {request.company} · {request.id}
          </span>
        </span>
        <span className="status" data-status={request.status}>
          {request.status}
        </span>
      </button>
    </li>
  );
}

FeedbackRequest holds the record's ID, title, customer, product area, status and message. The row gets a record and an open callback. It never changes the status.

Why a native button? You get keyboard support for free. Because the button reveals related content, aria-expanded tells assistive tech whether that content is open. When the detail opens, its heading gets focus, and Back to requests sends focus back to the row you came from. The WAI-ARIA disclosure pattern explains the expanded-state part.

This works because our detail panel is read-only. If your rows hold checkboxes, menus or inline actions, you need a different structure, because each control needs its own valid target.

3. Store the ID, not the record

The inbox keeps three pieces of UI state:

const [query, setQuery] = useState("");
const [area, setArea] = useState("All");
const [selectedId, setSelectedId] = useState<string | null>(null);

const visible = requests.filter((request) => {
  const matchesArea = area === "All" || request.area === area;
  const text = `${request.title} ${request.company} ${request.id}`
    .toLowerCase();
  return matchesArea && text.includes(query.trim().toLowerCase());
});

const selected = loadState === "ready"
  ? visible.find((request) => request.id === selectedId)
  : undefined;

Why derive selected instead of storing it? A second copy of the record goes stale. If the parent sends an updated status for the same ID, the list and the detail both show it, because both read from the same records. React's state-structure guidance recommends this selected-ID approach.

Search and the area filter work together. Changing either one closes the detail panel here. That's a deliberate product rule: the open record always belongs to the visible results. If your product keeps the detail open while filtering, pick a different rule and write a test for it.

Render rows with key={request.id}. And during a redesign, watch the component type, position and keys around stateful parts of the screen. React ties state to a component's place in the render tree, so wrapping a stateful component in a new container can quietly reset it. More on that in preserving and resetting state.

In other words, keeping the same API calls isn't enough. The component tree matters too.

4. One state, two layouts

On a wide screen, the list and detail sit side by side. On a narrow screen, the detail takes over, and Back to requests returns to the list.

The inbox component owns the filters and selected ID in both layouts. CSS only changes what's visible. There are no separate desktop and mobile copies of state to drift apart:

.inbox-layout.has-detail {
  grid-template-columns: minmax(0, 1.1fr) minmax(0, 1fr);
}

@media (max-width: 760px) {
  .inbox-layout.has-detail {
    grid-template-columns: minmax(0, 1fr);
  }
  .has-detail .inbox {
    display: none;
  }
}

760px is simply where this layout stops fitting. Check where yours does. Long titles, translated labels, enlarged text and an open detail panel will find problems that a short desktop fixture never shows.

We also gave flex and grid children min-width: 0, let long text wrap, and kept the Back button in the normal document flow, so narrow layouts behave predictably.

5. Decide once, reuse everywhere

Before you spread the design to more pages, agree on a few shared decisions: text hierarchy, spacing, focus style, selection style and status labels. Map them to the tokens and components the product already has.

The example names its selection colors:

:root {
  --selection-bg: #eef3ff;
  --selection-border: #294fc2;
}

.request-row[aria-expanded="true"] {
  background: var(--selection-bg);
  border-inline-start-color: var(--selection-border);
}

.status[data-status="Planned"] {
  color: #594013;
  background: #fff2d7;
}

If your design system already has fitting tokens, use them. The new screen stays consistent with its neighbors, and later changes are easier to review.

Design the loading, empty and error states alongside the main screen, not after it. In this inbox, loading has its own message. An empty filter result offers Clear filters. A failed request offers Retry and keeps your search and filter.

Each state answers a different question. Is it working? Does anything match? Did the data load? So each one needs its own next step.

6. Test behavior, not only pixels

A screenshot catches clipped text, uneven spacing or an unreadable badge. It can't tell you that a row opens the right customer or that Retry kept your filters.

So the browser check runs the scenario from step 1 directly. These lines come from its Playwright script:

await page.getByLabel("Product area").selectOption("Reporting");
await page.locator(".request-row").first().click();

assert.equal(
  await page.locator("#request-detail h2").textContent(),
  "Export feedback to CSV"
);
assert((await page.locator("#request-detail").textContent())
  .includes("Northline"));

await page.getByRole("button", { name: "Back to requests" }).click();
assert.equal(
  await page.getByLabel("Product area").inputValue(),
  "Reporting"
);

The full script also covers keyboard activation and focus return, combined filters, a record update reaching the open detail, narrow layouts, loading, empty results and retry. All 14 checks passed in a local Chromium run, and the output logs the browser version and each check.

For screenshot comparisons, use fixed records, a fixed viewport and the same rendering environment every time. Look at the first image yourself before you accept it as a baseline. Playwright's visual-comparison docs cover baselines and environment differences.

These checks cover local UI behavior only. Real API integration, authorization, real devices and a screen-reader session are separate work.

7. Hand off decisions, not only files

A good handoff lists the changed components, why you made each design decision, the acceptance scenarios and the checks you ran. It also flags anything that needs another owner, like a new response field or a permission rule.

This matters most when design and frontend share responsibility for a working product. At UITOP we ran into this on LogiCore, a logistics platform where we handled both the design and the React/TypeScript development, including shipment tracking and warehouse inventory. Interface decisions there had to match how the operational data behaved, or the screens looked right and worked wrong.

So for a React UI refinement, start with one important workflow. Make its component and state decisions easy to review, run the agreed checks, and only then roll the patterns out across the product.

Questions

Can I keep a React redesign limited to the UI layer?

Yes, if you scope it to presentation components, styles and their existing callbacks. Write down the routes, record IDs, API contracts, permissions and state that must keep working. Then review the changed files and run the affected workflow. Telling an AI agent "UI only" doesn't verify the code it writes.

Should I define design tokens and shared components before updating the pages?

Look at what the app already uses first. Settle shared decisions on one representative workflow, including its error and narrow-screen states, then reuse them. Building a big new token system before checking the existing components can turn a small refinement into a migration.

How should a team structure large AI-generated designs for implementation?

Separate shared styles and components from page-specific content. Give each task one bounded screen or workflow, with its dependencies and acceptance scenarios. Check the exports against your real React architecture, because a large generated HTML file doesn't define component boundaries or data ownership.

How can I use screenshot comparison to review a React UI redesign?

Capture stable fixtures at agreed viewports and compare them against baselines a person has reviewed, in a consistent environment. Add interaction checks for record identity, filters, focus and actions. A screenshot can match perfectly while the workflow behind it is broken.

How can new features follow the existing brand guidelines?

Turn the guidelines into the tokens, component variants and content rules your codebase uses. Review one representative feature against those decisions before extending it. A reference image gives useful context, but the code needs explicit rules for typography, color, spacing and states.

Should I hire a UI/UX designer, a frontend developer, or someone who handles both?

Let the unresolved work decide. Flow and hierarchy decisions need design ownership. Component integration and state behavior need frontend ownership. When both are in scope, give the team shared acceptance criteria and one clear implementation reviewer. UITOP combines product design and frontend development, and we scope that work around the workflow and codebase that need attention.

Which workflow in your React app needs a design change, and which behavior has to stay the same?

title: Our AI agent bought an eSIM for its owner, then got the money back. Every step is on chain.
description:
On 15 October the owner of ARGUS, our personal AI agent, wrote to it in Telegram: buy me the cheapest eSIM for Turkey. A few seconds after the owner said /yes, the QR code was in the chat. Thirty-four minutes later the owner asked for a refund, and 0.31 USDC came back to the agent's wallet.

Nothing in the run was simulated. A real eSIM was issued by a real wholesaler and then cancelled, and both payments are transactions on Base you can open. Three things in it are worth telling: the agent refused the first request, the eSIM's secret never passed through the model, and the agent never touched ETH.

It refused the first request

The first message was "buy it and refund it right away". ARGUS did not do that. Buying something only to return it at once looks like a test or a mistake, and it asked what the owner actually wanted: buy and keep it, buy nothing, or a refund for a real reason. The owner chose to buy. The refund came later, as a separate request with its own reason ("I did not install it").

Both the purchase and the refund waited for the owner's /yes. ARGUS has four eSIM tools: esim_offers, esim_buy, esim_status and esim_refund. The two that move money match built-in approval patterns (*buy* and *refund*). A config file can add patterns but never remove them. A hard cap of 1 USDC per eSIM was checked against the seller's own payment terms before anything was signed.

The secret skips the model

The activation code is the traveller's secret: whoever has it can install the eSIM. So it goes from the seller to the owner's chat through the tool's code, around the language model. The model sees the profile number, the price and the transaction. The QR code and the activation code are not in its context, not in ARGUS's memory, and not in its purchase ledger. If no Telegram channel is connected, ARGUS says so and sends nothing.

No ETH, one signature

ARGUS paid over x402: the seller answered the order with 402 Payment Required and its terms, and ARGUS signed one EIP-3009 transfer authorization for exactly that amount. Coinbase's x402 facilitator put it on chain and paid the gas. The refund went the same way in the other direction: the seller node checked with the wholesaler that the eSIM had never been installed (0 bytes used), cancelled it, and signed the transfer back.

Step Transaction From → to USDC
Purchase 0x617efd7a…3ae0 ARGUS → seller 0.31
Refund 0x6dcfb7f0…ed4b seller → ARGUS 0.31

The agent's wallet started with 0.50 USDC and ended with 0.50 USDC. The wholesaler's balance ended where it started.

Then without a hint: found through a marketplace

In the first run ARGUS was pointed at a private seller. In the second, it was given nothing. It searched the modelmarket.dev hub for an eSIM seller, got the offers through the hub, and paid the seller directly. For the test we switched our public seller node from demo to selling, at cost, for 52 minutes, and back to demo right after.

The first attempt ended without a purchase, and that was the agent being right. The node's quote said demo: false, but the node was still called "modelmarket.dev demo seller", and ARGUS would not pay a seller with "demo" in its name. We renamed the node by its mode and labelled every offer [SELLS] or [DEMO] from the seller's own answer, with a rule that the label decides, never the name. The second attempt bought and refunded within 26 seconds (purchase, refund).

Two agents, one seller, and a hub that counts

A marketplace that only lists sellers cannot tell one that delivers from one that takes the money: the payment goes straight from the buyer to the seller. So the seller node now signs a receipt for every delivery and every refund, and the buyer may bring it to the hub with the transaction. The hub checks the signature against the key the seller's listing published, checks the transfer on Base, and counts a confirmed delivery. It keeps no amounts and no addresses in the clear, and a buyer can keep its purchases private.

We tested it in a nine-minute selling window with two different buyers. A coding agent in the owner's terminal ran the kit's one-command example buyer, and three minutes later ARGUS bought the same plan in Telegram. Both refunded. The seller's listing ended with {"confirmed": 2, "distinct_buyers": 2, "refunded": 2}.

What broke along the way

  • Telegram approvals could never succeed. The bot's update loop waited for each task to finish, so a task waiting for /yes never received it, and every approval timed out as a "no". The loop now keeps reading while a task runs.
  • The demo name. Above. The fix was to trust the seller's answer, not its name.
  • The hub's privacy filter blocked the quotes. A data allowance of 104857600 bytes looked like a national ID number to the hub's personal-data check. Integer byte counts are now treated as machine values.

Try it, or sell eSIMs to agents yourself

  • ARGUS, the agent: github.com/alexar76/argus. The full case with every transaction is in docs/use-case-esim-purchase-refund.md.
  • The seller's side, an eSIM operator kit with x402 payments, automatic refunds and signed receipts: github.com/alexar76/esim-operator-kit, with the cases page.
  • Our node at esim.modelmarket.dev is back in demo mode: it quotes and refuses orders. Selling needs an operator with a wholesale account, which the kit sets up with one command.

We build ARGUS and the eSIM operator kit. Every purchase in these tests was at cost, by us, and refunded; no customer was involved.

title: Before You Click Swap on AviorSwap: The Details Worth Checking
description:
Crypto interfaces have become more accessible, but I think one habit remains important regardless of how simple a platform looks: understanding a transaction before confirming it.

A swap may take only a few clicks, yet several details can affect the result.

That's one reason I find the user experience of exchange platforms such as AviorSwap worth discussing.

The amount you send is only half the picture

When exchanging tokens, it's natural to focus on the amount being sold. But the estimated amount received deserves just as much attention.

The final result can depend on the available liquidity, the exchange route, network conditions, and applicable fees.

A useful interface should make the expected output visible before confirmation. If the quote changes or the transaction has specific limitations, users should be able to understand those conditions.

The goal isn't to make every user an expert trader. It's to give people enough information to make an informed decision.

Network selection can matter

Another detail that can be easy to overlook is the blockchain network.

Assets with similar names may exist on different networks, and not every wallet or destination supports every network in the same way.

Before proceeding, I'd check that the selected asset and network match the intended transaction.

This is especially important for users who move between different blockchain ecosystems regularly.

What I look for in an exchange interface

AviorSwap operates in the crypto exchange space, where clarity around transaction details is an important part of the overall experience.

When evaluating a platform, I'd look for a few things:

  • A clear summary of the assets being exchanged.
  • An estimate of the amount to be received.
  • Information about fees and price impact.
  • Visible network details.
  • Understandable transaction status messages.

These details help users understand what's happening without needing to interpret every technical step.

Of course, a public interface alone doesn't tell us everything about how a platform performs during live transactions. Actual execution and security practices require separate evaluation.

Simplicity and transparency should work together

I like interfaces that don't overwhelm users with unnecessary information. At the same time, simplicity shouldn't mean hiding details that could affect a financial decision.

The best approach is to present essential information upfront and make deeper technical details accessible when needed.

This principle applies to crypto exchanges, payment applications, and almost any product that asks users to authorize an important action.

Final thoughts

A convenient swap interface is useful, but convenience shouldn't replace understanding.

Taking a moment to review the expected output, network, and fees can help users make more deliberate decisions.

title: Comparing satisfies, type annotations, and assertions through compiler output
description:
Use satisfies when a configuration value should meet a type while its individual properties remain convenient to use. Two common shortcuts are misleading, though: that it can never affect inference, and that it always rejects extra keys.

The comparison uses the same object under a type annotation, satisfies, and as, with emitted declarations and diagnostics as evidence. For this display configuration, the differences were:

Form Type when reading ready Missing waiting
: Notices `string number[]`
satisfies Notices string Error
as Notices `string number[]`

Inspect declarations as well as editor hints

The experiment ran on September 11, 2026, with macOS arm64, Node.js 24.15.0, and TypeScript 7.0.2. The compiler used strict: true, target: ES2022, module: ESNext, and moduleResolution: Bundler, with type checking and declaration emit. The display values are synthetic test data.

type Notices = Record<"ready" | "waiting", string | number[]>;
export const annotated: Notices = { ready: "Ready", waiting: [1, 2] };
export const checked = { ready: "Ready", waiting: [1, 2] } satisfies Notices;
export const asserted = { ready: "Ready", waiting: [1, 2] } as Notices;
console.log(checked.ready.toUpperCase());

checked.ready.toUpperCase() passed and printed READY. Calling the same method on annotated.ready produced TS2339 because the property could also be an array.

The emitted declarations explain that difference:

type Notices = Record<"ready" | "waiting", string | number[]>;
export declare const annotated: Notices;
export declare const checked: {
    ready: string;
    waiting: number[];
};
export declare const asserted: Notices;
export {};

checked retains the types of individual properties. The other two variables have the annotated Notices type. This makes satisfies useful when a configuration needs a shared compatibility check without requiring extra narrowing wherever a particular value is used. The TypeScript 4.9 documentation describes this use of compatibility checks while retaining a useful expression type.

An assertion can leave a missing property undetected 

type Notices = Record<"ready" | "waiting", string | number[]>;
const value = { ready: "Ready" } as Notices;
console.log(value.waiting);

This code passed type checking and printed undefined. Changing the assertion to satisfies Notices produced TS2741 for the missing waiting property. An assertion does not create that property.

This also does not mean every possible assertion is accepted. TypeScript can reject an assertion based on the relationship between the types. The finding here is narrower: it accepts this particular object despite the missing required key. As the official explanation of type assertions states, assertions do not validate or convert runtime values.

Context can affect inference 

export const plain = { enabled: true, count: 1 };
export const checked = { enabled: true, count: 1 } satisfies { enabled: boolean; count: number };
export const frozenType = { enabled: true, count: 1 } as const;

In the emitted declarations, plain.enabled was boolean, while checked.enabled was true. Both count properties were number. Context from the target type means literal inference is not necessarily identical.

With as const, frozenType.enabled became a readonly true, and frozenType.count became a readonly 1. This does not freeze the object at runtime either. If a configuration will be modified later, decide whether that property should remain the literal true or accept both boolean values, including false.

Extra keys are not always rejected

Writing { ready: "Ready", waiting: [1], typo: 1 } satisfies Notices directly produced TS2353 for the extra typo property. Assigning that object to a variable first changed the outcome:

type Notices = Record<"ready" | "waiting", string | number[]>;
const input = { ready: "Ready", waiting: [1], typo: 1 };
const value = input satisfies Notices;
console.log(value.typo);

This passed and printed 1. A value can satisfy the required structure while retaining additional properties. Restricting the keys of external data requires a runtime check separate from these type constructs.

For the local configuration in this experiment, use satisfies to catch mistakes while retaining operations specific to each value. Use an annotation to specify the type the variable should expose. Reserve as for places where other evidence supports the asserted type.

The T02 cases in the reproduction code and the execution record include both accepted declarations and deliberately invalid inputs. Do not assume diagnostic numbers or inference remain identical across compiler versions; compare declaration output when upgrading.

title: A Model-Free Continuous-Time RL Algorithm from Discrete-Time Off-Policy Data with End-to-End Guarantees
description:
arXiv:2610.28915v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In this paper, we study continuous-time reinforcement learning, where the state follows an unknown stochastic differential equation but only a fixed off-policy batch of discrete-time transitions is available. Standard discrete-time Q-learning becomes problematic as the sampling interval shrinks, because differences between action values vanish. Continuous-time alternatives, such as Deep Advantage Updating and martingale q-learning, preserve the action signal but jointly learn a value function and an action-dependent critic. Building on the PhiBE-Q formulation (arXiv:2606.21925), we develop a model-free PhiBE policy iteration (PhiBE-PI) framework that uses a single state-action critic while preserving the continuous-time action-ranking scale. At each iteration, the framework learns the critic directly from sampled increments and uses it to improve the policy. The same batch is reused throughout, without explicitly estimating the drift or diffusion. We further develop an implementation under linear function approximation and establish a local end-to-end suboptimality guarantee for the learned policy. Our analysis quantifies how errors from time discretization, function approximation, and finite-sample policy evaluation propagate through policy iteration. It accounts for the dependence of successive policies on the reused data, so the guarantee does not require a fresh batch at each iteration. Moreover, we identify a bias-variance trade-off: smaller sampling intervals improve the approximation to the continuous-time problem but can increase statistical error at a fixed sample size. Thus, finer time discretization does not necessarily lead to better policy performance.

title: Your AI Agent Does Not Need Root Access: A Guide to Agentic Orchestration
description:
TLDR

  • Agentic orchestration coordinates AI agents that choose their own next steps. It decides who acts, what they see, which tools they get, and when a person approves.
  • Traditional orchestration runs a fixed path, while agentic orchestration bounds a path the model picks as it runs. It needs more control, not less.
  • The five core patterns are sequential, parallel, routing, orchestrator and workers, and evaluator loops. Start with the simplest one that works.
  • Give each step the least autonomy that does the job. Go from a fixed rule to a model call to an agent only when the simpler option fails.
  • Production needs five controls around the agent: spend ceilings, scoped tools, approval gates, step limits, and tracing. Unmeshed covers these inside durable workflows, but it isn't an agent reasoning framework.

Agentic orchestration is the coordination layer that manages AI agents that choose their own next steps, deciding which agent acts, what context it gets, which tools it may use, and when a person must approve. It is orchestration for systems where the path is not fixed in advance.

Most explanations stop at that definition and a diagram of agents passing messages. The harder question is how much freedom each step should get. Gartner expects over 40% of agentic AI projects to be canceled by the end of 2027, citing cost, unclear value, and weak risk controls.

This guide covers what agentic orchestration is, how it differs from traditional orchestration, the core patterns, and the controls that keep agents inside safe limits. We'll also say where Unmeshed fits and where it doesn't.

1. What Is Agentic Orchestration?

Agentic orchestration is the coordination layer that manages AI agents that choose their own next steps, deciding which agent acts, what context it gets, which tools it may use, and when a person must approve.

The key word is choose. In a fixed workflow, a developer decides every step before the run starts. In an agentic system, a model decides some of them while the run is happening. Someone has to set the limits on that choice, and that someone is the orchestrator.

It helps to say what it is not. It isn't one big agent doing everything. It isn't a prompt chain with a fancier name. And it isn't an agent framework on its own, because a framework shapes how one agent reasons while orchestration governs how agents run together.

The orchestrator owns five decisions:

  • Which agent or tool acts next
  • What context each agent sees
  • Which tools each agent may call
  • When the run stops, retries, or escalates
  • When a person has to approve

2. How Is Agentic Orchestration Different From Traditional Orchestration?

Traditional orchestration runs steps along a path you define in advance. Agentic orchestration coordinates steps where an AI model decides the path as it runs, so the orchestrator has to bound that freedom with limits, approvals, and logging.

Traditional orchestration is what workflow engines and API orchestrators do. Our guide to AI orchestration covers the wider term, including pipelines and model routing. This post covers the narrower case where the path itself is not fixed.

Dimension Traditional Agentic
Who decides the path The developer, in advance The model, at runtime
Predictability Same input follows the same path Same input can take different paths
Typical failure A step errors out An agent loops, picks the wrong tool, or compounds an early mistake
Cost shape Fixed per run Varies with the steps the model chooses to take
What the orchestrator adds Retries and scheduling Limits, approvals, tool scoping, and tracing

That last row is the point. An agentic system doesn't need less orchestration. It needs more.

3. What Are Agentic Workflows, and How Do They Differ From Agents?

Agentic workflows are multi-step processes where AI models decide some of the steps inside a defined structure. An AI agent is a system that directs its own process and tool use. The workflow sets the boundary, and the agent acts inside it.

Anthropic draws the same line in its guide to building effective agents. Workflows orchestrate models and tools through predefined code paths, while agents let the model direct its own process and tool usage.

A workflow

  • The path is set in code
  • The model fills in content or makes bounded choices
  • It's easy to test, audit, and explain

An agent

  • The model picks the next action in a loop
  • It uses tools and feedback from each step to decide what to do
  • It's harder to predict and costs more per run

Most production systems mix both. A workflow handles intake, validation, and approvals, and an agent handles the one step that needs judgment. If you're choosing a framework for that agent step, our guide to agent frameworks compares six.

4. What Are the Core Agentic Orchestration Patterns?

The core agentic orchestration patterns are sequential, parallel, routing, orchestrator and workers, and evaluator loops. Each trades predictability against flexibility, and most production systems combine two or three of them.

Anthropic and Google Cloud describe overlapping sets. This table pulls the common ones together.

Pattern How It Works Main Risk
Sequential Agents run in a fixed order, and each one feeds the next One weak step weakens every step after it
Parallel Agents work at the same time, and the results are merged Conflicting outputs and higher token use
Routing A classifier sends each request to the best-fit agent Requests sent to the wrong agent
Orchestrator and workers A lead agent splits the task and delegates the pieces Runaway delegation and cost
Evaluator loop One agent drafts, another critiques, and the cycle repeats Loops that never converge

Google Cloud warns that a loop can run indefinitely if its exit condition is wrong. That's why every loop needs a maximum number of iterations.

Start with the simplest pattern that works. Sequential and parallel patterns run on fixed logic with no model choosing the route, so they cost less and behave more predictably. Reach for orchestrator and workers only when you truly can't know the steps in advance.

5. How Does Autonomous Agent Coordination Work?

Autonomous agent coordination is how multiple agents hand off work, share state, and avoid conflicting actions without a person directing each step. It depends on explicit handoff rules, one source of shared state, and hard stop conditions.

  • Handoffs: Define what one agent passes to the next and in what shape. Loose, free-text handoffs are where context gets lost.
  • Shared state: Keep one record of the run that every agent reads and writes, instead of each agent carrying its own copy.
  • Context scoping: Give each agent only the context its task needs. Google Cloud calls managing this flow context engineering.
  • Conflict control: If two agents can change the same record, decide which one wins before they ever run.
  • Stop conditions: Set step limits, timeouts, and a spend cap, so a stuck agent ends the run instead of draining it.

Shared state and stop conditions are infrastructure problems, not prompt problems. They're why agent infrastructure has become its own topic, and why runs need durable execution to survive a crash halfway through.

6. How Much Autonomy Should Each Step Get?

Give each step the least autonomy that still does the job. Use a fixed rule when the answer is known, a single model call when the input is messy, and an agent loop only when the steps can't be predicted in advance.

Think of autonomy as a dial, not a switch. Each notch adds flexibility, and it also adds cost, variance, and review work.

Level Use It When Example Cost and Review
Fixed rule The answer is known Is this request a duplicate? Lowest, nothing to review
Single model call The input is messy, but the output is bounded Classify a support email Low, spot check the output
Workflow with an agent step One step needs judgment, and the rest is fixed An agent researches a customer, then a rule decides what happens Moderate, review flagged runs
Fully autonomous agent The steps can't be predicted at all Open-ended research or coding Highest, needs strong limits

Gartner's guidance maps to the same dial. It recommends agents where decisions are needed, automation for routine workflows, and assistants for simple retrieval.

Most teams start too far to the right. The cheaper path is to begin with a rule, promote a step to a model call when the input gets messy, and promote it to an agent only when the simpler version fails.

7. What Controls Does Agentic AI Orchestration Need in Production?

Agentic AI orchestration needs five production controls, which are spend ceilings, scoped tool access, approval gates, step limits, and full tracing. They stop an agent's freedom from turning into cost overruns or actions nobody reviewed.

Gartner expects over 40% of agentic AI projects to be canceled by the end of 2027 because of escalating costs, unclear business value, or inadequate risk controls. Each control below answers one of those reasons.

  • Spend ceilings: Cap what each agent can spend, and throttle it or switch it to a cheaper model near the cap. Cost grows with every extra step a model takes, so see our guide to token efficiency for where the money goes.
  • Scoped tool access: Bind each agent to a fixed list of tools, enforced by the runtime and not by a line in a prompt.
  • Approval gates: Pause the run before any action that is expensive to reverse, such as a payment or a deletion. A human-in-the-loop step does this and resumes the run once a person approves.
  • Step limits: End the run after a maximum number of steps or minutes, so a loop can't run forever.
  • Full tracing: Log every model call, tool call, and cost. LLM observability shows what happened, and agent evals show whether the result was any good.

None of these controls live inside the agent. They sit around it, which is why AI agent governance is a workflow concern and not a prompt concern.

8. What Should You Look For in an Agent Orchestration Platform?

An agent orchestration platform should add durable state, retries, approvals, tool scoping, spend tracking, and an audit trail around whichever agent framework you use. It runs the agents. It does not replace their reasoning.

The market mixes three different things under one label. Frameworks shape how an agent reasons. Cloud suites bundle models and agent builders for one vendor's stack. Workflow engines run durable, governed processes around any of them. Know which one you're buying.

Criterion What To Ask
Durability Does a run survive a crash or a redeploy and resume where it stopped?
Tool scoping Does the runtime stop an agent from calling a tool it wasn't given?
Spend controls Can you set a ceiling per agent and see cost per run?
Human approval Can a run pause for sign-off and resume on its own?
Observability Can you inspect every model call, tool call, and retry?
Framework neutrality Can you keep the agent framework your team already uses?
Cost shape Does pricing grow with actions or stay predictable?

Watch for agent washing as well. Gartner estimates that only about 130 of the thousands of agentic AI vendors are real, because many rebrand chatbots and RPA without real agentic capability. Ask any vendor to show you the run history of a failed agent step.

For the engine layer, see our roundup of workflow orchestration tools.

9. When Should You Avoid Agentic Orchestration?

Avoid agentic orchestration when the steps are known in advance, when one model call solves the task, or when an error is costly and can't be reviewed. Gartner says many use cases sold as agentic don't need an agentic setup.

Gartner analyst Anushree Verma put it plainly: "Many use cases positioned as agentic today don't require agentic implementations."

Google Cloud's guide makes the same point. Tasks like summarizing a document, translating text, or classifying customer feedback usually don't need an agentic workflow.

Skip it when

  • The steps are known in advance
  • A single model call solves the task
  • A wrong action is expensive, and no one can review it first

Use it when

  • The steps can't be predicted ahead of time
  • The task needs tools and outside data across several steps
  • You can check the outcome and cap the spend
  • Risky actions can pause for a person to approve

Skipping it is a fine answer. A fixed workflow with one model step costs less, breaks less, and is easier to explain.

10. How Does Unmeshed Handle Agentic Orchestration?

Unmeshed handles agentic orchestration by running agent steps inside durable, governed workflows. Each agent is bound to a fixed set of tools, tracked against a spend ceiling, and logged, while rules and approvals handle the decisions a model shouldn't make.

What it covers

  • Workflows with durable execution, so agent state survives crashes and redeploys
  • Agent orchestration steps that run on the same engine as your fixed steps
  • Tool binding enforced by the runtime, so an agent can't call a tool it wasn't given
  • Per-agent spend ceilings that throttle the agent or move it to a cheaper model near the cap
  • A built-in decision engine for rules a model shouldn't decide on every run
  • Approval steps that pause a run and resume it once a person signs off
  • MCP native tools, model agnostic, and a full run history of every model call, tool call, and cost

What it doesn't do

  • It isn't an agent reasoning framework. Keep LangChain, CrewAI, or your own loop inside a worker, and Unmeshed makes each step durable, retried, and audited.
  • It doesn't train models, and it isn't an LLM gateway for routing across providers.

The practical difference

Teams usually stitch this together from a workflow engine, an approval tool, and a cost tracker. Unmeshed puts durable state, approvals, rules, spend tracking, and run history in one system, built by the creators of Netflix Conductor.

Let The Agent Reason. Let The Workflow Set The Limits.
Bind your agent to approved tools, cap its spend, and send risky actions to a person. See all three in one governed flow.
Set The Guardrails

In a Nutshell

Agentic orchestration isn't a choice between using agents and skipping them. It's a choice about how much freedom each step gets and what limits surround it.

Start with a rule. Add a model call where the input is messy. Add an agent only where the steps can't be predicted. Then put spend ceilings, scoped tools, approval gates, step limits, and tracing around it.

Gartner's cancellation forecast comes down to cost and missing controls as much as missing value. The projects most at risk are the ones with no limits around the agent.

title: Why catch-all email addresses can't be verified (and what to do instead)
description:
If you've ever run a list through an email verifier, you've probably seen a result labelled catch-all, accept-all or unknown. It's tempting to treat that as a bug in the tool. It isn't. It's a hard limit of how email works, and once you understand it you'll make better decisions about what to send to.

How verification works under the hood

A verifier never sends an email. It runs a short conversation with the recipient's mail server and stops just before the message would be delivered:

  1. Syntax check. Is anna@example.com even a well-formed address?
  2. DNS lookup. Does example.com publish MX records, i.e. does anything accept mail for this domain?
  3. SMTP handshake. Connect to the mail server and say who the mail is for: 
EHLO verifier.example
MAIL FROM:<probe@verifier.example>
RCPT TO:<anna@example.com>

The interesting part is the reply to RCPT TO:

250 2.1.5 OK                       -> mailbox accepted
550 5.1.1 User unknown             -> mailbox does not exist

Then the verifier sends QUIT. No message is ever transmitted. For most domains, that 250 versus 550 is a clean answer.

Where it breaks: catch-all domains

Some mail servers are configured to accept every address at the domain. Ask about a real mailbox and you get 250 OK. Ask about xk2j9q-not-a-person@example.com and you also get 250 OK.

Companies do this for legitimate reasons: so a typo in an address still reaches someone, so mail to ex-employees lands in a shared inbox, or because their security gateway accepts everything first and filters later.

From the outside, a real mailbox and an invented one now look identical. The usual detection trick is to probe a random address that almost certainly doesn't exist. If that gets 250, the domain is catch-all. But that only tells you the domain accepts everything. It tells you nothing about whether the one address you actually care about belongs to a person.

No SMTP-based check can resolve this. Any tool that confidently labels these addresses "valid" is guessing.

Other reasons you'll see "unknown"

  • Greylisting. The server temporarily rejects the first attempt (451 4.7.1) and expects a retry minutes later.
  • Rate limiting and blocks. Large providers throttle or refuse verification-style connections.
  • Timeouts. The server simply doesn't answer in time.

A good verifier retries some of these, but some addresses will stay undetermined, and that's the honest result.

What to do with catch-all addresses

  1. Keep them as a separate segment. Don't mix them into your "verified" list.
  2. Send to the most engaged ones first (people who opened or clicked recently) and watch your bounce rate.
  3. Cap the volume. Hard bounces above roughly 2% of a send are where mailbox providers start to push back.
  4. Use other signals. A recent reply, a signed-up account or an address you got directly from the person is worth more than any verifier result.

The pricing question

Here's the part I'd encourage you to check in whatever tool you use: do you get charged for results the tool can't actually determine? Many verifiers bill a catch-all or unknown result exactly like a confirmed one, and some count catch-alls as valid in their accuracy claims.

Disclosure: I work on ListCheckup, an EU-based email verifier. We label catch-all and unknown addresses separately and refund the credit for them, precisely because we can't honestly confirm them. There's a longer write-up on why catch-all domains can't be verified, and a 54-second video overview on YouTube.

If you've found other ways to handle catch-all segments, I'd love to hear them in the comments.

title: Asking What a Director Sees Can Change What Vision-Language Models Choose
description:
arXiv:2610.29318v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Vision-language models are now routinely tested on theory of mind: whether they can work out what another person sees, knows, and means. A common design asks the model to report that perspective and then to act for the person, and reads a correct report beside a wrong action as a failure to use the perspective. That reading rests on a quiet assumption: that asking for the report leaves the action unchanged. We show that it does not. In a rendered Director Task, a partition hides the largest block from a director who asks for "the largest block". Asking first which blocks the director can see raises the share of replies that choose this hidden block by 12 to 88 percentage points on six GPT models and by 17 on Qwen3.8-27B, even though the models mostly report correctly which blocks the director sees. Reasoning traces and prompt rewordings suggest why: the question shifts how the request is read, from the director's view toward the model's own. When the prompt states what the director knows and refers to, fewer than 1% of replies pair a correct report with a hidden-block choice. Any evaluation that elicits a perspective report before the action it scores needs a baseline without the question, and we deliver one: paired prompts that differ only in that question, a design any perspective-taking benchmark can adopt.

title: Implicit Function or Implicit Type? Demystifying Rust Closures
description:
Closure Note

Rust closures often feel like a mysterious monolith, but they were born to solve a fundamental need: first-class functions behavior with state capture.

In conventional linear execution, named functions are invoked immediately. Standard function pointers (fn()) let you store and call functions later, but they lack a crucial capability—they cannot capture or remember variables from their surrounding environment.

That is why closures were introduced to Rust. Although we casually refer to closures as "functions," it is much more accurate to think of them as concrete, compiler-generated types.

How Closures Work Under the Hood

When you write a closure, it captures the variables it needs from its enclosing scope. Behind the scenes, the Rust compiler:

Generates an anonymous, unique type for the closure.

Stores the captured variables inside fields of this generated struct.

Applies borrowing rules: By default, it uses "reborrowing" mechanics identical to regular function calls with reference arguments.

Implements function traits: The compiler automatically implements one of the core closure traits based on how the variables are captured:

Fn: Implemented if the closure only borrows captured variables immutably. It can be called multiple times.

FnMut: Implemented if the closure borrows any variables mutably. It can also be called multiple times, modifying state along the way.

FnOnce: The parent trait of the others. If the closure takes ownership of captured variables (such as via the move keyword) or consumes them, it implements FnOnce and can typically only be executed once.

The Role of the move Keyword

As counterintuitive, closure with move won't take ownership of the instances behind reference types. It just moves the variable into the closure. What is different from closure without move is that the outer variables (with owned or reference types) will be invalid after the closure is constructed.

Because of Rust's rigorous borrow checker, we frequently rely on the move keyword with closures to satisfy lifetime constraints—especially when spawning threads or returning closures from functions. Instead of borrowing variables from the stack, move forces the closure to take ownership of those variables, moving them directly into the compiler-generated struct.

While optimizing Rust code often involves careful lifetime management, mastering how closures handle memory under the hood is a rare and invaluable skill for writing high-performance systems.

title: Encoded but Unused: Bounding the Sources of VLM Errors
description:
arXiv:2610.29241v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In this paper, we investigate why vision-language models (VLMs) produce errors by decomposing them into two sources: visual-representation failures, in which the visual evidence required for the correct answer is not encoded, and visual-utilization failures, in which this evidence is encoded but not successfully used. We propose to estimate the visual-utilization failure rate using lightweight probes and derive theoretical bounds on the true rate that account for probe imperfections. We introduce VELens (Visual Evidence Lens), a rank-based probe that traces visual evidence for both a target object and its ground-truth attribute, such as color, material, or shape, across VLM layers. We evaluate VELens on over 6,000 images using LLaVA-1.6-7B and Qwen2.5-VL-7B. Our method achieves ROC-AUC scores of 0.95 and 0.91, respectively, and outperforms alternative probes in both low-resource and unseen-attribute settings. Using it to diagnose errors, we estimate that visual-utilization failures account for 84.4% of LLaVA errors and 70.0% of Qwen errors, with conservative lower bounds of 77.5% and 61.0%, respectively. Overall, our study identifies visual utilization as the dominant bottleneck in VLMs and suggests that a central opportunity for improvement lies in developing better mechanisms to locate, route, and use the visual information they already encode.
