title: From Augmentation to Synthetic Evidence: Evaluating Generated Chest Radiographs at Dataset Intake
description:
arXiv:2610.29152v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A generated chest radiograph can be useful as declared augmentation, but the same image becomes unsupported evidence when submitted as the record of a real examination. We study this problem by separating three questions: whether an image passes an automated quality check, whether an origin classifier flags it as generated, and whether a trusted record supports the claimed acquisition. In our experiments, Qwen selects up to 20 images from pools of 1,000 existing Cheff-identified or SynthCheX candidates. A receiver evaluates quality with MedGemma and predicted origin with a classifier on frozen DINOv3 features. Quality-based selection raises quality passes from 12 to 19 of 20 for Cheff-identified images and from 8 to 17 for SynthCheX. We find no evidence that selection improves passage through both checks: no selected Cheff-identified image passes both, while uniform, quality, and quality-constrained surrogate selection produce 2, 1, and 2 SynthCheX passes. On unprocessed test images, the origin classifier flags 4,677 of 5,000 SynthCheX images, but it also misclassify 110 of 2,297 NIH (real) images and 568 of 957 genuine images from another collection as fake. Our results further show that JPEG compression reduces SynthCheX-versus-NIH AUROC from 0.987 to 0.841. Even without processing, 152 SynthCheX images pass both pixel checks. These checks can filter submissions, but they cannot verify an acquisition claim. We strongly advocate that source and intended use must be recorded and checked separately for admission of chest radiographs in medical datasets.

title: Error Message Design: Share the Recovery When You Build in Public
description:
When you share error message design while building in public, show the failure, the explanation and the recovery step together. A screenshot of improved wording can invite useful criticism, but a small walkthrough lets peers judge whether the person using the product can actually continue the task.

Choose one recoverable failure and use invented sample data. Explain the intended task, what caused the failure and what the product preserves. Then ask a focused question about the next action. Keep feedback on the wording separate from evidence that someone successfully recovered in the working interface.

Pick a failure the person can do something about

Consider a fictional SaaS tool that imports a repair shop's parts list from a CSV file. The sample file has a column named Item code, but one row has no code. The importer rejects the file. That gives the developer a specific situation to show without exposing a customer's real inventory or using an actual failed upload as public material.

Start the post by explaining the task: add the sample parts to the product. Show the relevant sample column and the current response. A message such as “Import failed” gives the reviewer little to assess. They need to know whether the problem concerns the file format, a missing value or a failure inside the service.

The GOV.UK Design System's error-message guidance distinguishes validation problems from service problems the user cannot fix. That distinction matters in this example. A missing item code may be correctable in the file. An unavailable import service needs a different explanation and next step, rather than an instruction to repair valid data.

Write the proposed message against a known condition

For the fictional missing-code case, proposed wording could identify the sample row and column, explain that no items were imported and tell the person to add the missing code before uploading again. Each part needs to match the actual import behavior. If some rows were imported, saying none were added would create a new error.

Do not promise that retrying is safe without checking what the application does. A partial import may require the person to review existing records first. The message should communicate the state the system knows. If it cannot determine whether anything was saved, that uncertainty belongs in the recovery flow rather than being hidden by reassuring copy.

Use row numbers only when the interface and downloadable file use a consistent numbering convention. Does the header count as a row? Can blank lines change the reported number? In the public example, state the convention or point directly to the relevant sample value. Precision that sends someone to the wrong place is worse than a less compact explanation.

Keep the attempt visible during recovery

Show what happens after the error appears. Does the chosen file remain identified? Can the person inspect the problem before replacing it? Does a second upload clearly replace the first attempt? A message can sound clear in isolation while the surrounding interface makes it hard to understand which state is current.

GOV.UK's guidance also recommends preserving entered answers when validation errors appear. Applied to this fictional import, the review question is what useful context the product can retain. Retaining a file name or a summary of the attempt is different from storing an uploaded document indefinitely. Describe the behavior you actually implement.

Do not collect or publish extra sample information just to make the demonstration feel realistic. A few invented parts can expose the interaction. Real supplier names, purchase costs and customer details are unnecessary for a review of the missing-code message. If the sample cannot explain the failure without private records, redesign the example before sharing it.

Capture the whole recovery path

Prepare a short sequence with a clear beginning and end. Start from the import screen, choose the deliberately incomplete sample, show the error and then use the corrected sample. Finish at the state that confirms what was added. Keep the changed input visible enough that a reviewer can understand what caused the later success.

Label the demonstration as a staged sample. It shows that this path behaved as described under these conditions. It does not establish that new users understand the message, that every invalid file is handled correctly or that the importer is safe for production workloads. Those are separate questions with separate evidence needs.

If the sequence is only a prototype, say which parts are simulated. A clickable mockup that displays a success card has not completed an import. You can still ask peers to critique the wording and information order. Just avoid presenting a simulated completion as a working product result in the post, cover or caption.

Ask peers to explain the next action

Instead of asking whether the new message looks better, ask what they would do next after reading it. A useful response might reveal that the row reference is unclear, that the person expects to edit inside the application or that they are unsure whether anything has already been saved. Those are concrete gaps to investigate.

Ask respondents which part of the sequence led them to that interpretation. That keeps the discussion attached to the artifact. A suggestion to add a button may be valuable, but you still need to understand the confusion it would address. Otherwise, a small copy review can become a collection of unrelated feature requests.

For a community post, include the role you most want to hear from. Developers can identify inconsistent system states; someone who regularly imports parts lists may question the workflow itself. Both can help, but their observations answer different questions. Record that context instead of combining every reaction into a single verdict.

Separate a copy review from a recovery test

A person reading a screenshot can tell you how they interpret it. A person trying the task can show what they actually do. If you move from public discussion to a guided session, use the same defined sample and let the participant respond before explaining the intended path. Record any help you provide.

Suppose, in a hypothetical session, someone corrects the missing value but cannot find how to replace the file. That would direct attention to the upload interaction. It would not prove the revised wording is useless. Write the observation narrowly and revise the part of the flow that prevented the task from continuing.

Likewise, successful recovery in one sample session is evidence about that attempt, not a universal usability claim. Keep the conditions and remaining questions beside the result when you share the follow-up. The useful public update explains which uncertainty changed and which still needs work.

Share what the review changed

The follow-up should show the specific revision and its reason. Perhaps the fictional developer adds a clear replacement-file action and makes the import state explicit. Show that change with the same sample so readers can compare the flow. Avoid turning a few helpful comments into a claim that the community validated the entire product.

Buildside's public description connects founder progress with specific peer contributions; I build Buildside. This kind of bounded recovery review gives that contribution a concrete object. Someone can inspect one failure path and challenge its explanation without needing to become a customer or review the entire application.

Before publishing your next build update, choose one error your product can explain more honestly. Prepare the smallest sample that reveals it, show the recovery and ask what the reader would do next. Then use the response to improve the real task. The valuable progress is the clearer route back to useful work, with evidence that says exactly how far you have checked it.

title: Compute that takes any shape
description:
Workloads differ in how long they run, how much memory they take, and how much of the environment they control. That previously meant a different compute primitive for each job, so product iterations required provisioning infrastructure, not just working on a feature.

We built Vercel so that none of this has to be your problem. The compute layer is a single system with a simple job. Take any workload, assemble the machine it needs, swap configuration on the fly, and absorb burst capacity in real time.

We call this Fluid.

Builds ran on it first, then sandboxes, and now functions. If you've shipped on Vercel, you've been on Fluid without knowing it.

Fluid compute now runs over 15 million builds a day, 25 million sandboxes a week, and a trillion requests a month.

A history of compute

Changing a machine used to mean changing it by hand. You went down to the computer store, bought a hard drive or a stick of RAM, and swapped it in yourself.

Then you could rent bare metal when you needed it, and use it to serve a website, host a database, or send email.

Then the cloud let you request a machine in any configuration you wanted, choose its operating system, use it, and throw it away when you were done.

For agents, even the cloud is too slow. A standard VM can't provision fast enough to keep up with how they work, but this is where Fluid excels.

How a workload runs on Fluid

When a workload comes in, Fluid assembles a machine to fit its shape. If an agent needs to run code, Hive provides an isolated VM, usually one already warm, so it's ready instantly. Your own image boots on top as the environment. A Drive connects, and your files are right where you left them, because storage was never tied to the machine.

Each workload needs something different. A build is compute-bound, so it wants a beefy machine, heavy on CPU and memory. A function is IO-bound, loading specific code to run the instant a request lands, usually on a small VM. A sandbox is flexibility-bound, taking whatever configuration the work calls for with a Drive attached for user data.

Fluid compute is the execution model that all of this leans on. Many requests run on one instance, instead of each spinning up its own. Work starts immediately, and with Active CPU pricing, you pay for CPU only while your code is working, not while it waits on a database or a model.

Hive

Hive is the "hardware." We built it to control our own compute. It provisions the isolated machines every workload runs on. It picks the right machine for the job, keeps each one isolated in our multitenant environment, and does it at global scale. Hive gives every product one control-plane API, so our teams build on the same foundation instead of each maintaining their own.

Fluid images

Fluid images is the environment. Until now the OS was fixed. You ran the one the cloud gave you, not the one you chose. Now you push your own image to Vercel Container Registry, and run it across sandboxes and functions. In the background, Vercel converts images into a Fluid image in a format we call VHS (Vercel Hive Snapshot), the optimized boot format behind Dockerfile deploys and sandbox custom images, so it can resume rather than boot and a custom machine is ready in milliseconds. It uses the same technology behind Sandbox Snapshots, so optimizations in one product carry to the rest. v0 already uses it to build and run its own development environments.

Vercel Drives

Vercel Drives is the storage. Your files live in portable, durable storage that travels with the workload instead of being stranded on one machine's disk. Storage that outlives the compute attached to it is what makes the rest of the system work. Drives aren't bound to a single machine, you can swap the compute underneath it and pick up exactly where you left off in the next session. Drives attach to sandboxes today, in private beta, and extend to the rest of Fluid from there.

One system underneath

These are different shapes of the same system, not separate platforms. Because it's one compute layer underneath every product, a gain in boot time, isolation, scheduling, or caching lands across functions, sandboxes, and builds at once, instead of being rebuilt three times. New shapes of compute can be added without rebuilding the foundation. You don't end up with separate primitives that drift apart.

And it's real, not a diagram: Hive provisions a full VM in milliseconds and brings your filesystem state along with it, so you get isolation stronger than an isolate or a container, without paying for it in startup time.

The agent workload

For an agent to move fast, it needs the right machine, and it needs it immediately. The faster the machine assembles, the faster the agent works.

An agent runs untrusted code, so the machine needs a secure boundary. It brings its own tools, so the machine needs its own environment. And because an agent spins up and tears down constantly, its state has to outlive the compute. Fluid assembles that machine immediately, and then a fresh one for the next task.

For years, the machine was a fixed thing, and you fit your work to it.

In Fluid you describe the work, and the machine forms around it.

title: SAPD: Learning from Agent Experience without Environment Interaction
description:
arXiv:2610.27847v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Scaling the training of Large Language Model (LLM) agents typically requires a large collection of executable environments, whose construction, maintenance, and operation constrain the expansion of training experience. Existing offline trajectories offer an opportunity to reuse interaction experience, yet effectively refining the current policy without revisiting these environments remains challenging: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) can lead to catastrophic forgetting, while online reinforcement learning requires real-time interaction with the environment. To address this challenge, we propose Step-Advantage Policy Distillation (SAPD), a method for learning from offline trajectories using relative step advantages. SAPD decomposes multi-turn trajectories into individual decision contexts for on-policy distillation, allowing the student to generate responses conditioned on recorded histories, and introduces relative step advantage signals to stabilize training. The entire process requires neither new environment observations nor additional multi-turn interactions. Experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop, and Search-based QA show that SAPD improves performance across different teacher configurations, mitigates catastrophic forgetting compared with SFT, and runs at least $4.7\times$ faster per training step than online OPD. We will release our code soon.

title: LIFT: Scoped Constraints for Evaluating and Training Instruction Following
description:
arXiv:2610.28819v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Common instruction following (IF) benchmarks, such as IFEval, evaluate the ability of language models (LMs) to follow simple constraints that can easily be verified programmatically. These same constraints, in turn, are used as reward signals for reinforcement learning. This design may lead to reward hacking of constraints, pushing models away from the main task. Recent attempts to address this resulted in benchmarks with richer constraints, but required expert labor, remained closed-access, and cannot be easily extended. We present Lift-Bench, an IF benchmark that asks a model to draft a document given a topic and a structured outline. Constraints are scoped to certain document sections, providing finer control over constraint density. Lift-Bench includes both verifiable and judged constraints, as well as a training counterpart, Lift-Train. Importantly, Lift-Bench provides both main task and instruction-following constraints, mitigating shallow reward hacking. On experiments with multiple models, we find that frontier models struggle with the harder subsets of our benchmark and analyze model performance along multiple axes. We also find that training on Lift-Train is much less susceptible to reward hacking than training on the common IFTrain. Lift-Bench and Lift-Train are publicly available, as well as the data generating pipeline.

title: Tuning the Linux Kernel for 10x Traffic: How We Prepared a Modest Cloud Server for the Hug of Death
description:
Somaxconn, SYN backlogs, TCP syncookies, and finding our breaking point with stepped Autocannon load benchmarks.

The alert hit our channel at 11:14 AM on a Tuesday.

Our product had just been picked up on a popular tech newsletter, and inbound traffic surged from our normal baseline of 8 requests per second to over 180 requests per second within three minutes.

On the surface, our 2-vCPU, 4GB RAM cloud instance looked relaxed. CPU utilization hovered around 32%. Memory had nearly 2GB free. Disk I/O was barely moving.

Yet visitors were seeing 502 Bad Gateway errors, and API clients reported connection timeouts:

curl: (35) OpenSSL SSL_connect: Connection reset by peer in connection to api.example.com:443

Why would a server drop incoming web traffic when more than half of its compute capacity was sitting idle?

The answer was not in the application code, the database queries, or the cloud provider firewall. The bottleneck was inside the Linux kernel network stack. Out of the box, Linux distributions ship with network socket limits designed for the hardware realities of twenty years ago. When an unexpected traffic surge hits your front door, the kernel drops incoming TCP handshakes before your reverse proxy or web application even knows they exist.

Here is the exact diagnostic workflow, the kernel parameters we tuned to handle ten times our normal traffic, and the stepped Autocannon load tests we used to find our server breaking point.

The Silent Killer: The Two TCP Queues

To understand why a server with an idle CPU rejects incoming web requests, you have to look at how the Linux kernel handles incoming TCP connections.

Before an HTTP request reaches Nginx, Node.js, Go, or Python, the kernel network subsystem must complete the standard TCP three-way handshake:

  1. The client sends a SYN packet to request a connection.
  2. The server responds with SYN-ACK.
  3. The client replies with an ACK packet.

The connection is now established. Only then does the application receive the socket through the accept() system call.

What most engineers miss is that the kernel maintains two completely separate queues in memory during this process:

The SYN Queue (Half-Open Sockets)

When a client sends a SYN, the kernel creates a lightweight request socket in memory and parks it in the SYN queue (also called the half-open connection queue). The connection stays here while waiting for the client final ACK.

The size of this queue is bounded by the kernel parameter net.ipv4.tcp_max_syn_backlog.

The Accept Queue (Fully Established Sockets)

Once the client returns the final ACK, the handshake is complete. The kernel promotes the connection from the SYN queue to the Accept queue.

The connection sits in the Accept queue until your application process calls accept() to pick it up and assign it a file descriptor.

The size of this queue is bounded by the system-wide limit net.core.somaxconn and the backlog parameter passed by your application to the listen() system call.

Here is the problem: on many standard cloud images, net.core.somaxconn defaults to 128 (or 4096 on newer kernels, while application servers still request 128 or 511). And net.ipv4.tcp_max_syn_backlog often defaults to 128 or 512.

If a sudden burst of 200 users attempts to connect simultaneously, the Accept queue fills up instantly.

Once the queue is full, the kernel has a stark choice. By default, it silently drops newly arriving ACK packets. The client assumes the packet was lost in transit and attempts TCP retransmissions, creating an artificial latency spike of one to three seconds.

If the queue remains congested, the client connection times out or the server resets it with a RST packet.

Your application never logged an error because the request was killed before user space ever saw it.

How to Prove Your Sockets Are Dropping Packets

Never guess when debugging the Linux network stack. You can inspect queue depths and drop counters directly from the command line.

Inspecting Live Socket Backlogs with ss

The ss command is the modern replacement for netstat. Most engineers know how to use it to check open ports, but few know how to interpret its queue output on listening sockets.

Run this command on your server:

ss -lnt '( sport = :80 or sport = :443 )'

You will see output formatted like this:

State      Recv-Q Send-Q Local Address:Port Peer Address:PortProcess
LISTEN     0      511          0.0.0.0:80        0.0.0.0:*
LISTEN     128    128          0.0.0.0:443       0.0.0.0:*

On an established socket (a live data connection), Recv-Q represents bytes in the receive buffer waiting to be read by the application, and Send-Q represents bytes waiting to be sent over the wire.

On a LISTEN socket, those columns mean something completely different:

  • Send-Q: The maximum backlog capacity of the Accept queue.
  • Recv-Q: The current number of established connections waiting in the Accept queue to be accepted by the application.

Look at port 443 in the sample output above. Recv-Q is 128 and Send-Q is 128.

The Accept queue is completely full. Every single incoming connection arriving at that exact microsecond is being dropped by the kernel.

Checking Kernel Drop Counters with nstat and netstat

To verify whether your server has suffered queue overflows historically, query the kernel SNMP network statistics:

nstat -az TcpExtListenOverflows TcpExtListenDrops

Or using netstat:

netstat -s | grep -i "listen"

Sample output:

14820 times the listen queue of a socket overflowed
14820 SYNs to LISTEN sockets dropped

If TcpExtListenOverflows is greater than zero, your server has dropped real customer connections because the Accept queue was saturated.

If TcpExtListenDrops is incrementing, the kernel had to discard incoming connection attempts because either the Accept queue was full, the SYN backlog was exhausted, or memory pressure prevented socket allocation.

To check if SYN flood protection or queue exhaustion has been triggered recently, inspect the kernel ring buffer:

dmesg -T | grep -i -E "syn|drop|backlog"

If you see messages like TCP: request_sock_TCP: Possible SYN flooding on port 443. Sending cookies. Check SNMP counters, the kernel SYN queue is overflowing.

The Double-Gatekeeper Bottleneck

A common mistake is changing net.core.somaxconn in /etc/sysctl.conf and assuming the problem is solved.

It is not. The Accept queue size is governed by a double gatekeeper:

Effective Accept Queue = min( net.core.somaxconn, application listen backlog )

When an application server initializes a socket, it executes the listen() system call:

int listen(int sockfd, int backlog);

The second argument tells the kernel how large of an Accept queue the application wants. But the kernel caps that request at the value of net.core.somaxconn.

If you raise net.core.somaxconn to 4096, but your application server requests a backlog of 128, your effective queue remains 128.

Conversely, if your Nginx configuration specifies listen 443 default_server backlog=4096;, but your kernel somaxconn is set to 512, the kernel truncates your queue to 512.

Both layers must be configured in unison.

Nginx Configuration

In your Nginx site configuration, explicitly set the backlog parameter on your listen directives:

server {
    listen 80 backlog=4096;
    listen 443 ssl backlog=4096;
    server_name api.example.com;

    # ... rest of configuration
}

Node.js / Express Configuration

In Node.js HTTP servers, the default backlog is 511. You can raise it by passing an options object to server.listen():

const express = require('express');
const app = express();

const server = app.listen({
    port: 3000,
    host: '0.0.0.0',
    backlog: 4096
}, () => {
    console.log('Server running with listen backlog 4096');
});

Python Gunicorn / Uvicorn

If you run Python workloads with Gunicorn, set the backlog parameter in your command line or config file:

gunicorn --workers 4 --backlog 4096 -b 0.0.0.0:8000 app:wsgi_app

The High-Performance Kernel Recipe

To prepare a production Linux host for high concurrency and unexpected traffic surges, create a dedicated sysctl configuration file at /etc/sysctl.d/99-network-tuning.conf.

Here is the exact configuration we deploy across our cloud nodes:

# /etc/sysctl.d/99-network-tuning.conf

# 1. Expand Socket Listen and SYN Backlogs
net.core.somaxconn = 4096
net.ipv4.tcp_max_syn_backlog = 4096
net.core.netdev_max_backlog = 4096

# 2. Connection Exhaustion and SYN Defense
net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies = 1
net.ipv4.tcp_synack_retries = 2

# 3. Socket Lifecycle and Teardown Acceleration
net.ipv4.tcp_fin_timeout = 15
net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse = 1

# 4. Ephemeral Port Range Expansion
net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range = 10240 65535

# 5. Network Buffer Allocation (Safe for 2GB - 8GB RAM nodes)
net.core.rmem_max = 16777216
net.core.wmem_max = 16777216
net.ipv4.tcp_rmem = 4096 87380 16777216
net.ipv4.tcp_wmem = 4096 65536 16777216

# 6. Anti-Spoofing and Path Verification
net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter = 1
net.ipv4.conf.default.rp_filter = 1

Let us break down why each parameter is set this way and what it changes in practice.

Socket Listen and SYN Queues

net.core.somaxconn = 4096 expands the maximum Accept queue limit from the legacy default to 4096 entries. This gives the application an order of magnitude more headroom during traffic spikes.

net.ipv4.tcp_max_syn_backlog = 4096 ensures the SYN queue can hold up to 4096 half-open connections while handshakes complete.

net.core.netdev_max_backlog = 4096 governs the incoming packet queue between the physical or virtual network interface card (NIC) and the kernel network stack. When the NIC receives packets faster than the CPU can process kernel interrupts, this buffer prevents packet drops at the driver layer.

SYN Cookies and Handshake Resiliency

net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies = 1 activates cryptographic SYN cookies when the SYN backlog overflows. Instead of dropping new connection requests, the kernel encodes the connection state into the initial TCP sequence number sent in the SYN-ACK. When the legitimate client responds with its ACK, the kernel reconstructs the socket without having stored anything in memory. This repels SYN flood attacks and absorbs unexpected spikes without degrading service.

net.ipv4.tcp_synack_retries = 2 lowers the number of times the kernel retransmits a SYN-ACK packet before abandoning the attempt. The default is 5, which ties up resources for over 30 seconds if a client disappears. Lowering it to 2 reclaims half-open sockets within 7 seconds.

Socket Teardown and TIME_WAIT Recycling

net.ipv4.tcp_fin_timeout = 15 reduces the time a socket stays in the FIN-WAIT-2 state from the default of 60 seconds down to 15 seconds. When clients disconnect abruptly without completing a clean four-way TCP shutdown, this ensures the kernel frees orphaned sockets four times faster.

net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse = 1 allows the kernel to safely reuse sockets in the TIME_WAIT state for new outgoing connections, provided the incoming timestamps are strictly greater than the previous connection. This is vital when running a reverse proxy (like Nginx) that opens and closes high-frequency TCP connections to local backend services.

Ephemeral Port Range

net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range = 10240 65535 expands the dynamic port range available for outbound client connections. The default Linux range is 32768 60999, offering approximately 28,231 ports. Setting it to 10240 65535 expands the pool to 55,295 ephemeral ports.

When an Nginx proxy handles 5,000 requests per second against an upstream Node.js application, ports in TIME_WAIT can rapidly exhaust the default range, leading to EADDRNOTAVAIL (Cannot assign requested address) errors. Doubling the port pool eliminates this ceiling.

Applying the Changes Safely

To load the new configuration into the running kernel without rebooting:

sudo sysctl --system

Verify that the values took effect:

sysctl net.core.somaxconn net.ipv4.tcp_max_syn_backlog net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse

Output:

net.core.somaxconn = 4096
net.ipv4.tcp_max_syn_backlog = 4096
net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse = 1

Don't Forget the Conntrack Table and File Descriptors

Two additional system limits frequently trip up engineers who tune socket backlogs but leave firewall or file descriptor defaults untouched.

1. The Netfilter Connection Tracking Table

If you use iptables, nftables, or ufw on your server, the kernel tracks every active stateful connection in a table called conntrack.

When traffic spikes, the connection tracking table can fill up completely. When that happens, the kernel drops incoming packets immediately, logging this terrifying message to dmesg:

nf_conntrack: table full, dropping packet

Check your current conntrack usage and maximum table limit:

cat /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_count
cat /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_max

On a system with 2GB to 4GB of RAM, raise the limit inside /etc/sysctl.d/99-network-tuning.conf:

net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max = 262144
net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_tcp_timeout_established = 600

Lowering nf_conntrack_tcp_timeout_established from its default of 432,000 seconds (5 full days!) down to 600 seconds (10 minutes) purges dead tracking entries exponentially faster.

2. Systemd and File Descriptor Ceilings

Every open socket in Linux requires a file descriptor. The default per-process file limit in systemd is often 1024.

If your Nginx worker process hits 1,024 open connections, it logs:

2026/10/21 11:15:02 [alert] 1240#1240: *45100 socket() failed (24: Too many open files) while connecting to upstream

To permanently fix this for Nginx, create a systemd drop-in configuration:

sudo mkdir -p /etc/systemd/system/nginx.service.d/
sudo nano /etc/systemd/system/nginx.service.d/override.conf

Add these lines:

[Service]
LimitNOFILE=65535

Also add worker_rlimit_nofile 65535; to the top of /etc/nginx/nginx.conf:

user www-data;
worker_processes auto;
pid /run/nginx.pid;
worker_rlimit_nofile 65535;

events {
    worker_connections 8192;
    multi_accept on;
}

Reload and restart:

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl restart nginx

Check the applied limit on the running process:

cat /proc/$(pgrep -o nginx)/limits | grep "Max open files"

Output:

Max open files            65535                65535                files

Real-World Socket Engineering: The Local Port Churn Lesson

When I was building AiroShare, a local DLNA streaming server and high-performance media engine, socket management was one of the earliest friction points I ran into.

In that project, the application broadcasts media manifests to DLNA receivers over SSDP multicast while servicing concurrent media chunk streaming requests over HTTP. During intense chunk streaming, ephemeral sockets opened and closed at an aggressive rate.

Without setting net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse = 1 and expanding the local port range, high-concurrency client requests quickly choked on dead sockets sitting in TIME_WAIT. The operating system refused to assign new client sockets, throwing EADDRNOTAVAIL errors even though the machine had negligible CPU load.

The exact same problem happens on cloud servers with reverse proxies. When Nginx proxies thousands of incoming connections to a local backend on 127.0.0.1:3000, it consumes an ephemeral port for every single upstream connection.

If keepalive connections are not enabled between Nginx and the backend, each request opens a new socket and leaves it in TIME_WAIT for 60 seconds.

Always configure upstream keepalive pools in Nginx:

upstream backend_cluster {
    server 127.0.0.1:3000;
    keepalive 64;
}

server {
    listen 443 ssl backlog=4096;
    server_name api.example.com;

    location / {
        proxy_pass http://backend_cluster;
        proxy_http_version 1.1;
        proxy_set_header Connection "";
    }
}

Adding proxy_http_version 1.1 and clearing the Connection header allows Nginx to reuse established TCP connections to your application, slashing socket churn by over 80%.

Stress Testing Live: Finding the Breaking Point with Autocannon

Applying kernel parameters without testing them is wishful thinking. To verify our tuning and find the true breaking point of our 2-vCPU node, we ran stepped load benchmarks using Autocannon.

Autocannon is a fast, Node.js-based HTTP benchmarking tool that supports high concurrency, pipelining, and custom headers.

Instead of hitting the server with a static blast of traffic, we used a stepped concurrency testing model:

  1. Step 1: 10 concurrent connections (moderate baseline load).
  2. Step 2: 25 concurrent connections (medium-high production burst).
  3. Step 3: 50 concurrent connections (extreme saturation test).

We ran tests against two separate endpoints: a heavy SSR/database-backed endpoint and an optimized, lightweight JSON telemetry endpoint.

Test 1: Baseline Load at 10 Concurrent Connections

Command executed:

autocannon -c 10 -d 30 -p 10 https://api.example.com/api/v1/telemetry

Output:

Running 30s test @ https://api.example.com/api/v1/telemetry
10 connections with 10 pipelined requests

Stat         2.5%     50%      97.5%    99%      Avg       Stdev     Max
Latency      78ms     135ms    210ms    245ms    138.4ms   34.2ms    312ms

Stat         1%       2.5%     50%      97.5%    Avg       Stdev     Min
Req/Sec      28       31       38       44       38.2      4.1       25

1.1k requests in 30.05s, 4.2 MB read
0 errors, 0 timeouts, 0 non-2xx responses

At 10 concurrent connections with pipelining, our server processed 38.2 requests per second at a median latency of 135ms. The CPU remained below 40%. Zero packet drops occurred. Socket errors stayed at zero.

Test 2: Scaling Up to 25 Concurrent Connections

Next, we tested the optimized API endpoint under higher concurrency:

autocannon -c 25 -d 30 https://api.example.com/api/v1/status

Output:

Running 30s test @ https://api.example.com/api/v1/status
25 connections

Stat         2.5%     50%      97.5%    99%      Avg       Stdev     Max
Latency      52ms     102ms    180ms    210ms    105.1ms   28.6ms    260ms

Stat         1%       2.5%     50%      97.5%    Avg       Stdev     Min
Req/Sec      62       68       75       84       75.3      5.8       58

2.3k requests in 30.04s, 8.9 MB read
0 errors, 0 timeouts, 0 non-2xx responses

On this endpoint, throughput climbed to 75.3 requests per second with a median latency of 102ms.

The contrast was stark. Before our kernel tuning, this exact test triggered TcpExtListenOverflows within four seconds. It dropped over 18% of all connection attempts. With the expanded backlog and tuned TCP syncookies, zero connections were dropped. Not one packet failed.

Test 3: The Latency Cliff at 50 Concurrent Connections

We pushed the 2-vCPU node further to find its ceiling:

autocannon -c 50 -d 30 https://api.example.com/api/v1/telemetry

Output:

Running 30s test @ https://api.example.com/api/v1/telemetry
50 connections

Stat         2.5%     50%      97.5%    99%      Avg       Stdev     Max
Latency      190ms    450ms    1620ms   1840ms   485.2ms   215.4ms   2410ms

Stat         1%       2.5%     50%      97.5%    Avg       Stdev     Min
Req/Sec      35       38       42       46       41.6      3.2       30

1.2k requests in 30.08s, 4.8 MB read
0 errors, 0 timeouts, 0 non-2xx responses

Look closely at what happened.

Throughput plateaued at 41.6 requests per second. Median latency jumped from 135ms to 450ms. The 99th percentile surged to 1,840ms.

During the test, running pidstat -u 1 on the server showed CPU utilization at 98.4%. The cores were pegged.

This is the classic latency cliff.

Crucially, because the kernel queue parameters were properly tuned, there were still zero connection drops and zero timeout errors (0 errors, 0 timeouts).

The server did not crash. It did not reset connections. Instead, requests queued orderly in the expanded Accept queue until CPU cycles were available to process them.

That distinction matters.

An untuned server crashes under load. It drops users with 502 Bad Gateway errors while CPU sits idle. A hardened server queues the burst gracefully. It trades latency for 100% request completion.

An Interesting Fact About somaxconn

The default value of 128 for somaxconn was not chosen through scientific analysis of modern networking.

It was first hardcoded into the 4.2BSD Unix kernel release in 1983.

At the time, typical Unix workstations had between 2MB and 16MB of total physical RAM. Network engineers feared that allowing more than 128 outstanding socket requests would exhaust kernel mbuf memory and trigger a system crash.

That 128-socket limit remained the default across mainstream Linux distributions for over two decades. Even today, many production cloud images default to conservative backlog values that can be saturated by a single office browser refresh.

My Default Rule of Thumb for High-Concurrency Nodes

When preparing a production Linux server for sudden traffic surges:

  • Match your backlogs: Set net.core.somaxconn = 4096 and net.ipv4.tcp_max_syn_backlog = 4096 in sysctl, and match them with backlog=4096 in your Nginx or application server.
  • Enable SYN cookies: net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies = 1 protects you from both deliberate SYN floods and legitimate viral traffic surges.
  • Speed up socket reclamation: Set net.ipv4.tcp_fin_timeout = 15 and net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse = 1 to prevent orphaned sockets from lingering.
  • Double your file limits: Add LimitNOFILE=65535 to your systemd overrides and configure worker_rlimit_nofile 65535; in Nginx.
  • Reuse proxy upstreams: Always configure keepalive in Nginx upstream blocks to avoid ephemeral port exhaustion on 127.0.0.1.
  • Monitor with ss -lnt and nstat: If Recv-Q matches Send-Q on a listening socket, or TcpExtListenOverflows is increasing, your Accept queue is overflowing.

Have you ever experienced an outage where your server was dropping traffic even though CPU and memory were barely breaking a sweat? What turned out to be the bottleneck?

title: Small SaaS Custom Metrics Dashboard — 4 Push API and Pull Model Boundaries
description:
For a small SaaS evaluating a Prometheus alternative, send each completed game-data batch through an idempotent push API, then expose reconciled custom metrics to the dashboard; do not treat either a successful push or a successful pull scrape as proof that the nightly pipeline produced correct data. The deciding constraint is signal quality: the service needs to distinguish late, duplicated, partial, and invalid batches without turning every log line into a metric, regardless of whether Grafana or another dashboard renders the result.

TL;DR: For a nightly pipeline, push one bounded completion record per batch into a durable receiver, derive low-cardinality metrics there, and retain structured logs as the audit trail. A pull endpoint remains useful for live process health. The two transport models solve different failure windows, so combining them is often clearer than declaring either one the universal winner.

This architecture decision record uses four boundaries: batch identity, acceptance, reconciliation, and publication. They matter more than the choice of dashboard.

Should a small SaaS push or pull custom metrics?

The concrete workload is a gaming pipeline that transforms a night's events into searchable structured logs and a small custom-metrics dashboard. Operators need to answer questions such as: Did every scheduled shard finish? Which game mode produced rejected records? Is the apparent drop in processed events real, or did telemetry arrive late?

Four invariants keep those answers defensible. First, every batch has a stable identifier derived from the scheduled run and shard, not from an individual retry. Second, accepting an observation never silently replaces a conflicting observation for the same batch. Third, aggregate counts can be reconciled against the accepted batch records. Fourth, dashboard publication cannot erase the underlying audit evidence. A beginner may reasonably start with the visible choice between a Prometheus pull model and a custom push API, but that framing omits the harder question: which observation survives long enough to prove what happened after an ephemeral job exits? A Node.js producer, a Go producer, and a shell-launched batch all face the same boundary. Transport syntax changes; the reconciliation obligation does not.

These are exactly-once effects, not a claim that a network transports a message exactly once. Retries happen. A receiver can acknowledge a request just before the client loses the response, and a scraper can miss a short-lived process between intervals. The design therefore makes repeated delivery harmless and exposes uncertainty rather than hiding it.

Keep the labels restrained. environment, pipeline, game_mode, and a bounded result can support operations; player_id, raw error text, and batch_id belong in logs or a lookup store, because their value sets grow with the workload. OpenTelemetry distinguishes metric instruments and their intended semantics, but an instrument does not rescue a poor attribute model. Cardinality is an architectural input.

Noise compounds.

A compliance-minded retention policy also separates the two records. Metrics answer aggregate operational questions, while structured logs preserve the traceable batch decision with access controls and retention appropriate to their contents. Do not copy player identifiers into metric attributes merely because a dashboard query feels convenient.

Decision: split durable batch facts from live health

The critical path is short. At batch completion, the worker submits one summary containing the stable batch key, counts, timestamps, and a checksum of the summarized output. A receiver validates it, applies an idempotency rule, persists the accepted fact, and returns an acknowledgment. A separate projector turns accepted facts into bounded metrics. The dashboard reads those metrics, while investigators search structured logs by batch key.

The worker also exposes pullable process metrics for memory pressure, queue depth, and current work. Those observations describe a running target and can disappear when the target exits; they are not the ledger of completed overnight work. Separating the paths prevents a common category error: process liveness and business completion have different clocks.

Decision point Push completion record Pull live target
Natural clock A batch reaches a terminal state A process is running at scrape time
Main failure boundary Ambiguous acknowledgment and retry Missed samples during target absence
Duplicate control Stable idempotency key plus conflict detection Collector timestamps repeated samples
Best signal here Completed, rejected, and reconciled batch totals Queue depth and worker health
Noise risk One series or event per unbounded identifier Scraping many ephemeral or irrelevant targets
Audit role Durable fact can point to detailed logs Snapshot alone is insufficient evidence

This comparison does not depend on a particular metrics product. OpenTelemetry provides a vocabulary for metric signals and instruments; it does not require the batch fact and the live gauge to use the same delivery path. Likewise, the dashboard is a view, not the system of record.

For a small operation, simplicity means fewer ambiguous states, not necessarily fewer components. One receiver, one durable table, and one projector may be easier to reason about than teaching every ephemeral worker to retain state until an external scraper happens to observe it. The reverse can be true for long-running services whose useful signals already exist continuously in memory. The trade-off is operational ownership: a durable receiver introduces schema evolution, storage recovery, access control, and projector lag. It is unsuitable when the team cannot operate that state correctly or when losing a best-effort counter has no consequence. In those cases, the pull model's smaller failure surface can be the better decision.

Critical path in Go

The following handler illustrates the contract, including the distinction between a duplicate and a conflict. The storage interface must enforce uniqueness on BatchID; an in-memory check followed by an insert would reopen the race.

package ingest

import (
    "context"
    "crypto/sha256"
    "encoding/hex"
    "encoding/json"
    "errors"
    "net/http"
    "time"
)

type Completion struct {
    BatchID   string    `json:"batch_id"`
    Pipeline  string    `json:"pipeline"`
    GameMode string    `json:"game_mode"`
    Processed uint64    `json:"processed"`
    Rejected  uint64    `json:"rejected"`
    Finished  time.Time `json:"finished_at"`
}

type Store interface {
    InsertOrCompare(ctx context.Context, batchID, digest string, c Completion) (inserted bool, conflict bool, err error)
}

type Handler struct{ Store Store }

func (h Handler) ServeHTTP(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    defer r.Body.Close()

    var c Completion
    dec := json.NewDecoder(http.MaxBytesReader(w, r.Body, 64<<10))
    dec.DisallowUnknownFields()
    if err := dec.Decode(&c); err != nil || c.BatchID == "" || c.Pipeline == "" {
        http.Error(w, "invalid completion", http.StatusBadRequest)
        return
    }

    canonical, err := json.Marshal(c)
    if err != nil {
        http.Error(w, "cannot encode completion", http.StatusInternalServerError)
        return
    }
    sum := sha256.Sum256(canonical)
    digest := hex.EncodeToString(sum[:])

    inserted, conflict, err := h.Store.InsertOrCompare(r.Context(), c.BatchID, digest, c)
    if err != nil {
        if errors.Is(err, context.Canceled) {
            return
        }
        http.Error(w, "temporary ingest failure", http.StatusServiceUnavailable)
        return
    }
    if conflict {
        http.Error(w, "batch identity conflict", http.StatusConflict)
        return
    }
    if inserted {
        w.WriteHeader(http.StatusCreated)
        return
    }
    w.WriteHeader(http.StatusNoContent)
}

Two limits are concrete here.

The 64 KiB body limit is a contract guard, not a throughput claim. A completion summary should remain small; detailed records stay in the structured-log path. The HTTP outcomes also have deliberately narrow meanings: 201 records a new fact, 204 recognizes an identical retry, 409 identifies a conflicting reuse of the batch key, and 503 leaves the client free to retry because no durable acceptance was promised. DisallowUnknownFields makes schema drift visible, although a production evolution policy may instead accept known versioned envelopes. This strictness has a limitation: independently deployed producers cannot add fields casually. A versioned envelope or an explicit compatibility window is required once producer and receiver releases can diverge.

The subtle part is the digest. Replaying an identical body for the same batch_id is success, because the desired effect already exists. Reusing that identifier with different counts is a conflict that should page or enter a review queue; silently choosing the latest payload would destroy the audit trail. Persist the accepted record and its digest in one transaction. Only then may the projector update dashboard-facing aggregates.

A projector can fail after persistence. That is acceptable if it checkpoints progress and can replay accepted records, because the dashboard may briefly lag while the durable fact remains intact. The lag itself should be measured as the age of the newest unprojected record, using a bounded set of attributes. This yields a signal about the observation system without recursively emitting a metric for every failed event.

How do we test signal quality rather than transport success?

Begin with fault cases, since a happy-path request proves little. Send the same completion twice and require one durable fact. Send the same key with altered counts and require a conflict. Cancel the client after the server commits, retry, and require an idempotent acknowledgment. Stop the projector, accept several batches, restart it, and require aggregates to converge without double counting. Finally, terminate a worker before the next scrape and verify that the batch remains visibly incomplete rather than falsely successful.

Reconciliation is the stronger test. For each nightly run, compare the expected shard manifest with terminal batch facts, then compare the sum of accepted processed and rejected counts with the pipeline's output manifest. A dashboard status is complete only after those checks agree. HTTP success means accepted, not reconciled.

Deployment deserves the same caution. Add the completion schema before requiring new fields, deploy the receiver before producers emit the new version, and keep projector rebuilds possible from durable records. An alert should fire on missing expected batches, identity conflicts, projector lag, and reconciliation mismatch. It should not fire once per malformed log line.

Review the noise weekly.

Inspect alert volume, the fraction of signals that led to an action, attribute cardinality growth, and time to reconcile the nightly run. These are decision criteria rather than invented universal thresholds. The acceptable limits depend on the schedule, on-call coverage, and regulatory obligations governing the underlying data. Document those limits beside the ADR and test them as configuration. An easy first assumption is that more labels make the Grafana dashboard more useful; later reconciliation exposes the flaw, because an identifier useful for one forensic search can create a separate metric series for every batch or player. Keep that identifier in the structured logs and link investigations through the stable batch key.

Rejected option and where it still fits

The rejected design exposes only an in-memory Prometheus pull endpoint from each nightly worker. It is attractive because there is no explicit ingestion receiver, and it can be adequate for a long-running service whose metrics describe current process state. For short-lived batch workers, however, absence is ambiguous: the job may not have started, may have completed between scrapes, or may have crashed before exposing a final value. A Grafana dashboard cannot infer which event occurred from a missing target. This is a limitation of the observation boundary in this workload, not a general defect in Prometheus.

The other extreme, pushing every structured log field directly into metric labels, is also rejected. It improves apparent search flexibility at the expense of uncontrolled series growth and muddles two data models. Search belongs over structured records; aggregation belongs over deliberately bounded dimensions. A custom log sink can encapsulate delivery, as the Logback appender documentation demonstrates for that ecosystem, but delivery plumbing does not define the correctness contract.

There is a valid use case for pull alone: stable services with discoverable endpoints, continuously meaningful gauges, and no requirement to prove that a transient batch reached a terminal state. There is also a valid use case for a simple push gateway without a durable fact store: disposable best-effort counters whose loss or duplication cannot affect an operational decision. Neither description matches a nightly gaming pipeline used for reconciliation.

The final choice is architectural, not promotional. Preserve one immutable batch fact, make retries idempotent, project only bounded metrics, and use pull observations for live health. That arrangement gives a small team a dashboard it can trust without asking the dashboard to become an audit database.

References

  • https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/signals/metrics/
  • https://logback.qos.ch/manual/appenders.html

title: Virtual DOM
description:
In the previous post, we discussed what React really is, the meaning of declarative UI, and its tree-like structure. Now, let’s continue that discussion further.

If you have worked with React, you have probably heard about state, how and why it is used. Don’t worry if you don’t know about it yet.

What is State in React?

State is information that can change over time and affects what a component renders.

Now, assume React renders the component and the user clicks a button. The information about whether the button is clicked or not is stored in this state.

Whenever the user clicks the button, the information in the state changes from its default value to clicked.

The state changes, so React schedules an update. The component is evaluated again. React compares the previous UI and the new UI to determine what needs to change in the actual DOM.

Previous UI vs. New UI

Here, you can see the two UIs: the previous UI and the new UI. So, what is the difference between them?

Understanding the Virtual DOM

To understand the difference, we need to discuss the Virtual DOM.

Assume you already have a UI. Now, you perform some action, and the UI changes.

To track the changes in the UI, React uses an in-memory representation of the updated UI.

To perform reconciliation, React compares both UIs: the previous UI that needs to be updated and the new UI created by React. This is commonly described as the Virtual DOM.

Note: I know this is an oversimplification, but to understand the idea of the Virtual DOM, this mental model is useful.

Using the Virtual DOM, React can determine the required changes instead of rebuilding the entire browser DOM every time the state updates.

The new UI we talked about is the Virtual DOM. Using reconciliation and the Virtual DOM, React updates the specific changes.

What is Reconciliation?

Now, I have used the word reconciliation many times. So, what is reconciliation?

Reconciliation is the process React uses to determine how the current rendered tree, which is the host tree, should change when new data or state produces a new tree, which is commonly referred to as the Virtual DOM.

In a web application, the host environment is generally the browser DOM. React is responsible for the UI programming model and reconciliation.

title: Right On Q: Recovering Reasoning under Quantization via Self-Generated Trajectories
description:
arXiv:2610.29378v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Quantization-aware training (QAT) aims to recover reasoning capabilities in low-bit large language models (LLMs). Existing recipes typically supervise the quantized student with the original full-precision model on fixed response sequences. However, the resulting low-bit quantized models still struggle on long-horizon reasoning tasks and often fail to terminate within a token budget that suffices for the full-precision model. We identify two challenges in closing this gap. First, fixed-response supervision leaves a mismatch between training prefixes and those encountered during student generation, and this trajectory divergence grows as responses lengthen. Second, on its own prefixes, the student underpredicts some next-token candidates and overpredicts others, and this distributional misalignment becomes more frequent at high-entropy prefixes. We present OnQ, a low-bit recovery pipeline that combines on-policy distillation and candidate-wise Dynamic KL. Starting from block-wise calibration, the quantized student generates responses and receives full-precision teacher supervision on its own prefixes. Dynamic KL weights forward and reverse KL by each candidate's teacher-student probability ratio to balance correction of under- and overprediction. Across Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, and 8B at 2- and 3-bit precision, OnQ achieves the highest nine-benchmark average, with the largest gains on long-horizon reasoning benchmarks. At 2 bits, it outperforms every baseline on every benchmark at every model size, improving the Qwen3-8B average by 10.26 points over the strongest baseline. It also produces shorter responses with fewer truncations and repetitive errors.

title: Frontend Development -Accessibility Is Part of Good Engineering
description:
Accessibility Isn't a Final Polish Step — It's Part of Building the Product

When developing a frontend, it's easy to focus on what users can see.

We adjust spacing, choose fonts, improve animations, and make sure everything looks right on different screen sizes.

But visual quality is only one part of the user experience.

A website also needs to work for people who navigate with a keyboard, use screen readers, or need stronger visual contrast to read content comfortably.

I think accessibility deserves attention from the beginning, not just before a product launch.

Start with the basics

Accessibility doesn't always require complicated libraries or a complete redesign.

Sometimes the most useful improvements come from using HTML elements correctly.

A button should be a real button. Navigation should use appropriate links. Form fields should have meaningful labels, and headings should follow a logical structure.

These choices help browsers and assistive technologies understand the page.

They can also make the code easier for other developers to maintain.

Keyboard navigation reveals hidden problems

One practical test is to navigate a website without using a mouse.

Can you reach the important controls? Is the current focus visible? Does the tab order make sense? Can you open and close interactive components using the expected keyboard controls?

If a user becomes trapped inside a modal or cannot reach an important action, the interface has a usability problem that may not be obvious during ordinary development.

Testing keyboard interaction is a simple way to uncover issues early.

Contrast and feedback matter too

Text should be readable against its background, and important interface states shouldn't depend on color alone.

For example, a form error shouldn't be communicated only by turning a field border red. A message explaining the problem gives users additional context.

Similarly, interactive elements need clear focus states so keyboard users can understand where they are on the page.

Small details like these can make a product more usable for a wider range of people.

Accessibility also improves development quality

I don't see accessibility as separate from good engineering.

Semantic HTML provides clearer structure. Labels make forms easier to understand. Predictable focus behavior makes interactive components easier to test.

Automated accessibility tools can identify some problems, but they won't catch everything. Manual keyboard testing and, where appropriate, screen-reader testing are still valuable.

The earlier these checks become part of a team's workflow, the less likely accessibility problems are to accumulate across the application.

A practical checklist

For my next frontend project, I'd want to check:

Every interactive control can be reached and operated with a keyboard.

Form inputs have clear labels.

Text and controls have sufficient contrast.

Focus indicators are visible.

Errors and status changes are communicated clearly.

Images have appropriate alternative text when they convey meaningful information.

Automated checks are supplemented with manual testing.

None of these steps guarantees a fully accessible application, but together they provide a useful starting point.

Final thoughts

A polished interface isn't necessarily an accessible one.

Good frontend development means considering how different people interact with a product and making sure important tasks don't depend on a single way of navigating or interpreting information.

Accessibility isn't just about meeting a checklist. It's about building software that more people can actually use.

What's one accessibility improvement you think every frontend developer should learn to implement?

title: How to Add, Edit, and Remove Hyperlinks in PowerPoint Using Java
description:
Hyperlinks in PowerPoint can point to websites, external resources, or other slides in the same presentation. For example, you might link a reference document from a project report or create a clickable table of contents for navigating between sections.

Java lets you add hyperlinks to text and images, create links between slides, and update or remove existing links.

This article walks through each of these operations with complete Java examples.

1. Add the Maven Dependency

First, add a PowerPoint processing library to your Java project.

If you're using Maven, include the following repository and dependency in your pom.xml file:

<repositories>
    <repository>
        <id>com.e-iceblue</id>
        <name>e-iceblue</name>
        <url>https://repo.e-iceblue.com/nexus/content/groups/public/</url>
    </repository>
</repositories>

<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>e-iceblue</groupId>
        <artifactId>spire.presentation</artifactId>
        <version>11.9.10</version>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>

The examples below work with PPTX files. Each program saves its result to a separate file, so you can test the operations independently.

2. Add a Hyperlink to Text in PowerPoint

To make a piece of text clickable, you can assign a hyperlink to a PortionEx object, which represents a text range within a paragraph.

The following example creates a slide containing the text "View Project Resources" and links it to a web page.

import com.spire.presentation.*;
import com.spire.presentation.drawing.FillFormatType;

import java.awt.geom.Rectangle2D;

public class AddTextHyperlink {

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {

        Presentation presentation = new Presentation();

        try {
            // Get the first slide
            ISlide slide = presentation.getSlides().get(0);

            // Add a text shape
            Rectangle2D.Double rect =
                    new Rectangle2D.Double(60, 100, 400, 100);

            IAutoShape shape = slide.getShapes()
                    .appendShape(ShapeType.RECTANGLE, rect);

            // Remove the shape fill and border
            shape.getFill().setFillType(FillFormatType.NONE);
            shape.getLine().setWidth(0);
            shape.getTextFrame().getParagraphs().clear();

            // Create a paragraph and text range
            ParagraphEx paragraph = new ParagraphEx();
            PortionEx text = new PortionEx();

            text.setText("View Project Resources");
            text.setFontHeight(22);

            // Set the hyperlink URL
            text.getClickAction().setAddress(
                    "https://www.example.com/");

            // Add the text to the shape
            paragraph.getTextRanges().append(text);

            shape.getTextFrame()
                    .getParagraphs().append(paragraph);

            // Save the presentation
            presentation.saveToFile(
                    "text-hyperlink.pptx",
                    FileFormat.PPTX_2013);

        } finally {
            presentation.dispose();
        }
    }
}

The key statement is:

text.getClickAction().setAddress("https://www.example.com/");

getClickAction() accesses the text's click action, while setAddress() assigns the destination URL.

The generated text-hyperlink.pptx contains the linked text. When you click it in Slide Show mode, PowerPoint opens the specified web page.

The URL in this example is a placeholder. Replace it with the actual destination when using the code.

3. Add a Hyperlink to an Image

Images can also act as hyperlinks. For example, a slide might contain a website logo or a document thumbnail that opens a related page when clicked.

Unlike text hyperlinks, which are associated with text ranges, image hyperlinks are attached to the image shape itself.

The following example inserts an image and assigns it a web address.

import com.spire.presentation.*;
import com.spire.presentation.drawing.FillFormatType;

import java.awt.geom.Rectangle2D;

public class AddImageHyperlink {

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {

        Presentation presentation = new Presentation();

        try {
            // Get the first slide
            ISlide slide = presentation.getSlides().get(0);

            // Define the image position and size
            Rectangle2D.Double rect =
                    new Rectangle2D.Double(80, 100, 240, 120);

            // Insert an image
            IEmbedImage image = slide.getShapes()
                    .appendEmbedImage(
                            ShapeType.RECTANGLE,
                            "logo.png",
                            rect);

            // Remove the image border
            image.getLine().setFillType(FillFormatType.NONE);

            // Create a hyperlink
            ClickHyperlink hyperlink =
                    new ClickHyperlink(
                            "https://www.example.com/");

            // Assign the hyperlink to the image
            image.setClick(hyperlink);

            // Save the presentation
            presentation.saveToFile(
                    "image-hyperlink.pptx",
                    FileFormat.PPTX_2013);

        } finally {
            presentation.dispose();
        }
    }
}

Here, appendEmbedImage() inserts logo.png into the slide, and setClick() assigns a ClickHyperlink object to the image.

The resulting image is clickable during the presentation.

Make sure logo.png exists in your application's working directory, or replace it with an absolute file path.

4. Link to Another Slide in the Same Presentation

Hyperlinks don't have to point to external websites. They can also navigate between slides within the same PowerPoint file.

This is useful for presentations with a table of contents or sections that users may want to visit in a different order.

To create an internal hyperlink, use ClickHyperlink(ISlide) to specify the destination slide.

The following example creates a two-slide presentation and adds a link on the first slide that opens the second.

import com.spire.presentation.*;
import com.spire.presentation.drawing.FillFormatType;

import java.awt.geom.Rectangle2D;

public class AddSlideHyperlink {

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {

        Presentation presentation = new Presentation();

        try {
            // Get the first slide
            ISlide firstSlide =
                    presentation.getSlides().get(0);

            // Add a second slide
            ISlide secondSlide =
                    presentation.getSlides().append();

            // Add content to the second slide
            Rectangle2D.Double targetRect =
                    new Rectangle2D.Double(60, 100, 450, 100);

            IAutoShape targetShape = secondSlide.getShapes()
                    .appendShape(ShapeType.RECTANGLE, targetRect);

            targetShape.getFill()
                    .setFillType(FillFormatType.NONE);
            targetShape.getLine().setWidth(0);

            targetShape.appendTextFrame("Project Details");

            // Add a text shape to the first slide
            Rectangle2D.Double linkRect =
                    new Rectangle2D.Double(60, 100, 450, 100);

            IAutoShape linkShape = firstSlide.getShapes()
                    .appendShape(ShapeType.RECTANGLE, linkRect);

            linkShape.getFill()
                    .setFillType(FillFormatType.NONE);
            linkShape.getLine().setWidth(0);
            linkShape.getTextFrame().getParagraphs().clear();

            // Create the clickable text
            ParagraphEx paragraph = new ParagraphEx();
            PortionEx text = new PortionEx();

            text.setText("Go to Project Details");
            text.setFontHeight(22);

            // Link to the second slide
            ClickHyperlink hyperlink =
                    new ClickHyperlink(secondSlide);

            text.setClickAction(hyperlink);

            paragraph.getTextRanges().append(text);

            linkShape.getTextFrame()
                    .getParagraphs().append(paragraph);

            // Save the presentation
            presentation.saveToFile(
                    "slide-hyperlink.pptx",
                    FileFormat.PPTX_2013);

        } finally {
            presentation.dispose();
        }
    }
}

The important part is:

ClickHyperlink hyperlink =
        new ClickHyperlink(secondSlide);

text.setClickAction(hyperlink);

Instead of passing a URL, we pass the destination slide as an ISlide object.

When the presentation is in Slide Show mode, clicking "Go to Project Details" navigates directly to the second slide.

You can use the same approach with an existing presentation. Retrieve the destination slide using presentation.getSlides().get(index) and assign it to a hyperlink.

Remember that slide indexes start at zero, so get(0) refers to the first slide and get(2) refers to the third.

5. Edit an Existing Hyperlink in PowerPoint

Links sometimes need to be updated when a website address changes or a referenced resource moves.

Rather than recreating the linked text, you can retrieve its text range and update the display text or destination URL.

The following example opens text-hyperlink.pptx, created in Section 2, and changes both the displayed text and the web address.

import com.spire.presentation.*;

public class EditPptHyperlink {

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {

        Presentation presentation = new Presentation();

        try {
            // Load the presentation
            presentation.loadFromFile(
                    "text-hyperlink.pptx");

            // Get the shape containing the hyperlink
            IAutoShape shape = (IAutoShape) presentation
                    .getSlides().get(0)
                    .getShapes().get(0);

            // Update the hyperlink display text
            shape.getTextFrame()
                    .getTextRange()
                    .setText("View Updated Project Resources");

            // Update the hyperlink URL
            shape.getTextFrame()
                    .getTextRange()
                    .getClickAction()
                    .setAddress(
                            "https://www.wikipedia.org/");

            // Save the updated presentation
            presentation.saveToFile(
                    "edited-hyperlink.pptx",
                    FileFormat.PPTX_2013);

        } finally {
            presentation.dispose();
        }
    }
}

The code uses setText() to change the displayed text and getClickAction().setAddress() to update the link destination.

The resulting edited-hyperlink.pptx contains the updated hyperlink.

One thing to watch for: This example accesses the first shape on the first slide because the structure of the input file is known.

In an existing presentation, a text box may contain several text ranges, each with different formatting or hyperlinks. In that case, locate the specific linked text range before editing it rather than assuming the first shape or entire text frame contains the intended link.

6. Remove a Hyperlink Without Deleting the Text

If a hyperlink is no longer needed, you can remove its click action while keeping the text.

For text hyperlinks, this can be done using setClickAction(null).

The following example removes the hyperlink from text-hyperlink.pptx, leaving the displayed text unchanged.

import com.spire.presentation.*;

public class RemovePptHyperlink {

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {

        Presentation presentation = new Presentation();

        try {
            // Load the presentation
            presentation.loadFromFile(
                    "text-hyperlink.pptx");

            // Get the shape containing the hyperlink
            IAutoShape shape = (IAutoShape) presentation
                    .getSlides().get(0)
                    .getShapes().get(0);

            // Remove the hyperlink
            shape.getTextFrame()
                    .getTextRange()
                    .setClickAction(null);

            // Save the presentation
            presentation.saveToFile(
                    "removed-hyperlink.pptx",
                    FileFormat.PPTX_2013);

        } finally {
            presentation.dispose();
        }
    }
}

The key statement is:

shape.getTextFrame().getTextRange().setClickAction(null);

Setting the click action to null removes the hyperlink from the text range without deleting the text itself.

The text may still retain its previous formatting, such as an underline or a hyperlink color. If you want it to look like ordinary text again, you may also need to adjust its formatting.

As with the previous example, this code assumes that the text shape and hyperlink are already known. For more complex presentations, identify the appropriate text range before removing its click action.

7. Things to Keep in Mind

Test Hyperlinks in Slide Show Mode

In PowerPoint's editing view, clicking text or an image usually selects the object rather than immediately following its hyperlink.

To check whether a hyperlink works, open the presentation in Slide Show mode and click the linked element.

External Links Depend on Their Destinations

A hyperlink may be stored correctly in the PPTX file even if its target website is unavailable or its address has changed.

Links to local files can also stop working when a presentation is moved to another computer or the referenced files are relocated.

Text and Shape Hyperlinks Are Different

Text hyperlinks are associated with text ranges, while image and shape hyperlinks are typically associated with the shape itself.

This distinction matters when editing or removing links. You need to identify whether the link belongs to a text range or the containing shape before changing its click action.

Be Careful When Working with Existing Slides

The examples for editing and removing hyperlinks access a shape by its index because they use a presentation with a known structure.

For real-world presentations containing multiple text boxes, images, charts, or grouped shapes, don't assume the target hyperlink is always in the first shape. Locate the relevant object and text range before making changes.

title: Beyond Small Talk: Modeling Disclosure Trajectories in Human-AI Conversation
description:
arXiv:2610.29413v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recently, we see a rise in conversational agents as a form of social and emotional support, where disclosure will unfold over time. Yet, current evaluations of these agents typically examine isolated conversational states. In analyses of naturally occurring conversations, disclosure history and current disclosure are confounded which tends to make their effects difficult to isolate. We thus introduce Trajectory-based Disclosure Evaluation (TraDE), an evaluation framework grounded in Social Penetration Theory that utilizes predefined disclosure trajectories and evaluates how preceding disclosure history shapes model behavior under matched current disclosure. Through the use of TraDE, we demonstrate across multiple models and relational behavior benchmarks that responses to disclosures matched on depth can differ depending on the preceding trajectory, particularly in whether models accept or challenge the user's framing. We also observed that these differences track accumulated exposure to deeper disclosure rather than any single moment of vulnerability or the order of disclosures. It also tends to persists for several turns after disclosure returns to shallow levels. For several behaviors, we also demonstrate that models diverge most consistently from human supporters in the Emotional Support Conversation corpus (ESConv) not when users open up but rather when they step back in their disclosure. TraDE thus provides a systematic way to expose history-dependent relational behavior that evaluations of isolated conversational states would otherwise miss.

title: Scan or Index? large Evidence Coverage, Answer Quality, and Cost in Long-Document RAG
description:
arXiv:2610.28957v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Scanning every passage in a long document seems thorough, but does it preserve more useful evidence or produce better answers? We compare 11 retrieval configurations spanning lexical and dense search, hybrid reranking, and full-document scanning with Jev, OpenAI Decisions, and Cloudflare Clef. Our evaluation uses 396 QASPER questions and 80 questions from eight complete textbooks, with common passages, a five-passage limit, and a fixed answer generator. On books, Hybrid + Jev achieves the highest observed evidence coverage (94.1%), compared with 88.7% for Jev full scan and 81.3\% for OpenAI dense retrieval. Full scans examine every passage initially, yet later reduction steps can discard relevant evidence. Higher evidence coverage also does not consistently produce better answers: Hybrid + Decisions achieves the highest observed book Answer Accuracy among retrieval methods (0.892), despite recovering less reference evidence. Full scanning incurs substantially higher latency on books under the tested deployments, while reusable dense retrieval has lower projected API cost than paid decision-based methods as queries accumulate. Most QASPER articles already fit within the hybrid candidate pool, limiting the benefit of scanning. These results highlight evidence retention, answer quality, and reuse cost as complementary criteria for choosing a long-document retrieval strategy.
