description:
Rusty Inbox is a free, open-source desktop email client for Linux, Windows and macOS. Its mail engine is written in Rust and its interface in Qt 6 / QML, so the window opens in a fraction of a second and stays light on memory. It works with any IMAP/SMTP account — Gmail (with an app password), Fastmail, iCloud, Yahoo, cPanel hosting — sorts the inbox into people, notifications and newsletters, and every action works from the keyboard. The source is on GitHub under MIT or Apache 2.0, and the app has its own page here: Rusty Inbox.

I built it because I live in my inbox, on a Linux desktop, and every mail client I tried was one of two things: fast but bare, or polished but a web app shipped inside its own copy of a browser. I wanted the polish without the browser. This post is the build story — the architecture, the decisions that kept it fast, and what it took to ship one codebase to three operating systems.

What does Rusty Inbox do?

  • Smart Inbox. Mail from people comes first. Notifications, newsletters and calendar invitations go into their own groups, which you can fold away.
  • Unified mailboxes across every account, with per-account Sent, Drafts and Done.
  • Undo Send and Send Later. Messages wait in a local outbox; a failed send retries by itself and stays under Scheduled.
  • Drafts that sync to your provider's Drafts folder, templates, and per-account signatures.
  • Done, Snooze, Pin and bulk actions (select all or a range), each with undo.
  • Keyboard first: J/K to move, E Done, S snooze, R/A/F reply, reply all, forward, C compose, Ctrl+Enter send.
  • Desktop native: tray icon with an unread dot, notifications, mailto: links, a single running instance, and live theming — on Omarchy the colours and font follow omarchy theme set.
  • One-click import from Thunderbird: accounts, servers and saved passwords.
  • Local and private: a SQLite cache on your machine, no telemetry, no cloud relay.

How is Rusty Inbox built?

Rusty Inbox is two layers that never wait on each other. The engine, rusty-inbox-core, is a plain Rust library with no UI code: IMAP sync with async-imap over rustls, SMTP with lettre, MIME parsing with mail-parser, and a SQLite cache through rusqlite. The desktop app is Qt 6 / QML, connected to Rust through cxx-qt. A single QObject — the bridge — sits between them.

Layer What it does Built with
Interface Inbox, reader, composer, settings Qt Quick / QML
Bridge JSON in, Qt signals out cxx-qt
Engine Sync, send, drafts, search, import Rust, Tokio
Storage Threads, messages, outbox, settings SQLite

The rule that makes it feel fast is simple: the interface only ever reads local data synchronously, and everything that touches the network reports back later as a signal. When you open a thread, QML asks the bridge for what is already in SQLite and draws it immediately. Sync runs on a small Tokio runtime inside the app and emits a signal when new mail lands. Scrolling and typing never block on a server.

At the time of writing the project is about 7,300 lines of Rust and 3,800 lines of QML, with 64 automated tests.

Five decisions that kept it fast and reliable

1. Pool IMAP connections per account

Logging in to IMAP is the slowest thing a mail client does, and some providers throttle accounts that log in too often. The engine keeps a small pool of authenticated connections per account, checks a pooled connection with a cheap liveness probe before reuse, and hands it back when the job is done. Opening a folder reuses a warm session instead of a fresh TLS handshake and login.

2. Undo Send is an outbox, not a timer

Pressing Send does not send. It writes the message to a local outbox table with a send_at time — now plus the undo window, or the time you picked for Send Later. Undo simply turns the row back into a draft. A background loop claims due rows and sends them; if the server fails, the row is marked failed, kept under Scheduled and retried. Because the outbox lives in SQLite, a crash or a closed laptop never loses a message.

3. Smart Inbox reads headers, not content

Sorting mail into people, notifications and newsletters does not need AI or a server. The signals are already in every message: a List-Unsubscribe or List-Id header means a newsletter, a calendar part means an invitation, and Precedence: bulk or a sender like noreply@ means an automated notification. Everything else is a person. It is deterministic, instant, and runs entirely on your machine.

4. Render HTML mail in a sandbox

HTML email is untrusted content. Each message renders in its own iframe with the sandbox attribute and no allow-scripts, so no script in an email ever runs. Links open in your default browser instead of inside the app. The rest of the interface is native Qt Quick; a web view is used only for message bodies.

5. Import from Thunderbird by reading its own files

Most people switching mail clients come from Thunderbird, and re-typing server settings is where they give up. Rusty Inbox reads the Thunderbird profile directly — the account settings in prefs.js and the saved passwords in logins.json, decrypted with the key in NSS key4.db — so accounts, servers and passwords come over in one click (when the profile has no primary password).

Shipping one codebase to Linux, Windows and macOS

Qt and Rust both cross-compile well, so the work was packaging, not porting. A GitHub Actions pipeline builds every release:

  • Linux: an AppImage and a Flatpak bundle, plus an Arch Linux PKGBUILD in the repo that builds from source.
  • Windows 10/11: an installer and a portable zip.
  • macOS 12+: a .dmg for Apple Silicon and Intel.

An install script picks the right package for your system and updates it when you run it again.

How do I install Rusty Inbox?

Download a package from GitHub Releases, or build it yourself with Rust 1.85+ and Qt 6.8+ (Qt Quick, Quick Controls 2 and Qt WebEngine):

git clone https://github.com/karem505/rusty-inbox && cd rusty-inbox
cargo build --release
./target/release/rusty-inbox

Then open Settings → Accounts. Most providers are detected from the address alone; for Gmail, create an app password and use it as the password. Coming from Thunderbird, choose Import from Thunderbird.

What I took from building it

Speed in a desktop app is mostly an architecture decision, not an optimisation pass: keep the UI on local data, push every slow thing behind a signal, and the app feels instant on any machine. The same thinking applies to the business software I build for companies — internal tools that open instantly and never make people wait on a spinner. If that is the kind of system your team needs, that is what my digital transformation consulting is for.

FAQ

Is Rusty Inbox free?
Yes. It is open source under MIT or Apache 2.0, with no paid tier and no account to create.

Does Rusty Inbox work with Gmail?
Yes, over IMAP and SMTP. Create a Google app password and use it as the account password.

Is Rusty Inbox a Thunderbird alternative?
It is a faster, keyboard-first inbox, and it imports your Thunderbird accounts, servers and saved passwords in one click.

Does Rusty Inbox collect data?
No. It has no analytics, crash reporting or servers of its own. It talks only to the mail servers you add.

What is Rusty Inbox built with?
A Rust mail engine (async-imap, rustls, lettre, mail-parser, SQLite, Tokio) and a Qt 6 / QML interface connected through cxx-qt.

Try it, star it, or open an issue: github.com/karem505/rusty-inbox.

Originally published at aboelmakarem.pro.

title: Tell HN: I unknowingly broke the PHP RCE embargo. I am sorry.
description:
I posted here about the then-upcoming PHP RCEs related to CVE-2026-109618 & CVE-2026-109619. I appreciate this has had considerable knock-on effects with the schedule for co-ordinated disclosure, and created additional workload.

I am truly sorry. I take full responsibility for my actions.

It was not remotely my intention to cause any of the subsequent side effects.

At the time of posting, I didn't know about any embargo. My contact had told me there was no embargo, and her contact had told her the same thing.

As someone who follows the 4-weekly PHP release cycle and compiles it from source, my intention was to alert others in a similar position to be aware of the importance/urgency of the updates.

That clearly backfired in a pretty wild fashion. I have learned my lesson.

Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50193416

Points: 83

title: Migrate from VAST 2 or 3 when a supported capability justifies the work.
description:
Originally published on VASTLint. This article is part of the Migrate video standards with evidence series.

An old VAST version is a reason to review a delivery contract. It is not a business case on its own. The case becomes concrete when a campaign needs a capability that the current route cannot reliably provide, or when repeated custom handling costs more than a supported upgrade.

Start by identifying the requirement that is blocked. It might concern creative identification, an interactive experience, verification or a media handoff. Then trace the whole route from the ad server through wrappers to the player or insertion system. Changing the first response cannot upgrade every downstream component.

Choose the capability before choosing the version.

The IAB Tech Lab VAST page links the published specifications and related addenda. Use the version supported by your destinations and the feature you actually need. VAST 4.x includes capabilities that are useful for modern delivery, but support for a version label is not evidence that every optional capability has been implemented.

Write an acceptance sentence in the campaign brief. For example, the same registered creative identifier must survive the ad-server response and appear in the agreed delivery report. That sentence gives engineering a test and operations a decision. A requirement to use the latest version gives neither team a measurable outcome.

Ask partners to confirm the specific structure they accept and the behavior they support. Keep sample responses and their approval. Record exceptions by destination rather than forcing all partners into a single untested response format.

Check whether the 2024 addendum meets the narrower need.

A full version migration is not always necessary. The VAST CTV Addendum 2024 describes extensions for bringing selected capabilities to older VAST routes. An extension is useful only where the receiving systems recognize and process it as intended.

Compare two scoped proposals: a supported addendum route for the immediate requirement, and a broader VAST 4.x migration. Include development, partner review, regression testing and future maintenance in both estimates. An addendum can reduce the first change while leaving some legacy complexity in place.

Do not insert a native element from a newer schema into an arbitrary older location and assume that an extension reader will find it. Follow the published structure and the receiving partner's documented contract. Save an example that the partner has actually processed successfully.

Treat a version change as a content change.

Changing the root version attribute is not a conversion procedure. Elements, required metadata and interpretation need to match the target specification. Review the complete document against the published VAST 4.3 specification when that is the agreed target, including the wrappers that lead to the final creative.

Keep the same intended advertisement in the before and after records. A clean empty response may be a legitimate no-ad response, but it does not establish that the campaign creative migrated successfully. Compare media, duration, identifiers, click behavior, tracking and verification requirements explicitly.

Run the original and candidate through VASTLint and retain both outputs. Review new findings instead of deleting fields until the report looks clean. Some fields may be required by the destination even when a more general document check permits their absence.

Test the route that will receive paid traffic.

Run the candidate through the actual ad-server and wrapper path, then through the approved player or insertion workflow. Check asset selection, playback, the expected events and the destination report. Record the environment and the time of the test so the result can be reproduced.

Include a working legacy creative as a control. Add failure cases for an unavailable asset and an unsupported optional feature. The purpose is to verify the agreed fallback and escalation, not simply demonstrate one successful happy path.

Limit the first release to a small, observable allocation. Keep the previous routing configuration and a rollback trigger that the operator can execute. A migration needs someone watching the campaign results, particularly when the new route changes reporting as well as delivery.

Budget against the problem the migration can solve.

Suppose, purely as a planning example, twelve campaign handoffs each require an hour of manual identifier reconciliation. A proposed change may target that twelve-hour task. It does not follow that all twelve hours disappear, because exceptions, validation and reporting work may remain.

Measure a comparable group after the change. Count unresolved identifiers, manual corrections and time spent by role. If the requirement instead concerns acceptance of a new format, retain the partner approval and subsequent delivery record. Do not present planned impression allocation as measured recovered revenue.

The same discipline can justify postponing a migration. If the current supported route meets the immediate requirement and the broader upgrade has no committed consumer, invest in the bounded change first. Record the limitation so it is revisited when the product requirement changes.

Make the approved route reusable.

Store the accepted version, optional capabilities, partner exceptions and sample test records with the integration configuration. Use that record when a second campaign arrives. Include an owner and a review trigger for SDK, ad-server or destination changes.

Use VASTLint at the document handoff and retain runtime checks for the destination. The commercial benefit is a capability that the business can repeatedly deliver with known acceptance conditions. A newer version number becomes useful when it supports that result.

title: SpacetimeDB AX Audit: A Review for AI Agents
description:
SpacetimeDB's homepage is written for AI agents. Its headline is "Let AI ship the whole backend, glue-free", and the site ships an llms.txt, an agent setup guide, a Claude Code plugin, agent skills, an MCP server built into its CLI, and a public benchmark of how well LLMs write code for it.

In our tests, a coding agent built a working, live-updating app on SpacetimeDB with no help from us. It used none of that tooling. And when we asked agents which backend to use for a web app, they picked Convex or Supabase.

SpacetimeDB is a database that is also your server, made by Clockwork Labs. We put it through our agent experience (AX) audit, following our AX audit method. The audit has four stages:

  • Awareness: does the model know SpacetimeDB without searching?
  • Discoverability: can an agent find SpacetimeDB when it's looking for a tool like it?
  • Reputation: does the agent speak well of SpacetimeDB, and recommend it over other options?
  • Integration: can the agent build a working proof of concept with SpacetimeDB?

How we tested

All testing used Claude Opus 5.5 (claude-opus-5-5) in Claude Code 2.1.285, on 7 October 2026. Every session started in a fresh, empty folder with no project files, memory, MCP servers, skills or plugins. Awareness questions ran with no tools at all, and discoverability and reputation questions with web search and web fetch only. The integration ran in a fresh Claude Code profile with no settings, plugins or history, with every command approved by us. We ran each prompt once, so treat these results as one developer's experience rather than a benchmark.

Scores at a glance

The model knows SpacetimeDB well, but as the game backend it was in 2025. It doesn't know the 2026 rebrand, the push into web apps or the agent tooling. Agents find it straight away for multiplayer games, but for web apps it comes second to Convex, and agents recommend Convex or Supabase over it. In the integration, the agent installed it, built a live page and hid private data without any help from us.

  • Awareness: OK (3 / 4) — Knows the games database well; doesn't know the rebrand, the web push or the agent tooling
  • Discoverability: OK (3 / 4) — Top pick for multiplayer games; second to Convex for web apps
  • Reputation: POOR (2 / 4) — Recommended for games; loses to Convex and Supabase for web apps
  • Integration: GOOD (4 / 4) — Live app with private data, correct answers and no human steps
  • Overall: OK (3 / 4) — Agents build well on it, but don't choose it for the web apps it now targets

See our AX audit rubric for how we score each stage. The overall score is the average of the four.

Awareness: does the model know SpacetimeDB?

Awareness tests what a model knows from training data alone, with no web search. SpacetimeDB has been public since 2023 and reached 1.0 in March 2025, so we expected the model to know it. The open question was whether it knew what SpacetimeDB has become in 2026.

OK (3 / 4) — Knows the games database well; doesn't know the rebrand or agent tooling

  • FAIL: Unknown, or confused with something else
  • POOR: Recognises the name, details vague or invented
  • OK: Accurate description from memory
  • GOOD: Accurate, and recommended unprompted

We started with two questions that don't name SpacetimeDB. Each answer below comes from a fresh session with no tools.

That's the opposite of SpacetimeDB's idea, which is to put game state and logic in the database. When we described that idea without the name, the model picked SpacetimeDB at once:

Asked "What is SpacetimeDB (spacetimedb.com)?", it gave an accurate description of the product as it was around its 1.0 launch, including the Clockwork Labs and BitCraft background. It didn't mention 2.0, the web push, C++ support or any agent tooling, and it called the product "open source" under a licence that "converts to a permissive license". SpacetimeDB's FAQ calls it source-available, and the AGPL it converts to isn't a permissive licence.

Then we asked about the new brand and the homepage tagline, and asked how to connect an agent to it over MCP:

The model didn't invent anything, and it said when it didn't know. Its picture of SpacetimeDB is the game backend from before 2.0.

  • Awareness: OK (3 / 4) — Knows the games database well; doesn't know the rebrand, the web push or the agent tooling

What SpacetimeDB can do about it

Training data catches up slowly, so the fix is content that teaches the next training cut about 2.0. Posts and guides that pair the name with the new pitch ("SpacetimeDB, a reactive backend for web apps and AI agents") will help, as will a short page explaining that "Spacetime" and "SpacetimeDB" are the same product. Using one name everywhere would remove the doubt the model had about the rebrand.

Discoverability: can an agent find SpacetimeDB?

Discoverability tests whether an agent with web search finds the product when it's looking for something like it. We ran three six-question "funnels", one session each. Each funnel starts with a broad problem and narrows towards SpacetimeDB one question at a time, then names it at question 6. We recorded the first question where SpacetimeDB appeared.

OK (3 / 4) — Top pick for games; second to Convex for web apps

  • FAIL: Only appears when named
  • POOR: Only appears with its own positioning language
  • OK: Appears for a specific description of the problem
  • GOOD: Top choice for broad problem descriptions

Each funnel asks from a different angle. Funnel A is a web developer, the audience SpacetimeDB 2.0 is aimed at. Funnel B is a game developer, the audience it started with. Funnel C builds apps by prompting a coding agent, which is who its homepage now speaks to.

Funnel Who's asking First question Where SpacetimeDB first appeared
A A web developer "I'm building a collaborative web app in React, a bit like a shared whiteboard with chat…" Question 3, as the runner-up to Convex
B A game developer "I'm making a multiplayer game in Unity. What should I use for the server side?" Question 2, as the top pick
C Someone building with Claude Code "I build apps mostly by prompting Claude Code. What backend should I have it use…" Question 3, as a footnote

For game developers, SpacetimeDB was the answer from the second question to the last:

For the web app in funnel A, SpacetimeDB appeared at question 3, when we asked for server logic inside the database, ACID transactions and query subscriptions. The agent's opening line was "Only two tools meet all four of your requirements: Convex and SpacetimeDB. For your app I'd choose Convex." Convex stayed the pick until the end. Then question 5 used SpacetimeDB's homepage tagline, and the search found Convex instead:

Funnel C is the one SpacetimeDB's new homepage is written for. Here are its six questions, asked in one session, with the start of each answer.

Question 3 described SpacetimeDB's agent tooling almost item by item. The agent ran a search for "SpacetimeDB MCP server llms.txt agent skills AI", found a community MCP server and the benchmark page, and concluded the official tooling wasn't there. It only found the plugin, the MCP server and llms.txt after we named SpacetimeDB and it read the homepage. It also noticed a weakness of the benchmark: "The benchmark scores are at the ceiling. Opus 5.5 and two GPT-6 models all score 99.5%."

  • Discoverability: OK (3 / 4) — Top pick for multiplayer games; second to Convex for web apps

What SpacetimeDB can do about it

Make the MCP server and agent skills findable by search

The agent searched for SpacetimeDB's MCP server, llms.txt and agent skills by name and found a community MCP server instead. A docs page titled in plain words, such as "Using SpacetimeDB with AI coding agents: MCP server, agent skills and llms.txt", would give that search an official result.

Put the taglines where search engines index them

Searches for "reactive backend platform" returned pages about Convex, and searches for "glue-free" and "ship the whole backend" returned nothing. The agent found both phrases on spacetimedb.com only after we named the product. Using them in page titles, the docs and launch posts would let a tagline search land on SpacetimeDB.

Win the web app recommendation

For web apps and agent-built apps, Convex was the agent's answer from the first or second question, before it had searched anything. The web articles it read were vendor round-ups of backends for AI coding agents, and SpacetimeDB wasn't in the ones it opened. Guides and comparisons written for web developers would give agents something to cite there.

Reputation: do agents recommend SpacetimeDB?

Reputation tests what the agent thinks once SpacetimeDB is named, including whether it recommends it over competitors and whether it gets the facts right. We ran seven questions, each in a fresh session with web search. Convex and Supabase were the two products the agent named most often before it found SpacetimeDB, five answers each, so we used them for the head-to-heads. (We've audited Supabase's own agent experience before, in Supabase vs PlanetScale.)

POOR (2 / 4) — Recommended for games; loses to Convex and Supabase for web apps

  • FAIL: Not recommended, or core facts wrong
  • POOR: Heavy caveats, facts unreliable
  • OK: Recommended for specific scenarios, facts mostly right
  • GOOD: Recommended over alternatives, facts right

Is SpacetimeDB good for web apps?

Four of the five verdict questions were about web apps, the market SpacetimeDB 2.0 is aimed at, and all four went against it. The agent kept SpacetimeDB for very high-frequency shared state and recommended Convex or Supabase for everything else. The one game question got a clear yes.

Question Verdict
What do you think of SpacetimeDB for a real-time web app? "For a typical web app I'd lean against it."
SpacetimeDB over Convex for a collaborative TypeScript and React app? No: "I'd pick Convex."
SpacetimeDB over Supabase for the same app? No: "For most collaborative web apps I'd pick Supabase"
A 3-person team building a B2B SaaS dashboard "Short answer: no."
An indie studio making a multiplayer Unity game "Yes, shortlist it"
Main risks of adopting SpacetimeDB (name only) All data held in memory, little public production evidence beyond BitCraft, the licence, and a single company behind it
Pricing and licensing vs Convex and Supabase (name "Spacetime" only) Accurate, with the one-production-instance licence limit as the main warning

SpacetimeDB vs Convex and Supabase

Both head-to-heads used the same scenario, a real-time collaborative web app built in TypeScript and React. Here's the answer against Convex:

The facts were mostly right, including when we used only the name. The pricing and licensing answer read SpacetimeDB's pricing page and its licence file and got every plan, price and licence term right. The answer on risks identified the product from its bare name, and its storage limits match SpacetimeDB's limits page. Here's how its main claims checked out. The two errors came from pages the agent read instead of SpacetimeDB's own.

What the agent said What's true
Version 2.7 is the latest ("2.7 in June 2026") That came from an unofficial mirror of the GitHub repository. The latest release is 2.10.2, from 29 September 2026
SpacetimeDB has "fewer built-in extras like file storage" The docs show files stored as binary columns in tables
"The docs list joins and COUNT(*), but not GROUP BY, SUM/AVG, ORDER BY, window functions, subqueries or CTEs." True. The SQL reference lists COUNT as the only aggregation
SpacetimeDB "admitted it had found and fixed problems" in its benchmarks True. Its May 2026 benchmarking post apologises for numbers that were "misleading"

Five of the seven answers cited the same unofficial mirror of SpacetimeDB's repository, and two took the out-of-date version number from it. The answer that compared SpacetimeDB with Supabase never opened spacetimedb.com. In our own check afterwards, we found a Spacetime vs Supabase comparison page on SpacetimeDB's site that it didn't reach.

  • Reputation: POOR (2 / 4) — Recommended for games; loses to Convex and Supabase for web apps

What SpacetimeDB can do about it

Answer the web app objections where agents look

Every web app verdict came back to the same few concerns, which were reporting queries, webhooks, file storage, auth and a smaller ecosystem. Some were wrong, such as file storage, and some were right, such as the SQL limits. A docs page that addresses each one for web developers, including how to build reporting with only COUNT in SQL, would give agents something to quote back.

Write comparisons that agents can use as a recommendation

The agent quoted SpacetimeDB's own Convex post as evidence against it ("Even SpacetimeDB's team says so."). A comparison page that names the web apps SpacetimeDB is the better choice for would give agents a reason to recommend it for those apps.

Keep the official sources ahead of copies

The mirror's out-of-date version number reached two answers. Release notes and the current version on pages that rank, such as the docs home and the GitHub README, would help the official sources win those searches.

Integration: can an agent build with SpacetimeDB?

Integration tests whether an agent can install the product and build a "hello world" with as little human help as possible. We gave it four CSV files for a fictional business (50 customers, 30 products, 300 orders with 742 line items) and asked it to:

  1. Set up SpacetimeDB and get a local instance running.
  2. Load the CSV data into a database and make sure it can query it.
  3. Answer a question using the database: which region had the most revenue in the last three months, and who were its top three customers?
  4. Build a web page that shows revenue per region live, then refund one order and prove the page updated without a reload.
  5. Stop client apps reading customer email addresses, and prove it.

We ran it in Claude Code's default permission mode, approving each command, so we could stop the agent from reading anything outside its folder. The integration ran in a brand-new Claude Code profile, so SpacetimeDB's plugin and skills would have loaded normally if the agent had installed them.

GOOD (4 / 4) — Live app with private data, correct answers and no human steps

  • FAIL: No working hello world
  • POOR: Works, but needed several human steps
  • OK: Works with short human steps and minor workarounds
  • GOOD: End to end, headline feature included, at most one human step

Installing: four and a half minutes, no help

The agent knew which product we meant and how to install it. It downloaded the official install script, read the top of it, and ran it. It then started a local server, made the local server the CLI's default, and tested the setup with a throwaway test project, which it deleted afterwards.

Loading the data, guided by the CLI's rules file

The agent wrote server code that defines four tables, storing money as whole cents, and loader functions that refuse to load the same table twice. It then wrote a Python script that sent the CSV rows to those functions. The row counts matched the files. It found that order is a reserved word in SpacetimeDB's SQL and renamed the tables to plurals.

Its main reference for SpacetimeDB's TypeScript API was the rules file that spacetime init writes into every new project, as AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md and Cursor rules. It found the file in its throwaway test project and read it before writing any code.

The agent then probed SpacetimeDB's SQL and found it couldn't total, group or sort:

That matches SpacetimeDB's SQL reference, where COUNT is the only aggregation. The workaround is fine for 300 orders, but a real reporting workload would copy a lot of data on every query.

The hello world: a correct answer

The answer matched the figures we calculated from the CSVs: $212,620.84 for North, excluding refunds. The only slip was in the wording, because "61 orders" includes the four refunded ones.

The live page: updated 23 ms after the refund

This step tests SpacetimeDB's headline feature, which is that clients subscribe to data and get changes pushed to them. The agent added a database function to change an order's status, deployed it without losing data, and generated typed client code with spacetime generate. It then built a small web page with SpacetimeDB's TypeScript client library that subscribes to the orders and customers tables.

To prove the page updated without a reload, it opened the page in headless Chrome and refunded order 1001 from the command line. Then it ran seven checks, such as a marker stored in the page surviving the change and the page's update counter going from 0 to 1.


Both figures match our own: West went from $225,607.88 to $219,182.69.

Hiding customer emails: a private table and a public view

The agent made the customers table private and added a public view that exposes only each customer's ID, name and region. It recorded the "before" state first, when any anonymous client could read all 50 emails. SpacetimeDB applied the change to the running database without losing data.

We checked it ourselves as an anonymous client. Reading the customers table returned "no such table: customers. If the table exists, it may be marked private.", and the view returned names and regions without emails.

What it used, and what it didn't

Finally, we asked which SpacetimeDB docs and agent tools it had used:

Step Agent time
Install and run locally 4.5 min
Load the data 7 min
Hello world Under a minute
Live page and refund 7 min
Hide emails 4 min

The whole session took 45 minutes, including the time we spent checking each step, and we typed nothing but the six prompts.

  • Integration: GOOD (4 / 4) — Live app with private data, correct answers and no human steps

What SpacetimeDB can do about it

Point the rules file at the rest of the agent tooling

The rules file that spacetime init writes was the only piece of SpacetimeDB's agent tooling the agent used. A short section in that file on the plugin, spacetime mcp and agent-setup.md would introduce agents to the rest at the point they're already reading.

Document the reporting pattern

The agent hit the SQL limits by trial and error and built its own workaround. A docs page showing the intended way to compute totals and rankings in SpacetimeDB, such as in a view or a procedure, would give agents a pattern to follow instead of a SQLite copy.

What this means for SpacetimeDB

SpacetimeDB is a good product for an agent to build on. Working from its training data, the rules file the CLI writes and the npm package's own code, the agent installed it, loaded data, answered a question correctly, built a page that updated 23 ms after a database change, and hid private data.

The problems come before an agent starts building:

  • From memory, agents know SpacetimeDB as a game backend, and its new tagline sounds like Convex to them.
  • For web apps, agents recommend Convex or Supabase. SpacetimeDB lost both head-to-heads and the SaaS question.
  • Agents searching for its MCP server, skills and llms.txt found a community MCP server instead.

Guides for web developers, comparison pages that recommend SpacetimeDB for specific kinds of app, and an agent tooling page that ranks for those searches would each address one of these.

title: I let Stripe grade my tests: building a billing simulator where no expected value comes from my own code
description:
Built for the TestSprite Hackathon, Season 4. Live: tera-orpin-three.vercel.app · Code: github.com/PugarHuda/tera

Founders are afraid to touch pricing, and they are right to be. Move a customer from $29 to $79 on day 17 of a 31-day month and Stripe writes two proration lines you have probably never computed by hand: an "Unused time" credit of −$14.03 and a "Remaining time" charge of $38.23, on top of the $79 renewal. Add a coupon that was applied once, a tax rate that is inclusive, a trial, or a subscription in Stripe's new flexible billing mode, and the invoice your customer sees is no longer something you can predict from the pricing page.

Tera simulates it first. You give it a customer timeline (subscribe, change seats, upgrade, apply a coupon, pause, cancel) and it returns every invoice to the cent, plus the webhook events Stripe will send for it. This post is not really about the simulator, though. It is about the question every test suite eventually has to answer: who decides what the right answer is?

The rule: the engine never writes its own expectations

The easiest way to get a green test suite for a billing engine is to run the engine, save its output, and assert that it does not change. That suite is worthless the day the engine is wrong, because it was wrong when the snapshot was taken too.

So Tera has one rule. Every expected value is derived by hand from the billing rules, written next to its arithmetic, and then replayed in a real Stripe test-mode account with test clocks. Scenario S05 in golden/scenarios.json looks like this:

"math": "remaining 15/31: -round(2900*15/31)=-1403, +round(7900*15/31)=3823",
"expect": [{ "date": "2027-02-01", "lines": [-1403, 3823, 7900], "total": 10320 }]

A script creates the same customer in Stripe, advances a test clock through the timeline, reads back Stripe's invoices and diffs them line by line against both the hand-derived values and Tera's engine. Only when all three agree is the scenario marked verified, and the evidence (invoice ids, test clock id) is committed to the repo. Today there are 130 golden scenarios and all 127 timelines among them match Stripe to the cent. The other three are migration scenarios with no invoices to replay.

When Stripe disagreed with my hand derivation, Stripe won, and I kept the receipts. A coupon applied in the same second as subscribing discounts the next invoice, because Stripe finalizes the first one at creation. A repeating coupon for 3 months lasts three calendar months, not three invoices. A percent discount on a proration comes off the rounded gross. None of those were in my head when I started.

Letting Stripe find the cases I did not think of

Hand-written scenarios only cover what you already suspect. So Tera also runs differential fuzzing: a seeded generator produces random customer timelines, with month-end anchors, Feb 29, random times of day, trials, seat and plan changes, coupons and both tax behaviours. Each one runs through Tera and through Stripe, and any difference is a finding.

Every finding goes through the same pipeline: a targeted Stripe probe to isolate the rule, a new hand-derived golden scenario that pins it, then the engine fix. The fuzzer runs nightly in CI with fresh seeds, in both of Stripe's billing modes. The rules it surfaced are some of the most interesting in the repo. Stripe prorates the unit price to 12 decimals before multiplying by seats, so a credit of exactly 11257.5 lands a cent under the tie. In flexible mode every credit refunds its original debit with the gross and the discount rounded separately.

This week the same approach caught a real gap in usage-based billing. A code audit found the engine silently dropping metered usage on an immediate cancellation. Seven live probes gave the rules: tier lines run only up to the tier the usage reaches, a metered item has no unused-time line, and cancelling with invoice_now bills the usage so far. A follow-up fuzz batch for metered prices then found that Stripe still sends a $0 final invoice after an unused last period. It also found a stale usage window in my own replay script.

Where TestSprite fits

Stripe is the oracle for the engine. TestSprite is the gate for everything a user actually touches.

  • 28 UI tests on every pull request, run by the TestSprite GitHub App against that PR's own Vercel preview. Branch protection requires the TestSprite V3 check. Each test asserts hand-derived amounts in the browser: "Invoice 2 totals $103.20", not "an invoice is shown".
  • The tests live in the repo. Every plan is a JSON file in testsprite/plans/ and every test has hand-written Playwright code in testsprite/code/. A CI check compares both with the cloud project and fails on drift. That matters because an auto-healing run can quietly rewrite stored code, for example pinning a preview URL or loosening an assertion to two words.
  • API tests against the preview, too. TestSprite gives backend tests no target URL, so a small script stores each API test with its base URL pointing at the PR's preview, runs it with auto-heal off, and puts production back.
  • Triage that uses the oracle. When TestSprite V3 fails, a workflow downloads the failure bundle, replays the golden scenarios behind that test on the same preview, and compares them with Stripe's recorded invoices. One PR comment then says either "engine still matches Stripe, so this is a UI regression" or which invoice the engine now gets wrong.
  • A nightly money-math canary on production, plus Playwright user journeys, Schemathesis fuzzing of the OpenAPI spec, Arazzo workflows, Lighthouse budgets and Stryker mutation testing on every PR.

TestSprite caught a real bug before merge on PR #18. A price added in the builder billed $0.00 instead of ¥4,500, because the builder put a metered price first. The fix went in, and the check went green.

What went wrong, honestly

The workspace ran out of TestSprite credits twice during the hackathon. When that happens the check reports "Not enough credits" without running a single test. Nine pull requests hit that wall; the ones that shipped were merged by the repository admin after every other check had passed. They are not hidden: docs/LOOP.md is generated from the GitHub API and lists every PR and every commit's TestSprite verdict. Five went red on real test results, all fixed in the same PR, and nine were blocked by credits. A credit shortfall is not a test verdict, and treating it as one in either direction would make the ledger lie.

A second lesson: every new test layer I added found something about the previous layers. Schemathesis found the OpenAPI spec looser than the validator. Redocly Respect's strict schema checks found my conditional schemas rejecting properties their parent declared. Then my fix for that made Schemathesis unable to generate requests at all. Each layer is cheap. Not running the next one is what gets expensive.

If you build something similar

  1. Pick an oracle that is not your code. For billing it is Stripe's test clocks. For tax it could be a published calculator. For physics, a reference implementation.
  2. Derive expectations by hand and write the arithmetic next to them. Future you will need it when the oracle disagrees.
  3. Let the oracle generate the questions too (differential fuzzing), and turn every disagreement into a pinned example.
  4. Keep your end-to-end tests in the repo and check the cloud copy against it.

Try it: open the simulator on S05, change the upgrade date, and press Verify in Stripe. Your own timeline gets replayed in a fresh test clock and diffed to the cent.

AI disclosure: this post was drafted by an AI agent (Claude Code) from the project's own repository, evidence files and CI history, and published at the author's request. The project itself was built with the same agent.

title: When LLMs Manipulate: Measuring Behavioral, Social, and Temporal Effects
description:
arXiv:2610.27573v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can influence user trust and decision-making through subtle linguistic cues, yet the behavioral effects of manipulative outputs remain poorly quantified. We introduce a behavioral computing framework for measuring \textit{behavioral vulnerability}, defined as users' susceptibility to manipulative AI responses. Building on DarkPatterns-LLM benchmark, we generate controlled manipulative stimuli using Manipulation Gradient Descent (MGD), targeting biases associated with authority, urgency, and social proof. We analyze participant responses using the Multi-Stakeholder Impact Assessment Network (MSIAN) to model cross-user influence and the Temporal Harm Propagation Model (THPM) to characterize the persistence of behavioral effects over time. In a study involving 120 participants, manipulative framing produced significant changes in trust calibration and compliance ($p < 0.01$), with effects also propagating across social contexts. These findings highlight the need to extend LLM safety evaluation beyond model outputs to measurable behavioral consequences and provide a computational framework for quantifying individual, social, and temporal risks arising from manipulative AI interactions.

title: RaspAssistant as an Agentic Framework for Automating Adsorption Simulation Research in Porous Materials
description:
arXiv:2610.27572v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Porous-material adsorption studies require coordinated structure preparation, force-field selection, simulation, validation, and interpretation, making end-to-end automation difficult. We test whether RaspAssistant, a hierarchical multi-agent framework, can carry an adsorption study from force-field preparation through validation and downstream separation analysis. Across twelve multi-agent workflow-reproduction runs spanning four adsorption and separation benchmarks, overall scores ranged from 8.50 to 10.00 on a rubric evaluating workflow correctness, simulation validity, and analysis consistency. In a separate eight-case force-field extraction benchmark, the mean weighted score was 0.967, combining parameter agreement and RASPA readiness. In open-ended studies, the system diagnosed and refined an acetylene force field and, after validating a CO$_2$ force field against MFI experiments, screened 197 pure-silica zeolites that passed automated input checks. These results demonstrate autonomous workflow execution after task specification and input provision: RaspAssistant coordinates, validates, adapts, and documents extended adsorption-simulation workflows while exposing model sensitivity and methodological limitations for expert review.

title: How to Test a Tauri App End-to-End (No WebDriver Needed)
description:
You can test a Tauri app end-to-end without WebDriver by describing each step in plain language. TestDriver matches each description against screenshots of the installed app, so:

  • you test the same .deb your users install, with nothing compiled into it
  • you don't write or maintain selectors
  • your test reads like the steps you'd give a teammate

TestDriver generates and runs black-box end-to-end tests. It starts your app in a fresh virtual machine, looks at the screen and uses a real mouse and keyboard, so it never needs selectors or access to your code. Each test is a normal Vitest file, and every run is recorded as a replay.

The example installs Yaak, an open-source API client built with Tauri, sends a request and checks the response. The full project is on GitHub: testdriverai/example-tauri-app.

Why not WebDriver

Tauri's testing docs recommend WebDriver: WebdriverIO's @wdio/tauri-service, which by default needs tauri-plugin-wdio-webdriver compiled into your app, or tauri-driver directly on Windows and Linux. Both find elements with selectors into the webview's DOM:

// WebdriverIO-style selector (illustrative, not run)
await $('[aria-label="Send request"]').click();

TestDriver describes the same element the way a user sees it:

await testdriver.find("Send button (paper airplane icon) at the right end of the URL bar").click();

The selector breaks when the markup changes. The description only changes when the UI does.

Watch the full replay

Open the full replay to step through every action with its screenshot and log.

The test 

import { describe, expect, it } from "vitest";
import { TestDriver } from "testdriverai/vitest/hooks";

const YAAK_DEB =
  "https://github.com/mountain-loop/yaak/releases/download/v2026.9.0/yaak_2026.9.0_amd64.deb";

describe("Yaak (Tauri)", () => {
  it("sends a GET request and shows the JSON response", async (context) => {
    const testdriver = TestDriver(context);

    // Download and install the .deb. We start the app ourselves below.
    await testdriver.provision.installer({ url: YAAK_DEB, launch: false });

    // Pull in Tauri's Linux runtime dependencies (WebKitGTK, libsoup) and start Yaak.
    await testdriver.exec(
      "sh",
      "sudo apt-get update -qq && sudo DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive apt-get install -f -y -qq",
      240000,
    );
    await testdriver.exec("sh", "nohup yaak-app-client >/tmp/yaak.log 2>&1 &", 10000);

    // Start with an empty workspace. The first find waits for the window to appear.
    await testdriver.find('"Start fresh" card on the Yaak welcome screen', { timeout: 60000 }).click();

    // Create a new HTTP request.
    await testdriver.find('"New Request" button in the middle of the empty workspace').click();
    await testdriver.find('"HTTP" option in the New Request dropdown menu').click();

    // Enter a URL and send it.
    await testdriver.find('URL input with the placeholder "https://example.com" next to the GET method selector').click();
    await testdriver.type("https://httpbin.org/json");
    await testdriver.find("Send button (paper airplane icon) at the right end of the URL bar").click();

    // Wait for the response to arrive, then check what the app rendered.
    await testdriver.find("green 200 OK status label at the top of the response panel", { timeout: 30000 });
    const responseShown = await testdriver.assert(
      'the response panel shows a green 200 OK status and a JSON body containing "Sample Slide Show"',
    );
    expect(responseShown).toBeTruthy();

    const savedInSidebar = await testdriver.assert(
      'the sidebar lists the request as "httpbin.org/json" with a 200 status badge',
    );
    expect(savedInSidebar).toBeTruthy();
  });
});

How it works

Install and launch the release build

provision.installer() downloads the .deb and installs it on a fresh Linux sandbox. The two exec() calls install Tauri's Linux runtime (WebKitGTK and libsoup) and start the app.

Describe elements by what users see

Each find() takes a description that names the label, the look and the position, such as "Send button (paper airplane icon) at the right end of the URL bar". Add a landmark when a label alone could match more than one element. See locating elements.

Wait for results, then assert

find() with a timeout keeps looking until the element appears, so the test waits for the app to start and for the 200 status without a fixed sleep. assert() then checks a plain-language statement against the screen and returns true or false. See making assertions.

Run it yourself

Clone the example repo, or set up TestDriver in your own project and run the test:

npx testdriverai init
npx vitest run tauri-app.test.mjs

To test your own Tauri app:

  • Point provision.installer() at your release .deb (tauri build writes it to src-tauri/target/release/bundle/).
  • Start your binary in the second exec() call. dpkg -L <package> shows its name.
  • On Windows, pass os: "windows" to TestDriver() and point the installer at your .msi or .exe.

FAQ

Do I need tauri-driver, WebdriverIO or a plugin?
No. TestDriver drives the installed app from the screen, so nothing is added to your Tauri project.

Do I need test IDs?
No. Steps are matched on screenshots, so there are no data-testid attributes to add or keep in sync.

Can I run it in CI?
Yes. It's a normal Vitest file and the app runs in TestDriver's cloud sandbox. See CI/CD.

Originally published on the TestDriver blog.

title: LTEM: LLM-Friendly Table-Enhanced Markdown for Table Understanding and Generation
description:
arXiv:2610.29188v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Tables in real-world documents, including scientific papers, financial reports, and statistical summaries, frequently use merged cells, multi-level headers, and sectioned layouts. Yet the lightweight formats LLMs handle best (Markdown, CSV) cannot express these structures, while expressive formats (HTML, LaTeX) impose excessive token cost and parsing complexity. To enable systematic analysis of this trade-off, we introduce a taxonomy decomposing table structure into six atomic features (F1-F6) and corresponding complexity levels (L1-L6), and construct STB (Synthetic Table Benchmark), a controlled benchmark with 1,089 tables systematically distributed across complexity levels. Using this framework, we propose LTEM (LLM-friendly Table-Enhanced Markdown), a formally specified, minimal extension of Markdown that explicitly encodes spans and hierarchical headers. Experiments across five state-of-the-art LLMs show that LTEM achieves accuracy comparable to HTML, offers a favorable accuracy-token trade-off relative to HTML and LaTeX, and produces substantially fewer invalid responses than LaTeX; for table generation, LTEM is comparable to MultiMarkdown though HTML is best. We release our taxonomy, benchmark, and format specification to support future research on LLM-table interaction.

title: Near-Duplicate Support Tickets 2026: Go Vector Threshold Review
description:
At 03:07, the page says that answers over the logistics support archive have started citing the same incident repeatedly. The on-call opens one trace and sees three PDF tickets about a delayed container, all admitted as separate evidence even though two are near copies created by an email export. The least complex useful response is a similarity gate with three outcomes: accept a clearly new ticket, suppress a clear duplicate, and send the uncertain middle to review. Do not turn one similarity threshold into an automatic delete button.

TL;DR: normalize and embed each ticket with the same pipeline, search only within an operationally meaningful candidate set, and treat similarity as a ranking signal rather than truth. Keep both sides of every decision, the model and preprocessing version, the score, the chosen boundary, and the reviewer outcome. Page on user-visible retrieval damage or sustained decision drift, not on a lone high score.

This matters before generation. Retrieval-augmented generation combines retrieved external material with generation; if duplicated tickets occupy several retrieval slots, the evidence presented downstream is narrower than the result count implies. The pager should therefore fire on the consequence: repeated evidence, missing distinct incidents, or a review queue that can no longer meet its service objective.

Quiet is not healthy.

What should have fired before the answer repeated itself?

The earlier signal is a change in the gate's decisions, segmented by the dimensions that can alter ticket language: carrier, route, document template, language, and ingestion version. A global average can stay calm while one newly deployed PDF template strips spaces or repeats headers, moving an entire cohort across the review boundary. Dashboards are weak evidence here. I want the page to name the affected cohort, the first bad deployment or corpus window, and a few decision identifiers that can be replayed without exposing ticket text.

A useful event is compact but reconstructable. Record a content hash for exact-copy handling, stable identifiers for the candidate pair, the embedding and normalizer versions, similarity, gate outcome, and timestamp. Keep the raw PDFs under the archive's existing access and retention controls; telemetry does not need their contents. Exact hashes catch byte-identical exports cheaply, while vector similarity handles paraphrases and formatting changes. Those are different mechanisms and should have separate counters.

Track the distribution, not merely the mean. Counts entering new, review, and duplicate, plus reviewer reversals for each outcome, expose a threshold that has drifted. A rise in duplicate decisions may be legitimate after a bulk import. The same rise paired with reviewers repeatedly splitting those pairs is evidence of bad suppression.

How should Go dedupe near-duplicate support tickets for review?

Cosine similarity for nonzero vectors is the dot product divided by the product of their magnitudes. Higher scores mean the representations point in a more similar direction; they do not prove that two tickets describe the same operational event. Two reports can share every phrase about a delayed shipment yet refer to different containers, days, or customers. Conversely, an update may add a resolution while still belonging to the original incident.

No score proves identity.

The gate below uses explicit lower and upper boundaries. It assumes the vectors were produced by one pinned embedding pipeline and rejects dimension mismatches and zero vectors instead of manufacturing a score. The policy compares a new ticket only with candidates selected by metadata such as tenant and a bounded event window; comparing every shipment with the entire archive creates plausible but operationally irrelevant neighbors.

package dedupe

import (
    "errors"
    "math"
)

type Decision string

const (
    New       Decision = "new"
    Review    Decision = "review"
    Duplicate Decision = "duplicate"
)

type Policy struct {
    ReviewAt    float64
    DuplicateAt float64
}

func Cosine(a, b []float64) (float64, error) {
    if len(a) == 0 || len(a) != len(b) {
        return 0, errors.New("vectors must have equal, nonzero dimensions")
    }

    var dot, aa, bb float64
    for i := range a {
        dot += a[i] * b[i]
        aa += a[i] * a[i]
        bb += b[i] * b[i]
    }
    if aa == 0 || bb == 0 {
        return 0, errors.New("cosine is undefined for a zero vector")
    }
    return dot / (math.Sqrt(aa) * math.Sqrt(bb)), nil
}

func (p Policy) Decide(score float64) (Decision, error) {
    if p.ReviewAt < -1 || p.DuplicateAt > 1 || p.ReviewAt >= p.DuplicateAt {
        return "", errors.New("invalid policy boundaries")
    }
    switch {
    case score >= p.DuplicateAt:
        return Duplicate, nil
    case score >= p.ReviewAt:
        return Review, nil
    default:
        return New, nil
    }
}

There are deliberately no universal numbers in that policy. A copied subject line, boilerplate carrier disclaimer, or OCR artifact can change the score distribution, as can any change to chunking or embeddings. Boundaries belong in versioned configuration and must come from labeled pairs that resemble current traffic. The upper boundary should reflect the cost of hiding a distinct logistics incident; the lower one should reflect the cost and capacity of human review.

This approach has limits. It is not suitable as the sole decision mechanism when regulations or contractual controls require a human to preserve every report, when the archive is too small to produce representative labeled pairs, or when exact business identifiers already determine identity without ambiguity. In those cases, deterministic matching or mandatory review is the better boundary. The trade-off is plain: a wider review band protects recall but spends analyst time and delays indexing, while a narrow band lowers latency by accepting more classification risk.

Do not compare isolated chunks and then discard the document relationship. A PDF header can be nearly identical across thousands of tickets. Build the decision from ticket-level evidence, preserve identifiers such as shipment or case references as structured features, and give reviewers both complete documents with the matching passages highlighted. A vector match proposes a case; an auditable workflow decides it.

Calibrate with incidents, not convenient examples

Start with labeled pairs sampled from the same path production will use. Include exact exports, paraphrased reports, follow-up messages, shared templates, OCR damage, and hard negatives: similar wording attached to distinct shipment identifiers. Split calibration and evaluation by time or incident group so revisions of one ticket do not leak into both sides and make the gate look cleaner than it is.

Then sweep candidate boundaries and count operational errors. A false duplicate can remove the only evidence of a separate lost shipment. A false new decision consumes index space and may crowd retrieval results. A review decision costs analyst attention and adds latency. Those costs are asymmetric, so a single aggregate accuracy number cannot choose the policy.

Use a replay set when the normalizer, PDF extraction, chunk construction, or embedding version changes. Run the proposed pipeline beside the current one, compare transitions among all three outcomes, and inspect the pairs that cross a boundary. Deploy the decision version with the indexed vectors; mixing new queries with old vectors produces a test you did not design. If either pipeline cannot reproduce its own stored decision from the retained inputs and version metadata, rollback and replay are guesses.

The review interface needs two distinct actions: confirm the same incident, or keep both and record why. That reason can become a future evaluation slice, for example same_template_different_container. Reviewers also need an escape hatch for linked but nonduplicate tickets, because a follow-up report may be valuable retrieval evidence even when it belongs to the same incident family.

Keep both.

Instrument the action path

After the noisy page, add instrumentation where a decision changes the corpus, not only where similarity is computed. The trace should connect PDF ingestion, exact-hash lookup, candidate selection, vector scoring, gate outcome, reviewer action, index mutation, and the retrieval result that later feeds an answer. One correlation identifier across those stages lets the on-call move backward from a repeated citation to the exact gate decision.

The service should fail closed around irreversible actions. A vector timeout can route a ticket to retry or review; it should not silently label the ticket new or duplicate. Invalid vectors and mismatched versions are errors. Queue age deserves an alert when it threatens the promised review latency, while individual review-band matches are normal work and should not wake anyone.

A compact operational record might look like this:

type GateEvent struct {
    DecisionID        string
    IncomingTicketID  string
    CandidateID       string
    ContentHashMatch  bool
    NormalizerVersion string
    EmbeddingVersion  string
    Similarity        float64
    Outcome           Decision
    ReviewedOutcome   Decision
}

Keep metric labels bounded. Ticket IDs belong in trace events or protected logs, not metric dimensions. Metrics can safely aggregate by policy version, outcome, source format, and a controlled cohort vocabulary. The page then links to sampled decision IDs, while the chart remains usable under load.

The decisive checks are end to end: the proportion of retrieved results occupied by one duplicate family, distinct incident coverage in a labeled query set, reviewer reversal rates, and review age. Generation quality cannot repair missing evidence. If deduplication suppresses a distinct ticket before retrieval, the answerer never sees it.

The threshold can create its own incident

Move the upper boundary downward and apparent duplicate removal rises, but so does the chance of hiding separate events that happen to use the same logistics template. Move it upward and reviewers or retrieval results absorb more copies. Widen the middle band and decision quality may improve while latency grows. There is no free setting.

For rollout, shadow the new policy, inspect boundary crossings, then canary it on a defined cohort with a rollback condition tied to reviewer reversals and retrieval coverage. Preserve suppressed documents rather than deleting them, and make the index mutation idempotent so replaying a decision does not create another copy. The runbook should say which decision version to disable, how to drain pending reviews, and how to restore suppressed ticket references.

The false-positive cost deserves the final word. An aggressive threshold can make a quiet dashboard by erasing the disagreement that should have reached a human, and in logistics that disagreement may be the difference between two similar complaints and two separate shipments needing action. A useful page fires when the system is losing distinct evidence or cannot process uncertainty in time. Everything else is a graph to inspect after breakfast.

Pages need consequences.

Further reading

  • Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks: https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401

title: Testing Crossplane Compositions with Chainsaw: kind Without Credentials, Then a Prod-Like Environment
description:
TL;DR. On top of part 2's offline render tests I added two Kyverno Chainsaw layers. One applies every composition to a throwaway kind cluster with no cloud credentials on every pull request, so nothing real gets created. The other applies the same use cases with real credentials to a prod-like environment, which mirrors production but can run a branch, and waits for Ready and verified cloud state. A third job upgrades existing composite resources (XRs) to the PR's compositions. I chose Chainsaw over Uptest, and the new layers found real bugs that every render test had passed.

This is an opinionated write-up of what worked for me as a solo DevOps engineer, in one company's setup. Treat it as experience to weigh, not as the one right answer.

This is part 3 of a series on Crossplane:

  1. Crossplane Black Boxes for Developer Self-Service
  2. Writing and Testing Crossplane Compositions in KCL
  3. This article

Why

Part 2 ended with render tests: every composition is rendered offline against JSON fixtures and diffed against recorded expected output. That catches KCL logic errors in milliseconds. It cannot catch anything that needs a reconcile loop: one XR waiting for another to resolve, a provider writing a Secret, a composition that only finishes on its second pass, or deletion leaving nothing behind.

Before this work, the only live check was a post-sync job waiting on permanent "canary" XRs. It ran after merge, and only after a successful sync, so a failed sync left that revision untested and nobody was told.

I had put Chainsaw aside once, because my only clusters were shared, the wrong place for test XRDs. That is specific to my case: a dedicated test cluster is a fine answer in general, and with many contributors a dedicated cluster plus Uptest is the safer choice. Reviewing part 2, a reader from the Crossplane community suggested a cheaper middle layer: a local kind cluster with no cloud credentials. Applying an XR there creates nothing real, so the isolation and cost problems disappear.

What

Layer Tool Where Proves
1. Render KCL + fixtures no cluster, CI on every PR the composition renders the expected resources
2. Applied to a cluster Chainsaw throwaway kind cluster, no cloud credentials, CI on every PR XRs apply, gates hold across reconciles, composed resources are right, deletion is clean
3. For real Chainsaw prod-like environment, with real credentials, before merge the cloud accepts it: IAM, real IDs, Ready, verified state, deletion

The permanent canaries stay. They are the only check of each environment's own project and IAM, of XRs that live through provider and composition upgrades, and of drift no PR caused. The post-sync job is gone, replaced by an alert that fires when a canary stays not Ready, or Ready but unverified, for 30 minutes.

One set of use cases

There is one XR manifest per kind in a use-cases/ directory, and both Chainsaw layers apply them, so they can't drift. Negative cases stay inline in the kind tests, because the prod-like layer applies everything in that directory.

Which layer owns a check

The rule I settled on: put each check in the cheapest layer that can see it.

Owner What goes there
Render every field value, every variant, every assert (one failing scenario per assert), verified status from mocked observations
kind only what needs a cluster: references resolving across XRs, gates over several reconciles, a provider writing a Secret, an assert surfacing as Synced=False, deletion leaving no managed resource behind
Prod-like what only the cloud decides: IAM, API acceptance, real IDs, Ready, real verified state

Every composition has at least one render fixture and one kind test. A field asserted in both layers is a second place to update, so I don't add those.

How

kind without credentials

The kind job installs the same Crossplane version, providers, functions and compositions as the real clusters, from the same directories. Cloud providers can't authenticate, so reconciling a managed resource (MR) fails at the cloud API, leaving no status.atProvider and no Ready, while provider-kubernetes works normally.

That breaks every composition that finishes on its second pass, such as a grant waiting for its identity. A small script writes status.atProvider on the cloud MR, in the real provider's ID format; a provider whose observe always fails never overwrites it. The mocks live in the tests and never in the compositions, where a test-only branch would ship to every environment.

A trimmed test looks like this:

apiVersion: chainsaw.kyverno.io/v1alpha1
kind: Test
metadata:
  name: bucket
spec:
  steps:
    - name: apply
      try:
        - apply:
            file: ../../use-cases/bucket.yaml
        - assert:
            resource:
              apiVersion: platform.example.com/v1alpha1
              kind: Bucket
              metadata:
                name: example-bucket
              status:
                (conditions[?type == 'Synced'] | [0].status): 'True'
    - name: observed
      try:
        - script:
            content: ../../lib/mock-observed.sh Bucket example-bucket
        - assert:
            file: assert-verified.yaml

A run takes about five minutes, and its largest phase is setup: all providers becoming healthy takes roughly 100 to 135 seconds. Tests run in parallel, so the run takes as long as its slowest test. Draft PRs skip the job, and marking the PR ready starts the first run.

The Crossplane install and the compositions are separate GitOps applications, so a PR changing both can roll out in either order. Such a PR also runs both skewed pairs: new compositions on the old install, and the reverse.

Prod-like environment, from a developer's machine

The prod-like layer applies the same use cases, waits for Ready and verified state, then deletes everything. Three decisions shaped it.

It runs before merge. The compositions sync to every environment automatically, so a test after merge reports a break already in production. Branch-testing there already runs the PR's compositions.

It runs from a developer's machine, not CI. Running in CI would need that environment pinned to the PR first, and that means a workflow running PR code with rights to repoint a GitOps application. I didn't want CI to hold that right, so the script refuses to run unless three things hold:

  • the cluster context provisions into that environment's own project;
  • the branch tracks its own remote branch, has nothing uncommitted and is pushed;
  • the environment's application is synced to exactly that commit.

Every cloud-facing name is unique to the run. The compositions use the XR's name as the cloud resource name. With fixed names, two runs would fight over one resource, and a run could adopt an existing resource with the same name and then delete it during cleanup. A render step copies the use cases with a per-run suffix on every name and reference.

Fourteen kinds run in dependency chains, and a consumer is applied only after what it references is Ready and verified. Kinds configured once per database instance are excluded, because a test copy would fight the real one and its delete would remove it. The alert kind's test rule is rendered so it can never fire. Every gateway the route kind accepts is shared with other services, so instead of throwaway routes it gets the branch test of a real route.

Why Chainsaw and not Uptest

Uptest is Upbound's tool for exactly this job, and it uses Chainsaw internally. I read its own templates before choosing.

On kind, Uptest waits for the wrong thing. Without credentials nothing becomes Ready, which is what Uptest waits on. The kind layer proves composed fields, absences and negative cases, which Chainsaw asserts declaratively and Uptest would need as hand-written shell hooks.

On a shared cluster, Uptest's lifecycle is unsafe for me. In the version I read:

  • every apply downloads and runs a helper script from the project's main branch, unpinned;
  • its import step scales every provider's runtime config to zero replicas and back, restarting those providers for the whole cluster;
  • delete, by default, waits for every managed resource on the cluster to go away.

With import and update turned off, what is left is apply, wait for Ready, delete. That is a few Chainsaw steps over the same use cases.

What the new layers found

Three composition bugs that every render test had passed:

  1. A service account composition reported allVerified: true before anything was observed. The list of resources to verify was empty on the first reconcile, and all([]) is true.
  2. An alert composition with no log-based metric composed nothing to verify, so it reported verified with nothing checked.
  3. A readiness gate observed the secret's name instead of the referenced bundle's name. When the two differed, the gate watched an object that doesn't exist, and the dependent resource was never created.

Each one became a render scenario first, then a fix.

A hole in the render harness. A failing scenario passed on any non-zero exit, so a scenario that tripped a different assert, or failed on a broken fixture, still passed. The harness now records the error type and assert message for each failing scenario and diffs them in CI.

Gotchas

  • A provider is Installed before its CRDs exist. The revision installs managed resource definitions, and a controller creates each CRD afterwards. Gating setup on Installed failed a run with no matches for kind. Wait for Healthy.
  • A mocked status must satisfy the CRD schema. The status subresource accepts an invalid patch, but every later full-object update is then rejected. That includes the garbage collector removing its own finalizer, so cleanup hangs. The mock script now validates the whole object with a server-side dry run first.
  • Delete with Foreground propagation. With Background, the namespace is deleted alongside the composed objects. Each object needs a ProviderConfigUsage in that namespace to finalize, so the namespace deadlocks.
  • Foreground is still not enough. The garbage collector blocks the owner only on dependents already in its cache, so an MR can outlive its XR. Each test's first step has a cleanup that waits for every managed kind to go; cleanup runs in reverse, so it runs last.
  • Assert every composed resource before the test ends. Otherwise cleanup can delete the XR while a reconcile is still applying, and the resource created in that window outlives it. This only appeared when I raised parallelism, because load widens the window.
  • Interrupted runs leave real resources. Chainsaw documents cleanup after a failed step, not after a killed process, and laptops get interrupted. The script reports earlier leftovers before starting and prints its run ID on Ctrl-C, and a daily orphan-detection job covers cloud resources whose XR is gone.

Upgrade testing

Everything above tests a change on fresh XRs. Many breaks hit XRs that already exist: a new composition revision re-renders them, a renamed composed resource is deleted and recreated, a removed field disappears. So when the compositions change, the kind workflow runs one more job:

  1. Install the main branch's tree and run its tests without cleanup, so their XRs stay.
  2. Install the PR's tree over them.
  3. Fail if any XR or composed resource was recreated (UIDs compared), or an XR is no longer synced and verified.

An intended recreation goes in a reviewed list file. As a negative control, renaming one composed resource failed exactly that kind's XRs. The job adds about eight minutes.

When a changed field makes the cloud provider replace the external resource, the MR keeps its UID, so that case is covered by the prod-like branch test and the permanent canaries instead.

Checklist

  • [ ] One use-case manifest per kind, shared by the kind and prod-like layers.
  • [ ] Each check lives in the cheapest layer that can see it.
  • [ ] Mocks only in tests, in the real provider's ID format, validated against the CRD schema.
  • [ ] Foreground deletion, plus an explicit wait for every managed kind before namespace delete.
  • [ ] Every composed resource asserted before the test ends.
  • [ ] The prod-like layer runs before merge, on unique names, only against the PR's exact commit.
  • [ ] Upgrade job: main's tree first, then the PR's, with no unexpected recreations.

References

  • Kyverno Chainsaw: https://kyverno.github.io/chainsaw/
  • Upbound Uptest: https://github.com/crossplane/uptest
  • kind: https://kind.sigs.k8s.io/
  • Kubernetes foreground deletion: https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/architecture/garbage-collection/#foreground-deletion

I wrote this article with the help of Claude, an AI assistant. I reviewed and edited it by hand, and it is based on my own hands-on experience.

title: UNIVERS: Learning UNIversal Voxel-wise Embedding via Randomized Synthesis for generalizable one-shot landmark localization
description:
arXiv:2610.29098v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: One-shot landmark localization in volume scans with varying fields of view (FOVs) is challenging. While existing self-supervised learning methods have shown promising performance, they rely on contrastive learning built upon augmented views of the same image, which inherently limits their generalization in cross-modality scenarios. This motivates research on cross-modality embedding learning using paired multi-modality images. However, existing methods suffer from not only limited training data, but also the requirement of multi-stage iterative training. To address these limitations, we propose UNIVERS, an end-to-end trainable framework that learns UNIversal Voxel-wise Embedding via Randomized Synthesis. Our framework leverages diverse pseudo-data synthesized from organ shape templates, with randomization applied to semantic layout, visual appearance, FOV, and spatial pose. Coupled with cross-domain discriminative voxel-wise contrastive learning, this domain randomization strategy forces the network to disregard domain-specific biases and learn features that are robust against variations in imaging contrast, resolution, and spatial context. Consequently, the trained model enables one-shot landmark localization in multi-modality volume scans with arbitrary FOVs. In this study, the efficacy of the proposed method is demonstrated by applying it to the task of localizing the adrenal glands, which are paired, small, and irregular endocrine organs. In particular, comprehensive experiments are conducted on three challenging adrenal gland datasets. The experimental results demonstrate that UNIVERS consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art (SOTA) one-shot landmark localization approaches, with particularly prominent advantages in cross-modality scenarios. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/Kendra9999/UNIVERS.
