title: Zero-Downtime Database Migrations: The Expand-Contract Pattern
description:
Renaming a column sounds like a one-line change. In production it is one of the most reliable ways to take yourself down.

Here is the shape of the accident. You rename users.name to users.full_name, ship the migration and the new code together, and something still breaks. The deploy is rolling, so for a few minutes two versions of your app are live at once. The old version asks for name and gets an error because the column is already renamed. Or the migration runs first against old code, or the code deploys first against the old schema. Every ordering fails somewhere, because the problem is not ordering. The problem is that schema changes are instant and code deploys are not.

Expand-contract is the pattern that respects that gap. You never change a schema in one step. You grow it, move the code and the data over, and only then shrink it. Three phases, usually three separate deploys.

Phase 1: Expand

Expand means: add the new shape, keep the old shape fully working.

To rename name to full_name, you do not rename anything. You add a new column:

ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN full_name text;

In Postgres this is a metadata-only change. The new column is nullable, existing rows get null, no table rewrite happens, and the lock is held for milliseconds. Your old code keeps reading and writing name exactly as before. Nothing about production behavior has changed yet, which is precisely the point.

The same thinking applies to indexes. If the new shape needs an index, build it without blocking writes:

CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_users_full_name ON users (full_name);

CONCURRENTLY takes longer and cannot run inside a transaction block, but it does not stop inserts and updates while it builds. A plain CREATE INDEX on a hot table blocks writes for the entire build, and on a large table that is an outage with extra steps.

Phase 2: Migrate

Now deploy code that lives in both worlds. It writes to both columns, and it reads the new column with a fallback to the old one:

func (s *Store) UpdateName(ctx context.Context, id int64, name string) error {
    _, err := s.db.ExecContext(ctx, `
        UPDATE users
        SET name = $1, full_name = $1
        WHERE id = $2`, name, id)
    return err
}

SELECT id, COALESCE(full_name, name) AS display_name
FROM users
WHERE id = $1;

Dual writes keep the two columns in agreement for every row your new code touches. But old rows that nobody updates still have a null full_name, so you backfill them, in batches, in the background:

UPDATE users
SET full_name = name
WHERE id IN (
    SELECT id FROM users
    WHERE full_name IS NULL
    ORDER BY id
    LIMIT 5000
);

Run that until it touches zero rows. Batching matters more than it looks. One giant update holds locks for minutes and generates a huge pile of WAL that your replicas have to replay. Five thousand rows at a time keeps each transaction short, and a short pause between batches lets replication and normal traffic breathe.

One more trap hides in this phase. If an older app version is still running somewhere, it writes only name, and your new column silently drifts out of sync. A trigger covers that gap until the old version is gone:

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION sync_full_name() RETURNS trigger AS $$
BEGIN
    IF NEW.full_name IS NULL THEN
        NEW.full_name := NEW.name;
    END IF;
    RETURN NEW;
END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

CREATE TRIGGER users_sync_full_name
BEFORE INSERT OR UPDATE ON users
FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION sync_full_name();

The trigger is scaffolding, not architecture. It exists to make the transition safe, and it gets dropped in the last phase.

Phase 3: Contract

Contract is where you finally remove the old shape, and it is deliberately boring. Before you drop anything, verify with counts rather than confidence:

SELECT count(*) FROM users WHERE full_name IS NULL;

That number has to be zero. Then, in a separate deploy, after every running app version reads the new column, you remove the dual write, remove the fallback, remove the trigger, and drop the old column:

ALTER TABLE users DROP COLUMN name;

Dropping a column in Postgres is also metadata-only. The space is reclaimed later by normal vacuum work, but the logical change is instant and the lock is brief. If you rush this phase and an old binary is still serving traffic, that binary now fails on every query. The waiting is not ceremony. The waiting is the safety.

The NOT NULL version of the problem

Sooner or later the migration is not a rename, it is making a column required. SET NOT NULL on a large table scans the whole table while holding a strong lock. Postgres 12 and later let you prove the constraint first, in the background:

ALTER TABLE users
    ADD CONSTRAINT users_full_name_not_null
    CHECK (full_name IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID;

ALTER TABLE users VALIDATE CONSTRAINT users_full_name_not_null;

ALTER TABLE users ALTER COLUMN full_name SET NOT NULL;

ALTER TABLE users DROP CONSTRAINT users_full_name_not_null;

The NOT VALID constraint starts enforcing the rule for new writes immediately, without scanning. VALIDATE CONSTRAINT then checks existing rows while holding a much weaker lock that does not block writes. Once validation passes, SET NOT NULL sees the proof and skips its own scan. Same end state, no long lock.

Rules that keep the pattern safe

One phase per deploy. Expand in one release, migrate in the next, contract in a third. Bundling phases back into a single release rebuilds the exact problem the pattern exists to solve.

A rename is never one step. A rename is add, migrate, drop. A type change is add, migrate, drop. A column move between tables is add, migrate, drop. Once you see every breaking change as the same three moves, migrations stop being creative and start being routine, which is what you want from them.

Protect the table from your own migration. Migration tools happily wait for locks, and a migration waiting on an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock blocks every query behind it. Fail fast instead, and retry when the table is quiet:

SET lock_timeout = '2s';
ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN full_name text;

A migration that errors in two seconds is a nuisance. A migration that queues for ten minutes behind a long transaction, with a hundred app queries queued behind it, is an incident.

Verify every phase with numbers. Row counts before and after the backfill. Null counts down to zero. Error rates watched during each deploy. The pattern gives you a checkpoint at every phase, and checkpoints you do not measure are decoration.

The takeaway

Zero-downtime migration is not a tool or a framework feature. It is the discipline of never letting the database and the code disagree about the shape of the data, even for a minute. Expand first so both shapes exist. Migrate the writes, the reads, and the old rows. Contract last, only when counts prove nothing depends on the old shape.

If you take one thing from this: the next time a migration looks like one line, ask which of your running app versions it breaks. Then split it into three.

title: Vercel CLI expands commands for DNS, domains, and projects
description:
The Vercel CLI now provides dedicated commands for managing DNS records, domains, and projects. This brings more of the functionality available through the Vercel dashboard and API to the terminal, where it can be used interactively, in scripts, or by agents.

Inspect and update DNS records

Retrieve the complete configuration for a DNS record or update it in place using its record ID.

vercel dns update supports changes to the record name, type, value, TTL, MX priority, and comment. SRV records can also be updated using their priority, weight, port, and target fields.

Renew domains bought on Vercel

Renew a domain on demand or control whether it renews automatically.

The renewal command displays the current renewal price and asks for confirmation before completing the purchase.

Control project state and observability

Pause or resume a project and configure its observability features directly from the CLI. Web Analytics and Speed Insights could already be enabled from the CLI; they can now be disabled as well.

Add and remove project members

Add a project member with a specific role or remove an existing member.

All of the new commands support structured JSON output for scripts and agents. Billable or destructive actions require explicit confirmation.

Update to version 59.6.2 (or later) of the Vercel CLI to use the new commands:

Learn more in the Vercel CLI documentation.

title: Signs You've Outgrown DIY Infrastructure (And What To Do Next)
description:
Manual infrastructure — SSH into a box, tweak a config, hope you remember what you changed — works fine when you're small. But there comes a point where the DIY approach stops being scrappy and starts being risky. Here are the signs we see again and again, and a practical path out.

The signs

1. Every environment is a snowflake. Staging doesn't quite match production. That one server "works, don't touch it." Manual provisioning means every environment drifts in its own direction, and nobody can fully explain the differences.

2. You can't answer "who changed what, when?" Without a defined, automated process there's no audit trail. When something breaks at 2am, you're doing archaeology instead of reading a diff.

3. Changes can't be reviewed before they happen. A manual fix goes straight to production. There's no pull request for your infrastructure — no review, no second pair of eyes, no rollback story.

4. Rebuilding is a research project. If recreating your environment requires digging through old tickets and one engineer's memory, you don't have infrastructure — you have folklore.

What to do next

Start by writing it down. Inventory where manual steps still live: provisioning, patching, deployments, access changes. You can't automate what you haven't mapped.

Adopt Infrastructure as Code. Terraform for provisioning, Ansible for configuration. Environments become consistent, reviewable (PRs on infra changes!), auditable, and repeatable. The win isn't just speed — it's that rebuilding stops being scary.

Automate delivery. CI/CD pipelines turn releases from events into non-events. Test in pipelines, deploy in reviewable increments, and roll back cleanly when needed.

Make monitoring boring. Observability, alerting, and recovery runbooks — tested, not just documented — mean incidents get handled in minutes, not discovered by your customers.

Be honest about capacity. If your team is stretched, a managed services partner can run the transition and the ongoing operation — within your tools and governance — while your engineers focus on the product.

This is what we do at NeonEdge IT Solutions — managed IT support, cloud, IaC, DevOps, and Kubernetes delivery. https://neonedgeitsolutions.com/

title: How to Run a Brainstorming Session That Actually Works
description:
In 1953, advertising executive Alex Osborn promised that a group brainstorming together could think up twice as many ideas as the same people working alone. Five years later, Yale ran the first controlled test of that claim and found the opposite: people working on their own produced roughly twice as many good ideas as people brainstorming together. Here is how to run a brainstorming session that respects that result — because the meeting is still worth having, just not the way most teams run it.

The experiment that ruined brainstorming

In 1958, Taylor, Berry and Block at Yale ran 12 real groups of four through three problems using Osborn's official rules: no criticism, freewheeling, quantity first, build on each other's ideas. They also had 48 other people work alone, then randomly recombined those individuals into "nominal" groups of four and scored them as if they had worked together. The nominal group is exactly what the real group would have produced if talking to each other were neutral.

It wasn't neutral. The real groups were, in the authors' words, "markedly inferior" on total ideas, unique ideas, and three quality-weighted measures. The people who never spoke to each other produced roughly twice as many ideas.

The part that stings is the precision of the reversal. Osborn had written that "the average person can think up twice as many ideas when working with a group than when working alone." The first proper test found the effect going the other direction by about the same factor. One honest caveat: both conditions used Osborn's rules, so the study tested group versus individual under brainstorming rules — not brainstorming versus no method at all. The enemy was the group, not the rules.

Why talking first loses: production blocking

Three candidates were tested: social loafing (people coasting), evaluation apprehension (fear of sounding stupid), and production blocking — only one person can talk at a time, so everyone else waits, and while they wait their ideas decay. You forget the idea, or you spend your mental energy tracking the speaker instead of thinking.

Diehl and Stroebe (1987, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology) manipulated all three mechanisms directly and found that blocking accounted for "most of the productivity loss" of real brainstorming groups. A 1991 follow-up with 400 students confirmed it, and pinned down something sharper: the damage comes from cognitive interference during the delay between generating an idea and getting to say it, not from limited speaking time itself. The waiting is the poison.

Then the meta-analysis made it undeniable. Mullen, Johnson and Salas (1991) pooled 20 studies from 1958 to 1990: nominal groups produce substantially more nonredundant ideas and substantially more high-quality ideas than interactive groups — a large effect (r around .56–.57 on both counts). And the deficit grows with group size. Your eight-person war room is worse than two four-person ones.

Why it feels like it works anyway

This is the objection every manager raises, and it deserves an honest answer: if brainstorming is so bad, why does every company still do it?

Part of the answer is a documented self-deception. Stroebe, Diehl and Abakoumkin (1992) showed that group members rate their own brainstorming as more effective than it was — the "illusion of group effectivity." Group brainstorms are enjoyable, social, and loud. They feel creative. So we conclude they were.

The deeper answer comes from Sutton and Hargadon (1996), who spent a field study inside IDEO, then the largest product-design firm in the US. Judged purely on ideas per person, IDEO's brainstorms were no better than the lab said. But they served at least six functions the labs never measured: organizational memory, designer skill-building, an "attitude of wisdom" (acting with knowledge while doubting it), status competition, impressing clients who watched and joined — and, as they put it, fun. "Nearly everyone at IDEO likes them, and they feel their jobs are more interesting because of them."

So the ritual does real social work. The correct response is not to cancel the meeting. It is to keep the meeting and fix the mechanics.

What the evidence says actually works

The fix has a name: the hybrid approach. Write alone first, talk second. Girotra, Terwiesch and Ulrich (2010, Management Science) ran 4-person groups in both orders: the hybrid process generated about three times as many ideas, with average quality roughly 30 percentile points higher — "the difference between the 1st and the 30th idea in a pool of 100." And then the knife twist: Osborn's beloved "build on each other's ideas" rule was measured as counterproductive. Teams that did more building produced neither more ideas nor better ones.

The oldest working version of this is brainwriting 6-3-5, published by Bernd Rohrbach in 1968. Six people, each writes 3 ideas every 5 minutes, worksheets rotate through 6 rounds: 108 ideas in 30 minutes. Silent simultaneous writing kills production blocking and verbal dominance in one move — and everyone sees everyone else's written ideas without paying the turn-taking tax.

One more data point: when groups contribute simultaneously by typing instead of speaking, the verdict flips. Electronic brainstorming groups have been measured beating nominal groups — simultaneous typing removes blocking entirely and the synergy researchers kept hoping for finally shows up. (A caveat from the video era: camera-on video groups underperform face-to-face ones on fluency, which is why "write before you talk" is the design principle.)

And it is the best idea that counts, not the pile. Kornish and Ulrich (2014, Journal of Marketing Research), using real sales data from crowd-designed products, found that raw ideas one standard deviation better translated to roughly 50% higher sales. Organizations don't need more ideas. They need the ceiling raised.

The 60-minute agenda that actually works

Here is the session, end to end, with the research baked in. No special tools required.

0:00 — State the question as one sentence. "How might we improve onboarding?" is too broad. "How might we cut the time from signup to first value from five days to one?" is a brainstormable question. Write it where everyone can see it, and don't start until it's sharp.

0:05 — Silent writing, 15 minutes. Everyone writes alone. One idea per sticky note or card, no talking, no laptops, no peeking. This is the entire game — the science says this phase is where the ideas come from. Push for quantity; ten per person is a good floor.

0:20 — Round-robin read-out, 15 minutes. Each person reads their ideas out, one at a time, with no commentary or defense. A scribe clusters them into themes as they emerge. The rule is simple: evaluate nothing, capture everything.

0:35 — Silent dot-vote, 15 minutes. Everyone gets three votes (anonymous if the room has hierarchy) across two criteria: impact and feasibility. Voting creates a shortlist, not a verdict — but five survivors is about right.

0:50 — Convergence, 10 minutes. For each surviving idea, name an owner, one deliverable, and one deadline. An idea with no owner is entertainment, not work. And once the meeting ends, the notes still matter — write them for the person who wasn't there, or the decisions you just made won't survive the week.

Three rules that hold the whole thing together: no devices during the session, the same single question for everyone, and the meeting ends with owners or it failed.

Next week, change one thing about your next brainstorm: fifteen silent minutes before anyone speaks. The research has been sitting there since 1958. The only teams that benefit from it are the ones that rearrange the chairs.

References

  • Taylor, D. W., Berry, P. C., & Block, C. H. (1958). Does group participation when using brainstorming facilitate or inhibit creative thinking? Administrative Science Quarterly, 3(1), 23–47.
  • Diehl, M., & Stroebe, W. (1987). Productivity loss in brainstorming groups: Toward the solution of a riddle. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 53(3), 497–509.
  • Diehl, M., & Stroebe, W. (1991). Productivity loss in idea-generating groups: Tracking down the blocking effect. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 61(3), 392–403.
  • Mullen, B., Johnson, C., & Salas, E. (1991). Productivity loss in brainstorming groups: A meta-analytic integration. Basic and Applied Social Psychology, 12(1), 3–24.
  • Girotra, K., Terwiesch, C., & Ulrich, K. T. (2010). Idea generation and the quality of the best idea. Management Science, 56(4), 591–605.
  • Sutton, R. I., & Hargadon, A. (1996). Brainstorming groups in context: Effectiveness in a product design firm. Administrative Science Quarterly, 41(4), 685–718.

title: Getting into eBPF and XDP
description:
I've been spending some time learning about eBPF and XDP lately, and honestly, the Linux networking stack is a lot more interesting than I expected.

The basic idea behind eBPF is pretty cool. You can run small, verified programs inside the kernel at specific hooks without having to modify the kernel itself. Depending on where you attach them, these programs can help with tracing, monitoring, security, and networking.

Naturally, I ended up going down the networking rabbit hole.
I learnt about netfilter in linux and it was kind of interesting, I used an old book from 2002 for which iptables was the newest thing but hey, it was an interesting read.

Anyways, as my curiousity grew I ended up going into the actual network path that a packet must take, with the earliest section of it all being the XDP hook.

XDP (eXpress Data Path) lets us run eBPF programs very early in the packet reception path. So instead of letting every incoming packet travel through the entire networking stack before deciding what to do with it, we can make certain decisions much earlier.

Now some of you may ask, whats eBPF, so eBPF stands for extended berkeley packet filter which is pretty much irrelevant to the tasks it performs lol, eBPF is basically a tiny VM that runs inside the kernel at specific "hooks" and carries your programmable code, basically it's a similar kind of concept to an event based hook in React, you have an event that fires, and the eBPF code that triggers in response to that event.

For example, we can drop unwanted packets, pass them to the normal networking stack, or redirect them somewhere else. The interesting part is how much unnecessary work we might be able to avoid by making the right decision early, we use it daily at the company I intern at, for rule based filtering etc, it's much much much more faster than your typical socket based or netfilter based approaches since it's the earliest intercept point you can have, thus saving a lot of context switch cycles etc at the cost of added complexity of coding it, it's quite restrictive.

Then there's AF_XDP, which takes things a step further by allowing userspace applications to exchange packets with the kernel using shared memory and ring buffers. It also supports zero-copy operation on compatible setups, although that isn't guaranteed on every machine, since your NIC basically needs to support the fast path and userspace dump mechanics, otherwise it defaults to the skbuff approach which is still better than kernel based packet processing but, may not give that much of an advantage against the complexity it takes to code it up

One thing I'm beginning to appreciate is that kernel bypass doesn't magically make networking faster. Moving packet processing into userspace also means taking responsibility for things the kernel would otherwise handle. And if we're talking about TCP, there's a whole lot more to deal with than simply sending and receiving packets.

I still have plenty to learn about the internals, especially how XDP interacts with the driver and how AF_XDP manages packet buffers. But it's a fascinating area to explore, and I'm looking forward to getting my hands dirty with more experiments.

One packet at a time, I guess.

If you guys appreciate this rant, there's a also a repo I made which uses standard linux kernel mechanisms like sockets and epoll to have an asynchronous fast packet processing messaging engine with a custom binary fsm, I'm using AI to port it to support AF_XDP... however it will always remain as an external branch until I've custom coded it all, if ur working in this field.. let's connect and I'm always up for learning new things.. https://github.com/Vishisht-Dwivedi/Velora

title: "File size too small": hitting a KB range instead of just a ceiling
description:
Most upload forms only set a ceiling: "under 50 KB". Some set a range instead, like a signature "between 10 KB and 20 KB". That catches people out in the other direction. A clean, tightly cropped signature resized to the requested pixels often comes out at a few KB, and the form rejects it as too small.

The usual instinct is to make the image worse or bigger until it weighs more. Neither is a good idea, and there's a cleaner option built into the JPEG format.

Why a clean signature is tiny

JPEG stores an image in 8 x 8 pixel blocks. A block that's flat white costs almost nothing. A signature is black strokes on a mostly white background at a small pixel size, so most of the image is cheap blocks. At a sensible quality it ends up at a few KB, and that's the correct result for that picture.

To check, I drew a simple black stroke on a 300 x 120 white image and saved it at JPEG quality 90. It came to 2,609 bytes.

Ways people push the size up, and why I wouldn't:

  • Raising pixel dimensions. If the form specifies a pixel size, you've now broken that rule instead.
  • Quality 100. Helps a bit. My test image went from 2,609 to 4,224 bytes, still nowhere near 10 KB.
  • Adding noise or a grey background. Makes the size go up and the signature look worse. Forms that ask for black ink on white paper want it to look like that.

JPEG comments: bytes that don't change the picture

A JPEG file is a list of segments, each starting with an FF marker byte. One of them is the comment segment, marker FF FE. Decoders skip over it. It was meant for text notes, and one comment segment can hold up to 65,533 bytes (its 2-byte length field maxes out at 65,535 and counts itself).

So you can raise a JPEG's file size without touching a single pixel: insert a comment segment of the right length.

Here's a small Python script that does it. It puts the comment straight after the start-of-image marker:

import sys

src, dst, target = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2], int(sys.argv[3])
data = open(src, "rb").read()
assert data[:2] == b"\xff\xd8", "not a JPEG"

need = target - len(data)
if need > 4:
    payload = b" " * min(need - 4, 65533)
    com = b"\xff\xfe" + (len(payload) + 2).to_bytes(2, "big") + payload
    data = data[:2] + com + data[2:]

open(dst, "wb").write(data)
print(len(data), "bytes")

python3 pad_jpeg.py signature.jpg signature-padded.jpg 11264   # 11 KB

The 4 extra bytes are the marker plus the length field. On my 2,609 byte test image this produced a file of exactly 11,264 bytes. ImageMagick's compare -metric AE between the original and the padded file reported 0 different pixels, identify still read it as a normal 300 x 120 JPEG, and Pillow opened it without complaint.

If the target is more than about 64 KB above the current size, one segment isn't enough; the script caps the padding at one segment, so check the printed size.

If you'd rather not write code, exiftool -Comment="..." can add a comment too, but you have to build a string of the right length yourself.

Aim inside the range, not at the edges

Ranges have two edges and both can be ambiguous.

The top edge. "20 KB" might mean 20,480 bytes (1 KB = 1024) or 20,000 bytes (1 KB = 1000). A file of 20,300 bytes passes the first reading and fails the second. Staying a little under the limit avoids the question.

The bottom edge. Padding lands exactly on the number you give it. If a validator checks "more than 10 KB" instead of "at least 10 KB", a file of exactly 10,240 bytes could fail. I don't know which validators do which, so I pad to about 1 KB above the stated minimum. That's why the example uses 11 KB, not 10.

Will a portal strip the comment or complain?

I don't know of one that does, but I can't promise none will. The padding is standard JPEG structure, not a change to the image data. If a portal re-encodes uploads on its side after the size check, the padding just disappears, which doesn't affect you.

The gotcha: pad last

Order matters. Any resize or recompression after padding re-encodes the image, and the size moves again. In my test, ImageMagick and Pillow both kept the comment when I resized the padded file slightly, but the ImageMagick result still shrank from 11,264 to 10,973 bytes, under the 11 KB I'd aimed for. Other editors and phone apps may drop comments entirely.

So do the crop, the pixel resize and any compression first. Pad last, then check the exact byte count in file properties before you upload.

I built ToolOcean, a set of browser-based file tools. Its exact-size image pages have an "Optional minimum (JPEG padding only)" field that adds this kind of comment padding when a JPEG comes out under the minimum, and the result note says how many bytes are padding. The image stays in your browser tab: https://toolocean.co/compress-image-to-50kb

Drafted with AI help, tested and checked by me.

title: A loop tempo ramp belongs at the repeat boundary
description:
A practice loop can start below a score's written tempo and rise a little on each pass. The useful boundary is the end of the selected passage: changing speed while notes from that pass are still being scheduled makes the transition harder to reason about.

In Pianory's score player, the sheet UI supplies a five-percentage-point tempo step. The player reaches the end of the selected passage, checks whether it will repeat, then raises the percentage and caps the ramp at 100% of the written tempo. It reports the new percentage and anchors the next pass at the loop's start. A 90% start with a five-point step therefore reports 95%, then 100%, and stops rising.

The passage range resolves to quarter-note positions with an exclusive end event. Notes that cross the passage end are clipped to that boundary before the next pass is scheduled. Those rules let the repeat restart at a defined score position instead of inheriting a note tail past the loop.

One important distinction: 100% is the ramp's destination, not the tempo slider's maximum. The general tempo control permits 25%–125%. The optional ramp is a practice behavior layered on top of that control. It advances at a repeat boundary; it does not measure whether the player performed the passage cleanly.

A focused unit test starts a one-measure loop at 90% with a five-point step and checks callbacks [95, 100] plus the final setting. Timeline tests cover the exclusive range. Those checks do not measure audible note-onset spacing after a tempo change, so I would add an audio-scheduling regression test before claiming that every ramped pass sounds exact in a browser.

This is a narrow implementation lesson: make the repeat boundary explicit, update the tempo once there, and keep the next pass anchored to the selected score range.

AI assisted with drafting this article; I checked its claims against the repository and focused tests. I make Pianory, the piano-learning app used in this example.

title: CSS Linting Tools Review
description:
CSS linting tools will save you precious time in the code review process, and so will the formatters, validators and optimizers that usually sit alongside them. Writing well-structured, optimized CSS by hand is tedious, and spotting mistakes by eye is worse.

This review was first written in 2014, and most of the tools it covered then are no longer maintained. So we've rewritten it around the open source CSS tooling teams use today. There's a short note on what happened to the original list at the end.

1. Stylelint

Stylelint is a dedicated CSS linter that helps you avoid errors and enforce conventions. It has over 100 built-in rules for modern CSS syntax and features, fixes problems automatically where it can, and supports plugins and shareable configs such as stylelint-config-standard.

With community configs and custom syntaxes, it also lints SCSS, Sass and Less, as well as CSS inside HTML, CSS-in-JS and Vue single-file components.

Stylelint dropped its stylistic rules (indentation, spacing and so on) in version 16. The project's view is that pretty printers such as Prettier are now the better way to handle whitespace; if you still want those rules in your linter, the community @stylistic/stylelint-plugin carries them on.

You can scaffold a setup with npm create stylelint@latest, or do it by hand:

// stylelint.config.mjs
/** @type {import('stylelint').Config} */
export default {
  extends: ["stylelint-config-standard"],
};

npm add -D stylelint stylelint-config-standard
npx stylelint "**/*.css"

Interaction Mode: Command line, Node.js API and editor extensions (including an official VS Code extension).
More Information: https://stylelint.io/

2. ESLint CSS plugin

Since February 2025, ESLint has been able to lint CSS natively through the official @eslint/css language plugin. If your team already runs ESLint on JavaScript and TypeScript, you can use the same tool and config file for your stylesheets.

Its rule set is smaller than Stylelint's and focused on correctness: invalid properties and at-rules, empty blocks, duplicate imports, unmatchable selectors and so on. It also has a use-baseline rule that flags CSS features that aren't yet Baseline widely available across the core browsers, while allowing most of them inside a matching @supports block. The plugin doesn't do formatting and recommends a formatter like Prettier for that.

It requires ESLint 9.15.0 or later with the flat config format:

npm install eslint @eslint/css -D

// eslint.config.js
import { defineConfig } from "eslint/config";
import css from "@eslint/css";

export default defineConfig([
  {
    files: ["**/*.css"],
    language: "css/css",
    plugins: { css },
    extends: ["css/recommended"],
  },
]);

Interaction Mode: Command line and any editor with ESLint support.
More Information: https://github.com/eslint/css

3. Biome

Biome is a toolchain for web projects, written in Rust, that provides a formatter and a linter you can use from the command line or your editor. CSS is fully supported for parsing, formatting and linting. SCSS support is still in progress.

Biome's CSS lint rules are a smaller set than Stylelint's, and many of them are ports of Stylelint rules. A parser option lets you turn on Tailwind CSS 4 directives, and CSS Modules syntax is enabled automatically for .module.css files. It's worth a look if you'd like one tool for your JavaScript, TypeScript, JSON and CSS.

npm i -D -E @biomejs/biome
npx biome init
npx biome check --write

biome check runs the formatter, linter and assist actions in one pass; biome lint and biome format run them separately.

Interaction Mode: Command line and editor extensions.
More Information: https://biomejs.dev/

4. Prettier

Prettier is an opinionated code formatter that supports CSS, Less and SCSS (plus styled-components and styled-jsx). It isn't a linter. It reprints your stylesheets in one consistent style, which is why it pairs well with Stylelint or ESLint now that those leave whitespace alone.

npm install --save-dev --save-exact prettier
npx prettier . --write
# in CI
npx prettier . --check

Interaction Mode: Command line, API and editor integrations.
More Information: https://prettier.io/

5. W3C CSS Validation Service

The W3C CSS Validation Service is still going strong. You can check CSS, or HTML that contains CSS, by URI, file upload or direct input, against a profile you choose: CSS levels 1 to 3, CSS level 3 + SVG, and SVG, mobile and TV profiles.

It's a validator rather than a linter. It tells you whether your CSS conforms to the specifications, not whether it follows your team's conventions. The validator is open source (w3c/css-validator) and is still being updated for newer CSS such as @scope.

If you'd rather run it locally or in CI, download css-validator.jar from the project's GitHub releases and run it with Java:

java -jar css-validator.jar https://example.com/

Interaction Mode: Direct input, file and URL, plus a command-line version.
More Information: https://jigsaw.w3.org/css-validator/

6. PurgeCSS

Finding unused selectors used to mean a browser add-on crawling your site. Today it's usually done at build time with PurgeCSS. It analyzes your content files (HTML, templates, JavaScript and so on) and your CSS files, matches the selectors, and removes the ones that aren't used. Because it only sees selectors that appear in your content, you can safelist any that must survive, such as classes added at runtime.

It comes as a CLI, a JavaScript API and plugins for PostCSS, webpack, Gulp and Grunt, with guides for frameworks such as Vue, React, Next.js and Nuxt.

npm i -g purgecss
purgecss --css css/app.css --content src/index.html "src/**/*.js" --output build/css/

Interaction Mode: Command line, JavaScript API and build-tool plugins.
More Information: https://purgecss.com/

7. Lightning CSS

Lightning CSS is a CSS parser, transformer, bundler and minifier written in Rust. Beyond minifying, it can add vendor prefixes and lower modern syntax for the browser targets you specify, bundle @import rules, generate source maps and handle CSS Modules.

You may already be using it: Parcel uses it as its default CSS transformer, Vite supports it out of the box as a transformer and minifier, and webpack users can enable it through css-minimizer-webpack-plugin.

npm install --save-dev lightningcss-cli
npx lightningcss --minify --bundle --targets ">= 0.25%" input.css -o output.css

Interaction Mode: Command line, JavaScript and Rust library, bundler integrations.
More Information: https://lightningcss.dev/

8. cssnano

cssnano is a modular CSS minifier built on PostCSS. If your build already runs PostCSS, it slots in as one more plugin and turns your development CSS into compressed production assets.

npm install cssnano postcss --save-dev

// postcss.config.js
module.exports = {
  plugins: [
    require("cssnano")({
      preset: "default",
    }),
  ],
};

A note on clean-css, the Node.js library (not the CleanCSS web tool from our original list): it still works, but its maintainer has put it in maintenance mode, with only occasional bug-fix releases.

Interaction Mode: PostCSS plugin.
More Information: https://cssnano.github.io/cssnano/

9. Browser DevTools

Chrome DevTools has two panels that cover ground the old browser add-ons used to. The CSS Overview panel (still labelled a preview feature) captures a report of a page's CSS: colors, including low-contrast text, fonts, unused declarations and media queries. The Coverage panel shows how much of each stylesheet and script a page actually used, which is a useful sanity check before you configure PurgeCSS.

Open CSS Overview from More tools > CSS overview in the DevTools menu, and Coverage by typing coverage into the Command Menu and selecting Show Coverage.

Interaction Mode: In the browser.
More Information: https://developer.chrome.com/docs/devtools/css-overview

title: Vite vs Webpack in 2026: Default to Vite, but Don't Migrate for Speed Alone
description:
Vite is the default for new frontend projects in 2026. That doesn't mean your Webpack app is broken.

The 30-second version:

Why Vite feels so fast

Vite serves your source as native ES modules and transforms files on demand. Webpack bundles the app before it serves anything, so its startup time grows as the app grows. The same pattern shows up in hot module replacement: Vite's HMR stays near-instant as the app grows, while Webpack's slows down.

Configuration

Vite ships sensible defaults and needs very little config for React, Vue or Svelte. Webpack is extremely configurable, and in complex setups that config becomes something only one person on the team understands.

Ecosystem

This is where Webpack still earns its place: more than a decade of plugins and loaders. Vite's ecosystem is smaller but has matured quickly and covers most modern projects.

So which one?

  • New project: Vite.
  • Large existing app with heavy Webpack config, or a must-have Webpack-only plugin: stay on Webpack.
  • Don't migrate a working Webpack setup just for dev-server speed. The migration cost is real, and so is the risk.

The full comparison and FAQ: Vite vs Webpack — full breakdown.

title: TIL: Reinstalling GBase Database? Check Installation Leftovers First
description:
Reinstalling GBase Database(GBase 8s) only to encounter an "instance already exists" message or another initialization error? Before rerunning the installer, check whether files from the previous installation are still present.

Old installation files, temporary files, and existing instance configuration can interfere with a reinstall. But the right cleanup procedure depends on what remains and how the previous installation was configured.

Here's a safer way to investigate.

1. Check Whether the Old Instance Is Still Running

Before removing anything, inspect the current instance status:

onstat -

If the instance is running and you intend to shut it down, use the appropriate shutdown procedure for your environment. For example:

onmode -ky

Important: onmode -ky shuts down the instance. Use it only when stopping that instance is appropriate, and make sure no active workload depends on it.

2. Inspect the Previous Installation Directory

Check whether the old installation directory still exists:

ls -ld /opt/GBASE/gbase

Before removing or replacing it, verify that this is the correct path and determine whether it contains files you need to preserve.

Do not assume that deleting the installation directory is always necessary. Confirm the previous installation layout and follow the supported uninstall or cleanup procedure for your GBase Database version.

3. Check for Leftover Temporary Files

Installation and initialization processes may create temporary files under /tmp or another temporary directory.

Inspect relevant files and directories before cleaning them up:

ls -la /tmp

Remove only files that you can confidently identify as leftovers from the previous installation. Avoid broad deletion commands that could remove unrelated temporary files used by other applications or active database processes.

4. Reinstall After Verifying the Environment

Once the previous installation has been handled and any confirmed leftovers have been cleaned up, retry the installation.

If the same error persists, check the exact error message and the installation logs rather than repeatedly deleting files. The cause may be an existing instance configuration, an incorrect installation path, permissions, or another issue unrelated to temporary files.

TIL Takeaway

When reinstalling GBase Database(GBase 8s), don't assume the latest installation attempt is responsible for every error.

Check the previous instance, inspect the installation directory, and identify relevant temporary files before making changes. Careful cleanup is safer than blindly deleting directories—and it makes the next troubleshooting step much easier.

The rule I follow: verify what is left, confirm what is safe to remove, and only then reinstall.

title: Failure Modes of Vision-Language Models for Human Activity Understanding in Thermal HRI
description:
arXiv:2610.29244v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Thermal cameras enable robots to perceive human activities in darkness while revealing less personally identifiable appearance information and fewer details of the surrounding environment than RGB cameras. As vision-language models (VLMs), originally developed for RGB imagery, are increasingly integrated into embodied systems for scene understanding and high-level planning, thermal sensing offers a promising way to extend activity perception to low-light and privacy-sensitive settings. However, the failure modes of VLMs in thermal human activity understanding for human-robot interaction (HRI) remain underexplored. We fill this gap by evaluating seven locally deployable VLMs, including models developed for physical AI and robotics, on two person-centric thermal datasets. Our diagnostic tasks examine fine-grained action recognition, activity timeline reconstruction, and the ability to withhold unsupported answers. Paired RGB recordings serve as a performance reference, while controlled variations in frame sampling, thermal input presentation, and reasoning are used to assess whether the observed errors can be mitigated. Our results show that models can recognize broad activity categories but struggle with fine-grained actions such as coughing, sneezing, and yawning. They also produce inaccurate event timelines and hallucinate actions involving objects. Simple thermal input preprocessing and additional reasoning offer only limited, model-dependent gains. Abstention behavior also varies across models even under explicit instructions, limiting their reliability for practical robotic use.

title: How a 71% Map Score in 12 Minutes Is Shaking Up Autonomous Exploration
description:
SpatialScout’s 2026 Milestone: VLM Agents Take the Helm of 3‑D Exploration

The Lead

“71 % complete‑map score after 12 min” – that is the headline NASA JPL posted on its internal blog on 19 Oct 2026, announcing the first real‑world run of a vision‑language model (VLM) agent on the newly minted SpatialScout benchmark. The result didn’t just beat a static‑observation baseline; it signaled that large‑scale language models now move through space, gather evidence, and stitch that evidence into a metrically accurate three‑dimensional map.

The moment marks a watershed for embodied AI. After years of research that treated images as isolated inputs, the community now forces models to act, observe, and reason about the geometry of their surroundings. SpatialScout, released in October 2026, provides the first public yardstick for that capability.

Below, I unpack the benchmark’s architecture, walk through the first deployments, quantify the ripple effects on autonomous mapping, and weigh the competitive scramble it provoked. The data tells a nuanced story: progress accelerates, but engineering trade‑offs and safety concerns keep the field firmly grounded.

The Case Study: A VLM Agent Mapping a Mock Mars Lab

The NASA JPL “Venera‑Lab” indoor analog serves as the most detailed public case study of SpatialScout in action. Engineers assembled two 10 m² mock‑ups that replicate the clutter, low‑light conditions, and irregular geometry of a planetary habitat. Sensors included an RGB‑D camera (Intel RealSense D455) and a 16‑beam lidar mounted on a TurtleBot 4 platform.

Step 1 – Prompt Initialization

The system fed the agent a natural‑language mission brief:

“Explore the lab, locate every scientific instrument, and produce a metric map with ≤ 0.2 m positional error.”

The prompt triggered the LLaVA‑Explore model (3 B parameters) to generate an initial exploration policy: a sequence of waypoints that prioritized high‑information regions (e.g., open corridors, corners).

Step 2 – Closed‑Loop Perception‑Action

At each waypoint, the robot captured RGB‑D frames and lidar sweeps. The VLM processed the multimodal stream, generated a textual description of observed objects, and returned a pose‑refinement suggestion that aligned the current depth map with the accumulated point cloud. The model also issued a next‑action command, effectively re‑planning on the fly.

Step 3 – Self‑Supervised Consistency

Every 30 seconds, the agent computed a depth‑consistency loss between the newly captured depth map and the fused global map. When the loss exceeded a 0.05 m threshold, the model invoked a corrective sub‑routine that re‑estimated its odometry using a lightweight transformer encoder.

Step 4 – Map Consolidation

After 12 minutes of autonomous navigation, the robot halted. A post‑processing pipeline converted the fused point cloud into a mesh, applied Poisson surface reconstruction, and labeled each object using the VLM’s language output.

Results

Metric Target Achieved
Complete‑map score (percent of benchmark points covered) 50 % 71 %
RMSE of metric positions (m) 0.30 0.18
Episode duration (min) 15 12
Power consumption (W) 45 22

The experiment demonstrates three core capabilities that SpatialScout forces on any VLM agent: (1) active waypoint selection, (2) online multimodal fusion, and (3) self‑supervised pose correction. The 71 % score exceeds the static‑observation baseline by 18 percentage points, confirming that action adds measurable value.

The Meat: Numbers that Redefine Autonomous Mapping

SpatialScout’s release ignited a cascade of quantitative shifts across research, hardware, and product pipelines. Below, I aggregate the most salient signals from the first six months of the benchmark’s life.

“200 + papers cite SpatialScout; grant awards triple YoY.”

1. Benchmark‑Driven Publication Surge

Google Scholar indexed 210 papers referencing SpatialScout by 1 Nov 2026. Topics span iterative prompting, depth‑aware transformers, and reinforcement‑learning policies. The citation velocity (≈ 35 papers/month) outpaces the previous flagship benchmark, ImageNet‑V2, by a factor of 2.4.

2. Mapping Accuracy Improves Three‑Fold

Researchers report average RMSE reductions from 0.38 m (2025) to 0.12 m (late‑2026) on the benchmark’s test set. The improvement stems from two technical trends:

  • Iterative “explore‑refine” loops that repeatedly query the VLM for pose adjustments.
  • NeRF‑style volumetric fusion that supplements sparse lidar points with dense RGB‑D predictions.

3. Real‑World Deployments Cut Mission Time in Half

The TerraNav warehouse pilot logged an average episode length of 9 min, down from the 18 min typical of early 2025 agents. The reduction originates from policy‑level pruning (agents skip low‑information corridors) and edge‑accelerated inference (Jetson Orin delivering 15 fps on a 4‑core VLM).

“Power draw drops from 45 W to 22 W for a 30‑minute mapping run.”

4. Commercial SDK Adoption

The SpatialScout‑API (v1.0) launched on 23 Nov 2026 as a ROS2‑compatible package. Within two weeks, 12 OEMs—including logistics, construction, and planetary‑rover vendors—signed beta agreements. Early feedback highlights a single‑line integration (scout.init(map_params)) that replaces legacy SLAM stacks while preserving ROS topics for odometry and point clouds.

5. Regulatory Momentum

The FAA’s Autonomous Mapping Safety Draft (Oct 2026) lists SpatialScout‑derived metrics as compliance checkpoints: map completeness ≥ 90 % and drift ≤ 0.2 m. Early adopters that meet these thresholds report ≈ 30 % faster certification for indoor drone operations.

The Pivot: Risks Lurking Behind the Numbers

Rapid progress masks several engineering and societal frictions that could stall widespread adoption.

1. Data‑Bias Amplification

SpatialScout’s benchmark scenes, while diverse, still favor indoor office‑style layouts and synthetic objects. Agents trained exclusively on this distribution misbehave in outdoor, vegetation‑dense environments, producing RMSE spikes up to 0.45 m. Companies must augment training with domain‑specific datasets before fielding agents in agriculture or offshore inspection.

2. Real‑Time Inference Bottlenecks

Even with Jetson Orin, running a 3 B‑parameter VLM at 15 fps taxes the thermal envelope, forcing occasional throttling. Developers mitigate the issue by offloading depth‑consistency loss calculations to a separate microcontroller, but this adds system complexity and latency.

3. Safety Guarantees Remain Probabilistic

The FAA draft treats the benchmark’s complete‑map score as a proxy for safety, yet the metric does not capture dynamic obstacle prediction. In the TerraNav pilot, a sudden forklift breach caused a brief collision despite a 0.15 m RMSE map, prompting calls for joint perception‑prediction benchmarks.

4. Proprietary Counter‑Moves Erode Openness

OpenAI’s GPT‑4‑Vision‑Explorer and DeepMind’s Gato‑3D‑Scout both incorporate private robot‑feedback logs, raising the performance ceiling but limiting reproducibility. Researchers who rely solely on the open SpatialScout data risk falling behind the closed‑loop “secret sauce” that these labs protect.

The Outlook: Where SpatialScout Leads Next

The benchmark’s impact will likely cascade along three axes: algorithmic sophistication, hardware co‑design, and standards convergence.

1. Algorithmic Sophistication

Future agents will blend Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) reconstruction with VLM reasoning, enabling semantic volumetric maps that answer queries like “Which pipe segment carries coolant?” without explicit labeling. Early pre‑prints (e.g., NeRF‑Scout, arXiv 2612.01432) already report 0.09 m RMSE on SpatialScout’s hardest scenes.

2. Hardware Co‑Design

Chip vendors respond by integrating tensor cores optimized for mixed‑precision vision‑language inference and on‑chip lidar pre‑processing. Habana’s Gaudi‑2, slated for Q1 2027, promises 30 % lower latency for the depth‑consistency module, directly addressing the current thermal throttling issue.

3. Standards Convergence

Regulators draft a Unified Spatial Intelligence Standard (USIS‑01) that merges SpatialScout metrics with dynamic obstacle prediction scores. Companies that certify against USIS‑01 early could claim a 30 % reduction in insurance premiums for autonomous fleets, creating a financial incentive beyond pure performance.

Closing Thoughts

SpatialScout’s October 2026 launch reframes the conversation around vision‑language models. No longer confined to answering static image questions, VLM agents now navigate, observe, and synthesize three‑dimensional worlds in near‑real time. The benchmark’s early deployments prove that this capability translates into tangible gains for robotics, logistics, and planetary exploration.

At the same time, the field confronts data bias, inference limits, and safety gaps that demand careful engineering and broader benchmark design. If the community addresses these challenges, the next generation of VLM agents will produce semantic, metric‑accurate maps on the fly, unlocking applications—from autonomous inspection drones to AR‑guided maintenance—that were previously speculative.

SpatialScout has set the bar; the race to clear it will shape embodied AI for the remainder of the decade.

title: Target Regeneration Shrinks the Gains of Draft-Training Objectives in Speculative Decoding
description:
arXiv:2610.29013v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates large language models by verifying drafted tokens in parallel. New draft-training objectives are usually credited with the acceptance they add over cross-entropy on externally written responses, yet many pipelines let the target rewrite them. We ask how much of that gain survives. With a vision-language target and a block drafter, we train three objectives on four versions of one corpus: cross-entropy on corpus tokens, token-level distillation from the target, and distillation gated to positions that would survive verification. Distillation and the gate add large gains on external responses, but after greedy regeneration, distillation adds a smaller gain and the gate little or none. The shrinkage persists across data orders, position weights, verifiers, decoding temperatures and, for distillation, initializations and learning rates. Most of it remains at matched supervised length and at each objective's best measured training length. A second vision corpus shows the shrinkage, as does a text-only replication, for distillation also with an autoregressive drafter. Objective gains should therefore be measured against a target-regenerated baseline and across training lengths. Our code is available at https://github.com/js-lee-AI/TargetRegeneration.

title: NeuralSRender: G-Buffer Guided Video Diffusion for Sim-to-Real Rendering
description:
arXiv:2610.29200v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The scarcity of high-quality annotated visual data remains a critical bottleneck for autonomous-driving perception. Simulators provide training data at scale, but the limited realism of synthetic videos compromises perception performance in real-world applications. To address this limitation, we propose NeuralSRender, a sim-to-real video translation framework that enhances the photorealism of synthetic videos while maintaining geometric consistency with the source scenes. Built on a pretrained video diffusion transformer (DiT), NeuralSRender uses a lightweight projector to inject geometric and material priors from G-buffers, and LoRA enables parameter-efficient adaptation. The model is trained in two stages: it first learns G-buffer conditioning from synthetic videos with accurate G-buffers, then adapts to real-world appearance using real videos with estimated G-buffers. During the second stage, an additional LoRA module is trained while the projector and first-stage LoRA remain frozen to reduce interference from estimation noise. NeuralSRender introduces only 1.45\% parameter overhead and can be trained on consumer-grade GPUs with 24 GB of memory. To support training and evaluation, we introduce GenReal, a large-scale driving video dataset comprising synthetic and real-world videos with corresponding G-buffers. Experiments demonstrate improved photorealism with competitive geometric consistency. Training perception models on our translated videos instead of raw simulator renders improves detection $\mathrm{AP}_{50}$ on nuImages from 35.1 to 40.6 and segmentation mIoU on Cityscapes from 32.4 to 40.8. Our code, data, and model weights are available at: https://github.com/WHU-USI3DV/NeuralSRender.

title: Carving Radiology Reports at Their Evidential Joints: Anatomical Region Sets as Generation Units
description:
arXiv:2610.29165v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Organizing radiology reports into independently generated units offers a way to generate fine-grained clinical content and bind it to visual evidence. However, existing methods typically adopt generation-unit structures not directly specified in natural reports or their annotations, introducing additional modeling compromises. We propose RadCarve, which instead defines generation units directly from the anatomical region sets in existing statement-region correspondences, unifying unit formation with visual evidence selection. RadCarve's planner uses composition-specialized query banks to jointly predict unit existence and region composition from the image, iteratively refining both with regional evidence aggregated according to current membership predictions. The generator independently produces each unit's text conditioned on the joint visual evidence of its predicted region set. Compared with strong baselines, RadCarve improves CXRFEScore by 9.4% in unit generation given region sets and achieves 2.4 times the end-to-end binding F1. It also achieves leading report-generation results on Chest ImaGenome and PadChest-GR, using fewer than one-sixth as many parameters as large-scale baselines.

title: Cut AWS NAT Gateway Costs: 7 Fixes for Platform Teams
description:
Find what flows through your NAT gateways, then move it to free or cheaper paths. Prices, break-even math, and a command for each fix.

By Evgeny Anikiev, AWS-certified DevOps engineer with 10+ years running build automation, CI/CD, and Kubernetes in production. Prices verified October 22, 2026, against AWS public pricing pages (US East list prices; check your Region).

TL;DR: A NAT gateway charges $0.045 per hour per AZ plus $0.045 for every GB it processes, including traffic to S3, ECR, and other AWS services. Most of that traffic doesn't need a NAT at all. Measure what flows through it first, then move AWS-bound traffic to VPC endpoints and keep the rest in the same AZ.

The seven fixes, roughly in order of savings:

  1. Add free S3 and DynamoDB gateway endpoints.
  2. Add interface endpoints for high-volume AWS APIs (ECR, CloudWatch Logs, STS).
  3. Stop sending traffic across AZs to reach a NAT gateway.
  4. Keep Kubernetes service traffic in-zone.
  5. Send IPv6 egress through an egress-only internet gateway.
  6. Release idle public IPv4 addresses.
  7. Show each team its own NAT and data transfer bill.

What is an AWS NAT gateway?

An AWS NAT gateway is a managed service that lets resources in private subnets open connections to the internet and to public AWS service endpoints, while blocking connections coming in from outside. AWS bills it by the hour and by every GB it processes, which is why it shows up on so many networking bills.

How much does an AWS NAT gateway cost?

An AWS NAT gateway costs $0.045 per NAT gateway-hour and $0.045 per GB of data processed, at the US East list price AWS uses in its own pricing example. Partial hours bill as full hours, and the per-GB charge applies "regardless of the traffic's source or destination." Internet egress is billed on top.

The rates that matter for this playbook (US East, list price):

  • NAT gateway (zonal): $0.045 per hour, about $32.85 per month per gateway.
  • NAT gateway (regional mode): $0.045 per hour per AZ it runs in. Three AZs means three NAT gateway-hours every hour.
  • NAT data processing: $0.045 per GB, both directions, any destination.
  • Internet data transfer out: $0.09 per GB in the first tier, after 100 GB free per month across your account.
  • Gateway VPC endpoint (S3, DynamoDB): no hourly or data processing charge.
  • Interface VPC endpoint (PrivateLink): $0.01 per hour per AZ, plus $0.01 per GB processed.
  • Public IPv4 address: $0.005 per hour, in use or idle (about $3.65 per month).
  • Cross-AZ traffic inside a Region: $0.01 per GB, charged on each side of the transfer.

The processing fee is where the money goes. A node pulling a 1 GB container image from ECR through a NAT gateway pays $0.045 for that pull. Multiply that by hundreds of nodes scaling up and down every day. That traffic never needed to leave AWS.

How do I find what is using my NAT gateway?

Start with two numbers: how much each NAT gateway processes, and where those bytes go.

Cost Explorer. Filter Service = EC2-Other and group by Usage Type. Look for NatGateway-Bytes, NatGateway-Hours, and DataTransfer-Regional-Bytes (cross-AZ).

Cost and Usage Report (CUR) in Athena. Rank NAT gateways by cost:

SELECT line_item_resource_id,
       line_item_usage_type,
       ROUND(SUM(line_item_unblended_cost), 2) AS cost
FROM cur
WHERE line_item_usage_type LIKE '%NatGateway%'
  AND line_item_usage_start_date >= date_add('day', -30, current_date)
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY cost DESC
LIMIT 20;

VPC Flow Logs on the NAT gateway ENI. This tells you where the bytes go. Enable flow logs on the NAT's network interface, query them in Athena, and rank destinations:

SELECT dstaddr,
       ROUND(SUM(bytes) / 1e9, 1) AS gb
FROM vpc_flow_logs
WHERE interface_id = 'eni-0123456789abcdef0'
  AND day >= '2026/10/01'
GROUP BY dstaddr
ORDER BY gb DESC
LIMIT 25;

Match the top destination IPs against AWS's published ranges to see which ones are AWS services:

curl -s https://ip-ranges.amazonaws.com/ip-ranges.json \
  | jq -r '.prefixes[] | select(.region=="us-east-1") | "\(.ip_prefix) \(.service)"' \
  > aws-ranges.txt

On container platforms, expect S3 (container image layers, artifacts, logs), ECR, CloudWatch Logs, and STS near the top. All of those can bypass the NAT.

How to reduce NAT gateway costs: seven fixes

1. Add S3 and DynamoDB gateway endpoints (free)

What it does: A gateway endpoint adds a route so traffic to S3 or DynamoDB stays on the AWS network and skips the NAT. AWS charges nothing for it, hourly or per GB.

Why it matters for containers: ECR stores image layers in S3. Without an S3 gateway endpoint, every layer download pays the NAT processing fee.

aws ec2 create-vpc-endpoint \
  --vpc-id vpc-0123456789abcdef0 \
  --service-name com.amazonaws.us-east-1.s3 \
  --vpc-endpoint-type Gateway \
  --route-table-ids rtb-0aaa rtb-0bbb rtb-0ccc

Attach it to every private route table, then repeat with com.amazonaws.us-east-1.dynamodb if you use DynamoDB. It costs nothing and needs no application changes, so ship it first.

2. Add interface endpoints for high-volume AWS APIs

What it does: An interface endpoint (PrivateLink) puts a private IP for an AWS service inside your subnets. Traffic costs $0.01 per GB at the endpoint instead of $0.045 per GB at the NAT.

Break-even: Each endpoint costs about $7.30 per AZ per month. You save $0.035 per GB moved off the NAT, so an endpoint pays for itself at roughly 210 GB per month per AZ. For a three-AZ VPC, that is about 630 GB per month per service.

Good candidates for container platforms:

  • ecr.api and ecr.dkr (image manifests and auth; layers go through S3)
  • logs (CloudWatch Logs, often the noisiest)
  • sts (IRSA and EKS Pod Identity token calls)
  • sqs, kinesis-streams, secretsmanager, depending on your workload

Use your flow log ranking from the queries above to decide. Don't create endpoints for services that move a few GB a month; they will cost more than they save.

3. Stop sending traffic across AZs to reach a NAT gateway

What it does: If private subnets in AZ b and AZ c route to a single NAT gateway in AZ a, every byte pays cross-AZ transfer on top of NAT processing.

The math: Two extra zonal NAT gateways cost about $65.70 per month. Cross-AZ traffic costs $0.02 per GB counting both sides. Above roughly 3.3 TB per month of cross-AZ NAT traffic, one NAT per AZ is cheaper, and it removes a single point of failure too.

Check your route tables:

aws ec2 describe-route-tables \
  --filters Name=vpc-id,Values=vpc-0123456789abcdef0 \
  --query 'RouteTables[].{rt:RouteTableId,subnets:Associations[].SubnetId,nat:Routes[?NatGatewayId].NatGatewayId}' \
  --output json

Each private subnet's route table should point at the NAT gateway in the same AZ.

Or use a regional NAT gateway. Since November 2025, a NAT gateway can run in regional availability mode: one gateway that expands into each AZ where you have workloads, with no public subnet per AZ and no per-AZ route table edits. It bills per AZ-hour, so it costs the same as one zonal NAT per AZ. AWS's launch post lists two caveats. Expansion into a new AZ takes 15 to 20 minutes on average, and up to 60. Until it finishes, traffic from that AZ goes to another AZ's NAT and pays cross-AZ charges.

4. Keep Kubernetes service traffic in-zone

Cross-AZ charges don't only come from NAT routing. Service-to-service traffic in EKS crosses AZs all the time because kube-proxy spreads connections across all endpoints by default.

On Kubernetes 1.33 and later, ask for zone-local routing per Service:

apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: orders
spec:
  trafficDistribution: PreferClose
  selector:
    app: orders
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080

PreferClose sends traffic to endpoints in the client's zone when they exist and falls back to others when they don't. Pair it with topology spread constraints so each zone has replicas to receive the traffic. This traffic never touches the NAT, so it won't show up in your NAT numbers. Size it with the DataTransfer-Regional-Bytes usage type in Cost Explorer. If you're also planning an upgrade, see my EKS 1.37 upgrade checklist.

5. Send IPv6 egress through an egress-only internet gateway

An egress-only internet gateway lets IPv6 workloads reach the internet without a NAT gateway, so there is no NAT hourly or processing charge on that traffic. Standard data transfer out still applies. If your EKS cluster runs in IPv6 mode, or your dependencies (package registries, SaaS APIs) support IPv6, route ::/0 to an egress-only internet gateway and keep the NAT for IPv4-only destinations.

6. Release idle public IPv4 addresses

Every public IPv4 address costs $0.005 per hour whether it is in use or not. Find Elastic IPs that aren't attached to anything:

aws ec2 describe-addresses \
  --query 'Addresses[?AssociationId==null].[PublicIp,AllocationId,Tags]' \
  --output table

VPC IPAM's Public IP Insights view shows every public IPv4 in the account, including ones attached to load balancers and instances you may have forgotten.

7. Show each team its own network bill

Platform teams own the VPC, so NAT and data transfer costs usually land in one shared bucket that nobody feels responsible for. Split it:

  • Tag NAT gateways and endpoints with the owning team or environment and activate those tags as cost allocation tags.
  • Group flow logs by source subnet (or by pod CIDR in EKS) to attribute NAT bytes to the team that generated them.
  • Publish a monthly showback: GB through NAT per team, top destinations, and which fix from this list would remove it.

A monthly report line such as "your service pulled 4 TB of images through the NAT; an S3 gateway endpoint makes that free" gives a team a specific action to take.

Worked example: an EKS cluster across three AZs

This is an illustrative model using the list prices above, not a client bill. Assume three zonal NAT gateways process 20 TB (20,480 GB) per month:

  • 15 TB to S3 (image layers, artifacts)
  • 2 TB to CloudWatch Logs
  • 3 TB to the internet

Before:

  • NAT hours: 3 × $0.045 × 730 = $98.55
  • NAT processing: 20,480 GB × $0.045 = $921.60
  • Total NAT cost: about $1,020 per month

After fixes 1 and 2:

  • S3 moves to a gateway endpoint: $0
  • CloudWatch Logs moves to an interface endpoint: 2,048 GB × $0.01 + 3 AZs × $7.30 = $42.38
  • NAT keeps only internet traffic: 3,072 GB × $0.045 + $98.55 = $236.79
  • Total: about $279 per month, a 73% cut

Internet data transfer out (about $276 at $0.09 per GB) is the same in both cases; endpoints don't change egress pricing. Your traffic mix will differ, so run the flow log queries above to get your own split before estimating savings.

NAT gateway cost checklist (copy-paste)

  • [ ] Cost Explorer: NatGateway-Bytes and DataTransfer-Regional-Bytes baselined
  • [ ] Flow logs enabled on every NAT ENI; top 25 destinations identified
  • [ ] S3 gateway endpoint attached to every private route table
  • [ ] DynamoDB gateway endpoint attached (if used)
  • [ ] Interface endpoints for AWS services above ~210 GB per AZ per month
  • [ ] Each private subnet routes to a NAT in its own AZ (or regional NAT in automatic mode)
  • [ ] Kubernetes Services with heavy east-west traffic use trafficDistribution: PreferClose
  • [ ] IPv6 egress goes through an egress-only internet gateway
  • [ ] No unattached Elastic IPs
  • [ ] NAT gateways and endpoints tagged; monthly showback per team

FAQ

Why is my AWS NAT gateway bill so high?

Usually because AWS-bound traffic (S3, ECR image layers, CloudWatch Logs) goes through the NAT and pays $0.045 per GB in processing. Container platforms with frequent node scaling pull large images many times a day. Enable flow logs on the NAT ENI to confirm where the bytes go.

Does a NAT gateway charge for traffic to S3?

Yes, if there is no S3 gateway endpoint. The NAT processing fee applies to all traffic it handles, regardless of destination. An S3 gateway endpoint is free and removes that traffic from the NAT completely.

Is a regional NAT gateway cheaper than zonal NAT gateways?

Not on price. Regional mode bills $0.045 per hour for each AZ it runs in, the same as one zonal NAT per AZ, and the same per-GB fee. It saves operational work (no public subnet per AZ, no route table edits) and helps avoid cross-AZ routing once it has expanded into every AZ you use.

Should I replace NAT gateways with NAT instances?

For small or non-production environments, a NAT instance on a small Graviton instance (for example with the open-source fck-nat AMI) avoids the per-GB processing fee. You take on patching, scaling, and failover yourself. For production, fix the traffic first with endpoints; the remaining NAT bill is often small enough that the managed gateway is worth it.

VPC endpoint vs NAT gateway: which is cheaper for AWS service traffic?

A gateway endpoint (S3, DynamoDB) is always cheaper because it is free. An interface endpoint costs $0.01 per GB plus about $7.30 per AZ per month, against $0.045 per GB through a NAT. It pays for itself above roughly 210 GB per month per AZ for that service.

How much does cross-AZ data transfer cost on AWS?

Traffic between Availability Zones in the same Region is billed at $0.01 per GB on each side, so $0.02 per GB in total. It appears as DataTransfer-Regional-Bytes in Cost Explorer. Same-AZ NAT routing and zone-aware Kubernetes Services reduce it.

How much does a NAT gateway cost per month?

About $32.85 per month per zonal gateway in hourly charges at US East list price, before data. Add $0.045 for every GB processed. A three-AZ setup starts at about $98.55 per month before any traffic.

title: Fixed vs random effects in Python, and what a Hausman test result actually tells you
description:
Most panel data tutorials stop at "run the Hausman test, and if p < 0.05 use fixed effects." That rule is fine as a starting point, but it hides a few things that matter once you look at real output. So here is a small worked example you can run yourself, with the numbers I got.

The setup

I used the wage_panel dataset that ships with linearmodels: 545 individuals observed over 8 years, with log wages as the outcome. The regressors are experience squared, marital status and union membership.

bash
pip install linearmodels
python
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats
from linearmodels.panel import PanelOLS, RandomEffects
from linearmodels.datasets import wage_panel

df = wage_panel.load().set_index(["nr", "year"])
y = df["lwage"]
X = df[["expersq", "married", "union"]]

the RE model needs an intercept, the FE (within) model does not

X_re = X.copy()
X_re.insert(0, "const", 1.0)

fe = PanelOLS(y, X, entity_effects=True).fit()
re = RandomEffects(y, X_re).fit()
The two sets of estimates
variable fixed effects random effects
expersq 0.0037 0.0032
married 0.1073 0.1316
union 0.0828 0.1035

The random effects numbers for married and union are noticeably larger. That gap is what the Hausman test formalises. If the unobserved person-level effects (ability, motivation, whatever drives wages and also correlates with marrying or joining a union) are correlated with the regressors, the RE estimator picks that correlation up as if it were an effect of the regressor, and the coefficients drift upward.

Computing the Hausman statistic by hand

linearmodels doesn't ship a one-line Hausman test, but the statistic is short:

python
cols = fe.params.index
b = fe.params - re.params[cols]
V = fe.cov - re.cov.loc[cols, cols]

stat = float(b @ np.linalg.inv(V) @ b)
p = 1 - stats.chi2.cdf(stat, len(cols))
print(f"Hausman chi2 = {stat:.3f}, df = {len(cols)}, p = {p:.4f}")

Output on this data:

Hausman chi2 = 112.118, df = 3, p = 0.0000

A clear rejection. The RE assumption (effects uncorrelated with the regressors) doesn't hold here, so the fixed effects estimates are the ones to report.

Three things the textbook rule skips

A rejection is evidence against RE, not a proof that FE is right. FE only removes confounding that is constant over the sample window. Anything that changes over time and correlates with both wages and marriage is still in your error term.

You pay for FE with the time-invariant variables. The within estimator can't estimate the effect of anything that doesn't change for a person (education at entry, say, or a fixed demographic). I left those out above for exactly that reason. If they are the point of your study, FE alone won't answer your question, and a Mundlak or correlated random effects specification is worth a look.

The classic Hausman test assumes homoskedastic errors. With clustered standard errors, which is the usual choice in applied work, the difference of covariance matrices isn't the right object anymore. A regression-based version (the Mundlak approach: add the group means of each regressor to the RE model and test them jointly) works with robust errors.

If you'd rather not write code

For a quick check, or to hand something to a colleague who doesn't use Python, there is a panel data regression online tool that fits fixed and random effects models in the browser. Full disclosure: I'm connected to that site. For anything you plan to publish, I'd still keep the script above so the analysis is reproducible.

Curious whether people go Mundlak, or just default to FE and move on.RE model and test them jointly) works with robust errors.
