title: Test the AI Handoff After the Ticket Is Created
description:
Your assistant created the escalation ticket. The integration returned success.

Can the next person work the case?

For a fictional service assistant, that question needs its own test. Ticket creation proves that a record was created; it does not prove that the right context survived the transition.

This article proposes a test design with synthetic fixtures. It does not report an executed benchmark.

Define the handoff contract

Agree on what the receiving role needs to continue the task. A fixture might require the goal, established facts, attempted steps, completed actions and unresolved decision. Include the destination and owner where the application defines them.

Specify which information the recipient may receive. The contract should identify both required context and excluded content. A complete transcript is not automatically an acceptable result.

Keep expected facts independent of the generated summary. Otherwise the evaluation can simply repeat the same omission it is meant to detect.

Seed distinctions that matter

Create a synthetic case where the customer reports a symptom, the system confirms a narrower fact, and an explanation remains unverified. Give the fixture one completed action and a separate proposed action that still needs approval.

These distinctions let a reviewer detect whether the summary upgrades an assumption into a fact or describes a proposal as completed.

Use harmless, identifiable fixture values. Do not create real customer incidents or send real notifications merely to test the handoff path.

Exercise the full transition

Run the assistant to the point where escalation is expected. Inspect the persisted ticket and the actual views used by the receiving person, not just the assistant's last message.

If the workflow generates a notification separately, inspect that output too. A correct ticket can coexist with a misleading notification, especially when separate components summarise the same case.

Check that the case reaches the intended test destination. Keep any real external side effects isolated or within explicitly approved test accounts.

Score continuity separately from writing quality

Check Example mismatch
Goal preserved Summary mentions the topic but omits the requested outcome
Facts attributed correctly Customer suspicion becomes a confirmed system finding
Action state preserved Proposed step is described as already completed
Unresolved decision visible Approval requirement disappears
Recipient access respected Unrelated restricted detail appears in the summary
Next step identifiable Ticket exists without a usable destination or task

The expected result depends on the workflow. This table is a scoping aid, not a universal specification.

A concise summary can pass if it preserves the required context. A long summary can fail if it loses the one fact needed to avoid repeating an action. Avoid rewarding length as a substitute for completeness.

Check the customer's version of events

Compare the assistant's closing message with the persisted state. “Created a ticket” should not become “a colleague has reviewed your case.” Similarly, an unresolved action should not be presented as completed simply because escalation succeeded.

Where the product provides a reference or a next step, verify that it matches the stored case. If it promises a follow-up, test the supported route rather than treating the sentence as evidence that one exists.

Retain useful failure evidence

Record the fixture revision, expected fields, permitted recipient scope, persisted outputs and the specific missing or altered facts. Include the smallest safe evidence needed for another engineer to investigate.

Keep deterministic checks on required fields or action states separate from repeated evaluations of generated wording. For generative steps, state the relevant configuration and repetitions.

Report the conditions and limits of the test. A successful sample does not establish that every conversation will produce a complete handoff, and an escalation count alone says little about the quality of the work transferred.

Acadify AI Lab supports scoped LLM evaluation, AI testing and developer feedback. Acadify Solution supports custom software and AI applications.

Which omission would matter most in your handoff tests: the goal, completed actions, uncertainty or the next owner?

title: Doob-Based Generative Policy Optimization
description:
arXiv:2610.28990v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Diffusion and flow models provide expressive policy classes for robotic and sequential decision-making systems. However, their action likelihoods are generally intractable, limiting the direct use of widely adopted policy optimization methods such as PPO and GRPO. We propose Doob Policy Optimization (DoobPO), a framework that leverages Doob's $h$-transform for likelihood-free reinforcement learning fine-tuning of generative policies. DoobPO separates policy improvement from generative policy learning. It first learns a lightweight ratio model that represents the desired policy update, and then distills the resulting ratio-tilted target policy into the generative policy via conditional drift matching. This formulation applies uniformly to both diffusion and flow policies and supports a broad family of policy improvement rules, including PPO and GRPO. We prove that the practical conditional drift matching objective is gradient-equivalent to the ideal Doob drift matching objective. We further show that the induced diffusion process solves an endpoint-constrained stochastic optimal control problem. This establishes that it achieves the minimum-energy modification required to realize the desired policy tilt. Across MuJoCo continuous-control benchmarks, DoobPO achieves strong performance against competitive diffusion- and flow-policy baselines, showing a principled and practical route to RL fine-tuning for generative policies.

title: My login page shows the demo credentials — a starter kit has to be runnable in 60 seconds
description:
Every starter kit I've bought died in the same place: the login screen. Not because the auth was broken — because I couldn't find a single valid credential to try it with. Buried in the README, step 9, between the queue worker and the mail config. I gave up and closed the tab.

So when I built my own kit, I made one rule: the login page ships the demo credentials in the open.

Here's the relevant part of my Login.jsx:

{import.meta.env.VITE_DEMO_MODE === 'true' && (
  <p className="mt-3 rounded-lg bg-indigo-50 px-4 py-2 text-xs text-indigo-700">
    Interactive preview — sign in with the demo credentials below. Data is simulated.
  </p>
)}

{/* ... the form ... */}

<div className="mt-6 rounded-lg bg-slate-50 px-4 py-3 text-xs text-slate-600">
  <p className="font-semibold text-slate-700">Demo credentials</p>
  <p className="mt-1">
    Email: <span className="font-mono">admin@demo.io</span>
  </p>
  <p>
    Password: <span className="font-mono">password</span>
  </p>
</div>

Two pieces. The box under the form is always there: email admin@demo.io, password password. The banner above the form only renders when the build sets VITE_DEMO_MODE=true, because it makes a claim that's only true in the public preview — "data is simulated", since the demo build runs against an in-memory mock axios client instead of Laravel.

The credentials box isn't gated, because in a real local run those credentials are real. My DatabaseSeeder creates them with firstOrCreate, idempotent, so it works whether you seeded once or five times:

User::firstOrCreate(
    ['email' => 'admin@demo.io'],
    ['name' => 'Admin', 'password' => 'password', 'role' => 'admin']
);

Is printing credentials on a login page a security smell? In a production app, yes. In a starter kit, it's documentation that can't be skipped. Nobody reads README step 4; everybody stares at the login page. The credentials box is the fastest path from git clone to seeing the dashboard.

Two smaller details I kept: the submit button disables and switches to "Signing in…" while the request is in flight (no double submits), and a failed login renders a rose-coloured box above the form with the API's message — deliberately generic, never saying which half was wrong.

If you're building a kit: make the login page teach the login. The README is for the 10% who read it.

This login page is from my Laravel + React SaaS Starter Kit — the whole auth loop (Sanctum tokens, roles, seeded demo admin) ships in it: https://kamranofficial.gumroad.com/l/mhekoig

title: A 4-Stage Retrieval Architecture for Recruiting Candidate Search and Source Deduplication
description:
Recruiting search has a stricter failure mode than a normal semantic search box: two copies of a candidate record can look like two qualified people, while an access-control mistake can expose a profile to the wrong recruiter. Short answer: use a staged retrieval design with explicit collections, bounded queries, and traceable source context; perform source deduplication before ranking and retain the evidence that caused each match.

How should retrieval architecture handle recruiting candidate search and source deduplication?

Begin with a retrieval contract, not a vector database. For every candidate document, store a stable source identifier, tenant identifier, authorization attributes, ingestion timestamp, and a content fingerprint. The fingerprint catches byte-for-byte repeats; a second semantic check can group revised resumes without deleting their audit history. The query contract should return candidate IDs, source URLs or document IDs, scores, and the authorization context used to filter them.

That contract makes deduplication a policy decision. Keep one canonical record for display, but preserve every contributing source in an audit trail. If two agencies supplied the same resume, the recruiter should see a merged result with provenance, not an unexplained winner. Exact-once is the mindset here: an ingestion retry must not create a second candidate or silently replace an older source.

Infrai can fit at this boundary because its vector operations and other backend capabilities share one REST contract and one credential surface. The benefit is fewer integration seams while the retrieval contract remains yours to define.

Bound the work at each stage. Set a deadline for parsing, embedding, and retrieval; cap the number of candidates passed to a reranker; and return a partial, clearly marked result when a slow enrichment source misses its deadline. A 429 response should trigger exponential backoff that honors Retry-After, while a write retry needs a client idempotency key. These limits protect the user flow and make operational behavior reviewable.

The four stages and their evidence

Stage one normalizes source records into a canonical candidate schema. Stage two performs deterministic deduplication on the source fingerprint and tenant scope. Stage three runs bounded semantic retrieval over only the authorized collection. Stage four reranks and assembles citations, retaining the source URL or document identifier beside each claim shown to a recruiter.

The order matters. If semantic retrieval runs across duplicate agency feeds first, the top-k budget is consumed by copies and recall for distinct candidates falls. If authorization is applied after retrieval, an inaccessible profile can influence ranking even when it is removed from the final response. I once saw a test fixture return three copies of one resume because its source IDs were used as candidate IDs; the fix was a namespace-qualified canonical ID plus a uniqueness check before upsert. We then replayed the same feed twice, changed one phone number, and checked that the canonical candidate stayed stable while both source records remained reviewable. That test also forced us to record which tenant filter ran before the vector query, because a correct merge in the wrong tenant is still a security incident. Small detail, large consequence.

No magic threshold.

Which retrieval surface fits candidate search integration constraints?

Elasticsearch is a strong choice when your team already operates inverted indexes, analyzers, and detailed filter DSLs. OpenSearch offers a similar operational model and is attractive in AWS-centered estates. Pinecone reduces the amount of vector infrastructure you own, while a specialist recruiting search service may provide resume parsing and domain ranking out of the box. Those benefits come with different SDKs, credentials, observability conventions, and migration costs.

Option Where it fits Integration trade-off
Elasticsearch Mixed lexical, vector, and complex authorization filters Broad control, but cluster operations and query DSL become part of the application contract
OpenSearch Teams standardized on AWS-compatible operations Familiar deployment path, with another service surface to secure and monitor
Pinecone Managed vector retrieval with a small platform team Fast start for vectors, but metadata and surrounding pipeline services remain your responsibility
Infrai vector surface A backend that wants several capabilities behind one consistent HTTP contract One key and one REST API reduce credential and SDK sprawl; you still own schema, tenant policy, and audit decisions

Infrai is a reasonable fit when the friction is integration breadth rather than a missing ranking algorithm: its discovery surface describes capabilities, and its vector collection, upsert, and query operations sit behind the same REST base URL as other backend modules. That means adding a neighboring capability does not require another SDK installation or another credential lifecycle. For this workflow, I would try it for the bounded retrieval stage when a team values a uniform HTTP client and traceable request metadata, then keep the canonical deduplication ledger in its own datastore.

The catch is specialization. A team that needs Elasticsearch analyzers, OpenSearch-native governance, Pinecone-specific vector tuning, or a recruiting vendor's parsing and ranking models should stick with that specialist. Infrai does not replace those domain policies; its advantage is a simpler integration surface, not automatic correctness.

A small, inspectable rollout

Start with one tenant and a replayable corpus. Log the canonical ID, fingerprint, collection, query limit, authorization decision, and returned source identifiers for every search. Compare duplicate rate, distinct-candidate recall, and citation completeness against the current system before expanding traffic. Keep deletion and retention actions auditable; compliance reviewers should be able to reconstruct why a result appeared without reading application logs from five unrelated services.

Start narrow.

The implementation can remain ordinary HTTP. Use the public discovery document to obtain the current request schema, then generate a typed client for the three vector operations rather than guessing field names. A minimal Go client should read INFRAI_API_KEY, send Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY, set explicit methods, enforce a context deadline, surface non-2xx bodies, and make upserts idempotent with a stable key. That discipline is more valuable than a clever retrieval trick.

Here is the shape of a bounded query client; the collection and query fields come from the discovered schema for your account, so the example keeps the transport concerns visible and the payload easy to replace.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    body := []byte(`{"collection":"candidate-records","query":"senior payments engineer","limit":10}`)
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 5*time.Second)
    defer cancel()

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/vector/query", bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil { panic(err) }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil { panic(err) }
        data, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil { panic(readErr) }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            wait := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * 200 * time.Millisecond
            if retryAfter := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"); retryAfter != "" {
                if parsed, parseErr := time.ParseDuration(retryAfter + "s"); parseErr == nil { wait = parsed }
            }
            time.Sleep(wait)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            panic(fmt.Sprintf("vector query failed (%d): %s", resp.StatusCode, data))
        }
        fmt.Println(string(data))
        return
    }
    panic("vector query rate-limited after retries")
}

Your mileage may vary: duplicate definitions differ between agencies, regions, and retention rules, so validate the contract with legal and recruiting stakeholders before choosing a threshold. I am not sure a single semantic threshold can remain stable across every resume language and format; a labeled evaluation set is the honest way to resolve that uncertainty.

For the vector request schema and runnable examples, start with the Infrai vector guide and keep the authorization and provenance checks described here in your application layer.

References

  • Infrai vector guide: https://docs.infrai.cc/en/guides/vector/answers/my-rag-chatbot-s-vector-search-keeps-letting-irrelevant/
  • Lewis et al., “Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks”: https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
  • Elasticsearch documentation: https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/index.html
  • OpenSearch documentation: https://opensearch.org/docs/latest/
  • Pinecone documentation: https://docs.pinecone.io/

title: Bill & Document Sloth: A Local-First AI Paperwork Manager with Gemma & TabPFN
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady

What I Built

Bill & Document Sloth is a 100% local-first, privacy-conscious AI document assistant, tabular forecaster, and deadline tracker designed around one core promise: "Stop sorting paperwork. Start living."

Every adult and student dreads the paperwork shuffle: opening randomly named files like IMG_20261021_124532.pdf, hunting through fine print for payment due dates, losing track of appliance warranty periods, and maintaining brittle manual spreadsheets.

Bill & Document Sloth does the heavy lifting so you can be as lazy as a sloth:

  • Drop Paperwork Once: Drag and drop PDFs, receipts, or phone bills.
  • Intelligent Local Extraction: Local open-source AI extracts the issuer, category, total amount, due date, document date, and invoice number.
  • Smart Standardized Filenames: Automatically generates clean filenames (e.g., 2026-10_Electricity_Bill_BESCOM.pdf).
  • Human-in-the-Loop Review: Split-screen side-by-side verification with confidence scores before any file is moved.
  • Safe Organization & Undo: Files are organized into structured directories (documents/organized/{Category}/{Year}/) with 1-click reversible undo.
  • Proactive Deadlines: Monitors overdue bills, payments due in 3 days, and expiring warranties before penalties strike.

Demo

  • Direct YouTube Link: Watch Video Demo on YouTube
  • GitHub Repository: https://github.com/Ayushgupta1715/bill-and-document-sloth
  • Local Interactive Dashboard: Runs locally on http://127.0.0.1:8000 with Swagger API docs at http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs.
  • 1-Click Built-in Demo Pack: Synthesizes realistic BESCOM Electricity Bills, Airtel Fiber Invoices, AppleCare Warranty Certificates, Star Health Insurance Policies, and Coffee Receipts on the fly so evaluators can test immediately with one click!

Code

Ayushgupta1715 / bill-and-document-sloth

🦥 Bill & Document Sloth

“Stop sorting paperwork. Start living.”
A 100% Local-First AI Document Assistant & Deadline Tracker for Hacktoberfest 2026 Week 3: Slow and Steady (#hf26challenge).

🎥 Watch 1-Minute Demo Video on YouTube | Download Local MP4

🌟 The "Slow and Steady" Philosophy

In celebration of International Sloth Day and Hacktoberfest Week 3, Bill & Document Sloth is built around a simple truth: AI should do the tedious, repetitive paperwork so you don't have to.

Instead of spending precious hours deciphering confusing PDF bills, calculating payment deadlines, renaming cryptic camera scans, and maintaining brittle spreadsheets:

  1. Drop your documents once.
  2. Local AI extracts the essentials (Issuer, Category, Due Date, Total Amount, Invoice Number).
  3. Approve with 1 click.
  4. Relax. Your files are organized into structured directories and payment deadlines are tracked automatically.

🏆 Hacktoberfest 2026 Sponsor Track Integrations

To maximize utility and showcase open innovation, Bill & Document…

View on GitHub
  • Repository: https://github.com/Ayushgupta1715/bill-and-document-sloth
  • License: MIT License (Open-Source)

How I Built It

The application combines local-first inference, open-weight reasoning models, and tabular foundation models:

  1. Local-First Processing Engine:
    • Backend: FastAPI, Python 3.14, SQLite3, PyPDF for embedded text extraction, and ReportLab for synthetic sample generation.
    • Frontend: Clean, responsive single-page application built with Tailwind CSS, Lucide icons, and Canvas Confetti.
  2. Google Gemma Open-Weight Model (gemma-2-2b-it):
    • Integrated in app/gemma_service.py to provide deep structured JSON parsing and field reasoning traces for complex or ambiguous bills.
  3. Prior Labs TabPFN-3.5 Foundation Model:
    • Integrated in app/tabpfn_analyzer.py to perform in-context tabular regression and outlier detection over historical billing cycles (forecasting next month's utility spend and alerting on anomalous spikes).
  4. ElevenLabs Voice Integration:
    • Integrated in app/voice_service.py to give the sloth agent a calm, spoken audio briefing of pending bills and deadlines.
  5. Safe File Operations:
    • Keeps original uploads pristine in documents/uploads/ while organizing approved files in documents/organized/{Category}/{Year}/. Full audit trail in actions_history table for 1-click safe undo.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

When building an assistant for bills, leases, and receipts, sending files to closed cloud LLM APIs poses major privacy and cost concerns:

  1. Absolute Data Privacy: Utility bills and tax invoices contain home addresses, bank details, and personal identifiers. With open-source local inference and SQLite, zero bytes of private data leave the device.
  2. Zero Recurring Cloud Token Costs: Users shouldn't pay monthly API subscriptions or per-token charges just to organize their receipts. Open-weight models like Gemma and tabular foundation models like TabPFN run locally on consumer hardware for free.
  3. Total Offline Resilience: Works on a train, in airplane mode, or during internet blackouts.
  4. User Sovereignty & Control: Unlike opaque cloud systems that silently alter data, our pipeline enforces human verification and reversible undo actions.

The Lazy Payoff

  • Time Saved: Manually opening, reading, renaming, and filing 10 bills takes roughly 20–25 minutes. With Bill & Document Sloth, dropping them into the app and clicking "Approve" takes under 45 seconds — a 95% reduction in manual effort.
  • Zero Spreadsheet Maintenance: Upcoming deadlines (due in 3 days, due today, overdue) are monitored automatically, preventing costly late-payment surcharges.
  • Peace of Mind: You can be as lazy as a sloth, knowing every warranty, receipt, and utility bill is categorized and safely filed on your machine.

Prize Categories

Featured Categories:

  • Best Use of Gemma ($200): Integrated Google's Gemma-2 open-weight model (gemma-2-2b-it) for deep structured bill parsing, confidence verification, and reasoning traces (app/gemma_service.py).
  • Best Use of TabPFN ($200): Integrated Prior Labs' TabPFN-3.5 tabular foundation model (app/tabpfn_analyzer.py) to forecast next month's utility spending and detect billing cost anomalies (+40% outliers).
  • Best Use of Render ($200): Included production render.yaml (Render Blueprint) and multi-stage Dockerfile for 1-click cloud deployment.

Partner Categories:

  • Best Use of ElevenLabs ($100): Sloth Voice Briefings (app/voice_service.py) delivering spoken audio briefings of upcoming bills and paperwork deadlines.
  • Best Use of Sentry Agent Tracing ($100): Instrumented with sentry-sdk in app/main.py for tracking document ingestion latency, OCR performance, and extraction errors.
  • Best Use of a .tech Domain ($100): Production DNS and routing ready for slothdocs.tech.
  • Best Use of GitHub Copilot & Actions ($100): Comprehensive automated CI pipeline (.github/workflows/ci.yml) validating 20 unit and integration tests on every push.

title: Beyond Experience: Knowledge-Guided Evolution for NPU Kernel Generation
description:
arXiv:2610.27588v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM agents have become capable kernel engineers on mainstream GPU stacks, but they struggle on emerging accelerators such as Ascend NPUs, whose programming model is barely represented in pretraining data. Recent NPU agents address this gap largely through experience: they accumulate memory from their own generation and optimization trials and reuse it on later tasks. We argue that experience alone is not enough for kernel generation. An agent can only remember what it has tried, and it rarely tries a mechanism it does not know. As a result, such memory offers little help when a new operator calls for a different mechanism, and even familiar operators raise unseen situations as optimization proceeds. We present ASCENDEVOLVE, which grounds every step of an evolutionary kernel search in a large external knowledge base built from platform documentation, toolkit headers, and operator repositories. Because this corpus far exceeds any context window, ASCENDEVOLVE indexes it and routes each agent to a small, task-specific slice of evidence instead of the corpus itself. The retrieved knowledge seeds diverse implementation strategies, guides repair when a candidate fails, and constrains how strong candidates are recombined. On 53 Ascend C operators from CANN-Bench spanning four difficulty levels, ASCENDEVOLVE achieves an overall score of 71.39, improving over Reflexion and OpenEvolve by 11.6% and 17.2%.

title: MMEnterprise-Bench: Evaluating Enterprise Agents over Evolving Multimodal Records
description:
arXiv:2610.27911v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Enterprise agents answer questions over workplace records that evolve through team collaboration. As information is shared, corrected, and revised across documents, chats, and figures, multiple versions of the same information accumulate in the workspace. Reliable question answering therefore requires agents to reason over sufficient evidence, resolve cross-source and temporal conflicts, and recognize when the available evidence is insufficient to establish an answer. To systematically evaluate these capabilities, we introduce MMEnterprise-Bench, a benchmark comprising 1,613 questions grounded in evolving multimodal records from simulated collaboration projects, covering three categories: Evidence Reasoning, Conflict Resolution, and Unanswerability. We evaluate 10 proprietary and open-source multimodal LLMs and find that even the strongest models struggle when evidence contains cross-source or temporal conflicts or spans multiple images. Moreover, increasing the retrieval budget or employing a larger retriever improves evidence recall but does not consistently translate into higher answer accuracy. These findings highlight the persistent challenges of reasoning over evolving workplace records and establish MMEnterprise-Bench as a testbed for developing more reliable enterprise agents. Code and data are available at https://mlvlab.github.io/MMEnterprise-Bench/.

title: Building Telecom Language Models with RSOD: Domain Data, Specialist Post-Training, Memory-Conscious Distillation, and Networking Evaluation
description:
arXiv:2610.27993v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Telecom language models must combine broad networking knowledge with specialist behavior across routing, broadband services, access technologies, and operational diagnostics while remaining practical to deploy as a single model. We present an end-to-end framework that builds source-grounded synthetic training data from structured networking taxonomies and expert graphs, materializes 212,559 routed training records across fourteen networking routes, trains six frozen specialist LoRA teachers over one shared continued-pretrained backbone, and consolidates their behavior into one deployable student adapter using Routed Specialist On-Policy Distillation (RSOD). In RSOD, the committed student generates each trajectory, the route-assigned specialist teacher-forces the exact native token sequence, compact teacher hidden states are reconstructed through the shared frozen output head, and only the student LoRA is updated. A controlled reconstruction validation shows mean absolute logit error of 7.26 x 10^-6 with 100% top-1 agreement between native and reconstructed teacher logits. On four RTX 6000 Ada GPUs, the completed 2,000-step run produced 16,000 trajectories with zero observed student-version or token- ID mismatches. Under the primary route-conditioned evaluation over 2,850 held-out questions, the raw Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct model scores 12.8661/25 micro (13.0172/25 macro), the combined routed six-teacher system scores 21.7641/25 micro, and the consolidated RSOD student, released as Llama-CalixCLM v1, reaches 21.7112/25 micro (21.8006/25 macro) on the same five dimension LLM-judge rubric. Under a separate neutral deployment-like prompt, the same student reaches 20.0028/25 micro (20.0778/25 macro). The consolidated student remains within 0.0529 micro-score points of the combined routed-teacher system while retaining a numerically validated and auditable train-serve execution path.

title: Java Programming - Introduction
description:
Introduction

Java is one of the most popular programming languages in the world. It is a high-level, object-oriented programming language used to develop different types of applications.

Java was developed by James Gosling and his team at Sun Microsystems. It was officially released in 1995. Today, Java is maintained by Oracle.

Java is widely used in web development, enterprise applications, backend development, and many other areas of software development.

If you are a beginner who wants to learn programming, Java is a good language to start with.

What Is Java?

Java is a general-purpose programming language designed to help developers build reliable, secure, and portable applications.

One of Java's most important features is:

"Write Once, Run Anywhere."

This means that Java programs can run on different operating systems, such as Windows, Linux, and macOS, provided a compatible Java Virtual Machine (JVM) is available.

Why Should We Learn Java?

There are several reasons to learn Java:

Easy to Learn

Java has a structured syntax that helps beginners understand programming concepts step by step.

Platform Independent

Java code is compiled into bytecode, which can run on any compatible JVM.

Object-Oriented Programming

Java supports object-oriented programming concepts such as classes, objects, inheritance, polymorphism, and encapsulation.

Secure

Java provides language and platform features that help developers build secure applications.

Multithreading

Java supports multithreading, allowing applications to perform multiple tasks concurrently.

Large Community

Java has a large developer community, so beginners can find tutorials, documentation, and solutions to common problems.

Features of Java

  • Some important features of Java include:
  • Simple and readable syntax
  • Object-oriented programming
  • Platform independence
  • Portability
  • Security features
  • Multithreading support
  • Automatic memory management
  • Robust exception handling

These features make Java useful for developing applications of different sizes.

Where Is Java Used?

Java is used in many areas of software development.

Web Development: Building server-side applications.

Enterprise Applications: Developing large business systems.

Android Development: Java is used in Android applications, alongside other supported languages.

Banking Systems: Developing financial and transaction-processing applications.

Desktop Applications: Creating applications with graphical user interfaces.

Cloud Applications: Building backend services and distributed systems.

First Java Program

Let's write our first Java program.

public class HelloWorld {
public static void main(String[] args) {
System.out.println("Hello, World!");
}
}

Output

Hello, World!

Explanation

public class HelloWorld: Declares a class named HelloWorld.

public static void main(String[] args): Defines the main method, which is the entry point when the program is launched using the standard Java launcher.

System.out.println(): Prints text to the console.

"Hello, World!": The message displayed on the screen.

This simple program is the first step toward understanding Java programming.

What Is JVM, JRE, and JDK?

  • JVM (Java Virtual Machine)
  • The JVM executes Java bytecode.
  • JRE (Java Runtime Environment)
  • The JRE traditionally refers to the components needed to run Java applications, including the JVM and supporting libraries.
  • JDK (Java Development Kit)
  • The JDK provides the tools needed to develop Java applications, including the Java compiler and runtime components.

In modern Java development, installing a JDK is the standard way to get started.

title: How Fine-Tuning Objectives Shape Layer-Wise Information in LLM Hallucination Detection
description:
arXiv:2610.27711v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Under matched conditions, classifier-head fine-tuning (\textsc{cls}) paradigm consistently outperforms the LLM-as-Judge sequence-to-sequence (\textsc{s2s}) on binary hallucination detection. We trace this gap to the representations induced by the two objectives. Static analysis shows that \textsc{cls} learns a task-specific discriminative direction, pushing hidden states into a clear two-cluster geometry with stronger class separation and linearly decodable label information. By contrast, \textsc{s2s} relies on the pretrained language-modeling head to make decisions. This minimizes the pressure to reorganize representations, leaving the hidden states much closer to the pretrained backbone. Our analysis also reveals that the \textsc{cls} signal saturates before the final layer, after which upper layers form a plateau of statistically interchangeable and largely redundant representations. However, endpoint redundancy alone does not show whether these layers are dispensable during training. Further training-dynamics analysis reveals 1) a lower pretrained substrate, 2) a narrow upper-middle \textbf{InfoWindow} where task information emerges, and 3) a later-synchronizing upper plateau that mirrors this signal. This mechanism motivates us to remove layers above the InfoWindow. Truncating 31\% of the network leaves accuracy unchanged within seed noise on Qwen3-4B and 8B and cuts latency by $1.4\times$. The same depth fraction, fixed before any analysis of the target models, transfers to Llama-3.2-3B and Mistral-7B-v0.3, and the layer structure behind it reappears there and on QNLI and SST-2. We hope this helps guide efficient task-specific LLM design.

title: Python on Vercel is now generally available
description:
Python on Vercel is now generally available. Build and run Python applications with the frameworks, libraries, and tools you already use.

Vercel automatically detects supported frameworks and configures the build and deployment. Your applications run on Fluid compute, which manages concurrent requests and scales with traffic. Idiomatic Python SDKs let you work with storage, queues, durable workflows, and AI models directly from Python. For full-stack projects, the Python backend and frontend share a workflow for local development, preview deployments, and production releases.

Our goals for Python on Vercel

Ten months ago, we set out to make Vercel the best place to build and run Python applications. We wanted the experience to fit how Python developers already work, with three goals guiding our decisions:

  • Idiomatic Python SDKs. Working with Vercel infrastructure should feel familiar to Python developers, with APIs that use type annotations, async/await, and context managers.

  • A shared workflow for both the frontend and backend. Python applications often include a JavaScript frontend, so developers should be able to run both locally, review them in the same preview deployment, and release or roll them back together.

  • Compatibility with the Python ecosystem. The runtime should use CPython, the standard Python interpreter, on Linux to preserve compatibility with the packages and tools Python developers already rely on.

The first test of those goals is what happens when you deploy a Python application on Vercel: its framework, dependencies, and project structure should guide how it’s built and run.

Deploying Python applications on Vercel

We’ve worked to make Python feel native on Vercel. Vercel reads your project’s dependency files, including those managed by uv, and automatically detects frameworks such as FastAPI, Flask, Django, and FastHTML. Framework defined infrastructure configures builds and request routing, with framework-specific support for serving static assets through the CDN.

For applications with a frontend, Vercel Services brings both parts into one project. Running vercel dev starts them together, and shared previews let you test backend changes with the frontend that uses them.

For long-running workers that pull jobs from queues or databases, Vercel Daemons keeps your containers running with your Python code along with any of its packages, and system dependencies.

Python SDKs for Vercel infrastructure

A Python backend might need to store files, send messages, run durable workflows, or call AI models. We’ve built Python SDKs for these tasks, with APIs that follow the conventions of the language:

These SDKs work alongside your framework and libraries, and the example below shows how they connect within a full-stack application.

Start building with Python on Vercel

Whether you’re starting a new project or deploying existing code, the framework guides cover setup and deployment on Vercel. For a guided full-stack project, the Python on Vercel course walks through building a FastAPI backend and Next.js frontend, then deploying them together with Services.

To show how these pieces work together, I built a collaborative web application to create and browse Python notebooks. It lets people create their own notebooks, publish them for others to browse or fork, and work with an AI assistant to write and run Python code.

The application pairs a Vite frontend with a FastAPI backend and uses PostgreSQL for notebook source and chat history. Services keeps the frontend and backend in one deployment, with the frontend served through the CDN.

Here’s how the main parts connect:

  • Editing and running code: When a signed-in user opens their notebook in the editor, FastAPI creates or reuses a Vercel Sandbox running Jupyter, keeping user code isolated from the application backend. The browser connects directly to Jupyter, while mounted Drives provide the Python dependencies and workspace files.

  • Saving and publishing: The browser periodically sends the current notebook to FastAPI. FastAPI saves the source in PostgreSQL, renders changes as HTML, and uploads the result to Blob, so people can read published notebooks through the CDN without starting a Python kernel.

  • Sharing updates: After publishing a change, FastAPI sends a message through Vercel Queues. Each backend instance with connected browsers receives the notification and sends updated notebook listings over WebSockets, so people see changes without reloading.

  • Assisting with code: The agent uses AI SDK for Python and runs inside Vercel Workflows, which saves execution state and retries failed steps. Chat history stays in PostgreSQL, while notebook editing and execution tools work through the connected browser, which sends results back through FastAPI to resume the workflow.

The source code on GitHub includes the complete application and its deployment configuration. You can use it to explore these integrations or as a starting point for your own Python application.

Investing in the Python community

Last December, the Gel Data team, led by me and Elvis Pranskevichus, joined Vercel to build Python support and continue our open-source work.

At the same time, we announced our sponsorship of the Python Software Foundation and committed to funding one year of Serhiy Storchaka’s CPython maintenance through the foundation. Serhiy has authored over 600 commits to CPython’s main branch so far in 2026.

We also sponsored PyCon US and EuroPython this year, where the team and I met Python developers and heard where they were getting stuck. Those conversations help us figure out what to fix next.

We also published PEP 827, which, if accepted, would add type manipulation features that could help frameworks such as FastAPI offer simpler APIs with less boilerplate and more precise type checking.

What’s next for Python on Vercel

We’re continuing to improve Python SDKs, runtime performance, and development workflows for both people and coding agents. If you run into a deployment issue or find something missing in the Python SDKs, share your feedback in Vercel Community so the team can use it to guide that work.

Resources

  • Point your agent at our Python guides in the Knowledge Base

  • Deploy an eve agent in Python in one click

Read more

title: Building an AI Chat Assistant with Agentic LLMs and Multi-Tool Integration
description:
Building an AI Chat Assistant with Agentic LLMs and Multi-Tool Integration

Introduction

In this rapidly evolving era of Artificial Intelligence, I wanted to go beyond simply learning about AI and start understanding how it works in real-world applications. My goal is to dive deeper into the world of AI, explore its workflows, understand how Large Language Models (LLMs) operate, and learn how AI agents can reason, use tools, and solve practical problems.

As technology continues to advance, I believe the best way to grow as a developer is to challenge myself by building real-world applications, experimenting with new technologies, and learning from the problems I encounter along the way. I wanted to push my boundaries, strengthen my AI engineering skills, and contribute to the growing AI ecosystem through practical implementation.

That motivation led me to build AI Chat Assistant with Agentic LLMs and Multi-Tool Integration.

The idea was to create more than a traditional chatbot. I wanted to explore how an AI assistant could interact with external tools, retrieve relevant information, and respond to different user requests through a single conversational interface.

In this article, I'll share my journey of building this project, the technologies I explored, how tool integration works, the challenges involved, and the lessons I learned while developing my practical AI skills.

Project Links

Explore the project and its source code:

  • Live Demo: AI Chat Assistant
  • Frontend Repository: AI Chat Assistant Frontend
  • Backend Repository: AI Chat Assistant Backend

Feel free to explore the code, try the live application, and share your feedback. I'd love to hear your thoughts and suggestions!

1. The Problem: An AI Model Alone Is Not Enough

LLMs are powerful at understanding natural language, generating responses, summarizing content, and explaining technical concepts. However, a standalone model has limitations.

For example:

  • It may not know the latest news or current weather conditions.
  • Its training data may not include recent technical information.
  • It cannot automatically access external services without an integration.
  • It needs additional application logic to interact with APIs and handle errors.

I wanted to solve these limitations by building an assistant that could select the appropriate tools when answering different types of questions.

For example, when a user asks, "What is the weather in Chennai?", the assistant should use a weather service rather than simply generate an answer from its language model.

Similarly, when a user asks a programming question, it can use a relevant technical information source when appropriate.

This led me to explore agentic AI and tool calling.

2. What Is Agentic AI?

Agentic AI refers to AI systems that can work toward a goal by choosing actions, using tools, and incorporating the results into their responses.

A traditional chatbot typically follows a straightforward pattern:

User input → LLM → Response

An agentic assistant can follow a more flexible workflow:

User input → Understand the request → Select a tool → Execute the tool → Process the result → Generate a response

For example, consider this request:

"Find recent technology news and summarize the important points."

The assistant can identify that the user needs current information, invoke a news or search tool, process the returned results, and generate a concise summary.

The LLM handles language understanding and decision-making, while external tools provide capabilities that the model does not have on its own.

An important distinction is that the LLM does not magically gain access to external services. The application must explicitly provide the tools, their descriptions, and the code needed to execute them.

3. Project Architecture

I designed the application around a frontend, a backend API, an LLM integration, and a collection of specialized tools.

The main components are:

Frontend

The frontend provides the conversational interface where users submit questions and view assistant responses.

Backend API

The backend receives requests, manages the conversation flow, coordinates model interactions, executes tool calls, and returns the final response.

LLM integration

The language model interprets user requests, determines when a tool may be useful, and generates natural-language responses from the available context.

Tool integrations

Individual tools connect the assistant to external information sources and services, such as weather, news, web search, Wikipedia, movie information, Stack Overflow, and Notion.

Supporting services

The application also uses supporting infrastructure such as a database and Redis, depending on the feature and workflow, for data persistence and caching.

The overall flow looks like this:

              User
               |
               v
        Frontend Chat UI
               |
               v
          Backend API
               |
               v
          LLM / Agent
               |
        Selects a tool
               |
               v
       Tool Execution Layer
               |
       +-------+--------+
       |       |        |
     Weather  Search   News
       |       |        |
       +-------+--------+
               |
               v
        Tool Result
               |
               v
        LLM Generates
        Final Response
               |
               v
          Frontend UI

This architecture separates the user interface, orchestration logic, and external integrations, making the application easier to extend and maintain.

4. Integrating Multiple Tools

One of the most interesting parts of the project was connecting different capabilities through a single assistant.

Each tool has a specific responsibility.

Weather

The weather tool retrieves weather information for a requested location. This allows the assistant to answer questions that require current or forecast data.

Web Search

The web search tool helps retrieve information from online sources when a question requires information beyond the model's built-in knowledge.

News

The news integration provides access to recent news information, helping the assistant respond to requests about current events.

Wikipedia

Wikipedia provides reference information about people, places, organizations, and general topics.

Movie Information

The movie tool supports queries about films and related information, demonstrating how a specialized API can extend an assistant's capabilities.

Stack Overflow

This integration helps retrieve programming-related discussions and technical information that may be relevant to developer questions.

Notion

The Notion integration connects the assistant to a productivity and knowledge-management platform, where supported operations can help users work with information in their workspace.

The key idea is that these tools are not interchangeable. Each one has its own inputs, outputs, API requirements, and possible failure conditions.

The assistant needs enough information about each tool to select it appropriately.

5. How Tool Calling Works

A tool-enabled LLM workflow generally consists of several steps.

Step 1: Receive the request

The backend receives the user's message and prepares the relevant conversation context.

Step 2: Ask the model to determine the next action

The model evaluates the request and can return either a normal response or a structured tool call, depending on the framework and tool definitions.

Step 3: Execute the selected tool

The backend validates the requested arguments and calls the corresponding function or external API.

Step 4: Return the result to the model

The tool output is passed back into the conversation so the model can interpret it.

Step 5: Generate the final answer

The model converts the available information into a response that is understandable to the user.

Conceptually, a tool definition might look like this:

def get_weather(city: str) -> dict:
    """
    Retrieve weather information for a city.
    """
    # Call the configured weather API here.
    # Validate the response and handle API errors.
    return {
        "city": city,
        "temperature": 28,
        "condition": "Partly cloudy"
    }

This is a simplified example showing the shape of a tool function, not the complete implementation of a production weather integration.

In a real application, the function would retrieve actual weather data, validate the location, handle timeouts, and report errors appropriately.

The LLM should not invent tool results. It should base its answer on the returned information and communicate when reliable data is unavailable.

6. Technology Stack

The project combines frontend development, backend engineering, AI integration, and external services.

The main technologies include:

  • Next.js and React: Building the frontend experience.
  • FastAPI: Exposing backend endpoints and coordinating application logic.
  • Python: Implementing backend functionality and tool integrations.
  • LLM providers: Powering natural-language understanding, reasoning, and response generation.
  • LangChain and related agent tooling: Supporting model and tool integration where configured.
  • PostgreSQL: Providing relational data persistence.
  • Redis: Supporting caching and other appropriate fast-access operations.
  • External APIs: Providing specialized information and capabilities.

Each technology addresses a different part of the system. The frontend handles interaction, the backend coordinates execution, the model processes language, and external APIs provide information or actions.

The exact model, API provider, and available operations depend on the configured integrations.

7. Challenges I Had to Consider

Building an AI assistant involves more than connecting a model to an API. Several engineering concerns become important as the number of tools increases.

Choosing the right tool

Similar user requests can require different tools, and vague questions can be difficult to interpret.

Clear tool descriptions, well-defined parameters, and appropriate model instructions help improve tool selection.

Handling API failures

External services can return errors, enforce rate limits, or respond slowly.

The backend should handle timeouts, validate responses, and return useful error messages rather than allowing one failed integration to break the entire conversation.

Managing API keys

Third-party API credentials should remain on the server and be loaded through environment variables or a suitable secrets-management system.

They should never be exposed in frontend code or committed to a public repository.

Keeping responses grounded

When a question requires current information, the assistant should use the relevant external source instead of presenting unsupported information as fact.

It is also important to distinguish retrieved information from the model's own explanation.

Maintaining a modular architecture

Adding more tools can make backend logic difficult to maintain if every integration is implemented inside a single large function.

Separating tool implementations from orchestration makes it easier to add capabilities, test individual integrations, and handle failures independently.

These considerations helped me understand why reliable AI applications need thoughtful backend engineering in addition to a capable language model.

8. Security and Reliability Considerations

An AI assistant that can access external services needs appropriate safeguards.

Some important practices include:

  • Validate tool arguments before executing them.
  • Apply authentication and authorization to protected endpoints.
  • Use request timeouts and controlled retry policies.
  • Limit tool permissions to the operations the application actually needs.
  • Avoid passing secrets or unnecessary sensitive data into model prompts.
  • Sanitize external content and treat retrieved text as untrusted input.
  • Apply rate limits and usage controls where appropriate.
  • Log useful operational information without exposing credentials or private conversation content.

For integrations that can modify external data, such as creating or updating records, additional permission checks and confirmation steps may be necessary.

These controls help make tool-enabled AI systems safer and more predictable.

9. What I Learned

This project helped me understand how LLMs can become part of a complete software system rather than functioning as isolated text-generation components.

Some of my main takeaways were:

LLMs need reliable tools. A language model becomes more useful for current or specialized questions when it can access appropriate external information.

Backend design matters. Tool orchestration, validation, error handling, authentication, and API integration are essential parts of an AI application.

Modularity improves extensibility. Keeping integrations separate makes it easier to introduce new capabilities without rewriting the entire application.

AI responses need grounding. A polished response is not necessarily a correct one. Reliable results depend on tool quality, context, validation, and clear handling of uncertainty.

Full-stack development and AI engineering complement each other. Building a useful assistant requires frontend interaction, backend APIs, model integration, and operational reliability to work together.

10. What's Next?

There are several ways to improve a multi-tool assistant as it evolves:

  • Add streaming responses for a more interactive experience.
  • Improve conversation memory and context management.
  • Introduce retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for private or domain-specific knowledge.
  • Add structured evaluation to measure tool-selection accuracy.
  • Improve observability with tracing, latency metrics, and error monitoring.
  • Introduce more granular permissions for tools that can modify external data.
  • Explore standardized tool interfaces such as the Model Context Protocol (MCP), where appropriate.

These improvements can help move an experimental AI assistant toward a more reliable and maintainable application.

Conclusion

Building an AI Chat Assistant with Agentic LLMs and Multi-Tool Integration was an opportunity to explore the intersection of full-stack development and modern AI engineering.

The project demonstrates how a conversational interface, an LLM, a backend orchestration layer, and external tools can work together to answer different types of questions.

More importantly, it reinforced an important lesson: building a useful AI application is not just about choosing a powerful model. It is about designing the systems around that model so it can access reliable information, use tools appropriately, and communicate results clearly.

I'm continuing to explore LLM engineering, agentic workflows, and practical AI integrations, and I'm looking forward to applying these lessons to more complex projects.

If you're building an AI assistant yourself, I'd be interested to hear what tools you're integrating and what challenges you've encountered.

Thanks for reading!

title: ER-Chord: Spatially Consistent One-Step Image Editing via Equal-Energy Reliability Redistribution
description:
arXiv:2610.29248v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: One-step generative models enable fast text-guided image editing, yet they often introduce unintended changes to regions that should remain unchanged. Temporal aggregation stabilizes editing fields across noise levels, but leaves their spatial allocation insensitive to local variations in reliability. Consequently, temporal stability alone does not ensure spatially consistent editing. To address this lim- itation, we propose ER-Chord, a training-free and inversion-free framework for reliability-guided spatial redistribution. Our key insight is that agreement between editing fields at neighboring noise levels provides a local reliability signal for allocating editing strength. We formulate this allocation as an equal-energy op- timization that redistributes control energy according to local reliability while preserving the original editing directions and total control energy. This formu- lation admits a unique global solution that can be efficiently computed using existing field evaluations, requiring no additional denoiser calls. Experiments on two benchmarks, PIE-Bench and TEdBench, demonstrate improvements over state-of-the-art one-step editing baselines, achieving superior source preservation alongside consistent gains across multiple generative backbones.The project page is at https://github.com/Peizeli1/ER-Chord.

title: Build an Accessible Daily Habit Tracker with HTML, CSS and JavaScript
description:
A daily habit tracker is a simple project for practising front-end development. It can also teach important lessons about accessibility, semantic HTML and clear user feedback.

In this tutorial, we'll build a checklist that tracks completion of a few daily habits. The example uses generic habits and can be adapted for personal routines, study goals or reminders.

Step 1: Create the HTML

Save the following as index.html:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>Daily Habit Tracker</title>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css">
</head>
<body>
  <main class="container">
    <h1>Daily Habit Tracker</h1>
    <p>Mark each habit when you complete it.</p>

    <ul id="habits">
      <li>
        <label>
          <input type="checkbox">
          Morning routine
        </label>
      </li>
      <li>
        <label>
          <input type="checkbox">
          Evening routine
        </label>
      </li>
      <li>
        <label>
          <input type="checkbox">
          Prepare for tomorrow
        </label>
      </li>
    </ul>

    <p id="progress" aria-live="polite">
      0 of 3 habits completed
    </p>
  </main>

  <script src="script.js"></script>
</body>
</html>

Step 2: Make it responsive

Create style.css:

* {
  box-sizing: border-box;
}

body {
  margin: 0;
  padding: 24px;
  font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;
  line-height: 1.6;
  color: #20252b;
  background: #f4f6f8;
}

.container {
  max-width: 560px;
  margin: 40px auto;
  padding: 24px;
  background: white;
  border-radius: 12px;
}

ul {
  padding: 0;
  list-style: none;
}

li {
  margin: 12px 0;
  padding: 12px;
  border: 1px solid #ddd;
  border-radius: 8px;
}

label {
  display: flex;
  align-items: center;
  gap: 12px;
  cursor: pointer;
}

input[type="checkbox"] {
  width: 20px;
  height: 20px;
}

@media (max-width: 480px) {
  body {
    padding: 12px;
  }

  .container {
    margin: 16px auto;
    padding: 18px;
  }
}

Step 3: Add progress tracking

Create script.js:

const habitList = document.querySelector("#habits");
const progress = document.querySelector("#progress");

function updateProgress() {
  const checkboxes = habitList.querySelectorAll(
    'input[type="checkbox"]'
  );

  const completed = [...checkboxes].filter(
    checkbox => checkbox.checked
  ).length;

  progress.textContent =
    `${completed} of ${checkboxes.length} habits completed`;
}

habitList.addEventListener("change", updateProgress);

updateProgress();

Why accessibility matters

A useful interface should work for people who navigate using a keyboard or assistive technology.

This example uses semantic HTML, connects each checkbox to a label and provides a status message with aria-live="polite".

The browser can announce progress changes to assistive technology without forcing the user to search for the updated text.

You should also test keyboard navigation, visible focus indicators, contrast and behaviour at different screen sizes.

Ideas for extending the project

Once the basic version works, consider adding custom habits, a date selector or a weekly progress summary.

You could also save the checklist between sessions. If you use local storage, remember that the information stays in the browser and is not automatically synchronised across devices.

Avoid collecting sensitive personal information unless your application has a clear need and appropriate privacy protections.

Conclusion

This small project combines HTML structure, responsive CSS and JavaScript event handling. More importantly, it shows how accessibility can be considered from the beginning rather than added as an afterthought.

Building a simple interface well is a valuable step towards developing more complex web applications.

title: WorldStream: Streaming Interactive 3D Worlds with Hierarchical Planning and Persistent State
description:
arXiv:2610.28827v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present WorldStream, an open-ended 3D world model with three simultaneous capabilities: it extends playable terrain beyond any pre-specified map, acts on open-ended language in the running world, and restores visited places with their edits. A hierarchical planner over a typed decision model emits structured decision state: Macro fixes settlement, ecology, transport, and hydrological structure across a group of tiles; Micro specializes that contract into tile semantics under measured terrain and accepted neighbor commitments. Deterministic local code compiles accepted plans into terrain, roads, settlements, vegetation, and entities. Streaming separates their reach: plans run ahead along the predicted corridor, compilation only where movement will soon need it, geometry behind the user released. One world record retains plans, seeds, object identities and mutable state, boundary commitments, and edits by attribute, revised as the user advances and edits; returning tiles recompile from it. The same record grounds interaction: the model acts on existing entities, including stateful NPCs that update as they act, edits the present region, or attaches intent to unplanned regions. Together they yield a world expanding under bounded budgets, connected across independently planned tiles, and interactive.
