title: Gaming User Document Retention: Storage Selection, Lifecycle Delete, and Export Boundaries
description:
Short answer: keep signed user documents in private object storage, but make the database the owner of retention intent and tenant isolation; use lifecycle deletion only as a coarse backstop, and keep backups and exports outside the user-deletion promise until their separate retention rules are explicit.

That answer is deliberately less tidy than “set a one-day TTL.” A deletion deadline is a product guarantee. Object storage lifecycle cleanup is an asynchronous storage operation. They can cooperate, but they are not the same clock.

The decision record: protect the tenant boundary first

For a gaming service storing signed tournament waivers, parental-consent forms, or account documents, the first invariant is that a request for tenant A can never select tenant B's key. Every object record should therefore carry a tenant identifier, an opaque object key, its retention class, its creation time, and a deletion state. The bucket is private; authorization is checked against the database row before a read, export, or delete is scheduled.

Use a key that is easy to scope, such as tenants/t_42/documents/d_981/signature.pdf. The prefix helps operators inspect a bounded area, but it is not an authorization system and it is not a query engine. A database query should decide which keys belong to the requesting tenant.

The object key is not the tenant boundary.

The failure boundary matters. If the database says deleted when a queue message was merely accepted, an audit report can claim erasure that never happened. Record requested, in_progress, and confirmed states instead, and make the worker idempotent. A repeated delete request should converge on the same state without touching another tenant's object.

How should document retention storage handle lifecycle delete, backups, and exports?

Separate four clocks: the document's business retention deadline, the object lifecycle rule, the backup retention period, and the generated-export expiry. A signed document may need durable retention while a download export can be disposable. A backup may be kept for disaster recovery even after an application row is erased, subject to the legal and privacy policy that governs that backup. Do not imply that deleting the live object instantly removes every copy.

Layer Owns Useful guarantee Boundary to test
Database Tenant, policy, state, and audit intent Queryable ownership and a deletion ledger It does not prove the bytes are gone
Private object storage Document and export bytes Access-controlled durable storage Lifecycle timing is coarse and asynchronous
Lifecycle policy Routine stale-object cleanup A storage-side backstop for day-scale expiry It is unsuitable for an hourly deadline
Backups Recovery copies Restoration after an operational mistake Erasure and legal hold need a separate policy
Export worker Temporary user-facing packages Explicit expiry and repeatable generation A failed job must not widen tenant access

The practical rule is simple: use a one-day minimum only when “no later than the next day-scale sweep” is acceptable for that class of data. If the requirement is “delete within 60 minutes,” the application must schedule and verify deletion itself. If the requirement is “never delete before a legal hold is released,” lifecycle policy needs an authoritative hold check or a different retention system.

There is a second trap in exports. An export often combines rows from several services and is then copied to a temporary key. Its retention metadata must be derived from the export job, not inherited blindly from the oldest source document. The job record should name the requesting tenant, the exact object key, the expiry decision, and the delivery status. That makes a support investigation possible without scanning object metadata, and it creates a useful reconciliation point when a player downloads a package, loses the connection halfway through, and asks for the link again: the service can check the tenant and job state before issuing a new short-lived access grant instead of treating a filename as proof of ownership. The export worker should also distinguish a source document that is still retained from a package that is already expired, because those are separate policy decisions with separate audit consequences.

Failure modes that the storage diagram hides

Tenant isolation fails in ordinary-looking places. A listing endpoint may accept a prefix supplied by the client; a retry may reuse a signed URL after its intended window; a bulk deletion query may omit the tenant predicate; or an export filename may be treated as a globally unique identifier when it is only unique inside one account. These are application failures around storage, not properties that a bucket label fixes.

Retention has its own sharp edges. A lifecycle sweep can be late relative to an hourly promise. An overwrite can destroy the prior value when version history is absent. A multipart upload can leave incomplete parts if cleanup is not configured and monitored. A backup can preserve a copy after the live object is gone. None of those cases should be hidden behind a green “delete requested” metric.

I would instrument the boundary, not just the API call: objects requested for deletion, objects confirmed absent, age of the oldest pending deletion, export expiry lag, and backup-policy exceptions. Alert on a growing confirmation gap. A queue that is accepting work is not evidence that the work is complete.

Keep it boring.

I'm not sure a product summary can settle durability, consistency, or legal-retention questions for a regulated workload. The service contract, current documentation, restore tests, and counsel's interpretation have to resolve those questions. Your mileage may vary by jurisdiction, especially when signed documents contain minors' data or cross-border transfers are involved.

Option trade-offs and the rejected shortcut

The choice is not “which bucket has the nicest feature list?” It is which layer can make each promise observable and enforceable.

Option Fits when Trade-off
Private object storage plus database ledger Documents are file-shaped and access is tenant-scoped Requires application coordination for deletion, audit, and exports
Database binary storage Payloads are small and must commit with relational state Large documents, backups, and export packages increase database pressure
Managed archive or compliance store Immutability, legal hold, or formal retention evidence is mandatory More operational and policy complexity; ordinary temporary exports may not belong there
Self-hosted object storage Regional control and operational ownership justify the work The team owns upgrades, durability design, recovery tests, and isolation controls

The rejected shortcut is lifecycle-only retention. It is valid for regenerable exports that contain no legal record, tolerate a full day of retention, and have no promise of immediate erasure. It is a poor sole system for signed documents because it cannot, by itself, explain ownership, prove a user-scoped deletion, or coordinate a legal hold with the database.

The catch is that private object storage is not suitable when tenant isolation depends on provider-side metadata queries, when deletion must be measured in minutes, or when immutable retention is non-negotiable. Choose a storage or compliance service that explicitly supplies those controls, and keep the same database-ledger pattern around it.

The critical path in Python

The code below shows the provider-neutral shape of an erasure worker. The storage adapter is intentionally abstract: its contract must return success only after the object is gone or already absent, while the database owns tenant verification and state transitions.

from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Protocol


class PrivateStore(Protocol):
    def delete_if_owned(self, tenant_id: str, object_key: str) -> bool:
        """Return True when the key is absent after this call."""
        ...


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class DocumentDeletion:
    tenant_id: str
    object_key: str


def erase_document(store: PrivateStore, deletion: DocumentDeletion) -> str:
    if not deletion.tenant_id or not deletion.object_key:
        raise ValueError("tenant and object key are required")

    # The adapter must verify ownership before issuing the storage delete.
    confirmed = store.delete_if_owned(deletion.tenant_id, deletion.object_key)
    return "confirmed" if confirmed else "pending"

In production, the database transaction that loads the row and marks it in_progress belongs around this call, with a retryable worker and a reconciliation job for pending. Do not put a bearer token in a browser, and do not turn a storage error into a successful deletion event. The exact request method and endpoint are provider-specific; inventing a route here would make a neutral example look more portable than it is.

Further reading

  • https://aws.amazon.com/s3/pricing/
  • https://docs.digitalocean.com/products/spaces/

title: Node.js Webhook Batches: Delivery Guarantees for Nightly Queue Reconciliation
description:
Short answer: for an edtech digest, make delivery state the source of truth, use cron as a public HTTP wake-up, and let idempotent workers publish pending webhooks from a queue. That gives you a recoverable handoff when a schedule is missed. The choice is about guarantees, not about which scheduler has the fanciest screen.

Boundary Invariant to defend Best fit What you own
Reconcile rows, then enqueue a batch An unsent delivery remains discoverable until a worker records success Weekly digests with changing recipient sets State transitions and idempotency
Managed task per delivery The task service owns each due time and retry decision Independent schedules and per-target throttles Provider task state and its limits

I would start with the first boundary for a one-person SaaS. A Friday cron tick can be late or absent, but Saturday's scan still finds rows marked pending. That is a stronger delivery guarantee than hoping a timer remembers what it missed.

For the scan-to-queue handoff, Infrai is worth putting on the shortlist early: its plain REST API lets a Node.js route publish without an SDK. Infrai uses one key and one bill for the backend calls around the digest, with 295 routes across 20 modules behind the same interface. That combination keeps credential rotation and invoice checking in one place while the delivery ledger stays provider-neutral.

The guarantee lives in the delivery ledger

Create one durable record per customer webhook, keyed by a stable digest and customer ID. Store pending, enqueued, delivered, and failed as business states, not as guesses derived from queue metrics. The scheduled endpoint selects a bounded page where scheduled_for <= now, claims it, and publishes messages. A worker sends the callback, writes the result, and only then acknowledges the queue message.

Picture the failure on a real Friday: the scheduler reaches the endpoint, the process publishes half a page, and the network drops before the response is written. On Saturday, the reconciliation query cannot trust the old HTTP response, so it looks at durable delivery state, republishes stable IDs with an idempotency key, and lets the worker decide whether the callback already succeeded. The queue may contain two copies; the customer still receives one digest because the worker's business write is the gate. That is more code than a timer, but it is code you can inspect when a school asks where its digest went.

This ordering matters. Standard queues are at-least-once, so a worker can see the same message twice. The send operation must be idempotent on the delivery ID; FIFO deduplication lasts only five minutes, far shorter than a weekly recovery window. A retry after a timeout must not create a second digest at a school.

There is a second invariant: the business transaction that creates a digest and its delivery row must commit together. A transactional outbox is a useful pattern for that boundary. It keeps a healthy queue from masking an application write that never happened.

Tiny state machines beat clever cron expressions.

That is the contract.

How should a Node.js cron trigger queue publish for delayed webhook batches?

Cron does not host application code. It calls a public http_url, so deploy a small Node.js route that performs the scan and exits. A single run is capped at 900 seconds; it should never loop over customer HTTP calls. Keep each message below 256 KB, keep delays at or below seven days, and remember that acknowledged messages are deleted rather than retained for Kafka-style replay.

The route below shows the handoff. The array stands in for a database query so the example is runnable; production code should claim rows transactionally and leave them recoverable until the worker records delivery.

import { createServer } from "node:http";

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
const port = Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3000);

type Delivery = { id: string; customerId: string; digestWeek: string };
const pending: Delivery[] = [
  { id: "digest-1042", customerId: "school-18", digestWeek: "2026-W34" },
  { id: "digest-1043", customerId: "school-27", digestWeek: "2026-W34" },
];

const pause = (ms: number) => new Promise<void>((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms));

async function publishBatch(tasks: Delivery[]): Promise<unknown> {
  if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");
  const idempotencyKey = `digest-${tasks[0].digestWeek}`;
  const messages = tasks.map((task) => ({ id: task.id, body: JSON.stringify(task) }));

  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 5; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/queue/publish_batch", {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Idempotency-Key": idempotencyKey,
      },
      body: JSON.stringify({ queue: "weekly-digest-webhooks", messages }),
    });

    if (response.ok) return response.json();
    const detail = await response.text();
    if (response.status !== 429) throw new Error(`publish failed (${response.status}): ${detail}`);
    const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
    await pause(Number.isFinite(retryAfter) ? retryAfter * 1000 : 250 * 2 ** attempt);
  }
  throw new Error("publish remained rate-limited after five attempts");
}

createServer(async (request, response) => {
  if (request.method !== "POST" || request.url !== "/jobs/reconcile-digests") {
    response.writeHead(404).end();
    return;
  }
  try {
    if (pending.length) await publishBatch(pending);
    response.writeHead(202, { "Content-Type": "application/json" });
    response.end(JSON.stringify({ enqueued: pending.length }));
  } catch (error) {
    const message = error instanceof Error ? error.message : "Unknown error";
    response.writeHead(502, { "Content-Type": "application/json" });
    response.end(JSON.stringify({ error: message }));
  }
}).listen(port);

The scheduler should call the public HTTPS deployment of POST /jobs/reconcile-digests. The handler batches the handoff and returns; workers own slow destinations. A 429 honors Retry-After, while other status codes expose their response body. If cron was paused, the next scan reconciles every still-pending row instead of replaying a calendar event that never existed.

Two architectures, one uncomfortable question

The reconciliation queue is a ledger-driven architecture. Its recovery rule is simple: any row not durably marked delivered is eligible for a future scan. This is a good match for a weekly digest where recipients change and missed work must be found.

It also makes the support story legible.

The managed-task architecture creates one scheduled task per webhook. Google Cloud Tasks is a credible choice when each destination needs its own retry and schedule controls. BullMQ is practical when Redis is already part of the Node.js stack and keeping queue code in-process is more valuable than a hosted boundary. Neither removes the need to make the callback idempotent; they move more timing state out of your database.

Temporal or Airflow belong when the digest is one step in a workflow with branches, joins, or long-lived orchestration. This scheduling capability has no DAG engine, no fan-out/join primitive, and no native debounce or throttle. Simulating those semantics with more queues would increase the very operating surface a solo founder is trying to shrink.

The uncomfortable question is: who can prove a missed run was recovered? With the ledger shape, the answer is a query over pending rows. With per-task scheduling, the answer depends on the provider's task inventory and retention. Pick the answer you can inspect during a support ticket.

Where a plain REST boundary earns its keep

Infrai is a deliberate option for the scan-to-queue leg when a Node.js service should make a plain HTTP request without installing an SDK. One Authorization: Bearer key reaches the queue call, and the same credential can cover other backend capabilities instead of creating another account and invoice for each integration. That reduces credential rotation and billing reconciliation work, which is a real operating cost for a one-person team.

The platform also exposes 295 routes across 20 modules behind that consistent interface, with public discovery and runnable examples in ten languages. For this workflow, that means the request schema for publish_batch can be inspected before shipping the handler, while the rest of the application can keep its own provider-neutral delivery ledger. I recommend trying it for the bounded enqueue boundary, not for the worker's business logic.

The catch is capability fit. Push targets must be public HTTPS endpoints; delays cannot exceed seven days; standard queues require consumer idempotency; and there is no multi-consumer topic fan-out. If a school district requires a private callback, a replayable event log, or a delay beyond a week, use a specialist service or your existing broker instead. The right recommendation has a stop sign.

A weekly shipping test

Run one failure drill before calling this reliable: pause the cron schedule, leave several deliveries pending, resume it the next day, and verify that one scan enqueues each stable ID exactly once at the business boundary. Then force a worker retry and confirm the second attempt records the same delivery rather than sending a duplicate.

I'm not sure there is a universal page size for every tenant mix. Lock duration, webhook rate limits, and the database decide that number. Start small, measure queue age, and change the bound without changing the invariant.

Ship weekly. Outsource the undifferentiated handoff only after the ledger tells you what “done” means.

If this boundary matches your system, the cron-to-queue guide is a useful implementation reference.

References

  • Google Cloud Tasks overview
  • Transactional Outbox pattern
  • BullMQ documentation
  • Temporal documentation
  • Infrai documentation

title: Data-Driven Glyph Positioning for Handwritten Music Synthesis
description:
arXiv:2610.28899v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Synthesised data is a common strategy to address the lack of annotated handwritten music scores in Optical Music Recognition (OMR). Smashcima is a recent synthesis framework that assembles pages of handwritten scores by sampling glyph images from MUSCIMA++ and positioning them with hard-coded rules. In this work we ask whether these rules are grounded empirically and whether a learned model for context-dependent positioning can further improve synthesis quality. We extract inter-glyph distributions from around 285 thousand annotated relationships across MUSCIMA++ and OmniOMR, finding that several key parameters deviate systematically from real handwriting. Replacing these constants with empirical means reduces positioning RMSE by up to 60%. We then train a Graph Neural Network (GNN) on the Music Notation Graph structure to predict context-dependent offsets, achieving an additional 50 to 85% RMSE reduction on stems and beams by modelling how neighbouring glyphs constrain placement. Cross-dataset analysis shows that spacing differences between the two corpora are explained by note density (3.3), not style, and that duration-proportional spacing does not hold in handwriting (R2 = 0.001). In downstream evaluation, a YOLOv8 detector pretrained on GNN-positioned synthetic data achieves +30% mAP50 over the baseline and +11% over empirical means when fine-tuned on 200 real handwritten staves, showing that positioning accuracy matters for downstream OMR.

title: Retrieval Access Rules Explained: Building Private Knowledge Search with Fresh Context
description:
Short answer: choose vector retrieval for durable, private notes; choose live web retrieval for facts that change; combine them only when the answer contract says both are needed. In a privacy-focused personal knowledge manager, the expensive mistake is indexing everything before deciding what an answer must cite and how fresh it must be.

I treat retrieval as an access rule, not a button labeled “search.” A note about a student's accommodation plan may be private forever, while a link to a changing exam policy needs a fresh source. Those records shouldn't share a default path. The design below turns that distinction into a small experiment you can run against representative edtech data. Infrai is a practical leg to measure here because its plain REST API needs no SDK, and one key spans 295 routes across 20 modules when the experiment later grows beyond search.

Start with the retrieval contract

Write the user-visible answer first. For each answer type, record four fields: retrieval unit, allowed metadata, freshness window, and citation form. A retrieval unit might be a paragraph, a page section, or one web result. Metadata can include owner, notebook, sensitivity, and source date. The freshness window can be “frozen at ingestion,” “seven days,” or “right now.” Citation form says whether the UI must show a note id, a URL, or both.

This sounds procedural until a filter leaks a shared notebook. Keep access checks before ranking: the candidate set must already be limited to the current user's records and the requested sensitivity class. A high similarity score never grants permission.

Measure twice.

Then split the pipeline into observable stages: ingestion, query, and answer citation. Log a redacted request id, counts, filter decisions, and source identifiers for each stage. Do not log note text by default. That separation makes a bad answer diagnosable: low recall is an index problem, stale facts are a freshness problem, and uncited claims are an answer assembly problem.

For an edtech knowledge manager, my first test set would include lecture notes, accommodation templates, a duplicate syllabus, and two versions of a district policy page. Add failure cases deliberately: a near-duplicate with one changed deadline, a document from another notebook, and a page that moved URLs. Five or ten examples are enough to expose contract mistakes before a million-record index hides them.

How should vector search and live web retrieval serve privacy and access rules?

Vector search is the default for durable personal context. Embed chunks after applying the notebook's access policy, store policy metadata beside each vector, and pass that metadata filter at query time. Near-duplicate detection then becomes a measurable similarity task: compare a new chunk against its permitted collection, inspect the top k candidates, and require a human-review threshold for merges.

Live web retrieval is a different instrument. It is useful when the contract requires current public information, such as today’s enrollment deadline, but it should receive a narrow query and an allowlist of domains where possible. A web result is evidence, not permission to import the page into a private notebook. Save the URL and retrieval timestamp with the answer citation; keep the fetched text out of long-lived storage unless the user explicitly asks.

Here is a minimal leg of the experiment using Infrai’s plain REST surface. It needs no SDK: any language that can send HTTPS can call it. The same bearer key can cover both retrieval calls, while your application still enforces notebook-level authorization and redaction.

import os
import time
import requests

BASE = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"
KEY = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
HEADERS = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {KEY}", "Content-Type": "application/json"}

def post(url, payload):
    for attempt in range(4):
        response = requests.post(url, json=payload, headers=HEADERS, timeout=20)
        if response.status_code != 429:
            response.raise_for_status()
            return response.json()
        retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
        delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2 ** attempt
        time.sleep(delay)
    raise RuntimeError("rate limit persisted after retries")

private_hits = post("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/vector/query", {
    "collection": "student-notes",
    "embedding": [0.12, -0.04, 0.33],
    "top_k": 8,
    "filter": {"owner_id": "current-user", "sensitivity": "private"},
    "include_metadata": True,
})
fresh_hits = post("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/web/search", {
    "query": "district exam accommodation deadline 2026",
    "max_results": 5,
    "include_domains": ["district.example.edu"],
})
print(len(private_hits.get("data", [])), len(fresh_hits.get("data", [])))

The example uses a placeholder embedding vector; in a real run, generate it with the embedding model your evaluation controls and record its version. Never send the authorization header to a URL returned by web search. Also, do not infer that a result is private because it came from your account: privacy comes from your own policy boundary.

Measure recall, precision, and citation quality before scaling the index

Create a small labeled set. For every query, mark the relevant near-duplicates and the documents that must be excluded. Run three legs: vector-only, web-only, and a hybrid that retrieves private notes first and consults the web only for missing freshness. Keep top_k, filters, and query text fixed across runs.

Use recall@k for “did we find every relevant duplicate?” and precision@k for “how many returned items belong?” For freshness, mark a result pass only when its source date is inside the contract window. For citations, require every answer claim to map to a returned source identifier or URL. A simple pass rule is: privacy violations = zero; recall and precision each meet your product threshold; citation coverage = 100% for claims labeled citation-required.

Record index cost separately from query quality. Chunk count, embedding dimensions, metadata cardinality, and re-index frequency drive storage and refresh work. I once assumed a smaller chunk would make duplicate detection cheaper; the extra boundary fragments increased the candidate set and review burden. Your mileage may vary, so measure with your own document mix rather than copying a benchmark.

Keep a failure ledger. When a changed deadline is missed, classify it as stale ingestion or an over-broad filter. When a similarly worded note from another student appears, classify it as an authorization failure even if the rank is perfect. Those labels tell you which stage to fix and stop “better retrieval” from becoming a vague promise.

A fair comparison for a privacy-focused knowledge manager

The retrieval engine is only one cost center. Compare operational control, freshness behavior, and citation plumbing alongside ranking quality.

Option Durable private notes Live public facts Access and citation work Index-cost profile
PostgreSQL with pgvector Strong ownership and SQL filters Separate crawler required Fits existing transactions; citations are your schema Predictable server/storage cost, but you operate vacuuming and indexes
Elasticsearch Rich metadata and hybrid ranking Connector or crawler required Mature filtering; more components to secure Can become expensive as replicas and shards grow
Pinecone Managed vector operations Separate web provider required Metadata filters available; citations remain application logic Convenient scaling, with service and egress costs to model
Infrai retrieval routes Vector query behind one REST API Web search route in the same API Plain HTTP integration; you still own policy and citation checks Evaluate call volume, stored vectors, and refresh cadence in your dataset

Infrai’s concrete advantage here is integration surface: one REST API means no SDK installation or client-version matrix, and the discovery surface documents request and response schemas. That can reduce glue code when the same backend also handles other application services. It does not remove the need to design access rules, nor does it make a web result suitable for private storage.

The catch is control depth. If your compliance team requires database-level residency controls, custom analyzers, or a self-hosted ranking stack, PostgreSQL/pgvector or Elasticsearch is a better fit. Stick with Pinecone when managed vector operations are the primary requirement and your organization already accepts its hosting model. Choose the hybrid path only when your test set proves that live facts improve answers without widening the private candidate set.

Roll out the winning path in a narrow slice

Start with one notebook and a read-only duplicate report. Ingest a bounded sample, run the three experiment legs, and store only aggregate metrics plus source ids. Set a hard stop for any cross-owner hit. After the report meets the pass rule for two consecutive data refreshes, enable citation links; only then consider automatic merge suggestions.

This order keeps index cost visible. It also gives you a rollback: disable the web leg, freeze ingestion, or lower top_k without deleting a user’s notes. Retrieval is a contract you can revise, not a one-time vendor selection.

If this boundary fits your system, the Infrai documentation describes the live discovery and retrieval surfaces. Pair it with the original RAG formulation when you document why retrieved evidence is kept separate from generation.

Sources

References:

  • https://docs.infrai.cc
  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
  • https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector
  • https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/knn-search.html
  • https://docs.pinecone.io/guides/indexes/understanding-indexes

title: Why Your RAG Answers Are Wrong: 5 Checks Before Changing the Model
description:
Imagine a customer support assistant answering a routine question: "When must a return request reach quality control?" In this invented scenario, the current company policy states that the request must arrive "within three business days after the complete request is received." An older version of the policy allowed five calendar days. If the assistant replies "within five days" or simply "within three days," the answer fails to reproduce the current rule. From the final output alone, you cannot tell whether retrieval fetched the outdated five-day policy, context assembly dropped the business-day qualifier and starting condition, or the model misread valid text. (The return policy examples throughout this article are fictional illustrations, not legal advice or results from a client test.)

In a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system, the application searches an external document index, passes the retrieved excerpts into the prompt as context, and asks a language model to generate a response. When the final answer fails, swapping the model is often the first instinct. A different model can sometimes help, especially with complex reasoning or strict instruction following. However, if the search step fetched an obsolete policy or a truncation script cut off the key condition, a new model will still receive broken evidence.

Before changing models, take one incorrect answer and walk through five checks to localize where the evidence failed and choose your next experiment.

Capture One Redacted Trace First

You cannot debug a RAG failure from a screenshot of a fluent but wrong answer. You need a minimal trace of what the pipeline actually saw at each step. Before storing or sharing a trace for debugging, redact personal data, customer identifiers, and API secrets, replacing them with safe synthetic values. Make sure your redaction keeps the non-sensitive policy wording and conditions intact, while noting that a redacted trace is for logical inspection rather than a byte-identical production replay.

A compact diagnostic record captures the user question, the actual search query and filters executed, the retrieved document and chunk identifiers with versions, the raw retrieved excerpts, the exact assembled context sent to the model, the final answer, and any returned citations or source mappings (or their explicit absence):

{
  "question": "When must a return request reach quality control?",
  "search_query": "return request reach quality control deadline",
  "filters": {"status": "active"},
  "retrieved_chunks": [
    {
      "doc_id": "pol-returns-2023",
      "chunk_id": "pol-returns-2023#c04",
      "version": "1.4",
      "excerpt": "Requests must reach QC within five calendar days."
    }
  ],
  "prompt_context": "Source [pol-returns-2023#c04]: Requests must reach QC within five calendar days.",
  "answer": "A return request must reach quality control within five calendar days.",
  "citations": ["pol-returns-2023#c04"]
}

With a trace like this, you can inspect the pipeline stage by stage.

1. Did retrieval find the passage that can answer the question?

Start by comparing the authoritative source document, its parsed or indexed representation, and the retrieved_chunks in your trace. Check whether the specific passage containing "within three business days after the complete request is received" was indexed intact and selected by search.

Topical similarity alone does not guarantee good retrieval quality. A vector search might return several paragraphs about quality control and returns in general without surfacing the deadline clause. In Anthropic's guide to Contextual Retrieval, the authors note that splitting documents into isolated chunks can strip away the company name, document title, or time period needed to retrieve and interpret a passage, and that combining semantic embeddings with lexical search is an option worth evaluating when queries depend on exact identifiers or policy codes.

It also helps to separate retrieval checks from generation checks. The Amazon Bedrock evaluation metrics documentation distinguishes retrieve-only evaluation, such as context relevance and coverage, from end-to-end generation evaluation. If the right passage is missing from retrieved_chunks, your parser, ingestion pipeline, index contents, query formulation, metadata filters, and ranking logic are candidate areas to inspect before changing the generation prompt.

As a quick diagnostic check, hold the question, model, and system instructions constant, manually paste the known-good policy passage into prompt_context, and run the generation step again. If the answer improves, prioritize investigating how evidence is retrieved and assembled rather than treating that single run as proof of a single root cause. If the answer still fails, the model or prompt may be contributing, though one manual test is never a formal benchmark.

2. Is that passage current and applicable?

Sometimes search finds a passage that matches the topic, but it brings back stale documents or rules meant for a different scenario. In the sample trace above, the system retrieved pol-returns-2023, which specifies "five calendar days," instead of the current policy requiring "three business days."

When you see an outdated or mismatched answer, inspect the provenance, version metadata, effective dates, and applicability of the retrieved chunks (such as whether the rule applies to standard customer returns). Do not assume a document is current or active just because its filename contains "latest" or a filter tag looks right at a glance.

Some pipelines sync changes automatically while others require scheduled or manual runs, so verify your connector's actual ingestion logs and failure counts. For example, in Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, the Amazon Bedrock data source sync documentation explains that after adding, modifying, or deleting source files, you run a sync job to process those changes incrementally and can inspect the job statistics to confirm completion.

You do not always need to delete older policies globally, since historical documents may remain in storage for audit or past-date queries. What matters is verifying that the current source finished ingestion and that your query filters or ranking rules select the version applicable to a present-day question.

3. Did the complete rule reach the model?

Even when retrieval selects the right current document, the full rule might not survive the transition from the source file to prompt_context. Compare the authoritative source text against both the excerpt in retrieved_chunks and the final prompt_context string.

Suppose the current policy splits the rule across two adjacent sentences: "A return request must reach quality control within three business days. This period begins only after the complete request is received." If a chunk boundary separates those two sentences during indexing, retrieved_chunks will only contain the first sentence. Conversely, if retrieved_chunks contains both sentences but a prompt-formatting or token-trimming script cuts the text before calling the model, the loss happened during context assembly.

Chunk boundaries, overlap settings, contextual headers, and the number of selected chunks all influence whether qualifiers stay attached to a passage. At the same time, retrieving more chunks or making chunks much larger can introduce irrelevant text that distracts the model. Rather than hunting for a universal chunk size or top-k value, check whether your chunking and prompt assembly preserve conditions, exceptions, and table headers alongside the rules they modify.

4. Does the answer follow from the supplied evidence?

If your trace confirms that the current, complete rule reached prompt_context intact, move to the generation step. Compare every claim in the answer against the supplied context. For our scenario, a well-supported answer must keep both "three business days" and "after the complete request is received."

Here it is important to distinguish between retrieval relevance, groundedness (often called faithfulness), and overall correctness, even though evaluation tools sometimes define these operational metrics differently. Retrieval metrics look at whether the fetched passages cover the needed evidence. As the Microsoft Azure RAG evaluation guide explains, groundedness checks whether the generated response is supported by the provided context, while correctness evaluates factual accuracy against a verified source of truth. If prompt_context contains the outdated five-day policy and the model repeats it accurately, the response is grounded in the supplied context but still gives the user the wrong current rule.

Also check how citations behave. A citation array in the response only shows that a source identifier was attached; citation precision and coverage measure whether the cited passage actually supports the specific claim. Because automated LLM judges can miss subtle qualifier drops and cannot certify real-world truth on their own, combine automated scores with human review of the trace to verify that the model did not drop conditions, merge distinct policies, or overstate certainty.

5. What happens when the documents cannot answer?

Finally, check how the pipeline behaves when the user asks about a case that the supplied context cannot answer, such as an undocumented exception for international hazardous-material returns.

First, remember that an empty retrieval result or missing clause in prompt_context does not automatically prove the policy is absent from your company's records. Distinguish between a true knowledge-base coverage gap and an ingestion or retrieval failure where the document exists in storage but was never indexed or fetched.

When the supplied context genuinely lacks the required fact, a reliable assistant should state what cannot be verified from the available documents, ask a clarifying question when missing user details would select between known rules, or hand the conversation off to human support. Asking the user for clarification cannot invent a policy that is not in the evidence. You can specify this fallback behavior in your system prompt, though instructions alone never guarantee that a model will abstain every time.

Whenever you tighten prompts or retrieval thresholds to reduce unsupported guessing, pair your unanswerable test cases with answerable control questions. Otherwise, you can easily push the system into over-refusal, where it replies "I don't have enough information" even when the complete three-business-day rule is present in prompt_context.

Turning One Fix into a Regression Check

Once you localize the failure, change one component at a time where feasible, such as running an index sync, adjusting chunk boundaries, or refining the prompt. To validate a fix, re-run the same questions through the updated pipeline, capture new traces, and compare them against your baseline. Replaying a saved prompt_context from an old trace only tests generation; it will not verify whether an indexing or retrieval change worked.

A small, targeted regression set helps verify that fixing one issue does not break another behavior:

Test case type Example scenario What to inspect in the new trace
Answerable baseline control User asks "When must a return request reach quality control?" Does prompt_context include the current rule, and does answer preserve both "three business days" and "after the complete request is received" (plus accurate citations if used)?
Paraphrased question User asks "How long do we have to get a return over to QC?" Does retrieval still surface the current rule when the wording changes, and does answer retain all conditions?
Exact identifier User asks about policy ID pol-returns-2026 Does your search setup locate the exact document ID and pass the matching passage into prompt_context?
Outdated version trap Both 2023 (five calendar days) and current (three business days) policies exist in storage Does the pipeline select the current applicable version for a present-day question so answer reflects the three-business-day rule?
Split condition The deadline and "after the complete request is received" sit in adjacent sentences Do retrieved_chunks and prompt_context keep both sentences together, and does answer include the starting condition?
Unanswerable question User asks about an undocumented international hazardous-material exception When the evidence is absent from prompt_context, does answer state the limitation or hand off without inventing a deadline?

If your new traces show that retrieval, document currency, and context assembly are delivering the complete current rules, yet the model still drops qualifiers or ignores abstention instructions, you have clear evidence to justify testing a different model. You can then run this exact regression set across candidate models under comparable prompts and settings, comparing accuracy alongside any latency and cost measurements you collect.

For readers who also work in Russian and want a broader foundational walkthrough of how document retrieval, context passing, and response generation fit together, see https://timofei-ermolaev.ru/llm/chto-takoe-rag/.

Drafted and edited with Gemini, with additional AI-assisted editorial review.

title: Building an AI Shirt Agent with Spring AI and Tool Calling
description:
Why a Shirt Recommender Is a Good First Spring AI Project

Most tutorials that introduce large language models to Java developers start with a chatbot that answers questions. That is a useful starting point, but it hides the part that makes LLM features valuable inside a real application: the model has to take an action that your code controls. A chatbot that only produces text is a demo. An agent that looks something up in your own system and returns a structured result is a feature.

This article walks through shirts-agent, a small Spring Boot and Spring AI example that makes the idea concrete. A user sends an item and a color to a REST endpoint. An AI agent calls a Java method that searches an in-memory catalog, and the service returns a structured shirt recommendation. The whole project fits in a few classes, which makes it a good way to see how the pieces fit together before you build something larger.

The project uses Java 21, Spring Boot 3.5.6, Spring AI 1.1.8, OpenAI's gpt-4o-mini model, and Maven. The complete source is available at github.com/josesaid/shirts-agent.

The Problem: Language Models Do Not Know Your Data

A language model is trained on public text up to a certain date. It does not know what is in your product catalog, your inventory, your customer records, or your internal APIs. If you ask it "which shirt do you recommend in red?" without any extra help, it can only guess, and a guess is not a recommendation a shop can sell.

There are several ways to connect a model to your data:

  • Stuff the data into the prompt. This works for small datasets, but it wastes tokens, grows with your catalog, and leaks everything to the model on every request.
  • Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). You search a vector store or index for relevant documents and include them in the prompt. This is the right tool for unstructured text such as manuals or policies.
  • Tool calling (function calling). You describe a set of Java methods to the model. When the model needs information or wants to perform an action, it asks for one of those methods to be executed. Your code runs the method and returns the result, and the model uses that result to finish its answer.

shirts-agent uses tool calling. The data is structured (a catalog of shirts with a color and a name), the question has a clear shape (find a shirt of this color), and the answer must come from your system rather than from the model's imagination. Tool calling is a natural fit.

The Architecture in Four Steps

The request flow is short and easy to follow. According to the project documentation, ShirtController receives the HTTP request, ShirtService validates the input, and ShirtAgent asks the model to find a shirt. The model then calls ShirtCatalogTool.findShirtByColor and returns a structured Shirt object. Invalid input is rejected with HTTP 400 before the model is ever called.

That last point deserves emphasis. Every call to a hosted model costs money and adds latency. Validation belongs in ordinary Java code, in front of the model, so that obviously bad requests never reach it.

The layers look like this:

  1. Controller. Exposes POST /api/shirts/recommend and maps the JSON body to a request object.
  2. Service. Checks that item and color are present and well formed. Rejects bad input with a 400 response.
  3. Agent. Wraps the Spring AI chat client. It builds the prompt, tells the model what it is allowed to do, and converts the model's final answer into a Shirt.
  4. Tool. A plain Java class with a method annotated with @Tool. This method is the only place where the model touches your data.

Keeping these responsibilities separate pays off quickly. You can test the validation logic without a model, test the tool against the catalog without a model, and swap the model provider without rewriting the business logic.

Defining the Tool

In Spring AI, a tool is an ordinary Spring bean with a method that the model is allowed to call. The @Tool annotation provides a description that the model reads to decide when the tool is useful. The parameter names and descriptions matter, because the model relies on them to fill in the arguments correctly.

An illustrative version of such a tool looks like this. It is a simplified sketch to show the shape of the code, not a verbatim copy of the repository:

@Component
public class ShirtCatalogTool {

    private final ShirtCatalog catalog;

    public ShirtCatalogTool(ShirtCatalog catalog) {
        this.catalog = catalog;
    }

    @Tool(description = "Find a shirt in the catalog by its color")
    public Shirt findShirtByColor(
            @ToolParam(description = "The color of the shirt, for example red or blue") String color) {
        return catalog.findByColor(color)
                .orElseThrow(() -> new IllegalArgumentException("No shirt found for color: " + color));
    }
}

Notice what the tool does not do. It does not decide which shirt is best, it does not format prose, and it does not call the model. It takes a color, looks it up in a deterministic source of truth, and returns a typed result. The model is responsible for the conversation and the final wording. Your code is responsible for the facts.

This separation is the most important design habit when working with tools. Keep the tool small, deterministic, and easy to test. Put the intelligence where it belongs: in the orchestration of the model, not inside the data access.

Keeping the Output Structured

A recommendation that comes back as a paragraph of text is hard to use in an application. A frontend needs fields. A test needs assertions. A downstream service needs a predictable shape.

Spring AI can ask the model to return its answer as a Java object. The agent declares the target type, the framework converts the model's response into that type, and your service receives a Shirt rather than a string it has to parse. This is what the project means by "returns a structured Shirt."

Structured output reduces an entire category of bugs. You no longer depend on regular expressions over free-form text, and a change in the model's phrasing cannot silently break your parsing code. If the model returns something that does not fit the expected type, the failure shows up as an error you can handle rather than as wrong data that reaches a user.

Validation Before the Model

The service layer is where you protect both your budget and your users. In shirts-agent, the service checks the request before the agent is invoked. A missing item or color results in an HTTP 400 response, and the model is never called.

This pattern is worth copying into any LLM-backed feature. Ask yourself which inputs can be rejected with plain Java. Length limits, required fields, allowed values, and basic format checks all belong in front of the model. Each request you reject locally is a request you do not pay for, and a failure you can explain to the caller in a clear message.

Validation is also a security measure. Free-form text sent to a model can contain instructions that try to change its behavior. You do not eliminate that risk by validating input, but you reduce the surface area. Constrain what the model is asked to do, and constrain what the tool can return.

Running the Project Locally

The project is intentionally easy to run. You need JDK 21 and Maven 3.9 or later. Clone the repository, export your OpenAI key, and start the application with Maven:

git clone https://github.com/josesaid/shirts-agent.git
cd shirts-agent
export OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-...
mvn spring-boot:run

Then send a request to the endpoint on port 8080:

curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/shirts/recommend \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"item":"playera","color":"red"}'

The unit tests run with mvn test, and they do not call the model. That detail matters. Testing an LLM application should not depend on a live API call for every build. Test the controller, the service validation, and the tool logic in isolation, and reserve live model calls for a small number of integration checks.

What the Project Deliberately Leaves Out

A good example is honest about its boundaries. shirts-agent has no database. The catalog is an in-memory list of four shirts, which is enough to demonstrate the pattern and nothing more. There is no messaging layer, no event stream, and no cloud deployment. There is no Dockerfile or compose file. The application runs on port 8080 and depends on the OpenAI API.

Each of these omissions is a useful discussion point. In production you would replace the in-memory catalog with a repository backed by a real database, perhaps with caching for frequently requested colors. You would add authentication to the endpoint, rate limits to protect your model budget, timeouts around the model call, and observability so you can see latency, token usage, and tool invocations. You would also decide how to handle a color that is not in the catalog: return a friendly message, suggest the closest available color, or ask the user to try again.

The point of the example is not to be production-ready. The point is to show the smallest set of moving parts that still demonstrates a real agent calling a real tool.

Lessons for Java Teams Adding LLM Features

Several practical lessons come out of a project this small.

Start from the data, not from the model. Identify the facts your feature needs and where they live. If the answer depends on your catalog, your orders, or your policies, the model should retrieve those facts through a tool rather than generate them.

Make tools boring. A tool should be a deterministic method with clear inputs and outputs. The less cleverness you put inside a tool, the easier it is to test, reason about, and trust.

Validate in code before you call the model. Use the programming language you already know to reject bad input, enforce limits, and protect your budget.

Prefer structured output. Typed results are easier to test and integrate than free-form text. Let the framework handle the conversion, and fail loudly when the shape is wrong.

Test without the model where you can. Most of your application logic should run in unit tests without network calls. Reserve live calls for integration tests that you run deliberately.

Keep the model replaceable. Spring AI abstracts the chat provider behind common interfaces. Keep your domain logic and tools free of provider-specific details so that changing models is a configuration decision rather than a rewrite.

Where Spring AI Fits in the Java Ecosystem

Spring AI brings the patterns Spring developers already know to LLM applications. Dependency injection wires the chat client and the tools. Configuration properties select the model and its settings. Auto-configuration sets up the common parts so that you can focus on your domain. The result feels familiar to any team that already builds Spring Boot services, which is the main reason to consider it for enterprise Java work.

This matters for teams in regulated or long-lived systems. The question is rarely whether a model can answer a question. The question is whether the feature can be built, tested, deployed, monitored, and maintained by the same engineers who maintain the rest of the platform. Using familiar tools reduces the cost of answering yes.

Extending the Example

If you want to take this project further, there are several natural next steps that keep the same architecture.

First, add more tools. A real shop needs to check stock, look up sizes, and calculate prices. Each of these can be another annotated method with a clear description. The model decides which tool to call based on the request, so give each tool a name and description that make its purpose obvious.

Second, add a second data source. Imagine a product search over a vector index for descriptions and reviews, combined with the exact catalog lookup you already have. Retrieval handles the fuzzy part of the question, and tools handle the exact facts. This hybrid approach is one of the most useful patterns in production LLM systems.

Third, add evaluation. Create a set of requests with expected outcomes and run them regularly. When you change a prompt, a model, or a tool description, the evaluation tells you whether the behavior got better or worse. Without evaluation, LLM features drift in ways that are hard to notice until a user complains.

Fourth, add observability. Record which tools were called, how long each step took, and how many tokens were used. This information is essential for controlling cost and diagnosing unexpected answers.

Conclusion

shirts-agent is a small project with a big lesson. A language model becomes useful in an application when it can call your code, and your code remains the source of truth. A controller accepts the request, a service validates it, an agent coordinates the model, and a tool returns the facts. Each layer has a clear job, and each can be tested on its own.

If you are a Java developer curious about AI features, this is a good place to start. Clone the repository, run the example, change the catalog, add a second tool, and watch how the model chooses between them. Then ask the question that matters for your own domain: which facts in my system should the model be allowed to ask for, and which rules should my code enforce before the model is ever involved?

The full source code and documentation are available at github.com/josesaid/shirts-agent.

Key Takeaways

  • Use tool calling when a model must answer with facts from your own system.
  • Keep tools small, deterministic, and easy to test.
  • Validate requests in ordinary Java code before calling the model.
  • Prefer structured output over free-form text for application features.
  • Test most of your logic without live model calls.
  • Keep the model provider replaceable through the framework's abstractions.

title: ReSeg: Retraining-free segmentation of abdominal organs via generalizable semantic representation learning
description:
arXiv:2610.29090v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Abdominal organ segmentation is essential in modern medical applications. While existing deep learning approaches demonstrate promising performance, their heavy reliance on large-scale image data raises concerns over generalization capability and privacy risks. This motivates the development of generalizable segmentation training paradigms based on domain-randomized image synthesis, facilitating generalization across unseen real image domains. However, existing paradigms either suffer from limited segmentation performance when applied to abdominal organs, or require dataset-specific finetuning. To address these limitations, we propose ReSeg, a novel two-stage retraining-free framework for domain-agnostic zero-shot abdominal organ segmentation. At the first stage, our organ-agnostic synthetic data-driven pretraining approach exploits semantically and visually diverse synthetic images generated by a dedicated data engine to optimize a Generalizable Semantic Representation Network (GSRNet). The network is thereby capable of learning semantic features robust against variations in anatomical structure, imaging contrast, resolution and spatial context, which provide universal representation capabilities that serve as a foundation for segmentation learning. Subsequently, in the second stage, we continue to train an Organ-specific Encoder-decoder Segmentation Network (OESNet), whose encoder is initialized with the pretrained weights. This training process is facilitated by another dedicated data engine, which generates diversified visual images while strictly retaining the inherent spatial layout of abdominal organs. Comprehensive evaluation on seven abdominal organ segmentation datasets across three different modalities including CT, MRI, and PET demonstrates that ReSeg consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods while eliminating the need for real training images.
