title: Python Data structures
description:
Introduction

When you go to a grocery store, you don't throw eggs, milk, and apples loosely into a single giant box. You instead put the eggs in a carton, the milk in a jug, and the apples in a bag.
In programming, data structures are those containers. They are specialized ways of organizing and storing data in your computer's memory so that you can access, sort, and modify your information efficiently.

1. The Core Four Data Structures

Python has four built-in data structures that handle almost every data organization task you will encounter.

Lists

A list is an ordered, mutable collection of items enclosed in square brackets [], with elements separated by commas.

  • Ordered: Items maintain their position and can be accessed using an index, starting from 0.
  • Mutable: Items can be added, removed, or modified after the list is created.
  • Allows duplicates: A list can contain repeated values.
  • Supports different data types: A list can contain strings, integers, floats, booleans, and other objects.

Code Snippet:


# =====================================
# UNDERSTANDING LISTS IN PYTHON
# =====================================

# 1. Creating a list
shopping_list = ["Milk", "Eggs", "Bread"]

print("Original List:", shopping_list)

# 2. ORDERED - Accessing items using indexes
print("\nFirst Item:", shopping_list[0])
print("Second Item:", shopping_list[1])

# 3. MUTABLE - Adding a new item
shopping_list.append("Butter")
print("\nAfter Adding Butter:", shopping_list)

# 4. MUTABLE - Modifying an existing item
shopping_list[1] = "Cheese"
print("After Replacing Eggs:", shopping_list)

# 5. MUTABLE - Removing an item
shopping_list.remove("Bread")
print("After Removing Bread:", shopping_list)

# 6. ALLOWS DUPLICATES
shopping_list.append("Milk")
print("\nAfter Adding Duplicate Milk:", shopping_list)

# 7. Checking the number of items
print("Total Items:", len(shopping_list))

Output:

Common List Operations in Python

Operation Python Code Purpose
Create items = ["A", "B"] Creates a list.
Access items[0] Gets the first item.
Add items.append("C") Adds an item at the end of the list.
Insert items.insert(1, "C") Inserts an item at a specified index.
Modify items[0] = "D" Changes an existing item.
Remove items.remove("B") Removes the first matching item.
Delete items.pop() Removes and returns the last item.
Count len(items) Returns the number of items in the list.

Key Takeaway: Python uses zero-based indexing, meaning the first item is at position 0, not 1.

Tuples

A tuple is an ordered, immutable collection of items, typically enclosed in parentheses () and separated by commas.

Unlike lists, tuples cannot be modified after creation. This means you cannot add, remove, or replace individual elements within a tuple.

Key characteristics of tuples:

  • Ordered: Elements maintain their position and can be accessed using indexes, starting from 0.
  • Immutable: Elements cannot be added, removed, or reassigned after the tuple is created.
  • Allows duplicates: Tuples can contain repeated values.
  • Supports different data types: A tuple can store strings, integers, floats, and other Python objects.
  • Supports unpacking: Values can be assigned to individual variables.

Code Snippet:


# =====================================
# UNDERSTANDING TUPLES IN PYTHON
# =====================================

# 1. Creating a tuple
# Fixed GPS coordinates (Latitude, Longitude)
nairobi_coords = (-1.218, 36.889)

print("Original Coordinates:", nairobi_coords)

# 2. ORDERED - Accessing elements by index
print("\nLatitude:", nairobi_coords[0])
print("Longitude:", nairobi_coords[1])

# 3. UNPACKING - Assigning values to variables
latitude, longitude = nairobi_coords

print("\nUnpacked Latitude:", latitude)
print("Unpacked Longitude:", longitude)

# 4. IMMUTABLE - Attempting to modify a tuple
try:
    nairobi_coords[0] = -1.300

except TypeError:
    print("\nERROR: Tuples cannot be modified!")

# 5. LENGTH - Counting elements
print("\nTotal Elements:", len(nairobi_coords))

Output:

Lists vs Tuples in Python

Feature List [] Tuple ()
Ordered Yes Yes
Mutable Yes No
Allows duplicates Yes Yes
Indexing Yes Yes
Supports different data types Yes Yes
Add/remove elements Yes No
Common use Shopping lists, inventory, changing data Coordinates, fixed configuration values, records

Key Takeaway:

  • Lists: Use when you need an ordered collection of items that can be modified.
  • Tuples: Use when you need an ordered collection whose elements should remain unchanged.

Dictionaries

A dictionary is a mutable collection of data stored in key-value pairs, enclosed in curly braces {}.

Unlike lists and tuples, which primarily access elements using numerical indexes, dictionaries allow you to retrieve values using unique keys.

Each key acts as an identifier that maps to a corresponding value, similar to how a word in a physical dictionary maps to its definition.

Key characteristics of dictionaries:

  • Key-value pairs: Each element consists of a key and its associated value.
  • Mutable: You can add, update, or remove key-value pairs after creation.
  • Unique keys: Duplicate keys are not allowed. Assigning a value to an existing key replaces its previous value.
  • Insertion ordered: Dictionaries preserve the order in which keys are inserted (Python 3.7+).
  • Flexible data types: Values can contain strings, numbers, lists, tuples, or even other dictionaries.
  • Fast lookups: Dictionaries typically provide efficient access to values through their keys.

Code snippet:


# =====================================
# UNDERSTANDING DICTIONARIES IN PYTHON
# =====================================

# 1. Creating a dictionary
user_profile = {
    "username": "dev_alex",
    "age": 28,
    "clearance": "admin",
    "active": True
}

print("Original Profile:", user_profile)

# 2. ACCESSING VALUES USING KEYS
print("\nUsername:", user_profile["username"])
print("Clearance:", user_profile["clearance"])

# 3. SAFE ACCESS USING .get()
print("Department:", user_profile.get("department", "Not Assigned"))

# 4. MUTABLE - Adding a new key-value pair
user_profile["department"] = "Engineering"
print("\nAfter Adding Department:", user_profile)

# 5. MUTABLE - Updating an existing value
user_profile["clearance"] = "super_admin"
print("Updated Clearance:", user_profile["clearance"])

# 6. MUTABLE - Removing a key-value pair
user_profile.pop("age")
print("\nAfter Removing Age:", user_profile)

# 7. CHECKING IF A KEY EXISTS
if "username" in user_profile:
    print("\nUsername exists in the dictionary")

# 8. ITERATING THROUGH KEY-VALUE PAIRS
print("\n--- USER PROFILE DETAILS ---")

for key, value in user_profile.items():
    print(f"{key}: {value}")

# 9. COUNTING KEY-VALUE PAIRS
print("\nTotal Entries:", len(user_profile))

Output:

Lists vs Tuples vs Dictionaries in Python

Feature List [] Tuple () Dictionary {}
Ordered Yes Yes Yes (insertion order)
Mutable Yes No Yes
Allows duplicates Yes Yes Values: Yes; Keys: No
Access elements Numerical index Numerical index Unique keys
Supports mixed data types Yes Yes Yes
Add/remove elements Yes No Yes
Common use Shopping lists, inventory Coordinates, fixed records User profiles, configurations, structured records

Key takeaway:

  • Dictionaries are ideal when you want to store, organize, and retrieve related information using meaningful keys rather than numerical positions.
  • They are widely used in Python applications, JSON processing, APIs, data engineering, and configuration management.

Sets

A set is an unordered, mutable collection of unique elements, typically enclosed in curly braces {}.

Unlike lists and tuples, sets do not allow duplicate values. If an element appears more than once, Python automatically keeps only one occurrence.

Sets are particularly useful for removing duplicates, checking membership, and performing mathematical operations such as unions, intersections, and differences.

Key characteristics of sets:

  • Unordered: Elements do not have fixed positions or numerical indexes.
  • Mutable: You can add or remove elements after creating a set.
  • Unique elements: Duplicate values are automatically eliminated.
  • No indexing: You cannot access elements using positions such as my_set[0].
  • Hashable elements: Set elements must be hashable, such as integers, strings, or tuples containing hashable values. Lists and dictionaries cannot be direct set elements.
  • Efficient membership testing: Sets are useful for quickly checking whether an item exists in a collection.

Code snippet:


# =====================================
# UNDERSTANDING SETS IN PYTHON
# =====================================

# 1. CREATING A SET
# Duplicate employee ID 101 is automatically removed
unique_ids = {101, 102, 103, 101}

print("Original Set:", sorted(unique_ids))

# 2. MUTABLE - Adding a new element
unique_ids.add(104)
print("\nAfter Adding 104:", sorted(unique_ids))

# 3. UNIQUE ELEMENTS - Adding a duplicate
unique_ids.add(102)
print("After Adding Duplicate 102:", sorted(unique_ids))

# 4. MUTABLE - Removing an element
unique_ids.remove(103)
print("\nAfter Removing 103:", sorted(unique_ids))

# 5. MEMBERSHIP TESTING
if 101 in unique_ids:
    print("\nEmployee ID 101 exists in the system.")

# 6. SET OPERATIONS
morning_shift = {101, 102, 105}
evening_shift = {102, 104, 106}

# UNION - All unique employees across both shifts
print("\nUnion:", sorted(morning_shift | evening_shift))

# INTERSECTION - Employees in both shifts
print("Intersection:", sorted(morning_shift & evening_shift))

# DIFFERENCE - Employees only in the morning shift
print("Difference:", sorted(morning_shift - evening_shift))

# 7. COUNTING UNIQUE ELEMENTS
print("\nTotal Unique IDs:", len(unique_ids))

Output:

Note: I used sorted() to display the elements in ascending order, making the output easier to follow. It returns a sorted list without changing the original set. Sets themselves do not guarantee an iteration order.

Comparison of Python Collections

Feature List [] Tuple () Dictionary {} Set {}
Ordered Yes Yes Yes No
Mutable Yes No Yes Yes
Allows Duplicates Yes Yes Keys: No, Values: Yes No
Supports Indexing Yes Yes Key-based access No
Add/Remove Elements Yes No Yes Yes
Common Use Shopping lists, inventory Coordinates, fixed records User profiles, configurations Unique IDs, removing duplicates

Key takeaway: Use sets when you need to store unique values, remove duplicates, perform membership checks efficiently, or compare collections using mathematical set operations.

For example, in data analytics, sets can help identify customers appearing in two datasets, detect unique product IDs, and compare records between different data sources.

2. Cheat Sheet: When to Use Each One

Choosing the right structure keeps your program fast and free of bugs. Use this simple rule of thumb:

Data Structure Best Used For... Example
List [] Collections of data that need to stay in order and might change later. A list of task names in a to-do app.
Tuple () Fixed, read-only data that must stay safe from accidental changes. Days of the week or config settings.
Dictionary {} Complex data that needs descriptive labels for fast lookups. A product page with price, color, and size.
Set {} Finding unique values or running math checks like finding overlaps. Tracking unique visitors to a website.

3. Practical Example: The Event Registration Manager

Let's bring all four data structures together into a single program that manages guest attendance for a tech conference.

Code snippet:

# ------------Event Registration Manager--------------------
# 1. TUPLE: Fixed event information that should never change
EVENT_INFO = ("Global Tech Summit", "Main Arena", "Day 1")

# 2. LIST: The active queue of arriving VIPs (we need order and flexibility)
vip_queue = ["Sarah", "Michael", "David"]
vip_queue.append("Elena")  # A new VIP arrives and is added to the end

# 3. DICTIONARY: Attendee profiles for quick lookup by ticket ID
attendee_profiles = {
    "TK-890": {"name": "Sarah", "type": "VIP", "checked_in": True},
    "TK-432": {"name": "John", "type": "Standard", "checked_in": False},
    "TK-112": {"name": "Michael", "type": "VIP", "checked_in": True}
}

# 4. SET: Tracking unique industries represented (no duplicates allowed!)
industries_present = {"Finance", "Healthcare", "Tech", "Finance"} # 'Finance' is repeated

# --- PROCESSING THE EVENT DATA ---
print(f"--- WELCOME TO THE {EVENT_INFO[0].upper()} ---")
print(f"Location: {EVENT_INFO[1]} | Schedule: {EVENT_INFO[2]}\n")

# Looking up a profile using a Dictionary Key
search_ticket = "TK-890"
guest_name = attendee_profiles[search_ticket]["name"]
print(f"Ticket Lookup: Ticket {search_ticket} belongs to {guest_name}.")

# Displaying the VIP order from our List
print(f"Next VIP in line to speak: {vip_queue[0]}")

# Displaying our Set (Notice how the duplicate 'Finance' is automatically gone)
print(f"Unique industries attending today: {industries_present}")

Output:

  • Tuple Protection: EVENT_INFO guarantees that nobody can accidentally overwrite the event name or location mid-program.
  • List Flexibility: vip_queue preserves the order of arrivals and lets us pull or add speakers dynamically.
  • Dictionary Speed: attendee_profiles allows us to instantly pull up a specific person's profile using their ticket code without scanning the entire database.
  • Set Cleanliness: industries_present cleans our metadata automatically, ensuring we only see a list of unique industries without any repeating clutter.

Conclusion

Data structures are the architectural backbone of clean code. By mastering lists, tuples, dictionaries, and sets, you no longer just write code instructions—you map out data intentionally. This structural organization is exactly how massive platforms like Spotify manage playlists (lists), handle user accounts (dictionaries), and eliminate duplicate song recommendations (sets).

title: React Bottom Sheet for the Web: Snap Points, Drag, Keyboard
description:
TL;DR

A React bottom sheet for the web is a draggable dialog pinned to the bottom of the screen, so build it on a DOM dialog primitive: Base UI's Drawer (maintained) or vaul (unmaintained per its README, still the most complete option on Radix). Pass snap points as fractions from 0 to 1 in a stable array, let the body scroll only at the last point, raise the sheet above the on-screen keyboard with the visualViewport API, and pad the part that touches the bottom edge with env(safe-area-inset-bottom). The free Wingo UI Drawer does all of this on top of vaul 1.1.2.

Search for a React bottom sheet and many of the top results are React Native packages such as @gorhom/bottom-sheet, which reach the browser only through React Native Web. This guide is about the React bottom sheet web apps need: a real dialog in the DOM, pointer events, position: fixed, an on-screen keyboard that covers half the screen and a home indicator under your Save button. It covers the five parts that decide whether a sheet feels native on a phone (snap points, drag to dismiss, nested sheets, the keyboard and the safe area), with code for vaul and for the free Wingo UI Drawer, which is built on it.

Which React bottom sheet library works on the web?

For apps that render to the DOM, vaul and Base UI's Drawer are the two serious choices, because both sit on a dialog primitive: focus trapping, Escape and the accessible title come with them. As of October 2026, from the npm registry and each project's docs:

Library Built on Snap points Nested sheets Latest release
vaul Radix Dialog Fractions or px strings Drawer.NestedRoot 1.1.2, Dec 14, 2024
Base UI Drawer Base UI Dialog Fractions, px or rem Yes, styled with CSS variables @base-ui/react 1.8.0, Sep 4, 2026
react-modal-sheet Motion Fractions or px, including 0 (closed) and 1 Not documented 5.6.0, Mar 27, 2026
react-spring-bottom-sheet react-spring, react-use-gesture A function of the content's min and max height Not documented 3.4.1, Jun 1, 2022

Three facts the table cannot show change the decision. Vaul's README says "This repo is unmaintained", and no release has shipped since December 2024; its peer range still includes React 19, and the Wingo UI Drawer runs on it with React 19.3. react-spring-bottom-sheet's peer range stops at React 18. react-modal-sheet's README says it "doesn't include any built-in accessibility properties", so focus trapping and dialog semantics are yours to add.

If your project already uses Base UI, the default for new shadcn/ui projects since July 2026, use its Drawer: it is maintained and covers snap points, nesting and the keyboard (Drawer.VirtualKeyboardProvider). On Radix, vaul is still the most complete option, and the rest of this guide is about the gaps you cover around it.

How do vaul drawer snap points work?

Vaul drawer snap points are stops on the way up, listed from least to most visible: a number is a fraction of the screen height (0.45 is 45%), a string is pixels ("320px"). The sheet renders at full height and is translated down to the active point. Three details trip people up in vaul 1.1.2:

  1. Fractions from 0 to 1. The type comment says "Array of numbers from 0 to 100", but the code multiplies each number by the window height, so 50 means fifty screens. Write 0.5.
  2. Pixels only. A string goes through parseInt, so "30rem" becomes 30 pixels.
  3. Hoist the array. Vaul re-runs its snap effect whenever snapPoints changes identity, so an inline literal re-snaps the sheet on every parent render.

Then decide what scrolls. Below the last point the body should stay still, so an upward swipe drags the sheet instead of scrolling a list the user can only half see. fadeFromIndex picks the point where the overlay starts to dim; it defaults to the last one, so a half-open sheet leaves the page bright.

Make the React bottom sheet modal when it holds a task. Pass modal={false} when the page behind must stay usable, like a results list over a map:

"use client";

import { useState } from "react";
import { Drawer, type DrawerSnapPoint } from "@/components/ui/drawer";

// fractions of the screen height, least visible first; one array for the app's lifetime
const SNAP_POINTS: DrawerSnapPoint[] = [0.45, 1];

type Apartment = { id: string; title: string; rent: string };

export function MapResults({ apartments }: { apartments: Apartment[] }) {
  const [snap, setSnap] = useState<DrawerSnapPoint | null>(SNAP_POINTS[0]);
  return (
    <Drawer
      defaultOpen
      modal={false}
      dismissible={false}
      snapPoints={SNAP_POINTS}
      activeSnapPoint={snap}
      onActiveSnapPointChange={setSnap}
      title="Apartments in Chicago"
      description={`${apartments.length} results in the map area`}
    >
      <ul className="flex flex-col gap-3">
        {apartments.map((a) => (
          <li key={a.id} className="flex justify-between gap-3 text-[15px]">
            <span className="truncate">{a.title}</span>
            <span className="font-semibold tabular-nums">{a.rent}</span>
          </li>
        ))}
      </ul>
    </Drawer>
  );
}

With snap points, dismissible={false} stops the sheet at its first point, so the list can never be dragged away behind the map. The Drawer keeps one array per distinct list of points even when you pass a literal, lets the body scroll only at the last point, and steps to the next point on a tap on the handle.

How does drag to dismiss decide when to close?

By distance or speed, measured when the finger lifts. Without snap points, vaul closes the sheet when you let go past 25% of its height (closeThreshold, default 0.25) or flick it faster than 0.4 pixels per millisecond; anything less eases back over 500ms on cubic-bezier(0.32, 0.72, 0, 1). With snap points it settles on the nearest point, a flick moves one point in its direction, and a flick faster than 2 pixels per millisecond closes the sheet or opens it fully. The harder part is when a drag should not start at all. Vaul 1.1.2 refuses one:

  • from inside a scrollable element that is not at its top, so a long list scrolls first;
  • for a moment after the content scrolled (scrollLockTimeout: 100ms in the code, although the type comment says 500ms);
  • while text is selected, from a native <select>, or from anything inside [data-vaul-no-drag];
  • in the first 500ms after opening.

Left and right drawers skip the scroll and timing checks. For content with its own horizontal gestures (a carousel, a map, a range slider) set handleOnly, so only the handle drags. And give every drag a visible alternative: Escape, a tap on the dimmed page and a close button. The Wingo UI Drawer leaves the close button off bottom sheets by default, so pass showClose (panels and dialogs always have one).

The demo below is a listings page. Filters opens a sheet with price, condition and category filters and a pinned button with the result count.

Live demo: Drawer. The original article embeds an interactive demo here (Tap Filters, then drag the sheet down: let go past a quarter of its height or flick it and it closes, a shorter drag settles back. Scroll the categories first: the sheet only drags once the list is back at the top). Try it live on wingo-ui.com or open the Drawer docs. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add drawer

How do you nest bottom sheets?

Open the second sheet from inside the first and push the first one back, like iOS. In vaul that is Drawer.NestedRoot, rendered inside the parent's Drawer.Content; it throws when it has no parent drawer, and as the child opens it shrinks the parent 16px narrower, lifts it 16px and follows the child's drag. It moves the parent only from its own onOpenChange, so a child opened by setting open from state leaves the parent flat.

The Wingo UI Drawer detects nesting from context. A drawer rendered inside another drawer's content uses the nested root on its own and pushes the parent for controlled opens too:

"use client";

import type { ReactNode } from "react";
import { Button } from "@/components/ui/button";
import { Drawer, DrawerBody, DrawerClose, DrawerContent, DrawerFooter, DrawerHeader, DrawerRoot, DrawerTrigger } from "@/components/ui/drawer";

export function DeliveryAddress({ addresses, newAddressForm }: { addresses: ReactNode; newAddressForm: ReactNode }) {
  return (
    <DrawerRoot>
      <DrawerTrigger asChild>
        <Button variant="soft" size="sm">Change</Button>
      </DrawerTrigger>
      <DrawerContent>
        <DrawerHeader title="Delivery address" description="Arrives in 1-2 business days" />
        <DrawerBody>
          {addresses}
          {/* inside the first sheet's content, so it nests and pushes the first one back */}
          <Drawer
            title="New address"
            trigger={<Button variant="ghost" fullWidth>Add a new address</Button>}
            footer={
              <DrawerClose asChild>
                <Button size="lg" fullWidth>Save address</Button>
              </DrawerClose>
            }
          >
            {newAddressForm}
          </Drawer>
        </DrawerBody>
        <DrawerFooter>
          <DrawerClose asChild>
            <Button size="lg" fullWidth>Deliver here</Button>
          </DrawerClose>
        </DrawerFooter>
      </DrawerContent>
    </DrawerRoot>
  );
}

Stop at two levels. On a 390px screen a third sheet is a page, so navigate to one.

What happens when the keyboard opens inside a bottom sheet?

The keyboard covers the sheet unless something moves it. On Safari for iOS, and on Chrome for Android since version 108, the keyboard resizes only the visual viewport (Chrome's announcement), so an element at position: fixed; bottom: 0 stays behind it. Vaul's repositionInputs, on by default, listens to visualViewport resize events: while a field has focus it raises the sheet by the height the keyboard covers and shrinks it when it no longer fits above the keyboard.

Two rules make that work in practice:

  • Do not focus a field on open. The Wingo UI Drawer focuses the sheet itself, so the keyboard does not cover half the sheet before anyone has read it; Tab moves on to the first control. When typing is the whole task, such as renaming a list, pass onOpenAutoFocus, call event.preventDefault() and focus the field yourself.
  • Use 16px text in inputs (text-base md:text-sm). iOS Safari zooms into a focused field with smaller text.

Turn repositionInputs off when the sheet handles the keyboard itself, for example a chat composer that follows the keyboard with the Pro useKeyboardInset hook.

How do you keep a bottom sheet clear of the home indicator?

Let the page reach the screen edges with viewport-fit=cover (in Next.js, viewportFit: "cover" in the root layout's viewport export), then pad the part of the sheet that touches the bottom edge with max(env(safe-area-inset-bottom), 16px). The max() keeps 16px of air on devices that report an inset of 0. Pad only the last part: the footer when there is one, otherwise the scrolling body, so its last row can scroll above the indicator. Cap the height at 92dvh so a strip of the page stays visible to tap. On a plain vaul drawer:

"use client";

import type { ReactNode } from "react";
import { Drawer } from "vaul";

type SheetProps = { trigger: ReactNode; title: string; children: ReactNode; actions: ReactNode };

export function BottomSheet({ trigger, title, children, actions }: SheetProps) {
  return (
    <Drawer.Root>
      <Drawer.Trigger asChild>{trigger}</Drawer.Trigger>
      <Drawer.Portal>
        <Drawer.Overlay className="fixed inset-0 z-40 bg-black/40" />
        <Drawer.Content
          aria-describedby={undefined}
          className="fixed inset-x-0 bottom-0 z-50 flex max-h-[92dvh] flex-col rounded-t-[28px] bg-popover outline-none"
        >
          <Drawer.Handle className="mt-2.5" />
          <Drawer.Title className="px-5 pt-3 pb-2 text-[17px] font-semibold">{title}</Drawer.Title>
          <div className="min-h-0 flex-1 overflow-y-auto overscroll-contain px-5">{children}</div>
          {/* the part that touches the bottom edge pads the home indicator */}
          <div className="flex flex-col gap-2 px-5 pt-3 pb-[max(env(safe-area-inset-bottom),16px)]">{actions}</div>
        </Drawer.Content>
      </Drawer.Portal>
    </Drawer.Root>
  );
}

The Wingo UI Drawer pads whichever part comes last. Its variant="floating" instead sits 8px above the safe area with every corner rounded, the look the Action Sheet uses for its iOS variant. The same insets for tab bars, FABs and toasts are in our Tailwind safe area insets tutorial.

Which bottom sheet should you use for each job?

There is no single bottom sheet UI React apps should use for everything. Pick by the job:

Component Use it for Built on Access
Drawer Forms, filters, pickers, results over a map; a side panel or a dialog from 768px (desktop) vaul Free
Action Sheet A short list of actions about one thing, with a separate Cancel and await show() Drawer Pro
Family Drawer A floating sheet that morphs between views, such as a menu and a confirmation vaul Free
Sheet A side panel on desktop that becomes a bottom sheet on phones (mobileSide="bottom") Radix Dialog and motion Free

The Action Sheet also works imperatively: mount an ActionSheetProvider once, take const actionSheet = useActionSheet() in a component, and in a click handler await actionSheet.show({ actions }) resolves with the chosen action's id, or null on Cancel or a dismiss. An action whose onSelect returns a promise keeps the sheet open with a spinner in its row; the sheet closes when the promise resolves, and the row shakes and stays ready to retry when it rejects.

Live demo: Action Sheet. The original article embeds an interactive demo here (Tap the ⋯ button on the listing: the iOS sheet floats above the home indicator with Cancel in its own card. Delete listing shows a spinner in its row until its promise resolves). Try it live on wingo-ui.com or open the Action Sheet docs. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add action-sheet

The Family Drawer keeps one floating sheet and animates its height between views, which suits a short flow like a menu that leads to a confirmation.

Live demo: Family Drawer. The original article embeds an interactive demo here (Tap Try it out and pick an option: the floating sheet morphs to the height of the new view. Drag it down or tap outside to close it). Try it live on wingo-ui.com or open the Family Drawer docs. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add family-drawer

In the registry (release 1.7.0), 39 other items import the Drawer, including the Popover, Select, Dropdown Menu and Dialog, which open as bottom sheets below 768px. Every sheet in an app drags, snaps and pads the same way.

What should you do next?

Install the free Drawer with npx wingo-ui@latest add drawer, open your app at 390px and drag a sheet closed with its list scrolled halfway. For the switch between a centered card and a sheet, read the shadcn responsive dialog tutorial; for touch targets, safe areas and the rest of the phone rules, the mobile-first React components guide and the Mobile UI in React category. The Action Sheet is part of Wingo UI Pro.

Components in this post

  • Drawer (Free): The library's bottom sheet on vaul: drag to dismiss, snap points, nesting, and a side panel or dialog on desktop. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add drawer
  • Family Drawer (Free): A floating bottom drawer that morphs smoothly between stacked views, inspired by the Family app. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add family-drawer
  • Action Sheet (Pro): The iOS action sheet: a short list of actions about one thing, with a title, red destructive rows and a separate Cancel, plus await show(). Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add action-sheet
  • Sheet (Free): A panel that slides in from any edge on a spring: filters, a cart, an inspector or the phone navigation menu, swipeable to close on touch. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add sheet

FAQ

Can I use @gorhom/bottom-sheet in a React web app?

Only through React Native Web: it is a React Native library that needs Reanimated and Gesture Handler. In a Next.js or Vite app that renders to the DOM, use vaul or Base UI's Drawer, which are built on accessible dialog primitives.

Is vaul still maintained?

No. As of October 2026 its README says the repo is unmaintained, and the last release is 1.1.2 from December 14, 2024. It still declares React 19 support; Base UI's Drawer is the maintained alternative.

Why do my vaul snap points not work with values like 50?

Vaul multiplies each number by the screen height, so numbers must be fractions from 0 to 1 (0.5 for half the screen), even though a type comment says 0 to 100. Strings are read as pixels, so write "320px", never rem.

How do I stop a vaul drawer from dragging when I swipe a carousel inside it?

Set handleOnly so only the handle drags the sheet, or add the data-vaul-no-drag attribute to the carousel's root element. Vaul already ignores drags that start on a native select or while text is selected.

Is the Wingo UI Drawer free?

Yes. The Drawer, Family Drawer and Sheet are free and the Action Sheet is Pro. npx wingo-ui@latest add drawer copies the component into your project with the Button, hooks and helpers it imports.

This article was originally published on the Wingo UI blog: React Bottom Sheet for the Web: Snap Points, Drag, Keyboard. The original has the live, interactive demos and is kept up to date.

title: Open weight takes 71.5% of tokens and 23% of spend
description:
AI Gateway Production Index — October 2026

Every month, AI Gateway routes tens of trillions of tokens between production applications and AI labs. That traffic gives us a view of what AI usage actually looks like in today's enterprise, and we publish it here monthly. See the Production Index reports from July, August, and September.

October 2026 summary

  • Open-weight models now process more than seven in ten gateway tokens and account for nearly one in four dollars. Their share of spend has more than quadrupled since June.

  • September’s gateway spend was about 13 times December’s, while the average price per token was 47% lower. Almost one in three teams changed their most-used lab in September, an index record.

  • Nearly 70% of September’s gateway spend on Chinese models went through US-based providers, up from less than 10% in December.

  • Jev was the fastest-adopted model in AI Gateway history, reaching 35% of paid teams in its first two weeks, but it accounted for just 0.27% of gateway spend over that same period. Opus 5.5 took more than one in ten gateway dollars in its own first two weeks, the largest spend share of any September model launch.

Frontier spend up 900%, spend share down 22%

In August, open-weight models processed the majority of AI Gateway token volume for the first time. The money is now following. Open weight’s share of spend has more than quadrupled over the last three months, from one in twenty gateway dollars in June to nearly one in four in September.

Open weight's growth is coming from both ends of its price range, and it mirrors the wider gateway. The cheapest models drive token growth, while the expensive models drive spend.

Led by Kimi K3, models priced at least four times the open-weight average cost per token accounted for about two-thirds of the increase in open-weight spend.

In contrast, DeepSeek-v4.1-Flash alone processed nearly half of all September tokens but took just 2.6% of spend. Its price per token was about a fifth of the open-weight average.

Customers are increasing budgets on both sides of the market. Since December, spend on frontier models has grown tenfold; spend on open-weight models has grown more than seventyfold.

In September, 68% of teams that put more money into open-weight models did the same for closed-weight models. And more than two in five teams already paying for frontier models spent more on them than in August, the highest share this year.

Spending on the frontier is still growing, but spending on alternatives is growing faster. A company can spend more with a frontier lab while relying on it for fewer workloads, so the lab gets more money, but a smaller part of the customer’s business.

AI spend increases 13x while the cost per token halves

Market share is changing hands inside a market that is getting much bigger and cheaper.

September's gateway spend was about 13 times December's, an increase of 1,180%, while the average price per token fell 47%. The median paid customer active in both December and September more than doubled its spend.

Teams are spending more, but labs have to keep winning their business. In September, nearly one in two teams changed their most-used model. And almost one in three changed their most-used lab, an index record.

Even teams with lower token volumes use a wide mix of models. Since December, teams that processed at least 10 million tokens over that period used an average of 15 different models. The average rose to 26 for teams processing at least 100 million tokens, and 42 for those processing at least a billion.

The model is becoming a replaceable part of a much larger investment. Companies can continuously improve their AI products and workflows while changing which models power them. They can spend more on AI without becoming more dependent on any one lab.

Chinese models are big business for American providers

More than two-thirds of September’s gateway spend on Chinese-origin models went to US-based providers, up from less than a tenth in December. The Chinese lab builds the model; the American provider runs it and sells access.

DeepSeek’s models processed 58% of all gateway tokens for 6.6% of spend. More than four in five of those tokens were served by DeepSeek itself, yet two in five dollars spent on its models went through US-based providers.

Moonshot AI, the Beijing-based lab behind Kimi, accounted for 3.6% of gateway tokens and 13.2% of spend in September. US-based providers served nine in ten of those tokens.

Z.ai, also based in Beijing and the creator of GLM, accounted for 7.2% of all tokens and 4.5% of spend. US-based providers served seven in ten.

Customers can use Chinese models through access sold by American providers. For teams that put more money into Chinese models in September, an average of 53% of their spending on those models went through US-based providers and 41% through China-based ones.

The same Chinese model can compete with US-based models while generating revenue for US-based providers.

September model launch scorecard: Jev, Opus 5.5, and GPT-6

Whether a model launch is successful depends on what you measure: how broadly it’s tried, how much usage and spend it receives, or what share of its initial users return. We ranked every model launch in September with at least two weeks of data by these metrics; the tables show the top ten for each. The full scorecard is at the end of the report.

Jev is the most-adopted and most-called model

In its first two weeks, Jev reached more than a third of paid teams, nearly double the reach of Sonnet 5.5 in second place. This is the fastest adoption of any model in AI Gateway history.

Jev also received the most requests of any model in September, even though it launched halfway through the month. Of the teams that tried Jev in week one, 55.6% returned in week two, the fifth-highest retention rate.

Jev is a decision model. Compared with typical language-model requests, a Jev request is faster, cheaper and uses a fraction of the tokens. So although its adoption was fast and broad, it accounted for just 1% of the month’s tokens and 0.15% of spend.

In September, Jev quickly became a popular model for production while remaining a tiny part of the inference bill.

Opus 5.5 takes more than one in ten gateway dollars

The launch that received the most dollars was Opus 5.5, with more than twice the share of any other September launch, followed by GPT-6 Astra and DeepSeek-v4.1-Flash.

Opus 5.5 caught on quickly, with almost nine in ten dollars coming from teams already using Opus 5. Existing customers were trying the new release while the wider Opus family was losing market share.

Across all versions, Opus accounted for almost a third of gateway dollars in September, down from one in two in August. Anthropic’s overall share fell below half of total gateway spend for the first time, dropping from 63.7% to 43.9%.

Luna brought users back; Astra brought spend

GPT-6 Luna reached nearly three out of every twenty paid teams in its first two weeks, in third place behind Jev and Sonnet 5.5. But its return rate was the highest of the month; almost two-thirds of the teams that tried it in its first week came back in the second.

GPT-6 Astra reached a smaller audience but took more budget. In its first two weeks, it accounted for about one in twenty gateway dollars; Luna accounted for less than one in a hundred. Luna reached almost three times as many teams while Astra captured more than five times the share of spend.

OpenAI is attracting more customers with Luna, but capturing far more money with Astra, even though fewer teams use it.

Full September scorecard

Previous AI Gateway Production Index reports

  • May 2026

  • June 2026

  • July 2026

  • August 2026

  • September 2026

About this report

This report uses anonymized, aggregate traffic routed through Vercel AI Gateway through September 2026.

A few notes on measurement:

  • Token volume includes input, output, reasoning, cached-input and cache-creation tokens.

  • Spending is estimated at published list prices; actual bills may differ. Average price per token is estimated spending divided by token volume.

  • Open-weight classifications follow the current AI Gateway model list, a broader definition than in earlier reports.

  • Switching rates compare paid teams with at least 10 million paid tokens in both months. “Most-used” is measured by paid tokens.

  • Provider location means company headquarters.

  • Launch metrics cover external paid teams during each model’s first 14 days. Reach uses paid teams active from the start of the launch month through the data cutoff. Spend share uses total paid gateway spending during the model’s window. Return rate is the share of first-week teams that used it again in week two.

  • Model counts cover December–September, with each version counted separately. Team-size thresholds use total input and output tokens over that period.

  • All figures use the most recent data and protocol available; prior months may be revised as methodology is updated.

title: RiO-DETRv2: Geometry-Aware Uncertainty Modeling Meets Real-Time Oriented Object Detection Transformer
description:
arXiv:2610.29159v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: RiO-DETR is the first real-time end-to-end transformer for oriented object detection, yet further localization gains require a more expressive box representation. Although distributional regression has succeeded in horizontal DETRs, extending it to oriented detection introduces geometry-misaligned boundary modeling and topology-inconsistent orientation refinement. We present RiO-DETRv2, a geometry-aware uncertainty modeling framework for real-time oriented object detection. To resolve the geometry mismatch, Object-Aligned Boundary Distribution Refinement represents box boundaries as probability distributions in an object-aligned coordinate system and progressively refines them across decoder layers. For better orientation topology consistency, we introduce Circular-to-Local Angular Residual Refinement that transitions from global periodic search to local fine-grained estimation. Unified OBB Quality-Aligned Learning further aligns classification, boundary and angular refinement with complete-OBB localization quality. Together, these designs improve localization without compromising efficiency, achieving a better balance between speed and accuracy. Specifically, RiO-DETRv2-l/x achieves 53.7/54.1 mAP50-95 on DOTA, outperforming RiO-DETR-l/x by 1.2/1.5 points with nearly unchanged computational cost. Code is available at https://github.com/RicePasteM/RiO-DETRv2.

title: Two Android ML tests that could never fail, and a TFLite check that can
description:
Two tests in my Android app could never fail. One only counts the labels; the other compares the output with an
answer file that holds no answers. And both of them look at this picture:

The app runs a Keras model exported to LiteRT, the new name of TensorFlow Lite. This post is about one rule: a check
proves something only if you have seen it fail. Here is how mine could not, and the check I would build instead.

Two tests that could not fail

The classification test asks only this of the result
(ClassificationE2ETest.kt, line 66):

assertTrue("Expected top-5 results",
    success.output.size in 1..5)

Any five labels pass, including the five least likely ones the app shows
(part 1
explains why it shows those).

The detection test looks better. It reads a golden file, the saved answer a test compares against, and matches each
expected box by its label and its overlap. Here is the golden file
(detection_golden.json,
its note cut to fit):

{
  "_note": "Golden generation skipped: ...",
  "model": "ssd_mobilenet_v1_detect.tflite",
  "image": "images/test_image.jpg"
}

The note in full reads "Golden generation skipped: No module named 'ai_edge_litert'". No boxes. The match loop runs
once per expected box, so with none it checks nothing, and the size check becomes "at least zero"
(DetectionE2ETest.kt, lines 130 to 131).
The script that should write the answers wrote this placeholder and carried on.

The check that can fail

1. Get the notebook's answer

Start from a real photo with a known answer. KerasHub's own example uses a California quail, and "quail" is class 85
in ImageNet, the label set these classifiers use
(imagenet_utils.py).
Its example downloads the photo with keras.utils.get_file, and on 22 October 2026 Wikimedia answered
403 -- Forbidden. That photo is CC BY-SA 3.0, too, not public domain. So I downloaded a public-domain one from the
U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service,
cropped it square, and loaded it from disk. With my exported preset in the example's place:

image = keras.utils.load_img("california_quail.jpg")
classifier = keras_hub.models.ImageClassifier.from_preset(
    "mobilenet_v3_small_100_imagenet",
    activation="softmax",
)
preds = classifier.predict(np.array([image]))
top_labels = keras_hub.utils.decode_imagenet_predictions(preds)

predict() runs the preset's own preprocessing, so this is the answer the model was built to give. On a computer's
CPU it gave quail 10.30, partridge 3.94, prairie chicken 3.77, black grouse 3.57 and ruffed grouse 3.43. One surprise:
those are raw scores. Despite activation="softmax", the 1,000 scores summed to 162.5, not 1.

2. Check the .tflite file in Python first

Run the .tflite file on the array the Keras model sees after preprocessing (KerasHub's hint is
model(model.preprocessor(x))), with the interpreter code from the
keras.io guide. Then compare the two outputs the way KerasHub's own export
tests do
(test_case.py):

abs_diff = np.abs(keras_val - litert_val)
mean_abs_diff = np.mean(abs_diff)
max_abs_diff = np.max(abs_diff)

On the quail photo they agreed: max_abs_diff 1.1e-05 and mean_abs_diff 1.9e-06 over the 1,000 scores, with the
same five labels in the same order and quail at 10.31 in both. If the file disagrees with the notebook here, the phone will too, and the bug is
in the export, not the app.

3. Hold the phone to the saved answer

Save the five labels and scores as the golden file, or for detection the boxes as label, score, x1, y1, x2,
y2: the keys my detection test already reads. Push the same photo to the phone and keep the test's matching rule:
the same label, and a box overlap of 0.5 or more, measured as IoU (the area two boxes share divided by the area they
cover together). Two guards make it a test that can fail:

  • An empty or missing golden file fails. It never counts as a pass.
  • The same pixels go in. The preset crops the photo to a square before it resizes it, and my app stretches it. Use a square photo, or crop it first.

Here it is failing

I copied my app's preprocessing into Python (resize to 224 by 224, then the preset's numbers) and fed the same file
the same square photo. Quail still came first, at 10.11 instead of 10.31, but prairie chicken and partridge swapped
places. A check that compares the ordered five labels fails right there, with the right numbers in the sidecar: what
is left is the resize step. That is the rule working, on a computer's CPU; I did not run the phone for this post.

What I have not solved

How close is close enough? My app's resize alone moved the top score by 0.2 and swapped two labels, before any
quantization (weights stored in fewer bits to make the file smaller). KerasHub's thresholds are set by hand, per model
and per output, and I do not have a rule for picking one. If you have one, I would like to read it.

The two tests are still in the repo as they were at commit b8d3e2f (3 July 2026). The scores and differences above come from a run
on 22 October 2026 with keras 3.15.1, keras-hub 0.32.0, litert-torch 0.10.0 and ai-edge-litert 2.3.0.

Next: five ways the export itself breaks, each with its public record →

title: Designing clearer link labels for short-drama discovery
description:
A short clip often becomes the entry point to a full drama. The next step should be simple: learn what the title is about, then see where the full story can be watched. In practice, search results can mix official platform pages, mirrors, clips, and unrelated uploads. When a discovery site puts all of these behind identical buttons, the destination becomes a surprise.

Treat link origin as useful context

An outgoing link should tell the visitor what kind of destination to expect before they click. For a short-drama guide, a label such as "Official platform" or "Third-party upload" is more useful than a generic "Watch now" button. The destination itself still matters, so the label should sit close to the link rather than being buried in a disclaimer.

This is also a content-model problem. A drama page can keep its story summary separate from its viewing links. That makes it possible to update a destination without rewriting the synopsis and to add context to each link without changing the title's description. If the destination cannot be verified, the page should avoid presenting it as official.

Make the limitation visible

Link labels do not guarantee availability or rights. Viewing pages can move, disappear, or vary by region. A guide can be honest about what it knows and still be useful: explain the story, identify the outbound destination, and let the reader decide what to open.

I work on Dravyra, an independent short-drama discovery guide. We distinguish official platform links from third-party uploads and keep story summaries separate from viewing destinations. Dravyra is not affiliated with the platforms it links to. This is a small example of a broader UX principle: tell people where a link goes, especially when the destination changes the meaning of the click.

title: Running a 4B model in 6 GB and training 3B parameters on a laptop
description:
What worked, what didn’t, and what the numbers actually mean.

I’m Gökhan Çava, an independent developer. I published LCGA Local, a source-only research package for local AI on small GPUs. This is the short technical story behind the release, including the parts that did not work.

The constraint: 6 GB of VRAM

The test machine is an RTX 3050 Laptop GPU with 6 GB of VRAM. That is enough for a small model, but not enough to load a 4B model in bf16 alongside a normal KV cache and a desktop session. The release contains two different answers to that constraint.

Serving: Qwen3-4B at a 4.5 GB peak

The serving path uses Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 in int8 with layer streaming and one bf16 layer slot. It is deliberately boring engineering: keep the resident working set below the limit, move weights in as needed, and avoid allocating the whole model at once.

Measured on the 6 GB RTX 3050 Laptop:

  • 4,513 MB peak VRAM
  • ~3.4 tok/s decode
  • 18.8 s first run, 2.4 s warm start
  • One-command entry point: "python llm.py" ("sohbet.cmd" on Windows)

This is not fast by datacenter standards. It is useful for local chat, experimentation, and checking whether a 4B model fits at all.

RAG: citations without a giant vector database

The RAG layer is CPU-only BM25 over a 326-document Wikipedia-derived corpus (4.57 MiB). It returns a passage and a citation, and it declines when the corpus does not support an answer.

On the internal exp48 evaluation (50 covered prompts plus 20 controls):

  • Retrieval: 50/50
  • Single-source answers: 50/50
  • Keyword overlap: 49/50
  • Citations: 50/50
  • Controls answered: 0/20

The one keyword miss is not a factual failure: the answer used the correct Turkish synonym "Büyük Okyanus" instead of the literal "Pasifik". The baseline keyword score was 42/50.

The important limit: this is a small, hand-built evaluation, not a public benchmark. The manual review was performed in the session by the agent and the developer, not by an independent human reviewer. The repository says so in "results/exp48_manual_review.md".

Training: all 3.09B parameters on the same 6 GB GPU

The M5 experiment asks a different question: can the same laptop update the full parameter set of a 3B model, not a LoRA adapter?

Using block streaming and Adafactor, M5 updates all 3.09B parameters on the 6 GB RTX 3050 Laptop:

  • 150-step demo
  • Cross-entropy: 2.5034 → 2.3242
  • 7.67 s/step
  • 4.93 GB peak VRAM

This is a demo, not a convergence study. A 150-step run is enough to show that the memory path works; it is not enough to claim a useful fine-tune. The full report is in "M5_RAPOR.md".

What did not work: the sparse-attention result

The repository also contains the LCGA block-sparse attention experiments. The current quality result is negative: in the measured setup, dense attention reached 12.46 PPL and the sparse variant reached 16.56 PPL. The release includes that result rather than hiding it. The serving and training work is independently useful; the sparse-attention idea still needs more work.

What is in the release

  • Local chat and serving code
  • CPU RAG and a 326-document corpus
  • M1–M5 and P1 training experiments and reports
  • CUDA-graph and research artifacts
  • 79 CPU/parity/cache/RAG tests
  • Press kit and honest limits

What is not in the release

Model weights, checkpoints, caches, and "tools/llama.cpp" are excluded. Qwen3-4B must be downloaded separately. The code is MIT-licensed; the RAG corpus is CC BY-SA 4.0 with attribution in "data/rag/README.md".

Links

  • Repository: https://github.com/byjameson/lcga-local
  • Release: https://github.com/byjameson/lcga-local/releases/tag/v0.1.0
  • Press kit: https://github.com/byjameson/lcga-local/blob/main/PRESS.md

If you run this on a smaller GPU, or if you find a mistake in the evaluation, open an issue. Negative results and corrections are welcome.

title: An Explicit Feedback Contract for Iterative ML-Agent Harnesses
description:
arXiv:2610.28798v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Iterative ML agents develop models by editing code, running experiments, reading a validation score, and choosing what to try next. In current harnesses this loop is served by an exact validation score returned after every attempt, which leaves the validation split open to adaptive selection. In this work, we introduce an explicit feedback contract for ML-agent harnesses, which specifies what an agent may observe, when iteration should stop, and when the test split may be touched. The contract releases a validation score only when a submission clears a noise threshold computed from the paired standard error, so no margin has to be tuned. We ran experiments on click-through-rate prediction, learning to rank, and a control task with no signal to find. The control is the sharpest case, because the true gain there is zero by construction: an agent reading exact scores ended by reporting a gain of 0.0157, while under the contract it reported 0.0033. On both real tasks the contract narrows the validation-test gap, and test performance is slightly higher rather than lower. The largest difference is in when the agents stop. Exact feedback used its entire budget of thirty submissions on two of the three tasks, including the one where nothing can be learned, while the contract halted after four to twelve. A run that exhausts its budget is usually read as diligence. It is better read as a symptom: when the feedback channel is unbounded, noise keeps supplying improvements to chase.

title: AviorSwap - Why Clear Transaction Status Matters
description:
Pending, Confirmed, or Failed? Crypto Apps Need Better Status Messages

One thing that can make a crypto application stressful to use is not knowing what's happening after clicking a button.

The transaction has been submitted, but nothing seems to change. Is it still processing? Did the network reject it? Should the user try again?

These are simple questions, yet answering them correctly requires thoughtful engineering and interface design.

A transaction has more than two states

In a traditional web application, users often expect an action to finish almost immediately.

Blockchain transactions work differently. Depending on the network and the operation, there may be several steps between initiating an action and seeing the final result.

A useful interface might distinguish between:

Preparing: The application is gathering the information needed for the transaction.

Awaiting approval: The wallet is waiting for the user to approve a request.

Submitted: The transaction has been broadcast.

Pending: The transaction is waiting for inclusion or further confirmation.

Confirmed: The transaction meets the application's confirmation criteria.

Failed: Reliable information indicates that the operation did not succeed.

These states aren't universal, and some applications may need additional ones. What matters is that each message reflects what the system actually knows.

Why generic errors can create bigger problems

Imagine a user submits a swap and the application displays a timeout.

The timeout might mean that the interface stopped receiving a response. It doesn't necessarily prove that the transaction was never submitted.

If the user immediately repeats the action, they could unintentionally initiate another transaction.

A better interface explains that the outcome is uncertain and provides a safe way to check the original transaction's status.

This is a good example of why error handling is more than a frontend detail. It can affect how users behave when something unexpected happens.

Looking at AviorSwap from a UX perspective

AviorSwap provides a useful context for thinking about exchange interfaces and the communication required around financial operations.

When evaluating a crypto exchange, I'd pay attention to how it communicates pending transactions, confirmations, failures, and the information users need to investigate a transaction.

I would also want to know whether the displayed status comes from reliable transaction data rather than simply from a frontend button state.

These are evaluation criteria, not claims about the performance of AviorSwap's live transaction workflow.

What developers can do better

A few practical improvements can make a difference:

Use precise language. Don't label a transaction successful before the required confirmation criteria are met.

Preserve transaction references. Where available, provide a transaction hash so users can investigate its status.

Avoid unsafe repetition. Make it easy to check an existing transaction before initiating another.

Explain the next step. Tell users whether they should wait, review a wallet request, or investigate a confirmed failure.

Final thoughts

Users don't expect every transaction to finish instantly. They do expect an application to communicate clearly.

For me, good transaction-status design is about reducing uncertainty without promising more than the underlying system can guarantee.

What's more frustrating when using a crypto app: waiting for confirmation or receiving an error message that doesn't explain what happened?

title: Clinical radar heart sounds with echocardiographic phenotypes of ventricular dysfunction and valvular disease
description:
arXiv:2610.29267v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Radar heart sounds capture cardiac mechanical activity without contact, while echocardiography characterizes ventricular and valvular function. Paired measurements connect these signals to structural heart disease, yet such data remain sparsely represented in public resources. Here we present 537 radar heart-sound recordings paired with one echocardiographic report for each of 162 patients. The cohort covers three overlapping phenotypes: left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) below 50%, regional wall-motion abnormality and at least moderate valvular regurgitation, present in 38, 43 and 39 patients, respectively. Original complex signals, processed radar heart sounds and temporal quality segmentation support signal-to-phenotype analysis. Technical validation retains 95.93% of signal duration and confirms reproducible waveform reconstruction. Patient-level five-fold evaluation achieves a mean outer-test AUROC of $0.770\pm0.138$ for reduced LVEF, identifying mechanical information associated with ventricular systolic dysfunction. This resource supports research linking non-contact cardiac mechanical signals to echocardiographic structural and functional phenotypes.

title: Propose, Then Confirm: How We Let an AI Change Real Business Data Without Fear
description:
I run a small coworking space in Burgas, Bulgaria, with my wife. I also build OhMyDesk, the software we run it on.

Most of the admin in a small space happens on the go. Someone walks in and wants a desk tomorrow. A member pays in cash. A bill for coffee beans arrives. You are standing at the door with a phone, not at a desk with a dashboard.

So we added an AI operator to the Telegram bot that already sent us booking alerts. You type what you need in plain words. It answers questions about your space, and it can do the work.

That second part is scary. An AI that answers questions can be wrong and you shrug. An AI that writes to your bookings and invoices can be wrong and you lose money or a customer.

Here is the pattern that let us ship it anyway.

The rule: the model never writes, it only proposes

Every action goes through two steps.

  1. Propose. The AI reads your live data and builds a concrete change. For example: "Book Alex on Desk 2 (Room 1), Tue 30 Jun, 1 day, 8 EUR."
  2. Confirm. The chat shows that change with a Confirm button. Only the tap saves it.

A real booking looks like this:

You:  Book a free desk for June 30
Bot:  There's 1 free desk on June 30. That's Desk 2 (Room 1).
      Who should I book it for?
You:  Alex
Bot:  Book Alex — Desk 2 (Room 1), Tue 30 Jun · 1 day · 8 EUR
      [Confirm]
Bot:  ✅ Booked Alex on Desk 2 (2026-06-30).

Four messages. No forms. And the AI never had the power to save anything by itself.

If you build an agent that touches real data, I think this is the single most useful rule. Below are the lessons that came with it.

Lesson 1: Make the proposal concrete

A vague proposal is useless. "I will book a desk for Alex" does not let you catch a mistake. Which desk? Which day? At what price?

So every staged action shows the full result: who, what, when and how much. The human checks the same facts they would check on a paper form. If the date is wrong, you see it before it matters.

A good test: could a tired person at 8 a.m. spot the error in two seconds? If not, the proposal needs more detail.

Lesson 2: Ask instead of guess

When a request is missing something, the AI asks. "Who should I book it for?" "Which desk?"

It is tempting to let the model fill gaps with its best guess. Don't. A guess that looks confident is worse than a question. The question costs one message. The wrong guess costs an awkward call to a member.

Lesson 3: Keep short follow-ups in the same thread

People reply with fragments. "10:00." "Desk 4." "Yes, her."

If your agent treats each message as a new request, a fragment like "Desk 4" means nothing. Worse, it might start a new action. We made sure a short follow-up stays attached to the open conversation. The time or desk number fills the missing slot in the proposal already on the table.

This sounds small. In practice it is the difference between a chat that feels natural and one that feels like a broken form.

Lesson 4: Never let the model make up a number

Operators ask things like "revenue this month versus last" or "how many desks are free this week."

A language model will happily produce a plausible number. That is the worst possible failure for a business tool, because nobody checks a number that looks right.

So answers are grounded in the space's live data. If the data is not there, the answer says so. And each space only ever sees its own data. The AI cannot read another space's records.

Lesson 5: A stray message must be harmless

Telegram is a busy app. People type in the wrong chat. They paste text by accident. Kids grab phones.

With propose-then-confirm, a random message can at worst produce a proposal you ignore. It cannot cancel a booking or mark an invoice paid on its own. That gave us the confidence to let the bot do real work, not only answer questions.

Lesson 6: Speak the operator's language

Our customers are small spaces across Europe. Many prefer to type in their own language.

The operator can write in English, Bulgarian, Russian or most other European languages, and the bot replies in the same language. Since the action itself is structured (a date, a desk, an amount), the language of the chat does not change what gets saved.

Lesson 7: Draft, don't send

Some actions should stop one step earlier. An invoice is one of them.

When you ask the AI to draft an invoice, it saves a draft on the Invoices page. It does not send anything to the member. You review it and send it yourself. Money sent to the wrong person in the wrong amount is very hard to take back, so the human keeps the last word.

What the AI can do today

For context, this is the list of actions the operator can stage, each behind a Confirm tap:

  • book, cancel, or mark a desk booking paid;
  • mark an invoice paid, which also records the payment;
  • freeze or reactivate a dedicated desk plan;
  • log an expense with amount, category and date;
  • let or vacate a private office;
  • capture a new lead;
  • draft an invoice for a member or a one-off guest.

It also answers questions like who is in today, which plans end soon, and which leads have gone quiet.

If you are building an agent that writes data

A short checklist, whatever your domain:

  1. The model proposes. A human confirms. Nothing else can save.
  2. Show the full change in the proposal: who, what, when, how much.
  3. Ask when a detail is missing. Never guess silently.
  4. Keep short replies attached to the open request.
  5. Ground every number in real data. Say "I don't know" when it is not there.
  6. Scope every request to one customer's data.
  7. For anything that leaves the building (emails, invoices), stop at a draft.

None of this needs a better model. It needs a smaller job for the model and a clear button for the human.

If you want to see how it looks in a real product, the OhMyDesk AI Autopilot page has a short demo. The rest of the product is on ohmydesk.app.

I would love to hear how others handle this. Do you let your agents write data directly, or do you keep a human tap in the loop?

title: Second Thoughts: Exploring and Planning through Comparative Imagination in World Models
description:
arXiv:2610.28779v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: World models let agents compare imagined outcomes before acting, but an agent must still decide which alternatives to explore and when a proposed plan should replace its learned policy. We introduce SDI (Sibling Disagreement in Imagination), which connects these decisions through a shared actor-based reference. SDI compares action sequences imagined from the same model state, using repeated rollouts of the actor's own sequence to measure variation under fixed behavior. This reference scales both the spread across candidate returns, which provides an exploration signal, and a proposed plan's predicted advantage, which governs action acceptance. The agent executes a planned action when its advantage exceeds the reference variability by a fixed factor; otherwise, it follows the actor. SDI reuses the base agent's world model, actor, and critic without requiring an additional disagreement ensemble. Exploration and planning guide training data collection, while evaluation uses the learned actor alone. Across Meta-World, Adroit, and DM-Control, SDI achieves a higher observed task-average score than every compared baseline in each suite and matches or exceeds the strongest baseline's performance on 15 of 18 tasks. Component ablations and robustness analyses further examine the roles of exploration, planning exposure, and action acceptance. Paired evaluations from identical simulator states show that the gate improves both recovery from actor failures and preservation of successful behavior relative to ungated planning, while substantially reducing return degradation. Together, these results support comparing imagined alternatives against a shared actor reference as a unified approach to exploring and planning with world models.

title: AviorSwap - Why User Experience Matters in Decentralized Finance
description:
DeFi Needs More Than Innovation — It Needs a Better User Experience

Decentralized finance has introduced new ways to exchange assets, interact with smart contracts, and participate in blockchain ecosystems. But I think one challenge remains: making these tools understandable for people who aren't blockchain experts.

A product can have interesting technology behind it and still struggle if users don't understand how to interact with it.

Complexity Is Still a Barrier

Traditional financial applications have spent years simplifying common tasks. Users expect clear instructions, predictable navigation, and understandable transaction summaries.

DeFi introduces additional concepts, including wallet connections, gas fees, network selection, token approvals, and transaction confirmations.

For experienced users, these may be familiar steps. For newcomers, they can create uncertainty.

I believe the goal shouldn't be to hide the technology. It should be to explain it in a way that makes important decisions easier.

Where Platforms Like AviorSwap Fit In

AviorSwap operates in the crypto exchange space, where users need to navigate assets, exchange options, and transaction details.

When evaluating a platform like this, I'd focus on how clearly it communicates the process.

Can users understand which assets they're exchanging? Are applicable fees visible before confirmation? Is the selected network clear? Can users understand what happens when a transaction is pending?

These questions are important because a smooth experience involves more than the number of features a platform offers.

Of course, evaluating a public website is different from testing every transaction workflow, so these are the criteria I'd use rather than claims about performance.

Good UX Can Help Prevent Mistakes

In financial applications, confusing interfaces can have consequences beyond frustration.

A user might select the wrong network, misunderstand a token approval, or assume that a pending transaction has failed.

Thoughtful design can help reduce these risks through clear labels, informative warnings, useful confirmation screens, and accurate status updates.

The best interfaces don't force users to become technical experts before completing basic tasks. Instead, they provide the right information at the right moment.

Simplicity Without Losing Transparency

There's a balance between making an application simple and removing information users need.

I like interfaces that keep the main workflow straightforward while allowing people to explore additional details when necessary.

For DeFi products, this means making common actions accessible without hiding fees, risks, or transaction conditions.

That approach can benefit beginners while still giving experienced users access to more detailed information.

Final Thoughts

I think the next stage of DeFi adoption depends not only on technical innovation but also on how well products communicate with their users.

Platforms such as AviorSwap provide an opportunity to think about how exchange experiences can become more understandable, transparent, and accessible.

Technology creates possibilities, but the user experience determines how easily people can navigate them.

title: From Comparison to Selection: Enhancing Cross-Scale Generalization of Pointer Networks Trained with Reinforcement Learning for Capacitated Drone Delivery Routing
description:
arXiv:2610.27936v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) enable fast, flexible last-mile and emergency delivery, but their routing remains challenging as the number of clients varies. Classical approaches based on mixed-integer programming and heuristics can scale poorly or require problem-specific design, motivating learning-based alternatives. Reinforcement learning is particularly promising, provided a single policy can generalize across problem sizes without retraining. Although attention-based Pointer Networks are inherently size-agnostic, their solution quality degrades under both upscaling and downscaling. Using the Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem (CVRP) as a controlled proxy, with fixed capacity reflecting drone payload constraints, we investigate this degradation and identify three contributing factors: shifts in node density, attention dispersion, and dilution of the mean-pooled graph context. We systematically compare architecture-wide, encoder-side, and decoder-side modifications to address these limitations and propose a learned, permutation-invariant graph-context aggregation mechanism, implemented as a weighted average and as Set2Set. Results reveal distinct requirements for transfer in each direction: entropy-based attention scaling reduces the CVRP20-to-CVRP100 performance gap by 1.41 percentage points, while the proposed aggregation methods achieve the largest improvement on the more challenging CVRP100-to-CVRP20 transfer, approximately 0.9 percentage points. Exploiting this complementarity, we introduce an approach selector that chooses the best model for each training-target size pair. The selector reduces cost relative to the reference model across all nine seen train-test pairs and eight of nine pairs involving unseen sizes (CVRP35, CVRP75, and CVRP200), achieving improvements of up to 3.2 percent.
