title: Measure First, Then Allocate: Calibrated Rollout Budgets for MCP Agents in Reinforcement Learning
description:
arXiv:2610.28785v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Training tool-using language models requires costly interaction, yet identical rewards within a rollout group provide no group-relative learning signal. We use reward disagreement to guide harness evaluation and the allocation of rollouts for policy training in Model Context Protocol (MCP) environments. We first introduce Discord, which tests harness edits using exact paired inference and decision-preserving early stopping: only disagreeing paired outcomes favor one harness over another. This insight motivates prospective allocation in BRACE (Bank-calibrated Rollout Allocation under Correlated Episodes). BRACE combines historical task evidence, uncertainty in task success rates, and a correlated reward model to forecast mixed-reward groups before allocating generation budget. Controlled harness experiments favor Discord, while live MCP experiments expose a retention-cost trade-off. At three Qwen3-VL model scales, BRACE exceeds the strongest plotted baseline peaks with fewer new training rollouts; historical-bank collection is counted separately. It also leads the compared methods on BFCL and NESTFUL without further training. Ablations probe the bank, estimator, and allocation score; prospective evaluation checks forecast calibration. These results support forecasting reward contrast before generation.

title: Different Defects, Different Effects: A Controlled Audit of Face Recognition Training Data
description:
arXiv:2610.28766v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The development of face recognition has been strongly supported by the availability of large-scale training datasets. Among them, MS-Celeb-1M has played an important role by providing millions of facial images from nearly 100K identities. However, the size and heterogeneity of such datasets increase the likelihood of annotation errors, redundant samples, and other forms of data inconsistency. This motivated the introduction of refined versions, such as MS1MV2 and MS1MV3, aimed at improving the quality of the training data. Despite these cleaning efforts, we show that several types of training-data defects remain in MS1MV3. By proposing complementary data-auditing strategies, we identify five defect categories: exact and near-duplicate images, split identities, crop errors, multiple-face ambiguity, and invalid content. We then assess the effect of correcting these defects under a controlled face-recognition training protocol based on IResNet-50 and ArcFace. The results show that targeted interventions can preserve, and in some cases improve, recognition performance while requiring fewer optimization steps to reach the performance of the original training set. Duplicate removal provides the clearest overall benefit, while split-identity merging and invalid-content removal also improve training efficiency. Overall, the results indicate that the effect of dataset cleaning depends strongly on the type of defect being addressed and provide further evidence that training-data quality remains an important and comparatively underexplored factor in large-scale face recognition. The training manifests and code used in this work will be released upon acceptance.

title: CSD: Common-Support Distillation for Cross-Tokenizer Knowledge Transfer
description:
arXiv:2610.28895v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Cross-tokenizer logits distillation enables knowledge transfer across model families, allowing students to learn from stronger or more specialized teachers. However, differences in vocabulary and segmentation make teacher and student next-token distributions difficult to align. Existing logits-based methods are easy to integrate into standard distillation pipelines, but often rely on restrictive heuristics or tokenizer-pair-specific choices. They may restrict supervision to shared vocabulary subsets, require manually selecting different objectives for different tokenizer pairs, or match only the observed chunk and its complement rather than individual alternative continuations. We introduce Common-Support Distillation (CSD), a unified logits-based framework that constructs a shared support between the teacher and student at each aligned input chunk and matches the induced distributions with a single objective. For one-to-one alignments, CSD uses explicit common-token pairs as the shared support. For other alignments, it constructs a virtual support whose probabilities are computed using the autoregressive chain rule. A residual event captures probability mass outside the explicit support, ensuring that both induced distributions remain normalized. Across four teacher-student settings comprising Llama-3.2-1B and Gemma3-1B-PT students with Qwen and Phi teachers, CSD consistently achieves the highest average performance among the evaluated cross-tokenizer methods, outperforming the strongest alternative by up to 1.8 points and surpassing both continued pretraining and same-tokenizer distillation. For Llama-3.1-8B, CSD improves average accuracy over the strongest evaluated baseline by up to 4.2 points for the base student and 1.6 points for the instruction-tuned student.

title: How to Build a Finance AI Agent With Audit Trails, Controls, and Human Oversight
description:
Here’s a truth about building AI agents for finance that nobody puts in the tutorial: the agent intelligence is maybe 30 percent of the work. The audit trail, the access controls, the human oversight checkpoints, the compliance documentation, that’s the other 70 percent. And that 70 percent is what determines whether your agent runs in production or gets killed in the compliance review before it processes a single transaction.

We learned this the expensive way on our first finance AI agent deployment. Built a beautiful underwriting agent. Elegant reasoning. Clean tool use. Impressive accuracy on test data. The compliance team looked at it for two hours and rejected it because they couldn’t answer one question: “If a regulator asks why the agent recommended denying this loan application, can you show them the exact data and reasoning that produced that recommendation?”

We couldn’t. The agent worked. It just didn’t prove it worked. And in finance, working without proving it is the same as not working.

This article is the guide we wish existed when we started. It covers the audit trail architecture, the access control design, the human oversight implementation, and the code patterns that make a finance AI agent not just functional but auditable, controllable, and compliant.

If you’re building agents that touch money, customer data, or regulatory workflows, this is the engineering that separates a demo from a deployment.

The audit trail isn’t logging. It’s the primary deliverable

Most developers think of audit trails as application logging. Write some events to a log file. Query them when something goes wrong. That’s not what finance compliance requires.

A finance audit trail must capture what data the agent received, what reasoning it applied, what tools it called, what each tool returned, what decision it reached, how confident it was, and what action it took, for every single transaction. And it must store this immutably for seven to ten years in a format that a non-technical regulator can review.

Here’s the data model:

from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from datetime import datetime
from enum import Enum
from typing import Optional
import hashlib
import json


class EvaluationType(Enum):
    DETERMINISTIC = "deterministic"
    AI_ASSISTED = "ai_assisted"
    HUMAN_REVIEWED = "human_reviewed"


class ActionType(Enum):
    AUTO_APPROVED = "auto_approved"
    AUTO_DENIED = "auto_denied"
    ESCALATED = "escalated"
    PENDING_REVIEW = "pending_review"


@dataclass
class AuditRecord:
    """Immutable record of every agent decision."""
    record_id: str
    timestamp: datetime
    agent_id: str
    agent_version: str

    # What was evaluated
    transaction_id: str
    transaction_type: str
    input_data_hash: str          # SHA-256 of exact input
    input_data_snapshot: dict      # Frozen copy of input state

    # How it was evaluated
    evaluation_type: EvaluationType
    rules_applied: list[str]       # Rule IDs for deterministic checks
    model_version: Optional[str]   # For AI-assisted evaluations
    prompt_hash: Optional[str]     # For reproducibility

    # What was concluded
    decision: ActionType
    confidence: Optional[float]
    reasoning_chain: list[dict]    # Step-by-step reasoning

    # What happened next
    escalated_to: Optional[str]
    human_reviewer: Optional[str]
    human_decision: Optional[str]
    human_override_reason: Optional[str]
    human_decision_timestamp: Optional[datetime]

    # Integrity
    previous_record_hash: Optional[str]  # Chain integrity
    record_hash: str = field(init=False)

    def __post_init__(self):
        """Compute hash for tamper detection."""
        content = json.dumps({
            'record_id': self.record_id,
            'transaction_id': self.transaction_id,
            'input_data_hash': self.input_data_hash,
            'decision': self.decision.value,
            'timestamp': self.timestamp.isoformat(),
            'previous_hash': self.previous_record_hash
        }, sort_keys=True)
        self.record_hash = hashlib.sha256(content.encode()).hexdigest()

Two fields in this model deserve specific attention.

input_data_hash and input_data_snapshot serve different purposes. The hash proves that the data hasn’t been modified since the decision was made. The snapshot preserves the exact data state at decision time, because the source data in the ERP may change after the agent evaluated it, and the regulator needs to see what the agent saw, not what the database currently contains.

previous_record_hash creates a chain where tampering with any historical record breaks the hash chain on every subsequent record. This isn’t blockchain, it’s a simple integrity mechanism that makes after-the-fact modification detectable.

The storage architecture matters:

class AuditStore:
    """Append-only audit storage with hot and cold tiers."""

    def __init__(self, hot_store, cold_store, retention_years=7):
        self.hot = hot_store      # PostgreSQL - last 90 days, fast queries
        self.cold = cold_store    # S3 + Parquet - long-term, cost-efficient
        self.retention = retention_years

    async def append(self, record: AuditRecord) -> str:
        """Write to hot store. Never update. Never delete."""
        # Verify chain integrity
        last_record = await self.hot.get_latest(record.agent_id)
        if last_record and record.previous_record_hash != last_record.record_hash:
            raise IntegrityError("Chain broken - previous hash mismatch")

        await self.hot.insert(record)
        return record.record_hash

    async def archive(self, older_than_days=90):
        """Move aged records to cold storage. Hot store stays fast."""
        records = await self.hot.get_older_than(older_than_days)
        await self.cold.write_parquet(records)
        # Mark as archived in hot store - never delete
        await self.hot.mark_archived(records)

The append-only constraint is non-negotiable. No updates. No deletes. No “soft deletes.” If a record needs correction, you append a correction record that references the original. The original stays forever.

The access control layer: least privilege isn’t optional

The agent’s service account should have exactly the permissions it needs and nothing more. This sounds obvious. In practice, it’s the control that most teams get wrong because scoping permissions precisely requires understanding every data access and system interaction the agent performs.

class AgentPermissions:
    """Define and enforce what the agent can access and do."""

    def __init__(self, agent_role: str):
        self.role = agent_role
        self.permissions = self._load_permissions(agent_role)

    def _load_permissions(self, role: str) -> dict:
        """Each agent role has explicit read/write scopes."""
        roles = {
            "ap_processor": {
                "read": [
                    "invoices",
                    "purchase_orders", 
                    "goods_receipts",
                    "vendor_master",        # Read vendor info
                    "approval_matrix",      # Read routing rules
                ],
                "write": [
                    "invoices.status",       # Update processing status
                    "invoices.match_result", # Record match outcome
                    "approval_queue",        # Route for approval
                ],
                "blocked": [
                    "payments.execute",     # Cannot trigger payments
                    "vendor_master.modify", # Cannot change vendor data
                    "general_ledger",       # No GL access
                    "payroll",              # No payroll access
                    "treasury",             # No treasury access
                ],
                "amount_ceiling": 100_000,  # Escalate above this
            },
            "underwriting_analyst": {
                "read": [
                    "loan_applications",
                    "credit_bureau_data",
                    "financial_documents",
                    "compliance_rules",
                ],
                "write": [
                    "applications.risk_assessment",
                    "applications.recommendation",
                    "escalation_queue",
                ],
                "blocked": [
                    "applications.approve",  # Cannot approve loans
                    "applications.deny",     # Cannot deny loans
                    "disbursement",          # No access to funds
                ],
                "amount_ceiling": None,  # All amounts escalate
            }
        }
        return roles.get(role, {"read": [], "write": [], "blocked": []})

    def check_access(self, operation: str, resource: str) -> bool:
        """Enforce permission before every system interaction."""
        if resource in self.permissions.get("blocked", []):
            raise PermissionDenied(
                f"Agent role '{self.role}' is blocked from '{resource}'"
            )

        allowed_resources = self.permissions.get(operation, [])
        if resource not in allowed_resources:
            raise PermissionDenied(
                f"Agent role '{self.role}' lacks '{operation}' on '{resource}'"
            )
        return True

The blocked list is as important as the read and write lists. Explicitly defining what the agent cannot access, even when those resources exist in the same system, creates a documented boundary that compliance teams can review. An AP processing agent that has no path to the payroll system, the treasury system, or the general ledger is an agent whose blast radius is bounded by design.

The amount_ceiling field is the operational authority limit. Transactions above this threshold escalate to a human regardless of how confident the agent is. The ceiling is a business decision, not a technical one, set by the finance leadership based on the organisation’s risk tolerance.

Human oversight: the checkpoint architecture

Human-in-the-loop for finance agents isn’t “a human can review if they want.” It’s a set of defined checkpoints where the agent must stop, present its work, and receive human authorisation before proceeding.

class OversightCheckpoint:
    """Defines when and how the agent pauses for human review."""

    def __init__(self, rules: list[dict]):
        self.rules = rules

    async def evaluate(
        self, 
        transaction: dict,
        agent_assessment: dict,
        audit_trail: list[AuditRecord]
    ) -> CheckpointDecision:
        """Determine if human review is required."""

        for rule in self.rules:
            if self._matches(rule, transaction, agent_assessment):
                return CheckpointDecision(
                    requires_human=True,
                    reason=rule["reason"],
                    reviewer_role=rule["reviewer_role"],
                    context=self._assemble_context(
                        transaction, agent_assessment, audit_trail
                    ),
                    sla_hours=rule.get("sla_hours", 24)
                )

        return CheckpointDecision(requires_human=False)

    def _matches(self, rule, transaction, assessment) -> bool:
        """Check if this transaction triggers a checkpoint."""
        checks = {
            "amount_exceeds": lambda: (
                transaction.get("amount", 0) > rule.get("threshold", 0)
            ),
            "confidence_below": lambda: (
                assessment.get("confidence", 1.0) < rule.get("threshold", 0.85)
            ),
            "new_counterparty": lambda: (
                transaction.get("counterparty_history_days", 999) < 
                rule.get("minimum_days", 90)
            ),
            "exception_type": lambda: (
                assessment.get("exception_type") in 
                rule.get("escalation_types", [])
            ),
            "regulatory_flag": lambda: (
                assessment.get("regulatory_flags", []) != []
            ),
        }

        check_fn = checks.get(rule["condition"])
        return check_fn() if check_fn else False

    def _assemble_context(self, transaction, assessment, trail) -> dict:
        """Give the human everything they need to make a decision."""
        return {
            "transaction_summary": transaction,
            "agent_recommendation": assessment.get("recommendation"),
            "agent_confidence": assessment.get("confidence"),
            "agent_reasoning": assessment.get("reasoning_chain"),
            "relevant_history": self._get_relevant_history(transaction),
            "applicable_rules": assessment.get("rules_checked"),
            "escalation_reason": assessment.get("escalation_reason"),
            "suggested_action": assessment.get("suggested_action"),
            "audit_trail": [r.record_id for r in trail[-5:]],  # Last 5 steps
        }


# Checkpoint rules configuration
CHECKPOINT_RULES = [
    {
        "condition": "amount_exceeds",
        "threshold": 100_000,
        "reason": "Transaction exceeds autonomous authority limit",
        "reviewer_role": "senior_finance",
        "sla_hours": 4
    },
    {
        "condition": "confidence_below",
        "threshold": 0.85,
        "reason": "Agent confidence below threshold",
        "reviewer_role": "domain_specialist",
        "sla_hours": 8
    },
    {
        "condition": "new_counterparty",
        "minimum_days": 90,
        "reason": "Counterparty has less than 90 days of history",
        "reviewer_role": "risk_analyst",
        "sla_hours": 24
    },
    {
        "condition": "regulatory_flag",
        "reason": "Transaction flagged for regulatory review",
        "reviewer_role": "compliance_officer",
        "sla_hours": 4
    },
]

The _assemble_context method is where the oversight becomes genuinely useful rather than merely procedural. A human reviewer who receives “please review this transaction” makes a worse decision than one who receives the transaction data, the agent’s recommendation, the reasoning chain, the applicable rules, and the suggested action. The context assembly is what makes human oversight efficient, the human starts with understanding, not investigation.

The sla_hours field is the detail that operational teams care about. A checkpoint without a response deadline creates a queue that grows without bound. The SLA ensures that escalated transactions are reviewed within a defined window, and transactions that aren’t reviewed within the SLA trigger secondary escalation.

Putting it together: the compliant agent loop

Here’s how the components compose into a complete agent execution loop:

class FinanceAgent:
    """A finance agent that's auditable, controlled, and supervised."""

    def __init__(self, tools, permissions, checkpoints, audit_store, llm):
        self.tools = tools
        self.permissions = permissions
        self.checkpoints = checkpoints
        self.audit = audit_store
        self.llm = llm

    async def process(self, transaction: dict) -> ProcessingResult:
        trail = []

        # Step 1: Deterministic compliance checks first
        compliance_result = await self._run_compliance_checks(transaction)
        trail.append(await self._audit(
            transaction, "compliance_check", 
            EvaluationType.DETERMINISTIC, compliance_result
        ))

        if not compliance_result.passed:
            return ProcessingResult(
                status="compliance_failed",
                details=compliance_result.failures,
                audit_trail=trail
            )

        # Step 2: AI-assisted assessment where judgment is needed
        assessment = await self._run_ai_assessment(transaction)
        trail.append(await self._audit(
            transaction, "ai_assessment",
            EvaluationType.AI_ASSISTED, assessment
        ))

        # Step 3: Check if human oversight is required
        checkpoint = await self.checkpoints.evaluate(
            transaction, assessment, trail
        )

        if checkpoint.requires_human:
            trail.append(await self._audit(
                transaction, "escalated",
                EvaluationType.AI_ASSISTED, 
                {"reason": checkpoint.reason}
            ))
            return ProcessingResult(
                status="pending_human_review",
                context=checkpoint.context,
                reviewer=checkpoint.reviewer_role,
                sla=checkpoint.sla_hours,
                audit_trail=trail
            )

        # Step 4: Execute within authority
        self.permissions.check_access("write", f"{transaction['type']}.status")

        if transaction.get("amount", 0) > self.permissions.permissions.get(
            "amount_ceiling", float("inf")
        ):
            trail.append(await self._audit(
                transaction, "amount_escalation",
                EvaluationType.DETERMINISTIC,
                {"ceiling": self.permissions.permissions["amount_ceiling"]}
            ))
            return ProcessingResult(
                status="escalated_amount_ceiling",
                audit_trail=trail
            )

        # Step 5: Execute and document
        action_result = await self._execute_action(transaction, assessment)
        trail.append(await self._audit(
            transaction, "action_executed",
            EvaluationType.DETERMINISTIC, action_result
        ))

        return ProcessingResult(
            status="completed",
            action=action_result,
            audit_trail=trail
        )

    async def _audit(self, transaction, step, eval_type, data) -> AuditRecord:
        """Every step gets an immutable audit record."""
        record = AuditRecord(
            record_id=generate_uuid(),
            timestamp=datetime.utcnow(),
            agent_id=self.agent_id,
            agent_version=self.version,
            transaction_id=transaction["id"],
            transaction_type=transaction["type"],
            input_data_hash=hash_data(transaction),
            input_data_snapshot=freeze(transaction),
            evaluation_type=eval_type,
            rules_applied=data.get("rules", []),
            model_version=self.llm.model_version if eval_type == 
                EvaluationType.AI_ASSISTED else None,
            prompt_hash=data.get("prompt_hash"),
            decision=data.get("decision", ActionType.PENDING_REVIEW),
            confidence=data.get("confidence"),
            reasoning_chain=data.get("reasoning", []),
            escalated_to=data.get("escalated_to"),
            human_reviewer=None,
            human_decision=None,
            human_override_reason=None,
            human_decision_timestamp=None,
            previous_record_hash=await self.audit.get_latest_hash(
                transaction["id"]
            )
        )
        await self.audit.append(record)
        return record

The execution order matters. Compliance checks run first, deterministic, binary, fast. If the transaction fails a regulatory requirement, there’s no point running the AI assessment. The AI assessment runs second, only for transactions that need interpretive evaluation. The checkpoint evaluation runs third, comparing the transaction characteristics and agent confidence against the oversight rules. The action execution runs last, only for transactions that passed compliance, received a confident assessment, and didn’t trigger a checkpoint.

Every step produces an audit record. The complete chain for a single transaction typically contains four to six records, each linked to the previous by hash. A regulator reviewing a decision can trace the complete chain: what data came in, what compliance checks passed, what the AI assessed and why, whether a human reviewed it, and what action was taken.

The testing that makes compliance teams comfortable

The code above gets you an architecture. The testing below gets you the approval to deploy it.

# Golden test set: known-outcome transactions for regression testing
class ComplianceRegressionSuite:
    """Run against every agent update, every prompt change, every model version."""

    def __init__(self, golden_set_path: str, drift_threshold: float = 0.02):
        self.golden_set = load_golden_set(golden_set_path)
        self.threshold = drift_threshold  # Max 2% decision drift

    async def run(self, agent: FinanceAgent) -> RegressionResult:
        results = []
        for case in self.golden_set:
            actual = await agent.process(case.transaction)
            results.append({
                "case_id": case.id,
                "expected_decision": case.expected_decision,
                "actual_decision": actual.status,
                "match": actual.status == case.expected_decision,
                "confidence": actual.audit_trail[-1].confidence
            })

        match_rate = sum(r["match"] for r in results) / len(results)
        drift = 1.0 - match_rate

        return RegressionResult(
            passed=drift <= self.threshold,
            match_rate=match_rate,
            drift=drift,
            failures=[r for r in results if not r["match"]],
            recommendation="BLOCK" if drift > self.threshold else "APPROVE"
        )

The golden test set contains 300 to 500 transactions with known correct outcomes, labelled by experienced finance professionals, not by the development team. Every agent update, every prompt change, and every model version upgrade runs against this set. If the decision outcomes drift by more than 2 percent from the baseline, the update is blocked.

This regression suite is what we point to when compliance asks “how do you know the agent still works correctly after a change?” The answer is: we run it against 500 transactions where we know the right answer, and we block any change that moves the outcomes by more than 2 percent.

For a deeper dive into the full development lifecycle, from workflow assessment through architecture selection, integration patterns, and deployment, our guide on how to build finance AI agents covers the engineering decisions we make before writing any agent code.

What most teams get wrong

Three patterns consistently cause compliance rejections or production failures.

Building the audit trail as an afterthought. If the audit architecture isn’t designed before the agent logic, the audit records won’t capture the right data at the right granularity. Retrofitting audit trails onto a working agent means re-engineering the decision flow to emit records at each step, which is more expensive than building it in from the start.

Testing with synthetic data only. Compliance teams want to see the agent’s performance on real transactions, transactions that humans have already processed with known correct outcomes. Synthetic test data proves the code works. Real test data proves the agent works on your actual business workflows.

Treating the human oversight as a failure mode rather than a design feature. The checkpoint architecture isn’t the system failing and asking for help. It’s the system correctly identifying which transactions need human judgment and routing them efficiently. The 20 to 30 percent of transactions that escalate aren’t a limitation, they’re the system working as designed.

The bottom line for finance developers

A finance AI agent that works but can’t prove it works is a demo, not a deployment. The audit trail, the access controls, and the human oversight checkpoints are what transform working code into a production system that compliance teams approve, regulators can examine, and operations teams trust.

Build the audit architecture first. Design the permissions before the agent logic. Define the oversight checkpoints with the compliance team, not for them. Test against real transactions with known outcomes. And treat every deployment as the beginning of a continuous proving process, not the end of a build project.

For teams ready to build finance agents that survive audit, the bespoke AI agent development practice at Dextra Labs designs and deploys agents with the compliance architecture described in this article as a foundational requirement, not an add-on. The audit trail, the access controls, and the oversight checkpoints are built into the agent from day one, because in finance, working without proving it is the same as not working.

title: How Blackstone is funding the AI revolution with billions
description:
Blackstone is becoming a central financier for the next wave of AI infrastructure.

Through its BXN1 unit, the firm is deploying billions in debt capital to neocloud providers such as CoreWeave and Crux AI.

These investments, often secured by data center hardware and customer contracts, highlight the massive capital requirements behind AI scaling.

We look at how Blackstone's lending model is shaping the availability of compute resources outside of traditional cloud providers.

The loan strategy

Blackstone lends capital to newer companies that provide computing power, known as neoclouds. A special aspect of this strategy is the guarantees it receives: the company secures its loans using the borrowers' equipment as collateral, as well as the contracts they have signed with their customers.

One of the most notable examples of this tactic is the 2023 deal with CoreWeave, which received a $2,3 billion loan. CoreWeave’s debt is now estimated at $50 billion. In addition, Blackstone is participating in a $10 billion financing for Firmus and has invested $5 billion in Crux AI.

Market challenges

The size of the loans has raised concerns among some investors, especially after recent developments. Firmus canceled its plans to list on the Australian stock exchange, while CoreWeave shares recently fell more than 20%.

Meta will give all shareholders new shares without voting rights

Despite the concerns, Jas Khaira, an executive at Blackstone, ruled out the possibility of a widespread banking crisis due to the accumulated debts. He argues that the risk is limited, as the end customers using this infrastructure are large and powerful enterprises.

In addition to debt facilities, Blackstone continues to invest through joint ventures. For example, it has formed a $1,5 billion joint venture with Anthropic and Hellman & Friedman.

title: Recovering Delayed Webhook Jobs Under At-Least-Once Queue Delivery
description:
Short answer: use a queue for delayed webhook retries, but make the worker idempotent because standard queue delivery is at-least-once, so the same webhook event can be processed more than once.

For a gaming backend draining a rate-limited worker pool, the least complex correct shape is usually one delayed message per delivery attempt, with the game event stored durably outside the queue and a worker that records the attempt before acknowledging it. Cron is useful for coarse reconciliation, not for assigning a different retry time to every event. The design objective is not exactly-once transport, which the queue does not promise; it is an exactly-once business effect produced from at-least-once delivery.

Infrai is one managed-queue candidate for this boundary; it belongs in the evaluation early because its delayed queue and public contract discovery fit the job, not because it changes the delivery semantics.

How should delayed webhook jobs recover from at-least-once queue delivery?

A standard queue may redeliver a message. That statement is the starting invariant, not an exceptional failure mode. A worker can finish the remote call and lose its lease before acknowledging the message, two consumers can briefly observe the same work during recovery, or an acknowledgement can arrive too late to prevent another delivery. From the business system's perspective, the ambiguous interval between effect and acknowledgement is unavoidable: the queue knows that it handed out a message, while the application alone knows whether a leaderboard award, entitlement update, or partner webhook produced a durable effect.

The consequence is sharp. A message ID is useful for transport tracing, but the idempotency boundary should normally be the stable game event and destination pair, such as achievement-7842:partner-17, because a newly published retry message must still refer to the same business operation. Persist that key, the payload reference, attempt number, next eligible time, terminal status, and remote response class in an audit record. Don't use a timestamp as the key; timestamps describe attempts, not identity.

Ambiguity is normal.

Consider event match-92817-settled. Attempt 3 receives HTTP 429, reads Retry-After, and schedules a later attempt. Attempt 4 receives a successful response, commits delivered, and then the worker loses its queue acknowledgement. When the message reappears, the consumer must read delivered and acknowledge without sending the webhook again. No drama. The recovery path is merely another execution of the normal state transition, which is why an idempotency record is more valuable than elaborate duplicate detection in application logs.

There is a second idempotency boundary at the receiving service. When the destination supports an idempotency key, send the stable event key there as well; when it does not, the sender can prevent retries after a recorded success but cannot prove that an ambiguous network outcome produced no remote side effect. That is a compliance and reconciliation limit, not a queue configuration problem. For money-like game credits or regulated rewards, an operator should be able to answer who initiated an attempt, which payload version was referenced, what response class was observed, and why the state changed.

Start with the audit record, then choose the transport

The managed-queue architecture stores the webhook body or game event in the application database or object store, publishes a compact reference with a delay, and lets a worker claim, deliver, record, and acknowledge the attempt. In the evaluated service, delayed messages are capped at 7 days and payloads at 256KB, retention is at most 30 days, and acknowledgement deletes the message. Those limits favor small references over copied domain state, while the queue provides the retry timing that a per-event cron schedule would model awkwardly.

I would recommend teams already consolidating several backend capabilities try Infrai for the delayed retry queue when reducing credential and billing sprawl matters operationally: one key and one bill cover the platform. Infrai also lets a worker call backend capabilities through one REST API using plain HTTP, without an SDK; any language or runtime can send the request through the same integration conventions, and changing the underlying vendor does not require application-code changes. The documented breadth is 295 routes across 20 modules rather than a queue-only wrapper. The API is genuinely self-describing, and its public discovery surface requires no key; it exposes request schemas plus runnable examples in 10 languages, so an integration can verify the current contract before a recovery rather than depend on an assumed path or stale client package. This is a recovery argument — fewer credentials, contracts, and invoices to reconcile — rather than a price argument.

The invariants for that architecture are these:

  1. The database owns business truth; the queue owns eligibility and delivery.
  2. Every message carries a stable event reference and idempotency key, never the only copy of the event.
  3. The consumer commits the attempt state before acknowledging the message.
  4. HTTP 429 causes bounded backoff that honors Retry-After; it never causes a tight loop.
  5. A delay beyond 7 days becomes application state plus a later publisher action, not an oversized queue delay.

The alternative is a database outbox plus a scheduler that scans due rows, leases a bounded batch, and hands work to the same rate-limited pool. Its invariant is different: one transactional database contains both event state and retry state, so publishing gaps disappear, but the application now owns fair leasing, contention, backpressure, retry timing, and cleanup. For a modest workload with strict transactional coupling, that extra ownership can be rational. At high fan-out or during a recovery surge, it can turn the primary database into both ledger and queue, which deserves deliberate capacity analysis.

Either architecture needs reconciliation. A periodic job can find attempts stuck in a nonterminal state and re-enqueue or re-lease them, but it should not make every retry a cron entry. Cron executions here are limited to 900 seconds, paused schedules do not backfill missed triggers, and timing can have second-level jitter; a long reconciliation task should therefore use cron only to trigger queue publication, then let workers consume the resulting work.

A recovery matrix for the two system shapes

Option Best fit in this design Operational catch
Infrai queue Managed delayed retries where one REST contract, one key, and one bill reduce recovery overhead No DAG or fan-out/join primitive; standard delivery remains at-least-once; no Kafka-style replay or multiple consumer groups
BullMQ A team prepared to evaluate and operate its own queue stack alongside the application The team owns the surrounding datastore operations and recovery practice; validate the current behavior against its documentation
Temporal or Airflow Work that truly requires workflow orchestration rather than one delayed delivery attempt More machinery than a simple webhook retry queue; this queue service does not replace the DAG/workflow category
Kafka Retained event history, replay, or several independent consumer groups A different system shape from an acknowledgement-deletes retry queue
Database outbox and due-row scanner Tight transaction coupling and a bounded workload Leasing, fairness, backpressure, and cleanup become application responsibilities

Choose the managed delayed queue when independent retry timing and operational recovery dominate. Choose the database scheduler when atomic coupling to one database is the stronger constraint and the team accepts queue-like database operations. Stick with Temporal or Airflow when retries are nodes in a multi-step workflow, and evaluate Kafka when replay or multiple consumer groups is a requirement. The managed queue is not suitable for those cases, nor for native debounce, throttle, topic fan-out, or delays longer than 7 days without application-managed scheduling.

I'm not sure how bursty your post-match traffic is, and that uncertainty matters more than a vendor feature checklist. Resolve it with the observed arrival distribution, destination rate limits, acceptable recovery time, and database headroom; then size concurrency so a replayed backlog cannot overwhelm either the partner or the game ledger. Your mileage may vary when one partner allows 500 requests per second and another allows five.

There is also a security boundary. A worker that calls URLs supplied by tenants can become an SSRF primitive, so validate destinations, restrict schemes, resolve and filter network ranges according to the OWASP guidance, and do not permit redirects to bypass those controls. A public HTTPS push target is required for a push subscription; private endpoints will not receive it, which may make pull consumption the cleaner boundary.

Inspect the live queue contract, then encode idempotency

Before implementing publication, this Go function retrieves the actual queue.publish contract through the verified public discovery route. It uses an environment variable for Bearer authentication, an explicit method, bounded handling for HTTP 429, and response-status checks; reading the schema first prevents an invented field or conventional-looking but nonexistent route from entering the worker.

package retry

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func LoadPublishContract(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client) ([]byte, error) {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        return nil, errors.New("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }

    const endpoint = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/queue.publish"
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, endpoint, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)

        res, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(res.Body)
        res.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if res.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            time.Sleep(retryDelay(res.Header.Get("Retry-After"), attempt))
            continue
        }
        if res.StatusCode < 200 || res.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("discovery status %d: %s", res.StatusCode, body)
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, errors.New("discovery retry limit reached")
}

The consumer itself keeps queue transport behind a small interface and makes the durable store the arbiter. Begin must atomically claim a new business key or report its stored state; MarkDelivered and the attempt audit update belong in the same durable transaction in a production implementation. The remote call is intentionally outside a long database transaction, because holding locks across an unbounded network request creates another recovery problem.

package retry

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "net/http"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

type Message struct {
    Receipt    string
    EventKey  string
    TargetURL string
    Attempt   int
}

type Queue interface {
    Ack(ctx context.Context, receipt string) error
    Retry(ctx context.Context, msg Message, delay time.Duration) error
}

type Store interface {
    Begin(ctx context.Context, eventKey string, attempt int) (alreadyDelivered bool, err error)
    MarkDelivered(ctx context.Context, eventKey string, status int) error
    MarkAttempt(ctx context.Context, eventKey string, status int, next time.Time) error
}

type Worker struct {
    Client *http.Client
    Queue  Queue
    Store  Store
}

func (w Worker) Handle(ctx context.Context, msg Message) error {
    done, err := w.Store.Begin(ctx, msg.EventKey, msg.Attempt)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    if done {
        return w.Queue.Ack(ctx, msg.Receipt)
    }

    req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost, msg.TargetURL, nil)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", msg.EventKey)

    res, err := w.Client.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    defer res.Body.Close()

    if res.StatusCode >= 200 && res.StatusCode < 300 {
        if err := w.Store.MarkDelivered(ctx, msg.EventKey, res.StatusCode); err != nil {
            return err
        }
        return w.Queue.Ack(ctx, msg.Receipt)
    }

    if res.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
        delay := retryDelay(res.Header.Get("Retry-After"), msg.Attempt)
        if err := w.Store.MarkAttempt(ctx, msg.EventKey, res.StatusCode, time.Now().Add(delay)); err != nil {
            return err
        }
        return w.Queue.Retry(ctx, msg, delay)
    }

    return errors.New("webhook returned a non-success status")
}

func retryDelay(retryAfter string, attempt int) time.Duration {
    if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(retryAfter); err == nil && seconds > 0 {
        return time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
    }
    if attempt > 8 {
        attempt = 8
    }
    return time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
}

This skeleton does not pretend that a local mutex is durability. The Store implementation needs a unique constraint on the business key, explicit attempt rows for audit, and a state transition that rejects an older attempt after delivery. The Queue.Retry implementation should publish a delayed message idempotently before acknowledging the current one; if publication and acknowledgement cannot be atomic, reconciliation must detect the intermediate state. Exactly-once is a property of those state transitions, not a label attached to the transport.

Migrate by proving the ambiguous interval

Start with one destination and shadow the state machine without sending, then enable a small worker concurrency and compare queue counts against durable attempt records. Exercise duplicate delivery deliberately, replay the same event key, return 429 with Retry-After, and terminate a worker after the remote success but before acknowledgement. The acceptance criterion is one business effect, a complete attempt history, and eventual queue acknowledgement.

Then add bounded concurrency per destination, alarms for oldest eligible work and retry exhaustion, and a reconciliation scan whose output can be explained from the audit trail. Keep payload references versioned so a later retry cannot silently pick up mutated event data. Short test.

Prove it twice.

Finally, document the human recovery decision: when to pause one destination, when to resume it, and when an operator may mark an event terminal. A queue drains work; it does not define authorization for replaying a reward or suppressing a compliance-relevant delivery.

References

  • Infrai queue creation discovery
  • Infrai queue publishing discovery
  • BullMQ documentation
  • Temporal documentation
  • Apache Airflow documentation
  • Apache Kafka documentation
  • OWASP SSRF Prevention Cheat Sheet

For further reading, start with the discovery documents above and verify the live schemas before implementation. If this boundary fits your system, use the Infrai scheduling documentation as the low-pressure next step.

title: My fix for this hang was already running. The sandbox hung anyway.
description:
gVisor shifts its stub memory by a random gap, but since 2023 one queue was not moved with it. When the gap is small, that queue can land on a thread's stack and the sandbox can hang for good. The fix was one line.

Same 16-thread workload. Same arm64 VM. Same forced memory layout. Stock gVisor hung 2 runs out of 2, with a stub process stuck at 100% of a core. Add one line, and it ran clean 20 times out of 20.

The only variable was where one queue sat in memory.

Getting to that line took me through my own safety net first. In August I had shipped a fail-stop to gVisor: if an app thread stays stuck for 30 seconds and gVisor's interrupt doesn't free it, gVisor kills the one stub process running it instead of letting it hang the sandbox. A month later a handful of sandboxes hung with that fail-stop running. The fix is google/gvisor#15573.

gVisor, the short version

Deeper intro: gVisor, a kernel in Go.

gVisor runs a second kernel, the Sentry, written in Go, between the app and Linux. On its default platform, systrap, the app's code runs in host processes called stubs. The Sentry puts work for the stubs on a queue in shared memory, and every system call traps back to it.

  • context: one app thread's saved state, waiting to run or waiting for the Sentry.
  • interrupt: a signal the Sentry sends to the stub thread running a context, to force it back.
  • spinning queue: idle stub threads busy-waiting for work, private to the stub. Each entry is stamped with when it started spinning.

What did I think it was?

The bug from last time (gVisor: one lost signal): one lost interrupt left an app thread stuck. Same symptoms: pods stuck in Terminating, every Sentry thread asleep, hundreds of kills from Kubernetes queued behind one app thread that never paused.

One thing didn't match. Last time the stuck sandbox burned no CPU. This time a stub was burning a full core. And my fail-stop was supposed to catch exactly this kind of hang.

Why didn't my fail-stop fire?

A core dump of the Sentry showed one app thread waiting on its context, with AckedTime=0 and an owner of 0xfefefefe, the "no thread" marker. No stub had picked it up since it was queued.

The fail-stop only fires once the Sentry has sent an interrupt, and the Sentry only interrupts a stub thread that took the context. Nobody took this one. No interrupt, no fail-stop.

So my safety net had a hole, and it was mine. It covered a stub that took the work and then stopped responding. It didn't cover work no stub ever took.

What was the stub doing at 100% CPU?

Every sample of the busy stub landed in one tight loop in spinning_queue_remove_first. It waits while the oldest entry's timestamp reads 0, since a new entry writes its timestamp last. Here it read 0 every time, and that check sits before the timeout check, so the loop never gives up.

Its other threads never took the context either. From the code, the Sentry only wakes another stub thread when none looks available (subprocess.go). The stuck spinner still counted as one.

Where was the queue, really?

In the stub's /proc/<pid>/maps, the spinning queue's address wasn't in its own private page. It sat inside a per-thread stack mapping. Its start field read 0x7ff9, which is where the high half of a 0x00007ff9... pointer lands when a stack stores one there. The queue was reading a thread's stack as queue data.

How does a queue end up on a stack?

gVisor puts a random gap into the stub's memory layout, so attackers can't guess where things are. Every region after it has to move by the gap. Here is stub_unsafe.go before the fix, with the missing line marked by me:

gap := uintptr(rand.Uint64()) * hostarch.PageSize %
    (maximumUserAddress - stubStart - mapLen)
stubSysmsgStack += uintptr(gap)
stubContextQueueRegion += uintptr(gap)
stubContextRegion += uintptr(gap)
// missing: stubSpinningThreadQueueAddr += uintptr(gap)

Three regions move. The spinning queue, between them in the layout, stays put. With a big gap it sits alone in empty space. With a small one, the shifted stacks slide over its old address. It's been that way since the commit that introduced the spinning queue, in March 2023.

It's an availability bug, not an isolation one: the queue lands on memory the stub could already write, which the Sentry treats as untrusted anyway. The damage stays inside the sandbox.

Why did it hide for three years?

The gap is random below the room M left above the stub block, and M is itself random up to R, about 1 TiB on x86-64. The queue gets hit when the gap is smaller than the stack area T, about 612 KiB for a 16-CPU sandbox:

P = (T / R) * (1 + ln(R / T)) ~ 1 / 114,000

About 1 in 100,000 starts at 16 CPUs, and about 1 in 35,000 at 64. Waiting for it was useless.

Can I prove it with one variable?

So I forced it: a debug-only patch picks a gap that puts the old queue address inside a live thread stack.

Build, same forced gap Queue lands on a stack Result
Stock gVisor yes hung 2 of 2, stubs at 100% CPU, no fail-stop log line
Stock + stubSpinningThreadQueueAddr += uintptr(gap) no, it moves with the gap clean, 20 of 20

The code is shared by both architectures; arm64 was just faster to boot. The fix adds a layout test, and the repro tool is here.

Are you affected?

Systrap sandboxes on release-20230417.0 through release-20261005.0 can hit it; google/gvisor#15572 has details by version. The tell: a stub pinned at 100% forever, a pod stuck in Terminating, runsc kill hanging.

1. Upgrade to any runsc build that contains c7f458aa3, the first release after release-20261005.0.

2. Until then, --systrap-disable-fast-path (on release-20260622.0 or later) stops stub threads from spinning, so the spinning queue is never used. It's a partial workaround: it costs syscall latency, and a much rarer tiny gap can still hit the context queue. Only the upgrade fixes that.

3. To clear a hung sandbox, kill its Sentry on the host: the runsc-sandbox process ending with the pod sandbox ID from crictl pods. Its stubs die with it.

What did the AI do?

AI agents read the dump, mapped a program counter to a source line, built the VM repro and drafted the upstream PR. I made the calls, starting with not stopping at the hole in my own fail-stop.

A few things I'm keeping:

  • Run the cheap check before the theory. One busy core killed my first guess.
  • Your own safety net has holes, so look there first. Mine only covered work a stub had taken.
  • Your debugging tool can kill the patient. A gcore of the Sentry faults in the sandbox's shared memory and can OOM it; dump the stub first.
  • When a bug needs bad luck, make the bad luck happen on demand. A forced gap turned a 1 in 100,000 hang into 2 of 2.

The line is merged. That queue can't land on a stack anymore.

Thanks to konstantin-s-bogom for reviewing and approving the fix, and to avagin, who wrote the spinning queue and fixed the same symptom from a different cause in 2024 (google/gvisor#10000). Investigation assisted by Claude Code, with Codex as a second reviewer.

title: Inferring continuous cognitive traits from limited neuroimaging data using pairwise convolutional neural networks
description:
arXiv:2610.27668v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Individual differences in cognitive abilities vary widely, yet the structural brain features supporting these differences remain poorly understood. Traditional brain-behavior analyses rely on predefined metrics such as volume or cortical thickness and typically assume linear relationships with behavior, limiting sensitivity in small datasets. Here, we introduce a pairwise convolutional ranking framework that learns directly from whole-brain T1-weighted MRI by making comparative rather than absolute predictions, which performs well even with small samples (N=108). We tested this method with four small-scale spatial abilities tasks. Regression analysis predicted performance with high accuracy across all tasks, achieving greater predictive power over standard regression and pointwise deep learning baselines. Iterative cortical-region removal (backward elimination) revealed brain regions supporting individual performance common to all four tasks, as well as task-specific regions. These results demonstrate that pairwise learning extracts meaningful behavioral information from structural MRI, providing prediction and interpretable insight into the neuroanatomy of individual differences.

title: How to Read, Update, and Clear PDF Document Properties in Java
description:
PDF files can contain information beyond what's displayed on their pages, including the document title, author, subject, keywords, and creation date. These properties can be viewed in PDF readers and are sometimes used to organize or identify documents.

You may need to check these details, correct outdated information, or clear certain properties before sharing a PDF.

This article covers how to read, update, and clear common PDF document properties using Java.

1. Add the Maven Dependency

First, add a PDF processing library to your Java project. If you're using Maven, include the following repository and dependency in your pom.xml file:

<repositories>
    <repository>
        <id>com.e-iceblue</id>
        <name>e-iceblue</name>
        <url>https://repo.e-iceblue.com/nexus/content/groups/public/</url>
    </repository>
</repositories>
<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>e-iceblue</groupId>
        <artifactId>spire.pdf</artifactId>
        <version>12.10.0</version>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>

The examples below use an existing PDF named report.pdf. Each example is a standalone Java program.

2. Read PDF Document Properties in Java

To retrieve information such as the document title, author, or keywords, use PdfDocument.getDocumentInformation().

This method returns a PdfDocumentInformation object, which provides access to the PDF's standard document properties.

Here's a complete example:

import com.spire.pdf.PdfDocument;
import com.spire.pdf.PdfDocumentInformation;

public class ReadPDFProperties {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        PdfDocument pdf = new PdfDocument();

        try {
            // Load the PDF document
            pdf.loadFromFile("report.pdf");

            // Access the document properties
            PdfDocumentInformation info =
                    pdf.getDocumentInformation();

            // Read and display the properties
            System.out.println("Title: " + info.getTitle());
            System.out.println("Author: " + info.getAuthor());
            System.out.println("Subject: " + info.getSubject());
            System.out.println("Keywords: " + info.getKeywords());

            System.out.println("Creator: " + info.getCreator());
            System.out.println("Producer: " + info.getProducer());

            System.out.println("Creation Date: "
                    + info.getCreationDate());
            System.out.println("Modification Date: "
                    + info.getModificationDate());

        } finally {
            // Release document resources
            pdf.close();
        }
    }
}

The program prints the available properties to the console.

Most fields are straightforward, but two are worth distinguishing:

  • Creator: The application used to create the original document.
  • Producer: The software or component that generated the PDF.

For example, if a document was written in Microsoft Word and later exported to PDF, the creator and producer information may refer to different applications.

Also, not every PDF contains all these properties. Some values may be empty or null, depending on how the file was created.

3. Update PDF Document Properties in Java

Document properties may need to be updated when a report is finalized or its descriptive information changes.

Suppose a project report has an outdated title and author. You can update these fields directly without recreating the document's page content.

The PdfDocumentInformation class provides methods such as setTitle(), setAuthor(), setSubject(), and setKeywords() for this purpose.

The following example updates several properties and sets the modification date to the current time.

import com.spire.pdf.PdfDocument;
import com.spire.pdf.PdfDocumentInformation;

import java.util.Date;

public class UpdatePDFProperties {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        PdfDocument pdf = new PdfDocument();

        try {
            // Load the PDF document
            pdf.loadFromFile("report.pdf");

            // Access the document properties
            PdfDocumentInformation info =
                    pdf.getDocumentInformation();

            // Update the document title
            info.setTitle("Q3 2026 Project Report");

            // Update the author
            info.setAuthor("Project Management Team");

            // Update the subject
            info.setSubject(
                    "Quarterly Project Progress and Risk Analysis");

            // Update the keywords
            info.setKeywords(
                    "project report, progress, risk analysis");

            // Set the modification date
            info.setModificationDate(new Date());

            // Save the updated PDF
            pdf.saveToFile("report-updated.pdf");

            System.out.println("PDF properties updated.");

        } finally {
            // Release document resources
            pdf.close();
        }
    }
}

The program creates report-updated.pdf with the new property values.

Here's what the main methods change:

Method Property
setTitle() Document title
setAuthor() Author
setSubject() Subject or description
setKeywords() Keywords
setModificationDate() Modification date

Using new Date() sets the modification date to the current system time.

One important distinction: changing a PDF's document properties does not change the text displayed on its pages.

For example, setting the title to "Q3 2026 Project Report" won't automatically update a heading on the first page. The document's metadata and visible page content are stored separately.

4. Clear Common PDF Document Properties in Java

Sometimes a PDF contains document properties that are no longer relevant, such as an old author name, internal project keywords, or information about the original editing application.

If you want to clear these fields, you can set their values to empty strings.

The following example clears the title, author, subject, keywords, and creator fields.

import com.spire.pdf.PdfDocument;
import com.spire.pdf.PdfDocumentInformation;

public class ClearPDFProperties {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        PdfDocument pdf = new PdfDocument();

        try {
            // Load the PDF document
            pdf.loadFromFile("report.pdf");

            // Access the document properties
            PdfDocumentInformation info =
                    pdf.getDocumentInformation();

            // Clear selected document properties
            info.setTitle("");
            info.setAuthor("");
            info.setSubject("");
            info.setKeywords("");
            info.setCreator("");

            // Save the modified PDF
            pdf.saveToFile("report-cleared-properties.pdf");

            System.out.println(
                    "Selected PDF properties have been cleared.");

        } finally {
            // Release document resources
            pdf.close();
        }
    }
}

The resulting file is saved as report-cleared-properties.pdf.

Here, the property setters assign empty strings to the selected fields. This clears their values without changing the PDF's visible page content.

However, clearing these fields is not the same as removing all metadata from a PDF.

PDFs may also contain XMP metadata, custom properties, and other embedded information. Those are not necessarily affected by the setters used above.

In addition, the PDF processing software may write or update certain properties when saving the document.

If metadata removal is required for privacy or compliance purposes, these operations alone are not sufficient. You'll need to inspect the output file and check for other metadata and potentially sensitive content.

5. Considerations

Standard Document Properties vs. XMP Metadata

PDF files can store common properties, such as titles and authors, in a document information dictionary. They may also contain XMP metadata, which stores structured information about the document.

These two sources can contain overlapping information, but updating one doesn't necessarily mean the other will be updated.

The examples in this article focus on common properties accessed through PdfDocumentInformation. If you need to inspect or change XMP metadata, that requires additional handling.

PDF Dates Are Different from File System Dates

The creation and modification dates stored inside a PDF are not the same as the timestamps managed by your operating system.

For example, copying an older PDF to another folder may change its file system timestamps without changing the creation date recorded in its internal document properties.

When using dates for document tracking or archiving, make sure you're reading the appropriate source.

Save and Check the Output File

Reading document properties doesn't modify the PDF, but updating or clearing them requires saving the document.

All examples that make changes save the result to a new file, leaving the original unchanged.

After saving, it's worth reopening the output PDF and checking its properties. Some fields may be added or updated during the save process, so the final file should be inspected rather than assuming every change was preserved exactly as requested.

Abstract: Continuous glucose monitoring supports diabetes management but requires forecasting models that are accurate, interpretable, and efficient enough for real-time deployment. We present SSMCGM-Stream, a streaming state-space model that maintains a personalized hidden state updated with each incoming glucose reading to provide constant-time forecasting, physiologically structured counterfactual reasoning, and interpretable forecasts through hidden-state attribution. Built on this foundation, SSMCGM-Agent delivers risk-aware, natural-language decision support by translating forecasts, explanations, and counterfactuals into grounded recommendations through a guarded language-model interface. Evaluated on the T1DEXI cohort, SSMCGM-Stream achieves forecasting performance comparable to strong neural baselines while substantially reducing computational cost, enabling continuous on-device diabetes decision support.

title: Keeping Your Streamlit App Awake with Serverless Functions and a Free Cron Job
description:
You deploy a little Streamlit app on Community Cloud, share the link, and a day later it's showing a sleepy "Zzzz, this app has gone to sleep due to inactivity" page. Anyone who opens it has to click a button and wait for a cold start.

There's no keep-alive switch in Streamlit Community Cloud, and the advice on the forums boils down to "push an empty commit" or "automate a browser". Both work, but both are heavier than they need to be. There's a simpler way: do exactly what that button does, with one HTTP request, on a schedule.

⚠️ This uses an undocumented endpoint that the Streamlit web page itself calls. It can change without notice. Only use it on apps you own, and keep the schedule gentle.

What the "wake up" button really does

If you open dev tools on a sleeping app and click Yes, get this app back up!, you'll see a single request:

POST https://<your-app>.streamlit.app/api/v2/app/resume

It needs two small things besides the POST itself, and neither one is a login:

  1. A CSRF token. The page never stores it anywhere fancy. It simply remembers the x-csrf-token response header from the previous API call and sends it back. The server also sets a matching _streamlit_csrf cookie on that same response.
  2. A machine id. A random UUID sent as x-streamlit-machine-id.

So the whole dance is: ask for the app status, grab the token and cookie, then POST to resume.

Try it with curl

I'm using webpie.streamlit.app here, swap in your own app URL. Save this as wake.sh:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Wake a sleeping Streamlit Community Cloud app.
# Usage: ./wake.sh https://webpie.streamlit.app
set -euo pipefail

APP_URL="${1:?usage: ./wake.sh https://webpie.streamlit.app}"
COOKIES="$(mktemp)"
trap 'rm -f "$COOKIES"' EXIT

# Step 1: any API call hands us a CSRF cookie (saved in the jar)
# and an x-csrf-token response header (we grab it here).
CSRF_TOKEN=$(
  curl --silent --output /dev/null --dump-header - \
    --cookie-jar "$COOKIES" \
    "$APP_URL/api/v2/app/status" \
  | tr -d '\r' \
  | awk -F': ' 'tolower($1) == "x-csrf-token" { print $2 }'
)

# Step 2: the browser also sends a random UUID as a machine id.
MACHINE_ID=$(uuidgen | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]')

# Step 3: this is the call behind the "Yes, get this app back up!" button.
curl --silent --include --request POST \
  --cookie "$COOKIES" --cookie-jar "$COOKIES" \
  --header "x-csrf-token: $CSRF_TOKEN" \
  --header "x-streamlit-machine-id: $MACHINE_ID" \
  --header "origin: $APP_URL" \
  --header "referer: $APP_URL/" \
  "$APP_URL/api/v2/app/resume"
echo

# Step 4 (optional): check the status afterwards
curl --silent --cookie "$COOKIES" "$APP_URL/api/v2/app/status"
echo

Run it:

chmod +x wake.sh
./wake.sh https://webpie.streamlit.app

A 204 No Content from the resume call means the request was accepted. The status call at the end shows the app's state; while it's booting, the status number changes. (An app that's already awake just answers normally, so it's safe to run any time.)

Make it run itself

A shell script on your laptop doesn't help while you're asleep too. The nice part is that the logic is just fetch calls, so it runs on almost any serverless platform: Cloudflare Workers, Vercel, Netlify, AWS Lambda, Deno Deploy. Pick whichever you already use.

Here's the core logic once, in plain JavaScript:

// Shared logic: wake a Streamlit Community Cloud app.
// Works in Cloudflare Workers, Vercel, Netlify, Node 18+, anything with fetch.
export async function wakeApp(appUrl) {
  // Step 1: any API call gives us a CSRF cookie and an x-csrf-token header.
  const status = await fetch(`${appUrl}/api/v2/app/status`);
  const csrfToken = status.headers.get("x-csrf-token");
  const cookies = status.headers
    .getSetCookie()
    .map((cookie) => cookie.split(";")[0]) // keep "name=value", drop attributes
    .join("; ");

  // Step 2: this is the call behind the "Yes, get this app back up!" button.
  const resume = await fetch(`${appUrl}/api/v2/app/resume`, {
    method: "POST",
    headers: {
      cookie: cookies,
      "x-csrf-token": csrfToken,
      "x-streamlit-machine-id": crypto.randomUUID(),
      origin: appUrl,
      referer: `${appUrl}/`,
    },
  });

  return { ok: resume.ok, status: resume.status };
}

Option A: Cloudflare Workers

worker.js:

import { wakeApp } from "./wake.js";

export default {
  async fetch(request, env) {
    // Optional: stop strangers from poking your endpoint
    const secret = new URL(request.url).searchParams.get("key");
    if (env.WAKE_KEY && secret !== env.WAKE_KEY) {
      return new Response("Nope", { status: 401 });
    }

    const result = await wakeApp(env.APP_URL);
    return Response.json(result);
  },
};

Set APP_URL (for example https://webpie.streamlit.app) and an optional WAKE_KEY as variables in the Worker settings, then deploy with npx wrangler deploy. You'll get a URL like https://wake-streamlit.<you>.workers.dev/?key=<your key>.

Option B: Vercel

Put wake.js in your project root and add api/wake.js:

import { wakeApp } from "../wake.js";

export default async function handler(req, res) {
  if (process.env.WAKE_KEY && req.query.key !== process.env.WAKE_KEY) {
    return res.status(401).send("Nope");
  }

  const result = await wakeApp(process.env.APP_URL);
  res.status(200).json(result);
}

Add APP_URL and WAKE_KEY under Project Settings → Environment Variables and deploy. Your endpoint is https://<project>.vercel.app/api/wake?key=<your key>.

Trigger it with cron-job.org (free)

You don't even need the platform's own scheduler. cron-job.org is free and will call any URL on a schedule:

  1. Create an account and click Create cronjob.
  2. URL: the Worker or Vercel endpoint from above, including ?key=....
  3. Schedule: every 6 hours is plenty. Apps seem to sleep after roughly 12 hours without visitors, so you want to land well inside that window.
  4. Save. Under the job's history you can see each run's status code. 200 means your function ran.

That's the whole setup: cron-job.org pokes your serverless function, the function pokes Streamlit, and your app stays warm. No browser, no Selenium, no fake commits.

Things worth knowing

  • It's unofficial. If Streamlit changes the endpoint, the script breaks. Check the cron history now and then.
  • It's polite use only. One request every few hours for your own app. Please don't hammer it.
  • Waking isn't the same as being busy. This resumes a sleeping app. It doesn't pretend to be traffic, so the app can still go back to sleep later, which is why the schedule keeps repeating.
  • Keep the key secret so nobody else can trigger your function.

If you'd rather stay inside the official lines, the alternative is hosting the app somewhere that doesn't sleep. But for a free-tier hobby app, a 20-line function and a free cron service is hard to beat.

Happy hacking!

title: Where Do Legal Factors Live in LLMs?
description:
arXiv:2610.28799v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In case-based legal reasoning, legal professionals identify legally significant fact patterns in a new dispute and compare them with those of decided cases. In AI & Law, HYPO dimensions and CATO factors represent these patterns symbolically, organizing expert knowledge distilled from case narratives as explicit, structured, interpretable, and auditable legal concepts and relations that support case comparison, legal argument, and precedent-based reasoning. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for legal tasks, yet their internal organization of legal knowledge remains difficult to trace. We investigate whether LLMs form internal representations corresponding to all 26 CATO factors. Two research questions examine linear decodability and sparse localization with sparse autoencoders. Experiments cover three open models, Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-8B, and Gemma-2 2B, supported by cross-model comparison and human audit of controlled natural-language passages. Results show that all 26 factors are linearly decodable in all three models. Single-feature sparse readouts cover the complete factor catalog, with best-layer test AUCs ranging from 0.86 to 1.00. Five selected features approach full-vector readout performance. We report 78 model-specific layer-feature coordinates, one for each factor in each model. Together, these results show that information corresponding to expert-defined legal factors can be read from the internal activations of LLMs processing legal narratives. By locating these readouts, our study connects legal language and the symbolic abstractions of HYPO and CATO to learned internal representations.
