title: CVE-2026-107823: How a Crafted Username Becomes MariaDB Security Metadata
description:
CVE-2026-107823: How a Crafted Username Becomes MariaDB Security Metadata

Vulnerability overview

CVE-2026-107823 is the lowest-scored flaw in the October 2026 MariaDB Server set at 7.2 under CVSS v3.1, and it is the one most likely to be misread as a rounding error beside the higher numbers in the same release. The flaw is a privilege escalation inside the database itself, disclosed in CSA Singapore alert AL-2026-144 together with CVE-2026-107814, CVE-2026-107815, CVE-2026-107818 and CVE-2026-107821.

Mechanism and exploitation conditions

The advisory describes the mechanism precisely. An authenticated user who holds both CREATE USER and CREATE VIEW WITH GRANT OPTION can create a crafted username containing additional view metadata. The parser then interprets part of that username as security metadata, which can allow the attacker to escalate database privileges.

This is metadata smuggling across a boundary the parser assumed was safe. Usernames are usually treated as identity labels, not as containers that can carry structured content into a privileged parsing path. When the same string is read twice with different grammar, the second read can accept what the first read merely stored.

The prerequisites are the story here. An attacker needs a working authenticated session, CREATE USER and CREATE VIEW WITH GRANT OPTION. A least-privilege deployment grants none of these to application accounts. A development or reporting account that was given CREATE USER for convenience hands over the first half of the chain, and WITH GRANT OPTION in view creation adds the second.

Impact

Successful exploitation elevates database privileges. In practice that means the attacker moves from an account with limited scope to one that can read or modify objects it was never intended to touch, and potentially to administrative capability over the instance.

The blast radius extends past the compromised schema. A database account with elevated privileges can enumerate other tenants on a shared instance, inspect stored procedures, and reach linked servers. Credential material stored in tables becomes readable, which is often the shortest path to systems outside the database.

Affected products and scope

Affected versions are 10.6.1 through 10.6.27, 10.11.1 through 10.11.18, 11.4.1 through 11.4.12, 11.8.1 through 11.8.8, 12.3.1 through 12.3.2, and 13.0.1. The advisory does not name a public proof of concept and does not report active exploitation, so prioritisation should rest on privilege grants rather than on threat-actor signals.

Exposure context

A ZoomEye query for vul.cve="CVE-2026-107823" returned no indexed assets at the time of writing, which is unsurprising for a privilege-escalation flaw that does not announce itself in a banner. A broader fingerprint query, app="MariaDB", returns 5111720 assets. Neither number identifies vulnerable hosts, and a zero CVE count is not evidence that no instance is affected.

ZoomEye search: https://www.zoomeye.ai/searchResult?q=YXBwPSJNYXJpYURCIg%3D%3D

Remediation and mitigations

Apply the vendor update for your branch and confirm the build string afterwards. Then treat the grant surface as the real control.

Inventory accounts with CREATE USER, and treat CREATE VIEW WITH GRANT OPTION as an administrative capability rather than a reporting default. Remove GRANT OPTION from view-definition accounts unless delegation is genuinely required. Separate application identities from schema-management identities so that a compromised application cannot craft usernames in the first place.

Detection is awkward because the exploit resembles normal DDL activity. Alert on creation of usernames containing unusual delimiters or long structured suffixes, and on view creation by accounts that normally only read. Review grants quarterly as a standing control, not as a one-off response to this advisory.

References

  • CSA Singapore alert AL-2026-144: https://www.csa.gov.sg/alerts-and-advisories/alerts/al-2026-144/
  • NVD entry for CVE-2026-107823: https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2026-107823

title: B2B portalından ERP'ye sipariş göndermek: Idempotency, outbox ve kredi limiti kontrolü üzerine geliştirici notları
description:
Bayilerin ve kurumsal müşterilerin kendi özel fiyatlarıyla sipariş verdiği bir B2B portalı dışarıdan bakınca basit bir e-ticaret sitesine benzer: ürün listesi, sepet, onay butonu. Ama arka tarafta durum çok farklıdır. Stok, fatura, cari hesap ve risk limiti ERP'dedir; iletişim geçmişi, fırsatlar ve upsell planı CRM'dedir; portal ise ikisinin arasında, her iki sistemin de doğru kabul ettiği tek bir gerçeği müşteriye göstermeye çalışır. Ben, Koray Yalçın olarak CRM mimarisi, lead yönetimi ve pazarlama otomasyonu üzerine çalışırken en çok zaman kaybettiren hataların arayüzde değil, tam bu entegrasyon katmanında ortaya çıktığını gördüm.

Bu yazıda B2B portal projesini iş tarafından değil, siparişi ERP'ye ulaştıracak kodu yazan geliştiricinin gözünden ele alıyorum: neden portalın ERP veritabanına doğrudan bağlanmaması gerektiği, çift sipariş nasıl önlenir, outbox deseni ne işe yarar, kredi limiti kontrolü nerede yapılmalı ve fiyat listeleri nasıl önbelleğe alınır. Belirli bir ERP'yi (SAP, Logo, Mikro) ya da belirli bir mesaj kuyruğunu savunmuyorum; ilkeler hepsinde aynı.

1. İlk kural: Portal ERP veritabanına SQL atmaz

Küçük ekiplerde en hızlı çözüm gibi görünen şey, portal uygulamasının ERP'nin veritabanına bir okuma-yazma kullanıcısıyla bağlanmasıdır. İlk hafta çalışır. Sonra şu sorunlar birer birer gelir:

  • Şema bağımlılığı: ERP güncellemesi bir tablo adını ya da alan tipini değiştirdiğinde portal sessizce bozulur.
  • İş kurallarının atlanması: ERP'nin kendi arayüzünden girilen siparişte çalışan doğrulamalar, tetikleyiciler ve numaralandırma mantığı doğrudan INSERT ile tamamen devre dışı kalır.
  • Performans: Yoğun saatte portaldan gelen fiyat sorguları, muhasebe ekibinin gün sonu raporlarıyla aynı veritabanı kaynaklarını paylaşır.
  • Güvenlik: İnternete açık bir uygulamanın, şirketin finansal çekirdeğine geniş yetkili bir bağlantısı olur.

Doğru yapı, portal ile ERP arasına bir entegrasyon katmanı koymaktır. Bu katman ERP'nin resmi API'sini, web servisini ya da onaylı içe aktarma mekanizmasını kullanır; portal ise yalnızca bu katmanla konuşur. Arada bir mesaj kuyruğu (RabbitMQ, Kafka ya da bulut sağlayıcınızın yönetilen kuyruğu) bulunması, ERP yavaşladığında veya bakımdayken siparişlerin kaybolmadan beklemesini sağlar.

2. Siparişin yaşam döngüsünü baştan tanımlayın

Kod yazmadan önce bir siparişin hangi durumlardan geçebileceğini netleştirmek, sonraki bütün tartışmaları kısaltır. Tipik bir durum makinesi şöyle görünür:

TASLAK -> GONDERILDI -> ERP_KUYRUGUNDA -> ERP_ONAYLADI -> SEVK_EDILDI -> FATURALANDI
                     \-> FINANS_ONAYI_BEKLIYOR -> (ONAY) -> ERP_KUYRUGUNDA
                     \-> REDDEDILDI
ERP_KUYRUGUNDA -> ERP_HATASI -> (yeniden deneme) -> ERP_KUYRUGUNDA

Burada önemli olan iki şey var. Birincisi, portal siparişi "gönderildi" diye işaretlediği anda ERP'de sipariş oluşmuş değildir; müşteriye gösterilen ifade de buna uygun olmalıdır ("Siparişiniz alındı, onay bekleniyor" gibi). İkincisi, her durum geçişi kaydedilmelidir. Bir bayi "siparişim nerede?" diye aradığında müşteri temsilcisinin bakacağı yer bu geçmiştir.

3. Çift siparişi önlemek: Idempotency anahtarı

B2B'de çift sipariş, B2C'deki kadar masum değildir. Tek bir sipariş satırı birkaç palet hammadde olabilir. Çift kaydın en yaygın sebepleri bellidir: kullanıcı butona iki kez basar, mobil ağ yanıtı yarıda keser ve uygulama isteği tekrarlar, kuyruk tüketicisi mesajı işledikten sonra onay vermeden çöker ve mesaj yeniden teslim edilir.

Çözüm, her sipariş için istemci tarafında üretilen bir idempotency anahtarıdır. Sepet onay ekranı açıldığında bir UUID üretilir ve sipariş isteğiyle birlikte gönderilir. Sunucu tarafında bu anahtar benzersiz kısıtla saklanır:

CREATE TABLE portal_orders (
  id               BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  idempotency_key  UUID NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  customer_code    TEXT NOT NULL,
  status           TEXT NOT NULL,
  erp_order_no     TEXT,
  created_at       TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

Aynı anahtarla ikinci istek geldiğinde yeni sipariş oluşturulmaz; ilk siparişin durumu döndürülür. Aynı mantık entegrasyon katmanının ERP'ye yazdığı noktada da gerekir. ERP'nin sipariş kaydında harici referans alanı varsa (çoğunda "belge no", "harici referans" ya da benzeri bir alan bulunur) portal sipariş kimliği oraya yazılır ve ERP'ye göndermeden önce bu referansla kayıt olup olmadığı kontrol edilir. Böylece kuyruk mesajı iki kez işlense bile ERP'de tek sipariş oluşur.

4. Outbox deseni: Veritabanı ile kuyruk arasındaki boşluk

Klasik hata şudur: uygulama siparişi kendi veritabanına yazar, ardından kuyruğa bir mesaj atar. Veritabanı işlemi başarılı olur ama kuyruk çağrısı ağ hatası verirse sipariş portalda görünür, ERP'ye hiç gitmez. Ters sırada yaparsanız bu kez ERP'ye giden ama portalda olmayan bir sipariş oluşabilir.

Transactional outbox deseni bu boşluğu kapatır. Sipariş kaydı ile "gönderilecek mesaj" kaydı aynı veritabanı işlemi içinde yazılır:

def submit_order(conn, order, idempotency_key):
    with conn.transaction():
        order_id = insert_order(conn, order, idempotency_key, status="GONDERILDI")
        conn.execute(
            "INSERT INTO outbox (aggregate_id, event_type, payload) VALUES (%s, %s, %s)",
            (order_id, "OrderSubmitted", to_json(order)),
        )
    return order_id

Ayrı bir yayıncı süreç outbox tablosunu düzenli okur, mesajları kuyruğa iletir ve başarıyla iletilenleri işaretler. Yayıncı çökerse mesaj tabloda bekler; tekrar ayağa kalktığında kaldığı yerden devam eder. Bu yöntem "en az bir kez teslim" garantisi verir; bu yüzden bir önceki bölümdeki idempotency kontrolü zorunlu bir eştir. İkisi birlikte, pratikte "tam bir kez etki" sonucunu üretir.

5. Kredi limiti kontrolü nerede yapılmalı?

B2B portalının perakende e-ticaretten en belirgin farkı, ödemenin çoğu zaman sipariş anında değil vadeli olarak yapılmasıdır. Bu da her siparişte müşterinin açık hesap riskini, vadesi geçmiş borcunu ve tanımlı kredi limitini kontrol etmeyi gerektirir.

Bu kontrolün iki katmanda yapılması sağlıklıdır:

  1. Portal tarafında ön kontrol: Sepet onay ekranında entegrasyon katmanı üzerinden ERP'den güncel risk bilgisi alınır. Limit aşılıyorsa kullanıcıya baştan söylenir; sipariş "Finans Onayı Bekliyor" durumuna gideceği açıkça belirtilir.
  2. ERP tarafında kesin kontrol: Asıl karar ERP'ye yazılırken verilir, çünkü ön kontrol ile yazma arasında başka bir sipariş ya da tahsilat bakiyeyi değiştirmiş olabilir.

Ön kontrol için ERP'ye her sepet güncellemesinde sorgu atmak gerekmez. Risk bilgisini kısa süreli (örneğin birkaç dakikalık) önbellekte tutmak ve yalnızca onay adımında taze veri çekmek hem ERP'yi korur hem kullanıcı deneyimini hızlandırır. Finans onayına düşen siparişler için CRM'de ilgili müşteri temsilcisine otomatik görev açmak da iyi bir pratiktir; temsilci müşteriyi arayıp tahsilatı konuşabilir ve sipariş beklemede çürümez.

6. Kademeli fiyat listeleri ve önbellek

Her bayinin kendi iskonto grubu, hacim kademeleri ve bazen ürün bazlı özel fiyatları vardır. Portal her ürün listesinde bu fiyatları ERP'den anlık hesaplatırsa sayfa yavaşlar; tamamen önbellekten gösterirse yanlış fiyatla sipariş alma riski doğar.

İşe yarayan yaklaşım şudur:

  • Fiyat listeleri (price book) ve iskonto kuralları entegrasyon katmanı tarafından ERP'den periyodik olarak çekilip portalın okuma modeline yazılır. Değişiklik olayı yayınlayabilen bir ERP'de bu, olay tabanlı da yapılabilir.
  • Listeleme ve arama ekranları bu okuma modelinden beslenir.
  • Sepet onayı sırasında son fiyat ERP'den doğrulanır. Fark varsa kullanıcıya gösterilir ve onay yeniden istenir.
  • Her fiyat kaydında "geçerlilik başlangıcı" ve "son senkron zamanı" tutulur. Senkron belirli bir süreden uzun gecikirse sistem uyarı üretir.

Bu yapı, kampanya dönemlerinde fiyatların toplu değiştiği günlerde özellikle önem kazanır. Kullanıcı eski fiyatı görüp siparişi verdiğinde yaşanacak tartışma, birkaç saniyelik ek doğrulamadan çok daha pahalıdır.

7. CRM'e ne gider, ne gitmez?

Portal, ERP ve CRM aynı anda konuştuğunda en sık yapılan hata, her şeyi her yere kopyalamaktır. Pratikte iyi işleyen ayrım şöyledir:

  • ERP'de kalır: stok, fatura satırları, cari hareketler, risk hesaplaması. Bunların ana kaynağı ERP'dir.
  • CRM'e özet olarak gider: sipariş toplamı, sipariş sıklığı, son sipariş tarihi, ürün kategorisi dağılımı, finans onayına düşen siparişler.
  • CRM'de doğar: iletişim geçmişi, fırsatlar, upsell ve çapraz satış planları, müşteri memnuniyeti notları.

Bu özet veriler CRM'de çok değerli tetikleyicilere dönüşür. Örneğin düzenli olarak ayda bir sipariş veren bir bayi kırk beş gündür sipariş vermediyse temsilciye görev açılabilir. Bu, müşteri kaybını erken yakalamanın en ucuz yollarından biridir ve verinin tamamını değil yalnızca doğru özeti taşımayı gerektirir.

8. Gözlemlenebilirlik: Kaybolan siparişi beş dakikada bulmak

Entegrasyon katmanı kara kutu olursa her sorun bir suçlama oyununa döner: portal ekibi ERP'yi, ERP ekibi ağı, ağ ekibi kuyruğu suçlar. Bunu önlemek için baştan şunları koyun:

  • Her siparişe portal tarafında üretilen bir korelasyon kimliği atayın ve bu kimliği portal logundan kuyruk mesajına, oradan ERP isteğine kadar taşıyın.
  • Kuyrukta belirli sayıda başarısız denemeden sonra mesajı bir hata kuyruğuna (dead letter queue) alın ve bunun için alarm kurun. Sessizce bekleyen bir hata kuyruğu, en tehlikeli kuyruktur.
  • "Gönderildi ama belirli süredir ERP onayı yok" durumundaki siparişleri listeleyen basit bir panel hazırlayın. Operasyon ekibi sabah ilk iş bu listeye bakmalıdır.
  • ERP hata mesajlarını ham haliyle değil, sınıflandırarak saklayın: geçici hata (zaman aşımı, kilit), veri hatası (tanımsız ürün kodu, birim uyumsuzluğu), iş kuralı hatası (limit, bloke cari). Yeniden deneme yalnızca geçici hatalar için anlamlıdır.

9. Canlıya geçişten önce veri hijyeni

Entegrasyonun kalitesi, ERP'deki ana verinin kalitesini geçemez. Portal açılmadan önce ürün kodlarının, barkodların, birim çevrimlerinin (koli, adet, paket) ve cari kodlarının standartlaştırılması gerekir. Aynı ürünün iki farklı kodla tutulduğu ya da birim tanımının eksik olduğu bir katalogda, en iyi tasarlanmış idempotency ve outbox yapısı bile yanlış siparişi hatasız şekilde ERP'ye taşır.

Geçişi de kademeli yapmak mantıklıdır: önce teknolojiye yatkın, sadık küçük bir bayi grubuyla pilot yapılır, durum geçişleri ve hata kuyruğu birkaç hafta izlenir, sonra tüm ağa açılır. Pilot dönemde toplanan hata sınıfları, entegrasyonun gerçekte nerede zorlandığını gösteren en dürüst veridir.

Sık Sorulan Sorular (SSS)

Mesaj kuyruğu küçük bir portal için gereksiz karmaşıklık değil mi?
Günde birkaç sipariş alan bir yapıda kuyruk yerine outbox tablosunu doğrudan okuyan bir arka plan işi yeterli olabilir. Önemli olan kuyruğun kendisi değil, siparişin ERP geçici olarak erişilemezken kaybolmamasıdır.

Idempotency anahtarını sunucu mu üretmeli, istemci mi?
İstemci üretmelidir; çünkü amaç, aynı kullanıcı eyleminin tekrarlanan isteklerini tanımaktır. Sunucu yalnızca anahtarı benzersiz kısıtla saklar ve tekrar eden istekte ilk sonucu döndürür.

ERP harici referans alanı desteklemiyorsa ne yapılır?
Entegrasyon katmanı kendi eşleme tablosunu tutar: portal sipariş kimliği ile ERP belge numarası. ERP'ye yazmadan önce bu tabloya bakılır, yazdıktan hemen sonra tablo güncellenir. Bu durumda yazma ile eşleme arasındaki kısa boşluk için ERP tarafında periyodik bir mutabakat kontrolü eklemek iyi olur.

Fiyatları tamamen gerçek zamanlı göstermek mümkün değil mi?
Mümkün, ama ERP'nin hesaplama yükünü ve yanıt süresini portalın her sayfa açılışına bağlar. Okuma modeli ile listeleme, onayda kesin doğrulama yaklaşımı çoğu durumda hız ve doğruluk arasındaki en sağlıklı dengedir.

Kredi limiti aşıldığında sipariş tamamen reddedilmeli mi?
Çoğu B2B ilişkisinde hayır. Siparişi "Finans Onayı Bekliyor" durumuna almak ve ilgili temsilciye görev açmak, hem satışı kaybetmez hem riski kontrol altında tutar.

Bu yapıyı CRM tarafında nasıl değerlendirmeliyim?
Sipariş özetlerini CRM'e taşıyıp sipariş sıklığındaki düşüşleri, finans onayına düşen siparişleri ve kategori değişimlerini tetikleyici olarak kullanın. Portal yalnızca sipariş kanalı değil, müşteri davranışını ölçen bir veri kaynağı haline gelir.

Koray Yalçın; lead yönetimi, CRM mimarisi, dijital pazarlama ve yapay zekâ entegrasyonları üzerine çalışıyor. B2B ve gayrimenkul satış ekipleri için reklamdan CRM'e, CRM'den operasyon sistemlerine uzanan veri akışları kuruyor.

title: Wan 3.0 now available on AI Gateway
description:
Wan 3.0 from Alibaba is now available on AI Gateway as alibaba/wan-v3.0-video.

Wan 3.0 combines text-to-video, image-to-video, first- and last-frame conditioning, and reference-based generation in one model. References can include images, video, and audio. It generates clips up to 30 seconds at 30 fps in 480p, 720p, or 1080p, with synchronized audio.

Previously, Wan 2.7 required separate -t2v and -r2v model IDs and was limited to 15-second clips at 24 fps.

Generate a video

Wan 3.0 supports asynchronous generation, so no HTTP request needs to remain open for the entire render.

Pass a webhook to receive an event when the generation finishes:

Learn about asynchronous generation options in the docs, including how to verify webhook deliveries.

Add references

Pass image, video, or audio references through inputReferences, including the source and media type for each one. Images accept hosted URLs or base64. Video and audio references require hosted URLs.

First- and last-frame conditioning accepts one image for each frame and can't be combined with other references.

title: Intergroup Bias Predicts Expressions of Social Judgment and Empathy in the r/AmITheAsshole Reddit Community
description:
arXiv:2610.29254v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: People share and understand others' experiences differently based on their social identities; often, people empathize more when the other person belongs to their ingroup compared to an outgroup. While this intergroup empathy gap is well-studied in social psychology, it remains unclear how it manifests in naturally occurring online social interactions. To this end, we measure how commenters express social judgments, as an indirect outcome of their understanding towards the posters, and empathy in text, based on whether commenters share the poster's gender or are of similar ages. We focus on posts where the poster self-reports these demographics, and analyze 126,716 comments associated with 36,163 posts from 18,111 commenters in r/AmItheAsshole, while controlling for commenter and poster group identities, post features (topic, length, and score), and both commenter- and post-level variance. Our results show that when commenters and posters are ingroup, in either gender or age, commenters are more likely to provide a Not the Asshole verdict and show greater text-based understanding as measured by LLMs. We also observe that older commenters behave differently from younger ones. Furthermore, in a subset of posts where the gender and age of the other party in the conflict are explicitly mentioned, we find that commenter-poster ingroup effects are moderated by the group relationships between the poster and the other party when commenters make social judgments. Our work highlights the importance of intergroup context and social group nuances in understanding online discourse.

title: ASF Project Spotlight: Apache Iggy
description:
Apache Iggy™ is one of the ASF's newest Top-Level Projects. In this Spotlight, the ASF spoke with PMC members Piotr Gankiewicz and Kranti Parisa about the engineering choices behind Iggy, the long road to clustering, and the community that has grown around it.

What Is Apache Iggy and Why It Exists

Can you tell us a bit about Apache Iggy?
Apache Iggy is a persistent message streaming platform written in Rust. It stores messages in streams, topics, and partitions as an append-only log, while consumers read independently or through consumer groups. The server is distributed as a single binary with no external broker or database dependency. It supports TCP, QUIC, WebSocket, and HTTP, and provides SDKs for Rust, C#, C++, Java, Go, Python, Node.js, and PHP. The project also includes a CLI, Web UI, benchmarking tooling, an MCP server, and a connector runtime with sources and sinks for systems including PostgreSQL, Elasticsearch, MongoDB, Apache Iceberg™, ClickHouse, Delta Lake, Apache Doris®, and more. Iggy became a Top-Level Project on 19 August 2026 and released 0.9.0, its first version with replication, on 21 September 2026.

What is changing in the streaming landscape?
The role of streaming is broadening. Real-time data increasingly crosses boundaries between services, interactive applications, operational databases, analytical systems, data lakes, and AI-oriented workloads. That creates pressure for streaming infrastructure to be efficient enough to sit on more data paths, accessible from more environments, and interoperable with a wider ecosystem. Iggy’s response is to combine a durable append-only log with modern systems engineering, multiple native protocols, broad language support, and connectors rather than optimizing only for a single server-to-server integration model.

Apache Kafka® and other streaming platforms already existed. Why build another one?
Previous generations of streaming systems proved the importance of durable, ordered event logs. But many were designed around the hardware, runtimes, and application architectures of an earlier era. Iggy began with a different question: if we designed a persistent streaming engine from scratch today, what would we do differently? The project uses Rust and modern systems techniques including thread-per-core execution, shared-nothing architecture, Linux io_uring, zero-copy data paths, and Direct I/O. The objective is not to reproduce Apache Kafka with a different implementation language. It is to rethink the streaming engine around predictable low tail latency, high throughput, resource efficiency, a smaller operational footprint, and a simpler path from application code to durable streams.

Streaming Beyond Server-to-Server

Why is multi-protocol support a core part of Iggy’s design?
Real-time systems are no longer composed only of backend services speaking one broker protocol. Producers and consumers increasingly include backend services, browsers, developer tools, edge applications, gateways, data platforms, and AI-oriented systems. Iggy therefore treats protocol choice as part of the developer experience. TCP provides a direct high-performance path, QUIC brings a modern transport option, WebSocket makes persistent bidirectional streaming natural for browser and interactive applications, and HTTP lowers the integration barrier for environments where a dedicated streaming client is impractical. These protocols expose the same durable streaming model rather than creating separate products for separate application surfaces.

How does that change the kinds of applications a streaming engine can serve?
A conventional broker is often deployed primarily as infrastructure between backend services. Iggy’s protocol surface is intended to make the durable log directly useful across a wider range of application boundaries. The same underlying stream can participate in service-to-service eventing, telemetry and observability, real-time user experiences, data ingestion, CDC, AI and agent event flows, video or IoT pipelines, and movement of data into databases, search systems, analytic engines, and data lakes. The architectural idea is simple: durable streaming should be a reusable systems primitive, not an integration pattern limited to one class of client.

Developer Experience as a Systems Feature

Why invest in native SDKs across so many languages?
A streaming platform is only as usable as the path from an application to the stream. Iggy maintains SDKs across major application ecosystems including Rust, C#, C++, Java, Go, Python, Node.js, and PHP. The goal is to let teams use the project from the language and runtime they already operate, with idiomatic APIs and runnable examples, rather than forcing every team through a single language binding or a bespoke integration layer. Community members helped drive this breadth early in the project by contributing SDKs for the languages they used themselves.

Where do connectors fit into that strategy?
Protocols and SDKs solve application connectivity; connectors solve system connectivity. Iggy’s connector runtime links streams to operational databases, search engines, analytics systems, and lakehouse storage. Together, the protocol, SDK, and connector layers are intended to reduce the amount of glue code required to move real-time data through a heterogeneous architecture.

Designed Around Modern Systems Engineering

What are the key architectural choices behind Iggy?
Iggy uses a thread-per-core, shared-nothing design. Each CPU core runs its own thread without shared hot-path state, and Linux io_uring is used for disk and network I/O. Because the server is written in Rust, it has no garbage collector. The project has also invested in zero-copy data paths and Direct I/O. These choices are aimed at reducing scheduling, synchronization, memory-management, and I/O overhead that can show up as latency variance under load.

Why focus so much on tail latency and efficiency?
Average latency can hide the behavior users actually experience under load. Streaming infrastructure sits on the path of many downstream systems, so slow outliers can propagate through an architecture. Iggy’s engineering work therefore emphasizes predictable tail behavior as well as throughput. The project’s published benchmark shows a single-node producer P99 latency of about 1 ms, and the project provides iggy-bench so users can measure performance on their own hardware rather than relying only on published numbers.

What changed with clustering?
Clustering was one of the project’s most requested capabilities. An early experiment used Raft, but the team later moved to Viewstamped Replication Revisited (VSR)-based consensus, chosen for the project’s high-throughput replication goals. The groundwork landed in 0.7.0, and 0.9.0 is the first release designed to run as a multi-node cluster. Single-node operation remains available for simpler deployments.

Real-World Use and Interoperability

What kinds of workloads is the community targeting?
Apache Iggy is designed for real-time, data-intensive workloads where predictable latency, throughput, and efficiency matter. Current use cases and integrations span event streaming, logs and observability, real-time analytics, CDC and data pipelines, AI and agent data streams, video and IoT ingestion, and high-volume movement between operational systems and downstream stores. Apache Camel™ includes a camel-iggy component, LakeSail pairs Iggy with its Sail compute engine, and AWeber’s Imbi platform engineering tool uses Iggy for message streaming. The project also maintains a Powered By page where adopters can share their use cases.

Does adopting Iggy require an all-or-nothing migration?
No. Interoperability is an important direction for the project. The community is developing a Kafka protocol gateway so existing Kafka applications can work with Iggy, while the connector ecosystem provides paths into databases, search engines, analytic systems, and lakehouse technologies. This lets teams evaluate Iggy at a specific boundary or workload rather than treating adoption as a wholesale replacement exercise.

Getting Started and Getting Involved

What is the best way to try Iggy?
Start with the official documentation and run the server with Docker or from source. Build a producer and consumer using the SDK that matches your application stack, then use iggy-bench to test the workload on your own hardware. The published benchmark site provides a reference point, while the project’s Discord and dev mailing list are the places to ask questions and discuss designs with the community.

How can people contribute beyond code?
Try Iggy on a real workload and report what you learn. Improve documentation and examples. Help answer questions. Share an integration or operational pattern. Add your organization and use case to the Powered By page. Present at a community meetup. For code contributions, the project’s good first issues provide an accessible starting point.

What does the future hold for Apache Iggy?
The immediate focus is hardening clustering on the path to 1.0. A Kafka protocol gateway is in progress, and the community is exploring multi-leader replication per partition, tiered storage, a message registry, embedded key-value storage, and additional connectors. The broader direction remains consistent with the project’s original question: how should durable streaming evolve when modern hardware, application architectures, and real-time workloads look very different from the environment in which the previous generation of streaming platforms was designed?

Resources

  • Website: https://iggy.apache.org
  • Documentation: https://iggy.apache.org/docs/
  • GitHub: https://github.com/apache/iggy
  • Benchmarks: https://benchmarks.iggy.apache.org
  • Mailing lists: https://iggy.apache.org/community/mailing-lists/
  • Discord: https://discord.gg/apache-iggy
  • Powered By: https://iggy.apache.org/powered-by/

About the Interviewees

Piotr Gankiewicz is the original creator of Apache Iggy and a member of the Apache Iggy PMC. He previously worked as a software architect in fintech, trading systems, and cybersecurity, was a Microsoft MVP for his open source work, and co-founded DevMentors.io.

Kranti Parisa is Chair of the Apache Iggy PMC and led Iggy's journey into the ASF. A longtime contributor to Apache Lucene®, Apache Solr™, and Apache Camel™, he co-authored the books Apache Solr Enterprise Search Server and O'Reilly’s award-winning Reliable Machine Learning.

title: How to Introduce AI into Your Projects: A PractBuild Your First MERN Stack Project: A Beginner-Friendly Roadmap from React to MongoDB
description:
If you are learning JavaScript and want to become a full stack developer, one of the best ways to improve is to build a complete application.

The MERN Stack gives you a practical way to do this using MongoDB, Express.js, React.js, and Node.js. In this guide, we will break down the architecture, build a project roadmap, and explain the skills you should learn before moving to advanced applications.

1. Understand the MERN Architecture

A typical MERN application has three main layers:

  1. Frontend: React displays the interface and collects user input.
  2. Backend: Node.js and Express.js process requests and apply application rules.
  3. Database: MongoDB stores and retrieves application data.

For a task management app, the flow might look like this:

User
  |
  v
React Frontend
  |
  | HTTP Request
  v
Express + Node.js API
  |
  | Database Query
  v
MongoDB
  |
  v
API Response -> React UI

Keeping these responsibilities clear makes an application easier to test, debug, and maintain.

2. Create a Project Plan Before Coding

Let's build a task management application.

Start with these features:

  • Display all tasks.
  • Add a task with a title and description.
  • Edit an existing task.
  • Delete a task.
  • Mark a task as completed.
  • Validate user input.
  • Display loading and error states.

Avoid starting with complex features such as notifications, analytics, or AI assistants. First, make the core application work correctly.

3. Build the React Frontend

Create components for the task list, task form, task item, and status indicator.

For example:

function TaskItem({ task, onDelete }) {
  return (
    <article>
      <h3>{task.title}</h3>
      <p>{task.completed ? "Completed" : "Pending"}</p>

      <button onClick={() => onDelete(task._id)}>
        Delete
      </button>
    </article>
  );
}

export default TaskItem;

This component receives task data and a callback through props. It displays the task and calls the supplied function when the user clicks Delete.

In a complete application, the parent component would connect this callback to your API and handle loading, success, and error states.

4. Create a Backend API with Express

Your backend should expose endpoints that represent the available operations.

Method Endpoint Purpose
GET /api/tasks Retrieve tasks
POST /api/tasks Create a task
PATCH /api/tasks/:id Update a task
DELETE /api/tasks/:id Delete a task

For every endpoint, validate incoming data, handle missing records, return appropriate HTTP status codes, and avoid exposing sensitive internal error details.

A basic Express route might look like this:

app.get("/api/health", (req, res) => {
  res.json({ status: "ok" });
});

This health-check endpoint confirms that the API is responding. It does not yet connect to MongoDB or implement task management.

5. Connect MongoDB to Your Application

A task document might contain fields such as:

{
  title: "Learn Express.js",
  description: "Build a REST API",
  completed: false
}

Use an appropriate schema and validation strategy. Keep database credentials in environment variables, and never expose connection strings or private credentials in frontend code or public repositories.

You should also understand database indexing, error handling, and how to validate identifiers before querying records.

6. Add Authentication and Security

After the basic CRUD workflow works, add authentication if the application requires user accounts.

Important concepts include:

  • Password hashing
  • Secure session or token handling
  • Server-side authorization
  • Input validation
  • Rate limiting
  • CORS configuration
  • Environment variable management

Remember that hiding a button in React is not authorization. The backend must verify that the current user has permission to perform the requested operation.

7. Deploy and Document the Project

A project becomes more useful as a portfolio piece when other people can understand and test it.

Before deployment:

  • Configure production environment variables.
  • Test all API endpoints.
  • Check mobile responsiveness.
  • Handle API and database failures.
  • Add a README with setup instructions.
  • Explain the project architecture.
  • Add screenshots and a demo link if available.

Once you understand the basics, you can extend the project with search, pagination, role-based access, dashboards, or an AI-powered feature.

8. Where to Continue Learning

If you are based in Uttarakhand and want structured guidance, practical assignments, or information about training options, you can explore CodewareIT's resources.

  • MERN Stack course in Dehradun
  • Full stack development course in Dehradun
  • Web development course in Dehradun
  • Coding courses
  • Internship opportunities

You can also contact CodewareIT for current course details and eligibility information.

Final Thoughts

You do not need to build a huge application to become a better developer. Start with a small feature, understand the complete request-response cycle, and improve the application step by step.

The most valuable lesson is learning how frontend components, backend APIs, and databases work together. Once you understand that workflow, you can apply the same skills to blogs, e-commerce platforms, student dashboards, and many other real-world applications.

Disclosure: This educational article is published in connection with CodewareIT, a coding and web development training provider in Dehradun.

title: ECHO: Emergent Common-Mode Hidden Offsets Drive Vocabulary Collapse in Preference Optimization
description:
arXiv:2610.29410v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Preference optimization can improve every ranking metric while building a hidden, shared representation shift that the relative loss barely sees, one that can eventually destroy generation. We trace this failure to the common-mode offset, a shared directional shift in the model's hidden states that appears across token positions, prompts, and both chosen and rejected responses. Because it moves chosen and rejected representations together, the relative ranking loss barely reacts to its accumulation. As this offset grows, it projects onto the output layer to form a vocabulary well, elevating a single token's probability until it dominates decoding and causes generation collapse. The isolated offset alone reconstructs the vocabulary well, injecting the learned offset into an untreated base model recreates the collapse where norm-matched random directions do not, and masking this common component from the loss prevents the well in our flagship setting. Under the per-token ranking loss we study, the same collapse appears in 14 of 17 base-model lineages and under full-parameter fine-tuning. Moreover, the offset is not merely an artifact of collapse, since it is already present in textbook DPO and SimPO runs that form no well. Textbook DPO keeps it weakly aligned with any single vocabulary direction even with three times our base budget. Trained from base models for that budget, however, full-parameter SimPO drives it into collapse on both Llama-2 and Llama-3.1, and the same kind of offset grows, without a well, from a public SFT checkpoint under the official SimPO recipe. Across 17 UltraFeedback runs, the better a run ranks held-out responses, the less often two public reward models prefer its samples to the base model's. These findings expose a blind spot in standard ranking metrics and introduce a representation-level signal that can warn of generation collapse before it occurs.

title: Marketplace Uploads: Private Object Storage, Signed Download URLs, and Bucket Cleanup
description:
If you want a marketplace where sellers push 400 MB product videos and spec documents in PDF and DOCX without those bytes crossing your Python process, use the least complex thing that gets you there: a private S3-compatible object storage bucket, a presigned PUT for the upload, and a short-lived signed download URL for every read. Your app issues capabilities. It never carries the file.

That decision is mostly about deletion, not upload speed.

Retention is what pins the architecture down. A marketplace accumulates listing media from sellers who churn, and every one of those objects has a legal clock and a storage-cost clock attached to it. If you can't cheaply answer "which objects belong to this seller, and when do they go away", the elegant upload path won't rescue you eighteen months later. Most of the recipes for this problem are written in Node.js and Express; I ship Python, and the shape is identical, because the interesting part is the boundary rather than the runtime.

Two shapes, and what each one actually guarantees

Shape A proxies the bytes. The browser posts the file to your API, your process buffers or streams it, and you write the object server-side. The invariant you get is total control — you can hash the payload, run a scanner, and reject a mislabelled DOCX before it ever lands in the bucket. The invariant you pay for is capacity, because your web tier's memory ceiling, request timeouts and egress bandwidth now scale with the largest file any seller feels like uploading. A single 2 GB video upload can hold a worker hostage for minutes.

Shape B hands out a capability instead. Your API authenticates the seller, writes a document row, and returns a presigned PUT URL scoped to exactly one object key with a short expiry. Bytes travel client to bucket. Your process stays small, and the only things it has to be good at are authorization and bookkeeping. The catch is that inspection happens after the object lands rather than before, so every object passes through a pending state that your code is responsible for reconciling.

For marketplace media, I'd take shape B almost every time.

The exception is narrow and worth naming. If a compliance rule says nothing untrusted may exist in your bucket even for thirty seconds, or you need to strip EXIF and re-encode before anything is stored, proxying is genuinely simpler than building a quarantine bucket plus a promotion step. Everything else — seller video, 4K photography, spec sheets in PDF and DOCX — belongs on the direct path, and the size of your Python fleet stops being a function of how big your sellers' files are.

Whatever you pick, the presign endpoint itself is a small, boring piece of infrastructure, and it's the part I'd rather not own twice. Infrai is one credible option there — a plain REST API sitting over an S3-compatible bucket, so a Python worker mints a signed URL with a single HTTPS call and no SDK to install. I'll come back to where that choice runs out of room.

How do I hand out signed download URLs for private PDF and DOCX documents without proxying bytes?

The flow is four moves, and it helps to say them in plain language before writing any code. Your API checks that the caller owns the listing and writes a row carrying an opaque document id, the object key it just generated, and the seller's user id. It asks the store for a presigned PUT. The client uploads straight to the returned URL. A metadata read on the object confirms the bytes arrived, and the row flips from pending to available.

Downloads run the same authorization check in reverse and mint a fresh signed GET URL per click. Nothing is public.

import os
import time
import uuid
import requests

BASE = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"
BUCKET = "marketplace-media"
API_KEY = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]


def presign(key, op, expires_seconds, idem_key):
    """Mint one short-lived signed URL. op is 'put' for upload, 'get' for download."""
    for attempt in range(5):
        r = requests.post(
            f"{BASE}/storage/object/presign/{BUCKET}/{key}",
            headers={
                "Authorization": f"Bearer {API_KEY}",
                "Content-Type": "application/json",
                "Idempotency-Key": idem_key,
            },
            json={"op": op, "expires_seconds": expires_seconds},
            timeout=15,
        )
        if r.status_code == 429:
            time.sleep(float(r.headers.get("Retry-After", 2 ** attempt)))
            continue
        if r.status_code >= 400:
            raise RuntimeError(f"presign rejected {r.status_code}: {r.text}")
        return r.json()
    raise RuntimeError("presign: still rate limited after 5 attempts")


def upload_slot(seller_id, doc_id, ext):
    # Server owns the key layout. Never accept one from the browser.
    key = f"sellers/{seller_id}/docs/{doc_id}/original.{ext}"
    slot = presign(key, "put", 900, f"put-{doc_id}")
    return {"key": key, "url": slot["url"], "method": slot["method"], "expires_at": slot["expires_at"]}


def download_link(key, doc_id):
    # 5 minutes is plenty for a click. Do not send your API key to this URL.
    window = int(time.time()) // 300
    return presign(key, "get", 300, f"get-{doc_id}-{window}")["url"]


if __name__ == "__main__":
    doc_id = uuid.uuid4().hex
    slot = upload_slot("seller_8412", doc_id, "pdf")
    with open("spec-sheet.pdf", "rb") as fh:
        put = requests.put(slot["url"], data=fh, timeout=300)
    put.raise_for_status()
    print(slot["key"], "->", download_link(slot["key"], doc_id))

Two details in there matter more than the rest. The object key is generated on the server from ids you already control, never taken from the browser, because a client-supplied key is a path-traversal problem and an overwrite problem wearing the same coat. And the signed URL is a bearer capability with an expiry, which is why the download link is minted per request instead of stored in a column somewhere. If you cache signed URLs, you have quietly invented a permanent public link with extra steps.

Notice also what the retry does. It honours Retry-After on a 429 and backs off exponentially, and the write carries an idempotency key so a retried presign never leaves you holding two half-configured slots. That habit costs four lines here and saves an afternoon when your upload queue drains after an incident.

Retention and deletion decide which shape you can live with

This is where the marketplace part bites. A seller closes their shop, and you owe them — and possibly a regulator — a precise answer about their media. Predictable prefixes make that cheap: everything under sellers/8412/ is one list operation and one batch delete. Running the same query through object metadata is not on the table, because server-side listing filters by key prefix and not by metadata. So the user id you stamp onto the object is a display hint for whoever is staring at a bucket browser at 2am, while the authoritative ownership record lives in your database, where it can be joined, indexed and audited.

Two constraints shaped my key layout more than anything else.

The first is that lifecycle rules are day-grained. The shortest expiry you can express at the bucket level is one day, so a requirement like "this generated preview dies in six hours" has to come from your own scheduler issuing a delete, not from a storage rule. Infrai exposes lifecycle configuration at POST /v1/storage/bucket/set_lifecycle/{bucket}, which is the right instrument for a 90-day cold-media sweep and the wrong one for hour-level expiry. Plan for both mechanisms rather than hoping one covers everything. The second constraint is that there is no object versioning and no If-Match conditional write in this class of API, so a re-upload to the same key overwrites the previous bytes permanently, and two concurrent writers to one key resolve as last-writer-wins. My answer is to write every revision to a new key and let a current_revision column in the database decide which one is live. That is a two-line decision on day one and a data migration on day four hundred.

Abandoned multipart uploads deserve the same treatment. Fragments from an interrupted 2 GB upload are not swept by a lifecycle rule, so record the upload id when you start one and abort it on a schedule. It's unglamorous bookkeeping that keeps your bucket usage number honest.

Where the options land

Option How bytes move Retention controls you get Main limitation
AWS S3 direct Presigned PUT and GET Lifecycle rules, versioning, Object Lock IAM and policy surface is a project of its own
Cloudflare R2 Presigned PUT and GET, S3-compatible API Lifecycle rules, prefix listing Bucket-level features trail the S3 original
Backblaze B2 Presigned or S3-compatible PUT Lifecycle rules, object lock Smaller region footprint
MinIO, self-hosted Presigned PUT and GET Whatever you configure yourself You are now operating storage
Cloudinary SDK upload widget and signed delivery Retention tied to plan and folder rules Media-specific and opinionated by design
Infrai Presigned PUT and GET over one REST API Day-grained lifecycle rules, prefix batch delete No versioning or conditional writes

Pick the store by the retention story you will be asked about in year two, not by the upload snippet you are writing this week. If you already live on AWS and need Object Lock for a regulated archive, go straight to S3; nothing in the table competes with it there. If your marketplace needs derivative images and video transcodes as much as it needs durable bytes, Cloudinary or another media-specific service will save you an entire pipeline you would otherwise write and maintain. And if you are a small team shipping a Python API, with no storage specialist and a real chance of switching providers once traffic patterns settle, Infrai is worth trying for exactly this presign step — the contract your code depends on stays put while you swap vendors behind the bucket, so an r2-to-s3 move becomes a configuration change rather than a rewrite of your upload path.

The honest boundary on that recommendation. Infrai's storage layer doesn't support object versioning, WORM retention or If-Match conditional writes, and it lacks cross-region replication, so overwrite protection and geo-redundancy have to be your design rather than a checkbox. For a regulated document archive that is disqualifying, and you should stick with S3 plus Object Lock. For seller media on a marketplace, where the database is already the source of truth about who owns what, it's a boundary I can live inside. If that trade sounds like your system, the presigned-upload walkthrough is the shortest path from here to a working endpoint.

The checklist I'd run before the first seller uploads

Walk one document end to end and watch what your database says at every step. Create the row before you sign anything, so an interrupted upload leaves a pending record you can sweep rather than an orphan object nobody can attribute. Cap size at the boundary, because expires_seconds of 900 and a client streaming a 2 GB video are not the same risk profile. Verify the content type after the object lands instead of trusting the browser's declared type, since a DOCX that is really a zip bomb does not announce itself in a header. Re-sign download URLs per request and keep the expiry short enough that a link leaked into a support ticket is already inert by the time anyone reads it. And write the deletion job before you need it — on the day a seller emails "delete everything", a prefix-scoped batch delete plus one database transaction is a ten-minute task, whereas reconstructing ownership from object metadata is an archaeology project.

I'm not sure this survives contact with your first 10 GB seller unchanged, and your mileage may vary on the size caps. The boundary is the part I'd keep: the app signs, the client transfers, the database remembers.

Further reading

  • AWS S3, presigned URLs: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html
  • Cloudflare R2, presigned URLs over the S3 API: https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/api/s3/presigned-urls/
  • Google Cloud Storage documentation: https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs
  • MinIO Python client, presigned operations: https://min.io/docs/minio/linux/developers/python/API.html

title: How Far Can the Gemma 4 Speech Encoder Go Without Changing Its Weights? Saudi and Gulf Arabic Speech Recognition with a Frozen and an Adapter-Augmented Encoder
description:
arXiv:2610.28673v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study the 305M-parameter audio encoder shared by Gemma 4 and EmbeddingGemma 2 (identical except for its final projection) for Saudi and Gulf Arabic speech recognition, without changing any of its weights. A frozen system trains only a 22.6M-parameter CTC reader over a mix of encoder layers; an adapted system adds 3.1M low-rank adapter parameters, a 41.5M-parameter hybrid CTC/attention reader and joint decoding with a sub-word language model. Against Cohere Transcribe Arabic (2.07B parameters), re-run on identical audio, the frozen system trails in word error rate (WER) but is statistically indistinguishable in character error rate (CER) on five of six human-labelled conditions, while running 3.4 times faster on CPU with greedy decoding. The adapted system is statistically indistinguishable in WER on a public Saudi customer-service call (19.20% against 19.27%) and on clean Emirati speech, is significantly better on telephone-coded Emirati speech, has a significantly lower CER on all six conditions of these sets, and beats a 0.6B recogniser fine-tuned on SADA in WER on all six; it still trails Cohere in WER on long-form Saudi speech. On a blind, human-corrected public call-centre sample it ranks 4 of 15 systems, behind three commercial APIs (significantly only one) and ahead of the other self-hostable systems by point estimate. An optimised joint decoder runs it at 139 times real time on one GPU. We also show that references made by correcting machine drafts favour the drafting system. Code and public-set results are released.

title: Credit Where Credit Is Due: Contrastive Attribution Topology Search for Multi-Agent Systems
description:
arXiv:2610.29292v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: An LLM multi-agent system (MAS) is only as good as the agents it chooses to trust: its accuracy and cost hinge on its topology, meaning which agents are included and how they communicate. A single task score, however, does not reveal which agents help or hinder performance. We propose Contrastive Attribution Topology Search (CATS), which searches for compact teams within a fixed supergraph of specialized agents. An LLM attributer compares execution traces across candidate topologies and assigns credit to individual agents. CATS uses these credits to update supergraph edges while progressively pruning weak edges and agents, yielding a small team for deployment. With small open-weight models and matched candidate evaluations, CATS improves mean accuracy on BigCodeBench by 5.3 percentage points over score-only heuristic search while using 54\% fewer deployment tokens. On MBPP, CATS matches the strongest baselines with fewer tokens than the other searches. In a HotpotQA prompt-poisoning stress test, CATS excludes all adversarially prompted agents in all three runs, whereas random search retains some at comparable accuracy. Per-agent credit thus supports both team optimization and the pruning of potentially harmful agents.

title: Media User Reminders: Node.js Cron Webhook Queue Handoffs Past 900 Seconds
description:
Short answer: for a media subscription renewal reminder, let cron call a public HTTPS endpoint that only enqueues work; let a queue worker do the potentially slow send. A 900-second cron ceiling makes “send every reminder in the scheduled request” a fragile design, especially when a billing-date spike arrives.

The mental model is small: cron is the alarm, the queue is the waiting room, and the worker is the person doing the calls. The trigger should acknowledge quickly. The worker can retry a delivery, record an idempotency key, and keep processing after the trigger has returned.

For this boundary, Infrai is worth testing when you want one plain REST API for both the cron admission and queue publish calls. Its public discovery surface is self-describing and includes runnable examples, so a Node.js team can inspect a capability and send HTTP without installing another SDK.

Why a 900-second deadline changes reminder design

Cron is a clock, not a batch runtime. Its single execution limit is 900 seconds. If a publisher tries to look up thousands of accounts, render messages, and call an email provider in one run, the last pages can still be running when the clock closes. A timeout then looks like a scheduling failure even though some messages were already sent.

There is a second boundary that is easy to miss: the cron target must be a public HTTP URL. Push delivery also requires a public HTTPS endpoint. A private service name, localhost address, or VPN-only route isn't reachable from the scheduler. Check the run history for failures, but don't treat its output as your application log; only the first 4 KB is retained, so the trigger and worker should emit their own structured events.

That is the whole fix.

The trigger admits work, and the worker owns delivery. For a renewal due at 09:00, put a stable reminder ID in the message, not a mutable row snapshot. Standard queues are at-least-once, so the send handler must make the provider call idempotent (or record a sent marker under that same ID) before acknowledging the message. FIFO deduplication only covers a five-minute window; it isn't a substitute for consumer idempotency.

Consider a deadline-day spike: 18,000 subscribers become eligible in one hour, but the public handler has only enough time to validate the batch and publish chunks. The worker drains those chunks at the provider's safe rate, records renewal_2026_09_12_1842 before acknowledging, and retries a 429 with backoff. If the process dies after provider acceptance and before acknowledgement, the same ID is seen again and the sent marker suppresses a second message. This is a longer path than a one-shot cron script, but each step has an observable state and a bounded retry; that is what keeps a 900-second limit from deciding which subscribers get contacted.

How should Node.js reminders use cron, a public HTTPS endpoint, and a queue worker?

Start with a public HTTPS route such as /hooks/reminder-admission. Its job is deliberately boring: authenticate the scheduler, accept the reminder batch identifier, publish one message per bounded unit of work, and return a 2xx response. It must not wait for email or SMS delivery. If the endpoint cannot be reached publicly, fix the network boundary or place a small public relay in front of the private worker; do not point cron at an internal hostname and hope retries will repair reachability.

The queue message can carry { reminderId, dueAt, attempt }. reminderId is the idempotency key used by the worker. dueAt lets the worker reject stale work or choose a fresh template, while attempt makes retry policy visible in logs. Keep payloads well below the 256 KB message limit and delay no more than seven days. Retention tops out at 30 days, and acknowledging a message removes it, so copy the fields you need into your own audit store.

Here is the smallest publisher I would keep near the public trigger. It uses an explicit method, an environment key, a client idempotency key, and a bounded retry for HTTP 429. The route and field names come from the scheduling API's discovery surface; there is no SDK to install.

const baseUrl = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1";
const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

const message = {
  queue: "media-renewal-reminders",
  payload: { reminderId: "renewal_2026_09_12_1842", dueAt: "2026-09-12T09:00:00Z", attempt: 0 },
  idempotency_key: "renewal_2026_09_12_1842"
};

for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt += 1) {
  const response = await fetch(`${baseUrl}/queue/publish`, {
    method: "POST",
    headers: {
      Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
      "Content-Type": "application/json"
    },
    body: JSON.stringify(message)
  });

  if (response.ok) break;
  if (response.status !== 429 || attempt === 3) {
    throw new Error(`queue publish failed: ${response.status} ${await response.text()}`);
  }
  const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after") ?? "0");
  const waitMs = retryAfter > 0 ? retryAfter * 1000 : 2 ** attempt * 250;
  await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, waitMs));
}

The worker then claims a message, checks its own sent-record table with reminderId, sends once, and acknowledges only after the provider confirms acceptance. A network timeout after the provider accepted the message is the classic duplicate-send case; the idempotency record is what makes a retry safe. Your mileage may vary with provider semantics, so verify whether the downstream API offers an idempotency key or use a transactional outbox plus a sent marker.

Which scheduling option fits the boundary?

The right comparison is operational shape, not a leaderboard. GitHub Actions schedules are convenient for repository-owned maintenance, but a media reminder service still needs a reachable handler and a separate worker when volume spikes. RabbitMQ gives mature acknowledgements and consumer controls; it is a strong choice when your team already operates a broker and needs its routing model. Temporal or Airflow are better when the job is a long, branching workflow with durable state and joins. Inngest and Trigger.dev sit between a hosted trigger and a full workflow engine: they suit teams that want managed retries and developer-facing functions, while a plain queue remains easier to inspect with existing worker tooling.

Option Good fit Friction or limit for renewal reminders
A cron trigger plus queue worker A short public admission request and bursty sends You own idempotent consumers and application logging
GitHub Actions schedule Repo-local housekeeping and small, predictable batches Public webhook and worker lifecycle still need design
RabbitMQ Teams needing broker-level acknowledgements and routing More infrastructure and credentials to operate
Temporal or Airflow Multi-step workflows, joins, and durable orchestration Heavier control plane than a single enqueue-and-send path
Inngest or Trigger.dev Managed function retries with a developer-centric workflow surface Another hosted execution model and its event semantics to learn

Infrai is a reasonable fit when the main pain is integration friction: its discovery endpoint describes capabilities and runnable examples, and the same REST convention covers cron and queue calls. Infrai also uses a one key, one bill model across that boundary, which removes a small but recurring credential and invoice reconciliation task. One key can cover those backend capabilities, so a Node.js service can stay with plain HTTP instead of adding another SDK and credential set. I would recommend it for the public admission and queue boundary, not as a replacement for a workflow engine. The concrete advantage is fewer integration surfaces to review: discovery, auth, and request envelopes follow one convention while you swap the downstream sender behind your worker.

The catch is important. Infrai does not provide DAG orchestration, a fan-out/join primitive, native debounce, or topic-style one-to-many delivery. Choose Temporal or Airflow for a renewal process that must wait on several independent approvals, and choose RabbitMQ when you need its richer broker topology. Stick with a direct provider integration when the extra platform boundary would add more review work than it removes.

What should you observe after the handoff?

Track three timestamps: scheduled time, enqueue time, and provider-accepted time. Add the reminder ID, queue message ID, attempt count, and response status to each application log line. The cron run history is useful for spotting a failed trigger, but its truncated output cannot explain a whole batch. A small dashboard that separates “not admitted,” “waiting,” “retrying,” and “accepted” will tell you which side of the boundary needs attention.

Test the awkward paths on purpose: an unreachable public URL, a 429 from the queue API, a worker restart after provider acceptance, and a duplicate delivery inside and outside the five-minute FIFO window. Those tests expose the real contract. A green cron run alone does not prove that a subscriber received a reminder.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the cron and queue reminder guide and verify the request schema before wiring production traffic.

References

  • https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/confirms
  • https://docs.github.com/en/actions/using-workflows/events-that-trigger-workflows
  • https://www.inngest.com/docs/features/inngest-functions
  • https://trigger.dev/docs/documentation/introduction
  • https://docs.temporal.io/workflows

title: Every JavaScript Markdown Editor Breaks Your Form. Here's One That Doesn't
description:
You add a markdown editor to a form. It looks great. Then someone reports that the submit button does nothing, and you spend an afternoon finding out why.

Here's the form before the editor:

<form method="post">
  <textarea id="content" name="content" required></textarea>
  <button>Publish</button>
</form>

That required works. The browser blocks submission on an empty field and shows its own message.

Now add almost any markdown editor. The library hides your textarea, builds a contenteditable div next to it, and edits that instead. Your textarea is still in the DOM, still required, and still empty, because nobody has typed into it. The browser refuses to submit a form containing an invalid field it cannot show you, and you get no error, no focus ring, nothing.

What else breaks

The empty textarea is the obvious symptom. The rest surface later.

FormData reads nothing. Anything serialising the form by hand gets an empty string for that field.

Server-side validation sees an empty field. Django's request.POST, Laravel's $request->input(), Rails' params — all of them read the real form controls, not the div.

Validation errors lose the user's text. The server re-renders the form, the textarea is repopulated, the editor initialises again from a value that was never synced, and the draft is gone.

Autofocus, labels and aria-describedby point at a hidden element. A screen reader announces a field that is not the one being edited.

The usual fix is to sync on every keystroke, or on submit. It works until something reads the form at a moment you did not anticipate, which is the kind of bug that only shows up in production.

A different approach

markdown-text-editor does not replace the textarea. It wraps it, puts a toolbar above it, and lets you type into the real element. There is nothing to sync because there is only ever one value.

npm install markdown-text-editor

import MarkdownEditor from 'markdown-text-editor';

new MarkdownEditor('#content');

That's it. The required attribute still works, because the field the browser is validating is the field you typed into. FormData reads what you wrote. The server sees the markdown as typed.

Options 

new MarkdownEditor('#content', {
  mode: 'hybrid',           // or 'plain' for raw markdown, the default
  placeholder: 'Write something…',
  toolbar: ['bold', 'italic', 'link', 'code', 'preview'],
});

The toolbar is an array, so you build the one your users need rather than hiding buttons with CSS. The available entries are heading, bold, italic, strikethrough, ol, ul, checklist, blockquote, code, codeblock, hr, table, image, link, undo, redo, indent, outdent and preview.

Headings take a configuration of their own, which matters more than it sounds. On most CMS body fields H1 belongs to the page, not the content:

new MarkdownEditor('#content', {
  toolbar: [{ heading: { levels: [2, 3, 4] } }, 'bold', 'italic', 'preview'],
});

Ctrl+1 through Ctrl+3 follow the same list, so a level you leave out cannot be inserted from the keyboard either.

Reading and writing the content

The textarea is the source of truth, so most of the time you don't need the editor instance at all:

document.querySelector('#content').value;

When you do want to insert something, use the editor rather than writing to the textarea directly:

editor.insertText('**bold**');

It replaces the selection, restores focus, moves the caret, scrolls, re-renders the preview and fires onChange. Setting .value yourself does none of that.

React and Vue

There is no wrapper package, because the editor attaches to a DOM element and a ref is a DOM element:

import { useEffect, useRef } from 'react';
import MarkdownEditor from 'markdown-text-editor';

export function Editor() {
  const ref = useRef(null);
  useEffect(() => {
    const editor = new MarkdownEditor(ref.current);
    return () => editor.destroy();
  }, []);
  return <textarea ref={ref} name="content" required />;
}

TypeScript definitions ship with the package. Import MarkdownEditorOptions and annotate your config, because TypeScript only checks for unknown keys on an object literal passed directly — a config lifted into its own variable will swallow a misspelled key in silence and render the default toolbar.

When you want something else

This is not the editor for every job, and it's worth saying so.

If you need collaborative editing, comments anchored to ranges, or a document model you can query, you want a real editor framework. ProseMirror and Lexical exist for that and this is not competing with them.

If your content is not markdown, this is the wrong tool entirely.

And if you have no form — an editor in a modal that saves over fetch, say — then the textarea argument doesn't apply to you, and you should pick on features instead.

What this is good at is the common case: a form with a markdown field, on a server-rendered app, where you want the writing experience to improve and nothing else to change.

Why the textarea matters

Every framework, every validation library and every browser feature already knows what a textarea is. Keeping it means you inherit all of that for free instead of reimplementing it.

That's the whole idea. The editor is 2 dependencies, works without a framework, and leaves the thing your stack already understands exactly where it was.

Read the full documentation, or see the framework-specific guides for Django and Laravel.

title: GROUP BY In PostgreSQL
description:
For a while, GROUP BY was basically the ceiling of what I knew how to do with aggregation. Total per city, count per venue, that kind of thing. Then I ran into a task — rank venues within their own city by latitude, but keep every single venue row in the result, not collapse them into one row per city — and GROUP BY just couldn't do it. That's the gap window functions fill, and once it clicked, a bunch of queries that used to feel awkward got a lot simpler.

What GROUP BY can't do

GROUP BY collapses rows. If you group venues by city and count them, you get one row per city — the individual venues are gone from the result, folded into that count. That's exactly what you want sometimes. It's exactly the problem other times, like when you want to know each venue's rank within its city, but still want every venue listed individually, not just a per-city summary.

Window functions keep every row 

SELECT
    name,
    city,
    RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY city ORDER BY latitude DESC) AS rank_in_city
FROM venues;

This returns one row per venue — nothing gets collapsed. Each row also gets a computed value attached to it, rank_in_city, based on how that venue compares to others in the same city. PARTITION BY city is doing something similar to what GROUP BY does conceptually, splitting the data into per-city buckets, but instead of collapsing each bucket into a single summary row, the window function computes something within each bucket and attaches it back onto every original row.

That's really the core difference worth holding onto: GROUP BY reduces row count, window functions don't.

The ones that come up most

ROW_NUMBER(), RANK(), and DENSE_RANK() all number rows within a partition, but they handle ties differently. ROW_NUMBER() gives every row a distinct number regardless of ties, arbitrarily breaking them. RANK() gives tied rows the same number, then skips ahead — two venues tied for rank 1 means the next one is rank 3, not 2. DENSE_RANK() also gives tied rows the same number, but doesn't skip — the next distinct value after a tie at 1 is 2, not 3.

LAG() and LEAD() compare a row to the row before or after it, within the same ordering:

SELECT venue_id, closed_on,
       LAG(closed_on) OVER (PARTITION BY venue_id ORDER BY closed_on) AS previous_closure
FROM closures;

This pulls, for each closure record, the date of that same venue's previous closure, sitting right there in the same row. Useful for things like "days since last closure" style calculations, where you need to compare a row to the one before it without writing a self join to do it.

SUM() OVER (...) gives you running totals — the same idea as a regular SUM, but computed cumulatively per row instead of collapsed into a single number.

Where this actually gets used

A common real request is "top N per category" — for this project, maybe "the two highest-latitude venues in each city." GROUP BY genuinely can't answer this on its own, because it would need to keep multiple rows per city, which defeats the whole point of grouping. The window function version:

SELECT name, city, latitude
FROM (
    SELECT name, city, latitude,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY city ORDER BY latitude DESC) AS rn
    FROM venues
) ranked
WHERE rn <= 2;

The inner query attaches a row number to every venue, restarting at 1 for each new city, ordered by latitude descending. The outer query then just filters down to rn <= 2. This pattern — window function inside, filter outside — is worth recognizing on sight, because "top N per group" comes up often enough that it's basically a template once you've seen it once.

Where this leaves you

Window functions solve a specific gap that GROUP BY leaves open: computing something per group while still keeping every individual row in the result, rather than collapsing down to one row per group. If a query needs a ranking, a comparison to a neighboring row, or a running total, and you catch yourself reaching for GROUP BY and getting frustrated that it's throwing away rows you actually needed, that's usually the signal a window function is what you actually want.

Next up: JSONB in practice — querying and indexing semi-structured data, which comes up constantly once you're syncing data from external sources.

title: MedBOE: Optimization-Based Estimation of Complete Patient Body Models from Whole-Body Medical Imaging
description:
arXiv:2610.28985v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: True whole-body medical imaging captures a patient from head to toe and provides comprehensive anatomical and/or functional information. This coverage enables reconstruction of the external body surface, yielding patient body models. However, scanner geometry (e.g., bore diameter), patient characteristics, and positioning can leave body regions missing (e.g., lateral arms/torso, hands, forearms, elbows), producing incomplete patient body models. Such incompleteness limits downstream medical analyses, including derivation of body-habitus metrics (BHMs), such as body volume and surface area, for injected radiotracer activity regimens, cardiometabolic risk assessment, and computational anatomical modeling for medical imaging simulation and radiation dosimetry. We present the Medical Body model Optimization-based Estimator (MedBOE), an automated, training-free framework for estimating complete patient body models from whole-body images with missing body regions. Our innovation is to leverage the Skinned Multi-Person Linear (SMPL) template, a parametric body mesh representing a broad range of body shapes and poses, in medical imaging. MedBOE aligns the SMPL template to the incomplete patient body models via attribute-guided optimization and estimates missing body regions through geometrically and volumetrically constrained deformation. We evaluated MedBOE using two public datasets: AutoPET (91 whole-body PET-CT images) and Human Implicit Tissues (HIT; 40 whole-body segmentations from MRI images). MedBOE achieved the best overall volumetric and geometric performance among evaluated methods. BHMs derived from MedBOE were within 2% error, suggesting low percentage errors for downstream analyses. MedBOE offers an automated, training-free method for estimating complete patient body models from whole-body images with missing body regions.
