title: Introducing Vercel for Slack
description:
Vercel Agent now works in Slack. Mention it the way you'd pull a teammate into a thread, and it reads the discussion, answers with the context of the platform running your app, and turns the team's decisions into changes you approve. Vercel for Slack is available today in Public Beta for Pro and Enterprise teams.

Work starts in conversation. An alert gets noticed in a channel, a fix gets agreed on in a thread, and then someone leaves Slack to do the work. With Vercel Agent, you can tag it in for answers about your infrastructure or hand it the work, all without leaving the conversation.

What is Vercel Agent?

When we introduced Vercel Agent, we called it an AI teammate for your development workflow. Today it's the first responder for your production apps. When something changes, it investigates your logs, metrics, and deployments, finds the root cause, and proposes a fix, often before anyone's opened a laptop. Give it a PR and it flags the regressions and risky changes that a passing CI run won't show.

In Slack, that agent joins the conversation itself. It is a core part of Vercel, so your deployments, build statuses, logs, metrics, code reviews, and PRs are in front of it before you've typed anything. Mention @Vercel in a channel, a thread, or a DM, and it answers like a teammate with every tab already open. And answering is only half of it, because once you know what's wrong, the agent can go fix it:

  • Diagnose issues: Investigate incidents, trace errors to the deploy that caused them, explain a cost spike, and answer questions about your codebase.

  • Code alongside your team: Fix failing builds and CI, review PRs with knowledge of how the code runs in production, and turn a thread's decision into a tested pull request.

  • Operate your projects: Roll back deployments, update configuration, manage feature flags, and resolve unusual usage before it becomes a bill.

The agent is read-only by default, and anything that changes code or configuration goes through a plan that you approve. Vercel for Slack brings that whole loop into the threads where you and your team are already discussing work.

Accelerating development with a conversation

Teams form decisions through collaboration. Incidents get triaged in a channel, code reviews are hashed out in threads, and features get scoped between standups. But once a thread settles on what needs to be done, the actions still need to be translated into tickets, terminal commands, and PR descriptions. Every handoff drops context, and the conversation that held the full picture becomes the thing everyone summarizes from memory. Vercel for Slack gives the agent the full context of the original conversation for every turn.

Answers in one place speed up the whole team

A deployment goes out at 1:42pm. By 1:51, checkout error rates are climbing and an alert lands in the platform engineering channel.

What used to happen next was a scatter. One responder opens logs to see how bad it is, another asks their coding agent to line up the anomaly up against the deploy timeline, a third starts reading the diff of the suspect PR. Each person investigates alone, in their own view of the same system, and the thread is where they reconcile by pasting screenshots, summarizing agent findings, and correcting each other as they establish the actual state of the situation. The minutes that matter get spent assembling the picture before anyone can act on it.

With Vercel for Slack, the first question goes to the agent, right in the thread.

"@Vercel, checkout errors spiked after the 1:42 deploy. What's going on?"

It sizes the blast radius, correlates the spike with the deployment, identifies the PR that shipped in it, and explains which change, in which file, caused which behavior. The answer arrives in the channel, where the whole team reads the same diagnosis at the same time.

Nobody has to re-run a teammate's investigation or wait for the recap, because everyone is looking at the same report. The engineer who knows the checkout code speaks to the change itself, the on-call weighs how many users are hit against how long a fix would take, and what's left for the thread is the decision, whether to roll back or fix forward.

Vercel Agent understands how your team already talks

The thread, channel, or DM is the beginning of the prompt itself. You don't have to re-explain anything that was already said, or pass in any context from your app or codebase. Bring it into a conversation like any other team member and it reads the room, picks up what the team has been discussing, and can act on it when asked.

One example of this was our iteration on Vercel Agent's plan card, the message it posts in Slack to request approval for the work it wants to do. The first version we tested internally was a wall of text, but when one of our engineers noticed that people were often approving actions without reading all of the details, we had a redesign thread that ran 47 replies deep on what a person needs to see before confirming an action on the group's behalf. Tagging Vercel Agent in at the end of that thread is what resulted in the card you see today.

By the time a PR from a conversation like this lands in a thread, the tests have already run and the preview deployment is live, so the team can start reviewing it in the conversation that kicked off the feature in the first place.

Vercel Agent reviews pull requests in the thread

Ask Vercel Agent for a review in the thread where the PR is being discussed, and the conversation is passed along with the request. What your team has been raising becomes context for what Vercel Agent checks, and its findings land back in the same thread, so discussing them, deciding, and fixing them is one loop instead of a trip to another tool.

One example from one of our own PR discussions was a review someone requested mid-thread. The agent came back with a bug sitting just outside the diff, the same title rendered twice in the UI.

A finding doesn't have to end as a comment. If the team agrees it should be fixed, the agent can patch the PR itself, and that change arrives the same way everything else does, as a proposal waiting on an approval.

Changes always go through a plan your team approves

When a thread lands on a change, Vercel Agent replies with a plan that says what will happen, in which project, and at what scope. Decisions in a channel form in fragments, across people and hours, and nobody types "DECISION:", so the plan is where all of that becomes one explicit thing to say yes to. Once approved, the agent does the work under its own identity, and the audit trail shows who asked, who approved, and what ran.

One example from our own threads was a cached page showing stale data after we shipped an update. Someone called for a cache purge scoped to just the specific pages, since it was peak hours, and asked the agent to set it up. The plan that came back matched the ask exactly, a purge of the specific path and its sub-paths with the rest of the site's cache left warm, and nothing ran until someone approved it.

Whether a thread ends in a diagnosis, a pull request, or a cache purge, the last step belongs to a person.

Getting started

The easiest way to get started is to simply ask Vercel Agent questions. Ask about the error you're chasing or the build that just failed, see what comes back, and let your team decide over time how much of the work the agent takes on. Until someone approves a plan, it's only ever reading.

Vercel for Slack is available in Public Beta for Pro and Enterprise teams. To start using Vercel Agent in Slack:

  • Open the Slack app in the Vercel Marketplace and click Connect Account.

  • Choose the Slack workspace to connect, then click Allow.

  • Mention @Vercel in a channel, a thread, or a DM.

  • Sign in to your Vercel account when it prompts you the first time.

See the Vercel for Slack docs for setup and permissions.

title: Our Own Jev: Typed Decisions in One Forward Pass, from an In-House Judge to Open LoRA Models
description:
arXiv:2610.29052v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A typed decision maps evidence, a question and a fixed set of options to a probability for every option, computed in one forward pass, by reading a language model's logits or a small head over its hidden states, instead of generating and parsing text. The commercial system Jev popularised this System~1 interface, and open reproductions have followed. We report two uses of the pattern. \emph{Part I} describes an in-house System~1 judge that triages about 148K agentic coding session records for a training corpus. It replaces a frontier LLM judge that cost on the order of \$1,000 per pass and whose stored labels matched a fresh two-judge consensus on only 26.9\% of the sessions where the two judges agreed; a self-hosted frozen backbone with a rank-16 LoRA adapter and a pointer head answers three typed questions in one forward pass, judges 1,000 sessions in about three minutes of one GPU, about \$0.06 at a reference rate and roughly 1\% of the frontier judge's cost, and keeps every session inside the organisation. \emph{Part II} asks whether a readout that adds no parameters can be competitive and whether training one helps. Applying the public Eikos recipe and corpus of about 25K decisions to three further backbones (1B, 2B and 35B), we read the frozen output layer of a LoRA-adapted decoder. On the 111 public hard items of JevBench our single-seed 35B, developed with those items in view, scores 79.3\%, not significantly different from the commercial reference (73.0\%, unadjusted $p=0.12$) and ahead of five open systems after Holm--Bonferroni correction; our 2B is ahead of all four kev checkpoints on the leaderboard. A single-seed ablation finds no detectable benefit from training the 26 letter rows of the output layer, and a retrain on a later corpus release moves the 2B's hard-tier accuracy by 11.7 points, which shows how little small evaluations resolve.

title: How to Check Feature Flags in Express Middleware in 2026 — SaaS Route Gating
description:
An Express middleware feature flag check should gate the Node.js API route on the server, cache the decision briefly, and leave the known-good notification path available. That gives the on-call one reversible action: disable risky delivery behavior without redeploying.

TL;DR: Poll a flag such as notification_bulk_send_v2, cache the last valid result briefly, and check the customer's entitlement separately. A flag is a release control, not authorization. For rollback safety, the old delivery path must remain deployable and observable until the new path has survived the rollback window.

This article uses Go because the control flow is easier to see without framework machinery. The same boundary fits Express middleware: lookup, cache, decide, then call the next handler or return a controlled response.

What should the on-call see when delivery fails?

Start at the page. It should identify the affected operation, the flag key, the deployed version, the last successful delivery time, and whether the fallback path is healthy. The operator needs enough context to choose between disabling a release path and investigating a provider failure. Those are different incidents.

The earlier signal is a sustained change in delivery outcomes split by flag state. A raw error count is weak: traffic changes can move it without changing reliability. Compare failures and attempts for the flagged path, and keep the old path's series beside it. Set the threshold from the service's error budget and traffic floor, not from a round number copied from another service.

There is an important system boundary here. Infrai's feature-flag client is polling-based, and its observability surface does not supply threshold notification delivery. Use the flag API for evaluation, then let Datadog monitors, Grafana Alerting, or Sentry alerts page on the delivery ratio. Datadog fits teams already correlating managed metrics and service telemetry; Grafana fits teams that want alert rules near their existing dashboards and data sources; Sentry fits application error triage better than general job-heartbeat monitoring. A heartbeat monitor such as Healthchecks.io should cover the separate case where the notification job never ran, because no delivery event exists to count.

No events means no ratio.

False positives have a real cost. Suppose the first failure after a quiet hour makes the short-window ratio look catastrophic: an automatic toggle can disable a healthy premium feature before enough attempts exist to support the conclusion. The old path then receives traffic, its queue depth changes, and the incident channel has to distinguish a real provider problem from a control action triggered by thin data. Require a minimum sample, use at least one longer confirmation window, page before automating rollback, and record the operator's decision in the incident timeline. The exact sample and window belong to the service's traffic model and error budget; inventing universal numbers would hide the trade-off.

How should Express middleware check a feature flag for Node.js route gating?

The invariant is blunt: no request reaches the new delivery handler unless both the release flag and the entitlement check pass. Browser flags may hide a button, but clients only poll and can be modified by the user. The server owns the decision.

This runnable program models the middleware boundary, a five-second cache, a boolean is_enabled lookup, and a separate plan check. Replace memoryFlags.IsEnabled with a provider adapter in production; keep the middleware contract unchanged.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "log"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "sync"
    "time"
)

const bulkSendFlag = "notification_bulk_send_v2"

type FlagSource interface {
    IsEnabled(context.Context, string) (bool, error)
}

type infraiFlags struct {
    apiKey string
    client *http.Client
}

func (f *infraiFlags) IsEnabled(ctx context.Context, key string) (bool, error) {
    baseURL := "https://api.infrai.cc"
    flagPath := strings.Join([]string{"", "v1", "flags", "is_enabled", url.PathEscape(key)}, "/")
    requestURL := baseURL + flagPath
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, requestURL, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return false, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+f.apiKey)

        resp, err := f.client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return false, err
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            resp.Body.Close()
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); parseErr == nil {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            select {
            case <-ctx.Done():
                return false, ctx.Err()
            case <-time.After(delay):
            }
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            resp.Body.Close()
            return false, fmt.Errorf("flag check returned %s", resp.Status)
        }
        var result struct {
            Data struct {
                Enabled bool `json:"enabled"`
            } `json:"data"`
        }
        err = json.NewDecoder(resp.Body).Decode(&result)
        resp.Body.Close()
        return result.Data.Enabled, err
    }
    return false, fmt.Errorf("flag check rate limited after retries")
}

type cachedFlag struct {
    mu      sync.Mutex
    source  FlagSource
    ttl     time.Duration
    value   bool
    expires time.Time
}

func (c *cachedFlag) enabled(ctx context.Context, key string) (bool, error) {
    c.mu.Lock()
    defer c.mu.Unlock()
    if time.Now().Before(c.expires) {
        return c.value, nil
    }
    value, err := c.source.IsEnabled(ctx, key)
    if err != nil {
        return false, err
    }
    c.value, c.expires = value, time.Now().Add(c.ttl)
    return value, nil
}

func entitled(r *http.Request) bool {
    return r.Header.Get("X-Plan") == "premium"
}

func gate(flag *cachedFlag, next http.Handler) http.Handler {
    return http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
        enabled, err := flag.enabled(r.Context(), bulkSendFlag)
        if err != nil || !enabled {
            http.Error(w, "feature unavailable", http.StatusServiceUnavailable)
            return
        }
        if !entitled(r) {
            http.Error(w, "premium plan required", http.StatusForbidden)
            return
        }
        next.ServeHTTP(w, r)
    })
}

func main() {
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if apiKey == "" {
        log.Fatal("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    flags := &cachedFlag{
        source: &infraiFlags{
            apiKey: apiKey,
            client: &http.Client{Timeout: 3 * time.Second},
        },
        ttl:    5 * time.Second,
    }
    mux := http.NewServeMux()
    mux.Handle("POST /notifications/bulk", gate(flags, http.HandlerFunc(
        func(w http.ResponseWriter, _ *http.Request) {
            w.WriteHeader(http.StatusAccepted)
        },
    )))
    log.Fatal(http.ListenAndServe(":8080", mux))
}

Five seconds is an example operating choice, not a universal constant. A shorter TTL speeds rollback but increases polling. A longer one reduces lookups but expands the period in which instances disagree after a toggle. Pick the maximum stale period your rollback objective permits, then add jitter in a multi-instance service so every process does not refresh at once.

The adapter makes an authenticated GET, reads the key from an environment variable, checks the HTTP status, and backs off on 429 while honoring a numeric Retry-After. Before deployment, compare its response struct with the public discovery schema returned for the capability. That schema is the contract to pin in an integration test.

Step 2: Choose the system shape before the vendor

Two architectures are viable.

Shape Invariant Best fit Main cost
Shared flag service plus local cache A last valid decision expires within the rollback objective Several services need one control plane Network and cache-staleness behavior must be designed
Application-owned configuration Config changes travel through the application's reviewed deployment path Few flags, strict change review, low operational breadth Rollback speed is tied to config distribution

Infrai is a deliberate option in the first shape. Its primary advantage here is breadth behind one REST contract: flags can sit beside other backend capabilities under one key instead of introducing another SDK and credential. The supporting advantage is operational inspectability: its public discovery surface describes request and response schemas and provides runnable examples, which reduces adapter guesswork. The platform snapshot exposes 295 capabilities across 20 modules, but breadth only matters if consolidation is one of your constraints.

Teams already standardizing several backend functions behind a plain REST boundary should try Infrai for the flag lookup and short-lived cache, because one contract removes a separate integration while preserving an application-owned gate. Do not choose it for sophisticated flag governance. There is no flag change audit log, evaluation analytics, parent-child dependency model, or recycle bin for deletion, so keep a naming/version convention and treat destructive cleanup as a reviewed operation.

Specialists deserve a fair look. LaunchDarkly is the stronger candidate when mature flag lifecycle and experimentation workflows drive the decision. Unleash is attractive when operating an open-source control plane is a requirement. ConfigCat favors a focused hosted flag product, while Flagsmith offers hosted and self-hosted paths. Verify the exact governance, SDK, polling, and audit behavior against each vendor's current documentation; those details change and they determine rollback safety more than a feature-count table does. The limitation is concrete: Infrai is not suitable when flag audit history, evaluation statistics, or dependent flags are mandatory. Pick the specialist whose current contract covers those requirements.

Step 3: Instrument the decision, not customer data

Emit one counter for attempts and one for failures, labeled with a bounded route name, release-path value, and coarse failure class. Do not put customer IDs, email addresses, flag payloads, or arbitrary error strings in metric labels. That keeps cardinality controlled and follows data minimization.

For boolean gates, use is_enabled. Use get_value only when the flag carries a configuration value such as a plan limit or UI variant. Keep authorization separate in both cases. Also preserve a request or delivery id through the handler so retries can be deduplicated by the notification worker; toggling a flag does not make an at-least-once delivery path idempotent.

Instrument both outcomes. If the disabled branch returns early without a counter, the dashboard will make the rollback look like disappearing traffic rather than an intentional control action.

Step 4: Rehearse rollback and deletion

Before rollout, exercise four cases: enabled and entitled, enabled and not entitled, disabled, and flag lookup unavailable. The example fails closed because bulk notification delivery is a premium write action. A read-only cosmetic variant could reasonably serve its stable default instead. Write that choice in the runbook.

Then rehearse the rollback with the old handler still present. Confirm that cached decisions converge inside the declared window, the old path can absorb traffic, and duplicate deliveries are rejected using the delivery id. Do not delete the old flag during the rehearsal. Infrai flag deletion has no recycle bin, so retirement should be a later, reviewed change after all callers and dashboards have stopped referring to the key.

The final decision rule is narrow: use a shared service when multiple applications need a fast, consistent rollback control and can tolerate bounded polling staleness. Keep configuration application-owned when reviewability matters more than independent rollback speed. Choose a specialist when audit history, evaluation statistics, dependencies, or experimentation are requirements.

Further reading

  • Martin Fowler: Feature Toggles
  • LaunchDarkly documentation
  • Unleash documentation
  • ConfigCat documentation
  • Flagsmith documentation
  • Healthchecks.io documentation
  • GDPR Article 5: data minimization

If this boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai capability sheet and inspect the live flag schema before writing the adapter.

title: Set per-user budgets on AI Gateway
description:
You can now use AI Gateway budgets to set a dollar spending limit for each user on your team.

The limit covers spend from every API key attributed to the user, along with their app tokens. After it's reached, AI Gateway rejects new requests until the budget resets or is increased.

This is useful for controlling spend from coding agents and other workloads that run without supervision, and prevents one user from consuming all of the team's shared budget.

Set user budgets

Open the Users view on the Budgets page to set two kinds of user budgets:

  • Default budget: If set, applies separately to every person without a custom budget, including users added later. Each user gets their own allowance rather than sharing one limit across the team.

  • Custom budget: Applies to one person and overrides the default. Removing it returns that user to the default budget.

Both default and custom budgets reset monthly by default, but you can change them to reset daily, weekly, or not at all. Budgets also support usage alerting via email to notify when you are at 50%, 75%, and/or 100% of your allocation.

User budgets don't replace API key, project, or team budgets. A request must remain within every budget that applies to it. Reaching any applicable limit blocks new requests.

API keys are attributed to the user who created them by default. If a key belongs to a production application or another shared workload, attribute it to the team from the API Keys page to keep its spend out of the key creator's budget. Keys created prior to the user budget feature release were attributed to the team for backwards-compatibility, so rotate to new keys if you wish to have current usage fall under the user scope.

Set budgets from the CLI

Upgrade to the latest Vercel CLI with vercel upgrade. You need Vercel CLI 59.6.2 or newer for user budgets, then set a default or custom user budget:

Identify a member by their email address, username, or user ID.

Team owners can manage user budgets, and can also grant other members AI Gateway Budget Manager permissions from team member settings. Spend using Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) credentials doesn't count toward user budgets.

Update to the latest Vercel CLI with vercel upgrade to get started, and learn more in the AI Gateway budgets documentation.

title: Vercel Ship 2026 recap
description:
For a decade, Vercel has shaped how the web is built. Now, we’re doing the same for agents. The companies that win the next decade will build on infrastructure designed for agents from the start, and thousands of people gathered across London, Berlin, New York, Sydney, and San Francisco to do just that at Vercel Ship 2026.

Agentic infrastructure

Guillermo Rauch (CEO, Vercel) opened Ship SF with a vision for the next era of software and agentic infrastructure: interfaces generated for any task in front of you, agents that reproduce and fix bugs autonomously, and software that takes production context and continuously improves itself.

Agentic infrastructure has three parts:

  • Vercel is where you build and deploy your own apps and agents. We give you every tool you need to build and run apps and agents in production, securely, at scale.

  • Vercel is where coding agents deploy that software. When you ask your harness where to deploy, you get Vercel, because Vercel is built for the way agents work. We have over 200 CLI commands that your agent can use to operate our entire platform.

  • Vercel itself is automated by agents. Vercel runs your apps in production, handling traffic, traces, observability, and anomalies. That data gives our agents the context they need to investigate autonomously, and then surface pull requests, not just alerts.

Agentic Infrastructure is for developers

In his opening keynote, Guillermo pointed to claims that AI would replace developers, then used Vercel's own data to prove them wrong. In the last 12 months:

  • The number of developers on Vercel has grown 3x

  • The number of new projects developers ship has doubled

  • The number of their agent-triggered deployments has increased 28x

"We built Vercel for developers," he said, "because they are the difference between a world full of slop and a world full of software worth using."

Backends on Vercel

In the next keynote, Malte Ubl (CTO, Vercel) showed how frontends, APIs, backend services, containers, MCP servers, and background workers can all run on Vercel, with support for custom runtimes and system dependencies.

He then announced that Python is now generally available on Vercel. Run FastAPI, Flask, or Django with standard CPython, PyPI dependencies, uv, and pyproject.toml. With Vercel Services, your frontend and backend deploy together, with previews of the full app.

Malte also introduced Vercel Daemons, now in public beta, for continuously running background workers. Deploy your code or container image, set the number of instances, and Vercel keeps them running and replaces them if they fail. Bring Celery, Dramatiq, Temporal workers, or your existing worker processes.

Vercel is for shipping agents

Tomo Occhino (CPO, Vercel) walked through the Agent Stack and its latest updates. The Agent Stack gives you everything you need to build, run, and scale agents in production.

  • Vercel Drives, now generally available for Sandbox, gives agents persistent workspaces. Code, data, and saved memory survive across runs, so you can change runtimes or compute without rebuilding the workspace.

  • eve, our open-source framework for building agents, now has persistent memory across sessions, extensions for installing tools and skills, and agent creation and deployment from the Vercel dashboard.

  • Vercel Connect is generally available, with more than 1,000 connectors. And MCP Events, now in public beta, lets agents respond to events from MCP servers. Connect handles subscriptions, renewals, and secure delivery.

  • AI Gateway now lets you set budgets for API keys, projects, individuals, and teams. You can also choose US-only inference to keep model processing in the United States, or enable Zero Data Retention so providers don’t retain your prompts or responses. He also introduced Vercel Token Pass, now in early access for Pro teams. Get $80 in GLM 5.3 and Kimi K3 token credit for $30/month, with more models coming soon.

Vercel for enterprise

Jeanne Grosser (COO, Vercel) focused on what happens when everyone in a company can build. Engineers, marketers, analysts, and sellers need a common place to deploy, with controls over who can ship, who can access an app, which systems agents can use, and how much they can spend. Company building is now agent building.

Vercel for Enterprise brings those controls together, with two additions announced:

  • Bring Your Own Cloud on AWS is now generally available. Your application functions run in your own AWS account, within your security and network boundaries.

  • Enterprise-Managed Authorization for Vercel Connect launched in public beta. With supported services and your identity provider configured, agents can act on employees’ behalf without asking each person to authorize every connection separately.

Watch the full day of programming

Ship week in San Francisco

The rest of Ship SF brought more than 2,700 developers, founders, and technical leaders to the Palace of Fine Arts for talks, workshops, startup studio sessions, and agent labs.

Ship day sessions

  • Assaf Elovic from Ora showed how his team tests whether websites work for agents by sending real agents to sign up, integrate, and pay, then tracing every step. Ora built that fleet on eve and used Is-Agentic to score a live site.

  • Katelyn Lesse from Anthropic covered the work that starts after an agent is running: keeping it fast and improving its performance across thousands of production sessions with Claude Managed Agents on Vercel.

  • Prashant Ratanchandani from Meta Superintelligence Labs joined Tomo to discuss building products including Muse on Vercel.

  • Matt Lewis from Vercel and Mala Neti from Slack explained how we built v, our internal agent, around Vercel’s own data and working practices. Connect and Passport secure its access, and Slack gives employees a place to use it where their work already happens.

  • Max Peters from Adapta broke down the router behind Brazil’s largest generative AI platform. Built on AI Gateway, it serves 168 models through one integration, selects a model in under 200 milliseconds, and handles more than three million requests a day with automatic failover and per-user budgets.

  • Sarah Sachs from Notion and Malte Ubl discussed how AI is changing the software teams build and the context agents need to do useful work.

  • Olawale Oladehin from AWS walked through production patterns for agents on AWS and Vercel, from self-correcting agents to multi-agent orchestration, and how BYOC lets teams run application functions within their own AWS environment.

  • Philip Miseldine and Sophia Levens from SAP showed how SAP is using v0, eve, and json-render to build generative interfaces, with a focus on consistent design and government requirements.

  • Aaron Brown and Arty Vohmincevs from Mercor explained how hundreds of employees build internal tools without losing control of access or spending. Apps inherit a managed identity layer, while AI Gateway gives the team visibility into model usage and budgets.

  • Yury Izrailevsky from ClickHouse traced the company’s path from an open-source analytics database to a platform spanning observability, AI engineering, and managed Postgres. His focus was how open source earns developer trust and helps infrastructure expand into new workloads.

Panel: Fast AI

Diogo Almeida, co-founder and CEO of TypeSafe AI, the company behind Jev, and Andrew Feldman, founder and CEO of Cerebras, joined Vercel for a discussion on model reliability, latency, and cost. The panel brought together the model and hardware sides of fast inference, from specialized models to wafer-scale chips.

Closing fireside with Tobi Lütke

Guillermo sat down with Tobi Lütke, CEO of Shopify, for "The Third Customer," a conversation about building for a world where agents research, compare, and buy products on people’s behalf.

Guillermo Rauch: What excites you about agentic commerce?

Tobi Lütke: It’s early, but the opportunity goes beyond handling purchases people already make. Think about project-based commerce: planning Halloween decorations for your house, or a 3D-printing project with your kids, then ordering everything to arrive before the weekend. Agents can help people follow through on things they otherwise wouldn’t have had time to do.

Guillermo Rauch: Where does that leave traditional storefronts?

Tobi Lütke: There’s still room for exceptional shopping experiences. A distinctive, thoughtful storefront can grow, just as a well-executed boutique can. The businesses that will struggle are the ones offering an undifferentiated experience. Quality and originality still matter.

Guillermo Rauch: How is AI changing engineering at Shopify?

Tobi Lütke: We now think of ourselves as verification engineers, building harnesses and acceptance tests that make changes verifiable. We’re rewriting our storefront renderer from Ruby to Rust, where we can compare the output byte for byte before switching over. We also celebrate simplification and code deletion. At a company hackathon, our internal Slack agent, River, topped the code-deletion leaderboard by a wide margin.

Guillermo Rauch: What should developers in this room go build?

Tobi Lütke: Explore the catalog APIs. They give you access to products from Shopify merchants, so you can build new commerce experiences without first recruiting both sides of a marketplace. Product discovery, recommendations, and curation are real business opportunities. People will pay for tools that help them find what they need.

Ship week San Francisco

Fast Forward hackathon

The day before Ship, Vercel and Meta hosted Fast Forward, with support from Shopify and Neon Postgres. Builders worked across three tracks: agents that keep working after you step away, multimodal apps, and immersive VR experiences.

Founder dinners, executive conversations, and Partner Day

Founders, partners, and enterprise leaders gathered throughout the week for dinners, Partner Day, and conversations on building with AI. The executive program focused on what happens when anyone with an idea can build, and how do you govern what ships.

Ship 2026 in London

Ship day keynotes

  • Tomo introduced the Agent Stack, bringing model access, durable execution, sandboxed compute, and messaging together for production agents.

  • Hedi launched Vercel Connect in public preview, giving agents scoped access to external tools and data without storing long-lived provider credentials in environment variables.

  • Shar demoed eve, our open-source agent framework. Each agent lives in a directory, with instructions in Markdown and tools in TypeScript. Durable execution, approvals, subagents, and evals are already wired in.

  • Jeanne introduced Vercel for Enterprise Apps and Agents, including Vercel Passport in public beta for protecting internal apps with your identity provider, and Bring Your Own Cloud on AWS in private beta.

Ship week London

Our first Ship outside the U.S. ran five days of events leading into the keynote, and an ice cream truck spent the week working its way across the city.

Built in London hackathon

Two hundred builders shipped agents on Codex and Vercel in a hackathon with OpenAI. Three projects stood out. Stella hunts down unclaimed grants for London SMBs, Oscar is a co-pilot that sharpens your prompts before you send them to a model, and Phone Jail blocks distractions and roasts you when you reach for your phone anyway.

Media, Founder, VC, and CTO dinners

Reporters traded story ideas over a media dinner. Twelve founders talked through the future of AI in EMEA at a VC dinner. And a dozen CTOs from teams including Marks & Spencer and Currys went off the record on what it takes to build and scale agents in the enterprise.

Day Zero builder night

Day Zero, the day before the keynote, turned into a 400-person builder night. Enterprise teams Mentimeter, Okta, and MongoDB joined Vercel in a packed room alongside partners DeepMind, ElevenLabs, and Cursor.

AI Social Club

A 160-deep waitlist formed for Malte's talk A New Stack for a New Era of Software, followed by Guillermo and Deliveroo's Will Shu's chat on building the agentic enterprise.

Ship day sessions

  • André Balleyguier from Anthropic showed Claude Managed Agents on Vercel, where Anthropic hosts the agent loop while every command the agent runs executes inside a Vercel Sandbox you own, keeping its filesystem, processes, and network egress in your environment.

  • Tomas Jansson from Currys/Elkjøp showed how his team evolved a Nordic retailer's ecommerce stack from storefronts toward shopping agents in three phases, anchored by a Next.js migration that cut time to first byte by 40%. The end state is one where customer intent replaces navigation.

  • Matan Kushner from Vercel broke down how Vertex, Vercel's support agent, now automates 91% of support tickets and saves 5,000 engineer-hours a month without degrading as its context grows.

  • Jas Sagoo and Sam Bellen from Auth0 made the case that getting an agent into production depends more on identity than on model quality. They demoed four standards-based identity patterns on the Vercel AI SDK, Token Vault, CIBA approvals, agents as first-class principals, and on-behalf-of delegation, so every action is scoped and traces back to a human decision instead of a shared API key.

  • Abhi Sivasailam from Vercel went deep into d0, Vercel's internal data agent built on eve, which runs analyses in a sandbox and now gets 45% of its questions from other agents, rather than people.

  • Romain Huet from OpenAI showed developers how to ship faster by delegating whole tasks to Codex Cloud Agents on Vercel, and made the case that as agents become users of your product, you design for agent experience with scoped API keys, markdown docs, and plugins.

  • Michał Pierzchała from Callstack demoed a QA agent that runs mobile apps on real devices, explores user flows on its own, and posts screenshots, recordings, and logs to pull requests on every PR.

  • Alex Holt from ElevenLabs paired the ElevenLabs Speech Engine with the AI SDK to build a voice agent that can reply in under a second, take interruptions mid-sentence, and switch language mid-conversation.

  • Malavika Balachandran Tadeusz from Vercel showed the mechanics of how software can ship itself, extending the agent loop past development into testing, observability, and experimentation with primitives like Vercel Flags and Skills.

Panel: Agents in production

Jeanne Grosser, COO of Vercel, moderated a panel on taking agentic workloads from prototype to production with some of the EU's top CTOs and AI leaders from frontier labs. A few highlights:

Arthur Viegers (Cursor): Autonomy should track risk, and the better an agent can assess the risk of a change, the more you can let it run on its own. Shopify and Amplitude already auto-review and merge 60-70% of low-risk PRs with no developer time, while a two-line change to authentication still goes to a human.

André Balleyguier (Anthropic): To decide what an agent can do on its own, judge each action by how reversible it is and how large its blast radius is, then contain it accordingly, for example inside a self-hosted sandbox. As you grant more autonomy, observability and evals become the things that keep it safe.

Ryan den Rooijen (Currys): The predicted death of stores never arrived, and Currys leads its markets by betting on humans. The open question for agentic commerce is which shopping journeys customers want an agent to handle and which they still want a person for.

Nicolas Le Pallec (AKQA): AI-native customer experience replaces navigation with intent. Reaching it takes three layers: a way to capture true customer intent, a brand brain that stores brand and product data for AI systems to retrieve, and generative UI that composes pages on the fly instead of serving static ones.

Fireside chat with Harry Stebbings

The day ended with a fireside chat between Guillermo and Harry Stebbings from 20VC. Below are excerpts from the lightning round at the end of the discussion.

Guillermo Rauch: What are the attributes of a founder you want to back?

Harry Stebbings: The profile has changed completely. It used to be a sales-led CEO who could fundraise and grow customers, where personality and sales carried the company. Now I want an engineering- and product-led founder.

Guillermo Rauch: Can you teach someone to become a voice for their industry?

Harry Stebbings: You can, but it's hard. You have to do it for six months straight. It's a muscle you build, and you have to commit to it every day and every hour.

Guillermo Rauch: When anyone can produce content and software, how do you stand out?

Harry Stebbings: You come up with a new format, a new intro, a new way to tell the story and shape the work. The content itself has shifted too. We used to do shows about leadership and hiring, and nobody cares about that anymore. What lands now is a founder and AI. Those are the two things.

Ship 2026 in Berlin

The Berlin event opened at the Old Mint, “Alte Münze”, where coins were once hammered by hand, before machine automation took over. It is also where the JavaScript logo was born, and where Guillermo Rauch (CEO) met Malte Ubl (CTO) for the first time at JSConf EU.

Software is moving the same way, from hand to machine, and Vercel is paving the way for building in the agentic era. Over 500 people gathered from across Germany to do just that at Ship 2026 in Berlin.

Ship day sessions

  • Suyog Rao from Vercel announced AI SDK 7. The AI SDK is now downloaded over 16 million times a week. Version 7 turns it into a toolkit for building and running agents that reason, call tools, run across many turns, and work across files and sandboxes, all behind one provider-agnostic interface with no lock-in.

  • Philip Miseldine from SAP showed how the company rebuilt its design system to be composable, so people and agents assemble interfaces from the same parts, with v0 running across its build, deliver, and decide stages.

  • Building with AI SDK 7 brought three speakers on stage. Lars Grammel, the primary engineer behind the update, went deep on the release, with the new harness layer and generation beyond text as the headline additions. Carsten Høyer from AKQA demoed the Starbucks ChatGPT app as a "generative store" that composes branded results from Starbucks' own products and visual identity, flipping the funnel so customers pull the brand into their conversation instead of visiting its site. Stephen Batifol from Black Forest Labs showed where the Flux image models fit in an agentic stack: sub-second generation and editing today, heading toward real-time generation and world models.

  • Arthur Viegers from Cursor showed how coding agents move from autocomplete to working across an entire codebase on their own.

Panel: CTOs on AI and growth

Chris Williams (Head of Forward Deployed Engineering, Vercel) moderated a CTO panel on building and scaling as the cost of creation trends toward zero. A few highlights:

Sven Rosemann (Flaconi): AI won't fix a broken business model, so the work is still operational excellence. He compares ecommerce to a decathlon, you win by being top-tier across every discipline at once. What's changing is discovery, which is moving into chat, so Flaconi is investing in the data foundation that makes its catalog retrievable by agents, betting that buying and checkout eventually happen there too.

Tjaž Silovsek (Astra AI): venture funding is no longer a prerequisite. For many ideas, you ship, find distribution, and iterate instead. Astra reached 10 million users and $25M ARR fully bootstrapped, with a small team kept fast by a stable foundation and agents given a lot of autonomy while kept as safe as possible.

DACH Partner Award

Vercel presented its first-ever DACH Partner Award to Valtech, for the exceptional impact and delivery, strategic thinking and team enablement it brought to clients. The presentation also thanked the event's sponsors: Auth0, Storyblok, Cursor, SAP, Accenture Song, Blazity, and JVM.

Ship 2026 in New York

Ship week New York

Ship NYC was the most in-demand of any stop yet with over 3,000 people registered. Founders, partners, leaders, and builders gathered for five days of hackathons, executive receptions, workshops, and more, with Ship day at the center.

Built in NYC

The week opened with Built in NYC, a hackathon co-hosted by Vercel and Anthropic alongside Sentry, Auth0, Resend, and Supabase. More than one hundred people joined us for an afternoon of building and demoing agents on Vercel.

VC, CTO, and VIP dinners

Jeanne DeWitt Grosser and Nick Bogaty gathered the leaders shaping AI-native development at a VIP reception. Founders traded notes on the future of agents over a VC dinner. At Per Se, Guillermo, Jeanne, Tom, and Malte took CTOs and CIOs for a closed-door conversation on where traditional architectures start to break in the agent era.

AI Social Club

AI executives and senior leaders assembled at Moss for a fireside chat led by Tom Occhino with William Anderson (CTO, Bloomberg Media), Jeremy Bunting (VP Engineering, Serhant), and Ali Patterson (Staff Design Program Manager, DoorDash). They discussed what's working, what's not, and where agentic infrastructure is driving meaningful outcomes for enterprises.

Ship day sessions

  • Ryan Coyne from SERHANT. walked through S.MPLE, a real estate agent built on Vercel that drove a 144% increase in commission income in its first full year.

  • Brandon Bloom from Brex gave its expense-audit agent a bash-only shell so it manages its own context instead of drowning in tool responses, cutting tool calls and token usage by 75%.

  • Ari Schapiro and Chris Sev from Auth0 demoed how to give an agent scoped, revocable power instead of a master key, with standards-based identity patterns like Token Vault and out-of-band human approval, live on the Vercel AI SDK.

  • Jenny Wang from Alta and Maxwell Osborne from PUBLIC SCHOOL NYC showed how Alta's AI styling app runs on Vercel, generating an avatar a second and 250M+ outfits so far. Together they built a custom version for PUBLIC SCHOOL's New York Fashion Week relaunch.

  • Charlton Roberts from FLORA showed three creative-production workflows running on Vercel Sandboxes. They collapsed 18 bespoke tools into two by letting the agent run and write its own code against the AI SDK.

  • Prasad Wangikar from Stripe broke down how to give agents spending power and capture agent-driven revenue using emerging protocols like MCP, UCP, and x402 for the machine-to-machine economy.

  • Shaown Nandi from AWS discussed how Vercel and AWS work together, with native AWS databases and OpenSearch available in the Marketplace and models through the AI Gateway, proven out by The Weather Company's 350M+ users.

Panel: Internal apps and agents in production

Jeanne moderated a panel on building and deploying internal agents with technical leaders on who should build, what governance looks like, and how teams can move from experiment to production. A few highlights:

Andy Martin (MJH Life Sciences): The way to win the shadow-IT battle is to constrain the stack and stay permissive inside it. His AI Accelerator trains non-engineers, marketers, and early-career staff to build internal apps on a deliberately tight stack of Claude Code, Vercel, and GitHub, with ephemeral preview deployments as the guardrail. As he put it, "If it becomes the Department of No, you will have people working around you."

Greg Chan (SERHANT): The cleanest way to structure agents is to mirror a human software team. Product-manager agents write requirements in Linear, engineering agents generate specs, and build-and-QA agents take it from there, so engineers become leads running multiple streams. To keep output safe, SERHANT runs evals for hallucination and compliance, including a custom model for Fair Housing Act rules.

Victor Oliveros (ZoomInfo): Embedding v0 inside your own product lets your customers build their own workflows. At ZoomInfo, 40,000+ of them do, turning the voice of the customer into a pull request. Agents analyze recorded calls and open PRs, so the product team decides what ships instead of synthesizing feedback. They pair Vercel's deployment guardrails with ZoomInfo's context-graph permissions, so each agent only touches data its user can see.

Fireside chat: Building agentic storefronts

Tom sat down with Vanessa Lee (VP of Product, Shopify) to discuss where commerce and software go next. Below are highlights:

Tom Occhino: Vercel and Shopify have shipped something new together. What is it?

Vanessa Lee: We boiled Hydrogen down to the parts of commerce that are genuinely hard (analytics, optimistic cart UI, variants) and made them work with any framework. So if you're on Next.js on Vercel, Shopify's commerce primitives now drop in, with an integration in the Vercel Marketplace. Read more here.

Tom Occhino: You also opened the Catalog API. What does it unlock?

Vanessa Lee: There's never been a good open product-search API. We have billions of products and millions of merchants, so we built one, the only widespread shopping API, made for commerce. It lets anyone embed shopping anywhere. Someone in my Toronto running group used v0 to build a site with a leaderboard and the weather, and the Catalog API surfaced products from nearby stores. Commerce stops being a destination and becomes part of what you build.

Tom Occhino: Shopify and Vercel both obsess over reducing friction. Why does that matter so much?

Vanessa Lee: Early on, Tobi's insight was that tools shape the market. The TAM was never limited by demand, it was limited by how hard the tools were to use. Make building easier and more people build. There's resourcefulness in the general population that's just untapped, and lowering the friction is what releases it.

Closing keynote with Ivan Zhao

We closed out Ship in New York with a conversation between Guillermo Rauch and Ivan Zhao (CEO, Notion). A few highlights:

Guillermo Rauch: You've started telling designers to design for the API first and the UI last. Why?

Ivan Zhao: Because your next customer isn't only a human, it's a human and an agent, and agents are blind. They don't see your interface, they read your semantics and your API. The most enduring software has always been a data structure anyway, the spreadsheet, or our block, a data structure that happens to have a UI. So design the structure and the meaning first, the interface last. A great tool for developers turns out to be a great tool for agents.

Guillermo Rauch: Vercel and Notion are both aggressively model-agnostic, Switzerland in the model wars. Why?

Ivan Zhao: The models leapfrog each other every few weeks, so picking a side is a losing game. We route automatically by the intelligence a task needs, frontier models for coding, smaller and faster ones for support and summarization. What excites me most is that as more use cases stop needing frontier intelligence, you can shape smaller models to your product and win back speed and cost. And speed creates discontinuities, a model five times faster can change the kind of interface you'd even design.

Guillermo Rauch: When a billion knowledge workers are agents, how does that reshape us?

Ivan Zhao: We can't fully see it, and that's the point. First-order effects are easy, the iPhone was an iPod plus a phone plus a browser. The second-order effects are the ones that surprise you, like what social media did to teenagers. We shape our tools, and then our tools shape us. With software that can think, the second-order effects are the ones we won't predict.

Guillermo Rauch: Taste or velocity, keep one.

Ivan Zhao: Taste. It's the distillation of wisdom from a lot of shots on goal.

Ship 2026 in Sydney

The Sydney event opened at Machine Hall, a 1930s electrical substation that ran the city's trams and wharves for half a century. Over 200 people gathered there to build for the agentic era at Ship Sydney.

Ship week Sydney

The week kicked off with the AI SYD meetup, where developers, AI engineers, and the Sydney technical community joined for an evening of lightning talks and networking. At the AI Social Club, senior leaders gathered at Shell House for a talk from Malte Ubl and a fireside with Suyog Rao and David Hyman (Founder, monō ai) on how agentic infrastructure is driving meaningful outcomes for enterprises.

Ship day sessions

  • Belen Garcia Fava and Vivek Katial from Heidi Health showed how their team ships fast in a regulated space with agents and Vercel, and made the case that trust is engineered, not granted.

  • Robin Yoong from Cursor created an eve agent by voice alone. Three models coded in parallel, and a spoken approval shipped it to Vercel.

  • Nonny Bell (Startup Manager APAC, Vercel) moderated a panel with Matthew Blode (AI Engineer, Linktree), Aarush Issar (GM AI Engineering, Auto & General Australia), and Leonardo Borges (Chief Engineer Gen AI, CommBank) on how their teams are adopting AI agents in production.

  • JJ Lecocq (Sales Director AUNZ, Vercel) led a discussion on how organizations are reshaping people, culture, and structure for AI.

Ship what's next

Thanks for joining us for Ship 2026 in London, Berlin, New York, Sydney, and San Francisco. We'll see you in May for Ship 2027.

title: WaFIR: Wavelet-Fourier Mixture-of-Experts with Subband-Adaptive Routing for Blind All-in-One Image Restoration
description:
arXiv:2610.29108v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Blind all-in-one image restoration must adapt a shared model to heterogeneous and sometimes mixed degradations without a task label at test time. We introduce WaFIR, a decoder module that decomposes features into Haar subbands, summarizes each subband with a compact Fourier descriptor, and routes it to prompt-conditioned spectral modulation experts. Unlike image-level frequency conditioning, WaFIR makes routing decisions at the subband level, enabling frequency-specific processing while retaining the task context learned by the backbone. Under a unified training and evaluation protocol for denoising, deraining, and dehazing, WaFIR improves average PSNR over the three tasks by 0.48 dB over the PromptIR baseline and by 0.38 dB over the recent Up-Restorer. Matched-capacity and routing controls show that the gain is not explained by additional parameters alone. On unseen noise intensities, descriptor-based routing is more robust than a discrete label-conditioned alternative and remains on par under compound degradations, while routing analyses show stable subband-dependent expert use across degradation types. These results support subband frequency structure as an interpretable complement to prompt-based conditioning for blind image restoration. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/WaFIR/README.md

title: Policy-Mask: Budget-Aware Adaptation of Diffusion Features to Discriminative Tasks
description:
arXiv:2610.28889v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Selecting intermediate features from a frozen diffusion model for discriminative tasks is non-trivial because the useful signal is distributed across the denoising trajectory, network depth, and channels. In practice, this requires choosing a timestep, a block, and a channel subset. Existing methods either fix these choices by hand or optimize only a few extraction hyperparameters, most often the timestep, then reuse the same rule across inputs and budgets. We introduce Policy-Mask, a budget-conditioned policy trained on the downstream objective that jointly selects all three under a prescribed channel budget. Without normalization, the channel-score contribution grows with the number of selected channels and dominates the timestep and block updates. We normalize it by subset cardinality, keeping the three policy heads on comparable scales and stabilizing joint training. At matched budgets, Policy-Mask improves over fixed extraction and feature-filter baselines across segmentation, classification, and semantic correspondence, reaching 38.9 mIoU on ADE20K, 75.4% top-1 on CIFAR-100 at 128 dimensions, and 76.3 PCK@0.1 on SPair-71k. Component-wise ablations show that block selection materially affects downstream accuracy, and the highest recorded channel-budget score occurs at 256 retained channels, identifying a practical operating point for compact diffusion representations. We further adapt Policy-Mask to diffusion transformers, including PixArt-$\Sigma$ and SD3.5 MMDiT, by replacing U-Net channels with image-token hidden dimensions.

title: When Can LLM Reasoning Reliably Reuse Intermediate Results?
description:
arXiv:2610.27662v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Sampling complete solutions gives large language models more chances to solve a problem, but each attempt starts again. For tasks with several subproblems, all required answers must be correct in the same attempt. Retaining intermediate results can avoid repeating correct work, but errors in those results may affect later attempts. We study when this reuse is reliable and how much computation it requires. For local retries that stop when no candidate passes within the retry budget, we give conditions for correct completion and bound the average number of attempts. We also show how checking cost and the chance of passing a check affect total computation. Experiments across eight reasoning models examine composite mathematics and arithmetic. Across four DeepSeek models, average success on the second subproblem is 36.2 percent without first-subproblem context, 57.2 percent with its answer, and 58.3 percent with its reasoning and answer. These scores measure second-subproblem coverage and include continuations made when selection fails. Arithmetic experiments show that similar first-attempt accuracies can lead to very different coverage after repeated attempts. Code is available at https://github.com/SempraETY/Intermediate-State-Reuse.

title: Build a Simple Water Quality Monitoring Dashboard with JavaScript
description:
Water-quality monitoring is a useful example of how web development can connect data with real-world systems.

A dashboard can display measurements such as pH and water temperature, show the time of the latest reading, and flag values that need review.

In this tutorial, we will build a small front-end prototype using HTML and JavaScript. The example uses simulated readings, not real sensors.

What are we building?

Our dashboard will:

  • Display a pH reading.
  • Display a water-temperature reading.
  • Show when the readings were updated.
  • Reject invalid sensor values.
  • Indicate when a reading falls outside configurable example limits.

Important: The example limits below are for demonstrating software logic only. They are not a validated pool-safety standard and must not be used to determine whether water is safe to swim in.

Step 1: Create the HTML

Create a file named index.html:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>Water Quality Dashboard</title>
</head>
<body>
  <main>
    <h1>Water Quality Dashboard</h1>

    <section aria-labelledby="ph-heading">
      <h2 id="ph-heading">pH reading</h2>
      <p id="ph-value">Waiting for data...</p>
      <p id="ph-status" aria-live="polite"></p>
    </section>

    <section aria-labelledby="temp-heading">
      <h2 id="temp-heading">Water temperature</h2>
      <p id="temp-value">Waiting for data...</p>
      <p id="temp-status" aria-live="polite"></p>
    </section>

    <p id="updated"></p>
  </main>

  <script src="script.js"></script>
</body>
</html>

Step 2: Add the JavaScript

Create script.js:

const phValue = document.querySelector("#ph-value");
const phStatus = document.querySelector("#ph-status");

const tempValue = document.querySelector("#temp-value");
const tempStatus = document.querySelector("#temp-status");

const updated = document.querySelector("#updated");

// Illustrative thresholds for this demo only.
const demoLimits = {
  phMin: 6.5,
  phMax: 8.0,
  temperatureMin: 10,
  temperatureMax: 40
};

function isValidNumber(value) {
  return typeof value === "number" && Number.isFinite(value);
}

function renderReading(data) {
  if (
    !isValidNumber(data.ph) ||
    !isValidNumber(data.temperature)
  ) {
    phValue.textContent = "Invalid reading";
    phStatus.textContent = "Check the incoming data.";

    tempValue.textContent = "Invalid reading";
    tempStatus.textContent = "Check the incoming data.";

    updated.textContent = "";
    return;
  }

  phValue.textContent = data.ph.toFixed(2);
  tempValue.textContent = `${data.temperature.toFixed(1)} °C`;

  const phInDemoRange =
    data.ph >= demoLimits.phMin &&
    data.ph <= demoLimits.phMax;

  const temperatureInDemoRange =
    data.temperature >= demoLimits.temperatureMin &&
    data.temperature <= demoLimits.temperatureMax;

  phStatus.textContent = phInDemoRange
    ? "Within demonstration range"
    : "Outside demonstration range";

  tempStatus.textContent = temperatureInDemoRange
    ? "Within demonstration range"
    : "Outside demonstration range";

  updated.textContent =
    `Updated: ${new Date(data.timestamp).toLocaleString()}`;
}

const simulatedReading = {
  ph: 7.2,
  temperature: 26.5,
  timestamp: Date.now()
};

renderReading(simulatedReading);

Step 3: Understand the data flow

The dashboard receives an object containing measurements and a timestamp.

The renderReading() function first validates the values. It then updates the page using textContent, which avoids interpreting the readings as HTML.

Finally, it compares the readings with the example thresholds and displays a status message.

In a real application, the simulated object could be replaced with data from an API or an IoT gateway.

What would a production system need?

A real water-monitoring system would need more than a front-end dashboard:

  • Calibrated sensors and documented measurement accuracy.
  • Secure communication between devices and the server.
  • Validation for missing, stale or implausible readings.
  • Appropriate thresholds based on the application and relevant guidance.
  • Error handling and alerts for sensor failures.
  • Regular maintenance and verification against suitable testing methods.

A dashboard should never claim that pool water is safe solely because a few sensor readings appear normal.

Conclusion

This small project demonstrates how JavaScript can turn structured measurements into a readable dashboard. It also highlights a key principle of monitoring software: presenting data clearly is important, but validating the source and understanding the limitations are equally important.

From simulated sensor projects to real IoT applications, good monitoring starts with reliable data and honest reporting of uncertainty.

title: Structuring a Japan Entity: Godo Kaisha vs Kabushiki Kaisha vs Branch Office for Tech Companies
description:
Key Points

  • Tax treatment is identical between a Godo Kaisha (GK) and a Kabushiki Kaisha (KK) — the real differences are formation cost, governance overhead, and how each is perceived by conservative counterparties, not tax exposure.
  • A branch office isn't a separate legal entity at all — it's the same legal person as your foreign parent, which means the parent's liability is effectively unlimited, not capped.
  • Several major US tech companies operate their Japan presence as a GK, which undercuts the assumption that a KK is required for enterprise credibility.
  • The decision that actually matters is liability isolation and future fundraising plans, not which entity type "sounds" more established.

Introduction

A founder I advised was ready to spend the extra time and money on a Kabushiki Kaisha specifically because he'd heard a GK "looks like a shell company" to Japanese enterprise buyers. He hadn't checked that Amazon Japan, Google Japan, and Apple Japan all operate through a Godo Kaisha structure. The credibility gap he was budgeting for barely exists at the scale that actually matters to enterprise buyers — what matters more is whether the entity limits liability and fits your fundraising plans.

This article — building on localization, buying-cycle, and compliance groundwork — covers the three realistic structures for a foreign tech company entering Japan: Godo Kaisha, Kabushiki Kaisha, and branch office. None of this is a substitute for Japan-qualified legal and tax counsel; treat it as the map that tells you which questions to bring to that counsel.

Three Structures, One Real Decision

Think of a branch office like operating without your own company at all — a satellite office phone-connected directly to headquarters, where every liability call still rings back to the parent. A GK or KK, by contrast, is its own legal person: liabilities generally stop at the entity, the same way a US LLC or corporation limits the parent's exposure.

The problem this framing solves: founders often start from "which entity is most prestigious" when the actual first question is "do we want liability isolation at all, and are we planning to raise institutional capital in this entity."

Godo Kaisha (GK)

Japan's closest equivalent to an LLC. Cheaper (roughly ¥62,000–¥102,000 in registration costs) and faster to set up (1–2 weeks) than a KK, largely because it skips notarizing the articles of incorporation and the related formalities a KK requires. Governance is flexible — profit distribution doesn't have to track ownership percentage the way a KK's does — and financial reporting obligations are lighter.

Kabushiki Kaisha (KK)

Japan's joint-stock company structure, the one most conservative Japanese banks, large enterprise customers, and government counterparties default to expecting. Costs more (roughly ¥182,000–¥222,000) and takes longer (2–3 weeks) because of notarization and stricter governance requirements, and it's the only one of the three that supports issuing shares in the way institutional VCs expect.

Branch Office

Not a separate legal entity — an extension of the foreign parent, registered with the Legal Affairs Bureau, requiring at least one Japan-resident representative. Because it's legally the same person as the parent, the parent's liability exposure is effectively unlimited, and the branch is taxed only on Japan-source income rather than under the entity-level tax treatment a GK or KK receives.

Comparison: Godo Kaisha vs Kabushiki Kaisha vs Branch Office

Criteria Godo Kaisha (GK) Kabushiki Kaisha (KK) Branch Office
Setup cost ¥62,000–¥102,000 ¥182,000–¥222,000 ¥97,000–¥127,000
Setup time 1–2 weeks 2–3 weeks 3–4 weeks
Legal status Separate legal entity Separate legal entity Same legal person as parent
Liability exposure Capped at the entity Capped at the entity Effectively unlimited (parent liable)
Tax treatment Identical to KK Identical to GK Japan-source income only
Can issue shares / raise VC No Yes No
Enterprise/bank perception Improving, but still less default-expected than KK Default expectation for conservative counterparties Weakest — reads as "testing the market," not committed
Best for Solo founders, small teams, no near-term VC plans Institutional fundraising, conservative enterprise/government sales Short-term market testing, representative activity only

Bottom line: default to a GK unless you have a specific, near-term reason to need share issuance or maximum conservative-counterparty credibility — and treat a branch office as a short-term testing vehicle, not a long-term operating structure, given its liability profile.

Pros and Cons

Advantages of Getting the Entity Choice Right Early

  • GK's cost and speed advantage compounds: the savings versus a KK are modest in absolute terms but the faster timeline matters when a specific enterprise deal's contracting phase is waiting on your entity being live.
  • KK's fundraising optionality is real, not cosmetic: if institutional Japan-based VC is genuinely on your roadmap, a KK avoids a costly conversion later.
  • A branch office is genuinely useful for its narrow purpose: testing whether a specific deal or market segment justifies a full entity, without committing to Japan-entity overhead first.

Disadvantages and Risks

  • Converting a GK to a KK later is a real project, not a formality: if your fundraising plans are more than speculative, deciding this upfront avoids a legal restructuring exercise mid-growth.
  • A branch office's unlimited-liability exposure is easy to underweight when the initial motivation is just "let's get something registered quickly" — the parent's exposure doesn't feel real until it is.
  • KK's governance overhead is a genuine ongoing cost, not just a setup cost: stricter reporting and auditing requirements persist for the life of the entity, not just at formation.

Is This Right for You?

Choose Godo Kaisha if:

  • You're a solo founder or small team without near-term institutional fundraising plans in Japan.
  • You want liability isolation without KK's governance overhead.
  • Enterprise/government credibility isn't yet a proven blocker in your specific sales motion — several major foreign tech companies operate as a GK without issue.

Choose Kabushiki Kaisha if:

  • You have concrete, near-term plans to raise institutional capital in the Japan entity itself.
  • Your primary buyers are conservative counterparties (traditional banks, large legacy enterprises, government) where KK is the explicit default expectation.

Choose a branch office only if:

  • You're testing a specific opportunity short-term and are not ready to commit to full entity overhead.
  • You've explicitly accepted the parent's unlimited-liability exposure as a deliberate tradeoff, not an oversight.

Implementation Approach

Phase 1: Decide the Structure (Weeks 1–2)

  1. Confirm your fundraising timeline — if institutional capital in the Japan entity is a near-term reality, default toward KK.
  2. Confirm your buyer profile — if conservative enterprise/government counterparties are your near-term primary target, weigh KK's perception advantage against GK's cost/speed advantage.
  3. Get a Japan-qualified corporate lawyer and tax accountant involved before filing, not after — entity choice interacts with tax and visa considerations covered in later phases.

Phase 2: Register the Entity (Weeks 2–5, depending on structure)

  1. File Articles of Incorporation (GK/KK) or branch registration documents with the Legal Affairs Bureau.
  2. Appoint a Japan-resident representative — required regardless of structure, and this person's visa status needs to be confirmed before filing, not during.
  3. Open a corporate bank account — a step that frequently takes longer than the registration itself for a newly-formed entity with no operating history.

Phase 3: Post-Registration Compliance Setup (Weeks 4–8)

  1. Register for corporate tax, consumption tax, and any applicable local taxes.
  2. Set up statutory bookkeeping appropriate to your entity type — KK's requirements are stricter than GK's.
  3. Confirm alignment with the APPI and data-residency posture covered in Data Residency and APPI Compliance, since your entity structure interacts with where you're legally accountable for compliance.

Phase 4: Operate and Revisit (Month 3+)

  1. Revisit the GK-to-KK conversion question once fundraising plans firm up — don't treat the initial choice as permanent if circumstances change materially.
  2. Reassess entity structure if you expand into the regulated sectors (finance, government-adjacent) discussed in Data Residency and APPI Compliance, where counterparty expectations may shift the calculus.

Cost Considerations

Cost Type What to Budget For Typical Range
GK formation Registration, notarization (minimal), filing fees ¥62,000–¥102,000 (~$400–$700)
KK formation Registration, notarization, filing fees ¥182,000–¥222,000 (~$1,200–$1,500)
Branch office registration Legal Affairs Bureau filing, representative appointment ¥97,000–¥127,000 (~$650–$850)
Legal and tax advisory Japan-qualified counsel for entity selection and setup $3,000–$10,000 one-time
Ongoing compliance (KK) Stricter statutory auditing and reporting Higher recurring cost than GK — model against your accounting provider's quote
Ongoing compliance (GK) Lighter statutory reporting Lower recurring cost than KK

ROI signal: the cost delta between GK and KK is small relative to a single enterprise contract — don't let formation cost alone drive the decision. Let fundraising plans and buyer-profile expectations drive it, and treat the cost table as a tiebreaker, not the primary input.

Questions to Ask Your Team

  1. "Do we have a genuine, near-term plan to raise institutional capital in the Japan entity itself, or is that speculative?"
  2. "Is KK's perception advantage actually blocking a specific deal today, or is this an assumption nobody's tested?"
  3. "If we choose a branch office for speed, have we explicitly accepted the parent's unlimited-liability exposure as a deliberate tradeoff?"
  4. "Who is our Japan-resident representative, and is their visa status confirmed before we file?"
  5. "Have we connected this entity decision to the APPI/data-residency posture from Data Residency and APPI Compliance, or are we treating them as unrelated decisions?"

Conclusion

The prestige argument for a Kabushiki Kaisha is weaker than it looks — major foreign tech companies operate their Japan presence as a Godo Kaisha, and tax treatment between the two is identical. Choose based on your actual fundraising plans and buyer profile, not on which name sounds more established. Treat a branch office as a short-term testing vehicle given its unlimited-liability exposure, not a long-term operating structure, and get Japan-qualified counsel involved before filing, not after.

Further Reading

  • JETRO — Setting Up a Business in Japan
  • Verybest Law Offices — Comparison of Entities
  • Nagashima Ohno & Tsunematsu — Japanese Tax Considerations of Registering "Representative in Japan"

If this helped, a like and a follow are appreciated — and if you've solved this differently, drop a comment, I'd like to hear it.
