title: A Client Stole My Proposal and Hired Someone Cheaper to Build It — Here's the Paid-Scoping Fix
description:
A pattern that comes up constantly in freelance communities: you spend real hours on a detailed proposal (architecture, scope, pricing) to win a client, they go quiet after the call, and a few weeks later their project ships — built exactly on top of what you sent them, just by someone cheaper.

The usual advice is "charge for the proposal." True, but it's incomplete — the part that actually determines whether a client says yes or walks is how you structure that paid step. Three things that made the difference for me:

1. Split the pitch into two documents, not one

Most people send a single combined doc: why-us and the exact technical plan, in one file. That's exactly what makes it easy to lift — the client has everything they need to brief a cheaper freelancer the moment you hit send.

Instead, split it:

  • Capability pitch (free to share): who you are, the expected outcome, rough timeline and price range. No architecture, no step-by-step plan.
  • Execution blueprint (gated): the actual "how we'd build it" — only exists after a paid scoping step.

A client who ghosts after the free pitch never had the material to hand to someone else in the first place.

2. Make the paid step a real invoice, not a verbal policy

"We charge for scoping" said out loud on a call is not the same as a dated invoice for a named deliverable ("Technical scope & architecture document — Project X"). If a dispute ever happens, "here's the signed quote and the paid invoice for this specific document" is a real paper trail. "We had a call and I mentioned we charge for that" is not.

I use my own invoice generator for this — a scoping fee is a line item like any other, it just happens to be deliverable #0.

3. Frame the fee as creditable, not an extra cost

State up front: this fee becomes a credit toward the project if you hire me. This kills the "why would I pay for a proposal" objection, because the honest answer becomes "you're paying for this research either way — this way you keep the value if we move forward." It reduces a scoping fee from "extra friction" to "you were always going to pay for this, I'm just making it explicit and fair."

The part people skip: put it in writing before the blueprint goes out

None of this works as a verbal understanding. Before I send the gated blueprint, the client has signed something — doesn't need to be a lawyer-drafted contract, a one-page mutual agreement covering confidentiality and the credit terms is enough to make the paid-scoping step mean something if it's ever tested. I use a free NDA generator for exactly this — fill in two names, done in under a minute, no account needed.

And if you're scoping a full services contract (not just an NDA) after the paid phase converts into real work, a contract checklist scanner catches the clauses people forget — payment terms with a real late fee, IP assignment tied to a specific moment, an acceptance deadline. I wrote about the 6 clauses that actually matter in more detail previously.

What this doesn't fix

A bad-faith client who's willing to pay a small scoping fee and still shop your blueprint around afterward isn't stopped by any of this — nothing short of a strong contract and a lawyer stops that. What this does fix is the much more common case: the tire-kicker who was never going to pay for anything, filtered out before you've sunk two unpaid days into their "quick proposal."

title: Passing Unit Tests Is a Trap: Your AI Agent Isn't Ready for Production
description:
Photo By: Growtika

We've all seen the dashboard go green: unit tests passing, API endpoints returning 200s, integrations working without a glitch. In traditional software engineering, that's usually a reassuring sign. But with AI agents, a clean test suite can create a false sense of security, right until an agent makes an unexpected decision that damages production data.

The problem isn't necessarily broken code. Traditional software QA was built around predictable execution paths. Autonomous agents complicate that model because they can choose different routes toward the same goal.

"With traditional software, you test a function, same input, same output, every time. Determinism is your friend," explains Pramin Pradeep, CEO of BotGauge. "With an agent, the execution path itself is a variable."

"With an agent, the execution path itself is a variable."

An agent's actions can change depending on its environment, available tools, and information encountered mid-task. As Pradeep puts it, "You have to test the system’s judgment, not just its outputs."

That distinction exposes a limitation of conventional unit and integration testing. You can have perfectly functioning database drivers and API clients without knowing whether an agent will use them appropriately.

It might call tools in the wrong order, overwrite records unnecessarily, or retry a failed transaction until it creates duplicate entries.

"Unit tests would pass all of those scenarios because each tool functioned correctly in isolation," Pradeep explains. "The failure lives in the sequencing and judgment, how the agent orchestrates its tools and that is invisible to tests that only look at individual components."

Developers therefore need to think beyond assertions tied to specific function calls. "Stop asserting specific actions and start asserting properties of the outcome," Pradeep advises.

Instead of demanding one predetermined execution sequence, tests should verify that the agent accomplishes its objective without violating permissions, creating unauthorized side effects, or proceeding when escalation is necessary. "Think of it as contract testing for agent behavior."

The goal is to establish invariants that remain true regardless of which execution path the agent chooses.

Six Failure Modes Worth Breaking Your Agent For

Before granting production access, Pradeep identifies six failure modes developers should deliberately investigate: scope creep, permission escalation, irreversibility, goal misgeneralization, credential handling, and silent failure.

The last two categories are particularly concerning when failures remain difficult to detect.

An agent resolving customer tickets might discover a shortcut that technically satisfies its completion metric while ignoring the customer's actual problem. Another might encounter an unexpected condition and continue producing plausible-looking results instead of reporting that something went wrong.

"Test each of these deliberately, with adversarial inputs designed to push the agent toward the failure mode," Pradeep says. "Do not wait to discover them in production."

Testing should also extend beyond the agent's instructions to the environment in which it operates. "Chaos testing, applied to the agent’s environment."

That means injecting API timeouts, returning malformed data, revoking permissions during execution, and introducing incorrect information from another agent.

Does the system retry safely? Does it recognize unreliable inputs? Can it recover without a corrupting state?

"Does the agent fail loudly rather than silently? Does it produce a recoverable state rather than a corrupted one? Does it escalate to a human when it cannot proceed safely?"

Those questions reveal whether an agent can handle real-world disruptions rather than merely succeed under ideal conditions.

Autonomous QA Isn't the Same as Red Teaming

Continuous testing becomes increasingly important once agents encounter conditions developers never anticipated.

"Conventional test suites cover the cases you imagined. Production surfaces the cases you did not," Pradeep explains.

But automated functional testing and adversarial evaluation serve different purposes.

Autonomous QA as a Solution (AQaaS), the approach BotGauge provides, combines automated test generation, execution, and maintenance with human-defined objectives. It supports functional coverage across applications, APIs, and evolving software environments.

However, Pradeep acknowledges an important limitation.

"Where it reaches its limits is when the system under test is itself an AI agent," he says. "This is where red teaming becomes essential."

Functional QA evaluates whether software performs intended operations. Red teaming deliberately challenges an agent's boundaries, examining whether it escalates permissions, bypasses safeguards, or continues operating when it should stop. "Two different disciplines, both necessary."

That distinction matters because automatically generating more functional tests doesn't necessarily reveal how an autonomous system behaves under adversarial pressure.

Who Tests the AI That's Testing the AI?

Using AI to evaluate another AI system introduces a further problem: how do developers know the validator is reliable?

Pradeep recommends three structural constraints: model separation, scope asymmetry, and ground truth anchoring.

The testing system should use a different model family from the agent under evaluation, operate with more restricted permissions, and have consequential findings checked against independently verifiable evidence.

"The QA agent is not the final word. It is the first filter."

Human engineers remain essential for investigating unfamiliar failures, authorizing irreversible production actions, and interpreting risks that require business context.

Before deployment, Pradeep also recommends action-level tracing, behavioral baselines, infrastructure-enforced permission boundaries, escalation procedures, and a kill switch.

But those safeguards cannot substitute for deliberately challenging the agent before release. "Before anything goes to production, run a full end-to-end red team exercise."

That means finding weaknesses, correcting them, and verifying that the fixes hold under renewed testing.

"Red team first. Fix what it finds. Then instrument, trace, and safeguard. In that order."

Green unit tests still matter. They establish whether the underlying components work.

For autonomous systems, though, passing those tests isn't proof of production readiness. It's the starting point for discovering what happens when the agent encounters conditions nobody planned for.

title: Signals and Queries: Token-Efficient Agentic Context Discovery
description:
arXiv:2610.29326v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: User-facing LLM agents must identify which behavioral policies apply at each turn, but evaluating every policy with an LLM is costly. We introduce Signals and Queries (S&Q), a lightweight first-stage relevance filter developed for Parlant 4.0 that removes at least 30% of candidate policies before downstream evaluation while preserving high recall. For each policy, an LLM generates activating examples and hard negatives offline. An independent logistic classifier trained on their embeddings then predicts relevance using embeddings and vector dot products, with no per-turn LLM calls. This shifts expensive relevance evaluation to a smaller candidate set, while allowing each policy's classifier to be updated independently. Evaluated against 9,144 LLM-judge relevance labels covering 254 $\tau^2$-bench conversation prefixes and 36 airline policies, S&Q achieves higher precision than top-K and cosine-threshold retrieval at every evaluated recall level, with consistent results across two embedding providers. These findings support inexpensive, per-policy classification as a practical first stage for reducing downstream evaluation workload in customer-facing agents.

title: The best Minecraft modpack for low-end PCs and laptops (2026)
description:
If Minecraft Java stutters on your laptop, the fix is almost never "buy a new PC". The vanilla renderer is old, and a handful of community mods replace the slow parts. Together they often double or triple your frame rate on integrated graphics, with no change to how the game plays.

Why vanilla Minecraft runs badly on weak hardware

Minecraft Java does a lot of work on one CPU core: rebuilding chunk meshes, ticking entities and drawing things you can't even see. On a laptop with integrated graphics, that turns into low FPS, long freezes when you load new terrain, and a fan that never stops.

Performance mods fix this in three ways: a faster renderer, less wasted work (not drawing what's hidden), and lighter memory use.

The core performance mods (Fabric)

Mod What it does
Sodium Replaces the rendering engine. The single biggest FPS gain.
Lithium Optimises game logic (mob AI, physics, chunk ticking) without changing behaviour.
FerriteCore Cuts RAM use, which matters most if you only have 8 GB.
ImmediatelyFast Speeds up drawing of the HUD, text, item frames and signs.
Entity Culling Skips drawing mobs and block entities behind walls.
More Culling Skips more hidden block faces, such as leaves.
BadOptimizations Small, safe tweaks to lighting and sky updates.
Dynamic FPS Drops the frame rate when the game is in the background, so laptops stay cool.

Every one of these is free on Modrinth. You don't need OptiFine: Sodium is faster, and Iris adds shader support on top if you want it later.

Settings that matter most on a low-end PC

  1. Render distance 8 to 10. Each step adds a lot of chunks. Simulation distance 6 to 8 helps the CPU.
  2. Graphics: Fast. Fancy leaves and transparency cost a lot on integrated GPUs.
  3. Turn off clouds and entity shadows. Small but free wins.
  4. VSync off, FPS cap around your screen's refresh rate.
  5. Give Java 3 to 4 GB of RAM, not more. Too much RAM can make garbage collection pauses worse on an 8 GB machine.

The two-minute option: a ready-made pack

Picking versions that work together is the annoying part. Lodestone Boost is our free pack for Minecraft 1.21.11 on Fabric. It bundles the mods above plus Iris, Zoomify and dynamic lights, with low-end starting settings. It contains no mod files itself: your launcher downloads each mod from Modrinth, and every author is credited.

Install it with the Modrinth App or Prism Launcher by importing the .mrpack file.

FAQ

Do performance mods work on servers?

Yes. Client-side mods like Sodium don't change gameplay, so they work on vanilla servers, including most big public servers. Always check a server's rules first.

Is Sodium better than OptiFine?

For raw FPS on modern versions, yes in most tests. Sodium plus Iris covers what most people used OptiFine for.

How much RAM should I give Minecraft?

For a performance pack, 3 to 4 GB is plenty. Content-heavy packs need 6 GB or more.

Will this work on a Chromebook or Mac?

On Apple Silicon Macs, yes, through Prism Launcher or the Modrinth App. Chromebooks need Linux support turned on and results vary.

Originally published on Lodestone. The free Lodestone Boost pack (Fabric 1.21.11, every mod downloaded from Modrinth, every author credited) is at https://jackiscool.com/shop/p/lodestone-boost/. Unofficial fan project, not affiliated with Mojang or Microsoft.

How to Auto-Update an updated_at Column: MySQL ON UPDATE vs a Database Trigger vs the ORM
description:
Disclosure: I build Schemity, a desktop ERD tool - this post is from our blog and uses it for the examples.

TL;DR: A DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP fills updated_at only once, at insert. On MySQL, add ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP to the column; on PostgreSQL, SQL Server and SQLite, write a trigger; or let the ORM set it, which works on every database but misses every write that does not go through the ORM. Pick the database side when scripts, admins or other services write to the table, and the ORM side when only one application does.

Whether updated_at should be set by the database or by the ORM comes down to one question: does anything besides your application write to the table? The database side means MySQL's ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP column clause or a trigger everywhere else; the application side means Rails timestamps, Django's auto_now, Eloquent or Prisma's @updatedAt. A column default alone never moves after the row is created.

The short version: if anything other than your application writes rows (a migration backfill, a support engineer in psql, a second service, a bulk update_all), keep it in the database. If one application owns every write, the ORM is simpler and portable. The rest of this post is what each option does on the edge cases that decide it, and the schema changes that break each one later without an error. Every database behaviour below was run on MySQL 8.4.11, PostgreSQL 18.3, SQL Server 2022 and SQLite 3.54.0 in throwaway containers; the ORM behaviour is quoted from each framework's documentation or source.

Why DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP is not enough

Most schemas start the same way. On MySQL:

CREATE TABLE orders (
    id BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    status VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    created_at TIMESTAMP(6) NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(6),
    updated_at TIMESTAMP(6) NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(6)
);

Both columns get the insert time. After that, updated_at is an ordinary column, and an UPDATE orders SET status = 'paid' leaves it exactly where it was. A default is a value for a missing column at insert, on every database. Keeping a "last changed" time current is a separate job, and each database gives you a different tool for it.

How to auto update updated_at column: the three options

MySQL ON UPDATE PostgreSQL trigger ORM (auto_now, @updatedAt, Rails timestamps)
Available on MySQL TIMESTAMP and DATETIME only Any database with triggers (SQL Server and SQLite below) Any database
An UPDATE that changes nothing Column unchanged Column moves Rails sends no UPDATE; Django's save() moves it
An UPDATE that sets updated_at itself Your value is kept Your value is overwritten Rails and Prisma keep it, Django's auto_now overwrites it
Raw SQL and scripts Covered Covered Not covered
Bulk updates Covered Covered Eloquent sets it; Django QuerySet.update() and Rails update_all do not
Renaming the column The clause follows the column Next UPDATE fails Change the model
Where it shows up In the column definition In a trigger, outside the table In application code

The rows that decide it are the bulk and raw writes, and the rename, so each option gets its own section.

MySQL: ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP

MySQL is the only one of the four with a column clause for this:

updated_at TIMESTAMP(6) NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(6) ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(6)

It fires only when a row's values actually change. UPDATE orders SET status = 'new' on a row whose status is already new reports 0 rows changed and leaves updated_at alone, which matches the MySQL manual: an auto-updated column "remains unchanged if all other columns are set to their current values". An UPDATE that sets updated_at explicitly keeps the value it was given, which is how a data fix can backdate a row on purpose. The clause works on DATETIME as well as TIMESTAMP, and with fractional seconds the precision has to match on both sides: CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(6) for a TIMESTAMP(6) column.

The trap is in later migrations. ALTER TABLE orders MODIFY updated_at TIMESTAMP(6) NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(6) replaces the whole column definition, and since it does not repeat the clause, the clause is gone. MySQL accepts the statement without a warning. Before it, information_schema.columns.EXTRA read DEFAULT_GENERATED on update CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(6); after it, DEFAULT_GENERATED. The column keeps its old values and stops moving, and nothing notices until someone asks why a row edited yesterday says it was last changed in March. RENAME COLUMN, by contrast, keeps the clause.

PostgreSQL, SQL Server and SQLite: a trigger

PostgreSQL has no column clause, so the column is kept current by a BEFORE UPDATE trigger:

CREATE FUNCTION set_updated_at() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
BEGIN
    NEW.updated_at := now();
    RETURN NEW;
END;
$$;

CREATE TRIGGER orders_set_updated_at BEFORE UPDATE ON orders
    FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION set_updated_at();

PostgreSQL also ships the same thing as an extension, moddatetime, in contrib: CREATE EXTENSION moddatetime; then CREATE TRIGGER ... BEFORE UPDATE ON orders FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION moddatetime(updated_at);. It saves writing the function and accepts only timestamp or timestamptz columns.

Three behaviours differ from MySQL, and all three were reproduced on 18.3:

  • It fires on every UPDATE, changed or not. UPDATE orders SET status = status moves updated_at. Adding WHEN (OLD.* IS DISTINCT FROM NEW.*) to the CREATE TRIGGER gives MySQL's no-op behaviour back; an explicit value is still overwritten.
  • It overwrites an explicit value. UPDATE orders SET updated_at = '2020-01-01' stores the current time instead, with the plpgsql function and with moddatetime. A backfill that needs to set historic times has to disable the trigger first.
  • now() is the start of the transaction, not the moment of the update. Every row a long transaction touches gets the same time. Use clock_timestamp() in the function if you need the wall clock.

SQL Server and SQLite use an AFTER UPDATE trigger that runs a second UPDATE on the same row. That second update does not fire the trigger again because recursive triggers are off by default on both (is_recursive_triggers_on = 0, PRAGMA recursive_triggers returns 0). On SQL Server:

CREATE TRIGGER orders_set_updated_at ON orders AFTER UPDATE AS
BEGIN
    SET NOCOUNT ON;
    IF UPDATE(updated_at) RETURN;
    UPDATE o SET updated_at = SYSUTCDATETIME()
    FROM orders o JOIN inserted i ON i.id = o.id;
END;

And on SQLite:

CREATE TRIGGER orders_set_updated_at AFTER UPDATE ON orders
WHEN NEW.updated_at IS OLD.updated_at
BEGIN
    UPDATE orders SET updated_at = strftime('%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%f', 'now') WHERE id = NEW.id;
END;

Both keep an explicit value, and both still move the column on a no-op UPDATE. The SQL Server guard has a catch: UPDATE(updated_at) is true whenever the column is in the SET list, even with its old value, so an ORM that writes every column on save makes this trigger return every time and the column never moves. Drop the guard if your ORM does that.

The weakness of a trigger is that it names the column in a place the column does not know about. Rename updated_at to modified_at and PostgreSQL accepts the rename, then fails the next UPDATE on the table with record "new" has no field "updated_at" from the plpgsql function, or "orders" has no attribute "updated_at" from moddatetime. Dropping the column does the same. The migration succeeds; the first write after the deploy is what fails. SQL Server fails the same way after sp_rename, which at least prints a caution. SQLite is the exception: it rewrites the trigger body on RENAME COLUMN, though a dropped column still breaks the next UPDATE with no such column: NEW.updated_at. A generated column is no way out here, since it cannot call now().

The ORM: auto_now, @updatedAt and Rails timestamps

Rails, Django, Laravel's Eloquent and Prisma all set updated_at themselves, in application code, so the same model works on every database and the behaviour is visible in the codebase. The cost is every write that does not go through that code path, and the frameworks document where that is:

  • Django: auto_now is "only automatically updated when calling Model.save()", not by QuerySet.update().
  • Rails: update_all "does not trigger Active Record callbacks or validations", so it does not touch updated_at either.
  • Prisma: @updatedAt is "implemented at Prisma ORM level", so a raw SQL UPDATE leaves it alone.
  • Eloquent is the exception for bulk writes: its query builder's update() adds updated_at to the values, so Order::where(...)->update([...]) sets it. A DB::table('orders')->update() does not.

Add a manual fix run in a SQL console, a nightly script, or a second service written in another language, and updated_at is right for some writes and stale for others. That is acceptable when the column is for display. It is not when an incremental export, a cache, or a sync job reads WHERE updated_at > :last_run, because a stale row is a row that sync never sends.

Which should you use: MySQL ON UPDATE, a trigger or the ORM?

  • One application owns every write, and updated_at is informational: let the ORM do it. It is portable and it lives next to the model.
  • Anything reads updated_at to decide what changed (sync, export, cache invalidation): put it in the database, because the database sees every write. On MySQL that is the column clause; elsewhere a trigger, with the WHEN clause if no-op updates should not count. Database-side fixes coverage, not ordering: now() is when a transaction started, so a long transaction that commits after a sync run can stamp rows earlier than that run's :last_run. Query with an overlap, such as updated_at > :last_run - interval '5 minutes', and make the sync idempotent.
  • Both at once is harmless when the column is for display: MySQL and the SQLite trigger keep the value the ORM wrote, and a PostgreSQL trigger replaces it with its own now(). For sync, pick one clock, the database's, since the application servers' clocks and time zones are not the database's.

Whichever you choose, the column's behaviour now depends on something the CREATE TABLE may not show, which is what makes it easy to lose in a later migration.

How Schemity keeps updated_at in the schema

To design the next one without losing this, the schema, not the application, has to carry the decision. Schemity is database design software that reads your live database, shows the impact of every schema change before it runs, and keeps the diagram as a file in Git.

On MySQL, the clause is part of the column in the diagram. Import SQL and the live reader both read ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, and the field dialog has an "On update, set to the current time" tick on TIMESTAMP and DATETIME columns. Because the diagram holds it, every MODIFY in the migration SQL Schemity writes restates it, so changing the column's type or default does not quietly drop it the way a hand-written MODIFY does. Converting a MySQL diagram to another database leaves the clause out and says so in the conversion notes (ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(6) "is left out: PostgreSQL has no column that sets itself on update"), rather than writing a column that looks the same and stops moving.

With the default removed and the tick left on, the planned migration still carries the clause:

On PostgreSQL, the mechanism lives outside the table, and the diagram is honest about that. Import SQL keeps CREATE EXTENSION moddatetime and writes it back as CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS moddatetime; setup SQL that runs before the tables, but the trigger and its function are not part of a table in the diagram: they are counted among the skipped statements, and updated_at reads as a timestamptz column with its now() default.

When you rename or drop updated_at in a diagram connected to the database, impact analysis reads the table's triggers from the catalogue and names each one, with the warning that it fails the next time it runs if it uses what changed. That is the error above, shown before the migration rather than after the deploy.

When you design the next table, the template every new entity starts from is the place to settle the columns once: created_at and updated_at with their types and defaults, so the question of how updated_at stays current is asked for every table rather than remembered for some.

Related reading

Why a trigger and not a generated column is the right tool for now() is in generated column vs trigger. For the type of the column itself, timestamp or timestamptz, see timestamp vs timestamptz. SQLite drops a table's triggers during a table rebuild, which is how an updated_at trigger disappears in changing a SQLite column type. And the MySQL round-trip benchmark is where Schemity's own loss of ON UPDATE was found and fixed.

title: ##How to Create an App Service on Microsoft Azure
description:
Introduction

Cloud computing has become an important part of modern technology, allowing individuals and organizations to build, deploy, and manage applications over the internet without having to maintain all the physical infrastructure themselves. One of the services that makes this possible is Microsoft Azure, a cloud computing platform that provides different tools for hosting websites and web applications.

Azure App Service is a Platform as a Service (PaaS) offering that allows developers to host web applications without having to manage the underlying servers or operating systems. It supports several programming languages and frameworks, making it useful for both beginners and experienced developers who want to deploy applications to the cloud.

In this article, I will walk through the process of creating an Azure App Service using the Microsoft Azure Portal. I will explain the configuration steps, show how to create the resource, and demonstrate how to access the deployed service. This practical guide is intended for beginners who want to gain hands-on experience with Microsoft Azure and understand how web applications can be hosted in the cloud.

Prerequisites

Before creating an App Service on Microsoft Azure, make sure you have the following:

  • A Microsoft Azure account: You need an account to access the Azure Portal.
  • An active Azure subscription: This allows you to create and manage resources on Azure.
  • A web browser: You can use Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, or any supported browser to access the Azure Portal.
  • An internet connection: A stable internet connection is required to access and manage your Azure resources.

Once these requirements are ready, you can proceed to create your first App Service using the Microsoft Azure Portal.

Step 1: Sign in to the Microsoft Azure Portal

To get started, open your web browser and visit the Microsoft Azure Portal. Sign in using your Microsoft account credentials. If you do not have an account, you will need to create one before proceeding.

After signing in successfully, the Azure Portal dashboard will appear. From here, you can access and manage the different cloud services provided by Microsoft Azure.

Step 2: Create a Resource Group

Before creating an App Service, I first created a Resource Group in Microsoft Azure. A Resource Group is a logical container used to organize and manage related Azure resources.

To create a Resource Group, I used the search bar at the top of the Azure Portal and searched for Resource groups. I selected the service from the search results and clicked Create.

On the creation page, I selected my Azure subscription and entered a name for the Resource Group. I also selected a region available to my subscription.

After entering the required details, I clicked Review + create to validate the configuration. Once validation was successful, I clicked Create to deploy the Resource Group.

After the deployment was complete, I opened the Resource Group to confirm that it had been created successfully.

Step 3: Create an App Service

After creating the Resource Group, the next step is to create an App Service in Microsoft Azure.

To do this, I used the search bar at the top of the Azure Portal and searched for App Services. I selected App Services from the search results and clicked Create, then selected Web App.

On the creation page, I started configuring the web application by entering the required details. I selected my Azure subscription and chose the Resource Group I created in the previous step.

Next, I entered a unique name for the web application and selected the appropriate publishing option, operating system, and runtime stack based on the application I wanted to host. I also selected an available region and configured the App Service Plan.

After completing the required settings, I proceeded to the next stage to review the configuration before creating the App Service.

Step 4: Verify the App Service Deployment

After reviewing the configuration and clicking the Create button, Azure began deploying the App Service. I waited for the deployment process to complete.

Once the deployment was successful, Azure displayed a notification confirming that the resource had been created. I then clicked Go to resource to open the App Service Overview page.

On the Overview page, I could see the details of my newly created App Service, including its name, resource group, and other configuration information.

This step helped me confirm that the App Service had been created successfully and was available for further configuration.

Step 5: Access the App Service

After confirming that the App Service was created successfully, the next step was to access it through the Microsoft Azure Portal.

On the App Service Overview page, I located the Default domain link, which provides the URL for accessing the web application. I clicked the link to open the website in my browser.

This allowed me to check whether the web application could be accessed through its Azure URL. The page displayed depends on whether application code has been deployed to the App Service.

This step helped me understand how Azure provides a web address through which a hosted application can be accessed over the internet.

Step 6: Open Advanced Tools

After creating the App Service, the next step was to access Advanced Tools in Microsoft Azure. These tools provide access to additional management and diagnostic features for the web application.

To do this, I opened my App Service in the Azure Portal and navigated to the Development Tools section in the left-hand menu. I selected Advanced Tools and clicked Go to open the Kudu management interface in a new browser tab.

This interface provides tools for inspecting and managing files associated with the App Service.

Step 7: Access the Website Root Directory

After opening the Advanced Tools interface, I navigated to the website's root directory, where the application's files are stored.

I opened the Debug Console and selected the appropriate console option available for my App Service. I then navigated to the site folder and opened the wwwroot folder.

The wwwroot directory is commonly used as the website's content directory in a Windows Azure App Service. It is where the website's main files, such as HTML, CSS, and JavaScript files, can be stored.

Step 8: Add and Save the Website Code

After locating the website's root directory, I added the HTML code for my web application. The HTML code defines the structure of the webpage, while CSS can be used to style its appearance and JavaScript can provide interactive functionality.

I saved the website file in the appropriate directory so that the App Service could serve the content when the website was accessed through its default domain.

After saving the file, I returned to the website's URL in my browser and refreshed the page to check whether the changes were visible.

Step 9: Test the Website

After saving the HTML, CSS, and JavaScript code, I returned to my Azure App Service's default domain and refreshed the webpage. The Gen Z Bible application appeared successfully in the browser.

I tested the application to confirm that the page loaded correctly and that its features were working as expected. This confirmed that my website content was accessible through the Azure App Service URL.

This practical exercise helped me understand how to host a web application on Microsoft Azure and make it accessible through the internet.

Conclusion

Creating an App Service on Microsoft Azure was a practical learning experience that helped me understand how web applications can be hosted in the cloud. I learned how to create a resource group, configure and deploy an App Service, access Advanced Tools, and upload my website files to the wwwroot folder.

After saving my Gen Z Bible application, I visited the App Service's default domain and confirmed that the website was running successfully.

This practical exercise has improved my understanding of Microsoft Azure and cloud computing. It also gave me more confidence in exploring other Azure services and deploying web applications in the future.

title: Multi-Objective Protein Optimization via Modular Diffusion Steering
description:
arXiv:2610.28943v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Protein engineering often requires improving several properties simultaneously, motivating the search for high-performing sequences that represent useful fitness tradeoffs. Discovering these sequences is challenging because the design space is combinatorially large and experimental campaigns often permit only a few rounds of batched measurements. We introduce \textit{MODS}, a modular framework for multi-objective protein optimization via inference-time diffusion steering. For each proposal, MODS samples augmented Chebyshev scalarization weights and a fitness-surrogate ensemble member to define a scalar steering reward. Varying the weights directs generation toward different objective tradeoffs, while varying ensemble members diversifies the predictions used for guidance. Because MODS expresses multi-objective acquisition through scalar rewards, it can be paired with different diffusion models and compatible steering procedures. After each evaluation batch, MODS updates the surrogates without retraining the generative model. We evaluate MODS on six protein optimization tasks using predictive oracles trained on experimental assay data, with two diffusion models and two steering procedures. MODS achieves competitive final hypervolume across all six tasks with both diffusion models, and substantially outperforms the best evaluated baseline on several tasks. Our results demonstrate a flexible and effective approach to multi-objective protein optimization with limited feedback.

title: Your agent forgot a decision you made last week. Mine did too.
description:
Your agent forgot a decision you made last week. Mine did too.

Last month my team reversed a queue decision. Nobody could say why we
had picked the first design, what evidence it rested on, or who had
signed off on the replacement. The old design was still half-wired in
as a "fallback", quietly depending on the thing we had just replaced.
We found out in production.

Vector RAG remembers text. It does not remember decisions — what
was chosen, what it rested on, what contradicted it, and what replaced
it. So I built a tiny local graph for exactly that: memgraph.

What it does

One zero-dependency Node.js CLI. No network, no server, no embeddings.
The store is a single JSON file you can commit next to your code.

memgraph init
memgraph add --type decision --title "Use Postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY for the queue" --source "ADR-014"
memgraph add --type fact --title "NOTIFY payloads cap at 8000 bytes" --source "Postgres docs"
memgraph link m-002 m-001 --relation contradicts
memgraph add --type decision --title "Switch the queue to Redis Streams" --source "ADR-019"
memgraph supersede m-001 m-003 --reason "payload cap makes NOTIFY the wrong tool"

Three questions it answers, fast:

  • Why did we decide this? memgraph why m-003 — source, supporters, contradictions, supersession.
  • Is anything stale or contradictory? memgraph check — unresolved contradictions, live nodes resting on superseded ones, sourceless claims.
  • What do we believe? memgraph list — every node, with superseded ones marked.

memgraph check exits 1 when it finds an error, so it works as a CI
gate: a PR that introduces a contradiction, or keeps depending on a
superseded decision, fails before it merges.

Demo

The repo ships a small team graph — a queue decision, the fact that
killed it, its replacement, and one leftover fallback still depending
on the dead design:

sh examples/run-demo.sh

memgraph check on that graph reports exactly two problems: the
fallback reader depends on a superseded decision, and one open
question has no source. The contradiction between the payload-cap
fact and the old decision does not get flagged — the old decision
was superseded, so that contradiction is resolved history, not a
live conflict.

One honesty note

A graph is only as good as what you record. memgraph cannot tell you
whether a source is true — it tells you where every claim came from
and whether the graph still holds together. A decision with no source
is a rumor with formatting; that is why check flags it. And when a
decision changes, supersede it — don't delete it. Deleting history is
how teams end up re-litigating the same choice every six months.

Repo: https://github.com/techdevfun/memgraph — MIT, zero dependencies,
Node.js 18+.

title: Taming Cascading Failures: Building a Production-Grade Async Circuit Breaker in Python
description:
In modern distributed systems, dependencies fail. Databases hit connection limits, payment gateways suffer network partitions, and microservices experience latency spikes during garbage collection or CPU throttling. While transient faults are inevitable, how your application reacts determines whether a localized hiccup remains minor or escalates into a platform-wide outage.

When a downstream service degrades, waiting for long socket timeouts and immediately retrying failed requests is catastrophic. In an asynchronous Python architecture powered by asyncio and httpx, thousands of coroutines execute concurrently. If a dependency slows down from 20ms to a 10-second timeout, caller connection pools saturate, memory balloons as pending tasks queue on the event loop, and upstream gateways time out. This chain reaction is a cascading failure.

Worse yet, naive retry loops trigger a retry storm. Even if the struggling downstream briefly recovers, hundreds of application instances waiting to retry will hammer it at the exact same moment—the thundering herd problem—immediately knocking it offline again.

Popularized by Michael Nygard in Release It!, the Circuit Breaker pattern prevents cascading failures by wrapping external calls in a stateful proxy that monitors error rates. When consecutive failures cross a safety threshold, the breaker trips open, rejecting subsequent requests in memory (fail-fast) without touching the network. After a cool-down period, it allows a controlled number of canary probes through to verify recovery before restoring traffic.

In this guide, we will architect and build async-circuit-breaker-engine—a production-grade, strictly typed asynchronous Circuit Breaker in Python 3.11+ using asyncio.Lock, AWS Full Jitter Exponential Backoff, and native JSON structured telemetry.

Section 1: Anatomy of the Circuit Breaker Pattern

At its core, a Circuit Breaker is a deterministic finite state machine (FSM) with three states: CLOSED, OPEN, and HALF_OPEN.

stateDiagram-v2
    direction LR
    [*] --> CLOSED
    CLOSED --> CLOSED : Call Succeeds (reset failures = 0)
    CLOSED --> OPEN : consecutive_failures >= failure_threshold
    OPEN --> OPEN : Elapsed < recovery_time_seconds (Fail-Fast < 1ms)
    OPEN --> HALF_OPEN : Elapsed >= recovery_time_seconds (Canary Probes)
    HALF_OPEN --> CLOSED : Probes Succeed (successes >= half_open_max_calls)
    HALF_OPEN --> OPEN : Any Probe Fails (re-trip & reset timer)

The Three Operational States

  1. CLOSED (Normal Operation): Requests flow freely to the upstream service. On success, consecutive_failures resets to 0. On an expected failure (httpx.HTTPError, asyncio.TimeoutError, or 503 Service Unavailable), consecutive_failures increments by 1. Reaching failure_threshold trips the breaker to OPEN and records the monotonic timestamp _opened_at.
  2. OPEN (Immediate Fail-Fast): Protective load shedding is active. Every incoming call is rejected in under 1 millisecond by raising CircuitBreakerOpenException in memory before any network socket is allocated. This preserves event-loop capacity and gives the downstream service time to recover.
  3. HALF_OPEN (Canary Probing): Once recovery_time_seconds elapses, the breaker transitions to HALF_OPEN on the next incoming request and enforces a strict concurrency cap (half_open_max_calls):
    • Only up to half_open_max_calls canary requests reach the upstream service; excess concurrent requests are rejected immediately with CircuitBreakerOpenException.
    • If all half_open_max_calls probes succeed consecutively, the circuit closes (CLOSED).
    • If even a single probe fails, the circuit immediately trips back to OPEN and restarts the recovery timer.

Section 2: Why Simple Retries Kill Systems: Enter Full Jitter Backoff

Even with a circuit breaker, clients catching CircuitBreakerOpenException or upstream errors need to know when to retry. Standard exponential backoff scales wait times deterministically by powers of two:

T = base_backoff * (2 ** retry_attempt)

However, deterministic exponential backoff still causes correlated retry spikes. Imagine 500 concurrent requests failing during the same 50ms network blip at t = 0s. With a 0.5s base backoff, all 500 clients sleep for 0.5s and collide at t = 0.5s, then sleep 1.0s and collide again at t = 1.5s. Deterministic backoff merely shifts the thundering herd forward in synchronized waves.

To break synchronization across concurrent workers, AWS architecture research introduced Full Jitter Exponential Backoff. Instead of sleeping for the exact exponential cap, we sample uniformly between 0 and the capped exponential value:

sleep_time = random.uniform(0, min(max_backoff, base_backoff * (2 ** retry_attempt)))

By spreading retry delays uniformly across [0, cap], Full Jitter dissolves synchronized traffic spikes into a flat, manageable stream of requests.

Section 3: System Design & Architecture

Our repository, async-circuit-breaker-engine, enforces modular separation of concerns and strict Python 3.11+ static typing:

async-circuit-breaker-engine/
├── AGENTS.md                  # Engineering standards
├── README.md                  # Quickstart & overview
├── requirements.txt           # Runtime & test deps
├── config.py                  # Frozen Pydantic v2 config
├── exceptions.py              # Exception hierarchy
├── circuit_breaker.py         # Core FSM, Lock & JSON logger
├── mock_service.py            # FastAPI upstream simulator
├── main.py                    # 5-phase lifecycle demo
└── test_circuit_breaker.py    # Async concurrency test suite

Key Architectural Decisions

  • Concurrency Safety via asyncio.Lock: Cooperative multitasking introduces race conditions whenever coroutines yield at await points. Guarding state evaluation (_before_call) and transitions (_on_success, _on_failure) with asyncio.Lock guarantees atomic mutations and prevents excess coroutines from slipping through HALF_OPEN.
  • Immutable Configuration with Pydantic v2: Using ConfigDict(frozen=True) prevents runtime mutation while validating boundary constraints (ge=1, gt=0.0) at startup.
  • Signature Preservation with ParamSpec and TypeVar: Decorating an async function with @circuit_breaker preserves its parameter and return types for mypy and pyright.

Section 4: Implementation Deep-Dive

4.1 Immutable Configuration and Explicit Exceptions

In config.py, CircuitBreakerConfig defines operational thresholds using a frozen Pydantic v2 model:

from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, Field

class CircuitBreakerConfig(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(frozen=True)

    failure_threshold: int = Field(default=3, ge=1)
    recovery_time_seconds: float = Field(default=10.0, gt=0.0)
    half_open_max_calls: int = Field(default=2, ge=1)
    base_backoff: float = Field(default=0.5, gt=0.0)
    max_backoff: float = Field(default=5.0, gt=0.0)

In exceptions.py, custom errors inherit from CircuitBreakerError, and CircuitBreakerOpenException attaches recovery metadata (remaining_seconds and backoff_seconds):

class CircuitBreakerError(Exception):
    def __init__(self, message: str, circuit_name: Optional[str] = None) -> None:
        self.message = message
        self.circuit_name = circuit_name
        super().__init__(self.message)

class CircuitBreakerOpenException(CircuitBreakerError):
    def __init__(
        self,
        message: str,
        circuit_name: Optional[str] = None,
        remaining_seconds: float = 0.0,
        backoff_seconds: float = 0.0,
    ) -> None:
        self.remaining_seconds = remaining_seconds
        self.backoff_seconds = backoff_seconds
        super().__init__(message=message, circuit_name=circuit_name)

4.2 Native JSON Structured Telemetry

In circuit_breaker.py, JsonStructuredFormatter serializes every circuit event into single-line JSON containing timestamp, circuit_name, state, event, and latency_ms:

class JsonStructuredFormatter(logging.Formatter):
    def format(self, record: logging.LogRecord) -> str:
        payload: dict[str, Union[str, float, int, None]] = {
            "timestamp": datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(),
            "circuit_name": getattr(record, "circuit_name", "unknown"),
            "state": getattr(record, "state", CircuitState.CLOSED.value),
            "event": getattr(record, "event", record.getMessage()),
            "latency_ms": round(float(getattr(record, "latency_ms", 0.0)), 3),
        }
        for field in ("consecutive_failures", "half_open_successes", "backoff_seconds", "error_type"):
            if (val := getattr(record, field, None)) is not None:
                payload[field] = val
        return json.dumps(payload, ensure_ascii=False)

4.3 State Machine Synchronization (_before_call, _on_success, _on_failure)

Inside CircuitBreaker, calculate_backoff computes the Full Jitter delay, while _before_call, _on_success, and _on_failure synchronize state transitions under self._lock:

    def calculate_backoff(self, retry_attempt: Optional[int] = None) -> float:
        attempt: int = self._retry_attempt if retry_attempt is None else max(0, retry_attempt)
        cap: float = min(self.config.max_backoff, self.config.base_backoff * (2**attempt))
        return random.uniform(0.0, cap)

    async def _before_call(self) -> None:
        async with self._lock:
            if self._state == CircuitState.OPEN:
                elapsed: float = (time.monotonic() - self._opened_at) if self._opened_at else 0.0
                if elapsed >= self.config.recovery_time_seconds:
                    self._state = CircuitState.HALF_OPEN
                    self._half_open_successes = 0
                    self._half_open_in_flight = 0
                    self._emit_log(event="state_transition_open_to_half_open")
                else:
                    remaining: float = max(0.0, self.config.recovery_time_seconds - elapsed)
                    backoff: float = self.calculate_backoff(self._retry_attempt)
                    self._retry_attempt += 1
                    self._emit_log(event="call_rejected_circuit_open", level=logging.WARNING, backoff_seconds=backoff)
                    raise CircuitBreakerOpenException("Circuit OPEN", self.name, remaining, backoff)

            if self._state == CircuitState.HALF_OPEN:
                if self._half_open_in_flight >= self.config.half_open_max_calls:
                    backoff = self.calculate_backoff(self._retry_attempt)
                    raise CircuitBreakerOpenException("HALF_OPEN max calls reached", self.name, 0.0, backoff)
                self._half_open_in_flight += 1

    async def _on_success(self, latency_ms: float) -> None:
        async with self._lock:
            if self._state == CircuitState.HALF_OPEN:
                self._half_open_in_flight = max(0, self._half_open_in_flight - 1)
                self._half_open_successes += 1
                if self._half_open_successes >= self.config.half_open_max_calls:
                    self._state = CircuitState.CLOSED
                    self._consecutive_failures = 0
                    self._half_open_successes = 0
                    self._retry_attempt = 0
                    self._emit_log(event="state_transition_half_open_to_closed", latency_ms=latency_ms)
            else:
                self._consecutive_failures = 0
                self._retry_attempt = 0
                self._emit_log(event="call_succeeded", latency_ms=latency_ms)

    async def _on_failure(self, exc: BaseException, latency_ms: float) -> None:
        async with self._lock:
            self._consecutive_failures += 1
            backoff: float = self.calculate_backoff(self._retry_attempt)
            self._retry_attempt += 1
            if self._state == CircuitState.HALF_OPEN or self._consecutive_failures >= self.config.failure_threshold:
                self._half_open_in_flight = 0
                self._half_open_successes = 0
                self._state = CircuitState.OPEN
                self._opened_at = time.monotonic()
                self._emit_log(event="state_transition_to_open", latency_ms=latency_ms, level=logging.ERROR, backoff_seconds=backoff, error=exc)

Incrementing self._half_open_in_flight inside _before_call under self._lock guarantees that if 50 coroutines arrive simultaneously as the recovery timer expires (half_open_max_calls=2), only 2 claim probe slots while 48 fail fast.

4.4 Typed Async Decorator @circuit_breaker

Using ParamSpec (P) and TypeVar (R), @circuit_breaker wraps any coroutine while preserving its type signature:

P = ParamSpec("P")
R = TypeVar("R")

def circuit_breaker(
    func: Optional[Callable[P, Awaitable[R]]] = None,
    *,
    name: Optional[str] = None,
    config: Optional[CircuitBreakerConfig] = None,
) -> Union[Callable[P, Awaitable[R]], Callable[[Callable[P, Awaitable[R]]], Callable[P, Awaitable[R]]]]:
    def decorator(target_func: Callable[P, Awaitable[R]]) -> Callable[P, Awaitable[R]]:
        breaker: CircuitBreaker[P, R] = CircuitBreaker(name=name or target_func.__qualname__, config=config)
        return breaker(target_func)

    return decorator(func) if func is not None else decorator

Section 5: Benchmarking and Proving Concurrency Resilience

In test_circuit_breaker.py, test_concurrent_calls_race_condition primes a breaker (failure_threshold=3) with 2 prior failures—right at the edge of tripping—and fires 50 concurrent coroutines via asyncio.gather:

    results = await asyncio.gather(*(border_failing_call() for _ in range(50)), return_exceptions=True)
    mock_errors = [r for r in results if isinstance(r, MockServiceException)]
    open_errors = [r for r in results if isinstance(r, CircuitBreakerOpenException)]

    assert breaker.state == CircuitState.OPEN
    assert len(mock_errors) == 1
    assert len(open_errors) == 49

Next, after waiting for recovery_time_seconds, it launches 50 concurrent coroutines into HALF_OPEN (half_open_max_calls=2), proving that self._lock allows only 2 canary probes to execute while rejecting the remaining 48.

Running pytest -v confirms all 6 unit, fail-fast timing (< 5ms), backoff bounds, and concurrency tests pass:

pytest -v
collected 6 items

test_circuit_breaker.py::test_state_closed_to_open_after_threshold PASSED [ 16%]
test_circuit_breaker.py::test_fail_fast_behavior PASSED                  [ 33%]
test_circuit_breaker.py::test_recovery_to_half_open_and_closed PASSED    [ 50%]
test_circuit_breaker.py::test_half_open_reopens_on_single_failure PASSED [ 66%]
test_circuit_breaker.py::test_concurrent_calls_race_condition PASSED     [ 83%]
test_circuit_breaker.py::test_jittered_backoff_bounds PASSED             [100%]

============================== 6 passed in 2.41s ===============================

Section 6: Real-World Execution: What It Looks Like in Production

Inspecting the JSON telemetry emitted during an outage highlights the latency protection of fail-fast shedding. While upstream failures take 105.0 ms before tripping the breaker to OPEN, subsequent blocked requests fail fast in 0.12 ms without touching the network:

{"timestamp": "2026-10-22T15:10:01.319Z", "circuit_name": "payments_upstream_circuit", "state": "CLOSED", "event": "call_failed", "latency_ms": 104.88, "consecutive_failures": 2, "backoff_seconds": 0.7421}
{"timestamp": "2026-10-22T15:10:01.425Z", "circuit_name": "payments_upstream_circuit", "state": "OPEN", "event": "state_transition_closed_to_open", "latency_ms": 105.0, "consecutive_failures": 3, "backoff_seconds": 1.6295}
{"timestamp": "2026-10-22T15:10:01.425Z", "circuit_name": "payments_upstream_circuit", "state": "OPEN", "event": "call_rejected_circuit_open", "latency_ms": 0.12, "consecutive_failures": 3, "backoff_seconds": 2.9104}
{"timestamp": "2026-10-22T15:10:04.630Z", "circuit_name": "payments_upstream_circuit", "state": "HALF_OPEN", "event": "state_transition_open_to_half_open", "latency_ms": 0.0, "consecutive_failures": 3}
{"timestamp": "2026-10-22T15:10:04.668Z", "circuit_name": "payments_upstream_circuit", "state": "CLOSED", "event": "state_transition_half_open_to_closed", "latency_ms": 18.012, "consecutive_failures": 0}

Dropping response time from 105.0 ms to 0.12 ms represents an 875x latency reduction, keeping event loops responsive under heavy degradation.

Section 7: Production Considerations & Edge Cases

  1. In-Memory vs. Distributed State with Redis: Process-local state (asyncio.Lock) adds near-zero overhead (< 0.15ms) with no external single point of failure. However, across 100 stateless workers with failure_threshold=5, an upstream could absorb 500 hits before every worker trips locally. For fleet-wide synchronization, back state transitions with atomic Redis Lua scripts.
  2. Sliding Windows vs. Consecutive Counters: Consecutive counters excel at catching hard outages, but an upstream failing 75% of the time might interleave 1 success every 3 failures, resetting the counter before tripping. For brownouts, use a ring-buffer sliding window that trips when the error rate exceeds a percentage threshold (e.g., > 50% over 50 calls).
  3. Exception Filtering (Never Penalize HTTP 4xx): Client errors like 400 Bad Request or 404 Not Found reflect invalid caller input, not downstream unavailability. Configure expected_exceptions to only count 5xx server errors (500, 502, 503, 504), 429 Too Many Requests, and transport timeouts (httpx.TimeoutException).

Conclusion & Call to Action

Resilience is not about preventing failures; it is about containing their blast radius. By combining an asyncio.Lock-guarded state machine, Full Jitter Exponential Backoff, strict Python 3.11+ typing (ParamSpec / TypeVar), and JSON structured telemetry, async-circuit-breaker-engine protects your microservices from cascading failures and thundering herds.

  • Explore and star the GitHub repository: https://github.com/marlete23/async-circuit-breaker-engine
  • Clone the repo, run python main.py to watch the 5-phase lifecycle live, and run pytest -v to verify concurrency resilience!

title: Weakly Supervised Fish Segmentation through Point-Supervised Tracking and Motion-Informed Language
description:
arXiv:2610.29047v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Understanding the properties of fish populations is increasingly important. Analyzing fish length, width, and mass is integral to maintaining healthy stock in the aquaculture industry, while counting wild fish populations supports marine conservation and coastal reef restoration efforts. Deep learning-based segmentation models offer a promising means of obtaining such information at scale. Most of these models, however, require costly and time-consuming per-pixel segmentation labels for training, which can take up to two minutes per fish to annotate manually. To address this inefficiency, we propose a weakly supervised segmentation pipeline that requires only point-labeled data (one click per fish) to produce accurate segmentation masks. Our pipeline consists of four stages. First, a point-supervised tracker predicts point annotations for each frame. These points are then converted into motion-informed language expressions, which guide a language-conditioned segmentation model (LMPM++) to capture temporal consistency and produce candidate segmentation masks. Finally, optical flow and background subtraction are applied as post-processing filters to suppress noise from incorrect segmentations. Experiments on the DeepFish dataset show improvement in foreground mean intersection over union (mIoU) as compared to baseline models.

title: Gemini 2.5 Flash "no longer available to new users" (404)
description:
The error:

{
  "error": {
    "code": 404,
    "message": "This model models/gemini-2.5-flash is no longer available to new users. Please update your code to use models/gemini-3.8-flash for the latest features and improvements. We recommend you to use the Interactions API (https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/get-started).",
    "status": "NOT_FOUND"
  }
}

Tested on: @google/genai: 2.27.0 · API key: new, free tier (AI Studio) · Node / OS: 24.14.0 / Windows 11 Pro · Date: October 7, 2026

This isn't your code, and it isn't your key's permissions. Google has retired the 2.x models for keys and projects that didn't use them before. That's why the same code keeps working on a colleague's old key and fails on yours, or works on your laptop and fails in a new deployment with a fresh key.

I called every older model name with a brand-new key. There are three different messages, depending on how old the model is:

Model Message
gemini-2.5-flash, gemini-2.5-pro, gemini-2.5-flash-lite 404 "no longer available to new users"
gemini-2.0-flash, gemini-2.0-flash-lite 404 "no longer available" (gone for everyone)
gemini-1.5-flash, gemini-1.5-pro 404 "is not found for API version v1beta, or is not supported for generateContent"

Each 404 for a 2.x model names its own replacement:

You asked for The error suggested
gemini-2.5-flash gemini-3.8-flash
gemini-2.5-pro gemini-3.1-pro-preview
gemini-2.5-flash-lite gemini-3.5-flash-lite
gemini-2.0-flash gemini-3.8-flash
gemini-2.0-flash-lite gemini-3.5-flash-lite

The model list doesn't warn you

If you check ai.models.list() first, you'll still find gemini-2.5-flash, gemini-2.5-pro and gemini-2.5-flash-lite in it, listed as supporting generateContent. Then the call 404s. So "it's in the list" doesn't mean your key can use it: only a real call tells you.

The fix

Change the model name. These worked with the new free key:

const res = await ai.models.generateContent({
  model: 'gemini-3.5-flash', // or 'gemini-3.5-flash-lite'
  contents: 'hi',
});

✅ gemini-3.5-flash and gemini-3.5-flash-lite both answered normally with the same key that got the 404.

To stop this happening at the next retirement, you can use the moving alias instead of a version number. gemini-flash-lite-latest answered, and the response's modelVersion showed it was serving gemini-3.5-flash-lite:

const res = await ai.models.generateContent({ model: 'gemini-flash-lite-latest', contents: 'hi' });
console.log(res.modelVersion); // gemini-3.5-flash-lite

The cost of an alias: the model behind it changes without notice, so output and pricing can shift under you. Log modelVersion so you can see when it does.

Don't jump straight to the suggested model

The 404 for gemini-2.5-flash says to use gemini-3.8-flash. Every time I tried it that evening, it returned 503 "This model is currently experiencing high demand" or timed out, and gemini-flash-latest did the same. Meanwhile, older models kept answering. The newest model is the busiest one. Test the replacement before you ship it.

And for the Pro suggestion (gemini-3.1-pro-preview): on the free tier its quota is 0, so switching to it turns your 404 into a 429. That one is covered in Gemini API 429 RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED: why your limit is 0.

What didn't work

❌ Checking models.list() before calling. The retired 2.5 models are still listed for a key that can't use them.

❌ Using the exact model the error recommends, as is. gemini-3.8-flash returned 503 or timed out every time I called it, and the recommended Pro model has no free-tier quota at all.

💡 Same idea, different provider Groq retired its Llama models the same way, with a model_not_found error: Groq API error 413, 429 and model_not_found.

How this was tested

A free Google AI Studio key on October 7, 2026 (a new one: it got the "to new users" 404), with @google/genai 2.27.0 on Node 24.14.0 (Windows 11). Every model was called once with a one-word prompt and maxOutputTokens: 1. The model list came from ai.models.list() with the same key. I didn't have an older key to confirm that the 2.5 models still work for existing users. That part is what the error message itself says ("to new users"), not something I saw. Google retires models on its own schedule, so check the date above.

The code for every case above is public, so you can run it yourself: gemini-429 in nk-repro.

Originally published, with updates as new versions ship, at nilaykabariya.blog. Written with AI assistance; every error and fix was reproduced on a real machine before it was written up.

title: Why is AI-generated language so hard to understand?
description:
arXiv:2610.29162v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: There is a widespread sense that AI-generated text has recently become harder to understand. In this study, we investigate a set of psycholinguistic features that are known to correlate with human processing difficulty (e.g., object relative clauses, long syntactic dependencies, low-frequency n-grams). Using a novel corpus of AI-generated text across diverse domains, we find that AI models use these difficult features more often than paraphrases generated by round-trip translation. Compared with human writing, all nine frontier and near-frontier models use more inanimate subjects with animate verbs and more low-frequency n-grams, and most also use longer dependencies, more stacked nouns, and more reduced object relatives in conversation; we also demonstrate substantial variation across model families. We propose and test a hypothesis as to why: while human language is optimized for successful communication, AI-generated text is increasingly optimized for other goals like math, code, and reasoning, in which there is a pressure for \textit{information density} rather than successful communication. We provide a proof-of-concept for this hypothesis by fine-tuning a language model under a length penalty, which leads to a divergence from human-like linguistic behavior. Our findings highlight the axes of misalignment between linguistic processing demands in humans and LLMs, and point toward possible remedies.

title: How To Qualify Consulting Leads
description:
How To Qualify Consulting Leads

As a principal frontend engineer and conversion architect, I have encountered numerous instances where standard off-the-shelf templates and generic forms fail to effectively qualify consulting leads. The primary reason for this failure lies in the lack of personalized approach and in-depth understanding of the client's specific needs and pain points. Generic templates often rely on a one-size-fits-all methodology, which neglects the unique requirements and objectives of each potential client.

Upon closer examination, it becomes apparent that the conventional methods of lead qualification are inadequate due to their inability to account for the complexities and nuances of each client's situation. This oversight can result in a significant loss of potential business opportunities, as unqualified leads can consume valuable time and resources without yielding tangible results.

To overcome these challenges, I have identified three concrete engineering takeaways that can enhance the lead qualification process:

  1. Implement a bespoke lead qualification framework: Develop a customized framework that takes into account the specific needs and objectives of your consulting services. This framework should be designed to capture the unique pain points and requirements of each potential client, allowing for a more accurate assessment of their qualifications.
  2. Utilize advanced data analytics and machine learning algorithms: Leverage data analytics and machine learning algorithms to analyze the behavior and characteristics of potential clients. This can help identify patterns and trends that are indicative of qualified leads, enabling more effective targeting and qualification.
  3. Integrate personalized and interactive elements into the lead qualification process: Incorporate personalized and interactive elements, such as tailored questionnaires and dynamic assessments, to engage potential clients and gather more accurate information about their needs and objectives. This can help build trust and establish a more meaningful connection with potential clients, ultimately leading to more effective lead qualification.

By incorporating these engineering takeaways into your lead qualification process, you can significantly improve the accuracy and effectiveness of your consulting lead qualification efforts. Vareli breaks this down in the complete analysis:
https://vareli.info/blog/how-to-qualify-consulting-leads
