title: The seed is just the oldest record, and other things I got wrong about a YantrikDB merge bug
description:
On 2026-10-16, antonius888 opened issue #253 on YantrikDB, the Rust memory engine for AI agents I maintain. In one think() consolidation pass, five memories from four unrelated topics (two delegated-task prompts, a fact about DPI community tools, two Bitwarden facts) were folded into one consolidated record whose text began "Hermes dashboard autostart: TWO mechanisms...". None of the five had anything to do with dashboard autostart.

yantrikdb-hermes-plugin runs the engine in-process as a memory backend for the Hermes agent framework, and its on_pre_compress hook writes a "compression gist" into the store before a conversation chunk gets trimmed: importance 0.75, metadata {"source": "compression_summary", "pre_compression": true, ...}. antonius888's gists ran over 1,300 characters, up to about 1,400.

What they posted:

  • Consolidation multiplies an absorbed record's importance by 0.3 (consolidate.rs:1191), so a 0.6 record comes out at 0.18. Their absorbed records landed between 0.18 and 0.24.
  • Over many think() passes (the engine only commits a handful of consolidations per pass by default), the store had built up 84 distinct consolidation targets: {2: 31, 10: 22, 3: 8, 1: 5, 6: 5, 4: 4, 5: 3, 8: 3, 7: 2, 9: 1}. The 22 at exactly 10 are sitting on the max_cluster_size hardcoded at the call site, consolidate.rs:774.
  • Ten pending "redundancy" triggers, urgency 0.988 to 0.997. Of the three quoted with scores, the 0.9973 one paired a gist with an unrelated 1C ERP fact written in Russian. The 0.9915 one was two different "Strata install" gists, which might honestly be near-duplicates, and the 0.9890 one was also gist against gist.

They proposed four fixes (exclude summaries from clustering, cap a gist's similarity influence, promote the pre_compression tag to a column, cap gist length) and had already added a local env var, YANTRIKDB_COMPRESSION_GIST, to turn the write off.

Two things I had wrong

I replied the same day, on engine 0.23.2, with a theory for why the entity-overlap guard in find_clusters didn't stop this. That guard has been in the engine since April (commit a27ab9f, the v0.4.2 to v0.4.4 core sync). It skips a candidate when both records have extracted entities and the sets share nothing, which keeps "Alice is CEO" from merging with "Sarah is CTO". My theory was that a gist's entity set covers everything it summarized, so it's never disjoint from anything and the guard can't fire.

That describes a record the plugin doesn't write. Here's the end of _compose_compression_gist on the plugin's main:

intent = (first_user or "").strip().replace("\n", " ")[:200]
outcome = (last_assistant or "").strip().replace("\n", " ")[:200]
n = len(middle)
if outcome:
    return (
        f"[compression-summary, {n} turns] "
        f"intent: {intent} | outcome: {outcome}"
    )

First 200 characters of the first user turn, first 200 of the last assistant turn, inside a fixed template. Nothing from the middle of the conversation gets read. That tops out around 450 characters on main, and v0.27.0, the release antonius888 was running, has the same cap. So 1,300-character gists match neither. I asked in the thread whether their copy of the hook had been modified. I still don't know.

The second mistake was one I'd been carrying around in my head, and I only caught it re-reading the Rust for this post. I'd been picturing the engine choosing the gist as a cluster's seed because it sits near so many other vectors. Seed choice has nothing to do with similarity:

// Sort by creation time (return indices)
let mut indices: Vec<usize> = (0..memories.len()).collect();
indices.sort_by(|&a, &b| memories[a].created_at.total_cmp(&memories[b].created_at));

let mut used = HashSet::new();
for (seed_pos, &i) in indices.iter().enumerate() {
    if used.contains(&i) { continue; }
    let mut cluster = vec![i];
    used.insert(i);
    // ... candidates are later records in time order, checked against
    // time window, entity-overlap guard, then cosine similarity

The earliest unused record becomes the next seed. A gist seeds a cluster only when it happens to be the oldest unused record in its neighborhood.

Where the merged text comes from matters more. The consolidation target is a brand-new record built by extractive_summary, which sorts members by importance, highest first, and leads with the top one's text. Ordinary facts in a store like this sit around 0.5 to 0.6. A gist is 0.75, so whenever one lands in a cluster, as seed or member, its text will very likely open the merged record.

The "Hermes dashboard autostart" record from the top isn't a gist (gists always start with the literal [compression-summary,), so I'm not pinning that one on gists. Same mechanism, though: the highest-importance member named a cluster that was mostly about other things.

The embedder

On 2026-10-17, a day after my first reply, I posted a partial correction: the gist is a real but secondary factor, and I think the main cause is the embedder.

I'd installed the published yantrikdb==0.23.2 wheel into a clean venv and, on a fresh store, scored text modeled on the report by calling the engine directly, once with the default embedder and once with potion-multilingual-128M:

pair default embedder potion-multilingual-128M
unrelated Russian↔Russian (1C/Bitwarden/gist/FoodTorg) 0.83–0.93 0.14–0.47
unrelated English↔English 0.04–0.23 0.21–0.33
Russian gist ↔ English gist 0.17 0.46

The default, potion-base, is the static, English-only model bundled in the wheel. Unrelated Cyrillic text scores 0.83 to 0.93 against other unrelated Cyrillic text, well over the 0.6 clustering threshold. That alone is enough to explain the gist-to-1C trigger, clusters filling to the size-10 cap, and the importance loss.

The last row is where the gist does contribute. Under the multilingual model, a Russian gist and an English gist still score 0.46, and the only thing they share is the [compression-summary, N turns] intent: ... | outcome: ... scaffolding. Every gist carries it, which gives gists a similarity floor with each other that ordinary facts don't have, and is a likelier story for the two gist-to-gist triggers than anything in their content.

Switching embedders has its own wall. On a store that already holds data, set_embedder_named() refuses and points you at db.reembed(), which isn't callable from Python (#241). My test also bypassed the plugin's config path, so I can't vouch for it end to end. Through the plugin, YANTRIKDB_EMBEDDER also needs YANTRIKDB_EMBEDDING_DIM set or it raises, and the plugin README documents a second route, YANTRIKDB_EMBEDDER_MODEL2VEC=minishlab/potion-multilingual-128M, which needs the model2vec package. Either way it means a fresh store and a re-import; consolidated originals keep their full text, so nothing is lost.

I committed to three follow-ups: make reembed() callable from Python; warn when stored text is mostly outside the embedder's language instead of degrading silently; and on the plugin side, a config switch for the gist write plus keeping gists out of the seed role.

The question I owed wolf-crazy

wolf-crazy, who already has one merged fix in this repo, picked up the seed-role piece today. Gists stay eligible as members and never become the seed. Their useful find: MemoryWithEmbedding, the struct find_clusters already works on, carries a metadata field filled from decrypted JSON at two construction sites, so there's no schema change and no extra decrypt. The proposed shape is an Option<&dyn Fn(&MemoryWithEmbedding) -> bool> parameter, None by default, so every other caller keeps today's behavior. That includes patterns.rs:327 and the Python binding at py_consolidate.rs:45, the _find_clusters antonius888 named in the report. (Checking that one, I noticed it passes None for the entity map, so the guard my first theory was about doesn't even run on that path.)

Their claims checked out against origin/main at 1d48d09 earlier today — the files involved hadn't changed since before the issue was even filed.

They asked one direct question: key the predicate off the pre_compression tag already in the metadata blob, or promote it to a real column first?

The reply that verified their work, posted under my account, was written as triage and pushed that data-model call to me instead of making it in a comment. When I sat down to write this, I still hadn't answered wolf-crazy.

So here's my answer: use the tag.

The reason sits a few dozen lines above where find_clusters gets called, at consolidate.rs:727-731:

let memories: Vec<MemoryWithEmbedding> = memories
    .into_iter()
    .filter(|m| m.metadata.get("consolidated_from").is_none())
    .collect();

Records tagged consolidated_from are dropped before clustering starts, so the next pass doesn't re-merge a summary with its own sources. A metadata key already decides clustering eligibility in the same file, and reading pre_compression for seed eligibility is the same kind of decision. A column earns its cost once there are enough opt-out knobs to want to query or index them. Right now there are two, both in a blob we already decrypt. If more show up I'll be migrating a live table with encrypted metadata on it, which won't be fun, and I'd still rather pay that later than pay for it now. Someone with more production migrations behind them could fairly call that backwards.

What I don't have an answer for is the other half. Keeping gists out of the seed role changes which record a cluster is measured against. It doesn't touch extractive_summary, which will still put a 0.75 gist at the front of any cluster it joins as a member, and with that template floor, gists join clusters easily. The plugin's source calls 0.75 "higher than baseline; this is a deliberate save." Lowering it, skipping gists when picking the lead, or dropping them from clustering the way consolidated_from records are dropped would each undo something chosen on purpose. I haven't picked one, and wolf-crazy's PR shouldn't wait on it.

Pranab Sarkar, Independent Researcher

title: The Show-Up Attack: When Subagents Win Over Their Supervisor
description:
arXiv:2610.27574v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multi-agent systems are increasingly deployed to coordinate multiple large language model (LLM) agents. However, this also creates new attack surfaces: malicious agents may have chances to exploit the coordination. In this paper, we propose and study the \textit{show-up attack}, in which a malicious subagent manipulates the supervisor into involving it in tasks beyond its assigned scope. To evaluate this risk, we propose SUA-Arena, which implements 6 attack strategies and contains 188 test cases. Then, we evaluate 6 frontier LLMs and find that all of them are vulnerable to show-up attacks. For example, GPT-5.6-Sol as a supervisor suffers an ASR of up to 0.93. Mitigation strategies such as prompting and restricted communication fail to reduce the risk consistently. These results show that multi-agent systems need explicit mechanisms for enforcing authority boundaries.

title: Vercel Drives is now generally available
description:
Vercel Drives is now generally available for Vercel Sandbox on Hobby, Pro, and Enterprise.

A Drive is persistent storage that you mount as a directory in a Vercel Sandbox. Its files remain available after the sandbox stops, so later runs and other sandboxes can access them by mounting the same Drive.

Use Drives to preserve an agent’s workspace or file-based memory across runs, or to make datasets, models, dependencies, and build artifacts available across sandboxes.

You can also fork a Drive into independent writable Drives. Forks inherit the source Drive's data, region, and maximum size, then store their own changes. Parallel workers can start with the same files and make changes without affecting the original or one another.

Learn more in the Drives documentation.

title: How our agents build on-brand pages with design.md
description:
Across Vercel, we use coding agents to design and build pages that have to look and feel like Vercel. The typography, color, and composition all need to carry the same judgment that we put into the pages we already ship ourselves.

We recently wrote about product-design, our skill that teaches agents how we design when they work in our codebases. The skill lives in each repository alongside the code that it governs, explaining how agents can find and understand our design system as well as product guidelines for whatever they are building.

This works great when agents are working in our codebases, where everything the skill needs is right there. But what about reports, proposals, and the one-off pages that still have to look like Vercel but get made in tools that can't read any of those files? For us, the answer was design.md, one public file any agent can load.

How we approached building design.md

What made product-design work well was that the design system and product guidelines were sitting right there in the repository for agents to read. We needed a way for agents and tools outside that environment to reach the same knowledge, so that the pages coming out the other end would still look like something we designed ourselves. That set two requirements:

  • A single public URL that anyone can point their agents at, regardless of the environment they run in.

  • Guidance covering everything that made product-design useful in the first place, from brand, layout, and copywriting to the design system, responsiveness, and information architecture.

The naive approach we tried first was to simply port product-design into a public prompt, collapsing the skill's reference files into one file any agent could read from a URL. The problem we found was that while the prompt described our visual language just fine, every model reading it interpreted that description differently, generating vastly different pages from the same guidance.

Part of this comes from the fact that design language is subjective. Phrases like "keep the layout clean" can really mean anything. What is "clean"? Beyond that, the bigger problem was everything else the prompt left behind. Inside our codebases, an agent reads product-design surrounded by real components and shipped examples of the things it describes. But a public prompt includes none of that, leaving every model to rebuild our style from just words alone.

So what we needed to do was distill what that environment provided into a single file, and the only way to know whether we were getting closer was to look at the pages coming out. We set the port aside and started writing a new file from scratch, this time testing every change against a repeatable set of eval prompts.

We wrote seven of them, pulled from real use cases and paired with mock inputs:

  • Usage and performance report

  • Renewal proposal

  • Benchmark report

  • Interactive planning page

  • Build-versus-buy brief

  • Security governance brief

  • Presentation deck

The prompts stayed fixed while the file changed, so any difference in the output traced back to the guidance.

The first comparison

These evals gave us a way to measure both what the file was actually doing and how it was being interpreted by different agents. For our first test, we wanted to know whether design.md would actually change what a model produced at all. We ran the renewal proposal eval twice in the same environment with the same model, once without design.md and once with it loaded, keeping the prompt, data, and viewport identical in both runs.

Without design.md, the model generated a generic SaaS dashboard. But with it, the page led with the renewal recommendation itself, pulled the commercial evidence into one grid, put peer values on a single scale so they could actually be compared, and kept supporting detail available without letting it compete with the summary. This allowed us to conclude that the file changed the page’s structure and hierarchy as well, not just the styling like we originally found, giving us enough signal to keep building the guidance like this, one rule at a time.

The three parts that make the system work

As we tested and rebuilt design.md, the scope evolved into a three-part system that made the entire thing work:

  • design.md supplies guidance that shows agents how to frame the reader's job, structure evidence, and choose a composition.

  • A public stylesheet that defines a bounded, documented vocabulary of classes and tokens.

  • An evaluation loop turns repeated human feedback into better guidance and deterministic checks.

Each of these layers covers a different slice of the work that creates a high-quality, on-brand Vercel page. The judgment that gets encoded in design.md gives agents guidance on:

  • Shaping a page for both a quick executive read and a detailed audit.

  • Writing copy with concrete claims and honest caveats.

  • Composing hierarchy, typography, and color so that evidence and prose support each other.

  • How to publish as Vercel, down to the asset rules for our wordmark and the triangle logo.

design.md also names the recurring generated-design patterns that we never want to see, allowing agents to recognize and avoid them far more reliably by giving the patterns names.

We created a stylesheet because agents kept inventing their own typography, spacing, and layout, so we took those decisions away from the model entirely. The stylesheet packages our design system's primitives, such as headers, tables, stat strips, and chart styles, as CSS that any page can use via a public URL. Then design.md documents the class names and tokens that the stylesheet provides, allowing the agent to build the page with those names in the HTML instead of reinventing them.

Another benefit to this is that the agent never actually reads the stylesheet itself. The stylesheet loads when the page renders in your browser, so none of the code enters the model's context, saving more room for design guidance instead.

Last, the evaluation loop is what helps make the other two pieces work. Deterministic checks are used to help catch mechanical failures, such as a table that ignores the width available to it, while people judge the subjective parts that can't be automated, like hierarchy, composition, and whether the page actually gives the reader what they came for.

How guidance made it into the file

Every line of guidance in design.md earned its place through the eval loop. We generated pages from fixed scenarios, reviewed what came back, encoded the corrections we accepted, and reran the scenarios to see whether each change stuck, since a change that helped one artifact could quietly hurt another. Nothing got in any other way.

Scenarios and rounds

Each of the seven prompts becomes a scenario, meaning the prompt is frozen together with its mock inputs and render settings. The renewal proposal, for example, always runs with the same fake customer data with the same viewport settings, keeping design.md as the only thing that changes between runs. A round means generating a fresh page from every scenario against the current version of the file. Full rounds cover all seven scenarios on both Claude Opus 4.8 and Codex with GPT-5.5.

If we want to investigate something specific, such as a rule change that only affects tables, we can rerun the affected scenarios or a single model, keeping iteration loops tight.

Generating all seven pages together also made them easy to compare side by side, and what stood out was that design.md wasn't pushing every page toward one template. The interactive planning page put its controls front and center, because someone opens a planning page to change the numbers and see what happens. The renewal proposal instead led with the recommendation and the commercial comparison behind it, because its reader is deciding whether to renew. Every page used the same Vercel typography, color, and spacing, but each one was structured around what its reader came to do.

Reviewing every run

To review the pages each round produced, we built a local app that displays full-page renders and runs blind A/B comparisons. This app eventually became our eval harness, running each scenario and storing the results. Each stored run keeps the prompt, inputs, model configuration, the version of design.md it used, the screenshots, and whatever feedback the reviewer left about it. Reviewers record every correction against the exact run that produced it.

Turning corrections into rules and checks

Each correction a reviewer records gets landed in the narrowest place that can consistently enforce it. Judgment changes go into design.md as prose, reusable mechanics go into the stylesheet, and anything that we can check mechanically becomes a deterministic check in code. Problems with the harness itself stay in the harness, and when a single model fails in a way the others don't, we keep it out of the rules until it repeats.

Take one of the early renewal proposals. Its commercial terms table came back squeezed to the same width as the prose, even though the page had room for the table to be twice as wide.

During review, we flagged that evidence tables should use the full width available to them. But when looking through previous outputs, we found this same failure everywhere. So this correction ended up going into two places:

  • A rule in design.md stating the intended behavior.

  • A deterministic check in code that catches the same layout failure the next time it appears.

Once this landed, later renewal proposal prompts resulted in pages with correct full-width tables. To verify changes like this one, we reran the affected scenarios after encoding them. At milestones we went further, running blind A/B rounds that put the updated design.md against an earlier version of the file to decide whether to keep, revise, or revert each change.

Measuring whether it worked

Building the file had taken well over 200 runs, counting full rounds, targeted checks, dry runs, and all of the dead ends. Alongside the human reviewers, a model judge wrote critiques for each round, and every round's feedback went into improving the next run.

After all of those runs, we wanted to know whether the corrections we had encoded were actually preventing the failures they were written for. So we picked three desktop scenarios, and for each one we had Codex with GPT-5.5 generate the page twice, once with design.md loaded and once without. We kept the first attempt from every generation, with no re-rolls. Then we ran our deterministic checks over all six pages and counted how many times a known failure, like a table that ignores its available width, showed up in each set. The pages generated with design.md had 39 of those failures. The pages generated without it had 91, which works out to 57% fewer in this test.

Those numbers come with two caveats. The checks can only catch failures we have already seen and written down, so this test says nothing about whether a page is well designed overall. Six pages is also far too small a sample to make claims about quality or reliability, and every one of them, with or without the file, still had at least one failure serious enough to block shipping. But what the test does well is tell us that once we name a failure and encode it, that failure tends to stay gone.

How design.md stays current

The eval loop got the file shipped, but what keeps it current is real usage. Inside our Slack, that usage comes through @design-agent, an agent built on eve that we use for anything from design critiques and copy alternatives to icon recommendations and report sites built from pasted data. Instead of setting up a prompt or hunting down source files, you just mention the agent in a thread. For website requests, it loads the current design.md, builds the page against the published stylesheet, and posts a full-page screenshot and deployment URL back to the thread. Unlike our fixed scenarios, each of these threads captures a real request, a real output, and whatever feedback or steering followed, showing us how the guidance performs out in the wild.

Every week, we gather all of that feedback in one place, the Slack threads along with comments from GitHub reviews and Figma. Automation groups the comments that keep repeating, and each repeated complaint becomes a proposed change. A person then reviews each proposal, checks whether the system already handles it, and decides where the accepted fix belongs, whether that is @design-agent, the product-design skill, design.md, the stylesheet, or a deterministic check. And if people start asking for a kind of page we have never tested, that request becomes a new eval scenario.

To know whether any of this is working, we count how often each kind of complaint shows up in similar work over time. Once we encode a fix, that count should start falling. When it does not, something about the fix is wrong. The rule might be unclear, it might not be loading when it is needed, the stylesheet might not have a primitive that can express it, or it might need a deterministic check instead of prose.

Build your own

You can build the same loop yourself, starting with one recurring artifact and one manual comparison.

1. Pick one repeated artifact

Use a recent task with a real reader and real inputs, like a proposal, performance report, benchmark, or microsite. Avoid broad goals such as "make it on-brand." Before generating anything, write down a short rubric. A good one checks that the supplied facts survived, that the reader's decision is clear, and that the correction you keep making by hand actually got resolved.

2. Save the baseline first

Generate the page once without any new design context, and save the prompt, inputs, configuration, and a screenshot. Keep that first output even if it looks rough, unless the harness itself failed. You cannot tell whether new context helped without a before.

3. Start from your last ten corrections

Collect the feedback you keep giving in design reviews, pull requests, or Slack, and rewrite each correction as something observable. That means writing Let evidence tables use the full available width instead of Make the table feel less cramped, since only one of those can be checked.

Put the decisions in one file with sections for scope, reader and task, observable decisions, and available primitives. That file is your first design.md.

4. Constrain repeatable mechanics

If your outputs keep inventing their own typography, spacing, or layout, publish a stylesheet and document the exact classes and tokens the agent may use. Keep your judgment in prose, and push the repeatable mechanics into CSS or deterministic checks.

5. Run one matched comparison

Generate the page one more time with the same input, model, and viewport, but now with your file loaded. Shuffle it with the baseline and score both against your rubric without knowing which is which.

You do not need a runner or a model judge to start, a single trial can reveal the large, obvious failures. To measure reliability, run multiple independent first-attempt trials (Anthropic's guide to evals for agents) and report how often the result holds.

6. Encode the correction

Review the output alongside whatever follow-up prompts you have to send, and then ask:

  • What did the user have to repeat or steer manually?

  • Is a rule missing or unclear?

  • Can the stylesheet express the correction?

  • Is the failure mechanical enough to check in code?

  • Does the correction generalize beyond this output?

Update the guidance instead of hand-tuning the generated page. Your next comparison tells you whether first attempts actually improved.

Add tooling after the manual loop starts paying off:

  • Include scenarios where the guidance should and should not apply.

  • Keep a small holdout hidden while editing.

  • Record model and guidance versions.

  • Automate mechanical checks.

  • Use multiple blind reviewers.

However far you take the automation, keep final changes human-reviewed.

Then keep the loop running. Collect feedback on a cadence, and watch whether each kind of complaint actually becomes less common after you change the guidance. A passing evaluation matters less if people keep correcting the same mistake in production.

And if you want working examples, ours are public. We load design.md into tools like v0, Codex, and Claude every day to make artifacts that feel like Vercel, and the eve design agent template will get you a Slack design agent like the one we run.

title: i couldn't see what my agents were doing, so i built a neat standup service
description:
I use a mix of agents from different platforms. one codes, one designs, one does research, a few run on a schedule. Each platform tends to be siloed, gated, private - and rightly so - keeping its' history and state squarely inside its own app... so often I found find my morning routine to involve logging into Claude, Codex, Grokot, etc and starting off by asking them for status.

These siloed tools are a common part of a competitive software landscape. As new tools emerge on an almost weekly basis with new capabilities, the place where work was happening and the velocity around it kept shifting from one platform to another.

So i built fleeet, a little board where my agents leave a short note when they finish something. Every task runs through fleeet (via a skill - redacting, sanitizing and simplifying the update) and auto-posting it. In the morning I can review my board on fleeet.space, or directly ask Claude "what did my agents do yesterday?" and fetch the report via MCP-UI.

Like the best daily standups, it's kept intentionally light and skimmable.

How it works

it's deliberately small. there are four events:

  • session_start
  • heartbeat
  • blocked (a question plus 2–3 options, so i can unblock it in seconds)
  • session_end (shipped, handed off, abandoned, or failed)

Each event has a run id, agent name, a task title (≤ 50 chars) and a one-line summary (≤ 64 chars). the schema is public in the repo.

The fun puzzle was deciding when an agent should speak up. Post on real work, skip no-ops, don't heartbeat every few seconds, and every start gets an end. honestly, the hardest part wasn't the server. it was teaching agents to say one useful sentence.

Any agent, Any vendor

There are three ways in, all posting the same events:

  • A skill, which is instructions the agent follows
  • An MCP server at fleeet.space/mcp
  • A zero-dependency CLI. if the agent can run a command, it can post. if the post fails, the CLI spools events locally to ./.fleeet/events.jsonl

I'm running it with claude code, codex, cursor, chat bots and scheduled scripts. Agents can also read the board back through MCP, so you can ask one what the others did.

Privacy

The kit never reads your files, env vars or git history. The board only sees what the agent writes. On top of that, the skill tells agents not to post secrets, code or personal stuff, the CLI skips things that look personal, and the server strips keys, emails and code on the way in.

I'd rather an agent post nothing than post something it shouldn't.

What it isn't

It's not a SaaS product.
It's not an orchestrator. It doesn't start or steer agents.
It's not a transcript logger, and it's not tied to one vendor.
It's the standup, not the meeting recording.

Open source

The kit (skill, schema, CLI, MCP setup) is Apache-2.0: github.com/nan-labs/fleeet. The hosted board at fleeet.space is a separate service right now, but I'm moving the UI components over to a self-hostable version at nan-labs/fleeet-server so anyone can run their own if they want.

It's early and I'm the only maintainer, so issues and ideas are very welcome. Thanks for reading!

title: SailPoint IdentityIQ Rules Explained: Where BeanShell Fits
description:
If you are learning SailPoint IdentityIQ (IIQ), rules are where configuration ends and code begins. IIQ rules are small pieces of BeanShell (Java-like scripting) that run at specific points in IIQ's processing, so you can handle the cases that out-of-the-box configuration cannot.

What a rule is

A rule is a script stored as a Rule object in IIQ. IIQ calls it at a defined hook, such as while reading data from an application or before sending a change to a target system. The rule receives input variables from IIQ (for example the application, the account data or the identity) and returns a value or modifies an object.

Rule types you will meet early

  • Correlation rule: decides which identity an account belongs to when simple attribute matching is not enough.
  • Customization rule: adjusts account data as it is read during aggregation, for example cleaning up values.
  • Build Map rule: shapes raw rows from delimited-file or JDBC sources into account attributes.
  • Identity attribute rule: calculates an identity attribute from one or more sources.
  • Before and After Provisioning rules: change a provisioning plan before it is sent, or act after it completes.

Why BeanShell matters for jobs

Most real IIQ projects onboard applications that do not fit the defaults. Interviewers often ask you to explain a correlation rule or debug a failed aggregation, which means reading and writing BeanShell. You do not need to be a senior Java developer, but you do need to be comfortable with variables, conditions, loops and IIQ's objects.

Tips when you start writing rules

  • Keep each rule small and focused on one job.
  • Log what the rule receives and returns while testing.
  • Test against a small set of accounts before running a full aggregation.
  • Reuse logic through rule libraries instead of copying code.

Full guide with examples: SailPoint IIQ rules and BeanShell explained. If you want structured, hands-on practice, see the SailPoint IIQ course at IAM Careers.

title: A Mechanistic Study of Automated Failure Attribution in LLM-based Agentic Systems
description:
arXiv:2610.28811v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Agentic systems have demonstrated strong capabilities on complex tasks by enabling multiple interacting large language model (LLM)-based agents to collaborate and execute subtasks in parallel. However, this collaborative structure introduces new challenges for reliably evaluating and diagnosing system failures, particularly failure attribution: tracing a system's execution to identify the agent step responsible for an incorrect final outcome. Because manually performing this task is time- and labor-intensive, recent work has turned to LLMs as judges to automate the process, referred to as automated failure attribution (AFA). These approaches assume that a sufficiently capable model can infer the failing step directly from an interaction transcript. In practice, however, direct prompting often performs poorly, which motivates follow-up work that explores various ways to improve AFA performance, including alternative prompting strategies and inference-time interventions. In this paper, we examine a more fundamental question: whether this weak behavioral performance reflects a genuine capability limitation. Using linear probes applied to internal activations, we uncover a significant \emph{knows-but-won't-say gap:} models encode sufficient information to attribute a failure correctly but fail to explicitly output the responsible step. Building on this finding, we propose \emph{grafting}, a simple manual intervention that exploits knowledge already encoded in the model to improve AFA performance without requiring ground-truth labels at inference time. Extensive evaluations across multiple LLMs and benchmark settings demonstrate that grafting consistently outperforms direct-prompting approaches, underscoring the potential of leveraging latent model knowledge for more reliable failure attribution. Our code is available at https://github.com/wendyzheng22/mi4afa.

title: Beyond Binary Labels: Diagnostic Evaluation of LLM Safety with Prompt-Level Rubrics
description:
arXiv:2610.29225v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Current LLM safety benchmarks predominantly rely on binary safe or unsafe labels, lacking explanatory depth and suffering from low consistency across automated judges. To address this, we introduce DiagSafe, a diagnostic evaluation framework that moves beyond binary classification by employing prompt-level rubrics. Grounded in globally applicable AI safety policies, each rubric provides explicit criteria along two dimensions: safety, which targets concrete harms with specific exemptions to suppress false positives, and usefulness, which independently evaluates instruction fulfillment. To ensure a robust and realistic evaluation, we construct a bilingual (English-Chinese) benchmark grounded in a comprehensive 84-label safety taxonomy, consisting of two subsets: DiagBase, which covers single- and multi-turn prompts with direct harmful queries and template-based jailbreaks, and DiagAttack, which embeds harmful intents into complex instruction-following tasks to form challenging instruction attacks. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DiagSafe significantly enhances the reliability of LLM-as-a-judge evaluation, achieving 95.34% agreement with human annotations -- substantially higher than the 69%-87% achieved by the baselines -- and high inter-judge consistency (Cohen's $\kappa$ = 0.864). Furthermore, applying our framework reveals that leading LLMs differ markedly in their unsafe rates, and each model also exhibits unique vulnerabilities along different dimensions. In addition, we observe that models are particularly susceptible in Chinese and multi-turn contexts. Ultimately, DiagSafe provides a reliable and explainable tool for auditing and optimizing LLM alignment.

title: A General Topological Symmetry Index for Critical Orbits In Neural Network Loss Landscapes
description:
arXiv:2610.28864v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A systematic understanding of the global structure of neural-network loss landscapes remains challenging due to their high dimensionality. Symmetries arising from network architectures and learning objectives provide a way to investigate aspects of this structure. Although a growing number of studies have drawn attention to these symmetries, a systematic characterization of them, as well as of the critical orbits they give rise to, remains incomplete. To address this gap, in this work we establish a topological symmetry index, based on the methodologies from the family of equivariant degree theories, to decode these symmetries. The frameworks apply to arbitrary network architectures and include methods applicable to degenerate critical orbits. The index detects the isotropy of the critical points and quantifies the corresponding net topological contributions. Several examples, including softplus MLPs, Transformers, and equivariant neural networks, are presented to illustrate the computations.

title: The Clean Plate Problem: How Multi-Stage Builds and Distroless Images Cut Container Attack Surfaces to Zero
description:
A few weeks ago, I ran an audit on a backend microservice container running in our staging cluster.The application itself was a compiled Go binary that took up less than 20 MB of disk space. But when I ran docker images, the resulting image weighed in at nearly 1 GB.Even worse, when I attached an interactive terminal into that running container:Bashdocker exec -it payment-service /bin/bash
I found a full-blown Debian Linux environment sitting inside. Compilers, package managers (apt), network downloaders (curl, wget), and an active root shell were all sitting right next to our core application logic.If an attacker managed to find a remote code execution (RCE) bug in that service, I hadn’t just handed them an app bug—I had handed them an entire Linux workstation inside our VPC.Here is how modern container workflows solve this using two industry patterns: Multi-Stage Builds and Distroless Images.1. Multi-Stage Builds: The Restaurant Kitchen AnalogyThink about eating at a restaurant.In the kitchen, the chef uses heavy knives, cutting boards, vegetable peelers, mixing bowls, and blazing stoves. When the waiter brings your order to the dining table, you get a clean plate with the finished meal.You would never expect the waiter to dump the chopping board, raw vegetable peels, greasy pans, and meat scraps directly onto your table.Yet that is exactly what a single-stage Dockerfile does.+-----------------------------------------------------------+
| SINGLE STAGE (Messy Kitchen + Food Shipped Together) |
| Compilers + SDKs + Git + Headers + Source Code + Binary |
| Image Size: ~900 MB |
+-----------------------------------------------------------+
When building an application in Go, Rust, C++, Java, or even Node.js, you need heavy build tools: compilers, package managers, development headers, and build caches. But your production environment only needs the final compiled binary or transpiled assets.The Fix: Multi-Stage SeparationA multi-stage build uses multiple FROM instructions in a single Dockerfile. Each FROM starts a brand-new stage, letting you copy only the artifacts you want from earlier stages.Here is what that looks like in practice:Dockerfile# -------------------------------------------------------------

STAGE 1: "The Kitchen" (Builder stage with compilers and SDKs)

-------------------------------------------------------------

FROM golang:1.23-alpine AS builder

WORKDIR /build

Cache dependency downloads

COPY go.mod go.sum ./
RUN go mod download

Copy source and compile down to a standalone binary

COPY . .
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -o /build/payment-api .

-------------------------------------------------------------

STAGE 2: "The Dining Table" (Final production runtime)

-------------------------------------------------------------

FROM alpine:3.20

WORKDIR /app

Copy ONLY the compiled binary from Stage 1

COPY --from=builder /build/payment-api /app/payment-api

EXPOSE 8080
CMD ["/app/payment-api"]
The Difference:Single-Stage Image: ~900 MB (Go compiler, source code, build caches, git).Multi-Stage Image: ~15 MB (Tiny Alpine OS layer + compiled binary).Why It Matters:During high-traffic autoscaling events, Kubernetes doesn't have to pull 1 GB images across the network to spin up new pods. A 15 MB image pulls in less than a second, saving cloud bandwidth costs and speeding up recovery times.2. Distroless Images: Stripping Down to the ChassisDropping image size to 15 MB with Alpine is a huge step forward, but from a security perspective, Alpine still ships with an interactive shell (/bin/sh) and a package manager (apk).To understand why this is a risk, consider an analogy:A standard family car comes with air conditioning, leather seats, a radio, a trunk, and a glovebox. A Formula 1 race car strips out everything that doesn't make the car go fast: no back seat, no radio, no air conditioning, no trunk.A Distroless image (originally created by Google) takes that Formula 1 approach to containers. It contains only your application and its minimal runtime dependencies (like glibc or SSL root certificates).It explicitly omits:Package managers (apt, apk, yum)System utilities (curl, wget, ls, grep)Interactive shells (/bin/sh, /bin/bash)Standard Base (Ubuntu/Debian): [ Shell + Tools + Package Manager + App ]
Alpine Base: [ Shell + apk + Minimal OS + App ]
Distroless Base: [ App + Direct Runtime Libs ONLY ]
A Real-World Security ScenarioImagine a critical vulnerability (like an RCE or file-upload exploit) is discovered in a patient records microservice.Scenario A: The Container Runs on Standard UbuntuThe attacker exploits the application bug and executes an arbitrary command.They run curl or apt-get install nmap directly inside the container.They download an external botnet or reconnaissance script.They explore the local container filesystem using ls -la and read configs.They use the running container as a jump box to pivot into the rest of your private network.Scenario B: The Container Runs on DistrolessThe attacker exploits the bug and tries to invoke /bin/sh.The operating system responds:Plaintextexec: "/bin/sh": stat /bin/sh: no such file or directory
The attacker tries calling curl or wget to pull remote tools. Neither exists.The exploit fails because there is no execution environment inside the container to run unauthorized binaries.The Gold Standard: Multi-Stage + DistrolessIn production systems handling sensitive workloads, you can combine both techniques. You build in a full developer SDK environment, but ship on Google's static Distroless image:Dockerfile# Stage 1: Build the code in a full compiler environment
FROM golang:1.23 AS builder

WORKDIR /src
COPY . .
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -o /app/server .

Stage 2: Deploy to Google's Distroless static runtime

FROM gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12

Copy the binary from the builder stage

COPY --from=builder /app/server /server

Distroless provides a built-in non-root user (UID 65532: nonroot)

USER nonroot:nonroot

EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["/server"]
What You Get:Tiny footprint: Image sizes drop to the bare minimum required for execution.Non-root by default: Runs under user nonroot, neutralizing container escape techniques that rely on root privileges.No shell attacks: Traditional living-off-the-land techniques (using installed utilities like curl or bash) are impossible.Clean vulnerability scans: Tools like Trivy or Snyk show zero CVEs for unneeded OS packages, because those packages were never installed in the first place.Comparison SummaryConceptWhat It IsProblem It SolvesProduction ImpactMulti-Stage BuildA Dockerfile using multiple FROM stages to separate build tools from runtime artifacts.Bloated image sizes caused by compilers, test suites, and package caches.Cuts storage needs, saves cloud network transfer costs, and speeds up auto-scaling.Distroless ImageA base image containing only the app and direct dependencies—no shell, no package manager.Attackers using internal container shells and OS utilities to pivot into your private network.Eliminates package vulnerabilities and neutralizes shell-based exploit payloads.Wrapping UpBuilding clean containers isn't just about saving a few hundred megabytes of disk space. It fundamentally changes the threat model of your workloads in the cloud.If your production container doesn't need a compiler to run, don't ship one. And if it doesn't need an interactive shell to serve traffic, strip the shell out entirely.Keep the kitchen in the build stage, and bring only the clean plate to production.

title: The Suite Is Green Only Because the Agent Ran the Tests In One Fixed Order
description:
Last week an agent added a test for a new token-bucket helper and reported done: the whole suite ran green, including its own new case. When I ran that file by itself, the test failed immediately. It had passed in CI only because an earlier test in the same module populated a shared in-memory registry; the new case read that leftover state instead of creating its own fixture. CI always executes files in the same fixed glob order, so the green never tested independence.

The agent trusted the signal it could see: the runner returned success on every pass, and nothing in its loop asked it to open the file alone or shuffle the order. The failure was invisible precisely because the green came from cooperation, not isolation.

Why sequential green cannot prove independence

One process is shared across files. Most runners load the module graph once and execute files in sequence, so module-level state survives from one test to the next. A singleton cache, a global registry, or a fixed random seed set during import is still there when the next file runs.

A predecessor writes state, the new test reads it. Test A registers a record; test B asserts that record exists. B passes because A ran first, not because the helper behaves correctly against a fresh default.

Fixed glob order makes the dependency permanent. CI enumerates files the same way on every run, so A always precedes B. The hidden edge never surfaces in the ordinary sequential pass.

The agent never probes the gap. Its loop repeats the same command that returns green. Running the file alone or randomizing order is an extra step nobody scheduled, so the leak survives as a passing test.

What order pollution usually looks like

A module-level mutable singleton. An in-memory cache, connection pool, or global registry populated by an earlier test and read by a later one, instead of being constructed inside each setup.

Import-time fixed state. A random seed or clock frozen at import, or a shared fixture object imported as a constant rather than built per test.

A teardown that patches over the leak. A reset in afterEach that clears just enough for the next file to pass, which masks the dependency instead of removing it. The next shuffle still breaks.

New tests written against the warmed world. The agent observes a registry that already contains data from prior examples and asserts against that observed shape, rather than constructing an empty baseline first.

The cheap gate that catches it

Run the changed file in isolation first. Before accepting green, execute only the file the agent touched. If it fails alone, the case depends on a predecessor and is not coverage.

Then shuffle the full suite with fresh workers. Run the same suite with randomized order and a fresh process per file. Order-sensitive pollution breaks on a shuffle far more often than on a clean sequential pass.

Each test builds its own fixture inside setup. No import-time mutable global, no reading state a prior test left behind. A test that only passes after a specific predecessor is a leak, not coverage; make it independent rather than adding a compensating reset.

Re-run a few times rather than once. A single green sequential run proves little; a handful of shuffled, isolated passes give real confidence.

The same gap on a stateful endpoint

The blind spot appears without a test runner at all. An agent verifies an endpoint against staging that already carries leftover rows from a previous call, reports the response looks right, and misses that a clean tenant returns a different shape. The warmed instance masks the missing case the way fixed file order masks the failing test. The reliable check compares the live response against the contract on a clean baseline instead of a warmed-up instance. That local-first, source-of-truth loop is the one we built into Powerduck: a green or warmed response never counts as proof that the shipped surface matches the spec.

What I check before accepting a green suite

  1. Did the new test run alone, or only as part of the fixed-order suite?
  2. Does it build its own fixture inside setup, or read a module-level global?
  3. Has the suite been run with randomized order and fresh per-file workers?
  4. On a stateful API, was the check done on a clean baseline, or on warmed staging?

Green in one fixed order proves the files cooperate. It never proves each one stands alone, and that distinction is exactly what an isolated, shuffled pass exposes.

title: Keeping Vector Retrieval Stable While Your Knowledge Base Is Still Loading
description:
Keeping Vector Retrieval Stable While Your Knowledge Base Is Still Loading

At 3:17 AM, your agent platform stops responding. Ingestion workers are retrying document chunks. Retrieval latency has spiked from 80ms to 4 seconds. The HNSW index is fine. The problem is that ingestion and retrieval are fighting over the same PostgreSQL pages, and neither path has backpressure logic. This is the production failure that tutorials skip.

I am evaluating Tencent/WeKnora as an external integrator, using its stated document-to-RAG, agent, and self-maintaining Wiki scope. The design below is a proposed PostgreSQL retrieval boundary, not a claim about WeKnora's current implementation or measured performance.

Keep ingestion outside the answering path

Separate document parsing, chunking, and embedding into asynchronous workers. Those workers write versioned chunks into PostgreSQL. Retrieval reads only published document versions; generation receives retrieved text and provenance, never responsibility for repairing ingestion.

For agent memory, use the same boundary: proposed memories enter ingestion rather than becoming searchable immediately. Otherwise, an agent can retrieve its own unvalidated output and reinforce it.

My proposed generation benchmark topology places an optional relay at https://b-lost.com/v1, B-Lost's gateway endpoint. It remains outside embedding generation and database timing. Availability, authentication, and model compatibility must be verified before running that baseline; no relay measurements are claimed here.

That separation matters: changing an embedding model requires a new embedding space and reindexing, whereas changing a generation endpoint should not.

The failure that tutorials miss

Consider a production incident reconstruction, not a reported WeKnora outage: concurrent ingestion workers begin inserting into an already large HNSW index. Insert latency rises, workers retry, and retrieval tail latency follows.

HNSW updates can contend on internal index-page locks, but "the index is locked" is not a sufficient diagnosis. Correlate PostgreSQL wait events (pg_stat_activity.wait_event_type, wait_event) with ingestion concurrency, WAL volume, buffer pressure (shared_buffers exhaustion), and query plans. Storage saturation (IOPS ceiling, write queue depth) and unrelated transaction locks can produce similar symptoms. Check pg_stat_statements for insert durations and pg_locks for blocking queries.

The immediate response is bounded ingestion concurrency (semaphore or worker pool size), bounded batches (500-1000 rows per transaction, not 50,000), and exponential retry backoff with jitter, not more workers. For an initial bulk import, loading before building HNSW often reduces write amplification. An existing serving table needs a separately scheduled CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY to avoid blocking reads.

A second failure often appears as "bad vectors." With inner-product ranking, inconsistent embedding normalization lets vector magnitude distort relevance. With cosine distance, ordinary positive rescaling does not change ranking. Check model revisions (OpenAI text-embedding-3-small vs ada-002), truncation (padding vs truncating to 768 dimensions), zero vectors (NaN propagation from malformed input), and filters before blaming normalization. Validate that ingestion and retrieval use identical preprocessing.

One runnable retrieval boundary

This example requires Python 3, psycopg[binary], PostgreSQL, and pgvector 0.8 or newer. Save it as retrieve.py. Run python retrieve.py init once, then python retrieve.py query tenant-uuid embedding.json search words. The JSON file must contain a 768-number array from the same embedding model used during ingestion.

import json
import math
import os
import sys

import psycopg
from psycopg.rows import dict_row

DSN = os.environ["DATABASE_URL"]
SCHEMA = """
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector;
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS memory_chunk (
    id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    tenant_id uuid NOT NULL,
    content text NOT NULL,
    embedding vector(768) NOT NULL,
    search_document tsvector GENERATED ALWAYS AS
        (to_tsvector('english', content)) STORED
);
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS memory_tenant
    ON memory_chunk (tenant_id);
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS memory_embedding_hnsw
    ON memory_chunk USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops)
    WITH (m = 16, ef_construction = 128);
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS memory_search
    ON memory_chunk USING gin (search_document);
"""

def normalize(values):
    values = [float(x) for x in values]
    if len(values) != 768 or not all(map(math.isfinite, values)):
        raise ValueError("Expected 768 finite values")
    norm = math.sqrt(sum(x * x for x in values))
    if norm == 0:
        raise ValueError("Zero embedding")
    return [x / norm for x in values]

def rrf(rankings, k=60, limit=10):
    if k < 1:
        raise ValueError("k must be positive")
    scores, documents = {}, {}
    for ranking in rankings:
        seen = set()
        for rank, row in enumerate(ranking, start=1):
            key = row["id"]
            if key in seen:
                continue
            seen.add(key)
            documents[key] = row
            scores[key] = scores.get(key, 0.0) + 1.0 / (k + rank)
    ordered = sorted(scores, key=lambda key: (-scores[key], key))
    return [
        {**documents[key], "rrf_score": scores[key]}
        for key in ordered[:limit]
    ]

with psycopg.connect(DSN, row_factory=dict_row) as conn:
    if sys.argv[1] == "init":
        conn.execute(SCHEMA)
    else:
        tenant = sys.argv[2]
        with open(sys.argv[3]) as source:
            vector = json.dumps(normalize(json.load(source)))
        text = " ".join(sys.argv[4:])
        conn.execute("SET LOCAL hnsw.ef_search = 100")
        conn.execute("SET LOCAL hnsw.iterative_scan = strict_order")
        conn.execute("SET LOCAL hnsw.max_scan_tuples = 20000")
        dense = conn.execute("""
            SELECT id, content
            FROM memory_chunk
            WHERE tenant_id = %s::uuid
            ORDER BY embedding <=> %s::vector
            LIMIT 50
        """, (tenant, vector)).fetchall()
        lexical = conn.execute("""
            SELECT id, content
            FROM memory_chunk,
                 websearch_to_tsquery('english', %s) AS q
            WHERE tenant_id = %s::uuid AND search_document @@ q
            ORDER BY ts_rank_cd(search_document, q) DESC, id
            LIMIT 50
        """, (text, tenant)).fetchall()
        print(json.dumps(rrf([dense, lexical]), indent=2))

Apply the same validation and normalization during ingestion. Treat this schema as the retrieval kernel; document versions and publication state belong in the surrounding ingestion contract. Run initialization separately from serving traffic. Add connection pooling (pgbouncer in transaction mode, or application-level pools with pool_size=20, max_overflow=10) to prevent connection exhaustion under load.

Spend latency where recall needs it

Filtered approximate search is the central trade-off. HNSW may encounter many neighboring vectors belonging to other tenants before finding enough eligible rows. Iterative scanning (hnsw.iterative_scan = strict_order) helps, but its scan budget (hnsw.max_scan_tuples) is finite. For small tenant datasets (under 10,000 rows), an exact distance sort over tenant-filtered rows may be faster and more complete than approximate search with high filtering overhead.

RRF combines lexical and semantic ranks without pretending their raw scores share a scale. It rescues identifiers and exact phrases that embeddings sometimes miss, but cannot recover candidates absent from both lists. Test retrieval quality by measuring recall@10 against a labeled eval set, not by eyeballing results.

Finally, tenant predicates are not authorization. Derive tenant identity from authenticated context (JWT claims, session middleware) and enforce database isolation where appropriate (row-level security policies if tenants must share tables). Compare approximate results against exact tenant-filtered search while ingestion runs. That comparison distinguishes a fast query from a retrieval system an agent can trust.

What's the hardest choice you've made?

The question that keeps me up is this: when do you stop treating ingestion as best-effort background work and start throttling user-facing features to preserve database stability? I've seen teams add circuit breakers that pause document uploads when retrieval p99 crosses 500ms, and I've seen teams accept 2-second retrieval during bulk imports because agents can wait. Both choices are defensible. Both have failed under unexpected load.

What's your architecture? Have you hit the wall where approximate search stopped being approximate enough, or where exact search became too slow? What did you change, and what did you wish you'd known six months earlier?

title: How to launch an 8-GPU RTX PRO 6000 instance on EcoHash
description:
An eight-GPU instance in EcoHash's Atlanta region gives you a whole node: eight RTX PRO 6000 GPUs with 96 GB of VRAM each, 200 vCPUs, 1,352 GB of RAM, and up to 5,260 GiB of temporary local scratch space. You can start with an EcoHash container image or bring the stack you already use.

This walkthrough covers the choices that matter before you launch, how to connect afterward, and where to put files you need to keep. Open GPU Instances in the console to follow along. You will need an account with enough credit for the configuration you select.

Choose Atlanta and all eight GPUs

Click Launch Instance, give the instance a name, and select atl for Atlanta. Under GPUs per Instance, choose 8x.

The configuration summary now shows the whole node dedicated to this instance. The eight GPUs provide 768 GB of total VRAM, with 96 GB on each GPU. That is memory distributed across eight devices; your serving or training software must support using multiple GPUs to take advantage of it.

Selecting eight GPUs allocates the whole node. Check the resource summary for your chosen region.

Pick a container for the work you want to run

The EcoHash Images tab offers several starting points. Their names include the installed software versions, so check the dropdown rather than relying on a tag from an old tutorial.

Use the inference image for vLLM, Jupyter for notebooks, or a base image for your own stack.

  • GPU Inference: vLLM configured for the RTX PRO 6000. This is the starting point for serving an LLM. It is a large image, so the first launch on a node may spend several minutes downloading it.
  • GPU Base: a CUDA and PyTorch environment for installing your own software. Choose the CUDA version your workload needs.
  • CUDA Bare: a CUDA 13.0 image without a framework, for building your environment from a smaller starting point.
  • GPU Jupyter: JupyterLab and an ML environment for browser-based notebook work.

The optional Startup Command runs when the instance starts. Use it to launch your application or model server. If you leave it blank, the image's default command applies. Make sure that command keeps the container running.

Bringing your own image

Open Images under Registry and click Add Image. Enter a display name and the full image reference, including its tag. For example, registry.example.com/team/eval:v1.0 is the format; replace it with your real registry and image.

A public image needs only its reference. Private images also need credentials with pull access.

For a private registry, provide its username and a read/pull access token. The form displays guidance for the registry you enter. AWS ECR login tokens expire after 12 hours and cannot be saved for this workflow; use a public ECR repository or arrange for EcoHash's account to have pull access.

Before saving the image, check these requirements:

  • Architecture: build for linux/amd64. On an Apple Silicon Mac, include --platform linux/amd64 in your docker buildx build command.
  • CUDA: use CUDA 13.0 or earlier for the configuration described here.
  • GPU support: your framework and CUDA extensions must support Blackwell sm_120. Check the specific build you are using, especially if you compile extensions yourself.
  • SSH: EcoHash configures SSH automatically for Debian, Ubuntu, and Alpine-based images. Include OpenSSH yourself for other base distributions.

Save the image, return to the launch form, and select it under Custom / Registry.

Set up SSH and an HTTP endpoint

Enable SSH access and add your public SSH key in the launch form. Keys are applied when the instance starts, so do this before launching. Keep the matching private key on your own computer.

If you want to call a model server or another HTTP application, enable Expose a public service URL and enter the port your application listens on inside the container, such as 8000.

The endpoint forwards to the HTTP port inside your container.

Your application must listen on 0.0.0.0, not only on 127.0.0.1. A process bound to localhost can run normally inside the container while remaining unreachable through the public URL.

Choose the runtime and attach storage

Select No end time if you want the instance to run until you terminate it. The form explains the credit hold and hourly deductions. This setting does not keep an instance running after the account runs out of credit.

Alternatively, choose a fixed estimated duration if you want an automatic end time. Read the billing summary before launching; it changes with the number of GPUs and the duration you select.

Attach persistent storage before starting work you need to keep.

A cloud drive attaches to one instance at a time. A shared filesystem can be attached to several instances. Both are retained after the compute instance ends. Choose a cloud drive for files used by this instance, or a shared filesystem when several instances need the same datasets, weights, or results.

Treat /workspace as temporary. Its local scratch data is erased when the instance ends, including when it stops because your account balance runs out. Write results you need to keep to an attached cloud drive or shared filesystem.

Review the GPU count, image, SSH keys, service port, duration, and storage attachments. Then click Launch. Allow extra time for the first download of a large container image.

Connect and check your application

Once the instance is running, its detail page shows the SSH command, the public URL if you enabled one, and a web terminal you can open in the browser. Copy the SSH command from that page rather than constructing the hostname or port yourself.

In the terminal, run:

nvidia-smi

For this configuration, the output should list eight RTX PRO 6000 GPUs. Check that your application can see all eight before starting a long job.

The public URL requires your console login or an EcoHash API key. To call it from a script, send the key in an Authorization: Bearer header. Paths after /service pass through to your application: /service/v1/models reaches the container as /v1/models.

For a vLLM server exposing that route, copy the instance's public URL and test it with:

export ECOHASH_SERVICE_URL="https://api.ecohash.com/gpu-instances/INSTANCE_ID/service"
# Set ECOHASH_API_KEY in your environment before running this request.
curl --fail-with-body "${ECOHASH_SERVICE_URL%/}/v1/models" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer ${ECOHASH_API_KEY}"

Replace INSTANCE_ID with your instance ID, or use the full URL copied from the console. A ready vLLM server should return a model list. For another application, use one of its own HTTP routes instead.

If the request fails, check that the application has finished starting, listens on 0.0.0.0, and uses the same port you entered in the console. Also confirm that your request includes a valid API key.

Before ending the session, confirm that your outputs are on persistent storage. Terminate the instance when you are finished to stop compute charges.

Open GPU Instances to configure a node, or read more about launching an instance and container images.

title: MemDev-Bench: Does Memory Help Code Agents?Benchmarking Memory Systems over Real Repository Histories
description:
arXiv:2610.27524v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Code agents increasingly work on evolving real repositories, and memory systems aim to help them reuse earlier experience. However, such experience is diverse and evolving, so it remains unclear how memory systems organize it and thereby affect code agents. Existing benchmarks cannot answer this reliably because they lack either temporally valid histories or control over prior-task relevance. In this paper, we present MemDev-Bench to evaluate how memory systems affect code agents over diverse repository histories. It pairs each task with relevance-annotated earlier tasks from the same repository to build histories with controlled relevance. We also build an automated pipeline that reliably makes these earlier tasks executable and verifiable, producing 4,869 historical tasks for 555 base tasks. Based on MemDev-Bench, our systematic evaluation of memory systems across diverse development scenarios yields three main findings. (1) Memory mainly improves fine-grained localization and editing, increasing functional correctness. (2) Memory also causes failures on otherwise solvable tasks even with related history, and unrelated history tends to increase such failures. These failures mainly stem from agents reusing memory without reassessing its applicability. (3) Compared with using memory systems, directly providing agents with raw historical trajectories substantially reduces their steps. Further analysis suggests that agents save these steps by reusing process information that compressed memories tend to omit. These results suggest that future memory systems should preserve process information and reassess memory applicability against current task context.

title: Pair-Free Coarse-to-Real Video Generation via Real-to-Coarse Image Supervision
description:
arXiv:2610.28954v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Coarse-to-real (C2R) video generation converts coarse animation, simulation, or game-rendered videos into photorealistic videos while preserving scene layout, camera motion, and dynamics. Training such models requires aligned (coarse, realistic) video pairs, which are expensive to create and confine prior systems to narrow synthetic domains. We exploit a simple asymmetry: paired videos are hard to obtain, but paired real-to-coarse images are easy to construct with existing editing and 3D reconstruction tools. Using these image pairs, we train the DINO-R2C model to transfer realistic images to coarse images in DINO feature space, and apply it frame-wise to ordinary real videos to synthesize pseudo-coarse videos. The C2R# model then learns to generate each real video from its pseudo-coarse counterpart, free from needing (coarse, realistic) video pairs. At inference, the DINO-R2C model is discarded and actual coarse videos drive the C2R# model directly. Thus, our pair-free training scales with any real-video corpora rather than with paired synthetic videos. We will release the model and project webpage at https://gonzalognogales.github.io/coarse2real-sharp/.

title: Query Feedback and Teaching for Stable and Certifiable Language Generation
description:
arXiv:2610.28918v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Language generation in the limit studies whether a learner observing an enumeration of an unknown target language can eventually generate only valid, previously unseen elements. We study stability, introduced by Kalavasis, Mehrotra, and Velegkas (2025), which requires the generator's infinite output set to eventually remain unchanged, and introduce the stronger notion of certifiability, which requires the generator to determine from its observations that its current output is valid. Drawing on teaching sets in learning theory, we introduce a hierarchy of teaching dimensions for generation under three increasingly strict success criteria: correctness, stability, and certifiability. These dimensions measure the minimum number of selected examples whose appearance guarantees the corresponding success condition. We also study stability and certifiability in the membership-query model of Charikar and Pabbaraju (2025). We characterize stable and certifiable generation, both with and without query feedback, and establish their relationships with uniform generation and identification in the limit. In particular, we give a finite-witness characterization of stable generation, analogous to Angluin's tell-tale characterization of identification, resolving a gap left open by Kalavasis, Mehrotra, and Velegkas (2025). We further compare these generation notions with identification in the limit and contrast their teaching requirements on well-studied language families, including regular and erasing pattern languages.

title: Building SEO Into a Website From Day One: A Practical Checklist for Developers and Designers
description:
Most SEO problems are not content problems. They are build problems: sites shipped with duplicated titles, JavaScript-rendered headings, five-megabyte hero images, and a robots.txt someone copied from a tutorial in 2016. Retrofitting SEO onto a finished site costs far more than building it in from the start. This checklist covers the technical foundations that developers and designers can bake into every project from day one.

1. Start With Semantic HTML

Semantic markup tells search engines — and assistive technology — what each part of a page means. Use one <h1> per page, keep heading levels in order, and reach for <header>, <nav>, <main>, <article>, and <footer> instead of a soup of <div> elements.

<main>
  <article>
    <h1>Custom Website Design for Small Businesses</h1>
    <section>
      <h2>Our Design Process</h2>
      <p>...</p>
    </section>
  </article>
</main>

A crawler reading this structure understands the page hierarchy instantly. A page built from nested divs with styled spans forces it to guess.

2. Meta Tags and Open Graph, Every Time

Every indexable page needs a unique <title> and meta description, plus Open Graph tags so shared links look intentional on social platforms:

<title>Local SEO Services in Karachi | Bright Studio</title>
<meta name="description" content="We help Karachi businesses rank in Google Maps and local search. See our process and results." />
<meta property="og:title" content="Local SEO Services in Karachi" />
<meta property="og:description" content="Rank higher in Maps and local search." />
<meta property="og:image" content="https://example.com/og-cover.jpg" />
<link rel="canonical" href="https://example.com/local-seo/" />

If your stack generates pages from templates or a CMS, build these fields into the template with sensible fallbacks — never ship a site where twelve pages share one title.

3. Set a Performance Budget and Enforce It

Core Web Vitals are a ranking input, and they are decided during the build, not after. Agree on a budget before writing code: for example, Largest Contentful Paint under 2.5 seconds on a mid-range phone, total page weight under 1.5 MB, and JavaScript kept as lean as the design allows. Then measure during development with Lighthouse, not the night before launch. The usual budget-killers are unoptimized images, too many web fonts, and third-party scripts added "just in case."

4. Add Structured Data Where It Earns Its Place

JSON-LD structured data helps search engines understand entities and can unlock rich results. Add the types that match the site: Organization or LocalBusiness sitewide, Article for posts, FAQPage where real FAQs exist, and BreadcrumbList on deeper pages.

<script type="application/ld+json">
{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "LocalBusiness",
  "name": "Bright Studio",
  "url": "https://example.com/",
  "telephone": "+92-300-0000000",
  "address": { "@type": "PostalAddress", "addressLocality": "Karachi", "addressCountry": "PK" }
}
</script>

Validate every template with Google's Rich Results Test before launch — a syntax error silently discards the whole block.

5. Get robots.txt and the Sitemap Right

Your robots.txt should guide crawlers, not block your own assets by accident:

User-agent: *
Allow: /
Disallow: /wp-admin/
Sitemap: https://example.com/sitemap.xml

Generate the XML sitemap automatically from your CMS or build pipeline so it updates when pages change, include only canonical, indexable URLs, and submit it in Google Search Console on launch day.

6. Plan Internal Linking in the Architecture

Internal links distribute authority and tell crawlers which pages matter. Design them into the site structure: service pages linked from the homepage and navigation, related articles linked from each post, and descriptive anchor text instead of "click here." A simple rule that works: every important page should be reachable within three clicks of the homepage, and no page should be an orphan with zero internal links pointing to it.

7. Treat Images as a Performance and SEO Asset

Compress images before upload, serve modern formats (WebP or AVIF), and always set explicit width and height attributes to prevent layout shift. Use responsive sizes so phones do not download desktop assets:

<img src="office-800.webp"
     srcset="office-480.webp 480w, office-800.webp 800w, office-1200.webp 1200w"
     sizes="(max-width: 600px) 480px, 800px"
     width="800" height="533"
     alt="Design team reviewing website mockups in the Karachi office"
     loading="lazy" />

Write alt text that describes the image for someone who cannot see it — that is its purpose — and let filenames be descriptive too (team-meeting.webp, not IMG_4021.webp).

Launch-Day Final Checks

Before handing over the site: crawl it with a free tool to catch broken links and duplicate titles, confirm the staging site's noindex or password protection is removed, test the contact forms, and verify analytics and Search Console are connected. Fifteen minutes of checks prevents the classic disaster of a beautiful new site that Google cannot see.

None of this requires an SEO specialist in the room — it requires treating search as a build requirement, the same way you treat responsive design. Teams that build this way, including the web team at MSJ Digital (https://msjdigital.agency/custom-website-design/), find that SEO stops being a rescue job and becomes a launch feature.

Written by MSJ Digital — a digital agency in Pakistan building fast, search-ready websites for growing businesses.

title: Cara Mahasiswa Dapat $100 Kredit Azure Gratis (Tanpa Kartu Kredit!)
description:
