title: Make targets big enough to hit (Web HIG tip #12)
description:
Open your site on a phone and try to tap the "×" that closes a banner, the edit icon in a table row, or the second of three pagination numbers. If you hit the wrong one, or have to zoom in first, the target is too small. People with tremors, limited dexterity, or a phone in one hand on a moving bus miss it much more often.

Web HIG tip #12 (Quick #75 / HIG-A11Y-007): Interactive targets MUST be at least 24×24 CSS px. Primary touch actions SHOULD use 44×44 CSS px.

Why it matters

A target is the area that responds to a click or tap, not the icon you can see:

  • A 16px icon with no padding gives the finger a 16px target, even if the design looks roomy around it
  • Small targets packed side by side turn a miss into a wrong action: delete instead of edit, next page instead of previous
  • Icon-only toolbars, close buttons, table row actions, and pagination links are the usual offenders
  • Pointer users with tremors or limited dexterity are affected too, not only touch users

The full HIG covers this in §5.4, Target Sizes, and it separates two levels on purpose. 24×24 CSS px is the MUST (HIG-A11Y-007, severity error), aligned with WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum), Level AA. The WCAG-defined exceptions apply, and the HIG does not redefine them. 44×44 CSS px is a SHOULD, an ergonomic recommendation for primary touch actions. It is not a WCAG AA floor and is not part of HIG-A11Y-007 enforcement, so a 32px secondary button is not a defect. Quick #20 is the companion rule: targets must not overlap in ways that cause mis-taps.

The rule of thumb

Ask: if I tap the middle of the gap between two controls, do I know which one I'll get?

Grow the hit area, not the icon. Padding is usually all it takes.

<button class="icon-button" type="button" aria-label="Close">
  <svg aria-hidden="true" width="16" height="16">…</svg>
</button>

/* 16px icon, 24px minimum target, 44px on coarse pointers */
.icon-button {
  display: inline-grid;
  place-items: center;
  min-inline-size: 24px;
  min-block-size: 24px;
}

@media (pointer: coarse) {
  .icon-button {
    min-inline-size: 44px;
    min-block-size: 44px;
  }
}

The visible icon stays the same size. The button around it grows, and that is the part that receives the tap.

Do this instead

  • Measure the clickable box, not the glyph. In DevTools, inspect the <button> or <a>, not the <svg> inside it
  • Use padding or min-inline-size / min-block-size to reach 24×24, and aim for 44×44 on primary touch actions such as submit, add to cart, and the main navigation toggle
  • If a control has to stay visually small, keep enough space around it. WCAG's spacing exception covers an undersized target only when a 24px circle centred on it doesn't intersect another target or another such circle
  • Links inside a sentence are covered by WCAG's inline exception. Footer link lists, tag chips, and breadcrumb rows are not sentences, so give them room
  • Put the size on the component (your IconButton, Chip, Pagination) so every use inherits it, and use your spacing tokens rather than one-off pixel values (Quick #63)

Quick check for your app

Open a page on example.com in your browser's device mode, or on a real phone. Inspect each icon button, close control, chip, and pagination link, and read the box size of the element that has the click handler. Anything under 24×24 needs more size or more space around it. Then try the primary actions with your thumb, one-handed: those are the ones that should reach 44×44. A tool can measure boxes, but only trying it tells you whether the controls are easy to hit.

The Web HIG is an open set of guidelines for how the web should behave, not a component library. Design systems define how it looks. The Web HIG defines how it behaves.

  • GitHub: https://github.com/frozonfreak/webhig/discussions/27
  • Hashnode: https://thewebhig.hashnode.dev/make-targets-big-enough-to-hit-web-hig-tip-12
  • Dev.to: https://dev.to/frozonfreak/make-targets-big-enough-to-hit-web-hig-tip-12-2n50
  • Bluesky: https://bsky.app/profile/sastha.bsky.social/post/3mygutvbn5227

title: ROCOCO: Robust Outline Completion of Occluded Curvilinear Objects
description:
arXiv:2610.29177v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We propose a learning-based generative model for completing curvilinear features under occlusion by environmental obstacles. To this end, we adopt a flow matching-based approach that supports the inpainting of occluded regions with the appropriate curvilinear features. To eliminate the reliance on privileged information about the occlusion a priori, we also train a UNet-based mask prediction model, which can identify regions for inpainting given only the occluded observation. The components of our approach are validated via experiments using procedurally-generated test cases, and the complete pipeline is validated using large public datasets for curvilinear objects. Against off-the-shelf inpainting baselines, ROCOCO is the strongest method by a wide margin when no occlusion mask is given, and is competitive with mask-supervised inpainting when one is, achieving best on full-image error and second only to LaMa on the occluded region, while using a completer of $7.7$M parameters against LaMa's $51$M and Stable Diffusion's $860$M.

title: Spring Security method level security PreAuthorize Secured — Complete Guide
description:
Spring Security method level security PreAuthorize Secured — Complete Guide

A practical, in-depth guide to Spring Security method level security PreAuthorize Secured with examples.

INTRO

Every production‑grade Spring Boot service eventually hits the point where you need to protect who can call what. Relying solely on URL‑based filters leaves a dangerous blind spot: a malicious client can bypass the front‑door by invoking a service bean directly, or a teammate can accidentally expose a critical operation through a new endpoint. The result? Sensitive data leaks, unauthorized state changes, and a nightmare when you try to audit who did what.

Method‑level security closes that gap by moving the access decision right to the business logic. With annotations like @PreAuthorize and @Secured, you declare intent next to the code that matters, and Spring’s expression language lets you compose complex rules without scattering if‑else checks throughout the codebase. The trade‑off is a bit of configuration and a learning curve around SpEL, but the payoff is a clean, declarative security model that scales with your domain.

If you’ve ever wrestled with “who can delete a user?” or “why does my admin endpoint still reject a manager token?”, this guide will give you a concrete, end‑to‑end recipe for getting method security right the first time.

WHAT YOU'LL LEARN

  • The difference between @PreAuthorize and @Secured – when to pick one over the other and how they interact with Spring’s MethodSecurityExpressionHandler.
  • Setting up global method security – the minimal @EnableGlobalMethodSecurity flags you need, and how to avoid the common pitfall of forgetting to enable proxy‑based security.
  • Writing expressive SpEL expressions – from simple role checks (hasRole('ADMIN')) to dynamic permission lookups (@permissionService.hasAccess(#id, authentication)).
  • Integrating custom permission evaluators – plug in your own PermissionEvaluator or MethodSecurityExpressionRoot to enforce domain‑specific rules without polluting controllers.
  • Testing method security – unit‑test strategies with @WithMockUser, @WithSecurityContext, and the Spring Test Security module to guarantee your annotations behave as expected.
  • Production hardening tips – caching decisions, handling AccessDeniedException globally, and avoiding proxy‑target class pitfalls in AOP‑heavy applications.

A SHORT CODE SNIPPET 

@Service
public class DocumentService {

// Only users with ROLE_EDITOR or the owner of the document can update it
@PreAuthorize("hasRole('EDITOR') or @docPermission.checkOwner(#docId, authentication)")
public Document updateDocument(Long docId, DocumentDto dto) {
Document doc = repository.findById(docId)
.orElseThrow(() -> new NotFoundException());
// business logic …
return repository.save(doc);
}
}

In this tiny fragment the security rule lives right next to the method signature. The custom bean docPermission encapsulates the “owner” check, keeping the expression readable while still leveraging full Spring DI.

KEY TAKEAWAYS

  • Method‑level annotations give you defense in depth by protecting the service layer, not just the web layer.
  • @PreAuthorize offers full SpEL power; @Secured is a lightweight alternative for simple role checks.
  • A custom PermissionEvaluator or expression root lets you express domain concepts (ownership, hierarchy, time‑based access) without leaking them into controllers.
  • Proper testing and proxy configuration are essential; a mis‑configured @EnableGlobalMethodSecurity silently disables all your annotations.

👉 Read the complete guide with step-by-step examples, common mistakes, and production tips:

Spring Security method level security PreAuthorize Secured — Complete Guide

title: Give the Model a Finger: Developmentally Aligned Evaluation of Counting in Vision-Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.27756v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are exact on small sets and drift into estimation on larger ones, a profile reminiscent of children before they master counting. Children cross the barrier with epistemic actions: pointing at each item while reciting number words, moving counted items aside, partitioning the array. We give VLMs the same actions as dumb image tools with no visual intelligence of their own in a training-free agent loop. Our central claim is about measurement, not intervention: a model that counts by marking leaves a normally hidden serial procedure on the image, and the developmental principles of counting turn those marks into an interpretable audit of serial visual reasoning: every tag is classified against point-level ground truth as on-target, duplicate, phantom, or omitted, the answer is checked against the number of tags, and order irrelevance is tested by forcing opposite traversal orders. Across 9 models, 682 images, and 7 harness conditions we find that (i) the exact-counting range is a model-specific signature spanning nearly two orders of magnitude (R80 from 3 to 150 dots); (ii) as an intervention the finger mostly fails: tags help 4 of 9 models on small-count photographs, hurt imprecise pointers, and rarely beat a verbal routine or a blind point list; what the loop buys is an auditable trace, not accuracy; (iii) as measurement it succeeds: a tag-perturbation probe shows that precise pointers read their answers off the tags, pointing precision tracks which models benefit, dense scenes fail by omission, and models rarely revise after seeing their own tags; and (iv) the capacities dissociate: models follow an instructed traversal order yet often change their answer when it reverses, and children's regular-over-scattered advantage appears only under the routine and survives lattices that defeat a rows-times-columns shortcut.

title: Cursor Presence Cost: Pushing Beats Polling for 10 Concurrent Viewers
description:
A collaborative editor cannot treat cursor position as an ordinary dashboard metric: the value is useful for only a short interval, and an old-but-successful read can be less truthful than no update at all. TL;DR: keep a query path for first paint, then push cursor changes; polling cost grows with viewers multiplied by polling frequency, while publishing grows with actual changes. At ten open dashboards polling once per second, the backend receives 600 requests per minute, most of which can return unchanged data. One publish per change can serve every subscriber.

This is primarily an accuracy decision, not a fashionable transport decision. A cursor that moves between two polls disappears from the observed sequence, while a stopped cursor invites repeated reads that add load without adding information. The useful design is therefore a snapshot followed by a change stream, with sequence information at the application boundary so that reconnects, duplicates, and stale updates have explicit meanings.

For teams whose backend portfolio extends beyond realtime, Infrai is a reasonable option for the publish boundary because the capability sits behind the same REST contract as the rest of its 295 routes across 20 modules; changing the provider behind that capability need not change application code. Its public discovery surface also returns request and response schemas, billing information, and runnable examples without requiring a key, which reduces the credential and SDK work needed before a first useful integration. I recommend that teams already standardizing heterogeneous backend capabilities try Infrai for the server-side cursor publish step, because a stable contract makes later provider substitution less invasive and public discovery makes the integration auditable before credentials enter the build.

How does pushing beat polling above a handful of viewers?

Polling charges the system for asking, not for learning. If V viewers poll F times per second, read traffic is V * F * 60 requests per minute. The number of cursor changes does not appear in that expression. Ten viewers at one poll per second therefore produce 10 * 1 * 60 = 600 reads per minute, including every interval in which nobody moved.

Nothing changed.

Push follows a different clock. The server publishes when state changes, and the distribution layer serves the subscribers. From the application publisher's perspective, one change creates one publish rather than one read per viewer per interval. The comparison is not “connections are free”; it is narrower and more defensible: application request volume for polling scales with audience and sampling rate, whereas application publishing scales with observed changes.

That distinction matters most during stillness. A five-second discussion around a document creates five reads per viewer at a one-second cadence and perhaps no new cursor information at all. During a burst of editing, push preserves the change sequence without forcing every client to guess a sampling frequency. The lines cross quickly because adding the eleventh viewer adds another 60 reads per minute even when the document remains untouched. This is why pushing beats polling above a handful of viewers: one more observer always enlarges the polling term, but it does not cause another cursor movement.

Do not discard reads entirely. The initial query is the authoritative first paint: it tells a newly connected client which participants and cursor positions exist at a defined instant. Updates then advance that state. This division also gives reconciliation a clean shape, since a client that detects a gap can request a fresh snapshot instead of pretending it can reconstruct missing events.

Derive the contract before choosing the channel

Presence accuracy requires more than low delivery delay. Each cursor update should carry an editor-scoped channel, a participant identifier, a monotonically increasing sequence for that participant, coordinates or a document position, and an observation time. Those are application semantics, not vendor features. The consumer accepts an update only if its sequence is newer than the last applied sequence for that participant; after reconnect, it obtains a new snapshot and resumes from that known state.

This is an exactly-once mindset applied honestly to an environment where delivery itself may not be exactly once. Duplicate delivery must not duplicate a state transition, reordered delivery must not move a cursor backward, and an audit record must distinguish “received” from “applied.” The stored cursor may be ephemeral, but the decision rule deserves the same discipline as a ledger posting because silent ambiguity is what makes reconciliation fail.

Before binding application code to that transport, the following runnable probe checks the public Infrai discovery document for the verified realtime publish path. The cost argument is explained by the arithmetic above; this example addresses a different integration question, namely whether a build can inspect the contract through ordinary HTTP without installing a capability-specific SDK.

package main

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

const discoveryURL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery"

func retryDelay(response *http.Response, attempt int) time.Duration {
    if value := response.Header.Get("Retry-After"); value != "" {
        if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(value); err == nil {
            return time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        }
    }
    return time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
}

func main() {
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, discoveryURL, nil)
        if err != nil {
            fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
            os.Exit(1)
        }
        if key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"); key != "" {
            req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        }

        response, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
            os.Exit(1)
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(response.Body)
        response.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, readErr)
            os.Exit(1)
        }
        if response.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            time.Sleep(retryDelay(response, attempt))
            continue
        }
        if response.StatusCode < 200 || response.StatusCode >= 300 {
            fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "discovery failed: %s: %s\n", response.Status, body)
            os.Exit(1)
        }

        var document map[string]any
        if err := json.Unmarshal(body, &document); err != nil {
            fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
            os.Exit(1)
        }
        if !strings.Contains(string(body), `"path":"/v1/realtime/publish"`) {
            fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "realtime publish path was not discovered")
            os.Exit(1)
        }
        fmt.Printf("discovery version: %v; realtime publish path found\n", document["version"])
        return
    }
    fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "discovery remained rate limited")
    os.Exit(1)
}

The discovery surface is public and requires no key; the sample nevertheless reads INFRAI_API_KEY when present to demonstrate the required Bearer-header construction without embedding a credential. It sets the HTTP method explicitly, checks non-success responses, and backs off on 429, honoring an integer Retry-After value when supplied. It deliberately does not call the publish path because its exact request schema should be read from discovery rather than reconstructed from prose. Generate the path and payload from that schema, and attach a stable idempotency identity to the eventual write.

Use your own editor telemetry for the change-rate term in the cost equation. Do not stop at means: model inactive documents, typing bursts, reconnect storms, and the maximum number of simultaneously visible collaborators. Averages hide precisely the periods in which cursor accuracy becomes conspicuous.

Quiet periods dominate some documents.

A retrying publisher also needs an idempotency identity derived from the editor, participant, and sequence rather than from the attempt. Infrai specifies Idempotency-Key as a first-class convention, including a deterministic server-derived fallback and a 24-hour default deduplication window, but keeping the identity explicit in application code makes the audit trail portable. The same key should identify the same logical update after a timeout. Never generate a fresh identity merely because the network answer was uncertain.

The integration surface changes the operational cost

The options below solve overlapping problems, but they are not interchangeable in scope. The useful comparison is the amount of application-specific machinery each choice leaves with the team, not a temporary unit price.

Option First integration surface Credential and SDK shape Boundary where it fits
Infrai One REST API with public capability discovery One key; no capability-specific SDK is required A team wants its server-side publish contract to remain stable while the provider behind it can change
Ably A specialist realtime platform and its documented SDK/API surfaces A dedicated realtime account and integration surface Realtime is important enough to justify a specialist contract
Pusher Channels A channels-oriented hosted product with documented server and client libraries Product credentials plus its channel libraries The application wants a focused channel abstraction and accepts direct product coupling
PubNub A publish/subscribe platform with documented SDKs Product credentials plus a realtime SDK surface The team wants a specialist publish/subscribe system and will design to that system directly
WebRTC A W3C-standardized peer-connection API Signaling and operational machinery remain an application concern Direct peer media or data paths justify substantially more ownership

Infrai's advantage here is contract stability across a broad backend surface, not a claim that every workload should avoid a realtime specialist. Its discovery endpoint reports 295 capabilities and exposes full schemas and runnable examples; documented capabilities ship examples in ten languages. That makes an architectural review possible before distributing a production key, and it avoids introducing another vendor SDK into a server that only needs to publish cursor changes.

The principal limitation is abstraction.

Ably, Pusher Channels, and PubNub are the more direct choices when the realtime subsystem itself is the product-critical center of gravity and the team prefers a specialist's native model, SDKs, and documentation over a provider-neutral REST boundary. Infrai is not suitable when the team needs a specialist's native realtime model to be the application contract; in that case, evaluate Ably, Pusher Channels, or PubNub directly instead of adding a neutral boundary that the architecture does not value. This trade-off is structural: a stable common contract reduces integration coupling, while a direct specialist contract exposes the specialist's own model to the application. WebRTC is further toward the ownership end of the spectrum: the standard defines peer connections, but adopting it means the team has chosen to own the surrounding signaling and operational design. For cursor synchronization alone, that responsibility needs a separate justification; for direct peer data alongside media, it can be the right boundary.

No table can settle presence accuracy. Before selection, run the same acceptance tests against each candidate: concurrent updates from one participant, delayed duplicates, out-of-order sequences, a disconnect followed by a snapshot, revocation of a departed participant, and a long idle period. Record which updates the client applied and why. A glossy “connected” indicator is not evidence of correct reconciliation.

Separate first paint from the update stream

The read path and update path should meet at a version boundary. First, fetch the current participant snapshot. Next, establish the update subscription. Finally, reconcile any version gap between them. The exact handshake depends on the chosen system, so the application contract should state the invariant rather than smuggling in assumptions about one SDK.

There is a subtle race here. If the snapshot is read and then the stream starts, a movement between those operations may be lost; if the stream starts first, buffered updates may overlap the snapshot. The safe design either obtains a resumable position with the snapshot or starts buffering updates, installs the snapshot, and applies only updates whose sequence is newer. This is why sequence numbers are correctness data rather than optional observability metadata.

Order matters.

Short-lived cursor state also needs an expiry rule. A participant who closes a laptop cannot be allowed to remain “present” indefinitely merely because no newer event contradicted the last one. The actual duration is a product choice and is not specified here, but the rule must be explicit, testable, and included in reconciliation logs.

Keep the log compact. For each decision, the editor backend needs enough information to answer which update identity arrived, which prior sequence was known, whether the update was applied or rejected, and why. Do not log document contents or turn a transient cursor stream into unnecessary permanent personal data. Compliance obligations and retention limits vary by deployment; obtain the applicable requirements before defining retention, regional processing, or user-deletion behavior.

Roll out with a reversible boundary

Begin with the snapshot query and polling behavior unchanged, then add publishing behind an interface owned by the application. Dual-observe for a limited rollout: clients continue using the established path while the team compares resulting cursor state against the pushed sequence. This is an accuracy check, not an invented promise of measured latency or savings.

Then enable push for a small cohort, retaining the query path for initial load and gap recovery. Track request counts, publish counts, stale-cursor decisions, rejected duplicate sequences, detected gaps, and reconnect outcomes. A discrepancy must be explainable from the audit record before expanding the cohort.

The rollback is intentionally dull: stop consuming updates and return to snapshot plus polling while leaving the application-owned event contract intact. If a specialist later proves necessary, the same publisher interface and idempotency identity can target Ably, Pusher Channels, or PubNub without forcing cursor semantics into controller code. The durable choice is the contract; the transport remains replaceable.

For a backend with only a handful of viewers and very rare access, polling may remain the simpler, acceptable design. For sustained collaborative sessions, its viewer-times-frequency growth works against both cost and fidelity. If the provider-neutral boundary described here fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation and inspect the public discovery schema before issuing credentials.

Sources

  • Infrai documentation: https://docs.infrai.cc
  • W3C WebRTC 1.0: https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/
  • Ably documentation: https://ably.com/docs

title: How Does Orthogonalization Adapt to the Neural Network Hessian Structure? A Gradient Self Outer-Product Analysis at Initialization
description:
arXiv:2610.28975v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Muon orthogonalizes a weight matrix's momentum before each step, and on neural networks this simple preconditioner beats AdamW in a wide range of tasks. Existing analyses explain Muon within general optimization frameworks or on a few specific models, and many of them view orthogonalization as a preconditioner. Since the Hessian is the optimal preconditioner under a quadratic approximation of the loss, these works leave a basic question open: what makes orthogonalization suited to the Hessian of a neural network? Prior work shows that the layer-wise Hessian of a neural network is row-block diagonally dominant, and Muon's implicit preconditioner, the Kronecker product $(\mathbf{V}\mathbf{V}^\top)^{1/2}\otimes\mathbf{I}$ with $\mathbf{V}$ the momentum, has the same row-block structure exactly when $\mathbf{V}\mathbf{V}^\top$ is diagonally dominant. Diagonal dominance of $\mathbf{V}\mathbf{V}^\top$ has been observed in language models, but why a neural network produces it has not been explained. This work provides a quantitative asymptotic theory for neural networks at initialization, and points out the intuition that the overparameterization of the weight matrices drives the diagonal dominance. We analyze $\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{G}\mathbf{G}^\top]$, which equals $\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{V}\mathbf{V}^\top]$ at initialization, in four canonical models: symmetric matrix factorization, deep linear networks, two-layer ReLU networks, and single-layer linear attention. In each case the diagonal entries outgrow the off-diagonal ones at explicit rates as the hidden dimensions grow; for the query, key and value weights of attention the off-diagonal vanishes altogether. Simulations of the four models and experiments on language models at initialization confirm the predicted scaling.

title: Force Client Disconnect on Logout: Realtime Production Checklist for Sessions
description:
A logout button must end the server session and the live connection. For a live poll running during a support session, the least complex correct sequence is: revoke the realtime token, disconnect the authenticated client identity, record the result, and only then finish the HTTP logout response.

Choice Existing socket ends now Old token cannot reconnect Operational burden
Revoke token only No Yes Low
Disconnect identity only Yes No Low
Revoke, then disconnect identity Yes Yes Low
Track and close individual socket IDs Only the IDs found Depends on separate auth logic High

TL;DR: use revocation plus identity-level disconnect. Token revocation closes the future; identity disconnect closes the present. For a backend that already speaks HTTP, a plain REST surface is attractive because there is no realtime administration SDK or client-library version to carry. Infrai is one option with verified token-revoke and user-disconnect operations under one API key. Pusher Channels, Socket.IO, Ably, and PubNub deserve consideration too, but their control models and hosting boundaries differ.

How should Express force a realtime client disconnect on logout?

Revocation changes what a credential may do after the revocation takes effect. It does not, by itself, prove that a connection authenticated earlier has been torn down. An open transport can outlive the browser session that created it. That is the gap the logout handler has to close.

Two calls. One identity.

The reverse shortcut is broken as well. Disconnecting today's socket while leaving its credential valid lets the same client reconnect. Mobile retries, a second browser tab, or ordinary reconnect logic can make that happen immediately. The two actions solve different time windows, so treating either one as a substitute creates a race.

Identity is the hinge. A token issued to an anonymous transport handle gives the server nothing durable to target when an account logs out. The token needs to carry the real authenticated client identity used by the disconnect operation. For a support chat widget with an attached live poll, that identity should follow the signed-in participant, not a tab-local socket ID. This also defines the security boundary: logout invalidates the credential and removes every active connection represented by that identity. If the product supports multiple independently managed devices, use a device-scoped authenticated identity from the start. Do not bolt device semantics onto a socket ID after launch; that apparent shortcut trades one identifier during issuance for a permanent mapping table during every logout.

The two criteria that actually decide the design

The first criterion is coverage across time. I would reject any design review that cannot answer both questions in one breath: what stops the connection that is open now, and what stops the revoked credential from opening the next one? A neat client-side close() call answers neither reliably. The browser can disappear before it sends the request, and a hostile client can ignore it.

The second is one identity from issue through logout. Measure glue here. Count the mappings a team must maintain between application user, session, token, connection, and vendor user. Every extra lookup is another stale record during logout. An identity-level administrative disconnect avoids keeping a private socket registry just to enforce session lifecycle.

Logging is part of the behavior, not garnish. Record the application session identifier, authenticated client identity, revocation outcome, disconnect outcome, request or correlation identifier, and timestamp. Never log the bearer token. When a customer says the poll kept updating after logout, support should be able to establish which controls ran without asking engineering to reconstruct a socket timeline.

Keep the log statement after both calls settle. A generic logged_out: true event written before the realtime controls run is misleading: it proves only that the HTTP route was entered. Also decide failure policy explicitly. For a security-sensitive logout, an upstream control failure should surface as a real error and remain visible to retry machinery; returning success while a known live connection remains is a poor contract.

A small Express boundary that stays testable

The request-body schemas for administrative calls are vendor contracts, so the route should not scatter those payloads through controller code. Put them behind a narrow adapter generated or implemented from the provider's current schema. The Express handler can then enforce ordering, error propagation, and audit behavior without pretending all realtime services accept the same JSON.

import express, { type Request, type Response } from "express";

type LogoutSubject = Readonly<{
  sessionId: string;
  realtimeToken: string;
  clientIdentity: string;
}>;

type InfraiBodies = Readonly<{
  revoke: Readonly<Record<string, unknown>>;
  disconnect: Readonly<Record<string, unknown>>;
}>;

interface RealtimeAdmin {
  revokeToken(): Promise<{ requestId: string }>;
  disconnectIdentity(): Promise<{ requestId: string }>;
}

interface Sessions {
  requireLogoutSubject(request: Request): Promise<LogoutSubject>;
  destroy(sessionId: string): Promise<void>;
}

interface AuditLog {
  info(event: Readonly<Record<string, string>>): void;
}

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");
const baseUrl = process.env.INFRAI_BASE_URL;
if (!baseUrl) throw new Error("INFRAI_BASE_URL is required");

function parseBody(name: string): Readonly<Record<string, unknown>> {
  const value = process.env[name];
  if (!value) throw new Error(`${name} is required`);
  return JSON.parse(value) as Readonly<Record<string, unknown>>;
}

const bodies: InfraiBodies = {
  revoke: parseBody("INFRAI_REVOKE_BODY"),
  disconnect: parseBody("INFRAI_DISCONNECT_BODY"),
};

async function post(path: string, body: Readonly<Record<string, unknown>>) {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt += 1) {
    const result = await fetch(`${baseUrl}${path}`, {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
      },
      body: JSON.stringify(body),
    });

    if (result.status === 429 && attempt < 3) {
      const retryAfter = Number(result.headers.get("retry-after"));
      const delayMs = Number.isFinite(retryAfter)
        ? retryAfter * 1_000
        : 250 * 2 ** attempt;
      await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delayMs));
      continue;
    }

    const payload = (await result.json()) as { request_id?: string };
    if (!result.ok) {
      throw new Error(`Realtime control failed (${result.status}): ${JSON.stringify(payload)}`);
    }
    return { requestId: payload.request_id ?? "not-returned" };
  }
  throw new Error("Rate-limit retry budget exhausted");
}

const realtime: RealtimeAdmin = {
  revokeToken: () => post("/realtime/token/revoke", bodies.revoke),
  disconnectIdentity: () => post("/realtime/user/disconnect", bodies.disconnect),
};

export function buildApp(
  sessions: Sessions,
  audit: AuditLog,
): express.Express {
  const app = express();

  app.post("/logout", async (request: Request, response: Response) => {
    const subject = await sessions.requireLogoutSubject(request);
    const revoked = await realtime.revokeToken();
    const disconnected = await realtime.disconnectIdentity();

    await sessions.destroy(subject.sessionId);
    audit.info({
      event: "realtime_logout_enforced",
      sessionId: subject.sessionId,
      clientIdentity: subject.clientIdentity,
      revokeRequestId: revoked.requestId,
      disconnectRequestId: disconnected.requestId,
    });

    response.status(204).end();
  });

  return app;
}

Set INFRAI_BASE_URL to the documented versioned API base. The two JSON environment values must be populated from the current discovery schemas for the authenticated subject; they are not license to invent a { token } or { userId } field. This constraint looks fussy, but fake payloads are worse than visible configuration. The example calls POST /v1/realtime/token/revoke and POST /v1/realtime/user/disconnect, uses Bearer authentication, sets explicit methods, checks statuses, and keeps credentials out of source.

The adapter must treat a 429 as backpressure: honor Retry-After when present and otherwise use bounded exponential backoff. It must also surface non-success response bodies. Do not spin, swallow a 4xx, or convert every failure into a fake success. Since these are control operations rather than content creation, the important retry property is convergence toward “revoked and disconnected,” while the application still avoids launching duplicate retry workers for one logout.

I benchmark this boundary by counting network round trips and required state, not by inventing latency claims. There are exactly two administrative calls because there are two security effects. Parallelizing them saves one dependency edge but weakens the easy-to-audit order. I choose revoke first: once it succeeds, no fresh connection using that token should win the race while disconnect is in flight. That is a concrete trade-off, not a claim that sequential calls are faster.

Order wins here.

Where the other options fit better

Pusher Channels is a credible fit when its authenticated-user model and server-side termination workflow already match the application. Its documentation exposes termination of a user's connections as an administrative operation. That keeps the intent close to identity-level disconnect, but a team should still verify how credential invalidation is handled in its own authentication path. One control is not automatically both controls.

Socket.IO is the runner-up I would choose when owning the realtime servers is a feature. Its server API can find sockets and disconnect them, and rooms can express user membership. The trade-off is operational: the application owns the identity convention, multi-node coordination, and credential/session policy. That is useful control for a custom protocol. It is extra glue for a small widget.

Ably documents token revocation, including revocation scoped through token attributes. It is worth evaluating when its token model is already the center of the system. PubNub documents access-token revocation through its Access Manager. In both cases, ask the same blunt question before choosing: what documented administrative action terminates connections that authenticated before revocation? If the answer relies on waiting for expiry, it does not meet an immediate-logout requirement.

The comparison is less about feature counts than ownership boundaries:

  • Choose a plain REST administration surface when time-to-first-call and minimal dependency churn matter most.
  • Choose Pusher Channels when its user-authentication and termination model already fits the product.
  • Choose Socket.IO when the team wants to own servers and connection policy.
  • Evaluate Ably or PubNub when their token and access-management models align with an existing deployment, then test the open-socket case explicitly.

No vendor choice repairs a vague identity model. Test with two tabs under one identity, log out in one, and verify that both active connections end and that the revoked token cannot reconnect. Then repeat while forcing a 429 and a non-success response from each administrative call. Those four checks reveal more than a long feature matrix.

Production decision

The production checklist is short because the invariant is sharp. Issue realtime credentials for a genuine authenticated identity. On logout, revoke the credential before disconnecting that identity. Destroy the application session, emit an audit event containing outcomes rather than secrets, and make failures observable.

Client cleanup still has value for UI responsiveness, but it is not enforcement. The server owns enforcement.

For the live poll, define reconnect behavior separately: a newly authenticated session may reconnect and backfill poll state according to the application's event model, while a logged-out session has no valid path back. Do not confuse recovery for an authorized client with continued delivery to a revoked one.

Further reading

  • Socket.IO server API: disconnecting sockets
  • Pusher Channels: terminate user connections
  • Ably: revoke tokens
  • PubNub: revoke tokens
  • W3C WebRTC 1.0

title: Cache Locally, Recompute Selectively for Streaming Video Understanding
description:
arXiv:2610.29229v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Streaming video understanding (SVU) requires video-LLMs to process incoming video continuously while answering user queries with low latency. Recent methods reduce query-time cost by prefilling frames into KV caches during idle time and reusing the cached KVs at query time. To bound per-frame computation over unbounded video streams, these methods restrict the context available during prefill. This creates a fundamental context mismatch: the restricted context may omit information needed to properly contextualize video tokens, yet, still contain information irrelevant to the eventual query, which is unknown during prefill. We propose FrameBlend, a simple yet effective plug-and-play method to address this mismatch through selective KV recomputation, without requiring any additional training. At query time, FrameBlend re-prefills selected video tokens using query-relevant context and replaces their cached KVs with recomputed ones. Crucially, this recomputation enables shorter attention windows during idle-time prefill, substantially reducing prefill cost while improving accuracy. Experiments across three SVU frameworks and five streaming and offline benchmarks demonstrate accuracy gains of up to 3.9 pp. On RVS-Ego, FrameBlend reduces per-frame prefill FLOPs by over 20% and total processing time by 14-59% for retrieval-based frameworks, including the cost of query-time recomputation. These results demonstrate that a simple change in how contextualization is distributed between idle time and query time can improve the accuracy-efficiency trade-off for SVU.

title: Dissimilarity-Based Markov Decision Processes for Stabilizing State Distributions
description:
arXiv:2610.29024v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reinforcement learning for stochastic systems typically optimizes expected cumulative rewards, while reliable and repeatable behavior also depends on how the state distribution evolves over time. Optimizing expected return alone does not guarantee that this distribution converges to a desired target or remains stable. This paper develops a theoretical framework for learning policies that stabilize state distributions. We formulate the problem as a Dissimilarity-based Markov Decision Process (DMDP), in which the policy acts on the current state distribution and the objective measures its dissimilarity to a target distribution. We establish sufficient conditions under which the optimal policy makes the target distribution asymptotically stable. To support policy learning, we introduce a finite-dimensional representation of distributions and show how stability guarantees for its parameter dynamics extend to the underlying state distributions. We further develop certificates for the learned policies, including their deployment using estimated distribution parameters. These results quantify how learning and estimation errors affect the guarantees and identify conditions under which learned policies retain asymptotic stability. For practical implementation, we combine distribution estimates and target-dependent rewards with PPO and SAC. A computable example on a linear system illustrates the proposed theoretical certificates. Furthermore, experiments on a HalfCheetah task demonstrate the benefits of distribution feedback and explicit target matching for regulating the velocity distribution.

title: RL-IF: Tracking Non-local Training Data Influence for Online Reinforcement Learning
description:
arXiv:2610.28883v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Online reinforcement learning (RL) has achieved significant success in decision-making tasks, but modern online RL remains highly sensitive to the quality of training experience. Understanding the contribution of individual training instances is therefore central to data-centric RL, with applications ranging from experience selection to policy interpretation. Existing data attribution methods for online RL primarily focus on local influence within a single training round, overlooking the non-local data influence across multiple training rounds. In this work, we formalize data attribution in online RL through a trajectory-level leave-one-out quantity, RL-LOO, which measures how one training sample influences a downstream target after subsequent online updates have taken place. We then derive RL-IF, a first-order estimator that propagates data influence through both optimization effects and policy-induced sampling effects, and provide theoretical guarantees on its approximation accuracy under smoothness assumptions. Our analysis further disentangles these two effects and shows both theoretically and empirically that the full RL-IF estimator can often be well approximated using the optimization effect alone. Building on this observation, we develop RINSE, a practical data filtering method for online RL. Experiments on standard control benchmarks and an RLHF-style toxicity-mitigation setting show that RINSE improves training efficiency and final performance over standard PPO and local attribution baselines. These results suggest that RL-IF provides a practical and principled framework for understanding and improving online RL.

title: Vercel applications are protected from Next.js August 2026 security vulnerabilities
description:
Summary

Two vulnerabilities affecting Next.js were disclosed in the August 2026 Security Release. Next.js applications hosted on Vercel are protected and require no customer action.

Next.js August 2026 vulnerabilities

Next.js disclosed the following critical vulnerabilities:

  • GHSA-2xp9-vwfh-vxw4 originates in the upstream libheif dependency and can lead to unauthenticated remote code execution when Image Optimization processes a crafted AVIF input.

  • CVE-2026-75604 (GHSA-p293-qw3h-jr36) can lead to unauthenticated remote code execution on Windows-hosted Next.js servers in applications using the Pages Router and App Router without Cache Components.

After the AVIF vulnerability was identified, Vercel applied protections to its managed Image Optimization service.

Impact on Vercel deployments

Applications hosted on Vercel are protected. No upgrades, configuration changes, or redeploys are required.

  • Once the AVIF vulnerability was identified, Vercel disabled AVIF optimization across its managed Image Optimization service. AVIF inputs are served as-is and do not pass through the affected processing path.

  • The second vulnerability only affects servers using a Windows filesystem. Vercel's Next.js runtime uses Linux and is not affected.

Resolution for self-hosted applications

Self-hosted Next.js applications should upgrade to the appropriate patched version.

For applications running Next.js 15.x or earlier:

For applications running Next.js 16.x:

In the patched releases, AVIF images are not resized or optimized. They are served as-is until a fixed libheif version is available. There is no workaround for the Windows vulnerability; affected servers should upgrade immediately.

Python is now generally available

Applications in any language with containers

The Vercel container runtime lets you deploy applications written in any language, packaged with the OS libraries and executables they need. Since container support entered Public Beta, 5,000 teams have shipped 150,000 container deployments on Vercel.

Containers deploy as Vercel Functions on Fluid compute, scaling with traffic and using Active CPU pricing, which doesn’t charge for idle time spent waiting for API responses, database queries, or LLM inferencing. title: Don't hold span.enter() across an .await: a wrong-trace-id bug in async Rust
description:
While investigating our logs I found a classic async Rust trap where logs contained both resuls from polling by internal service and also messages as result of incoming API calls to our system. Logs from one request could carry the trace id of a different request. The cause was one line in a axum middleware.

TLDR

  • Do not hold the guard from span.enter() across an .await.
  • Use .instrument(span) on the future instead. It enters the span on every poll and leaves it on every yield.
  • Test it with two requests that interleave on one thread, and check that each log line sits in exactly one span.

The code that looked fine

An axum middleware that gives every request a trace id:

pub async fn trace_id_middleware(req: Request<Body>, next: Next) -> Response {
    let trace_id = Uuid::new_v4().to_string();
    let span = info_span!("api_request", trace_id = %trace_id);
    let _enter = span.enter();          // <- the problem

    let mut req = req;
    req.extensions_mut().insert(trace_id);

    next.run(req).await
}

It compiles, and with one request at a time it works. Under concurrent load the logs got mixed up.

Why it breaks

span.enter() returns a guard. While the guard is alive, the span is "current" on that thread. That is a thread-local setting, not a property of your future.

When the handler hits an .await and yields, the guard is still alive inside the suspended future, so the thread still has this request's span as current. The runtime then polls another request on the same thread. That request's logs, and any span it creates, now sit under the first request's span.

The tracing docs warn about this. It is easy to miss because nothing fails: you only see logs with the wrong context.

The fix 

use tracing::Instrument;

pub async fn trace_id_middleware(req: Request<Body>, next: Next) -> Response {
    let trace_id = Uuid::new_v4().to_string();
    let span = info_span!("api_request", trace_id = %trace_id);

    let mut req = req;
    req.extensions_mut().insert(trace_id);

    next.run(req).instrument(span).await
}

.instrument(span) wraps the future. Each time the future is polled it enters the span, and when it yields it leaves it. The span is current only while this request's code is actually running.

No more:

let _guard = span.enter();

Rather:

some_future.instrument(span).await

Test it

Add a test with two requests that interleave on one thread, and check that every log line sits inside exactly one api_request span, the right one. Then put span.enter() back once and confirm the test fails. A test that passes on the buggy code proves nothing.

The same idea in a polling loop

We have loops that peek a message from a queue, store it, and then acknowledge it. Each message has a trace id minted at peek time. Passing it by hand into every log call is easy to forget, so each message now runs inside its own span:

let span = message_span("DDK", &collection, &peek_trace_id);
async {
    // ... parse, persist, acknowledge ...
    tracing::Span::current().record("message_id", msg_id.as_str());
    // ...
}
.instrument(span)
.await;

Two details:

  • Declare the field as tracing::field::Empty when you create the span, and fill it in later with Span::current().record(...) once the value is known.
  • Inside the async block, continue is not allowed. The early exits became return, which ends this message and lets the loop move on to the next tick.

Takeaways

  1. In async code, never keep a span.enter() guard alive across an .await.
  2. Put the span on the future with .instrument(span).
  3. Test with interleaved tasks on a single thread, and check the full span scope of each event, not just the innermost span.
  4. Break the code on purpose once to see the test fail.

title: Introducing Run SDK: secure eval for your agents
description:
Agents increasingly write TypeScript programs to coordinate tools and process their results. Once those programs touch real applications, some steps require authentication, while others need human approval.

Executing that code with eval gives it the same access as the application around it, including its secrets and internal services, and leaves no durable way to pause at those boundaries.

Today, we're releasing the Run SDK, a package for executing untrusted JavaScript and TypeScript without giving it direct access to your application or system. Applications expose narrow host functions and can interrupt execution for authentication or human-in-the-loop approval. The program resumes after a decision without repeating completed work.

A small interface to the host

The Run SDK evaluates JavaScript or type-stripped TypeScript in a fresh QuickJS context inside a worker thread, with no direct route to Node.js or the network.

The application exposes selected operations through hostFunctions. These are regular functions that become callable globals inside the sandbox:

Here, the generated program knows about store.listOrders(). The database client and its credentials remain in the application.

Calls cross the sandbox boundary through serialization. A host function may return a promise, so existing service clients can sit behind this interface without being passed into the sandbox.

You can try this in the playground. Code you run there can only reach the host functions on the page.

Code mode in practice

The Run SDK is the internal module powering code mode tool execution in the AI SDK. Giving an agent a program changes the unit of work. One model response can describe the calls and the logic connecting them:

The two requests happen concurrently, and invoice filtering stays local to the program. Only the useful result returns to the application.

This is a good fit for agents that work across several internal services. A research agent can combine search results before answering. A support agent can inspect an account without putting an entire billing response back into its context.

The same package can power a code interpreter or a product feature that accepts customer-defined transformations. In both cases, the application chooses the available data and operations.

Host functions work best when they map to actions in your product, like refunding an order. Exposing orders.refund(id) gives the application a clear place to check the user and the order. A generic request function would make that authority much harder to reason about.

Native support for human-in-the-loop and auth

Reading invoices is different from issuing a refund. When generated code reaches a sensitive operation, the host function can interrupt execution:

When the run is interrupted, the result includes a signed token the application can save with an approval request and use to resume the run when a decision arrives.

Resuming replays the program, but settled host function calls use their recorded results. Host function work completed before the interruption does not run again. The interrupted function receives the approval and continues from there.

This mechanism also works when a workflow must wait for authentication. The application owns the waiting period; the worker does not need to remain alive.

Running within limits

A sandbox still needs to account for code that loops forever or produces an oversized result. createRunner() sets shared limits:

Limits can also be set per run. The defaults cover the QuickJS heap and the values crossing the host boundary; applications can tighten them for their workload.

Each invocation receives a new QuickJS context. Dynamic evaluation is disabled and built-in prototypes are hardened. This boundary applies to the generated program, while host functions remain trusted application code and must perform their normal authorization checks.

The Run SDK is intended for JavaScript computation inside an application. Workloads that require an operating system, package installation, or process-level isolation should use Vercel Sandbox instead.

Extracting the execution layer

The first version of this runtime lived inside just-bash as js-exec, backed by QuickJS. It let agents write TypeScript against the shell's virtual filesystem and command set.

We extracted that layer into the Run SDK and replaced the Node-shaped environment with application-defined host functions. We tested the underlying mechanism in eve, using it to run agent-generated TypeScript against real tools. It now powers code mode in the AI SDK where existing AI SDK tools are mapped to host functions, while the Run SDK handles their sandboxed execution.

Getting started

The Run SDK supports Node.js 22.13+ and Bun. You will need pnpm or another package manager installed on your local development machine.

Check out the documentation and API reference.

title: Towards Realistic Models of Change: A Causal Perspective on Decision-Making and Dynamical Systems
description:
arXiv:2610.28803v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: While statistical learning has made remarkable progress in recent decades, driven by large datasets and data-driven protocols that have transformed scientific practice, it still faces a key limitation: it struggles to generalize beyond the data it has seen, often failing under distribution shift. Causality offers a promising solution: causal models focus on the underlying mechanisms of change rather than surface-level associations, enabling robust reasoning under external interventions. This allows systems not only to learn from data, but also to reason about hypothetical scenarios, adapt to new environments, and inform better decisions. This thesis explores how these approaches can inform each other, in two parts.
  The first part examines algorithmic recourse, that is, identifying which changes an individual can make to overturn an unfavorable decision. We propose an alternative perspective to the established framework, arguing for a more realistic cost function, a reformulation of the problem in causal terms, and the inclusion of a temporal dimension in policy evaluation.
  The second part focuses on dynamical systems, extending the notions of causal interventions and effects to discrete and continuous stochastic processes. We show that the equilibria of these processes, and how they change following an intervention, can be linked to Structural Causal Models (SCMs), viewed as compressed representations of the underlying temporal dynamics. We argue for the relevance of such temporal causal models, since in real-world scenarios actions take time to produce their effects.
  The common goal of both parts is practical: the utility, robustness, and trustworthiness of these models depend critically on their ability to realistically represent the underlying phenomena.

This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge: Week 3

🦥 What I Built: SlothSort

Tomorrow is International Sloth Day, and sloths have life figured out: move at your own pace, conserve energy, and let automation do the tedious heavy lifting so you don't have to.

Every developer and knowledge worker knows the dread of opening their ~/Downloads or Desktop folder: a terrifying graveyard of chaotic filenames:

  • Receipt_Uber_Eats_Oct14.pdf
  • IMG_20261019_142311.jpg
  • contract_nda_mutual_signable_oct.pdf

Cleaning this manually takes endless clicking, dragging, and cognitive fatigue.

SlothSort is a zero-effort desktop and download tidier that channels your inner sloth:

  1. Drop or Paste Clutter: Toss in messy filenames, downloads, or unorganized project files.
  2. Local Gemma 2 Semantic Intelligence: Google's open-weight Gemma 2 (running 100% locally via Ollama) inspects context, categorizes files, and renames them to clean, consistent, ISO/semantic standards (e.g., 2026-10_Invoice_AcmeCorp.pdf).
  3. Lazy Voice Debrief with ElevenLabs: Listen to a soothing, witty sloth audio debrief celebrating how much effort you saved today.
  4. 1-Click Execution Script: Provides an auto-generated bash script (organize.sh) so you can execute the sorting on your machine in one terminal command.

🎥 Video Demo & Walkthrough

▶️ Watch the full walkthrough on YouTube: https://youtu.be/TANmvRYIfnw

📸 Screenshots

SlothSort running 100% on-device with Gemma 2 sorting queue, ElevenLabs voice debrief player, and 1-click terminal execution script.

🔒 Why Open Innovation Matters

The Hacktoberfest prompt asks: Why does open innovation matter for what you built?

For personal file management, open-weight, on-device AI is not just a nice-to-have; it's a non-negotiable requirement:

  1. Absolute Privacy on Sensitive Files: Desktop clutter is full of private data — bank statements, unreleased source code, medical invoices, passwords, and client NDAs. Sending this metadata to commercial cloud LLMs creates catastrophic privacy risks. With Gemma 2 running locally via Ollama, zero bytes ever leave your laptop.
  2. $0 API Costs Forever: Commercial cloud LLM tokens add up quickly when organizing hundreds of files. With open-weight models, you set it up once and clean your folders an unlimited number of times for free.
  3. Offline Resilience: Whether you're on a long flight without Wi-Fi or working in a remote cabin, your sloth organizer works completely offline.

  • Framework: Next.js 16 (Turbopack, App Router) with Tailwind CSS and TypeScript.
  • Open-Source AI Core: Google Gemma 2 (gemma2:9.2B) served locally through Ollama (http://localhost:11434), producing structured JSON categorization plans.
  • Voice AI: ElevenLabs Multilingual v2 generating soothing, sloth-themed audio debriefs.

title: MINER: Modeling Inter- and Intra-Person Variance for Reidentification
description:
arXiv:2610.28941v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Clothes-Changing Person Re-Identification (CC-ReID) remains challenging due to drastic appearance shifts across outfits. Most prior works devise biometric signal-extraction heuristics to enhance inter-person variance, e.g., using segmentation masks, while leaving intra-person variance uncontrolled. We present MINER, a simple model-agnostic framework that suppresses garment bias by contrasting hard examples and adaptively balancing dataset-dependent intra- and inter-person variance. Extensive experiments show that MINER improves retrieval across CC-ReID benchmarks, achieving state-of-the-art performance on four datasets and ranking among the leaders in all three tracks of the open TVRID RGB-Depth ReID challenge.

title: Privacy-preserving inference on hosted models: a learned input-embedding transform for frozen Qwen3.8-27B
description:
arXiv:2610.27817v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Every prompt sent to a hosted language model is readable by whoever runs it. We study whether the prompt can remain on the client while the host receives transformed vectors that stand in for it. A language model converts text to vectors exactly once, with a public lookup table; we perform that step locally and pass the vectors through a small trained network (55.6M parameters) before they leave the perimeter. The host runs a frozen 27B model (Qwen3.8-27B) on the transformed vectors and never receives text or token ids. We train the transform against the frozen model as a fixed judge, combining a forward-KL utility term with an auxiliary term that pushes each vector away from its original direction. On 1,490 MMLU questions held out from training, the transform costs 1.5 points of accuracy (80.7% vs. 82.3%), breaking 68 of the 1,226 questions the unmodified model answers correctly (5.5%), while 30.1% of content tokens no longer decode to their original token under a nearest-neighbour lookup.

title: WordPress Feels Slow? Profile Plugins and Queries Before You Buy More Hosting
description:
A slow WordPress page is not automatically a hosting problem. Before you upgrade, split the time into three buckets: PHP/plugin execution, database query time, and network time to first byte. If query time is low and PHP time is high, a bigger database does not help. If query time is high, a faster CPU can hide a missing index for a while. Profile before you upgrade.

Step 1: Measure a stable baseline

Use a staging copy with the same plugins and data. Measure the uncached page for profiling, then measure the cached page separately.

URL="https://staging.example.com/"

for i in 1 2 3 4 5; do
  curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{time_starttransfer}' "$URL"; echo
done

Do not trust one run. Use the median of several runs. If the page is cached, the uncached number is the one that tells you about plugins and queries.

Step 2: Log page time, query count, and query time

Add this to wp-config.php while profiling:

define('SAVEQUERIES', true);

Create wp-content/mu-plugins/wp-profile.php:

<?php
add_action('shutdown', function () {
    if (!defined('SAVEQUERIES') || !SAVEQUERIES) {
        return;
    }

    global $wpdb;

    $total = 0.0;
    $slow = [];

    foreach ((array) $wpdb->queries as $q) {
        $seconds = (float) $q[1];
        $total += $seconds;

        if ($seconds >= 0.05) {
            $slow[] = [
                'sql' => $q[0],
                'seconds' => round($seconds, 4),
                'caller' => $q[2],
            ];
        }
    }

    error_log(sprintf(
        'WP_PROFILE page=%ss query=%ss queries=%d slow=%s',
        timer_stop(0),
        round($total, 4),
        count($wpdb->queries),
        wp_json_encode($slow)
    ));
});

Load the page, then read the PHP error log. Remove the constant and the mu-plugin after profiling. SAVEQUERIES adds overhead and should not stay on in production.

Step 3: Sweep plugins on staging

Do not do this on production. Deactivate all active plugins, then activate one at a time and measure the same URL.

cd /path/to/wordpress

measure() {
  for i in 1 2 3; do
    curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{time_starttransfer}' "$1"; echo
  done | sort -n | sed -n '2p'
}

wp plugin list --status=active --field=name > /tmp/active-plugins.txt
wp plugin deactivate --all

while read -r plugin; do
  wp plugin activate "$plugin"
  echo "$plugin $(measure https://staging.example.com/)"
  wp plugin deactivate "$plugin"
done < /tmp/active-plugins.txt

wp plugin activate $(cat /tmp/active-plugins.txt)

Skip plugins that the site needs to boot. Also test with the default theme if you suspect the theme. A plugin that adds a small query can still add a large external HTTP call on every page load.

Step 4: Read the slow queries

Open the log line that starts with WP_PROFILE. Take the SQL from the slow array and run EXPLAIN in MySQL:

EXPLAIN SELECT post_id
FROM wp_postmeta
WHERE meta_key = 'example_key';

Look for:

  • type=ALL on a large table
  • a large rows estimate
  • Using temporary
  • Using filesort

Add an index only after you check the real query pattern and test write performance. An index that helps one report can hurt checkout or editorial saves.

Step 5: Check autoloaded options

Large autoloaded options are loaded on every request. Find the largest ones:

SELECT option_name, LENGTH(option_value) AS bytes
FROM wp_options
WHERE autoload = 'yes'
ORDER BY bytes DESC
LIMIT 20;

Do not delete rows blindly. Identify stale options from plugins you no longer use, then remove them through the plugin or a backup-backed cleanup.

Step 6: Check transients

Expired transients can pile up in wp_options. List the largest:

SELECT option_name, LENGTH(option_value) AS bytes
FROM wp_options
WHERE option_name LIKE '%transient%'
ORDER BY bytes DESC
LIMIT 20;

If you see many expired transients, clean them from the database or with a maintenance routine you control.

Step 7: Decide what to buy

  • Query time high, page time high: fix queries, indexes, or autoloaded data before buying a bigger database.
  • Query time low, page time high: profile plugins, theme hooks, external HTTP calls, and PHP workers.
  • Time to first byte high before WordPress runs: look at DNS, TLS, network, and host-level caching.
  • Only logged-in admin pages are slow: profile admin hooks, not the front end.

Hosting upgrades are useful when the profile shows a real resource limit. They are a poor substitute for a missing index or a plugin that calls a remote API on every request.

AumCreate is a one-person WordPress shop in Singapore. It does custom WordPress development and deployment setup. If you want help turning this profile into a fix, the services page is here: AumCreate services.

title: Better Policies, Worse Verifier Audits
description:
arXiv:2610.29029v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Verifier stacks increasingly sit inside post-training and test-time compute loops. We study a specific control loop: a component verifier is evaluated on fresh policy outputs against the full success label and refreshed when that aggregate score falls. For a conjunctive target $y = F \wedge M$, its on-policy AUC is $(1-q)A_{\mathrm{own}} + qA_{\mathrm{cross}}$, where $q = \Pr[F=1 \mid y=0]$. As the policy masters $F$, $q$ can rise toward one, removing weight from $F$-failures and rewarding information about $M$. We call this on-policy audit collapse. We derive a sharp identified set, a complete-erasure threshold, and the exact point at which the audit can prefer a worse component verifier; its population optimum is the full-outcome predictor, not the component oracle. An exact oracle exhibits the collapse, a natural multi-label text control shows inversion can select a head with lower canonical $F$-AUC at the observed failure mixture, and a prediction-registered ECG study shows that acting on the audit can reduce off-policy $F$-AUC, transfer the damage to an unseen generator, and increase downstream constraint violations. Preserving own-failure support prevents the damage. Matching label-complexity bounds and a controlled-mixture audit give the corresponding repair: audit the component on its own failures, and keep those failures in the refresh distribution.

title: Let Agents Design How They Search: Automatic Interface Optimization for Agentic Search
description:
arXiv:2610.29250v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Agentic search depends on the interface through which a language-model agent accesses and explores a corpus. Existing interface designs are fixed by hand and applied unchanged to every corpus, although effective designs may depend on the corpus. We introduce SearchWeaver, a framework for automatic search interface optimization guided by downstream search performance. A proposer uses execution trajectories and task rewards to jointly revise corpus artifacts, executable tools, and usage instructions. This pro cess optimizes what information is prepared in advance, which operations tools perform, and which decisions remain with the search agent. With GPT-5.4-nano, the optimized interfaces improve answer accuracy from 71.6% to 78.4% on BrowseComp-Plus and average nDCG@10 from 45.7 to 55.0 across four BRIGHT subsets over Direct Corpus Interaction. These findings highlight the value of jointly optimizing corpus artifacts, executable tools, and usage instructions to develop effective search interfaces.

title: Introducing Vercel Drives: persistent storage for agents
description:
Agents often handle complex work that continues across runs. As that work evolves, they may need a new environment with different tools, runtimes, or compute. They should be able to continue working with the same files when they change environments.

We built Vercel Drives to keep an agent’s files independent of its execution environment. It is now generally available for Vercel Sandbox. Agents can mount the same drive in a new environment configured for the next task and continue where they left off.

Persisting state with a drive

Create a drive once, then mount it when you create a sandbox. From the CLI:

Or from the Sandbox SDK:

In this example, everything under /workspace persists on the drive. Everything else belongs to the sandbox. The next sandbox that mounts the drive finds the repository, and anything else the agent wrote there, where the previous run left it.

The drive keeps the agent’s files independent of the sandbox running it. An agent can resume work in a new sandbox or switch runtimes without transferring its workspace. Other sandboxes can mount the same drive.

Sharing state across sandboxes

Agents can prepare files on a drive once and reuse them across sandboxes. If one agent builds a dataset on a drive, other agents can mount read-only copies to analyze the data or generate reports without rebuilding the dataset. They use the shared files as input and save their results separately.

Agents can also fork a drive to explore different approaches independently. Each fork starts with the drive’s contents and provides its own writable workspace. Agents can try different transformations of the dataset in parallel without changing the original or affecting one another. Forks don’t merge back into the original drive.

Forking is generally available.

Get started

Vercel Drives is now generally available for Vercel Sandbox on all plans.

Drives default to 1 TiB, or 1 GiB on Hobby, with up to 16 TiB available. See the documentation for configuration, snapshots, and limits, or the changelog for what changed at GA.
