title: Connection Pooling for PostgreSQL Under Real Concurrency
description:
Here's a number worth staring at. In a benchmark Andres Freund ran while working on Postgres connection scalability, one active connection doing simple reads managed 33,457 transactions per second on an otherwise idle server. Add 10,000 connections that do nothing at all, and the same single connection dropped to 14,496 TPS. Nothing else changed. The idle connections weren't running queries. They were just there.

That's the part of connection pooling most teams never think about. They treat pool size as a knob on one service: bump max from 10 to 50 because the API felt slow, ship it, move on. But Postgres doesn't see your services. It sees one flat pile of backend processes, and every service, every replica, every cron job, and every half-finished rolling deploy adds to the same pile.

So let's do this properly. Not "what should max be," but "how do you split one database's real capacity across everything that talks to it, and keep it split when the cluster autoscales at 3pm on a Friday."

What a Postgres connection actually costs

Postgres uses a process-per-connection model. Every client connection gets its own backend process, forked by the postmaster, with its own slot in shared memory and its own row in pg_stat_activity. That's very different from a thread-per-connection database, and it's why the question "how many connections can Postgres handle?" has a more interesting answer than you'd expect.

There are three separate costs, and people usually blame the wrong one.

Memory is smaller than folklore says. You'll read "10MB per connection" in a lot of blog posts. Freund's analysis on the Citus blog measured it properly and found the per-connection overhead is below 2 MiB when the server is configured sensibly, with huge_pages on. That's not free, but it's not the reason your database fell over either. (The shared-memory side is also allocated up front: max_connections sizes the lock tables and process slots at startup, which is one reason changing it needs a restart.)

Snapshots were the real bottleneck, and they got fixed. Every statement takes a snapshot to decide which row versions it can see. Before Postgres 14, building that snapshot meant walking the state of every backend, including the idle ones. In Freund's CPU profile, with one active connection next to 5,000 idle ones, the bottleneck sat squarely in GetSnapshotData(). His fix landed in Postgres 14, and the before/after is dramatic: with 48 active connections and 10,000 idle, throughput went from 369,845 TPS to 1,115,740 TPS on the same hardware (2x Xeon Gold 5215).

Active concurrency is the cost that never goes away. Here's the thing Postgres 14 didn't change and can't change: if 400 connections are all running queries at the same time on a 16-core box, they're fighting over 16 cores, the same buffer pool, the same locks, and the same disk queue. Context switching goes up, cache hit rates go down, lock waits pile on. More concurrent work past the point of saturation doesn't make the database do more. It makes every query slower.

That last point is the whole article in one sentence. Idle connections are now cheap. Active connections are still expensive. Your pooling strategy should be about capping active concurrency at the database, not about hoarding slots.

The formula everyone quotes, and what it really means

The HikariCP wiki's "About Pool Sizing" page is one of the most-cited pieces of writing on this topic, and it opens with a result from Oracle's Real-World Performance group: reducing the connection pool size alone, with no other change, cut application response times from around 100ms to around 2ms. Smaller pool, faster app.

Then it gives its starting-point formula:

connections = ((core_count * 2) + effective_spindle_count)

A few details matter here and get lost in the retelling:

  • core_count is the database server's physical cores, not the app server's, and not hyperthreads.
  • effective_spindle_count is how many disk operations can be in flight usefully. On SSD or NVMe, people typically plug in 1 as a starting point. The "extra" connections beyond cores only exist to cover time a backend spends blocked on I/O.
  • The wiki's own example is a 4-core server with one disk: (4 * 2) + 1 = 9, rounded to 10. It claims that setup comfortably serves 3,000 front-end users running simple queries at 6,000 TPS.

And the wiki is explicit that this is a starting point, not a law. Treat it as an order-of-magnitude anchor.

The detail that matters most here: that formula tells you the size of the pool for the whole database. It does not tell you what to put in one service's config. If you have a 16-core database, the formula says somewhere around 33 connections should be actively working at once. If you have eight services each running six replicas, and each replica's pool is sized "by the formula," you've just told the database it should expect 1,584 of them. That's how teams end up quoting HikariCP correctly and still melting their database.

Your real pool size is a multiplication

Let's make it concrete. The following is a hypothetical system, but the shape will look familiar: four workloads on one Postgres primary with 16 physical cores and max_connections = 200.

Workload Replicas (steady) Pool max per replica Connections at steady state
api (Node, pg) 12 10 120
worker (Go, pgxpool) 6 16 96
reporting 2 10 20
cron + migrations + humans with psql varies varies ~5
Total 241

It's already over 200 at steady state, and nothing is misbehaving. Each team picked a reasonable-looking number. Two of those numbers are literally library defaults: pg.Pool defaults max to 10, and pgxpool defaults MaxConns to the greater of 4 or runtime.NumCPU(), so a worker pod on a 16-vCPU node gets 16 without anyone deciding that.

Now add the two things that make this worse at the worst possible moment.

Rolling deploys. A Kubernetes Deployment's maxSurge defaults to 25%. During a rollout, old and new pods coexist, so your 12 API replicas can briefly be 15. That's 30 more connections, and they show up exactly when you're deploying, which is also when you're least prepared to debug FATAL: sorry, too many clients already.

Autoscaling. The HPA scales on CPU or custom metrics. It has no idea your database has a connection budget. When traffic spikes, it'll happily add pods, and each new pod can fill its whole pool as soon as traffic reaches it. The database gets more connections at the exact moment it's getting more load.

And don't forget the slots you can't use. Postgres reserves superuser_reserved_connections (default 3) for superusers, and since Postgres 16 there's also reserved_connections (default 0) for roles granted pg_use_reserved_connections. Those exist so you can still get in and fix things when the app has eaten every other slot. Keep them. Your app budget is max_connections minus those reservations minus whatever replication, monitoring, and migration tooling need.

So the honest formula for a direct-to-Postgres setup is:

sum over services of (pool_max * max_replicas * (1 + surge))
    + ops_and_tooling
    <= max_connections - superuser_reserved_connections - reserved_connections

Notice it uses max_replicas, the HPA ceiling, not today's replica count. If you size against the steady state, the budget holds right up until you need it.

Size each service with Little's Law, not vibes

If the database-wide number comes from cores, where does the per-service number come from? From how long each request actually holds a connection.

Little's Law says the average number of items in a system equals arrival rate times time in the system: L = lambda * W. For a connection pool, L is how many connections are busy on average, lambda is how often the service checks one out, and W is how long it keeps it.

Take a worked example, again with hypothetical numbers. Say one API replica handles 200 requests per second at peak, and each request holds a connection for about 15ms (query time plus the round trips in between, from checkout to release):

busy connections = 200 req/s * 0.015 s = 3

Three connections busy on average. A pool of 10 per replica gives you a lot of headroom for bursts and slow queries. A pool of 50 gives you nothing except the ability to hurt the database when things go wrong.

The useful insight isn't the arithmetic. It's that W is the variable you control, and it's usually the one that's out of whack. If that same service holds a connection for 150ms instead of 15ms, it needs ten times the connections for the same traffic. And the most common reason W balloons isn't slow SQL. It's code like this:

// Looks fine. Holds a Postgres connection across an HTTP call.
const client = await pool.connect();
try {
  await client.query('BEGIN');
  const order = await client.query('SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = $1 FOR UPDATE', [id]);
  const charge = await paymentGateway.charge(order.rows[0]); // 300-2000ms, network
  await client.query('UPDATE orders SET status = $1 WHERE id = $2', ['paid', id]);
  await client.query('COMMIT');
} catch (err) {
  await client.query('ROLLBACK');
  throw err;
} finally {
  client.release();
}

That transaction pins a connection (and a row lock) for the full duration of a third-party network call. Under load, the pool drains, and every other request queues behind payment latency. Bumping max doesn't fix it. It just moves the queue into Postgres, where it now also holds row locks. Do the external call outside the transaction, and let the database connection live only as long as the database work.

Postgres has a guardrail for the worst version of this: idle_in_transaction_session_timeout terminates sessions that sit idle inside an open transaction longer than the limit. It's off by default. Turning it on per role is cheap insurance.

Configure the client pool like you mean it

Library defaults are tuned for "works on a laptop." Under real concurrency, a few of them bite hard.

In node-postgres, connectionTimeoutMillis defaults to 0, which means no timeout. When the pool is exhausted, pool.connect() and pool.query() just wait. Forever. Your request timeout fires upstream, the client retries, and now you've got two waiters instead of one. Here's a pool that fails fast instead:

db.ts

import pg from 'pg';

export const pool = new pg.Pool({
  host: process.env.PGHOST,
  database: process.env.PGDATABASE,
  user: process.env.PGUSER,          // one role per service, see below
  max: 10,                           // sized from the budget, not from a hunch
  connectionTimeoutMillis: 2_000,    // fail fast when the pool is empty
  idleTimeoutMillis: 10_000,         // the default, stated on purpose
  maxLifetimeSeconds: 1_800,         // recycle so connections rebalance after failover/scale
  application_name: 'api',           // shows up in pg_stat_activity
});

// An idle client can error (e.g. the server restarted). Without a
// listener, that error is unhandled and can crash the process.
pool.on('error', (err) => {
  console.error('idle pg client error', err);
});

// Export these as metrics. waitingCount > 0 for long = pool is the bottleneck.
export function poolStats() {
  return {
    total: pool.totalCount,
    idle: pool.idleCount,
    waiting: pool.waitingCount,
  };
}

pool.waitingCount is the most underrated metric in Node database code. If it's regularly above zero, requests are queueing for connections inside your app. That's fine in short bursts; it's exactly where you want the queue to be. If it's pinned high, you've either got a W problem (connections held too long) or a genuinely undersized pool, and the Little's Law math tells you which.

On the Go side, the trap is different. database/sql defaults SetMaxOpenConns to 0, which means unlimited. Nothing in your service stops it from opening one connection per concurrent goroutine that touches the database. If you're using pgxpool directly, set the limits explicitly instead of inheriting runtime.NumCPU() from whatever node the pod landed on:

db.go

cfg, err := pgxpool.ParseConfig(os.Getenv("DATABASE_URL"))
if err != nil {
    return nil, err
}
cfg.MaxConns = 16                        // explicit: from the budget, not NumCPU
cfg.MinConns = 2
cfg.MaxConnLifetime = 30 * time.Minute
cfg.MaxConnIdleTime = 5 * time.Minute
cfg.ConnConfig.RuntimeParams["application_name"] = "worker"

pool, err := pgxpool.NewWithConfig(ctx, cfg)

The nested-checkout deadlock

One more client-side footgun, and it's a nasty one because it looks like the database is hung. If a single request can hold two connections at once (for example, it opens a transaction, then calls a helper that does pool.query() outside that transaction), then a pool can deadlock itself: every connection is held by a request that's waiting for a second connection that will never come free.

The HikariCP wiki gives the minimum pool size that avoids this: Tn * (Cm - 1) + 1, where Tn is the max number of concurrent threads and Cm is the max connections any one of them holds at once. With 8 threads each holding up to 3, that's 17. The better fix is to not do it: pass the transaction's client down instead of reaching back into the pool.

Give every service its own role

One cheap move pays off in three places. Instead of every service connecting as app, give each one its own Postgres role.

CREATE ROLE api_svc       LOGIN CONNECTION LIMIT 150;
CREATE ROLE worker_svc    LOGIN CONNECTION LIMIT 100;
CREATE ROLE reporting_svc LOGIN CONNECTION LIMIT 20;

-- Per-role guardrails, applied at session start, no app code needed
ALTER ROLE api_svc       SET statement_timeout = '5s';
ALTER ROLE api_svc       SET idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '10s';
ALTER ROLE reporting_svc SET statement_timeout = '120s';
  1. CONNECTION LIMIT turns the budget into enforcement. A misconfigured reporting deploy can exhaust its own 20 slots and get errors, instead of exhausting the whole database and taking the API down with it.
  2. Per-role settings replace per-connection SET. This matters a lot once PgBouncer's transaction mode enters the picture, because SET doesn't survive there. ALTER ROLE ... SET is applied when the server connection starts, so it works through the pooler.
  3. Visibility. Combined with application_name, you can finally answer "who is using my connections?" in one query: 
SELECT usename, application_name, state, count(*)
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE backend_type = 'client backend'
GROUP BY usename, application_name, state
ORDER BY count(*) DESC;

If that query shows 180 connections in state idle and 6 in active, you've just learned that your database isn't busy, it's crowded. That's the signal for the next step.

When the math doesn't close: PgBouncer

At some point the budget stops working. You've got too many services, too many replicas, or serverless functions that each want their own connection, and the sum of pools is fundamentally bigger than what Postgres should hold. That's when you put a pooler between the apps and the database.

PgBouncer is the standard answer. It's lightweight (the docs cite about 2 kB of memory per client connection by default), and its key trick is that client connections and server connections are separate numbers. Thousands of app connections can map onto a few dozen real Postgres backends.

The pooling mode decides how aggressively that mapping happens:

  • session (the default): a server connection is assigned for the lifetime of the client connection. Safe, fully compatible, and it barely reduces server connections at all if your app pools hold connections open.
  • transaction: a server connection is assigned only for the duration of one transaction, then returned. This is where the multiplexing actually happens, and it's what you want for the "many services, one database" problem.
  • statement: returned after every statement. Multi-statement transactions aren't allowed. Rarely what you want.

A transaction-mode config for our hypothetical system might look like this:

pgbouncer.ini

[databases]
; per-database cap on real Postgres connections, across all users
appdb = host=10.0.0.5 port=5432 dbname=appdb max_db_connections=60

[pgbouncer]
listen_addr = 0.0.0.0
listen_port = 6432
auth_type = scram-sha-256
auth_file = /etc/pgbouncer/userlist.txt

pool_mode = transaction
max_client_conn = 5000        ; app-side connections PgBouncer will accept
default_pool_size = 20        ; server connections per (user, database) pair
reserve_pool_size = 5         ; extra server conns under load...
reserve_pool_timeout = 3      ; ...after a client waited this many seconds
max_prepared_statements = 200 ; protocol-level prepared statements in txn mode

query_wait_timeout = 30       ; client waiting for a server conn gives up
server_idle_timeout = 600
server_lifetime = 3600

Two things worth pointing out. First, default_pool_size is per user/database pair, so the one-role-per-service move from earlier now gives each service its own isolated server-side pool inside PgBouncer. Second, max_db_connections sits on top as a hard ceiling for the whole database, which is exactly the "one shared budget" idea expressed as config.

The app-side pools don't go away. Each pod still keeps a small pool of connections to PgBouncer, and those can be generous, since a client connection to PgBouncer is cheap. The expensive resource, a real Postgres backend, is now rationed in one place.

What transaction mode breaks

Transaction pooling isn't free, and the PgBouncer docs are blunt about it: clients must not rely on session-level state, because consecutive transactions can land on different server connections. Their compatibility table lists what never works in transaction mode:

  • SET / RESET (session settings leak or vanish; use ALTER ROLE ... SET or SET LOCAL inside a transaction instead)
  • LISTEN (notifications go to whichever backend you happened to be on)
  • WITH HOLD cursors
  • SQL-level PREPARE / DEALLOCATE
  • Temp tables with PRESERVE ROWS or DELETE ROWS (only ON COMMIT DROP is safe)
  • LOAD
  • Session-level advisory locks (pg_advisory_lock); the transaction-level pg_advisory_xact_lock variants are fine

The session-level advisory lock one deserves a warning, because it fails silently:

Warning
If a job runner uses pg_advisory_lock() for leader election behind PgBouncer in transaction mode, the lock is taken on one server connection and the "unlock" may run on another. The lock can outlive the job, or another instance can grab a different backend and believe it's the leader. Point those workloads at a session-mode pool or straight at Postgres.

A practical pattern is two PgBouncer databases pointing at the same Postgres: one in transaction mode for request/response traffic, one in session mode (per-database pool_mode is allowed in the [databases] section) for migrations, LISTEN-based consumers, and anything that needs session state.

Prepared statements used to be the deal-breaker

For years, the standard advice was "turn off prepared statements if you use PgBouncer in transaction mode," because a statement prepared on one backend doesn't exist on the next. PgBouncer 1.21 changed that: with max_prepared_statements set to a non-zero value, PgBouncer tracks protocol-level prepares and re-prepares them transparently on whichever server connection the client lands on. Through 1.23 that setting defaulted to 0 (off); since 1.24 it defaults to 200.

The catch: it only covers protocol-level prepared statements, the kind drivers send through the extended query protocol. A literal PREPARE foo AS ... in SQL is still invisible to PgBouncer and still breaks. And if you're on a managed pooler or an older PgBouncer, check the version before assuming it works.

PgBouncer has its own ceiling

PgBouncer is single-threaded. One process uses one CPU core, no matter how big the box is. For most setups that's plenty, but a very busy pooler can become the bottleneck itself. Since 1.12 you can run several processes on the same port with so_reuseport = 1 and let the kernel spread client connections across them, and newer versions add peer_id plus a [peers] section so cancellation requests reach the right process.

Here's the gotcha that brings us right back to the start of this article: each PgBouncer process has its own pools. Four processes with default_pool_size = 20 can open up to 80 server connections per user/database pair, not 20. Run PgBouncer as a sidecar in every app pod and you've rebuilt the original multiplication problem with extra steps. The pooler only centralizes the budget if it's actually central, or if you divide the per-process limits by the number of processes.

Watching the budget

Once the pooler is in place, you've got two queues to watch: the one inside each app (waitingCount in node-postgres, Stat() in pgxpool) and the one inside PgBouncer. Connect to the admin console and run:

SHOW POOLS;

The columns that matter are cl_active (clients linked to a server connection, or idle with nothing waiting), cl_waiting (clients waiting for one), sv_active / sv_idle (server connections in use or parked), and maxwait (how long the oldest waiting client has been waiting). A healthy transaction-mode pool under load looks like a lot of clients, a small number of active server connections, and cl_waiting that blips and drains. A maxwait that keeps climbing means the database-side budget really is too small for the work, or, more often, that some transaction is holding its server connection far too long.

On the Postgres side, the pg_stat_activity query from earlier is still your ground truth. The number you care about isn't count(*). It's count(*) WHERE state = 'active', compared against your core count.

Where this leaves you

If I had to compress all of this into one opinion, it's this: raising max_connections is almost never the fix. It's the database equivalent of widening the highway entrance while leaving the bridge the same width. Postgres 14 made idle connections cheap, so a bigger number won't crash you the way it used to, but it also won't give you more throughput, because throughput is bounded by cores and I/O, not slots.

The playbook, in order of how cheap it is:

  1. Count what you've actually got: sum pool_max * max_replicas * surge across every service and compare it to the real budget.
  2. Shorten W. Get network calls out of transactions, set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout, and fix nested checkouts. This often shrinks the needed pool by more than any tuning.
  3. Set explicit client pool limits and a connection-acquire timeout, and graph the waiting count.
  4. Give each service its own role with a CONNECTION LIMIT and per-role timeouts.
  5. When the sum still doesn't fit, put PgBouncer in transaction mode in front, with max_db_connections as the single shared ceiling, and route session-dependent workloads around it.

Queues are fine. You're always going to have one somewhere. The whole game is choosing where it lives, and the right answer is in your app or your pooler, where waiting is cheap, not inside Postgres, where every extra waiter makes everyone else slower.

Originally published at andriiboyko.com.

title: EASformer: Environment-Action-State Alignment for Industrial Generative Ranking
description:
arXiv:2610.27691v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Modern industrial ranking systems increasingly adopt generative recommendation (GR) paradigms, in which user behavior sequences and non-sequential (NS) features are tokenized and jointly modeled by Transformer-style backbones. This unified formulation provides a scalable interface for modeling long histories and heterogeneous features. However, sequence and NS representations often carry asymmetric semantics: historical representations may combine environment context with observed-action semantics, whereas candidate-side NS representations contain no observed action but incorporate richer supplementary context, such as user-item interaction features and recent behavior lists. Direct interaction between such representations can make query-key dot products compare different semantic objects, limiting meaningful cross-token interaction. To fill this gap, we propose EASformer, an Environment-Action-State disentangled architecture for industrial app ranking. EASformer constructs an explicitly aligned context environment space shared by historical and non-sequence tokens, while disentangling user actions from historical token and candidate-specific context form non-sequence tokens. Based on this aligned space, EASformer enables complementary historical action retrieval and state-conditioned action prediction. Furthermore, the disentangled design supports a Cloze-style self-supervised objective by masking historical actions and reusing the candidate prediction pathway. On an offline benchmark from a real-world industrial app marketplace, EASformer achieves an AUC of 0.89411, yielding a 0.88% relative improvement over the deployed baseline. Online A/B tests further support this advantage, with relative eCPM lifts of 1.26% and 3.94% across two real-world ranking scenarios.

title: Three font files preload on every page of our site, and on five of the six I measured one of them has nothing to render
description:
CogniPrep's root layout loads three font families, from two different mechanisms:

import { GeistSans } from 'geist/font/sans';
import { GeistMono } from 'geist/font/mono';
import { Space_Grotesk } from 'next/font/google';

const spaceGrotesk = Space_Grotesk({
  subsets: ['latin'],
  variable: '--font-space-grotesk',
  display: 'swap',
  preload: true, // Preload to prevent font flash in header
  adjustFontFallback: true,
});

All three variable classes go on <html>:

<html className={`${GeistSans.variable} ${GeistMono.variable} ${spaceGrotesk.variable}`}>

and globals.css turns them into Tailwind v4 theme tokens:

@theme {
  --font-sans: var(--font-geist-sans), ui-sans-serif, system-ui, sans-serif, ...;
  --font-mono: var(--font-geist-mono), ui-monospace, SFMono-Regular, 'SF Mono', Menlo, ...;
  --font-brand: var(--font-space-grotesk), var(--font-geist-sans), ui-sans-serif, ...;
}

That reads like a tidy three-tier type system: body, code, brand. Here is what the browser is actually asked to fetch.

Three preloads, 163 KB, on every page 

curl -s https://cogniprep.app/ | grep -o '<link rel="preload"[^>]*woff2[^>]*>'

Three hits, and the sizes:

File Bytes Family
Geist_Variable-s.p.*.woff2 69,652 Geist Sans, weights 100 to 900
GeistMono_Variable.p.*.woff2 71,368 Geist Mono, weights 100 to 900
0c89a48fa5027cee-s.p.*.woff2 22,320 Space Grotesk, latin subset

163,340 bytes of woff2 at rel=preload, which is the browser's "fetch this before you need it" priority, on /, /pricing, /blogs, /games/<provider> and /login. I checked all five: identical three preloads, because the thing that triggers a next/font preload is the font being referenced by the layout that wraps the route, not a glyph being painted.

One of them paints nothing on most pages

The only way to use Geist Mono here is the font-mono utility, so counting it in the delivered HTML counts the font's entire job on that page:

for p in / /login /pricing /blogs /about /signup; do
  printf "%s %s\n" "$p" "$(curl -s https://cogniprep.app$p | grep -o 'font-mono' | wc -l)"
done

/        112
/login     0
/pricing   0
/blogs     0
/about     0
/signup    0

The homepage's 112 are one string counted twice: 56 in the rendered markup and the same 56 in the RSC payload that follows it, every one of them a two-digit index beside a provider name (<span class="font-mono text-xs text-white/30">01</span>). The other five pages use it zero times, and still pay 71,368 bytes of preload: 44% of the font budget on those pages, fetched at high priority, to render nothing at all.

Across the app, 40 files reference font-mono, and they are all the same genre of text: a user id on the profile page, a support ticket reference, an error digest in the error boundary, a kbd hint in the search box. Real uses, all of them, and none of them worth a preload on a sign-up form.

While I was in there: the token with no utility

Tailwind v4 generates a utility for every @theme key, so --font-brand should give us font-brand. Search the live stylesheet:

# the big stylesheet is 245,213 bytes
grep -c '\.font-brand{' big.css   # 0
grep -o '\-\-font-brand:[^;]*' big.css
# --font-brand:var(--font-space-grotesk), var(--font-geist-sans), ui-sans-serif, ...

The variable ships. The class does not, because Tailwind v4 only emits utilities it sees used, and all four places that want the brand font do this instead:

<span style={{ fontFamily: 'var(--font-brand)' }}>CogniPrep</span>

Four components: the public footer, the dashboard header, the auth layout and the shared brand lockup. The inline style works, so nothing is broken, which is exactly why it survived. The cost is that a @theme entry that exists to generate a utility now exists to generate a variable that four files read by hand.

And the subset that is not a subset

We asked for subsets: ['latin']. The emitted CSS has three @font-face blocks for Space Grotesk:

Unicode range Bytes Preloaded
latin 22,320 yes
latin-ext 18,924 no
vietnamese 6,772 no

This is next/font/google behaving correctly and counter to how the option reads. subsets controls what gets a preload hint, not what gets declared. The other two faces sit in the stylesheet with their unicode-range and are fetched only if a character in that range is painted. For a site whose public copy is English, those two files are a rounding error that never downloads. Worth knowing before you file a bug about it.

One more detail from the same CSS, for anyone chasing layout shift: two of the three families get a metrics-adjusted fallback and one does not.

@font-face{font-family:GeistSans Fallback;src:local(Arial);
  ascent-override:94.56%;descent-override:27.76%;size-adjust:106.28%}
@font-face{font-family:Space Grotesk Fallback;src:local(Arial);
  ascent-override:89.71%;descent-override:26.62%;size-adjust:109.69%}

Geist Mono has no fallback face at all, just a stack ending in monospace. With font-display: swap on all three, a slow font fetch means sans and brand text swaps into a size-matched Arial and mono text swaps into whatever the OS calls monospace at its own metrics. For the amount of mono text on this site that is the right trade, and it is another argument for the font not being in the critical path.

What I would change

  1. Take Geist Mono out of the root layout. It is 71 KB preloaded for a user id and a ticket reference. Either declare --font-mono as a plain system stack (ui-monospace, SFMono-Regular, Menlo, monospace), which is what the fallback already renders on a slow connection, or load it with preload: false so it is fetched when a page that uses it asks.
  2. Measure preloads per page, not per config. Everything above came from one grep against production HTML. The config file said "three fonts"; only production says "three fonts, on every route, before paint".
  3. Leave the brand font alone. 22 KB for the wordmark on every page is real, but the wordmark is on every page, in the header and the footer, and the fallback metrics mean the swap does not move the layout. That one is paying for itself.

The general shape of this: preload on a font is a statement about the whole route group, and the route group is "everything the layout wraps". If a font is used by 1 page in 6, it does not belong in the layout that wraps all 6.

See it

Every number above is measurable from a terminal against the live site. Open DevTools, filter Network by Font, and load the homepage (three woff2, one of which renders those small provider numbers), then the login page and the pricing page, where the same three arrive and the monospace one has no character to draw. The wordmark in the header and footer of the about page is the Space Grotesk face, set by an inline style rather than a Tailwind class, and the blog index is the biggest document of the six I measured, at 674,168 bytes of HTML, if you want a page where 71 KB of unused font is not the largest thing in flight.

title: How to Run a Local LLM on a Laptop With 8 GB of RAM
description:
Running modern artificial intelligence models locally usually conjures images of expensive multi-GPU desktop rigs. However, recent advances in model quantization and lightweight inference runtimes have made it entirely feasible to run local llm low ram setups on modest hardware, such as an 8 GB RAM laptop.

While you will not be executing massive 70-billion parameter models on a standard consumer laptop, you can successfully run smaller, highly optimized models locally. This approach keeps your data private, works completely offline, and costs nothing in API fees. This guide covers how to prepare your hardware, choose the right models, and execute them efficiently within strict memory limits.

Understanding the Constraints of 8 GB RAM

Before executing any commands, it is crucial to understand where system resources go. On an 8 GB laptop, your operating system typically consumes between 2 GB and 3 GB of RAM just sitting idle. That leaves roughly 5 GB of RAM available for your LLM and any other running applications.

Memory bandwidth is the primary bottleneck on consumer laptops. Integrated graphics and standard system memory share the same memory bus, which means token generation speeds will be slower than on dedicated hardware. To make this work, you must use quantized models. Quantization reduces the precision of model weights, typically from 16-bit floating-point down to 4-bit integers. This drastically shrinks the memory footprint of the model with only a minor degradation in output quality.

Choosing the Right Runtime and Models

The most efficient way to manage local inference on resource-constrained hardware is through Ollama or llama.cpp. These tools handle memory mapping and can offload computation efficiently. For an 8 GB RAM machine, you should strictly target models in the 1 billion to 3 billion parameter range, quantized to 4 bits or 5 bits.

Good candidate models include:

  • Llama 3.2 (3B): Offers strong reasoning capabilities for its size and fits comfortably within a low memory budget.
  • Phi-3.5 Mini (3.8B): Microsoft's compact model performs exceptionally well on coding and logic tasks.
  • Qwen 2.5 (1.5B or 3B): Extremely fast execution speeds on low-end hardware with solid multilingual support.

A 3B model quantized to 4 bits (often denoted as Q4_K_M) requires approximately 2 GB to 2.5 GB of RAM. This leaves enough headroom for your operating system to avoid thrashing into swap memory.

Step-by-Step Setup Guide

Follow these steps to set up a local inference environment using Ollama on your machine. This process assumes a standard installation on macOS, Linux, or Windows via WSL2.

First, download and install Ollama from the official source or use your package manager. Once installed, start the background service.

To ensure your laptop does not run out of memory, pull a model specifically sized for low-resource systems. Open your terminal and execute the following command:

ollama run qwen2.5:3b

If you want to verify memory usage while the model is loaded, you can check your system monitor or run the list command in a separate terminal window:

ollama list

You can interact with the model directly in the terminal. To optimize performance further, you can adjust the context window size. By default, some models allocate space for 8,192 or 16,384 tokens, which consumes unnecessary RAM. You can create a custom model file to restrict the context window to 2,048 tokens, preserving memory for generation:

FROM qwen2.5:3b
PARAMETER num_ctx 2048

Save this text in a file named Modelfile, then build and run it locally:

ollama create small-qwen -f ./Modelfile
ollama run small-qwen

By capping the context window, you prevent the KV cache from expanding uncontrollably and causing your system to freeze due to out-of-memory errors.

Performance Optimization and Best Practices

Running an LLM on 8 GB of RAM requires discipline regarding your host system. Close memory-heavy applications like web browsers with numerous tabs open before launching your inference runtime.

If you notice severe lag or system stuttering, the model is likely exceeding your available physical RAM and spilling over into virtual memory on your storage drive. Solid-state drives mitigate this slowdown somewhat, but disk read and write speeds are still orders of magnitude slower than physical RAM. If this occurs, switch to a smaller 1.5B parameter model like qwen2.5:1.5b.

Monitor your CPU and memory usage using built-in utilities like Task Manager on Windows, Activity Monitor on macOS, or htop on Linux. Keeping an eye on these metrics helps you find the exact balance between model capability and system stability.

A Practical Option for Windows Users

If you are looking for a complete application setup rather than managing raw terminal commands, there are various desktop clients designed to interface with local runtimes. One practical option for Windows users who want a local AI companion with a Live2D face is YUNA, which you can find at https://ko-fi.com/s/45662d5cc0. This tool provides an alternative interface for running local models without requiring manual script configuration every time you want to chat.

Disclosure: I am the developer of YUNA, the software mentioned in the last section.

title: How to Evaluate a Polarion Alternative: Traceability, Workflows, and Deployment
description:
When requirements, tests, approvals, and delivery work are tracked in disconnected places, teams have to reconcile status manually and can lose visibility into ownership and traceability. The practical way to choose a replacement for Polarion is to evaluate how well each platform supports your full delivery lifecycle—not just its task views.

Start by listing the records your teams need to connect, then compare configuration and governance needs, check deployment constraints, and test the platform using a representative project. The three platforms below illustrate different priorities: configurable delivery workflows, formal lifecycle traceability, and collaborative requirements definition.

Compare platforms by lifecycle fit

Platform Best suited to Deployment options in the source Project and workflow fit Requirements and test fit
ONES.com Product, R&D, and complex delivery teams Cloud, private cloud, on-premise, and air-gapped Configurable fields, statuses, issue types, layouts, link types, workflows, Agile planning, reporting, and automation Shared project and knowledge context, with test management for connected delivery processes
Polarion ALM Large-scale, regulated, and traceability-focused development Cloud and on-premise Structured lifecycle processes, configurable permissions, workflow automation, and reusable project data Requirements authoring, change control, traceability, and centralized test management
Jama Connect Collaborative requirements planning and review Cloud Review-oriented collaboration and structured project records Requirements relationships, approvals, and review evidence

1. Map the lifecycle records that must stay connected

List the objects your teams need to manage and relate. Depending on the lifecycle, these may include requirements, user stories, risks, defects, tests, approvals, releases, and supporting knowledge.

Then identify the relationships that matter. For example, a team may need to follow a requirement through implementation and verification, or understand how a change affects related tests and release progress. A platform should make the necessary relationships visible without requiring parallel spreadsheets or manual status reconciliation.

2. Separate configuration needs from process complexity

Some organizations need formal, predefined controls for regulated work. Others need a configurable framework that supports different delivery methods across teams. These are related but distinct questions: a complex process does not automatically mean every team needs the same workflow.

Compare the configuration points that affect your operating model: fields, statuses, issue types, layouts, permissions, workflow rules, link types, and automation. Also consider how teams will coordinate planning, reporting, and collaboration alongside requirements and tests.

When configurable project workflows are the priority

ONES.com is relevant when teams want a configurable project management foundation for planning and delivery across product, engineering, QA, and other functions. It supports configurable work items and workflows, Agile planning, reporting, automation, and shared project and knowledge context. Its deployment options include cloud, private cloud, on-premise, and air-gapped models.

This flexibility means teams should agree on governance standards before configurations spread across departments. Project templates, permissions, fields, and statuses need enough consistency to support shared reporting while leaving room for project-specific needs.

When formal traceability is the priority

Polarion ALM is designed for product development where requirements, approvals, tests, changes, and releases need to remain connected. Its strengths include requirements authoring and management, traceability, configurable permissions and workflows, centralized test management, and cloud or on-premise deployment.

For a broader platform evaluation, also assess how it supports portfolio coordination, team-level planning, reporting, and collaboration outside the core ALM process.

When requirements reviews are the priority

Jama Connect focuses on helping product and engineering stakeholders define, review, approve, and relate requirements. Its review processes and linked records can help make ownership, decisions, and approval evidence easier to follow. The source describes it as a cloud platform.

If the organization also needs broad delivery workflows or multiple deployment models, check whether a requirements-centered platform covers the complete lifecycle or whether it needs to work alongside other systems.

3. Check deployment and governance before designing workflows

Confirm deployment constraints early. Cloud can reduce infrastructure responsibility, while on-premise, private cloud, or air-gapped options may better match an organization’s security, infrastructure, or data-governance requirements. Availability differs by platform, so verify that the required model is supported before investing time in detailed configuration.

Also clarify who can view and change governed information, how workflows are controlled, and whether multiple teams or business units need shared standards. These requirements affect both platform fit and the effort needed to maintain configurations.

4. Evaluate with a representative project

Use a real project sample that includes changing requirements, cross-team dependencies, review gates, test activity, and reporting needs. Walk through the lifecycle from requirement to implementation, verification, and release, using the records and relationships your team identified earlier.

Check whether the platform supports the complete operating process or only works well in a simplified demonstration. Note where teams would need manual reconciliation, separate records, or additional governance decisions. This gives stakeholders a consistent basis for comparing platforms against their actual requirements.

Choose based on the work your teams need to coordinate

ONES.com is oriented toward configurable project and R&D delivery workflows; Polarion ALM is oriented toward formal lifecycle control and requirements-to-test traceability; Jama Connect is oriented toward collaborative requirements definition and review. The right fit depends on which of those needs is central and how each platform handles the rest of your lifecycle.

Make the decision against a representative project, governance model, deployment requirement, and end-to-end delivery process. That is more reliable than choosing from feature counts or isolated demonstrations.

title: Lazy‑Loading Reasoning Chunks in Documedic CDSS
description:
Lazy‑Loading Reasoning Chunks in Documedic CDSS

Documedic is a clinical decision support system (CDSS) that delivers AI‑generated recommendations to clinicians through a web interface built with NestJS, React, PostgreSQL, and the OpenRouter API. One of the most visible performance bottlenecks in a CDSS is the size of the reasoning data that accompanies each recommendation. The reasoning is a multi‑paragraph explanation of how the AI arrived at a decision, and it is often several kilobytes long. When every recommendation is loaded eagerly, the initial bundle size grows, the page takes longer to render, and the user experience suffers, especially on mobile devices. This is where cdss pays off in practice.

The Problem

  • Large payloads – A typical reasoning chunk can be 5–10 KB of plain text. When a clinician opens a patient case, dozens of recommendations may be displayed, each with its own reasoning.
  • Slow initial render – React must download and parse all of the reasoning text before it can paint the UI. On a 3G connection, this can add several seconds to the load time.
  • Resource waste – Most clinicians read only a handful of recommendations. Loading all reasoning data upfront means the browser downloads data that may never be viewed.

The Solution: Lazy‑Loading Reasoning Chunks

Documedic solves this problem by deferring the download of reasoning until it is needed. The approach is a three‑layer architecture:

  1. Backend API – A NestJS controller receives a request for a specific recommendation ID. It calls OpenRouter to generate the reasoning, stores the result in PostgreSQL, and returns a JSON payload containing only the recommendation text.
  2. Frontend Lazy Component – The React app uses React.lazy and Suspense to load a ReasoningChunk component on demand. The component fetches the reasoning from the backend when it becomes visible.
  3. IntersectionObserver Trigger – An observer watches the ReasoningChunk placeholder. When the user scrolls near the chunk, the observer triggers the fetch, ensuring the network request is made only when the user is likely to read the content.

Backend Implementation

The NestJS controller is minimal. It receives the recommendation ID, calls the OpenRouter client, writes the reasoning to PostgreSQL, and returns the recommendation text. Getting cdss right early saves rework later.

// src/recommendations/recommendations.controller.ts
import { Controller, Get, Param } from '@nestjs/common';
import { RecommendationsService } from './recommendations.service';

@Controller('recommendations')
export class RecommendationsController {
  constructor(private readonly service: RecommendationsService) {}

  @Get(':id')
  async getRecommendation(@Param('id') id: string) {
    const rec = await this.service.getRecommendation(id);
    return { text: rec.text };
  }
}

The service layer handles the OpenRouter call and database interaction.

// src/recommendations/recommendations.service.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { OpenRouterClient } from '@openrouter/client';
import { PrismaService } from '../prisma/prisma.service';

@Injectable()
export class RecommendationsService {
  private readonly openRouter = new OpenRouterClient({ apiKey: process.env.OPENROUTER_KEY });

  constructor(private readonly prisma: PrismaService) {}

  async getRecommendation(id: string) {
    // Retrieve cached reasoning if present
    const cached = await this.prisma.recommendation.findUnique({ where: { id } });
    if (cached) return cached;

    // Generate reasoning via OpenRouter
    const { text } = await this.openRouter.generate({ prompt: `Explain recommendation ${id}` });

    // Persist to PostgreSQL
    return this.prisma.recommendation.create({ data: { id, text } });
  }
}

The Prisma schema defines a simple table:

model Recommendation {
  id   String @id
  text String
}

Frontend Implementation

On the client side, the Recommendation component renders the recommendation text and a lazy‑loaded placeholder for the reasoning.

// src/components/Recommendation.tsx
import React, { useRef, useEffect, useState, Suspense } from 'react';

const ReasoningChunk = React.lazy(() => import('./ReasoningChunk'));

export const Recommendation: React.FC<{ id: string; text: string }> = ({ id, text }) => {
  const placeholderRef = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const [visible, setVisible] = useState(false);

  useEffect(() => {
    const observer = new IntersectionObserver(
      ([entry]) => {
        if (entry.isIntersecting) setVisible(true);
      },
      { rootMargin: '200px' },
    );
    if (placeholderRef.current) observer.observe(placeholderRef.current);
    return () => observer.disconnect();
  }, []);

  return (
    <div className="recommendation">
      <p>{text}</p>
      <div ref={placeholderRef} className="reasoning-placeholder">
        {visible && (
          <Suspense fallback={<div>Loading reasoning…</div>}>
            <ReasoningChunk recommendationId={id} />
          </Suspense>
        )}
      </div>
    </div>
  );
};

The ReasoningChunk component performs the fetch when it mounts. Good cdss keeps the rest of the workflow predictable.

// src/components/ReasoningChunk.tsx
import React, { useEffect, useState } from 'react';

export const ReasoningChunk: React.FC<{ recommendationId: string }> = ({ recommendationId }) => {
  const [reasoning, setReasoning] = useState<string>('');

  useEffect(() => {
    fetch(`/api/recommendations/${recommendationId}`)
      .then((res) => res.json())
      .then((data) => setReasoning(data.text));
  }, [recommendationId]);

  return <pre>{reasoning}</pre>;
};

Resulting User Experience

  • Fast first paint – The recommendation text is rendered immediately; the reasoning placeholder is a lightweight <div>.
  • On‑demand data – The network request for the reasoning is made only when the user scrolls close to the chunk, saving bandwidth.
  • Consistent performance – Even on slow connections, the UI remains responsive because heavy text is loaded asynchronously.

Integration with the CDSS Workflow

When a clinician opens a patient case, the page loads a list of recommendations. Each recommendation is rendered with the component above. The lazy‑loading strategy keeps the initial payload small, allowing the clinician to focus on the most critical information without waiting for all AI explanations to download. When the clinician decides to explore a recommendation further, the reasoning appears seamlessly, preserving the flow of clinical decision support.

Conclusion

Documedic’s lazy‑loading of reasoning chunks is a concrete example of how careful architectural choices can improve the performance of a medical AI CDSS. By combining NestJS, React, PostgreSQL, and OpenRouter, the system delivers high‑quality AI explanations without compromising the speed clinicians expect from a clinical decision support tool.

Related reading

  • Encounter lifecycle enforcement in Documedic CDSS
  • Hardening Document Extraction in a NestJS CDSS

title: Reflection AI's Beam now available on AI Gateway for free
description:
Beam from Reflection AI, previously available in stealth as stealth/cat-jam, is now available on AI Gateway. Beam is free to use for a limited time during the launch period when serviced by Reflection AI.

Beam is an low latency US open-weight reasoning model for coding and agentic tasks, with weights released under Apache 2.0. Beam supports tool calling and structured outputs, with a 1M-token context window for code, documents, and conversation history. Reasoning effort is adjustable. Beam is designed for speed, activating only 23B of its 501B parameters per token and avoiding tokens a task doesn't need, so it tends to reach answers sooner than larger open models.

There are 2 ways to access Beam for free:

  • Using the standard model name (reflection/beam with provider reflection). When the free period ends, the model slug will automatically transfer over to pricing with no downtime.

  • Using the -free suffix to the standard name (reflection/beam-free). The model will stop serving when the free offer ends.

To use it in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and more, install the latest Vercel CLI and run setup:

Then select reflection/beam or reflection/beam-free in the agent. See the coding agents guide for details.

Try Beam in the model playground.

AI Gateway provides a unified API for calling models, tracking usage and cost, and configuring retries, failover, and performance optimizations for higher-than-provider uptime. It includes built-in custom reporting, Zero Data Retention support, budgets for API keys, routing rules, and more.

AI Gateway reflects provider pricing with no markup and does not charge a platform fee on inference, including on Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) requests.

title: Language Impairment as a Lens onto Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.28992v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Although large language models (LLMs) encode language in highly distributed spaces, they remain vulnerable to focal disruptions---a phenomenon strikingly similar to how localized brain damage causes clinical aphasia in humans. To investigate this theoretical tension, we ask whether LLMs possess a functional structure analogous to the human language system, by introducing a novel mechanistic interpretability framework inspired by aphasia. Through two complementary approaches, classifier-guided lesioning and continuous activation steering, we systematically induce aphasia-like breakdowns in LLMs. We find that language functions can be successfully isolated to discrete structural circuits and continuous representational vectors, yet these functions remain densely entangled with significant circuit overlap and vector similarities across distinct aphasic profiles. Furthermore, while steering generalizes robustly across downstream tasks, structural lesioning remains asymmetrically constrained. By bridging neuropsychology and mechanistic interpretability, we demonstrate that LLMs, functionally analogous to biological brains, rely on a densely entangled architecture that can be systematically mapped through clinically-informed interventions.

title: Conditional Imaging for Privacy-Preserving Visual Sensing
description:
arXiv:2610.28835v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Conventional visual sensing faces a fundamental dilemma: information that should remain private today may need to be recovered tomorrow. This challenge is becoming increasingly important as cameras become pervasive in our daily surroundings. Existing safeguards either protect visual content only after an image is formed or suppress information during capture in ways that prevent its later recovery. Here, we show through an information-theoretic analysis that privacy and recoverability cannot be achieved simultaneously in static optical systems. Information preserved in a measurement for later reconstruction also remains available to an observer of that measurement, limiting the privacy such systems can provide. To overcome this limitation, we introduce conditional imaging, an imaging approach that changes the optical state for every captured frame. The measurement alone conceals the scene, while knowledge of the corresponding physical system state enables its reconstruction. We analyze how the optical parameters determine the information that can be recovered and use this analysis to guide the design of a camera prototype. We evaluate the system on a captured dataset of human faces using increasingly powerful attempts to recover the scene, from direct visualization and computational inversion to learned reconstruction and identity recognition. Our experiments show that conditional imaging preserves identity in authorized reconstructions while withholding visual information from observers without access to the system state. By making the physical state of the camera part of the information needed for reconstruction, conditional imaging enables visual information to be protected at the point of capture while remaining recoverable for future authorized use.

title: Solving the Dual-Write Problem: Implementing an Async Transactional Outbox with Idempotent DLQ in Python
description:
Every distributed backend eventually confronts a deceptively simple requirement: persist a state change in a relational database and notify an external service via an HTTP webhook or message broker. In an e-commerce checkout flow, a service inserts a record into an orders table and immediately dispatches an order.created webhook to a billing or fulfillment consumer.

Executing those two operations sequentially inside a single request handler introduces the Dual-Write Problem—one of the most common sources of silent data corruption in microservice architectures:

  1. Commit-First Failure (Lost Events): The service commits the order to the database and then issues an HTTP POST to the webhook endpoint. If a transient DNS failure, timeout, or 502 Bad Gateway occurs—or if the process crashes right after COMMIT—the order is recorded and charged, but the downstream service never receives the event.
  2. Publish-First Failure (Phantom Events): Emitting the webhook before committing the database transaction is equally dangerous. If a constraint violation or deadlock triggers a ROLLBACK, downstream services act on a phantom order that never existed in the database.
  3. In-Transaction Network I/O (Lock Contention): Holding an open database transaction across an outbound HTTP call ties up locks during network latency and still fails if the final commit errors after the webhook returns 200 OK.
  4. Blind Retries Without Idempotency (Duplicates): When a timeout occurs after the receiver processes the request but before the HTTP response arrives, naive retries re-send the payload, causing double charges and duplicate shipments.

To eliminate dual writes without the availability penalties of Two-Phase Commit (2PC), production systems combine the Transactional Outbox Pattern with Cryptographic Idempotency and an automated Dead-Letter Queue (DLQ).

In this tutorial, we will architect a complete, strictly typed Python 3.11+ reference system using asyncio, aiosqlite in Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) mode, httpx, Pydantic v2, and FastAPI.

Section 1: Anatomy of the Transactional Outbox Pattern

The core insight behind the Transactional Outbox pattern is converting an unsafe cross-network dual write into a single local ACID transaction. Instead of calling the remote webhook during order creation, the business transaction persists both the domain entity (orders) and the domain event (outbox) inside the same database engine.

flowchart TD
    Client["Client Application"] -->|"1. OrderCreate"| Tx["SQLite ACID Transaction (BEGIN IMMEDIATE)"]

    subgraph SQLite_WAL["SQLite Database (WAL Mode + Foreign Keys)"]
        Tx -->|"INSERT"| OrdersTable[("Table: orders")]
        Tx -->|"INSERT (status = PENDING)"| OutboxTable[("Table: outbox")]
        DLQTable[("Table: dead_letter_queue")]
    end

    OutboxTable -->|"2. Poll Batch (PENDING -> PROCESSING)"| Dispatcher["OutboxDispatcher (asyncio + httpx)"]
    Dispatcher -->|"3. HTTP POST /webhooks + Header: Idempotency-Key"| Consumer["FastAPI Webhook Consumer"]

    Consumer -->|"200 OK (Processed or Deduplicated)"| SuccessUpdate["UPDATE outbox SET status = PUBLISHED"]
    SuccessUpdate --> OutboxTable

    Consumer -->|"5xx / Timeout (retry_count < max_delivery_attempts)"| RetryUpdate["Increment retry_count + Exponential Backoff + Revert to PENDING"]
    RetryUpdate --> OutboxTable

    Consumer -->|"5xx / Timeout (retry_count >= max_delivery_attempts)"| QuarantineTx["Atomic Quarantine Transaction"]
    QuarantineTx -->|"UPDATE status = DEAD_LETTER"| OutboxTable
    QuarantineTx -->|"INSERT poison event"| DLQTable

The Four-State Event Lifecycle

Every event stored in the outbox table progresses through a strictly enforced state machine defined by the EventStatus enumeration in models.py:

  • PENDING: Initial state assigned inside the atomic transaction alongside the orders insertion.
  • PROCESSING: Lease state applied atomically when OutboxDispatcher claims a batch (batch_size), preventing concurrent poll cycles from picking up in-flight records.
  • PUBLISHED: Terminal success state reached once the receiver responds with HTTP 200 OK.
  • DEAD_LETTER: Terminal quarantine state reached when an event exhausts max_delivery_attempts. The dispatcher atomically updates outbox to DEAD_LETTER and copies the event into dead_letter_queue, preventing Head-of-Line blocking.

Section 2: Cryptographic Idempotency with Canonical SHA-256 Hashing

Because the Transactional Outbox pattern provides At-Least-Once delivery, an event can be delivered more than once if a connection drops after the consumer processes the payload.

Generating a random UUID inside the HTTP client before each retry fails to guarantee deduplication because the key changes on every attempt. Likewise, hashing raw JSON strings directly is brittle: different dictionary key orderings or whitespace ({"a": 1, "b": 2} vs {"b":2,"a":1}) produce completely different hashes for identical domain data.

In models.py, we solve this deterministically by canonicalizing the JSON payload—sorting keys lexicographically and stripping whitespace—before computing a 64-character hexadecimal SHA-256 digest:

def canonicalize_json_payload(payload: Union[dict[str, Any], str, BaseModel]) -> str:
    if isinstance(payload, BaseModel):
        parsed_data: Any = payload.model_dump(mode="json")
    elif isinstance(payload, str):
        parsed_data = json.loads(payload)
    elif isinstance(payload, dict):
        parsed_data = payload
    else:
        raise TypeError(f"Unsupported payload type: {type(payload).__name__}")

    return json.dumps(parsed_data, sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":"), ensure_ascii=False)


def compute_idempotency_key(payload: Union[dict[str, Any], str, BaseModel]) -> str:
    canonical_json: str = canonicalize_json_payload(payload)
    return hashlib.sha256(canonical_json.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()

This digest is persisted in outbox.idempotency_key (UNIQUE) and transmitted in the Idempotency-Key HTTP header on every delivery attempt.

Section 3: Architecture & System Layout

The project is organized into modular components with strict Python 3.11+ static typing (Union, Optional, Callable) and frozen Pydantic v2 settings (ConfigDict(frozen=True) in config.py):

async-transactional-outbox-dlq/
├── AGENTS.md           # Engineering standards and architectural rules
├── README.md           # Quickstart and architecture overview
├── ARTICLE.md          # Technical deep-dive tutorial
├── requirements.txt    # Runtime and test dependencies
├── config.py           # Immutable AppConfig and structured JSON log formatter
├── models.py           # Pydantic v2 schemas, EventStatus, and SHA-256 canonicalizer
├── database.py         # Async SQLite WAL initialization and ACID transactions
├── dispatcher.py       # Background OutboxDispatcher worker with backoff and DLQ
├── mock_consumer.py    # FastAPI idempotent webhook server with failure injection
├── main.py             # Live 4-cycle end-to-end console demonstration
└── test_outbox.py      # Async pytest verification suite

Why SQLite with Write-Ahead Logging (WAL)?

Standard SQLite rollback journals lock the database file during writes, triggering SQLITE_BUSY errors when a background worker polls while business transactions write. In database.py, every connection initializes WAL mode and referential integrity:

async def configure_connection(conn: aiosqlite.Connection) -> None:
    conn.row_factory = aiosqlite.Row
    await conn.execute("PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL;")
    await conn.execute("PRAGMA foreign_keys=ON;")
    await conn.execute("PRAGMA synchronous=NORMAL;")
    await conn.execute("PRAGMA busy_timeout=5000;")

In WAL mode, writes are appended sequentially to a write-ahead log (*-wal), allowing concurrent business writes and OutboxDispatcher reads/updates to proceed without blocking one another.

Section 4: Implementation Deep-Dive

4.1 Atomic Business and Outbox Persistence (database.py)

In create_order_with_outbox_event(), we open the SQLite connection with manual transaction control (isolation_level=None) and execute BEGIN IMMEDIATE;. Both orders and outbox rows are inserted within the same transaction; any exception triggers an immediate ROLLBACK:

    await conn.execute("BEGIN IMMEDIATE;")
    try:
        await conn.execute(
            "INSERT INTO orders (id, customer_email, amount, status, created_at) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?);",
            (order_record.id, order_record.customer_email, order_record.amount, order_record.status, order_record.created_at),
        )
        if failure_injector is not None:
            failure_injector()

        await conn.execute(
            """
            INSERT INTO outbox (
                id, event_type, payload_json, idempotency_key,
                status, retry_count, last_error, created_at, updated_at
            ) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?);
            """,
            (
                outbox_event.id, outbox_event.event_type, outbox_event.payload_json,
                outbox_event.idempotency_key, outbox_event.status.value,
                outbox_event.retry_count, outbox_event.last_error,
                outbox_event.created_at, outbox_event.updated_at,
            ),
        )
        await conn.execute("COMMIT;")
        return order_record, outbox_event
    except Exception:
        await conn.execute("ROLLBACK;")
        raise

The optional failure_injector callback allows tests to inject an exception right between the two INSERT statements to prove that neither row survives a partial failure.

4.2 Batch Polling and Async Dispatching (dispatcher.py)

OutboxDispatcher.process_batch() atomically claims up to batch_size events in PENDING state, transitions them to PROCESSING, and posts each payload using httpx.AsyncClient:

        headers: dict[str, str] = {
            "Content-Type": "application/json",
            "Idempotency-Key": event.idempotency_key,
            "X-Event-Id": event.id,
            "X-Event-Type": event.event_type,
        }
        response = await client.post(
            self._config.consumer_endpoint,
            content=event.payload_json.encode("utf-8"),
            headers=headers,
        )
        if response.status_code == 200:
            await mark_event_published(event_id=event.id, db_path=self._config.db_path)
            return EventStatus.PUBLISHED

4.3 Exponential Backoff and Atomic DLQ Quarantine (database.py & dispatcher.py)

When an HTTP error or 5xx status occurs, record_event_failure_or_quarantine() increments retry_count. While new_retry_count < max_delivery_attempts, the event reverts to PENDING and sleeps using exponential backoff (base_backoff * (2 ** (retry_count - 1))).

Once new_retry_count >= max_delivery_attempts, the event is atomically quarantined into dead_letter_queue and marked DEAD_LETTER:

        if new_retry_count >= max_delivery_attempts:
            await conn.execute(
                "UPDATE outbox SET status = ?, retry_count = ?, last_error = ?, updated_at = ? WHERE id = ?;",
                (EventStatus.DEAD_LETTER.value, new_retry_count, error_message, now, event.id),
            )
            await conn.execute(
                """
                INSERT INTO dead_letter_queue (id, original_event_id, payload_json, failure_reason, quarantined_at)
                VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?);
                """,
                (dlq_record.id, dlq_record.original_event_id, dlq_record.payload_json, dlq_record.failure_reason, dlq_record.quarantined_at),
            )
            await conn.execute("COMMIT;")
            return EventStatus.DEAD_LETTER, new_retry_count, dlq_record

4.4 Idempotent FastAPI Consumer (mock_consumer.py)

The FastAPI server (POST /webhooks) uses InMemoryIdempotencyStore protected by an asyncio.Lock. If an Idempotency-Key was already processed, it increments delivery_hits and returns 200 OK without repeating the side effect. Passing ?simulate_failure=true forces an HTTP 500 error to test retry exhaustion and DLQ isolation.

Section 5: Benchmarking and Verification Suite

The test suite in test_outbox.py uses pytest, pytest-asyncio, and httpx.ASGITransport to validate all six architectural invariants:

  • test_atomic_transaction_order_and_outbox_success: Confirms active WAL mode and atomic insertion into orders and outbox.
  • test_atomic_rollback_on_failure: Forces a mid-transaction error and verifies 0 rows remain in both tables after ROLLBACK.
  • test_sha256_idempotency_key_deterministic: Confirms identical SHA-256 digests across reordered keys and whitespace variations.
  • test_dispatcher_publishes_pending_event: Verifies PENDING -> PUBLISHED transition upon 200 OK.
  • test_dispatcher_retries_and_quarantines_to_dlq: Simulates repeated 500 responses until retry_count reaches max_delivery_attempts (3) and verifies insertion into dead_letter_queue.
  • test_consumer_idempotency_deduplication: Sends duplicate webhook requests and verifies side_effects_count == 1.

Section 7: Production Considerations & Enterprise Scaling

  1. SQLite WAL vs. PostgreSQL (FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED): SQLite in WAL mode excels for single-node microservices and edge deployments sharing a local volume. When scaling horizontally across multiple stateless worker replicas on PostgreSQL, claim batches with SELECT ... WHERE status = 'PENDING' ORDER BY created_at ASC LIMIT 10 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED so concurrent workers never contend on the same rows.
  2. DLQ Replay Workflows: Once a downstream outage or schema bug is fixed, an administrative replay script can atomically delete the dead_letter_queue entry and reset the parent outbox row to status = 'PENDING', retry_count = 0. Preserving the original idempotency_key guarantees safe replay.
  3. Migrating from Polling to Change Data Capture (CDC): When throughput grows beyond tens of thousands of events per second or sub-20ms latency is required, keep the exact same transactional outbox table and replace the polling loop with Debezium tailing the database write-ahead log directly into Apache Kafka.

Conclusion & Call to Action

By combining ACID local transactions in SQLite WAL mode, an asynchronous OutboxDispatcher with exponential backoff, canonical SHA-256 idempotency keys, and automatic Dead-Letter Queue quarantine, we have completely eliminated the Dual-Write Problem.

title: PhyMo: Learning Physical Dynamics with Accurate and Continuous Motion from Multi-View Videos
description:
arXiv:2610.29107v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recovering dynamic 3D scene geometry, appearance, and the physical motion states that govern scene evolution from multi-view videos is important yet challenging. A key difficulty is that appearance can be deceptive. Under rendering supervision alone, a model may fit the observed images by changing color or opacity to compensate for inaccurate deformation, rather than recovering the true evolving geometry and motion. This issue is especially severe in scenes with fast or locally complex motion, where inaccurate trajectories can still produce plausible images over the observed frames, but lead to unreliable reconstruction and discontinuous future prediction. In this paper, we propose PhyMo, a framework for learning evolving dynamics from multi-view videos. We introduce a Motion-Aware Trajectory Representation that drives the model to recover accurate motion from deformation, rather than relying on appearance shortcuts to explain observed motion. On top of this, we propose a Continuous Motion Evolution module with bidirectional kinematic continuity constraint to promote temporally consistent evolution of displacement, velocity, and acceleration. Together, these designs yield geometrically faithful interpolation and continuous motion extrapolation. Experiments on four dynamic scene benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art performance.

title: Multi-level Encoder with Global Topic for Task-oriented Dialogue Summarization
description:
arXiv:2610.29097v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Task-oriented dialogue summarization aims to automatically extract key information to generate domain summaries to improve service efficiency and quality. Task-oriented dialogue is inherently logical and surrounds specific topic. How to effectively capture the dialogue topic and the most salient information becomes one of the major challenges of this task. In this paper, we propose a task-oriented dialogue summarization model utilizing a multi-level encoder with global topic (MLEGT). This model discovers temporal and spatial dependencies through a multi-level encoder, while simultaneously obtaining a simple yet effective global topic in the process of graph construction. It not only captures the crucial details but also breaks the long-range limit and discover the intrinsic structure across the dialogue. Then, a global topic guided pointer mechanism is added into the summrizer to capture ignored but important information, which is helpful to improve the accuracy of the summary. A comprehensive study of two public datasets, including a real-world large-scale Chinese police interrogation dataset and a medical reporting service dataset proves the superiority of our method on several strong baselines.

title: C$^2$U in RAG: Compositional Concept Unlearning in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
description:
arXiv:2610.29223v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation can expose unwanted concepts through retrieved evidence even when the generator is moderated. We study query-side concept suppression with a fixed encoder and document index. Compositional Concept Unlearning (C$^2$U) routes a profile-derived direction through an augmented atom bank, adding only a bounded edited-minus-original delta to the raw query. Across five datasets, four encoders, and three seeds, the validation-selected configuration reduces pooled binary target Hit@5 by 4.25 percentage points with non-positive control degradation and target-exposure changes. Under the evaluated query transforms, it suppresses target density without increasing budgeted control-query exposure. Separately, ArXiv four-concept composition improves over an averaged-direction comparator after independent validation gates and first-use test evaluation.

title: Your Tests Pass Against Source — That Is Why the Published Package Lost an Export
description:
Two weeks ago a patch I reviewed bumped a shared package from 2.1.0 to 2.2.0. Every test in the repo was green, the CI badge was green, and the changelog claimed the renamed formatting helper was exported as formatBudget. The first consumer to upgrade hit formatBudget is not a function at runtime, on a path our own tests never touched. The agent that made the change had moved the helper between files, fixed the in-file import, watched the suite stay green, and called it done. The built dist/ barrel still pointed at the old location, so the published tarball never carried the symbol under the documented name.

The reason nobody caught it before release is structural: in a monorepo with a path alias, the test runner resolves formatBudget straight to the edited TypeScript file. A missing re-export in the package barrel is invisible in that resolution. The suite validates that the modules inside the repo agree with each other. It says nothing about the tarball a consumer downloads.

Source-run tests test the source, not the ship

The package boundary only exists after build. A dev compiler and path alias resolve imports to the working files on disk. The boundary a consumer crosses — built output, the published barrel, tree-shaken exports, declared dependencies — does not exist while the tests run against source.

Green means internal agreement, not published correctness. A passing suite proves the edited file and the test that imports it agree. It cannot prove the built artifact re-exports the symbol, that the barrel lists it, or that a clean install finds it.

The agent has no reason to suspect the gap. The tool it trusts most — the test runner — returns confidence, and nothing in its loop asks it to prove the result against the artifact it is about to ship. So it reports green and moves on.

Monorepo hoisting hides the rest. A package that forgot to declare a dependency can still import it locally because another package in the workspace already hoisted it to the root node_modules. The broken declaration surfaces only on a clean install.

The cheap gate: consume what you publish

Build before you check the surface. Run the package build first, then import from dist — or from a packed tarball — in a short smoke check that imports every public export the documentation lists. Place this check after the build step, not before; running it against source reproduces the exact blind spot.

A 20-line barrel-import check catches the common failures. It surfaces a missing re-export, a renamed export left behind in the old file, an accidental removal of a documented symbol, and a bad declaration that hoisting masked. None of these appear in ordinary unit tests.

Verify on a clean install. Install the packed tarball in an empty directory and import from there, instead of relying on the workspace's hoisted dependencies. A clean install is the environment a consumer actually has.

Ask for the right report after a public-surface change. After a rename, move, or removal of a documented export, "tests green" is incomplete. The acceptance answer should state that the built artifact exists, that every documented export imports from dist, and that a clean-install import succeeded.

The mirror gap on the API side

The same blind spot appears without a build step. The handler compiles, unit tests pass, and the code looks correct, but the live response renamed or dropped a field because nobody diffed the actual response against the contract. Source-level confidence cannot see what a deployed endpoint returns to a client. The reliable check compares the live response against the spec rather than trusting the handler that compiled. That local-first loop is the one we built into Powerduck: the contract stays the source of truth, and a green build never counts as proof that the shipped surface matches it.

What I check before a public release

  1. Did this change touch a public export or a documented symbol, or only internal logic?
  2. Did any check run against dist or the packed tarball after build, or only against source?
  3. Did we import every documented export from the built artifact in a clean-install context?
  4. On the API side, did anyone diff the live response against the spec, or only read the handler code?

A green suite measures agreement inside the repo. The consumer lives outside it. Until you verify against the built artifact — or, for an API, against the live response — green means the source looks right, not that the shipped thing works.
