title: MariaDB's FILE Privilege Is a Filesystem Primitive: CVE-2026-107814 and CVE-2026-107818
description:
MariaDB's FILE Privilege Is a Filesystem Primitive: CVE-2026-107814 and CVE-2026-107818

Vulnerability overview

The Cyber Security Agency of Singapore published alert AL-2026-144 on 16 October 2026 describing five MariaDB Server vulnerabilities fixed by the project. Two of them share a cause that a patch note makes easy to skim past. CVE-2026-107814 and CVE-2026-107818 are both rated 8.4 under CVSS v3.1, and both turn an ordinary database grant into the ability to write files that the operating system later trusts.

The other three flaws in the same release are CVE-2026-107815 at 8.5, CVE-2026-107821 at 8.0 and CVE-2026-107823 at 7.2. This analysis concentrates on the pair that abuses the FILE privilege, because their exploitation prerequisites are the ones most likely to be present in routine database estates.

Mechanism and exploitation conditions

CVE-2026-107814 allows a database user holding the FILE privilege to write startup dot-files such as .bash_profile into the $HOME directory of the database service account. The written file is inert until a human opens a login shell for the mysql account, at which point the shell reads the profile and executes its contents. The flaw is therefore a persistence mechanism dressed as a file-write issue, and the trigger is administrative behaviour rather than an automated cron job.

CVE-2026-107818 follows a related path. A user with the FILE privilege can create /run/mysqld and inject attacker-controlled environment values into the restarted service. That path is conditional: it depends on the secure-file-priv configuration permitting writes to /run/mysqld. Where administrators have left secure-file-priv empty, file writes across the filesystem are unrestricted and the condition is trivially satisfied.

Neither flaw requires remote code execution against the server binary. The FILE privilege is normally treated as a data-export convenience, granted to reporting accounts that stage query output on disk. Once granted, it becomes a filesystem primitive with the effective permissions of the mysqld process.

Impact

The immediate consequence is code execution in the context of the database service account, reached through a shell profile or through environment injection into a service restart. From that position an attacker can read the full data directory, harvest credentials embedded in configuration, and reach any system the database account can access over the network.

Operational risk concentrates on two populations. The first is shared database platforms where FILE was granted broadly to support operational scripts. The second is hosts where the service account shares $HOME with human login behaviour, such as manually administered virtual machines. Container images that never spawn a login shell reduce the trigger surface for CVE-2026-107814 without addressing CVE-2026-107818.

Affected products and scope

The advisory lists MariaDB Server versions 10.6.1 to 10.6.27, 10.11.1 to 10.11.18, 11.4.1 to 11.4.12, 11.8.1 to 11.8.8, 12.3.1 to 12.3.2 and 13.0.1. That spans six maintained branches, so branch-level patch inventory matters more than a single version comparison.

The advisory does not state which upstream engine component each fix touched, and it does not describe a proof of concept. Treat both as unknown rather than as evidence of low risk.

Exposure context

A ZoomEye query for the database fingerprint app="MariaDB" returns 5111720 matching assets. That figure describes deployment scale for identification purposes: it counts hosts whose banners identify MariaDB, not hosts confirmed to be running an affected build or to have granted FILE.

ZoomEye search: https://www.zoomeye.ai/searchResult?q=YXBwPSJNYXJpYURCIg%3D%3D

Remediation and mitigations

Upgrade to the current release in your branch, following the vendor guidance to update promptly. Because six branches are affected, verify the exact build string after upgrading instead of assuming a package manager did the right thing.

Where an upgrade cannot be scheduled immediately, attack the prerequisites. Audit every account holding the FILE privilege with SHOW GRANTS and revoke it where the business case is a query export that can be redirected. Set secure-file-priv to a dedicated directory. Review filesystem permissions on the service account home so that the account cannot write shell profiles, and give /run/mysqld ownership and mode expectations that exclude arbitrary environment injection.

References

  • CSA Singapore alert AL-2026-144: https://www.csa.gov.sg/alerts-and-advisories/alerts/al-2026-144/
  • NVD entry for CVE-2026-107814: https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2026-107814
  • NVD entry for CVE-2026-107818: https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2026-107818

title: The Wall: How a Wi-Fi driver killed the server dream
description:
Eight percent packet loss, a kernel panic, and the €15 answer that was hiding in plain sight

The morning after Frankie came alive, I wrote a backup script.

A hundred lines of bash that would SSH into the Oracle VM, check that PostgreSQL was healthy, check that disk space was above 5 GB, check that load was below 4.0. If everything passed, it would pull a pg_dump, gzip it, and store it on Frankie's 120 GB disk. Two dumps kept. Everything older deleted. A safeguard, not an archive. Geographic redundancy: the VM in Frankfurt, Frankie on Kefalonia. The job would run at 04:00, when the island sleeps and the WiFi air is quiet.

I finished the script at 23:00. I ran one test before bed.

ping -c 100 8.8.8.8

Sixty percent loss.

That was from across the room. I moved Frankie next to the router. Eighty-eight percent signal. Two hundred seventy megabits per second negotiated rate. Locked to 2.4 GHz, powersave disabled.

ping -c 100 8.8.8.8

Nine percent loss.

The b43 driver, the open-source driver for the Broadcom BCM4321, has a hard ceiling. I spent the next three hours proving it.

The ceiling

The internet is full of tuning advice for b43. Disable powersave. Lock to 2.4 GHz. Force legacy rates with iw. Add module options. I did all of it.

I disabled powersave in NetworkManager. I locked the connection to 802.11b/g with nmcli. I installed iw and forced legacy-2.4 bitrates. I moved the machine until it was touching the router. The signal indicator showed full bars. The negotiated rate showed 270 Mbit/s, a figure that is impossible on 2.4 GHz channel 1 with 20 MHz width, which means the router was using 40 MHz channel bonding, a mode b43 handles badly.

I forced 20 MHz width. I forced lower rates. I added options b43 nohwcrypt=1 qos=0 to /etc/modprobe.d/b43.conf.

ping -c 100 8.8.8.8

Nine percent loss. Round-trip times spiking to 86 milliseconds. The driver was not failing because of configuration. The driver was failing because it is the driver. The b43 codebase for the BCM4321 rev 05 has a ceiling, and that ceiling is 8 to 10 percent packet loss at full signal.

This is not a signal problem. This is a driver problem.

The escape hatch that was not

Every forum thread about the BCM4321 ends the same way. "Just use the proprietary wl driver." I tried.

I installed bcmwl-kernel-source. I blacklisted b43, bcma, ssb. I rebooted.

The kernel panicked. dmesg showed wl_module_init call stacks. The wl driver crashes on init with this kernel, on this hardware, after the 193-package upgrade that fixed everything else. The upgrade that brought b43 to life did not make wl viable. They are mutually exclusive on this machine, and wl loses.

I reverted. Removed the blacklist, reloaded b43, reconnected. Nine percent loss. But at least it connected.

What nine percent means

Nine percent packet loss does not matter for browsing. Falkon retries. Pages load. It does not matter for SSH: type a command, if a packet drops, the terminal hangs for half a second, then recovers. It does not matter for writing this article in Geany, which is entirely offline.

But nine percent matters for an unattended 04:00 backup job pulling a multi-gigabyte PostgreSQL dump over SSH. A dropped packet in the middle of an scp does not recover cleanly. The transfer hangs. The cron job fails. The safeguard is not safe. A backup that fails silently is worse than no backup, because it gives you false confidence.

I tested this. I ran the script manually. It failed twice in three attempts. The third attempt completed, but the transfer took fourteen minutes for a 1.2 GB dump because TCP was constantly retransmitting. Over a wired connection, the same transfer would take four minutes.

Frankie could not be a server over WiFi. Not because the WiFi was weak, but because the driver was honest about its limits.

The €15 answer

A USB Ethernet adapter costs €15. Any USB 2.0 to RJ45 adapter works on Linux without drivers. Plug it in, the kernel sees eth0, DHCP fires, ping shows zero percent loss. The backup script works. The cron job works. Frankie becomes the server it was meant to be.

I do not have the adapter yet. On the island, it might take a week to find one. Until then, Frankie is in limbo. The script is written. The cron is ready. The machine waits.

The pivot

If Frankie cannot come to the work over WiFi, and the adapter is not here yet, then Frankie's role must change. I stripped the server plan. No headless conversion. No 04:00 cron. No Tailscale tunnel. Frankie stays in the GUI, running LXQt, waiting.

The options without the adapter are real but limited. Frankie can be a learning sandbox: break it, reinstall it, try Arch, try Ansible, try Docker. The WiFi flakiness does not matter because the work is local. Frankie can be a distraction-free writing machine: Geany, Vim, Markdown, no browser, no notifications. Frankie can babysit an Arduino or an ESP32 over USB. The machine does not need internet; it needs a serial port and a screen.

But none of these are what Frankie was meant to be. Frankie was meant to be a server. A backup anchor. A quiet machine in the corner that pulls a dump while I sleep.

That future costs €15. Not €1,500 for a new laptop. Not €500 for a used ThinkPad. €15 for a USB Ethernet adapter that removes the wireless variable entirely.

Sometimes the cheapest solution is the one you pay for.

The infrastructure, right now:

  • Local dev: Frankie, 2008 MacBook Air, Lubuntu, LXQt, no GPU acceleration, b43 WiFi with 9% loss, mbpfan tuned to 55/60

  • Production database: Oracle Cloud Always Free ARM VM, PostGIS 16, pgRouting

  • Site: Cloudflare Pages, global CDN

  • Tiles: GitHub Pages, PMTiles

  • Builds: GitHub Codespaces

  • Email: Resend SMTP, daily VM health reports at 08:00 EEST

  • The backup script: Written, tested, failing. Waiting for a cable.

There is no procurement department. There is no EU grant. There is one person, a drawer of old hardware, and a shopping list with one item on it.

Frankie is alive. But Frankie is not yet a server.

title: Cold Chain, Cold Comfort: What the Danfoss Case Says About Buying Exposed Equipment
description:
Cold Chain, Cold Comfort: What the Danfoss Case Says About Buying Exposed Equipment

The French supermarket attack of 11 October 2026 is usually filed under incident response. It belongs equally in procurement. Every controller in the affected class was bought, installed and configured by somebody, and the configuration that put a control panel on a public address was a purchasing and commissioning decision before it was a security one.
The exposure data makes that case more sharply than any policy document.

What was purchased

Danfoss confirmed its equipment was targeted in the attack on cooling systems at hundreds of French supermarkets. Its statement separated the fleet into two groups: AK-SM800 and AK-SC355 controllers that no longer receive security updates, and AK-SM800A controllers running outdated firmware. The StoreView panel is the interface in front of those controllers.
Both groups share a property that no datasheet advertises. They can be reached on the public internet, and a portion of them were. Censys counted 2,991 exposed StoreView panels on 11 October, 1,825 of them in France, and by 14 October the French figure had fallen 71% to 537.
The version distribution describes a purchasing pattern as much as a patching pattern. On 11 October, 74% of French exposed instances ran below 4.3.1, the release covering CVE-2025-41450, CVE-2025-41451 and CVE-2025-41452. Poland sat at 81%, Romania at 80% and Belgium at 76%. The current release is 5.3.2.
A fleet with three quarters of its exposed units behind a fix that shipped over a year earlier is not a fleet with a patching backlog. It is a fleet whose owners did not know they held a patching obligation, which is a contract problem.

The measurement that belongs in a tender

An independent engine cannot read a firmware version, but it can establish whether a class of equipment tends to face the internet. That is a question a buyer can ask before signing.
The ZoomEye header query run on 22 October 2026 is one way to obtain the evidence:
| Query | Result |
| --- | --- |
| http.header="Danfoss" | 260 |
| http.header="Danfoss" && port="80" | 120 |
| http.header="Danfoss" && port="443" | 132 |
| http.header="Danfoss" && country="NL" | 54 |
| http.header="Danfoss" && country="US" | 28 |
| http.header="Danfoss" && country="DE" | 25 |
| http.header="Danfoss" && country="FR" | 1 |
What a buyer should not do is read 260 as a quality verdict on the vendor. It is a count of assets emitting a particular header. What a buyer can do is use the technique on the class of equipment actually being considered, record the result, and ask the supplier why a device with a web management interface appears on the public internet at all.
The Netherlands figure of 54 against a French figure of 1 four days after a French incident is a useful thought experiment in that conversation. The header string does not concentrate where the incident happened; it concentrates wherever those devices were installed and configured with public reachability.

The three questions a specification should force

The incident supplies the questions, and they are not the usual security questionnaire items.

  1. Does the device need a public address to function? A refrigeration control panel that supports remote maintenance is not the same product as one that requires a public interface. If the vendor's answer is that internet connectivity is optional, the commissioning decision becomes the operator's to defend.
  2. What is the supported-version lifetime, in writing? Danfoss divided its fleet into models still receiving updates and models that no longer do. A buyer who does not know which side of that line a purchased controller sits on has bought an indefinite obligation with a finite vendor commitment.
  3. Who patches it, and with what outage? The Claroty demonstration of CVE-2025-41450 and CVE-2025-41451 chained to remote code execution and falsified temperature readings describes a device whose compromise is measured in stock loss. The patch for it competes with a refrigeration loop that cannot be safely restarted at will. That trade-off belongs in the contract, not in the incident review.

Why disconnection is a purchasing signal

Censys concluded that operators disconnected panels rather than patched them, because all three version categories shrank by roughly 70%, including the ones already on patched releases. That is a rational choice for a single site under pressure. Across a market it is a signal that the equipment's maintenance model does not accommodate firmware updates.
A buyer reading that signal has three options, and only one of them is comfortable. Accept the model and budget for disconnection as a routine control. Accept the model and negotiate an update window into the maintenance contract. Or buy equipment whose update path does not require a cold-chain risk assessment.
None of this requires naming a vendor as negligent. The three CVEs were patched, the versions were published, and the vendor stated which models remain supported. The gap sits in the space between a shipped fix and a fleet that could apply it.

A practical procurement checklist

For the next refrigeration, HVAC or building-management procurement round:

  • Search the public internet for the equipment class before signing, using a fixed query and recording the date.
  • Ask for the supported-version end date of every controller model in the bid, not the product family.
  • Ask what the vendor's remote-access architecture requires, and whether the panel can sit behind a broker rather than on a public address.
  • Write a firmware update window into the maintenance contract, with an agreed outage tolerance for the refrigeration loop.
  • Re-run the external query after commissioning and compare it with the pre-purchase baseline. The last item is where a tool like ZoomEye earns its place in a procurement file: not as a compliance tick, but as evidence that the configuration is what the specification said it would be.

The uncomfortable takeaway

The French operators who disconnected their panels in 72 hours acted faster than their contracts had prepared them to act. The equipment worked, the fixes existed, and the mechanism to apply them did not.
That is the part of this incident worth carrying into a supplier negotiation. Exposure counts are volatile and engine-dependent. A maintenance model that expects a controller to be patched on a live refrigeration loop is a durable thing to fix.

References

  • Infosecurity Magazine, "France: Internet-Exposed Danfoss Controllers Drop 71% After Cyber-Attack", https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/france-expose-danfoss-controllers/
  • Censys, "Frostbitten in France: A Danfoss StoreView internet exposure report", https://censys.com/blog/frostbitten-in-france-a-danfoss-storeview-internet-exposure-report/
  • ZoomEye search syntax baseline, https://zoomeye.ai/agent.md

title: HypTI: Hyperbolic Geometry-Aware Multimodal Feature Fusion Framework for Dementia Detection Based on Tabular-Image Data
description:
arXiv:2610.27941v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: AI-assisted dementia detection usually requires multimodal fusion of diverse data, such as clinical tabular assessments and neuroimaging data. However, most existing approaches perform feature fusion in Euclidean space. This overlooks the geometric structure of representation, including hierarchical organization in clinical assessments and multi-scale anatomical patterns in neuroimaging data. Recent studies have proved hyperbolic space provides a natural geometry for modelling hierarchical and multi-scale structures due to its exponentially expanding space. Motivated by these, we propose HypTI, a hyperbolic geometry-aware multimodal fusion framework for dementia detection based on clinical tabular assessments and MRI scans. HypTI extends hyperbolic representation learning to an underexplored tabular-MRI setting, jointly modelling clinical tabular, MRI scans, and cross-modal interactions in hyperbolic space. Specifically, clinical tabular variables are represented through learnable Lorentz prototypes to capture hierarchical relationships among assessments, while MRI scans are encoded using ROI-guided multi-scale representation learning to capture anatomical patterns across brain regions and spatial scales in Lorentz space. The multimodal representations are integrated through an adaptive fusion module generates subject-specific scale and shift coefficients to dynamically modulate and integrate the multimodal embeddings, enabling effective patient-level tabular-image representation learning for dementia detection. Experiments on OASIS-3 dataset show that the proposed framework achieves strong performance compared with representative approaches.

title: The best workflow engine is a programming language
description:
The idea of orchestrating long-running, stateful logic on top of unreliable, stateless infrastructure isn't new. We've had message queues, job runners, microservice choreographies, and full-blown workflow engines for a long time. What we never had was a version of it that felt good to write.

I'd spent about six months working on a fork of Temporal, mostly on weekends, trying to turn it into a serverless answer with DX that felt more Vercel-native. Eventually it dawned on me that to ship that experience, I'd need to own the execution environment too. So I dropped the fork, joined Vercel, and started hacking on a new framework from scratch alongside Nathan Rajlich.

Code is already a DAG

A workflow is a DAG, a directed acyclic graph. Before Temporal (and Cadence before it), nearly every workflow framework made you draw that DAG by hand. Apache Airflow is the canonical example. You describe your pipeline as an explicit graph of tasks and dependencies, and your actual logic gets buried inside the nodes."

That always felt backwards to me. We already have a tool for expressing "do this, then that, and these in parallel, and branch here." It's called a programming language. An abstract syntax tree is a DAG. Software itself is a DAG.

I knew that in the abstract, but it didn't truly hit me until I saw Temporal, where you write what looks like normal sequential code and the engine makes it durable underneath. It was the dream all along.

What running Temporal taught me

Temporal is great once your infrastructure exists. I was starting from scratch, and setting it up meant:

  • Standing up Temporal Cloud (or self-hosting the server: Frontend, History, Matching, and Worker services, plus a Cassandra/Postgres/MySQL backend and sharding).

  • Running your own worker fleet: Temporal never executes your code. Your workers poll the server and run your workflows and activities. In practice that's a Kubernetes cluster you own.

  • Wiring it all together: task queues, activity registration, client config.

  • Managing the workers yourself: scaling, uptime, restarts, and the build-and-deploy pipeline for the worker processes.

  • Setting up encryption: workers talk to the control plane over the internet, so you're configuring mutual TLS and a data converter to encrypt payloads before they leave your environment.

Once all of that was in place, the workflow dream mostly became real. But I wanted something easy to start that could still scale as my project grew into production.

Versioning in-flight workflows

Beyond owning the worker build-and-deploy process myself, there was a harder problem. If I changed my workflow code while runs were still in flight, I was kind of stuck. There were no longer any workers running the old, correct version of that code. Replay would hit my new code with an old event history and break on a non-determinism error.

The official answer is the patching API (patched() / GetVersion). You branch your code on a change ID and march it through a multi-stage deprecate-then-remove lifecycle as old runs age out of retention. It works, but it means evolving workflow code very carefully. Over enough changes, the workflow code rots into a thicket of version flags.

I couldn't explain Temporal signals

Whenever I tried to show running Temporal demos to friends, signals / queries / updates turned into the single most confusing part. They're three separate primitives for getting data in and out of a running workflow, each with its own rules. Queries can't block, signals are fire-and-forget and get buffered, and you have to know when to reach for which. The concepts did land but it wasn't very intuitive. To me, that was a DX smell. If I can't explain the human-in-the-loop primitive without a whiteboard, it's too complicated. That's why Workflow SDK replaces all three with a single primitive, the hook.

What Workflow SDK looks like today

With Workflow SDK, you write one file of normal code. "use workflow" marks an orchestrator; "use step" marks a unit of side-effecting work. In between it's just await, try/catch, Promise.all, loops, and conditionals.

A few things fall out of that one file:

  • No DAG file: The compiler reads the directives and splits the code into workflow and client/step bundles. The graph is your control flow.

  • Retries: Uncaught errors retry by default. Throw new FatalError(...) to stop. Throw new RetryableError(..., { retryAfter }) for custom backoff. Set fn.maxRetries = n to tune.

  • Ad-hoc webhooks: const webhook = createWebhook() creates a real, callable URL inside a running workflow, in a single line. The run parks until someone hits it, with no route or handler.

  • Hooks: Webhooks are sugar over a more general primitive. Create a hook with createHook<T>(), await it, and the data someone sends is what comes back. This one concept replaces signals, queries and updates

Here's an ad-hoc webhook end to end. An approval that can pause for seconds or for weeks, with nothing extra to deploy.

A library, not a platform

Traditional engines make you bring infrastructure to the framework. Workflow SDK brings the framework to infrastructure you already have.

DBOS had the right idea

While I was working out how to actually build this, I studied every workflow engine I could find. The one that stood out was DBOS, an open-source durable execution library that runs almost entirely client-side. The only thing its server needs is Postgres.

Workflow SDK adopts that shape. There's no bespoke orchestrator to self-host or pay for, and no new stateful system to operate. The only infrastructure it needs is infrastructure you already run: your app, a database, a queue. All the heavy lifting happens in the library.

The backend is swappable

Workflow SDK pushes the idea past one database. The whole thing is a spec, a way of writing workflows, steps, and hooks that any infrastructure can back. You mix and match the substrate to fit your stack:

  • Redis / Kafka / etc. for your streams

  • Postgres / Cassandra / the file system / Turso / Durable Objects / etc. for durability

  • Vercel Queues / SQS / Cloudflare Queues / etc. for your queue

The runtime only ever talks to a single interface, the World, which covers storage, queuing, auth, and streaming. Swapping any layer never touches your workflow code.

In fact, we maintain a first-party Postgres world inspired by DBOS, using Postgres for durability, queueing, and streaming. And in every world, there's no worker fleet and no control plane. A framework integration exposes two plain HTTP endpoints that deploy like the rest of your app.

Even the Vercel backend is "just" a CRUD API

The Vercel Workflow Server, the thing that backs workflows on Vercel, is stateless and does no compute or orchestration at all. It's just like the Postgres world, but extended with Vercel's authentication and multi-tenancy. A CRUD API, nothing more. It even runs as a regular Vercel deployment. All the heavy lifting, all the actual workflow logic, lives in the open-source, Apache-licensed client-side library, which can be extended freely.

So the "managed" offering isn't a black box you're locked into. It's just another World, one implementation of a spec you can read, fork, and extend. The data format isn't bespoke either. You can swap out any piece of the stack.

Some patterns lean on the platform

I should be upfront. A few of Workflow SDK's design choices are shaped by how Vercel executes code. The clearest example is versioning, the same code-evolution problem that makes traditional engines so painful.

Our answer is to pin each run to the specific deployment that started it. The run keeps executing against the exact copy of the code it began on, so changing your workflow never breaks in-flight runs. It's a clean solution, but it was only easy to build because Vercel already keeps immutable deployments around for long periods. The official Postgres world doesn't track and route versions this way yet. Encouragingly, community worlds have already implemented the spec as intended. Platformatic's version-safe durable workflows on Kubernetes is a great example.

And I think that's exactly the right trade. Pinning moves the complexity of versioning off the developer writing workflows and onto the infrastructure. That burden lands on the world author, the infra provider, and us as the framework authors. If everyone using a framework hits the same hard problem and has to solve it themselves in the same painful ways, the framework has failed them. A good framework moves that complexity upstream.

Steps should be free

Performance is the next big problem for us to solve. Invoking a step isn't cheap. Each step involves networking and a trip over a queue to durably commit its result correctly. For correctness, that's the right thing to do. But it works against the pitch that distributed computing should feel like function calls.

When you write ordinary code, you don't think twice about the overhead of a function call. It's so fast it's effectively free. But if every step carried a heavy overhead, the abstraction leaks. You start rationing steps, reasoning about granularity, declining to turn a small function into a checkpoint because it's "not worth a step."

So the goal is blunt: steps should be free.

In the ideal version of this, you could take any function in an existing codebase, add "use step", and everything would just work, with no serialization constraints and no performance penalty.

That dream drives us.

What if any developer could turn a plain function into something with the performance, networking, observability, and availability of a standalone microservice, but using just two words: "use step"? That would change how we write code.

Workflow v5 (in beta at the time of writing) already delivers up to a 5x performance improvement with no change to the user-facing API, and v6 will push it further while making third-party worlds just as fast. We're sharing details as we go in this GitHub discussion, and you can start testing today with npm install workflow@beta.

I set out to build a durable framework that feels like writing ordinary code, runs on the infrastructure you already have, and is fast enough that you never think twice about reaching for a step. It's real today, and we're building the rest of it in the open.

Come build Workflow SDK with us

If designing durable systems under real-world constraints sounds like fun, the Workflow team at Vercel is hiring.

See open roles.

title: Validate VEX on the way out, not on the way in
description:
A tool that both reads and writes VEX documents ends up with one struct carrying two opposite obligations. A document I issue is a claim somebody downstream will act on, so anything ambiguous has to be refused before it reaches disk. A document a supplier issued last quarter is a fact, and refusing to parse it hides exactly the statements someone needs in order to fix them. The mistake is serving both duties with one validator called from both sides.

I ran into this building vexdesk, a small Go tool that sits between a bill of materials and a VEX document: it reads what syft or trivy already wrote, works out which OSV advisories could touch the components, and turns my decisions into OpenVEX. From 11 September 2026 the EU Cyber Resilience Act expects manufacturers to answer the "is my product affected" question in writing, quickly, for every product they ship. That changes what these files are. They stop being an artefact of an internal process and become something a customer receives, stores, and compares against the one before it.

That last word carries the whole argument. Comparison is the only reason to be lenient on read, and it is a sufficient one.

Reading: refuse only what is not a document

The read path has exactly one job: decode. Whether the document obeys the rules is information, not a gate.

// Parse reads a document that has already been issued. It does not validate: a
// document published last quarter is a fact, and refusing to read it would hide
// exactly the statements someone needs to see in order to fix them. Writing
// stays strict; reading does not.
func Parse(data []byte) (*Document, error) {
    var doc Document
    if err := json.Unmarshal(data, &doc); err != nil {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("openvex: %w", err)
    }
    if doc.Context == "" && len(doc.Statements) == 0 {
        return nil, errors.New("openvex: not a VEX document: it has neither @context nor statements")
    }
    return &doc, nil
}

The single check left in there is not a conformance check. A payload with neither @context nor statements is not a malformed VEX document, it is some other JSON file, almost always because the wrong path was typed on the command line. Telling you that is helpful. Telling you that a vendor's not_affected is missing a justification code, and then refusing to open the file, is not: the finding you wanted to look at is inside the file you just declined to read.

The payoff shows up in the diff command, which is what a recipient of a new document actually wants:

$ vexdesk diff released/vex-2.0.0.json vex.json
3 change(s), 4 claim(s) unchanged

CHANGE       ADVISORY      PRODUCT                                      DETAIL
new          FIXTURE-0005  pkg:npm/cogwheel@4.1.0                       under_investigation
restated     FIXTURE-0004  pkg:npm/cogwheel@4.1.0                       affected → fixed
rejustified  FIXTURE-0001  pkg:golang/github.com/example/widget@v1.2.3  justification vulnerable_code_not_in_execute_path → component_not_present

The comparison runs claim by claim, one vulnerability against one product. For that to work, both sides have to be loadable, including the old one I issued before I tightened my own rules, and including the one from a supplier whose generator is sloppier than mine. A strict parser would make the second document in that pipeline unreadable precisely when it matters most.

Writing: refuse anything that leaves a reader guessing

On the way out the posture inverts. Validate is called from exactly one place, the constructor, and it is unforgiving.

func (d *Document) Validate() error {
    var errs []error
    if strings.TrimSpace(d.Author) == "" {
        errs = append(errs, errors.New("document: author is required"))
    }
    if len(d.Statements) == 0 {
        errs = append(errs, errors.New("document: a document with no statements says nothing"))
    }
    for i, s := range d.Statements {
        if err := s.Validate(); err != nil {
            errs = append(errs, fmt.Errorf("statement %d: %w", i, err))
        }
    }
    return errors.Join(errs...)
}

Two details there are deliberate. Errors are joined rather than returned on the first failure, because somebody fixing a decisions file wants the whole list, not one problem per run. And each statement error is wrapped with its index, because "vulnerability name is required" is useless without knowing which of forty statements it belongs to.

not_affected is where the rule earns its keep

The statement-level check that matters most is the one on not_affected, since that is the verdict nobody rechecks:

case NotAffected:
    // One of the closed set of codes, always. Prose explains a decision to
    // the person reading this document; only the code lets a reviewer, a
    // diff or another tool compare it against every other not_affected.
    // An impact statement is welcome alongside it, never instead of it.
    switch {
    case s.Justification == "" && strings.TrimSpace(s.ImpactStatement) != "":
        errs = append(errs, fmt.Errorf(
            "not_affected has an impact_statement but no justification: prose does not stand in for one of %v",
            justifications))
    case s.Justification == "":
        errs = append(errs, fmt.Errorf("not_affected requires a justification, one of %v", justifications))
    case !slices.Contains(justifications, s.Justification):
        errs = append(errs, fmt.Errorf("justification %q is not one of %v", s.Justification, justifications))
    }

The first case took a real argument with myself to keep. A sentence like "the affected parser is only reached from the admin importer, which this build does not include" is genuinely more informative to a human than the code vulnerable_code_not_in_execute_path. It is also unusable by the diff above. A reviewer putting this quarter's document next to last quarter's can see that a code changed; nobody can tell whether two paragraphs of prose express the same conclusion. So the code is mandatory and the prose is encouraged next to it, and the error message lists the accepted codes rather than sending the author off to find the spec.

The symmetric rules follow from the same test: can you act on this without asking me a question. affected requires an action_statement, because telling a customer they are affected and nothing else gives them no move to make. A justification on any status other than not_affected is refused outright: a code attached to fixed looks like it means something and does not.

Note that none of this is enforced on read. A supplier document that breaks every one of these rules parses fine and diffs fine, and that is what splitting the paths buys.

The identifier comes from the statements 

// New assembles a document and validates it. The identifier is derived from the
// statements, so the same decisions produce the same document id — a rebuild in
// CI does not look like a new document every time.
func New(author string, at time.Time, tooling string, statements []Statement) (*Document, error) {
    doc := &Document{
        Context:    Context,
        Author:     author,
        Timestamp:  at.UTC().Format(time.RFC3339),
        Version:    1,
        Tooling:    tooling,
        Statements: statements,
    }
    doc.ID = deriveID(statements)
    if err := doc.Validate(); err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    return doc, nil
}

deriveID is a hash of the marshalled statements, nothing else. A random UUID would have been one line shorter and would have made every CI run produce a document that looks new. The timestamp moves on every build and should; identity should not. If my decisions did not change, the @id does not change, and a recipient automating against these files can tell a reissue from a revision without reading the body.

That makes the placement of the validation matter in a way that is easy to miss: the ID is assigned before Validate runs, so a rejected document never escapes with a plausible-looking identifier attached. There is no partially-constructed Document lying around for a caller to grab and write out anyway.

No issuer, no document

The vex command refuses to run without -author. The library would refuse too, a few hundred milliseconds later, after reading the SBOM and the advisory directory, so the flag check is redundant in the strictest sense. I keep it because the reason is not about flags. A VEX document without an issuer cannot be trusted by its reader: an anonymous not_affected is a claim with nobody behind it, which is worth less than no claim at all. Checking it at the edge says that out loud, and checking it again in Validate means it holds no matter who calls the package.

What I would do differently

Leniency on read currently means silence on read. The information is available, since Validate is exported and I could run it against a parsed supplier document, but nothing in the read path surfaces it, so a document with a bare impact_statement and no code passes through unremarked. I would add that as a report rather than a refusal: parse, diff, and separately say "this document breaks three rules I would not have let myself emit." Accepting a flawed document and failing to mention the flaws are two different decisions, and I conflated them.

Two smaller things. Version is hardcoded to 1 while the @id moves with the statements, which leaves two identity-shaped fields following different rules. And because deriveID hashes only the statements, the same claims issued under a different author produce the same identifier, defensible enough since the ID names a set of decisions and the author is a separate field, but it is a property I arrived at rather than chose...

The general shape has held up, though, and I think it is not specific to VEX. Any format you both consume and produce wants the validator on one side only. Strict where you are the author and responsible for what the reader can do with it; permissive where somebody else already made their choices and all you can do is read them.

Originally published on polycratia.com — where I write about payment systems, crypto rails and marketplace backends.

title: A Practical CI/CD Pipeline: Build Once, Tag by Commit, Deploy Anywhere
description:
A good CI/CD pipeline is boring. Every change goes through the same steps, deploys look the same every time, and rolling back takes seconds.

This post builds a minimal pipeline for a containerised app using GitHub Actions. The principles also apply to other CI systems and cloud providers.

Principles first

  1. Build once. Create a single artefact (a container image) and promote that same artefact through staging and production. Don't rebuild per environment, or you're not testing what you ship.
  2. Make artefacts immutable. Tag images with the commit SHA. Avoid deploying latest, because you can't tell what it is or roll back to it reliably.
  3. Keep config out of the image. Environment variables and secrets come from the environment at runtime.
  4. Automate the check after deploy. A deploy isn't done until a health check passes.

Step 1: Test and build on every push 

# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: ci

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 20
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run lint --if-present
      - run: npm test

  build:
    needs: test
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
      packages: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3
      - uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
      - uses: docker/build-push-action@v6
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:${{ github.sha }}
          cache-from: type=gha
          cache-to: type=gha,mode=max

Pull requests run tests only. Merges to main also build and push an image tagged with the exact commit.

Step 2: A small, secure Dockerfile 

FROM node:20-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM node:20-alpine
WORKDIR /app
ENV NODE_ENV=production
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
USER node
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]

Multi-stage builds keep the final image small, and USER node avoids running as root.

Step 3: Deploy the exact image

How you deploy depends on your platform (ECS, Kubernetes, Cloud Run, a VM with Docker, and so on). The pattern is the same: tell the platform to run the image tagged with this commit SHA.

  deploy-staging:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: staging
    steps:
      - name: Deploy image
        run: |
          echo "Deploying ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:${{ github.sha }} to staging"
          # replace with your platform's command, for example:
          # kubectl set image deployment/app app=ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:${{ github.sha }}
      - name: Wait for health check
        run: |
          for i in {1..20}; do
            if curl -fsS https://staging.example.com/healthz; then exit 0; fi
            sleep 5
          done
          echo "Health check failed" && exit 1

  deploy-production:
    needs: deploy-staging
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production        # add required reviewers in repo settings
    steps:
      - name: Deploy the same image
        run: echo "Deploying the same SHA to production"

Using GitHub Environments lets you add required approvals for production and keep secrets separate per environment.

Step 4: Add a real health endpoint 

app.get("/healthz", async (req, res) => {
  try {
    await db.query("SELECT 1");     // check critical dependencies
    res.status(200).json({ status: "ok" });
  } catch {
    res.status(503).json({ status: "unhealthy" });
  }
});

Keep it fast and cheap. Platforms use it to decide whether to send traffic to a new version, and your pipeline uses it to decide whether a deploy succeeded.

Step 5: Rollback is just another deploy

Because every image is tagged with a commit SHA, rolling back means deploying the previous known-good SHA. No rebuild required.

# example: redeploy the previous version
kubectl set image deployment/app app=ghcr.io/org/app:<previous-sha>

Practice this before you need it. A rollback you've never tried isn't a plan.

Beyond the basics

  • Secrets: prefer short-lived credentials via OIDC (for example, GitHub Actions to AWS, Azure or GCP) over long-lived keys stored in secrets.
  • Infrastructure as code: manage cloud resources with Terraform or similar, reviewed through pull requests.
  • Progressive delivery: canary or blue/green releases reduce the impact of a bad deploy.
  • Observability: logs, metrics and alerts tied to each release, so you can see when a deploy changed behaviour.
  • Database migrations: make them backward-compatible so old and new versions can run side by side during a rollout.

Checklist

  • [ ] One build, promoted across environments
  • [ ] Images tagged by commit SHA, never latest
  • [ ] Config and secrets injected at runtime
  • [ ] Health check gates every deploy
  • [ ] Manual approval for production
  • [ ] Rollback tested

What does your deployment pipeline look like, and what's the one thing you'd change?

Further reading: Cloud DevOps Solutions

title: Building Multi-Tenant SaaS Help Center Retrieval — A 4-Stage Citation Contract
description:
The hard choice in a multi-tenant SaaS help center is not “which vector database is fastest?” It is deciding how much freshness and control your citation contract can tolerate. Short answer: keep a durable, tenant-filtered index for stable content, add a live retrieval path for fast-changing pages, and make both produce the same citation-shaped result. That lets the answer layer remain boring and auditable.

I start with the answer a support user will see, then work backward. A citation must identify the tenant, source document, revision, and the exact text span used. If a result cannot carry those fields, it is not ready for generation, no matter how relevant its embedding looks.

The constraint is a retrieval contract

Write the contract before picking an endpoint. Mine has four invariants: every query is scoped to one tenant; every chunk has a stable source and revision; freshness is explicit; and an answer cites only chunks returned by retrieval. Those rules prevent a surprisingly common failure where a global index returns a plausible paragraph from another customer.

Infrai fits the durable branch when you want one REST API for this vector work and adjacent backend jobs. The public discovery surface is self-describing, so the adapter can inspect the documented method and path instead of baking provider-specific assumptions into each tenant.

The retrieval unit matters too. A whole article is easy to cite but noisy for reranking. A tiny sentence has sharp relevance but loses context. In practice, I use a section-sized chunk with a parent document id, heading path, locale, ACL, and updated_at. Your mileage may vary; chunk size depends on how your help center authors write.

Keep ingestion, querying, and citation as separate observable stages. Log tenant id and request id at each boundary, plus candidate count and the selected source ids. Do not log the full customer text by default. That is a compliance decision, not a performance trick.

How should multi-tenant SaaS help center retrieval handle freshness and citation tracing?

There are two viable shapes.

The durable path ingests published content into a tenant-partitioned vector collection. It gives predictable filtering, repeatable evaluation, and a clean revision history. The live path fetches or searches the current help-center source at query time, then ranks those passages alongside durable candidates. It catches an article edited five minutes ago, but it adds network variability and another place to enforce tenant permissions.

Their shared invariant is the citation envelope. A candidate should look conceptually like this:

candidate = {
    "tenant_id": "t_42",
    "document_id": "doc_918",
    "revision": "r17",
    "heading_path": ["Billing", "Invoices"],
    "text": "...",
    "source_url": "https://help.example.test/billing/invoices",
    "updated_at": "2026-08-31T09:20:00Z",
    "retrieval_path": "durable",
}

The answer service accepts only this envelope. It can merge durable and live candidates, deduplicate by document and revision, and attach citations without guessing where a sentence came from. A short-lived live result that lacks a revision should be marked ineligible for citation, even if it helps reranking.

Ship it carefully.

Where a narrow API surface helps

For a team that wants this split without installing an SDK for every backend concern, Infrai is a deliberate option. Its breadth is behind one consistent REST surface: discovery reports 295 routes across 20 modules, and a single key can cover the vector operations alongside other backend capabilities. That can reduce adapter code when the same service also owns notifications or scheduled ingestion.

For the durable branch, the documented vector surface covers collection creation, upsert, query, and deletion. Generate request details from the public discovery document instead of copying assumptions between tenants. The useful advantage here is the uniform contract, not a claim that one index will fit every workload. Infrai also puts 295 routes across 20 modules under one key, so an ingestion worker does not need a new vendor credential when it adds a scheduling or notification step. One REST API means plain HTTP from any language, with no SDK installation required.

This is the small discovery probe I use during startup. It is intentionally read-only; the production writer still validates its tenant metadata before calling a vector write route.

import os
import time
import requests

def load_discovery():
    for attempt in range(4):
        try:
            response = requests.get(
                "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery",
                headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['INFRAI_API_KEY']}"},
                timeout=10,
            )
            if response.status_code == 200:
                return response.json()
            if response.status_code != 429 or attempt == 3:
                raise RuntimeError(f"discovery failed: HTTP {response.status_code}: {response.text}")
            retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
            time.sleep(float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2 ** attempt)

Here is the boundary I keep in code: the provider client returns candidates, while my application owns tenant filters and citation validation.

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class Candidate:
    tenant_id: str
    document_id: str
    revision: str
    text: str
    source_url: str

def citation_ready(candidate: Candidate, tenant_id: str) -> bool:
    return (
        candidate.tenant_id == tenant_id
        and bool(candidate.document_id)
        and bool(candidate.revision)
        and bool(candidate.source_url)
        and bool(candidate.text.strip())
    )

That small check is where cross-tenant leakage gets stopped. It also makes a provider swap less dramatic because the downstream contract does not change.

How do the common alternatives compare?

The comparison is about system shape, not a universal leaderboard. Pinecone is a managed vector index, Weaviate is an open-source and managed vector database, and Elasticsearch combines mature lexical search with vector capabilities. All can participate in a durable path; the surrounding operational model is the differentiator.

Option Durable index fit Live/fresh path Citation-control implication
Pinecone Managed vector retrieval with tenant metadata filters Usually an application-owned fetch or re-index step Keep revision and source fields in metadata; validate them before generation
Weaviate Flexible self-hosted or managed collection model Application can combine collection search with source fetch More deployment choices mean more policy to standardize
Elasticsearch Hybrid lexical/vector retrieval in an existing search stack Strong fit when the source is already indexed and refreshed Mapping and analyzer changes become part of the citation audit trail
Infrai vector surface One REST contract for collection create, upsert, query, and delete Pair vector results with an application-owned live fetch Discovery and consistent envelopes simplify the adapter boundary; tenant policy remains yours

No row removes the need for a labeled evaluation set. Before rollout, label a small sample per tenant with the expected supporting passage, then measure recall at the candidate stage and citation accuracy at the answer stage. I once treated a high top-k score as proof of grounding; the first revision-heavy test showed that stale, well-phrased chunks can still win. That was a design correction, not a model problem.

Roll out the two paths without losing the audit trail

Start durable-only for a narrow set of published articles. Store the retrieval path, revision, and source ids with every generated answer. Add the live branch behind a flag for tenants whose content changes hourly, and compare citation coverage against the same labeled set. Keep a kill switch that selects durable candidates when the live source is unavailable; the answer should then say it is based on the last indexed revision.

The catch is operational ownership. A live fetch is not suitable when your source has strict latency budgets, offline regions, or no stable revision identifiers. Stick with a durable-only specialist such as Elasticsearch when lexical controls and existing cluster operations are the primary constraint. Conversely, a live branch earns its cost when “current policy” matters more than a fixed response time.

If your boundary fits the uniform REST approach, start with the Infrai documentation and confirm the current discovery schemas before wiring ingestion. The decision rule is simple: choose the path that preserves freshness, control, and citation evidence together; combine both when the feature needs durable and live context.

Sources

  • https://docs.infrai.cc
  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
  • https://docs.pinecone.io/
  • https://weaviate.io/developers/weaviate
  • https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/dense-vector.html

title: How to Use Parallel Data for Multilingual Pretraining
description:
arXiv:2610.28838v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: High-quality human-translated parallel corpora can improve cross-lingual transfer, but are typically too small for large-scale pretraining. Machine-translated web corpora help overcome this limitation, making parallel data available at pretraining scale. Standard multilingual pretraining, however, samples source documents and their translations independently, without explicitly using their parallel structure. We investigate how to use the parallel structure of the data to improve multilingual pretraining by concatenating each document with its translation in the same training sequence. We compare this parallel pretraining (PPT) approach with standard pretraining (SPT), training models from scratch at matched token budgets. Surprisingly, despite the benefits of parallel data reported in prior cross-lingual work, PPT alone does not consistently improve language understanding over SPT. Our further analysis suggests that although PPT builds a strong cross-lingual foundation, as shown by its better use of shared information across languages, the mismatch between parallel training contexts and single-language task inputs limits its gains in general language understanding. This finding motivates a two-stage approach following the pretraining-fine-tuning paradigm: we first use PPT to build a cross-lingual foundation, then continue with SPT to adapt it to standard language modeling. In both high-resource and low-resource settings, the two-stage approach consistently improves general language understanding and cross-lingual task performance over standard pretraining alone at matched training budgets.

title: To Keep or Not to Keep: Learning KV Cache Retention in Disaggregated LLM Serving Systems
description:
arXiv:2610.28637v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Disaggregated \textsc{LLM} serving separates prefill and decode across node pools, placing a network fabric between \textsc{KV}-cache computation and consumption. This breaks a key assumption of classical cache policies: a miss no longer incurs only local recomputation, but also network transfer to the decode node. Likewise, admitting a block to the global cache requires an additional transfer, so poor retention decisions waste both memory and bandwidth. We present \textbf{KVLearn}, a learning-based framework for cost-aware \textsc{KV}-cache retention in disaggregated serving. KVLearn includes: (i) a lightweight Prefix Reuse Predictor (\textsc{PRP}) that estimates reuse probability from structural and temporal prefix features without modifying model weights; (ii) a Cost-Aware Retention Score (\textsc{CARS}) that converts reuse probability into keep/admit decisions using recomputation, transfer, and storage costs; and (iii) an Adaptive Threshold Controller (\textsc{ATC}) that adjusts admission thresholds online from observed hit rates and memory pressure. We integrate KVLearn into a globally disaggregated serving topology and evaluate it on text and multimodal workloads, including large image/video-derived \textsc{KV} blocks with heterogeneous reuse patterns. KVLearn reduces end-to-end time-to-first-token by up to 56% versus No-Cache, 38% versus LRU-Pool, and 33% versus Mooncake-style baselines, while cutting inter-node \textsc{KV} transfer volume by up to 53% versus LRU-Pool. On MM-Session, throughput remains within ${\sim}5%$ of oracle. Code is available at https://github.com/FastLM/KVLearn.

title: October 21 Security Roundup: PHP2Shell's Backstory, Java, HTTP/3, Node, Railway and OVH
description:
21 October 2026 was a long day for security teams. PHP patched two critical vulnerabilities, Oracle issued an out-of-band alert for Java, Node.js closed ten vulnerabilities and Railway disclosed access to customer secrets. The day before, OVHcloud's command-line tool had been shipped with malware.

This post is a roundup of that day. Each section says what happened and what you should do. The technical deep dive on the PHP bugs is in a separate post: Two Critical RCEs in PHP: CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Video: Pixel Shorts ¬∑ Yesterday, in short.

At a glance

Topic Identifier What to do
PHP2Shell CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619 ¬∑ CVSS v4.0 9.2 Move to 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35; restart PHP-FPM and Apache
Java (JSSE) CVE-2026-91403 ¬∑ CVSS 9.1 Update the JDK or replace blocked.certs
HTTP/3 QPACK CVE-2025-64702 (quic-go), CVE-2026-12523 (quiche) quic-go 0.57.0, quiche 0.29.3, lsquic 4.9.0; disable HTTP/3 on Bun
Node.js 10 CVEs, worst is CVE-2026-111497 (Brotli, RCE) 22.23.4, 24.22.1 or 26.12.1
Railway Incident QH8L8B3E Rotate every environment variable and API token stored on Railway
OVHcloud CLI 0.11.0 ‚Äì 0.15.0 (19 October) If you installed it that day, rotate every secret on disk and use 0.16.0

PHP2Shell: from 2024 to today

2024: the first sign

According to the PHP Foundation, the first signs appeared in 2024. A PHP core developer contracted by the Foundation noticed the out-of-memory (OOM) problem while fixing another issue from Quarkslab's 2024 audit. No concrete attack vector was found at the time, and issues with clear impact took priority.

In the following months the security team drafted several fixes. As The Next Web reports, one broke backward compatibility, one introduced a new DoS risk and one required changes across thousands of extensions. The small, consensus-driven team could not pick one. The Foundation called this a "structural failure" and says decisions will now be made by majority.

August 2026: rediscovered with AI

This summer two teams independently found a working attack path:

  • Calif: According to the Wall Street Journal, a Calif researcher found the flaw with GPT-5.6 Sol as part of OpenAI's "Patch the Planet" program.
  • Wiz Research: According to Wiz, the first finding came on 19 August, unauthenticated RCE was confirmed against Drupal and WordPress on 20‚Äì21 August, and the reports went to PHP on 24 August. Wiz says it used Wiz Atlas, Gemini 4 Argon and GPT-5.6 Sol.

PHP acknowledged the reports on 21 September and started a coordinated fix.

17‚Äì21 October: the leak and the patch

Date What happened
17 October Amazon Threat Intelligence saw a PHP2Shell attempt in its MadPot honeypots, four days before disclosure. How the actor got the details is unknown.
20 October The CVE IDs circulated on forums and social media with a wrong release time and a wrong score (10.0). PHP moved its pre-announcement to 19:30 UTC.
20 October Calif mistakenly published a video of its working PoC. The Foundation says it revealed "limited additional details".
21 October 07:41 UTC Chainguard published patched images more than six hours early. The Foundation said this disregarded coordinated disclosure.
21 October 14:00 UTC 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35 released.
21 October watchTowr saw exploitation attempts in its honeypots; Cloudflare saw attack traffic against customers and shipped WAF rules. No confirmed successful compromise has been reported.

Names of alleged leakers are circulating on social media. I could not find them in any primary source, so they are not here.

How to apply the PHP fix correctly

1. Check the PHP your site actually runs

If a server has several PHP versions, php -v in the terminal shows only the default CLI. The PHP-FPM pool or Apache module serving your site can be a different version.

php -v                 # CLI PHP
php-fpm8.4 -v          # the FPM your site uses (adjust the version)
ls /etc/php/           # all installed versions (Debian/Ubuntu)

If unsure, put a temporary phpinfo() page on the site, check "Server API" and the version line, then delete it.

2. Update the package

Debian and Ubuntu (distribution packages): Distributions usually backport security fixes into the old version number. If the number did not change, look for the CVE in the changelog.

sudo apt update
sudo apt install --only-upgrade 'php8.4*'
apt changelog php8.4-fpm | grep -E '109618|109619'

Ond≈ôej Sur√Ω's repository (deb.sury.org): This repository follows PHP's upstream version numbers. It also has new packages for 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1 dated 21 October. I checked their changelogs myself: the patch was written by PHP developers and carries the note "Minimal mitigation for EOL version". It buys time for 8.1 and older; the real fix is moving to 8.2 or later.

AlmaLinux: Patched packages are in the AlmaLinux 8, 9 and 10 repositories.

sudo dnf update 'php*'

Docker: Rebuild your image on the new version tag (e.g. FROM php:8.4.27-fpm) and restart the containers. A docker pull alone is not enough; containers started from the old image keep running old code.

Shared hosting and control panels: Your provider applies the update. Ask in writing which version you are on.

3. Restart

PHP-FPM workers and Apache processes run the code they loaded into memory. The fix is not live until they restart.

sudo systemctl restart php8.4-fpm
sudo systemctl restart apache2      # if you use mod_php

4. Interim settings

The interim settings php.net lists (session.upload_progress.enabled = 0, memory_limit = -1, a low post_max_size, and fatal_error_backtraces = 0 on PHP 8.5) do not make a server safe; they close some paths. Details are in the earlier post. If you don't use upload progress, keeping it off after patching does no harm; I left it off on my server.

On my own server

I installed the builds that landed in the CloudPanel repository on the evening of 21 October: 8.5.12 (17:29) and 8.4.27 (18:56). The check on 22 October:

$ php-fpm8.5 -v
PHP 8.5.12 (fpm-fcgi) (built: Oct 21 2026 07:08:08) (NTS)
$ php-fpm8.4 -v
PHP 8.4.27 (fpm-fcgi) (built: Oct 21 2026 07:08:08) (NTS)

Java: CVE-2026-91403

According to OpenJDK's 21 October advisory, eight intermediate CA certificates were compromised. The component is security-libs/javax.net.ssl (JSSE), scored 9.1 under CVSS 3.1. JDK 8, 11, 17, 21, 25 and 27 are affected; OpenJFX is not. Oracle issued it as a separate Security Alert, outside the regular October CPU.

  • Standalone JDK/JRE: Update to the latest release.
  • If you can't update: Drop in the new $JDK_HOME/lib/security/blocked.certs (blacklisted.certs on JDK 8; back up any entries you added), or enable revocation checking: 
-Dcom.sun.net.ssl.checkRevocation=true -Dcom.sun.security.enableCRLDP=true
  • OS-provided OpenJDK: On Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora, Red Hat and Arch, updating the system certificates is usually enough. Update FreeBSD and Homebrew packages directly.

If you don't know how many JDKs you have, count them first: CI agents, IDEs and runtimes bundled inside applications each need their own update.

HTTP/3: QPACK memory amplification

FoxIO published a class of memory amplification flaws in QPACK, HTTP/3's header compression (summary by The Hacker News). Affected stacks cap the compressed input but not the decoded header list, or apply the cap too late. Seven of the ten HTTP/3 stacks tested were affected. No authentication is needed; a small request can make the server allocate far more memory.

Stack Status
quic-go (Caddy, Traefik, cloudflared) Fixed in 0.57.0 ¬∑ CVE-2025-64702
Cloudflare quiche Fixed in 0.29.3 ¬∑ CVE-2026-12523
lsquic (LiteSpeed, OpenLiteSpeed) Fixed in 4.9.0
Wireshark (dissector) 4.6.2 / 4.4.12 ¬∑ CVE-2025-13945
Bun, h3 (hyperium), aioquic/mitmproxy Unpatched at disclosure
IIS, Envoy, ngtcp2/nghttp3, Google quiche Not affected per FoxIO

Interim mitigations for unpatched stacks: don't expose Bun's HTTP/3 server, run mitmproxy with --set http3=false, and set a limit with max_field_section_size in h3. No in-the-wild exploitation was reported at disclosure.

Node.js: 21 October security releases

On 21 October Node.js fixed 10 CVEs across the 22.x, 24.x and 26.x lines: 4 high, 3 medium, 3 low. The fixed releases are 22.23.4, 24.22.1 and 26.12.1.

High severity:

  • CVE-2026-111497: out-of-bounds write in the Brotli decoder that allows remote code execution (RCE).
  • CVE-2026-105483: TLS certificate hostname check bypass when an IP address is written with fullwidth digits.
  • CVE-2026-106069: TLS hostname check bypass when the host loosely resolves to an IP address.
  • CVE-2026-105482: dns.resolve truncates names containing a NUL character.

Among the medium ones, CVE-2026-106074 stores the entropy cache of crypto.randomUUID() and randomInt() in snapshots and SEAs, so processes started from the same snapshot can repeat values. Node.js 20 and 25 are end-of-life and got no fix; apps on those lines need a major upgrade.

node -v

Railway: access to environment variables

On 21 October Railway detected anomalous activity in the systems that store customer environment variables. According to GitGuardian's summary, an unauthorized party may have accessed encrypted values and, for some, decrypted ones. Railway links it to a series of attacks on platform companies aimed at compromising AI inference providers.

Per the status page, builds were paused platform-wide, OAuth sessions were invalidated, bucket credentials were rotated and on 22 October at 04:17 UTC all Railway API tokens were revoked. On the morning of 22 October, Pro and Enterprise builds were running slowly and Hobby builds were not yet enabled.

If you use Railway:

  1. Rotate keys in the upstream services first (AWS, GCP, GitHub, AI providers), then update the values in Railway.
  2. Rotate sealed variables too; the disclosure doesn't say whether they were in scope.
  3. Rotate private registry credentials.
  4. Review the logs of services that use these credentials. Railway published guides for AWS, GCP and GitHub.
  5. Create a new Railway API token; the old ones no longer work.

Claims that crypto assets stored on Railway were also drained are circulating on social media; I could not confirm them from a primary source.

OVHcloud CLI: a supply-chain attack

According to BleepingComputer, attackers took over a developer's GitHub account and replaced files in existing OVHcloud CLI releases. Versions 0.11.0 through 0.15.0 served malicious files on 19 October between roughly 14:47 and 16:21 (sources state the time zone differently; the window is about 94 minutes).

  • The malware is an infostealer that collects secrets from disk. It includes a hidden preinstall.js loader and a second stage fetched through a Solana memo dead drop. OpenSourceMalware links it to an operation called GlassWorm.
  • Affected platforms: macOS (Intel, ARM), Linux (x86_64, ARM64) and Windows x86-64. Builds from source and Docker images were not affected.
  • The releases could be changed without passing CI/CD because GitHub's release immutability setting was off. OVHcloud has turned it on.
  • 0.10.0 and 0.16.0 are clean.

This is not a customer data breach; there are no reports of access to OVHcloud infrastructure or customer databases. But if you installed or updated the CLI in that window on 19 October, the advice from OVHcloud CEO Octave Klaba is clear: change every secret on that machine.

Today's checklist

  • [ ] PHP: is your site's PHP-FPM on 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35? If not, update, then restart PHP-FPM and Apache.
  • [ ] PHP 8.1 and older: install the minimal patch and plan the move to 8.2 or later.
  • [ ] Java: update every JDK/JRE or replace blocked.certs.
  • [ ] HTTP/3: check your quic-go, quiche and lsquic versions; disable HTTP/3 on Bun.
  • [ ] Node.js: 22.23.4, 24.22.1 or 26.12.1.
  • [ ] Railway: rotate every environment variable, registry credential and API token.
  • [ ] OVHcloud CLI: if you installed 0.11‚Äì0.15 on 19 October, rotate your secrets and move to 0.16.0.

title: Vienna rent prices per sqm by district: October 2026 (live ImmoScout24 data)
description:
Disclosure: I built the Apify Actors used to collect this data. This post was written with AI assistance.

Vienna's median asking rent is €22.72 per m² in October 2026, about €1,590 a month for a typical flat. The most expensive district is Innere Stadt (1010) at €26.74 per m², followed by Donaustadt (€26.67); the cheapest is Simmering (1110) at €18.77.

If you are comparing Vienna districts before a move, negotiating a lease or building a market model, the number you want is rent per square metre by district, and the listing pages do not show it. This report computes it from live ImmoScout24.at rental listings, for all 23 districts, and I will publish a new edition regularly so you can see the change.

Rent per m² by district

Orange: the three most expensive districts. Green: the three cheapest. The grey figure is the change against the previous edition (this is the first edition, so there is none yet, shown as a dash).

Rent per m² by flat size: under 40 m² cost the most

  • under 40 m²: €28.05 per m² (median rent €900 a month, 52 listings)
  • 40-60 m²: €22.72 per m² (median rent €1,099 a month, 281 listings)
  • 60-90 m²: €21.53 per m² (median rent €1,598 a month, 301 listings)
  • 90 m² and up: €22.80 per m² (median rent €3,148 a month, 381 listings)

The under 40 m² band is the most expensive per square metre (€28.05) and the 60-90 m² band the cheapest (€21.53). A small flat is a cheaper flat per month, not per square metre, so compare districts using flats of the same size.

How this was measured

  • Source: the ImmoScout24 Austria Scraper on Apify, run on 2026-10-22 with a fixed input: all 23 Vienna postcodes, rent, flats, sorted newest first, the newest 50 listings per district (1015 listings in total after removing duplicates, implausible rows and listings beyond the agency cap). The portal itself listed 3,880 rental flats in Vienna that day (column "Rental flats on the portal").
  • Asking rents, not contracts: these are the rents advertised by landlords and agents, as ImmoScout24 shows them (monthly rent including operating costs). Signed contracts, old tenancies and regulated rents are lower.
  • City median: each listing is weighted by how many rental flats its district has on the portal, so small districts do not count as much as large ones.
  • No single advertiser decides a district: one agency or developer counts for at most 5 listings per district, because a developer who posts a whole new-build block on one day would otherwise set the median of its district (listings used per district: 30 to 50).
  • Aggregates only: no landlord names, streets or listing texts are used or published here.
  • Caveat 1: peripheral districts with a lot of new-build rental supply can rank higher than their address suggests; the data used here does not separate new-builds from older flats.
  • Caveat 2: the newest 50 listings are a sample of a district's market, not all of it. Differences of a euro between neighbouring districts are within noise; the gaps of five euros and more are not.

How to get this data yourself, every day

Everything above was collected by an Apify Actor from a fixed input, plus some arithmetic. You can run the same collection on your own Apify account in a couple of clicks:

  • ImmoScout24 Austria Scraper: $1.50 per 1,000 results on the free plan, you pay only for results delivered.

Collecting the data for this edition costs about $1.73 on Apify's free plan (you pay per result delivered, nothing for a search that returns nothing), so a monthly refresh costs about the same.

Daily monitor in three steps:

  1. Open the Actor, paste an input like the one below, and switch on Only new (onlyNew). The first run returns everything; every later run returns only what no earlier run of the same watch list delivered, and skipped items are not charged.
  2. Save the input as a task and put it on a schedule (for example the cron expression 0 7 * * *, every day at 07:00 UTC).
  3. Send the result where you work: e-mail, Slack or Google Sheets, from the task's Integrations tab. 
{
  "locations": [
    "Wien"
  ],
  "transaction": "rent",
  "propertyType": "flat",
  "sortBy": "newest",
  "maxListingsPerSearch": 100,
  "onlyNew": true,
  "monitorKey": "vienna-rent-flats"
}

Want the numbers for your own street, price range or flat size? Open the ImmoScout24 Austria Scraper on Apify, set the district and filters, and run it: the input form is prefilled, one click starts a run, and the dataset comes back as CSV, Excel or JSON.

Next edition: follow me here on dev.to to get the next Vienna rent update, and run the monitor above if you would rather have the new listings in your inbox the same morning they appear.

title: JUICE: Unified Multimodal Modeling in Pretrained Representation Spaces
description:
arXiv:2610.28801v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Most unified multimodal models treat images and text asymmetrically: a pretrained language model generates text, an attached diffusion head generates images, and outputs that contain both are produced in a fixed order, so the first output cannot adapt to the second. We ask whether both modalities can instead be generated by one process that is trained on them jointly from scratch. Pretrained encoder spaces hold both modalities in one continuous form and carry knowledge learned at scale, and recent work finds them effective as generative targets for vision and language. We therefore model the joint distribution directly in these spaces. We introduce JUICE (Joint Unified multimodal modeling In Continuous Encoder spaces), a single flow matching Transformer over frozen image and text representations, in which each modality has its own noise level. Which modalities are clean and which are generated then decides the task: image generation, captioning, visual question answering, or joint generation. Controlled pretraining runs test each design choice. At equal guidance, generating text as continuous states leaves image generation intact (48.41 GenEval, against 47.86 for a model trained only for text-to-image generation), while captions lose some exact wording. Training on joint and conditional denoising together beats either alone, and semantic encoder spaces beat VAE latents and raw pixels as targets. At 2.1B parameters, with no language model initialization and at 224x224, JUICE reaches up to 0.88 on GenEval and 73.1 on VQAv2. By sampling both modalities from the joint distribution (coupled sampling), it can also draw a route on a map while writing out the matching moves. On mazes with several valid solutions, joint success rises from 54.6% with independent sampling to 93.7%, and no modality has to go first. On visual spatial planning, JUICE solves 99.8% of maps at its training sizes.
