Google Cloud Contact Center as a Service

Announcement

Google Cloud CCaaS 6.22

We've released version 6.22 of Google Cloud CCaaS.

The timing of the update to your instance depends on the deployment schedule that you have chosen. For more information, see Deployment schedules.

Feature

Transcript separation for chat

You can now configure Google Cloud CCaaS to deliver a separate transcript file for each participant segment in a chat, instead of one combined transcript per session. Under Settings > Chat > Chat Transcript, select Per Segment in Transcript Separation to generate individual transcript files for each agent, virtual agent, or supervisor who joins the chat—helpful for identifying which participant handled each part of a transferred or escalated conversation. Your consumers still receive a single, full-chat transcript regardless of this setting.

For more information, see Chat transcripts and chat history.

By default, this capability is inactive. Contact Google Cloud Support to turn it on for your instance.

Feature

Campaign-based scheduled callbacks

Agents can now schedule a callback during an outbound campaign call. The callback belongs to the campaign, not to an individual agent, and the dialer calls the consumer back in the time slot they chose. Administrators set slot length, capacity, booking window, and expiry for each campaign, and supervisors can track upcoming, completed, and expired callbacks from the campaign list.

For more information, see Campaign management.

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue where direct access point (DAP) greeting messages played twice when a call was deflected to an internal phone number due to queue overcapacity.

  • Fixed an issue where session metadata for top-level menu paths and selected menus was incorrectly displayed in English instead of the user's configured language.

  • Fixed an issue where a failed Salesforce lookup was incorrectly treated as having no matches, which resulted in the creation of duplicate records.

  • Fixed an issue where inbound transfer restrictions remained in force even after being hidden in the administrator interface, causing queues to become silently unreachable for transfers.

  • Fixed an issue where hold music continued to play throughout a call recording after a warm transfer was completed.

  • Fixed an issue where outbound virtual agent audio was prematurely truncated during multi-message turns.

  • Fixed an issue where the Real-time Monitoring Queues report didn't accurately count skill-matched agents for skills-based queues, often displaying zero available agents despite their availability.

  • Fixed an issue where calls deflected to an external phone number after entering a queue were incorrectly recorded as abandoned by the customer.

  • Fixed an issue where the credit card tokenizer was missing from the SmartActions menu during outbound callback calls.

  • Fixed an issue where mandatory call dispositions were discarded if an agent's voice connection dropped but their session remained active.

  • Fixed an issue where the text resize menu in the chat widget wasn't scrollable at 400% browser zoom, which prevented users from accessing all available text size options.

  • Fixed an issue where the system incorrectly prevented saving automatic call redirection settings when the target was a virtual agent-operated queue.

  • Fixed an issue where duplicate call records were created for a single inbound call, causing incorrect wait times to appear in the real-time queue view.

  • Fixed an issue where empty data attributes caused an error in the agent interface during call connections.

  • Fixed an issue where the Transfer Restrictions destination picker provided no feedback when a queue was ineligible, making it indistinguishable from a typo or search error.

  • Fixed an issue where incoming calls were rejected with a SIP 603 error due to high database latency and connection timeouts.

  • Fixed an issue where the documentation for the Apps API and call session metadata schema didn't define the top-level parentId and finishReason fields.

  • Fixed an issue where certain inbound call failures were incorrectly reported as a busy signal.

  • Fixed an issue where the event processor service crashed during scaling or rebalancing of the system.

  • Fixed an issue where the conversation ID was missing from chat events during active sessions.

  • Fixed an issue where report exports didn't download or remained stuck in a processing state indefinitely.

  • Fixed an issue where agents could transfer calls to queues that were already closed if their transfer list was loaded while the queue was still open.

  • Fixed an issue where queued chats were assigned to agents after the end-user had become unresponsive without being prompted to check in.

  • Fixed an issue where voice calls cold-transferred to an over-capacity queue generated duplicate reporting records and incorrect queue wait times if the callback leg failed.

  • Fixed an issue where direct inbound calls deflected to voicemail during after-hours played three separate audio prompts sequentially.

  • Fixed an issue where a single call was simultaneously assigned to two different agents if the pickup coincided with the cascade timer expiry.

  • Fixed an issue where direct inbound calls weren't projected to agents in a breakthrough-enabled status if another call was already waiting in their queue.

  • Fixed an issue where a gray empty area appeared below the chat container in the agent adapter when the iframe width was narrower than 449px.

  • Fixed an issue where several Kubernetes and Google Cloud service accounts were granted overly broad permissions, which could have allowed for unauthorized privilege escalation.

  • Fixed an issue where an agent's status sequence was recorded in the incorrect order following a brief connection loss during an active chat.

  • Fixed an issue where selecting a contact during a native campaign call didn't automatically open the corresponding record in the CRM.

  • Fixed an issue where AI-generated Smart Disposition suggestions were inconsistently displayed for outbound calls during the wrap-up period.

  • Fixed an issue where call recordings became distorted or garbled when multiple holds were placed during a call.

  • Fixed an issue where audio uploads were accepted based on the file extension rather than the actual file content, which caused call disconnections when incompatible formats were played.

  • Fixed an issue where the call duration timer in the external call adapter didn't match the In-call status timer in the agent desktop for inbound calls.

  • Fixed an issue where the sentiment score was incorrectly displayed in the call adapter for calls escalated from a virtual agent, even when the Sentiment Analysis setting was disabled.

  • Fixed an issue where duplicate reporting rows were generated for call and wrap-up durations due to concurrent system events.

  • Fixed an issue where agents couldn't sign in or refresh their status if their account was linked to a deleted or unknown status.

  • Fixed an issue where the Manager API documentation for agent activity logs omitted 17 chat routing and activity values, leading to incomplete reporting data for customers.

  • Fixed an issue where IVR custom callback numbers for certain international regions, including Norway and Denmark, were incorrectly dialed with a +1 prefix.

  • Fixed an issue where metadata for calls deflected between virtual agent assignment and connection wasn't exported to the Cloud Storage bucket.

  • Fixed an issue where virtual agent to human chat escalations experienced delays of up to 300 seconds during agent assignment.

  • Fixed an issue where the Answer button didn't appear for dial-by-extension calls when other calls were already waiting in an agent's queue.

  • Fixed an issue where a supervisor's name didn't appear in the chat widget when joining a conversation using the monitor then barge workflow.

  • Fixed an issue where ending a chat session in one browser tab didn't automatically close the chat widget in other open tabs.

title: Building a Scalable Audit & System Logging Architecture for Healthcare Applications
description:
A practical approach to separating business audit events from technical system logs for better debugging, observability, and accountability.

When people think about healthcare software, they usually think about Electronic Health Records (EHRs), appointment scheduling, billing systems, prescriptions, or patient portals.

Those features are obviously important—but after several years working on backend systems, I've learned that one of the most valuable components isn't visible to users at all.

It's logging.

Users don't notice it.

Product demos rarely mention it.

But the moment something goes wrong in production, it becomes one of the first places every engineer looks.

Questions like these suddenly become critical:

  • Why did this request fail?
  • Who updated this record?
  • What changed?
  • Was it a system issue or a user action?
  • When did it happen?
  • Can we reproduce it?

Without a well-designed logging strategy, answering those questions often means digging through databases, reproducing issues, or relying on guesswork.

With a good logging architecture, the answers are usually only a few searches away.

In this article, I'd like to share a logging architecture pattern that separates Audit Logs from System Logs, why that distinction matters, and some practical lessons I've learned while designing enterprise backend applications.

Why Logging Matters in Healthcare

Healthcare applications manage some of the most sensitive information in any industry.

Every day, systems perform operations like:

  • Updating patient demographics
  • Scheduling appointments
  • Recording medications
  • Signing clinical encounters
  • Updating insurance information
  • Managing laboratory results

Each operation changes business data that someone may need to investigate later.

Imagine receiving a production ticket that simply says:

The patient's insurance information changed yesterday.

The first question isn't **how **to fix it.

The first question is:

What actually happened?

A good logging strategy should make that easy to answer.

Audit Logs vs. System Logs

One of the biggest mistakes I see is treating audit logs and system logs as the same thing.

Although both record events, they solve completely different problems.

Audit Logs

  • Record business events
  • Who changed the data?
  • Business accountability
  • User activity
  • Compliance

System Logs

  • Record technical events
  • How did the application behave?
  • Technical troubleshooting
  • Request lifecycle
  • Performance & debugging

Think of it like this:

  • Audit Logs tell the story of the business.
  • System Logs tell the story of the application.

Keeping these responsibilities separate makes both systems much easier to maintain.

High-Level Architecture

Instead of allowing every controller or service to generate logs independently, one common approach is to centralize the logging process.

                Client

                  │

                  ▼

        HTTP Request Received

                  │

                  ▼

     Request Processing Layer

      ┌────────────┴────────────┐

      ▼                         ▼

System Logging           Business Logic

                                  │

                                  ▼

                    Audit Event Dispatcher

                                  │

               ┌──────────────────┼──────────────────┐

               ▼                  ▼                  ▼

         Domain A           Domain B           Domain C

               └──────────────────┼──────────────────┘

                                  ▼

                 Search & Analytics Platform

This separation keeps business logic focused on business problems while allowing logging to evolve independently.

System Logging

System logs describe how the application behaves.

Every incoming request typically generates a system log regardless of whether business data changes.

Typical metadata includes:

  • HTTP Method
  • Endpoint
  • Authenticated User
  • Organization ID
  • Client IP
  • Timestamp
  • Request ID / Correlation ID
  • Request Parameters
  • Response Status
  • Execution Time
  • Exception Details

A simplified pipeline looks like this:

Incoming Request --> Collect Request Metadata --> Execute Business Logic --> Capture Response --> Generate System Log --> Search Platform

Capturing request metadata before executing business logic is especially valuable.

Even if an exception occurs later, engineers still have enough context to investigate what happened.

Audit Logging

Audit logging has a different purpose.

Not every request deserves an audit event.

Viewing a dashboard usually doesn't.

Updating a patient record probably does.

Instead of placing audit logic throughout the application, a centralized dispatcher can determine whether an action should generate an audit event.

A simplified flow looks like this.

Business Operation --> Audit Dispatcher --> Determine Business Domain --> Module A/B/C --> Compare Previous State --> Generate Audit Event --> Store Event

Each module owns only the logic related to its own domain.

For example:

  • Create Record
  • Update Record
  • Delete Record
  • Restore Record

This keeps the architecture modular and avoids duplicating logging logic across multiple controllers or services.

Choosing a Search Platform

As applications grow, log volume increases rapidly.

Searching millions of log entries using relational databases alone can become inefficient.

Search and analytics platforms such as Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, or similar technologies are designed specifically for this workload.

Benefits include:

  • Full-text search
  • Fast filtering
  • Near real-time indexing
  • Time-based queries
  • Aggregations
  • Dashboards
  • Scalable storage

Instead of storing logs alongside transactional data, indexing them separately makes production investigations significantly faster.

Benefits of Separating Audit & System Logs

After adopting this architecture, organizations often notice several practical improvements.

Faster Debugging

Engineers spend less time reproducing issues because request history is already available.

Better Accountability

Business actions become traceable.

Teams can understand who performed an action, what changed, and when it happened.

Easier Production Support

Support teams can investigate incidents without involving developers in every case.

Improved Observability

System logs provide visibility into:

  • API failures
  • Background jobs
  • Integration issues
  • Slow requests
  • Exceptions

Cleaner Architecture

Business logic remains focused on business functionality instead of logging implementation.

Performance Considerations

Logging should improve observability—not reduce application performance.

Some practices that have worked well include:

Log meaningful business events.

Avoid storing sensitive information.

Keep payloads concise.

Index commonly searched fields.

Rotate or archive old logs.

Consider asynchronous logging for high-volume systems.

Good logging should be informative without becoming expensive.

Common Logging Mistakes

Some mistakes appear repeatedly across enterprise applications.

❌ Mixing audit logs with system logs.

❌ Logging passwords or authentication tokens.

❌ Logging every single request without a purpose.

❌ Making logs impossible to search.

❌ Ignoring retention and archival strategies.

A thoughtful logging strategy is just as important as the logging technology itself.

Lessons Learned

One lesson has stayed with me throughout multiple backend projects:

Logging should never be treated as something you add after a feature is finished.

It should be part of the system architecture from the beginning.

Good logging doesn't only help developers.

It helps support engineers.

It helps administrators.

It helps operations teams.

And ultimately, it improves confidence in the software itself.

Looking ahead, I also think AI will change how we interact with logs.

Instead of manually searching thousands of entries, AI systems will be able to summarize incidents, identify unusual behavior, explain failures in natural language, and assist engineers during production investigations.

For healthcare systems, where reliability and accountability are essential, that evolution is particularly exciting.

Final Thoughts

Logging isn't the feature users ask for.

It's the feature engineers appreciate when everything else goes wrong.

Separating Audit Logs from System Logs creates a cleaner architecture, simplifies troubleshooting, and improves long-term maintainability.

Whether you're building healthcare software, SaaS products, or enterprise platforms, investing in a thoughtful logging strategy will pay dividends long after the feature has shipped.

Because in production systems, understanding what happened is often just as important as making sure it never happens again.

Discussion

How do you approach logging in your applications?

  • Do you separate audit logs from system logs?
  • Have you adopted centralized logging?
  • Which search platform are you using—Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, Loki, Splunk, or something else?

I'd love to hear how other teams are solving these challenges.

title: Image generation API compared: 11 models, the same 3 prompts, real outputs
description:
Originally published on the QuickSilver Pro blog.

QuickSilver Pro sells a dozen image-generation models behind one OpenAI-compatible endpoint, /v1/images/generations. They are billed per image, and the price per image ranges widely: $0.003 for FLUX.1 Schnell, $0.07 for Seedream 5.0 Pro. The question is what the extra money buys.

So on 2026-10-20 we gave 11 of them the same three prompts and looked at every image.

Model Price per image
GPT Image 2.5 Flare $0.018
GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst $0.018
GPT Image 2 $0.01
Seedream 5.0 Pro $0.07
Seedream 4 $0.055
Qwen Image 3.0 $0.04
FLUX.2 Pro $0.027
FLUX.2 Klein $0.02
FLUX.1 Schnell $0.003
SDXL Turbo $0.003
Bria FIBO 1.5 $0.055

Prices as of 2026-10-20; current prices are on the pricing page.

Nano Banana Pro is also in the catalog; it is not part of this test.

How we tested

Three prompts, each testing something different:

  1. Text on packaging: Product photo of a matte black coffee bag standing on a wooden table. The front label reads "NORTHWIND ROASTERS" in large white capital letters, and below it, in smaller text, "Ethiopia Yirgacheffe" and "250 g". Soft studio lighting, shallow depth of field.
  2. Exact composition: Flat vector illustration on a plain white background: exactly three red apples on the left side of the image, and exactly one blue cup on the right side. Nothing else in the image.
  3. Photoreal scene: Photorealistic photograph of a small wooden cabin beside a mountain lake at dawn, mist over the water, a red canoe tied to a wooden dock in the foreground, pine trees, no people.

Every request used the same parameters: size="1024x1024", n=1, nothing else. Each model ran each prompt once. We then ran the composition prompt a second time on every model, one request at a time, to get a cleaner latency figure and a second sample. We judged every image by eye: for the label, whether all three lines are spelled exactly right; for the illustration, whether there are exactly three apples on the left and one cup on the right; for the scene, whether every element in the prompt is there and physically plausible.

Results

Model Median latency Text on packaging Three apples, one cup Photoreal scene
GPT Image 2.5 Flare 11.5 s All correct 2 of 2 All elements
GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst 17.5 s All correct, plus a line we did not ask for 2 of 2 All elements
GPT Image 2 20.2 s All correct 2 of 2 All elements
Seedream 5.0 Pro 40.8 s All correct, brand name smaller than asked 1 of 1 All elements
Seedream 4 6.4 s All correct 1 of 1 All elements, very saturated colours
Qwen Image 3.0 5.0 s All correct 1 of 2 (four apples once) All elements
FLUX.2 Pro 8.9 s All correct 1 of 2 (two apples once) All elements
FLUX.2 Klein 1.3 s All correct 0 of 2 (two apples both times) Canoe overlaps the dock
FLUX.1 Schnell 0.7 s Brand correct, small text garbled 1 of 2 (two apples and two cups once) Canoe lying on the dock
SDXL Turbo 4.1 s Garbled 0 of 2 Two canoes, neither at the dock
Bria FIBO 1.5 8.9 s "Yirgachefee", plus two lines of invented text 1 of 1 All elements

Latency is the median of four requests per model, measured from one client. The second composition run was not saved for Seedream 4, Seedream 5.0 Pro and Bria FIBO 1.5, so those have one sample. All 33 requests in the main run succeeded.

What stands out:

  • Text is mostly solved, except at the cheap end. Eight of the eleven models wrote all three lines of the label correctly. FLUX.1 Schnell and Bria FIBO 1.5 got the brand name right and garbled or misspelled the smaller lines; SDXL Turbo produced lettering that is not words.
  • Counting is where models differ. Only the three GPT Image models drew three apples and one cup in both runs. Qwen Image 3.0, FLUX.2 Pro and FLUX.1 Schnell got it right once and wrong once, so a single good image does not mean the model follows counts reliably. FLUX.2 Klein drew two apples both times.
  • The photoreal scene was easy for nearly everyone. Eight of eleven images had every element in a plausible arrangement. The failures were physical: a canoe merged into the dock, a canoe lying on top of it.
  • Latency spans nearly two orders of magnitude. FLUX.1 Schnell answered in under a second; Seedream 5.0 Pro took 28 to 51 seconds per image.

Text on packaging

GPT Image 2.5 Flare GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst Qwen Image 3.0
FLUX.2 Klein Bria FIBO 1.5 SDXL Turbo

Three apples on the left, one cup on the right

GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst Seedream 5.0 Pro Bria FIBO 1.5
Qwen Image 3.0 (first run) FLUX.2 Pro (first run) SDXL Turbo

Cabin, lake and red canoe

GPT Image 2.5 Flare Seedream 5.0 Pro FLUX.2 Pro
Qwen Image 3.0 FLUX.2 Klein SDXL Turbo

What the API actually returns

The models do not all answer a request the same way, and code that works with one can break on another:

  • Size is not always what you ask for. We asked for 1024x1024 every time. Seedream 4 returned 1280x1024 every time we checked. GPT Image 2 picks its own aspect ratio at about 1.57 megapixels: 1774x887 for the apples (twice), 1536x1024 for the lake, 1312x1199 for the coffee bag. Every other model returned 1024x1024.
  • Some models return a link instead of the image. GPT Image, Qwen Image, FLUX and SDXL Turbo put the image in b64_json. Seedream 4, Seedream 5.0 Pro and Bria FIBO 1.5 return a download URL in url instead, and still did when we passed response_format="b64_json". We did not test how long those links stay valid, so download the file straight away.
  • The format differs too. FLUX, SDXL Turbo and the Seedream models returned JPEG; GPT Image, Qwen Image and Bria returned PNG. Check the file's first bytes rather than assuming an extension.

Code that handles both response shapes:

import base64
import urllib.request

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.quicksilverpro.io/v1",
    api_key="YOUR_QSP_KEY",
)

result = client.images.generate(
    model="gpt-image-2.5-flare",
    prompt="Flat vector illustration: three red apples on the left, one blue cup on the right, plain white background.",
    size="1024x1024",
    n=1,
)

image = result.data[0]
if image.b64_json:
    data = base64.b64decode(image.b64_json)
else:  # Seedream and Bria return a download link instead
    data = urllib.request.urlopen(image.url).read()

with open("apples.png", "wb") as f:
    f.write(data)

Which one to use

  • GPT Image 2.5 Flare if the image has to match the prompt: correct text and correct counts in every run, at $0.018 per image and about 11 seconds. Sunburst gave the same accuracy here, more slowly, and added a line of text we did not ask for; GPT Image 2 is cheaper at $0.01 but slower and does not keep the size you request.
  • Qwen Image 3.0 or FLUX.2 Pro for good text and photoreal scenes in five to nine seconds, if you can retry when a count comes out wrong.
  • FLUX.2 Klein or FLUX.1 Schnell when speed and volume matter more than precision: drafts, thumbnails, many variations to choose from. Klein even got the label text right, in about a second.
  • Seedream 5.0 Pro produced accurate, natural-looking images, but at $0.07 and 28 to 51 seconds per image it is the most expensive and slowest model in this test.

The whole test, about 50 images including reruns and checks, cost about $1.45 at QuickSilver Pro prices on 2026-10-20.

Limits of this test

One or two images per model per prompt is a very small sample: the composition prompt showed that the same model can get it right on one run and wrong on the next, so treat every cell in the table as one observation, not a rate. Quality was judged by one person looking at the images, and "looks natural" is a matter of taste. We used default settings only; several of these models accept extra parameters (quality, seeds, prompt rewriting) that we did not try. Latency was measured from one client on one day, and in the first run all eleven models were working at the same time. Run your own prompts before choosing: every image request appears in your dashboard with its cost.

For setup in other languages and SDKs, see the quickstart and the model list.

title: ArcFlow: Training Flow Policies for Multiple Solver Budgets
description:
arXiv:2610.28788v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Flow-matching policies adjust inference cost through the number of solver steps, but reinforcement learning at a single fixed solver budget can hide degradation at cheaper deployment budgets and even erase useful one-step behavior present in a pretrained policy. We introduce Action-Ratio-Clip Flow (ArcFlow), a deployment-aware algorithm for training one flow policy across a specified range of solver budgets. ArcFlow combines action-aligned supervision, budget exposure, and worst-budget checkpoint selection. For reconstruction objectives, its bridge aggregates temporal probes into one surrogate ratio and one PPO-style clip per action, with a boundary residual exactly equal to deployed one-step reconstruction error. Cycling exposes the shared field to the deployment range, and selection optimizes its performance floor. For native velocity objectives, multi-budget endpoint supervision applies the same principle without replacing the native update. Both realizations preserve the architecture and deployment-time cost. Across DM Control, manipulation, and locomotion, ArcFlow attains the highest mean one-step return among five flow-policy baselines on 25 of 30 tasks under each method's reported training settings. Component studies identify complementary improvements from boundary supervision, the fixed-grid bridge, budget exposure, and deployment selection. These results establish deployment-budget-aware training as an effective route to strong low-step control with one policy serving multiple inference costs.

title: Think-Capture: Active 3D Geometry Acquisition for Spatial Reasoning in Vision-Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.29232v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) excel at 2D recognition but often fail to maintain consistent 3D relations across sparse viewpoints, leading to spatial hallucinations under occlusion and perspective changes. Existing methods commonly fuse all frames with dense geometry, incurring substantial computation and context overhead while encouraging blind reliance on imperfect estimators. We present Think-Capture, a query-conditioned framework that first identifies task-critical objects and then acquires their geometry on demand. A 3D toolkit lifts zero-shot masks into a common coordinate frame, and a Symbolic 3D State Abstraction compresses object and camera states into structured text. Hierarchical Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) trains the VLM on cases in which geometry either helps or misleads, teaching it when to use tool evidence and when to fall back on visual cues. Think-Capture-4B reaches 54.4% on MindCube-Tiny (+21.5 points over its backbone), 39.1% on the MMSI-Bench positional subset (+7.9), and 42.8% on ViewSpatial (+5.2). It also remains robust under coordinate and mask perturbations. The full stack fits one 24 GB GPU and serves as an asynchronous high-level reasoner on an Agibot G1. Our code is available at https://github.com/819346675/Think-Capture.

title: Automated Multi-Agent Organization Design: From Architecture Search to Organizational Learning
description:
arXiv:2610.27531v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Agentic system design is increasingly shifting from hand-crafted prompts and workflows toward automated search over agentic programs and interaction structures, with multi-agent systems receiving growing attention. Yet a central question remains unresolved: when does an automatically generated multi-agent structure exhibit a functionally meaningful division of responsibility? We argue that automated multi-agent design should move beyond searching for effective architectures toward identifying which responsibilities are functionally necessary, how they should be allocated, and when they should change. To explore this, we propose Automated Multi-Agent Organization Design (AMOD), which treats organization itself as a first-class design object, explicitly modeling how agent teams are composed, what functional responsibilities the agents assume, how they coordinate, and how collective decisions are made. We formulate AMOD as an execution-driven design loop. For each task, an automated designer instantiates an organization by assigning functional responsibilities and coordination rules to a set of agents. After execution, task outcomes, intermediate artifacts, and interaction traces are examined to identify which responsibilities may be missing, duplicated, or ineffective, and the organization is revised accordingly. We also propose testing discovered responsibilities by removing them, replacing them with generic roles, or changing their assignment under matched resource budgets, with complementary evaluations. AMOD provides a principled foundation for evidence-based and adaptive multi-agent organization design.

title: CUA-Recovery: Benchmarking Error Recovery in Long-Horizon Computer-Use Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.27645v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As computer-use agents (CUAs) move to long-horizon workflows spanning multiple applications, undetected errors can silently corrupt persistent state and cause cascading failures in subsequent actions. Reliable error detection and recovery have become critical bottlenecks for building robust CUAs. However, existing benchmarks focus primarily on end-to-end task performance, providing limited insight into whether agents can detect and recover from errors during execution. The few benchmarks that evaluate recovery rely largely on manually injected errors, which may not reflect the types or horizons of failures induced by real agent policies. We introduce CUA-Recovery, a benchmark comprising test and training suites across multiple desktop applications. We construct it using ReRail, a framework for synthesizing long-horizon tasks and trajectories in a persistent desktop environment. ReRail composes MyPCBench tasks into new long-horizon workflows with executable ground truth, collects verifier-confirmed failures from multiple policies, and turns them into verified recovery trajectories. CUA-Recovery comprises a human-verified test suite of 2,250 erroneous states over 100 tasks and a training suite of 8.6K trajectories over 377 tasks. Evaluation on the test suite shows that agents struggle both to recognize inherited errors and to complete the task. Across six agents and six takeover depths, Error Awareness Rate (EAR) reaches at most 44.0% and Pass@3 at most 25.5%. After fine-tuning Qwen3.5-35B-A3B on the training suite, its average EAR rises from 19.9% to 35.2% on held-out recovery states, and its Rubric Score goes from 5.0% to 16.1%. It also gains 15.3 points on MyPCBench and 10.8 points on Odysseys for Pass@3, showing that the training trajectories help both with recovery and with completing tasks from a clean start. Our code is available at https://github.com/xu-hu-2002/CUA-Recovery.

title: Interaction-Gated Time-Frequency Learning for Parameter-Efficient PPG-Based Heart Rate Estimation
description:
arXiv:2610.28693v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Photoplethysmography (PPG) enables low-cost and non-invasive heart rate (HR) monitoring but remains sensitive to waveform distortion, physiological variability, and measurement interference. Temporal waveform characteristics and frequency-domain periodicity provide complementary information for HR estimation; however, effectively exploring and integrating these representations within a compact model remains challenging. This paper proposes TF-IG, a parameter-efficient interaction-gated time-frequency learning framework for PPG-based HR estimation. TF-IG employs a dual-branch architecture in which a temporal branch captures pulse morphology via dilated depthwise-separable convolutions, while a frequency branch extracts cardiac periodicity information from bounded log-spectrogram representations. To combine the two domains, we introduce an interaction-gated fusion module that explicitly models feature agreement and discrepancy, while also learning feature-wise weights to balance temporal and spectral information. A parameter-shared regression head further maps the temporal, spectral, and fused representations into the final HR prediction space. Experiments on the benchmark BIDMC PPG and Respiration Dataset using a subject-exclusive training, validation, and test protocol show that TF-IG achieves a mean absolute error (MAE) of 1.227 BPM, a root mean square error (RMSE) of 2.060 BPM, a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.9934, and 92.28 percent of estimates within 3 BPM, while remaining parameter-efficient with only 84.6K parameters. Ablation results further demonstrate the complementary contributions of the temporal and frequency branches, interaction-gated fusion, and shared regression head. These results indicate that explicitly modeling cross-domain interactions provides an effective accuracy-complexity trade-off for lightweight PPG-based HR estimation.

title: Transformers as Generic Deep Neural Networks: Exact Compilation, the Cost of Removing Activation-Activation Products, and Multi-Agent Attention Clustering
description:
arXiv:2610.28958v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Transformers are deployed as a special model class. Neural processing units (NPU) add dedicated operators for attention and normalization, and quantization relies on Transformer-specific algorithms. We show the computation does not force this. Every Transformer block, with attention, LayerNorm and a GELU MLP, compiles exactly into a generic deep neural network built from fixed affine maps, routing and the square, sigmoid and inverse square root, plus GELU or its sigmoid approximation. Without activation-activation products, every transform-wise compilation adds at least $N^2$ scalar nonlinear evaluations per head for dense scores. Keeping that one operation type removes this cost; its elementwise form, present on every surveyed NPU, suffices with the sigmoid and inverse square root. For top-$k$ attention with exchangeable tail scores, we prove that exact or conditional-mean tail mass gives an unbiased, minimum-mean-square-error estimate of the attention distribution, while tail drop is conditionally biased. When queries or agents cluster, centroids choose the keys first, reducing the number of computed scores from $N^2$ to $Nk$ per head. On DeiT-Tiny, MambaIRv2-Light and Pythia-70M the compiled models match their references with all keys, standard post-training quantization applies, and the exact tail-mass estimate beats tail dropping with half as many keys on DeiT-Tiny and, for $k\le8$, on Pythia-70M.

title: Understanding Target Probability Reuse in Speculative Decoding
description:
arXiv:2610.29210v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Speculative decoding uses a target model to verify a tree of draft tokens in parallel. We study whether the resulting next-token distributions can help select the next tree. For unrestricted target models, we show that guaranteed exact reuse requires a distribution computed at the next round's complete context. We characterize when retaining this distribution requires sacrificing accepted tokens and establish conditions under which this loss persists across decoding rounds. Across six targets, we find that reranking first-token branches with a separately computed distribution at the current context improves expected acceptance over draft ranking, especially with small tree budgets. Drawing the first token from this distribution before allocating the tree further improves expected acceptance over pruning a preselected tree, even at equal mean tree size. In our experiments, both selection rules also decode faster than draft ranking when the separate target pass overlaps standalone drafting. Our findings show that making target probabilities available before tree allocation can improve the efficiency of speculative decoding. Our code is available at https://github.com/js-lee-AI/TargetRows.

title: A KAN-based Non-linear Factorization for Embedding Layer Compression
description:
arXiv:2610.29424v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Among existing embedding compression approaches, low-rank factorization provides a simple and mathematically principled solution by approximating the embedding matrix with a reduced-rank decomposition. However, its practical effectiveness is often limited, as the resulting linear bottleneck constrains representational capacity. To overcome these limitations, we propose an enhanced factorization scheme that increases expressive power by introducing learnable non-linear projections within the compressed embedding layer. Our method is inspired by the Kolmogorov Arnold Networks (KAN) paradigm, which replaces fixed linear transformations with learnable univariate functions. Despite promising results in other domains, applications of KANs in NLP remain scarce and have so far been largely limited to final or task specific layers, rather than core representational components such as embedding layers.
  We evaluate the proposed approach by integrating the compressed embedding layer into the Skip-gram framework and comparing it against a standard low-rank baseline under matched parameter budgets on the Word Analogy and Semantic Similarity benchmarks. We further introduce an effective initialization strategy from a pre-trained, uncompressed embedding layer. The behavior of the model is analyzed both immediately after initialization and after a brief post-initialization refinement phase, considering training with the standard Skip-gram objective as well as variants augmented with distillation from the original embedding layer. Overall, our results show that augmenting low-rank factorization with learnable non-linear projections effectively mitigates the limitations of linear bottlenecks, yielding more faithful compressed embeddings under fixed dimensionality and suggesting a promising direction for embedding layer compression beyond purely linear methods.

title: Recurring User Alerts API Explained — 4 Cron Rules for Monthly Weekly Timezone Webhooks
description:
A rate-limited worker pool makes recurring user reminders an API and queueing problem before it becomes a cron problem. Keep the user's calendar intent, turn each due occurrence into a small job, and let workers drain that queue at a known rate. That adds some latency during a burst, but it protects delivery from a burst that exhausts the pool. The same rule applies to monthly and weekly reminders: cron starts the dispatch, while the worker budget decides how quickly the notifications leave the system.

Short answer: store an IANA timezone with the weekly or monthly rule, send a signed public webhook that only records and enqueues an occurrence, and make the worker idempotent. Treat latency and cost as explicit operating choices rather than promises hidden in a cron expression.

Begin with the worker constraint

A cron tick says “start,” not “how much work can run now.” In a B2B SaaS product, a tenant may schedule a digest for the same local minute as many other tenants. Imagine a Monday morning where hundreds of tenants become due together while the same worker pool is processing imports and exports. If every callback renders a template and waits for a provider, the burst consumes connection slots before the scheduler can report success. The scheduler should call an authenticated endpoint, the endpoint should persist an occurrence key, and a queue should hand work to rate-limited consumers. The callback returns after durable enqueue; template rendering and provider calls stay out of the request path. That split makes the latency-versus-cost decision visible: reserve capacity for fast dispatch, or accept queue age and batch the work.

I use (schedule_id, scheduled_for) as the business idempotency key. Queue delivery is commonly at least once, so a retry must map to the same job instead of sending a second reminder. A message identifier alone is too weak: the identifier can change while the user's intended occurrence has not.

Keep the rule visible in operations. Queue age, callback latency, duplicate suppression, and worker utilization tell you whether the pool is draining. CPU by itself does not.

One sentence matters here: bursts are normal.

What should a weekly or monthly reminder API promise about timezone webhooks?

The API should promise calendar intent, not a frozen UTC timestamp. “Tuesday at 09:00 in Europe/Berlin” should remain a local-time rule when daylight-saving rules change. Store the IANA identifier, local wall-clock time, frequency, and a policy version; compute the next UTC instant as derived state and recompute it after each accepted occurrence. A fixed offset such as +01:00 cannot describe future timezone transitions.

Monthly schedules need a declared policy for a date that does not exist. Reject it, clamp to the last day, or choose the next valid day. Any of those can be defensible; silently selecting one makes support and compliance reviews painful. Your mileage may vary when a tenant's sending window or provider quota is stricter than the worker pool.

The public webhook is a narrow bridge, not the reminder engine. Sign the exact raw body with a timestamped HMAC, reject stale timestamps, compare digests in constant time, persist the occurrence, and then return a success response. RFC 2104 defines the keyed-hash construction; the freshness window is an application policy that should match clock-skew and replay-retention decisions.

import hashlib
import hmac


def valid_signature(raw_body: bytes, header: str, secret: bytes, now: int) -> bool:
    try:
        sent_at_text, supplied = header.split(".", 1)
        sent_at = int(sent_at_text)
    except ValueError:
        return False

    # Five minutes is an example policy; choose a window for your clocks.
    if abs(now - sent_at) > 300:
        return False

    signed = f"{sent_at}.".encode() + raw_body
    expected = hmac.new(secret, signed, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
    return hmac.compare_digest(expected, supplied)

The handler still has to enforce tenant authorization and an idempotency constraint. Authentication answers “who called?”; the occurrence key answers “have I accepted this calendar event already?”

Where do webhook and queue designs fail under load?

The first failure mode is useful work inside the callback. Rendering, calling an email or SMS provider, and waiting for a response couples an internet-facing timeout to every downstream dependency. Return after the ledger write and enqueue; let workers own retries, backoff, suppression checks, and provider-specific rate limits.

The second is an unexamined pause policy. Some schedulers skip occurrences while a schedule is paused, while a business may expect one compensating reminder after resume. Record the pause interval and choose explicitly between “send once after resume” and “skip missed occurrences.” Do not let a retry accidentally decide that policy.

The third is a calendar edge case hidden in a parser. Test a weekly rule across a daylight-saving transition, a monthly rule near the end of a short month, and a leap-day rule. Use a fixed test clock and compare the stored local intent with the derived UTC instant after each transition.

I have spent enough time on OTP and email delivery to distrust a green HTTP response by itself. A 2xx only proves that the bridge accepted a request; it does not prove that a message was delivered. Track scheduled, enqueued, acknowledged, delivered, and suppressed states, and keep reminder content out of logs because destinations and timezone choices are personal data.

How should latency, cost, and endpoint boundaries shape the choice?

Decision Latency-leaning option Cost-leaning option
Dispatch Poll frequently and reserve worker capacity Batch due occurrences on a slower cadence
Retry Short backoff with a dead-letter review path Fewer attempts with explicit operator review
Calculation Derive each next occurrence immediately Derive it when a worker claims the schedule
Security Signature, replay cache, and tenant limits Signature with a smaller replay store

The trade-off is concrete. A public HTTPS webhook is a good boundary when the ingress can be authenticated and monitored. It is not suitable for a private-only service unless a public gateway forwards into the private worker plane. A queue with at-least-once delivery is a poor fit for a side effect that cannot be made idempotent; use a workflow system or an application-level ledger when the process needs joins, long-running compensation, or an audit trail across steps.

Do not make a unit price the main decision. Measure queue wait, callback time, duplicate rate, and worker utilization with the same tenant mix you expect in production. I'm not sure any single scheduler's “timezone support” label tells you how it handles invalid monthly dates, pause recovery, or replay, so require those behaviors in an acceptance test.

A small rollout that keeps the calendar honest

Start with one tenant and a staging endpoint. Generate weekly and monthly occurrences around a daylight-saving change, a short month, and a leap day. Replay each signed callback and verify that the ledger creates one job for one occurrence.

Then cap concurrency below the provider's documented limit, watch queue age, and exercise the pause and resume policy. Roll out by tenant cohort. Keep the calendar policy version beside each schedule so a later policy change does not silently rewrite existing intent.

The durable design is deliberately plain: calendar data, an occurrence ledger, a narrow webhook, and a worker loop. Cron is only the trigger.

References

  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2104
  • https://cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/overview
  • https://www.iana.org/time-zones

title: An RSS feed grew to 500 items and my crawler got flagged as broken 📰
description:
I didn't change a line of code. The feed changed, and Google News had been saying no the whole time.

Hi! I'm Tim, a self-taught developer in Nairobi. I build small data tools that run as Apify Actors, serverless jobs that people pay for per result.

Apify runs every public Actor once a day with its default input. The run has to finish within 5 minutes and return at least one result. If it fails three days in a row, the Actor gets an "under maintenance" label on its Store page.

This week one of mine got that label: a news crawler that reads RSS feeds, fetches each new article, pulls out the clean text, and remembers what it has already returned so a scheduled run only gives you what's new.

Over the last 30 days, 24 of its runs passed and 3 timed out.

Let's find out why! 🔍

⏱️ Reproducing the daily test

The daily test uses the default input, which for this crawler is an empty form. With no sources given, it falls back to four built-in ones: a Google News search plus the TechCrunch, Electrek and Engadget feeds.

So I ran exactly that on my machine and timed it:

Source Items found Articles saved
Google News search 100 0
TechCrunch (keyword filter) feed didn't load from my connection 0
Electrek 500 500
Engadget (keyword filter) 1 1

580 seconds. Nearly twice the limit, and the two big problems are right there in the table.

📜 Problem 1: the feed was 500 items long

Electrek runs on WordPress, where a feed shows the latest 10 items by default. This one lists 500, and my code never asked how long a feed was. It fetched every item:

for (const source of sources) {
    let items;
    try {
        items = await discover(source);
    } catch (err) {
        log.warning(`Discovery failed for ${source.name}`, { error: (err as Error).message });
        continue;
    }
    for (const item of items) {
        const article = await fetchAndParse(item.url);
        // ...dedupe, save, charge
    }
}

The crawler is polite: it waits at least a second between requests to the same site. That's the right thing to do, but it means 500 articles from one site take at least 500 seconds before anything else happens.

Dedupe didn't help either. It runs on the parsed article (canonical URL, title, publish time and a hash of the body), so even an article the crawler had already seen got fetched again before it could be skipped.

🚪 Problem 2: Google News says no

The Google News source produced 100 links and 0 articles. Here's the start of news.google.com/robots.txt:

User-agent: *
Disallow: /
Allow: /$
Allow: /?
Allow: /home$
Allow: /home?
Allow: /home/
Allow: /nwshp$
Allow: /topics/
Allow: /publications/
Allow: /stories/
...

Everything is disallowed except the homepage and a few HTML sections. The RSS search feed lives under /rss/search, and every article link in it is a news.google.com/rss/articles/... redirect. None of those paths are allowed.

My crawler checked robots.txt before fetching each article, and correctly refused all 100. But it never checked before fetching the feed itself. So it read a feed it wasn't allowed to read, then politely declined every link in it.

By those rules, the Google News source can't return a single article. It only ever cost time.

(Further down, the same file has a block that disallows everything for GPTBot, ClaudeBot, PerplexityBot and a few other AI crawlers by name.)

🐢 Problem 3, found while fixing: timeouts got three retries

While testing the fix, TechCrunch article pages kept timing out from my connection. The fetch helper retried transient failures three times with backoff, and it treated a timeout like any other transient error.

With a 15-second timeout, that's 4 attempts plus backoff: about a minute for one page. A site that's having a bad day could eat the whole 5 minutes on its own.

🔧 The fixes

1. Check only the newest N items per feed

A new maxArticlesPerSource input, default 20. Items are sorted newest first, then cut:

const maxPerSource = Number.isInteger(input.maxArticlesPerSource) && input.maxArticlesPerSource! > 0
    ? input.maxArticlesPerSource!
    : DEFAULT_MAX_ARTICLES_PER_SOURCE; // 20

const newestFirst = (a: { publishedAt: string | null }, b: { publishedAt: string | null }) =>
    (Date.parse(b.publishedAt ?? '') || 0) - (Date.parse(a.publishedAt ?? '') || 0);

if (items.length > maxPerSource) {
    items = [...items].sort(newestFirst).slice(0, maxPerSource);
}

For a monitor that runs on a schedule, the newest 20 is what you want anyway. Anything older was either returned by an earlier run or is old news.

2. Check robots.txt at the door too

Feeds now go through the same robots.txt check as articles, and Google News sources are skipped with a reason instead of failing quietly:

export async function discover(source: Source): Promise<DiscoveredItem[]> {
    if (source.type === 'google-news') {
        throw new Error("Skipped: Google News doesn't allow automated access to its RSS feeds (robots.txt). Add the publishers' own RSS feeds instead.");
    }
    const feedUrl = source.feedUrl;
    if (!(await isAllowedByRobots(feedUrl))) {
        throw new Error(`Skipped: the site's robots.txt doesn't allow automated access to ${feedUrl}`);
    }
    const feed = await fetchFeed(feedUrl);
    // ...
}

Google News also left the default sources. Most publishers have their own feed, often at /feed or /rss, and those are the ones to use.

3. One retry for a timeout, and a per-site limit

A page that timed out once gets one more try, not three:

} catch (err) {
    const timedOut = (err as Error).name === 'TimeoutError' || /timeout/i.test((err as Error).message);
    if (attempt === MAX_RETRIES || (timedOut && attempt >= 1)) throw err;
    await sleep(2 ** attempt * 500);
}

And after 2 failed articles from the same site, the rest of that site is skipped for this run:

for (const item of items) {
    const site = siteOf(item.url);
    if ((failuresBySite.get(site) ?? 0) >= MAX_FAILURES_PER_SITE) {
        skippedDisallowedOrFailed++;
        continue;
    }
    // fetch, and on failure: failuresBySite.set(site, failures + 1)
}

The articles aren't lost. They're still in the feed tomorrow, when the site may be answering again.

4. "Nothing new" is a result

There was one more trap waiting. The daily test needs at least one result, but this crawler's whole point is to return only new articles. A second run on the same day, or a quiet news day, could return nothing at all and look broken.

So a run with nothing new now saves one row saying so, and doesn't charge for it:

if (stored === 0) {
    await Actor.pushData({
        title: 'No new articles in this run (not charged)',
        note: skippedDuplicate > 0
            ? `All ${skippedDuplicate} articles found were already returned by an earlier run.`
            : 'The sources returned no articles that could be fetched and read.',
        discovered,
        skippedDuplicate,
        skippedDisallowedOrFailed,
        skippedSources,
        discoveredAt: new Date().toISOString(),
    });
}

If you're scheduling a monitor, an empty result and a broken run look the same from the outside. A row that says why tells them apart.

🧪 After

Run Where Time Result
Empty input, first run my machine 82 s 21 articles
Empty input, same storage again my machine 122 s 1 row: "All 21 articles found were already returned by an earlier run."
A Google News + TechCrunch input my machine 38 s 1 row, with the Google News skip reason in it
Empty input Apify 29 s 25 articles (Electrek 20, TechCrunch 3, Engadget 2)

The repeat run was slower because TechCrunch was timing out from my connection. The per-site limit kicked in after two failures, and it still finished well inside the limit. On Apify's servers, TechCrunch answered fine.

🎯 What I learned

  • Inputs you don't control will grow. A feed, an API page, a sitemap. If the loop has no cap, the run time doesn't either.
  • Check robots.txt at the entry point, not just the pages. My crawler was careful about every article and careless about the feed that listed them.
  • A timeout is not a hiccup. Retrying a 15-second timeout three times turns one slow page into a lost minute.
  • "Nothing new" deserves a row. For anything that runs on a schedule, say why the result is empty.
  • A daily health check is a free alarm. The code hadn't changed since August. The world around it did, and the check is what told me.

The crawler is back to finishing in under a minute, and the under-maintenance label should clear after the next daily test.

title: Node.js Backend SMS OTP Login: Send and Verify Code for Airline Alerts
description:
When an airline changes a gate or cancels a flight, an OTP login and a disruption alert are two different trust problems. The login code is short-lived authentication data. The alert is operational communication that may contain a booking reference. Treating both as “send an SMS” creates the wrong boundary.

Short answer: use a hosted SMS OTP send-and-verify path for the login, then put abuse controls in your Node.js application. Add a cooldown, an IP and device limit, a country allowlist, and a delivery-status poller. Keep the alert template and passenger data under your application’s ownership. A provider can move the message; it should not silently become the system of record for your rules.

Infrai is a plausible fit here when one REST surface needs OTP delivery beside storage, scheduling, or observability. Its breadth reduces integration glue; it does not move ownership of passenger data or processor contracts out of your application.

What should own the message and the code?

The useful decision is not which API has the prettiest SDK. It is where data is retained, which processor sees it, and who can delete or replay it.

For a marketplace-style seller notification, the application should own the event, recipient consent, template version, and idempotency record. For an airline disruption flow, substitute passenger consent, itinerary state, and a notification audit record. The SMS service should receive the minimum needed to deliver the current message. Do not put the entire itinerary into the OTP request or the alert body.

The boundary also explains why a hosted OTP endpoint is attractive for the main login path: token generation and verification do not need to be rebuilt in application code. The application still owns the policy around that endpoint. A five-minute code lifetime, a resend cooldown, and a per-account attempt ceiling are product decisions, not properties to assume from a delivery API.

How should a Node.js backend send SMS OTP login codes?

Yes. The smallest useful implementation has three states: cooldown, pending, and verified. A request enters cooldown immediately after a send is accepted. Verification moves it to verified; a failed or expired attempt returns a useful error without allowing an unlimited resend loop.

This example keeps provider calls behind two narrow functions. Their inputs are deliberately explicit, so the rest of the service does not depend on a provider-specific SDK. The concrete request body and response schema belong to the selected provider’s current documentation; do not copy field names from an old integration into production.

type OtpState = "cooldown" | "pending" | "verified";

type OtpSession = {
  state: OtpState;
  expiresAt: number;
  nextSendAt: number;
  attempts: number;
};

const sessions = new Map<string, OtpSession>();
const COOLDOWN_MS = 30_000;
const CODE_TTL_MS = 5 * 60_000;
const MAX_ATTEMPTS = 5;

export function canRequestCode(key: string, now = Date.now()): boolean {
  const session = sessions.get(key);
  return !session || now >= session.nextSendAt;
}

export function startLocalSession(key: string, now = Date.now()): OtpSession {
  if (!canRequestCode(key, now)) {
    throw new Error("otp_cooldown");
  }

  const session: OtpSession = {
    state: "cooldown",
    expiresAt: now + CODE_TTL_MS,
    nextSendAt: now + COOLDOWN_MS,
    attempts: 0,
  };
  sessions.set(key, session);
  return session;
}

export function recordVerificationAttempt(key: string, now = Date.now()): void {
  const session = sessions.get(key);
  if (!session || now >= session.expiresAt) throw new Error("otp_expired");
  session.state = "pending";
  session.attempts += 1;
  if (session.attempts > MAX_ATTEMPTS) throw new Error("otp_attempt_limit");
}

The map is only a compact example of the policy. A real backend needs a shared store with an expiry, plus an atomic increment for attempts. It also needs a key that combines account, normalized phone, IP, and a device signal. Otherwise an attacker can rotate one dimension and avoid the limit.

The provider-facing part should use the documented POST /v1/sms/otp and POST /v1/sms/verify operations when those are the chosen hosted path. Keep the bearer key in process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY; use an explicit POST; check every status; and attach a client-generated idempotency key to a retriable write. On 429, honor Retry-After and back off. Never retry a write in a tight loop.

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

export async function providerRequest(
  operation: "otp" | "verify",
  body: unknown,
  idempotencyKey: string,
): Promise<unknown> {
  const url = operation === "otp"
    ? "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/sms/otp"
    : "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/sms/verify";
  const response = await fetch(url, {
    method: "POST",
    headers: {
      Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
      "Content-Type": "application/json",
      "Idempotency-Key": idempotencyKey,
    },
    body: JSON.stringify(body),
  });

  const payload: unknown = await response.json();
  if (!response.ok) {
    throw new Error(`sms_provider_${response.status}: ${JSON.stringify(payload)}`);
  }
  return payload;
}

The wrapper is intentionally boring. It does not pretend that an HTTP 200 means a handset received anything. After a send, poll the documented SMS status or events operation for visibility. There are no webhook pushes in this capability, so polling limits how quickly a larger email-plus-SMS orchestration can react.

Which provider fits a trust-sensitive alert flow?

The shortlist should include specialists, not only broad backend platforms. Twilio is a strong choice when its mature communications tooling and channel ecosystem are the priority. Vonage is a reasonable alternative when its messaging APIs and regional coverage fit the deployment. AWS SNS fits teams already standardizing on AWS primitives and accepting more application-owned orchestration. Their exact retention, residency, subprocessor, and contract terms still need review for the countries where passengers live.

Option Integration shape Best fit Boundary to verify
Infrai REST surface across backend modules One key and one contract for a small service SMS processor, region, retention, and polling behavior
Twilio Specialist communications APIs Channel depth and established messaging workflows Product-specific residency and subprocessor terms
Vonage Specialist messaging and verification APIs A route and coverage model that matches the deployment Regional delivery and retention terms
AWS SNS AWS-managed messaging primitive Teams already operating inside AWS More orchestration remains application-owned

An integrated backend surface is useful for a different reason. Infrai exposes communication capabilities alongside other backend modules under one REST API, and its public discovery surface documents schemas and runnable examples. That can remove glue when the same service already needs storage, scheduling, or observability. It does not erase the processor boundary: the SMS provider remains involved in delivery, and the application remains responsible for geographic controls, deletion policy, and the contractual residency question.

I would try Infrai for the login OTP and delivery-status part of a small Node.js service when one consistent API matters more than choosing a single-channel specialist. The breadth is the primary benefit; the supporting benefit is one integration surface for adjacent backend work. I would choose Twilio, Vonage, or a direct regional provider instead when a regulated route, a contractual country guarantee, or richer real-time communications orchestration is the deciding requirement.

Do not use the platform as evidence that an SMS message is resident in a particular country. A provider abstraction cannot manufacture an audio, SMS, or processor guarantee that its contracts do not provide. For an email fallback, build the email verification-code flow in your application: there is no managed email OTP endpoint in this capability set. Email suppression and authentication controls are separate work, not an automatic fallback.

What changes at scale?

First, replace the in-memory map with a shared expiring store and make “send once per cooldown window” atomic. Second, persist a notification record containing the event id, template revision, recipient hash, provider request id, and deletion deadline. Third, poll status with bounded backoff and stop after a terminal state or a business-defined timeout. The poller should be resumable; a process restart must not create a second OTP.

The country allowlist belongs beside those controls. So does a per-country cost circuit breaker. Neither geographic fencing nor country-specific spend protection is built into the SMS path described here. A carrier delivery failure is an operational signal, not permission to resend five times.

The trade-off is visible. Hosted OTP gets a beginner-friendly login path shipped quickly, while application-side controls add code and operational state. The state is small on paper, but in production it spans the 30-second cooldown, the five-minute code lifetime, five verification attempts, a country policy, a delivery poller, and a deletion deadline. Those values are examples of application policy, not promises to infer from a provider response; tune them against the threat model and passenger support flow. Specialist messaging vendors may provide deeper communications features, but they also add another key, SDK, processor review, and integration boundary. Pick the boundary you can audit.

Keep the rule simple.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai API documentation and verify the current schemas, processor terms, and delivery behavior before wiring it into a login.

Sources

  • Infrai machine-readable documentation index
  • NIST SP 800-63B Digital Identity Guidelines
  • RFC 7489: DMARC
  • Twilio Verify API documentation
  • Vonage Verify API overview
  • Amazon SNS mobile text messaging documentation

title: Create a simple form and style it with FSCSS
description:
A short walkthrough: HTML structure, FSCSS for layout and chrome, then optional polish with tokens and the form module. Everything compiles to plain CSS.

1. Markup first

Keep the form boring and accessible. FSCSS does not replace labels or name attributes.

<form class="contact" action="#" method="post">
  <h1 class="contact__title">Contact</h1>
  <p class="contact__lead">We’ll reply within one business day.</p>

  <label class="field">
    <span class="field__label">Name</span>
    <input class="field__input" type="text" name="name" autocomplete="name" required>
  </label>

  <label class="field">
    <span class="field__label">Email</span>
    <input class="field__input" type="email" name="email" autocomplete="email" required>
  </label>

  <label class="field">
    <span class="field__label">Message</span>
    <textarea class="field__input field__input--area" name="message" rows="4" required></textarea>
  </label>

  <button class="btn" type="submit">Send</button>
</form>

2. Load FSCSS

Prototype (CDN runtime):

<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/fscss@1.2.6/runtime.min.js" defer></script>
<link type="text/fscss" href="form-page.fscss">

Or compile:

npm install -g fscss@1.2.6
fscss form-page.fscss form-page.css

<link rel="stylesheet" href="form-page.css">

3. Style with layout helpers and tokens

stack, px / py, rounded, and friends (1.2.5+) keep the sheet short. See shorthands.

/* form-page.fscss */
:root {
  --bg: #0b1020;
  --surface: #121a30;
  --border: #22304f;
  --text: #e6edf7;
  --muted: #9fb0d0;
  --accent: #6366f1;
  --radius: 12px;
}

body {
  m: 0;
  min-h: 100vh;
  center: both;
  p: 24px;
  bg: var(--bg);
  color: var(--text);
  ff: system-ui, sans-serif;
}

.contact {
  w: 100%;
  max-w: 400px;
  stack: 16px;
  p: 24px;
  bg: var(--surface);
  border: 1px solid var(--border);
  rounded: 16px;
}

.contact__title {
  m: 0;
  fs: 1.35rem;
}

.contact__lead {
  m: 0;
  color: var(--muted);
  fs: 0.9rem;
}

.field {
  stack: 6px;
}

.field__label {
  fs: 0.8rem;
  color: var(--muted);
}

.field__input {
  w: 100%;
  px: 12px;
  py: 10px;
  rounded: var(--radius);
  border: 1px solid var(--border);
  bg: #0a0f1e;
  color: var(--text);
  font: inherit;
}

.field__input:focus {
  outline: 2px solid var(--accent);
  outline-offset: 2px;
}

.field__input--area {
  resize: vertical;
  min-h: 100px;
}

.btn {
  mt: 4px;
  px: 16px;
  py: 10px;
  border: 0;
  rounded: var(--radius);
  bg: var(--accent);
  color: #fff;
  font: inherit;
  fw: 600;
  cur: pointer;
}

.btn:hover {
  filter: brightness(1.08);
}

What you get after compile: normal flex column + gap, axis padding, radius, and colors—no framework runtime.

4. Optional: reusable button with @define 

@define btn(bg: #6366f1){`
  display: inline-flex;
  align-items: center;
  justify-content: center;
  padding: 10px 16px;
  border: 0;
  border-radius: var(--radius, 12px);
  background: @use(bg);
  color: #fff;
  font-weight: 600;
  cursor: pointer;
`}

.btn {
  @btn(var(--accent))
}

.btn-ghost {
  @btn(transparent)
  border: 1px solid var(--border);
  color: var(--text);
}

5. Optional: form.fscss module

When you want float labels and shared field chrome instead of hand-rolled classes:

@import((form-root, form-group, form-input, form-label, form-float, form-btn-primary) from form)

@form-root()
@form-float(.form-group, .form-input, .form-label)

Markup pattern (input before label, placeholder=" " for :placeholder-shown tricks) is documented with the module. Use selective imports so you only pull what the page needs.

6. Optional: semantic styling with pattern() (1.2.4+) 

pattern(0.55: "soft dark form card", `
  background: #121a30;
  border: 1px solid #22304f;
  border-radius: 16px;
  padding: 24px;
`)

.contact {
  soft dark form card
  stack: 16px;
  max-w: 400px;
}

Good for role-based phrases; keep critical layout in explicit rules so the form stays predictable.

7. Try it in the IDE

  1. Open fscss.devtem.org/ide
  2. Paste the HTML into an index.html and the FSCSS into form-page.fscss
  3. Ctrl+Enter to compile, preview to check focus states
  4. Export when you’re ready

Checklist

  • Labels associated with controls (wrapping <label> or for / id)
  • :focus styles visible on keyboard
  • Tokens on :root so themes don’t require rewriting fields
  • Production: compiled CSS only, not the runtime
  • Shorthands: https://fscss.devtem.org/shorthands
  • Docs: https://fscss.devtem.org/docs
  • IDE: https://fscss.devtem.org/ide
  • npm: fscss@1.2.6

A simple contact form is a good first FSCSS page: one column (stack), a few fields, one button—and the same file can grow into tokens, @define, or a form module without changing the HTML structure.
