title: How v0 authenticates to Snowflake without exposing the user's OAuth token
description:
AI-generated applications often need to authenticate to external services on behalf of their users. That creates a problem: generated code shouldn't have access to the user's credentials.

We faced that decision when building the v0 Snowflake integration. It lets users connect Snowflake, inspect schemas, query data, and generate applications that run against their warehouses. That generated code has to authenticate to Snowflake, but it is written by a model and runs without human review, and prompt injection can steer it into exfiltrating whatever it can read, so the user's OAuth token should never enter the environment the code runs in.

We solved this with a Snowflake request proxy for v0 sandboxes, built on the Vercel Sandbox firewall. The sandbox can run normal Snowflake clients, but the real credential is resolved at request time in a server proxy outside the sandbox runtime. This lets existing Snowflake clients work inside the sandbox without exposing the user's credential to generated code.

The harder problem was deciding where the proxy could safely inject the credential. The obvious implementation, replacing a placeholder token wherever it appears, introduces another credential leak.

Isolation doesn't protect secrets

v0 runs generated applications in isolated sandboxes. Isolation protects the rest of the system from untrusted code, but it doesn't protect secrets inside the sandbox.

If a generated app can read a token from the filesystem, that token can be copied into logs, returned in an API response, embedded into generated client code, or sent to another host. Sandbox isolation limits what the application can access, but it does not help once the credential itself is available inside the sandbox.

For Snowflake, the credential represents the Snowflake role the user connected with. v0 should be able to help the user explore and build with data they are authorized to access, but generated code should not receive raw provider credentials just because it needs one.

Every Snowflake request goes through the proxy

The sandbox cannot talk to Snowflake directly. When code inside it sends a request to the user's Snowflake account host, the sandbox firewall forwards that request to the v0 Snowflake proxy:

The firewall terminates TLS with a certificate authority unique to each sandbox, which lets the proxy read and rewrite traffic that would otherwise be encrypted. The sandbox trusts that certificate authority automatically, so the Snowflake SDK and CLI run with their default certificate validation, OCSP included. The proxy then verifies the sandbox's OIDC token, looks up the v0 chat the sandbox belongs to, restores the user session bound to that chat, and retrieves a fresh Snowflake credential for that user.

The sandbox does not choose where a token-bearing request is sent. The proxy derives the Snowflake account host from the server-side credential and rejects invalid account URLs, keeping the credential scoped to the connected Snowflake account rather than trusting host information supplied by generated code.

Compatibility without credential exposure

As a stopgap, the first version of the integration wrote the user's real token into the sandbox's Snowflake token files. The proxy replaced that approach. Ideally, we would remove token files from the sandbox entirely, but Snowflake clients expect credentials in different locations depending on the authentication flow.

Some requests, such as Snowflake SQL API calls, authenticate with an Authorization: Bearer header. Other client flows read local token files and send the token as part of a login request. Once the client has authenticated, subsequent requests use Snowflake-issued session tokens, and the proxy passes those requests through untouched.

To preserve compatibility, v0 still writes a token-shaped placeholder into the sandbox. The placeholder is a fixed, public, 72-byte string that grants no access, and its only job is to let existing Snowflake SDK and CLI flows behave as if a token exists. The proxy never authorizes a request based on the placeholder itself. Instead, the proxy authorizes the request using the sandbox's server-side identity and its binding to the user's chat.

The real OAuth token, the reusable credential that represents the user, is never written into the sandbox. Snowflake does issue session tokens that live inside the sandbox after login, but each of those belongs to a single authenticated session.

Those sessions are short-lived in practice. The Snowflake helper in generated apps destroys its connection after each query, which ends the session right away. Closing the chat does not end a session on its own, but tearing down the sandbox takes the token with it, and Snowflake expires the session server-side after four hours of inactivity by default. When a request reaches the proxy, it decides whether and where to attach the credential.

Why blind replacement fails

The first version of the proxy searched each request for the placeholder and swapped in the real token wherever it appeared:

The problem is that generated code controls parts of the request, including where the placeholder can appear. A SQL statement, for example, is caller-controlled data. If a query contains the placeholder as a string literal, blind replacement turns that query into one containing the real OAuth token. If the database then returns that string, the real token comes back into the sandbox as query output, and the proxy would have leaked the token it was built to keep out.

Stricter matching does not close the hole. The proxy shouldn't inject a credential based on attacker-controlled text. Instead, it needs to know which field in each Snowflake request carries authentication.

Injecting credentials only into authentication fields

Snowflake requests reach the proxy in three shapes, and each shape puts authentication in a different place.

For Snowflake SQL API requests, the proxy sets the OAuth token on the Authorization: Bearer header. The body remains caller-controlled SQL and is not rewritten. If the placeholder appears in the SQL payload, the proxy rejects the request before it reaches Snowflake and logs it as placeholder misuse.

For Snowflake login requests, the proxy parses the JSON request body, sets the token structurally at the login token field, and serializes the body again. If the placeholder remains anywhere else in the request body, the proxy fails closed.

Post-login session requests authenticate with Snowflake-managed session tokens, so the proxy has nothing to inject.

Failing closed

The proxy rejects any request where:

  • The sandbox is not bound to a chat

  • No user-scoped credential can be obtained

  • The Snowflake account host cannot be derived

  • The placeholder appears outside an approved authentication field

  • A structured login body cannot be parsed safely

Requests are also bounded before inspection so that compressed or oversized bodies cannot turn the proxy into an unbounded parser. Every proxied request emits an observability event with the upstream outcome, status, duration, and injection location. This surfaces misuse and integration failures without exposing secrets.

Handling refresh and deploy

Token refresh cannot depend on an ambient browser cookie, because proxy requests originate from the sandbox, not from the user's browser session. v0 binds the user session to the sandbox instead, and the proxy mints and refreshes OAuth credentials from that binding.

The publish path uses Snowflake CLI flows with the same credential boundary. Deploy can write the placeholder into credential files, but never the real token.

After deployment, the application runs in Snowpark Container Services and authenticates as its own service user, with a token that Snowflake manages and rotates automatically, mounted at /snowflake/session/token. The user's OAuth token and the v0 proxy are no longer involved.

The resulting security boundary

For users, none of this is visible. Connect Snowflake, ask v0 to inspect schemas or build an app, preview the result, and deploy when it's ready.

The security model rests on five rules:

  • Credential injection happens only at each endpoint's authentication fields

  • Requests that use the placeholder outside an authentication field are rejected and logged

  • Token-bearing requests go only to the connected Snowflake account host

  • Credentials are minted and refreshed server-side

  • Generated code uses Snowflake without ever reading the user's OAuth token

In its first 15 days in production, the proxy attached credentials server-side for roughly 13,000 requests and recorded zero placeholder-misuse rejections.

Although we built this proxy for Snowflake, the same problem applies to other integrations: generated code often needs to authenticate without receiving the user's long-lived credential. The important part is to inject credentials only into protocol-defined authentication fields, rather than rewriting arbitrary request data.

The v0 Snowflake integration is now available in beta. Get started by reading the integration docs.

Read more

title: GBase Database Batch Silent Installation: How to Troubleshoot Deployment Failures
description:
Batch deployment makes it easier to install GBase Database(GBase 8s) across multiple servers. But when a silent installation fails on several machines at once, a small configuration mistake can quickly become a deployment-wide problem.

The key is to stop the rollout, identify the failure on a single machine, and validate the fix before continuing.

Here is a practical troubleshooting workflow for failed batch silent installations.

1. Stop the Next Batch Immediately

If multiple servers start reporting installation failures, pause the remaining deployment tasks.

Continuing to deploy with the same configuration can spread the problem to more machines and make troubleshooting harder.

Keep a record of which nodes have completed installation successfully, which have failed, and which have not yet been processed. Avoid modifying verified nodes unless there is a clear reason to do so.

2. Reproduce the Failure on a Single Machine

Choose one failed server and rerun the silent installation using the same response file and parameters used in the batch deployment.

./ids_install -i silent -f /opt/bundle.properties -DLICENSE_ACCEPTED=TRUE

Capture the complete command output and inspect the installation logs. Identify the first error rather than focusing only on the final failure message.

The goal is to determine whether the problem comes from the installation parameters, the target server's environment, or a conflict with existing files and services.

If the failure cannot be reproduced on the selected machine, compare its configuration with the other failed nodes before making changes.

3. Check Four Common Causes of Batch Installation Failures

Response File or Path Problems

A response file that works on one server may be missing, corrupted during transfer, or stored at a different path on another server.

Check that the file exists and is readable:

ls -l /opt/bundle.properties

If the same response file is distributed to multiple servers, verify that its contents match the intended configuration. Pay particular attention to installation paths, selected components, and other environment-specific parameters.

Missing Dependencies or Environment Differences

Servers in the same deployment batch are not always identical. Differences in installed packages, operating system configuration, permissions, or environment variables can cause the same silent installation to succeed on one machine and fail on another.

Compare a failed node with a known-good node. Use the installation logs to identify missing dependencies or environment-related errors before changing system settings.

Port or Directory Conflicts

An installation may encounter conflicts with existing files, directories, or services on the target machine.

Check whether the intended installation directory already contains files from a previous attempt. Also verify that the configured database port is not already in use.

For example, inspect the installation directory:

ls -ld /opt/GBASE/gbase

If a port conflict is suspected, check the actual port configured for the target instance and identify the process using it. Do not assume every server uses the same port configuration.

Insufficient Disk Space

A batch deployment may fail only on certain servers because their available disk space differs.

Check the installation filesystem:

df -h /opt

If the installer uses a separate temporary filesystem, check that filesystem as well. Package extraction and temporary files may require additional space beyond the final installation footprint.

4. Fix One Machine Before Resuming the Batch

Once you identify the root cause, correct it on the selected server and repeat the installation or recovery procedure as appropriate.

Before resuming the rollout, verify that:

  • The silent installation completes successfully.
  • The installed files have the expected ownership and permissions.
  • The database instance can be initialized and started using the documented procedure.
  • The configured port and connection settings work as expected.

Remember that successful software installation does not necessarily mean the database instance is ready for use. Validate the relevant instance initialization and connection steps separately.

After the test machine passes these checks, resume deployment in small batches and monitor the results before increasing the rollout size.

5. Make the Next Batch Deployment More Reliable

A repeatable GBase Database deployment process should include a few safeguards:

  • Validate first: Test the response file and installation procedure on a single representative server.
  • Check prerequisites: Verify operating system requirements, dependencies, disk space, permissions, and port availability before deployment.
  • Keep configurations consistent: Use a controlled response file and explicitly document any server-specific differences.
  • Deploy incrementally: Increase batch size only after the previous batch passes validation.
  • Record failures: Keep installation output, relevant logs, and the affected server's configuration for later comparison.

These practices help distinguish problems in the deployment procedure from differences between individual servers.

Final Thoughts

When batch silent installation of GBase Database fails, resist the temptation to rerun the entire deployment immediately.

Stop the rollout, reproduce the error on one machine, identify the first failing step, and validate the fix before proceeding. A controlled, incremental deployment is much safer than allowing the same unknown problem to spread across every server.

The principle is simple: validate one machine, verify one batch, and scale only when the results are consistent.

title: Designing PostgreSQL HA with Patroni, etcd, and HAProxy in Multi-Zone Linux Clusters
description:
Originally published on the HostingPodium Enterprise Engineering Blog.

Free SRE & Developer Diagnostics: Test your stack live with our Global DNS Propagation Checker & SSL Health Auditor, Free Website Speed & Core Web Vitals Checker, or explore all 9 Free Webmaster & Cloud Engineering Tools.

This guide explains how to construct a zero-data-loss PostgreSQL HA cluster with Patroni, etcd, and HAProxy across three Linux zones, covering configuration, kernel tuning, and operational runbooks.

Scope

This guide details a production-grade PostgreSQL high-availability (HA) stack built on Patroni, etcd, and HAProxy. The target environment is a three-zone deployment on RHEL 9 or AlmaLinux 9, each zone hosting a dedicated compute node. The design guarantees zero data loss under a single-zone outage, enforces split-brain protection at the consensus layer, and provides deterministic client routing via health-checked TCP load balancing.

Cluster topology

The logical layout consists of:

Component Instances per zone Purpose
etcd 1 Consensus store for Patroni metadata
Patroni + PostgreSQL 1 Primary or replica, runs synchronous replication
HAProxy 1 (optional active-passive pair) Client entry point, performs TCP health checks

All nodes share a private VLAN (10.0.0.0/24) for inter-process traffic and a public VLAN for client access. The HAProxy virtual IP (VIP) is allocated from the public subnet and is moved by keepalived on failover.

etcd consensus layer

etcd runs as a three-member cluster, one member per zone. The --initial-cluster-state flag is set to new on first boot, and --initial-cluster-token is a UUID unique to the deployment. To prevent split-brain, the --auto-compaction-retention is set to 1h and the election timeout is tuned to 5 seconds.

# /etc/etcd/etcd.conf
ETCD_DATA_DIR="/var/lib/etcd"
ETCD_NAME="etcd-$(hostname)"
ETCD_INITIAL_ADVERTISE_PEER_URLS="https://$(hostname -I | awk '{print $1}'):2380"
ETCD_ADVERTISE_CLIENT_URLS="https://$(hostname -I | awk '{print $1}'):2379"
ETCD_INITIAL_CLUSTER="etcd-node1=https://10.0.0.11:2380,etcd-node2=https://10.0.0.12:2380,etcd-node3=https://10.0.0.13:2380"
ETCD_INITIAL_CLUSTER_STATE="new"
ETCD_INITIAL_CLUSTER_TOKEN="$(cat /etc/etcd/token)"
ETCD_CLIENT_CERT_AUTH="true"
ETCD_PEER_CLIENT_CERT_AUTH="true"
ETCD_CERT_FILE="/etc/etcd/ssl/etcd.pem"
ETCD_KEY_FILE="/etc/etcd/ssl/etcd-key.pem"
ETCD_TRUSTED_CA_FILE="/etc/etcd/ssl/ca.pem"
ETCD_QUOTA_BACKEND_BYTES=8589934592   # 8 GiB
ETCD_ELECTION_TIMEOUT=5000
ETCD_HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL=250
ETCD_AUTO_COMPACTION_RETENTION=1h

All etcd traffic is encrypted with TLS 1.2+. The quorum size of three ensures that any two zones can form a majority, satisfying the majority rule for Raft.

Patroni configuration

Patroni reads its state from etcd and controls PostgreSQL via pg_ctl. The configuration file is identical on each node, with zone-specific values injected through environment variables.

# /etc/patroni/patroni.yml
scope: pg-ha-cluster
namespace: /db/
name: $(hostname)
restapi:
  listen: 0.0.0.0:8008
  connect_address: $(hostname -I | awk '{print $1}'):8008
etcd:
  host: https://10.0.0.11:2379,https://10.0.0.12:2379,https://10.0.0.13:2379
  protocol: https
  cacert: /etc/patroni/ssl/ca.pem
  cert: /etc/patroni/ssl/patroni.pem
  key: /etc/patroni/ssl/patroni-key.pem
bootstrap:
  dcs:
    ttl: 30
    loop_wait: 10
    retry_timeout: 10
    maximum_lag_on_failover: 1048576   # 1 MiB
    postgresql:
      use_pg_rewind: true
      parameters:
        wal_level: replica
        max_wal_senders: 10
        max_replication_slots: 10
        wal_keep_size: 1024          # MiB
        synchronous_commit: on
        synchronous_standby_names: "*"
        hot_standby: on
        max_connections: 500
        shared_buffers: 4GB
        effective_cache_size: 12GB
        work_mem: 64MB
        maintenance_work_mem: 512MB
        checkpoint_timeout: 5min
        checkpoint_completion_target: 0.9
  initdb:
    - encoding: UTF8
    - locale: en_US.UTF-8
    - data-checksums
  pg_hba:
    - host all all 10.0.0.0/24 md5
    - host replication all 10.0.0.0/24 md5
    - host all all 0.0.0.0/0 reject
  users:
    admin:
      password: "$(cat /etc/patroni/secrets/admin.pass)"
      options: [CREATEDB]
postgresql:
  listen: 0.0.0.0:5432
  data_dir: /var/lib/pgsql/13/data
  bin_dir: /usr/pgsql-13/bin
  authentication:
    replication:
      username: replicator
      password: "$(cat /etc/patroni/secrets/replicator.pass)"
    superuser:
      username: postgres
      password: "$(cat /etc/patroni/secrets/postgres.pass)"

Key Patroni Bootstrap & Synchronous Replication Parameters

  • synchronous_standby_names="*" forces every replica to acknowledge writes, guaranteeing zero data loss as long as a quorum of replicas remains reachable.

  • maximum_lag_on_failover=1MiB prevents a lagging replica from being promoted.

  • wal_keep_size=1024 reserves enough WAL for a full-zone outage.

HAProxy routing

HAProxy runs in TCP mode on a dedicated VIP (10.0.1.100). It performs a health check against the Patroni REST API; only nodes reporting state: "running" and role: "master" are advertised as primary. Replicas are exposed on a separate port for read-only workloads.

# /etc/haproxy/haproxy.cfg
global
    log /dev/log    local0
    maxconn 5000
    daemon
    tune.ssl.default-dh-param 2048
    ssl-default-bind-ciphers PROFILE=SYSTEM
    ssl-default-server-ciphers PROFILE=SYSTEM
    ssl-default-bind-options no-sslv3 no-tlsv10 no-tlsv11
    nbproc 2
    cpu-map 1 0-3
    cpu-map 2 4-7

defaults
    mode tcp
    log global
    timeout connect 5s
    timeout client 30s
    timeout server 30s
    option tcplog
    retries 3

frontend pgsql_front
    bind 10.0.1.100:5432
    default_backend pgsql_primary
    acl is_read path_beg /read
    use_backend pgsql_replica if is_read

backend pgsql_primary
    option httpchk GET /master
    http-check expect status 200
    server pg1 10.0.0.21:5432 check port 8008 inter 2s rise 2 fall 3
    server pg2 10.0.0.22:5432 check port 8008 inter 2s rise 2 fall 3 backup
    server pg3 10.0.0.23:5432 check port 8008 inter 2s rise 2 fall 3 backup

backend pgsql_replica
    option httpchk GET /replica
    http-check expect status 200
    server pg1 10.0.0.21:5432 check port 8008 inter 2s rise 2 fall 3 disabled
    server pg2 10.0.0.22:5432 check port 8008 inter 2s rise 2 fall 3
    server pg3 10.0.0.23:5432 check port 8008 inter 2s rise 2 fall 3

Failover is driven by keepalived moving the VIP to the node whose Patroni instance reports role: "master". The health-check interval of 2 seconds yields sub-second detection of primary loss.

Kernel and system parameters

Linux kernel tuning focuses on network buffers, shared memory limits, and file descriptor counts. The following sysctl settings are applied on every PostgreSQL node:

Parameter Value Rationale
net.core.somaxconn 4096 Allows HAProxy to accept many concurrent connections.
net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse 1 Reduces TIME_WAIT buildup under heavy client churn.
vm.max_map_count 262144 Required for large shared memory segments used by PostgreSQL.
kernel.shmmax 68719476736 68 GiB – matches shared_buffers plus overhead.
kernel.shmall 16777216 Number of pages (8 KiB each) to support shmmax.
fs.file-max 1000000 Ensures PostgreSQL can open the required number of sockets and files.

Persist the values in /etc/sysctl.d/99-pg-ha.conf and reload with sysctl --system.

Synchronous replication strategy

Patroni is configured for synchronous_commit=on and synchronous_standby_names="*". In a three-zone deployment this means the primary must receive acknowledgment from both replicas before confirming a transaction. The write latency typically rises by 2-4 ms, measured with pgbench -c 50 -j 4 -T 60. The trade-off is acceptable for workloads that cannot tolerate data loss.

In the event that a replica becomes unreachable, Patroni automatically demotes the primary to asynchronous mode after a configurable failover_timeout (default 30 seconds). This prevents a permanent write stall while preserving data integrity once the missing replica rejoins.

Failover and recovery runbook

  • Detect primary loss: HAProxy health check fails, keepalived triggers VIP move.

  • Patroni election: Remaining nodes consult etcd; the node with the lowest name wins the Raft election and assumes role: "master".

  • Promote replica: Patroni runs pg_ctl promote. PostgreSQL replays pending WAL up to the last synchronous commit.

  • Validate quorum: Verify SELECT pg_is_in_recovery(); returns false on the new primary and SELECT * FROM pg_stat_replication; shows both replicas in sync.

  • Update HAProxy: Health check endpoint /master now returns 200, HAProxy routes traffic to the new primary within two seconds.

  • Re-integrate failed zone: Once the node is back online, start etcd, let it join the Raft cluster, then start Patroni. It will register as a replica and begin streaming WAL.

  • Post-failover audit: Capture etcdctl endpoint status --write-out=table and patronictl list output for compliance records.

If the failed zone contained the original primary and its data directory is corrupted, initiate a fresh base backup using pg_basebackup -D /var/lib/pgsql/13/data -Fp -Xs -P -R from the current primary before re-joining.

Observability stack

Metrics are collected via Prometheus exporters:

  • etcd exporter on port 2379/metrics

  • Patroni exporter (built-in) on port 8008/metrics

  • PostgreSQL exporter on port 9187

  • HAProxy exporter on port 9101

Alertmanager Rules & Quorum Loss Thresholds 

# alerts.yml
- alert: PostgreSQLPrimaryDown
  expr: patroni_role{role="master"} == 0
  for: 30s
  labels:
    severity: critical
  annotations:
    summary: "Primary PostgreSQL instance is down"
    runbook: "https://internal.runbooks/pg-primary-failure"

- alert: EtcdQuorumLost
  expr: etcd_server_has_leader == 0
  for: 15s
  labels:
    severity: warning
  annotations:
    summary: "Etcd cluster has lost quorum"
    runbook: "https://internal.runbooks/etcd-quorum"

Logs are shipped to Elasticsearch via Filebeat; each component tags logs with service=postgresql|etcd|haproxy for easy correlation.

Trade-offs

  • Latency vs. durability: Synchronous replication adds 2-4 ms per transaction; asynchronous mode reduces latency but permits data loss if the primary crashes.

  • Complexity of etcd: Managing a Raft cluster adds operational overhead compared to a simple file-based DCS, but it eliminates split-brain scenarios that can arise with ZooKeeper or Consul under network partitions.

  • HAProxy vs. PgBouncer: HAProxy offers TCP-level health checks and VIP failover, whereas PgBouncer provides connection pooling but cannot move a VIP without additional tooling.

  • Resource footprint: Running three full PostgreSQL instances with 4 GiB shared buffers each consumes ~12 GiB RAM per node; sizing must account for OS, etcd, and HAProxy overhead.

Operational checklist

  • Validate TLS certificates on etcd, Patroni, and HAProxy before deployment.

  • Run etcdctl endpoint health on each member; expect 100 % success.

  • Confirm patronictl list shows one master and two replicas.

  • Execute pgbench -c 10 -j 2 -T 30 and record 95th-percentile latency; must stay below 10 ms under baseline load.

  • Test failover by stopping patroni on the master; verify VIP moves and new master promotion within 30 seconds.

  • Inspect Prometheus alerts after each test; no pending critical alerts should remain.

  • Back up etcd snapshots daily with etcdctl snapshot save /backups/etcd-$(date +%F).db.

Following this checklist on a weekly cadence keeps the HA stack within SLA limits and provides early detection of configuration drift.

Summary

The combination of Patroni, etcd, and HAProxy delivers a deterministic failover path, strict split-brain avoidance, and zero-data-loss guarantees for PostgreSQL workloads spread across three availability zones. By adhering to the kernel parameters, replication settings, and runbook steps outlined above, operators can meet sub-second recovery objectives and maintain consistent performance under load.

title: I Migrated a Cloudflare Agents Workspace and Measured Everything: What Changes When the Storage Format Changes?
description:
The difference was not the table names.

TL;DR

On October 20, 2026, Cloudflare Agents switched its Workspace implementation from @cloudflare/shell to @cloudflare/computer. The change is not just a new API name. It changes how files are stored. The old implementation stored one row per path, with the file contents base64-encoded in that same row. The new one separates inodes and chunks, storing content-addressed blobs in 512 KiB pieces.

I ran the old and new implementations in the same Durable Object and compared the data before and after migration.

  • The tables are different, so old files are invisible after switching without migration. They are still there, though.
  • Storing a whole file in one row changes the size limit and performance. The old implementation hit a limit at about 6 MiB, and its 1 MB read/write cycle was 13.5 times slower.
  • The schema is versioned, so it migrates forward automatically but cannot go backward.
Aspect Old @cloudflare/shell New @cloudflare/computer
Tables cf_workspace_<namespace> vfs_* / _vfs_*
Representation of one file One row (path TEXT PRIMARY KEY) Inode + 512 KiB chunks
Where content lives Base64 in the same row's content column Blob addressed by SHA-256
Observed file-size limit About 6 MiB without R2 No single-row limit; content is chunked
1 MB write + read 87.25 ms 6.45 ms
Same content at two paths Stored twice Both paths share one blob row
Reopen with old implementation Works Fails with EIO

Test code: GitHub repository

Here is the main point upfront.

The old and new implementations differ in storage format, not API. Once you understand that, the reason files disappear after switching without a migration, why the file-size limit changes, why the new implementation is faster, and why you cannot switch back all follow from the same underlying change. The migration guide says to copy files manually because the tables differ. The deeper difference is their structure, not their names.

This article expands on my talk about migrating a Cloudflare Agents Workspace with measurements I could not fit into the presentation. It is for people using Cloudflare Agents who are preparing to move to @cloudflare/computer.

1. The announcement

On October 20, 2026, Cloudflare posted this changelog:

Think and Agent Skills now use the workspace from @cloudflare/computer as well as the filesystem tools.
@cloudflare/shell is deprecated, and so is Think's createExecuteTool. These will no longer be developed nor supported from today onwards.

On the same day, Cloudflare published @cloudflare/think@0.21.0, @cloudflare/computer@0.6.0, and agents@0.29.0. @cloudflare/shell also received version 0.5.0 that day to announce its deprecation. npm's deprecated flag applies retroactively to earlier versions too, so 0.4.3 shows the same warning.

The migration guide itself had landed earlier, in PR #2564 on October 14. It did not arrive at the same time as the announcement.

The Changelog also says:

This is a breaking change. @cloudflare/computer stores files in different tables from @cloudflare/shell, and there is no automatic data migration between workspace formats.

“Different tables.” That is where I started. Let's see how different they are.

2. The old Workspace stored one file per row

A Workspace is where an agent stores its files. A model interacts with them through read, write, edit, and ls; the files themselves live in Durable Object SQLite.

The old @cloudflare/shell schema is included in the migration guide:

CREATE TABLE cf_workspace_default (
  path             TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  parent_path      TEXT NOT NULL,
  name             TEXT NOT NULL,
  type             TEXT NOT NULL CHECK(type IN ('file','directory','symlink')),
  mime_type        TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'text/plain',
  size             INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  storage_backend  TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'inline' CHECK(storage_backend IN ('inline','r2')),
  r2_key           TEXT,
  target           TEXT,
  content_encoding TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'utf8',
  content          TEXT,
  created_at       INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT (unixepoch()),
  modified_at      INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT (unixepoch())
);

It is straightforward: the path is the primary key, and the metadata and content live in the same row. The content column holds file contents, base64-encoded for binary files.

Large files are handled separately. The default threshold is 1,500,000 bytes. Files above that threshold are moved to R2, leaving only an r2_key in the row. If no R2 bucket is provided, the implementation logs a warning and keeps the file inline:

if (size >= this.threshold && !r2)
  console.warn(`[Workspace] File ${path} is ${size} bytes but no R2 bucket was provided. Storing inline.`);

This “put everything in one row” design matters later.

3. The new Workspace separates inodes and chunks

The new @cloudflare/computer uses several tables:

Table Stores
vfs_dirents Parent inode + name → child inode
vfs_nodes Inode metadata (type / mode / mtime / size / link_target)
vfs_chunks Inode + chunk index → blob SHA-256
vfs_blobs SHA-256 → size and last-reference time
vfs_blob_bytes SHA-256 → actual bytes
vfs_meta schema_version and revision counter

Path resolution walks vfs_dirents from the root (inode = 1). File contents are split into 512 KiB chunks, each stored in vfs_blob_bytes as a blob keyed by SHA-256:

const CHUNK_SIZE = 524288;

The tables start with vfs_ or _vfs_, so they do not collide with cf_workspace_*. Both formats can coexist during migration.

From here, I measured what follows from the structural difference.

4. Consequence #1: switching does not make old files visible

I put both implementations on the same Durable Object. Splitting them across two DO namespaces would not test migration on the same storage. I switched between them inside one class.

I wrote 13 items with the old implementation, initialized the new one, and tried reading them:

Read through old Workspace before switch → {found: true, length: 23}
Initialize new Workspace
Read /workspace/notes.md through new     → ENOENT no such file
Read /notes.md through new               → ENOENT no such file
New-side tree                            → [{path: "/workspace", type: "dir"}]

The new implementation could not see the files.

If I stopped here, the article would say “the data is gone.” That would be quick—and wrong.

Add two controls

“Not visible through the new implementation” does not tell us whether the original write failed. In the same run, I verified that the old Workspace could still read the file both before and after switching:

Read through old before switch        → {found: true, length: 23}
Read through old after switch         → {found: true, length: 23}
Rows in cf_workspace_default          → 14 (same as before)

The old implementation could still read the file after the switch. The row count had not changed either.

The data was not gone. The new implementation was looking somewhere else. A table listing showed both formats coexisting:

cf_workspace_default
computer_execution_runtime
sqlite_sequence
vfs_blob_bytes   vfs_blobs    vfs_changes   vfs_chunks
vfs_dirents      vfs_manifests  vfs_meta    vfs_nodes
_vfs_fetch_cursor  _vfs_mounts  _vfs_push_cursor
_vfs_sync_operations  _vfs_sync_skips  _vfs_watermark

I also learned that all vfs_* tables are created as soon as you call new Workspace(). They do not wait for the first filesystem operation. The schema_version was 10.

5. Consequence #2: the size limit changes when everything fits in one row

The old implementation base64-encodes file contents and puts them in one cell. A 4 MB file becomes 5,592,408 base64 characters.

Meanwhile, the Durable Objects Limits page says:

Item Documented limit
Maximum string, BLOB, or table row size 2 MB
KV key size Key and value combined cannot exceed 2 MB

A 4 MB file should not fit in the old Shell. I predicted that while designing the benchmark and prepared files of 1 KB, 100 KB, 1 MB, and 4 MB.

They all worked.

My prediction was wrong.

4 MB → storage_backend=inline, content_encoding=base64,
       content_len=5,592,408 → read-back SHA-256 matches
8 MB → Error: string or blob too big: SQLITE_TOOBIG

I got the same result in local Miniflare and a deployed production Durable Object.

Measurement: where is the actual limit?

Stepping through the library would only reveal its implementation constant, not the underlying limit, so I called ctx.storage.sql and ctx.storage.kv directly to find the boundary. Each probe used a new Durable Object.

Largest accepted  8,388,627 bytes
Smallest rejected 8,388,628 bytes

8 MiB is 8,388,608 bytes. TEXT, BLOB, and a KV value all failed at the same boundary.

That is four times the documented 2 MB. I repeated probes around the boundary on a new Durable Object and got the same result. I reported it in cloudflare-docs#34502. Since I could not rule out 2 MB being the guaranteed limit and 8 MiB merely an implementation allowance, I did not open a PR asserting a new limit; I attached a reference branch instead.

Why does the old implementation stop at 6 MiB?

The old Shell hit its own boundary below the raw SQL limit:

Largest file accepted by shell.writeFileBytes  6,291,408 bytes (8,388,544 base64 chars)
Smallest rejected                             6,291,409 bytes (8,388,548 base64 chars)

Base64 expands the content by about 4/3, so that works out to roughly 6 MiB of file data.

I could not explain why the Shell fails earlier than raw SQL at 8,388,627 bytes. I reproduced its DDL, indexes, INSERT statement, ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE clause, and base64 string, then ran them against the same Durable Object. Raw SQL accepted the value. I also suspected that UPSERT might duplicate the value through excluded, but an UPSERT against an existing row accepted the same size.

The stack trace points to the Shell's INSERT:

Error: string or blob too big: SQLITE_TOOBIG
  at Object.run (index.js:367:17)
  at Workspace.writeFileBytes (index.js:652:22)

I stopped there. For practical purposes, remember that “without R2, the old Shell's file-size limit is about 6 MiB.”

The new Computer splits content into 512 KiB chunks, so this particular wall is gone. Files of 8 MB, 16 MB, and 32 MB all worked. Chunking may look like a performance design, but it also changes the size limit.

6. Consequence #3: base64 conversion on every operation is slower

I hit an oddity here: Date.now() does not advance inside a Worker. In production, even a 4 MB write was recorded as 0ms. It advanced in local Miniflare, so at first I thought I was misreading the production logs.

I measured from outside instead. I sent one request that repeated the operation 60 times and a control request that did nothing, then divided the difference by 60. The table shows the median of seven runs:

Size Old Shell New Computer
1 KB 1.58 ms -0.75 ms
100 KB 4.92 ms 0.80 ms
1 MB 87.25 ms 6.45 ms

I cannot draw conclusions from the 1 KB and 100 KB results. As the negative value shows, the differences are buried in HTTP round-trip variance.

At 1 MB, the gap was clear: 13.5×. The old Shell base64-encodes a 1 MB file into one row on every write and decodes it on every read, adding overhead. My measurement includes the write and the read together, so I cannot say which one is slower on its own.

7. Consequence #4: content addressing enables deduplication

The new implementation uses the blob's SHA-256 as its primary key. The same bytes can be shared by files anywhere in the tree.

I wrote the same 512 KiB of content to two paths and counted rows in vfs_blobs:

Initial blob count                 → 0
Write identical content to path 1  → 1
Write identical content to path 2  → 1  (no increase)
Control: write different content  → 2  (increases)

Without the control, I could not distinguish deduplication from an implementation that never added a blob at all. The different byte sequence confirmed that a second row is created when the content differs.

The old implementation stores content per path, so putting the same file in two places uses storage twice.

8. Consequence #5: there is nowhere to put some metadata

The old FileInfo has mimeType, createdAt, and updatedAt. The new WorkspaceStatResult has only these fields:

{ name, inode, mode, mtime, size, isFile, isDirectory, isSymbolicLink }

There is no API in workspace.fs to read or write MIME types. There is only one timestamp, mtime.

The migration guide also says this metadata is not retained:

Things the copy does not keep:

  • created_at and modified_at. Computer stamps the time of the copy.
  • mime_type. Computer does not store a MIME type per file.

In my measurements, every migrated file's mtime was the time the copy ran. It is not just that the data is “not retained”; the new schema has nowhere to store it.

9. Consequence #6: you can move forward, but not backward

The new implementation versions its schema. Its initialization code looks like this:

const onDiskVersion = db.one("SELECT v FROM vfs_meta WHERE k = ?", "schema_version")?.v ?? 0;
if (onDiskVersion > 10) throw createWorkspaceError("EIO", `Unsupported workspace filesystem schema version ${onDiskVersion}`);
if (onDiskVersion > 0 && onDiskVersion < 10) runMigrations(db, onDiskVersion, 10);

Migrations run forward automatically. There are nine registered migrations, from v1 to v10.

There is no migration backward.

Rather than deploying an old version, I changed the on-disk schema_version to 11 to simulate a database newer than the binary, then ran the same initialization path:

Current schema_version                 → 10
Control: reconstruct with same version → {read: "hello"}
Set schema_version to 11
Open again with older binary            → EIO Unsupported workspace filesystem schema version 11
Set schema_version back to 10
Can it open now?                        → {read: "hello"}

What I measured is that the binary cannot open a database whose on-disk schema_version is newer than the version it supports. This means “you cannot roll back” only if a new release raises the schema version. It has already been raised nine times, so it is reasonable to expect that it could happen again.

Neither the migration guide nor the Changelog mentions this. There is one sentence in the implementation document 03_filesystem_schema.md:

Open() refuses to run if the binary is older than the on-disk schema_version.

The old data remains, so if migration fails you can still read from the old tables. The inability to roll back is the less recoverable part.

10. Running the migration guide's script

Now that I understood the structural difference, I ran the migration.

The guide provides a copy function named copyShellWorkspace(). It walks the old Workspace with glob("/**") and writes the files through the new fs API. The destination is under /workspace, which Think also uses as its working directory.

I ran the script without changing it. My test data included UTF-8 Japanese text, TypeScript in a nested directory, JSON for exact-content comparison, 64 KB of binary data generated with a deterministic pseudorandom sequence, an empty directory, and four symlinks covering relative, absolute, and root-escaping targets.

comparison → {
  total: 13, missing: [], typeChanged: [],
  contentMismatch: [], extra: []
}

All 13 items existed after migration, their types had not changed, and the 64 KB binary's SHA-256 matched. The empty directory remained too. I got the same result in local wrangler dev and in a deployed production environment.

I also verified that the hash comparison could actually detect a mismatch. I changed one bit in a byte sequence and confirmed that it produced a different hash: af2ba40f… versus 73734ea1…. A comparison that cannot detect a mismatch does not prove that two files match.

I checked one assumption the script relies on as well. A comment says, “glob returns rows ordered by path, so parents come before children.” If that were false, writeFile could run before mkdir. In my tests, results were sorted lexicographically, so each parent appeared before its children.

Symlinks need one extra check

When I followed each link individually, one of them failed:

Link Target in Shell Target after migration Can follow it?
/links/rel.md ../notes.md /workspace/notes.md Yes
/links/abs.md /notes.md /workspace/notes.md Yes
/links/dotdot.md /src/../notes.md /workspace/src/../notes.md Yes
/links/esc.md /../notes.md /workspace/../notes.md ENOENT

/workspace/../notes.md resolves to /notes.md, which is outside the migration destination /workspace.

The cause is in the script's resolveTarget():

// Shell resolves a relative target against the link's directory and never
// goes above `/`.
function resolveTarget(link: string, target: string): string {
  if (target.startsWith("/")) return target;   // Absolute paths pass through
  const parts = link.split("/").slice(1, -1);
  for (const part of target.split("/")) {
    if (part === "..") parts.pop();
    else if (part !== "" && part !== ".") parts.push(part);
  }
  return `/${parts.join("/")}`;
}

The @cloudflare/shell implementation (resolveSymlink) also sends absolute paths through normalizePath. normalizePath stops .. at the root, so /../notes.md becomes /notes.md in Shell. The migration script passes the path through unchanged. When it prefixes /workspace, the target escapes that directory.

The conditions are narrow. Relative paths all migrate correctly. Absolute paths containing ., //, or .. that does not go above the root also work. The only failure is an absolute path containing .. that goes above the root.

The script does not report an error. symlink() saves the target without validating it, and following it stops at the root rather than throwing. This is like a legal dangling link on POSIX. The copy completes successfully.

A path/type/hash comparison will not catch this. The link exists, so it is not missing. Its type is still symlink, so the type matches. It has no file content, so it is not included in the hash comparison. My own comparison script reported missing: [], contentMismatch: []. To catch this, you have to follow and read the link:

await to.fs.readFile(linkPath, "utf8");   // ENOENT if the target cannot be followed

A second issue is that the migration is not safe to rerun:

First migration  → ok
Second migration → EEXIST path exists: /workspace/links/abs.md

mkdir({ recursive: true }) silently succeeds for an existing directory. writeFile overwrites unless exclusive is specified. symlink(target, path) has no equivalent of a force option; if the path already exists, it always throws EEXIST. That matches Node's fs.symlink behavior and is not a library bug.

The guide's onStart example sets a flag after copying completes. If the copy fails partway through, the flag is never set and the next startup fails again on the same link. Remove the link before recreating it:

const link = at(entry.path);
if (await to.fs.readlink(link).then(() => true, () => false)) {
  await to.fs.rm(link);
}
await to.fs.symlink(at(target), link);

I reported these two issues in cloudflare/agents#2645. Before filing, I checked for duplicates and found that both had been raised in earlier reviews. One did not survive a PR replacement; the other had been marked resolved based on the incorrect assumption that absolute paths were already rebased. Checking first meant I did not present either as a new discovery.

If your Workspace has no symlinks, you will not hit this part.

11. Persistence survives hibernation

The storage format changed, but the files still live in Durable Object SQLite. I checked whether they survive restarts.

“Readable from another request” is not enough evidence. The same instance might still be in memory and return the file from there. I generated a crypto.randomUUID() in the constructor and included it in the response. If that value changes, the Durable Object is a new incarnation.

                     bootId                                  Read
1. Write             1cadfbdd-7595-4879-94c1-43abca4688c0   ok
2. Read immediately  1cadfbdd-7595-4879-94c1-43abca4688c0   ok   (same)
3. After 15 seconds  e4f5f2ab-3d7d-4389-8e2d-ee32fdd97b02   ok   (changed)
4. After 150 seconds c602f7f1-c9f6-465e-9b36-0c3259706d64   ok   (changed again)

Reads 3 and 4 came from different incarnations. The file content included the old bootId from when it was written, showing it was the same data.

I decided which fields to record before running the test: a case number for writing back the verdict, bootId to show whether a restart happened, env to distinguish local from production, sha256 and size to identify the file, the operation's elapsed time, and ok and error fields that hold results instead of throwing exceptions.

This control proved useful. After redeploying, my first immediate read succeeded, but the bootId was unchanged. The DO was still in memory and running the old code; it had not restarted. Without the control, I might have concluded that the file persisted across a restart. I waited 15 seconds and tried again, then confirmed that the bootId changed and the file was still readable.

How long until hibernation?

I varied the wait time and checked bootId. The zero-second wait was the control:

Wait (s)  Restarted  Read
      0   No         ok   (control)
      3   No         ok
      6   No         ok
      9   No         ok
     11   Yes        ok
     13   Yes        ok
     15   Yes        ok

The boundary is between 9 and 11 seconds, matching the documentation's “hibernate after 10 seconds of inactivity.”

12. Before you migrate

  • Count your symlinks. Run glob("/**") and count entries with type === "symlink". If there are none, the official script should work as-is.
  • If you have links, follow and read them after migration. Path/type/hash comparisons will not catch the issue.
  • Check for files larger than 6 MiB. If the old implementation stored them in R2, pass the same r2 bucket and name during migration.
  • Deploy assuming you cannot roll back. Once the new schema has been written, an older @cloudflare/computer cannot open that Durable Object.
  • Do not delete the old data immediately. The old tables remain, so wait to DROP TABLE until your comparison is done.

The dependency arrangement changes too. In @cloudflare/think@0.20.2, @cloudflare/shell was a direct dependency; you did not install it yourself. In 0.21.0, @cloudflare/computer is a peer dependency. The mechanism behind “I upgraded and my Workspace is empty” is right there.

13. Conclusion

The storage format changed, and the rest followed from it:

  • Different tables → files are invisible after switching without a migration, but the old tables remain and the old Workspace can still read them.
  • One row versus chunks → the old implementation hits a limit at about 6 MiB; the new one accepts files of 32 MB.
  • Base64 conversion on every operation → a 13.5× difference in the 1 MB read/write test.
  • Content-addressed blobs → the same content at two paths takes one blob row.
  • Fewer metadata columns → there is nowhere to store mime_type or created_at.
  • A versioned schema → it migrates forward automatically and cannot be opened by an older implementation after the version changes.

The migration guide says to copy files manually because the tables differ. The difference is not just the table names; it is the structure. Understanding that structure tells you what to verify before you migrate.

I also found two mismatches with the documentation. The Durable Object SQLite value limit I tested was 8 MiB, not 2 MB, and the user-facing docs do not mention that an older implementation cannot open a Durable Object after its schema has been upgraded.

The most surprising result was that a 4 MB file worked. I had predicted the result from the official limit and got it wrong. Because I had trusted the documented number, I no longer trusted my other predictions once it failed. I ended up measuring both the size limit and performance myself. That took more time than the migration itself.

References

  • Think agents now use a @cloudflare/computer workspace — The announcement, the lack of automatic migration, and deprecation of createExecuteTool.
  • Migrating from @cloudflare/shell to @cloudflare/computer — Both schemas and the copy script discussed in §10.
  • cloudflare/computer docs/03_filesystem_schema.md — All vfs_* table definitions, chunk size, and schema version behavior.
  • Durable Objects — Limits — The documented 2 MB row-size limit tested in §5.
  • Durable Objects — Lifecycle — Sources for the 10-second hibernation and 70–140-second eviction behavior.
  • cloudflare/computer#217 / #219 — Acknowledgment that writing to R2 and namespaces are not supported yet.
  • cloudflare/agents#2645 — Report about the symlink migration script in §10.

title: Beyond Correct Answers: How Compositional Cues Shape Visual Judgments
description:
arXiv:2610.28843v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Visual question answering requires models to assign attributes and relations to the correct objects, a problem known as visual binding. Structured prompts make these assignments explicit through labeled fields. Yet an improvement from the full prompt does not reveal which labels help or how they interact. First, we isolate field-label effects across ten models and six tasks by holding the image and claim fixed. These comparisons reveal differences that overall accuracy can hide. With a relation label present, adding object-role labels helps Qwen3 but hurts Qwen2 on Spatial. Second, we compare auxiliary hints that preserve or swap the question's role assignments against a no-hint baseline. Across two image sets, Qwen3's advantage with preserving hints mainly reflects errors caused by swapped hints. Preserving hints remain near baseline. Field order further affects the harm. Third, we test clearer hint wording and direct selection of the relation shown in the image. Clearer hints improve text matching but do not consistently improve visual judgments. In contrast, relation selection partly reduces errors for some hints in Qwen3 and GPT-4.1-mini.

title: Screen Sizes & Viewport Cheat Sheet for 2026
description:
Screen Sizes & Viewport Cheat Sheet for 2026

Every responsive bug report starts the same way: "it looks broken on my phone." Then you spend ten minutes hunting for that phone's viewport width — one site lists the panel resolution, another lists a viewport from two generations ago, and a third just says "various."

This is the cheat sheet I keep coming back to: the device viewports worth testing in 2026, the framework breakpoints next to them, and the three numbers — resolution, viewport, DPR — that developers constantly mix up. All values below are portrait CSS-pixel references. Treat heights as references, not guarantees: mobile browser bars, keyboards and zoom change the visible height, while width stays comparatively stable.

Phone viewports worth testing

Eleven models cover nearly every width your layout will meet in production, from the narrow 360px Android baseline to the 440px Pro Max class. The full model-by-model reference lives in the iPhone viewport sizes table and the device screen sizes index.

Device CSS viewport Panel resolution DPR
Galaxy S25 360 × 780 1080 × 2340 3
iPhone SE (3rd gen) 375 × 667 750 × 1334 2
Galaxy S25 Ultra 384 × 832 1440 × 3120 3.75
iPhone 14 390 × 844 1170 × 2532 3
iPhone 16 393 × 852 1179 × 2556 3
iPhone 17 402 × 874 1206 × 2622 3
Pixel 10 412 × 923 1080 × 2424 2.625
iPhone Air 420 × 912 1260 × 2736 3
Pixel 10 Pro 427 × 952 1280 × 2856 3
iPhone 16 Plus 430 × 932 1290 × 2796 3
iPhone 17 Pro Max 440 × 956 1320 × 2868 3

Patterns worth internalizing:

  • Modern iPhones cluster tightly. Everything from the iPhone 14 to the 17 sits between 390 and 440 CSS pixels wide, all at DPR 3. If your layout survives 390, 402 and 430, it survives the current iPhone line.
  • Android is wider at the edges. The base Galaxy line still reports 360px — the narrowest mainstream target, and the one that exposes cramped toolbars and rigid dialogs first.
  • DPR is not always a whole number. The Pixel 10 ships at 2.625 and the S25 Ultra at 3.75. Hard-coding "retina = 2x or 3x" assumptions into image pipelines is how blurry hero images happen; serve srcset steps and let the browser pick.
  • Shared widths hide differences. Several models share a viewport width while differing in height, DPR and safe areas. A matching reference is a starting point for testing, not proof two devices render identically.

Tablets and laptops, briefly

Tablet viewports overlap small-laptop widths, which is why "tablet layout" and "small desktop layout" so often collide around 1024px.

Device / class CSS viewport / workspace Panel resolution
iPad mini (A17 Pro) 744 × 1133 1488 × 2266
Classic iPad reference 768 × 1024 —
iPad (10th gen) / iPad Air 11" 820 × 1180 1640 × 2360
iPad Pro 11" (M4) 834 × 1210 1668 × 2420
iPad Pro 13" (M4) 1032 × 1376 2064 × 2752
Budget laptop (WXGA) 1366 × 768 1366 × 768
MacBook Air 13" (M3) 1470 × 956 2560 × 1664
MacBook Pro 14" (M4) 1512 × 982 3024 × 1964
1080p panel at 125% scaling 1536 × 864 1920 × 1080

Two things to notice. First, laptop "workspace" values are scaled: a 2560 × 1664 MacBook Air panel gives CSS a 1470 × 956 layout space, and OS scaling — not the panel — decides what your media queries see. Second, the classic 768 × 1024 iPad reference refuses to die; it is still a useful portrait test width even though current iPads report larger viewports.

Tailwind vs. Bootstrap breakpoints

Both frameworks are mobile-first min-width systems, but their thresholds only agree at 768px. The side-by-side reference, with a live checker that tracks your current width against both systems, is the responsive breakpoint checker.

Tier Tailwind Bootstrap
Base 0–639px (base) 0–575px (xs)
Small sm 640px sm 576px
Medium md 768px md 768px
Large lg 1024px lg 992px
Extra large xl 1280px xl 1200px
Largest 2xl 1536px xxl 1400px

Practical consequences:

  • A layout that switches to two columns at Bootstrap lg (992px) does so 32px earlier than the same layout at Tailwind lg (1024px). Porting components between the two without adjusting expectations shifts every boundary.
  • Tailwind expresses its thresholds in rem (640px = 40rem at the default root size), Bootstrap in px. If a user changes their browser's root font size, rem-based breakpoints move and px-based ones don't — a classic source of "works on my machine."
  • Test the pixel below each threshold, not just the threshold itself: 639, 767, 1023, 1279 and 1535 are where the old layout makes its last stand.

If you only keep one testing set, make it 360, 393, 430, 768, 1024, 1366, 1536 and 1920 — narrow Android, common iPhone, large phone, tablet portrait, tablet landscape, small laptop, large laptop and desktop. The reasoning behind that set is laid out in the common screen resolutions reference.

Check your own device, live

Tables tell you what a device should report. Your actual browser may disagree — because of zoom, OS display scaling, an installed web app shell, or a keyboard eating half the screen. When a bug is on your desk, measure the real thing:

  1. Open the viewport size checker on the device in question.
  2. Read three values: viewport (window.innerWidth × innerHeight), DPR (window.devicePixelRatio), and the active Tailwind/Bootstrap range.
  3. Resize or rotate and watch the values update; then paste the report straight into the bug ticket, so QA reproduces at your width instead of guessing.

For screenshot and image bugs, multiply the CSS slot by the live DPR: a 360px-wide slot on a DPR 3 phone needs a 1080px asset to stay sharp, and exporting at the panel resolution "to be safe" just ships megabytes nobody asked for.

The three numbers everyone confuses

Most screen-size confusion is one paragraph away from disappearing:

Physical resolution is the panel's pixel grid — 1179 × 2556 on an iPhone 16. It describes hardware. Your CSS never sees it directly. CSS viewport is the area the page renders into, in CSS pixels — 393 × 852 on that same phone. Media queries, breakpoints and layout respond to this number and only this number. DPR is the ratio between them: how many physical pixels paint one CSS pixel. It drives image sharpness (and screenshot dimensions), but it does not change which breakpoint is active.

So when a spec sheet brags about a huge resolution, divide by DPR before you panic: what lands in your stylesheet is the viewport. And when a user reports a "tiny" screen, ask for their viewport and DPR — not their panel resolution — before you touch a single media query.

TL;DR

Test widths, not devices: 360–440px covers current phones, 768–1032px covers tablets, and scaled laptop workspaces matter more than panel resolutions. Keep resolution, viewport and DPR in separate mental buckets, verify your own browser live instead of trusting spec sheets, and always check the pixel just below the breakpoint.

title: Online Open-World Wafer Defect Discovery using Hyperdimensional Computing
description:
arXiv:2610.28949v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Conventional wafer defect analysis relies on offline, closed-world classifiers that fail to detect novel, unseen defect signatures emerging during continuous semiconductor manufacturing. To address this, we propose WaferHDC, an online open-world wafer defect discovery framework based on hyperdimensional computing (HDC). The memory-centric architecture of WaferHDC enables rapid anomaly detection and grouping of recurring failures into compact hypervector representations. This allows the memory space to dynamically scale with new defect modes without retraining a static classifier or archiving entire raw wafer history. WaferHDC first models normal spatial distributions, then dynamically groups recurring failures into persistent defect memory without labels or predefined class counts. It outperforms the strongest online baseline by 13.3 p.p. in adjusted Rand index and 10.5 p.p. in normalized mutual information on the industry-standard WM-811K dataset. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of WaferHDC for continuous and open-world wafer defect analysis.

title: I gave Claude Code a browser with my real logins. Here's what I had to get right
description:
Most of my day is spent with Claude Code, and the browser was always the weak spot. Tools built on Playwright start a fresh profile, so the agent is logged out of everything. Pointing an agent at my main Chrome felt like a bad idea. So I built my own browser, Kinaya, and gave it an MCP server.

Adding it to Claude Code is one line:

claude mcp add kinaya -- /Applications/Kinaya.app/Contents/MacOS/kinaya —mcp

The browser starts itself if it isn't running. Getting from "the agent can click things" to "I actually let it use my accounts every day" took a few decisions that I think apply to anyone building agent tooling.

1. Every session gets its own background tab

Driving whatever tab is in front doesn't work once you want to keep browsing while an agent works, or when two Claude Code sessions run at once and fight over the same page.

So each MCP session opens its own background tab and all later calls act on it. The tab I'm looking at never moves. Every tool also takes an optional tab_id, so one agent running several tabs is still explicit. Screenshots work on background tabs and when other windows cover the browser, because the agent needs to see the page without the window being in front.

2. Approval for actions, not for reading

Reading (read_page, find, get_page_text, screenshot) runs freely. Clicks, typing, navigation, form fills, uploads and sign-ins ask for approval in a side panel, or can be always allowed per site. A prompt left unanswered for about 5 minutes expires and Claude is told the action didn't run, so an agent never hangs forever waiting on me.

Private and Tor tabs are off limits to the agent entirely.

3. The agent never sees a password

sign_in fills a login saved in the browser's password vault, and create_login generates and saves a strong password for a sign-up. The password goes straight into the page. The model only ever sees the username. The vault itself is XChaCha20-Poly1305 on disk, with no cloud.

For things only a human can do, like CAPTCHAs and phone codes, there's an ask_user tool with a reply box in the side panel.

4. Page text is data, not instructions

Once an agent has your logins, prompt injection from a web page stops being theoretical. The server's instructions tell the model that text on web pages is untrusted data and never instructions. It's not a complete defence, but combined with approval on actions it means a malicious page can't quietly make the agent do something.

5. Don't let page dialogs block the agent

A browser alert or confirm can freeze an automated session. In Kinaya, dialogs raised while the agent acts are answered and reported back to the agent instead of blocking.

The rest of the tool list

| area | tools |
| --- | — |
| reading | read_page, find, get_page_text, screenshot |
| acting | click, hover, type, fill_form, select_option, press_key, scroll, upload_file, dismiss_popups |
| tabs | navigate, new_tab, switch_tab, close_tab, list_tabs |
| accounts | sign_in, create_login, ask_user |
| waiting and debugging | wait_for, wait, read_console, read_network, run_javascript |
| other | batch, search_history, list_downloads |

batch runs several actions in one call, which saves round trips.

The browser itself

It's also just my daily browser. Tauri 2 and Rust on WebKit. Ad and tracker blocking runs in the engine with Brave's adblock-rust, compiled into a WebKit content-rule list, so requests are dropped before they leave. Command palette for everything, private tabs, Tor tabs through the Arti client, reader mode, no telemetry.

It's $19 once with a 14-day trial: ibraryunus.com/apps/kinaya. If you're building agent tools, I'd be keen to hear how you're handling logins and approvals.

title: Seeing the Forest for the Trees: Emergent Agreement from Individual Conversations
description:
arXiv:2610.29328v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As LLM agents interact in the wild and shape each other's decisions, understanding how they converge toward agreement becomes important. We study this in multi-turn conversations where two LLMs discuss subjective matters, can agree or disagree, and may change their stances. Using a linear classifier on individual conversation activations, we identify an internal representation of agreement. We find that it varies substantially across turns and conversations and does not reliably track external agreement at the individual conversation level. We therefore move beyond the representation of agreement in individual conversations, by aggregating the agreement representation across conversations. Externally, this aggregate view reveals a simple structure: when pooled across conversations, agreement can be predicted well with a Markov process, with agreement at each turn being a direct function of agreement at the previous turn. Similarly, when internal agreement is aggregated, it couples with the external Markov agreement through a power-law mapping, exposing Markovian dynamics in internal representations. Additionally, we find that after a change of stance, models express agreement externally before their internal representations reflect the same shift. These results reveal a joint structure between internal and external agreement that emerges only when internal features are aggregated across conversations. Code available at https://github.com/technion-cs-nlp/SeeingTheForestForTheTrees.
