title: DGCM-SSFA: Dual-Granularity Cross-Modulation and Sparse Strip Frequency Attention for Efficient 3T-to-7T MRI Synthesis
description:
arXiv:2610.29141v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Synthesizing high-fidelity 7T MRI from routinely acquired 3T scans offers a practical pathway to enhanced neuroimaging without the prohibitive cost of ultra-high-field scanners. While existing deep learning approaches have achieved promising results, state-of-the-art methods typically rely on either large-scale architectures exceeding 45 million parameters or computationally intensive ensemble strategies, limiting their practicality in resource-constrained clinical environments. In this work, we propose a compact multi-domain attention framework, termed DGCM-SSFA, that achieves competitive synthesis quality with only 11M parameters. The proposed architecture integrates two complementary modules into a U-Net Transformer backbone. First, a Dual-Granularity Cross-Modulated Feature Modulator (DGCM) is embedded at multiple hierarchical levels to enhance local edge and texture details through Sobel-guided spatial attention and depthwise frequency-aware channel attention with cross-branch gating. Second, a Sparse Strip Frequency Attention (SSFA) module at the bottleneck captures global spatial context via strip-pooled attention with near-linear complexity, while simultaneously performing FFT-based spectral modulation in the frequency domain. These two modules operate synergistically with the backbone's native channel attention, forming a triple-granularity feature refinement pipeline. Extensive experiments on the UNC and BNU 3T-to-7T MRI datasets across T1w and T2w modalities demonstrate that DGCM-SSFA achieves strong structural fidelity, attaining an SSIM of 0.8431 on BNU T2w---approaching the best benchmark value of 0.8624---and 0.8100 on BNU T1w, while using substantially fewer parameters than Transformer-based alternatives such as ResViT (123.4M) and FS-RWKV (45.4M).

title: Building AI Research Teams for Autonomous Discovery of Linear Attention Architectures
description:
arXiv:2610.28887v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Autonomous agents can increasingly propose ideas, modify code, and run experiments, creating an opportunity to accelerate scientific discovery using teams of collaborative AI researchers. To escape local minima in the discovery, we propose to encourage orthogonal exploration by constructing the team using agents with varying expertise. However, realizing this design requires more than diverse backgrounds. When experiments are costly, a team can test only a limited number of ideas, thereby creating the need to balance exploration and exploitation when selecting a subset of researchers to propose and execute new experiments. Furthermore, each result should shape what the team tries next. We therefore ask how AI researchers with different scientific backgrounds can build on one another's findings and sustain progress under a limited experimental budget. To address these challenges, we build a team of persistent AI researchers, each grounded in a different discipline, who keep private research histories, share experimental evidence, and receive research opportunities through adaptive allocation. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this design by deploying the team to search for linear attention architectures, where it outperforms GDN2 at 1.3B scale on language modeling, common-sense reasoning, and synthetic and real-world retrieval tasks. In controlled comparisons, removing any single organizational component from our design yields markedly weaker discoveries: without disciplinary backgrounds, the search plateaus early; without private histories, researchers make less progress despite identical shared evidence; and uniform selection falls short of adaptive allocation within the same budget. These results suggest that sustained autonomous discovery depends not only on stronger agents, but also on who explores, what they remember, and how research effort is allocated.

title: Private Exports: Caching Signed Download Links to Reduce Presign Rate-Limit Requests
description:
Short answer: object storage fits private fintech exports, but large-file throughput depends on keeping page refreshes away from the presign path. Cache each still-valid signed download URL in the backend, preserve the export job and object key, and retry presign generation with bounded exponential backoff instead of signing again on every click.

A 4 GB statement archive should spend its time moving from object storage to the customer, not making the application mint another authorization artifact because a browser tab refreshed. The link is control-plane work; the file transfer is data-plane work. Treating both as one request path creates a rate-limit problem that more transfer capacity won't solve.

How should a fintech export page cache signed download URLs under presign rate limits?

Key the cache by tenant, user authorization scope, export job, and object key. Return a cached URL only while it has a conservative validity margin; otherwise, let one backend worker generate the replacement while concurrent requests wait for that result. Don't cache by object key alone. In a fintech system, that shortcut can cross an access boundary even when the underlying object remains private.

The export record is the durable center of the flow. It should hold the job state and object key after generation completes. The signed URL is disposable state layered on top. A page refresh can then read the same completed record and reuse its current link rather than starting a new export or presign call. This separation also prevents an impatient user clicking five times from creating five large archives.

Keep the expiry margin explicit. I'm not sure what margin is right for every workload because it depends on link lifetime, clock skew, and how long a download may sit before it starts; load tests with realistic file sizes and client geography should settle it. The important part is to expire the cache before the URL itself, not at the same instant.

One request wins.

Cache first.

The following Python script calls the verified presign path without inventing a request body or response field. Set INFRAI_API_ROOT to the API's versioned root and pass tenant, user, export, bucket, and key arguments. The example demonstrates scoped cache keys, one in-flight signer per key, a short reuse window, HTTP 429 handling, Retry-After, and jittered exponential backoff. Any other 4xx response is surfaced rather than treated as success.

import json
import os
import random
import sys
import threading
import time
from urllib.error import HTTPError
from urllib.parse import quote
from urllib.request import Request, urlopen


class RateLimited(Exception):
    def __init__(self, retry_after: float | None = None):
        self.retry_after = retry_after


API_ROOT = os.environ["INFRAI_API_ROOT"].rstrip("/")
API_KEY = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
CACHE_SECONDS = 30
cache: dict[str, tuple[float, dict]] = {}
locks: dict[str, threading.Lock] = {}
locks_guard = threading.Lock()


def lock_for(cache_key: str) -> threading.Lock:
    with locks_guard:
        return locks.setdefault(cache_key, threading.Lock())


def request_signed_link(bucket: str, key: str) -> dict:
    path = "/storage/object/presign/{}/{}".format(
        quote(bucket, safe=""), quote(key, safe="/")
    )
    request = Request(
        API_ROOT + path,
        method="POST",
        headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {API_KEY}"},
    )
    try:
        with urlopen(request, timeout=15) as response:
            if not 200 <= response.status < 300:
                raise RuntimeError(f"HTTP {response.status}")
            return json.load(response)
    except HTTPError as error:
        detail = error.read().decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
        if error.code == 429:
            retry_after = error.headers.get("Retry-After")
            raise RateLimited(float(retry_after) if retry_after else None)
        raise RuntimeError(f"HTTP {error.code}: {detail}") from error


def get_link(tenant: str, user: str, export: str, bucket: str, key: str) -> dict:
    cache_key = f"{tenant}:{user}:{export}:{bucket}:{key}"
    cached = cache.get(cache_key)
    if cached and cached[0] > time.monotonic():
        return cached[1]

    with lock_for(cache_key):
        cached = cache.get(cache_key)
        if cached and cached[0] > time.monotonic():
            return cached[1]

        for attempt in range(5):
            try:
                result = request_signed_link(bucket, key)
                cache[cache_key] = (time.monotonic() + CACHE_SECONDS, result)
                return result
            except RateLimited as error:
                if attempt == 4:
                    raise
                base = error.retry_after or min(2**attempt, 16)
                time.sleep(base + random.uniform(0, base * 0.25))

    raise RuntimeError("retry loop ended unexpectedly")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(json.dumps(get_link(*sys.argv[1:6]), indent=2))

For more than one application process, replace the in-memory map and locks with shared equivalents that provide an atomic winner. The cache key might look like tenant_81:user_204:export_991:ledger.csv; the exact identifiers are yours, but every authorization dimension must be present. A cached link should never outlive a permission change without an invalidation strategy. That compliance detail is easy to miss because the URL still works exactly as designed.

Separate presign pressure from large-file throughput

Large-file performance needs two measurements. First, count application requests that reach the presign operation per completed export. Second, measure the actual object transfer independently. If refresh spam raises the first number while bytes delivered stays flat, tuning multipart transfer or adding application workers attacks the wrong side of the system.

Retries can amplify the same mistake. A browser retry, an API gateway retry, and a worker retry can multiply one click into several signing attempts unless they share stable request identity. Presign generation is the narrow operation here, so coalesce identical requests and cap retry attempts. Honor Retry-After when it is supplied; otherwise use exponential backoff with jitter. Fast retry loops are traffic generators wearing a reliability label.

Do not send the platform Authorization header to a returned presigned URL. The signed URL carries its own temporary authorization, and the object must remain private or signed-only. The application should redirect the authorized user to that URL or return it to the client, then get out of the large-file byte path unless policy requires the application to proxy every byte.

The edge case I would test first is refresh during expiry: 30 tabs ask for the same finished export while its cached link enters the safety margin. The correct result is one replacement signing operation, not 30. Also test a permission revocation during that window, a job that has finished but whose link cache is empty, and repeated requests while the export is still running. Those tests expose authorization and state-machine gaps long before a throughput chart does.

Picture the request sequence rather than the average: export export_991 finishes, its private object key is committed to the job record, and a customer opens the page on a slow connection. The first authorized page request signs the object and places the result in a tenant-and-user-scoped cache. The browser refreshes twice, a mobile session opens the same export, and a gateway retries one request. All four follow-up requests should read the same cached result; none should rebuild the CSV, and none should independently hit the presign operation. When the cache enters its early-expiry margin, one shared lock elects a replacement request while the others wait. If that request receives 429, it honors Retry-After or applies bounded exponential backoff with jitter. At every step, the durable job record still points to one object. This is the difference between controlling a burst and merely moving it downstream.

Back off.

How do storage options compare after request amplification is controlled?

The right comparison is not which logo serves a byte fastest in an unspecified region. It is how much provider-specific control the team needs, and whether a shared backend surface is worth the capability boundaries it introduces.

Option Integration shape Best fit Reason to choose something else
AWS S3 Direct provider integration Teams standardized on the S3 control plane A shared interface is more valuable than provider-specific integration
Cloudflare R2 Direct provider integration Teams that have already chosen R2 The workload must also move across several supported storage vendors through one contract
Alibaba Cloud OSS Direct provider integration Teams committed to OSS One application contract across vendors matters more
Tencent Cloud COS Direct provider integration Teams committed to COS One application contract across vendors matters more
Google Cloud Storage Direct provider integration GCS is a hard requirement It is outside Infrai's current vendor coverage
Infrai One REST surface over R2, S3, OSS, and COS A team wants one credential and consistent conventions for multiple backend capabilities Native-only storage controls or an unsupported provider are required

Infrai is a strong option when integration overhead is the constraint: its public discovery surface describes each capability with request and response schemas, billing metadata, and runnable examples, so wiring storage starts by reading the operation contract rather than installing another SDK. It also puts multiple backend capabilities behind one key and one bill. For this flow, the relevant verified operation is POST /v1/storage/object/presign/{bucket}/{key}; discover its live schema before constructing the request, and keep the returned link in the application cache described above.

That advantage doesn't make it the automatic choice. Stick with AWS S3, Cloudflare R2, Alibaba Cloud OSS, or Tencent Cloud COS directly when provider-specific controls are central to the design. Choose Google Cloud Storage when GCS support is mandatory. AWS EFS solves a different problem: it is a managed file system, so it should not be treated as a drop-in answer to a signed object-download workflow.

What capability boundaries change the export design?

Private, expiring downloads are supported, but permanent public links and static-site hosting are not: there is no public or public-read ACL, and public_url remains null. That's a sound boundary for this use case, yet it rules out using the same path as a public image host. Browser-direct uploads also need separate planning because self-service CORS configuration is not exposed.

There is no object versioning or object lock. An accidental overwrite therefore isn't recoverable through this surface, and financial records that require WORM retention need an external design. There is also no If-Match conditional write, so strict concurrent exclusion belongs in a queue or database transaction. These aren't footnotes for a fintech workload; they determine which records may be placed behind the abstraction.

Operationally, lifecycle expiration has a one-day minimum. That works for daily cleanup, not hour-level deletion. Multipart fragments have no automatic cleanup rule, metadata cannot be searched server-side because listing only filters by prefix, and accumulated exports require explicit monitoring of bucket usage and object counts. Cross-region automatic replication and cross-cloud bulk migration tooling are absent. Trial credit cannot pay for persistent writes.

The catch is clear: use this pattern for private export artifacts whose authorization lives in the application and whose cleanup can tolerate daily granularity. It is not suitable for immutable regulatory archives, public asset hosting, GCS- or B2-dependent deployments, self-managed browser CORS, or workloads that require native cross-region replication.

Roll out with counters, state, and cleanup

Start with one export type and preserve the old download path during rollout. Add an export state machine such as requested, running, completed, and expired; save the object key once; then place signed-link reuse in front of presign generation. A stable request identifier should follow a repeated user action through the application so retries do not create duplicate export jobs.

Watch four counters: export jobs created, completed objects, presign attempts, and cache hits. Their relationships matter more than a single total. If page traffic rises but completed objects and presign attempts remain nearly steady, coalescing is doing its job. Your mileage may vary on the cache window, especially for customers who begin multi-gigabyte downloads long after opening the page.

Finally, schedule lifecycle cleanup with the one-day minimum in mind and audit object counts as well as bytes. Rollback should disable link reuse without deleting job state or object keys. That gives the team a compact change surface: the heavy data path stays in object storage while the application gains control over refresh spam, retries, authorization, and expiry.

description:
You can now build bots that hold end-to-end encrypted 1:1 and group conversations on XChat with the new XChat adapter for Chat SDK.

title: Three small browser tools, three different correctness problems
description:
A calculator can look polished and still be wrong. An inventory estimate can use the right formula against the wrong stock figure. A worksheet can print a neat answer key that belongs to a different set of questions.

Wizekin's three new browser tools made these differences concrete. Here are the implementation decisions behind a handmade pricing calculator, an inventory reorder calculator, and an arithmetic worksheet generator.

1. State what a percentage is a percentage of

For handmade pricing, “add 30% profit” is ambiguous. A markup is measured against cost. A margin is measured against selling price.

For a unit cost of 7.30:

const markupPrice = 7.30 * 1.30;       // 9.49
const marginPrice = 7.30 / (1 - 0.30); // about 10.43

Selling fees introduce another dependency on the final price. If the channel takes 5% of the selling price plus 0.30 per item, and the target margin is 30%, solve for price:

function sellingPrice(unitCost, fixedFee, margin, feeRate) {
  const denominator = 1 - margin - feeRate;
  if (denominator <= 0) {
    throw new Error('Margin plus percentage fee must be below 100%.');
  }
  return (unitCost + fixedFee) / denominator;
}

sellingPrice(7.30, 0.30, 0.30, 0.05); // 11.692307...

The function takes fractions, not whole percentage numbers. The UI accepts 30 and 5, then converts them. That boundary needs to be explicit.

The fixed-fee assumption matters too: one item per transaction. A multi-item order needs its order-level fee allocated across the items. Shipping, tax, failed output, and material allowance also need named assumptions rather than hidden defaults.

The free CraftCost Studio includes a complete batch example and separates labor cost from the profit remaining after the entered costs.

2. Use the right stock figure

A simple reorder point is average daily demand multiplied by supplier lead time, plus safety stock. But comparing it only with stock on the shelf can ignore an incoming shipment or reserved units.

const reorderPoint = dailyDemand * leadDays + safetyStock;
const inventoryPosition = onHand + onOrder - allocated;
const shouldReorder = inventoryPosition <= reorderPoint;

With demand of four units per day, seven lead days, and ten safety units, the reorder point is 38. If there are 25 units on hand, ten incoming, and five allocated, position is 30.

An order quantity needs another decision: the target coverage. Seven extra days gives a target of 4 * (7 + 7) + 10, or 66. This model suggests 36 units when the reorder condition is met.

The useful tests include equality at the reorder threshold, zero demand, and allocations exceeding on-hand stock. Zero demand should produce an explicit “undefined” stock-cover result, not an infinite-looking number that reads like a recommendation.

StockSimple Studio exposes each assumption. It is a planning calculator, not a demand forecast or an accounting valuation service.

3. Generate the question and answer together

For exact-division practice, rejection-sampling random dividends until they happen to divide evenly is unnecessary. Choose a nonzero divisor and a quotient, then construct the dividend:

const divisor = 8;
const quotient = 10;
const dividend = divisor * quotient; // 80
const question = { dividend, divisor, answer: quotient };

The range now describes divisor and quotient. The dividend can be larger, which the UI needs to explain.

Each question object contains its answer. Both the worksheet and the answer page render from the same objects. A seeded random generator makes a sheet reproducible from its settings, while changing the seed produces another sequence. Repeated questions can still occur; deterministic does not mean unique.

LessonSheet Studio uses this approach for printable arithmetic practice and separate answer pages. It does not collect student records or claim curriculum certification.

Keep the calculations independent of the page

All three tools put calculation functions in a shared module that Node can test without loading a browser. Useful assertions check identities: the calculated craft profit has the intended margin; inventory position reconciles; every exact-division question satisfies dividend === divisor * answer.

Browser testing then covers the things those assertions cannot: reset controls, labels, saved-state behavior, and narrow-screen layouts. In this release, browser testing caught a reset control shadowing form.reset, and a note field that was accidentally required. Passing arithmetic tests did not catch either issue.

Maker disclosure: these are Wizekin tools, developed with AI assistance. The public tools are free. Separate offline workspace editions have been prepared, but their paid listings are not live at publication time. There are no traffic, income, or maintenance guarantees.

title: Guilt by Association: Semantic Leakage Drives Associative Gender Bias
description:
arXiv:2610.28944v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Semantic leakage occurs when a concept in the prompt steers model generation about an entity, even though the concept is irrelevant to it (e.g., a person who likes yellow is said to work as a school bus driver). It has mostly been studied in settings where the concept is directly attributed to the entity the model is asked about. This leaves open whether leakage is a flawed heuristic, where the model builds a profile of that entity, or a much broader associative tendency, e.g., working across seemingly unrelated entities. We argue for the latter: even after removing the attribution of the concept to the specific entity, leakage persists. Next, we extend this idea to gender bias. While work on gender bias in LMs typically looks at cases where the stereotyped concept is attributed to an entity, our findings suggest that a concept may steer outputs with its mere presence in the scene. We show this using gendered concepts under two conditions: when the subject engages with the concept, and when the concept just sits in the scene. We find that both shift model generation toward the stereotype to a similar extent. Together, our results suggest that semantic leakage drives a form of bias that is overlooked by current evaluations.

package com.github.paohaijiao.biz.report;

import com.github.paohaijiao.JOption;
import com.github.paohaijiao.axis.JCategoryAxis;
import com.github.paohaijiao.axis.JValueAxis;
import com.github.paohaijiao.code.JTrigger;
import com.github.paohaijiao.config.JPdfConfig;
import com.github.paohaijiao.demo.constant.JQuickConstant;
import com.github.paohaijiao.enums.JChartType;
import com.github.paohaijiao.executor.JQuickPdfFactory;
import com.github.paohaijiao.factory.JChartRendererFactory;
import com.github.paohaijiao.series.JLine;
import org.junit.Test;

import java.io.File;
import java.io.FileOutputStream;
import java.io.IOException;

/**
 * 统一信用报告 —— 风格 02：折线图（墨绿）
 *
 * <p>以 {@code report/credit_report_02_line.txt} 为模板，把折线图渲染成 SVG 后
 * 绑定到模板中的 {@code ${svg}} 占位符，输出到 {@code D:\test\creditreport\02_line.pdf}。</p>
 *
 * @author Martin
 * @version 1.0.0
 */
public class JQuickCreditReport02LineTest {

    public static final String path = JQuickConstant.path;

    @Test
    public void report02Line() throws IOException {
        JOption option = new JOption();
        option.title().text("信用评级趋势").subtext("2020-2023年度（单位：万元）");
        option.tooltip().trigger(JTrigger.axis);
        JCategoryAxis xAxis = new JCategoryAxis();
        xAxis.data("2020年", "2021年", "2022年", "2023年");
        option.xAxis(xAxis);
        option.yAxis(new JValueAxis());
        JLine revenue = new JLine();
        revenue.name("营业收入").data(8560, 12340, 18920, 25680);
        JLine profit = new JLine();
        profit.name("净利润").data(1240, 2150, 3890, 5420);
        option.series(revenue, profit);

        String svg = JChartRendererFactory.renderChart(JChartType.LINE, option);

        File dir = new File(path + "creditreport");
        if (!dir.exists()) {
            dir.mkdirs();
        }
        FileOutputStream fileOutputStream = new FileOutputStream(path + "creditreport/02_line.pdf");
        JPdfConfig config = new JPdfConfig();
        // 开启 flex 行布局：图表与其右侧的指标说明面板在宽度允许时并排，而不是换行堆叠。
        config.getLayoutConfig().setFlexLayout(true);
        JQuickPdfFactory factory = new JQuickPdfFactory(config);
        factory.bind("svg", svg);
        byte[] bytes = factory.executeResource("report/credit_report_02_line.txt");
        fileOutputStream.write(bytes);
        fileOutputStream.close();
    }
}

Step 3 — run it

The class is a JUnit test, so run it with Maven:

mvn -pl jquick-pdfx test -Dtest=JQuickCreditReport02LineTest

…or call the test method from a main wrapper if you want a plain entry point:

public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
    new JQuickCreditReport02LineTest().report02Line();
}

Output: 02_line.pdf

How it works

Binding a chart SVG into the template

The chart is not a bitmap — JChartRendererFactory.renderChart(...) returns an SVG string, and the template embeds it with a single <svg> element bound to ${svg}. That means the chart stays vector-sharp at any zoom level, and it participates in normal flow layout instead of being stamped on top of the page.

  • Declare only the width on <svg>; the height is derived from the chart's aspect ratio, so the chart never stretches vertically.
  • Open config.getLayoutConfig().setFlexLayout(true) if the template centers the chart with display:flex.
  • Bind the SVG string with factory.bind("svg", svg) — bind() is pure data injection and never re-parses markup. 
String svg = JChartRendererFactory.renderChart(JChartType.LINE, option);
JQuickPdfFactory factory = new JQuickPdfFactory(config);
factory.bind("svg", svg);
byte[] bytes = factory.executeResource(TEMPLATE);

Making the table fill the text area

Tables default to content width, which leaves a ragged right margin on a formal document. Setting width:100% on the <table> makes it span the full text area; percentage widths on the first row's cells then distribute the remaining space across columns.

  • Set width:100% on <table> and give explicit widths only to the leading columns.
  • Label columns need around 100px so labels like Taxpayer ID do not wrap.
  • Leave the last column without a width so it absorbs rounding remainder. 
<table style="width:100%; fontSize:9pt">
  <tr>
    <td style="width:100px; padding:5px">'Taxpayer ID'</td>
    <td style="padding:5px">${taxNo}</td>
  </tr>
</table>

Template syntax cheat sheet

Syntax Meaning
<td style="padding:4px; border:1px solid #C3CDD8"> Cell styling. A <td> holds text only — no nested blocks.
factory.bind("k", v) Injects plain text into the context; markup inside a value is dropped.
'literal text' A single-quoted string is a literal — whatever is inside is printed verbatim.
${var} An expression. It must sit outside the quotes: 'No: '${docNo}.
<table style="width:100%"> Spans the full text area; give explicit widths only to the leading columns.

Gotchas worth remembering

  • Compute money with BigDecimal, round once, and derive 大写 from the rounded value.
  • Flex children whose fixed widths exceed the text area wrap instead of sitting side by side.
  • ${var} must sit outside single quotes — 'No: ${docNo}' prints the placeholder literally.
  • <image src="..."> never evaluates ${...}; write a literal path.

Output

Wrap up

You now have a template file, a Java class and a PDF — all three reproducible from a clean clone. Swap the placeholder blocks for real data (or for real seal images) and the layout does not move.

title: DuplexLedger: Benchmarking Transactional Memory in Full-Duplex Speech Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.27581v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Full-duplex speech agents must update persistent memory while listening and speaking, yet it remains unclear which events should be stored, revised, or excluded. Existing benchmarks isolate interaction timing from memory outcomes, obscuring the state transitions behind a correct answer. We introduce DuplexLedger, a bilingual benchmark of 1,094 persistent sessions aligning four full-duplex scenarios with event-level Write/Update/Ignore/Retain supervision, explicit pre/post memory states, and 6,564 same-session questions and checks. Evaluating five full-duplex models reveals an interaction-memory gap: no system combines strong boundary control with coherent final-state memory, and the best final-state fact coverage is 2.01%. We propose ACT-Mem, an 8.92M-parameter sidecar comprising an event controller, a versioned transactional ledger, and a typed retriever coupled with a frozen MiniCPM-o 4.5 backbone. On 219 held-out sessions, ACT-Mem increases latest-value accuracy from 4.11% to 8.68% while reducing stale assertions and distractor adoption. It improves interaction boundaries but slows interruption stopping. These results motivate selective, auditable full-duplex memory rather than indiscriminate transcript retention. Code is available at https://github.com/lyx-researcher/DuplexLedger.

title: Microfrontends previews now link across repositories
description:
Microfrontends can now link Preview Deployments across repositories when their Git branch names match exactly.

In a monorepo, projects share the same Git repository, commits, and branches, so Vercel can automatically link their previews. Cross-repository projects have separate commit histories and branches in separate repositories. With this update, Vercel matches Git-connected projects by branch name and links their corresponding previews.

For example, when you preview the new-checkout branch of one project, requests to other projects in the Microfrontends group will use their new-checkout previews when available. This makes it easier to review coordinated changes across repositories in one preview experience.

This feature is enabled by default for new Microfrontends groups. You can manage it in your Microfrontends settings. Learn more about how deployment routing works for Microfrontends.

title: AWS RDS Explained: Launch, Secure, and Scale a Managed Database
description:
By Vishal Patil | #vishalcloudjourney

Running a database on your own EC2 instance means you are also the DBA. You patch the OS, schedule backups, set up replication, and wake up when the disk fills. Amazon RDS (Relational Database Service) takes that operational work off your plate so you can focus on your application. In this hands-on guide, you'll launch a MySQL database on RDS, lock it down, connect from EC2, test automatic failover, and learn how to scale reads.

What Is Amazon RDS?

Amazon RDS is a managed service for relational databases. You choose the engine and size, and AWS handles the heavy lifting.

Supported engines: Amazon Aurora (MySQL and PostgreSQL compatible), MySQL, PostgreSQL, MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server, and Db2.

What AWS manages for you

  • Hardware provisioning and OS patching
  • Automated backups and point-in-time recovery
  • Database software patching during a maintenance window
  • Multi-AZ failover
  • Monitoring through CloudWatch

What you still manage

  • Schema design, queries, and indexes
  • Security groups, network placement, and user access
  • Choosing instance size and storage
  • Cost control

Note: With standard RDS you don't get SSH or OS-level access to the underlying host. That's the trade-off for a managed service.

What You Will Build

  • A security group setup where only your EC2 app server can reach the database
  • A private MySQL RDS instance with encryption and automated backups
  • A connection from EC2 to the database
  • A Multi-AZ standby and a failover test
  • (Optional) A read replica

Architecture:

EC2 app server (ec2-app-sg) → RDS MySQL primary (rds-sg, AZ-a)
                                  ↓ synchronous replication
                              RDS standby (AZ-b), takes over on failure

Key Concepts in 60 Seconds

  • DB instance: The managed database server you pay for.
  • DB subnet group: The subnets (in at least two AZs) where RDS is allowed to place your database.
  • Multi-AZ: A standby copy in another AZ, kept in sync, that takes over automatically if the primary fails. It's for availability, not for read scaling.
  • Read replica: An asynchronously updated copy used to scale read traffic.
  • Automated backups: Daily backups plus transaction logs, kept for 1 to 35 days, enabling point-in-time restore.
  • Snapshot: A manual backup that stays until you delete it.
  • Endpoint: The DNS name your application uses to connect. Always use the endpoint, never an IP.

Prerequisites

  • An AWS account with permissions for RDS, EC2, and VPC
  • A VPC with subnets in at least two AZs (the default VPC works)
  • A running EC2 instance (Amazon Linux 2023) to act as your app server, or you can launch one in Step 4

Cost note: RDS bills while the instance is running, and Multi-AZ roughly doubles the instance cost. Check the current Free Tier terms for your account and follow the cleanup section at the end.

Step 1: Create the Security Groups

Use two security groups so the database is reachable only from your app server.

App security group (ec2-app-sg) attached to your EC2 instance

  • Inbound: SSH (22) from your IP, or use EC2 Instance Connect or Session Manager

Database security group (rds-sg)

  • Inbound: MySQL/Aurora (3306) from ec2-app-sg (select the security group as the source, not 0.0.0.0/0)

This is the single most important RDS security habit: never open your database port to the internet.

Step 2: Check the DB Subnet Group

  1. Go to RDS → Subnet groups.
  2. The default VPC already has a default subnet group covering its subnets.
  3. For your own VPC, create a subnet group and add subnets from at least two AZs.

Step 3: Create the Database

  1. Go to RDS → Databases → Create database.
  2. Choose Standard create and engine MySQL.
  3. Template: Free tier or Dev/Test, depending on what your account shows.
  4. Settings:
    • DB instance identifier: mydb-rds
    • Master username: admin
    • Credentials: choose Managed in AWS Secrets Manager (recommended), or set a strong password yourself
  5. Instance configuration: a small burstable class such as db.t4g.micro or db.t3.micro.
  6. Storage:
    • Type: General Purpose SSD (gp3), 20 GiB
    • Enable storage autoscaling with a sensible maximum
  7. Connectivity:
    • VPC and subnet group: your chosen ones
    • Public access: No
    • VPC security group: rds-sg
  8. Additional configuration:
    • Initial database name: appdb
    • Automated backups: enabled, retention 7 days
    • Encryption: enabled (this must be chosen at creation)
    • Deletion protection: on for anything important
  9. Click Create database. It takes a few minutes to reach Available.
  10. Open the database and copy its Endpoint.

Step 4: Connect from EC2

  1. Connect to your EC2 instance (launch one with ec2-app-sg in the same VPC if you don't have one).
  2. Install a MySQL client: 
   sudo dnf install -y mariadb105
  1. Connect using the RDS endpoint: 
   mysql -h <your-rds-endpoint> -u admin -p

If you used Secrets Manager, open the secret in the console and choose Retrieve secret value to get the password.

  1. Create a table and add data: 
   USE appdb;
   CREATE TABLE visitors (id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(50));
   INSERT INTO visitors (name) VALUES ('Vishal'), ('AWS Builder');
   SELECT * FROM visitors;

You now have a working managed database that only your app server can reach.

Step 5: Turn On Multi-AZ

  1. Select your database and click Modify.
  2. Under Availability, choose Create a standby instance (Multi-AZ).
  3. Choose Apply immediately and confirm.

RDS creates a standby in another AZ and keeps it synchronized. Your endpoint stays the same.

Step 6: Test Failover

  1. Select the database, then Actions → Reboot.
  2. Check Reboot with failover? and confirm.
  3. Watch the Events tab and the database's AZ. The standby is promoted, and the AZ changes.
  4. Re-run your SQL query. Your data is still there, and the same endpoint works.

Expect a short interruption (typically a minute or two) while DNS flips to the new primary. Your application should retry failed connections.

Step 7 (Optional): Add a Read Replica

  1. Select the database and choose Actions → Create read replica.
  2. Give it an identifier such as mydb-rds-replica.
  3. Once available, point read-heavy queries at the replica's endpoint and keep writes on the primary.

Replication is asynchronous, so replicas can lag slightly behind the primary.

Multi-AZ vs Read Replica

Multi-AZ Read Replica
Purpose High availability and failover Read scaling
Replication Synchronous Asynchronous
Takes traffic normally No (standby only) Yes (reads)
Automatic failover Yes No (manual promotion)

Security Best Practices

  • Keep Public access set to No and place the DB in private subnets.
  • Allow access only from application security groups.
  • Use Secrets Manager for credentials and rotate them.
  • Enable encryption at rest (KMS) and enforce SSL/TLS connections.
  • Turn on deletion protection and automated backups.
  • Use IAM to control who can modify or delete DB instances.

Cost Tips

  • Pick the smallest instance that meets your needs and resize later.
  • Use Multi-AZ for production, but not for throwaway labs.
  • Stop or delete dev databases you aren't using. (A stopped RDS instance is automatically started again after 7 days.)
  • Delete old manual snapshots you no longer need.
  • Consider Reserved Instances for steady, long-running databases.

Common Issues and Fixes

Problem Likely cause Fix
Connection times out rds-sg doesn't allow 3306 from your app's SG Add the inbound rule with ec2-app-sg as source
Can't connect from your laptop Database is private (public access: No) Connect through EC2, a bastion, or Session Manager
Access denied for user Wrong username or password Re-check credentials or the Secrets Manager value
Unknown database Initial DB name wasn't set Run CREATE DATABASE appdb;
Storage full warnings Autoscaling off or limit reached Enable storage autoscaling or increase size

Clean Up

To avoid charges:

  1. Delete the read replica first (if you created one)
  2. Turn off deletion protection, then delete the DB instance
  3. Decide whether to keep a final snapshot (it costs storage) and whether to delete automated backups
  4. Delete leftover manual snapshots
  5. Delete the security groups and the EC2 instance if no longer needed
  6. Delete the Secrets Manager secret if you created one just for this lab

Conclusion

Amazon RDS lets you run production-grade relational databases without managing servers, patches, or backups by hand. With private networking, Multi-AZ, and automated backups, you get a secure and resilient foundation in minutes. Next, try adding a read replica, enabling Performance Insights, or moving to Aurora to see how far managed databases can go.

If you found this helpful, let's connect and keep learning together.

Connect with me

  • LinkedIn: vishalpatil-devops-aws
  • dev.to: @vishal_patil_aws
  • GitHub: VishalPatil-DevOps-AWS

vishalcloudjourney

title: Revision graphs are not image approval: 12 small Node tests
description:
When an image goes through several small wording changes, a folder full of similarly named exports quickly becomes difficult to review. Which candidate came from the untouched source? Which one was based on an earlier edit? Did someone accidentally describe a revision as its own parent? Those questions are about the revision record, not the pixels. A small JavaScript check can identify some metadata inconsistencies without pretending to approve the image itself.

This is a project-associated, AI-assisted technical article. The complete module and tests below were executed locally with twelve passing Node test cases. The examples are synthetic. The code does not read image files, perform OCR, detect manipulation, assess permissions, or establish that a screenshot is authentic. A clean result only means the supplied revision records pass this particular consistency contract.

Model a revision as an explicit relationship

Each record has an identifier, a parent identifier, and a note. A null parent identifies an independent root. A candidate points to the record it was derived from rather than merely repeating a filename. This makes branches possible: two alternative wording choices can both point to the same source. A later review can then distinguish alternatives without assuming that the highest revision number is automatically the approved version.

The identifier is intentionally restricted to a short lowercase string containing letters, digits, underscores, or hyphens. It is a record key, not a filesystem path or an external URL. The note explains the role of the record in ordinary language. Neither field proves that a corresponding file exists. Your surrounding workflow still needs to associate a record with the correct artifact and preserve the original rather than silently overwriting it.

Choose a small contract before writing the check

The function rejects a non-array input and bounds the list to one thousand records. It reports malformed rows, invalid or duplicate identifiers, missing parent references, blank notes, and cycles. Multiple independent roots are allowed because a review packet may contain several authorized examples. This is not intended as a universal asset management schema; it is a deliberately narrow starting point that can be understood in one sitting.

Duplicate identifiers deserve special treatment. The first occurrence is kept in the lookup map, and later occurrences are reported and ignored for relationship traversal. That choice avoids silently replacing an earlier record with a later one. A caller should treat any returned issue as a reason to inspect the packet, not as an invitation to automatically repair the data. Guessing which duplicate was intended can destroy the very history the record is supposed to preserve.

Detect cycles without approving the content

For every indexed record, the checker walks through parent references until it reaches a root or an unknown key. A small set tracks the keys visited during that walk. Revisiting a key indicates a cycle, including the simple case of a record naming itself as its parent. The approach favors clarity over cleverness and is reasonable for the bounded list used in this demonstration.

The straightforward traversal can repeat work across records, so its worst case is quadratic in the number of records. The one-thousand-record limit makes that cost explicit, but it is not a promise about every deployment environment. If your workflow grows substantially, consider memoized traversal or a dedicated graph representation. Measure the actual workload instead of assuming this teaching example is an optimized production service.

Keep the function pure and its output modest

The implementation creates its own map and sets without modifying the input array or its records. One test verifies that behavior by comparing a structured clone before and after inspection. Preserving input matters when the same record packet is later displayed to a reviewer or saved as evidence of what was submitted. An inspection helper should not quietly rewrite the history it was asked to inspect.

Issue objects contain an index or identifier and a short code. They do not echo the entire note, which may contain context that a caller does not want in a generic diagnostic log. A production application still needs its own logging and privacy policy. This example demonstrates a restrained output shape; it does not establish that every possible use of the function is safe or that the supplied notes contain no sensitive information.

The complete module

The first file exports only the inspection function. It has no network requests, filesystem operations, browser automation, or package dependencies. A successful return does not grant permission to publish an image, and an error does not show that an image is malicious. The output concerns only the consistency of the metadata relationships represented by this function.

// Metadata consistency only. Does not read files or approve image edits.
export function inspectChain(records) {
  if (!Array.isArray(records)) throw new TypeError('records must be an array');
  if (records.length > 1000) throw new RangeError('at most 1000 records');
  const issues = [];
  const byId = new Map();
  for (const [index, row] of records.entries()) {
    if (!row || typeof row !== 'object' || Array.isArray(row)) {
      issues.push({ index, code: 'invalid_record' });
      continue;
    }
    if (typeof row.id !== 'string' || !/^[a-z0-9_-]{1,64}$/.test(row.id)) {
      issues.push({ index, code: 'invalid_id' });
      continue;
    }
    if (byId.has(row.id)) {
      issues.push({ index, code: 'duplicate_id' });
      continue;
    }
    byId.set(row.id, row);
  }
  for (const [id, row] of byId) {
    if (row.parent !== null && (typeof row.parent !== 'string' || !byId.has(row.parent))) {
      issues.push({ id, code: 'missing_parent' });
    }
    if (typeof row.note !== 'string' || !row.note.trim()) {
      issues.push({ id, code: 'missing_note' });
    }
    const seen = new Set();
    let current = id;
    while (byId.has(current)) {
      if (seen.has(current)) {
        issues.push({ id, code: 'cycle' });
        break;
      }
      seen.add(current);
      const parent = byId.get(current).parent;
      if (parent === null) break;
      current = parent;
    }
  }
  return issues;
}

Test the ordinary cases and the awkward edges

The tests include a root, a branch, duplicate keys, a missing parent, self and two-node cycles, an empty note, an invalid identifier, malformed rows, non-array input, an oversized list, and multiple roots. There is also an explicit non-mutation check. These cases describe the contract more clearly than a single example that happens to pass. They make it easier to see which outcomes are intentional and which are not implemented.

Run the second file with node --test revision-chain.test.mjs from the directory containing both files. The local run used for this article passed all twelve test cases with zero failures. That is evidence for these synthetic cases, not a security audit or an exhaustive proof. Add regression tests when you change the schema or discover a meaningful edge case in your actual workflow.

Connect the record to a manual screenshot review

Suppose a team needs to edit screenshot wording in an instructional graphic after the editable source is lost. Preserve an untouched source, record the exact replacement phrase, and give each generated candidate its own revision record. If the actual application or source design is available, a fresh export may be the better choice. The revision graph should support that decision rather than force every task through pixel editing.

AI Image Text Editor is one browser resource for the image step: https://image-text-editor.online/ . Its public homepage describes JPG, PNG and WebP inputs up to ten megabytes, selected text regions, and up to eight selections in one task. New users can start with free credits; edits consume credits. The service uses nearby lettering and background as references, so spelling, alignment, and surrounding detail still need review. This module is not integrated with that service and does not benchmark its output.

Separate consistency, correctness, and authorization

A revision packet can be perfectly consistent while every image in it contains the wrong wording. A reviewer still needs to compare the actual candidate with the approved request and inspect nearby details. They should check the result at its final display size, where resizing or compression may reveal a readability problem that was not obvious in the editor. A polished preview is not evidence that a label is factually correct.

Permission is a separate question again. Use authorized or synthetic examples, avoid unnecessary sensitive uploads, and clearly label altered screenshots when readers could mistake them for original records. Visual text replacement is not secure redaction; metadata, filenames, surrounding context, and older copies can still reveal information. The modest benefit of this helper is organizational: it can make a review packet easier to understand while leaving the actual content and publishing decisions where they belong.

Complete test file 

import test from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
import { inspectChain } from './revision-chain.mjs';
const root = () => ({ id: 'source', parent: null, note: 'Untouched synthetic source' });
const codes = rows => inspectChain(rows).map(x => x.code);

test('one root is valid metadata', () => assert.deepEqual(inspectChain([root()]), []));
test('a branch preserves one source', () => assert.deepEqual(inspectChain([root(),
  { id: 'candidate_1', parent: 'source', note: 'First label correction' },
  { id: 'candidate_2', parent: 'source', note: 'Alternative wording' }]), []));
test('input is not mutated', () => {
  const data = [root()]; const copy = structuredClone(data); inspectChain(data); assert.deepEqual(data, copy);
});
test('duplicate identifiers are reported', () => assert.ok(codes([root(), root()]).includes('duplicate_id')));
test('missing parent is reported', () => assert.ok(codes([{ id: 'edit', parent: 'lost', note: 'Test' }]).includes('missing_parent')));
test('self cycle is reported', () => assert.ok(codes([{ id: 'edit', parent: 'edit', note: 'Test' }]).includes('cycle')));
test('two-node cycle is reported', () => assert.ok(codes([
  { id: 'a', parent: 'b', note: 'A' }, { id: 'b', parent: 'a', note: 'B' }]).includes('cycle')));
test('blank note is reported', () => assert.ok(codes([{ ...root(), note: ' ' }]).includes('missing_note')));
test('invalid id is reported', () => assert.ok(codes([{ ...root(), id: '../source' }]).includes('invalid_id')));
test('nonobject rows are reported', () => assert.ok(codes([null, []]).every(x => x === 'invalid_record')));
test('non-array input and oversized lists throw', () => {
  assert.throws(() => inspectChain({}), TypeError); assert.throws(() => inspectChain(Array(1001)), RangeError);
});
test('multiple independent roots are allowed', () => assert.deepEqual(inspectChain([root(),
  { id: 'second', parent: null, note: 'Another authorized example' }]), []));

title: Is Anyone Enforcing the Cartel? What Reinforcement Learning Teaches LLM Agents in Markets
description:
arXiv:2610.28787v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Evaluations of large language model (LLM) agents report that pricing agents collude at others' expense. Yet collusion is defined by enforcement: a cartel, in which competitors share monopoly profits, holds only if a member who cheats is punished. We introduce an audit that tests enforcement by forcing a member to cheat in counterfactual copies of a market, and use it to study what reinforcement learning (RL) teaches agents in pricing and trading. Small LLMs trained by RL learn what their training rivals reward, but only what they readily try. In self-play, they learn fixed rules ignoring their rivals; against a punishing rival, to be deterred; against a cheating rival, to match its cuts, never the costly price war that would deter it, which they rarely try. A war forced into training is learned, but mostly only where it was forced. Against their own copies, deterred and matching agents can earn the same cartel profits, but only matching ones can enforce them, and then thinly: as a by-product and only against large cuts. Q-learners enforce collusion only in pricing. Prompted LLMs reach cartel-like outcomes mostly through rules that ignore the market. Outcome measures cannot tell these cases apart; the audit can.

title: Why Custom Elementor Container Architecture Outperforms Page Builder Bloat (Achieving 95+ PageSpeed)
description:
Why Custom Elementor Container Architecture Outperforms Page Builder Bloat (Achieving 95+ PageSpeed)

For years, senior front-end engineers and performance advocates have criticized WordPress page builders — especially Elementor — for producing unmaintainable DOM soup, runaway JavaScript execution, and failing Google's Core Web Vitals (INP, LCP, CLS).

The criticism was well deserved. A typical off-the-shelf Elementor site built with legacy sections, columns, and 12 third-party addon packs (like Essential Addons or Ultimate Addons) easily exceeds 2,400 DOM nodes, loads 3.2MB of unminified JavaScript, and scores under 45 on mobile PageSpeed Insights.

However, when approached as an extensible component framework rather than a visual design crutch, modern Elementor can achieve sub-second Largest Contentful Paint (LCP < 1.0s) and guaranteed 95+ mobile performance scores.

At UCDREAMS, our engineering team specializes in high-speed, custom Elementor development. Here is how we architect clean-code container systems that scale.

1. Migrating to Native CSS Flexbox & Subgrid Containers

The root cause of page builder lag is nested DOM wrappers:

<!-- Legacy Bloat: 5 nested wrappers for a single headline -->
<div class="elementor-section">
  <div class="elementor-container">
    <div class="elementor-column">
      <div class="elementor-widget-wrap">
        <div class="elementor-widget elementor-widget-heading">
          <h2>Our Services</h2>
        </div>
      </div>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

By enabling Elementor's native Flexbox and CSS Grid containers and writing custom CSS utility classes, we flatten the DOM tree by over 65%:

<!-- Modern UCDREAMS Container Architecture -->
<div class="ucd-container ucd-flex-row">
  <h2 class="ucd-heading">Our Services</h2>
</div>

2. Dynamic Content Binding with ACF Pro (Advanced Custom Fields)

Most agencies make the mistake of hardcoding client copy, pricing tables, and testimonials directly into visual Elementor widgets. This makes content updates fragile and forces marketing teams into layout-breaking edits.

Instead, we engineer a decoupled CMS architecture:

  1. Custom Post Types (CPTs) store structured business data (team members, case studies, client reviews, pricing packages).
  2. Advanced Custom Fields (ACF Pro) manages typed data fields with strict input validation.
  3. Elementor Single Templates dynamically pull ACF tags without touching the DOM layout.

This allows marketing managers to update content from simple WP admin form fields in 30 seconds without ever touching the visual editor.

3. Core Web Vitals Optimization Checklist

To ensure every build achieves a 95+ score on Google PageSpeed Insights:

  • Conditional Asset De-Queuing: Using wp_dequeue_style() and wp_dequeue_script() to prevent Elementor frontend scripts from loading on pages where no widgets require them.
  • Inline Critical CSS: Extracting above-the-fold viewport styles and injecting them into the <head> while deferring non-critical CSS.
  • Modern WebP/AVIF Generation: Serving next-gen responsive image sizes with native srcset and fetchpriority="high" on hero images.
  • Sub-Second Server Caching: Enterprise edge caching with WP Rocket and Cloudflare APO.

title: Turn Input Predicates Into Boundary Cases Before Testing an API
description:
AI disclosure: An AI agent drafted this article by reading an existing Python example. The tables specify expected behavior from source; they are not test results. No API was called and no new test implementation is supplied.

A useful boundary case starts with the predicate the program evaluates. An error message is a clue, but its wording may be less precise than the condition that triggers it.

Consider a small support-drafting function. Before calling its request helper, it rejects a blank ticket, rejects a ticket whose length is greater than 8,000, and requires an output-token parameter between 1 and 2,048 inclusive.

These are limits of the example function. They do not establish the API service's limits or the capabilities of any model.

Hold the other inputs steady

To reason about one check, choose otherwise valid local inputs and vary only the item under discussion. If both the ticket and the numeric parameter are invalid, an early failure may hide the later condition.

For the ticket, the first question is whether its stripped value is empty. The length check then uses the original string, not the stripped version.

Proposed ticket case Expected result at the local ticket checks Why it is useful
Empty text Reject as empty Covers the obvious empty input.
Spaces or newlines only Reject as empty Exercises the stripped-value check.
Nonblank text of length 7,999 Pass these ticket checks Covers just below the upper boundary.
Nonblank text of length 8,000 Pass these ticket checks Establishes whether equality is allowed.
Nonblank text of length 8,001 Reject as too long Covers just above the boundary.

“Pass these checks” is deliberately narrow. It does not mean a model request succeeded, a reply was useful or any charge was established.

The example's error text says to keep the ticket “under” 8,000 characters, while its condition rejects only lengths greater than 8,000. A source-derived case at exactly 8,000 exposes that difference without guessing what the author intended.

The Python documentation defines len() in terms of the number of items. Here it is applied to a decoded string. Do not silently substitute archive size, UTF-8 byte count or a model's token count as the measurement.

Separate parsing from range validation

The command-line path first converts the output-token setting with int(). The function then applies its numeric range check.

Proposed parameter case Expected stage
A value that cannot be parsed as an integer Stop during conversion on the command-line path.
Integer 0 Reject at the function's range check.
Integer 1 Pass this range check.
Integer 2,048 Pass this range check.
Integer 2,049 Reject at the function's range check.

These are separate assertions. An integer-conversion failure does not exercise the upper-bound branch. A valid integer does not establish that it lies within the allowed range.

Keep expectations separate from observations

A case record should have distinct places for the source condition, the expected branch, the observed result and the evidence. Until the case has actually been executed under stated conditions, leave the observed result as not run.

If these cases are later implemented, the external request should be isolated so that passing the local checks cannot accidentally trigger a real call. That is a proposed testing boundary, not a claim that a test harness was built here.

This small matrix gives a reviewer something precise to challenge: equality at the limit, measurement units, conversion versus range validation, and the order of checks. It avoids using a generic “invalid input” case as a substitute for understanding which predicate was exercised.

title: Cursor Cloud Agents can now run in Vercel Sandbox
description:
Cursor Cloud Agents can now run in Vercel Sandbox instead of Cursor's hosted machines.

Cursor manages the agent harness and inference loop. Its Self-Hosted Machines APIs let you supply the execution environment where agents clone repositories, edit files, and run commands and tests. Self-Hosted Machines requires a Cursor Enterprise plan.

Vercel Sandbox provides that execution environment as an isolated Firecracker microVM for each agent request. Vercel Functions and Vercel Workflows form a durable control plane that claims queued agent requests, provisions workers, monitors sessions, and cleans up automatically.

With this architecture, you get:

  • A scale-to-zero worker pool without long-lived virtual machines

  • A dedicated, isolated Sandbox for every agent request

  • Durable retries when a worker or session fails

  • Short-lived, user-scoped credentials inside each Sandbox

title: Environment variables now use Config and Secret types
description:
When you add or edit an environment variable in Vercel, you now choose Config or Secret instead of using the Sensitive toggle. Existing variables marked Sensitive are automatically treated as Secrets and continue to work without migration.

  • Config: The value remains readable after saving for members with access. Use Config for non-sensitive values you may need to inspect later, such as variables with a public framework prefix.

  • Secret: The value remains available to your deployments and can be replaced, but members cannot view or retrieve it after saving. Use Secret for passwords, API keys, and tokens.

You can select an environment or Preview branch for each value. The environment variable list in the dashboard shows each variable’s type and where it applies.

Team policy changes

The Enforce Sensitive Environment Variables team policy is deprecated with this update. When enabled, it required every environment variable created by a team member to be Sensitive, including non-sensitive configuration. With Config and Secret types, members can choose the appropriate type for each variable.

A new Separate Production Secret Values policy is available in your Security settings. When enabled, the Production value for a Secret must differ from the values used for the same key in Preview, Development, and custom environments.

If your team had the legacy policy enabled, confirm whether the Separate Production Secret Values policy should be enabled for your team. The deprecated policy is no longer enforced by the Vercel CLI.

Set variable types from the CLI

To choose whether an environment variable is a Config or Secret from the CLI, pass --visibility config or --visibility secret to vercel env add or vercel env update:

The existing flags continue to work. When --visibility is omitted, --no-sensitive maps to Config and --sensitive maps to Secret. After adding or updating a variable, the CLI output shows its type under Visibility.

Learn more in the Environment Variables documentation.

title: One Trip.com URL, Five Pulls, Twelve Hours: 21 Different Hotels, Six Every Time
description:
I run a visa agency in Bali. The other half of my week goes into Apify Actors, and one of them reads Trip.com: a city, two dates and a guest count in, one row per hotel out, with the live nightly rate for exactly those dates.

Trip.com is the booking channel for most of Asia and it has no public web API, so a scraper is the only way in. The field I expected to cause trouble was the price. It didn't. What caused trouble was something I hadn't thought to check: which hotels the page shows you at all.

The same URL, five times, one day

My QA runs hit a hardcoded list URL so I can diff the output day over day. On 21 October 2026 five of them fired against a byte-identical URL:

https://www.trip.com/hotels/list?city=723&checkin=2026%2F11%2F20
  &checkout=2026%2F11%2F23&adult=2&children=0&curr=USD&locale=en-XX

Bali, three nights, two adults, USD. Pulls at 00:30, 07:48, 07:55, 08:20 and 12:10 — an 11-hour-40-minute span. Twelve hotel rows each, which is one page, 60 rows total.

Those 60 rows contained 21 distinct hotels. Six appeared in all five pulls. Nine appeared exactly once.

Appeared in Hotels Median nightly
5 of 5 pulls 6 $22
4 of 5 3 $30
3 of 5 3 $89
1 of 5 9 $52

Pairwise, the overlap decays with the gap between requests, and it decays cleanly:

Pair Gap Common rows
07:55 vs 08:20 25 min 12 / 12
07:48 vs 07:55 7 min 11 / 12
00:30 vs 07:48 7 h 8 / 12
08:20 vs 12:10 4 h 8 / 12
07:48 vs 12:10 4 h 7 / 12
00:30 vs 12:10 11 h 40 6 / 12

So this is not per-request randomness. Requests minutes apart come back identical or off by one row. Requests hours apart come back half different. That is the signature of a result set that is assembled and cached, then reassembled later — not a ranking you can treat as stable.

It replicates. Three pulls on 20 October against the 19–22 November window: the two fired a minute apart agreed 12 of 12, the one twenty hours earlier agreed 7 of 12 with both. Two pulls this morning, four hours apart, agreed 7 of 12 — a $260 Kempinski vanished, a $283 resort appeared.

What that does to a number you'd actually report

The prices held almost perfectly still. Across the six hotels present in all five pulls, the nightly rate moved in three of them, by exactly one dollar: $34→$35, $10→$11, $28→$27. Kenran Resort sat at $72 in all five, Moonloka at $16. If you track one named property, Trip.com is boringly consistent and this article is irrelevant to you.

Aggregate those same five pulls and the stillness disappears:

Pull Median nightly Mean nightly
00:30 $31.00 $51.60
07:48 $35.00 $62.80
07:55 $31.50 $61.40
08:20 $31.50 $61.30
12:10 $23.50 $39.00

The mean nightly rate for Bali swung from $39.00 to $62.80 — a 61% spread — on one day, from one URL, with essentially no price changing. Every dollar of that swing is sampling. The 12:10 pull happened to miss the expensive tail: no Anvaya at $110, no Kayon Jungle at $281, no ARNA at $90. The 07:48 pull caught all three.

Which direction it biases is not random either. The six properties that never moved are all in the cheap half — $9 to $72, median $22. The nine one-time visitors have a median of $52 and include $86, $98, $106 and $166. Page one has a sticky cheap core and a rotating expensive tail, and a "city average" built on page one inherits whichever part of that tail it happened to catch.

Asking for more rows is a different question, not a bigger answer

The obvious fix is to pull deeper. It works, but not in the way "more data, same answer" suggests. Three runs on Bangkok this morning, 21–24 November, same two adults, minutes apart:

  • 12 rows: median $38.50, mean $45.10
  • a second 12-row run three minutes later: 11 of 12 the same hotels, zero price differences, order reshuffled
  • 48 rows, thirty seconds after that: 48 distinct properties, median $53.50, mean $75.30

Median $38.50 against $53.50 on the same city, the same dates, the same minute. Page one is not a random sample — it is cheap-skewed, and each extra page walks you up the price distribution. The 48-row run also did not contain 2 of the 12 hotels the first run had just returned.

The practical rule I now use: if you want a city-level statistic, fix the row count and never compare two samples of different depth. If you want coverage, run it more than once and union on hotelId — the churn is working for you then, because five pulls of 12 gave me 21 properties, not 12.

import requests, statistics
from collections import defaultdict

TOKEN = "<APIFY_TOKEN>"
seen = defaultdict(dict)

for _ in range(5):  # five pulls, spaced hours apart by a scheduler
    rows = requests.post(
        "https://api.apify.com/v2/acts/lergassy~tripcom-scraper/run-sync-get-dataset-items",
        params={"token": TOKEN},
        json={"cityId": 723, "cityName": "Bali",
              "checkIn": "2026-11-21", "checkOut": "2026-11-24",
              "adults": 2, "maxHotels": 48, "currency": "USD"},
    ).json()
    for r in rows:
        if r.get("type") == "hotel" and r.get("price"):
            seen[r["hotelId"]] = r          # last write wins, one row per property

print(len(seen), "distinct hotels")
print("median", statistics.median(r["price"] for r in seen.values()))

Note the type == "hotel" filter. The last row of every run is a free notice row with the run's own accounting — rowsDelivered, chargedTotalUsd, timings. The 48-row Bangkok run reports {"rowsDelivered": 48, "chargedTotalUsd": 0.144} and finished in 28 seconds. Leave it in your dataframe and it becomes a hotel with no price.

Two price fields you should not multiply

While I had 451 priced rows from 22 runs sitting on disk, I checked the arithmetic between price (nightly) and totalPrice (the stay).

totalPrice was larger than price × nights in 451 of 451 rows. Median ratio 1.200, range 1.056 to 1.339. Two things are stacked in there: totalPrice is the number Trip.com prints as incl. taxes & fees, and price is rounded to a whole currency unit, which on a $9 room is an 11% rounding step on its own. I am not going to tell you the tax rate, because Trip.com ships a formatted total and a rounded nightly figure and splitting them is guessing. What I will say is that price * nights is never the number the guest pays, and the error is a fifth, not a rounding wobble.

The discount badges have a smaller version of the same gap. 373 rows carried an originalPrice, and it was above price in all 373 — median implied discount 29.4%. On the 364 rows that also carried an "N% off" tag in dealTags, the discount you compute from the two numbers beat the badge in 341 of them, median by 2.7 points: Lloyd's Inn says 61% off with $80 → $28 next to it, which is 65%. Use the badge as a label and compute your own number, and don't expect them to agree to the point.

The Actor is Trip.com Scraper — hotel cards with the live rate for your dates, property details, and the guest reviews off the hotel page, by city ID or by URL.

When this is the wrong tool

  • You need a booking. This reads public pages. There is no availability hold, no rate code and no reservation here.
  • You need every hotel in a city, exactly once. You will get there by unioning repeated runs, not by one run. If you need a guaranteed complete inventory as of a timestamp, Trip.com's page one will not give you one.
  • You need per-room rate plans. Each row carries the one room Trip.com chose to price for your dates — roomName, roomId — not the hotel's full rate table.
  • You need a tax breakdown. You get the pre-tax nightly figure and the all-in total. The split between them is not published as fields, and I'd rather ship two honest numbers than three invented ones.

If you keep one thing from this: before you trust a scraped ranking, pull it twice an hour apart and count the overlap. A field that disagrees with itself is obvious. A row set that quietly swaps half its members is not, and it moves your averages far harder than any price ever will.
