title: Designing a Fair AI Detection Feature: 7 UX Patterns That Prevent False Accusations
description:
Adding an AI detector to your product takes an afternoon. Designing it so it doesn't falsely accuse a real person takes much more thought.

A student who gets flagged for an essay they wrote, or a candidate rejected because a tool said "AI", is a real harm. It's also a support ticket, a trust problem and, increasingly, a compliance risk. This post collects UX and product patterns we recommend for any feature that uses an AI detection score, whichever provider you use.

Why this matters: false positives are real

  • In 2023, Stanford researchers (Liang et al., "GPT detectors are biased against non-native English writers") tested seven popular detectors on 91 TOEFL essays written by non-native English speakers. On average, the detectors misclassified 61.3% of those human-written essays as AI-generated, and almost all of the essays were flagged by at least one detector.
  • OpenAI withdrew its own AI text classifier in July 2023, citing its low rate of accuracy.
  • Formal, simple or heavily edited human writing can look statistically "predictable", which is exactly what detectors look for.

None of this means detection is useless. It means the interface around the score decides whether the feature is helpful or harmful.

Pattern 1: Show confidence levels, not verdicts

❌ AI-GENERATED in a red badge

✅ High likelihood of AI-generated text (review recommended)

A raw number like "87%" also misleads, because people read it as "87% of this was written by AI" or "87% chance this person cheated". Neither is true. Map the score into a few bands:

function presentScore(aiProbability) {
  if (aiProbability >= 85) {
    return { label: "High likelihood of AI", tone: "warning", action: "review" };
  }
  if (aiProbability >= 60) {
    return { label: "Mixed signals", tone: "neutral", action: "optional_review" };
  }
  return { label: "Low likelihood of AI", tone: "info", action: "none" };
}

Tune the thresholds for your use case. A plagiarism-sensitive exam needs different bands from a blog moderation queue.

Pattern 2: Refuse to score short text

Short texts don't carry enough statistical signal. ProofAI's API docs recommend at least 50 words, and many teams set a higher bar for high-stakes decisions.

const MIN_WORDS = 50;
if (wordCount(text) < MIN_WORDS) {
  return ui.show("Not enough text to analyze reliably. Add at least 50 words.");
}

Showing "not enough text" is honest. Showing a confident score on two sentences is not.

Pattern 3: Highlight passages, don't stamp documents

Most real documents are mixed. Someone might write the body themselves and use AI to polish the intro. If your provider returns per-segment scores (ProofAI's API returns a segments array), highlight passages instead of labelling the whole file:

function renderSegments(segments) {
  return segments.map(s => `
    <span class="seg seg--${s.color_label}" title="AI likelihood: ${s.ai_prob}%">
      ${escapeHtml(s.text)}
    </span>`).join("");
}

Reviewers can then ask a precise question ("Can you walk me through how you wrote this section?") instead of making a blanket accusation.

Pattern 4: Humans decide, the tool informs

Never wire a detection score directly into an automatic, high-impact action:

  • ❌ Auto-reject applications above 80%
  • ❌ Auto-fail assignments above a threshold
  • ✅ Add a "needs review" flag and send the item to a person
  • ✅ Combine the score with other evidence: drafts, version history, a short conversation, timed in-class writing

Log who reviewed each flagged item and what they decided. That audit trail protects both your users and your company.

Pattern 5: Explain it in the UI

A small "How is this calculated?" link does a lot of work. Say plainly:

  • What the score measures (statistical patterns common in AI-generated text)
  • What it doesn't prove (authorship or intent)
  • That results can be wrong, especially for short texts and non-native writing
  • How a person can appeal or add context

Pattern 6: Give people a way to respond

If you show a flag to the person who wrote the content, such as a student or candidate, give them a clear path:

  1. See which passages were flagged
  2. Add context or upload drafts
  3. Request human review

An appeal button costs little to build and prevents a lot of harm.

Pattern 7: Be careful with privacy

Detection means sending user content to a third party. Check:

  • Does the provider store submitted content or use it for training? (ProofAI states it doesn't store scanned content.)
  • Is the connection encrypted, and are API keys restricted to your domain?
  • Do your terms tell users their content may be checked?

Under rules like the EU AI Act's transparency obligations (applying from 2 August 2026) and India's amended IT Rules on synthetically generated content (in force since 20 February 2026), how you handle AI-related content is getting more regulatory attention. Being transparent with users is the safest default.

A quick checklist

  • [ ] Scores shown as confidence bands, not verdicts
  • [ ] Minimum length enforced
  • [ ] Passage-level highlighting where possible
  • [ ] No automatic high-impact decisions
  • [ ] "How this works" explanation in the UI
  • [ ] Appeal or "add context" path
  • [ ] Privacy and data-retention checked

Wrapping up

The detection model is only half the feature. The other half is the interface that decides how people act on it. If you get these patterns right, AI detection becomes a helpful review signal instead of a source of false accusations.

If you want to try these patterns with real scores, the ProofAI free detector works without login, and our API docs show the segment-level response format.

Have you ever been falsely flagged by an AI detector, or had to handle a complaint about one? We'd like to hear how it went in the comments. 👇

Disclosure: we're the team behind ProofAI at 4Born Solutions. This article was drafted with AI assistance and reviewed and edited by our team.

title: When Do Humans and Machines Truly Complement Each Other? Formal Conditions and Empirical Evidence for Human-AI Synergy
description:
arXiv:2610.27965v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Can humans and artificial intelligence cooperate such that their combination yields greater accuracy than either agent alone? This result, termed \emph{synergy} or \emph{complementarity}, is notoriously difficult to achieve, even when both agents possess significant independent accuracy. In this paper, we present a formal framework to model human-AI interaction through the lens of reliance patterns, which characterize the joint correctness structure of human and algorithmic decisions. We derive mathematically necessary and sufficient conditions for synergy, demonstrating that its emergence depends on the ability of either agent to identify and correct the errors of the other, what we call Human and Algorithmic Correction. Beyond its theoretical contribution, the proposed framework provides a foundation for the design and evaluation of knowledge-based decision support systems, where interaction policies must dynamically integrate heterogeneous sources of expertise. We demonstrate this through the analysis of seven clinical case studies. Our empirical results reveal a ``dominance trap,'' where a strong algorithmic advantage can paradoxically inhibit synergy by eroding human corrective intervention. We also show that synergy can persist even in the presence of cognitive biases, such as automation bias, provided there is functional de-correlation between human and AI errors. These results provide a formal foundation for key concepts in the human-AI systems literature and offer actionable insights for designing interaction-centric AI systems that foster complementarity.

title: A Single SQL Constraint Can Save Your Database From Bad Data — Do You Know Which One?
description:
Imagine you are building an order management system.

Your "customers" table contains 10,000 customers. Your "orders" table contains 500,000 orders.

Everything works perfectly.

Then one day, an application inserts an order for "customer_id = 99999".

The problem? Customer 99999 does not exist.

Your database now contains an order that cannot be linked to a valid customer.

Your reports may become unreliable. Your joins may not return the expected information. Your team may spend hours investigating a data-quality problem that could have been prevented.

The solution is not another SQL query. It is a database constraint.

Let's explore how SQL developers prevent these problems and learn some common SQL interview traps along the way.

  1. CREATE TABLE: Start With the Right Structure

First, create a customer table.

CREATE TABLE customers (
customer_id NUMBER PRIMARY KEY,
customer_name VARCHAR2(100) NOT NULL
);

Notice two important constraints:

  • "PRIMARY KEY" ensures that every customer has a unique, non-NULL identifier.
  • "NOT NULL" prevents a customer record from being inserted without a name.

Now create an orders table.

CREATE TABLE orders (
order_id NUMBER PRIMARY KEY,
customer_id NUMBER,
order_amount NUMBER(10,2)
);

At first glance, everything looks fine.

But there is a hidden problem.

Nothing in this table definition prevents an order from referencing a customer who does not exist.

How do we fix it?

  1. FOREIGN KEY: Protect Table Relationships

Add a foreign key.

ALTER TABLE orders
ADD CONSTRAINT fk_orders_customer
FOREIGN KEY (customer_id)
REFERENCES customers(customer_id);

Now the database enforces the relationship.

If someone tries to insert an order with a non-NULL customer ID that does not exist in "customers", the database rejects the operation.

Why is this important?

Because your database should not depend entirely on every application developer remembering to validate every relationship correctly.

Interview takeaway: A foreign key enforces referential integrity at the database level.

One important detail: a nullable foreign key can contain "NULL" unless the column is also defined as "NOT NULL".

  1. ALTER TABLE: Change Structure Without Recreating the Table

Business requirements rarely remain the same forever.

Suppose you now need to store customer email addresses.

Do you need to drop the table and create it again?

No.

ALTER TABLE customers
ADD email VARCHAR2(150);

The new column is added to the existing table, and existing rows are retained.

You can also use "ALTER TABLE" to add or remove constraints and modify columns, subject to database-specific rules and existing data.

In production, always review dependencies before changing a schema. A column modification or removal can affect reports, stored procedures, applications, and downstream data pipelines.

  1. DROP vs TRUNCATE vs DELETE: The SQL Interview Trap

An interviewer asks:

"You have a table containing 10 lakh records. You want to remove all records but retain the table structure. Which command would you use?"

Many candidates immediately answer "DELETE".

But let's understand the differences.

DROP — Remove the Table

DROP TABLE orders;

This removes the table itself, including its data and associated table objects such as indexes and constraints.

Use it only when the table is no longer needed.

TRUNCATE — Remove All Rows

TRUNCATE TABLE orders;

This removes all rows while retaining the table structure.

There is no "WHERE" clause, so you cannot use it to remove only selected records.

DELETE — Remove Selected Rows

DELETE FROM orders
WHERE order_amount < 1000;

This removes only rows matching the specified condition.

You can also delete all rows by omitting the "WHERE" clause.

Important Oracle interview tip: DDL statements such as "DROP" and "TRUNCATE" have implicit-commit implications. Do not assume you can roll them back like an ordinary uncommitted "DELETE".

Always verify the target table and understand the transaction behavior before running destructive commands.

  1. COMPOSITE PRIMARY KEY: When One Column Is Not Enough

Consider an order-items table.

A single order can contain several products, and the same product can appear in different orders.

CREATE TABLE order_items (
order_id NUMBER,
product_id NUMBER,
quantity NUMBER,
unit_price NUMBER(10,2),

PRIMARY KEY (order_id, product_id)

);

Why use two columns in the primary key?

Because the combination of "order_id" and "product_id" identifies each row.

For example:

  • "(101, 10)" identifies product 10 in order 101.
  • "(101, 20)" identifies product 20 in order 101.
  • "(102, 10)" identifies product 10 in order 102.

These combinations are different.

But inserting "(101, 10)" a second time would violate the composite primary key.

This concept is useful when designing junction tables, order details, and many-to-many relationships.

  1. CHECK CONSTRAINT: Prevent Invalid Values

Suppose an order amount must never be negative.

You can enforce that rule at the database level.

ALTER TABLE orders
ADD CONSTRAINT chk_order_amount
CHECK (order_amount >= 0);

Now an insert or update that violates the constraint is rejected.

One subtle detail: a "CHECK" constraint alone does not reject "NULL" values. If the amount must also be present, define the column as "NOT NULL" or add an appropriate constraint.

This is the kind of detail that separates memorizing SQL syntax from understanding how database rules actually work.

Your SQL Interview Challenge

Before you leave, try this question without looking up the answer.

You have two tables:

  • "customers", containing customer information.
  • "orders", containing customer orders.

You must prevent an order from referencing a customer who does not exist.

Which solution is best?

A. Create an index on "orders.customer_id".

B. Add a foreign key referencing "customers.customer_id".

C. Use "ORDER BY customer_id".

D. Add a "CHECK" constraint requiring "customer_id > 0".

Pause and decide before reading further.

Correct answer: B — Add a foreign key.

An index can improve access performance, but it does not enforce the relationship. Sorting rows does not enforce data integrity, and checking that an ID is positive does not establish that the customer exists.

A foreign key directly enforces the required relationship.

The key principle is simple:

Good database design makes invalid data harder to create.

Want to Master SQL DDL for Interviews?

We've covered the fundamentals, but there is much more to learn.

What happens when you need a many-to-many relationship? When should you use "ON DELETE CASCADE"? How do you modify existing constraints safely? What mistakes do interviewers expect SQL developers to avoid?

I've brought these topics together in a detailed guide on Sankalan Data Tech.

The complete tutorial covers:

  • "CREATE", "ALTER", "DROP", and "TRUNCATE" with practical examples
  • Primary keys, foreign keys, unique constraints, and check constraints
  • One-to-many and many-to-many relationships
  • Composite primary keys and junction tables
  • Constraints versus triggers
  • Common interview mistakes and follow-up questions
  • 21 SQL interview questions with answers

👉 Continue learning with the complete SQL DDL guide:

https://www.sankalandtech.com/Tutorials/sql-plsql-faq-interview/ddl-manage-tables-relationships-sql-faq.html

If you are preparing for a SQL developer, Oracle PL/SQL, or data engineering interview, work through the examples and understand the reasoning behind each constraint instead of simply memorizing syntax.

Save this post for revision, and test yourself on the interview questions in the full guide.

title: The Hidden Dangers of Free Proxies: A Deep Dive into Security Risks and Building Secure Alternatives
description:
Originally published on tamiz.pro.

For many developers, the allure of a "free proxy list" is a quick fix for bypassing geo-restrictions, scraping public data, or masking an IP address during early-stage testing. However, in the world of networking, there is no such thing as a free lunch. When you route your traffic through a server you do not control and that is provided for free, you are essentially handing the keys to your data stream to an anonymous third party. This article explores the underlying mechanisms that make free proxies dangerous and provides a technical blueprint for implementing secure, self-hosted alternatives.

  • The Architecture of a Proxy
  • The Threat Model of Free Proxies
  • Common Attack Vectors
  • The Economic Incentive: Why are they Free?
  • Building a Secure Alternative with Squid and WireGuard
  • Production Best Practices for Proxy Infrastructure
  • Frequently Asked Questions

The Architecture of a Proxy

To understand the risk, we must first understand the flow. A proxy server acts as an intermediary gateway between a client (your application) and a destination server (the API or website you are accessing).

In a standard request flow:

  1. The client sends a request to the proxy server.
  2. The proxy server forwards that request to the destination server.
  3. The destination server responds to the proxy.
  4. The proxy forwards the response back to the client.

From the perspective of the destination server, the request originated from the proxy's IP, not the client's. While this provides anonymity from the destination, it creates a single point of failure and a total point of visibility for the proxy operator. If the proxy is "transparent" or "anonymous," it may or may not hide your original IP via the X-Forwarded-For header, but the operator of the proxy server always sees the raw TCP stream.

The Threat Model of Free Proxies

When using a free proxy, your threat model expands significantly. You are no longer just worried about the destination server or the ISP; you have introduced a malicious actor into the middle of your request-response cycle.

The "Man-in-the-Middle" (MITM) by Design

A proxy is, by definition, a Man-in-the-Middle. While legitimate proxies use this for caching or filtering, a malicious free proxy uses it for interception. Because the proxy terminates the TCP connection from the client and initiates a new one to the server, it has full access to the payload of every unencrypted packet.

TLS Termination and SSL Stripping

Many developers assume that HTTPS (TLS) protects them from proxy risks. While TLS provides end-to-end encryption, a sophisticated proxy can attempt SSL Stripping. In this attack, the proxy intercepts the initial HTTP request and prevents the upgrade to HTTPS, serving the client a plaintext HTTP version of the site while maintaining an HTTPS connection with the actual server. If the developer's code doesn't strictly enforce HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security) or validate certificates, the proxy can read every password, API key, and session token in plaintext.

Common Attack Vectors

1. Packet Sniffing and Data Exfiltration

Free proxy operators often run packet sniffers like tcpdump or Wireshark on the proxy interface. Any data sent over HTTP, FTP, or SMTP is captured in real-time. Even with HTTPS, metadata (DNS queries, destination IPs, packet timing) is leaked, which can be used for fingerprinting the developer's infrastructure.

2. Payload Injection

Because the proxy controls the response body before it reaches the client, it can inject malicious code. For a web scraper, this might mean the proxy modifies the HTML to include a malicious script or redirects a download link to a malware-infected binary. For an API client, the proxy could modify JSON responses to trigger vulnerabilities in the client's parser (e.g., injecting oversized strings to cause a buffer overflow).

3. IP Reputation Poisoning

Free proxies are often shared by thousands of users, many of whom are using them for botnets or DDoS attacks. When you use these IPs, your traffic is associated with a "dirty" IP. This often leads to your legitimate requests being flagged by WAFs (Web Application Firewalls) like Cloudflare or Akamai, resulting in permanent IP bans for the proxy range and potential flagging of your own account if you are authenticated.

The Economic Incentive: Why are they Free?

Maintaining servers and bandwidth costs money. If a service is free, the data is the product. Proxy operators monetize their infrastructure through:

  • Selling Data: Logs of user activity, headers, and intercepted credentials are sold on dark-web forums.
  • Ad Injection: Injecting banners or scripts into HTTP responses to generate ad revenue.
  • Botnet Recruitment: Using the proxy as a distribution point for malware to infect the clients connecting to it.
  • Traffic Rerouting: Sending your traffic through other "partner" proxies to artificially inflate traffic numbers for certain sites.

Building a Secure Alternative with Squid and WireGuard

Instead of relying on public lists, developers should build a private proxy cluster. The most secure approach is to combine a VPN (WireGuard) for transport security and a Caching Proxy (Squid) for request management.

Prerequisites

  • A VPS (Ubuntu 22.04 LTS recommended)
  • Root access to the server
  • Basic knowledge of Linux networking

Step 1: Securing the Transport Layer with WireGuard

To prevent the proxy from being exposed to the open internet (and thus becoming a target for open-proxy scanners), we wrap it in a WireGuard VPN. This ensures only authenticated clients can even reach the proxy port.

# Install WireGuard
sudo apt update && sudo apt install wireguard -y

# Generate keys
wg genkey | tee privatekey | wg pubkey > publickey

Configure /etc/wireguard/wg0.conf:

[Interface]
PrivateKey = <Server_Private_Key>
Address = 10.0.0.1/24
ListenPort = 51820

[Peer]
PublicKey = <Client_Public_Key>
AllowedIPs = 10.0.0.2/32

Step 2: Installing and Configuring Squid

Squid is the industry standard for HTTP proxying. We will configure it to listen only on the WireGuard interface, making it invisible to the public web.

sudo apt install squid -y

Edit /etc/squid/squid.conf. We want to disable public access and only allow our VPN subnet:

# Define the WireGuard network
acl vpn_network src 10.0.0.0/24

# Allow access from the VPN network
http_access allow vpn_network

# Deny everything else
http_access deny all

# Change default port if desired
http_port 3128

# Hide the client IP (Make it an anonymous proxy)
forwarded_for off
request_header_access Via deny all
request_header_access X-Forwarded-For deny all

Step 3: Implementing the Client Connection

On the developer's machine, connect to the VPN and then route the application traffic through the proxy IP.

# Start WireGuard client
sudo wg-quick up wg0

# Test the proxy using curl
curl -x http://10.0.0.1:3128 https://api.ipify.org

By using this architecture, you have eliminated the MITM risk from third parties. The traffic is encrypted from your machine to your VPS via WireGuard, and the proxy is not accessible to the public, preventing it from being hijacked by botnets.

Production Best Practices for Proxy Infrastructure

For engineers scaling this to a production environment, consider these advanced configurations:

  1. Rotation via Load Balancer: If you are scraping, do not use one IP. Use a pool of small VPS instances and a load balancer (like HAProxy) to rotate requests across different exit nodes.
  2. Strict TLS Validation: Always use libraries that enforce certificate validation. In Python's requests, ensure verify=True (which is default). Never set verify=False when using a proxy, as this disables the only protection you have against SSL stripping.
  3. Monitoring and Logging: Implement Prometheus and Grafana to monitor proxy latency and error rates. High spikes in 403 Forbidden responses usually indicate that your proxy IP has been flagged and needs rotation.
  4. Avoid Long-Lived Sessions: If you are automating tasks, rotate your proxy identity frequently to avoid pattern detection by the destination server's behavioral analysis engines.

For more architectural patterns on secure networking, check out Tamiz's Insights for deep dives into system design.

Frequently Asked Questions

Q: Can't I just use a SOCKS5 proxy instead of HTTP?
SOCKS5 is more flexible as it handles any TCP/UDP traffic, not just HTTP. However, it doesn't provide the caching or header manipulation capabilities of Squid. The security risks remain the same: if the SOCKS5 server is "free," the operator can still sniff all unencrypted traffic passing through the socket.

Q: Is a commercial "Paid Proxy" safer than a free one?
Generally, yes, because there is a legal contract and a business model based on service availability rather than data theft. However, the operator still has the technical ability to see your traffic. The only way to ensure total privacy is to own the infrastructure (self-hosting).

Q: What is the difference between an Anonymous and an Elite proxy?
An Anonymous proxy hides your IP but tells the server it is a proxy (via the Via header). An Elite (or High Anonymity) proxy hides your IP and pretends to be a regular browser, omitting any proxy headers. While Elite proxies are better for bypassing blocks, they don't provide additional security against a malicious operator.

title: LatBridge: Efficient and Stable Model Replacement in Latent-Communication Multi-Agent Systems
description:
arXiv:2610.27813v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multi-agent systems rely on communication to complete tasks, and latent communication passes continuous representations to reduce text generation and re-encoding. However, multi-agent systems must reconfigure agent models, whereas existing latent-communication methods are built for fixed model combinations, so their interfaces may fail after replacement. Our pilot study confirms this interface failure and identifies the requirement for interface reuse after model replacement. We present LatBridge, which connects agent models through a shared Bridge and separate interfaces under a shared latent-communication protocol. After agent model replacement, LatBridge reuses unchanged interfaces, selects matching low-rank interfaces, and combines them through the Bridge, training only missing ones with all models frozen. The Bridge processes source representations in the basic mode and constructs target input without autoregressive generation in the accelerated mode. Experiments support effective communication after model replacement, with mean basic-mode accuracies of 14.8% on MATH and 27.3% on ALFWorld next-action prediction across eight small-model configurations. Analyses examine the factors supporting task accuracy and communication efficiency.

title: Why I built my coding-agent tooling as a local proxy instead of hooks
description:
There are dozens of coding agents out there now, with a new one every other week.

Using them extensively, both at work and on side projects, I kept having ideas about the requests they send, how I could optimize them, or build around them to improve my workflows:

  • What if a small local model checked them for secrets first?
  • What if I could see where my tokens actually go?
  • What if old tool output could be trimmed before it's sent again?

The sensible move was to pick one tool like Claude Code or Codex CLI, build on that tool's hooks, and call it a day.

In true side project fashion, that's not what happened.

Where to put it

Every coding agent has its own extension point: hooks, config, plugins. Build the same idea on each, and you're maintaining four versions that break whenever one of the tools changes.

But they all have one thing in common: whatever tool you use, it ends up sending requests to a model over HTTP. So that's where I put it. Torana is a local proxy that sits between the agent and the model provider.

Pointing an agent at it is usually one environment variable. For Claude Code:

ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL="$(torana endpoint anthropic)" claude

What that one decision forced

1. Build once, works in every tool. Since the proxy sees every request, anything built there works for Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode or Pi. The catch: they don't all speak the same API. Anthropic Messages, OpenAI Chat Completions and Responses all look different, so the proxy has to understand each format before anything can be built on top of it.

2. It has to run locally. The proxy sees everything: your code, your prompts, the files the agent reads, your keys. That's not something to send to someone else's server. Torana runs on your machine, and it's open source so you can check what it does.

3. It became a plugin system. I had more than one idea, so each idea is its own plugin. Plugins are compiled to WebAssembly, and you can write them in Go or Rust. A plugin that sees all your agent traffic shouldn't run just because it's installed, so nothing runs until you've reviewed its permissions and approved it.

What it cost

A proxy isn't free:

  • Each tool needs routing. Most take a base URL, but not all the same way. Codex, for example, needs its HTTP/SSE mode instead of websockets for plugins to see the responses.
  • Some things only the harness knows. A proxy sees requests, not the agent's UI. That's why Torana later grew an MCP server, so the agent can ask the proxy questions from inside the chat.
  • Prompt caching makes you careful. Change an old message, and the provider's cache for the whole conversation can be rebuilt. Any plugin that edits history has to pay for itself first.

What's next

Over the next few weeks I'll write up one decision at a time: what I built, why, and what it cost. MCP is next.

If you want to try it: https://torana.sh/?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=social&utm_content=origin-04 (open source: https://github.com/torana-edge/torana-edge)

title: LIC Plan Comparison Tool: FastAPI & React Workflow
description:
Problem

LIC agents in India often juggle dozens of plans while presenting them to clients. The traditional approach—static PDFs or spreadsheets—leads to duplicated effort, stale bonus data, and slow page loads when a new plan is added. A digital tool that loads only the necessary code for a chosen plan, while isolating runtime errors, directly addresses these pain points.

Implementation Overview

The DoAide InsureKit achieves this with a combination of FastAPI on the back‑end, React + Vite on the front‑end, and a PostgreSQL database that stores plan metadata and current bonus rates. The most visible technical improvement is route‑level code splitting coupled with an error boundary.

Route‑Level Code Splitting

Vite, the bundler used in this project, supports dynamic imports out of the box. Each top‑level route in the React app is defined as a lazily loaded component. For example, the PlanComparison page that renders the lic plan comparison table is imported like this:

import { lazy, Suspense } from "react";

const PlanComparison = lazy(() => import("./pages/PlanComparison"));

export default function App() {
  return (
    <Suspense fallback={<div>Loading...</div>}>
      <PlanComparison />
    </Suspense>
  );
}

When a user navigates to /compare, Vite bundles only the PlanComparison component and its dependencies into a separate chunk. The main bundle remains under 50 KB, reducing the initial payload and improving perceived performance for agents who need to switch between multiple plan views.

Error Boundary

Even with code splitting, a bug in one component could crash the entire UI. To mitigate this, the project introduces a custom error boundary that captures rendering errors and displays a fallback UI. The implementation looks like this:

class ErrorBoundary extends React.Component {
  state = { hasError: false };

  static getDerivedStateFromError() {
    return { hasError: true };
  }

  componentDidCatch(error, info) {
    console.error("ErrorBoundary caught an error", error, info);
  }

  render() {
    if (this.state.hasError) {
      return <h2>Something went wrong while loading the comparison.</h2>;
    }
    return this.props.children;
  }
}

export default function App() {
  return (
    <ErrorBoundary>
      <Suspense fallback={<div>Loading...</div>}>
        <PlanComparison />
      </Suspense>
    </ErrorBoundary>
  );
}

This pattern ensures that a failure in the premium calculator or a missing bonus rate does not affect the rest of the application. The boundary logs the error for developers and presents a user‑friendly message to the agent.

Back‑End Support

FastAPI powers the API endpoints that feed the comparison tool. A typical route looks like:

from fastapi import APIRouter
from pydantic import BaseModel

router = APIRouter()

class PlanRequest(BaseModel):
    plan_ids: list[int]
    age: int

@router.post("/compare")
async def compare_plans(req: PlanRequest):
    # Query PostgreSQL for plan details and bonus rates
    plans = await db.fetch("SELECT * FROM plans WHERE id IN :ids", ids=req.plan_ids)
    # Calculate premiums based on age and bonus
    results = [calculate_premium(p, req.age) for p in plans]
    return {"plans": results}

The calculate_premium function pulls the current bonus rate from the database, ensuring that the calculator always uses up‑to‑date data. Because the front‑end only loads the comparison component when required, the API is called only once per view, keeping server load low.

User Experience

From an agent’s perspective, the workflow is straightforward:

  1. Select Plans – In the sidebar, check the boxes of up to 10 LIC plans.
  2. View Comparison – The PlanComparison component renders a table with premium estimates, bonus rates, and a side‑by‑side comparison of LIC vs FD vs mutual funds.
  3. Adjust Parameters – A small form lets the agent change the age or term, triggering a fresh API call and re‑rendering only the affected rows.

Because the component is lazily loaded, the initial navigation to the comparison page takes under 200 ms on a 3G connection. If an error occurs (e.g., the database is temporarily unreachable), the error boundary displays a concise message instead of crashing the entire UI.

Technical Takeaways

  • Route‑level code splitting reduces bundle size and improves load times, a critical factor for agents working in bandwidth‑constrained environments.
  • Error boundaries localize failures, keeping the rest of the lic agent tool usable.
  • FastAPI + PostgreSQL provide a lightweight yet powerful backend that can handle complex premium calculations without latency.
  • Vite’s native support for dynamic imports means minimal configuration overhead.

These techniques together make the DoAide InsureKit a robust platform for LIC plan comparison, insurance calculation, and portfolio management.

Future Directions

The current implementation already includes SEO prerendering for each route. Adding server‑side rendering for the comparison component could further reduce time‑to‑first‑byte for agents who rely on slow mobile networks. Additionally, a GraphQL layer could expose a single endpoint for all plan data, simplifying the front‑end logic.

Conclusion

By combining route‑level code splitting, error boundaries, and a FastAPI backend, DoAide InsureKit delivers a fast, reliable lic plan comparison experience that meets the needs of Indian LIC agents, insurance advisors, and financial planners.

title: Python on Vercel is now generally available
description:
Python is now a first-class language and runtime on Vercel. Build APIs, full-stack applications, and AI agents with native Python SDKs and a shared development and deployment workflow for your Python backend and JavaScript frontend.

Python framework and runtime support

Vercel handles the infrastructure so you can focus on your application:

  • Automatic framework support: FastAPI, Flask, and Django applications are automatically recognized and configured, with framework-specific support for serving static assets through the Vercel CDN.

  • Native Python runtime and tooling: Vercel runs CPython on Linux and supports uv and pyproject.toml for dependency management.

  • Compute for APIs and workers: Scale request-driven applications with Fluid compute and run long-running pull-based workloads with Vercel Daemons.

Native Python SDKs

Within your application, Python SDKs let you build agents, run untrusted code, and orchestrate durable workflows.

  • Sandbox: Give your application or agent an isolated Linux VM on demand.

  • AI SDK for Python (Beta): Generate or stream model responses and call tools. Get started with uv add ai.

  • Workflow SDK for Python (Beta): Persist execution state and retry failed workflow steps.

  • Queues (Beta): Send and receive messages for background work.

  • Connect: Obtain credentials for calling external APIs.

  • Blob: Upload and retrieve files in object storage.

Use the SDKs individually or combine them in the same Python application.

Your frontend and backend, together

For full-stack applications, Vercel Services allows you to deploy your frontend and backends together in one project, with shared previews and atomic deployments and rollbacks. Within that project, you can view logs by service and connect backends privately through service bindings.

For a frontend in frontend/ and a FastAPI app defined in backend/main.py, add this vercel.toml at the repository root.

Requests under /api/ reach matching FastAPI routes with the path unchanged, while other requests reach the frontend. Run both services locally with vercel dev, then deploy them together from the same repository.

title: CVE-2026-89111: SSRF in a Multi-Tenant SDK and the OAuth Credentials Behind It
description:
CVE-2026-89111: SSRF in a Multi-Tenant SDK and the OAuth Credentials Behind It

A server-side request forgery in a cloud SDK sounds like a lower-tier finding until you consider what the SDK is holding. For CVE-2026-89111 in the SAP Cloud SDK for Python, the answer is OAuth2 client credentials in multi-tenant SAP Business Technology Platform environments.

The disclosure

CVE-2026-89111 is rated 10.0 and affects SAP Cloud SDK for Python versions below 0.45.2. The flaw is server-side request forgery. Public reporting reviewed here notes that no in-the-wild exploitation had been observed at the time of writing, which distinguishes it from the KEV-listed issues covered elsewhere in this series.

Severity without exploitation is still severity. A 10.0 SSRF in a library that handles tenant-scoped credentials deserves attention before someone builds an exploit.

Why SSRF in an SDK is different

SSRF in a web application lets an attacker make the server issue requests on their behalf, typically to internal endpoints the attacker cannot reach directly.

SSRF in a shared SDK is a different shape. The SDK runs inside the customer's application, and that application holds credentials issued for its tenant. If request construction can be influenced so that the credential-bearing call goes to an attacker-chosen destination, the outcome is credential exfiltration rather than internal port scanning.

The distinction matters for impact assessment. A traditional SSRF is an access bypass. This one is closer to a credential leak: the tenant's OAuth2 client secret, presented to the wrong host, is a durable compromise.

The multi-tenant dimension

The affected environment is described as multi-tenant BTP. Two aspects deserve emphasis.

First, credentials in this environment authorize access to services across a subscription. A leaked client credential is not a read-only token for one endpoint; its scope is defined by the service instance it was created for.

Second, SDKs are consumed by application developers rather than operated by platform teams. The library version in use is often decided by a dependency lock file and updated when someone runs an upgrade. That makes remediation a code change in every consuming application, distributed across teams.

This is why library vulnerabilities with credential impact age badly. There is no single appliance to patch, and the dependency may sit several levels deep.

Practical remediation

  1. Identify consuming applications. Search dependency manifests and lock files for the SDK. Container images reveal what actually shipped, which is often more accurate than repository manifests.
  2. Upgrade to 0.45.2 or later in each application, then rebuild and redeploy so the runtime image contains the fixed version.
  3. Verify at runtime. Log or assert the SDK version during startup. A repository that declares the fixed version and an image that contains the old one is a common mismatch.
  4. Rotate client credentials for tenant service instances where the vulnerable version was deployed in an environment that processes untrusted input.
  5. Review outbound traffic. If the SDK's request destinations are logged or observable, examine historical records for calls to unexpected hosts.

Step five is where an SSRF can be confirmed or ruled out in retrospect. Most organizations have proxy or egress logs that would show a credential-bearing request leaving for an unexpected destination, and few have looked at them for this reason.

The dependency problem this exposes

Credential-handling libraries occupy a privileged position in an application's dependency graph and are usually treated like any other package. They get updated on a release cadence, not a security one.

The practical improvement is to classify dependencies that hold credentials separately from those that do not, and apply a faster update policy to the first group. That is a policy change, not a tooling purchase, and it directly reduces the window in which a flaw like this one remains deployed.

References

  • SAP, Security notes portal (SAP Security Note for CVE-2026-89111; version 0.45.2 is the fixed release per public reporting).
  • NVD, CVE-2026-89111.
  • Week 42 2026 security summary citing the CVSS 10.0 rating and BTP credential scope: security report.

title: Vercel Connect now supports Secure Compute
description:
Vercel Connect now supports Secure Compute, allowing connectors to reach providers with IP allowlists, such as Salesforce and Snowflake.

With Secure Compute routing enabled, Connect’s provider requests use the selected network’s dedicated static IP addresses instead of Connect’s shared IPs. Requests to obtain and refresh access tokens follow that route; your app’s direct API routing is unchanged by this setting. Credential management stays the same, so you don’t need to store long-lived provider secrets in your app or build OAuth flows yourself.

To enable Secure Compute routing for a supported connector and all projects that use it:

  • Open your connector’s Settings in the Vercel dashboard.

  • Under Secure Compute Routing, choose an existing network.

  • If your provider uses an IP allowlist, add the selected network’s displayed IP addresses to it in the provider’s settings.

  • Save your changes in Connect.

Requests for initial connector creation and all provider discovery requests bypass the selected network and connect directly to providers. If the selected network is unavailable, routed requests fail instead of falling back to Connect’s shared IPs.

Read the Secure Compute routing documentation for configuration details.

title: Staged Continual Adaptation of Multimodal Foundation Models for Japanese Financial Documents
description:
arXiv:2610.27904v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Staged post-training of multimodal foundation models chains vision-language alignment, reasoning distillation, and domain tuning, yet how each phase trades capabilities against the others remains under-characterised. Tracking an 8.4B-parameter model from an un-fine-tuned baseline through three training phases on Japanese financial documents (evaluated on five text-input benchmarks), we find the phases interact non-additively: math-only distillation overwrites the financial knowledge acquired earlier even as procedural math skill survives, and the domain phase repairs more than it installs. A skip-phase ablation is best for domain knowledge but forfeits numerical-reasoning gains, so per-phase contributions are not decomposable and the best checkpoint is task-dependent, with implications for checkpoint retention and scheduling rather than added stages.

title: I’m building Haven Vault: an open source home for private files
description:
Some files deserve their own space: personal photos, important documents, and notes you want to keep private.

I’m building Haven Vault, an open source personal vault that encrypts your content in the browser and runs in your own Firebase project.

The goal is to make private storage comfortable enough for everyday use, with code you can inspect, run, and improve.

Explore Haven Vault on GitHub

Each installation is designed for a single owner. You control the deployment, and a separate vault passphrase is used to derive the key that decrypts your content locally.

The app already includes:

  • Encrypted files and notes, including filenames, item metadata, and thumbnails.
  • Collections, search, and favorites to help you find things again.
  • Photo zoom and panning, PDF previews, and text previews inside the app.
  • Grid and list views, plus trash for managing deleted items.
  • Passkey sign-in and configurable automatic locking.

One design decision worth sharing is the separation between signing in and unlocking the vault.

A passkey authenticates you and establishes access to the backend. Your vault passphrase decrypts the data in your browser. Being authenticated does not mean the encryption key is available.

That gives Haven three distinct states:

  1. Signed out.
  2. Signed in, with the vault locked.
  3. Signed in, with the vault unlocked.

This distinction also makes the experience less repetitive. Locking the vault clears local secrets and decrypted content while keeping an unexpired authentication session active. You can unlock again with your passphrase. Signing out ends the local authenticated session and attempts to revoke it on the server.

Automatic locking follows the same idea. Content is concealed immediately when the app goes into the background. A configurable grace period determines when the key is cleared and the vault locks; during that grace period, decrypted data remains in memory. There is also a separate inactivity timeout.

I want opening a document, checking another app, and returning to the vault to feel natural.

Haven uses React, TypeScript, Vite, Firebase, SimpleWebAuthn, and the Web Crypto API. The project’s source code is MIT licensed.

If you want to explore the interface, you can run the fictional demo without a Firebase account or environment file. With Node 22.12+ within the Node 22 release line and pnpm 12 installed:

git clone https://github.com/i-am-jyotirmaya/haven-vault.git
cd haven-vault
pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
pnpm dev

Then open the local demo.

The demo uses fictional content and cannot upload real files. To test the actual encrypted vault locally, there is a Firebase emulator workflow. Production deployment currently requires your own Firebase project with Blaze billing; the setup guide walks through it.

Haven is still evolving and has not received an independent security audit. There is no passphrase reset or built-in backup/export workflow, so keep independent originals. The security documentation explains the threat model and limitations, including the need to trust the browser and deployed application code.

I’m sharing it now because feedback from people using different devices, browsers, and workflows can shape what it becomes.

If you take it for a spin, I’d especially value:

  • A confusing setup step explained from a fresh perspective.
  • A mobile interaction or keyboard flow that could feel better.
  • A reproducible bug with fictional test data.
  • A small improvement to the documentation, accessibility, or tests.

A useful contribution can start with “this took me longer to figure out than it should have.” And if you spot something you’d enjoy fixing, the contribution guide is there to help you get started. For suspected vulnerabilities, please use the private reporting route described in the security documentation.

If this sounds like a project you’d enjoy using or building, have a look at the repository. I’d love to see which small improvements the community notices first.

What’s the one thing a personal vault needs to get right before you’d use it regularly?

title: ACE-Compression: An Ability-Centric Evaluation of Compressed Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.27913v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Model compression makes large language models deployable, but today's evaluation tells an incomplete story. Standard practice measures retained task performance and stops there. This misses a critical fact: compression perturbs the distributed knowledge embedded across billions of weights, and task scores alone cannot reveal which underlying abilities survive and which quietly collapse. To solve this question, we introduce ACE-Compression, an ability-centric evaluation framework. Instead of asking only "does the compressed model still answer correctly?", we ask "which of its core abilities remain intact?" Our framework probes four deployment-facing dimensions: procedural reasoning and constraint execution, knowledge grounding and truthfulness, social cognition and affective understanding, and persona fidelity and stylistic consistency. Across more than 35 compressed checkpoints from six open-weight LLMs-covering quantization and pruning-we find that compression redistributes ability profiles. Coarse, local, and surface-level signals often persist, while fine-grained, long-tail, and context-dependent abilities become fragile. Quantization consistently outperforms pruning in retention, but the practical meaning of that gap depends entirely on which ability an application requires. Based on our findings, deployers can choose compression methods by the ability profile their application needs, not just by a leaderboard average. And algorithm designers gain diagnostic signals to build compression methods that preserve what matters. We believe that ACE-Compression turns compression from a black-box accuracy drop into an interpretable intervention-one we can measure, understand, and ultimately improve.

title: Building a Nested LADDER for LLM Unstructured Post-Training Pruning
description:
arXiv:2610.28773v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Non-uniform allocation can improve post-training pruning of large language models, yet quality can still degrade sharply at high sparsity. To control degradation as sparsity increases, we introduce LADDER (Layer-Wise Allocation via Damage-Driven Evaluation and Refinement), which allocates sparsity incrementally. At each step, it evaluates pruning an additional fraction of weights from each eligible layer and commits the layer update that causes the least end-to-end degradation per removed parameter. This process produces non-uniform sparsity profiles and exactly nested masks across multiple budgets. We evaluate LADDER on five OPT, Llama, and Qwen models across 10-90% sparsity, using SparseGPT as its candidate-generation backend and comparing against uniform and adaptive allocation baselines. Results reveal a clear operating-regime trade-off: LADDER is comparable or slightly weaker at benign sparsity but becomes substantially more robust from 70% onward. This high-sparsity advantage largely persists after posterior distillation across four of five models and translates into improved retention of aggregate zero-shot accuracy.

title: TIL: GBase Database Connection Failed? Check sqlhosts First
description:
Today, I ran into a familiar problem: dbaccess couldn't connect to GBase Database(GBase 8s). The culprit wasn't a password or an obvious network failure. The hostname configured in sqlhosts didn't match the hostname resolution settings in /etc/hosts.

Here's how I tracked it down.

3 Quick Checks for GBase Database Connection Issues

1. Check the hostname in sqlhosts

cat "$GBASEDBTDIR/etc/sqlhosts.ol_gbasedbt1210"

Look at the hostname field in the connection entry. Make sure it matches the intended server address and instance configuration.

2. Check the system hostname

hostname

Compare the output with the hostname used in sqlhosts. A mismatch is worth investigating, especially after installation or hostname changes.

3. Check hostname resolution

cat /etc/hosts

Confirm that the hostname can resolve to the correct IP address. You can also test resolution directly:

getent hosts your-hostname

Replace your-hostname with the hostname configured in sqlhosts.

The key isn't that all three files or commands must display exactly the same text in every setup. It's that the hostname used by the connection configuration must resolve correctly to the intended server.

Why This Matters

When troubleshooting a GBase Database connection failure, it's tempting to start changing passwords, firewall rules, or network settings.

But if sqlhosts points to a hostname that resolves incorrectly—or doesn't resolve at all—the connection can fail before those other factors become relevant.

Start with the connection entry and hostname resolution. They're quick to verify and can save you from unnecessary troubleshooting.

TIL takeaway: When dbaccess reports a connection error, check sqlhosts and hostname resolution first. If they look correct, move on to instance status, port configuration, network reachability, and credentials.

One small configuration mismatch can look like a much bigger database problem.

title: T-DIG: Text-Conditioned Diversity for Image Generation
description:
arXiv:2610.29003v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Text-to-image (T2I) platforms typically return several images per prompt so users can explore different visual interpretations and choose one that matches their intent. However, T2I models are usually optimized for single-image quality which comes at a cost of multi-image diversity, limiting this exploration. Diversity is also contextual: one user wants variations in background, while another wants them in artistic style, and the same user may later want variations in clothing. The generated images should differ along whatever axis the user cares about. In this paper, we introduce T-DIG, a text-conditioned diversity framework for image generation and editing. T-DIG is an iterative framework comprising multiple modules that lets users type prompts, inspect default generations, request variations using natural language, and continue refining outputs until they're satisfied. At its core, T-DIG uses an LLM policy that produces K axis-conditioned prompts or edit instructions for a frozen generator or editor. We train this policy with GRPO using a text-conditioned diversity reward and alignment penalties. Because the image generator remains frozen, T-DIG applies to open-weight, distilled, and proprietary models. We also release the first dataset for text-conditioned prompt diversity in image generation, with the training and validation splits built from human-written axes and a test set drawn from real user interactions with T-DIG. T-DIG far exceeds baselines in improving text-conditioned diversity, while preserving base-prompt alignment across a variety of metrics and human judgements. We show that user-directed diversity exploration can be added to a wide range of image generation models, open and closed, without the need to access their weights. Website: https://image-study.org/t-dig/

title: TEMPL: A Resource-Efficient and Transparent Model-Free Framework for Pseudo-Label Generation in Material CT Scans
description:
arXiv:2610.28974v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The scarcity of large annotated datasets limits deep learning (DL) segmentation in material CT analysis. DL-based pseudo-labeling can help, but it is often computationally expensive and hard to interpret. We introduce a multi-stage, model-free framework that generates pseudo-labels directly from grayscale CT scans. It combines thresholding, morphological dilation, and a custom breadth-first search region-growing algorithm to produce polygonal annotations without pre-trained weights, labeled data, or a GPU. We compare it against the zero-shot Segment Anything Model (SAM), a fully supervised 3D U-Net, and classical baselines. On a dendrite dataset with ground truth, our method reaches 63.19% IoU versus 10.74% for zero-shot SAM, with four times the instance recall at 0.5 IoU (33.3% versus 8.3%). The supervised 3D U-Net serves as a reference ceiling that requires expert labels. On a silica sand specimen, YOLO models trained on our labels performed comparably to models trained on SAM labels in a qualitative comparison. Across 1,053 extracted grains, the median equivalent diameter was 163.8 micrometers, near the specimen's known 106 to 150 micrometers sieve range, compared with 219.5 micrometers for SAM, whose labels merge adjacent particles and add spurious detections. A sensitivity analysis shows a stable operating range for the key threshold and a sharp, predictable failure point linked to phase contrast. Our method needs 15s per image on a standard CPU versus 28s for SAM on a GPU. These results support our transparent approach as a tool for annotation bootstrapping and microstructural quantification in resource-limited settings.

title: Railway Says Some Customer Secrets May Have Been Decrypted. What Should Teams Do?
description:
A platform can encrypt a secret at rest and still face a serious incident if an attacker reaches a path that exposes its decrypted value. Railway's October 21 security notice says an unauthorized third party may have accessed encrypted customer environment variables and obtained the decrypted contents of some of them.[1]

Railway has not said that every customer was affected. Its initial analysis suggests the impact may be limited to a subset, while its precautionary recommendation applies to all users.[1] This is an evolving incident, so check Railway's notice and status page before acting on older summaries.[2]

What Railway has disclosed

Railway says the affected systems store customer environment variables. Those values can include API keys, database access, or credentials for private registries.[1] The company also says it believes the incident is part of a broader series of attacks against platform companies intended to reach AI inference providers. That is Railway's assessment, not a publicly described attack chain.[1]

Railway paused builds and deployments while investigating.[1] Its status updates on October 22 added response guides, including credential rotation and checks for unusual usage at connected services.[2] At 02:19 UTC on October 22, Railway said builds were still offline and some remediation steps requiring a redeploy would have to wait.[2]

The public notice does not explain how the third party gained access, how many accounts were affected, or which specific variables were exposed.[1] Railway says it will contact customers it confirms were affected.[1] Avoid treating either the possible subset or the platform-wide precaution as a confirmed count. The first is Railway's initial assessment; the second is its response advice.[1]

Rotate credentials at the service that issued them

Changing a value in a hosting dashboard does not necessarily invalidate the old credential. A leaked API token can remain usable until its issuing provider revokes it. A database password remains valid until the database accepts a new one and the old one is disabled.

For each secret stored in Railway, identify the system that issued it, then replace it there. Update the corresponding Railway variable when the platform allows it, and revoke the old value. Railway recommends rolling all environment variables, including API keys and private registry credentials.[1]

For database credentials, coordinate the change with the database itself. AWS defines rotation as updating the credential in both the secret store and the database or service that accepts it.[4] Changing only one side can leave the application or database using an outdated value.[4]

Prioritize credentials that can create bills, expose customer data, or grant broad access. Include AI provider keys, cloud access, database passwords, source-control tokens, and private package credentials if they were stored in the affected platform. Railway's notice explicitly includes environment variables and private registry credentials in its recommendation.[1]

Keep a short record of each credential: owner, issuing service, affected application, replacement status, and old-key revocation status. AWS recommends limiting access to secrets, monitoring their use, and rotating credentials as part of secret management.[3]

Check for use you do not recognize

Review the logs at the service that issued each credential, as Railway recommends reviewing service logs for unusual activity.[1] Look for requests, deployments, access locations, or usage patterns the team cannot explain. Railway's status page has published service-specific guides, including checks for unusual activity at AI providers, cloud accounts, databases, and other connected services.[2]

A lack of suspicious entries does not prove that a credential was not accessed. Logs may have limited retention or may not capture every relevant action. Treat log review as one part of the response, alongside replacement and revocation.

Plan for a paused deployment pipeline

A rotation is not complete if the running application still depends on the old value. But during Railway's response, teams could not deploy new versions while builds were paused. Railway's status page said some remediation steps required a redeploy and had to wait for builds to return.[2]

That creates an operational tradeoff: revoke an old credential immediately and risk breaking the live service, or keep it active while waiting to deploy the replacement. There is no universal answer. For a credential with clear signs of misuse, containment may outweigh availability. For a production database password with no safe way to update the running app, coordinate the change with the database and platform status, and use Railway's service-specific guidance.[2] Avoid making a rushed change that locks out the application without actually revoking the old credential.

The lesson is about the full secret lifecycle

Encryption at rest is important, but it is not the whole security boundary. Applications and platforms must eventually retrieve usable credentials to connect to databases, cloud accounts, registries, and APIs. The important questions are also who can access those values, how access is monitored, and how quickly a credential can be replaced and revoked.

AWS recommends limiting access to secrets, monitoring their use, and rotating credentials as part of secret management.[3] These controls cannot prevent every breach. They can reduce the number of systems a stolen credential can reach and shorten how long it remains useful.[3]

For developers, keep a secret inventory. Record which service issued each key, what it can access, how to revoke it, and which deployment depends on the replacement. AWS's guidance on limiting access and monitoring secret use supports planned secret management.[3]

Railway's disclosure is still developing. Treat its published guidance as the source for the platform response, and check the incident page for new updates before redeploying.[2]

Sources

[1] Railway, Security Disclosure: Wednesday October 21st
[2] Railway, Platform incident updates
[3] AWS, Secrets Manager best practices
[4] AWS, Rotate AWS Secrets Manager secrets

title: DynaWeave: Learning to Adapt through Dynamic Scenario Synthesis
description:
arXiv:2610.29443v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly use tools to complete tasks in stateful environments. However, many training environments remain largely static apart from changes caused by the agent's own actions, whereas external events introduced by other users, services, or sudden contingencies in real environments can invalidate ongoing plans. To address this gap, we introduce DynaWeave, an automated synthesis framework that transforms existing static tasks into verifiable dynamic scenarios. The framework generates exogenous events relevant to each task, covering changes in task requirements, environment state, and external information. It uses directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) to represent dependencies between events and an execution engine to activate them during agent interaction. A dynamic verifier revises only the evaluation checks affected by events that actually occur and retains all other checks. Using DynaWeave, we collect 2,095 verified interaction trajectories across 36 environments and use them for supervised fine-tuning of Qwen3.5 models. Experiments on Gaia2, CostBench, and ToolMaze show that DynaWeave achieves consistent improvements in overall performance across all three evaluated model sizes, increasing the task completion rate on CostBench by 67.34 percentage points and even exceeding the performance of Gemini-3.1-Pro-Preview on ToolMaze. These results support dynamic scenario synthesis as a practical approach to training agents to adapt to changing environments. Our code is available at https://github.com/Miaow-Lab/DynaWeave.

title: Offline Apprenticeship Learning for Human-Centric Environments
description:
arXiv:2610.28716v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Effective decision-making in human-centric environments such as Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITSs) and clinical healthcare requires policies that are adaptive, data-efficient, and ethically deployable. Apprenticeship Learning (AL) infers policies directly from expert demonstrations by recovering the underlying reward structure, enabling strictly offline learning without environment interaction. This dissertation develops a progression of offline AL frameworks organized around two challenges: reward modeling and demonstration quality. For reward modeling, EM-EDM clusters demonstrations by latent reward functions and induces cluster-specific policies, and THEMES partitions trajectories into temporally coherent sub-trajectories guided by a hierarchically learned reward regulator; across one educational and three clinical datasets, THEMES outperforms flat and hierarchical AL baselines. For demonstration quality, HALIDE integrates continuous quality signals into hierarchical policy induction, enabling principled reuse of mixed-quality data under distribution shift. CCHAL further attributes quality to individual decisions via Bayesian credit assignment, dual-arm criticality scoring that contrasts expert and non-expert behavior, and a Bradley-Terry contrastive IRL objective over failure trajectories, outperforming baselines including HALIDE on three clinical EHR datasets and an ITS dataset. Finally, a real-world classroom evaluation of StuEDM, an EDM-induced policy that preserves student agency and intervenes only on disagreement, shows significant learning gains over an Expert baseline and a higher pretest-adjusted posttest score than a CQL policy trained on a far larger corpus, while overriding students less than half as often. Together, this work establishes offline AL as a practical, data-efficient, and ethically viable paradigm for human-centric environments.

title: AI Gateway now supports asynchronous video generation
description:
Video generation on AI Gateway can now run asynchronously.

By default, generateVideo keeps one HTTP request to AI Gateway open until the result is ready. Because video generation can take seconds or minutes, that request can exceed request timeouts.

With asynchronous generation, your application can receive a webhook, poll for completion, or start a generation and retrieve the result in a later request.

Choose an option based on whether your process can keep running and whether your application can receive webhooks:

Existing generateVideo calls continue to work as before. All four options support text-to-video, image-to-video, reference-to-video, and other video inputs.

Upgrade the SDK

Install the latest versions of the AI SDK and AI Gateway provider:

Use asynchronous video generation

Wait for completion in a Workflow

An easy way to consume the completion webhook is a Workflow SDK. The workflow creates its own webhook URL, passes it to startVideo, and suspends until AI Gateway delivers the completion event. Install the Workflow SDK alongside the AI SDK:

While the video renders, the workflow run is suspended and resumes when AI Gateway delivers the terminal event.

Use a webhook with generateVideo

Pass webhook to generateVideo to wait for a completion event without polling. AI Gateway sends an event when the job completes or fails. The SDK waits for that event, fetches the generated videos, and resolves the original generateVideo call.

The calling process and webhook handler need a shared token and store so the delivery can be matched to the correct generation. generateVideo does not expose the signing secret for this job. See the webhook verification documentation for the complete receiver pattern.

Both the polling and webhook options for generateVideo return result.videos as GeneratedFile objects. The SDK downloads provider-hosted videos, making uint8Array, base64, and mediaType available in either job.

Poll with generateVideo

Add poll to an existing generateVideo call:

AI Gateway starts an asynchronous job, and the SDK sends a short status request at each interval until the job finishes. The calling process must remain running until generateVideo resolves, but no individual request to AI Gateway stays open for the full generation.

Start a job and retrieve it later

startVideo returns an operation as soon as AI Gateway accepts the job, without waiting for rendering to finish. Store that operation and pass it to getVideoStatus later from the same process or another one:

The operation is JSON-serializable, so it can be stored in a database or passed through a queue. Your application controls how long to keep checking the job because it has no built-in timeout.

You can also pass webhookUrl to startVideo to receive a completion event instead of checking the status. The start response includes the signing secret needed to verify the webhook.

Unlike generateVideo, getVideoStatus does not download hosted videos. It returns provider URLs or inline bytes. Hosted URLs can expire, so download any videos you need to keep.

Monitor asynchronous jobs

Every asynchronous generation appears on the AI Gateway Logs page as soon as it starts. Jobs show as Running while generation is in progress and update when they complete or fail.

Under Request Mode, select Async to show only asynchronous jobs. Opening an entry shows the job ID and the request details.

Only asynchronous requests create jobs. A standard generateVideo call appears as a single completed request after the video is ready.

For size limits, idempotency for retried job starts, webhook delivery retries, and other operational details, read the asynchronous video generation documentation or browse all video models.
