title: Auditing Conformal Prediction for Language Models Under Inference-Time Model Shift
description:
arXiv:2610.28937v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Conformal prediction (CP) for language models is typically evaluated under a matched protocol, in which calibration and deployment use the same post-training inference configuration, such as quantization mode and inference temperature. In deployment, these choices often differ from those used at calibration to meet memory or throughput constraints or serving policies. We argue that this exposes a limitation in current CP evaluation protocols for language models. We formalize the underlying phenomenon as inference-time model shift: a change in the conformal score distribution induced by inference configuration rather than by the input--label distribution, and theoretically characterize how it breaks split-conformal exchangeability even when the task distribution and trained model are unchanged. We then evaluate its consequences across 8 language models, 4 finite-label benchmarks, and 12 inference configurations. We find that matched evaluation can substantially overstate deployment-time coverage, and that the effect is heterogeneous across models and datasets. We argue that inference configuration should be reported as a first-class experimental axis in CP evaluations for language-model systems.

title: Don't Stop Long-Context Continual Pre-Training Too Early: An Empirical Scaling Law
description:
arXiv:2610.29352v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Long-context continual pre-training (LCCP) is widely used to improve long-context capability, but how its benefits scale with the number of tokens used for LCCP remains unclear. We investigate this question through modeling, monitoring, and validating the benefits of scaling LCCP. First, we establish an empirical additive power law relating long-context performance to model size and the respective token budgets of short-context pre-training and LCCP. Experiments across five model scales and more than one hundred short- and long-context budget configurations show that the fitted law reproduces the observed trends and extrapolates well to held-out model scales. Second, we introduce \textsc{Constant-Last4}, a training and observation protocol that averages the four most recent consecutive checkpoints from a constant-learning-rate run to enable stable monitoring along a single extensible training trajectory. Under this protocol, the same scaling-law form fits well and accurately predicts the LCCP performance trajectory of a 1.22B-parameter model trained on approximately 100B LCCP tokens. Finally, downstream evaluations along this trajectory show continued improvements in long-context performance, with no clear sign of saturation within the evaluated range. These gains persist after both 128K context extension and supervised fine-tuning, with benefits extending to long-context understanding and agentic tasks. Together, these results argue for continuing to scale LCCP rather than stopping early: its gains are stably observable along an extensible trajectory, quantitatively predictable, and transferable to downstream tasks.

title: SAIL: A Learnable Generalisation of Spatial Autocorrelation over Graph-Structured Data
description:
arXiv:2610.28806v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In vision and scientific domains involving spatial data, a key question is whether node feature values vary independently across space or form coherent spatial structures. Classical spatial autocorrelation statistics such as Moran's $I$ and Geary's $C$ quantify this phenomenon but operate on a single scalar variable with fixed neighbourhood weights, limiting their use for high-dimensional graph-like data. We introduce SAIL (Spatial Autocorrelation Index Learner), a differentiable framework that generalises spatial autocorrelation into a learnable operator by jointly learning feature projections defining candidate scalar fields and inter-node neighbourhood affinities. SAIL produces interpretable local and global spatial coherence descriptors, enabling supervised prediction and unsupervised discovery of spatial autocorrelation modes and hotspots. We show that SAIL exactly recovers classical spatial statistics under appropriate parametrisations and, for tasks driven by latent spatial autocorrelation, can approximate the Bayes-optimal predictor with an inductive bias matched to such tasks. Experiments on synthetic data and large-scale biomedical graphs demonstrate statistical correctness and discovery of spatial coherence with applications across vision, geospatial analysis, and biomedicine. The code repository is available at: https://github.com/pkeller00/SAIL.

title: AI-Generated UI Tests in Business Central, or How to Check That "Passed" Actually Means Something
description:
The test passed. The official bc-replay runner reports passed, and the Page Scripting pane says "Script completed without errors". But the record isn't in the database.

The problem and the usual approaches

These days, more and more processes are being automated with AI agents. It's becoming an essential part of how our work is changing. AI agents already write code, search for and check information, analyze an existing codebase, make plans, and draw conclusions from everything they've gathered. So a natural question comes up. How can we trust the result?

Teams want to be sure their features work. That has always been true, and for good reason. The product's reputation depends on it. It matters even more in business systems, where the customers are businesses themselves and a mistake can be expensive. And when it comes to checking features, the obvious answer is testing.

With AI agents, a developer can cover a new feature in detail with automated tests written in code. Manual QA can click through the feature and see how it works. Yes, it's slow, and you need to know exactly what was added (I describe how to make this part much better in another article). But this way we see how the system works with our own eyes. Automation QA gives you a visible result too.

Let's try to find an approach that doesn't need the statistics and metrics used to evaluate ML models, doesn't require you to know code syntax to read the tests, and doesn't make you check the feature by hand or write the same steps in code for an automated check.

Closer to the point

To trust a result, it's best to see it in a way that's simple and clear to everyone who works with the system. That means the UI.

Business Central already has a tool for replaying clicks. It's called Page Scripting. I record my clicks, the pane saves them to a YAML file, and from here on I'll call that file a plan. In CI, bc-replay runs the same plan. In the end, we get a ready-made answer.

In my approach, an AI agent writes these scenarios from start to finish. I'll cover exactly how it does that in a separate article. Here the question is whether you can take such a test's result at face value, even when official Microsoft tools run it.

I decided to check how reliable this approach is. During the experiments I saw, with my own eyes and on the same screen, both the green status "Script completed without errors" and a red BC error.

The Page Scripting pane. On the right, "Script completed without errors" and green check marks on every step. On the left, the red banner "The length of the string is 15, but it must be less than or equal to 10 characters", and BC is also asking whether to discard the unsaved changes.

Let's look at the problem cases I found and try to pick methods that can protect a test setup from false passed results. From here on, green means the test passed and red means it failed, the same colors you see in reports and CI. If you want more background on the topic, I've put it in the notes.

Three cases where the test passed but the step didn't run

I did the study on BC 28 and BC 29, on-prem and in a SaaS sandbox. I ran the plans with the official npx replay runner from the @microsoft/bc-replay package, which I'll just call the runner from here on, and with the Play button in the Page Scripting pane. Judging by the BC client code, both play the plan with the same player, so they give the same result. Fields with the AUT prefix belong to my test extension.

The first thing I had to add was a deterministic check that a new record really appeared in the database. On-prem, a separate check script with SQL access to the database did it. On SaaS, requests to the standard API did the same job. From here on I call this the independent data check, because it looks straight at the data, separately from the session that created it. I'll describe it in detail after the three cases.

Server validation banner

When the BC server rejects a value you entered, for example one that's too long for the field, it doesn't open a dialog and doesn't stop you from working with the page. Instead, a red bar with the error text appears above the form. I call it the server validation banner. A person sees it and fixes the value. A script just moves on.

The plan creates a new Customer and enters 15 characters into a Text[10] field. BC shows the red banner "The length of the string is 15, but it must be less than or equal to 10 characters" and saves the record without that value. The runner reports passed every time, with no warning at all. The player itself, if you read its result directly, records no error (error: null) and counts every step as replayed. You can see the banner in the screen recording the runner makes automatically for every run, but the field in the database is empty. The record was created, and Name was saved. Only the value that was too long never reached the database, and the "Not saved" status in the screenshot below refers to that value. The same plan with 9 characters saves the value. In the pane, the banner is on screen too, but what people read is the status, "Script completed without errors". Below is the shortened runner output for the first on-prem run.

# npx replay console
  1 passed

# results.xml (JUnit)
<testsuites … tests="1" failures="0" skipped="0" errors="0" …>

# replay-log.yml, the step with the 15 characters, no error in it
  - type: input
    target:
      - page: Customer Card
      - field: AUT Loyalty Code
    value: ARTLEN15XXXXXXX

The same plan and the same player as in npx replay, but without the final step that closes the page, because that step opens a dialog on top of the banner. The runner doesn't open the Page Scripting pane, so there's no pane on the right. The player reported no error and counted every step, even though BC shows the length banner and the status "Not saved", and the value from the Loyalty Code field never reached the database.

A filter with the value true

The player silently fails to apply a filter on a Boolean field with the value true. The list stays unfiltered, and the filter step is marked as done. In my case, the true came from the AI agent that built the plan. In my test environment, a plan filtered the Vendor List this way. The runner gave passed, and the last frame of the recording shows all six vendors.

  # the agent's plan, passed, but the filter isn't applied
  - type: input
    target:
      - page: Vendor List
      - scope: filter
        field: AUT Preferred
    value: true

A filter with the value true in the pane. The Preferred filter is added with no value, the list shows all vendors, and the pane marks the filter step green.

For the same filter the recorder writes value: 2, which is the option number in the list of values (0 empty, 1 No, 2 Yes). The pane again says "Script completed without errors", but now only one vendor is left in the list, as it should be. value: "Yes" works too. And if you change just the 2 to true in the recorder's output, the filter silently stops working again, so for a Boolean filter, write the option number, the way the recorder does.

  # the recorder's output, the filter works
  - type: input
    target:
      - page: Vendor List
        runtimeRef: b8r
      - scope: filter
        field: AUT Preferred
    value: 2            # 0 empty, 1 No, 2 Yes

A step the player doesn't understand

The player checks page and field names against the open page and fails honestly when they're wrong, for example "Field '…' was not found". But it doesn't check how the step itself is written, and it silently counts a step it doesn't understand as done. The easiest way to show this is with the type: key. Every step in a plan starts with it, and it tells the player what to do. For example, type: input means enter a value into a field. If you write step: instead of type:, the player doesn't run the step, but it doesn't fail either. The plan below creates an Item and fills in two fields. The step for the second field has the key step: instead of type:.

  - type: input
    target:
      - page: Item Card
      - field: Description
    value: =Parameters.'Description'   # value from the plan's parameters

  - step: input            # should be type:
    target:
      - page: Item Card
      - field: AUT Shelf No.
    value: =Parameters.'ShelfNo'

The Page Scripting recorder never writes it this way, and there's no official schema that would reject an unknown key. So this case and the previous one show up exactly when an agent writes the plan or someone edits it by hand. For generated plans, checking passed becomes a required part of the approach.

If the plan doesn't check the skipped step, the runner gives passed every time. The player treats the step: step as replayed, even though nothing happens in the client. The runner fails a run only when the player returned an error or replayed no steps at all, and warnings don't affect the result. So the run is green, and in the variant from the snippet above the Item exists, but the field is empty.

When every step is written this way, as in the screenshot below, no Item appears in the database. The Page Scripting pane shows this plainly, because every such step gets a green check mark. If the plan has a validate on the skipped field itself, the run turns red.

Every step of the plan is written with the key step. The pane says "Script completed without errors" and gives each step a green check mark, but the Items list filtered by the description from the plan is empty, so the Item was never created.

The player is just as quiet when it skips a step with a typo in the type (type: imput) or in the value key (vaule: instead of value:). In both cases the runner gave passed, the pane showed green check marks, and the field stayed empty. The same happens with check steps. More on that in the negative control section.

Methods that protect against a false passed

All three cases lead to one conclusion. A test result has to be confirmed by a check that doesn't depend on the session that produced it.

Independent data check

The independent data check reads the result straight from the database or through the API, not through the browser session that created it. It knows nothing about what the screen or the runner showed. Every plan writes a unique run tag into the record, for example into the customer's name, so the check looks for that exact record.

But the check itself can be wrong too. There are two basic mistakes worth guarding against from the start, and doing so barely complicates the setup.

  • The check looks in the wrong place. A query that returns "0 rows" may be looking at the wrong database or company, and then "no record" proves nothing. The fix is to count known data in the company before searching for the tag. This is the positive control, and that's what it's called in the code below. If it finds nothing, the check itself is broken, and we don't trust the run.
  • A mistake in the query itself. The positive control confirms the table is the right one, but it doesn't catch a mistake in the query's filter. What protects against that is a control plan, one where the data is guaranteed to be saved. For step: it's the same plan with type:, and for the banner it's the plan with 9 characters. In both cases, the check found the record with its value.

The result is the diagram below, and the check's verdict only means something at its third step.

The independent data check. If either of the first two steps fails, there's no conclusion about the run.

Back to how the check reads the data. The check itself is a script written in advance that can only read the data, and the agent can only run that script. How that access is set up depends on how your Business Central is deployed. As examples, here are the two approaches I used for the demo, SQL for on-prem and the API for a SaaS sandbox.

On-prem through SQL

In a container, the check script runs a SQL query straight against the database. In the snippet below, the first query is the positive control. It counts all the records in the table for the right company. The second query looks for the record by its run tag.

-- 1. positive control: the check can see the right company's table
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM [<company>$Customer$<base-app-id>];
-- 0 → the check is broken (wrong database / company / prefix), don't trust the run

-- 2. result check (length banner)
SELECT c.[No_], c.[Name], x.[AUT Loyalty Code$<ext-app-id>]
FROM [<company>$Customer$<base-app-id>] c
LEFT JOIN [<company>$Customer$<base-app-id>$ext] x ON x.[No_] = c.[No_]
WHERE c.[Name] = @RunTag;
-- after npx replay (passed): 1 row, AUT Loyalty Code empty

Run the check twice, once before the run and once after. Before the run, there must be no record with the tag yet, and the positive control shows how many records the table holds. After the run, the count must have grown by exactly the number of records the plan creates, and a search by tag must find exactly that record, with the value the plan entered. If there's no record with the tag, or the field is empty, but the runner gave passed, that passed is false. And if a record with the tag turns up before the run, the tag isn't unique and there's no conclusion.

SaaS through the API

For the cloud version, which Microsoft calls Business Central online, the documentation on extracting data says that "For Business Central online, the only supported option for reading data is using APIs". So on SaaS, the data check becomes a GET request to the standard API v2.0 on behalf of the test user. The first request in the snippet below is the positive control. It checks that the company returns at least one record. The second looks up the record by its run tag.

# 1. positive control: the company MUST return at least one record, otherwise the check is broken
GET https://api.businesscentral.dynamics.com/v2.0/<tenant>/<env>/api/v2.0/companies(<id>)/customers?$top=1&$select=number
Authorization: Bearer <test user's delegated token>

###
# 2. result check (length banner)
GET https://api.businesscentral.dynamics.com/v2.0/<tenant>/<env>/api/v2.0/companies(<id>)/customers?$filter=displayName eq '<run tag>'&$select=number,displayName,addressLine2
Authorization: Bearer <test user's delegated token>
# → 1 row, "addressLine2": ""   (runner: passed)

The proof here, as on-prem, is a missing record or an empty field after the positive control has passed. The check gets its token through its own app registration in Entra ID with delegated permissions, so it sees exactly what the test user sees.

The pane says "Script completed without errors" and gives all six steps a green check mark, while above the form there's the red banner "The length of the string is 60, but it must be less than or equal to 50 characters" and the status "Not saved". On top of the page, BC also shows the dialog "A modal dialog is open in another window". After this run, the API returns a new Customer with an empty addressLine2.

Pre-run plan check

By pre-run plan check I mean an automated check of the YAML plan's text without running it, the way a linter checks code. It sits in front of the runner and the pane, because neither of them checks the plan. This check stops an unknown key, a typo in the step type, typos in value: and operation:, and the value true in a filter. But it knows nothing about value length, so only the data check catches the banner. There's a minimal snippet at the end of the article.

A negative control for every validate

Not every change can be checked in the database. A lot of functionality doesn't change data at all. It only shows the data differently, like a filter on a list. For that, Page Scripting has validate, a check step you put in the plan alongside the actions. My measurements showed that validate works when it checks exactly the thing that broke. A check on the skipped field turned the step: run red ("Was expecting 'A1-01' but got ''"), and a check on the first row after the filter with the value true gave "Was expecting '20000' but got '10000'".

The same skipped step, but the plan checks the Shelf No. field with validate. The field is empty, and the pane turns red on exactly that check.

After the filter with the value true, the validate on the first row expects vendor 20000 but sees 10000. Here the pane honestly says "Script failed".

But a validate that has never failed is still a hypothesis. My measurements showed that the player silently skips a check with a typo in the type (type: validat) or in the operation: key, just as it skips actions. If you deliberately break the expected value in such a check, the run is still green, so the check might as well not be in the plan.

A check with a typo in the operation key and a deliberately wrong expected value, A1-02. The pane says "Script completed without errors", even though the last step has a red icon and the field holds A1-01.

So every such step needs a negative control. That's what I call a copy of the plan with the expected value broken on purpose. A run of that copy must fail on exactly that step and nowhere earlier. If it's green, the check doesn't work. This is the counterpart of the positive control in the data check. There we make sure the check sees known data. Here we make sure validate can fail.

  - type: validate
    target:
      - page: Item Card
      - field: AUT Shelf No.
    operation: "="
    value: =Parameters.'ShelfNo'   # A1-01
    # negative control: value: A1-02 → the run must fail on exactly this step

In my test environment I made a negative control for each of the two validate steps in the control plan (the one where the data is saved correctly) and ran each of them with the runner twice. All four runs failed on exactly the broken step, and every step before it passed. The error was the one you'd expect, "Was expecting 'A1-02' but got 'A1-01'". Meanwhile, the data check found a new Item with the correct value every time, and the same plan without the break came up green. So the red came from the check itself, not from the data. The player stops at the first red validate, so one negative control tests exactly one check.

The negative control in the pane. The expected value is deliberately changed to A1-02, the field holds the correct A1-01, and the last check step is the one that fails, while every step before it is green.

This technique has a limit. A negative control proves that the check runs and can fail, but it doesn't show whether the value depends on the behavior the requirement describes. So it's a cheap minimum. Mutating data or AL code is the stronger tool. dubcrab describes a similar technique, inverting the assertion, in Your green tests are lying, and the same author covers data mutation on his blog. LethAL does AL code mutation for BC. More on it in the notes.

How to apply this to your tests

The scripts from my test environment are tied to my setup, but the principle carries over to any Page Scripting run.

  1. Check the result directly with a database query and a positive control, so the check fails when it can't see a known record.
  2. Make a deliberately red run for every validate. Break the expected value, and that exact step must fail.
  3. Keep the video of the green run too, next to the data check result.
  4. Check the plan before running it, so an unknown key or the value true in a filter never reaches the runner or the pane.

A minimal plan check for item 4 can look like this.

// plan = the YAML plan, parsed with any parser (e.g. js-yaml)
const KNOWN = new Set(['navigate', 'invoke', 'input', 'filter', 'validate', 'close-page' /* + the types you actually use */]);
function checkPlan(plan) {
  const errs = [];
  plan.steps.forEach((s, i) => {
    if (s.type === undefined) errs.push(`step ${i + 1}: no 'type:' (keys: ${Object.keys(s).join(', ')})`);
    else if (!KNOWN.has(s.type)) errs.push(`step ${i + 1}: unknown type '${s.type}'`);
    if (s.type === 'input' && !('value' in s)) errs.push(`step ${i + 1}: input without 'value:'`);
    if (s.type === 'validate' && !('operation' in s)) errs.push(`step ${i + 1}: validate without 'operation:'`);
    for (const t of s.target ?? [])
      if (t.scope === 'filter' && ['true', 'false'].includes(String(s.value)))
        errs.push(`step ${i + 1}: the player will silently fail to apply filter '${t.field}' with the value ${s.value}; for a Boolean write Yes / No or the option number (2 = Yes)`);
  });
  return errs; // non-empty → don't start the runner
}

And write the task description you give to an agent or a person so that there's something to prove it with. It helps when the task describes

  • who acts, which data and preconditions, and where it starts and ends;
  • the observable outcome, meaning a document or a ledger entry. "The field was saved" isn't enough for this;
  • for each requirement, whether you check the UI or the data, which data check with a positive control covers it, and where the negative controls are;
  • what is out of scope.

If you want to practice and check this yourself, you could, for example, use the ready-made scenarios from the how-to articles on MS Learn and the test names in microsoft/BCApps.

What's next

A green status from the runner or the pane proves only that the player reached the end of the plan without an error. The independent data check with a positive control proves that the record really is in the database. The negative control proves that validate really checks something. The pre-run plan check proves that the plan reaches the player intact.

These methods work today on plain Page Scripting. The limit is that its player itself doesn't see BC's banners and dialogs, it doesn't check how a step is written, and you can't put a data check or a BC error check between the steps of a plan. More generally, I'd like to see something closer to how a person does the steps, as if they were walking through them in the browser themselves, with every stage and nuance. So let's try bringing in a browser automation tool. I'll share what came of it in the next article.

If you've run Page Scripting and seen green where there was no data, I'd like to hear how it went for you.

Notes. What Microsoft and the community already have

  • AL tests don't see the UI. TestPage runs inside BC, without a browser, so real dialogs are out of its reach. The author of LethAL, a tool that deliberately breaks AL code, writes that "Tests run without a GUI, so code behind a Confirm or a dialog may be unmeasurable" (LethAL README).
  • Page Scripting is meant not only for developers. Microsoft writes that "Customers, consultants, and testers can create repeatable user acceptance tests … without writing AL code" (roadmap entry RM573384).
  • Page Scripting in CI. bc-replay runs the same plan in CI (MS Learn), and AL-Go for GitHub supports it starting with v6.1. For a green run, AL-Go publishes no details. "If the page scripting tests succeed - the details are not published" (AL-Go release notes).
  • A plan without the recorder. Erik Hougaard built a plan from Page Metadata back in 2024 (hougaard.com), Andy Wingate generates AI variants of a recorded script (D365BC-vibe-page-scripting), and in rf9000/CreateScriptsForVideos an agent writes the plan.
  • The player's silent modes. FBakkensen described them in his bc-replay format reference, for example "no error, the row silently never inserts" (format reference). Checking data outside the UI and deliberately failing a check are both known techniques on their own. My part here is only to put them together for the BC UI and measure them on the runner, the pane, and two BC versions.
  • The blind spot of a UI scenario. FBakkensen writes that "bc-replay re-reads the bound Rec exactly as a TestPage does, so its oracle is blind to that fault class" (al-page-script skill). In other words, if a UI scenario re-reads the same record that TestPage does, it will miss the same bug that TestPage misses. That's one more reason to check the result outside the session that created it.
  • The same thing is noticed outside BC too. ACCELQ, a test tool vendor, writes about Dynamics 365 that "A passing UI test only proves the interface behaved correctly" (ACCELQ article).

title: State Management in Modern React: Zustand vs Redux Toolkit vs Context API
description:
title: "State Management in Modern React: Zustand vs Redux Toolkit vs Context API"
published: true
published_at: "2027-02-08T09:00:00+05:30"
description: "A practical engineering guide to State Management in Modern React: Zustand vs Redux Toolkit vs Context API. Learn core mechanics, production tradeoffs, and best practices."
tags: [react, javascript, frontend, webdev]
ai_disclosure_level: some_ai

In modern software development, State Management in Modern React: Zustand vs Redux Toolkit vs Context API is a critical subject that every serious engineer must understand. Whether building distributed backend systems, designing scalable databases, or optimizing developer productivity, mastering the underlying mechanics separates junior developers who guess from senior engineers who deliver reliable architectures.

In this deep dive, we break down why State Management in Modern React: Zustand vs Redux Toolkit vs Context API matters, examine common failure modes in production, and walk through concrete implementation patterns.

The Problem: Why Naive Approaches Fail

In earlier development workflows or smaller-scale projects, teams frequently overlook the subtleties of react architectures.

When systems scale, common bottlenecks emerge:

  1. Unpredictable Latency & Resource Starvation: High concurrency and unoptimized execution pipelines exhaust system resources, leading to degraded response times and thread pool stalls.
  2. Hidden Failure Cascades: Unhandled edge cases and lack of defensive invariants create silent data corruption that propagates across microservices.
  3. High Cognitive Overhead: As codebases evolve, poorly structured domain abstractions become difficult to maintain, test, and refactor.

To resolve these challenges, engineering teams must implement disciplined patterns focusing on:

  • Comparing Bundle Sizes: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • Boilerplate Reduction: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • Transient Updates Without Re-Renders: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • Devtools Integration: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.

Under the Hood: Architectural Overview

Understanding how State Management in Modern React: Zustand vs Redux Toolkit vs Context API functions beneath high-level abstractions is essential for diagnosing production anomalies.

+--------------------------------------------------------------+
| System Workflow: React Architecture                    |
|                                                              |
| [Incoming Workload] ---> [Validation & Boundary Layer]       |
|                                     |                        |
|                                     v                        |
|                     [Optimized Core Execution]               |
|                                     |                        |
|                                     v                        |
|                  [Resilient State / Output Store]            |
+--------------------------------------------------------------+

When designing systems around this pattern, prioritize:

  • Isolation of Concerns: Keep business invariants decoupled from transport protocols and third-party drivers.
  • Deterministic Resource Management: Bound memory allocations, connection pools, and worker concurrency to prevent out-of-memory crashes.
  • Observability & Metrics: Expose granular latency histograms, error rates, and throughput metrics to Prometheus/Datadog.

Practical Implementation

Here is a clean, production-oriented pattern demonstrating these principles in action:

// Production-Ready Pattern: State Management in Modern React: Zustand vs Redux Toolkit vs Context API
// Focus areas: Comparing bundle sizes, boilerplate reduction, transient updates without re-renders, devtools integration, and choosing the right tool for app complexity.

const http = require('http');

class ResilientService {
  constructor(options = {}) {
    this.timeoutMs = options.timeoutMs || 5000;
    this.concurrencyLimit = options.concurrencyLimit || 50;
    this.activeWorkers = 0;
  }

  async executeTask(context) {
    if (this.activeWorkers >= this.concurrencyLimit) {
      throw new Error('Service saturated: backpressure limit reached.');
    }

    this.activeWorkers++;
    const controller = new AbortController();
    const timeout = setTimeout(() => controller.abort(), this.timeoutMs);

    try {
      if (!context || !context.id) {
        throw new TypeError('Invalid task context: missing required ID.');
      }

      const result = await this.performWork(context, controller.signal);
      return result;
    } finally {
      clearTimeout(timeout);
      this.activeWorkers--;
    }
  }

  async performWork(context, signal) {
    if (signal.aborted) throw new Error('Task aborted due to timeout');
    return { id: context.id, success: true, processedAt: new Date().toISOString() };
  }
}

module.exports = { ResilientService };

Production Gotchas to Avoid

When deploying this architecture at scale, keep these three operational realities in mind:

  1. Beware of Unbounded Queues: Always place hard limits on in-memory buffers and connection queues. An unbounded queue simply hides backpressure until the process encounters an Out-Of-Memory (OOM) crash.
  2. Set Aggressive Timeouts: Never make external network or storage calls without explicit connection and read timeouts. A single hanging dependency can exhaust worker pools system-wide.
  3. Ensure Idempotency: Network packets get dropped and clients retry. Ensure that mutating operations can be executed multiple times safely without producing duplicate side-effects.

Summary Checklist

  • [x] Validate at the boundary: Ensure invalid states never penetrate deep domain layers.
  • [x] Enforce bounded resource limits: Protect memory, connections, and CPU threads against unexpected spikes.
  • [x] Log structured telemetry: Attach correlation IDs to log records for rapid root-cause analysis during outages.
  • [x] Design for failure: Always provide graceful fallbacks and fast-failure mechanisms when dependencies degrade.

title: Gate Initialisation versus Recurrent Dropout and Zoneout in Learning Long Dependencies: A Controlled Study of LSTM and GRU Networks on Synthetic Tasks
description:
arXiv:2610.29034v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Dropout and zoneout are routinely added to long short-term memory (LSTM) and gated recurrent unit (GRU) networks, but, to our knowledge, their placements have not been crossed with gate initialisation in a factorial design, and it is not known whether early gradient propagation tells which runs will learn long dependencies. We trained one-layer LSTMs and GRUs on the adding problem and on delayed recall in a factorial grid of 720 runs, crossing conventional and chrono gate initialisation with up to six recurrent regulariser placements at one rate each, with pre-specified follow-ups, and recorded how sensitive the final hidden state was to the input at every lag. Because both tasks supply fresh or exhaustive training data, the study measures the regularisers' effects on optimisation and does not assess generalisation from a finite training set. At lengths chosen to make conventional initialisation difficult, all 360 chrono-initialised runs reached the validation criterion within 5000 updates, as did 119 of 120 unregularised runs with a horizon about four times too short or too long, whereas conventionally initialised networks learned slowly or did not reach the criterion within the budget at the longer lengths. Under conventional initialisation, dropout generally delayed learning and zoneout helped only in some conditions. The early input sensitivity added little to predicting which conditions learn once the early validation loss was modelled per task, architecture and initialisation. Within conditions, a flatter early decay went with the seeds that learned, but in a pre-specified test the association was modest (concordance 0.61), condition-dependent and not robust to resampling seeds. The results support chrono initialisation, even with a rough horizon, on such tasks.

title: Omnilingual-MsASR: Benchmarking Multimodal, Multilingual, Long-Form Multi-Speaker ASR of Omni Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.29455v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Omni-modal large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable progress in audio and video understanding. However, existing models struggle with long-form, multi-speaker videos, especially in understanding the entire video and recognizing who says what and when. To characterize the capability limit of current omni LLMs and guide future model development, we introduce Omnilingual-MsASR, a multilingual, multimodal benchmark for long-form Multi-speaker Automatic Speech Recognition (MsASR) covering six languages, recordings up to 30 minutes, and scenarios with up to 20 speakers. Omnilingual-MsASR provides parallel audio and video inputs to evaluate models' cross-modal consistency and their ability to exploit complementary cues across modalities. Extensive evaluations of leading omni-modal LLMs reveal substantial performance bottlenecks, while their tcpWERs frequently exceed 100%. These findings highlight fine-grained temporal localization, speaker disambiguation, and cross-modal synergy as key challenges for future omni-modal foundation models. Our work is available at https://github.com/QwenLM/Omnilingua-Bench/tree/main/Omnilingua-MSpeaker.

title: Dirty flash vs clean flash: when your Galaxy actually needs a full wipe
description:
When people talk about flashing Samsung firmware with Odin, one question comes up in almost every thread: "Do I need to wipe my phone first?" The answer most people give — always wipe — is wrong as often as it's right. There's a real distinction between a dirty flash and a clean flash, and knowing which one your situation needs saves you from both data loss and pointless re-setup.

What the terms mean

A "dirty flash" is flashing new firmware over your existing installation without wiping user data — the phone keeps your apps, settings, and files, and the new system replaces the old one underneath. A "clean flash" wipes everything (the data partition) and starts the phone from a blank state, like it just came out of the box.

When a dirty flash is fine

If you're upgrading or reinstalling the same Android version family — say, moving from one build to a newer build of the same One UI version — a dirty flash usually works perfectly. The system partition gets replaced, your data partition stays untouched, and the phone boots with everything where you left it. This is also the right choice when you're re-flashing the same firmware to fix a boot problem: wiping data rarely fixes a corrupted system partition, and it costs you everything.

When you actually need a clean flash

There are three cases where wiping is the correct move. First, downgrading: going from a newer Android version back to an older one almost always needs a clean flash, because the newer version's data format can confuse the older system. Second, switching regions or carriers: moving between firmware variants with different CSC configurations can leave conflicting carrier settings behind. Third, persistent crashes or strange behavior after an update: if you've flashed and the phone still misbehaves, leftover data from the old system is the most likely cause, and a clean flash is the definitive test.

The part people get wrong

The wipe in Odin is controlled by the CSC file you load. A HOME_CSC preserves your data; a regular CSC wipes it. The mistake isn't choosing one or the other — it's choosing without backing up first. Phone storage is cheap to back up and expensive to lose: even when you're planning a dirty flash, back up your data before you start, because a flash can fail in ways that force a wipe afterward.

The safe workflow

One: back up everything you care about. Two: match the firmware to your model and CSC, exactly. Three: decide dirty or clean based on the three cases above — not on habit. Four: use HOME_CSC for dirty, CSC for clean, and don't toggle anything else you don't understand. Five: flash, then let the first boot take its time; it's building caches from scratch and interrupting it causes more problems than patience does.

Most flashing disasters aren't technical failures. They're people wiping a phone they didn't need to wipe, or not wiping one they should have — usually with no backup either way. Decide before you click Start.

For the firmware side of the process — finding the exact build for your model and region before you decide which kind of flash you need — SamFware keeps a library of official stock firmware organized by model and CSC code, with guides that walk through the whole flash from backup to first boot. SamFware is free to use, with no registration required.

title: GBase Database Silent Installation: 6 Common Errors and How to Fix Them
description:
Silent installation helps automate GBase Database(GBase 8s) deployment, but a failed installation can interrupt an otherwise straightforward process. In most cases, the first places to check are the response file, installation permissions, component dependencies, and available disk space.

Here are six common issues to investigate when ids_install -i silent fails.

1. License Acceptance Is Missing

A silent installation needs the license acceptance parameter. Check that your response file contains the following setting:

LICENSE_ACCEPTED = TRUE

Alternatively, pass the parameter directly to the installer:

./ids_install -i silent -f /opt/bundle.properties -DLICENSE_ACCEPTED=TRUE

If the license acceptance parameter is missing or incorrectly configured, the installation may stop before completing.

2. The Response File Path Is Incorrect

The installer cannot read parameters from a response file that does not exist or is inaccessible.

Check the file first:

ls -l /opt/bundle.properties

Confirm that the path specified by -f matches the actual file location and that the user running the installation has read permission.

For example:

./ids_install -i silent -f /opt/bundle.properties -DLICENSE_ACCEPTED=TRUE

If the command references the wrong directory or filename, correct the path before investigating more complicated causes.

3. The Installation Directory Has Incorrect Permissions

Directory permissions can prevent the installer from creating or updating files.

Inspect the target directory:

ls -ld /opt/GBASE/gbase

Check whether the installation process has the necessary permissions to write to the directory. If the directory already exists, also check its ownership and whether existing files could interfere with the installation.

Do not change ownership blindly. Choose permissions based on the installation procedure and the account intended to manage the database software.

4. Selected Components Have Missing Dependencies

A response file may specify multiple components through SELECTED_FEATURES. Some selected components may require additional dependencies or supporting packages.

If the installation fails during component setup:

  • Review the selected features in the response file.
  • Check the installation logs for dependency or package errors.
  • Install any required dependencies.
  • Remove unnecessary components from the selection if they are not needed for the current deployment.

Avoid removing components simply to make the installation pass. First identify the component responsible for the failure, then adjust the configuration accordingly.

5. There Is Not Enough Disk Space

A silent installation can fail if the target filesystem does not have enough free space for the installation files and temporary files.

Check available capacity:

df -h /opt

Also check the filesystem used for temporary files if the installer extracts packages under /tmp or another temporary directory.

If space is insufficient, clean up unnecessary files or select an appropriate filesystem with enough capacity. Remember that the installation package itself is not the only space requirement: extraction and installation can require additional temporary storage.

6. The Instance Initialization Runs as Root

Installing the GBase Database program and initializing a database instance are separate operations with different execution requirements.

Running ids_install as root is permitted. However, the instance initialization script must be run as the gbasedbt user.

If initialization is performed as root, files or directories may receive incorrect ownership, causing problems when the database instance is started or managed by gbasedbt.

Before starting the instance, verify that the relevant installation and instance files have the expected ownership. Follow the product's installation procedure to correct any ownership problems rather than repeatedly rerunning initialization commands.

A Practical Troubleshooting Order

When troubleshooting a failed GBase Database silent installation, check the following in order:

  1. Response file: Confirm that the file exists, is readable, and contains valid parameters.
  2. License acceptance: Verify LICENSE_ACCEPTED = TRUE or pass the command-line parameter.
  3. Permissions: Check the installation directory and the account running each step.
  4. Components: Review SELECTED_FEATURES and any dependency errors.
  5. Disk space: Check both the installation filesystem and temporary storage.
  6. Instance initialization: Make sure initialization is performed as gbasedbt, not root.

This order helps separate configuration problems from operating-system and instance-management issues.

Final Thoughts

Automating GBase Database deployment is not just about running ids_install -i silent. A reliable installation also depends on a valid response file, correct permissions, sufficient disk space, and proper separation between software installation and instance initialization.

When a silent installation fails, start with the response file and the installation logs before changing multiple settings at once. Identifying the first failing step is usually more effective than repeatedly rerunning the installer without knowing what went wrong.

title: I built SiteScope, a free technical SEO audit tool that ranks what to fix first
description:
For my college course I built SiteScope (vikramyadav.me), a free technical SEO audit tool. You enter a site, it crawls every page it can reach, and it tells you what to fix first. No sign-up needed to run an audit. If you want, you can create an account to have your sites re-audited daily or weekly.

The problem

Two things bugged me about free SEO checkers.

First, most test a single URL and hand back an unordered list. SiteScope follows internal links and the XML sitemap and checks every page it finds (up to 300 per audit). Then it ranks issues with one rule:

priority = severity × share of pages affected

A missing alt text on every page outranks a broken link on one page; a 5xx on half the site outranks both.

Second, a lot of sites load their content with JavaScript. SiteScope reads raw HTML, the way most AI crawlers do, so you can check whether your content needs JavaScript to show up. The tool itself uses no JavaScript framework. Every page, including the report, is server-rendered, because a tool that talks about JavaScript SEO should be readable by a crawler that runs none.

It also checks broken links, duplicate and near-duplicate pages (SimHash), the internal link graph (click depth, PageRank, orphan pages), titles, meta descriptions, H1s, canonicals, noindex and more. Reports download as PDF or JSON, and re-running an audit shows what was fixed and what is new since last time.

Tech stack

  • FastAPI (Python 3.12) with Jinja2 templates; audits run as FastAPI background tasks
  • PostgreSQL 16, where each finished result is one JSONB column
  • Docker Compose with an Nginx reverse proxy and Certbot
  • Azure VM: one small VM (2 vCPU, 1 GiB RAM) running two containers
  • Cloudflare for DNS and proxying
  • httpx + asyncio for crawling, BeautifulSoup for parsing, NetworkX for the link graph

What I learned

  • A URL fetcher is an SSRF hole. If a stranger can type any URL, they will try the cloud metadata service or localhost. The guard refuses private, loopback and reserved addresses, checks every redirect hop, and connects to the exact IP it checked, so DNS rebinding can't swap the address in between.
  • Don't trust a header anyone can send. My per-IP limit read Cloudflare's CF-Connecting-IP, but anyone hitting the server's IP directly could send that header with a new value each time. Now it only believes that header when the connection really comes from Cloudflare's IP ranges, and the limit lives in Postgres so a restart doesn't reset it.
  • Keep dependencies small on a small VM. NetworkX's PageRank pulled in numpy and scipy, so I wrote my own PageRank and tested it against the reference. The scheduled re-audits run as a background task inside the app, with no cron, Celery or Redis.
  • Severity alone gets the order wrong. Multiplying by the share of pages affected fixed it.
  • An SEO tool shouldn't create thin pages. Report pages send noindex and are disallowed in robots.txt.
  • DNS moves need care. Switching nameservers to Cloudflare replaces the whole zone, so I recreated the existing records first and issued SSL before turning on the proxy.

What's next

Some things are still open: score-drop emails are waiting on an SMTP provider, and external link checks stop at 200 links per audit.

Try it at vikramyadav.me and see the code on GitHub. Feedback welcome!

title: Actually, All Learnable Distribution Classes Are Privately Learnable
description:
arXiv:2610.28878v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We show that every class of distributions that is learnable up to arbitrarily small target error in total variation distance with finitely many samples is also learnable under ($\varepsilon, \delta$)-differential privacy up to arbitrarily small target error with finitely many samples. This proves a conjecture of Ashtiani. Previous work by Bun, Kamath, Mouzakis, and Singhal [arXiv:2402.00267] gave a weak refutation of this conjecture, showing that this implication is not true when learnability is defined with respect to a fixed target error. In contrast, we show that, under the standard definition of learnability, the conjecture is true.

title: Rain Dance AI: turn one or two portraits into a 15-second sunset video
description:
I built Rain Dance AI, a photo-to-video side project that puts one or two people into a 15-second sunset-pier scene. You supply the portraits; the site supplies the setting and sequence. There is no prompt box. I kept the format fixed so the first decision is who appears in the story, rather than how to describe a scene.

Solo takes one photo for the singer and adds a fictional adult partner. Duet takes two: the opening singer first, then the person waiting on the pier. Those labels describe roles, not gender. Each upload should show one consenting adult, with a clear face and visible outfit: JPEG, PNG or WebP, up to 10 MB. Both modes produce a vertical 9:16, 768p MP4. Paid orders use a delivery email instead of an account; the private order link lets you return to check progress, remaining uses and downloads.

The decision I want feedback on is the free four-second preview. It lets someone try their own photo before paying, but it only covers the opening. Preview and paid clips are generated separately, so the preview cannot promise the same face, clothing or movement in the final video. The playable example shows the full 15 seconds and its fictional-adult input portrait. I think both views are useful: a short personal preview answers a different question from watching an entire sample. Faces can drift, outfits can change, and a good opening frame does not establish consistency through the ending. The official recording is not included, and exact lip-sync is not guaranteed. Free previews are limited to one per browser workspace and one per network per day, subject to shared availability. The workspace allowance does not reset; the shared daily limit resets at midnight Asia/Shanghai. Allow about 15 minutes or longer.

Current USD packs are $9.90 for one video, $24.90 for three, and $49.90 for ten, with no subscription or expiry on unused videos. A confirmed technical failure restores the used allowance; dissatisfaction with a completed result is reviewed separately, without an automatic retry or refund. Uploaded photos are scheduled for deletion from our storage after seven days; interruptions can delay cleanup, and external processing has separate retention terms. Completed videos have no automatic expiry, and deletion can be requested through support. I still recommend downloading anything you want to keep.

Rain Dance AI is an independent project, unaffiliated with the artists behind the song. One UX question: what would you need beside a four-second preview to judge whether a separately generated 15-second video is worth buying?

title: HumanCentric-Scenes-AI: A Human-Curated Multimodal Dataset of AI-Generated Human-Centric Scenes Across Surveillance, Occupational Portraits, AI-Edited Images, and Short-Form Video
description:
arXiv:2610.29045v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We introduce HumanCentric-Scenes-AI, a human-curated dataset of 296 AI-generated stimuli that depict people across four contexts in which people encounter AI-generated media. The Surveillance subset contains 85 AI-generated CCTV-style images. The Occupations subset contains 128 AI-generated occupational portraits in a balanced paired design covering 64 occupations with one female and one male version of each. The AI-edited subset contains 27 real photographs in which a region was altered or replaced by a generative model. The Video subset contains 56 AI-generated short videos. We curated the images and videos manually over multiple rounds to make them as photorealistic as possible. For each stimulus we release the file, the generation prompt where recorded, and per-stimulus metadata. We report depicted-gender distributions from an initial set of 134 generations without a specified gender and compare them with U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics occupational gender shares. We report edit-region size and its association with zero-shot detection difficulty for the AI-edited subset. We report image-quality distributions for the Surveillance subset and subject-category coverage for the Video subset. HumanCentric-Scenes-AI is intended first for human-perception research, and also for calibration of AI-detection classifiers and bias analysis of generative models.

title: E8-QAT: Efficient 2-Bit Quantization-Aware Training with Implicit Lattice Codebooks
description:
arXiv:2610.27699v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Low-bit quantization reduces the memory footprint of large language models, but preserving accuracy with efficient training remains challenging. Scalar quantization encodes weights independently, while explicit-codebook vector quantization introduces costly search during training. We propose E8-QAT, a 2-bit quantization-aware training framework that uses the $E_8$ lattice as an implicit eight-dimensional codebook. It jointly quantizes weight groups through arithmetic projection without storing or searching an explicit codebook during the training forward pass. A 2-bit core encoding and sparse extension preserve the selected lattice points exactly, adding less than 0.1\% to core index storage. On Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, E8-QAT matches the performance of the full-precision model in terms of the average score across the four tasks. E8-QAT improves over the state-of-the-art baseline by 2.03\% on IFEval and by 1.51\% on LiveCodeBench, under the same data, schedule, and bit width. The 2-bit representation reduces peak memory by 80\% and supports a $4\times$ larger batch. At each representation's largest feasible batch, E8-QAT reaches $1.97\times$ the decoding throughput of BF16.

  • Using the standard name (i.e., zai/glm-5.3) with provider options to sort DigitalOcean as the preferred provider keeps working after September 8 and routes across every provider that serves the model, at their usual rates.

Because the promo name goes away when the offer ends, treat it as something you switch on for the window rather than hardcode. To keep the standard name in your code instead, pin the provider with order: ['digitalocean'] under providerOptions.gateway, which prefers DigitalOcean and falls back to the others if it cannot serve the request.

GLM-5.3 takes text input, with a 1M token context window and a maximum output of 128K tokens. Discounted requests appear in your spend dashboard and carry a trace like any other request.

Try GLM-5.3 in the model playground.

title: AI Automation for Small Businesses: 7 Practical Ways to Save Time Every Week
description:
"AI" sounds like something reserved for giant tech companies with huge budgets. In reality, some of the most valuable uses of AI today are small, practical automations that save small businesses hours every single week.

You do not need a robot workforce. You need to stop doing the same repetitive tasks by hand. Here are seven places to start.

1. Answering common customer questions

Every business gets the same questions again and again: hours, pricing, availability, delivery, booking. An AI assistant on your website or messaging channels can answer these instantly, 24/7, and hand over to a human when the question gets complicated. Customers get fast answers; your team gets its time back.

2. Lead follow-up

Speed wins deals. When a potential customer fills in a form and hears back two days later, they have often already chosen a competitor. Automation can send an instant, friendly first response, ask qualifying questions, and book the lead into your calendar while the interest is fresh.

3. Appointment reminders and confirmations

No-shows cost service businesses real money. Automated confirmations and reminders by email or message dramatically reduce them — and nobody on your team has to remember to send them.

4. Reports without the spreadsheet marathon

Weekly sales summaries, stock levels, website traffic, ad performance — if someone on your team spends Friday afternoon copying numbers into a report, that report can be generated automatically and delivered to your inbox.

5. Content drafts and social media

AI can draft social posts, product descriptions, and email newsletters from your notes, so you are editing instead of staring at a blank page. Consistency becomes much easier when the first draft writes itself.

6. Sorting and tagging enquiries

Support emails and form submissions can be automatically read, categorised, and routed — urgent issues to the top, quotes to sales, general questions to support. Nothing gets lost, and nothing waits in the wrong inbox.

7. Data entry between tools

Copying data from one system into another is pure waste. Connecting your tools so information flows automatically — from form to CRM to invoice — removes errors and hours of manual typing.

Where to begin

Start with the task your team complains about most. Automate one thing, measure the time saved, then move to the next. Small wins compound quickly.

This is exactly the kind of work we do at Cloudlift Tech. Our AI automation services are built for small and growing businesses: practical, affordable, and focused on measurable time savings — not hype. If you want to see which of your processes could be automated first, visit cloudlifttech.com and talk to our team.

The goal of automation is not to replace people. It is to give people their time back for the work only they can do.

title: Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Pay When Agents Serve Users? Testing Agent Scaling in Dual-Control Settings
description:
arXiv:2610.27655v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multi-agent systems (MAS) built from language models are deployed on the premise that collaboration beats a single-agent system (SAS), yet when it pays is unclear. The most systematic study to date gives a capability-saturation rule: coordination helps while the SAS is weak and hurts once it is strong, with the crossing near 45% single-agent accuracy. That rule was derived on autonomous benchmarks, where no user takes part. We test it where agents now work: in conversation with a user under a written policy, on $\tau^2$-bench, the dual-control benchmark. On its airline, retail and telecom domains we compare the stock SAS with a centralized MAS built from the same model for six models from three families, over about 7,950 simulated conversations, with one completion-token ledger per episode per system. The study was pre-registered with a public change log; the MAS is reported as built, with one validity bar unmet (its planner never saw the tool schemas). Under a fixed simulated user no cell shows a MAS benefit: the MAS is worse in 12 of the 13 valid cells and tied in the thirteenth, and the fitted gain is negative across the observed capability range (weighted mean -28 points, 95% CI [-44, -12]). On the two cells where the rule predicts a benefit, the MAS loses by 13 and 22 points, and without a budget ceiling it at best draws level at 5.5 times the SAS's token spend. The one gain appears on the cell nearest 45%, under a second simulator. Whether the gain declines with capability is unresolved (slope -0.41, 95% CI [-1.51, +0.68]), because model-by-domain effects dominate. The MAS does not detectably reduce wrongful database writes; it converts other failures into budget exhaustion and inaction. For agents that serve people, the SAS is the default; a multi-agent design must show compute-matched evidence from the setting itself. We release all trajectories, ledgers, prompts and code.

title: Toward Agentic AI for the 6G Physical Layer: From Algorithm Discovery to Verified Baseband Silicon
description:
arXiv:2610.27797v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: 6G will be designed faster than it can be built: AI-driven search already proposes physical-layer algorithms at machine speed, while carrying a single one onto embedded baseband silicon remains specialist work. That silicon imposes hard memory and numeric limits, but also exposes cost structures a GPU lacks, and a design flow that never runs on the target sees neither. We present an agentic workflow in which an LLM coding agent implements algorithms on a commercial baseband SoC, optimizes them down to agent-written vector assembly, and validates them on silicon. The agent is guided by a knowledge base of measured platform facts, checked at every step against evaluators it is instructed never to edit, and metered per phase. We showcase the workflow on an AI-discovered orthogonal time frequency space (OTFS) detector portfolio on the open 6G4All platform. It yields twelve kernels that run cycle-exactly on silicon, their optimized versions at 18k-405k cycles (30-660 $\mu$s) per frame. It also yields a new detector shaped by the chip's measured costs that needs 13.9% fewer cycles than the port of the discovered detector while matching its error rate, with a measured edge our evaluation cannot statistically resolve, a structure that a hardware-blind search objective had no reason to find. What is not specific to OTFS is the workflow: an LLM agent exploring an implementation space under real hardware limits, with the cost of every choice measured rather than assumed.
