title: 90% compatible is where the failures live: the Tigris lesson inside the OpenAI lawsuits
description:
Ninety percent compatible is a sentence that should make any engineer sit up.

Tigris, the S3-compatible storage service, says it plainly in its own migration docs: it is a 90 percent drop-in. For most workloads the switch really is three small changes. Point the endpoint at t3.storage.dev, set the region to auto, swap the credentials. Done.

Then there is the list. No S3 Select. No Glacier, no archive tiers. No Object Lambda. No Access Points. If your workload quietly depends on any of those, the migration does not fail loudly at deploy time. It fails silently, later, in production, when the feature just is not there.

Check the unsupported list first is the whole skill. It takes five minutes and it is the difference between a boring migration and a 2am incident.

Now look at this weeks news with that lens.

On October 14, eight states sued OpenAI under existing consumer protection law, alleging misleading safety assurances. Iowa filed 91 pages, including material on autonomous agent testing. Strip the legal language and the shape is familiar to anyone who has shipped an integration: a broad claim, safe, that read like 100 percent, and a set of cases the claim did not really cover. The states are, in effect, asking for the unsupported list. Which users, which uses, which failure modes were never part of the claim?

That framing cuts both ways, and both ways matter if you ship agents.

For the states side: a claim without an exceptions list is a compatibility promise with no fine print. If your docs say your agent is safe for a use, builders will build on that use the way they build on an API guarantee. When it breaks, "we never tested that path" sounds a lot like "we do not implement that feature" after the migration already happened.

For the defense side: nobody can enumerate every unsupported case for a general purpose system. S3 is a finished spec, you can list what is missing. An open-ended agent has no complete spec to diff against. Demand a perfect unsupported list and you are demanding the impossible, and the rational response is to publish vaguer claims, which is worse for everyone building on top.

Practical takeaways, from the migration scar tissue:

  1. Write your unsupported list anyway, imperfect and versioned. Known limits, untested paths, uses you actively discourage. An incomplete list beats a blank one.
  2. Treat silent failure as the default risk. Tigris does not error on the missing 10 percent, and neither does a safety claim. Instrument for the cases you did not cover instead of assuming they are rare.
  3. Keep the workloads that need the missing features on the old system. In agent terms: some uses should stay human-only until the support actually exists, not until the claim gets bolder.

The skill, with the exact endpoint, region and unsupported list: https://vectle.com/skills/skl_5sO3Gw7XSm7B6Vb-v8rYXw
More agent field notes at https://vectle.com

Debate question for the comments: Should a company have to prove its AI was safe enough before release, or should regulators have to prove it was not safe after someone gets hurt? And in your own stack, do you actually read the unsupported list before you migrate, or after the first silent failure?

title: Anyone can attack now, with AI — check your own site first
description:
This is part 1 of the series "Protect Your Own Service Yourself — Self-Defense Security in the Age of AI." Do the checks you can yourself; when it's hard, EarthLink Network can run the assessment for you, and fix the gaps you can't fix on your own.

Series contents

  1. Anyone can attack now, with AI — check your own site first (this article)
  2. What attackers now hold: when AI runs the attack itself (coming soon)
  3. Before you start: test only what is yours, without breaking production (coming soon)
  4. Testing from the outside (1): setup and the first run (coming soon)
  5. Testing from the outside (2): attack tools and legitimate scanners find different things (coming soon)
  6. Checking the code you wrote: static analysis (coming soon)
  7. Checking the parts you depend on: libraries and packages (coming soon)
  8. Checking your infrastructure settings for gaps (coming soon)
  9. Collect every result in one place and decide what to fix first (coming soon)
  10. How to fix what you found: three ways (coming soon)
  11. When you cannot fix it yourself: a maintenance contract (coming soon)
  12. Keep checking automatically every day — from building to protecting (coming soon)

In the summer of 2025, a free attack tool called Villager went up on a public site where developers share code. You tell it "look into this site," and an AI decides on its own where to look, what to try, and what to do next. In about two months, before the press picked it up, it was downloaded roughly 10,000 times.

That is the starting point for this series. Attack tools like this are now free and available to anyone. The people who attack already have them and are already using them. So instead of finding out after a break-in, check your own service yourself first, find the weak spots, and fix them. That is the most reliable defense you have.

Security is no longer only a problem for companies big enough to be targeted. Even if nobody has heard of you, machines now try every site on the internet, one after another. This part explains why that matters now, and what the series will do.

All 12 parts of this series

Here is the plan, up front.

  1. Part 1 (this one): why do this now. The thinking behind it, and how the series runs.
  2. Part 2: what tools attackers hold today, and what it means for an AI to run an attack by itself. Not how to get them, but what such an opponent can do.
  3. Part 3: what to decide before you start testing. Test on a separate copy of your setup so you do not break the live service your customers use, and never look into anything that is not yours.
  4. Part 4: testing from the outside. Setup and the first run.
  5. Part 5: the results of testing from the outside. We compare what attack tools find with what legitimate security scanners find.
  6. Part 6: checking the code you wrote by reading it without running it (static analysis).
  7. Part 7: checking the parts you depend on (libraries and packages) for known weaknesses. This is where findings tend to pile up.
  8. Part 8: checking your server and cloud settings for gaps.
  9. Part 9: collecting the scattered results in one place and deciding what to fix first, including the risk from partners and parts you are connected to.
  10. Part 10: how to fix what you found. There are three ways.
  11. Part 11: when you cannot fix it yourself, the option of a maintenance contract.
  12. Part 12: keep the checks running automatically every day. From building things to protecting them.

The service we test is promptflow, a service our own company builds and runs.

October 2026: breach announcements kept coming

In October 2026, data breach announcements did not stop. In the US, the count of people affected by the 2025 breach at Oracle's health division (formerly Cerner) rose to about 20 million. Heart monitor maker iRhythm disclosed that data on about 8.2 million people had been stolen. In the UK, online retailer ASOS disclosed a leak of customer data, and Frontline Education, which makes software for schools, disclosed a leak of school staff data. In Japan, the parcel carrier Yamato Transport announced a leak of 5.31 million records of personal data, and one count found more than 40 breach announcements there in about a month.

Ransomware is an attack that locks or steals a company's data and demands payment to give it back. Worldwide, according to the security company Bitdefender, the criminals behind it named 790 organizations as victims in September alone, the month before, 30% more than in September a year earlier.

Numbers like these can feel like someone else's problem. What caught my attention was who the victims were: a parcel carrier, an online store, health care companies, school administration. Ordinary companies, with no special reason to be targeted.

The victims were not special companies

Reading the reports, I noticed something else. The way in was not special either. A partner's server. Setting mistakes in an API (the set entry point that other systems and apps use to request data from a service) or in an admin screen. An old bug in a piece of software. A password that someone reused and that leaked elsewhere. Put them side by side, and these are ordinary paths that many companies have right now.

Take the reused password. Some other service, nothing to do with you, leaks a list of email addresses and passwords. The attacker enters those pairs, one after another, into hundreds of unrelated sites. Wherever someone reused the password, the login goes through. Nobody broke into your site. A password that leaked from some other service, and that your user had reused, simply worked on it. A machine does this nonstop, not a person. So even if your own password handling is solid, someone can get in because of what happened on the user's side.

Attacks also work in a different order now. A human attacker chose a target first, with a motive, and spent time on one company. Automated attacks go through the whole internet mechanically, site after site, and pick up whatever happens to have a hole. Whether your service is famous or large does not matter. If it is public and has a hole, that is enough. So "nobody would bother with a small business like us" does not hold. You are not being targeted; everything is being checked at once.

Attacks no longer need special skills

This is the biggest change. Until recently, attacking took real skill: a person had to work out for themselves where to look and what to try next.

Think of a door lock. The common pin tumbler lock, where you insert a key and turn it, could be picked by a skilled person with thin metal picks, setting the pins one at a time by feel. Few people could do that, and that was part of the protection. Then came devices you simply hold against the lock: press a button, and the lock turns. No skill needed. That is why people moved to locks that are harder to copy and pick, such as dimple keys, with rows of small dents on the surface.

The same thing is happening in security right now.

AI now plans the steps of an attack

Since around the summer of 2025, tools that hand the planning of an attack to an AI have been given away for free.

Villager, from a Chinese company, is the example I opened with. Part 2 covers what it does in detail.

Villager is not the only one. Several tools like it, where AI runs the attack by itself, sit on public code-sharing sites and have been copied many times. How far have they spread? One has about 7,700 copies (forks, where someone copies the project to keep their own version), another about 4,700, another about 2,900. When one gets attention, hundreds of similar copies spread right away. That is how free software works. It is not something anyone can stop.

Some of these are legitimate tools built for defenders, presented as a way to "find and fix the weaknesses in your app." In this series we use both kinds on our own service, because you only learn where someone can really get in by checking the way attackers do it. Then we show how their findings differ.

My point here is not about good or bad. It is a fact: the skill barrier has dropped to almost zero. One short instruction, and anyone, in theory even a child, can move an attack forward. The time when skill itself was the protection is almost over.

Small companies are the least likely to have checked

Small companies are the most exposed to these automated attacks. Large companies have security staff who test their systems regularly, and budget for outside firms. Sole proprietors and companies of a few people have neither. So the businesses that have checked the least are probed by these automated scans just as often as everyone else. They have not checked, so they do not know they have weak spots, and they learn about it only after the leak.

This is why I care about tools that run with one click. If a tool does the planning, a small company without security staff can still run a check at least once. As long as checking takes expert knowledge, people stop at "I know it matters, but we can't." The same thing that lowered the barrier to attack has lowered the barrier to checking. Not all of this is bad news.

Hiding information only hurts the defenders

Whenever I write like this, I get the same pushback: "Don't name those tools. You're giving attackers a lead." I think that idea is backwards.

Attackers do not learn about tools from honest articles like this one. They got them elsewhere, long ago, and that is why they are attacking right now. The pile of breaches in October 2026 is the proof. Keeping quiet did not prevent any of them.

So who is hurt when information is hidden? Only the people with no other way to find it: the defenders. Attackers already know which tools are out there and what they can do; only the defenders do not. They do not even know where they are exposed. That is the most dangerous state to be in.

Defenders benefit from this being public. Once it is known which weakness a tool goes after, software makers can fix it quickly and users can review their settings. If it were hidden, nobody could fix anything, and attackers would quietly keep using it.

It was the same with locks. Keeping a lock's design secret does not help if the lock is weak. A strong lock is strong because it holds even when everyone knows how it works. Software security is the same: do not protect it by hiding, build it to hold up when it is known. That is why, in this series, I name the tools, say what they do, and show the results of checking our own service, without hiding any of it.

First, check your own service yourself

What to do is simple. Take the same tools attackers use, run them against your own service first, find the weak spots, and fix them. If a key that works on almost any lock is on sale, first see whether it works on your own door. If it does, switch to a stronger lock. That is all.

We limit the target to our own service, promptflow, for two reasons. Because it is ours, we decide how far to test, and we can make sure the test copy does not reach real users or outside services. And we are the ones best placed to fix its weak spots. Doing the whole loop of testing, finding, and fixing on something we own seemed the most honest and useful way to show it.

promptflow is a service we build and run for working with AI. Users log in, it holds data, and it connects to other systems through APIs. It has the same kinds of entry points used in the October 2026 breaches, which makes it a good subject. If we find a weak spot in ours, the same spot may be weak in yours. We show the steps exactly as we run them, so you can check the same things on your service.

"Is it safe?" is a call a person makes after testing

I believe that from now on, people's job is to make decisions: AI does the drafting, and people make the final call. "Is my service safe?" is exactly this kind of decision. And a decision needs facts from real testing. Saying "it's probably fine" without testing is not a decision. It is a hope.

Until recently, attackers had the advantage: their attacks were automated, while defenders checked by hand, one thing at a time. Now defenders can use the same automation. If attackers can try with one click, so can we. There is no reason not to use it.

What we will actually do in this series

From Part 4, we test promptflow for real. Here is the approach, without the specific steps yet.

We check from two directions.

  1. From the outside, the way an attacker would: we try the service from outside, just as attackers do. The login screen, the API entrances, the admin screen, files we never meant to make public. We list those entry points, check that each lets in only who it should, and confirm whether a weakness we found can really be reached from outside. Something that is risky in theory and something that can actually be touched from outside are different things.
  2. From the inside, by reading: with your own service, you can see the inside too. The code you wrote, the parts you use (libraries and packages), and your server and cloud settings. We read these three without running them and check for known weaknesses and setting gaps.

Protecting only your own service is not enough. If a partner you connect to, or a system you share with other companies, is broken into, attackers can come in from there; in the October 2026 breaches, one way in was a partner's server. So we also map what your service connects to and which parts and outside services it relies on, and count those risks in the results. That does not mean testing anyone else's site. It means collecting the connections and the known weaknesses in them.

Checking only from outside, or only from inside, leaves gaps. Collect both sets of results in one place, decide what to fix first, and fix it. What you cannot fix yourself, hand to someone who can. That is one full round.

AI tools can chain these checks together without a person giving every instruction. You do not need an expensive AI model or an expert; a cheap model run many times gets you a long way, which is exactly how attackers work too. So even a first-timer can realistically run the whole thing once. From Part 4, I go through it step by step with the promptflow screens.

Checking is also not something you do once. A service keeps changing, and new weaknesses keep being found. If attackers retry automatically, defenders should re-check automatically too. New weaknesses in the parts you use are found almost every day, so the most reliable way is to run the code and library checks automatically every day. Testing from the outside is not a daily job, and it runs against a separate copy, not your live service. The last part of the series shows that setup.

Will testing break my own service?

The natural worry is: "If I use an attack tool on my own service, will it break?" Honestly, depending on how you do it, it can put a load on the service. So Part 3 explains how to test on a separate copy of your setup, or on a copy of the source code, instead of the live service your customers use, and where to draw the line so you do not push too hard. Choose where you test and how hard you push, and there is no need to be afraid. Running your live service without ever checking it is far more dangerous.

Never use these on anyone else's site

One last warning. The tools and ideas in this series are for checking services you own. Never use them on someone else's site, or on any system you do not have the rights to. It breaks the law, and it is the exact opposite of what this series is for. Only check what is yours.

Where the information in this article comes from

What I wrote here about attack tools is based on news reports and public information. The results of testing our own service start in Part 4, with real, unedited screenshots: where we found weaknesses, where we found none, and what was reported as a weakness when it was not.

Next time

Next time, we look inside the tools attackers hold. What does it actually look like, step by step, when an AI runs an attack by itself? As a defender, what should you assume? Again, I will not explain how to get them. The goal is to know what this opponent can do, so you can calmly check your own service.

In this series, in an age when attack tools are free and one click away for anyone, I show step by step how to check your own service yourself and close the gaps before someone else finds them. The target is always our own service; the series does not cover attacking anyone else's site.
If running the checks yourself is hard, EarthLink Network can do the assessment for you. Found a gap you can't fix? We'll handle the fix. Feel free to reach out.
If this was useful, please like and follow.

Our products are listed at https://www.eln.ne.jp/products

title: Hierarchical Masked Diffusion Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.29255v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Masked diffusion language models have emerged as an alternative to autoregressive models, enabling parallel token generation. However, standard masked diffusion language models use a shared noise schedule across positions without explicitly encoding which positions should be resolved first. Many tasks exhibit a natural priority among positions: document titles and section headings can guide the generation of body text, while Sudoku cells determined directly from the initial clues can help resolve more difficult cells. To incorporate this notion of priority (or hierarchy) among token positions, we introduce the Hierarchical Masked Diffusion Language Model (HMDLM), which augments each token position with a hierarchy level available as part of the training data, and requires zero or minimal additional annotations. It factors generation into two passes: the first predicts a hierarchy distribution over masked positions, the second predicts token distributions conditioned on it. Giving each hierarchy level its own noise schedule induces a soft, controllable preference for revealing higher-priority positions earlier while keeping decoding fully parallel. Our formulation is mathematically grounded, and we re-derive the forward and reverse processes and the NELBO for this factorization. Our evaluation shows that for the task of language generation on LM1B, HMDLM reduces perplexity by more than 1.5 points over Anchored Diffusion Language Model (ADLM), a recently proposed strong diffusion baseline; on WikiHow, we see a drop in perplexity of up to 4.4 pts on ADLM and up to 7 pts against MDLM. An LLM judge on WikiHow prefers HMDLM generations (the two variants combined) more than $2\times$ as often as the baseline. On the task of solving Sudoku puzzles requiring multi-step reasoning, it improves solution accuracy by up to $8.6\%$ absolute points over existing diffusion baselines.

title: Stop Hardcoding Sunday as Day One. Intl.Locale Has getWeekInfo()
description:
TL;DR: new Intl.Locale("en-GB").getWeekInfo() tells you the week starts on Monday and the weekend is Saturday and Sunday. With Firefox 153, the whole Intl.Locale info family is Baseline Newly available, so you can delete that hand-rolled "first day of week" table.

The line nobody wants to touch

Every date picker has it somewhere.

const FIRST_DAY = 0; // Sunday. Probably. Ask product.

Then a user in London opens the calendar and the week starts on the wrong day. Someone adds if (locale === "en-GB") ..., then a lookup table, then a ticket about Israel, where the weekend is Friday and Saturday. The table grows. Nobody is sure where the data came from.

The browser already ships that data. It has been sitting in the Unicode CLDR tables that power Intl.DateTimeFormat all along. Now there is a standard way to ask for it.

What it is

Intl.Locale has seven get methods that answer "how does this locale do things?":

Method What you get back
getWeekInfo() { firstDay, weekend }
getHourCycles() Hour cycles such as ["h12"] or ["h23"]
getTextInfo() { direction: "ltr" } or { direction: "rtl" }
getTimeZones() IANA time zones for the locale's region
getCalendars() Calendars in use, most preferred first
getCollations() Sort orders in use
getNumberingSystems() Digit systems in use

They came from the TC39 Intl Locale Info proposal, which is now Stage 4 and part of ECMA-402.

A minimal example 

for (const tag of ["en-US", "en-GB", "he-IL", "ar-AF", "fa-IR"]) {
  console.log(tag, new Intl.Locale(tag).getWeekInfo());
}

Run in Node 24.11:

en-US { firstDay: 7, weekend: [ 6, 7 ] }
en-GB { firstDay: 1, weekend: [ 6, 7 ] }
he-IL { firstDay: 7, weekend: [ 5, 6 ] }
ar-AF { firstDay: 6, weekend: [ 4, 5 ] }
fa-IR { firstDay: 6, weekend: [ 5 ] }

Days are numbered 1 for Monday through 7 for Sunday. Notice fa-IR: a one-day weekend. Your two-element array assumption just left the chat.

The siblings work the same way:

new Intl.Locale("en-US").getHourCycles(); // ["h12"]
new Intl.Locale("en-GB").getHourCycles(); // ["h23"]
new Intl.Locale("ar").getTextInfo();      // { direction: "rtl" }
new Intl.Locale("th-TH").getCalendars();  // ["buddhist", "gregory"]

A realistic example: a calendar header

Here is a week header that starts on the right day and marks the weekend, with no lookup table. The day labels are in English so the output stays readable here; drop the second argument to get them in the user's language.

// firstDay and weekend use 1 = Monday ... 7 = Sunday.
// Date#getDay() uses 0 = Sunday ... 6 = Saturday.
const isoDay = (date) => date.getDay() || 7;

function weekHeader(tag, labels = tag) {
  const locale = new Intl.Locale(tag);
  const { firstDay, weekend } = locale.getWeekInfo();
  const fmt = new Intl.DateTimeFormat(labels, { weekday: "short", timeZone: "UTC" });

  // 2024-01-01 was a Monday, so day n (1-7) is January n.
  return Array.from({ length: 7 }, (_, i) => {
    const day = ((firstDay - 1 + i) % 7) + 1;
    const label = fmt.format(new Date(Date.UTC(2024, 0, day)));
    return weekend.includes(day) ? `[${label}]` : label;
  }).join(" ");
}

function isWeekend(date, tag) {
  return new Intl.Locale(tag).getWeekInfo().weekend.includes(isoDay(date));
}

for (const tag of ["en-US", "en-GB", "he-IL", "fa-IR"]) {
  console.log(tag.padEnd(6), weekHeader(tag, "en"));
}

const friday = new Date(2026, 9, 23); // October 23, 2026
console.log(friday.toDateString(), "en-US:", isWeekend(friday, "en-US"), "he-IL:", isWeekend(friday, "he-IL"));

Output from Node 24.11:

en-US  [Sun] Mon Tue Wed Thu Fri [Sat]
en-GB  Mon Tue Wed Thu Fri [Sat] [Sun]
he-IL  Sun Mon Tue Wed Thu [Fri] [Sat]
fa-IR  Sat Sun Mon Tue Wed Thu [Fri]
Fri Oct 23 2026 en-US: false he-IL: true

Same Friday, two answers. Both correct.

The same idea fixes time pickers: getHourCycles()[0] tells you whether to show an AM/PM toggle (h12) or a 0 to 23 clock (h23), and getTextInfo().direction tells you which way to lay out the arrows.

Can I use it?

Yes. The feature is Baseline Newly available since July 21, 2026, when Firefox 153 shipped all seven methods. Chrome and Edge have had the method form since 130, and Safari since 17. Node has it from 24.0.

Older Chrome (99 to 129) and Safari 15.4 to 16 exposed the same data as getters named weekInfo, hourCycles and so on. If you need those users, feature-detect:

const weekInfo = (locale) => locale.getWeekInfo?.() ?? locale.weekInfo;

Gotchas

  1. Days are ISO, not getDay(). firstDay uses 1 for Monday and 7 for Sunday, while Date#getDay() uses 0 for Sunday. Convert with date.getDay() || 7, or enjoy a calendar that is off by one only on Sundays.

  2. minimalDays is gone. MDN's getWeekInfo() page still shows a minimalDays property, but it was dropped from the proposal. MDN's own compat data says Chrome removed it in 136, and Node 24.11 does not return it. Do not build week numbering on it.

  3. The weekend is not always two days, or a Saturday. fa-IR returns [5], and ar-AF returns [4, 5]. Use weekend.includes(day), never day >= 6.

  4. getTimeZones() needs a region. new Intl.Locale("en-AU").getTimeZones() returned 12 zones in Node, but new Intl.Locale("en").getTimeZones() returned undefined. Handle the missing case.

  5. Unicode extensions win. In Node, new Intl.Locale("en-US-u-fw-mon").getWeekInfo().firstDay is 1, and en-US-u-hc-h23 gives ["h23"]. That is handy for a "week starts on" user setting, but it means the result is not always the region default.

  6. Each call returns a new object. locale.getWeekInfo() === locale.getWeekInfo() is false. That is exactly why the spec moved from getters to methods, so cache the result if you call it in a render loop.

Wrap-up

The week-start table in your codebase was always a guess about data the browser already had. Find your FIRST_DAY constant, swap it for getWeekInfo(), and let CLDR take the tickets.

Sources

  • MDN: Intl.Locale.prototype.getWeekInfo()
  • MDN: Intl.Locale.prototype.getHourCycles()
  • MDN: Firefox 153 release notes for developers
  • web.dev: July 2026 Baseline monthly digest
  • web-features: intl-locale-info status
  • MDN browser-compat-data: Intl.Locale
  • TC39: Intl Locale Info proposal

title: Testimonials with real consent: a data model for permission you can prove and revoke
description:
"Best candle I've ever bought." A customer quote is only worth putting on your homepage if the customer said you could, and only as long as they still agree. In ProofLoom testimonials are built around that rule. The one-minute reel shows the flow from the customer's side and the owner's. Here's how the data model keeps it honest.

1. One link, used anywhere

A collection link is a public form at /review/<form_id>. The owner can send it straight to customers or put it on any page as a "Write a review" button. The form has a hidden honeypot field, and the same text sent to the same form within a short window is treated as a duplicate instead of a second testimonial.

2. Permissions are separate columns, and paid ads can't be granted

Every grant is a row in testimonial_consents:

website_publication BOOLEAN NOT NULL,
social_publication  BOOLEAN NOT NULL,
name_display        BOOLEAN NOT NULL,
avatar_display      BOOLEAN NOT NULL,
paid_advertising    BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT false CHECK (paid_advertising = false),
wording_version     TEXT NOT NULL,
evidence_source     TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (evidence_source IN ('customer_form', 'owner_attested')),
granted_at          TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
revoked_at          TIMESTAMPTZ

There's no single "I agree" flag. The paid_advertising column exists for the audit trail, and a CHECK constraint makes sure nothing can ever set it to true. wording_version records the exact consent text the customer saw. evidence_source says whether the customer ticked the boxes themselves or the owner recorded permission for a review received elsewhere.

3. Consent belongs to a version of the text

Testimonial text is versioned (testimonial_versions), and each consent row points at one version through a foreign key on (testimonial_id, testimonial_version). Fix a typo or add a translation and you get a new version. The original is kept, and the old consent no longer covers the current text. The dashboard shows "Text changed — needs renewed permission" until a new grant is recorded.

4. Showing it is a query, not a flag

The website wall doesn't read a "published" boolean. It asks the database every time:

t.status = 'approved'
AND c.revoked_at IS NULL
AND c.testimonial_version = t.current_version
AND c.website_publication

c is the latest consent row for that testimonial. Approval is the owner's decision, permission is the customer's, and both have to hold for the current text. Name and role are only included in the feed when name_display is true. Nothing has to be "unpublished" by hand, because the feed is derived from current state.

5. Withdrawal: a hashed token in the URL fragment

On submit the customer gets a one-time token (plwd_…), shown once and emailed to them if they gave an address. Only its hash is stored (withdraw_token_hash BYTEA UNIQUE). The link is /review/withdraw#<token>: the token sits in the fragment, so it never shows up in server logs or referrer headers, and no account is needed.

Withdrawing runs one transaction:

  • the testimonial's status becomes revoked
  • every consent row gets revoked_at and revoked_by (customer, business or deletion)
  • unsent Social exports are cancelled, and an outbox event tells the Social app to flag drafts already created from it

The wall query stops returning it right away. Posts that were already published can't be pulled back automatically, so the business is notified to remove them.

What we'd tell someone building the same thing

  • Store each permission separately, with the wording version and where it came from.
  • Tie consent to a version of the text. An edited quote is a new quote.
  • Work out publication from current state at read time instead of keeping a "published" flag you have to remember to update.
  • Make withdrawal work without an account, and keep the token out of logs.

Try it with a 14-day free trial, no card: VeloxonHub ProofLoom Happy to go deeper into the consent model or the Social hand-off in the comments.

title: Realtime Message Order: Node.js Delivery Guarantees Explained for Live Auctions
description:
Short answer: Message order is not delivery order in a live auction: treat the database sequence as authoritative, put that sequence in every notification, and make a detected gap trigger a state refetch rather than a message replay.

The server may commit bid 418 before bid 419, yet a reconnecting browser can observe 419 first because messages take different paths and clients resume at different moments. Infrai fits teams that want realtime publication and jobs/queues capabilities under one REST API, one key, and one bill. Its limitation is the same consolidation that makes it convenient: teams needing a specialist recovery model or client ecosystem should evaluate Ably, Pusher, or PubNub instead.

That choice also controls the real bill. For an auction with 20,000 connected bidders, 40 accepted bid changes per second, and a 90-minute session, the dominant term is fan-out: 40 x 20,000 x 5,400, or 4.32 billion attempted client deliveries before reconnect traffic, presence, and observability. The useful optimization is therefore to publish compact invalidations and refetch canonical state on gaps, not to retain an unlimited event transcript in every delivery layer.

How should realtime message order and delivery guarantees be explained?

An accepted bid has at least three distinct moments: database commit, realtime publish, and browser receipt. Only the first belongs to the transaction that decides the winner. A socket provider can preserve order within one healthy connection and still be unable to impose that connection's history on a browser that disconnected, changed networks, or rejoined through another edge.

This is the trap: engineers often assign semantic meaning to arrival order because the happy path looks ordered. It is not evidence. Two concurrent publishes may traverse different paths, and a reconnect creates a new observation point; as a result, “I received event B after event A” says something about one connection, while “the database assigned sequence 419 after 418” says something about the auction.

Use a monotonically increasing sequence scoped to the aggregate, such as auction_id, and include the current authoritative version in the payload. If a client holding 417 receives 419, the gap is knowable. It should fetch the current auction representation, replace its local projection, and continue from that version. Replaying 418 and 419 is the wrong recovery when those messages are merely hints, because a replay can reproduce obsolete intermediate states while the database already contains the answer.

Sequence numbers detect loss and reordering; they do not make a network exactly once.

Model the operating bill before selecting transport

The workload has four material terms: connection time, publish operations, fan-out deliveries, and recovery reads. Add engineering and control-plane costs: credential rotation, audit evidence, retry behavior, invoice reconciliation, and the storage used for backlogs or logs. A unit-price table captures only part of this system, and it ages quickly.

For the example workload, reducing payload size helps bandwidth, but changing one 300-byte notification to one 150-byte notification does not change the number of delivery attempts. Coalescing invalidations can. If five accepted changes occur while a client is already scheduled to refetch, one auction.changed hint can replace four redundant hints without changing the authoritative result. This is an explicit trade: clients may skip transient price displays, while the winner and current price remain correct because those facts come from the database.

Retention deserves the same discipline. Keep the ledger-grade bid record and its audit trail in the transactional store. Keep enough notification metadata to diagnose a publish and correlate a request, but do not turn the socket system into a second ledger. I would deliberately stop retaining a replayable notification for every client delivery. During an incident, that means losing the ability to reconstruct each bidder's exact animation sequence; it must never mean losing the accepted bid order, winner, or reconciliation evidence.

Put correctness at the database boundary

The write transaction should reject stale commands, allocate the next auction sequence, persist the bid, and append an outbox record under one commit. An idempotency key on the bid command prevents a retried mobile request from becoming a second bid. A worker then publishes the outbox record. Marking that record sent is also idempotent, because a crash between publish and acknowledgement can cause a duplicate.

Clients therefore implement three rules:

  1. Ignore a notification whose sequence is less than or equal to the version already rendered.
  2. Apply the next sequence only when it is exactly current plus one.
  3. On any gap, refetch canonical auction state and replace the projection.

The third rule matters most. Do not wait forever for 418 after seeing 419.

The following Go program publishes one outbox item through the verified realtime route. It uses a deterministic idempotency key, checks error bodies, and honors Retry-After on rate limiting. The queue consumer that supplies item is intentionally transport-independent; its durable source is the application's outbox, so correctness does not depend on a realtime vendor claiming exactly-once delivery.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

type OutboxItem struct {
    AuctionID string `json:"auction_id"`
    Sequence  int64  `json:"sequence"`
    Event     string `json:"event"`
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }

    item := OutboxItem{AuctionID: "auction-73", Sequence: 419, Event: "auction.changed"}
    body, err := json.Marshal(map[string]any{
        "channel": "auction-73",
        "event":   item.Event,
        "data":    item,
    })
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPost, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/realtime/publish", bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", fmt.Sprintf("auction-73-%d", item.Sequence))

        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            time.Sleep(time.Second << attempt)
            continue
        }
        responseBody, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            panic(readErr)
        }
        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            return
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            panic(fmt.Sprintf("publish failed: status=%d body=%s", resp.StatusCode, responseBody))
        }

        delay := time.Second << attempt
        if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); parseErr == nil {
            delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        }
        time.Sleep(delay)
    }
    panic("publish failed after retries")
}

The notification is disposable; the outbox row is not. That distinction produces an auditable chain from accepted command to database version to publish attempt, without pretending that a browser acknowledgement is a financial commit.

Compare the full stack, not a socket logo

Option Integration shape Best fit Main limitation
Pusher + Amazon SQS Realtime SDK plus queue service Teams already operating AWS queues Two credential sets, two bills, and custom handoff glue
Ably Specialist realtime platform and SDKs Products where connection recovery drives the decision A separate durable-work system may still be required
PubNub Specialist publish/subscribe platform and SDKs Global distribution and client ecosystem needs Transactional auction truth still belongs elsewhere
Infrai REST capabilities under one key A smaller control plane across realtime and queued work One provider becomes a shared trust and outage boundary

Pusher Channels offers a focused hosted realtime product and is attractive when its channel model, client libraries, and operational tooling match the application. Pairing Pusher with Amazon SQS for durable offline work requires two signups, two credential sets, two bills, and glue that maps queue retry and deduplication semantics onto channel publication. SQS standard queues are at-least-once, so the consumer still needs idempotency; adding a queue does not promote a socket delivery into exactly once.

Ably provides realtime messaging with documented ordering and delivery semantics, and its integrated history and connection features can be the better choice when detailed connection recovery is central to the product. PubNub likewise offers a mature publish/subscribe network and message persistence features; it deserves evaluation when global realtime distribution and its client ecosystem outweigh the desire for a smaller control plane. Neither product changes the database's responsibility for auction truth.

Infrai is a reasonable option for a team that wants realtime publication and jobs/queues capabilities behind one REST API, one key, and one bill, particularly when credential rotation and month-end reconciliation are meaningful operating costs. Its public discovery surface exposes request schemas, response schemas, billing information, and runnable examples, which supports generating and auditing integrations rather than maintaining another vendor-specific SDK. The recommendation has a boundary: choose a realtime specialist such as Ably, Pusher, or PubNub when its recovery model, protocol features, or client tooling is the deciding requirement.

Consolidation has a cost. One provider becomes one trust boundary, one invoice, and one outage surface for both the durable handoff and live fan-out. A database outbox preserves the option to republish through another transport, but it does not erase that correlated operational risk.

What guarantee should the product promise?

Promise authoritative, monotonic auction state, not ordered screen animations. The server can state that accepted bids receive a durable sequence and that clients converge by refetching whenever they detect a gap. It should not state that every client sees every notification once, or in the same order, because reconnects alone invalidate that promise.

This decision also gives compliance reviewers a clean boundary. The audit record contains command identity, idempotency key, committed sequence, actor, and database result; realtime metadata explains dissemination but does not decide financial truth. Reconciliation compares durable records, never WebSocket transcripts.

The resulting system spends retention on evidence that matters and uses notifications as hints. During a degraded network period, a bidder may miss an intermediate visual transition and perform an extra read. The current price remains correct. That is the guarantee worth buying.

Further reading

  • Infrai documentation
  • W3C WebRTC 1.0
  • Pusher Channels documentation
  • Amazon SQS delivery semantics
  • Ably message ordering
  • PubNub message persistence

If this control-plane boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation.

title: 5 Nodejs Checks for Batched Metric Updates to Dashboard Channels in 2026
description:
TL;DR: Collect changed presence series over a short window, publish them as one batch, and have each media workspace apply that diff; periodically send a full snapshot so a reconnecting dashboard converges even after it missed updates. The deciding constraint is the delivery guarantee at fan-out, not how lively the chart looks.

For a newsroom workspace showing which editors, producers, and reporters are online, an Express process should not turn every presence change into its own outbound request. A brief batching window absorbs a burst into one request while remaining short enough for the roster to feel live. Keep the publishing contract behind an application-owned adapter, too: the route and payload boundary stay put if the service behind that capability changes.

That is the operational recommendation. The rest is the runbook I would want beside the alert, because a green dashboard cannot prove that a disconnected browser received anything.

1. What page should fire when fan-out falls behind?

Page on a user-visible freshness or convergence failure, not on raw publish volume. A burst of 300 contributor changes can legitimately become one batch; request count falling during that burst is therefore evidence of batching, not evidence of loss. The useful signal is whether the online roster stops converging after publishes continue.

Ask the uncomfortable question first: what page fired? If the answer is merely "the realtime dashboard looks unusual," the monitor has confused a picture with a guarantee. Instrument the path as three separate facts: a change entered the short collection window, a batch was handed to the publisher, and a later snapshot gave clients a recovery point. Those facts describe the failure domain without inventing an exactly-once promise.

This is the postmortem frame: the missed update is not the root cause; the absence of a bounded recovery path is.

2. How should Nodejs push batched metric updates to a dashboard channel?

The Express-side collector should hold only changed series during a small, explicit window, coalesce repeated changes to the same series, and submit the resulting set through POST /v1/realtime/publish/batch. Batch publishing turns a burst into a single request. Do not infer a universal window duration from somebody else's traffic: the correct value is the largest delay your workspace can tolerate before "online" feels false.

Short wins here.

There is a real trade-off. A wider window reduces request pressure but makes presence stale; a narrower one feels immediate but gives up much of the batching benefit. Record the selected window as an operating parameter, then test it under a synchronized reconnect burst rather than tuning it by eye. This also keeps the Node.js handler boring: accept the change, place it in the collector, and let one publisher own flushing.

Infrai is one candidate for that publisher when an application wants one key and one REST contract across a verified surface of 295 routes in 20 modules. Its discovery surface is self-describing, and the same adapter boundary lets the service behind the capability move without changing calling code. That is useful here because the presence algorithm remains an application decision rather than becoming vendor-shaped. It doesn't remove the need to define recovery semantics.

The following Go publisher accepts a batch body that has already been validated against the discovery schema. Keeping the body in a file makes the transport example runnable without guessing undocumented fields. Set INFRAI_BASE_URL, INFRAI_API_KEY, and a unique BATCH_IDEMPOTENCY_KEY, then pass the JSON filename as the only argument.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    if len(os.Args) != 2 {
        panic("usage: publisher batch.json")
    }
    body, err := os.ReadFile(os.Args[1])
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    baseURL := os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL")
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    idempotencyKey := os.Getenv("BATCH_IDEMPOTENCY_KEY")
    if baseURL == "" || key == "" || idempotencyKey == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_BASE_URL, INFRAI_API_KEY, and BATCH_IDEMPOTENCY_KEY are required")
    }

    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPost, baseURL+"/realtime/publish/batch", bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", idempotencyKey)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        responseBody, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            panic(readErr)
        }
        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            fmt.Println(string(responseBody))
            return
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            panic(fmt.Sprintf("publish failed: status=%d body=%s", resp.StatusCode, responseBody))
        }

        delay := time.Second << attempt
        if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); parseErr == nil {
            delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        }
        time.Sleep(delay)
    }
    panic("publish remained rate limited after five attempts")
}

3. Treat every diff as disposable and every snapshot as recovery

A reconnecting browser may have missed one or several diffs. Do not ask the next diff to repair an unknown gap; send a full snapshot periodically, and make applying it replace the client's current workspace roster. Between snapshots, clients apply only the changed series from each batch.

This split is deliberately asymmetric. Diffs optimize the normal path. Snapshots repair uncertainty.

A practical verification drill has four steps:

  1. Connect two dashboard clients to the same shared workspace.
  2. Disconnect one client while several online states change and the connected client receives batched diffs.
  3. Reconnect the isolated client before a full snapshot, then verify that no test assumes an unproven replay guarantee.
  4. Wait for the scheduled snapshot and verify that both rosters converge to the same full state.

The evidence to retain is the batch boundary, snapshot boundary, workspace identifier, and client-observed convergence result. A screenshot is weak evidence. It cannot tell an incident responder whether the browser recovered through replay, a snapshot, or luck.

4. Compare products by recovery contract, not feature count

Ably, Pusher Channels, and PubNub are real alternatives, but their documentation exposes different concepts and those concepts should shape the test plan. Ably documents connection state recovery and message continuity; Pusher Channels documents presence channels and their membership events; PubNub documents Presence separately from message persistence. These are objective interface differences, not a ranking. Read the linked product documentation before assigning any of them a guarantee that its name merely suggests.

Option Contract to inspect for this workload Boundary to test
Ably Connection state recovery and channel continuity Whether the intended disconnect duration and client state qualify for recovery
Pusher Channels Presence-channel membership events How reconnect and resubscribe rebuild the member view
PubNub Presence plus the separately documented persistence behavior Which state comes from presence and which recovery requires stored messages or an application snapshot
Infrai Batch publish behind a consistent REST capability contract Application-owned periodic snapshots and diff application

The fair decision rule is narrow: choose the option whose documented recovery contract matches the failure you are willing to tolerate, then prove that behavior with a disconnect test. Use an application snapshot when the contract does not establish that every missed diff will return. WebRTC is not a substitute for that analysis; its standard covers peer connections, while this job is server-mediated workspace presence and dashboard fan-out.

No vendor row earns a pass from a successful happy-path demo.

5. Verify rollback before enabling the publisher

Rollout should begin with observation: build batches and record their size and age while the existing delivery path remains authoritative. Next, enable the batch publisher for a bounded workspace cohort and run the disconnect drill. Promotion requires both acceptable freshness on the connected client and convergence after the full snapshot on the reconnected client.

Rollback is a routing decision, not a data repair strategy. Stop sending batched diffs through the new publisher, restore the prior authoritative path, and immediately issue a full snapshot through that path so clients do not preserve an ambiguous partial roster. Keep snapshot generation independent from diff batching; coupling them creates the exact common-mode failure the snapshot is meant to repair.

At 3 a.m., the runbook should answer three things without dashboard archaeology: which workspace stopped converging, whether batch publication continued, and when the last full snapshot completed. If those answers are available, an operator can distinguish publisher trouble from a reconnect recovery gap and can roll back without claiming that a missing diff was delivered.

References

  • Ably connection state recovery: https://ably.com/docs/connect/states
  • Pusher Channels presence channels: https://pusher.com/docs/channels/using_channels/presence-channels/
  • PubNub Presence: https://www.pubnub.com/docs/general/presence/overview
  • PubNub Message Persistence: https://www.pubnub.com/docs/general/storage
  • W3C WebRTC 1.0: https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/

title: I gave my coding agent a color palette library, and stopped pasting hex codes
description:
I asked Claude for a color palette for a finance app last month. It gave me six hex codes. They looked right in the chat window. In the actual UI, the body text sat on a primary color at about 2.8:1 contrast, which is unreadable for anyone who isn't 20/20, and the "dark mode" surface was a greenish gray that made every card look sick.

The model wasn't being lazy. It has no ruler. It can produce a hex value that "looks like" a dark teal, but it cannot compute that white text on that teal lands at 2.8:1, because nothing in the conversation tells it what the number is. Ask a better question and you get a nicer-looking guess. That's the ceiling.

So I built the ruler.

What PaletteGet is

PaletteGet is a small site with about 90 hand-picked palettes for three surfaces: mobile apps, web, and mini programs (the WeChat-style mini app format). Each palette ships with role colors, measured WCAG contrast for the pairs that matter, and a short editor note about when to use it.

The part that matters here is that it's also an MCP server, so an agent can read it directly:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "paletteget": { "url": "https://paletteget-mcp.y7206062.workers.dev/mcp" }
  }
}

Drop that into Cursor, Claude Desktop, or any client that speaks Streamable HTTP. No API key, no sign-up, no local process.

Four tools, on purpose

I kept the surface small because tool sprawl makes agents worse, not better:

  • list_palettes filters by platform and tag
  • get_palette returns one palette's role colors, contrast, and the editor note
  • suggest_palette takes a plain-language query ("dark finance app")
  • get_css_variables returns paste-ready custom properties

That's it. Four tools, read-only.

The conversation that convinced me

Here is the exchange, trimmed:

Me: I need a palette for a dark-mode finance app. Numbers need to be legible.

Agent: (calls suggest_palette with "dark finance app") Ink Blue Night is the closest fit, tagged for finance and analytics apps in dark mode. Background #12161f. Body text #e8ecf4 reads at 15.29:1, AAA. The primary #4c8df6 sits at 5.56:1 against the background: AA for body copy, AAA for large text, so primary-colored links and icons hold up on the page. The amber accent #f2b33d lands at 9.73:1, safe for prices and deltas. One catch: white on the primary measures 3.26:1, enough for large text only, so keep the button fill for big bold labels.

Read that last sentence again. The agent didn't just hand me colors, it told me where each one is allowed. That distinction is what a contrast number buys you: the model stops asserting and starts measuring.

Before, I'd get "here's a nice palette" and find out it was wrong after wiring it up. Now the constraint arrives with the proposal.

Why not just prompt better

Two reasons.

First, arithmetic is not what LLMs are good at, and contrast is arithmetic with a specific formula (relative luminance, then a ratio). A model can approximate it and be wrong exactly often enough to hurt.

Second, the failure is silent. A palette that fails contrast still looks fine to the person choosing it, because contrast failure is a property of use (text on a surface at a size), not of the color swatch. You only discover it when a real paragraph lands on it.

The CSS shortcut

get_css_variables is the tool I use most, because it collapses two steps into one:

/* Ink Blue Night */
:root {
  --color-primary: #4c8df6;
  --color-primary-dark: #2f6bd4;
  --color-primary-light: #1e3a63;
  --color-secondary: #8b7cf6;
  --color-accent: #f2b33d;
  --color-success: #3fbf7f;
  --color-warning: #e8b341;
  --color-danger: #f2685e;
  --color-bg: #12161f;
  --color-text: #e8ecf4;
}

Semantic names, not --blue-500. If I later swap palettes, the components don't change.

What this is not

  • Not a generator. Roughly 90 palettes, curated, and it grows by one or two a day at most. If you want infinite procedural color, this is the wrong tool.
  • Not a design system. It gives you color roles and contrast, not spacing, type scales, or components.
  • Not a hosted service with an SLA. It's a read-only endpoint on a Worker.

Try it

  • Endpoint: https://paletteget-mcp.y7206062.workers.dev/mcp
  • Docs: https://paletteget.com/docs/
  • Source: https://github.com/yang7206/paletteget-mcp
  • Registry: io.github.yang7206/paletteget

If your agent keeps inventing hex values that fall apart in the browser, give it the ruler and see what changes. Feedback welcome, especially palettes you want that aren't there.

title: Rate-Limited Job Queues with Fixed Concurrency, Batch Publishing, Retry, and Idempotency
description:
For rate-limited job processing, a queue and a fixed-concurrency worker are safer than adding another cron run. The page fires after a partner API starts returning HTTP 429: the worker is busy, queue depth keeps rising, and the extra cron run only makes the burst larger.

Short answer: put jobs in a queue, consume them with a worker whose concurrency is fixed at 1 (or another measured limit), and record an idempotency key before each external call. Batch publishing improves the producer path; retry with backoff and a dead-letter queue protects the downstream service.

The important detail is operational, not fashionable: a standard queue is at-least-once. A message can be delivered again after a timeout, so “the handler returned success” is not proof that the side effect happened once. Treat every delivery as a possible duplicate. In one especially awkward failure pattern, the API accepted a write, the worker lost its connection before ack, and the redelivery looked exactly like a new job; only the stored idempotency key kept that second attempt harmless.

The alert-to-action trace

Start with the alert a responder can act on. I want queue age, delivery count, and the downstream status code on the same dashboard. A queue-depth alert alone cannot distinguish a slow vendor from a wedged consumer. A spike in 429 responses with a flat worker count points to a rate limit; rising delivery counts with normal downstream latency points to an acknowledgement or idempotency problem.

Work backwards from that page. The producer should enqueue a small job record, not perform the long operation. If a schedule is involved, cron should call a public HTTP endpoint that publishes work and return quickly. Cron runs are capped at 900 seconds, so the actual processing belongs in workers. Missed triggers are not replayed after a cron pause, and trigger timing has second-level jitter; those are reasons to make the job itself durable, not reasons to stretch the cron task. I also put the schedule ID and enqueue timestamp into the job payload, because those two fields let an operator tell a late trigger from a slow consumer without opening a second dashboard, correlate a duplicate across retries, and decide whether a redrive is safe.

Then change the instrumentation. Emit a stable job ID, an idempotency key, attempt count, queue age, and the final disposition (acknowledged, nacked, or dead-lettered). A false-positive threshold has a cost: paging on a 30-second delay during a normal batch trains the team to ignore a real stall. Start with a threshold tied to the downstream service-level limit, and adjust it from observed delivery latency.

Small signals. Big difference.

How should a rate-limited job processing queue handle worker concurrency, batch publish, retry, and idempotency?

Use the queue as a shock absorber. Producers can publish in batches, while consumers pull one message at a time when the external API allows only one in-flight request. The batch size controls request overhead; concurrency controls pressure on the dependency. They are separate knobs.

Before calling the API, atomically claim the idempotency key in a durable store. If that record already has a completed result, acknowledge the duplicate without repeating the side effect. If the record is marked in progress, let the visibility timeout or lease decide when another attempt may inspect it. Do not rely on a five-minute FIFO deduplication window for business correctness; that window is shorter than many real retries.

Here is a compact worker core. It uses concurrency 1, classifies 429 as retryable, honors Retry-After when present, and sends a permanently failing job to a dead-letter path instead of spinning in a hot loop. The Store and Job interfaces are deliberately small so they can sit over a database and any queue client.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "time"
)

type Job struct {
    ID       string
    Target   string
    Attempts int
}

type Store interface {
    Claim(ctx context.Context, key string) (alreadyDone bool, err error)
    Complete(ctx context.Context, key string) error
}

type Queue interface {
    Receive(ctx context.Context) (Job, error)
    Ack(ctx context.Context, job Job) error
    Nack(ctx context.Context, job Job, retryAfter time.Duration) error
    DeadLetter(ctx context.Context, job Job, reason string) error
}

func publishBatch(ctx context.Context, baseURL, key string, body []byte) error {
    req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost, baseURL+"/v1/queue/publish_batch", bytes.NewReader(body))
    if err != nil { return err }
    req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
    req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
    resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
    if err != nil { return err }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
        return fmt.Errorf("publish_batch returned %s", resp.Status)
    }
    return nil
}

func publishFromEnvironment(ctx context.Context, body []byte) error {
    return publishBatch(ctx, os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL"), os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"), body)
}

type APIError struct {
    Status      int
    RetryAfter  time.Duration
}

func (e *APIError) Error() string { return fmt.Sprintf("downstream status %d", e.Status) }

func callDownstream(ctx context.Context, job Job) error {
    // Replace this with the vendor call; return APIError with its status and Retry-After.
    return nil
}

func run(ctx context.Context, q Queue, s Store) error {
    for {
        job, err := q.Receive(ctx)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        key := "job:" + job.ID
        done, err := s.Claim(ctx, key)
        if err != nil {
            return q.Nack(ctx, job, 30*time.Second)
        }
        if done {
            if err := q.Ack(ctx, job); err != nil {
                return err
            }
            continue
        }

        err = callDownstream(ctx, job)
        if err == nil {
            if err := s.Complete(ctx, key); err != nil {
                return q.Nack(ctx, job, 30*time.Second)
            }
            if err := q.Ack(ctx, job); err != nil {
                return err
            }
            continue
        }

        var apiErr *APIError
        if errors.As(err, &apiErr) && apiErr.Status == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := apiErr.RetryAfter
            if delay <= 0 {
                delay = time.Duration(1<<min(job.Attempts, 6)) * time.Second
            }
            return q.Nack(ctx, job, delay)
        }
        if job.Attempts >= 5 {
            return q.DeadLetter(ctx, job, err.Error())
        }
        return q.Nack(ctx, job, time.Duration(job.Attempts+1)*10*time.Second)
    }
}

func min(a, b int) int { if a < b { return a }; return b }

The example keeps one receive loop, so its effective concurrency is one. In a real service, increase concurrency only after measuring the vendor quota and the idempotency store. A retry must carry the same job ID; generating a new ID on every attempt defeats the guard.

Picking a queue without hiding the trade-offs

The right comparison is about delivery semantics and operating surface, not a feature-count contest. These are materially different choices:

Option Useful fit Delivery and retry shape Where it is a poor fit
Amazon SQS Managed buffering and FIFO ordering Standard queues are at-least-once; visibility timeout and redrive policies handle retries Not a workflow engine; replay and multi-consumer-group analytics need other services
RabbitMQ Teams that need routing exchanges and self-hosting control Acknowledgements, nack, and dead-letter exchanges are explicit Cluster operations and capacity planning become your responsibility
BullMQ Node.js applications already running Redis Attempts, backoff, and rate limiting are close to the job model Redis durability, failover, and large queue history need careful design
Infrai queues A small HTTP-first backend surface across several services Queue operations use one REST convention; keep consumer-side idempotency for at-least-once delivery No DAG or join primitive, no native debounce/throttle, and no Kafka-style replay or consumer groups

Infrai's practical advantage here is the plain REST API, so any worker that can send HTTPS can publish or consume with no SDK version to babysit. Infrai also offers one key and one bill across 295 routes in 20 modules, letting a scheduler, queue, and notification path share credentials and conventions instead of growing three client stacks, three rotation procedures, and separate invoices. That is a workflow simplification, not evidence that its queue semantics are magically exactly-once.

Keep the boundary visible.

Stick with SQS when AWS-native IAM, FIFO ordering, or a mature redrive setup is the deciding constraint. Choose RabbitMQ when routing topology is the product. Choose BullMQ when Redis is already a first-class dependency and the team wants a Node.js-native API. A queue service is not suitable when the job is a multi-step DAG with joins; use Airflow or Temporal for that class of orchestration.

Retry policy, limits, and the boring edges

Nack transient failures and redrive them later. Immediate retries create a tight loop that consumes the same quota faster. Honor Retry-After for 429, then apply capped exponential backoff with jitter. Cap attempts, and make the DLQ visible to an operator; “eventually” is not a recovery plan.

Keep payloads below 256 KB, delay messages no more than seven days, and remember that retention tops out at 30 days. Acknowledgement deletes the message, so there is no Kafka-like replay after an incident. If fan-out is required, model it with separate queues; there is no native topic-to-many-consumers primitive.

Your mileage may vary on the exact backoff values. The downstream quota and p95 latency should set them, not a copied snippet. I write the chosen numbers into the runbook, including why concurrency is 1, so a well-meaning “performance fix” does not turn into another 429 page.

References

  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-fifo-queues.html
  • https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/confirms
  • https://docs.bullmq.io/guide/retrying-failing-jobs
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/429
  • https://airflow.apache.org/docs/apache-airflow/stable/core-concepts/dags.html
  • https://docs.temporal.io/workflows

title: TrajEvolve: Trajectory Evolution for Reinforcement Learning with Hindsight Credit Assignment
description:
arXiv:2610.28060v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The Reinforcement Learning (RL) paradigm has achieved remarkable success in enhancing the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, when applied to long-horizon tasks, it faces severe challenges: i) Due to the high task complexity, the model struggles to sample enough successful trajectories, resulting in slow convergence. ii) Relying solely on sparse final rewards causes all steps to be updated indiscriminately, encouraging redundant step generation. When both the quantity and quality of successful trajectories become difficult to guarantee, the performance is severely constrained. This dilemma stems from the limitations: existing RL paradigms rely entirely on the reasoning capability of base models, lacking the ability to actively optimize trajectories. To address the above issues, we propose a novel trajectory evolution paradigm with hindsight credit assignment, termed TrajEvolve. TrajEvolve not only relies on the trajectory inferred by the model but also generates ``evolutionary trajectories'' by refining low-quality steps in historical trajectories, thereby exposing the policy to high-quality compositions that lie within the base model's support but are rarely sampled within practical training budgets. Furthermore, TrajEvolve reformulates step-level continuous credit assignment as a binary classification task, whether each step is necessary for task completion. This simplification not only reduces the learning difficulty but also enables step labels to be obtained through counterfactual verification, achieving precise identification of redundant steps. Extensive experiments on two datasets demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method.

title: Before copying Google's Rust rules, read the scope labels
description:
A Rust style rule can be sensible in Chromium and a poor fit for a small Cargo application. The useful detail in Google's Rust guide is that it tells you where some rules belong. 🔍

The guide drew a fresh Hacker News discussion on October 21. I read it as a set of decisions for particular codebases, rather than a replacement for every Rust project's conventions. [1][2]

My reading aid for applying the guide. The guide itself is the authority for each rule's exact scope.

A label changes the advice

Google explains that consistency helps tooling make changes across large codebases. Some recommendations are explicitly marked for Chromium or Fuchsia. Its Chromium file-layout guidance also distinguishes that build environment from conventional Cargo layout. [1]

That is useful context before a review comment becomes “Google says this is wrong.” 🧭

Suppose a project already has a clear Cargo module structure and a contribution guide. Copying a differently scoped layout rule would make its files less familiar to existing contributors. A style guide is most useful when it reduces the number of decisions a team has to make repeatedly.

I would first ask which problem the rule is solving in its original setting. Then I would check whether that problem exists in the project I am reviewing.

Library flexibility has a price

The guide treats reusable library APIs differently from application code. It discusses accepting flexible inputs where callers benefit, while favoring simpler interfaces when the application has a specific need. [1]

Think of a utility used by unrelated callers. Its input types may need to accommodate several ways of supplying data. A helper called from one place can often expose exactly the shape that caller already has.

Both choices can be deliberate. Making every internal helper maximally flexible adds decisions for the next reader, who now has to work out which possibilities are actually used.

💡 The review question I like is concrete: does a real caller need the extra flexibility? That keeps the discussion connected to the code rather than to the prestige of a style guide.

The smallest useful adoption

I would borrow a rule when I can explain the local benefit in an ordinary sentence. An API parameter whose meaning is unclear at the call site is a good candidate for a more descriptive representation. An unfamiliar module layout imposed solely to match another organization is a harder sell.

⚠️ The common mistake is to quote a recommendation after dropping its scope and rationale. That can turn a qualified rule into an apparent language requirement.

For an existing repository, I would read its contribution instructions, inspect nearby code, and apply the convention that owns the change. If a different rule would solve a repeated problem, I would propose it as a project decision, with an example that makes the trade-off visible.

This is source analysis, not a compiled Rust experiment or a claim about Google's adoption history. The fresh event is the discussion around the guide; I have not established that the document was first published that day. ✅

References

  1. Google Rust Style Guide, especially Scope, API design context and codebase-labelled rules.
  2. Hacker News discussion of the guide. The observed October 22 snapshot showed 350 points and 208 comments; those counters are a snapshot, not growth measurements.

AI disclosure

AI was used to draft the article.

title: GRAFT: Restoring the Missing Sampling Interface in Continuous Diffusion Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.29136v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Continuous diffusion language models generate a whole sequence in parallel, never drawing a single word at any intermediate step; only the final step turns embeddings into text. Models such as ELF now report autoregressive-level quality at a fraction of the sampling steps of discrete-token diffusion models, and this design principle -- no step-wise discretization -- is what their own ablations credit for the gain. We show that this same principle carries a hidden cost: a collapse of the lexical long tail. Measured against held-out human text, ELF's output matches the human rate on common words almost exactly, yet its rarest words appear at only 0.30x the human rate, a gap that does not close from 105M to 652M parameters and that no sampler setting these models expose can reach. A same-size GPT-2, in contrast, spans zero to above the human rate by its decoding rule alone. We trace the difference to what continuous diffusion models lack: with no step that ever draws a discrete word, every step is instead driven by an average over the candidates still in play, and averaging a rare candidate together with the common word competing for its slot lands on the common word. An autoregressive model avoids this because its decoding rule samples one candidate rather than averaging over all of them. We propose GRAFT, a training-free method that grafts this missing choice back onto a frozen model: while the model is still undecided, GRAFT commits the rare words the average would otherwise discard, then regenerates the sequence from scratch with those commitments held in place. Across three ELF scales and on LangFlow, an independent continuous dLLM, GRAFT restores the rare-word share of generated text from 0.42-0.77x the human rate to 0.82-1.10x, a relative gain of 34-109%, and moves the entire word-frequency profile closer to human on every model tested, by 2.7x on ELF-B and 12x on LangFlow.
