title: GBase Database Installation Methods Compared: Which Is Most Efficient?
description:
Choosing the right installation method for GBase Database(GBase 8s) depends on more than installation speed. Interaction requirements, component customization, repeatability, and deployment scale all affect operational efficiency.

GBase Database supports several installation approaches, including one-click, typical, manual, and silent installation. Each serves a different purpose.

1. Comparing Four GBase Database Installation Methods

Installation method User interaction Component customization Batch deployment Best use case
One-click installation Low Medium Medium Quick environment setup and validation
Typical installation Very low Low Low Fast testing and basic validation
Manual installation High High Low without additional automation Customized production installation
Silent installation None during installation Medium to high, depending on the response file High Repeatable, automated batch deployment

The ratings above are relative and assume a standard installation workflow. Actual efficiency depends on the installation package, configuration requirements, and automation already available in your environment.

2. One-Click Installation: Quick Setup

One-click installation is useful when you need to establish a GBase Database(GBase 8s) environment quickly.

It reduces manual configuration steps and is suitable for initial validation, demonstrations, and basic environment checks.

However, convenience comes with trade-offs. Default parameters may not match production requirements, so review settings such as the installation path, character set, and database port before using the environment for more demanding workloads.

Choose one-click installation when speed and simplicity matter more than fine-grained control.

3. Typical Installation: Minimal Configuration

Typical installation is designed for users who want to get a basic environment running with minimal interaction.

It works well for quick tests, compatibility checks, and preliminary validation without extensive component selection.

The main limitation is customization. If your environment requires specific components or carefully controlled configuration, a typical installation may not provide enough flexibility.

Choose typical installation when you need a basic test environment with minimal setup effort.

4. Manual Installation: Maximum Control

Manual installation gives administrators more control over the installation process.

You can select components, specify installation paths, and make decisions that align with the target environment's operational requirements.

This flexibility is particularly useful for production deployments that require explicit configuration decisions. The trade-off is time: administrators must understand the installation steps and validate the resulting environment.

Manual installation can also be automated with additional scripting, so it is not inherently unsuitable for batch deployment. Without that automation, however, repeated manual installations require more effort and create more opportunities for configuration drift.

Choose manual installation when customization and direct control are the primary requirements.

5. Silent Installation: Consistency at Scale

Silent installation is the natural choice when deploying GBase Database across multiple servers with a standardized configuration.

Instead of answering installation prompts on every machine, you provide the parameters through a response file.

For example:

./ids_install -i silent \
  -f /opt/bundle.properties \
  -DLICENSE_ACCEPTED=TRUE

The response file makes installation parameters repeatable and easier to manage. Combined with deployment scripts, silent installation reduces repetitive interaction and helps maintain consistency across nodes.

It does not eliminate the need for validation. Target servers may differ in available disk space, dependencies, permissions, or port availability. These prerequisites should be checked before starting a batch deployment.

The efficiency advantage becomes more significant as the number of servers grows. There is no universal threshold at which silent installation becomes faster, but the time saved on repeated interactions and configuration checks can outweigh the initial effort of preparing and validating the response file.

Choose silent installation when repeatability, automation, and batch deployment are the main priorities.

6. How to Choose the Right Installation Method

For GBase Database deployment, a practical decision framework is:

  • Need a quick test? Use one-click or typical installation.
  • Need detailed control over a single production environment? Use manual installation.
  • Need consistent configuration across multiple servers? Use silent installation with a validated response file.
  • Need repeatable deployment at scale? Combine silent installation with prerequisite checks, logging, and incremental rollout.

These methods are not mutually exclusive. A team can validate a configuration with a simple installation first, refine the production settings through a controlled installation, and then automate repeated deployments using silent installation.

Conclusion

The most efficient GBase Database installation method is the one that matches your deployment requirements.

One-click and typical installation reduce setup effort. Manual installation provides greater control. Silent installation makes standardized, repeatable deployment easier to manage across multiple servers.

Rather than choosing one method for every situation, build a workflow around the strengths of each. Validate early, standardize the configuration, and automate only after the installation process is understood and tested.

title: SCODEL: Shared Canonical Ontology Definitions for Food Entity Linking and Ontology-Grounded Recipe Knowledge Graphs
description:
arXiv:2610.27637v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Identifying recipe entities and linking them to ontology concepts is fundamental for semantic recipe understanding. However, food mentions in recipes are often ambiguous, context-dependent, and lexically diverse, making ontology entity linking (EL) challenging. We propose SCODEL, a streamlined, model-agnostic approach based on a central idea: contextual food mentions and ontology concepts that refer to the same entity should learn the same canonical ontology-oriented definition. SCODEL uses these shared definitions as a semantic normalisation layer, providing complementary semantic information to existing EL models without requiring a new linking architecture. We further introduce ReciLinkD, the first benchmark for contextual food ontology entity linking in recipes. Experiments show that SCODEL consistently improves three modular EL models (ReFinED, GSM-EL, and BLINK): SCODEL x BLINK achieves the highest Hit@1 on seen concepts (88.33%), while SCODEL x GSM-EL achieves the highest Hit@1 on unseen concepts (83.15%), outperforming the strongest large language model (LLM) based EL baseline in each setting. Experiments on a biomedical ontology benchmark further demonstrate that SCODEL generalises beyond the food domain. Finally, we use SCODEL to ground food mentions at scale and construct an ontology-grounded recipe knowledge graph, demonstrating its utility for ontology-aware recipe retrieval and corpus-level food analysis.

title: Attention-based Classification for Indirect Prompt Injection
description:
arXiv:2610.28988v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks, in which adversarial instructions are embedded in external data processed by a language model, pose a significant threat to the integrity of deployed LLM agents. Attention Tracker (Hung et al., 2025) is a recently proposed white-box detection method that identifies prompt injection attacks by monitoring how a model's attention is distributed between user task tokens and data tokens, claiming dataset-agnostic detection via a scalar focus score threshold. In this paper, we provide the first evaluation of Attention Tracker in a realistic agentic IPI setting using the AgentDojo benchmark, finding that the dataset agnosticism claim does not hold. We find that in agentic environments, long structured tool outputs subvert the fundamental assumptions Attention Tracker makes about attention that the method depends on and produces near-chance detection on AgentDojo across most model families. We propose AttnDA, an extension replacing the scalar threshold with a Fisher Linear Discriminant Analysis classifier over the per-head focus score vector, and evaluate both methods in a cross-dataset setting spanning four benchmarks. AttnDA improves detection performance across agentic and tool-integrated benchmarks, though transfer to AgentDojo remains challenging regardless of classifier choice. A covariance ablation further shows that removing inter-head correlation structure substantially contributes to performance, with complex covariance assumptions causing significant degradation on cross-domain data. These results indicate that the attentional distraction signal underlying focus-score-based detection does not transfer reliably to agentic environments, and that learned linear classifiers over head-level attention features offer improved detection performance, provided training data from the target deployment domain is available.

title: Why I Practice Coding Interviews Out Loud
description:
For a long time I prepared for coding interviews by solving problems silently. I could solve medium problems on my own, then froze in real interviews. The problem was not the algorithms. It was talking while thinking.

Silent practice hides the real skill

In a live coding round, the interviewer is grading your communication as much as your code. They want to hear you clarify the problem, propose a brute-force approach, explain why it is slow and then improve it. If you have never practised narrating, the first time you do it is under pressure.

My routine now

  1. Read the problem aloud and restate it in my own words.
  2. Ask two clarifying questions, even if I think I know the answer (input size, edge cases, duplicates).
  3. Say the brute force first and its complexity.
  4. Talk through the optimisation before writing a line of code.
  5. Code while narrating what each block does.
  6. Test with one normal case and one edge case out loud.

I set a 35-minute timer for each problem.

Reviewing the session

After each run I review what I actually said. I started using ClapAssist for this, since it has a coding mode and gives a recap of the session, but a simple screen recording works too. The goal is to catch habits like going silent for two minutes or skipping complexity analysis.

What changed

Within three weeks my mock interview feedback shifted from "good solution, hard to follow" to "clear communicator." Same algorithms, very different result.

If you are grinding problems but struggling in real rounds, try practising out loud for a week. It is uncomfortable at first and then it becomes your biggest advantage.

title: GBase Database Silent Installation FAQ: 5 Common Questions Answered
description:
Silent installation makes it easier to automate GBase Database(GBase 8s) deployment across multiple servers. By using a response file to supply installation parameters, administrators can reduce repetitive input and improve configuration consistency.

If you're preparing to automate a GBase Database installation, these five frequently asked questions cover the basics.

Q1: What's the Difference Between Silent Installation and CLI Installation?

The main difference is how installation parameters are provided.

  • CLI installation: Uses a command-line interface and may still require interactive input, depending on the installer and installation mode.
  • Silent installation: Reads predefined parameters from a response file and runs without interactive prompts.

For example, a silent installation command may look like this:

./ids_install -i silent \
  -f /opt/bundle.properties \
  -DLICENSE_ACCEPTED=TRUE

This approach is useful when the same installation procedure needs to run repeatedly across multiple servers.

Q2: How Do I Generate a Silent Installation Response File?

A response file stores the parameters required by the installer, such as installation settings and selected components.

Depending on the installer version, you may be able to generate a response file with a command such as:

./ids_install -r /opt/bundle.properties

Alternatively, check whether the installation media includes a sample response file that you can copy and customize.

Before using the file in a deployment batch, verify that its syntax and parameter names match the documentation for your installation package. Test the completed file on a single server first.

Q3: Why Is LICENSE_ACCEPTED Required?

A silent installation cannot pause to ask the administrator to accept the license interactively. License acceptance must therefore be supplied in advance when required by the installer.

For example:

LICENSE_ACCEPTED = TRUE

Some installation packages also accept the setting as a command-line parameter:

-DLICENSE_ACCEPTED=TRUE

Follow the syntax supported by your installer and make sure you have reviewed and accepted the applicable license terms before proceeding.

Q4: Can I Use GBase Database Immediately After Silent Installation?

Not necessarily. Completing the software installation does not automatically mean that a usable database instance is running.

Depending on the installation package and selected workflow, additional steps may include:

  • Configuring the required environment variables.
  • Reviewing the instance's onconfig configuration.
  • Checking the connection settings in sqlhosts.
  • Initializing the database instance when initialization has not already been performed.
  • Starting the instance and validating connectivity.

For a manual installation, instance initialization may be a separate step performed by the gbasedbt user. Other installation workflows may handle some configuration or initialization tasks automatically.

Always check what the selected installation procedure has already completed before running additional initialization commands.

Q5: When Should I Use Silent Installation?

Silent installation is particularly useful in three scenarios.

Batch deployment: Install GBase Database across multiple servers using a standardized response file and deployment procedure.

Automation and CI/CD pipelines: Integrate database software installation into a repeatable operational workflow, with prerequisite checks and logging.

Consistent environments: Reduce differences caused by repeated manual input when development, testing, staging, or production environments require standardized installation parameters.

Silent installation does not guarantee identical environments by itself. Operating system packages, directory permissions, disk space, and port availability can still differ between servers. Validate these prerequisites before running a batch.

Final Thoughts

Understanding the response file, license acceptance, instance initialization, and deployment prerequisites makes GBase Database silent installation easier to manage.

Start with a tested response file, verify the installation on one server, and then expand to batch deployment. This approach improves repeatability while reducing the risk of spreading a configuration error across multiple machines.

title: Toán Tử (Operators) Trong Java
description:
Toán tử là những ký hiệu được sử dụng để thực hiện các phép toán và so sánh trong lập trình. Java cung cấp nhiều loại toán tử khác nhau, bao gồm: 

I. Toán tử số học (Arithmetic Operators)
II. Toán tử bit (Bitwise Operators)
III. Toán tử so sánh (Comparison Operators)
IV. Toán tử logic (Logical Operators)
V. Toán tử điều kiện (Conditional Operators)
VI. Toán tử gán (Assignment Operators)
Ảnh mô tả các loại toán tử trong java.<!--more-->

Ⅰ. Toán tử số học

Sử dụng cho các phép toán cộng, trừ, nhân, chia, modulo (lấy dư).

Toán tử

Mô tả

Ví dụ

+

Phép cộng

a + b

-

Phép trừ

a - b

*

Phép nhân

a * b

/

Phép chia

a / b

%

Phép chia lấy dư

a % b

++

Tăng thêm 1

a + 1

--

Giảm đi 1

a - 1

Ⅱ. Toán tử bit

Các toán tử bit thực hiện các phép toán trên các bit của số nguyên.

Toán tử

Mô tả

~

Phủ định NOT: Trả về giá trị phủ định của một bít. Chuyển đổi các bit 1 thành 0 và ngược lại.

&

Toán tử AND: So sánh từng bit của hai số. Kết quả là 1 chỉ khi cả hai bit đều là 1, 0 trong các trường hợp khác.

|

Toán tử OR: So sánh từng bit của hai số. Kết quả là 1 nếu một trong hai bit là 1, 0 trong trường hợp cả hai bit đều là 0.

^

Toán tử Exclusive OR: So sánh từng bit của hai số. Kết quả là 1 chỉ khi hai bit khác nhau, 0 trong trường hợp hai bit giống nhau.

>>

Dịch phải: Dịch các bit của số nguyên sang phải một số vị trí nhất định. Các bit trống được lấp bằng bit dấu (0 cho số dương và 1 cho số âm).

<<

Dịch trái: Dịch các bit của số nguyên sang trái một số vị trí nhất định. Các bit trống được lấp bằng bit 0.

Ⅲ. Toán tử so sánh

Các toán tử so sánh dùng để so sánh các giá trị và trả về kết quả dạng boolean.

Toán tử

Mô tả

Ví dụ

==

Bằng nhau

a == b

!=

Khác nhau

a != b

>

Lớn hơn

a > b

<

Nhỏ hơn

a < b

>=

Lớn hơn hoặc bằng

a >= b

<=

Nhỏ hơn hoặc bằng

a <= b

Ⅳ. Toán tử logic

Các toán tử logic làm việc với các toán hạng Boolean. Các toán tử quan hệ được sử dụng trong các cấu trúc điều khiển.

Toán tử

Mô tả

&&

Toán tử (AND) đọc là “Và”. Trả về giá trị:

True: nếu cả hai toán hạng đều là True.

False: nếu ít nhất một toán hạng là False.

||

Toán tử (OR) đọc là “Hoặc”. Trả về giá trị:

True: nếu ít nhất một toán hạng là True.

False: chỉ khi cả hai toán hạng đều là False.

^

Toán tử XOR đọc là “Hoặc ngoại trừ”. Trả về giá trị:

True: nếu chỉ một trong hai toán hạng là True.

False: nếu cả hai toán hạng đều là True hoặc cả hai đều là False.

!

Toán tử (NOT) đọc là “Không”. Trả về giá trị:

True: nếu toán hạng là False.

False: nếu toán hạng là True.

Ⅴ. Toán tử điều kiện

Toán tử điều kiện, còn được gọi là toán tử ba ngôi, là một loại toán tử đặc biệt trong Java được sử dụng để xác định điều kiện và trả về giá trị tương ứng dựa trên điều kiện đó. Nó là một cú pháp ngắn gọn để thay thế cho các câu lệnh if-else truyền thống. Bạn sử dụng cú pháp sau:

Cú Pháp 
<điều_kiện> ? <giátrị_khiđúng> : <giá_trị_khi_sai>

Giải thích các thành phần:

↳ <điều_kiện>: Biểu thức logic trả về giá trị true hoặc false.

↳ <giátrị_khiđúng>: Giá trị được trả về nếu <điều_kiện> là true.

↳ <giá_trị_khi_sai>: Giá trị được trả về nếu <điều_kiện> là false.

↳ Nếu điều kiện đúng: Trả về giá trị sau dấu ?.

↳ Nếu điều kiện sai: Trả về giá trị sau dấu :.

Main.java 
public class Main {

   public static void main(String[] args) {

      int age = 20;

      String message = (age >= 18) ? "Bạn đã đủ tuổi" : "Bạn chưa đủ tuổi";

            System.out.println(message); // In ra "Bạn đã đủ tuổi"

    }

}

Kết quả của chương trình là: 

Bạn đã đủ tuổi

Ⅵ. Toán tử gán

Toán tử gán mở rộng trong Java là những toán tử kết hợp phép toán và phép gán trong cùng một biểu thức. Giúp cho việc viết code ngắn gọn và dễ đọc hơn.

Toán tử

Mô tả

Ví dụ

=

Gán giá trị của toán hạng phải cho toán hạng trái.

c = 10

+=

Cộng và gán Thực hiện phép toán cộng giữa c và a, sau đó gán kết quả cho c.

c += a tương đương với c = c + a

-=

Trừ và gán Thực hiện phép toán trừ giữa c và a, sau đó gán kết quả cho c.

c -= a tương đương với c = c - a

*=

Nhân và gán Thực hiện phép toán nhân giữa c và a, sau đó gán kết quả cho c.

c *= a tương đương với c = c * a

/=

Chia và gán Thực hiện phép toán chia giữa c và a, sau đó gán kết quả cho c.

c /= a tương đương với c = c / a

%=

Lấy số dư và gán Thực hiện phép toán chia lấy phần dư giữa c và a, sau đó gán kết quả cho c.

c %= a tương đương với c = c % a

&=

AND và gán Thực hiện phép toán bitwise AND giữa c và a, sau đó gán kết quả cho c.

c &= a tương đương với c = c & a

^=

XOR và gán Thực hiện phép toán bitwise XOR giữa c và a, sau đó gán kết quả cho c

c ^= a tương đương với c = c ^ a

<<=

Dịch trái và gán Dịch trái c với số bit bằng giá trị của a, sau đó gán kết quả cho c

c <<= a tương đương với c = c << a

>>=

Dịch phải và gán Dịch phải c với số bit bằng giá trị của a, sau đó gán kết quả cho c

c >>= a tương đương với c = c >> a

title: Deep Dive: ITR Filing Optimization in DoAide TaxFile
description:
Problem

In India, taxpayers must choose between the old tax regime, which offers a range of deductions, and the new regime, which provides lower tax rates but no deductions. Selecting the optimal regime requires juggling multiple variables: gross income, HRA, capital gains, and specific deductions such as Section 80C and 80D. Manual calculation is error‑prone and time‑consuming, especially for freelancers and first‑time ITR filers.

DoAide TaxFile solves this by presenting a side‑by‑side comparison of the two regimes. The tool calculates the tax payable under each regime based on user‑entered data and displays the difference, allowing the user to see which option saves more money. This is where itr filing pays off in practice.

How It Works

The comparison feature is built around a simple FastAPI endpoint that accepts a JSON payload describing the taxpayer’s financial profile. The payload includes:

  • Gross annual income
  • HRA received and rent paid
  • Capital gains
  • Deductions claimed under Section 80C, 80D, and other applicable sections

The API validates the payload with Pydantic models, queries a PostgreSQL database for current deduction limits, and then performs the tax calculation using the tax slabs defined by the Income Tax Department. The result is a JSON object containing the tax payable under both regimes.

# app/api/compare.py
from fastapi import APIRouter
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from typing import Optional

router = APIRouter()

class RegimeRequest(BaseModel):
    income: float = Field(..., gt=0)
    hra: float = Field(0)
    rent: float = Field(0)
    capital_gains: float = Field(0)
    deductions_80c: Optional[float] = Field(0)
    deductions_80d: Optional[float] = Field(0)

@router.post("/compare-regime")
async def compare_regime(req: RegimeRequest):
    # tax calculation logic omitted for brevity
    old_tax = calculate_old(req)
    new_tax = calculate_new(req)
    return {"old": old_tax, "new": new_tax}

The calculate_old function applies the standard deduction, HRA exemption rules, and Section 80C/80D limits pulled from a deductions table in PostgreSQL. The calculate_new function applies the lower tax slabs and skips all deductions. Getting itr filing right early saves rework later.

On the front end, a React component built with Vite fetches the API and renders a comparison table. The component uses useState to hold the result and a simple fetch call to submit the form.

// src/components/RegimeCompare.jsx
import { useState } from "react";

export default function RegimeCompare() {
  const [payload, setPayload] = useState({
    income: 0,
    hra: 0,
    rent: 0,
    capital_gains: 0,
    deductions_80c: 0,
    deductions_80d: 0,
  });
  const [result, setResult] = useState(null);

  const handleSubmit = async (e) => {
    e.preventDefault();
    const res = await fetch("/api/compare-regime", {
      method: "POST",
      headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
      body: JSON.stringify(payload),
    });
    const data = await res.json();
    setResult(data);
  };

  return (
    <form onSubmit={handleSubmit}>
      {/* form fields omitted for brevity */}
      <button type="submit">Compare Regimes</button>
      {result && (
        <table>
          <thead>
            <tr>
              <th>Regime</th>
              <th>Tax Payable (₹)</th>
            </tr>
          </thead>
          <tbody>
            <tr>
              <td>Old</td>
              <td>{result.old}</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
              <td>New</td>
              <td>{result.new}</td>
            </tr>
          </tbody>
        </table>
      )}
    </form>
  );
}

The component is styled with Tailwind CSS, ensuring a responsive layout that works on both desktop and mobile devices. Good itr filing keeps the rest of the workflow predictable.

User Experience

When a user navigates to the Compare Regimes page, they first see a concise explanation of the two tax regimes. Below that is a form with labeled inputs for each financial parameter. As the user types, the form state updates in real time. Upon submission, the page displays a table comparing the tax payable under the old and new regimes.

If the old regime is cheaper, the table highlights the savings and suggests which deductions are most valuable. If the new regime is better, the table shows the lower tax amount and indicates that the user can forego deductions. The interface also provides a link to the Tax Saving Tips blog post for deeper guidance.

Implementation Details

  • Backend: FastAPI (Python 3.12), Pydantic for request validation, SQLAlchemy for database access, PostgreSQL for storing deduction limits.
  • Frontend: React 18, Vite for bundling, Tailwind CSS for styling, and the native fetch API for communication.
  • Deployment: The app is containerized with Docker and deployed to a cloud platform that scales horizontally. The API uses route‑level code splitting to keep the bundle size small, and an error boundary captures any runtime errors.
  • SEO: Each route is prerendered with its own <head> section, canonical tags, and JSON‑LD, ensuring the old vs new tax regime page ranks for relevant searches.

Conclusion

The old‑vs‑new regime comparison tool removes a significant barrier to efficient ITR filing. By automating the calculation and presenting the results in a clear, side‑by‑side format, DoAide TaxFile empowers Indian salaried professionals, freelancers, and first‑time filers to make data‑driven decisions. The underlying FastAPI/React architecture makes the feature reliable, maintainable, and easy to extend with additional tax rules in the future.

Further Reading

  • Marginal relief at ₹12L article
  • Delayed refund walkthrough

These resources are available in the blog section, which is automatically included in the sitemap for better discoverability.

title: Your HTML Pages Can Animate Like This Now! (No JavaScript Required)
description:
When navigating between HTML pages on traditional multi-page applications (MPAs), the browser reloads the page, causing an abrupt white flash or jump. For years, achieving fluid transitions meant building a Single Page Application (SPA) with React, Vue, or heavy client-side routing libraries.

That is no longer required. Modern browsers now support Native Cross-Document View Transitions, allowing smooth animations between separate, real HTML files using pure CSS.

In this tutorial, we will turn a multi-page luxury automotive site (Orion Motors) into an app-like experience with zero custom JavaScript.

1. The Core Rule: @view-transition

To allow separate HTML documents to participate in a cross-document view transition, both the outgoing and incoming pages must opt in.

If all your HTML pages share a single stylesheet (e.g., styles.css), you only need to write this single rule:

@view-transition {
  navigation: auto;
}

Note: This rule enables native cross-document transitions for eligible, same-origin navigations.

2. Customizing Global Page Transitions

When a view transition occurs, the browser creates temporary pseudo-elements representing the outgoing state (::view-transition-old(root)) and the incoming state (::view-transition-new(root)).

We can apply custom keyframe animations to these pseudo-elements to control our exit and entry effects:

/* Target the outgoing page */
::view-transition-old(root) {
  animation: 0.36s ease-in pageOut;
}

/* Target the incoming page */
::view-transition-new(root) {
  animation: 0.48s cubic-bezier(0.22, 1, 0.36, 1) pageIn;
}

/* Keyframe Animations */
@keyframes pageOut {
  to {
    opacity: 0;
    filter: blur(4px);
    transform: scale(0.98);
  }
}

@keyframes pageIn {
  from {
    opacity: 0;
    filter: blur(4px);
    transform: translateY(12px);
  }
  to {
    opacity: 1;
    filter: blur(0);
    transform: translateY(0);
  }
}

3. Shared Element Transitions with view-transition-name

Animating whole pages is great, but modern app UI relies on shared elements—like an image on a product card morphing smoothly into the main hero image of a detail page.

To achieve this:

  1. Give the element on Page A and the corresponding element on Page B the exact same view-transition-name.
  2. Ensure each name is unique per rendered page. 
/* Orion V12 Car Model */
.car-v12 {
  view-transition-name: orion-v12;
}

/* Orion S9 Car Model */
.car-s9 {
  view-transition-name: orion-s9;
}

/* Orion E7 Car Model */
.car-e7 {
  view-transition-name: orion-e7;
}

Refining Movement with ::view-transition-group

You can target the container managing the named transition (::view-transition-group) to customize timing, curves, and physics:

::view-transition-group(orion-v12),
::view-transition-group(orion-s9),
::view-transition-group(orion-e7) {
  animation-duration: 0.72s;
  animation-timing-function: cubic-bezier(0.16, 1, 0.3, 1);
}

Key Takeaways

  • @view-transition { navigation: auto; } enables native cross-document transitions across separate same-origin HTML files.
  • Use ::view-transition-old(root) and ::view-transition-new(root) to customize whole-page exit and entry styles.
  • Assign identical view-transition-name values to elements across pages to seamlessly morph images, headings, and cards.
  • Keep your architecture clean, fast, and accessible without shipping heavy client-side JavaScript routers.

Take Your CSS to the Next Level 🚀

If you want to build clean, responsive layouts like a senior developer even faster, I packaged these architectural patterns into a practical resource:

👉 Grab the Guide: Build Any Responsive Layout with CSS Grid & Flexbox

It is designed to take you from layout confusion to confidently building any complex layout you see online!

title: ART-MPG: Autoregressive R/T Manifold Path Guiding
description:
arXiv:2610.29049v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Specular chains concentrate important transport in small regions of path space and the structure depends on chain topology. We introduce ART-MPG, a compact neural model that samples chain length, an autoregressive reflection/transmission (R/T) string, and a direction from a topology-conditioned four-component von Mises-Fisher (vMF) mixture. We extend the repeated trial weighting in Manifold Path Guiding (MPG) by conditioning retry sampling on both chain length and the sampled R/T string, accounting for its known mass outside the stochastic re-hit trials. For a fixed proposal and target chain, this preserves the ideal expectation while reducing the expected retry count and reciprocal-estimator variance compared with retries conditioned on chain length alone. We distinguish the formal unbiasedness result from the capped and clamped renderer used in experiments. We evaluate fourteen scenes across a range of samples per pixel (SPP) against existing online and offline rendering algorithms. Our method consistently produces lower mean squared error at equal SPP than the online and offline baselines, with lower standard deviation across runs.

title: Combating Catastrophic Forgetting in Continual Domain Adaptation via Knowledge Recasting
description:
arXiv:2610.28892v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Adapting language models to new domains during post-training risks degrading previously acquired capabilities, a phenomenon commonly known as catastrophic forgetting. Existing mitigation methods largely treat forgetting as a consequence of excessive model drift. They therefore constrain updates by preserving old outputs, replaying old data, or regularizing changes to parameters and representations so that the updated model remains close to its previous state. We take a different view: Rather than pulling the updated model back toward its old state, we translate the new domain into the model's pre-existing knowledge space, making unfamiliar knowledge learnable through familiar procedures. Therefore, we propose Skill Schema Transport (SST), a post-training framework that transports new knowledge into the model's existing skill space. SST abstracts each example type into a skill schema, preserving its essential operations, dependencies, and verification steps while removing domain-specific surface forms. By recasting new examples as instances of reusable procedures, SST turns knowledge update from trajectory memorization into procedural reuse. In continual domain adaptation settings, SST consistently reduces forgetting while improving generalization to related tasks. Across two 3B instruction-tuned backbones, SST improves average final performance on streamed domains by 2.53 to 5.75 points over sequential post-training. It also lowers max-drop forgetting in all evaluated settings, with the largest reduction from 42.41 to 7.10 points on the Qwen-3B MATH stream, while substantially recovering the OOD degradation induced by sequential updates.

title: DriftNeRF: Cross-Ray Density Drifting for Sparse-View Neural Radiance Fields
description:
arXiv:2610.29106v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) synthesize photorealistic novel views from dense image collections, but degrade sharply when few views are available. We attribute a specific, measurable defect to the objective itself: the rendering loss is a sum over independent rays and contains no term comparing densities that different rays assign to the same region of space, so nearby 3D points can settle on contradictory densities while every training pixel is reproduced correctly. We make this quantity explicit by measuring cross-ray density disagreement directly during training, and show that it stays high in vanilla NeRF, falls only incidentally under frequency-based regularization, and moves together with held-out quality in the sparse regime. We then close the gap with DriftNeRF, a drop-in regularizer that instantiates the drifting-field template on density samples: a masked exponential kernel aggregates densities from nearby points on other rays into a stop-gradient consensus target, and the resulting drifting field penalizes unsupported disagreement while leaving agreed-upon boundaries intact. The regularizer reads only sampled positions, ray identifiers, and predicted densities, so it requires no pretrained model, external geometry, or additional images, and transfers across field parameterizations. On NeRF-Synthetic it reduces residual disagreement by an order of magnitude, and across NeRF-Synthetic, DTU, and LLFF it improves 3-view PSNR over the strongest MLP-NeRF baseline by 0.42-0.65 dB and remains competitive with sparse-view Gaussian pipelines under a matched protocol without their depth, flow, or covisibility preprocessing.

title: DetM-Tracker: Deterministic and Memory-Efficient VIS for Autonomous Industrial Inspection
description:
arXiv:2610.29212v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Autonomous industrial inspection requires strictly deterministic real-time inference under tight memory and computational constraints. However, existing Video Instance Segmentation (VIS) models suffer from prohibitive scaling: dense temporal memory grows with spatial resolution and sequence length, while fixed-capacity decoders fail to exploit the inherent sparsity of industrial scenes, creating a practical memory wall on resource-constrained edge platforms. We present DetM-Tracker, a streamlined VIS framework for autonomous industrial inspection, where target objects often exhibit highly similar appearance under constrained "micro" fields of view. DetM-Tracker eliminates architectural redundancy through three synergistic components: (1) Compact Scalar Memory, which condenses high-dimensional instance features into four-scalar descriptors, reducing temporal memory complexity from $O(T \cdot N \cdot R)$ to $O(T \cdot \hat{N})$. This mechanism effectively compresses frame-level representations into a bank of active instances, where $R$ denotes resolution, $N$ and $\hat{N}$ represent global and window-specific instance counts, respectively and $T$ the temporal window size; and (2) Dynamic Instance Channels, which adaptively allocate query capacity according to the actual number of visible objects; and (3) Entropy-Gated Skip Connection, which concentrates computational budget on high-uncertainty spatial regions to refine object boundaries in a single forward pass without auxiliary refinement heads. Our approach effectively bridges the gap between modern VIS models and the practical demands of industrial edge deployment, reducing inference latency by approximately 20$\times$ and VRAM consumption by 6$\times$ compared to state-of-the-art dense-feature baselines.

title: Act on Your Behalf, Beyond Your Authorization: Benchmarking LLM Agent Authorization Alignment
description:
arXiv:2610.27548v2 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: When an LLM agent acts on behalf of a user, it is expected to act within the authorization scope the user grants. Existing agent evaluations largely measure task completion or harmful consequences and can therefore overlook actions that violate this delegation without producing conventional safety or privacy harms. We introduce AuthorizationBench, a benchmark of authorization alignment grounded in documented real-world cases. A scalable construction pipeline produces 286 executable tasks spanning situational triggers, the presence or absence of direct harmful consequences, and ten application domains. We execute every task with four models at two reasoning-effort settings across three agent harnesses in an authorization-aware sandbox that keeps authorized and out-of-authorization paths executable and observable, yielding 6,864 trajectories. Agents act out of authorization in 19.2% of trajectories, with rates ranging from 10.5% to 26.6% across the 24 configurations. Task completion does not imply authorization. Increasing reasoning effort leaves the aggregate rate nearly unchanged, with effects varying across models. On controlled pairs, agents act out of authorization at similar rates with (17.9%) and without (20.8%) direct harmful consequences, and more often under benign pressures than malicious injections (23.5% versus 17.6%, p=0.002). Our results show that task capability, additional reasoning, and consequence-oriented safety evaluation do not by themselves ensure authorization alignment. Moreover, agents that consult the principal before completing a task exhibit lower rates of out-of-authorization behavior (14.0% versus 21.6%, p<0.001), pointing to a tension between agent autonomy and preserving users' decision authority that calls for further human-centered study. Dataset and code are available at https://github.com/PEACH-Research-Lab/AuthorizationBench .

title: How to Test an LLM App: Evals That Run in CI
description:
Collect about 50 real inputs, label each with the behaviour you expect instead of an exact answer, check what you can with plain code, use an LLM judge only for the rest and calibrate it against your own labels, then run the whole set on every pull request. That is enough to catch most regressions before users do.

Why a normal test suite is not enough

A unit test says the same thing every time. A language model does not. You can change one sentence in a prompt, swap a model version, or let a provider update weights quietly, and the feature still returns something that looks fine. Nothing crashes. The answers just get a little worse, and you find out from a user.

The fix people keep landing on is an eval set: a fixed collection of inputs you run through the feature and score every time something changes. It is the same idea as a test suite, with scoring instead of exact matches.

Start with about 50 real inputs

Several practitioner guides suggest starting small, somewhere between 30 and 60 cases. What matters more than the count is where the cases come from. Real messages from real users beat inputs that another model invented, because invented inputs tend to be tidy and real ones are not. If the feature is not live yet, ask a few people who would use it to write the messages they would actually send.

Label each case with the behaviour you expect. Refuse. Call this tool. Ask a clarifying question. Answer from the supplied document. Labels like these survive a prompt rewrite, while an exact expected sentence breaks the first time the wording changes. Once the feature is live, replace a slice of the set each quarter with real failures so it does not go stale.

Use plain code wherever it works

A surprising number of checks need no model at all. Is the output valid JSON? Does it match the schema? Did the right tool get called with the right arguments? Does the reply mention a forbidden word, or leak a string it should never contain? One practitioner reports that roughly a third to 40 percent of their checks are this kind, and another puts it closer to 60 or 70 percent for agents. The exact share depends on the product, but the direction is the same. These checks are fast, free and never disagree with themselves.

Promptfoo is a free open source runner that handles both kinds of check. A small config looks like this:

# promptfooconfig.yaml
prompts:
  - 'Convert the following English text to {{language}}: {{input}}'

providers:
  - openai:gpt-6-sol

tests:
  - vars:
      language: French
      input: Hello world
    assert:
      - type: contains
        value: 'Bonjour le monde'

  - vars:
      language: Spanish
      input: Where is the library?
    assert:
      - type: llm-rubric
        value: Output is a Spanish translation that asks where the library is

You run it with npx promptfoo@latest eval and open the results with npx promptfoo@latest view. The first test uses a plain substring check. The second hands a written rule to a judge model, which brings us to the part people get wrong.

Calibrate the judge before you trust it

An LLM judge is just another model with opinions. Before its scores gate anything, label about 50 cases yourself, let the judge score the same cases, and compare. One guide treats a disagreement rate above about 15 percent as a sign that the judge prompt needs work, and reports reaching around 91 percent agreement after a few hours of tuning. Repeat the check when the judge model changes.

If you compare two answers with a judge, run each pair twice with the order swapped and only count the results that agree. Models have a habit of favouring whichever answer they see first.

Make it a gate, then watch production

Promptfoo ships a GitHub Action that runs the eval on every pull request and posts the result as a comment. This is the workflow from its documentation. Save it under .github/workflows/ and add OPENAI_API_KEY as a repository secret (the token for comments is supplied automatically):

name: Prompt Evaluation

on:
  pull_request:
    paths:
      - 'prompts/**'

jobs:
  evaluate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      pull-requests: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '24'
      - uses: promptfoo/promptfoo-action@v1
        with:
          openai-api-key: ${{ secrets.OPENAI_API_KEY }}
          github-token: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
          prompts: 'prompts/**/*.json'
          config: 'prompts/promptfooconfig.yaml'

Change the paths to match your project. Then decide the rule: fail the build when an important score drops by more than a small margin. The same guide quotes a margin of 2 points, and a cost of about 42 cents and 90 seconds per run for its own suite. Your numbers will differ, but a few cases and a cheap model keep it small.

A fixed set only catches problems you already thought of. Sampling a small slice of yesterday’s real conversations and scoring them each night catches drift that the fixed set misses. Post the result somewhere the team will actually look. A score in a dashboard nobody opens does not count as having evals.

A one week plan

  • Day 1 and 2: collect 30 to 50 real inputs and write the expected behaviour next to each.
  • Day 3: write the plain code checks. Schema, tool name, forbidden strings.
  • Day 4: add a judge rubric for what code cannot check, then compare it with your own labels.
  • Day 5: add the run to CI and set the failure margin.
  • Afterwards: add every real failure you meet as a new case.

None of this needs a platform or a budget. It needs a file of cases and the habit of adding to it whenever something goes wrong.

Sources

The numbers above are rules of thumb from practitioner write ups, not benchmarks. See LLM Evals in 2026: A Practitioner’s Field Guide for the set size, judge agreement and CI figures, and the Promptfoo getting started guide for the config format.

Originally published at https://ahmadhsn1.github.io/blog/how-to-test-llm-app-evals-ci/

title: norregel: a preregistered benchmark of dated numeric values in Norwegian law
description:
arXiv:2610.29207v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: norregel asks language models for numeric values in Norwegian statutes, regulations and parliamentary decisions (NOK amounts, percentages, multiples of the National Insurance basic amount (G) and age limits), each at a stated date. The 916 items were extracted mechanically from Lovdata's open data, and each carries the dated history of its provision, so an answer can be classed as correct, outdated, wrong or uninterpretable. We report a first and a second preregistered run on the same items. In the first run (five models, listed publicly only after local analysis), H1, that outdated answers are more frequent for values that took effect after a model's cutoff, could not be tested in substance, and H2 and H3 were inconclusive; Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 4.6 answered 46.7% and 40.2% of the 880 primary items correctly. The second run was preregistered and published before any of its calls, and eight models were analysed. Its pooled primary test supported H1 under the preregistered decision rule (d = 17.8 percentage points, 95% interval [7.7, 28.9], p = 0.0001). In the preregistered sensitivity analysis S8, which counts as outdated only the most recent value that differs from the key, d was 3.9 [-3.6, 12.7] (p = 0.1754), an interval that contains 0. H1 was supported in every other preregistered sensitivity analysis, but S8 is the only one that gives both groups one target value, so we do not regard the support for H1 as robust. The share of outdated answers equal to that most recent value (H2) was 56.1% [46.6, 65.0], an interval that contains 0.5, and the pooled test of a lower share correct in Nynorsk than in Bokm{\aa}l (H3) was inconclusive. Several models, among them Haiku 4.5, gave mostly uninterpretable answers. Items and keys are withheld; item IDs, per-answer classes, code and results are on Zenodo.

title: Your Retry Policy Is Making Production Outages Worse
description:
When a downstream database or microservice experiences a brief latency spike, your application's retry logic is supposed to mask the glitch. Instead, in most production architectures, retries are the exact mechanism that turns a 5-second hiccup into a 45-minute cascading outage.

As documented in the AWS Builders' Library, retries are inherently selfish: when a client retries a failed call, it asserts that its request is important enough to demand more resources from a dependency that is already struggling to survive.

If your HTTP client uses fixed delays, standard exponential backoff without jitter, or retries across multiple layers of your stack, you haven't built resilience—you've built a synchronized load amplifier.

The Problem: Synchronized Herds and Layered Multiplication

Most engineers know that immediate retries (delay = 0) are dangerous, so they configure standard exponential backoff: wait 1s, then 2s, then 4s.

However, as Marc Brooker demonstrated in the AWS Architecture Blog research on Exponential Backoff and Jitter, standard exponential backoff only reduces how often a single client retries—it does not break synchronization across clients.

When a downstream service stalls for 500ms, 1,000 concurrent requests fail at the exact same millisecond:

  1. All 1,000 clients sleep for 1000ms (2^0 * 1000).
  2. Exactly one second later, all 1,000 clients wake up in lockstep and hammer the recovering server simultaneously, alongside normal incoming traffic.
  3. The server collapses again, and the synchronized wave repeats at 2000ms and 4000ms.

The Multiplicative Retry Trap: In a 5-tier microservice call chain where each service is configured with just 3 retries (1 initial + 3 retries = 4 attempts per hop), a single database timeout at the bottom triggers 4^4 = 256 requests (or up to 243x load at 3 attempts per layer across 5 layers) for a single user click.

The Common Mistake: Un-Jittered Backoff and Blind Error Retries

Consider a typical production wrapper around an HTTP or RPC call that passes most code reviews without question:

// ❌ Looks resilient, but causes synchronized retry storms under load
export async function fetchOrderDetails(orderId: string): Promise<Order> {
  const maxRetries = 3;
  const baseDelayMs = 1000;

  for (let attempt = 0; attempt <= maxRetries; attempt++) {
    try {
      const response = await httpClient.get(`/orders/${orderId}`, {
        timeout: 2000,
      });
      return response.data;
    } catch (error: any) {
      if (attempt === maxRetries) {
        throw error;
      }
      // 1. Retries ALL errors (including 400 Bad Request or 401 Unauthorized)
      // 2. Deterministic exponential delay keeps failing clients synchronized
      // 3. No global cap on how many retries the process is firing right now
      const delay = baseDelayMs * Math.pow(2, attempt);
      await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delay));
    }
  }
  throw new Error("Unreachable");
}

The Consequence in Production

When a deployment or database lock causes latency to cross the 2000ms timeout threshold:

  • Calling instances keep open sockets waiting, then fire synchronized retry waves at +1s, +2s, and +4s.
  • Even if you restart the overloaded downstream pods, the backlog of in-flight retries immediately crushes the new instances before their caches warm up—a classic positive feedback loop described in Google's SRE Book on Addressing Cascading Failures.

The Improved Approach: Full Jitter + Retry Budgets

To make retries safe in production, you need three controls working together:

  1. Full Jitter: Randomize the delay between 0 and the exponential cap (sleep = random(0, min(cap, base * 2^attempt))) to flatten synchronized spikes into a smooth, constant arrival rate.
  2. Strict Retryability Filtering: Only retry transient transport errors or explicit 429 / 503 statuses (respecting Retry-After headers when present).
  3. A Local Retry Budget (Token Bucket): Cap retries at a maximum percentage (e.g., 10%) of total outbound traffic. If the dependency is completely down, the budget drains and clients fail fast instead of amplifying the outage. 
// ✅ Production-safe: Full Jitter, Retry Budget (10% cap), and transient filtering
class RetryBudget {
  private tokens = 100;
  private readonly maxTokens = 100;
  private readonly retryCost = 10; // 1 retry costs 10x what a normal request deposits

  recordRequest(): void {
    this.tokens = Math.min(this.maxTokens, this.tokens + 1);
  }

  tryAcquireRetry(): boolean {
    if (this.tokens >= this.retryCost) {
      this.tokens -= this.retryCost;
      return true;
    }
    return false;
  }
}

const orderServiceBudget = new RetryBudget();

function isTransientError(status?: number, code?: string): boolean {
  if (code === "ECONNRESET" || code === "ETIMEDOUT") return true;
  return status === 429 || status === 502 || status === 503 || status === 504;
}

export async function fetchOrderDetailsSafe(orderId: string): Promise<Order> {
  const maxRetries = 3;
  const baseDelayMs = 200;
  const maxCapMs = 5000;

  orderServiceBudget.recordRequest();

  for (let attempt = 0; attempt <= maxRetries; attempt++) {
    try {
      const response = await httpClient.get(`/orders/${orderId}`, {
        timeout: 2000,
      });
      return response.data;
    } catch (error: any) {
      const status = error.response?.status;
      const canRetry =
        attempt < maxRetries &&
        isTransientError(status, error.code) &&
        orderServiceBudget.tryAcquireRetry();

      if (!canRetry) {
        throw error; // Fail fast if permanent error or retry budget is exhausted
      }

      // Full Jitter formula: random(0, min(cap, base * 2^attempt))
      const expCap = Math.min(maxCapMs, baseDelayMs * Math.pow(2, attempt));
      const fullJitterDelay = Math.floor(Math.random() * expCap);

      await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, fullJitterDelay));
    }
  }
  throw new Error("Unreachable");
}

Click to compare Full Jitter vs. Equal Jitter vs. Decorrelated Jitter
In AWS's simulation of 100 contending clients, Full Jitter reduced total server calls by more than 50% compared to standard exponential backoff while finishing faster. Here is when to pick each variant:
  • Full Jitter (random(0, min(cap, base * 2^attempt))): Best default choice. Lowest total server work and fastest completion time under high contention.
  • Equal Jitter (temp / 2 + random(0, temp / 2)): Guarantees a minimum sleep window (temp / 2) so a client never retries at 0ms, while still de-synchronizing the herd.
  • Decorrelated Jitter (min(cap, random(base, prevSleep * 3))): Stateless-free alternative that scales sleep based on the previous random wait time rather than a strict power of two.

Production Resilience Checklist

Before shipping any client SDK, queue consumer, or API gateway rule, verify your retry policy against these five rules:

  • [ ] Retry at a single layer in the stack: Disable automatic retries in inner microservice hops and ORM drivers if your API gateway or top-level caller already retries; let lower layers fail fast.
  • [ ] Always apply Full Jitter: Never deploy fixed-interval or pure 2^n backoff in systems with more than one concurrent caller.
  • [ ] Enforce a 10% Retry Budget: Use a token bucket so that if more than 10% of requests are failing, clients stop retrying and shed load immediately.
  • [ ] Require Idempotency Keys for mutations: Never enable automatic retries on POST or PATCH endpoints unless an idempotency key is passed and enforced atomically at the storage layer.
  • [ ] Propagate deadlines across hops: If an incoming request has a 2000ms timeout and already spent 1800ms in upstream processing, don't fire a retry that takes another 1500ms after the user has already disconnected.

The Takeaway

Retries are only effective when failures are transient, isolated, and rare. The moment a failure becomes systemic—such as a saturated connection pool or a degraded database replica—naive retries turn your own microservices into an internal botnet. Replace deterministic backoff with Full Jitter, restrict retries to a single architectural layer, and enforce a Retry Budget so your system knows when to stop digging.

Have you ever experienced a self-inflicted retry storm in production, and do you enforce retry budgets at the service mesh/gateway level or inside application code?

Sources & Further Reading

  • Exponential Backoff And Jitter – AWS Architecture Blog (Marc Brooker)
  • Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter – Amazon Builders' Library
  • Addressing Cascading Failures – Google Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) Book

title: Liquid Glass: Physical Optical Lensing & Glassmorphism UI Engine for Linux in Rust (WGPU)
description:
Most "frosted glass" or "glassmorphism" implementations on the web and Linux desktops boil down to a simple 2D box-blur shader layered over a background capture.

While that looks pleasant, it isn’t how real glass behaves. Real optical glass has curvature, refraction, chromatic dispersion (wavelength splitting), surface tension, and directional specular sheen.

Over the last few weeks, I’ve been building Liquid Glass: an open-source rendering engine and UI framework written in Rust, WGPU, and WGSL that brings true physical optical glass simulation to Linux desktop apps and Wayland widgets.

🔬 The Optical Physics Under the Hood

Instead of drawing flat quads with blurred backdrops, Liquid Glass computes analytical Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) per fragment:

1. Plano-Convex Snell Refraction

We compute the surface height $h(p)$ and its normal gradient $\nabla h(p)$ analytically across the geometry boundary:
$$N = \text{normalize}\begin{pmatrix} -\nabla h_x \ -\nabla h_y \ 1 \end{pmatrix}$$

Using Snell's Law ($IOR = 1.33 - 1.52$), light rays bend towards the optical center, producing true optical barrel distortion and magnification of underlying desktop wallpapers.

2. Spectral Chromatic Dispersion

Real glass splits white light into spectral wavelengths at curved meniscus boundaries. Liquid Glass offsets red, green, and blue texture sample coordinates proportionally to the surface refraction angle:

let r_offset = refract_vec * (1.0 - dispersion);
let g_offset = refract_vec;
let b_offset = refract_vec * (1.0 + dispersion);

This gives chamfered edges and button rims an unmistakable physical glow.

3. Directional Solar Rim Lighting & Specular Sheen

A dual-lobe Blinn-Phong specular reflection catches a simulated directional sunlight vector ([-0.6, -0.8]), producing bright 1.5px grazing meniscus catches.

⚡ Performance: 0.0% CPU When Idle

A common pitfall with custom Linux widgets and shaders is battery drain from uncapped render loops. Liquid Glass was architected for zero idle overhead:

  1. Kernel epoll_wait Blocking: When no audio is playing and no pointer is moving, the event loop stops spinning and sleeps in Wayland's event_queue.blocking_dispatch(). Top benchmark: 
   PID    USER  %CPU  %MEM  COMMAND
   241729 zius   0.0   1.2  glass-panel
  1. Single Quad Draw Call: The entire UI (capsule glass, vinyl grooves, music notes, equalizer bars, timeline, scrubber knob, transport buttons, speaker) is rendered in a single quad draw call inside WGSL.
  2. In-Memory Pre-Scaled Wallpaper Cache: Moving or dragging the widget samples wallpaper crops in sub-milliseconds without disk I/O.

🎨 Building UI Components with glass-ui

Building high-level interfaces shouldn't require writing raw WGSL shaders. The workspace includes glass-ui, providing pre-built interactive components:

  • GlassCard / GlassIsland: Physical glass containers with adjustable corner radius, curvature, and bevel.
  • GlassButton: Tactile spring-animated buttons with click compression (0.94x) and smooth recovery.
  • GlassToggle: Pill switch with spring-animated knob transitions.
  • GlassSlider: Draggable timeline scrubber with track rail, active fill, and thumb. 
use glass_ui::{GlassWidget, GlassCard, GlassButton, GlassToggle, GlassSlider};

let mut widget = GlassWidget::new();

// Floating container
widget.add_card(GlassCard::island(0.1, 0.1, 0.8, 0.8).blur(32.0));

// Interactive controls
widget.add_button(GlassButton::new(0.15, 0.25, 0.30, 0.10, "Play"));
widget.add_toggle(GlassToggle::new(0.50, 0.25, 0.15, 0.08, true));
widget.add_slider(GlassSlider::new(0.15, 0.50, 0.70, 0.05, 0.65));

// In your event loop:
widget.on_pointer_move(x, y);
widget.update(dt);
let surfaces = widget.collect_surfaces();
renderer.render(&surfaces)?;

🚀 Two Running Targets

  1. Floating Wayland Desktop Island (glass-panel): Uses zwlr_layer_shell_v1 on Hyprland/wlroots to float transparently over your wallpaper with real-time MPRIS media playback control. 
   cargo run -p glass-panel --release
  1. Cross-Platform Desktop Window (simple-window): Uses standard winit and wgpu to render a windowed UI component playground. 
   cargo run -p simple-window

🤝 Open Source & Contributing

We'd love community help expanding this into a full-featured desktop UI ecosystem:

  • Building new glass-ui components (GlassTextInput, GlassTooltip, GlassContextMenu).
  • Supporting more compositor protocols (KDE KWin blur, COSMIC compositor).

  • New showcase widgets (weather, clock, system monitor).

title: How to get Amazon's full Best Sellers top 100 for any category and marketplace as JSON
description:
I built this actor; it's a paid tool on Apify with a free trial credit.

Amazon's Best Sellers pages are the simplest public signal of what's selling: a top 100 per category, per marketplace, refreshed hourly. They're also annoying to collect. Each page only renders 30 of its 50 products and loads the other 20 when you scroll, the two pages live behind a pg= parameter, prices come in a different format on every marketplace, and Amazon blocks most datacenter IPs after a few requests.

I'm an 18-year-old engineering student, and I wrapped all of that in an actor called Amazon Best Sellers Scraper. This post shows how to call it from Python and Node, what the data looks like, and one small project: a daily rank tracker for a category.

How it works, briefly

An Amazon list page embeds all 50 ASINs of the page with their ranks in a data attribute and renders the first 30 product cards. The other 20 come from a background call the page's own script makes when you scroll; the actor makes the same call on the same session, so you get all 50 per page and all 100 per list. Prices are parsed per locale ($1,234.56 and 20,46 € both work), the currency is set per marketplace, and the left-hand menu is read so you can pull every subcategory in one run. No browser; plain HTTP through residential proxies in the marketplace's country.

Python example 

pip install apify-client

from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient("<YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN>")

run = client.actor("rel8ble/amazon-bestsellers-scraper").call(run_input={
    "categoryUrls": [
        "https://www.amazon.com/Best-Sellers-Electronics/zgbs/electronics/",
        "https://www.amazon.de/gp/new-releases/ce-de/",
    ],
    "maxItemsPerList": 100,
})

for p in client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items():
    print(p["marketplace"], p["rank"], p["asin"], p["price"], p["currency"], p["rating"], p["title"][:60])

Node example 

npm install apify-client

import { ApifyClient } from 'apify-client';

const client = new ApifyClient({ token: '<YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN>' });

const run = await client.actor('rel8ble/amazon-bestsellers-scraper').call({
    categoryIds: ['electronics'],
    domain: 'amazon.co.uk',
    listType: 'bestsellers',
    maxItemsPerList: 50,
    includeSubcategories: true,
});

const { items } = await client.dataset(run.defaultDatasetId).listItems();
for (const p of items) console.log(p.listName, p.rank, p.asin, p.price, p.currency, p.title);

What a result looks like 

{
    "rank": 1,
    "asin": "B08JHCVHTY",
    "title": "blink plus plan with monthly auto-renewal",
    "price": 11.99,
    "priceText": "$11.99",
    "currency": "USD",
    "rating": 4.4,
    "ratingsCount": 280900,
    "imageUrl": "https://images-na.ssl-images-amazon.com/images/I/31YHGbJsldL._AC_UL900_SR900,600_.png",
    "url": "https://www.amazon.com/dp/B08JHCVHTY",
    "listType": "bestsellers",
    "listName": "Best Sellers in Electronics",
    "categoryId": "electronics",
    "categoryPath": "Any Department > Electronics",
    "listUrl": "https://www.amazon.com/gp/bestsellers/electronics",
    "marketplace": "amazon.com",
    "page": 1,
    "scrapedAt": "2026-10-08T00:36:48.481Z"
}

A small project: a daily rank tracker

Schedule the actor once a day on the Apify platform (Schedules tab, pick the actor, paste the input), then append each day's dataset to a local SQLite table and chart any ASIN's rank over time:

import sqlite3, datetime as dt
from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient("<YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN>")
db = sqlite3.connect("ranks.db")
db.execute("""create table if not exists ranks(
    day text, marketplace text, list_url text, asin text, rank int, price real, rating real, ratings_count int, title text,
    primary key(day, list_url, asin))""")

# Latest finished run of the actor (the scheduled one)
runs = client.actor("rel8ble/amazon-bestsellers-scraper").runs().list(desc=True, limit=1).items
dataset_id = runs[0]["defaultDatasetId"]
day = dt.date.today().isoformat()

for p in client.dataset(dataset_id).iterate_items():
    db.execute("insert or replace into ranks values (?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?)",
               (day, p["marketplace"], p["listUrl"], p["asin"], p["rank"], p["price"], p["rating"], p["ratingsCount"], p["title"]))
db.commit()

# Which products climbed the most since yesterday?
for row in db.execute("""
    select t.asin, y.rank as yesterday, t.rank as today, t.title
    from ranks t join ranks y on y.asin = t.asin and y.list_url = t.list_url and y.day = date(t.day, '-1 day')
    where t.day = ? order by (y.rank - t.rank) desc limit 10""", (day,)):
    print(row)

One list a day is 100 results, or 15 cents, so a 20-category tracker runs for about $3 a month.

Things I learned building it

  • 30 vs 50: the "missing" 20 products per page aren't on page 2, they're lazy-loaded. If you scrape the HTML only, you get 60 of the 100 and a gap at ranks 31-50 and 81-100.
  • Prices: 97% of products on a 200-item test had one. The rest are subscriptions or out-of-stock items Amazon lists without a price.
  • Movers & Shakers, Most Wished For and Most Gifted currently render without a server-side product grid, so the actor only promises Best Sellers and New Releases. URLs of the other kinds are accepted and come back empty, with the reason in the run summary.
  • Residential proxies are the default. Datacenter IPs work for a while and then hit captchas; the actor retries on a fresh session, but residential is cheaper in retries than it costs in bandwidth (about 0.5 MB per page).

If something breaks or a field is wrong, the Issues tab on the actor page reaches me directly.

Amazon Best Sellers Scraper on Apify

title: ChronoSynth: Constraint-Aware Question Synthesis over Temporal Knowledge Graphs
description:
arXiv:2610.29339v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Knowledge graph question generation (KGQG) generates natural-language questions from structured graph evidence and a target answer. When the input graph is temporal, a valid question must also preserve the answer field, time condition, reference event, and temporal order that determine the answer set. Existing KGQG methods and prompting baselines can produce fluent questions that alter these conditions, causing temporal semantic drift. This paper studies temporal KGQG as a constraint-preserving graph-to-question problem and proposes ChronoSynth, a memory-augmented and constraint-aware generation framework. ChronoSynth first constructs a Temporal Intent State to make the intended question semantics explicit. It then retrieves compatible typed question patterns from an indexed pattern memory, adapts them to the input graph, and validates the generated question. Validation feedback guides revisions when a supported inconsistency is detected. Experiments on CRONQUESTIONS and MultiTQ demonstrate state-of-the-art generation performance, with ablations supporting the contributions of its components.

title: The Best Open Source Cloud Providers in 2026
description:
The open source cloud landscape covers a lot of ground. Some platforms give you a full IaaS stack with their own API surface. Others sit on top of existing hypervisors. A few implement the AWS API so your existing tooling carries over unchanged. The right choice depends on what you're replacing, what your team already knows, and whether you can afford to rebuild your operational model from scratch.

This is a practical comparison of the main options in 2026, written from our own vantage point as one of them. We've tried to be honest about where each tool fits and where it doesn't.

OpenStack

OpenStack is the oldest and most battle-tested open source cloud platform available. It covers compute (Nova), object storage (Swift), networking (Neutron), block storage (Cinder), identity (Keystone), and a dozen other services, each maintained as a separate project under the OpenStack Foundation. Telecoms, national research networks, and large enterprises run it in production at serious scale.

The operational complexity is real. Deploying OpenStack on anything other than a managed distribution requires substantial expertise, and keeping it running requires a dedicated team. If you are evaluating OpenStack for a team of five engineers, the maintenance overhead will consume more capacity than the platform returns.

OpenStack has its own API surface. Your AWS CLI, Terraform AWS provider, and eksctl workflows do not carry over. Teams switching from AWS need to learn a new operational model.

Best fit: Large organisations with dedicated infrastructure teams who need maximum flexibility and have no AWS tooling dependency.

Apache CloudStack

CloudStack is a mature IaaS platform originally developed by Cloud.com, open-sourced in 2010, and now under the Apache Foundation. It is simpler to deploy and operate than OpenStack and has been used by several commercial cloud providers as the underlying platform. The API is CloudStack's own, with some AWS EC2 API compatibility that covers basic instance management but not the full surface.

The community is smaller than OpenStack's and development pace has slowed, but the platform is stable and well-understood. For teams that need a proven IaaS layer without OpenStack's operational overhead, CloudStack is worth evaluating.

Best fit: Mid-size organisations building an internal cloud who want something more operationally accessible than OpenStack.

OpenNebula

OpenNebula is a European open source cloud platform with a strong following in HPC, research, and edge computing environments. It manages KVM, LXC, and Firecracker workloads and is designed to run on a lean footprint, making it viable on smaller hardware clusters where OpenStack would be overkill. It has its own API surface and a web interface that is considerably simpler to navigate than OpenStack's Horizon.

OpenNebula's community is smaller than either OpenStack or CloudStack, but the project is actively maintained and the documentation is good. For edge and research deployments where simplicity and low resource usage matter more than breadth of services, it is a credible choice.

Best fit: Research institutions, HPC environments, and edge deployments that need a lightweight IaaS layer.

Proxmox VE

Proxmox is a hypervisor management platform built on KVM and LXC, not a cloud platform in the IaaS sense. It gives you a web interface for managing virtual machines and containers across a cluster, along with Ceph integration for shared storage. It does not give you an API that applications call to provision infrastructure programmatically in the way that AWS, OpenStack, or CloudStack do.

Proxmox's star rose sharply after Broadcom's VMware acquisition triggered 800 to 1,500% price increases for standalone vSphere customers, and it is the most common destination for VMware refugees. The transition from vSphere to Proxmox is relatively straightforward for teams whose operational model is manual VM management through a web interface.

Teams who built their operational model on Terraform, eksctl, and the AWS CLI face a harder transition. Proxmox has no equivalent for those tools.

Best fit: Teams replacing VMware who manage VMs through a web interface rather than programmatically.

Ubicloud

Ubicloud (AGPL-3.0, Ruby, 12,300 GitHub stars) is a managed cloud service running on Hetzner and Leaseweb hardware that offers elastic compute, block storage, managed Postgres, Kubernetes, firewall, load balancer, and AI inference endpoints. Pricing runs 3 to 10x lower than equivalent AWS services, which is the primary pitch.

Ubicloud is a hosted service you access over the internet rather than software you deploy on hardware you own. For teams looking to cut their cloud bill without changing their operational model significantly, it is worth evaluating. For teams with data sovereignty requirements or air-gapped deployments, it is not the right answer because your data still lives on someone else's hardware.

Best fit: Teams on AWS who want to reduce their bill and can tolerate moving to a different hosted provider.

Spinifex

Spinifex (AGPL-3.0, Go, github.com/mulgadc/spinifex) is our product. It implements the AWS API surface — EC2, S3, IAM, EKS, ECS, ECR, VPC, EBS — on standard Linux bare metal, with no external control plane and no internet requirement.

The specific thing Spinifex does that none of the other platforms on this list do is preserve your AWS tooling investment. If your team has Terraform configs written against the AWS provider, eksctl workflows, IAM role structures, and scripts using the AWS CLI, those run against Spinifex with a single endpoint override, meaning far less rework to your operational model.

The performance case is documented in our OnLogic HX401 benchmark: CPU overhead runs 7% (sysbench single-thread: 1,358 events/s guest vs 1,456 bare metal). The docs also cover areas of active improvement.

Spinifex is the right answer for teams in air-gapped or sovereign environments, teams on edge hardware where AWS connectivity is unreliable, and teams with enough AWS tooling investment that rebuilding it on a new API surface is not a viable option. It is not the right answer for teams who need maximum breadth of services, or are primarily doing web-based VM management.

Best fit: Teams deploying to air-gapped facilities, edge hardware, or sovereign environments who have existing AWS tooling they want to preserve.

Choosing between them

The questions that narrow the field fastest:

Do you need AWS tooling compatibility? If your team has significant Terraform, eksctl, or AWS CLI investment, that eliminates OpenStack, CloudStack, OpenNebula, and Proxmox from the running. Ubicloud covers some AWS API surface but is a hosted service. Spinifex covers the core services required to run on hardware you own, with additional AWS service support added regularly.

Do you need to keep data on hardware under your direct control? That eliminates Ubicloud. The on-premise options are OpenStack, CloudStack, OpenNebula, Proxmox, and Spinifex.

Do you need to operate without internet connectivity? OpenStack can run air-gapped with sufficient effort, but it was not designed for it. Spinifex installs from a release tarball with no external dependencies and has no phone-home requirement.

Do you need to replace VMware with something familiar? Proxmox is the most direct path if your team manages VMs through a web interface. If your team provisions infrastructure programmatically, Proxmox does not cover what VMware gave you.

Given the many options for open source cloud providers, we encourage teams to research each option thoroughly to decide which option is best for them.

Full Spinifex documentation is at docs.mulgadc.com. For the other platforms: openstack.org, cloudstack.apache.org, opennebula.io, proxmox.com, ubicloud.com.

The quickest and easiest way to tell if Spinifex is the best option for you is through our hosted sandbox, which gives you 72 hours to try Spinifex without getting your own hardware involved. Sign up here: https://mulgadc.com/signup

title: Why Page Builders Ruin Custom HTML Designs (And How Zero-Wrapper Block Conversion Fixes It)
description:
Every front-end developer who has tried to bring a custom HTML/CSS mockup into WordPress has experienced the same quiet heartbreak. In the browser, the static HTML file looks razor-sharp. Ten minutes after moving it into a page builder or block converter, the navigation height is off by 6 pixels, the pricing table borders have vanished, a CSS Grid has collapsed into a single column, and half the inline SVGs refuse to scale.

Why does that happen—even when you copy the exact same CSS file into WordPress? The answer lies in DOM wrapper pollution and cascade order.

1. How Extra Wrappers Break Modern CSS

Modern CSS relies heavily on parent-child relationships: Flexbox, CSS Grid, direct child combinators (>), and adjacent sibling combinators (+). Consider a simple rule from a designer’s stylesheet:

body > header + main > .pricing-grid > article {
  display: flex;
  flex-direction: column;
  justify-content: space-between;
}

Look at what happens in a typical WordPress theme or page builder:

  • Full Site Editing wraps the page in <div class="wp-site-blocks">, wraps the header in <header class="wp-block-template-part"><header>..., and wraps the body in <div class="entry-content wp-block-post-content">. Now body > header + main never matches.
  • A page builder wraps every widget in 3 to 5 layers of .elementor-widget-container or .et_pb_module divs. Direct CSS Grid and Flex items cease to be children of the grid container.
  • WordPress’s own core/table block wraps every <table> in a <figure class="wp-block-table">, breaking .pricing > table.

2. How Kerf Keeps the Same DOM

When we engineered Kerf, we set a strict benchmark: success is not “does it look close,” but “is the rendered DOM the same DOM?”

  • Unwrapped document chrome: Kerf unwraps core/template-part and core/post-content at render time and copies your mockup’s <html> and <body> classes and data-* attributes onto the real document tags.
  • kerf/div renders one element with one set of attributes: A <section class="hero"> becomes a block that renders <section class="hero">. A <td> renders a <td>. Nothing is normalized or wrapped.
  • Additive-only core blocks: Headings (core/heading) and paragraphs (core/paragraph) use native WordPress blocks so you get rich text editing and Yoast/Rank Math compatibility without inserting wrapper elements.
  • Case-accurate inline SVG: PHP’s DOMDocument::loadHTML() normally lowercases viewBox to viewbox and linearGradient to lineargradient, breaking SVG scaling. Kerf restores canonical SVG camelCase and sanitizes against a strict DOM allowlist.

3. Proving It: Pixel-by-Pixel Image Subtraction

On the Kerf home page, we show the Copperline Studio template opened as a static HTML file on the left and rendered by WordPress after a one-click Kerf import on the right. When you blend the two 1440×900 screenshots with CSS mix-blend-mode: difference, identical pixels subtract to pure black (#000000).

Copperline Studio on WordPress — 134/134 selectors matched

The rendered WordPress page keeps every tag, class, stylesheet, and script in source order.

Want to test how your most complex stylesheet holds up? Launch the live WordPress Playground demo and drop in your ZIP to see your selector match score in seconds.
