title: Depth-guided Geometric Adaptation for Few-shot Image Classification
description:
arXiv:2610.28856v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Few-shot image classification (FSIC) frequently suffers from visual ambiguity, where background clutter and RGB appearance similarities hinder discriminative feature matching in data-scarce settings. To mitigate this, we propose DAFIC, a geometry-guided framework that incorporates monocular depth into representation learning, episodic adaptation, and dense support-query matching. DAFIC first learns geometry-aware token representations through RGB-D self-supervised pre-training. Subsequently, the Depth-guided Geometric Adaptation (DGA) module uses depth-derived geometry to refine patch representations with geometry-enriched class context while suppressing background interference. Spatial Bidirectional Patch Matching (SBiM) then performs bidirectional dense matching on the refined features, reducing sensitivity to spurious correspondences and background clutter. Extensive experiments on four benchmarks show that DAFIC achieves strong performance against existing methods, with ablation and robustness analyses supporting the effectiveness of coupling geometry-conditioned episodic adaptation with bidirectional matching for few-shot visual recognition.

Enterprise leaders have to figure out how to let everyone build, without giving up security or control.

Enterprise Apps and Agents

We built Enterprise Apps and Agents to solve these challenges at Vercel, and in June, we made it available to our customers. Enterprise Apps and Agents is a central control plane for governing every builder, app, agent, token, and dollar.

Today, we are expanding the platform:

A single control plane for governing enterprise AI

Enterprise Apps and Agents gives you a single deployment destination for both engineers and citizen developers, with central governance over access, providers, models, data retention, token budgets, integrations, and policies, managed through your existing IdP.

Vercel centralizes AI governance so that company policies can be applied consistently across control domains.

Apps and agents run on the same infrastructure that powers billions of production deployments, and Vercel gives you a single place for observability and security monitoring across every project, through analytics, audit logs, and the Security Dashboard.

Secure Compute provides private connectivity to enterprise systems, while BYOC on AWS lets your application functions run in your own AWS account under your permissions and network controls.

Deployment governance

Citizen developers and engineers use different tools. A marketer might use ChatGPT to build a landing page, an analyst might use Claude Code to run queries and build a report, and an engineer might use Codex, OpenCode, or fx.

No matter the harness, Vercel gives you a single deployment target, and connects to your existing IdP, so you can control who creates deployments.

How Klaviyo's built a secure internal app platform

Before Vercel, shipping a simple internal app at Klaviyo took two weeks of chasing IT, opening tickets for engineering, and following up with the platform team. They built an internal app-building platform on top of Enterprise Apps and Agents, and now anyone in the company can deploy an idea in three minutes. In their first two weeks on Vercel, 512 employees deployed 356 apps.

Access governance

Controlling who can deploy doesn't protect the apps, agents, and data that make it into production.

On Vercel, you can configure every deployment to be private by default, and with Vercel Passport, you can require employees to authenticate through your IdP before they can access internal apps.

Integration and data governance

Agents are only useful when they can access your systems and data, but that often means using long-standing environment varibles with wide-ranging permissions to your CRM, databases, Slack, and other systems.

Vercel Connect implements connectors with scoped access, and mints tokens for each agent task, meaning agents only access the specific context they need for the job. And now, with Enterprise-Managed Authorization, when employees sign into Vercel through your IdP, agents can use connected services automatically, without a separate authorization prompt.

Connect also integrates with Passport, so individual employee permissions also apply at the integration and data layer. If someone can't see data in a source system, they can't access it through an app or agent either.

Model and token governance

The average enterprise company using Vercel AI Gateway routes across 17 different models. Without a model router, that would require integrating with multiple separate providers, spreading API keys and budget management across platforms.

AI Gateway gives you access to hundreds of models through a single API, with no markup on cost, and Zero Data Retention keeps your data from being stored or trained on. You can also elect to route through US-only providers to maintain compliance.

How Mercor manages model governance at scale

Mercor connects AI labs with subject-matter experts who help train and evaluate models. Their engineers need access to hundreds of models to enable that work, but before migrating to Vercel, access was spread across direct integrations and third-party routers, making stolen credentials a huge risk, and token spend impossible to manage.

They moved their model routing to AI Gateway, and now engineers can access hundreds of models with a single, expiring secret, and they can set budgets per person or project.

In their first 10 days on AI Gateway, they processed 63 billion tokens without hitting any rate limits.

Centralized visibility and security

Vercel Observability gives you a single view for app and agent telemetry across every project, so you can easily manage performance and troubleshoot problems for both internal tools and customer-facing products.

The Security Dashboard flags risks across your team and apps, including missing MFA, unprotected preview deployments, long-lived credentials, and framework vulnerabilities. Each finding links to the settings needed to fix it.

Bring Your Own Cloud on AWS

BYOC on AWS is generally available. With BYOC, application functions execute in your AWS account, within your security and network boundaries.

Meta Superintelligence Labs runs on Vercel via BYOC, giving its AI teams the ability to test and deploy ideas quickly, inside their own AWS environment. Leaders at Meta said that in their first week on Vercel, they shipped a month worth of work.

From idea to global scale on one platform

Vercel let's everyone in your company build safely, and makes it easy for engineers to ship the best ideas at global scale, all on a single platform.

That is how we built Vertex, our customer support agent. We were previously using a vendor, but it couldn't answer all of our customers questions. When our support team built agents and skills to cover the gaps and increase our responses times, and we realized they had laid the foundation for the experience we wanted to deliver directly to our customers.

Our GTM engineering team took that foundation and made it production ready with evals and model failover.

Today, Vertex handles 91% of our customer support cases autonomously, processing thousands of tickets a week, and it runs on the same platform where the idea started.

Ship your best ideas, securely

title: Node.js GDPR Log Retention: 4 Boundaries to Delete User Data Safely
description:
A nightly media pipeline needs searchable failure evidence, but replay and rollback can quietly restore data that an erasure job already removed. That constraint changes the design: keep direct user identifiers out of application logs, separate the lookup needed for erasure from the log records, and make deletion state survive every rollback.

TL;DR: Treat log retention and user-data erasure as two different controls. Retention limits how long records exist. Erasure handles records that must disappear sooner. In Node.js, emit a versioned pseudonymous subject token, keep the reversible mapping outside the log system, delete that mapping and matching records through an auditable job, then test that a rollback cannot revive either one.

This is less convenient than logging an email address. Good. Convenience is how identifiers leak into exception strings, queue payloads, and copied debug fields.

How should GDPR log retention handle deleted user data?

The GDPR question is often phrased as a retention-period question: how long should application logs stay searchable, and how does the right to be forgotten apply? For an EU startup, the sharper operational question is where user data can return from after a valid erasure request. The log index is rarely the only copy. A media pipeline may read a nightly manifest, enqueue transformations, retry failed items, export an archive, and retain a replay input. Deleting a user's indexed events while leaving their identifier in any replayable input means the next run can emit the same data again. Good logging practices therefore start before retention: minimize fields at ingress, preserve a narrow lookup path for deletion, and enumerate every store or replay source that can reproduce an event. The legal basis, scope, exceptions, and response duties need qualified review for the actual service; an engineering design cannot decide those questions. It can make the resulting policy enforceable and testable.

The failure is temporal. Deployment version 42 removes a mapping and scrubs current records. A rollback to version 41 restores code that still logs raw ownerEmail, while an old queue message waits for retry. The software rollback worked; the privacy operation did not.

That is the risk.

Deletion state must move forward even when application code moves backward. Put tombstones and schema compatibility outside the application release artifact. An older release must either understand the current privacy envelope or refuse to process it. Never let it guess.

For the media pipeline, I would define four boundaries:

  1. Ingress replaces the account identifier with a scoped subject token before work reaches the queue.
  2. Workers log an allowlisted event shape, not arbitrary request objects or media metadata.
  3. Search storage and cold archives share an erasure manifest, including completion status.
  4. Replay checks the tombstone set before reading historical input or emitting fresh events.

Four is not a universal number. It is the smallest useful model for this pipeline because each boundary owns a different way deleted data can return. Schema version 2 in the example is also a local contract, not an industry standard.

Build the smallest logging surface

Start with types. A logger that accepts Record<string, unknown> is quick to ship and expensive to police. It lets every caller invent fields, so deletion becomes a hunt through unknown shapes.

The following TypeScript keeps the useful operational dimensions: pipeline run, stage, outcome, duration, and a scoped subject token. It deliberately omits filenames, URLs, free-form exception messages, and media captions. Those values can contain user data even when their field names look harmless.

import { createHash, randomUUID } from "node:crypto";

type PipelineStage = "ingest" | "transcode" | "index" | "publish";
type Outcome = "ok" | "retry" | "failed";

type PipelineEvent = Readonly<{
  schemaVersion: 2;
  eventId: string;
  occurredAt: string;
  runId: string;
  subjectToken: string;
  stage: PipelineStage;
  outcome: Outcome;
  durationMs: number;
  errorCode?: string;
}>;

const subjectToken = (tenantId: string, userId: string, secret: string): string =>
  createHash("sha256")
    .update(`${secret}:${tenantId}:${userId}`)
    .digest("hex");

export function pipelineEvent(
  input: Omit<PipelineEvent, "schemaVersion" | "eventId" | "occurredAt">
): PipelineEvent {
  return {
    schemaVersion: 2,
    eventId: randomUUID(),
    occurredAt: new Date().toISOString(),
    ...input,
  };
}

Hashing is not deletion, and a plain hash of a predictable user ID is weak pseudonymization. The secret scopes the token, while a separately controlled mapping or derivation-key lifecycle provides the erasure handle. The token remains personal data whenever it can still be linked back to a person, so do not treat this transform as an exemption from privacy controls.

Keep errors boring. Map known failures to stable codes such as SOURCE_UNREADABLE or TRANSCODE_TIMEOUT; send the original exception to a restricted diagnostic path only after applying the same field policy. A stack trace can carry request values. A generic serializer cannot know which substring matters.

Make erasure a state machine, not a delete button

A one-shot delete call gives weak evidence. The worker can time out after removing hot records but before updating an archive. Retrying must be safe, and operators need to distinguish “accepted” from “complete.”

I use an explicit state transition in the design, even if the first implementation has only one storage backend:

type ErasureState =
  | { status: "requested"; subjectToken: string; requestId: string }
  | { status: "tombstoned"; subjectToken: string; requestId: string }
  | { status: "purging"; subjectToken: string; requestId: string }
  | { status: "verified"; subjectToken: string; requestId: string };

interface LogStore {
  deleteBySubject(token: string): Promise<void>;
  countBySubject(token: string): Promise<number>;
}

async function purgeAndVerify(
  state: Extract<ErasureState, { status: "tombstoned" }>,
  stores: readonly LogStore[]
): Promise<ErasureState> {
  for (const store of stores) await store.deleteBySubject(state.subjectToken);

  const remaining = await Promise.all(
    stores.map((store) => store.countBySubject(state.subjectToken))
  );
  if (remaining.some((count) => count !== 0)) {
    return { ...state, status: "purging" };
  }

  return { ...state, status: "verified" };
}

Do not log the erasure request's raw identity from this code. Record its opaque request ID, state transition, policy version, and target-store result in a separate audit stream with its own access rules. Otherwise the mechanism designed to remove an identifier writes a new copy of it.

Retention still matters. It caps exposure and storage volume, but one global duration is usually a blunt instrument. Set periods by event class and documented purpose, then apply the shortest period that still supports the job. Security audit events, pipeline performance samples, and content-level diagnostics do not need identical fields or lifetimes.

The limitation is search fidelity. Removing free-form context makes novel failures slower to investigate, tokenization adds key-management work, and full-store verification can delay completion. This approach is not suitable when a team cannot inventory every replay source or keep old workers compatible with new tombstones; in that state, pause historical replay until the lifecycle is controlled. That is an explicit availability trade-off, not a hidden promise. It also does not determine which records a particular GDPR request legally requires a controller to erase. Policy owners must supply that decision, and the implementation must encode it without broadening the data collected.

Sampling does not solve this problem either. Head sampling decides before an operation completes; tail sampling can decide after observing more of the trace. Both reduce retained telemetry, but neither guarantees that a particular person's records were excluded or erased. Use sampling for signal volume. Use minimization, retention, and erasure for data lifecycle.

Test the rollback, not just the happy path

The valuable test begins after deletion. Seed two subjects across the live index, archive, retry queue, and replay input. Erase one. Then deploy the previous compatible worker version, replay the old batch, and assert three things: the erased token has zero searchable records, no new record is emitted for it, and the other subject remains searchable.

Fail closed on unknown schemas. If version 41 cannot interpret a version 42 tombstone, the queue item should park for review instead of running through legacy logging code. This costs availability for a narrow class of replay. I take that trade because a delayed media job is recoverable; resurrected personal data is much harder to contain.

Benchmark the controls separately. Measure ingestion overhead from tokenization, erasure completion latency across every store, replay throughput with tombstone checks, and query usefulness after fields are removed. Publish the test fixture and percentile method internally. A single average hides the exact tail where nightly batches and deletion jobs collide.

There is one nasty edge: key rotation. If token derivation changes without a version marker, the erasure job may search for today's token while old logs contain yesterday's token. Include a non-secret token version in the schema and retain only the key material needed by the active erasure window. Test every supported version.

What I would change at scale

At small volume, synchronous deletion across a few stores is understandable and easy to verify. At larger volume, use a durable erasure manifest, idempotent workers per storage class, and a final verifier that cannot mark completion until all required targets report zero matches. Partition work, but preserve one request-level state machine.

I would also move from per-event tombstone lookups to a local, frequently refreshed deny set with a strict freshness budget. That improves replay throughput, but introduces a delay between a request and enforcement at each worker. The acceptable budget is a policy decision, not a cache default.

Search quality will drop when raw filenames, URLs, and messages disappear. Compensate with stable enums and bounded dimensions, not a larger bag of strings. For this pipeline, stage, outcome, errorCode, runId, and duration buckets answer the operational questions without turning the index into a shadow user database.

The decision rule stays plain: a release is rollback-safe only when older compatible code cannot recreate erased telemetry from queues, archives, or replay inputs. Verify that property before optimizing ingestion or search. No dashboard can repair a broken lifecycle.

Sources and References

  • OpenTelemetry, “Sampling”: https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/sampling/

title: LocalAgent: Collaborative Agentic Verification for Fine-Grained Instance-Level Consistency
description:
arXiv:2610.29174v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have made rapid progress in general visual understanding, yet they still struggle with fine-grained instance-level consistency verification, where the goal is to determine whether two images depict the exact same physical object under varying viewpoints, illumination, and backgrounds. This task requires both global semantic perception and precise examination of subtle local evidence, since semantically similar objects may differ only in small suspicious regions. To address this challenge, we propose LocalAgent, a collaborative agentic framework that integrates the complementary strengths of a generalist MLLM and lightweight specialist verifiers. The MLLM first reasons globally to identify suspicious local regions, which are then delegated to a Local Evidence Verifier (LEV) toolkit for fine-grained appearance and geometric matching. LEV comprises Local Appearance Consistency (LAC), which estimates appearance similarity under illumination and color changes, and Local Geometric Correspondence (LGC), which estimates spatial correspondence under viewpoint changes. LEV returns structured scalar evidence that the MLLM integrates for the final decision. We further introduce an auxiliary-capped reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) strategy, in which answer correctness dominates auxiliary tool-use and format signals, enabling the policy to learn when verification is necessary. Experiments show that LocalAgent improves mean accuracy by 4.9% over the strongest CoT-RFT baseline while invoking a verifier on only 12.13% of samples and preserving the general multimodal capabilities of the underlying MLLM. The open-source repository is available at https://github.com/Firefly-zoo/LocalAgent-main.

title: Vercel and Shopify make agents first-class shoppers
description:
Agents already shop on the web, but they often use pages and tools originally built for people and search engines. Building a better shopping experience for agents means treating them as first-class shoppers, with product information they can read directly and tools designed for agents to shop.

Today, Vercel Shop, our open source Next.js storefront template for Shopify, is generally available. Teams can launch storefronts optimized for how people, search engines, and agents interact with them.

Vercel Shop is built on Shopify’s Hydrogen SDK. The SDK gives teams access to the store’s product catalog, cart and order management, payments, and checkout to build custom storefronts. Earlier this year, Vercel and Shopify announced plans to rebuild Hydrogen to work across JavaScript frameworks. Today, the rebuilt SDK is generally available.

Give agents the information and tools they need

Vercel Shop makes product pages available as machine-readable content, including price, availability, and options. The same product URL can serve a visual page to people or product information that agents can read without interpreting the page’s layout. The template also includes structured data embedded in pages and sitemaps to help search and answer engines discover and understand the products.

Shopify co-developed the Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP), which gives agents a standard way to search a store’s catalog, read product details, check availability, build a cart, and get a checkout link. Vercel Shop makes these capabilities discoverable at the merchant’s own domain, so agents can use MCP to search products and build carts without navigating the site.

Customize the experience for all customers

Vercel Shop brings the store’s product catalog, cart, and checkout together with a Next.js storefront, product information and shopping tools for agents, and a shopping assistant powered by eve. The storefront and assistant live in the same codebase, so teams can customize the store’s design and how the assistant helps shoppers.

Skills included in the template guide coding agents through setup, customization, and template updates. Teams can create an experience where shoppers browse product pages or ask the assistant to find products and add them to their cart. Both share the same cart, so shoppers keep what they’ve added as they move between experiences.

Storefronts built with Shopify and Vercel

Today, we launched our merch store at vercel.store with limited-edition drops. It’s built on Vercel Shop. The store’s shopping agent helps shoppers find products, add them to their cart, and continue to checkout.

Shopify, Next.js, and Vercel already power storefronts for brands including AG1, Bombas, and PAIGE. When PAIGE re-architected its ecommerce platform, it saw a 22% increase in revenue and a 76% increase in conversion over Black Friday and Cyber Monday, with no downtime.

Get started with Vercel Shop

Get started with Vercel Shop. Check the documentation to connect your Shopify store and configure the storefront.

title: My whole design system is one 30-line CSS file
description:
Here's my entire global stylesheet, in full:

@tailwind base;
@tailwind components;
@tailwind utilities;

body {
  @apply bg-slate-100 text-slate-800 antialiased;
}

/* Custom scrollbar */
::-webkit-scrollbar {
  width: 10px;
  height: 10px;
}

::-webkit-scrollbar-track {
  background: #f1f5f9;
}

::-webkit-scrollbar-thumb {
  background: #94a3b8;
  border-radius: 8px;
  border: 2px solid #f1f5f9;
}

::-webkit-scrollbar-thumb:hover {
  background: #64748b;
}

That's it. Three Tailwind directives, one body rule, and a styled scrollbar.

The kit's "look" doesn't come from this file. It comes from repeating the same utility combinations everywhere — rounded-xl bg-white p-6 shadow-sm is my card, text-sm font-medium text-slate-500 is my label. My StatCard component is literally that combo with four accent colour choices. The design system is a habit, not a file.

So why the scrollbar? Because the users table scrolls, and a default browser scrollbar next to an otherwise polished admin panel is the kind of thing that makes a buyer think "unfinished". Ten lines of CSS, one considered detail. Slate track, rounded thumb, darker on hover — it matches the palette instead of fighting it.

I deliberately did not add a component library, a theme file, CSS variables, or dark mode. Not because they're bad — because a starter kit should only ship what it actually uses. Architecture theatre is the fastest way to make a kit feel heavy. Thirty honest lines beats three hundred speculative ones.

The body rule does the real work anyway: bg-slate-100 for the app background, antialiased because un-anti-aliased text on a dashboard looks cheap. Two tokens, applied once, inherited everywhere.

If you're shipping a kit: resist the theme file. Repeat one good combo until it becomes your design system, and spend your CSS budget on the ten lines people actually notice.

This stylesheet ships in my Laravel + React SaaS Starter Kit — the whole frontend (React dashboard, auth pages, admin panel) included: https://kamranofficial.gumroad.com/l/mhekoig

title: AWS announces AWS Interconnect - last mile preview with Megaport
description:
AWS launches AWS Interconnect - last mile preview with Megaport, a fully managed connectivity offering that allows customers to connect their branch offices, data centers, and remote locations to AWS with just a few clicks, eliminating the friction and complexity of network setup. As a milestone collaboration between AWS and Megaport, AWS Interconnect - last mile combines AWS cloud innovation with Megaport operating one of the world's largest Software Defined Networks (SDN), with 1,200+ enabled data centers across 31 countries.

Through the AWS Management Console, customers can now instantly establish private, high-speed connections to AWS by simply choosing their preferred AWS Region, bandwidth speed, Direct Connect Gateway ID and partner subscriber ID. Once initiated, AWS generates an activation key to complete connectivity provisioning with Megaport. The launch simplifies the connectivity experience by pre-provisioning capacity and automating complex network configuration including BGP peering, VLAN configuration, and ASN assignment. At GA, customers will also be able to dynamically scale bandwidth from 1 Gbps to 100 Gbps through the AWS Console. The service is designed for high availability, with zero down-time maintenance, backed by a 99.99% SLA. 

AWS Interconnect - last mile is available in the San Jose (us-west-1) and N. Virginia (us-east-1) metros through Megaport. You can create a preview Interconnect using the AWS Management Console, Command Line Interface (CLI), or API. Partners can also easily adopt via a published open API package on GitHub. For more information, see the AWS Interconnect - last mile documentation and pricing pages.

title: Web Components: Shadow DOM
description:
Unleash the Power of Encapsulation: A Deep Dive into Web Components' Shadow DOM

Hey there, fellow web wizards! Ever feel like your CSS and JavaScript are playing a never-ending game of whack-a-mole, where a change in one place mysteriously breaks something completely unrelated somewhere else? If you’ve ever wrestled with global styles bleeding into your carefully crafted components or found yourself desperately trying to name things with obscure prefixes to avoid collisions, then you’re in for a treat. Today, we're diving headfirst into a super cool feature of Web Components that’s going to revolutionize how you build reusable UI elements: Shadow DOM.

Think of Shadow DOM as your own personal, private digital greenhouse. Inside, you can grow your components with their own unique ecosystem of styles and behaviors, completely insulated from the outside world. No more accidental styling wars, no more JavaScript interference! It’s like giving your components a force field of encapsulation, and it’s genuinely a game-changer.

Before We Get Our Hands Dirty: What You Should Know

While Shadow DOM is incredibly powerful, it's not like it materialized out of thin air. To truly appreciate its magic, it’s helpful to have a basic understanding of a few core concepts.

  • HTML, CSS, and JavaScript: You’re already a pro at this, right? Shadow DOM leverages these fundamental web technologies.
  • Web Components: Shadow DOM is a part of the Web Components suite, alongside Custom Elements and HTML Templates. If you're new to Web Components, I highly recommend getting a grasp on those first. Think of them as the building blocks, and Shadow DOM as the protective casing for those blocks.
  • The DOM (Document Object Model): You know that tree-like structure that represents your HTML? Shadow DOM creates a separate, hidden DOM tree attached to an element in the main DOM.

Don’t worry if you’re not an expert in all of these. We’ll cover what you need as we go. The main takeaway is that Shadow DOM works with the existing web platform, not against it.

What Exactly Is Shadow DOM?

At its heart, Shadow DOM is all about encapsulation. It allows you to attach a hidden, separate DOM tree to an element. This "shadow tree" is rendered separately from the main document's DOM (the "light DOM"). Crucially, the styles and scripts defined within the shadow tree are scoped only to that tree. They won't leak out and affect the rest of your page, and styles from the main document generally won't intrude unless you explicitly allow them.

Imagine you have a custom button component. Without Shadow DOM, if you style your button with a red background, that red background might accidentally apply to other buttons on your page that you didn't intend to style. With Shadow DOM, you can style that custom button with a bright red background inside its shadow tree, and the rest of your page remains blissfully unaware and unaffected.

The Magic Ingredient: The Shadow Root

To create a Shadow DOM, you need a "host" element. This is the element in your light DOM to which the shadow tree will be attached. Then, you use JavaScript to attach a shadow root to that host element. The shadow root is the entry point to your shadow tree.

Here’s a simple example:

// Get the host element from your light DOM
const hostElement = document.getElementById('my-custom-element');

// Attach a shadow root to the host element
// 'open' mode means you can access the shadow root from JavaScript
// 'closed' mode makes it inaccessible (less common for general use)
const shadowRoot = hostElement.attachShadow({ mode: 'open' });

// Now you can manipulate the shadowRoot as if it were a regular DOM node
shadowRoot.innerHTML = `
  <style>
    /* Styles are scoped to this shadow tree */
    button {
      background-color: dodgerblue;
      color: white;
      padding: 10px 20px;
      border: none;
      border-radius: 5px;
      cursor: pointer;
    }
    p {
      font-family: sans-serif;
    }
  </style>
  <p>This is inside the shadow DOM!</p>
  <button>Click Me (Shadow Style!)</button>
`;

And in your HTML:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
  <title>Shadow DOM Demo</title>
</head>
<body>
  <my-custom-element id="my-custom-element"></my-custom-element>

  <button>This button has global styles!</button>

  <script src="script.js"></script>
</body>
</html>

If you run this, you'll see the "Click Me" button styled with a blue background, while the other button outside the my-custom-element will have default browser styling (or whatever global styles you might have). The text inside the shadow DOM is also styled with a sans-serif font. Pretty neat, right?

Advantages: Why You'll Fall in Love with Shadow DOM

The benefits of Shadow DOM are numerous and impactful. Let's break down some of the most significant ones:

  • True Encapsulation (The Star of the Show!): This is the primary reason to use Shadow DOM. Styles and scripts are isolated. No more worrying about global CSS selectors clashing with your component’s styles. Your component’s internal structure is also protected from external manipulation unless you explicitly allow it. This makes building complex, reusable components a breeze.

    • CSS Scoping: Styles defined within the shadow tree only apply to elements within that shadow tree. This eliminates the fear of accidentally styling elements outside your component.
    • JavaScript Scoping: While JavaScript in the shadow DOM can access the global scope, global JavaScript can't easily access or manipulate elements inside the shadow DOM without explicit permission (via the shadow root's mode and by querying specific elements).

  • Reusability: Because components built with Shadow DOM are self-contained, they can be dropped into any project without fear of breaking other parts of the application. This is a developer's dream for creating consistent and maintainable UIs.

  • Maintainability: With clear separation of concerns, debugging becomes significantly easier. If a style is off, you know to look within the component's shadow DOM. If a behavior is broken, the scope of your investigation is much narrower.

  • Composability: Shadow DOM plays exceptionally well with other Web Components features like Custom Elements and HTML Templates. You can create highly complex components by composing simpler, encapsulated ones.

  • Browser Native Solution: Shadow DOM is a web standard supported by modern browsers. This means you don't need to rely on external libraries for this core functionality (though libraries can certainly enhance the Web Component development experience).

  • Reduced Code Complexity: By avoiding the need for complex naming conventions or CSS-in-JS solutions purely for scoping, your codebase can become cleaner and easier to understand.

The Flip Side: What to Be Mindful Of (Disadvantages)

While Shadow DOM is fantastic, it’s not a silver bullet. There are a few things to keep in mind that might be considered drawbacks:

  • Styling from the Outside Can Be Tricky: This is the flip side of encapsulation. If you need to style an element inside a shadow DOM from the outside (e.g., a parent component wanting to influence a child component's style), it's not as straightforward as a regular DOM element. You’ll need to use specific mechanisms like CSS custom properties (variables) or :host selectors with slotted content to achieve this. This can add a learning curve.

  • Initial Learning Curve: While the core concepts are simple, understanding the nuances of Shadow DOM, especially when it comes to styling and interacting with slotted content, can take some time and practice.

  • Accessibility Considerations: While browsers are getting better, ensuring accessibility for elements within shadow DOMs requires careful attention. You need to ensure proper ARIA attributes and semantic HTML are used within the shadow tree.

  • Browser Support (Less of an issue now, but worth noting): While modern browsers have excellent Shadow DOM support, very old browsers might not. For production applications targeting a broad audience, you might still need fallbacks or polyfills, though this is becoming increasingly rare.

  • Developer Tools Can Be a Bit More Complex: Inspecting elements within a shadow DOM in browser developer tools can feel a little different at first. You'll see a distinct "shadow root" section. Once you're familiar, it's easy, but it's an initial adjustment.

Diving Deeper: Key Features and Concepts

Let's unpack some of the more detailed aspects of Shadow DOM:

The Shadow Root and its Modes (open vs. closed)

As we saw earlier, attachShadow() can take a mode argument:

  • mode: 'open': This is the most common mode. It means that you can access the shadow root from JavaScript via element.shadowRoot. This is useful for debugging, testing, or when you need to programmatically interact with the shadow DOM from outside.

    const hostElement = document.getElementById('my-component');
const shadowRoot = hostElement.attachShadow({ mode: 'open' });
console.log(shadowRoot); // You can see the shadow root here!

  • mode: 'closed': In this mode, element.shadowRoot will return null. This offers stronger encapsulation, making it very difficult to access the shadow DOM from the outside. This is often used by built-in browser elements (like the <video> element's controls) to prevent external interference. For custom components, open is generally preferred for flexibility.

Rendering and the Shadow Tree

The content you add to the shadowRoot effectively creates a separate DOM tree. When the browser renders your page, it renders the light DOM and then, independently, renders the shadow DOM for each element that has one. This is why styles are scoped – the browser treats them as distinct rendering contexts.

Styling the Shadow DOM: The Power of :host and ::slotted()

This is where things get interesting when you want to communicate styles between the light and shadow DOM.

  • :host: This pseudo-class allows you to style the host element from within the shadow DOM.

    const shadowRoot = hostElement.attachShadow({ mode: 'open' });
shadowRoot.innerHTML = `
  <style>
    /* Style the host element itself */
    :host {
      display: block; /* Host elements are often inline by default */
      border: 2px dashed purple;
      padding: 10px;
    }
    /* Style the host element when it has a certain class */
    :host(.special) {
      background-color: lightyellow;
    }
  </style>
  <p>Content inside the host!</p>
`;

    And in your HTML:

    <my-custom-element></my-custom-element>
<my-custom-element class="special"></my-custom-element>

  • ::slotted(): This is used to style elements that are distributed into the shadow DOM via the <slot> element (which we'll touch on shortly).

    const shadowRoot = hostElement.attachShadow({ mode: 'open' });
shadowRoot.innerHTML = `
  <style>
    ::slotted(p) { /* Style any <p> elements slotted into this component */
      color: green;
      font-weight: bold;
    }
    ::slotted([slot="icon"]) { /* Style elements with the slot="icon" attribute */
      fill: red; /* Example for SVG */
    }
  </style>
  <slot></slot> <!-- Default slot -->
  <slot name="icon"></slot> <!-- Named slot -->
`;

    And in your HTML:

    <my-custom-element>
  <p>This paragraph will be green and bold!</p>
  <svg slot="icon">...</svg> <!-- This SVG will be red -->
</my-custom-element>

Slots: Injecting Content into Your Shadow DOM

The <slot> element is crucial for allowing the light DOM to project content into the shadow DOM. It acts as a placeholder within the shadow tree where external content can be rendered.

  • Default Slot: If you have an un-named <slot> in your shadow tree, it will render any child elements from the light DOM that don't have a slot attribute assigned to them.

  • Named Slots: You can give slots a name attribute. Then, in your light DOM, you can assign child elements to specific slots using the slot attribute with a matching name.

    <my-component>
  <span slot="header">My Custom Header</span> <!-- This goes into the named slot "header" -->
  <p>This is the default content.</p> <!-- This goes into the default slot -->
</my-component>

    And in the component's shadow DOM:

    <style>
  .container {
    border: 1px solid #ccc;
    padding: 15px;
  }
  h2 {
    color: navy;
  }
</style>
<div class="container">
  <slot name="header"><h2>Default Header</h2></slot> <!-- Named slot -->
  <div>
    <slot></slot> <!-- Default slot -->
  </div>
</div>

    This allows for flexible and reusable components where the consumer can provide their own content for specific parts of the component.

Putting It All Together: A More Realistic Example

Let's imagine creating a simple, reusable "fancy-card" component.

// fancy-card.js
class FancyCard extends HTMLElement {
  constructor() {
    super();
    const shadowRoot = this.attachShadow({ mode: 'open' });

    shadowRoot.innerHTML = `
      <style>
        :host {
          display: block;
          border: 1px solid #ddd;
          border-radius: 8px;
          padding: 16px;
          box-shadow: 0 4px 8px rgba(0,0,0,0.1);
          font-family: 'Arial', sans-serif;
          background-color: white;
          margin-bottom: 16px;
        }
        .card-header {
          font-size: 1.2em;
          font-weight: bold;
          margin-bottom: 12px;
          color: #333;
          border-bottom: 1px solid #eee;
          padding-bottom: 8px;
        }
        .card-content {
          color: #555;
          line-height: 1.6;
        }
        /* Style the slotted title if it's an h3 */
        ::slotted(h3) {
          margin-top: 0; /* Remove default margin for slotted h3 */
          color: #007bff; /* Make slotted h3 blue */
        }
      </style>
      <div class="card-header">
        <slot name="title">Default Card Title</slot>
      </div>
      <div class="card-content">
        <slot></slot>
      </div>
    `;
  }
}

customElements.define('fancy-card', FancyCard);

And in your HTML:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
  <title>Fancy Card Demo</title>
  <style>
    body {
      background-color: #f4f4f4;
      padding: 20px;
    }
    /* Global styles will NOT affect the card's internal elements */
    h3 {
      color: red !important; /* This will NOT affect the slotted h3 within fancy-card */
    }
  </style>
</head>
<body>

  <h1>Web Components with Shadow DOM</h1>

  <fancy-card>
    <h3 slot="title">My Awesome Feature</h3>
    <p>This is some descriptive content about our awesome feature. It leverages the power of Shadow DOM for robust encapsulation.</p>
    <p>You can add multiple paragraphs or any other HTML content here.</p>
  </fancy-card>

  <fancy-card>
    <span slot="title">Another Card Example</span>
    <p>This card uses a <span>span</span> for its title instead of an H3.</p>
  </fancy-card>

  <fancy-card>
    <!-- No slot="title" provided, so "Default Card Title" will be used -->
    <p>This card only has default content.</p>
  </fancy-card>

  <script src="fancy-card.js"></script>
</body>
</html>

In this example, you can see how the fancy-card component uses Shadow DOM to encapsulate its structure and styling. The slot="title" allows users to inject their own title content, and the ::slotted(h3) selector ensures that even if the user provides an h3 for the title, it gets styled appropriately within the shadow DOM. Crucially, the global h3 { color: red !important; } style has no effect on the h3 inside the fancy-card.

Conclusion: Embrace the Power of Encapsulation!

Shadow DOM is more than just a cool technical feature; it's a fundamental shift in how we think about building user interfaces on the web. By providing true encapsulation, it empowers developers to create modular, reusable, and maintainable components that are robust and less prone to conflicts.

While there's a learning curve, the benefits of embracing Shadow DOM – particularly when used in conjunction with Custom Elements and HTML Templates as part of the Web Components standard – are immense. It’s the key to building scalable and predictable web applications in the modern era.

So, go forth and experiment! Start building your own encapsulated components. The web just got a whole lot more organized and a lot less prone to CSS wars. Happy coding!

title: Quantum-JEPA: Quantum Born Priors for Latent-Action JEPA World Models
description:
arXiv:2610.27921v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A single observation can admit several plausible futures, making uncertainty an essential part of world modelling. However, quantum generative models remain underexplored for this task. We introduce Quantum-JEPA, a latent-action JEPA framework that learns distributions of future representations using a conditional quantum Born prior. Circuit measurements generate binary latent actions, which a shared predictor maps to alternative future representations. We train the quantum prior through the quality and diversity of these predictions using a sampled energy objective. Our model learns distinct continuations on constructed multimodal tasks and captures latent-action correlations that support coordinated multi-agent futures. On D3IL, a benchmark of diverse human demonstrations, our trained models generate multiple obstacle-crossing routes from a common starting point without observed motion. On the controlled tasks, our classical and quantum prior implementations improve prediction validity and distributional fidelity over the evaluated variational baselines. Our quantum priors combine competitive predictive quality with a parameter-efficient sampling structure: they avoid an exponentially sized categorical output layer while supporting correlated latent actions. We further validate finite-shot parameter-shift training, including training with readout noise. Unlike most prior work, which focuses on simulation, we also verify the feasibility of inference with trained priors on a real QPU. These results establish a trainable quantum component for JEPA future prediction and a basis for exploring quantum-enhanced world models at larger scales.

title: Big Claims, Small Margins: Do Reported GraphLLM Gains Survive Simple Baselines?
description:
arXiv:2610.28714v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM-based methods for node classification on text-attributed graphs (TAGs) routinely report state-of-the-art accuracy. We ask how these results compare with inexpensive baselines run on the same splits. On the splits of three recent studies, we tune four baseline representatives with validation-only selection and compare them with the highest mean that each paper reports for an LLM-based method in the matched setting. Correct & Smooth on TF-IDF features trails this reference by a median of 2.3 percentage points, and an MLP on frozen e5-large-v2 embeddings by 2.8 points. Correct & Smooth is within 3 points of the reference or better on 15 of 24 tasks, but the reference is significantly higher on 12 of 22 testable tasks, so several reported gains remain substantial. Reading released code next to the papers, we also document evaluation risks: selection of hyperparameters or checkpoints on the test set, labels of test-pool nodes used in training, baseline numbers reused without disclosure, and a text-label misalignment in a released Cora loader. Reports of the same method on the same split also differ by up to 12.5 points across papers whose configurations are not documented to match.

title: Implementing 2 Delivery Guarantees in Go — One Key Spans Realtime and Queues
description:
The operational constraint is simple: a typing indicator may disappear, but an order message cannot. Short answer: one key across realtime and queues buys a smaller integration surface, not identical delivery guarantees. Put durable notifications through a queue, publish transient state directly to a realtime channel, and keep both behind one integration only when its processor boundaries satisfy your data policy. With Infrai, the durable half and immediate half use the same credential, so the inbox-plus-publish pattern does not require two vendor integrations.

That convenience does not merge the guarantees. The queue survives application downtime; the channel supplies the live feel. One key also creates one place to investigate delivery, one bill, and one shared outage surface. Name that concentration risk before choosing it.

What does one key across realtime and queues actually buy?

For beginners, the answer is easier to retain when it is explained through failure. I have been paged for both missed scheduled work and duplicate deliveries. The tempting diagnosis is "the transport failed." The more useful invariant is narrower: every durable event needs a stable identity, and every consumer must be safe to run twice. Standard queues are at-least-once, so acknowledging a message and changing an order cannot be treated as one magical operation.

For an e-commerce inbox, I use two classes:

  • order.shipped, refund.requested, and receipt state go to durable storage or a queue before fan-out.
  • customer.typing goes straight to realtime because a stale indicator is worse than a missing one.
  • A read receipt needs a durable monotonic state if the product promises it across reconnects. The realtime copy is only the fast projection.

That distinction matters more than the logo on the transport. During a provider incident, retrying a typing event minutes later is incorrect. Retrying order.shipped is required, but only with the same event ID.

Step 1: Make the delivery contract executable

Start with an event envelope that has no vendor-specific types. This is the part of the design that lets the capability provider move without forcing a rewrite of business code.

package main

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "time"
)

type Event struct {
    ID        string          `json:"id"`
    Kind      string          `json:"kind"`
    Channel   string          `json:"channel"`
    CreatedAt time.Time       `json:"created_at"`
    Payload   json.RawMessage `json:"payload"`
}

func durable(kind string) bool {
    switch kind {
    case "order.shipped", "refund.requested", "message.read":
        return true
    case "customer.typing":
        return false
    default:
        panic("unclassified event: " + kind)
    }
}

func main() {
    e := Event{
        ID: "evt_order_8472_shipped_v1", Kind: "order.shipped",
        Channel: "order_8472", CreatedAt: time.Now().UTC(),
        Payload: json.RawMessage(`{"carrier":"parcel-post"}`),
    }
    fmt.Printf("durable=%t id=%s channel=%s\n", durable(e.Kind), e.ID, e.Channel)
}

Run it with Go 1.22 or later. The important behavior is the panic on a new, unclassified event. Quietly defaulting every new event to ephemeral delivery is how an innocent product change becomes a missing-notification incident.

Step 2: Queue first, then project live

For durable events, publishing to the channel is a projection after the queue accepts the envelope. The unified API exposes POST /v1/queue/publish and POST /v1/realtime/publish under the same Bearer credential. I would use the event ID as the idempotency key on writes; the platform specifies Idempotency-Key as a convention with a 24-hour default deduplication window. Consumer idempotency still stays in the application.

The following runnable program demonstrates that consumer boundary without inventing a vendor request body. It uses a local ledger, but the transaction belongs in the same database as the order state in production.

package main

import (
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "sync"
)

type Ledger struct {
    mu   sync.Mutex
    seen map[string]struct{}
}

func (l *Ledger) Apply(id string, change func() error) (bool, error) {
    l.mu.Lock()
    defer l.mu.Unlock()
    if _, ok := l.seen[id]; ok {
        return false, nil
    }
    if err := change(); err != nil {
        return false, err
    }
    l.seen[id] = struct{}{}
    return true, nil
}

func main() {
    ledger := Ledger{seen: map[string]struct{}{}}
    for attempt := 1; attempt <= 2; attempt++ {
        applied, err := ledger.Apply("evt_order_8472_shipped_v1", func() error {
            if attempt < 1 {
                return errors.New("database unavailable")
            }
            fmt.Println("order 8472 marked shipped")
            return nil
        })
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        fmt.Printf("attempt=%d applied=%t\n", attempt, applied)
    }
}

The output applies the state transition once and rejects the duplicate. Small result. Big invariant.

Retries at the HTTP edge need the same discipline: an explicit method, Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY, a stable idempotency key, response-status checks, and exponential backoff on 429 that honors Retry-After. Do not send a new event ID merely because the first response was lost.

Step 3: Draw the trust boundary before choosing one key

A common credential changes the integration boundary, not the legal or physical path of customer data. The unified API can handle capability selection and consistent authentication. The specialist provider behind the selected capability remains part of the processing path. A unified invoice is not a deletion guarantee.

Before putting order messages or read receipts through any aggregator, record four answers for each capability: permitted regions, maximum retention, deletion procedure, and every processor or subprocessor that can receive the payload. The public discovery surface returns capability metadata including regions, vendor readiness, and the default vendor without requiring a key. Use that to begin review, then verify the provider contract and current documentation. Do not infer residency from an API hostname.

This Go program fetches that discovery document with an explicit method, checks errors, and backs off on 429. It prints only realtime and queue capabilities, giving a reviewer a current starting point rather than a region guessed from marketing copy.

package main

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

type Capability struct {
    ID            string   `json:"id"`
    Regions       []string `json:"regions"`
    VendorsReady  []string `json:"vendors_ready"`
    DefaultVendor string   `json:"default_vendor"`
}

type Discovery struct {
    Capabilities []Capability `json:"capabilities"`
}

func main() {
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    var resp *http.Response
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery", nil)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        if key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"); key != "" {
            req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        }
        resp, err = client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            break
        }
        resp.Body.Close()
        delay := time.Second << attempt
        if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
            delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        }
        time.Sleep(delay)
    }
    if resp == nil {
        panic("discovery request was not sent")
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
        panic(fmt.Sprintf("discovery failed: %s", resp.Status))
    }
    var doc Discovery
    if err := json.NewDecoder(resp.Body).Decode(&doc); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    for _, capability := range doc.Capabilities {
        if strings.Contains(capability.ID, "realtime") || strings.Contains(capability.ID, "queue") {
            fmt.Printf("%s regions=%v ready=%v default=%s\n", capability.ID,
                capability.Regions, capability.VendorsReady, capability.DefaultVendor)
        }
    }
}

Queue retention is bounded at 30 days on this surface. That is an upper limit, not a reason to retain every payload for 30 days. Put the smallest useful body on the queue, keep authoritative order data in your system of record, and test deletion as an operational procedure. If policy demands a particular region or a contractual deletion SLA and the selected processor cannot prove it, use a direct specialist integration.

My recommendation: teams that want one Go-side contract for durable inbox events and immediate fan-out should try Infrai for the queue-plus-realtime boundary when its disclosed region and provider chain pass their review. The primary gain is that the contract stays stable if the capability vendor changes; the supporting gain is one credential and one investigation surface during an incident.

Step 4: Compare the concentration trade-off

The fair comparison is not "many SDKs bad, one API good." It is control-plane concentration against specialist depth.

Option Integration shape Trust-boundary question Better fit when
Unified API Queue and realtime capabilities behind one REST API and key Which ready vendor and region serve each capability? A stable cross-capability contract matters more than direct provider coupling
Ably Specialist realtime platform Do its region, retention, and processor terms match the event class? Realtime-specific product depth is the deciding factor
Pusher Channels Specialist channel integration Where is message data processed, and how is deletion handled? The team wants a focused channels product
PubNub Specialist realtime platform Which regional and retention controls apply to the chosen setup? The application needs a direct realtime-provider relationship
Amazon SQS plus a realtime provider Separate durable and live integrations Can the team govern two processor chains and credentials? Independent failure domains and direct cloud control justify more glue

This table deliberately makes no latency or uptime claim. Those require measurements under the application's traffic pattern. It also avoids treating WebRTC as an alternative to queued notifications: WebRTC defines peer communication primitives, while an order inbox still needs durable application state.

The unified option's advantage is breadth: public discovery reports 295 routes across 20 modules, and documented capabilities include runnable Go examples. Its corresponding limitation is concentration. If the single control surface is unavailable, both notification paths may be affected even if their semantics differ. Two direct providers cost more operational attention but can give separate credentials, contracts, escalation paths, and outage surfaces.

Where this pattern stops

Do not queue typing indicators. Do not call a successful realtime publish proof that a durable order transition exists. Do not claim that one key collapses the specialist provider's processor obligations into Infrai's; it does not.

The pattern also stops at requirements the capability metadata and contract cannot establish. Strict residency, bespoke retention, audited deletion deadlines, or a need for provider-specific realtime features can outweigh portability. In that case, Ably, Pusher, PubNub, or a queue such as Amazon SQS paired with a specialist channel may be the cleaner engineering choice.

For the remaining cases, the runbook is short: classify the event, queue durable state with a stable ID, make the consumer idempotent, fan out the projection, and keep transient presence off the durable path. Then rehearse the failure in both directions. A live publish can fail after the queue succeeds; a duplicate queue delivery can arrive after clients already saw the update.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation and inspect the current capability discovery before selecting a processor.

  • Official unified API documentation
  • Ably documentation
  • Pusher Channels documentation
  • PubNub documentation
  • Amazon SQS documentation
  • W3C WebRTC 1.0

title: A Parallel Multi-Dialect Arabic Dependency Treebank
description:
arXiv:2610.28823v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Dependency parsing resource development for Arabic has largely focused on Modern Standard Arabic, leaving dialectal Arabic comparatively under-resourced. We introduce MADARTB, the first large-scale parallel dependency treebank spanning five city dialects: Beirut, Cairo, Doha, Rabat and Tunis, and extending an existing parallel MSA version. In total MADARTB consists of 5,000 sentences annotated using the CATiB dependency scheme. We analyze syntactic similarity across all city dialects and MSA. Although global construction profiles exhibit high similarity across varieties, local syntactic structures frequently diverge, revealing substantial structural variation across dialects. We further establish a cross-dialect dependency parsing comparison using a supervised parser and four LLMs. The supervised parser achieves 87.5% LAS, while the best LLM setup trails at 85.7% LAS across all six varieties on the test set. We release our annotations and models publicly.

title: Google Gemini Turns Prompts Into Web Apps With Canvas and AI Studio Build Mode
description:
Google Gemini now provides two first-party ways to turn a natural-language prompt into a working web experience. Gemini Canvas is designed for rapid visual prototyping inside the Gemini interface, while Build mode in Google AI Studio generates a code-backed, full-stack web app that can be refined, shared, exported, or deployed to Google Cloud Run.

The distinction matters for businesses that want to test an idea quickly without treating every early experiment as a finished software product. Canvas can help turn a concept into a shareable prototype in minutes. AI Studio Build mode offers a more direct route from the same kind of prompt to an editable application codebase and a live deployment workflow.

Two Gemini paths from idea to web experience

Gemini Canvas focuses on fast prototypes

Canvas is Gemini's prompt-to-prototype workspace. A user selects Canvas below the prompt bar, describes what they want, and uses the Create option to generate a web page or another deliverable. Google positions the workflow around quickly creating apps, games, web pages, infographics, and similar artifacts.

This makes Canvas useful when the immediate question is whether an idea is understandable, visually useful, or worth pursuing. A manager could use it to sketch an internal calculator, create a simple customer-facing explainer, or demonstrate the flow of a proposed service without first commissioning a complete application.

Canvas is available to all Gemini users. Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers receive enhanced access through Gemini 3 and a larger token context. Its editing experience has an important limitation: text styling and formatting edits are desktop-only.

AI Studio Build mode adds code and deployment

For applications that need to move beyond an early prototype, Build mode in Google AI Studio provides a more complete development path. Users describe their goal, and Gemini, through the Antigravity agent, generates a codebase and a live preview. By default, a generated web app includes a React frontend and a Node.js backend.

Google's official AI Studio Build mode documentation describes a workflow in which users can generate an app, preview it, iterate on it, and deploy it. They can also link GitHub, start from an App Gallery example, import existing code, export a ZIP file, or push code to GitHub for external hosting.

That is a materially different proposition from a visual mockup. Build mode creates code that teams can inspect and extend, while Google Cloud Run provides a direct hosting target. Google also documents integrated secrets management and workspace tools as part of this end-to-end flow.

Area Gemini Canvas Google AI Studio Build mode
Primary role Rapid, visual-coding-style prototyping Code-backed full-stack app generation
Typical output Shareable app, game, web page, infographic, or similar artifact Web app with a live preview, or a native Android app
Default web stack Not specified in the supplied Canvas material React frontend and Node.js backend
Next-step options Iterate on a prototype within Gemini Share, edit code, use GitHub, export a ZIP, or deploy to Cloud Run

What this means for no-code evaluation

Gemini's new workflows overlap with a common reason businesses consider no-code tools: reducing the time between an idea and something people can see or use. But the supplied Google material supports a more specific comparison: Canvas and Build mode serve different stages of the same process.

Canvas is the better fit for validating an interface, communication asset, or lightweight app concept. Build mode is the stronger choice when the project needs an accessible codebase, backend logic, source control through GitHub, or a route to hosting. A prototype made in Canvas should not automatically be assumed to have the operational characteristics of a deployed Build mode application.

For decision-makers, that separation can prevent a common mistake: treating a persuasive demonstration as proof that an application is ready for real users, data, and business processes. The value of prompt-driven building is speed, but the choice of pathway should match the level of technical follow-through required.

Costs, integration choices, and practical uses

Google states that up to two AI Studio apps can be deployed to Cloud Run at no charge through its free tier. Hosting or deployment beyond that free tier can incur costs. This makes the service useful for initial experimentation, but a team should understand the hosting model before it moves a public or operationally important app into regular use.

Build mode is particularly relevant when an experiment must connect to existing development practices. GitHub linking supports collaboration, imported code creates a path for extending an existing project, and ZIP export leaves open the option of external hosting. Those capabilities mean a team is not restricted to a single prompt-generated preview once the project requires more hands-on development.

Potential practical uses supported by the platform's prompt, preview, refinement, and deployment workflow include:

  • Creating a prototype for an internal tool before committing to a larger build.
  • Building a simple web experience to test a new customer-facing idea.
  • Starting a web app that developers can review, modify, and manage through GitHub.
  • Using App Gallery examples as a starting point rather than beginning with a blank prompt.
  • Deploying an early application to Cloud Run after testing it in AI Studio.

The speed of generation does not remove implementation responsibilities. Google documents security considerations around deployment, including server-side handling of API keys. Businesses should therefore review generated code, decide how secrets will be managed, and confirm that the hosting and integration approach suits the app's intended use before relying on it in a live workflow.

Prompt-generated apps are most valuable when they connect to a real workflow rather than remain a demo. Scalevise can help assess the right use case, define requirements, and turn a prototype into a dependable implementation through practical AI adoption planning. That work can reduce rework before a team commits to deployment, integrations, or ongoing hosting costs. Request an AI consultancy to map your next prompt-to-app project.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the difference between Gemini Canvas and AI Studio Build mode?

Canvas is Gemini's workspace for quickly generating shareable prototypes and visual artifacts from prompts. AI Studio Build mode generates a code-backed application with a live preview and options to edit, export, share, or deploy it.

Can Google Gemini create a live website from a prompt?

AI Studio Build mode can generate a full-stack web app from a prompt and deploy it directly to Google Cloud Run. It can also export the app as a ZIP file or push it to GitHub for external hosting.

What technology does AI Studio Build mode use for web apps?

By default, AI Studio Build mode generates a web app with a React frontend and a Node.js backend.

Is Gemini Canvas free to use?

Canvas is available to all Gemini users. Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers receive enhanced access through Gemini 3 and a larger token context.

Does deploying an AI Studio app cost money?

Google offers a free tier for deploying up to two AI Studio apps to Cloud Run. Deploying or hosting beyond that free tier can incur costs.

Conclusion

Google Gemini's Canvas and AI Studio Build mode create a practical progression from prompt-driven experimentation to code-backed web application deployment. Canvas lowers the barrier to testing an idea, while Build mode provides the code, preview, collaboration, and Cloud Run deployment options needed for a more substantial next step. The opportunity is significant for teams that pair rapid generation with careful review of code, security, integrations, and hosting costs.

title: Automatic Differentiation with Constraints in Forward and Inverse Problems
description:
arXiv:2610.27888v2 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Approximate solutions of partial differential equations (PDEs) on unstructured grids can be represented on a graph. Numerical optimization involving stiff evolutionary and static PDEs often requires solving a large system of equations, which can be treated as a constraint. In this work, we present a fully differentiable graph-based implicit solver that incorporates this constraint. We evaluate its performance across four key tasks: a) linear and nonlinear forward modeling of evolutionary and static problems, b) solving inverse problems to estimate equation coefficients, c) solving inverse problems to estimate the right-hand side, and d) learnable graph coarsening to accelerate forward modeling. The stability and differentiability of our solver enable significant reductions in the complexity of forward modeling while efficiently addressing related inverse problems. These capabilities make it a powerful tool for different physics and engineering applications, in particular for geophysics, where inverse problems are commonly solved in order to reduce the model uncertainty.

title: Supabase: The Open Source Firebase Alternative
description:
A New Approach to the Problem

Supabase addresses the need for a scalable, open-source backend solution that rivals proprietary offerings like Firebase. By leveraging PostgreSQL, it provides developers with a robust database solution that supports various application types, from web to mobile to AI applications.

What is it and How it Works

Supabase is a Postgres development platform designed to offer Firebase-like functionality using open-source tools. It features a hosted Postgres database, authentication and authorization, auto-generated APIs (both REST and GraphQL), real-time subscriptions, file storage, and an AI + Vector/Embeddings Toolkit.

Architecture

Supabase operates as a hosted platform that can be accessed without installation. It can also be self-hosted for those who prefer local development. Key components include:

  • Postgres: A reliable object-relational database with extensive capabilities.
  • Realtime: An Elixir server that listens to database changes and broadcasts updates via websockets.
  • PostgREST: Transforms the PostgreSQL database into a RESTful API.
  • GoTrue: A JWT-based authentication API.
  • Storage API: Manages file storage and permissions.
  • pg_graphql: Exposes a GraphQL API.
  • postgres-meta: Manages Postgres instances through a RESTful interface.
  • Envoy: A high-performance edge and service proxy.

Key Capabilities & Developer Onboarding

Supabase offers a range of features that simplify the developer experience:

  • Auto-generated APIs: Automatically creates REST and GraphQL endpoints from your database schema.
  • Authentication: Simplifies user management with built-in JWT support.
  • Real-time subscriptions: Allows apps to receive updates instantly as data changes.
  • File storage: Easily manage files with permissions tied to Postgres roles.
  • AI toolkit: Facilitates the integration of AI and vector embeddings for advanced applications.

To get started, developers can sign up at the Supabase dashboard or clone the repository. The installation commands will depend on the chosen setup method, either hosted or self-hosted.

Who Should Use It & Integration Scenarios

Supabase is ideal for developers looking for a scalable backend solution without the constraints of proprietary services. It's particularly well-suited for:

  • Startups needing rapid development of web and mobile applications.
  • Teams looking to integrate real-time features into their applications.
  • Developers who prefer open-source tools over commercial alternatives.

However, it may not be suitable for teams requiring extremely high customization or those deeply embedded in other proprietary ecosystems.

Community Pulse: What Developers Are Saying

Despite its strengths, community feedback indicates some pain points. One notable issue was raised in Issue #26785, where developers reported problems with the API Gateway and PostgreSQL logging during local development. This highlights a potential area for improvement in the local development experience, which remains a challenge for some users.

Should You Try It?

Supabase stands out as a compelling alternative to Firebase, especially for developers seeking open-source solutions. Its recent updates, including the introduction of Supabase Pipelines in public alpha and support for ChatGPT authentication, reflect its commitment to evolving in response to community needs. If you need a robust backend for your applications, Supabase is worth considering.

title: An append-only, hash-chained audit log in SQLite, and a script to check it
description:
When a coding agent can ask for production access, the question afterwards is simple: who touched production, with what, and why? Styx answers it with an audit log on your machine. This post is about how that log is built, what it does and doesn't protect against, and a short script you can run to verify it.

What goes in

Every time an agent asks for access, and every time access is granted, used, denied, revoked or expires, one row is written. Connecting or removing a target, changing a policy and opening a pull request are rows too. Each row carries:

  • the actor: you, the system (a policy or a timer), or the agent by name
  • the target, the scope and the duration
  • the agent session and the worktree it came from
  • what triggered it: for a use, the command itself, like $ vercel deploy --prod
  • the policy that decided it, if one did
  • detail such as the agent's reason, and whether you verified with Touch ID, Windows Hello or your password

Before a row is written, anything shaped like a secret is scrubbed out of commands, reasons and labels, so a token an agent pasted into a command line doesn't end up in the log.

Append-only means the database says no

The log is a table in the local SQLite database. Triggers on the table abort any update or delete. Nothing in the app edits a row, and rows are only written through one function, AuditService.append. When a grant is revoked, Styx doesn't change the 'granted' row; it adds a 'revoked' row.

The chain

Each row has a sequence number, the hash of the row before it (prev_hash) and its own hash: a SHA-256 of the previous hash and the row's contents. Change any field of any row, or remove one from the middle, and the chain breaks from that point on.

Verifying it yourself

The app has no verify button yet, but the data is just a table. Export it read-only with sqlite3 (3.33 or later, for -json) and pipe it into Node:

sqlite3 -readonly -json ~/Library/Application\ Support/Styx/styx.db \
  "SELECT * FROM audit_entries ORDER BY seq" | node verify-audit.mjs

With this saved as verify-audit.mjs:

import { createHash } from 'node:crypto';

const chunks = [];
for await (const chunk of process.stdin) chunks.push(chunk);
const rows = JSON.parse(Buffer.concat(chunks).toString('utf8') || '[]');
const camel = (k) => k.replace(/_([a-z])/g, (_, c) => c.toUpperCase());

let prev = '';
for (const r of rows) {
  const row = {};
  for (const [k, v] of Object.entries(r)) if (k !== 'hash') row[camel(k)] = v;
  const canonical = JSON.stringify(row, Object.keys(row).sort());
  const hash = createHash('sha256').update(prev).update('\n').update(canonical).digest('hex');
  if (row.prevHash !== prev || hash !== r.hash) {
    console.log(`Chain broken at entry ${row.seq}`);
    process.exit(1);
  }
  prev = r.hash;
}
console.log(`Chain intact: ${rows.length} entries`);

It prints Chain intact with the number of entries, or the first row where the chain breaks. The database is at ~/Library/Application Support/Styx/styx.db on a Mac, %APPDATA%\Styx\styx.db on Windows and ~/.config/Styx/styx.db on Linux.

What the chain can't do

The chain shows that rows weren't edited one at a time after the fact. It doesn't stop someone who can write to your files from rewriting the whole log and recomputing every hash. If that matters to you, copy the latest hash somewhere else now and then; a later rewrite of the history before it won't match.

It's also a record, not a barrier. Styx is a guardrail, not a sandbox: agents run as you, and one that deliberately goes around Styx's tools isn't stopped by the log or by anything else in it. What the log gives you is a trustworthy account of everything that did go through Styx.

The code is Apache-2.0 at github.com/NicholasFlemmer/styx-app.
